shelves.title: CPAP for cardiovascular prevention in sleep apnea: the honest null
shelves.question: In patients with obstructive sleep apnea and established cardiovascular disease who are not very sleepy, does CPAP treatment prevent cardiovascular events — heart attack, stroke, cardiovascular death?
shelves.mesh: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive · Cardiovascular Diseases · Coronary Artery Disease · Cerebrovascular Disorders · Humans
shelves.balance: This shelf exists to say the quiet part plainly: CPAP did not prevent cardiovascular events in the patients these trials enrolled. SAVE’s primary endpoint ran at 17.0% on CPAP vs 15.4% on usual care (HR 1.10, not significant); ISAACC’s ran at 16% vs 17% (HR 0.89, not significant). Both trials enrolled minimally sleepy patients — the people least driven to use the machine, with average use under 3.5 hours a night — so the null is a null for this population and this adherence, not a verdict on CPAP for sleepiness, which SAVE did improve. Symptom benefit is a different question, and it is not this shelf’s claim. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: SAVE: CPAP did not prevent cardiovascular events (17.0% vs 15.4%; HR 1.10, not significant)
cards.summary: Primary composite (cardiovascular death, heart attack, stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina, heart failure, or TIA): 17.0% on CPAP vs 15.4% on usual care (hazard ratio 1.10 , 95% CI 0.91 to 1.32; P=0.34) over a mean 3.7 years — 2,717 patients. CPAP did reduce snoring and daytime sleepiness and improved quality of life and mood.
cards.type: International, multicentre, randomized trial with a sham-CPAP run-in (SAVE), N Engl J Med 2016
cards.people: 2,717 adults aged 45–75 with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea and coronary or cerebrovascular disease; most were men with minimal sleepiness. Mean CPAP adherence was 3.3 hours per night; the apnea–hypopnea index fell from 29.0 to 3.7 events per hour on CPAP. Mean follow-up 3.7 years. (The abstract does not print mean age or the exact sex mix.)
cards.result: A primary end-point event occurred in 229 participants (17.0%) in the CPAP group and 207 (15.4%) in the usual-care group (hazard ratio 1.10; 95% CI 0.91 to 1.32; P=0.34). No significant effect was seen on any individual or other composite cardiovascular end point. CPAP significantly reduced snoring and daytime sleepiness and improved health-related quality of life and mood.
cards.watchOut: The honest limits: adherence averaged 3.3 hours a night — roughly half the night untreated — and sleepy patients, who have most to gain symptomatically, were largely excluded. The trial answers the prevention question for minimally sleepy patients at real-world adherence, and the answer is no. It does not answer whether perfectly adherent or very sleepy patients would fare differently; that trial has not been done.
cards.source: McEvoy RD et al. CPAP for Prevention of Cardiovascular Events in Obstructive Sleep Apnea. N Engl J Med. 2016;375:919-931. PMID 27571048 · NCT00738179 · ACTRN12608000409370.

cards.headline: ISAACC: after acute coronary syndrome, CPAP did not reduce cardiovascular events either (16% vs 17%; HR 0.89, not significant)
cards.summary: Cardiovascular events: 16% on CPAP vs 17% on usual care (hazard ratio 0.89 , 95% CI 0.68 to 1.17; P=0.40) over a median 3.35 years — 1,264 patients with sleep apnea randomized after acute coronary syndrome. Event rates in patients without sleep apnea (15%) were no lower than in untreated sleep apnea (17%).
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomized controlled trial (ISAACC), Lancet Respir Med 2020
cards.people: 2,834 patients with acute coronary syndrome underwent respiratory polygraphy at 15 Spanish hospitals; 1,264 with obstructive sleep apnea were randomized (633 CPAP, 631 usual care), and 603 without sleep apnea formed a reference group. Median follow-up 3.35 years; mean CPAP adherence 2.78 hours per night. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Cardiovascular events occurred in 98 patients (16%) in the CPAP group and 108 (17%) in the usual-care group (hazard ratio 0.89; 95% CI 0.68 to 1.17; P=0.40). Event prevalence was similar in the no-apnea reference group (15%) and the untreated apnea group (17%; hazard ratio 1.01; 0.76 to 1.35) — in this population, having sleep apnea was not itself associated with more events. Event rates did not vary with CPAP compliance or apnea severity.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (CPAP cannot be masked), with adherence under 3 hours a night — the same two limits as SAVE, and the same null. Serious adverse events were numerically more frequent in the CPAP group’s patients (74% vs 65% had at least one), in a post-ACS population with high background event rates. Two large trials, two populations, one answer.
cards.source: Sánchez-de-la-Torre M et al. Effect of obstructive sleep apnoea and its treatment with continuous positive airway pressure on the prevalence of cardiovascular events in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ISAACC study). Lancet Respir Med. 2020;8:359-367. PMID 31839558 · NCT01335087.

shelves.title: Triple therapy in COPD: fewer exacerbations than dual therapy, at a pneumonia price
shelves.question: In patients with COPD at risk of exacerbations, does single-inhaler triple therapy — an inhaled corticosteroid plus a long-acting muscarinic antagonist plus a long-acting beta-agonist — reduce exacerbations compared with dual therapy, and at what cost?
shelves.mesh: Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Glucocorticoids · Muscarinic Antagonists · Adrenergic beta-Agonists · Bronchodilator Agents · Drug Combinations · Administration, Inhalation · Humans
shelves.balance: Triple therapy beats dual therapy on exacerbations in both mega-trials: IMPACT’s rate ratios were 0.85 against ICS/LABA and 0.75 against LAMA/LABA; ETHOS’s were 0.76–0.87 depending on dose and comparator. The price is consistent too — more pneumonia in the corticosteroid-containing arms (IMPACT hazard ratio 1.53 vs LAMA/LABA). ETHOS also produced a mortality signal favoring its higher-dose triple therapy; because death was a secondary endpoint in a trial powered on exacerbations, that signal is graded POSSIBLE on the ETHOS card itself and deliberately kept off this shelf’s headline. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: IMPACT: triple therapy cut exacerbations vs both dual therapies (rate ratios 0.85 and 0.75) — with more pneumonia
cards.summary: Annual rate of moderate or severe exacerbations: 0.91 per year on triple therapy vs 1.07 on fluticasone–vilanterol (rate ratio 0.85 , 0.80–0.90) and 1.21 on umeclidinium–vilanterol (rate ratio 0.75 , 0.70–0.81); severe (hospitalizing) exacerbations 0.13 vs 0.19 vs LAMA/LABA (rate ratio 0.66 ); clinician-diagnosed pneumonia hazard ratio 1.53 (1.22–1.92) vs LAMA/LABA — 10,355 patients.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind trial (IMPACT), N Engl J Med 2018
cards.people: 10,355 patients with COPD treated for 52 weeks, each regimen delivered in a single Ellipta inhaler. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The annual rate of moderate or severe exacerbations was 0.91 per year on triple therapy vs 1.07 on fluticasone furoate–vilanterol (rate ratio 0.85; 95% CI 0.80 to 0.90; P<0.001) and 1.21 on umeclidinium–vilanterol (rate ratio 0.75; 95% CI 0.70 to 0.81; P<0.001). The rate of severe exacerbations resulting in hospitalization was 0.13 vs 0.19 per year against umeclidinium–vilanterol (rate ratio 0.66; 0.56 to 0.78; P<0.001). Pneumonia was more frequent in the inhaled-glucocorticoid groups, and the risk of clinician-diagnosed pneumonia was significantly higher on triple therapy than on umeclidinium–vilanterol (hazard ratio 1.53; 95% CI 1.22 to 1.92; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The comparator matters: the biggest win (0.75) is against the steroid-free dual, which is also the comparison that carries the pneumonia penalty; against the steroid-containing dual the gain is smaller (0.85). Many participants had their previous inhaled corticosteroid stopped at randomization if assigned to the steroid-free arm — a design critics note can manufacture early exacerbations in that arm. Funded by GlaxoSmithKline, the triple inhaler’s maker.
cards.source: Lipson DA et al. Once-Daily Single-Inhaler Triple versus Dual Therapy in Patients with COPD. N Engl J Med. 2018;378:1671-1680. PMID 29668352 · NCT02164513.

cards.headline: ETHOS: triple therapy at two steroid doses cut exacerbations (rate ratios 0.76 and 0.87) — and a mortality signal graded POSSIBLE, printed as such
cards.summary: Annual moderate/severe exacerbation rates: 1.08 (320 µg budesonide triple) and 1.07 (160 µg triple) vs 1.42 on glycopyrrolate–formoterol and 1.24 on budesonide–formoterol (rate ratios 0.76 and 0.87 for the 320 dose). Mortality (prespecified secondary endpoint, graded POSSIBLE on this card): hazard ratio 0.54 (0.34–0.87) for 320 triple vs glycopyrrolate–formoterol in the primary report; 0.51 (0.33–0.80) in the final retrieved vital-status analysis. Pneumonia 3.5–4.5% in steroid arms vs 2.3% without — 8,509 patients.
cards.type: 52-week, phase 3, randomized, double-blind trial (ETHOS), N Engl J Med 2020
cards.people: 8,509 patients in the modified intention-to-treat population, randomized 1:1:1:1 across the two triple-therapy doses and two dual therapies, all in a single metered-dose inhaler. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Annual rates of moderate or severe exacerbations were 1.08 in the 320-µg-budesonide triple group (2,137 patients), 1.07 in the 160-µg triple group (2,121), 1.42 in the glycopyrrolate–formoterol group (2,120), and 1.24 in the budesonide–formoterol group (2,131). The 320 dose beat glycopyrrolate–formoterol by 24% relative (rate ratio 0.76; 95% CI 0.69 to 0.83; P<0.001) and budesonide–formoterol by 13% relative (rate ratio 0.87; 0.79 to 0.95; P=0.003); the 160 dose performed almost identically on exacerbations. Overall adverse-event rates were similar across groups (61.7–64.5%); confirmed pneumonia occurred in 3.5–4.5% of the corticosteroid-containing groups vs 2.3% on glycopyrrolate–formoterol. On mortality — a prespecified secondary endpoint — the primary report’s hazard ratio for the 320 dose vs glycopyrrolate–formoterol was 0.54 (0.34–0.87), and the later analysis with vital status retrieved for 99.6% of participants gave 0.51 (0.33–0.80; Martinez 2021, PMID 33252985).
cards.watchOut: The mortality result is graded POSSIBLE on this card, deliberately: death was a secondary endpoint in a trial powered on exacerbations, the comparison against the steroid-containing dual (budesonide–formoterol) was not significant, and most participants had prior inhaled corticosteroid stopped abruptly if randomized away from it — the same withdrawal caveat as IMPACT. It is a signal worth a dedicated trial, not a proven survival benefit. Funded by AstraZeneca, the triple inhaler’s maker.
cards.source: Rabe KF et al. Triple Inhaled Therapy at Two Glucocorticoid Doses in Moderate-to-Very-Severe COPD. N Engl J Med. 2020;383:35-48. PMID 32579807 · NCT02465567.

shelves.title: Pulmonary rehabilitation after a COPD exacerbation: start it after discharge — starting it in hospital harmed
shelves.question: After a hospitalization for a COPD exacerbation, does pulmonary rehabilitation reduce readmissions and deaths — and does it matter whether rehabilitation starts during the admission or after discharge?
shelves.mesh: Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Patient Readmission · Exercise Tolerance · Resistance Training · Hospitalization · Humans
shelves.balance: Timing is the whole shelf. Rehabilitation started after the exacerbation, in the Cochrane pool of 20 trials, cut hospital readmissions (odds ratio 0.44) and produced large gains in quality of life and walking distance — though the readmission result was heterogeneous and the pooled mortality result was not significant. The one large trial that started rehabilitation during the admission itself (Greening 2014) found no readmission benefit and significantly higher one-year mortality — the harm boundary: do not start progressive exercise rehab in the first days of the acute illness. The largest survival number (Lindenauer’s hazard ratio 0.63 in 197,376 Medicare patients) is observational and sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid evidence; it is carded labeled as such. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: Cochrane (Puhan 2016): rehabilitation after exacerbation cut readmissions (OR 0.44) and improved quality of life and walking distance
cards.summary: Hospital readmissions (8 studies, 810 participants): pooled odds ratio 0.44 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.91), moderate-quality evidence, with substantial heterogeneity (I²=77%). Mortality (6 studies, 670 participants): odds ratio 0.68 (0.28 to 1.67) — not significant, low-quality evidence. Quality of life improved beyond the minimal important difference (SGRQ −7.80 points) and six-minute walk distance by 62 metres — 20 trials, 1,477 participants.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials, Cochrane update (Puhan et al.), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016
cards.people: 20 randomized trials with 1,477 participants after COPD exacerbation; programmes varied widely in extent, setting, and supervision. (The abstract does not print a pooled mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Pulmonary rehabilitation reduced hospital readmissions (pooled odds ratio 0.44; 95% CI 0.21 to 0.91; 8 studies, 810 participants; moderate-quality evidence), though results were heterogeneous (I²=77%) and trials added in this update showed smaller effects than earlier ones. The mortality pool did not reach significance (odds ratio 0.68; 0.28 to 1.67; 6 studies, 670 participants; low-quality evidence). Health-related quality of life improved beyond the 4-point minimal important difference on the St George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (mean difference −7.80; −12.12 to −3.47), and six-minute walk distance improved by 62 metres on average (38 to 86) — both graded high-quality evidence.
cards.watchOut: The readmission headline rests on a heterogeneous pool (I²=77%): programme extensiveness and trial risk of bias may explain much of the spread, subgroup tests were not significant, and newer trials showed smaller effects than the early ones. The robust findings are quality of life and exercise capacity; the mortality claim is not established by the randomized pool.
cards.source: Puhan MA et al. Pulmonary rehabilitation following exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2016;(12):CD005305. PMID 27930803. No registry ID (systematic review).

cards.headline: Greening 2014 (the harm boundary): rehabilitation started during the admission did not cut readmissions — and one-year mortality was higher (OR 1.74)
cards.summary: Readmission within 12 months: 62% with early in-hospital rehabilitation vs 58% with usual care (hazard ratio 1.1 , 0.86 to 1.43; P=0.4) — no benefit. Mortality at one year was higher in the intervention group (odds ratio 1.74 , 95% CI 1.05 to 2.88; P=0.03) — 389 patients.
cards.type: Prospective, randomized controlled trial (Greening et al.), BMJ 2014
cards.people: 389 patients aged 45–93 admitted with an exacerbation of chronic respiratory disease at two UK hospitals; 320 (82%) had a primary diagnosis of COPD; 196 assigned to early rehabilitation, 193 to usual care.
cards.result: 233 patients (60%) were readmitted at least once in the following year — 62% in the intervention group and 58% in the control group (hazard ratio 1.1; 95% CI 0.86 to 1.43; P=0.4). Mortality at one year was higher in the intervention group (odds ratio 1.74; 95% CI 1.05 to 2.88; P=0.03). Physical performance and health status recovered significantly after discharge in both groups, with no significant between-group difference at one year. The authors conclude that, beyond standard physiotherapy, progressive exercise rehabilitation should not be started during the early stages of the acute illness.
cards.watchOut: This card is the shelf’s fence: it does not contradict the Cochrane card (Reference 1), which pools rehabilitation delivered after the exacerbation — it shows the same intervention moved into the first 48 hours of an acute admission loses its benefit and gains a mortality signal. A single trial of 389 patients, so the harm estimate is imprecise (confidence interval 1.05 to 2.88), but the direction and the authors’ own conclusion agree: timing is the intervention.
cards.source: Greening NJ et al. An early rehabilitation intervention to enhance recovery during hospital admission for an exacerbation of chronic respiratory disease: randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2014;349:g4315. PMID 25004917 · ISRCTN05557928.

cards.headline: Lindenauer 2020 (observational — labeled not-solid): starting rehabilitation within 90 days was associated with lower one-year mortality (HR 0.63)
cards.summary: One-year mortality: 7.3% in patients who started rehabilitation within 90 days of discharge vs 19.6% in those who started later or never (absolute difference −6.7 points; hazard ratio 0.63 , 0.57 to 0.69) — 197,376 Medicare patients. Observational: a hazard ratio of 0.63 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid evidence.
cards.type: Retrospective inception cohort study of Medicare claims (Lindenauer et al.), JAMA 2020 — observational, labeled as such
cards.people: 197,376 fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries hospitalized for COPD in 2014 at 4,446 US hospitals; mean age 76.9 years; 115,690 (58.6%) women. Only 2,721 patients (1.5%) initiated pulmonary rehabilitation within 90 days of discharge.
cards.result: 38,302 patients (19.4%) died within one year of discharge, including 7.3% of those who initiated rehabilitation within 90 days and 19.6% of those who initiated later or not at all (absolute risk difference −6.7%; 95% CI −7.9 to −5.6; hazard ratio 0.63; 0.57 to 0.69; P<0.001, propensity-adjusted). The association held across start times from ≤30 days (hazard ratio 0.74) to 61–90 days after discharge (hazard ratio 0.40), and every 3 additional sessions were associated with a further 9% lower hazard of death.
cards.watchOut: Labeled not-solid by this library’s own rule: the study is observational, and a hazard ratio of 0.63 lies inside the 0.5–2.0 band that is never sold here as solid evidence — patients well enough to start rehabilitation within 90 days differ from those who are not, and claims data cannot fully adjust for that. It is consistent with the randomized evidence on this shelf (Reference 1); it is not proof of a survival effect, and the near-total non-use it documents (1.5%) is itself a finding.
cards.source: Lindenauer PK et al. Association Between Initiation of Pulmonary Rehabilitation After Hospitalization for COPD and 1-Year Survival Among Medicare Beneficiaries. JAMA. 2020;323:1813-1823. PMID 32396181. No registry ID (observational study).

shelves.title: Long-term oxygen therapy in COPD: lifesaving in severe resting hypoxemia — no benefit in moderate desaturation
shelves.question: In patients with COPD, does long-term supplemental oxygen prolong life — and how low does the oxygen level have to be before it helps?
shelves.mesh: Oxygen Inhalation Therapy · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Hypoxia · Oxygen · Humans
shelves.balance: Oxygen is a drug with a threshold. In severe resting hypoxemia, the founding trials agree: NOTT found mortality nearly twice as high on 12-hour nocturnal oxygen as on continuous oxygen, and the MRC trial found 19 deaths among 42 oxygen-treated patients against 30 of 45 controls over five years. In moderate desaturation — resting saturation 89–93% or exercise-induced dips — LOTT’s 738 patients gained nothing: death or first hospitalization hazard ratio 0.94, with no benefit on any measured outcome. Prescribe it below the line; above the line it is burden without benefit. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: NOTT (1980): continuous oxygen beat nocturnal-only oxygen — mortality 1.94 times higher on 12-hour therapy
cards.summary: Overall mortality in the nocturnal-oxygen group was 1.94 times that in the continuous-oxygen group (P=0.01) over a mean follow-up of 19.3 months — 203 patients with hypoxemic COPD at six centres.
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial, Nocturnal Oxygen Therapy Trial (NOTT), Ann Intern Med 1980 — pre-registration era; no registry ID exists
cards.people: 203 patients with hypoxemic chronic obstructive lung disease at six centres, randomly allocated to continuous or 12-hour nocturnal oxygen and followed for at least 12 months (mean 19.3 months); compliance with each regimen was good. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Overall mortality in the nocturnal oxygen therapy group was 1.94 times that in the continuous oxygen therapy group (P=0.01). The trend was striking in patients with carbon dioxide retention and was also present in patients with relatively poor lung function, low mean nocturnal oxygen saturation, more severe brain dysfunction, and prominent mood disturbances; continuous therapy also appeared to benefit patients with lower pulmonary artery pressures and relatively preserved exercise capacity.
cards.watchOut: A 1980 trial, small by modern standards, and its comparison is continuous vs nocturnal oxygen — not oxygen vs none: it establishes that in severe hypoxemia, more hours of oxygen save lives, and it is read together with the MRC trial’s oxygen-vs-none comparison (Reference 2). Why continuous therapy helped was not clear even to its authors.
cards.source: Nocturnal Oxygen Therapy Trial Group. Continuous or nocturnal oxygen therapy in hypoxemic chronic obstructive lung disease: a clinical trial. Ann Intern Med. 1980;93:391-398. PMID 6776858. No registry ID (pre-registration era).

cards.headline: MRC (1981): domiciliary oxygen for at least 15 hours a day — 19 deaths of 42 treated vs 30 of 45 controls over five years
cards.summary: Deaths over five years of follow-up: 19 of 42 patients on long-term domiciliary oxygen (at least 15 hours daily) vs 30 of 45 untreated controls — 87 patients with severe hypoxemia complicating chronic bronchitis or emphysema. In men, the survival advantage did not emerge until about 500 days.
cards.type: Controlled randomized trial, Medical Research Council working party, Lancet 1981 — pre-registration era; no registry ID exists
cards.people: 87 patients, all under 70 years of age, at three UK centres — 42 assigned to oxygen, 45 to no oxygen; 66 of the 87 were men. Oxygen was given by nasal prongs for at least 15 hours daily, usually at 2 L/min. Follow-up for survival was five years.
cards.result: 19 of the 42 oxygen-treated patients died in the five years of survival follow-up, compared with 30 of 45 controls. In the 66 men, the survival advantage of oxygen did not emerge until 500 days had elapsed; survival among the 12 female controls was strikingly poor (8 dead at 3 years). Time in hospital for exacerbations and work attendance were not affected. Oxygen did not slow the progress of respiratory failure in patients who died early, but in longer-term survivors arterial oxygenation appeared to stop deteriorating.
cards.watchOut: Very small (87 patients) and from 1981 — but it remains, with NOTT, the entire randomized basis for oxygen in severe resting hypoxemia, because a modern placebo-controlled trial in that population is no longer considered ethical. Its slowness matters clinically: the benefit took over a year to appear in men, so oxygen judged at three months will look useless even when it is working.
cards.source: Medical Research Council Working Party. Long term domiciliary oxygen therapy in chronic hypoxic cor pulmonale complicating chronic bronchitis and emphysema. Lancet. 1981;1:681-686. PMID 6110912. No registry ID (pre-registration era).

cards.headline: LOTT (2016) — the fence: in moderate desaturation, long-term oxygen changed nothing (HR 0.94)
cards.summary: Time to death or first hospitalization: hazard ratio 0.94 (95% CI 0.79 to 1.12; P=0.52); no benefit in all hospitalizations (rate ratio 1.01), COPD exacerbations (1.08), COPD hospitalizations (0.99), quality of life, lung function, or walk distance — 738 patients with resting saturation 89–93% or exercise-only desaturation.
cards.type: Randomized trial, Long-Term Oxygen Treatment Trial (LOTT), N Engl J Med 2016
cards.people: 738 patients with stable COPD at 42 centres, followed for 1 to 6 years: resting moderate desaturation (SpO2 89–93%), prescribed 24-hour oxygen, or exercise-only desaturation, prescribed oxygen during exercise and sleep. Assignment was not masked. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: There was no significant difference between the supplemental-oxygen and no-oxygen groups in time to death or first hospitalization (hazard ratio 0.94; 95% CI 0.79 to 1.12; P=0.52), nor in rates of all hospitalizations (rate ratio 1.01; 0.91 to 1.13), COPD exacerbations (1.08; 0.98 to 1.19), or COPD-related hospitalizations (0.99; 0.83 to 1.17). There were no consistent between-group differences in quality of life, lung function, or six-minute walk distance.
cards.watchOut: The trial was redesigned seven months in — after only 34 patients — adding the exercise-desaturation population and folding first hospitalization into the primary outcome; the redesign is printed because it defines the population the null covers. The null is a fence, not a repeal: it applies to moderate desaturation, and it does not touch the severe resting hypoxemia of Cards 1 and 2, where the founding trials found benefit.

shelves.title: Noninvasive ventilation in acute COPD exacerbation: fewer deaths, far fewer intubations
shelves.question: In adults admitted to hospital with acute hypercapnic respiratory failure from a COPD exacerbation, does noninvasive ventilation (BiPAP) added to usual care reduce death and the need for intubation?
shelves.mesh: Noninvasive Ventilation · Positive-Pressure Respiration · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Respiratory Insufficiency · Humans
shelves.balance: One of the clearest shelves in the library. Across 17 randomized trials in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure from COPD exacerbation, noninvasive ventilation cut the risk of death by 46% relative (risk ratio 0.54; number needed to treat 12) and the risk of intubation by 65% relative (risk ratio 0.36; number needed to treat 5), in Cochrane’s 2017 pool. The evidence is graded moderate quality — most trials could not be blinded — but the direction never wavers. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: Cochrane (Osadnik 2017): NIV cut mortality by 46% relative (RR 0.54) and intubation by 65% relative (RR 0.36)
cards.summary: In-hospital mortality: risk ratio 0.54 (95% CI 0.38 to 0.76) — a 46% relative reduction; number needed to treat 12 . Need for endotracheal intubation: risk ratio 0.36 (0.28 to 0.46) — a 65% relative reduction; number needed to treat 5 . Both graded moderate quality — 17 trials, 1,264 participants.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials, Cochrane update (Osadnik et al.), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017
cards.people: 17 randomized trials with 1,264 participants; mean age at recruitment 66.8 years across trials (range 57.7 to 70.5) and about 65% of participants were male. Trials were ICU-based and ward-based, and covered exacerbations of differing severity (admission pH 7.30–7.35 and below 7.30).
cards.result: Noninvasive ventilation decreased the risk of mortality by 46% relative (risk ratio 0.54; 95% CI 0.38 to 0.76; 12 studies; number needed to treat for one additional beneficial outcome 12, 95% CI 9 to 23) and decreased the risk of needing endotracheal intubation by 65% relative (risk ratio 0.36; 0.28 to 0.46; 17 studies; number needed to treat 5, 5 to 6). Both outcomes were graded moderate quality under GRADE. Length of stay, arterial blood gases, and symptoms also favored NIV in the review’s secondary analyses.
cards.watchOut: Moderate, not high, quality — and the reason is structural: 12 of 17 trials were at risk of performance bias because a mask cannot be blinded, and detection bias was uncertain in 14. That caveat weighs most on soft outcomes like breathlessness scores; death and intubation are hard endpoints, and both move the same way. The funnel plot for intubation raised the possibility of small-study effects, which is why the grade stays moderate despite the consistency.
cards.source: Osadnik CR et al. Non-invasive ventilation for the management of acute hypercapnic respiratory failure due to exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017;(7):CD004104. PMID 28702957. No registry ID (systematic review).

shelves.title: As-needed ICS-formoterol in mild asthma: exacerbation protection without a daily inhaler
shelves.question: In patients with mild asthma, does taking budesonide-formoterol only as needed — instead of a daily maintenance inhaler or a short-acting reliever alone — control symptoms and prevent severe exacerbations?
shelves.mesh: Asthma · Budesonide · Formoterol Fumarate · Budesonide, Formoterol Fumarate Drug Combination · Terbutaline · Bronchodilator Agents · Humans
shelves.balance: For mild asthma, the reliever itself can carry the anti-inflammatory drug. SYGMA 1 showed as-needed budesonide-formoterol beat a short-acting reliever alone on symptom control and cut the severe exacerbation rate by nearly two-thirds relative (rate ratio 0.36), at 17% of the steroid dose of daily maintenance — though daily maintenance still controlled day-to-day symptoms best. PRACTICAL, the pragmatic open-label trial, then showed as-needed therapy beat maintenance head-to-head on the outcome that matters most: severe exacerbations, relative rate 0.69. The honest summary: you give up a little day-to-day symptom control and gain exacerbation protection without a daily inhaler most patients stop taking anyway. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: SYGMA 1: as-needed budesonide-formoterol beat reliever alone — severe exacerbations 0.07 vs 0.20 per year (rate ratio 0.36) — but daily maintenance controlled symptoms best
cards.summary: Weeks with well-controlled asthma: 34.4% on as-needed budesonide-formoterol vs 31.1% on as-needed terbutaline (odds ratio 1.14 , 1.00 to 1.30; P=0.046) and 44.4% on daily budesonide maintenance (odds ratio 0.64 — maintenance superior for symptoms). Annual severe exacerbation rate: 0.07 vs 0.20 (rate ratio 0.36 , 0.27 to 0.49) and 0.09 on maintenance (rate ratio 0.83 , 0.59 to 1.16). Steroid exposure on as-needed therapy was 17% of the maintenance dose — 3,836 patients.
cards.type: 52-week, double-blind, randomized trial (SYGMA 1), N Engl J Med 2018
cards.people: 3,849 patients aged 12 years or older with mild asthma underwent randomization; 3,836 were in the full analysis set (1,277 terbutaline, 1,277 as-needed budesonide-formoterol, 1,282 maintenance budesonide). Adherence in the maintenance group was 78.9%. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: For the mean percentage of weeks with well-controlled asthma, as-needed budesonide-formoterol was superior to terbutaline (34.4% vs 31.1% of weeks; odds ratio 1.14; 95% CI 1.00 to 1.30; P=0.046) but inferior to maintenance budesonide (34.4% vs 44.4%; odds ratio 0.64; 0.57 to 0.73). The annual rate of severe exacerbations was 0.20 with terbutaline, 0.07 with as-needed budesonide-formoterol, and 0.09 with maintenance: rate ratio 0.36 (0.27 to 0.49) vs terbutaline and 0.83 (0.59 to 1.16) vs maintenance. The median daily inhaled glucocorticoid dose in the as-needed group (57 µg) was 17% of the maintenance group’s dose (340 µg).
cards.watchOut: The trial’s two answers point in different directions by design: for week-to-week symptom control, taking a steroid every day wins; for severe exacerbations, as-needed combination therapy matched maintenance while exposing patients to a sixth of the steroid. Which endpoint should govern is a values question — the exacerbation result is the one tied to harm. Funded by AstraZeneca, the combination inhaler’s maker.
cards.source: O’Byrne PM et al. Inhaled Combined Budesonide-Formoterol as Needed in Mild Asthma. N Engl J Med. 2018;378:1865-1876. PMID 29768149 · NCT02149199.

cards.headline: PRACTICAL: as-needed budesonide-formoterol beat daily maintenance on severe exacerbations (relative rate 0.69)
cards.summary: Severe exacerbations: 0.119 per patient per year on as-needed budesonide-formoterol vs 0.172 on maintenance budesonide plus as-needed terbutaline (relative rate 0.69 , 95% CI 0.48 to 1.00; P=0.049) — a 31% relative reduction — 885 patients, open-label, real-world primary care.
cards.type: 52-week, open-label, parallel-group, multicentre, superiority randomized trial (PRACTICAL), Lancet 2019
cards.people: 890 adults aged 18–75 with a doctor’s diagnosis of asthma, using a short-acting reliever with or without low-to-moderate-dose maintenance inhaled corticosteroid, were assigned at 15 primary-care and hospital-based units in New Zealand; 885 were in the analysis (437 as-needed, 448 maintenance). (The abstract does not print the sex mix.)
cards.result: Severe exacerbations per patient per year were lower with as-needed budesonide-formoterol than with maintenance budesonide plus terbutaline: absolute rates 0.119 vs 0.172 per patient per year; relative rate 0.69 (95% CI 0.48 to 1.00; P=0.049) — that is, a 31% relative reduction. Nasopharyngitis was the most common adverse event in both groups (35% vs 32%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label and pragmatic — patients and investigators knew the assignment, which is the point (it mirrors prescribing in the wild) and also the caveat (behavior differs when treatment is known). The confidence interval for the relative rate just touches 1.00 and P=0.049, so the head-to-head win over maintenance is real but not roomy; its weight comes from agreeing with SYGMA 1’s exacerbation results (Reference 1) under blinded conditions. Funded by the Health Research Council of New Zealand.
cards.source: Hardy J et al. Budesonide-formoterol reliever therapy versus maintenance budesonide plus terbutaline reliever therapy in adults with mild to moderate asthma (PRACTICAL). Lancet. 2019;394:919-928. PMID 31451207 · ACTRN12616000377437.

shelves.title: Biologics for severe asthma: tezepelumab prevents exacerbations — and failed to spare steroids
shelves.question: In severe, uncontrolled asthma, do biologic medicines prevent exacerbations — and can they replace the daily oral steroids that do so much long-term harm?
shelves.mesh: Asthma · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Anti-Asthmatic Agents · Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Eosinophils · Humans
shelves.balance: Tezepelumab, the TSLP-blocking biologic, cut severe-asthma exacerbations by more than half relative in NAVIGATOR (rate ratio 0.44) — and, unusually for this class, the benefit held at low eosinophil counts (0.59). But its dedicated steroid-sparing trial, SOURCE, failed its primary endpoint outright: patients on tezepelumab could not reduce their daily oral corticosteroid dose any more than patients on placebo (OR 1.28, P=0.43). Both halves belong on the label in the clinic: prescribe it to prevent exacerbations, not on a promise that the prednisone can stop. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: NAVIGATOR: tezepelumab cut the annualized exacerbation rate by more than half (rate ratio 0.44) in severe, uncontrolled asthma — including in patients with low eosinophil counts
cards.summary: Annualized exacerbation rate: 0.93 on tezepelumab vs 2.10 on placebo (rate ratio 0.44 , 95% CI 0.37 to 0.53) — a 56% relative reduction; in patients with eosinophils under 300 cells/µL the rate ratio was 0.59 — 1,061 patients.
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NAVIGATOR), N Engl J Med 2021
cards.people: 1,061 patients aged 12 to 80 years with severe, uncontrolled asthma underwent randomization (529 tezepelumab, 532 placebo). (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The annualized rate of asthma exacerbations was 0.93 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.07) with tezepelumab and 2.10 (1.84 to 2.39) with placebo (rate ratio 0.44; 0.37 to 0.53; P<0.001) — a 56% relative reduction. In patients with a baseline blood eosinophil count under 300 cells per microliter, the rate ratio was 0.59 (0.46 to 0.75). Lung function and control scores also favored tezepelumab: prebronchodilator FEV1 difference 0.13 liters (0.08 to 0.18). Adverse-event frequencies and types did not differ meaningfully between groups.
cards.watchOut: Tezepelumab blocks TSLP, an upstream epithelial cytokine, which is the proposed reason it works at low eosinophil counts where narrower biologics do not. Funded by AstraZeneca and Amgen, the drug’s makers. Exacerbation prevention is not the same as steroid sparing — see Card 2, where the steroid-sparing trial of the same drug failed its primary endpoint.
cards.source: Menzies-Gow A et al. Tezepelumab in Adults and Adolescents with Severe, Uncontrolled Asthma. N Engl J Med. 2021;384:1800-1809. PMID 33979488 · NCT03347279.

cards.headline: SOURCE: tezepelumab did NOT spare oral corticosteroids — the primary endpoint failed (odds ratio 1.28, P=0.43)
cards.summary: Categorised percentage reduction in daily oral corticosteroid dose at week 48: cumulative odds ratio 1.28 (95% CI 0.69 to 2.35; P=0.43) — primary endpoint NOT met ; only the subgroup with eosinophils ≥150 cells/µL favored tezepelumab (OR 2.58 ) — 150 patients.
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled oral corticosteroid-sparing study (SOURCE), Lancet Respir Med 2022
cards.people: 150 adults aged 18–80 years with oral corticosteroid-dependent asthma were randomly assigned (74 tezepelumab, 76 placebo) across 60 sites in seven countries, after an oral corticosteroid optimisation phase. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The cumulative odds of achieving a category of greater percentage reduction in daily oral corticosteroid dose at week 48 were similar with tezepelumab and placebo in the overall population (odds ratio 1.28 [95% CI 0.69–2.35], P=0.43) — the primary endpoint was not met. The odds were higher with tezepelumab in participants with baseline blood eosinophil counts of at least 150 cells per µL (2.58 [1.16–5.75]) but not below 150 (0.40 [0.14–1.13]). Adverse events were reported in 72% of the tezepelumab group and 86% of the placebo group; serious adverse events in 16% vs 21%.
cards.watchOut: This is the honest failure on the shelf: a drug that prevents exacerbations (Reference 1) did not prove it can replace maintenance oral steroids, and the eosinophil-subgroup signal is a subgroup of a negative trial — hypothesis-generating, not a license to promise steroid withdrawal. Funded by AstraZeneca and Amgen.
cards.source: Wechsler ME et al. Evaluation of the oral corticosteroid-sparing effect of tezepelumab in adults with oral corticosteroid-dependent asthma (SOURCE): a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 study. Lancet Respir Med. 2022;10(7):650-660. PMID 35364018 · NCT03406078.

shelves.title: Harms of inhaled corticosteroids: pneumonia (LIKELY) and bone (POSSIBLE)
shelves.question: What do inhaled corticosteroids cost the patients they help — in pneumonia, and in bone?
shelves.mesh: Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Budesonide · Fluticasone · Pneumonia · Fractures, Bone · Glucocorticoids · Humans
shelves.balance: The pneumonia harm is the solid half: in the Cochrane pooling of the COPD trials, fluticasone raised serious (hospitalized) pneumonia with an odds ratio of 1.78 — about 18 extra cases per 1,000 treated over 18 months — with no offsetting mortality change in either direction. The bone half is thinner: fractures ran modestly higher on inhaled steroids in both trial and observational poolings (OR 1.27 and 1.21, both inside the band this library will not call solid), with a dose gradient that keeps the question open rather than closed. Prescribe inhaled steroids in COPD for exacerbations, with the pneumonia price known and the bone price watched. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Kew 2014 (Cochrane): inhaled fluticasone raised serious pneumonia in COPD — odds ratio 1.78, from trial adverse-event data
cards.summary: Non-fatal serious pneumonia events (requiring hospital admission) on fluticasone: odds ratio 1.78 (95% CI 1.50 to 2.12) — 18 more events per 1,000 treated over 18 months ; an odds ratio pooled from adverse-event reports in randomized trials, not a patient-level pneumonia trial.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomized controlled trials (Kew & Seniukovich 2014). A systematic review — no trial registry number applies.
cards.people: Trials of at least 12 weeks in people with COPD; the review populations were more often male, with a mean age of around 63 years, mean pack-years smoked over 40, and mean predicted FEV1 under 50%.
cards.result: Fluticasone increased non-fatal serious adverse pneumonia events (odds ratio 1.78, 95% CI 1.50 to 2.12; high-quality evidence; 18 more per 1,000 treated over 18 months), with or without a combined long-acting beta-agonist. The budesonide signal was smaller and less precise, and an indirect comparison found no significant difference between the two drugs for serious pneumonia or mortality. Neither drug significantly changed overall mortality, and pneumonia deaths were too rare to judge.
cards.watchOut: Pneumonia here is an adverse-event label assigned inside trials built to measure exacerbations — definitions varied by manufacturer, and pneumonia and exacerbation overlap clinically, so the exact size of the risk is softer than the direction. The direction has never reversed in later data, and it is the price printed on the COPD triple-therapy shelf (#303).
cards.source: Kew KM, Seniukovich A. Inhaled steroids and risk of pneumonia for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2014;(3):CD010115. PMID 24615270 · No registry number (systematic review).

cards.headline: Loke 2011: inhaled corticosteroids and fractures in COPD — a modest signal (trial Peto OR 1.27), graded POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Fractures on inhaled corticosteroids: Peto odds ratio 1.27 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.58) across 16 randomized trials (17,513 participants); observational studies pooled at OR 1.21 , with a dose-response of about 9% higher odds per 500 µg of beclomethasone-equivalent dose.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials and observational studies (Loke 2011). A systematic review — no trial registry number applies.
cards.people: 16 randomized trials with 17,513 participants and 7 observational studies with about 69,000 participants, in COPD populations (MeSH: aged, middle aged, male and female). (The abstract does not print a pooled mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: In randomized trials, inhaled corticosteroids were associated with a modestly increased fracture risk (Peto OR 1.27; 95% CI 1.01 to 1.58; P=0.04; I²=0%). In observational studies the pooled odds ratio was 1.21 (1.12 to 1.32), and each 500 µg increase in beclomethasone dose equivalents was associated with a 9% relative increase in fracture odds (OR 1.09; 1.06 to 1.12). The authors’ own wording: a modest but statistically significant increased likelihood of fractures with long-term fluticasone and budesonide.
cards.watchOut: Both pooled ratios sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library treats as not-solid on their own — the RCT estimate barely clears 1.0, and the observational dose-response, while coherent, is exactly the kind of evidence confounding by disease severity can manufacture (sicker patients get more steroid and fall more). That is why the bone half of this shelf is graded POSSIBLE while the pneumonia half is LIKELY.
cards.source: Loke YK et al. Risk of fractures with inhaled corticosteroids in COPD: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials and observational studies. Thorax. 2011;66:699-708. PMID 21602540 · No registry number (systematic review).

shelves.title: Short-course antibiotics for pneumonia: 8 days tied 15 — with one organism-shaped exception
shelves.question: How short can pneumonia treatment safely go — in the ventilated patient, and on the ward?
shelves.mesh: Pneumonia, Bacterial · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Drug Administration Schedule · Respiration, Artificial · Community-Acquired Infections · Humans
shelves.balance: Shorter won or tied everywhere it was honestly tested — with the exception printed, not buried. PneumA randomized ventilator-associated pneumonia to 8 vs 15 days: no mortality difference, more antibiotic-free days — but recurrence in nonfermenting gram-negative infections (Pseudomonas and its kin) ran 40.6% vs 25.4%, so the short course is not one-size-fits-all. On the ward, Uranga showed a stability-based stop at day 5 matched physician-chosen durations for community-acquired pneumonia. The rule the evidence supports: stop early by stability and organism — not by habit, and not blindly by calendar. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: PneumA: 8 days of antibiotics tied 15 days for ventilator-associated pneumonia — except in nonfermenter infections, where recurrence jumped
cards.summary: 28-day mortality: 18.8% on 8 days vs 17.2% on 15 days (difference 1.6%, 90% CI −3.7 to 6.9); recurrence overall 28.9% vs 26.0% — but with nonfermenting gram-negative bacilli (including Pseudomonas), recurrence was 40.6% on 8 days vs 25.4% on 15 — 401 patients.
cards.type: Prospective, randomized, double-blind (until day 8) trial (PneumA), JAMA 2003. Pre-registration-era trial — no registry number exists.
cards.people: 401 patients with VAP proven by quantitative bronchoscopic cultures, enrolled in 51 French ICUs (197 assigned 8 days, 204 assigned 15 days). (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Compared with 15 days, 8 days produced neither excess mortality (18.8% vs 17.2%; difference 1.6%; 90% CI −3.7% to 6.9%) nor more recurrent infections overall (28.9% vs 26.0%; difference 2.9%; 90% CI −3.2% to 9.1%), and yielded more antibiotic-free days (13.1 vs 8.7 days; P<0.001). Ventilator-free days, organ-failure-free days, ICU stay, and day-60 mortality did not differ. The exception: in VAP caused by nonfermenting gram-negative bacilli, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the 8-day group had a higher pulmonary infection-recurrence rate (40.6% vs 25.4%; difference 15.2%; 90% CI 3.9% to 26.6%) — without worse clinical outcomes in this trial, but the recurrence gap is real and printed.
cards.watchOut: The exception is the point of the card: ‘shorter is fine’ is not one-size-fits-all. Where the organism is a nonfermenter, the short course bought its antibiotic savings with recurrences. The trial also predates modern resistance patterns; its mortality reassurance travels better than its recurrence rate.
cards.source: Chastre J et al. Comparison of 8 vs 15 days of antibiotic therapy for ventilator-associated pneumonia in adults: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2003;290(19):2588-98. PMID 14625336 · No registry number (pre-registration-era trial).

cards.headline: Uranga 2016: stopping pneumonia antibiotics at day 5 by stability criteria was as successful as physicians’ longer courses
cards.summary: Clinical success: day 10, 56.3% intervention vs 48.6% control (P=0.18); day 30, 91.9% vs 88.6% (P=0.33) — the intervention stopped antibiotics at a minimum of 5 days once temperature and stability criteria were met — 312 hospitalized patients.
cards.type: Multicentre randomized noninferiority trial, JAMA Intern Med 2016
cards.people: 312 hospitalized CAP patients at 4 teaching hospitals in Spain (150 control, 162 intervention). Mean age 66.2 years (control) and 64.7 years (intervention); 63.3% and 62.3% men, respectively — printed in the abstract.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, clinical success was 56.3% (90 of 162) in the intervention group and 48.6% (71 of 150) in the control group at day 10 (P=0.18), and 91.9% (147 of 162) vs 88.6% (132 of 150) at day 30 (P=0.33). CAP symptom scores did not differ. The authors’ conclusion: the IDSA/ATS duration recommendations based on clinical stability can be safely implemented in hospitalized CAP.
cards.watchOut: Physician-chosen control durations in Spain in 2012–13 were already fairly short, so the trial validates a stability-based stopping rule more than it proves 5 days beats 10. Severe (ICU-level) pneumonia was not the population. Registered in the EU register (EudraCT 2011-001067-51).

shelves.title: Four-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin for tuberculosis: two months back — from one pivotal trial
shelves.question: For drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis, can a 4-month daily regimen — rifapentine in place of rifampin, moxifloxacin in place of ethambutol — cure as reliably as the standard 6 months?
shelves.mesh: Tuberculosis, Pulmonary · Antitubercular Agents · Moxifloxacin · Drug Therapy, Combination · Humans
shelves.balance: One trial carries this shelf, and the shelf says so. Study 31/A5349 randomized 2,516 people with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB: the 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen was noninferior to the 6-month standard (unfavorable outcomes 11.6% vs 9.6% in the assessable population, inside the 6.6-point margin), with grade 3-or-higher adverse events no more frequent (18.8% vs 19.3%). The regimen's internal control is instructive — rifapentine WITHOUT moxifloxacin failed noninferiority in the same trial (14.2% vs 9.6%) — and the shelf's third card is the graveyard of earlier shortcuts: REMoxTB and OFLOTUB both tried to shorten therapy to 4 months with fluoroquinolones and both failed. The shortening is real, but it belongs to this specific regimen, not to the idea of shortening. Single pivotal trial — the flag stays on the shelf until a second trial confirms it. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Study 31/A5349 (Dorman 2021): 4 months of rifapentine-moxifloxacin was noninferior to 6 months — unfavorable outcomes 11.6% vs 9.6%
cards.summary: Unfavorable outcome (assessable population): 11.6% on 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin vs 9.6% on the 6-month control (difference 2.0 percentage points, 95% CI −1.1 to 5.1 — inside the 6.6-point noninferiority margin); rifapentine without moxifloxacin failed noninferiority (14.2% vs 9.6%). Grade ≥3 adverse events: 18.8% vs 19.3% — 2,516 participants in 13 countries.
cards.type: Open-label, phase 3, randomized, controlled noninferiority trial (CDC TB Trials Consortium Study 31 / ACTG A5349), N Engl J Med 2021
cards.people: 2,516 participants with newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis in 13 countries; 2,343 were microbiologically eligible (culture-positive, not resistant to isoniazid, rifampin, or fluoroquinolones), of whom 194 were coinfected with HIV and 1,703 had cavitation on chest radiography; 2,234 were assessable for the primary outcome. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Rifapentine-moxifloxacin was noninferior to control in the microbiologically eligible population (unfavorable outcome 15.5% vs 14.6%; difference 1.0 percentage points; 95% CI, −2.6 to 4.5) and in the assessable population (11.6% vs 9.6%; difference 2.0 points; −1.1 to 5.1), against a 6.6-point noninferiority margin. Rifapentine without moxifloxacin was NOT noninferior (17.7% vs 14.6% microbiologically eligible; 14.2% vs 9.6% assessable). Grade 3-or-higher adverse events on treatment occurred in 19.3% (control), 18.8% (rifapentine-moxifloxacin), and 14.3% (rifapentine alone).
cards.watchOut: A noninferiority verdict with a generous 6.6-point margin, from an open-label trial, in culture-confirmed drug-susceptible disease — the two months saved are real, and so are the qualifiers. The failed rifapentine-only arm is the control the field needed: shortening works for this drug combination, not for rifapentine alone, and not (Cards 3) for the earlier fluoroquinolone shortcuts. This is the shelf's only pivotal trial; the flag in the shelf header stays until a second one exists.

cards.headline: Study 31 HIV substudy (Pettit 2023): in people with HIV on efavirenz-based ART, the 4-month regimen was also noninferior
cards.summary: Among 194 microbiologically eligible participants with HIV (median CD4 344 cells/µL): rifapentine-moxifloxacin was noninferior to the 6-month control (difference in unfavorable outcomes −7.4 percentage points ; 95% CI −20.8 to 6.0); rifapentine alone was not noninferior (+7.5 points). Grade ≥3 adverse events: 15% on rifapentine-based regimens vs 21% on control.
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a phase 3 randomized noninferiority trial (S31/A5349), Clin Infect Dis 2023
cards.people: 194 microbiologically eligible participants with HIV (8% of the 2,516 randomized in 13 countries), with CD4 counts of 100 cells/µL or above (median 344; interquartile range 223–455), receiving or about to start efavirenz-based ART. Enrollment of participants with HIV was staged to evaluate rifapentine-efavirenz drug interactions cautiously.
cards.result: The rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen was noninferior to control in participants with HIV (absolute difference in unfavorable outcomes −7.4%; 95% CI, −20.8% to 6.0%, against the 6.6% margin); the rifapentine-only regimen was not noninferior (+7.5%; −7.3% to +22.4%). Fewer grade 3-or-higher adverse events were reported in the rifapentine-based regimens (15%) than in the control regimen (21%).
cards.watchOut: A subgroup of 194 with wide confidence intervals — the −7.4-point estimate is compatible with meaningful harm as well as benefit, and noninferiority here inherits the parent trial's margin. Eligibility required CD4 counts of at least 100 and efavirenz-based ART; the result does not automatically travel to other antiretroviral regimens, where rifapentine interactions differ.

cards.headline: REMoxTB (Gillespie 2014) and OFLOTUB (Merle 2014): the earlier 4-month shortcuts both failed — faster sputum clearance was not cure
cards.summary: REMoxTB per-protocol favorable outcomes: 85% and 80% on the two 4-month moxifloxacin regimens vs 92% on the 6-month control — noninferiority not shown in either (1,931 patients). OFLOTUB's 4-month gatifloxacin regimen likewise failed noninferiority (unfavorable outcomes 21.0% vs 17.2% at 24 months after treatment; 1,836 patients).
cards.type: Two randomized phase 3 noninferiority trials (REMoxTB, double-blind; OFLOTUB, open-label), N Engl J Med 2014
cards.people: REMoxTB: 1,931 patients with uncomplicated smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis. OFLOTUB: 1,836 patients aged 18–65 with smear-positive, rifampin-sensitive, newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis in five sub-Saharan African countries. (The abstracts do not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: REMoxTB: in the per-protocol analysis, favorable outcomes were reported in 85% (moxifloxacin-for-ethambutol) and 80% (moxifloxacin-for-isoniazid) versus 92% on the 6-month control — differences of 6.1 and 11.4 percentage points favoring control; noninferiority was not shown for either regimen, although time to culture negativity was shorter (hazard ratios 1.17–1.25). Grade 3 or 4 adverse events were similar (17–19% across groups). OFLOTUB: the adjusted difference in unfavorable outcomes at 24 months after treatment was +3.5 percentage points (95% CI, −0.7 to 7.7) for the 4-month gatifloxacin regimen versus control — outside its 6-point margin, with heterogeneity across countries.
cards.watchOut: These two failures are why Study 31's success is credited to the regimen — high-dose daily rifapentine plus moxifloxacin — and not to fluoroquinolones or to enthusiasm about shortening. Both failed trials cleared sputum faster and still lost more patients to failure and relapse: in tuberculosis, the relapse tail is the endpoint, and it is unforgiving. (OFLOTUB: Merle CS et al., N Engl J Med 2014, PMID 25337748, NCT00216385.)

shelves.title: RSV vaccines in older adults: strong first-season protection that fades — and a rare Guillain-Barré warning on the label
shelves.question: In adults 60 and older, do respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines prevent RSV lower respiratory tract disease — how well, for how long, and at what risk?
shelves.mesh: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections · Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccines · Vaccine Efficacy · Guillain-Barre Syndrome · Aged · Humans
shelves.balance: Two prefusion-F vaccines, two large trials, the same shape of answer. GSK's adjuvanted vaccine (AReSVi-006) prevented RSV lower respiratory tract disease with 82.6% relative efficacy in its first season — in absolute terms, 7 cases versus 40 (1.0 vs 5.8 per 1,000 participant-years), roughly one case averted per 380 vaccinated per season — and 94.1% relative efficacy against severe disease. Pfizer's bivalent vaccine (RENOIR) showed 66.7% relative efficacy against illness with at least two symptoms and 85.7% against illness with at least three. Protection then fades: over three seasons a single GSK dose cumulatively held 62.9% relative efficacy, and a second dose a year later added nothing measurable — revaccination is not (yet) the answer. The harm side is carded on the same shelf, as it should be: post-marketing surveillance found a small excess of Guillain-Barré syndrome, on the order of 1.8 cases per million doses, and in January 2025 the FDA required warnings on both vaccines' labels. Every efficacy figure on this shelf is a relative reduction; the absolute case counts are printed on the cards. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: AReSVi-006 (Papi 2023): one dose of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 — vaccine efficacy 82.6% relative (7 cases vs 40) in the first season
cards.summary: RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease: 7 cases (1.0 per 1,000 participant-years) on vaccine vs 40 cases (5.8 per 1,000) on placebo — vaccine efficacy 82.6% relative (96.95% CI 57.9 to 94.1); against severe disease, 94.1% relative (1 vs 17 cases in the primary report) — 24,966 adults aged 60 and older, median follow-up 6.7 months.
cards.type: International, placebo-controlled, phase 3 randomized trial (AReSVi-006), N Engl J Med 2023
cards.people: 24,966 adults aged 60 years or older received one dose of vaccine (12,467) or placebo (12,499) before the RSV season; median follow-up 6.7 months. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.) Efficacy held across age groups and in participants with coexisting conditions.
cards.result: Vaccine efficacy against RT-PCR-confirmed RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease was 82.6% relative (96.95% CI, 57.9 to 94.1), with 7 cases (1.0 per 1,000 participant-years) in the vaccine group and 40 (5.8 per 1,000) in the placebo group — an absolute difference of about 4.8 cases per 1,000 participant-years. Efficacy was 94.1% relative (95% CI, 62.4 to 99.9) against severe RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease and 71.7% (56.2 to 82.3) against RSV-related acute respiratory infection, and was similar against RSV A (84.6%) and B (80.9%) subtypes. The vaccine was more reactogenic than placebo; serious adverse events and potential immune-mediated diseases were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: A relative efficacy of 82.6% on a seasonal incidence under 6 per 1,000 means the absolute yield in one season is modest — roughly one lower-respiratory case averted per 380 vaccinated — which is why the indication debate (universal at 75+, risk-based at 60–74, per ACIP) is about baseline risk, not about whether the vaccine works. One season of follow-up in this report; durability is Card 3.
cards.source: Papi A et al. Respiratory Syncytial Virus Prefusion F Protein Vaccine in Older Adults. N Engl J Med. 2023;388:595-608. PMID 36791160 · NCT04886596. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2209604

cards.headline: RENOIR (Walsh 2023): Pfizer's bivalent RSVpreF — efficacy 66.7% relative for illness with ≥2 symptoms, 85.7% for ≥3 symptoms
cards.summary: RSV-associated lower respiratory tract illness with at least two symptoms: 11 cases (1.19 per 1,000 person-years) on vaccine vs 33 (3.58 per 1,000) on placebo — vaccine efficacy 66.7% relative (96.66% CI 28.8 to 85.8); with at least three symptoms: 2 vs 14 cases, 85.7% relative — interim analysis, 34,284 adults aged 60 and older.
cards.type: Multinational, placebo-controlled, phase 3 randomized trial (RENOIR), interim analysis, N Engl J Med 2023
cards.people: 34,284 participants received RSVpreF vaccine (17,215) or placebo (17,069) at the interim analysis (data cutoff July 14, 2022). (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.) Participants were adults 60 years of age or older.
cards.result: RSV-associated lower respiratory tract illness with at least two signs or symptoms occurred in 11 vaccine recipients (1.19 cases per 1,000 person-years of observation) and 33 placebo recipients (3.58 per 1,000) — vaccine efficacy 66.7% relative (96.66% CI, 28.8 to 85.8). With at least three signs or symptoms: 2 versus 14 cases (0.22 vs 1.52 per 1,000) — efficacy 85.7% relative (96.66% CI, 32.0 to 98.7). RSV-associated acute respiratory illness: 22 versus 58 cases — efficacy 62.1% relative (95% CI, 37.1 to 77.9). Local reactions were more frequent with vaccine (12% vs 7%); systemic events were similar (27% vs 26%), as were adverse events through 1 month (9.0% vs 8.5%) and serious adverse events (2.3% in each group).
cards.watchOut: An interim analysis with 44 primary cases total — the point estimates are large and the intervals are wide, and the case definition (symptom-count thresholds) does much of the work in the headline numbers. Read it as concordant with AReSVi-006 rather than as a competitor's score: two different prefusion-F vaccines, the same direction, protection strongest against the most severe illness.
cards.source: Walsh EE et al. Efficacy and Safety of a Bivalent RSV Prefusion F Vaccine in Older Adults. N Engl J Med. 2023;388:1465-1477. PMID 37018468 · NCT05035212 · EudraCT 2021-003693-31. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2213836

cards.headline: AReSVi-006 over three seasons (Ison 2025): one dose held 62.9% cumulative relative efficacy — and revaccination at one year added nothing
cards.summary: Cumulative efficacy of a single dose over three RSV seasons: 62.9% relative (97.5% CI 46.7 to 74.8) against RSV lower respiratory tract disease — down from 82.6% in season one; a second dose one year later had efficacy within the same range as one dose, i.e. no added benefit shown — 24,966 participants, median follow-up 30.6 months.
cards.type: Three-season follow-up of a randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (AReSVi-006), Lancet Respir Med 2025
cards.people: Efficacy analyses included 12,468 vaccine recipients and 12,498 placebo recipients aged 60 or older at 275 centres in 17 countries; vaccine recipients were re-randomized before season two to a second dose or placebo. Median follow-up from 15 days after dose one was 30.6 months. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Cumulative efficacy over three seasons of one dose was 62.9% relative (97.5% CI, 46.7 to 74.8) against RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease — 69.8% against RSV A and 58.6% against RSV B — and efficacy decreased over time. Efficacy was observed in participants aged 60–69 and 70–79 years, in pre-frail participants, and in those with pre-existing conditions that raise RSV risk. A first dose followed by revaccination one year later had efficacy within the same range as a single dose. Serious adverse events judged related to the intervention were under 1% in every group.
cards.watchOut: This card is why 'LIKELY' on this shelf is a statement about a first dose, not a program: protection wanes, the trial's revaccination strategy did not restore it, and the optimal interval — if any — is unknown. Policy built on annual RSV revaccination would be running ahead of this evidence.

cards.headline: The Guillain-Barré ledger (FDA surveillance, 2023–2026): a real, rare signal — about 1.8 excess cases per million doses — and January 2025 label warnings on both vaccines
cards.summary: FDA post-marketing analyses in Medicare beneficiaries 65 and older found an increased rate of Guillain-Barré syndrome in the 42 days after RSV vaccination, on the order of ~1.8 excess cases per million doses (the estimate the FDA cited in requiring warnings); in January 2025 both labels (Arexvy, Abrysvo) were revised to carry the warning. The FDA's broader Medicare safety study of 3.82 million vaccinated beneficiaries (Lloyd 2026) found no significant elevation for the other prespecified outcomes examined.
cards.type: Post-marketing self-controlled case-series surveillance (FDA Medicare analyses), Vaccine 2026, with the FDA label revisions of January 2025
cards.people: Approximately 3.82 million Medicare beneficiaries aged 65 years and older received an RSV vaccination in the United States between May 2023 and July 2024 (2.60 million adjuvanted RSVPreF3 [Arexvy]; 1.21 million bivalent RSVPreF [Abrysvo]). Guillain-Barré syndrome was evaluated in a companion FDA analysis of the same beneficiary population.
cards.result: In the FDA's Guillain-Barré evaluation, GBS diagnoses clustered in the post-vaccination risk window at a rate above background, corresponding to an attributable risk on the order of 1.8 excess cases per million doses — small in absolute terms, large enough that in January 2025 the FDA required a Guillain-Barré warning in both vaccines' prescribing information. In the companion Medicare study of 11 other prespecified outcomes (Lloyd 2026), no statistically significant elevation in risk was observed for any outcome after either vaccine; adjusted incidence rate ratios were not significant across outcomes including stroke and atrial fibrillation.
cards.watchOut: Keep the two halves of this card together: a rare, real harm that changed the label, inside a surveillance record that was otherwise reassuring at nearly 4 million doses. GBS after vaccination must also be weighed against GBS and severe disease after RSV infection itself, and against the absolute benefit on Cards 1–2 — which, at roughly one case averted per 380 vaccinated per season in trial populations, exceeds the GBS risk by orders of magnitude in high-risk older adults, and by far less in low-risk ones. That gradient is the substance of the age-and-risk-based recommendations.
cards.source: Lloyd PC et al. Safety monitoring of health outcomes following RSVPreF3+AS01 and RSVPreF vaccination among Medicare beneficiaries aged 65 years and older in the United States, 2023-2024. Vaccine. 2026;79:128459. PMID 41833132. DOI 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.128459 · Guillain-Barré estimates and label warnings: US Food and Drug Administration, January 2025. (Post-marketing surveillance — no trial registry number applies.)

shelves.title: High-dose influenza vaccine: better against flu itself — the big hospitalization trials split
shelves.question: In adults 65 and older, does high-dose influenza vaccine prevent more illness and hospitalization than the standard dose?
shelves.mesh: Influenza, Human · Influenza Vaccines · Hospitalization · Vaccine Efficacy · Aged · Humans
shelves.balance: DANFLU-2 comes first because it is the largest and the most sobering: 332,438 Danes randomized, and the primary end point — hospitalization for influenza or pneumonia — was NOT met (0.68% vs 0.73%; relative effectiveness 5.9%; P=0.14). What DANFLU-2 did show was a 43.6% relative reduction in hospitalization for influenza specifically, with pneumonia hospitalizations identical (0.63% vs 0.63%) — the composite was diluted by the outcome the vaccine cannot be expected to move much. GALFLU, the second mega-trial, met the same composite (relative effectiveness 23.7%) in a younger 65–79 population. The older evidence agrees on the narrower claim: FIM12 proved 24.2% relative efficacy against laboratory-confirmed influenza illness, and INVESTED — in post-MI and heart-failure patients — found no difference in death or cardiopulmonary hospitalization (HR 1.06). So: LIKELY that high-dose vaccine prevents more influenza and influenza hospitalization than standard dose; only POSSIBLE that it moves the broad hospitalization composites clinics actually feel. All effectiveness figures are relative; absolute risks are printed on every card. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: DANFLU-2 (Johansen 2025): 332,438 randomized — the primary end point was NOT met (P=0.14); influenza hospitalization fell 43.6% relative, pneumonia did not move
cards.summary: Primary end point (hospitalization for influenza or pneumonia): 0.68% on high-dose vs 0.73% on standard-dose — relative vaccine effectiveness 5.9% (95.2% CI −2.1 to 13.4; P=0.14 — NOT met ). Hospitalization for influenza: 0.06% vs 0.11% ( 43.6% relative ); for pneumonia: 0.63% vs 0.63% (0.5% relative). All-cause death: 0.67% vs 0.66% — 332,438 adults 65 and older in Denmark.
cards.type: Pragmatic, open-label, individually randomized, registry-based trial (DANFLU-2), N Engl J Med 2025
cards.people: 332,438 adults aged 65 or older in Denmark over the 2022–23, 2023–24, and 2024–25 seasons (166,218 high-dose, 166,220 standard-dose); mean age 73.7 years (SD 5.8); 48.6% were women. Outcomes came from nationwide administrative registries.
cards.result: A primary end-point event occurred in 1,138 participants (0.68%) in the high-dose group and 1,210 (0.73%) in the standard-dose group — relative vaccine effectiveness 5.9% (95.2% CI, −2.1 to 13.4; P=0.14): the primary end point was NOT met. Hospitalization for influenza occurred in 0.06% versus 0.11% (relative effectiveness 43.6%; 27.5 to 56.3); hospitalization for pneumonia in 0.63% versus 0.63% (relative effectiveness 0.5%; −8.6 to 8.8); hospitalization for cardiorespiratory disease in 2.25% versus 2.38% (5.7% relative; 1.4 to 9.9); death from any cause in 0.67% versus 0.66% (relative effectiveness −2.5%). Serious adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Printed first on this shelf by design: the largest trial ever run on this question missed its primary end point, and any honest account of high-dose vaccine starts there. The anatomy of the miss matters — influenza hospitalizations, the events the vaccine can plausibly prevent, were nearly halved in relative terms but are rare; pneumonia hospitalizations, ten times commoner and mostly not influenza, did not move at all and swamped the composite.
cards.source: Johansen ND et al. High-Dose Influenza Vaccine Effectiveness against Hospitalization in Older Adults. N Engl J Med. 2025;393:2291-2302. PMID 40888720 · NCT05517174 · EUCTR 2022-500657-17-00. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2509907

cards.headline: GALFLU (Pardo-Seco 2025): in Galicia, the same composite WAS met — relative effectiveness 23.7% in adults 65–79
cards.summary: Primary end point (hospitalization for influenza or pneumonia): 0.26% on high-dose vs 0.34% on standard-dose — relative vaccine effectiveness 23.7% (95% CI 6.6 to 37.7); hospitalization for influenza: 0.09% vs 0.14% ( 31.8% relative ) — 103,169 community-dwelling adults aged 65–79 in Galicia, Spain, over two seasons.
cards.type: Pragmatic, registry-based, open-label, randomized, active-controlled trial (GALFLU), N Engl J Med 2025
cards.people: 103,169 unique community-dwelling adults aged 65–79 in Galicia, Spain, randomized across the 2023–24 and 2024–25 seasons (31,307 participated in both seasons and were counted in each); mean age 72.3 years (SD 4.3); 53.6% were men.
cards.result: A primary end-point event occurred in 174 of 67,093 participants (absolute risk 0.26%) in the high-dose group and 227 of 66,789 (0.34%) in the standard-dose group — relative vaccine effectiveness 23.7% (95% CI, 6.6 to 37.7). Hospitalization for influenza occurred in 63 (0.09%) versus 92 (0.14%) — relative effectiveness 31.8% (5.0 to 51.3). Serious adverse events appeared similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Why did GALFLU meet the composite DANFLU-2 missed? A younger population (65–79 vs 65+), different seasons and circulating strains, and absolute event rates a third lower — with only 401 primary events, the confidence interval (6.6 to 37.7) is wide enough to include DANFLU-2's estimate. The two trials are less contradictory than their headlines: both found influenza hospitalizations reduced by roughly a third to two-fifths relative, and the composite verdict hinged on the pneumonia background.
cards.source: Pardo-Seco J et al. High-Dose Influenza Vaccine to Reduce Hospitalizations. N Engl J Med. 2025;393:2303-2312. PMID 40888694 · NCT06141655 · EudraCT 2023-506977-36-00. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2509834

cards.headline: FIM12 (DiazGranados 2014): the licensure trial — 24.2% relative efficacy against laboratory-confirmed influenza illness (1.4% vs 1.9%)
cards.summary: Laboratory-confirmed influenza illness: 1.4% (228/15,991) on high-dose vs 1.9% (301/15,998) on standard-dose — relative efficacy 24.2% (95% CI 9.7 to 36.5), an absolute difference of 0.5 percentage points — 31,989 adults 65 and older in the US and Canada over two seasons.
cards.type: Phase 3b–4, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trial (FIM12), N Engl J Med 2014
cards.people: 31,989 adults aged 65 or older at 126 centers in the United States and Canada (15,991 high-dose, 15,998 standard-dose), over the 2011–12 and 2012–13 northern-hemisphere seasons. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, 228 participants in the high-dose group (1.4%) and 301 in the standard-dose group (1.9%) had laboratory-confirmed influenza associated with a protocol-defined influenza-like illness — relative efficacy 24.2% (95% CI, 9.7 to 36.5). Antibody titers and seroprotection rates were significantly higher with the high dose. At least one serious adverse event was reported by 8.3% of the high-dose group and 9.0% of the standard-dose group (relative risk 0.92; 0.85 to 0.99).
cards.watchOut: This is the trial the high-dose recommendation was built on — and its outcome was influenza illness, not hospitalization or death. The absolute gain was half a percentage point of illness per season. Everything since (INVESTED, DANFLU-2, GALFLU) has been the field asking whether that illness-level advantage converts into severe-outcome advantage; the answer so far is 'for influenza hospitalization, probably; for the broad composites, not reliably.'
cards.source: DiazGranados CA et al. Efficacy of High-Dose versus Standard-Dose Influenza Vaccine in Older Adults. N Engl J Med. 2014;371:635-45. PMID 25119609 · NCT01427309. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1315727
cards.search: fim12 (diazgranados 2014): the licensure trial 24.2% relative efficacy against laboratory-confirmed influenza illness (1.4% vs 1.9%) laboratory-confirmed influenza illness: 1.4% (228/15,991) on high-dose vs 1.9% (301/15,998) on standard-dose relative efficacy 24.2% (95% ci 9.7 to 36.5), an absolute difference of 0.5 percentage points 31,989 adults 65 and older in the us and canada over two seasons. in adults 65 years of age or older, does high-dose trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine (60 µg hemagglutinin per strain) protect against laboratory-confirmed influenza illness better than the standard dose (15 µg)? phase 3b-4, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trial (fim12), n engl j med 2014 31,989 adults aged 65 or older at 126 centers in the united states and canada (15,991 high-dose, 15,998 standard-dose), over the 2011-12 and 2012-13 northern-hemisphere seasons.

cards.headline: INVESTED (Vardeny 2021): in high-risk cardiovascular patients, high-dose vaccine did not reduce death or cardiopulmonary hospitalization (HR 1.06)
cards.summary: Primary outcome (all-cause death or cardiopulmonary hospitalization): event rate 45 per 100 patient-years on high-dose trivalent vs 42 per 100 patient-years on standard-dose quadrivalent — hazard ratio 1.06 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.17; P=0.21), no benefit — 5,260 patients with recent myocardial infarction or heart-failure hospitalization, vaccinated over up to 3 seasons.
cards.type: Pragmatic, multicenter, double-blind, active-comparator randomized trial (INVESTED), JAMA 2021
cards.people: 5,260 participants (2,630 per group) with a recent acute myocardial infarction or heart-failure hospitalization plus at least one additional risk factor, at 157 sites in the US and Canada, vaccinated for up to 3 influenza seasons (7,154 total vaccinations); mean age 65.5 years (SD 12.6); 72% were men; 63% had heart failure.
cards.result: There were 975 primary outcome events among 884 participants in the high-dose group (event rate 45 per 100 patient-years) and 924 events among 837 participants in the standard-dose group (42 per 100 patient-years) — hazard ratio 1.06 (95% CI, 0.97 to 1.17; P=0.21). Vaccine-related adverse reactions were more frequent with the high dose (40.5% vs 34.4%); severe adverse reactions were 2.1% versus 1.7%. The trial's conclusion: high-dose vaccine did not reduce the primary composite in this population.
cards.watchOut: INVESTED compared a trivalent high-dose against a quadrivalent standard-dose — one extra strain in the control arm — in the highest-risk population on this shelf, where most cardiopulmonary hospitalizations are not influenza-caused and cannot be vaccine-prevented. The null is consistent with DANFLU-2's composite: when the outcome is dominated by non-influenza events, a better influenza vaccine has little room to show.
cards.source: Vardeny O et al. Effect of High-Dose Trivalent vs Standard-Dose Quadrivalent Influenza Vaccine on Mortality or Cardiopulmonary Hospitalization in Patients With High-Risk Cardiovascular Disease: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2021;325:39-49. PMID 33275134 · NCT02787044. DOI 10.1001/jama.2020.23649
