shelves.title: Digital CBT for insomnia: Sleepio and its class — real effects, placebo-tested
shelves.question: Does cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia delivered by an app or website actually improve sleep?
shelves.mesh: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Humans · Internet · Sleep · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Digital CBT-I is the best-evidenced product on this slate: a placebo-controlled trial with large effects on sleep efficiency (Sleepio, d≈1.0 against an active placebo), the largest psychological-intervention trial of its era confirming a large insomnia effect at scale (OASIS, d=1.11), and a second program whose randomized gains persisted a full year (SHUTi). LIKELY, fenced to what was measured — self-reported sleep improvement in self-selected, internet-using adults with insomnia. No card compares the apps with sleeping pills; that is a different shelf’s question. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Sleepio’s placebo-controlled trial (Espie 2012, Sleep): online CBT raised sleep efficiency 20 points — three-quarters of users finished with sleep efficiency above 80%
cards.summary: 164 adults meeting proposed DSM-5 criteria for insomnia disorder (mean age 49; 120 women), randomized to online CBT (Sleepio: six sessions with an animated therapist, automated support, moderated community), imagery-relief placebo, or usual care. Sleep efficiency gain: +20% with CBT vs +6% placebo (d=1.06) and +6% usual care (d=0.95) , sustained at 8-week follow-up. Finishing with sleep efficiency >80%: 76% CBT vs 29% placebo vs 18% usual care ; >90%: 38% vs 6% vs 0%.
cards.type: Randomized, placebo-controlled, three-arm trial, Sleep 2012. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: ISRCTN44615689.
cards.people: 164 adults (120 women; mean age 49 years, range 18–78) from an online community in the UK, meeting proposed DSM-5 criteria for insomnia disorder: 55 assigned online CBT, 55 imagery relief therapy (placebo), 54 treatment as usual.
cards.result: On the primary endpoint of sleep efficiency, online CBT was associated with sustained improvement at post-treatment (+20%) relative to both treatment as usual (+6%; d=0.95) and imagery relief therapy (+6%; d=1.06), maintained at 8-week follow-up. 76% of CBT participants completed treatment with sleep efficiency >80%, compared with 29% (placebo) and 18% (usual care); 55% exceeded 85% and 38% exceeded 90%. Daytime functioning and Sleep Condition Indicator scores also improved substantially (d=0.77–1.20 on the indicator).
cards.watchOut: A rare thing in digital health: a real placebo arm, which matters because engaging apps harvest large placebo responses — and CBT still beat it by a wide margin. The fence is the sample: self-selected, internet-recruited UK volunteers, and an 8-week horizon. Whether effects persist for years is Card 3’s question (a different program’s answer).
cards.source: Espie CA et al. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial of online cognitive behavioral therapy for chronic insomnia disorder delivered via an automated media-rich web application. Sleep. 2012;35(6):769–781. PMID 22654196 · ISRCTN44615689. DOI 10.5665/sleep.1872

cards.headline: OASIS (Freeman 2017, Lancet Psychiatry): 3,755 students — digital CBT cut insomnia severity with a large effect (d=1.11) and nudged paranoia and hallucinations down
cards.summary: The largest randomized trial of a psychological intervention of its era: 3,755 university students with insomnia at 26 UK universities, randomized to digital CBT for insomnia (Sleepio) or usual care, single-blind. At 10 weeks the intervention reduced insomnia by an adjusted difference of 4.78 points [4.29–5.26] on the Sleep Condition Indicator (Cohen’s d=1.11), paranoia by 2.22 points (d=0.19), and hallucinatory experiences by 1.58 points (d=0.24); insomnia change statistically mediated the mental-health changes. No adverse events were reported.
cards.type: Single-blind randomized controlled trial with mediation analysis (OASIS), Lancet Psychiatry 2017. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: ISRCTN61272251.
cards.people: 3,755 university students with insomnia at 26 UK universities (1,891 digital CBT; 1,864 usual practice), assessed online at 0, 3, 10, and 22 weeks. The record’s abstract does not print an age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: Compared with usual practice, the sleep intervention at 10 weeks reduced insomnia (adjusted difference 4.78; 95% CI, 4.29 to 5.26; Cohen’s d=1.11; P<0.0001), paranoia (−2.22; 95% CI, −2.98 to −1.45; d=0.19; P<0.0001), and hallucinations (−1.58; 95% CI, −1.98 to −1.18; d=0.24; P<0.0001). Insomnia was a mediator of change in paranoia and hallucinations. No adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Two fences. The population is students — young, educated, digitally fluent — and the authors themselves say generalization beyond students requires testing. And keep the effect sizes in their lanes: the sleep effect is large (d=1.11); the psychosis-spectrum effects are small (d≈0.2), interesting as causal evidence about sleep’s role, not as a treatment claim for paranoia.
cards.source: Freeman D et al. The effects of improving sleep on mental health (OASIS): a randomised controlled trial with mediation analysis. Lancet Psychiatry. 2017;4(10):749–758. PMID 28888927 · ISRCTN61272251. DOI 10.1016/S2215-0366(17)30328-0

cards.headline: SHUTi at one year (Ritterband 2017, JAMA Psychiatry): internet CBT-I gains held — insomnia severity effect size grew to d=2.32 at 12 months
cards.summary: 303 adults with chronic insomnia randomized to SHUTi (a 6-week automated, interactive internet CBT-I program) or online patient education. All three primary outcomes favored SHUTi at every time point (group × time P<.001): insomnia severity, sleep-onset latency, and wake after sleep onset. Within-group effect sizes for SHUTi ran d=0.79–1.90 post-treatment and were maintained at 1 year — insomnia severity d=2.32, sleep-onset latency d=1.41, wake after sleep onset d=0.95 at follow-up.
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial with 1-year follow-up, JAMA Psychiatry 2017. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT01438697.
cards.people: 303 US adults with chronic insomnia who self-referred (mean age 43.3 years [SD 11.6]; 71.9% women); 151 randomized to SHUTi and 152 to online patient education; about half reported at least one medical or psychiatric comorbidity.
cards.result: Results for the 3 primary sleep outcomes showed a significant overall group × time interaction for all variables, favoring the SHUTi group (Insomnia Severity Index F=20.65, P<.001; sleep-onset latency F=6.01, P<.001; wake after sleep onset F=12.68, P<.001). Within-group effect sizes demonstrated improvements from baseline to post-assessment for SHUTi participants (range, Cohen d=0.79 [95% CI, 0.55–1.04] to d=1.90 [95% CI, 1.62–2.18]). Treatment effects were maintained at the 1-year follow-up.
cards.watchOut: SHUTi is not Sleepio — it is carded as the class’s durability evidence, and the comparison was patient education, not placebo or a sleeping pill, so expectancy contributes to these numbers. Within-group effect sizes at follow-up (the d=2.32 headline) also flatter: they measure change from a symptomatic baseline without the control group’s parallel change netted out. The randomized between-group result — significant on all primaries — is the durable claim.
cards.source: Ritterband LM et al. Effect of a Web-Based Cognitive Behavior Therapy for Insomnia Intervention With 1-Year Follow-up: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Psychiatry. 2017;74(1):68–75. PMID 27902836 · NCT01438697. DOI 10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2016.3249

cards.headline: Reading the digital CBT-I evidence together: the rare app that beat its placebo, at scale, with a year of durability
cards.summary: Three randomized programs converge: Sleepio beat a credible placebo on sleep efficiency (d≈1.0); Sleepio at 3,755-student scale cut insomnia severity with d=1.11; SHUTi’s between-group wins on all primary outcomes held at one year . No card here compares digital CBT-I head-to-head with sleeping pills or with face-to-face CBT-I — that comparison lives on the sleep slate’s future shelf (#499’s question) — and none measures falls, cognition, or other hard outcomes in older patients.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1–3 together and fences the claim to symptom improvement in self-selected adults.
cards.people: The populations of Cards 1–3: UK adults with insomnia disorder (placebo-controlled), UK university students with insomnia, and US adults with chronic insomnia, all self-selected and internet-delivered.
cards.result: Digital CBT-I improves self-reported sleep — efficiency, severity, latency, wake after sleep onset — versus placebo, usual care, and patient education, with large short-term effects and demonstrated 1-year durability. Populations were volunteers comfortable online; completion and engagement vary in routine practice, and real-world effects are usually smaller than trial effects for self-help interventions.
cards.watchOut: Insomnia severity here is self-reported by design — sleep diaries and questionnaires are the field’s standard outcomes, but they are subjective, and unblinded participants know whether they got the therapy. The placebo-controlled card (Reference 1) is what keeps this shelf’s grade high despite that.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–3 on this shelf (PMID 22654196; PMID 28888927; PMID 27902836).

shelves.title: Pneumococcal vaccines in older adults: vaccine-type disease prevented — pneumonia overall, not shown
shelves.question: Do pneumococcal vaccines prevent pneumococcal pneumonia and invasive disease in older adults?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Community-Acquired Infections · Humans · Pneumococcal Vaccines · Pneumonia, Pneumococcal · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Vaccines, Conjugate
shelves.balance: One very large trial anchors the conjugate claim: in CAPiTA (84,496 adults ≥65), PCV13 prevented 45.6% of vaccine-type pneumococcal pneumonia and 75.0% of vaccine-type invasive disease — and 5.1% (not significant) of pneumonia from any cause, which is the number that keeps the shelf honest. The older polysaccharide vaccine’s pooled record (Cochrane) supports protection against invasive disease, largely on non-randomised evidence, with no shown effect on all-cause pneumonia or mortality. Split stamp: LIKELY for the conjugate vaccine against vaccine-type disease; POSSIBLE for the polysaccharide vaccine’s broader claim. Proposed split stamp — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: CAPiTA (Bonten 2015, NEJM): the 13-valent conjugate vaccine prevented vaccine-type pneumonia (VE 45.6%) and invasive disease (VE 75%) in 84,496 older adults
cards.summary: 84,496 adults aged 65 or older randomised double-blind to PCV13 or placebo (Netherlands), mean follow-up 3.97 years. Per-protocol vaccine efficacy against first episodes of vaccine-type pneumococcal community-acquired pneumonia: 45.6% [95.2% CI 21.8–62.5] (49 vs 90 cases); against nonbacteremic/noninvasive vaccine-type pneumonia 45.0% [14.2–65.3]; against vaccine-type invasive pneumococcal disease 75.0% [41.4–90.8] (7 vs 28 cases). Efficacy persisted through the trial. Against community-acquired pneumonia from any cause , efficacy was 5.1% [−5.1 to 14.2] — not significant. Serious adverse events and deaths were similar; local reactions were more common with vaccine.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2015. Registry ID from the record’s own text: NCT00744263.
cards.people: 84,496 adults 65 years of age or older in the Netherlands, followed a mean of 3.97 years. The record’s abstract does not print a sex breakdown.
cards.result: In the per-protocol analysis of first episodes of infections due to vaccine-type strains, community-acquired pneumonia occurred in 49 persons in the PCV13 group and 90 persons in the placebo group (vaccine efficacy, 45.6%; 95.2% confidence interval, 21.8 to 62.5), nonbacteremic and noninvasive community-acquired pneumonia occurred in 33 persons in the PCV13 group and 60 persons in the placebo group (vaccine efficacy, 45.0%), and invasive pneumococcal disease occurred in 7 persons in the PCV13 group and 28 persons in the placebo group (vaccine efficacy, 75.0%; 95% CI, 41.4 to 90.8). In the modified intention-to-treat analysis, community-acquired pneumonia from any cause occurred in 747 persons in the PCV13 group and 787 in the placebo group (vaccine efficacy, 5.1%; 95% CI, −5.1 to 14.2). Numbers of serious adverse events and deaths were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The fence is in the trial’s own conclusion: PCV13 prevented disease caused by its 13 serotypes and did not detectably prevent pneumonia overall — because vaccine serotypes cause a minority of all pneumonia in older adults. Quote the 45.6% and the 75% as vaccine-type numbers, never as pneumonia numbers. The trial also predates the higher-valency conjugates (15-, 20- and 21-valent) that recommendations have since moved to on immunogenicity bridging; those products have no CAPiTA of their own.
cards.source: Bonten MJM et al. Polysaccharide conjugate vaccine against pneumococcal pneumonia in adults. N Engl J Med. 2015;372(12):1114–1125. PMID 25785969 · NCT00744263. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1408544

cards.headline: The polysaccharide vaccine’s pooled record (Cochrane, Moberley 2013): protection against invasive disease, no shown effect on pneumonia overall or mortality
cards.summary: The 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine (PPV23) is the older, broader, weaker technology: more serotypes, no conjugate carrier, no immunological memory. The Cochrane meta-analysis of its trials and observational studies concluded that the evidence supports PPV to prevent invasive pneumococcal disease in adults — the non-randomised evidence for that outcome pooled at OR 0.48 [0.37–0.61] — while finding the randomised evidence less clear in adults with chronic illness , and no evidence supporting routine use to prevent all-cause pneumonia or mortality : all-cause mortality pooled at OR 0.90 [0.74–1.09]. Adverse events were outside the review’s scope.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, CD000422), 2013. No registry ID applies to the review itself.
cards.people: Adults, predominantly older and at-risk populations, in randomised trials, controlled before-after and case-control studies of 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine across high- and low-income settings.
cards.result: The authors concluded that the meta-analysis provides evidence supporting the recommendation for PPV to prevent invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) in adults; that the evidence from randomised trials is less clear with respect to adults with chronic illness; and that the meta-analysis does not provide evidence to support the routine use of PPV to prevent all-cause pneumonia or mortality. PPV was not associated with substantial reductions in all-cause mortality (OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.09).
cards.watchOut: A pooled record with two different strengths of evidence for two different outcomes: the invasive-disease protection leans substantially on non-randomised studies, and the outcomes patients ask about first — pneumonia and death — are the ones with no shown benefit. Later conjugate products have largely displaced PPV23 in recommendations, but PPV23’s record is the standing warning against reading serotype-specific efficacy as pneumonia prevention.

cards.headline: Reading the pneumococcal evidence together: strong against vaccine-type disease, silent on pneumonia as a whole
cards.summary: The pattern across both technologies is the same one CAPiTA drew in a single trial: pneumococcal vaccines prevent disease caused by the serotypes they contain — conjugate efficacy 45.6% against vaccine-type pneumonia and 75% against vaccine-type invasive disease in one very large randomised trial; polysaccharide protection against invasive disease supported mostly by observational pooling — and neither has shown a reduction in all-cause pneumonia or mortality, the endpoints diluted by every other cause of a winter admission. The grade therefore splits by claim: the vaccine-type claim is as strong as single-trial evidence gets; the broader adult-protection claim for the polysaccharide vaccine is a grade lower and rests on non-randomised data.

It does not establish reductions in all-cause pneumonia or mortality for either. Serotype replacement and the shift to higher-valency conjugates are live context the carded records predate.
cards.watchOut: Cite ‘pneumococcal vaccination prevents pneumonia’ only with the word ‘vaccine-type’ attached and the CAPiTA all-cause figure (5.1%, not significant) within reach — the shelf’s whole point is the distance between those two statements.

shelves.title: Melatonin: jet lag vs insomnia — strong for jet lag, small for insomnia
shelves.question: Does melatonin help jet lag after crossing time zones, and does it help ordinary insomnia — and are those the same claim?
shelves.mesh: Antioxidants · Humans · Jet Lag Syndrome · Melatonin · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders · Sleep Wake Disorders · Sleep Disorders, Circadian Rhythm
shelves.balance: Two different questions share one bottle, and the evidence splits cleanly. For jet lag, the Cochrane review found 9 of 10 placebo-controlled trials positive when melatonin was taken close to the destination bedtime after flights crossing five or more time zones, with 0.5–5 mg similarly effective and a number needed to treat of 2 — a short-term circadian claim, graded LIKELY. For ordinary insomnia, the pooled effects are minutes, not hours: sleep onset latency fell by 4.0 minutes in the Brzezinski meta-analysis (17 studies, 284 subjects) and total sleep rose by 12.8 minutes; the later Auld review again found its most convincing signal in sleep-onset latency in primary insomnia (P=0.002) across only 12 randomised trials. The Ferracioli-Oda 2013 meta-analysis (sleep latency −7.06 minutes) is carded at its home on Shelf #116 and is not re-carded here. Split stamp: LIKELY for jet lag; POSSIBLE for insomnia sleep-onset. Proposed split stamp — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Herxheimer & Petrie 2002 (Cochrane): melatonin for jet lag — 9 of 10 trials positive, NNT 2, after flights crossing ≥5 time zones
cards.summary: Cochrane review of 10 randomised trials in airline passengers, airline staff or military personnel comparing oral melatonin with placebo (one trial also compared zolpidem). Nine of the ten trials found melatonin, taken close to the target bedtime at the destination (10pm to midnight), decreased jet lag from flights crossing five or more time zones. Daily doses of 0.5–5 mg were similarly effective, except that people fell asleep faster and slept better after 5 mg than 0.5 mg; doses above 5 mg appeared no more effective, and 2 mg slow-release performed relatively poorly. The review's number needed to treat was 2.
cards.type: Systematic review (Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2002). No registry ID applies to a systematic review.
cards.people: 10 randomised trials in airline passengers, airline staff or military personnel; the record does not print a pooled participant count, mean age, or sex mix.
cards.result: Nine of the ten trials found melatonin, taken close to destination bedtime, decreased jet lag after flights crossing five or more time zones; 0.5–5 mg similarly effective; NNT 2 per the review.
cards.watchOut: A 2002 review of small, older trials with subjective jet-lag ratings, for short-term travel use only. It says nothing about nightly insomnia treatment, long-term safety, or use in children — do not lend its jet-lag strength to the insomnia claim. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Herxheimer A, Petrie KJ. Melatonin for the prevention and treatment of jet lag. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2002;(2):CD001520. PMID 12076414

cards.headline: Brzezinski 2005: melatonin for insomnia — sleep onset 4.0 minutes faster, total sleep 12.8 minutes longer
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of 17 studies involving 284 subjects that met inclusion criteria, pooling sleep onset latency, total sleep duration and sleep efficiency. Melatonin significantly reduced sleep onset latency by 4.0 min (95% CI 2.5 to 5.4), increased sleep efficiency by 2.2% (95% CI 0.2 to 4.2), and increased total sleep duration by 12.8 min (the record's abstract is truncated at that point and prints no confidence interval for this outcome, so none is claimed). The underlying studies were highly heterogeneous in populations, insomnia definitions, doses and routes.

cards.result: Sleep onset latency −4.0 min (95% CI 2.5 to 5.4); sleep efficiency +2.2% (95% CI 0.2 to 4.2); total sleep duration +12.8 min.
cards.watchOut: Statistically real, clinically small: four minutes to fall asleep is not a treatment effect most patients can feel, and 284 subjects across 17 studies is a thin base. This card is the honest size of the insomnia claim. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Auld 2017: the most convincing melatonin signal is sleep-onset latency — in primary insomnia (P=0.002) and delayed sleep phase (P<0.0001)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of double- or single-blind randomised controlled trials of melatonin vs placebo in primary sleep disorders: of 5,030 citations, 12 trials were included, covering primary insomnia, delayed sleep phase syndrome, non-24-hour sleep-wake syndrome in blind people, and REM behaviour disorder. The most convincing evidence was for reducing sleep onset latency in primary insomnia (P=0.002) and delayed sleep phase syndrome (P<0.0001), and for regulating sleep-wake patterns in blind patients. The authors called for large-scale randomised trials. Effect sizes in minutes are not printed in the record's abstract and are not claimed here.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials, Sleep Med Rev 2017. No registry ID applies to a meta-analysis.
cards.people: 12 randomised trials in adults with primary sleep disorders; the record does not print a pooled participant count, mean age, or sex mix.
cards.result: Most convincing evidence: reduced sleep onset latency in primary insomnia (P=0.002) and delayed sleep phase syndrome (P<0.0001); sleep-wake regulation in blind patients.
cards.watchOut: Only 12 trials across four different disorders, and the abstract reports significance, not size. Direction is consistent with Brzezinski; magnitude remains minutes-scale until a large trial says otherwise. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: Sleep duration and health: the U-curve — an observational shelf
shelves.question: Are both short and long habitual sleep associated with higher mortality and cardiovascular events — and how solid is that association?
shelves.mesh: Cardiovascular Diseases · Cause of Death · Female · Humans · Male · Prospective Studies · Risk · Sleep · Sleep Wake Disorders · Time Factors
shelves.balance: Every number on this shelf is observational, and every pooled ratio sits between 1.05 and 1.47 — inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid evidence. The shape is consistent across three large dose-response meta-analyses: risk is lowest at about 7 hours, short sleep carries a mortality relative risk of 1.12 (Cappuccio) rising 6% relative per hour below 7 (Yin), and long sleep carries the larger signal — relative risk 1.30 for death (Cappuccio), 1.39 in Jike's long-sleep pool, and 1.47 at 11 hours in Kwok's spline. Long sleep is also the arm most plausibly explained by reverse causation: sick people sleep longer. Association, consistently shaped, causality unproven. Proposed stamp MAYBE (weak evidence) — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Cappuccio 2010 (observational): short sleep RR 1.12 and long sleep RR 1.30 for death — both inside the not-solid band
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies: 16 studies, 27 cohort samples, 1,382,999 participants, follow-up 4–25 years, 112,566 deaths; sleep duration by questionnaire, death by certification. Short sleep was associated with greater risk of death (RR 1.12; 95% CI 1.06 to 1.18) and long sleep likewise (RR 1.30; 95% CI 1.22 to 1.38), with significant heterogeneity for long sleep. OBSERVATIONAL: both ratios lie between 0.5 and 2.0, which this library's developer floor does not count as solid evidence.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies, Sleep 2010. Observational evidence — no registry ID applies.
cards.people: 1,382,999 male and female participants across 27 cohort samples; follow-up 4–25 years; the record does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Short sleep: RR 1.12 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.18) for all-cause mortality. Long sleep: RR 1.30 (95% CI 1.22 to 1.38).
cards.watchOut: Questionnaire sleep, not measured sleep; long sleepers differ from 7-hour sleepers in health, work and mood in ways adjustment cannot fully remove. A U-shape in cohorts is a description, not a prescription to sleep exactly 7 hours.
cards.source: Cappuccio FP et al. Sleep duration and all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. Sleep. 2010;33(5):585-592. PMID 20469800

cards.headline: Yin 2017 (observational, dose-response): lowest risk at ≈7 hours; mortality +6% relative per hour below 7, +13% relative per hour above
cards.summary: Dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies in generally healthy populations (searched to December 2016). U-shaped associations were found for all-cause mortality, total cardiovascular disease, coronary heart disease and stroke, with lowest risk at ≈7 hours per day, varying little by sex. For mortality, the pooled relative risk was 1.06 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.07) per 1-hour reduction below 7 hours and 1.13 (95% CI 1.11 to 1.15) per 1-hour increment above 7 hours. OBSERVATIONAL: all ratios are inside the 0.5–2.0 not-solid band.
cards.type: Systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies, J Am Heart Assoc 2017. Observational evidence — no registry ID applies.
cards.people: Prospective cohorts in generally healthy populations; the record's abstract does not print a pooled participant count, mean age, or sex mix.
cards.result: All-cause mortality: RR 1.06 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.07) per hour below 7 h; RR 1.13 (95% CI 1.11 to 1.15) per hour above 7 h. Total CVD: 1.06 and 1.12; stroke: 1.05 and 1.18, respectively.
cards.watchOut: Per-hour slopes look precise because the cohorts are enormous; precision is not causality. The same data cannot distinguish 'long sleep harms' from 'illness lengthens sleep.'

cards.headline: Kwok 2018 (observational): mortality risk climbs with each hour above 8 — RR 1.14 at 9 h, 1.30 at 10 h, 1.47 at 11 h
cards.summary: Systematic review, meta-analysis and spline analysis of prospective cohorts: 74 studies, 3,340,684 participants, 242,240 deaths among 2,564,029 participants reporting death events. Self-reported sleep over 8 hours was associated with higher all-cause mortality in a graded fashion (RR 1.14 [1.05–1.25] at 9 hours, 1.30 [1.19–1.42] at 10 hours, 1.47 [1.33–1.64] at 11 hours); no significant difference was identified for sleep under 7 hours in the linear model, while similar patterns appeared for stroke and cardiovascular mortality. Subjective poor sleep quality was associated with coronary heart disease (RR 1.44; 95% CI 1.09 to 1.90). OBSERVATIONAL: every ratio is inside the 0.5–2.0 not-solid band.

cards.headline: Reading the U-curve together: a consistent shape built entirely from cohorts — graded MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis of Cards 1–3. Three independent dose-response pools agree on the shape (nadir ≈7 hours; long-sleep arm larger than short-sleep arm) and on nothing stronger: no randomised trial has assigned sleep duration and measured mortality, and none is likely to. Jike 2018's long-sleep pool (137 cohorts, 5,134,036 participants) found the same pattern — mortality RR 1.39 (95% CI 1.31 to 1.47), stroke 1.46, cardiovascular disease 1.25 — all inside the not-solid band. The shelf's claim is therefore fenced: habitual sleep far from 7–8 hours marks higher risk; whether changing sleep changes risk is unknown.

cards.result: Consistent U/J shape across >5 million pooled participants; largest pooled ratio 1.47 — still below the library's 2.0 solid-evidence floor for observational harm.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote this shelf as 'sleeping 9 hours raises your death risk by 30%' without the word 'associated' and the observational fence. Marker vs mechanism is exactly what these data cannot settle.

shelves.title: Weekend catch-up sleep: the metabolic rescue that wasn't
shelves.question: Does sleeping longer on weekends undo the metabolic harm of weekday sleep restriction?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Circadian Rhythm · Energy Intake · Female · Humans · Insulin Resistance · Male · Sleep · Sleep Deprivation · Weight Gain · Young Adult · Cardiovascular Diseases · Prospective Studies · Accelerometry
shelves.balance: The one randomised test says no. In Depner 2019, 36 healthy young adults lived through repeated 5-hour weekday nights with an ad libitum weekend: they slept only about 1.1 hours more than baseline across the weekend, ate more after dinner and gained weight during restriction, and — once restriction resumed — whole-body, hepatic and muscle insulin sensitivity fell by roughly 9–27% relative to baseline, with circadian phase delayed. The weekend did not protect them. The large observational counterweight (Chaput 2024, 73,513 UK Biobank adults with wrist accelerometry, 8 years) found weekend catch-up sleep was not associated with mortality (HR 1.17 [0.97–1.41] for ≥2 hours) or incident cardiovascular disease (HR 1.05 [0.94–1.18]) — a null that sits inside the not-solid band in any case. Catch-up sleep may feel restorative; as a metabolic strategy it is unproven and, in the laboratory, insufficient. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Depner 2019 (randomised): weekend recovery sleep failed to prevent insulin-sensitivity loss — down ~9–27% when restriction resumed
cards.summary: Randomised laboratory study of 36 healthy young adults in three groups: control (9-hour sleep opportunities, n=8), sleep restriction without weekend recovery (5-hour opportunities, n=14), and sleep restriction with weekend recovery (5-day workweek pattern, 2 days ad libitum weekend, then 2 nights of restriction again, n=14). Insufficient sleep increased after-dinner energy intake and body weight in both restriction groups. During the weekend, the recovery group slept cumulatively ~1.1 h more than baseline and after-dinner intake fell versus restriction days — but on returning to restriction, circadian phase was delayed and intake and weight rose again. Whole-body insulin sensitivity fell ~13% in the no-recovery group during restriction; in the recovery group, whole-body, hepatic and muscle insulin sensitivity fell ~9%–27% during recurrent restriction versus baseline.
cards.type: Randomised controlled laboratory trial, Curr Biol 2019. The record's databank carries no registry ID and none is printed.
cards.people: 36 healthy young adults (control n=8; restriction n=14; restriction + weekend recovery n=14); the record does not print a mean age or exact sex counts; women slept less than men during the weekend per the abstract.
cards.result: Weekend recovery did not prevent metabolic dysregulation: insulin sensitivity fell ~9%–27% (whole-body, hepatic, muscle) during recurrent restriction vs baseline in the recovery group; ~13% whole-body fall in the restriction-only group.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-six young, healthy volunteers, 9 nights, laboratory conditions — a mechanism test, not a verdict on every real-world sleeper. But it is the only randomised evidence on the question, and its direction is unambiguous: the rescue did not occur.

cards.headline: Chaput 2024 (observational): device-measured weekend catch-up sleep — no association with mortality (HR 1.17) or cardiovascular disease (HR 1.05)
cards.summary: Prospective cohort of UK Biobank adults with wrist accelerometry: 73,513 participants for mortality and 70,518 for incident cardiovascular disease, mean follow-up 8.0 years. Weekend catch-up sleep (weekend minus weekday duration) was grouped as none, >0 to <1 h, ≥1 to <2 h, ≥2 h. In multivariable-adjusted models, catch-up sleep was not associated with mortality (≥2 h group HR 1.17 [95% CI 0.97 to 1.41]) or incident CVD (HR 1.05 [95% CI 0.94 to 1.18]); continuous dose-response analyses and analyses restricted to weekday sleep under 6 hours agreed. OBSERVATIONAL: both hazard ratios lie inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid evidence — in either direction.

cards.people: 73,513 UK adults (mortality analysis) with wrist accelerometry; mean follow-up 8.0 (SD 0.9) years; the record does not print a mean age or sex mix in the abstract.
cards.result: Mortality, ≥2 h catch-up vs none: HR 1.17 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.41). Incident CVD: HR 1.05 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.18). Null overall.
cards.watchOut: Accelerometry fixes the self-report problem of older catch-up studies but not confounding: people who can sleep in differ from people who cannot. A null association also cannot prove the weekend sleep did nothing for the weekday-restricted subgroup's metabolism — Depner's trial is the sharper instrument for that.

cards.headline: Reading the catch-up evidence together: one small trial says the rescue fails; one large cohort finds no outcome difference — the gap is a bigger trial
cards.summary: Synthesis of Cards 1–2. The randomised laboratory evidence (n=36) shows weekend recovery sleep does not prevent insulin-sensitivity loss, weight gain or circadian delay when weekday restriction resumes; the device-measured cohort evidence (n≈73,500) shows no mortality or cardiovascular association for catch-up sleep in either direction. What is missing — and is named here as the shelf's in-flight need — is an adequately powered randomised trial of weekend recovery sleep with metabolic endpoints in habitual short sleepers outside the laboratory; none was found in the 2026-11-08 currency sweep. Until one exists, the honest advice is that catch-up sleep is not a substitute for adequate weekday sleep.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study; closing card names the missing trial per the thin-shelf rule.
cards.people: No new participants; synthesis of Cards 1–2.
cards.result: Trial: metabolic harm not prevented. Cohort: no outcome association. Combined claim fenced to those two statements.
cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade Chaput's null into 'catch-up sleep is useless' (outcomes were mortality/CVD, not next-week metabolism) or Depner's laboratory null into 'never sleep in' (n=36, 9 nights). Each card fences the other.

shelves.title: Napping and cardiovascular events — long naps mark risk; short naps do not
shelves.question: Is daytime napping associated with cardiovascular disease and death — and does nap length change the answer?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cause of Death · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Risk Factors · Sleep · Time Factors
shelves.balance: This shelf is one large dose-response pool and its limits. Across 11 prospective cohorts (151,588 participants, mean 11 years), naps of 60 minutes or more were associated with cardiovascular disease (rate ratio 1.82 [1.22–2.71]) and with all-cause mortality (rate ratio 1.27 [1.11–1.45]), while naps under 60 minutes were associated with neither. The dose-response was J-shaped for cardiovascular disease. Every figure is observational: the mortality ratio sits inside the 0.5–2.0 not-solid band, and even the 1.82 cardiovascular ratio — the shelf's largest — stays below the developer's 2.0 floor for solid observational harm. Long naps most plausibly mark poor night sleep, apnea and illness rather than causing events. Proposed stamp MAYBE (weak evidence) — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Yamada 2015 (observational): naps ≥60 min — cardiovascular RR 1.82, mortality RR 1.27; naps <60 min — neither
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies (searched to December 2014): 11 cohorts, 151,588 participants, 1,625,012 person-years, mean follow-up 11 years, 60% women, 5,276 cardiovascular events and 18,966 deaths. Long daytime naps (≥60 min/day) were associated with higher cardiovascular disease (rate ratio 1.82 [95% CI 1.22 to 2.71], P=0.003) and higher all-cause mortality (rate ratio 1.27 [95% CI 1.11 to 1.45], P<0.001) versus not napping. Napping <60 min/day was not associated with cardiovascular disease (P=0.98) or mortality (P=0.08). The nap–cardiovascular dose-response was J-curved (P for nonlinearity=0.01). OBSERVATIONAL: the 1.27 mortality ratio is inside this library's 0.5–2.0 not-solid band, and 1.82 does not cross the 2.0 floor.
cards.type: Meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies, Sleep 2015. Observational evidence — no registry ID applies.
cards.people: 151,588 participants (60% women) across 11 prospective cohorts; mean follow-up 11 years; the record does not print a pooled mean age.
cards.result: Nap ≥60 min/day vs none: cardiovascular disease RR 1.82 (95% CI 1.22 to 2.71); all-cause mortality RR 1.27 (95% CI 1.11 to 1.45). Nap <60 min/day: no association with either outcome.
cards.watchOut: People nap long because they slept badly, have apnea, are ill, or are retired — the nap is the messenger. No trial has randomised nap length and measured events, and the cohorts cannot separate siesta cultures, night-shift recovery naps and illness naps.
cards.source: Yamada T et al. Daytime Napping and the Risk of Cardiovascular Disease and All-Cause Mortality: A Prospective Study and Dose-Response Meta-Analysis. Sleep. 2015;38(12):1945-1953. PMID 26158892

cards.headline: Reading the napping evidence together: length is the whole story the data can tell — and it is a marker story until proven otherwise
cards.summary: Synthesis built on Card 1, the shelf's single pooled source. The pattern is internally coherent — a threshold near 60 minutes, a J-curve, null findings below the threshold — which is why the shelf exists at all; but coherence inside observational data does not manufacture causality, and the developer's floor leaves both pooled ratios short of solid. The shelf's usable clinical content is narrow: a new habit of long daytime naps in an older adult is a prompt to look for apnea, poor night sleep and illness, not a proven cause to treat by nap restriction. No randomised evidence exists; none was found in the 2026-11-08 sweep.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. Single-source shelf; the limitation is printed on the card's face.
cards.people: No new participants; synthesis of Card 1.
cards.result: Long naps (≥60 min) mark higher cardiovascular and mortality rates in cohorts; short naps do not. Causality unestablished.
cards.watchOut: Single-pool shelf: if Yamada's pooling choices are wrong, the shelf is wrong. Graded MAYBE (weak evidence) for exactly that reason, and the stamp must travel with any quotation of the 1.82 figure.

shelves.title: Shift-work disorder: wake agents work modestly; the sleepiness remains
shelves.question: In shift-work disorder, do wake-promoting agents (modafinil, armodafinil) improve night-shift sleepiness and performance — and what role does light have?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Benzhydryl Compounds · Central Nervous System Stimulants · Disorders of Excessive Somnolence · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Modafinil · Sleep Disorders, Circadian Rhythm · Work Schedule Tolerance
shelves.balance: Two large placebo-controlled trials, one honest message: the wake agents help, modestly, and leave the disorder standing. Modafinil 200 mg before night shifts (209 patients, 3 months) lengthened nighttime sleep latency by 1.7 vs 0.3 minutes, improved clinical symptoms in 74% vs 36%, and cut reported accidents or near-accidents on the commute home (29% vs 54%) — yet treated patients remained excessively sleepy with impaired performance. Armodafinil 150 mg (254 workers, 12 weeks) raised mean sleep latency from 2.3 to 5.3 minutes vs 2.4 to 2.8 on placebo and improved clinician ratings (79% vs 59%). Neither drug harmed daytime sleep. For bright light — part of this shelf's question — no pivotal randomised trial in shift-work disorder was verified for carding; light remains a guideline-supported adjunct with indirect evidence, and the shelf says so rather than borrowing strength from the depression shelves. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Czeisler 2005 (NEJM): modafinil in shift-work sleep disorder — symptoms improved in 74% vs 36%, commute accidents 29% vs 54%, sleepiness persisted
cards.summary: Three-month double-blind trial: 209 patients with shift-work sleep disorder randomised to modafinil 200 mg or placebo before each night shift. Modafinil improved mean nighttime sleep latency from baseline by 1.7 (±0.4) vs 0.3 (±0.3) minutes (P=0.002); more patients improved clinically (74% vs 36%, P<0.001); lapses of attention on the Psychomotor Vigilance Test fell with modafinil while rising on placebo (P<0.001); and fewer modafinil patients reported accidents or near-accidents commuting home (29% vs 54%, P<0.001). Daytime sleep was not adversely affected; headache was the most common adverse event. The authors state plainly that treated patients continued to have excessive sleepiness and impaired performance.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2005. Pre-registration-era reporting: the record's databank carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 209 patients with shift-work sleep disorder (chronic excessive sleepiness at night work, insomnia by day); the record does not print a mean age or sex counts in the abstract.
cards.result: Nighttime sleep latency change: +1.7 vs +0.3 min (P=0.002). Clinical improvement: 74% vs 36% (P<0.001). Commute accidents/near-accidents: 29% vs 54% (P<0.001). Residual excessive sleepiness persisted on treatment.
cards.watchOut: A 1.7-minute latency gain is a laboratory improvement, not restored alertness — the trial's own conclusion fences the claim. Commute accidents were self-reported. The population had diagnosed shift-work sleep disorder, not ordinary night-shift tiredness.
cards.source: Czeisler CA et al. Modafinil for excessive sleepiness associated with shift-work sleep disorder. N Engl J Med. 2005;353(5):476-486. PMID 16079371

cards.headline: Czeisler 2009: armodafinil 150 mg — sleep latency 2.3→5.3 minutes vs 2.4→2.8 on placebo; clinician-rated improvement 79% vs 59%
cards.summary: 12-week randomised controlled study at 42 North American sleep facilities: 254 permanent or rotating night-shift workers with excessive sleepiness from chronic (≥3 months) shift work disorder of at least moderate severity (entry required mean sleep latency ≤6 minutes and daytime sleep efficiency ≤87.5%). Armodafinil 150 mg or placebo was taken 30–60 minutes before each night shift. Mean sleep latency rose from 2.3 (SD 1.6) to 5.3 (SD 5.0) minutes on armodafinil vs 2.4 (1.6) to 2.8 (2.9) on placebo (P<.001); clinical condition improved in 79% vs 59% (P=.001); diary sleepiness fell during laboratory nights, work nights and the commute home; memory and attention test performance improved. Daytime sleep by polysomnography was unaffected.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, Mayo Clin Proc 2009. Registry ID from the record's own databank: NCT00080288.
cards.people: 254 permanent or rotating night-shift workers with moderate-or-worse shift work disorder; the record does not print a mean age or sex counts in the abstract.
cards.result: Final-visit mean sleep latency: 5.3 (SD 5.0) min on armodafinil vs 2.8 (SD 2.9) on placebo (P<.001). Clinician-rated improvement: 79% vs 59% (P=.001).
cards.watchOut: Even after treatment, mean latency (5.3 minutes) sat near the severe-sleepiness range — the same partial-rescue pattern as modafinil. Industry-conducted shift-work trials measure laboratory nights; real-world safety outcomes (actual crash rates) were not endpoints.

cards.headline: Reading the shift-work evidence together: wake agents are a partial rescue — and light's trial evidence for this disorder is not carded because it is not pivotal
cards.summary: Synthesis of Cards 1–2. Modafinil and armodafinil each beat placebo on sleep latency, global clinical ratings, vigilance and self-reported commute risk, with effect sizes that leave patients measurably sleepy — a class claim of modest symptomatic benefit in diagnosed shift-work disorder, graded POSSIBLE. On bright light: timed light is biologically rational and guideline-endorsed for circadian shifting, but the verification pass for this shelf found no pivotal randomised light trial in shift-work disorder with hard alertness outcomes to card at library standard (the 2026 AASM systematic review, PMID 42925443, postdates the trials and is noted in the currency sweep). Light is therefore described here as an adjunct with indirect evidence — its depression evidence lives on Shelf #497 and must not be imported as shift-work proof.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. Light-evidence limitation printed on the card's face.
cards.people: No new participants; synthesis of Cards 1–2 (463 randomised workers in total).
cards.result: Wake agents: consistent, modest, placebo-beating benefit with residual sleepiness. Light in shift-work disorder: no carded pivotal trial.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial tested combined wake-agent + light + schedule strategies, rotating-shift workers outside sleep-clinic recruitment, or long-term cardiovascular safety. Do not generalise to all night workers.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–2 on this shelf (PMID 16079371; PMID 19880686).

shelves.title: Bright light therapy beyond seasonal depression: real in nonseasonal depression, unproven in dementia
shelves.question: Does bright light therapy help conditions other than seasonal affective disorder — nonseasonal depression, bipolar depression, dementia?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bipolar Disorder · Depressive Disorder · Dementia · Female · Humans · Major Depressive Disorder · Male · Phototherapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Beyond winter depression, light's record divides by diagnosis. In nonseasonal major depression, the CAN-BIND trial (Lam 2016, 122 patients) found light monotherapy (effect size d=0.80) and light-plus-fluoxetine (d=1.11) beat sham-plus-placebo while fluoxetine alone did not (d=0.24) — a single well-built trial, graded POSSIBLE. In bipolar depression, one 46-patient trial (Sit 2018) found midday bright light produced remission in 68.2% vs 22.2% on dim red placebo (adjusted OR 12.6), with no polarity switches — promising, small, single-centre in spirit, also POSSIBLE. The older meta-analysis (Golden 2005) agrees in direction for nonseasonal depression (effect size 0.53 across 3 studies) but found adjunctive light added nothing (effect size −0.01). In dementia, the Cochrane pool found no effect on cognition, sleep or behaviour, and the one large factorial trial's light effects (0.9 MMSE points) came packaged with melatonin arms — MAYBE (weak evidence). Split stamp as proposed. Proposed split stamp — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Lam 2016 (CAN-BIND): light alone (d=0.80) and light + fluoxetine (d=1.11) beat placebo in nonseasonal depression — fluoxetine alone did not (d=0.24)
cards.summary: Randomised, double-blind, placebo- and sham-controlled 8-week trial in 122 adults (19–60 years) with nonseasonal major depressive disorder of at least moderate severity, in four arms: light monotherapy (10,000-lux white light 30 min/d early morning + placebo pill, n=32), fluoxetine monotherapy (inactive ion generator + fluoxetine 20 mg/d, n=31), combination (n=29), and double placebo (n=30). MADRS change: light 13.4 (SD 7.5), fluoxetine 8.8 (9.9), combination 16.9 (9.2), placebo 6.5 (9.6). Combination (d=1.11; 95% CI 0.54 to 1.64) and light alone (d=0.80; 95% CI 0.28 to 1.31) were significantly superior to placebo; fluoxetine alone was not (d=0.24; 95% CI −0.27 to 0.74). Response: 75.9% combination, 50.0% light, 29.0% fluoxetine, 33.3% placebo. Remission: 58.6%, 43.8%, 19.4%, 30.0% respectively.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, JAMA Psychiatry 2016. Registry ID from the record's own databank: NCT00958204.
cards.people: 122 adults aged 19–60 with nonseasonal major depressive disorder of at least moderate severity, outpatient psychiatry clinics; the record does not print the sex mix in the abstract.
cards.result: MADRS change vs placebo: light d=0.80 (95% CI 0.28 to 1.31); combination d=1.11 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.64); fluoxetine d=0.24 (not significant). Combination NNT for response/remission ≈2 per the record.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 122 patients, 8 weeks — and the fluoxetine arm's failure to beat placebo should temper any reading of the light arms. Blinding a light box is intrinsically imperfect (patients can guess brightness). Replication is the missing step; graded POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, for that reason.
cards.source: Lam RW et al. Efficacy of Bright Light Treatment, Fluoxetine, and the Combination in Patients With Nonseasonal Major Depressive Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Psychiatry. 2016;73(1):56-63. PMID 26580307 · NCT00958204

cards.headline: Sit 2018: midday bright light for bipolar depression — remission 68.2% vs 22.2% (adjusted OR 12.6), no mood switches
cards.summary: 6-week randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial: 46 depressed adults with bipolar I or II disorder on stable antimanic medication (excluding hypomania/mania, mixed symptoms, rapid cycling), assigned to 7,000-lux bright white light (n=23) or 50-lux dim red placebo light (n=23) at midday. Remission (SIGH-ADS ≤8) at weeks 4–6: 68.2% bright light vs 22.2% placebo (adjusted odds ratio 12.6); endpoint depression scores 9.2 (SD 6.6) vs 14.9 (SD 9.2) (adjusted β=−5.91). No mood polarity switches occurred in either group. Sleep quality improved in both groups without a significant between-group difference.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, Am J Psychiatry 2018. Registry ID from the record's own databank: NCT00852592.
cards.people: 46 adults with bipolar I or II depression on stable antimanic therapy; the record does not print a mean age or sex counts in the abstract.
cards.result: Remission 68.2% vs 22.2% (adjusted OR 12.6); depression score 9.2 vs 14.9 at endpoint; zero polarity switches.
cards.watchOut: Forty-six patients: an odds ratio of 12.6 from 46 patients is a signal to replicate, not a settled effect — the confidence interval (not printed in the abstract) must be wide. Patients with rapid cycling or mixed features were excluded, exactly the patients in whom light-induced switching would matter most.

cards.headline: Golden 2005 (meta-analysis): bright light effect size 0.53 in nonseasonal depression — but 0.01 (null) as an antidepressant adjunct
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of light therapy for mood disorders (1975–2003); only 13% of located studies met inclusion criteria. Bright light reduced depression severity in seasonal disorder (8 studies, effect size 0.84; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.08) and in nonseasonal depression (3 studies, effect size 0.53; 95% CI 0.18 to 0.89). Bright light as an adjunct to antidepressant pharmacotherapy for nonseasonal depression was not effective (5 studies, effect size −0.01; 95% CI −0.36 to 0.34). The authors warn that many efficacy reports rest on non-rigorous designs.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, Am J Psychiatry 2005. No registry ID applies to a meta-analysis.
cards.people: Pooled randomised trials in mood disorders; the record does not print a pooled participant count, mean age, or sex mix.
cards.result: Nonseasonal depression, bright light: effect size 0.53 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.89), 3 studies. Adjunct to antidepressants: effect size −0.01 (95% CI −0.36 to 0.34), 5 studies — null.
cards.watchOut: The nonseasonal pool is three small pre-2003 studies, and the adjunct null directly tempers Lam's combination result a decade later: whether light adds to an antidepressant remains genuinely unsettled. Direction consistent; magnitude soft.
cards.source: Golden RN et al. The efficacy of light therapy in the treatment of mood disorders: a review and meta-analysis of the evidence. Am J Psychiatry. 2005;162(4):656-662. PMID 15800134

cards.headline: Forbes 2014 (Cochrane, dementia): no effect of light therapy on cognition, sleep, or challenging behaviour across 11 trials
cards.summary: Cochrane review of randomised trials of light therapy (any intensity/duration) vs control in dementia of any type or severity: 11 trials (13 articles) met inclusion criteria, though 3 could not enter the analyses for data reasons. The updated review found no effect of light therapy on cognitive function, sleep, challenging behaviour (e.g. agitation), or psychiatric disturbances. OBSERVATIONAL FLOOR NOTE: this is a null randomised pool, carded as the dementia fence — the absence of demonstrated benefit, in the population where circadian reasoning is most often invoked.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014. No registry ID applies to a systematic review.
cards.people: 11 randomised trials in people with dementia of any type/severity; the record does not print a pooled participant count in the abstract.
cards.result: No effect on cognition, sleep, challenging behaviour, or psychiatric symptoms in the pooled analysis.
cards.watchOut: Trial quality and light doses varied, and three eligible studies contributed no analysable data — 'no effect found' in a messy pool is weaker than a clean null. cards.headline: Riemersma-van der Lek 2008: whole-day bright light in care facilities — cognition decline slowed by 0.9 MMSE points, in a trial where melatonin did part of the work
cards.summary: Long-term double-blind 2×2 factorial trial (1999–2004) in 189 residents of 12 Dutch group care facilities (mean age 85.8 [SD 5.5] years; 90% women; 87% dementia): facilities randomised to whole-day bright (~1000 lux) or dim (~300 lux) light, participants to evening melatonin 2.5 mg or placebo, mean treatment 15 months (maximum 3.5 years). Light attenuated cognitive deterioration by 0.9 MMSE points (95% CI 0.04 to 1.71), a relative 5%; improved Cornell depression scores by 1.5 points (relative 19%); and attenuated growth in functional limitations by 1.8 points/year (relative 53%). Melatonin shortened sleep onset by 8.2 minutes and lengthened sleep by 27 minutes but worsened affect scores and withdrawn behaviour when given without light.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 2×2 factorial trial, JAMA 2008. Registry ID from the record's own databank: ISRCTN93133646.
cards.people: 189 elderly care-facility residents, mean age 85.8 years, 90% women, 87% with dementia, Netherlands.
cards.result: Light: MMSE deterioration attenuated by 0.9 points (95% CI 0.04 to 1.71); depression −1.5 Cornell points; functional-limitation growth attenuated 1.8 points/year. Melatonin: sleep onset −8.2 min, duration +27 min, with adverse affect effects alone.
cards.watchOut: Facility-level light randomisation in 12 facilities, effects at the edge of significance (CI 0.04 to 1.71), and a co-intervention (melatonin) with its own benefits and harms — this trial cannot carry a dementia light claim by itself, and Cochrane's wider pool (Reference 4) found nothing. MAYBE (weak evidence) is the honest grade for dementia.

cards.headline: Reading the light evidence together: depression — yes, modestly, twice; dementia — not shown
cards.summary: Synthesis of Cards 1–5. For nonseasonal major depression, one rigorous sham-controlled trial plus an older concordant meta-analysis support a real symptom benefit for morning bright light, alone or combined — POSSIBLE. For bipolar depression, a single small trial with a large remission gap and no switches — POSSIBLE, replication owed. For dementia cognition, sleep and behaviour, the Cochrane pool is null and the one positive factorial trial is small-margin and melatonin-confounded — MAYBE (weak evidence). Light is cheap and low-risk, which justifies clinical use ahead of proof in depression; it does not justify quoting the depression effect sizes for dementia care.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study; split claim printed on the card's face.
cards.people: No new participants; synthesis of Cards 1–5.
cards.result: Depression (nonseasonal + bipolar): consistent positive randomised signals, small bases. Dementia: pooled null with one confounded positive trial.
cards.watchOut: Sham conditions for light (dim light, ion generators) may not be inert, and none of the depression trials ran beyond 8 weeks. Durability, dose and timing optimisation are all unanswered.

shelves.title: Restless legs: iron first — and the augmentation price of dopamine agonists
shelves.question: In restless legs syndrome, does iron treatment (especially with low ferritin) improve symptoms, and how often do dopamine agonists cause augmentation over time?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Dopamine Agonists · Female · Ferric Compounds · Humans · Iron · Male · Maltose · Middle Aged · Pramipexole · Restless Legs Syndrome · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Iron first is a dose-and-status claim, not a slogan. The Cochrane pool (Trotti 2019; 10 studies, 428 participants) found iron beat placebo on restless-legs severity (IRLS mean difference −3.78 [95% CI −6.25 to −1.31], moderate-certainty). The dose story matters: 1,000 mg ferric carboxymaltose improved IRLS by 8.9 vs 4.0 points over placebo at day 28 (Allen 2011), while a single 500 mg dose did not separate from placebo at week 6 (Cho 2018) — under-dosing iron and declaring it failed is the trap this shelf exists to prevent. The harm half is the dopamine agonists: augmentation — symptoms starting earlier, spreading, intensifying on treatment — appeared in 42% of a long-term pramipexole cohort (mean onset 16.5 months) and in 20% with definite/highly-suggestive signs in a community dopamine-treated sample, accruing at roughly 8% per year. Split stamp: POSSIBLE for iron benefit; LIKELY for augmentation as a real long-term harm. Proposed split stamp — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Trotti 2019 (Cochrane): iron beat placebo on RLS severity — IRLS mean difference −3.78 points, moderate certainty
cards.summary: Cochrane review of controlled trials of oral or parenteral iron vs placebo, other medication or no treatment in adults with restless legs syndrome (searched to September 2017): 10 studies, 428 participants, follow-up 2–16 weeks; 9 compared iron with placebo and 1 with pramipexole. Pooling the 7 IRLS trials, iron produced greater improvement than placebo (mean difference −3.78; 95% CI −6.25 to −1.31; I²=66%; 345 participants), GRADE moderate certainty; adding an eighth study on a different scale kept the benefit (SMD −0.74; 95% CI −1.26 to −0.23). Against pramipexole in a single 30-patient study, severity reduction was similar (MD −0.40; 95% CI −5.93 to 5.13). Sleep quality did not differ significantly.
cards.type: Systematic review of controlled trials (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019. No registry ID applies to a systematic review.
cards.people: 428 adults with restless legs syndrome across 10 studies; the record does not print a mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: IRLS improvement, iron vs placebo: MD −3.78 (95% CI −6.25 to −1.31), 7 studies, 345 participants, moderate certainty. Quality of life (continuous): SMD 0.51 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.87) favouring iron.
cards.watchOut: Small trials (428 people total), short follow-up (≤16 weeks), and heterogeneity I²=66%. A mean 3.8-point IRLS gain is modest — iron is first-line because of the risk profile and the augmentation alternative (References 4–5), not because its effect is large.

cards.headline: Allen 2011: IV ferric carboxymaltose 1,000 mg — IRLS fell 8.9 vs 4.0 points at day 28; 25% still treatment-free at 24 weeks
cards.summary: 28-day multicentre randomised placebo-controlled preliminary trial: 46 RLS patients withdrawn from all RLS treatment; 24 received ferric carboxymaltose 500 mg in two doses 5 days apart (1,000 mg total) and 22 placebo, with crossover/open extensions and follow-up to 24 weeks. At day 28, IRLS fell by 8.9 (SD 8.52) on FCM vs 4.0 (SD 6.11) on placebo (P=0.040); 'very much or much improved' on CGI was 48.3% vs 14.3% (P=0.004); quality of life also improved significantly. Of the 24 initially iron-treated, 45% responded and 29% remitted (IRLS ≤10) at day 28, and 25% remained free of other RLS medication at 24 weeks. A single 1,000 mg dose on day 28 matched the divided dose; an extra 500 mg for non-responders added little. No significant adverse events.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial, Sleep Med 2011. The record's databank carries no registry ID and none is printed.
cards.people: 46 adults with restless legs syndrome, treatment-withdrawn at entry; the record does not print a mean age or sex counts in the abstract.
cards.result: IRLS change at day 28: −8.9 (SD 8.52) FCM vs −4.0 (SD 6.11) placebo (P=0.040). CGI much/very-much improved: 48.3% vs 14.3% (P=0.004). Remission (IRLS ≤10): 29% of iron-treated.
cards.watchOut: Forty-six patients, labelled 'preliminary' by its own authors, with open-label extensions after day 28. It establishes that the 1,000 mg dose can work; with Card 3 it establishes that dose is not a detail.

cards.headline: Cho 2018 (the dose fence): a single 500 mg ferric carboxymaltose dose did NOT beat placebo at week 6
cards.summary: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled study of a single 500 mg ferric carboxymaltose infusion in idiopathic RLS (patients off RLS medication ≥2 weeks). At week 6, neither primary outcome separated significantly: IRLS change −8.3 (±7.5) on FCM vs −4.8 (±8.7) on placebo (P=0.100); visual-analogue severity −23.4 (±24.1) vs −13.3 (±23.1) (P=0.077). No secondary outcome was significant at week 6. Of 32 iron-treated subjects in phase I, 7 (21.9%) remained free of further RLS medication at 30 weeks. No serious adverse effects. The authors contrast their null with the two prior well-controlled 1,000 mg trials and propose a clinically relevant total-dose threshold.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, Sleep Med 2018. The record's databank carries no registry ID and none is printed.
cards.people: Adults with idiopathic restless legs syndrome (32 treated with iron in phase I); the record does not print the total randomised N, mean age, or sex counts in the abstract.
cards.result: Week 6 IRLS change: −8.3 vs −4.8 points, P=0.100 (not significant). VAS severity: −23.4 vs −13.3, P=0.077 (not significant).
cards.watchOut: A small trial whose confidence intervals still include a useful effect — 'not significant' here is under-dosed and under-powered, not disproof of iron. Its library function is the fence: card the dose with the claim, always.

cards.headline: Lipford & Silber 2012 (cohort): augmentation in 42% on long-term pramipexole — median dose doubled as efficacy faded
cards.summary: Long-term cohort follow-up of 50 patients initially prescribed pramipexole (1998–2002), mean treatment duration 8 years (range 0.6–12). Augmentation developed in 42% of patients, after a mean of 16.5 months and no later than 4.1 years after starting. Pramipexole was completely effective in only 40% at follow-up (vs 67% initially), partially effective in 58%; median daily dose rose from 0.38 mg after stabilisation to 1.0 mg. Side effects occurred in 74%: daytime sleepiness in 56% (including sleep attacks while driving in 10%) and impulse control disorders in 10%. Nine patients (18%) discontinued (poor efficacy 4, impulse control disorders 2, augmentation 1, resolved symptoms 2); 28% needed added non-dopaminergic medication. OBSERVATIONAL cohort — frequencies describe this clinic population.
cards.type: Long-term cohort study (retrospective chart review, surveys, telephone interviews), Sleep Med 2012. Observational — no registry ID applies.
cards.people: 50 patients with restless legs syndrome on pramipexole, mean 8 years of treatment; the record does not print a mean age in the abstract.
cards.result: Augmentation: 42%, mean onset 16.5 months, all cases within 4.1 years. Complete efficacy fell from 67% to 40%; median dose 0.38→1.0 mg/day. Impulse control disorders: 10%.
cards.watchOut: Fifty patients from one centre's early pramipexole era, with augmentation assessed retrospectively — the 42% is an estimate with wide uncertainty, not a universal rate. Its weight comes from agreement with Card 5's larger community sample.
cards.source: Lipford MC, Silber MH. Long-term use of pramipexole in the management of restless legs syndrome. Sleep Med. 2012;13(10):1280-1285. PMID 23036265

cards.headline: Allen 2011 (community sample): definite/highly-suggestive augmentation in 20% of dopamine-treated RLS — accruing ≈8% per year
cards.summary: Cross-sectional survey of 266 patients with dopamine-treated restless legs syndrome recruited through their physicians, augmentation classified by NIH criteria. Overall, 20% had definitive or highly suggestive clinical indications of augmentation; only 25% reported no indications at all, and that no-indication group was the only one with a low mean IRLS (<15) and good outcomes, vs a mean IRLS of 23.6 in the augmentation group. Augmentation accrued at about 8% per year for at least the first 8 years of dopamine treatment (mean duration 2.7 [SD 2.4] years in the sample). Likely risk markers included more frequent and more uncomfortable pre-treatment symptoms and longer treatment duration. OBSERVATIONAL, single-survey ascertainment.
cards.type: Cross-sectional community survey study, Sleep Med 2011. Observational — no registry ID applies.
cards.people: 266 adults with dopamine-agonist/levodopa-treated restless legs syndrome; mean treatment duration 2.7 (SD 2.4) years; the record does not print a mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Definite/highly-suggestive augmentation: 20%. No augmentation indications: 25%. Accrual ≈8% per year over the first 8 years. Mean IRLS 23.6 with augmentation vs <15 without any indications.
cards.watchOut: One-time online survey with clinician recruitment — sicker patients may be over-represented, and 'highly suggestive' is softer than examination-confirmed augmentation. Two independent designs (References 4–5) pointing the same way is what earns the harm its LIKELY grade despite observational data.
cards.source: Allen RP et al. Restless legs syndrome (RLS) augmentation associated with dopamine agonist and levodopa usage in a community sample. Sleep Med. 2011;12(5):431-439. PMID 21493132

cards.headline: Reading the RLS evidence together: check iron, dose iron fully, and treat dopamine agonists as a loan augmentation collects on
cards.summary: Synthesis of Cards 1–5. Iron: a moderate-certainty pooled benefit (IRLS −3.78) that appears dose-dependent — 1,000 mg ferric carboxymaltose positive, 500 mg null — making ferritin assessment and full-dose replacement the shelf's first move. Dopamine agonists: effective short-term (their efficacy trials live elsewhere and are not re-carded), but augmentation emerges in roughly a fifth to two-fifths of long-term users within the first few years, alongside dose escalation, sleepiness and impulse control disorders in a tenth. The 2016 international task-force guideline (Garcia-Borreguero et al., Sleep Med 2016; PMID 27448465, cited here within the synthesis) recommends α2δ ligands as an augmentation-sparing first-line alternative and iron repletion for low stores — consistent with, and downstream of, the primary evidence carded above.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. Guideline cited within the synthesis only, not as a standalone card.
cards.people: No new participants; synthesis of Cards 1–5.
cards.result: Iron benefit: real, modest, dose-dependent. Augmentation: common, time-dependent, and the central long-term cost of dopaminergic therapy.
cards.watchOut: Ferritin thresholds for treatment are not settled by these records and are not printed here. Patients already augmented need specialist management (dose division, switch to α2δ ligand or rotigotine, or opioids in severe cases per the guideline) — beyond this shelf's evidence cards.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–5 on this shelf (PMID 30609006; PMID 21978726; PMID 29458749; PMID 23036265; PMID 21493132).

shelves.title: CBT-I vs sleeping pills, long-term: the pills stop working when they stop; CBT-I doesn't
shelves.question: Head-to-head and long-term, how does cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia compare with hypnotic medication?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Azabicyclo Compounds · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Female · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives · Male · Middle Aged · Piperazines · Polysomnography · Pyridines · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders · Temazepam · Zolpidem
shelves.balance: Four randomised head-to-head trials, spanning three hypnotics and 24 months, tell one story with unusual consistency. Acutely, CBT-I and medication both work: in Morin 1999 (78 older adults), wake-after-sleep-onset fell 63.5% on combined therapy, 55% on CBT-I, 46.5% on temazepam, 16.9% on placebo. The separation is durability: CBT-I gains were sustained to 24 months while temazepam-alone gains were not; Sivertsen 2006 found CBT-I superior to zopiclone at 6 months (sleep efficiency 90.1% vs 81.9%) with zopiclone indistinguishable from placebo on most outcomes; Jacobs 2004 found CBT beat zolpidem, with drug gains returning toward baseline after discontinuation; and Morin 2009 showed the best long-term remission (68%) came from combined therapy followed by CBT-I alone — continued zolpidem did worse (42%). No card on this shelf duplicates Shelves #231 (suvorexant drug trials) or #437 (digital CBT-I vs placebo): this shelf's question is the comparison itself. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Morin 1999 (JAMA): CBT-I, temazepam, both, or placebo in late-life insomnia — only the behavioural gains survived 24 months
cards.summary: Randomised placebo-controlled trial, 8 weeks of treatment with follow-up at 3, 12 and 24 months: 78 adults (50 women, 28 men; mean age 65 years) with chronic primary insomnia, assigned to cognitive-behaviour therapy (stimulus control, sleep restriction, sleep hygiene, cognitive therapy; n=18), temazepam (n=20), both (n=20), or placebo (n=20). All three active treatments beat placebo post-treatment, with a trend favouring the combination: percentage reduction in wake-after-sleep-onset was 63.5% (combined), 55% (CBT), 46.5% (pharmacotherapy), 16.9% (placebo). At follow-up, behaviour-therapy patients sustained their gains; drug-alone patients did not, and the combined group's long-term outcome was more variable. Subjects, significant others and clinicians all rated behavioural treatment more effective than drug alone, and satisfaction was higher.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled clinical trial, JAMA 1999. Pre-registration-era trial: the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 78 older adults (mean age 65 years; 50 women, 28 men) with chronic primary insomnia, single academic centre.
cards.result: Wake-after-sleep-onset reduction: combined 63.5%, CBT 55%, temazepam 46.5%, placebo 16.9%. Durability to 24 months: sustained with behavioural treatment, not with drug alone.
cards.watchOut: Small groups (n=18–20 per arm) and a benzodiazepine (temazepam) rather than a modern Z-drug — but Cards 2–4 repeat the durability pattern against zopiclone and zolpidem, which is why the shelf grades the pattern, not this trial alone.
cards.source: Morin CM et al. Behavioral and pharmacological therapies for late-life insomnia: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 1999;281(11):991-999. PMID 10086433

cards.headline: Sivertsen 2006 (JAMA): CBT beat zopiclone at 6 months — sleep efficiency 90.1% vs 81.9%; zopiclone mostly matched placebo
cards.summary: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Jan 2004–Dec 2005, Norway): 46 adults (mean age 60.8 years; 22 women) with chronic primary insomnia assigned to CBT (sleep hygiene, sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive therapy, relaxation; n=18), zopiclone 7.5 mg nightly (n=16), or placebo (n=12), treated 6 weeks and followed to 6 months, with ambulatory polysomnography and sleep diaries. CBT improved short- and long-term outcomes vs zopiclone on 3 of 4 measures; for most outcomes zopiclone did not differ from placebo. Sleep efficiency on CBT rose from 81.4% at baseline to 90.1% at 6-month follow-up, vs a fall from 82.3% to 81.9% on zopiclone; CBT patients spent more time in slow-wave sleep and less time awake at night. Total sleep time was similar across groups.

cards.result: Sleep efficiency at 6 months (polysomnography): CBT 90.1% (from 81.4%) vs zopiclone 81.9% (from 82.3%). CBT superior on 3 of 4 outcomes; zopiclone ≈ placebo on most.
cards.watchOut: The smallest trial on the shelf (n=46) — its zopiclone-null could be power, not proof. Direction and durability nonetheless match Morin 1999 and Jacobs 2004 exactly.

cards.headline: Jacobs 2004: CBT beat zolpidem for sleep-onset insomnia — drug gains returned toward baseline after the drug stopped
cards.summary: Randomised placebo-controlled trial in 63 young and middle-aged adults with chronic sleep-onset insomnia: CBT, pharmacotherapy (zolpidem), combination, or placebo. On most measures CBT was the most effective intervention: it produced the greatest changes in sleep-onset latency and sleep efficiency, yielded the largest number of normal sleepers after treatment, and maintained gains at long-term follow-up. Combined treatment gave no advantage over CBT alone. Pharmacotherapy produced only moderate improvements during administration, and measures returned toward baseline after discontinuation. Outcomes were sleep-diary latency/efficiency/total sleep time plus Nightcap home monitoring and daytime functioning. Exact per-arm figures are not printed in the record's abstract and are not claimed here.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled clinical trial, Arch Intern Med 2004. Pre-registration-era trial: the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 63 young and middle-aged adults with chronic sleep-onset insomnia; the record does not print a mean age or sex counts in the abstract.
cards.result: CBT superior on most measures, largest number of normal sleepers, gains maintained at follow-up; combination no better than CBT alone; zolpidem gains moderate and not maintained after discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: Sleep-onset insomnia only (not maintenance), younger patients than Cards 1–2, and effect sizes are described qualitatively in the record. The card claims the comparison's direction and durability — which the record states — and no invented numbers.

cards.headline: Morin 2009 (JAMA): adding zolpidem to CBT-I helped acutely — but the best 6-month remission (68%) came from stopping the drug and keeping CBT-I
cards.summary: Two-stage randomised trial in 160 adults with persistent insomnia (Canada, 2002–2005): 6 weeks of CBT alone vs CBT + zolpidem 10 mg nightly, then 6 months of extended therapy (monthly maintenance CBT or none; continued intermittent zolpidem + CBT, or CBT alone) and 6-month follow-up. Acutely, both arms improved sleep latency, wake-after-onset and efficiency (all P<.001), with a larger total-sleep-time increase on combination (P=.04); response (60% vs 61%) and remission (39% vs 44%) were similar. During extended therapy and follow-up, combined-start patients had higher remission (56% vs 43%; P=.05) — and the best long-term outcome was combined therapy followed by CBT alone: remission 68% (20/30) vs 42% (12/29) for those who continued zolpidem (P=.04).
cards.type: Randomised controlled two-stage trial, JAMA 2009. Registry ID from the record's own databank: NCT00042146.
cards.people: 160 adults with persistent insomnia at a university sleep centre; the record does not print a mean age or sex counts in the abstract.
cards.result: Acute remission: 39% CBT vs 44% CBT+zolpidem. Follow-up remission: 68% for combined→CBT-alone vs 42% for combined→continued zolpidem (P=.04).
cards.watchOut: The drug's acute contribution is real (sleep time) — this trial refutes 'pills never help' as firmly as it refutes 'stay on pills.' Subgroup denominators shrink by the final comparison (30 vs 29), so the 68/42 gap is the shelf's most fragile number.
