shelves.title: Deprescribing benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older adults: EMPOWER — ask the patient, with a taper in hand
shelves.question: Can direct patient education get long-term older benzodiazepine users to stop — safely and at scale?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Benzodiazepines · Contraindications · Female · Humans · Inappropriate Prescribing · Male · Patient Education as Topic · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders · Deprescriptions · Hypnotics and Sedatives
shelves.balance: EMPOWER is the rare deprescribing trial that worked by mailing the patient, not lecturing the doctor. Among 303 long-term benzodiazepine users aged 65–95, a brochure describing harms plus a stepwise taper produced discontinuation at 6 months in 27% vs 5% on usual care (risk difference 23% [95% CI 14% to 32%]; number needed to treat 4), with a further 11% reducing dose — and 62% of recipients started the cessation conversation themselves. The programme's larger successor, D-PRESCRIBE (489 patients), replicated the model through pharmacists for inappropriate medicines overall (43% vs 12% discontinued) including sedative-hypnotic users specifically (43.2% vs 9.0%). The systematic-review context (Reeve 2017) shows education-plus-taper interventions yielding discontinuation between 27% and 80% across studies, with mostly no worsening of sleep or withdrawal outcomes. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: EMPOWER (Tannenbaum 2014): a mailed brochure + taper stopped benzodiazepines in 27% vs 5% at 6 months — NNT 4
cards.summary: Cluster randomised trial (2010–2012): 30 community pharmacies randomised (15 intervention, 15 wait-list control); 303 long-term benzodiazepine users aged 65–95 enrolled before randomisation (148 intervention, 155 control); 261 (86%) completed 6-month follow-up. The intervention was a direct-to-patient deprescribing empowerment package describing benzodiazepine risks with a stepwise tapering protocol; discontinuation was ascertained from pharmacy renewal records. At 6 months, 27% of the intervention group had discontinued vs 5% of controls (risk difference 23% [95% CI 14% to 32%]; intracluster correlation 0.008; number needed to treat 4). An additional 11% (95% CI 6% to 16%) reduced dose. Sixty-two percent of recipients initiated a cessation conversation with their physician and/or pharmacist. No subgroup (age >80, sex, duration, indication, dose, prior taper attempt, polypharmacy ≥10) modified the effect.
cards.type: Cluster randomised trial (EMPOWER), JAMA Intern Med 2014. Registry ID from the record's own databank: NCT01148186.
cards.people: 303 community-dwelling long-term benzodiazepine users aged 65–95 years, recruited from 30 community pharmacies (Canada).
cards.result: Discontinuation at 6 months: 27% intervention vs 5% control (risk difference 23% [95% CI 14% to 32%]; NNT 4). Dose reduction in a further 11%.
cards.watchOut: Volunteers recruited through pharmacies may be more ready to stop than the average long-term user, and 6 months is not forever — relapse beyond the trial window is unmeasured here. The outcome is discontinuation, not a demonstrated fall in fractures or falls; the shelf claims the behaviour change the trial measured.
cards.source: Tannenbaum C et al. Reduction of inappropriate benzodiazepine prescriptions among older adults through direct patient education: the EMPOWER cluster randomized trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2014;174(6):890-898. PMID 24733354 · NCT01148186

cards.headline: D-PRESCRIBE (Martin 2018): the pharmacist-led sequel — inappropriate medicines stopped in 43% vs 12%; sedative-hypnotics 43.2% vs 9.0%
cards.summary: Cluster randomised trial in 69 Quebec community pharmacies (2014–2017): 489 patients aged ≥65 prescribed one of four Beers-criteria medicines (sedative-hypnotics, first-generation antihistamines, glyburide, NSAIDs); 34 pharmacies (248 patients) intervention, 35 (241) control; 437 (89%) completed the trial (mean age 75 years; 66% women). Intervention pharmacists sent patients an educational deprescribing brochure and their physicians an evidence-based pharmaceutical opinion. At 6 months, 43% (106/248) of the intervention group no longer filled the inappropriate prescription vs 12% (29/241) of controls (risk difference 31% [95% CI 23% to 38%]). Among sedative-hypnotic users specifically: 43.2% (63/146) vs 9.0% (14/155) discontinued (risk difference 34% [95% CI 25% to 43%]).

cards.headline: Reeve 2017 (systematic review): benzodiazepine/Z-drug withdrawal in older adults is feasible — discontinuation 27–80% with education + tapering
cards.summary: Systematic review of interventions to deprescribe benzodiazepines and other hypnotics in older adults (studies 1995–2015): 7 studies of benzodiazepine/Z-drug withdrawal met criteria. Discontinuation reached 64.3% in a melatonin-substitution study and 65.0% in a GP-targeted intervention; mixed interventions combining patient education with tapering (2 studies), pharmacological substitution with psychological support (1), and tapering with psychological support (1) yielded discontinuation between 27.0% and 80.0%. Five studies measured clinical outcomes after discontinuation: four found no difference in withdrawal symptoms or sleep quality, while one reported declining quality of life over 8 months in those who continued benzodiazepines vs those who stopped.
cards.type: Systematic review, Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2017. No registry ID applies to a systematic review.
cards.people: 7 intervention studies in adults aged ≥65 years; the record does not print a pooled participant count.
cards.result: Discontinuation rates 27.0%–80.0% depending on intervention; most studies found no worsening of withdrawal symptoms or sleep quality after stopping.
cards.watchOut: Seven heterogeneous studies with no pooled estimate — a feasibility map, not an effect size. Its role on this shelf is context and safety reassurance around Cards 1–2, whose randomised numbers carry the stamp.

cards.headline: Reading the deprescribing evidence together: the patient is the intervention — hand them the risks and the taper
cards.summary: Synthesis of Cards 1–3. Two cluster trials from the EMPOWER programme (792 patients combined) show the same manoeuvre working twice: put a concrete harm description and a stepwise taper directly in the patient's hands, and roughly a quarter to two-fifths of long-term older users stop within 6 months, at NNT ≈4 for EMPOWER, without a signal of harm in the wider review literature. The fence: both trials are Canadian, pharmacy-recruited, and from one programme, and discontinuation — not falls or cognition — is the proven outcome. Graded LIKELY for the discontinuation claim exactly as fenced. No EMPOWER card exists elsewhere in the library: the Beers shelf (#137) examines the criteria's evidence base, a different question, and does not card these trials.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. One-programme fence and #137 distinction printed on the card's face.
cards.people: No new participants; synthesis of Cards 1–3.
cards.result: Direct patient education + taper: discontinuation 27% vs 5% (EMPOWER) and 43.2% vs 9.0% in sedative-hypnotic users (D-PRESCRIBE).
cards.watchOut: Long-term users with dependence physiology, seizure risk or unstable psychiatric illness need supervised tapers beyond a brochure — EMPOWER enrolled community volunteers, not every long-term user. Do not quote the 27% as a guarantee for unselected clinic panels.

shelves.title: Later school start times and teen sleep: Seattle's natural experiment
shelves.question: When a school district delays start times, do teenagers actually sleep more — and does anything measurable improve?
shelves.mesh: Academic Performance · Adolescent · Analysis of Variance · Humans · Schools · Sleep · Students · Time Factors · Washington · Absenteeism · Sleep Stages
shelves.balance: Seattle did the experiment policy usually only debates: the district delayed secondary start times by nearly an hour, and researchers measured students objectively before and after. Median daily sleep rose by 34 minutes — gained by waking later, not by going to bed earlier, exactly as circadian biology predicts — median grades rose 4.5%, and attendance improved (Dunster 2018). The wider literature agrees in direction: Bowers & Moyer's meta-analysis (5 longitudinal and 15 cross-sectional comparison studies) found later start times associated with longer sleep, less daytime sleepiness and less tardiness, while warning that longitudinal primary research is thin. This is a natural experiment, not a randomised trial: one district, one pre/post comparison, concurrent changes uncontrolled. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Dunster 2018 (Seattle natural experiment): start delayed ~1 hour — median sleep +34 minutes, median grades +4.5%, attendance improved
cards.summary: Pre-/post-research study around the Seattle School District's decision to delay the secondary school start time by nearly an hour. Using objective measurement (wrist actigraphy in the study design as reported), the authors found an increase in daily median sleep duration of 34 minutes, associated with a 4.5% increase in students' median grades and an improvement in attendance. The sleep gain came from later waking with bedtime essentially unchanged — consistent with the authors' framing that adolescent bedtime is biologically set by the circadian clock, so a later start converts directly into more sleep rather than later nights.
cards.type: Natural experiment (pre-/post study of a district policy change), Sci Adv 2018. Not a randomised trial — no registry ID applies.
cards.people: High-school students in the Seattle School District studied before and after the start-time delay; the record's abstract does not print the actigraphy sample size, mean age, or sex mix, and none is claimed here.
cards.result: Median daily sleep duration: +34 minutes after the delay. Median grades: +4.5%. Attendance: improved (the record's abstract does not print an attendance effect size).
cards.watchOut: Pre/post in a single district: no concurrent control district, so secular trends, cohort differences and other district changes cannot be excluded. Grades and attendance are school-record outcomes, not health endpoints. The 34-minute sleep figure is the shelf's solid core; the grade figure is its most quotable and least controlled number.
cards.source: Dunster GP et al. Sleepmore in Seattle: Later school start times are associated with more sleep and better performance in high school students. Sci Adv. 2018;4(12):eaau6200. PMID 30547089

cards.headline: Bowers & Moyer 2017 (meta-analysis): later start times — longer sleep, less sleepiness, less tardiness, across 20 studies
cards.summary: Meta-analysis aggregating 5 longitudinal studies and 15 cross-sectional comparison-group studies of school start time and student outcomes. Later start times were associated with longer sleep durations; later starts were also associated with less daytime sleepiness (7 studies) and tardiness to school (3 studies). The authors explicitly counsel cautious interpretation: methodological considerations, including the need for more longitudinal primary research, limit the strength of inference. Effect sizes in minutes are not printed in the record's abstract and are not claimed here.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal and cross-sectional studies, Sleep Health 2017. No registry ID applies to a meta-analysis.
cards.people: Students across 20 studies (5 longitudinal, 15 cross-sectional comparison); the record does not print a pooled participant count, mean age, or sex mix.
cards.result: Later start times associated with longer sleep duration, less daytime sleepiness and less tardiness; authors advise cautious interpretation pending more longitudinal research.
cards.watchOut: Fifteen of twenty studies are cross-sectional comparisons between different schools — districts that delay starts differ from districts that don't. The meta-analysis supports Seattle's direction; it cannot independently prove causation.
cards.source: Bowers JM, Moyer A. Effects of school start time on students' sleep duration, daytime sleepiness, and attendance: a meta-analysis. Sleep Health. 2017;3(6):423-431. PMID 29157635

cards.headline: Reading the school-start evidence together: the sleep gain is real and mechanistically coherent; the academic gain is a promising association
cards.summary: Synthesis of Cards 1–2. The strongest claim this shelf supports: delaying secondary start times by about an hour increases objectively measured teen sleep by roughly half an hour, because wake time moves and bedtime does not — observed in Seattle and directionally consistent across 20 studies. The grade (+4.5% median) and attendance findings are genuine results of the Seattle study but rest on its uncontrolled pre/post design. No randomised trial of district start times exists, and the shelf is graded POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY for exactly that design ceiling — while noting that 'wait for an RCT' is not an available policy option for a question districts must decide annually.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. Design ceiling printed on the card's face.
cards.people: No new participants; synthesis of Cards 1–2.
cards.result: Sleep: +34 median minutes (Seattle, objective) with concordant meta-analytic direction. Grades/attendance: improved in Seattle; causality less secure.
cards.watchOut: Effects may differ where commutes, after-school work, sports schedules or elementary-start swaps bind differently. Seattle delayed secondary starts specifically; the shelf does not speak to delaying all grades.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–2 on this shelf (PMID 30547089; PMID 29157635).

shelves.title: MRSA pneumonia: linezolid vs vancomycin — better clinical cure in the one prospective trial, the same survival
shelves.question: For nosocomial pneumonia caused by MRSA, is linezolid better than dose-optimized vancomycin — on clinical cure, and on survival?
shelves.mesh: Pneumonia, Staphylococcal · Cross Infection · Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus · Linezolid · Vancomycin · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Humans
shelves.balance: Linezolid's advantage is real but narrow. The one prospective double-blind trial designed for MRSA pneumonia (ZEPHyR, 1,184 treated) found higher clinical success with linezolid in the per-protocol population (57.6% vs 46.6%) and less nephrotoxicity (8.4% vs 18.2%), but 60-day mortality was essentially identical (15.7% vs 17.0%) — and the superiority signal did not come from the intention-to-treat population. The earlier randomized program (Rubinstein 2001) found linezolid and vancomycin equivalent in gram-positive nosocomial pneumonia overall. The striking survival gap sometimes quoted for linezolid (80.0% vs 63.5%) comes from a retrospective subset analysis of those earlier trials — hypothesis-generating, and its mortality claim is exactly what ZEPHyR's prospective test failed to confirm. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: ZEPHyR 2012: linezolid beat vancomycin on clinical success in MRSA nosocomial pneumonia (57.6% vs 46.6%, per-protocol) — 60-day mortality was the same
cards.summary: ZEPHyR: linezolid beat vancomycin on per-protocol clinical success ( 57.6% vs 46.6% ), with the same 60-day mortality (15.7% vs 17.0%) and less nephrotoxicity (8.4% vs 18.2%).
cards.type: Prospective, double-blind, controlled, multicenter randomized trial (ZEPHyR), Clin Infect Dis 2012; vancomycin dose-optimized by trough levels
cards.people: 1,184 hospitalized adults with hospital-acquired or healthcare-associated MRSA pneumonia were treated; 448 (224 per arm) formed the modified intention-to-treat population and 348 (172 linezolid, 176 vancomycin) the per-protocol population. Treatment was linezolid 600 mg IV every 12 hours or vancomycin 15 mg/kg every 12 hours for 7–14 days. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: In the per-protocol population, clinical success at end of study was achieved by 95/165 (57.6%) on linezolid vs 81/174 (46.6%) on vancomycin (95% CI for the difference, 0.5% to 21.6%; P=.042). All-cause 60-day mortality was similar: 15.7% linezolid vs 17.0% vancomycin. Nephrotoxicity occurred more frequently with vancomycin (18.2%) than with linezolid (8.4%); overall adverse-event incidence was similar.

cards.headline: Rubinstein 2001: linezolid and vancomycin were equivalent in gram-positive nosocomial pneumonia overall
cards.summary: Rubinstein 2001: linezolid and vancomycin were equivalent in gram-positive nosocomial pneumonia — clinical cure 66.4% vs 68.1% .
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, multicenter trial, Clin Infect Dis 2001. Pre-registration-era trial — no registry number exists on the record
cards.people: 396 hospitalized adults with nosocomial pneumonia received linezolid 600 mg twice daily plus aztreonam (n=203) or vancomycin 1 g twice daily plus aztreonam (n=193) for 7–21 days. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: In evaluable patients, clinical cure rates were 71/107 (66.4%) for linezolid vs 62/91 (68.1%) for vancomycin, and microbiological success rates were 36/53 (67.9%) vs 28/39 (71.8%) — equivalent between groups. MRSA eradication rates and safety evaluations were similar, and no resistance to either drug was detected.

cards.headline: Wunderink 2003: the famous survival gap for linezolid (80.0% vs 63.5%) is a retrospective subset analysis — fenced as such
cards.summary: Wunderink 2003: the famous survival gap ( 80.0% vs 63.5% ) comes from a retrospective subset analysis — hypothesis-generating, and exactly what ZEPHyR’s prospective test failed to confirm.
cards.type: Retrospective analysis of data from two prospective randomized double-blind trials, Chest 2003 — not itself a randomized comparison for the MRSA question
cards.people: 1,019 patients with suspected gram-positive nosocomial pneumonia across 134 sites in the two parent trials, including 339 with documented S. aureus pneumonia and 160 with documented MRSA pneumonia (75 linezolid, 85 vancomycin in the survival analysis).
cards.result: In the MRSA subset, Kaplan-Meier survival was 80.0% (60/75) on linezolid vs 63.5% (54/85) on vancomycin (p=0.03), and the adjusted odds ratio for survival was 2.2 (95% CI 1.0 to 4.8; p=0.05) — a relative measure from a post-hoc subset. Clinical cure in the MRSA subset was 59.0% (36/61) vs 35.5% (22/62) (adjusted OR 3.3; 95% CI 1.3 to 8.3).
cards.watchOut: This is the card the shelf exists to fence. The subset was defined after the trials ran, the parent trials were not powered or randomized for MRSA pneumonia, and the adjusted survival interval (1.0 to 4.8) barely excludes no effect. When the question was later asked prospectively in ZEPHyR, the mortality difference vanished (15.7% vs 17.0%). Treat the 2003 survival signal as the hypothesis ZEPHyR tested — not as a finding.

cards.headline: Reading the linezolid–vancomycin pneumonia trials together
cards.summary: Linezolid is at least vancomycin’s equal for MRSA pneumonia and kinder to kidneys, but no prospective trial shows it saving more lives — POSSIBLE.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Adults with nosocomial (hospital-acquired or healthcare-associated) pneumonia, with the MRSA-documented subset as the shelf's focus.
cards.result: The fence: linezolid is at least vancomycin's equal for MRSA pneumonia (Rubinstein 2001 equivalence in the broader gram-positive population; ZEPHyR 2012 per-protocol clinical-cure advantage), kinder to kidneys (nephrotoxicity 8.4% vs 18.2% in ZEPHyR), and not shown to save more lives in any prospective test (ZEPHyR 60-day mortality 15.7% vs 17.0%). The retrospective survival signal (Wunderink 2003) is printed on its own card, labeled with its design, because it is still widely quoted as if it were a trial result. No in-flight randomized trial in the 24-month sweep is re-asking the head-to-head question.
cards.watchOut: A per-protocol superiority on clinical cure plus a null on mortality earns POSSIBLE, not more. Vancomycin harm in ZEPHyR was kidney injury despite trough-guided dosing — the comparison was against optimized vancomycin, not careless vancomycin.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID 22247123 (ZEPHyR), PMID 11170948 (Rubinstein 2001), and PMID 14605050 (Wunderink 2003), all carded on this shelf.

shelves.title: Ventilator-associated pneumonia: stop early by response — REGARD-VAP confirms the short-course answer PneumA first gave
shelves.question: For ventilator-associated pneumonia, can antibiotics be stopped after a short, response-guided course (about a week or less) instead of a fixed long course — without costing lives or inviting recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Pneumonia, Ventilator-Associated · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Drug Administration Schedule · Intensive Care Units · Intention to Treat Analysis · Humans
shelves.balance: The founding trial of this question — PneumA (Chastre 2003), 8 vs 15 days in 401 patients with culture-proven VAP — is not re-carded here: its home is Shelf 313, where its result (no mortality difference; recurrence 40.6% vs 25.4% in nonfermenting gram-negative infections on the short course) is already carded, and that organism-shaped exception is part of this shelf's fence. What this shelf adds is the modern confirmation. REGARD-VAP (2024, 461 patients) tested an individualized short course — stop at 3–7 days once fever resolved and the patient was stable — against usual care (median 14 days): the 60-day composite of death or pneumonia recurrence was 41% vs 44%, meeting noninferiority, with far fewer antibiotic side effects (8% vs 38% per-protocol). Singh 2000 supplies the older, narrower lesson: in ICU patients whose pulmonary infiltrates scored as low-likelihood pneumonia, a 3-day stop was safe and halved resistance/superinfection. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: REGARD-VAP 2024: an individualized short course (median 6 days) was noninferior to usual long-course care (median 14 days) for VAP — with a third as many antibiotic side effects
cards.summary: REGARD-VAP: a response-guided short course (median 6 days ) was noninferior to usual long-course care (median 14 days) on the 60-day composite of death or recurrence ( 41% vs 44% ), with a third as many antibiotic side effects.
cards.type: Multicentre, individually randomized, open-label, phase 4 noninferiority trial (REGARD-VAP), Lancet Respir Med 2024; outcome assessors masked
cards.people: 461 adults with VAP (CDC/NHSN criteria, ventilated ≥48 hours, on culture-directed antibiotics) in 39 ICUs in Nepal, Singapore, and Thailand; 232 assigned to individualized short-course treatment and 229 to usual care. Median age 64 years (IQR 51–74); 181 (39%) female. Short-course patients were assessed for fever resolution for 48 hours and hemodynamic stability, then stopped at ≤7 days (as short as 3–5); usual care was ≥8 days at clinician discretion.
cards.result: Median antibiotic duration for the index VAP episode: 6 days (IQR 5–7) vs 14 days (10–21). The primary outcome — the 60-day composite of death or pneumonia recurrence — occurred in 95/231 (41%) on short-course vs 100/229 (44%) on usual care (risk difference −3%; one-sided 95% CI −∞ to 5%), meeting the prespecified 12% noninferiority margin in both intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses; superiority was not established. In the per-protocol population, antibiotic side effects occurred in 17/211 (8%) on short-course vs 86/224 (38%) on usual care (risk difference −31%; 95% CI −37 to −25; p<0.0001).
cards.watchOut: The 12% noninferiority margin is wide, the trial is open-label, and the composite mixes death with recurrence — read it as 'a response-guided stop at about a week did not detectably worsen outcomes while cutting drug exposure and side effects,' not as proof that any fixed short number of days fits every organism. PneumA's nonfermenter exception (Shelf 313) still applies.
cards.source: Mo Y et al. Individualised, short-course antibiotic treatment versus usual long-course treatment for ventilator-associated pneumonia (REGARD-VAP): a multicentre, individually randomised, open-label, non-inferiority trial. Lancet Respir Med. 2024;12(5):399-408. PMID 38272050 · NCT03382548.

cards.headline: Singh 2000: when pulmonary infiltrates scored as low-likelihood pneumonia, stopping antibiotics at 3 days was safe — and resistance/superinfection fell from 35% to 15%
cards.summary: Singh 2000: in low-likelihood pulmonary infiltrates, a 3-day stop was safe — continuation beyond day 3 ran 28% vs 90% , mortality did not differ, and resistance/superinfection fell from 35% to 15%.
cards.type: Randomized trial using the Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score (CPIS), Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2000. Pre-registration-era trial — no registry number exists on the record
cards.people: 81 ICU patients with pulmonary infiltrates and CPIS ≤6 (low likelihood of pneumonia): 39 assigned to ciprofloxacin monotherapy with re-evaluation at 3 days (antibiotics stopped if CPIS remained ≤6) and 42 to standard therapy at treating physicians' discretion. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Antibiotics were continued beyond 3 days in 28% (11/39) of the experimental group vs 90% (38/42) on standard therapy (p=0.0001); among patients whose CPIS remained ≤6 at day 3, continuation was 0% (0/25) vs 96% (24/25). Mortality and ICU length of stay did not differ (the abstract reports no significant difference and prints no rates) despite significantly shorter, cheaper therapy. Antimicrobial resistance, superinfection, or both developed in 15% (5/37) on the experimental strategy vs 35% (14/37) on standard therapy (p=0.017).
cards.watchOut: This is not a trial of confirmed VAP — it is a trial of suspected VAP that probably was not pneumonia, which is exactly its lesson: the largest safe 'short course' is the one never started or stopped at reassessment. Do not cite it as evidence about treating proven VAP for 3 days.
cards.source: Singh N et al. Short-course empiric antibiotic therapy for patients with pulmonary infiltrates in the intensive care unit. A proposed solution for indiscriminate antibiotic prescription. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2000;162(2 Pt 1):505-11. PMID 10934078 · No registry number (pre-registration-era trial).

cards.headline: Reading the VAP duration evidence together — including the trial that lives on Shelf 313
cards.summary: The 8-vs-15-day anchor trial, PneumA, is home on Shelf #313 and is cited here, not re-carded; this shelf’s own trials extend it — response-guided stopping is noninferior — LIKELY.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Adults with ventilator-associated pneumonia (REGARD-VAP; PneumA on Shelf 313), and ICU patients with pulmonary infiltrates of low pneumonia likelihood (Singh).
cards.result: The fence: the 8-vs-15-day anchor, PneumA (Chastre 2003; 401 patients; 28-day mortality 18.8% on 8 days vs 17.2% on 15 days), is carded at its home on Shelf 313 under the one-home rule and is cited, not duplicated, here. This shelf's own cards extend it in two directions: REGARD-VAP shows a response-guided stop (median 6 days) is noninferior to usual long courses on death-or-recurrence at 60 days, with far fewer side effects; Singh shows the de-escalation logic reaches back to day 3 when the diagnosis itself is doubtful. The exception travels with the answer: in PneumA, VAP caused by nonfermenting gram-negative bacilli (including Pseudomonas) recurred in 40.6% on 8 days vs 25.4% on 15 days — short courses are response- and organism-guided, not calendar-blind. No in-flight trial in the 24-month sweep is positioned to overturn this; the open question is duration in nonfermenter and multidrug-resistant VAP specifically.
cards.watchOut: Shelf 313 and this shelf answer sibling questions (pneumonia duration on the ward and in the ventilated patient vs VAP strategy); cross-reference, don't merge. REGARD-VAP's usual-care arm (median 14 days) reflects practice in its settings — the noninferiority verdict is against that comparator, with its 12-point margin stated on the card.

shelves.title: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for early outpatient COVID-19: benefit in high-risk, null in standard-risk
shelves.question: Does early nirmatrelvir-ritonavir prevent hospitalisation or death in high-risk outpatients — and does it help standard-risk or vaccinated patients?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Antiviral Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · COVID-19 Drug Treatment · Disease Progression · Hospitalization · Lactams/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Leucine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split, proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane) — LIKELY in high-risk unvaccinated outpatients: in EPIC-HR, COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death by day 28 was 0.77% on nirmatrelvir-ritonavir versus 7.01% on placebo in patients treated within 3 days (an 89.1% relative risk reduction), and all 13 deaths in the final analysis were in the placebo group. MAYBE (weak evidence) in standard-risk or vaccinated patients: in EPIC-SR the primary symptom outcome did not differ (median time to sustained alleviation 12 versus 13 days, P=0.60) and hospitalisation or death was 0.8% versus 1.6% (difference -0.8 percentage points, 95% CI -2.0 to 0.4), a ratio inside the 0.5-2.0 band that is never presented as solid evidence on this library. The discordance by baseline risk is the shelf's central fact and stays two-handed. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: EPIC-HR: hospitalisation or death 0.77% versus 7.01% when treated within 3 days in high-risk unvaccinated outpatients
cards.summary: EPIC-HR: hospitalisation or death 0.77% vs 7.01% when treated within 3 days — an 89.1% relative reduction, about 6.3 points absolute, with all final-analysis deaths on placebo.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 2,246 symptomatic, unvaccinated, nonhospitalised adults at high risk for progression to severe COVID-19 underwent randomisation (1,120 nirmatrelvir-ritonavir and 1,126 placebo). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the planned interim analysis of patients treated within 3 days after symptom onset, COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death by day 28 was 0.77% (3 of 389) in the nirmatrelvir group, with 0 deaths, versus 7.01% (27 of 385) in the placebo group, with 7 deaths — a difference of -6.32 percentage points, described by the trial as an 89.1% relative risk reduction. Efficacy was maintained in the final analysis (difference -5.81 percentage points; 88.9% relative risk reduction), and all 13 deaths occurred in the placebo group. Viral load at day 5 was lower with nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (adjusted mean difference -0.868 log10 copies per millilitre). Adverse events were similar overall (any adverse event 22.6% versus 23.9%; serious adverse events 1.6% versus 6.6%); dysgeusia (5.6% versus 0.3%) and diarrhoea (3.1% versus 1.6%) were more frequent on treatment.
cards.watchOut: Participants were unvaccinated and at high risk, treated early in the pandemic era; the absolute benefit depends on that high baseline risk (7.01% on placebo) and does not transfer to lower-risk populations — see the EPIC-SR card.
cards.source: Hammond J et al. Oral Nirmatrelvir for High-Risk, Nonhospitalized Adults with Covid-19. N Engl J Med. 2022 Apr 14;386(15):1397-1408. PMID: 35172054. Registry ID: NCT04960202 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: EPIC-SR: no faster symptom relief, and hospitalisation or death 0.8% versus 1.6%, in standard-risk or vaccinated outpatients
cards.summary: EPIC-SR: symptom relief no faster ( 12 vs 13 days , P=0.60) and hospitalisation or death 0.8% vs 1.6% in standard-risk or vaccinated outpatients.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 1,296 participants underwent randomisation and were included in the full analysis population; 1,288 received at least one dose (654 nirmatrelvir-ritonavir and 634 placebo). Eligible patients were fully vaccinated with at least one risk factor for severe disease, or had no risk factors and had never been vaccinated or not been vaccinated within the previous year. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The median time to sustained alleviation of all targeted COVID-19 signs and symptoms was 12 days in the nirmatrelvir-ritonavir group and 13 days in the placebo group (P=0.60). Five participants (0.8%) in the nirmatrelvir-ritonavir group and 10 (1.6%) in the placebo group were hospitalised for COVID-19 or died from any cause (difference, -0.8 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.0 to 0.4). Adverse events were similar (25.8% versus 24.1%); the most commonly reported treatment-related events were dysgeusia (5.8%) and diarrhoea (2.1%).
cards.watchOut: The hospitalisation/death difference is small, its confidence interval crosses zero, and the corresponding ratio sits inside the 0.5-2.0 band — it must not be presented as solid evidence of benefit in this population. The trial's primary (symptom) outcome was null.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the same drug, opposite verdicts by baseline risk — high-risk benefit is LIKELY, standard-risk benefit is MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: The same drug, opposite verdicts by baseline risk — high-risk benefit LIKELY, standard-risk benefit MAYBE (weak evidence); Tier C split, proposed.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: EPIC-HR (2,246 high-risk unvaccinated outpatients) and EPIC-SR (1,296 standard-risk or vaccinated outpatients), both phase 2-3, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 5 days of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir started within 5 days of symptoms (EPIC-HR headline analysis within 3 days).
cards.result: Where placebo-group hospitalisation or death was 7.01%, nirmatrelvir-ritonavir reduced it to 0.77% (89.1% relative risk reduction, absolute difference about -6.3 percentage points, with all 13 final-analysis deaths on placebo). Where placebo-group risk was only 1.6%, the rates were 0.8% versus 1.6% (difference -0.8 percentage points, CI crossing zero) and symptom relief was no faster (12 versus 13 days, P=0.60). The proposed split stamp — LIKELY for high-risk unvaccinated patients, MAYBE (weak evidence) for standard-risk or vaccinated patients — is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Never merge the two trials into a single efficacy claim: baseline risk, vaccination status and era differ, and the standard-risk result is the honest counterweight to the high-risk result.

shelves.title: Oseltamivir for treating and preventing influenza
shelves.question: Does oseltamivir shorten influenza illness or prevent complications and transmission, on the full trial record?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Drug Evaluation · Enzyme Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Europe · Health Status · Influenza, Human/drug therapy/prevention & control · Japan
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two independent syntheses of the same manufacturer trial programme agree that oseltamivir shortens illness modestly in adults — by 16.8 hours in the Cochrane review of full clinical study reports (from 7.0 to 6.3 days) and by a median 25.2 hours in the Dobson individual-participant-data meta-analysis (97.5 versus 122.7 hours). They disagree on complications: Dobson found fewer lower-respiratory complications requiring antibiotics (4.9% versus 8.7%) and fewer hospital admissions (0.6% versus 1.7%), while Cochrane, working from the full study reports, found no significant effect on hospitalisation (risk difference 0.15%, 95% CI -0.78 to 0.91) and no significant reduction in serious complications, with the apparent pneumonia effect confined to self-reported, unverified pneumonia. Both agree on harm: nausea and vomiting are increased (Dobson risk differences +3.7 and +4.7 percentage points). Prophylaxis reduced symptomatic influenza in Cochrane's analysis (risk difference 3.05% in individuals; 13.6% in households) but not asymptomatic infection. Influenza vaccines are a different intervention and live on their own shelves (#321, #443, #451); nothing vaccine is carded here.

cards.headline: Cochrane (full study reports): oseltamivir shortened adult illness by 16.8 hours, with no significant effect on hospitalisation
cards.summary: Cochrane (full study reports): illness shortened by 16.8 hours [8.4 to 25.1] — 7.0 → 6.3 days — with no significant effect on hospitalisation .
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials (clinical study reports)
cards.people: 46 trials in the formal analysis, including 20 oseltamivir trials (9,623 participants) and 26 zanamivir trials (14,628 participants), in adults and children with confirmed or suspected exposure to naturally occurring influenza. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: For treatment of adults, oseltamivir reduced the time to first alleviation of symptoms by 16.8 hours (95% CI 8.4 to 25.1; P<0.0001) — from 7.0 to 6.3 days. There was no effect in asthmatic children; in otherwise healthy children the reduction was 29 hours (95% CI 12 to 47). Treatment of adults with oseltamivir had no significant effect on hospitalisations (risk difference 0.15%, 95% CI -0.78 to 0.91), and did not significantly reduce complications classified as serious or leading to study withdrawal (risk difference 0.07%, 95% CI -0.78 to 0.44). The reduction in self-reported, investigator-mediated, unverified pneumonia (risk difference 1.00%, 95% CI 0.22 to 1.49) was not significant in the five trials using a more detailed diagnostic form, and no trial defined pneumonia or reported radiologically confirmed pneumonia effects. Harms in adults: nausea (risk difference 3.66%; number needed to treat to harm 28) and vomiting (risk difference 4.56%; NNTH 22) were increased. In prophylaxis, oseltamivir reduced symptomatic influenza in individuals (risk difference 3.05%; NNTB 33) and in households (risk difference 13.6%; NNTB 7), with no significant effect on asymptomatic influenza (risk ratio 1.14, 95% CI 0.39 to 3.33).
cards.watchOut: All trials were manufacturer-sponsored; inadequate reporting put half the oseltamivir studies at high risk of selection bias, placebos may have contained active substances, and complication definitions were absent — which is why this review's complication verdicts are more sceptical than the published-paper literature.
cards.source: Jefferson T et al. Neuraminidase inhibitors for preventing and treating influenza in adults and children. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2014 Apr 10;2014(4):CD008965. PMID: 24718923. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Dobson IPD meta-analysis: symptoms 25.2 hours shorter, with fewer antibiotic-treated respiratory complications (4.9% versus 8.7%) and admissions (0.6% versus 1.7%)
cards.summary: Dobson IPD: median alleviation 97.5 vs 122.7 hours (25.2 hours shorter); antibiotic-treated respiratory complications 4.9% vs 8.7% — a claim the Cochrane review does not share.
cards.type: Individual-participant-data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 9 trials including 4,328 patients — adults treated with oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily or placebo for naturally occurring influenza-like illness in Roche-sponsored, double-blind trials. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat infected population, time to alleviation of all symptoms was 21% shorter in relative terms with oseltamivir (time ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.74-0.85; p<0.0001), with median times of 97.5 hours versus 122.7 hours (difference -25.2 hours, 95% CI -36.2 to -16.0); in the full intention-to-treat population the effect was attenuated (time ratio 0.85; median difference -17.8 hours). Lower respiratory tract complications requiring antibiotics more than 48 hours after randomisation were fewer with oseltamivir (risk ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.42-0.75; 4.9% versus 8.7%; risk difference -3.8%), as were hospital admissions for any cause (risk ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.17-0.81; 0.6% versus 1.7%; risk difference -1.1%) — both ratios at or inside the edge of the 0.5-2.0 band this library treats cautiously, printed here with their absolute rates. Nausea (9.9% versus 6.2%; risk difference 3.7%) and vomiting (8.0% versus 3.3%; risk difference 4.7%) were increased; there was no effect on neurological or psychiatric disorders or serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: This analysis pools the same Roche-sponsored trials the Cochrane review examined from full study reports, and reaches a more favourable complication verdict — the disagreement is about unpublished detail and outcome definitions, and both cards must be read together. Admission events were few (the 0.37 risk ratio rests on 0.6% versus 1.7%).

cards.summary: A day or less of illness bought; the complications claim is contested between the two best syntheses of the same trial programme — POSSIBLE.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the Cochrane review of 107 clinical study reports (46 trials analysed; 9,623 participants in oseltamivir trials) and the Dobson individual-participant-data meta-analysis (9 trials, 4,328 patients), covering substantially the same trial programme.
cards.result: Symptom shortening is the consistent finding (16.8 hours by Cochrane; median 25.2 hours by Dobson, in infected patients). Complications are the contested finding: Dobson reports fewer antibiotic-treated lower-respiratory complications (4.9% versus 8.7%) and admissions (0.6% versus 1.7%), while Cochrane finds no significant hospitalisation effect (risk difference 0.15%, CI crossing zero) and attributes the pneumonia signal to unverified, self-reported outcomes. Harms (nausea, vomiting) are agreed. That pattern — certain small symptomatic benefit, disputed complication benefit — is a POSSIBLE stamp. Prophylaxis against symptomatic influenza is supported by Cochrane (risk difference 3.05% individually, 13.6% in households) with no effect on asymptomatic infection.
cards.watchOut: Do not settle the complications dispute by picking the favourable synthesis; the shelf's claim is the dispute itself. Vaccine shelves (#321, #443, #451) are the home for influenza prevention by vaccination and are not re-carded here.

shelves.title: Antibiotics for acute COPD exacerbations
shelves.question: Do antibiotics improve outcomes in acute COPD exacerbations, and in which severity strata?
shelves.mesh: Ambulatory Care · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Disease Progression · Hospitalization · Intensive Care Units · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/classification/drug therapy/mortality · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The Cochrane synthesis of 16 trials (2,068 participants) found antibiotics reduced treatment failure in inpatients with severe exacerbations (risk ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.91) and in outpatients (risk ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.94) — both ratios inside the 0.5-2.0 band and therefore not presented as solid evidence on their own — but the outpatient effect lost significance when restricted to currently available drugs (risk ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.01). The single ICU trial (93 patients) showed a large effect on treatment failure (risk ratio 0.19) and on mortality (Peto odds ratio 0.21), while four inpatient trials showed no mortality effect (Peto odds ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.37 to 2.79) — the mortality figures are printed together, as required, and no general mortality claim is made. The founding Anthonisen trial found success in 68% of exacerbations on antibiotic versus 55% on placebo. Adverse events, especially diarrhoea, were more common with antibiotics. Maintenance COPD therapy lives at #303-#306; only exacerbation antibiotics are carded here.

cards.headline: Cochrane: antibiotics reduced treatment failure in inpatients and outpatients, but the outpatient effect vanished for currently used drugs
cards.summary: Cochrane: treatment failure reduced in inpatients (risk ratio 0.77 ) and outpatients ( 0.75 ) — both inside the 0.5–2.0 band — and the outpatient effect vanished when restricted to currently available drugs.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 16 trials with 2,068 participants with acute COPD exacerbations, analysed separately as outpatients (mild to moderate), inpatients (severe), and ICU patients (very severe). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In outpatients, antibiotics statistically significantly reduced treatment failure between 7 days and 1 month (risk ratio 0.75; 95% CI 0.60 to 0.94; low-quality evidence), but not when the analysis was restricted to currently available drugs (risk ratio 0.80; 95% CI 0.63 to 1.01). In inpatients, antibiotics reduced treatment failure (risk ratio 0.77; 95% CI 0.65 to 0.91; high-quality evidence), regardless of restriction to current drugs. The only ICU trial (93 patients) showed a large effect on treatment failure (risk ratio 0.19; 95% CI 0.08 to 0.45). On mortality: four inpatient trials showed no effect (Peto odds ratio 1.02; 95% CI 0.37 to 2.79), while the single ICU trial showed a statistically significant mortality effect (Peto odds ratio 0.21; 95% CI 0.06 to 0.72) and a shorter stay (mean difference -9.60 days). Length of stay otherwise did not differ. Adverse events were more frequent with antibiotics (Peto odds ratio 1.53; 95% CI 1.03 to 2.27), driven by diarrhoea (Peto odds ratio 2.62; 95% CI 1.11 to 6.17).
cards.watchOut: The headline risk ratios (0.75-0.77) sit inside the 0.5-2.0 band and are not solid evidence by this library's standard; the mortality benefit rests on one 93-patient ICU trial against a null in four inpatient trials, and trials span 1957-2012, including drugs no longer used.
cards.source: Vollenweider DJ et al. Antibiotics for exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012 Dec 12;(12):CD010257. PMID: 23235687. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Anthonisen 1987: exacerbation success 68% on antibiotic versus 55% on placebo, with deterioration halved
cards.summary: Anthonisen 1987: exacerbation success 68% vs 55% on placebo, with deterioration halved.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 173 patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease followed over 3.5 years, contributing 362 treated exacerbations (182 antibiotic and 180 placebo). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Exacerbations were defined by increased dyspnoea, sputum production, and sputum purulence, and followed at 3-day intervals; those resolving in 21 days were treatment successes. The success rate was 55% with placebo and 68% with antibiotic. Failure with deterioration occurred in 19% of placebo-treated and 10% of antibiotic-treated exacerbations. Peak flow recovered more rapidly with antibiotic treatment. Side effects were uncommon and did not differ between antibiotic and placebo.
cards.watchOut: A crossover-era trial from 1987 using broad-spectrum antibiotics of its time, counting exacerbations rather than patients as the unit; it founded the symptom-stratification approach (dyspnoea, sputum volume, purulence) but its effect size — a ratio inside the 0.5-2.0 band — is modest, consistent with the later Cochrane verdict.
cards.source: Anthonisen NR et al. Antibiotic therapy in exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Ann Intern Med. 1987 Feb;106(2):196-204. PMID: 3492164. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: antibiotics help most where exacerbations are most severe; the average effect is modest and stratum-dependent — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Antibiotics help most where exacerbations are most severe; the average effect is modest and stratum-dependent — POSSIBLE.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: a Cochrane synthesis of 16 trials (2,068 participants, searched to September 2012) and the 1987 Anthonisen trial (173 patients, 362 exacerbations).
cards.result: Across four decades the picture is consistent in shape and modest in size: treatment failure falls with antibiotics in inpatients (risk ratio 0.77) and, on all-trials analysis, outpatients (0.75), with Anthonisen's absolute success rates of 68% versus 55%; the outpatient effect is not significant for currently used drugs (0.80, CI crossing 1), inpatient mortality is null (Peto OR 1.02), and the large ICU effects (treatment failure 0.19, mortality 0.21) come from a single 93-patient trial. Hence POSSIBLE, with the severity gradient — not a blanket yes — as the claim. Diarrhoea and overall adverse events are the price (Peto ORs 2.62 and 1.53).
cards.watchOut: Ratios between 0.5 and 2.0 are not solid evidence on this library; the shelf's defensible statement is about where benefit concentrates (severe and ICU exacerbations), not that every exacerbation needs an antibiotic.

shelves.title: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation for obstructive sleep apnea
shelves.question: In CPAP-intolerant moderate-to-severe OSA, does upper-airway (hypoglossal) stimulation reduce apnea events and sleepiness?
shelves.mesh: Electric Stimulation Therapy/adverse effects · Hypoglossal Nerve · Lung · Oxygen/blood · Pharyngeal Muscles/innervation,physiopathology · Polysomnography · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The STAR study (126 implanted patients) is a single-group cohort, not a randomised comparison against no treatment: at 12 months the median apnea-hypopnea index fell 68% (29.3 to 9.0 events/hour) and the oxygen desaturation index fell 70% (25.4 to 7.4), with sleepiness and quality of life improved and a procedure-related serious adverse event rate under 2%. Its embedded randomised withdrawal sub-study is the controlled kernel: among responders, scores stayed flat with therapy maintained (AHI 8.9) and rebounded when therapy was switched off for a week (25.8 vs 7.6 events/hour, P<0.001), showing the measured effect belongs to the device. A single pivotal study with a one-week withdrawal test caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: STAR 2014: upper-airway stimulation cut the median AHI by 68% at 12 months (29.3 to 9.0 events/hour) in CPAP-intolerant patients — an uncontrolled cohort
cards.summary: STAR 2014: upper-airway stimulation cut the median AHI by 68% at 12 months ( 29.3 to 9.0 events/hour) in CPAP-intolerant patients — an uncontrolled cohort, with a randomised withdrawal proof.
cards.type: Prospective, multicentre, single-group cohort study with an embedded randomised therapy-withdrawal trial
cards.people: 126 participants with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea who had difficulty accepting or adhering to CPAP, surgically implanted with an upper-airway stimulation device; 83% were men, mean age 54.5 years, mean body-mass index 28.4.
cards.result: The median apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) at 12 months decreased 68%, from 29.3 events per hour to 9.0 events per hour (P<0.001), and the oxygen desaturation index decreased 70%, from 25.4 to 7.4 events per hour (P<0.001). Secondary measures (Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Functional Outcomes of Sleep Questionnaire, time with oxygen saturation below 90%) showed reduced effects of sleep apnea and improved quality of life. In the randomised withdrawal phase among responders, the mean AHI did not differ significantly from the 12-month score in the 23 participants maintained on therapy (8.9 vs 7.2 events/hour), but was significantly higher in the 23 participants whose therapy was withdrawn (25.8 vs 7.6 events/hour, P<0.001); oxygen desaturation results followed a similar pattern. The rate of procedure-related serious adverse events was less than 2%.
cards.watchOut: The main cohort had no control group and enrolled patients pre-selected for anatomy and CPAP failure; regression to the mean and selection cannot be excluded for the headline 68% fall — the one-week randomised withdrawal in 46 responders is the part of the design that isolates the device's effect.
cards.source: Strollo PJ Jr et al. Upper-airway stimulation for obstructive sleep apnea. N Engl J Med. 2014;370(2):139-149. PMID: 24401051. Registry ID: NCT01161420, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: A real device effect on apnea indices, proven by withdrawal — but a single pivotal study, so POSSIBLE.
cards.type: Synthesis

shelves.title: Surgery for obstructive sleep apnea in adults: multilevel and pharyngoplasty techniques
shelves.question: In adults with OSA who cannot use CPAP, does multilevel upper-airway surgery reduce apnea severity and sleepiness versus continued medical management?
shelves.mesh: Blood Pressure · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure/instrumentation · Oxygen/blood · Palate, Soft/surgery · Polysomnography · Self Report · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One small open-label randomised trial and one selected single-centre surgical trial programme support multilevel/pharyngoplasty surgery in CPAP-failure patients, but neither is large or blinded. SAMS (MacKay 2020, 102 adults) found combined palatal and tongue surgery beat ongoing medical management at six months on the apnea-hypopnea index (baseline-adjusted difference −17.6 events/hour) and Epworth Sleepiness Scale (−6.7 points), with two serious adverse events in the surgery group, including a postoperative myocardial infarction. SKUP3's modified uvulopalatopharyngoplasty cohort, drawn from its earlier randomised trial, sustained an AHI fall from 52.9 to about 24 at both 6 and 24 months in patients selected by Friedman stage and tonsil size. Promising and concordant, but preliminary — POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: SAMS 2020: multilevel surgery cut AHI by 17.6 events/hour more than medical management and sleepiness by 6.7 points at six months
cards.summary: SAMS 2020: multilevel surgery cut AHI by 17.6 events/hour more than medical management and sleepiness by 6.7 points at six months.
cards.type: Multicentre, parallel-group, open-label randomised clinical trial
cards.people: 102 adults with symptomatic moderate or severe obstructive sleep apnea in whom conventional device treatment had failed, enrolled 2014–2017 and randomised to multilevel surgery (51 — modified uvulopalatopharyngoplasty plus minimally invasive tongue volume reduction) or ongoing medical management (51); mean (SD) age 44.6 (12.8) years, 18 (18%) women; 91 (89%) completed the trial.
cards.result: The mean apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) was 47.9 at baseline and 20.8 at six months in the surgery group, and 45.3 at baseline and 34.5 at six months in the medical-management group (mean baseline-adjusted between-group difference at six months −17.6 events/hour [95% CI −26.8 to −8.4]; P<0.001), against a minimal clinically important difference of 15 events/hour. The mean Epworth Sleepiness Scale score was 12.4 at baseline and 5.3 at six months with surgery, and 11.1 and 10.5 with medical management (baseline-adjusted difference −6.7 [95% CI −8.2 to −5.2]; P<0.001), against a minimal important difference of 2 units. Two participants (4%) in the surgery group had serious adverse events (one myocardial infarction on postoperative day 5 and one hospitalisation for observation after hematemesis of old blood). The authors call this a preliminary study and ask for confirmation in additional populations and longer follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 102 patients, six months: the sleepiness outcome is patient-reported and unblinded, and a residual mean AHI of 20.8 is still moderate apnea — surgery reduced severity; it did not normalise breathing for the average patient.
cards.source: MacKay S et al. Effect of Multilevel Upper Airway Surgery vs Medical Management on the Apnea-Hypopnea Index and Patient-Reported Daytime Sleepiness Among Patients With Moderate or Severe Obstructive Sleep Apnea: The SAMS Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020;324(12):1168-1179. PMID: 32886102. Registry ID: ACTRN12614000338662 (Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry), stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: SKUP3 follow-up 2018: after modified UPPP in selected patients, AHI stayed down at 24 months (52.9 at baseline, 24.1 at two years) and sleepiness halved
cards.summary: SKUP3 follow-up 2018: after modified UPPP in selected patients, AHI stayed down at 24 months ( 52.9 → 24.1 ) and sleepiness halved — a follow-up report, labelled as such.
cards.type: Follow-up report (6 and 24 months) of a single-centre randomised trial cohort
cards.people: 65 patients with an apnea-hypopnea index ≥15, body mass index below 36, Epworth Sleepiness Scale ≥8 and Friedman stage I or II, who underwent modified uvulopalatopharyngoplasty including tonsillectomy after failing nonsurgical treatment; the parent SKUP3 trial randomised surgery against delayed surgery, and this report follows the operated cohort; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix. Dropout was 8% at six months and 20% at 24 months.
cards.result: The AHI decreased significantly from a mean (SD) of 52.9 (20.5) at baseline to 23.6 (20.2) after six months and 24.1 (20.9) after 24 months (P<0.001). Patients with tonsil size 2 and sizes 3 to 4 both had significant reductions in AHI at both follow-ups. The median Epworth Sleepiness Scale score decreased significantly from 13 (range 8–21) to 6.5 (1–18) after six months and 5 (2–17) after 24 months (P<0.001). Body-mass index remained unchanged, and there were significant modest correlations between the reductions in AHI and sleepiness after 24 months.
cards.watchOut: This record is the cohort follow-up of the randomised SKUP3 trial, not a randomised comparison at 24 months: the control group had crossed to surgery, one in five patients had dropped out by two years, and entry required favourable anatomy (Friedman stage I–II, BMI below 36), so the sustained halving of AHI applies to selected patients.

shelves.title: Shorter all-oral regimens for rifampin-resistant tuberculosis (TB-PRACTECAL)
shelves.question: Does a 24-week all-oral BPaL-based regimen beat the long standard of care for rifampin-resistant TB on efficacy and safety?
shelves.mesh: Antitubercular Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Moxifloxacin/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Rifampin/adverse effects,pharmacology · Tuberculosis, Multidrug-Resistant/drug therapy · Tuberculosis, Pulmonary/drug therapy · Linezolid/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: TB-PRACTECAL's stage-2 comparison found a 24-week all-oral BPaLM regimen (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin) noninferior to a 9-to-20-month standard of care — and on the modified intention-to-treat numbers, far fewer unfavourable outcomes (11% vs 48%; risk difference −37 percentage points) — with fewer grade 3-or-higher or serious adverse events (19% vs 59%). But recruitment was terminated early, the evaluable populations shrink fast across analyses (301 enrolled in stage 2; 128 in the modified intention-to-treat set; the per-protocol difference was −9 points), and the trial was open-label — one trial, so POSSIBLE. STREAM supplies the supporting arc: an earlier 9-to-11-month regimen was noninferior to the 20-month standard (favourable status 78.8% vs 79.8%), showing 'shorter' itself was sound while its injectable-era regimen has been superseded by the all-oral one. Drug-susceptible TB is Shelf #319 and latent TB Shelf #509; neither is re-carded here.

cards.headline: TB-PRACTECAL 2022: 24-week all-oral BPaLM was noninferior to 9–20-month standard care — unfavourable outcomes 11% vs 48% (modified ITT) — with fewer severe adverse events (19% vs 59%)
cards.summary: TB-PRACTECAL 2022: 24-week all-oral BPaLM was noninferior to 9–20-month standard care — unfavourable outcomes 11% vs 48% (modified ITT) — with fewer severe adverse events.
cards.type: Open-label, phase 2–3, multicentre, randomised, controlled noninferiority trial; recruitment terminated early
cards.people: Patients aged 15 or older with rifampin-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis in Belarus, South Africa and Uzbekistan; in stage 2, 301 patients entered the BPaLM (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin for 24 weeks) vs standard-care comparison, of whom 145 were evaluable intention-to-treat, 128 modified intention-to-treat and 90 per-protocol. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The primary outcome — an unfavourable status (death, treatment failure, discontinuation, loss to follow-up, or TB recurrence) at 72 weeks — occurred in the modified intention-to-treat analysis in 11% on BPaLM vs 48% on standard care (risk difference −37 percentage points, 96.6% CI −53 to −22), and in the per-protocol analysis in 4% vs 12% (risk difference −9 points, −22 to 4); the noninferiority margin was 12 points. In the as-treated population, grade 3-or-higher or serious adverse events occurred in 19% on BPaLM vs 59% on standard care.
cards.watchOut: Recruitment was terminated early and the analysis populations contract sharply (301 → 128 → 90): the spectacular −37-point modified-ITT difference leans on how unfavourable status (including discontinuation and loss to follow-up) accumulates over a 9–20-month comparator, and an open-label design can move exactly those components. The per-protocol figure (−9 points) is the soberer read.
cards.source: Nyang'wa BT et al. A 24-Week, All-Oral Regimen for Rifampin-Resistant Tuberculosis. N Engl J Med. 2022;387(25):2331-2343. PMID: 36546625. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02589782, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: STREAM 2019: a 9–11-month regimen was noninferior to the 20-month standard — favourable status 78.8% vs 79.8%; deaths 8.5% vs 6.4%
cards.summary: STREAM 2019: a 9–11-month regimen was noninferior to the 20-month standard — favourable status 78.8% vs 79.8%; deaths 8.5% vs 6.4% printed on the card.
cards.type: Phase 3 noninferiority trial (2:1 randomisation)
cards.people: 424 participants with rifampin-resistant tuberculosis susceptible to fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides, randomised to a short regimen (9 to 11 months, including high-dose moxifloxacin) or the 20-month regimen following the 2011 WHO guidelines; 383 in the modified intention-to-treat population and 321 per-protocol. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: A favourable status at 132 weeks (cultures negative at 132 weeks and previously, with no intervening positive culture or prior unfavourable outcome) was reported in 78.8% of the short-regimen group and 79.8% of the long-regimen group (adjusted difference 1.0 percentage point, 95% CI −7.5 to 9.5; P=0.02 for noninferiority at a 10-point margin), consistent per-protocol (adjusted difference −0.7 points, −10.5 to 9.1). Grade 3-or-higher adverse events occurred in 48.2% (short) vs 45.4% (long). QT or corrected-QT prolongation to 500 ms occurred in 11.0% vs 6.4% (P=0.14). Death occurred in 8.5% vs 6.4%, and acquired resistance to fluoroquinolones or aminoglycosides in 3.3% vs 2.3% — the mortality figures printed beside the efficacy figures, as this library requires.
cards.watchOut: STREAM's short regimen still contained an injectable aminoglycoside era's drugs and required fluoroquinolone/aminoglycoside susceptibility — it proves the shorter principle, not the current regimen; its death and QT figures lean, if anything, against the short arm.

cards.headline: Synthesis: six months, all oral, beats a year and a half of the old standard on tolerability — POSSIBLE on one early-stopped trial
cards.summary: Six months, all oral, beats a year and a half of the old standard on tolerability — POSSIBLE on one early-stopped trial.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: TB-PRACTECAL stage 2 (301 patients) and STREAM (424 randomised).
cards.result: Read together: shortening works (STREAM: 9–11 months noninferior to 20), and going all-oral works better (TB-PRACTECAL: unfavourable outcomes 11% vs 48% modified-ITT, severe adverse events 19% vs 59%, per-protocol difference a quieter −9 points). The direction is consistent and the human stakes of the old regimens (injections, deafness-era toxicities, 20 months of adherence) are not in dispute; the precision is. One early-terminated, open-label pivotal trial is why the stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY.

shelves.title: Baloxavir for influenza: one dose against the virus and the oseltamivir benchmark
shelves.question: Does single-dose baloxavir shorten influenza illness versus placebo — and versus oseltamivir — in healthy and high-risk outpatients (CAPSTONE-1/-2)?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Dibenzothiepins · Endonucleases/antagonists & inhibitors · Influenza, Human/drug therapy,virology · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Morpholines
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for symptom shortening vs placebo; not for superiority over oseltamivir): CAPSTONE-1 (1,064 infected patients in its phase 3 intention-to-treat-infected population) found single-dose baloxavir shortened time to symptom alleviation vs placebo (median 53.7 vs 80.2 hours; P<0.001), with a similar time to alleviation as oseltamivir and a greater day-1 viral-load reduction than either comparator. CAPSTONE-2, in high-risk outpatients, repeated the placebo result (median time to improvement 73.2 vs 102.3 hours, difference 29.1 hours) and again did not separate from oseltamivir (73.2 vs 81.0 hours, difference 7.7 hours with an interval crossing zero). The counterweight sits on CAPSTONE-1's own card: viral variants with reduced baloxavir susceptibility emerged in 9.7% of phase 3 baloxavir recipients. Oseltamivir's own treatment/prevention evidence is Shelf #583 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: CAPSTONE-1 2018: single-dose baloxavir beat placebo on time to symptom alleviation (53.7 vs 80.2 hours) and matched oseltamivir — but reduced-susceptibility variants emerged in 9.7% of recipients
cards.summary: CAPSTONE-1 2018: single-dose baloxavir beat placebo on time to symptom alleviation (53.7 vs 80.2 hours) and matched oseltamivir — with a reduced-susceptibility asterisk.
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, controlled trials (a phase 2 dose-ranging placebo-controlled trial, then a phase 3 placebo- and oseltamivir-controlled trial)
cards.people: Otherwise healthy outpatients with acute uncomplicated influenza; the phase 3 intention-to-treat-infected population was 1,064 patients aged 12 to 64 years treated in the 2016–2017 season with single weight-based baloxavir doses (40 or 80 mg), placebo, or oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days; 84.8–88.1% in each group had influenza A(H3N2). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The median time to alleviation of symptoms was 53.7 hours (95% CI 49.5 to 58.5) with baloxavir vs 80.2 hours (72.6 to 87.1) with placebo (P<0.001); in the phase 2 trial the median time was 23.4 to 28.2 hours shorter on baloxavir than placebo (P<0.05). Time to alleviation was similar with baloxavir and oseltamivir, while baloxavir produced greater viral-load reductions 1 day after dosing than placebo or oseltamivir. Adverse events were reported in 20.7% (baloxavir), 24.6% (placebo) and 24.8% (oseltamivir). Polymerase acidic protein variants with I38T/M/F substitutions conferring reduced susceptibility to baloxavir emerged in 2.2% (phase 2) and 9.7% (phase 3) of baloxavir recipients.
cards.watchOut: A symptom-hours endpoint in uncomplicated influenza in healthy outpatients — no hospitalisation or mortality outcome — and a resistance-emergence rate (nearly 1 in 10) that is the real long-term cost of a single-dose, single-target drug used widely.
cards.source: Hayden FG et al. Baloxavir Marboxil for Uncomplicated Influenza in Adults and Adolescents. N Engl J Med. 2018;379(10):913-923. PMID: 30184455. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02954354 (with JapicCTI 153090 for the phase 2 trial), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: CAPSTONE-2 2020: in high-risk outpatients, baloxavir again beat placebo (73.2 vs 102.3 hours to improvement) and again did not separate from oseltamivir (81.0 hours)
cards.summary: CAPSTONE-2 2020: in high-risk outpatients, baloxavir again beat placebo (73.2 vs 102.3 hours to improvement) and again did not separate from oseltamivir.
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled and oseltamivir-controlled phase 3 trial
cards.people: 2,184 outpatients aged 12 or older at 551 sites in 17 countries and territories, with influenza-like illness of less than 48 hours and at least one risk factor for influenza complications, randomised to single-dose baloxavir (730), placebo (729) or oseltamivir (725); the modified intention-to-treat population with RT-PCR-confirmed influenza was 1,163 (388 baloxavir, 386 placebo, 389 oseltamivir), of whom 48% had influenza A H3N2 and 42% influenza B. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The median time to improvement of influenza symptoms was 73.2 hours (95% CI 67.2 to 85.1) on baloxavir vs 102.3 hours (92.7 to 113.1) on placebo (difference 29.1 hours, 14.6 to 42.8; P<0.0001) and 81.0 hours (69.4 to 91.5) on oseltamivir (difference from baloxavir 7.7 hours, −7.9 to 22.7 — an interval including no difference). Adverse events were reported in 183 of 730 baloxavir patients (25%), 216 of 727 placebo patients (30%) and 202 of 721 oseltamivir patients (28%).
cards.watchOut: 'High-risk' here means outpatients with risk factors and symptoms under 48 hours — not hospitalised or severe influenza, for which neither CAPSTONE trial provides evidence; nearly half the randomised patients had no PCR-confirmed influenza and left the primary population.

cards.summary: One dose buys about a day of symptoms vs placebo, nothing proven over oseltamivir — LIKELY.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: CAPSTONE-1 (1,064 infected phase 3 patients; healthy outpatients) and CAPSTONE-2 (1,163 confirmed-influenza patients; high-risk outpatients).
cards.result: Two trials, two populations, the same shape: baloxavir shortens illness by roughly 26–29 hours against placebo (80.2→53.7 and 102.3→73.2 median hours), matches oseltamivir on symptoms in both, and clears virus faster on day 1. shelves.title: Molnupiravir for community COVID-19: two trials, two populations (PANORAMIC, MOVe-OUT)
shelves.question: Does molnupiravir help in COVID-19 — in unvaccinated high-risk adults (MOVe-OUT) and in a largely vaccinated community population (PANORAMIC)?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Antiviral Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · COVID-19/virology · Cytidine/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Hydroxylamines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · SARS-CoV-2/isolation & purification · Viral Load
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — unvaccinated high-risk adults (MOVe-OUT era) · LIKELY — no benefit in a largely vaccinated community population (PANORAMIC) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate: hospitalisation-or-death composite). MOVe-OUT (1,433 unvaccinated at-risk adults, 2021 era) found hospitalisation or death by day 29 in 6.8% on molnupiravir vs 9.7% on placebo (difference −3.0 percentage points; 1 vs 9 deaths), the effect larger at the planned interim analysis (7.3% vs 14.1%) than in the full cohort — a single trial whose own numbers softened as it completed, hence POSSIBLE. PANORAMIC (25,054 in the primary analysis, 94% with at least three vaccine doses) found hospitalisation or death in 1% vs 1% (adjusted odds ratio 1.06, 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.81 to 1.41) — a very large null that carries LIKELY for the population actually now treated. The discordance is the shelf: same drug, different immunity, different answer. Nirmatrelvir–ritonavir is Shelf #580 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: MOVe-OUT 2022: in unvaccinated at-risk adults, hospitalisation or death by day 29 was 6.8% vs 9.7% — with the interim analysis stronger (7.3% vs 14.1%) than the full result
cards.summary: MOVe-OUT 2022: in unvaccinated at-risk adults, hospitalisation or death by day 29 was 6.8% vs 9.7% — with the interim analysis stronger (7.3% vs 14.1%). (Tier C — hospitalisation-or-death composite; PROPOSED.)
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (planned interim analysis at 50% follow-up)
cards.people: 1,433 nonhospitalised, unvaccinated adults with mild-to-moderate laboratory-confirmed COVID-19, symptom onset within 5 days, and at least one risk factor for severe illness, randomised to molnupiravir 800 mg twice daily for 5 days (716) or placebo (717). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Hospitalisation for any cause or death through day 29 occurred in 48 of 709 molnupiravir participants (6.8%) vs 68 of 699 on placebo (9.7%) (difference −3.0 percentage points, 95% CI −5.9 to −0.1). At the planned interim analysis the difference had been larger: 28 of 385 (7.3%) vs 53 of 377 (14.1%) (difference −6.8 points, −11.3 to −2.4; P=0.001). Deaths through day 29: 1 on molnupiravir and 9 on placebo. In some subgroups (previous SARS-CoV-2 infection, low baseline viral load, diabetes) the point estimate favoured placebo. Adverse events occurred in 216 of 710 (30.4%) vs 231 of 701 (33.0%).
cards.watchOut: A single trial, stopped into its own success: superiority was declared at the interim look, and the completed cohort's effect (−3.0 points) is less than half the interim's (−6.8) — the standard early-stop inflation pattern, in a pre-vaccination, pre-Omicron-era risk landscape that no longer exists.
cards.source: Jayk Bernal A et al. Molnupiravir for Oral Treatment of Covid-19 in Nonhospitalized Patients. N Engl J Med. 2022;386(6):509-520. PMID: 34914868. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04575597, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PANORAMIC 2023: in a largely vaccinated community population, hospitalisation or death was 1% vs 1% — adjusted odds ratio 1.06, no benefit
cards.summary: PANORAMIC 2023: in a largely vaccinated community population, hospitalisation or death was 1% vs 1% — adjusted odds ratio 1.06, no benefit. (PANORAMIC is in The Lancet; its registry ID is sourced from its abstract.)
cards.type: UK national, multicentre, open-label, platform-adaptive randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 26,411 participants randomised (12,821 to molnupiravir plus usual care, 12,962 to usual care alone, 628 to other platform groups); the primary analysis population held 12,529 and 12,525 respectively. Participants were 50 or older, or 18 or older with relevant comorbidities, unwell with confirmed COVID-19 for 5 days or fewer in the community; mean age 56.6 years (SD 12.6); 24,290 of 25,708 (94%) had received at least three vaccine doses.
cards.result: Hospitalisation or death within 28 days occurred in 105 of 12,529 (1%) on molnupiravir plus usual care vs 98 of 12,525 (1%) on usual care alone (adjusted odds ratio 1.06, 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.81 to 1.41; probability of superiority 0.33), with no treatment interaction in subgroups. Serious adverse events were recorded in 50 of 12,774 (0.4%) vs 45 of 12,934 (0.3%), none judged related to molnupiravir.
cards.watchOut: Open-label — but the endpoint (hospitalisation or death) is the kind least movable by expectation, the event rates were low because vaccination had already done the heavy lifting, and an odds ratio of 1.06 in 25,000 patients excludes any large hidden benefit in this population.
cards.source: Butler CC et al. shelves.title: Antifibrotics for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: nintedanib and pirfenidone
shelves.question: Do nintedanib (INPULSIS-1/-2) and pirfenidone (ASCEND) slow the decline in lung function in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis versus placebo — and what do they cost in gastrointestinal harm?
shelves.mesh: Disease Progression · Enzyme Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis/drug therapy,physiopathology · Indoles/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Protein-Tyrosine Kinases/antagonists & inhibitors · Vital Capacity/drug effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two independent antifibrotic programmes, each placebo-controlled and replicated, slow lung-function decline in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Nintedanib cut the annual forced vital capacity (FVC) decline by 125.3 ml in INPULSIS-1 and 93.7 ml in INPULSIS-2; pirfenidone produced a 47.9% relative reduction in the proportion with a 10-point FVC decline or death in ASCEND. The price is gastrointestinal harm: diarrhoea in about 62% on nintedanib versus about 19% on placebo, and more gastrointestinal and skin events on pirfenidone. This shelf claims slowed decline only — ASCEND itself found no significant difference in death from any cause (P=0.10), and no mortality claim is made here.

cards.headline: INPULSIS 2014: nintedanib slowed FVC decline by 125.3 ml/year in INPULSIS-1 and 93.7 ml/year in INPULSIS-2 versus placebo
cards.summary: INPULSIS-1/-2 (2014): nintedanib slowed FVC decline — differences of 125.3 and 93.7 ml/year versus placebo.
cards.type: Two replicate 52-week, randomised, double-blind, phase 3 trials (INPULSIS-1 and INPULSIS-2) reported in one paper
cards.people: 1066 patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis randomly assigned in a 3:2 ratio to nintedanib 150 mg twice daily or placebo for 52 weeks across the two trials. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The adjusted annual rate of change in FVC was -114.7 ml with nintedanib versus -239.9 ml with placebo in INPULSIS-1 (difference 125.3 ml, 95% CI 77.7 to 172.8; P<0.001) and -113.6 ml versus -207.3 ml in INPULSIS-2 (difference 93.7 ml, 44.8 to 142.7; P<0.001). Time to first acute exacerbation did not differ in INPULSIS-1 (hazard ratio 1.15, 0.54 to 2.42; P=0.67) but favoured nintedanib in INPULSIS-2 (hazard ratio 0.38, 0.19 to 0.77; P=0.005) — a relative measure, discordant between the twin trials. Diarrhoea rates were 61.5% (nintedanib) versus 18.6% (placebo) in INPULSIS-1 and 63.2% versus 18.3% in INPULSIS-2; diarrhoea led to discontinuation in less than 5% of patients.
cards.watchOut: The exacerbation signal is inconsistent between the two replicate trials (hazard ratios 1.15 and 0.38), so the shelf rests on the FVC endpoint, which was consistent; FVC decline is a lung-function measure, not a survival outcome.
