cards.headline: ASCEND 2014: pirfenidone gave a 47.9% relative reduction in 10-point FVC decline or death at 52 weeks versus placebo
cards.summary: ASCEND (2014): pirfenidone gave a 47.9% relative reduction in 10-point FVC decline or death at 52 weeks (absolute proportions not printed in the abstract).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial
cards.people: 555 patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis randomly assigned to oral pirfenidone 2403 mg per day or placebo for 52 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, pirfenidone produced a relative reduction of 47.9% in the proportion of patients with an absolute decline of 10 percentage points or more in percent predicted FVC or who died, and a relative increase of 132.5% in the proportion with no decline in FVC (P<0.001 for the primary comparison) — both relative measures as reported in the abstract, which does not print the underlying absolute proportions. Pirfenidone reduced the decline in 6-minute walk distance (P=0.04) and improved progression-free survival (P<0.001). There was no significant difference in dyspnoea scores (P=0.16) or in death from any cause (P=0.10) or from idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (P=0.23) within ASCEND itself; a prespecified pooled analysis with two earlier phase 3 trials did favour pirfenidone for death from any cause (P=0.01). Gastrointestinal and skin-related adverse events were more common with pirfenidone but rarely led to discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: The headline 47.9% is a relative figure whose absolute proportions the abstract does not state, and the mortality signal comes only from pooling with earlier trials — one of which had missed its own FVC endpoint — so it is reported here as background, never as this shelf's claim.
cards.source: King TE Jr et al. A phase 3 trial of pirfenidone in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. N Engl J Med. 2014;370(22):2083-2092. PMID: 24836312. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01366209, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two drugs, three placebo-controlled trials, one consistent finding — antifibrotics slow FVC decline at a gastrointestinal price — LIKELY
cards.summary: Two drugs, three placebo-controlled trials, one consistent finding — antifibrotics slow FVC decline at a gastrointestinal price — LIKELY.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: INPULSIS-1/-2 (1066 patients, nintedanib) and ASCEND (555 patients, pirfenidone), all 52-week placebo-controlled trials in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
cards.result: Both programmes met their lung-function endpoints in every pivotal trial carded: FVC decline roughly halved on nintedanib (differences of 125.3 and 93.7 ml/year) and the categorical FVC-decline-or-death endpoint relatively reduced by 47.9% on pirfenidone. Harms are dominated by gastrointestinal effects (nintedanib diarrhoea about 62% versus about 19%). Neither drug is carded here as prolonging life: ASCEND's own mortality comparisons were non-significant. Nintedanib for systemic-sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease is a different question, drafted separately (Shelf #688), and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the ASCEND pooled mortality analysis as proof either drug prolongs survival; this shelf's claim is slowed decline in lung function.

shelves.title: CFTR modulators in cystic fibrosis: ivacaftor and the triple combination
shelves.question: Does ivacaftor improve lung function in G551D cystic fibrosis (STRIVE) — and does elexacaftor–tezacaftor–ivacaftor do the same for people with a single Phe508del allele?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aminophenols/adverse effects,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Cystic Fibrosis/drug therapy,genetics,physiopathology · Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator/genetics,metabolism · Drug Synergism · Forced Expiratory Volume/drug effects · Mutation
shelves.balance: LIKELY: In genotype-defined cystic fibrosis, CFTR modulation produces large, concordant lung-function gains in two placebo-controlled trials of different regimens. Ivacaftor improved percent predicted FEV1 by 10.6 percentage points versus placebo in G551D disease (STRIVE), and elexacaftor–tezacaftor–ivacaftor improved it by 13.8 points at week 4 and 14.3 points through week 24 in Phe508del–minimal-function disease (Middleton 2019), with exacerbation rates relatively lower by 55% and 63% respectively. The claims are genotype-specific: each trial covers only the population it enrolled.

cards.headline: STRIVE 2011: ivacaftor improved percent predicted FEV1 by 10.6 percentage points versus placebo in G551D cystic fibrosis
cards.summary: STRIVE (2011): ivacaftor improved percent predicted FEV1 by 10.6 percentage points versus placebo in G551D cystic fibrosis.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (48 weeks)
cards.people: 167 subjects aged 12 years or older with cystic fibrosis and at least one G551D-CFTR mutation, randomly assigned to ivacaftor 150 mg every 12 hours (84 assigned, 83 dosed) or placebo (83 assigned, 78 dosed). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The change from baseline through week 24 in percent predicted FEV1 was 10.6 percentage points greater with ivacaftor than placebo (P<0.001), noted by 2 weeks and maintained through week 48. Through week 48, subjects on ivacaftor were 55% less likely to have a pulmonary exacerbation than those on placebo (P<0.001) — a relative measure; the abstract does not print the absolute exacerbation rates. Respiratory-symptom scores were 8.6 points higher with ivacaftor (P<0.001), weight gain was 2.7 kg greater (P<0.001), and sweat chloride fell by 48.1 mmol per liter versus placebo (P<0.001). Serious adverse events were less frequent with ivacaftor than placebo (24% vs 42%).
cards.watchOut: A single-genotype trial (G551D, a small minority of cystic fibrosis): the result does not transfer to other genotypes, which is why the triple-therapy trial below enrolled a different population.
cards.source: Ramsey BW et al. A CFTR potentiator in patients with cystic fibrosis and the G551D mutation. N Engl J Med. 2011;365(18):1663-1672. PMID: 22047557. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00909532, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: CFTR modulation works where the genotype matches the drug — LIKELY, genotype by genotype
cards.summary: CFTR modulation works where the genotype matches the drug — LIKELY, genotype by genotype.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: STRIVE (167 subjects, G551D, ivacaftor, 48 weeks) and Middleton 2019 (403 patients, Phe508del–minimal function, triple therapy, 24 weeks).

shelves.title: Dupilumab for COPD with type 2 inflammation
shelves.question: In COPD with blood-eosinophil evidence of type 2 inflammation, does dupilumab reduce exacerbations versus placebo on top of inhaled triple therapy?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Eosinophils/immunology · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/drug therapy,immunology · Inflammation/classification,immunology · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use,adverse effects · Forced Expiratory Volume/drug effects · Inflammation/blood,drug therapy,etiology,immunology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two replicate phase 3 trials (BOREAS, 939 patients; NOTUS, 935 patients) in COPD with blood eosinophils of at least 300 per microliter on inhaled triple therapy found dupilumab reduced the annualised rate of moderate or severe exacerbations — rate ratios 0.70 (0.78 vs 1.10 per year) and 0.66 (0.86 vs 1.30 per year) — with FEV1 gains of about 82–83 ml at week 12. Both rate ratios sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid on a single trial; the stamp rests on two concordant blinded trials with absolute rates printed, not on either ratio alone. The population is biomarker-selected: nothing here applies to COPD without type 2 inflammation.

cards.headline: BOREAS 2023: dupilumab cut the annualised exacerbation rate to 0.78 versus 1.10 per year in eosinophilic COPD (rate ratio 0.70)
cards.summary: BOREAS (2023): dupilumab cut the annualised exacerbation rate to 0.78 vs 1.10 per year (rate ratio 0.70) in eosinophilic COPD.
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (52 weeks)
cards.people: 939 patients with COPD, a blood eosinophil count of at least 300 per microliter and elevated exacerbation risk despite standard triple therapy, randomised to dupilumab 300 mg (468) or placebo (471) subcutaneously every 2 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The annualised rate of moderate or severe exacerbations was 0.78 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.93) with dupilumab and 1.10 (0.93 to 1.30) with placebo (rate ratio 0.70, 0.58 to 0.86; P<0.001) — a relative measure, printed with its absolute rates; the ratio sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band. Prebronchodilator FEV1 rose by 160 ml versus 77 ml at week 12 (difference 83 ml; P<0.001), sustained through week 52. At week 52 the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire score improved by -9.7 versus -6.4 (difference -3.4; P=0.002). Adverse events leading to discontinuation, serious adverse events and adverse events leading to death were balanced between groups.
cards.watchOut: Biomarker-selected population (eosinophils at least 300 per microliter) already on triple therapy: the result does not extend to non-eosinophilic COPD, and the relative effect is modest in size.

shelves.question: Do mepolizumab (MENSA) and benralizumab (SIROCCO) reduce exacerbations in severe eosinophilic asthma versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Asthma/drug therapy,immunology,physiopathology · Drug Therapy, Combination · Eosinophilia · Forced Expiratory Volume
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two anti-IL-5-pathway antibodies each cut exacerbations in severe eosinophilic asthma in placebo-controlled trials. Mepolizumab reduced the exacerbation rate by 47% (intravenous) and 53% (subcutaneous) relative to placebo in MENSA; benralizumab reduced the annual exacerbation rate in SIROCCO with rate ratios of 0.55 (every 4 weeks) and 0.49 (every 8 weeks) in patients with eosinophils of at least 300 cells per microliter. Most of these relative measures sit inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band (the 0.49 ratio just crosses it); the stamp rests on two concordant blinded programmes, not on any single ratio. Tezepelumab, the other severe-asthma biologic in this library, is home on Shelf #309 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: MENSA 2014: mepolizumab reduced exacerbations by 47% (intravenous) and 53% (subcutaneous) relative to placebo in severe eosinophilic asthma
cards.summary: MENSA (2014): mepolizumab reduced exacerbations by 47% (intravenous) and 53% (subcutaneous) relative to placebo (absolute rates not printed in the abstract).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy trial (32 weeks)
cards.people: 576 patients with recurrent asthma exacerbations and evidence of eosinophilic inflammation despite high-dose inhaled glucocorticoids, assigned to intravenous mepolizumab 75 mg, subcutaneous mepolizumab 100 mg, or placebo every 4 weeks for 32 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The rate of exacerbations was reduced by 47% (95% CI 29 to 61) with intravenous mepolizumab and by 53% (37 to 65) with subcutaneous mepolizumab versus placebo (P<0.001 for both) — relative reductions; the abstract does not print the absolute exacerbation rates, and both figures sit inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band when expressed as ratios. Exacerbations needing an emergency department visit or hospitalisation were reduced by 32% (intravenous) and 61% (subcutaneous), also relative. At week 32, FEV1 rose by 100 ml (intravenous, P=0.02) and 98 ml (subcutaneous, P=0.03) more than placebo; St George's Respiratory Questionnaire improvement exceeded placebo by 6.4 and 7.0 points (minimal clinically important change 4 points). The safety profile was similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: A 32-week trial reporting relative reductions without absolute rates in its abstract: the absolute benefit depends on the patient's baseline exacerbation rate, which was high by design in this selected population.
cards.source: Ortega HG et al. Mepolizumab treatment in patients with severe eosinophilic asthma. N Engl J Med. 2014;371(13):1198-1207. PMID: 25199059. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01691521, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: SIROCCO 2016: benralizumab reduced the annual exacerbation rate versus placebo (rate ratios 0.55 every 4 weeks, 0.49 every 8 weeks) in high-eosinophil severe asthma
cards.summary: SIROCCO (2016): benralizumab reduced the annual exacerbation rate versus placebo (rate ratios 0.55 every 4 weeks, 0.49 every 8 weeks ) in high-eosinophil asthma.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (48 weeks)
cards.people: 1205 patients aged 12–75 years with severe asthma uncontrolled on high-dosage inhaled corticosteroids plus long-acting beta2-agonists, with at least two exacerbations in the previous year, at 374 sites in 17 countries, randomised to benralizumab 30 mg every 4 weeks (400), every 8 weeks (398), or placebo (407); the primary analysis population (eosinophils at least 300 cells per microliter) numbered 267 (placebo), 275 (every 4 weeks) and 267 (every 8 weeks). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: In the high-eosinophil population, benralizumab reduced the annual exacerbation rate over 48 weeks versus placebo (rate ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.71 with every-4-week dosing; 0.49, 0.37 to 0.64 with every-8-week dosing; p<0.0001 for both) — relative measures; the 0.49 ratio reaches the 0.5 threshold this library treats as solid, the 0.55 ratio sits just inside the caution band. Prebronchodilator FEV1 improved versus placebo (least-squares mean change 0.106 L every 4 weeks and 0.159 L every 8 weeks). Asthma symptoms improved with the every-8-week regimen (difference -0.25) but not the every-4-week regimen (-0.08). The most common adverse events were worsening asthma (13% benralizumab vs 19% placebo) and nasopharyngitis (12% vs 12%).
cards.watchOut: The headline efficacy population is the eosinophil-at-least-300 stratum; patients below that count were randomised but are not the population the primary result describes.
cards.source: Bleecker ER et al. shelves.title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension: macitentan and selexipag on morbidity and mortality
shelves.question: Do macitentan (SERAPHIN) and selexipag (GRIPHON) reduce the composite of death and pulmonary-hypertension complications versus placebo, on top of background therapy?
shelves.mesh: Endothelin A Receptor Antagonists · Endothelin B Receptor Antagonists · Exercise Tolerance · Familial Primary Pulmonary Hypertension · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Hypertension, Pulmonary/complications,drug therapy,mortality · Kaplan-Meier Estimate
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: both primary endpoints are morbidity/mortality composites with a death component). Two event-driven placebo-controlled trials found fewer composite events: SERAPHIN's primary endpoint occurred in 31.4% on macitentan 10 mg and 38.0% on 3 mg versus 46.4% on placebo (hazard ratios 0.55 and 0.70, relative measures), and GRIPHON's in 27.0% on selexipag versus 41.6% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.60). The composites were driven by worsening/progression and hospitalisation, not by death: GRIPHON found no significant mortality difference (100 deaths on selexipag vs 105 on placebo by study end), and no standalone mortality claim is made on this shelf.

cards.headline: SERAPHIN 2013: macitentan cut the morbidity/mortality composite to 31.4% (10 mg) and 38.0% (3 mg) versus 46.4% on placebo
cards.summary: SERAPHIN (2013): macitentan cut the morbidity/mortality composite to 31.4% (10 mg) and 38.0% (3 mg) vs 46.4% on placebo (death component not separately reported).
cards.type: Event-driven, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: 742 patients with symptomatic pulmonary arterial hypertension randomly assigned to placebo (250), macitentan 3 mg once daily (250), or macitentan 10 mg once daily (242); stable oral or inhaled pulmonary-arterial-hypertension therapy other than endothelin-receptor antagonists was allowed. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary composite endpoint (death, atrial septostomy, lung transplantation, initiation of intravenous or subcutaneous prostanoids, or worsening of pulmonary arterial hypertension) occurred in 46.4% on placebo, 38.0% on macitentan 3 mg and 31.4% on macitentan 10 mg. Hazard ratios versus placebo were 0.70 (97.5% CI 0.52 to 0.96; P=0.01) for 3 mg and 0.55 (0.39 to 0.76; P<0.001) for 10 mg — relative measures with the absolute event rates printed above; both sit inside or near the 0.5–2.0 caution band. Worsening of pulmonary arterial hypertension was the most frequent primary-endpoint event, so the composite benefit is not a demonstrated mortality benefit. Adverse events more frequent with macitentan were headache, nasopharyngitis and anaemia.
cards.watchOut: Tier C shelf: the endpoint is a composite whose commonest component is disease worsening; the abstract does not report the death component separately, so no mortality figure is carded.
cards.source: Pulido T et al. Macitentan and morbidity and mortality in pulmonary arterial hypertension. N Engl J Med. 2013;369(9):809-818. PMID: 23984728. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00660179, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: GRIPHON 2015: selexipag cut the death-or-complication composite to 27.0% versus 41.6% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.60), with no mortality difference
cards.summary: GRIPHON (2015): selexipag cut the death-or-complication composite to 27.0% vs 41.6% (hazard ratio 0.60) — with no mortality difference (100 vs 105 deaths).
cards.type: Event-driven, phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: 1156 patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension randomly assigned to placebo or selexipag in individualised doses (maximum 1600 micrograms twice daily), either untreated or on a stable endothelin-receptor antagonist, a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor, or both. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A primary-endpoint event (death from any cause or a pulmonary-arterial-hypertension complication) occurred in 41.6% on placebo and 27.0% on selexipag (hazard ratio 0.60, 99% CI 0.46 to 0.78; P<0.001) — a relative measure with absolute rates printed; disease progression and hospitalisation accounted for 81.9% of events. There was no significant difference in mortality: 105 patients in the placebo group and 100 in the selexipag group had died from any cause by the end of the study. Premature discontinuation for adverse events was 14.3% on selexipag versus 7.1% on placebo; common adverse events were prostacyclin-type effects (headache, diarrhoea, nausea, jaw pain).
cards.watchOut: Tier C shelf: four-fifths of the composite was progression and hospitalisation, and the trial's own mortality comparison was null — the card leads with both facts so the composite is never read as a survival benefit.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two event-driven trials agree on fewer composite events, driven by progression and hospitalisation — mortality unproven — LIKELY, PROPOSED (Tier C)
cards.summary: Two event-driven trials agree on fewer composite events, driven by progression and hospitalisation — mortality unproven — LIKELY, Tier C.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: SERAPHIN (742 patients, macitentan) and GRIPHON (1156 patients, selexipag), both event-driven placebo-controlled trials in pulmonary arterial hypertension, largely on background therapy.
cards.result: Both trials reduced their morbidity/mortality composites by similar relative amounts (hazard ratios 0.55–0.70 and 0.60) with absolute differences of 8.4–15.0 and 14.6 percentage points respectively, and in both the events were dominated by worsening disease and hospitalisation rather than death; GRIPHON's mortality counts (100 vs 105 deaths) were essentially identical. shelves.title: Long-term macrolides to prevent bronchiectasis exacerbations
shelves.question: In non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, does long-term low-dose macrolide therapy (azithromycin in EMBRACE; erythromycin in BLESS) reduce exacerbations — and at what cost in resistance and cardiac effects?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Azithromycin/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Bronchiectasis/etiology,physiopathology,prevention & control · Cystic Fibrosis/complications · Drug Administration Schedule · Forced Expiratory Volume/drug effects · Secondary Prevention
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials of different macrolides in non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis both reduced exacerbations: azithromycin three times weekly for 6 months cut the exacerbation rate to 0.59 versus 1.57 per patient (rate ratio 0.38) in EMBRACE, and erythromycin twice daily for 12 months reduced protocol-defined exacerbations (incidence rate ratio 0.57; 1.29 vs 1.97 per patient per year) in BLESS. The resistance cost is measured, not hypothetical: BLESS found macrolide-resistant oropharyngeal streptococci rose by a median of 27.7% on erythromycin versus 0.04% on placebo. The 0.38 ratio is beyond the 0.5 solidity threshold; the 0.57 ratio sits inside the caution band, and the stamp rests on the pair.

cards.headline: EMBRACE 2012: azithromycin three times weekly halved the exacerbation rate — 0.59 versus 1.57 per patient over 6 months (rate ratio 0.38)
cards.summary: EMBRACE (2012): azithromycin three times weekly cut the exacerbation rate to 0.59 vs 1.57 per patient over 6 months (rate ratio 0.38).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (6 months)
cards.people: 141 patients aged 18 years or older with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis on high-resolution CT and at least one pulmonary exacerbation requiring antibiotics in the past year, at three centres in New Zealand, assigned to azithromycin 500 mg three times a week (71) or placebo (70). cards.result: The rate of event-based exacerbations in the 6-month treatment period was 0.59 per patient on azithromycin versus 1.57 on placebo (rate ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.54; p<0.0001) — a relative measure beyond the 0.5 solidity threshold, with absolute rates printed. Prebronchodilator FEV1 did not differ significantly between groups (difference 0.04 L, -0.03 to 0.12; p=0.251), nor did the change in St George's Respiratory Questionnaire total score (difference -3.25, -7.21 to 0.72; p=0.108).
cards.watchOut: Six months of treatment in 141 patients with at least one prior exacerbation: lung function and quality of life were both null, and the trial does not measure the resistance cost that BLESS (below) quantifies.

cards.headline: BLESS 2013: erythromycin for 12 months reduced exacerbations (1.29 vs 1.97 per patient per year; incidence rate ratio 0.57) — and raised macrolide resistance by a median 27.7%
cards.summary: BLESS (2013): erythromycin for 12 months reduced exacerbations ( 1.29 vs 1.97 per patient per year ; incidence rate ratio 0.57) — and raised macrolide resistance.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (12 months)
cards.people: 117 currently nonsmoking adults with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis and two or more infective exacerbations in the preceding year, in an Australian university teaching hospital and referral network, randomised to erythromycin ethylsuccinate 400 mg twice daily (59) or placebo (58); 107 (91.5%) completed. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Erythromycin reduced protocol-defined pulmonary exacerbations overall (mean 1.29 [95% CI 0.93 to 1.65] vs 1.97 [1.45 to 2.48] per patient per year; incidence rate ratio 0.57, 0.42 to 0.77; P=.003) — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, with absolute rates printed — and in the prespecified subgroup with baseline Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection (mean difference 1.32; P=.02). Erythromycin reduced 24-hour sputum production (median difference 4.3 g; P=.01) and attenuated lung-function decline (difference 2.2 percent predicted for postbronchodilator FEV1 change; P=.04). The cost: macrolide-resistant oropharyngeal streptococci increased by a median of 27.7% on erythromycin versus 0.04% on placebo (difference 25.5%; P<.001).
cards.watchOut: The resistance outcome is in commensal oropharyngeal streptococci over 12 months — a real ecological cost signal, but not a direct measure of resistant clinical infections; cardiac (QT) effects were not an outcome of this trial.

cards.summary: Macrolides prevent bronchiectasis exacerbations — LIKELY — with a measured resistance price.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: EMBRACE (141 patients, azithromycin, 6 months) and BLESS (117 patients, erythromycin, 12 months), both double-blind placebo-controlled trials in non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis with prior exacerbations.

cards.watchOut: Quote the resistance finding with the benefit: a year of macrolide prophylaxis buys fewer exacerbations with measurably more resistant commensal flora.

shelves.title: Pleural procedures: intrapleural tPA-DNase for infection, and indwelling catheter vs talc for malignant effusion
shelves.question: Does intrapleural tPA plus DNase improve drainage and cut referrals for surgery in pleural infection (MIST2) — and does an indwelling pleural catheter relieve breathlessness and cut hospital days as well as talc pleurodesis in malignant effusion (TIME2, AMPLE)?
shelves.mesh: Deoxyribonucleases/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Fibrinolytic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Instillation, Drug · Intention to Treat Analysis · Linear Models · Lung/diagnostic imaging · Pleural Diseases/diagnostic imaging,drug therapy,mortality
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — tPA-DNase for pleural infection · LIKELY — catheter equals talc on breathlessness with fewer hospital days. For pleural infection, one blinded factorial trial (MIST2, 210 patients) found combined tPA–DNase improved drainage, cut surgical referral (4% vs 16%) and shortened hospital stay by 6.7 days versus placebo, while either agent alone was ineffective and DNase alone increased surgical referral (39% vs 16%) — a single trial, so the benefit caps at POSSIBLE. For malignant effusion, two trials (TIME2, 106 patients; AMPLE, 146 patients) agree an indwelling pleural catheter relieves breathlessness as well as talc pleurodesis while reducing initial and total hospital days and repeat procedures, at the cost of more (mostly device-related) adverse events.

cards.people: 210 patients with pleural infection randomly assigned for 3 days to double placebo, intrapleural tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA) plus DNase, t-PA plus placebo, or DNase plus placebo (48–51 patients per arm in the reported comparisons). cards.result: Pleural opacity (percentage of hemithorax occupied by effusion) fell more with t-PA–DNase than placebo (-29.5±23.3% vs -17.2±19.6%; difference -7.9%, 95% CI -13.4 to -2.4; P=0.005); neither agent alone differed significantly from placebo. Surgical referral at 3 months was 2 of 48 (4%) with t-PA–DNase versus 8 of 51 (16%) with placebo (odds ratio 0.17, 0.03 to 0.87; P=0.03) — a relative measure beyond the 0.5 solidity threshold — but 18 of 46 (39%) with DNase alone (odds ratio 3.56, 1.30 to 9.75; P=0.01). Hospital stay was 6.7 days shorter with combined therapy versus placebo (P=0.006). Adverse-event frequency did not differ significantly among groups.
cards.watchOut: One factorial trial: the combination result and the DNase-alone harm signal come from the same 210 patients, and the surgical-referral cells are small (2 vs 8 events) — the reason this half of the shelf caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: TIME2 2012: indwelling catheter equalled talc on breathlessness over 42 days (difference 0.16 mm) with a 0-day versus 4-day initial stay
cards.summary: TIME2 (2012): indwelling catheter equalled talc on breathlessness over 42 days (difference 0.16 mm), with a 0-day vs 4-day initial stay.
cards.type: Unblinded randomised controlled trial (1 year follow-up)
cards.people: 106 patients with malignant pleural effusion and no previous pleurodesis, recruited at 7 UK hospitals, randomised to an indwelling pleural catheter inserted as an outpatient with home drainage, or inpatient chest tube with talc slurry pleurodesis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Dyspnoea improved in both groups with no significant difference over the first 42 days (mean visual analogue scale 24.7 mm catheter vs 24.4 mm talc; difference 0.16 mm, 95% CI -6.82 to 7.15; P=.96; minimum clinically significant difference 10 mm). At 6 months dyspnoea favoured the catheter (difference -14.0 mm; P=.01). Initial hospitalisation was shorter with the catheter (median 0 days [IQR 0–1] vs 4 days [2–6]; P<.001). Further pleural procedures were needed by 3 (6%) catheter patients versus 12 (22%) talc patients (odds ratio 0.21, 0.04 to 0.86; P=.03). Adverse events were more frequent with the catheter: 21 of 52 versus 7 of 54 patients (odds ratio 4.70, 1.75 to 12.60; P=.002). Quality of life did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded by necessity (a home catheter cannot be disguised), with a patient-reported primary outcome — expectation effects cannot be excluded, though the hospital-day and reintervention outcomes are objective and point the same way.

cards.headline: AMPLE 2017: catheter patients spent fewer days in hospital overall (median 10.0 vs 12.0 days) with no difference in breathlessness or quality of life
cards.summary: AMPLE (2017): catheter patients spent fewer days in hospital overall (median 10.0 vs 12.0 days ), with no difference in breathlessness or quality of life.
cards.type: Open-label, randomised clinical trial (12 months follow-up)
cards.people: 146 patients with symptomatic malignant pleural effusion and no prior catheter or pleurodesis, recruited at 9 centres in Australia, New Zealand, Singapore and Hong Kong, randomised to indwelling pleural catheter (74) or talc pleurodesis (72); median age 70.5 years; 56.2% male; 2 patients withdrew before intervention and were excluded.
cards.result: The catheter group spent fewer days in hospital from procedure to death or 12 months (median 10.0 [IQR 3–17] vs 12.0 [7–21] days; P=.03; Hodges-Lehmann difference 2.92 days, 95% CI 0.43 to 5.84), mainly in effusion-related days (median 1.0 vs 4.0 days; P<.001). Fewer catheter patients needed further ipsilateral invasive drainages (4.1% vs 22.5%; difference 18.4%, 7.7% to 29.2%). There were no significant differences in breathlessness improvement or quality of life. Adverse events occurred in 22 catheter patients (30 events) versus 13 pleurodesis patients (18 events). The authors note the magnitude of the hospital-day difference is of uncertain clinical importance.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the headline difference is a median of 2 days over a remaining lifespan — statistically real, clinically modest; the trial itself flags that uncertainty.

cards.headline: Synthesis: drain infected fluid with the combination, not either agent alone; for malignant effusion the catheter trades device events for hospital days — split stamp
cards.summary: Drain infected fluid with the combination, not either agent alone; for malignant effusion the catheter trades device events for hospital days — Split: POSSIBLE (tPA-DNase) · LIKELY (catheter vs talc).
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: MIST2 (210 patients, pleural infection) and TIME2 (106 patients) plus AMPLE (146 patients), both malignant-effusion trials of catheter versus talc.
cards.result: Two separate pleural questions share one shelf because they share a procedure room. Infection: only the tPA-plus-DNase combination beat placebo on drainage, surgical referral (4% vs 16%) and stay (-6.7 days); DNase alone was worse than placebo on referral (39% vs 16%) — combination or neither. Malignant effusion: breathlessness relief was equal in both trials, while catheters consistently cut hospital days (initial stay 0 vs 4 days in TIME2; total 10.0 vs 12.0 median days in AMPLE) and repeat procedures (6% vs 22%; 4.1% vs 22.5%), with more adverse events. The currency sweep's SCOPE trial (saline lavage versus intrapleural enzyme therapy in pleural infection) is fenced here as a newer comparator question, not carded: it does not replace MIST2's placebo-controlled factorial evidence.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the two halves: MIST2's patients had infection and a surgical-referral endpoint; TIME2/AMPLE's had malignancy and a palliative endpoint. Stamps differ for that reason.

shelves.title: Azithromycin prophylaxis for COPD exacerbations
shelves.question: Does daily azithromycin for a year prevent COPD exacerbations versus placebo — and does thrice-weekly azithromycin in frequent exacerbators (COLUMBUS) replicate it, at what hearing and resistance cost?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Azithromycin/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Bacterial Infections/prevention & control · Drug Resistance, Bacterial · Macrolides/therapeutic use · Nasopharynx/microbiology · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/drug therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials of different azithromycin schedules in exacerbation-prone COPD both reduced exacerbations: daily azithromycin for a year delayed the first exacerbation (median 266 vs 174 days) and cut the exacerbation frequency (1.48 vs 1.83 per patient-year; hazard ratio 0.73) in the Albert trial (1142 patients), and thrice-weekly azithromycin cut the adjusted exacerbation rate (rate ratio 0.58; unadjusted 1.94 vs 3.22 per patient per year) in COLUMBUS (92 frequent exacerbators). Both relative measures sit inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band; the stamp rests on two concordant trials with absolute rates printed. The measured cost in the larger trial was hearing decrements (25% vs 20%); the resistance cost of a year of macrolide is quantified on the bronchiectasis shelf (#815), not in these COPD trials.

cards.headline: Albert 2011: daily azithromycin for a year delayed the first COPD exacerbation (median 266 vs 174 days) and cut frequency to 1.48 versus 1.83 per patient-year
cards.summary: Albert (2011): daily azithromycin for a year delayed the first COPD exacerbation (median 266 vs 174 days ) and cut frequency to 1.48 vs 1.83 per patient-year.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (1 year)
cards.people: 1142 participants with COPD at increased exacerbation risk, but without hearing impairment, resting tachycardia or apparent risk of QT prolongation, randomly assigned to azithromycin 250 mg daily (570) or placebo (572) in addition to usual care; 1-year follow-up was 89% and 90% respectively. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Median time to first exacerbation was 266 days (95% CI 227 to 313) on azithromycin versus 174 days (143 to 215) on placebo (P<0.001). Exacerbation frequency was 1.48 versus 1.83 per patient-year (P=0.01), with a hazard ratio for an exacerbation of 0.73 (0.63 to 0.84; P<0.001) — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, printed with its absolute rates. St George's Respiratory Questionnaire scores improved more on azithromycin (mean decrease 2.8±12.8 vs 0.6±11.4; P=0.004), and 43% versus 36% exceeded the minimal clinically important difference (P=0.03). Hearing decrements were more common on azithromycin (25% vs 20%; P=0.04). The trial states the effect on microbial resistance patterns was not known.
cards.watchOut: Patients with hearing impairment, resting tachycardia or QT-prolongation risk were excluded at entry — the hearing and cardiac safety picture in unselected COPD patients is worse than this trial can show.
cards.source: Albert RK et al. Azithromycin for prevention of exacerbations of COPD. N Engl J Med. 2011;365(8):689-698. PMID: 21864166. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00325897, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: COLUMBUS 2014: thrice-weekly azithromycin in frequent exacerbators cut the adjusted exacerbation rate (rate ratio 0.58; 84 vs 129 total exacerbations)
cards.summary: COLUMBUS (2014): thrice-weekly azithromycin in frequent exacerbators cut the adjusted exacerbation rate (rate ratio 0.58 ; 84 vs 129 exacerbations).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, single-centre trial (12 months)
cards.people: 92 patients aged 18 years or older with COPD who had received treatment for three or more exacerbations in the previous year, at a single centre in the Netherlands, assigned to azithromycin 500 mg three times a week (47) or placebo (45); 41 (87%) and 36 (80%) completed. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: 84 exacerbations were recorded on azithromycin versus 129 on placebo; the unadjusted rate was 1.94 (95% CI 1.50 to 2.52) versus 3.22 (2.62 to 3.97) per patient per year, and after adjustment azithromycin significantly reduced the exacerbation rate (rate ratio 0.58, 0.42 to 0.79; p=0.001) — a relative measure inside the caution band, with absolute rates printed. Serious adverse events were reported by 3 (6%) azithromycin patients versus 5 (11%) on placebo. The commonest adverse event was diarrhoea (9 [19%] vs 1 [2%]; p=0.015).
cards.watchOut: A small single-centre trial in an extreme frequent-exacerbator phenotype (three or more treated exacerbations in the prior year): its larger relative effect should not be read onto ordinary COPD populations.
cards.source: Uzun S et al. Azithromycin maintenance treatment in patients with frequent exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COLUMBUS): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet Respir Med. 2014;2(5):361-368. PMID: 24746000. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00985244, from the record's databank fields.

cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Albert 2011 (1142 patients, daily azithromycin, 1 year) and COLUMBUS (92 patients, thrice-weekly azithromycin, 12 months), both double-blind placebo-controlled trials in exacerbation-prone COPD.
cards.result: The larger trial sets the conservative estimate (1.48 vs 1.83 exacerbations per patient-year; hazard ratio 0.73) and the small frequent-exacerbator trial the larger one (adjusted rate ratio 0.58) — directionally concordant, both with absolute rates printed. shelves.title: Brensocatib for bronchiectasis
shelves.question: Does the DPP-1 inhibitor brensocatib prolong time to first exacerbation and reduce exacerbation rates in bronchiectasis — the phase 2 WILLOW signal tested at scale in the phase 3 ASPEN trial?
shelves.mesh: Benzoxazoles/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Bronchiectasis/drug therapy,metabolism · Dipeptidyl-Peptidases and Tripeptidyl-Peptidases/antagonists & inhibitors · Disease Progression · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Forced Expiratory Volume · Leukocyte Elastase/metabolism
shelves.balance: LIKELY: A phase 2 signal confirmed at phase 3 scale. In WILLOW (256 patients, 24 weeks), brensocatib prolonged time to first exacerbation (adjusted hazard ratios 0.58 at 10 mg and 0.62 at 25 mg versus placebo); in ASPEN (1721 patients, 52 weeks), the annualised exacerbation rate was 1.02 (10 mg) and 1.04 (25 mg) versus 1.29 on placebo (rate ratios 0.79 and 0.81), with 48.5% versus 40.3% remaining exacerbation-free at week 52. The phase 3 relative effects sit inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band and are modest — about 0.25 fewer exacerbations per patient-year — and the stamp reflects a replicated programme with absolute rates printed, not a large effect. Hyperkeratosis and, in WILLOW, dental and skin events were the notable harms.

cards.headline: WILLOW 2020: brensocatib prolonged time to first exacerbation in bronchiectasis (adjusted hazard ratios 0.58 at 10 mg, 0.62 at 25 mg)
cards.summary: WILLOW (2020): brensocatib prolonged time to first bronchiectasis exacerbation (adjusted hazard ratios 0.58 at 10 mg, 0.62 at 25 mg ).
cards.type: Phase 2, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (24 weeks)
cards.people: 256 patients with bronchiectasis who had had at least two exacerbations in the previous year, randomly assigned to placebo (87), brensocatib 10 mg once daily (82), or brensocatib 25 mg once daily (87). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The 25th percentile of time to first exacerbation was 67 days on placebo, 134 days on brensocatib 10 mg and 96 days on 25 mg; treatment prolonged time to first exacerbation (P=0.03 for 10 mg and P=0.04 for 25 mg versus placebo), with adjusted hazard ratios of 0.58 (95% CI 0.35 to 0.95) and 0.62 (0.38 to 0.99) — relative measures inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band. Incidence-rate ratios for exacerbations were 0.64 (0.42 to 0.98; P=0.04) at 10 mg and 0.75 (0.50 to 1.13; P=0.17) at 25 mg. Sputum neutrophil elastase activity fell with both doses. Dental and skin adverse events of special interest were more frequent with the 10-mg and 25-mg doses respectively than with placebo.
cards.watchOut: A 24-week phase 2 trial whose dose ordering is untidy (the 10-mg arm looked at least as good as 25 mg on time-to-event) — hypothesis-confirming for ASPEN, not a dose guide.
cards.source: Chalmers JD et al. Phase 2 Trial of the DPP-1 Inhibitor Brensocatib in Bronchiectasis. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(22):2127-2137. PMID: 32897034. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03218917, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: ASPEN 2025: brensocatib cut the annualised exacerbation rate to 1.02 (10 mg) and 1.04 (25 mg) versus 1.29 on placebo over 52 weeks
cards.summary: ASPEN (2025): brensocatib cut the annualised exacerbation rate to 1.02 (10 mg) and 1.04 (25 mg) vs 1.29 on placebo (rate ratios 0.79–0.81).
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised trial (52 weeks)
cards.people: 1721 patients with bronchiectasis (1680 adults and 41 adolescents) randomly assigned to brensocatib 10 mg once daily, brensocatib 25 mg once daily, or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The annualised rate of adjudicated pulmonary exacerbations was 1.02 (10 mg), 1.04 (25 mg) and 1.29 (placebo): rate ratios versus placebo 0.79 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.92; adjusted P=0.004) and 0.81 (0.69 to 0.94; adjusted P=0.005) — relative measures inside the caution band, with absolute rates printed. Hazard ratios for time to first exacerbation were 0.81 and 0.83, and 48.5% in each brensocatib group remained exacerbation-free at week 52 versus 40.3% on placebo. FEV1 declined by 50 ml (10 mg), 24 ml (25 mg) and 62 ml (placebo); only the 25-mg difference versus placebo was significant (38 ml; adjusted P=0.04). Adverse events were similar across groups except a higher incidence of hyperkeratosis with brensocatib.
cards.watchOut: The absolute gain is about a quarter of an exacerbation per patient-year at either dose, with no dose separation on the primary endpoint — a real but modest effect in a chronic daily therapy.
cards.source: Chalmers JD et al. Phase 3 Trial of the DPP-1 Inhibitor Brensocatib in Bronchiectasis. N Engl J Med. 2025;392(16):1569-1581. PMID: 40267423. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04594369 and EudraCT 2020-003688-25, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: WILLOW's signal survived ASPEN's scale — LIKELY, with modest phase 3 effect sizes stated plainly.

shelves.title: Roflumilast for severe COPD on top of inhaled therapy
shelves.question: Does oral roflumilast reduce exacerbations in severe COPD with chronic bronchitis already on inhaled combination therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-2 Receptor Agonists/therapeutic use · Aminopyridines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Benzamides/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Bronchodilator Agents/therapeutic use · Cyclopropanes/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The roflumilast signal on top of inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting beta-agonist therapy is directionally consistent but statistically fragile. REACT (1945 patients) missed its prespecified primary Poisson analysis (rate ratio 0.868; p=0.0529) and reached significance only in the predefined negative-binomial sensitivity analysis (0.858; p=0.0424); RE2SPOND (2354 patients) missed its primary endpoint outright (rate ratio 0.92; p=0.163), with benefit confined to a post hoc frequent-exacerbator/hospitalisation subgroup. Two trials pointing the same way with relative effects deep inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band earn POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. Harm is consistent: adverse-event withdrawals about 11% versus about 5% in both trials.

cards.headline: REACT 2015: roflumilast missed its primary analysis (rate ratio 0.868; p=0.0529) and reached significance only on the sensitivity analysis (0.858; p=0.0424)
cards.summary: REACT (2015): roflumilast missed its primary analysis (rate ratio 0.868; p=0.0529 ) and reached significance only on the sensitivity analysis.
cards.type: 1-year, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, multicentre phase 3-4 trial
cards.people: 1945 patients aged 40 years or older, with at least 20 pack-years of smoking, severe COPD with chronic bronchitis and at least two exacerbations in the previous year, at 203 centres in 21 countries, randomly assigned to roflumilast 500 micrograms once daily (973) or placebo (972) on top of fixed inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting beta2-agonist therapy; background tiotropium was allowed. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The rate of moderate-to-severe exacerbations was 0.805 per patient per year on roflumilast versus 0.927 on placebo: 13.2% lower by the primary Poisson analysis (rate ratio 0.868, 95% CI 0.753 to 1.002; p=0.0529 — not significant) and 14.2% lower by the predefined negative-binomial sensitivity analysis (0.823 vs 0.959; 0.858, 0.740 to 0.995; p=0.0424) — relative measures inside the caution band, with absolute rates printed. Adverse events were reported by 648 (67%) on roflumilast versus 572 (59%) on placebo, and adverse-event withdrawal was 104 of 968 (11%) versus 52 of 967 (5%). Deaths were 17 (1.8%) versus 18 (1.9%).
cards.watchOut: The shelf's strongest trial is positive only under its sensitivity analysis: any honest citation of REACT must carry p=0.0529 beside p=0.0424.

cards.summary: RE2SPOND (2016): roflumilast did not significantly reduce exacerbations overall (rate ratio 0.92; P=0.163 ).
cards.type: 52-week, phase 4, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial

cards.headline: Synthesis: two large trials, two missed primary analyses, one consistent direction — POSSIBLE, and the weakest stamp on this slate
cards.summary: Two large trials, two missed primary analyses, one consistent direction — POSSIBLE, the weakest stamp on this slate.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: REACT (1945 patients) and RE2SPOND (2354 patients), both 1-year double-blind placebo-controlled trials of oral roflumilast added to inhaled combination therapy in severe COPD with chronic bronchitis.
cards.result: Combined, 4299 patients produced relative exacerbation reductions of 13–14% (REACT, significance analysis-dependent) and 8.5% (RE2SPOND, non-significant) — no trial met its prespecified primary analysis. Inhaled triple therapy is home on Shelf #303 and roflumilast CREAM/FOAM for skin disease on Shelves #824/#829 — different formulation and diseases, not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Prescribers weighing this add-on should see the withdrawal gap (about 11% vs 5% in both trials) beside the borderline efficacy — tolerability, not efficacy, is the consistent finding.

shelves.title: Narcolepsy wake promotion beyond modafinil: solriamfetol and pitolisant
shelves.question: Do the newer wake agents reduce excessive sleepiness in narcolepsy versus placebo — solriamfetol in its phase 3 trial, pitolisant (an H3 inverse agonist) against placebo and modafinil — and does pitolisant also cut cataplexy?
shelves.mesh: Carbamates/therapeutic use · Narcolepsy/drug therapy,physiopathology · Phenylalanine/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Sleep Latency · Sleepiness · Wakefulness-Promoting Agents/therapeutic use · Benzhydryl Compounds/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Three double-blind randomised trials cover the two halves of the question. Solriamfetol (236 patients) beat placebo on both wakefulness (Maintenance of Wakefulness Test +9.8 and +12.3 minutes at 150 and 300 mg vs +2.1) and sleepiness (Epworth −5.4 and −6.4 vs −1.6). Pitolisant beat placebo on sleepiness in HARMONY (ESS difference −3.0, 95% CI −5.6 to −0.4) but did NOT show non-inferiority to modafinil in that 95-patient trial, and in the dedicated HARMONY-CTP trial it cut weekly cataplexy by 75% vs 38% on placebo (rate ratio 0.512, 0.43 to 0.60 — a relative measure, with the absolute weekly rates printed on its card). Three concordant blinded trials carry LIKELY; the honest limits are that pitolisant's sleepiness effect is smaller than solriamfetol's trial showed and its modafinil comparison is unresolved. Sodium oxybate for narcolepsy is Shelf #921 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Thorpy 2019: solriamfetol 150 and 300 mg beat placebo on both wakefulness (+9.8 and +12.3 vs +2.1 minutes) and sleepiness (ESS −5.4 and −6.4 vs −1.6)
cards.summary: Solriamfetol trial (2019): 150 and 300 mg beat placebo on both wakefulness ( +9.8 and +12.3 vs +2.1 minutes ) and sleepiness.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (12 weeks)
cards.people: 236 patients with narcolepsy (mean sleep latency under 25 minutes on the Maintenance of Wakefulness Test, Epworth Sleepiness Scale score 10 or more, usual nightly sleep at least 6 hours) randomised to solriamfetol 75, 150 or 300 mg or placebo; 231 formed the modified intention-to-treat population; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Solriamfetol 300 and 150 mg were positive on both coprimary endpoints: least-squares mean changes in Maintenance of Wakefulness Test latency were 12.3 (SE 1.4) and 9.8 (SE 1.3) minutes vs 2.1 (SE 1.3) on placebo, and Epworth scores changed by −6.4 (SE 0.7) and −5.4 (SE 0.7) vs −1.6 (SE 0.7) (all p<0.0001). At week 12, 78.2% (150 mg) and 84.7% (300 mg) reported overall improvement vs 39.7% on placebo (both p<0.0001). Adverse events at 5% or more across solriamfetol doses included headache (21.5%), nausea (10.7%), decreased appetite (10.7%), nasopharyngitis (9.0%), dry mouth (7.3%) and anxiety (5.1%). The 75 mg dose was not positive on the coprimary endpoints as reported.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks, with wakefulness measured on a laboratory test and sleepiness on a scale: the trial does not show effects on accidents, work performance or cataplexy, and the dose-response means the licensed lower doses cannot borrow the 300 mg results.
cards.source: Thorpy MJ et al. A randomized study of solriamfetol for excessive sleepiness in narcolepsy. Ann Neurol. 2019 Mar;85(3):359-370. PMID: 30694576. Registry ID: NCT02348593, stated in the record's abstract (phase 3 study number); the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: HARMONY 2013: pitolisant beat placebo on sleepiness (ESS difference −3.0) but did not show non-inferiority to modafinil
cards.summary: HARMONY (2013): pitolisant beat placebo on sleepiness (ESS difference −3.0 ) but did not show non-inferiority to modafinil.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, parallel-group, double-dummy trial (pitolisant vs placebo vs modafinil, 8 weeks)
cards.people: 95 patients with narcolepsy and Epworth score at least 14, recruited at 32 centres in five European countries and randomised to placebo (30), pitolisant up to 40 mg (32) or modafinil up to 400 mg (33), after a psychostimulant washout; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean Epworth reductions over 8 weeks were −3.4 (SD 4.2) on placebo, −5.8 (6.2) on pitolisant and −6.9 (6.2) on modafinil. Pitolisant was superior to placebo (adjusted difference −3.0, 95% CI −5.6 to −0.4; p=0.024) but not non-inferior to modafinil (difference 0.12, −2.5 to 2.7; p=0.250). Adverse events numbered 22 (pitolisant), 26 (modafinil) and 10 (placebo); severe treatment-related events numbered one with pitolisant (abdominal discomfort) and five with modafinil.
cards.watchOut: Small (95 patients) and short (8 weeks), and designed so the modafinil question is formally unanswered: a confidence interval from −2.5 to 2.7 Epworth points is compatible with pitolisant being modestly worse or modestly better than modafinil. Cataplexy was not this trial's endpoint — that is the next card's trial.

cards.headline: HARMONY-CTP 2017: pitolisant cut weekly cataplexy attacks by 75% vs 38% on placebo (rate ratio 0.512, relative)
cards.summary: HARMONY-CTP (2017): pitolisant cut weekly cataplexy attacks by 75% vs 38% on placebo (rate ratio 0.512, relative).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (7 weeks) — pinned at build to answer the drafted question's cataplexy half
cards.people: 106 patients with narcolepsy with cataplexy (at least 3 cataplexies per week, Epworth score 12 or more) randomised at 16 centres in nine countries to pitolisant up to 40 mg (54) or placebo (52), with 54 and 51 in the intention-to-treat analysis; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Weekly cataplexy rate fell by 75% on pitolisant (from 9.15 attacks per week at baseline to 2.27) vs 38% on placebo (from 7.31 to 4.52) — a rate ratio of 0.512 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.60; p<0.0001), a relative measure printed here with the absolute weekly rates beside it. Treatment-related adverse events were more common on pitolisant (15 of 54, 28%) than placebo (6 of 51, 12%) (p=0.048); there were no serious adverse events, and one case of severe nausea on pitolisant. The most frequent pitolisant adverse events were headache, irritability, anxiety and nausea.
cards.watchOut: Seven weeks in patients with frequent cataplexy: durability beyond the trial and performance in milder cataplexy are untested, and the headline 75% is a within-group relative fall — the placebo group's own 38% fall is why the absolute rates matter.

cards.summary: Two drugs, three blinded trials — wake promotion beyond modafinil is real, and pitolisant's cataplexy claim has its own trial — LIKELY.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: solriamfetol phase 3 (236 patients), HARMONY (95 patients) and HARMONY-CTP (106 patients).

shelves.title: Sodium oxybate for narcolepsy: cataplexy and sleepiness
shelves.question: Does sodium oxybate reduce cataplexy attacks and excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy versus placebo — the two blinded reports of the oxybate programme, with its controlled-substance burden on the shelf face?
shelves.mesh: Cataplexy/drug therapy · Central Nervous System Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Sodium Oxybate/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Cataplexy/epidemiology · Disorders of Excessive Somnolence/drug therapy,epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The two carded reports are two papers from ONE randomised programme — the same 228 patients with narcolepsy with cataplexy, analysed for cataplexy in one report and for sleepiness in the other — so this shelf has a single trial programme and caps at POSSIBLE however consistent the reports are. Within it, the results are strong and dose-related: median weekly cataplexy falls of 57.0%, 65.0% and 84.7% at 4.5, 6 and 9 g nightly, and at 9 g a median increase of over 10 minutes in wakefulness latency (p<.001) with significant sleepiness-score improvements at 6 and 9 g — on top of the stimulants most patients continued. Sodium oxybate is the sodium salt of gamma-hydroxybutyrate, a controlled substance with a tightly restricted distribution; that burden, and the twice-nightly dosing the drug's short action imposes, belong on the shelf face beside the efficacy. The lower-sodium formulation in a different disorder is Shelf #922 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Xyrem International Study Group 2005 (cataplexy report): sodium oxybate cut weekly cataplexy attacks by a median 57.0%, 65.0% and 84.7% at 4.5, 6 and 9 g
cards.summary: Sodium oxybate, cataplexy report (2005): cut weekly cataplexy attacks by a median 57.0%, 65.0% and 84.7% at 4.5, 6 and 9 g.
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial (8 weeks, dose-titration)
cards.people: 228 adult patients with narcolepsy with cataplexy at 42 sleep clinics, weaned from anticataplectic medications and randomised to 4.5, 6 or 9 g sodium oxybate nightly or placebo for 8 weeks, with weekly 1.5 g titration steps; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, nightly doses of 4.5, 6 and 9 g sodium oxybate produced statistically significant median decreases in weekly cataplexy attacks of 57.0%, 65.0% and 84.7% respectively, measured by patient daily diaries — a clear dose-response. Some adverse events also showed a dose-response relationship, and the weekly titration schedule was associated with fewer adverse events than previously reported in fixed-dose double-blind oxybate trials.
cards.watchOut: The percentages are median within-group falls in attacks, printed as the abstract reports them; the abstract gives no absolute weekly attack counts, so no absolute rate is printed here. Eight weeks, after withdrawal of prior anticataplectics — rebound during weaning can flatter the subsequent treatment contrast.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one programme, two symptom wins — strong within-trial effects, single-programme ceiling
cards.summary: One programme, two symptom wins — strong within-trial effects, single-programme ceiling — POSSIBLE.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: one randomised programme of 228 adults with narcolepsy with cataplexy, reported twice (cataplexy and sleepiness).
cards.result: Sodium oxybate is unusual in improving both of narcolepsy's major symptoms in the same programme — cataplexy attacks down by a median of up to 84.7% at 9 g and wakefulness latency up by over 10 minutes at 9 g — which is why the drug anchors narcolepsy care despite its burdens. The stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, because two reports of one 8-week programme are one piece of randomised evidence, and the newer wake agents on Shelf #920 now cover sleepiness (and, for pitolisant, cataplexy) without the controlled-substance apparatus. The currency sweep's once-nightly oxybate post hoc analyses are fenced here: a formulation programme, not a replacement for these anchors.
cards.watchOut: Do not cite the two 2005 reports as independent confirmations of each other in any downstream summary; they share every patient.

shelves.title: Idiopathic hypersomnia: lower-sodium oxybate
shelves.question: In idiopathic hypersomnia, does lower-sodium oxybate hold its benefit under randomised withdrawal — and does the parent compound, sodium oxybate, beat placebo in the same disorder?
shelves.mesh: Disorders of Excessive Somnolence/chemically induced,drug therapy · Idiopathic Hypersomnia/drug therapy · Sodium Oxybate/adverse effects · Sodium Oxybate/therapeutic use,adverse effects,administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind randomised trials of oxybate in idiopathic hypersomnia, of two formulations, now agree. The lower-sodium oxybate phase 3 trial (154 enrolled; 115 randomised into withdrawal) showed that switching to placebo for 2 weeks worsened Epworth scores while continuing the drug held them (least-squares mean difference −6.5, 95% CI −8.0 to −5.0), after open-label treatment had brought scores from 15.7 to 6.1. The 2025 sodium oxybate trial pinned from the currency sweep (45 patients, parallel placebo control) found an almost identical adjusted Epworth advantage (−6.86, −9.73 to −4.00) plus better severity scores and wakefulness latency. Two concordant blinded trials carry LIKELY for oxybate's effect on sleepiness in this disorder — with the caveats that one is a withdrawal design in open-label responders, the other is small and single-centre, and adverse events are frequent (nausea 22% in the large trial; any treatment-emergent event in 81.8% on sodium oxybate in the small one).

cards.headline: Dauvilliers 2022: under randomised withdrawal, placebo patients worsened while lower-sodium oxybate patients held — Epworth difference −6.5 points
cards.summary: Randomised withdrawal (2022): placebo patients worsened while lower-sodium oxybate patients held — Epworth difference −6.5 points .
cards.type: Phase 3, placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomised-withdrawal trial (after open-label titration and stabilisation)
cards.people: 154 adults aged 18–75 years with idiopathic hypersomnia at 50 specialist centres in six European countries and the USA began open-label lower-sodium oxybate; after titration and a 2-week stable-dose period, 115 were randomised to continue lower-sodium oxybate (56, individually optimised 2.5–9.0 g/night) or switch to placebo (59) for 2 weeks; the abstract does not state the randomised cohort's mean age.
cards.result: Epworth scores fell from a mean of 15.7 (SD 3.8) at baseline to 6.1 (4.0) by the end of the stable-dose period. During the 2-week double-blind withdrawal, scores increased (worsened) on placebo but remained stable on continued lower-sodium oxybate (least-squares mean difference −6.5; 95% CI −8.0 to −5.0; p<0.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events in the 154-person safety population included nausea (22%), headache (18%), dizziness (12%), anxiety (11%) and vomiting (11%). No deaths were reported.
cards.watchOut: A withdrawal design proves the drug is doing the work in people who already tolerated and responded to it during open-label treatment; it cannot estimate the effect of starting the drug in an unselected patient, and the randomised phase lasted only 2 weeks.
cards.source: Dauvilliers Y et al. Safety and efficacy of lower-sodium oxybate in adults with idiopathic hypersomnia: a phase 3, placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomised withdrawal study. Lancet Neurol. 2022 Jan;21(1):53-65. PMID: 34942138. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03533114, from the record's databank fields; EU Clinical Trials 2018-001311-79 is also stated in the record's abstract.

cards.headline: Dauvilliers 2025: sodium oxybate (the parent compound) beat placebo in idiopathic hypersomnia — Epworth difference −6.86 points, wakefulness latency +14.75 minutes
cards.summary: Sodium oxybate trial (2025): the parent compound beat placebo in idiopathic hypersomnia — Epworth difference −6.86 points .
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled trial (single centre) — found in the currency sweep and carded
cards.people: 45 adults aged 18–60 years with idiopathic hypersomnia (Epworth score 14 or more) at the National Reference Center for Hypersomnia in Montpellier, France, randomised to sodium oxybate (22; twice-nightly titration from 4.5 g to a maximum of 9 g) or placebo (23); 36 of the 45 were women and the mean age was 29.0 ± 7.5 years; 40 patients completed the study.
cards.result: At week 8 the adjusted Epworth difference favoured sodium oxybate (least-squares mean difference −6.86; 95% CI −9.73 to −4.00; p<0.0001), as did the Idiopathic Hypersomnia Severity Scale (−11.61; −16.63 to −6.59; p<0.0001) and Maintenance of Wakefulness Test latency (+14.75 minutes; 9.98 to 19.52; p<0.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events (nausea, headache and dizziness the named examples) were reported by 81.8% of sodium oxybate patients vs 26.1% on placebo. The authors note low-sodium oxybate is the sole FDA-approved treatment for this disorder; this trial tested the older full-sodium compound.
cards.watchOut: Small (45 randomised) and single-centre, with a very high adverse-event rate on active treatment that can partially unblind a sleepiness endpoint; it supports the lower-sodium trial's class conclusion but is not a second large trial.
cards.source: Dauvilliers Y et al. Efficacy and Safety of Sodium Oxybate in Adults With Idiopathic Hypersomnia: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Neurology. 2025 Jun 10;104(11):e213690. PMID: 40359459. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03597555, from the record's databank fields; EudraCT 2017-004122-15 is also stated in the record's abstract.

cards.headline: Synthesis: withdrawal and parallel designs, two formulations, one convergent answer on sleepiness
cards.summary: Withdrawal and parallel designs, two formulations, one convergent answer on sleepiness — LIKELY.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the lower-sodium oxybate withdrawal trial (115 randomised) and the sodium oxybate parallel trial (45 randomised).
cards.result: The two designs answer complementary questions — does stopping the drug lose the benefit (yes: −6.5 Epworth points of separation in 2 weeks) and does starting it beat placebo (yes: −6.86 points at 8 weeks, with objective wakefulness latency up by about 15 minutes) — and their near-identical effect sizes are the shelf's strength. A diary-based secondary report of the lower-sodium trial from the currency sweep adds sleep-time detail and is fenced, not carded: it is the same patients. Sodium oxybate in NARCOLEPSY is Shelf #921; the formulations and diagnoses must not be merged.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial runs beyond weeks, and idiopathic hypersomnia's other burdens — prolonged night sleep and sleep inertia — are secondary or unmeasured in both abstracts; the LIKELY is for sleepiness and severity scores, not for normalising the disorder.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dauvilliers Y et al. Lancet Neurol. 2022;21(1):53-65. PMID: 34942138; Dauvilliers Y et al. Neurology. 2025;104(11):e213690. PMID: 40359459. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Mandibular advancement devices vs CPAP for obstructive sleep apnea
shelves.question: In obstructive sleep apnea, does a mandibular advancement device match CPAP on sleepiness, blood pressure and health outcomes despite lowering the apnea–hypopnoea index less — the Phillips randomised crossover trial and the CRESCENT blood-pressure trial?
shelves.mesh: Automobile Driving · Blood Pressure Monitoring, Ambulatory/instrumentation · Computer Simulation · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure/instrumentation,methods,statistics & numerical data · Cross-Over Studies · Fatigue/etiology,physiopathology · Hypertension/etiology,physiopathology
shelves.balance: LIKELY — for comparable health outcomes, not for equal apnea control, and with no cardiovascular-event claim made on this shelf: Phillips 2013 (126 patients, crossover) found CPAP lowered the apnea–hypopnoea index more (4.5 vs 11.1 events/hour) but patients wore the device longer (6.50 vs 5.20 hours/night), and sleepiness, driving performance and disease-specific quality of life improved similarly on both. CRESCENT (220 randomised patients with hypertension and increased cardiovascular risk) found the device non-inferior to CPAP on 24-hour mean arterial pressure at 6 months (between-group difference −1.6 mm Hg, non-inferiority p<0.001 against a 1.5 mm Hg margin), with the device group's pressure actually falling 2.5 mm Hg while CPAP's did not change. Two randomised trials carry LIKELY for outcome comparability in patients who use the device. Whether treating sleep apnea prevents cardiovascular EVENTS is Shelf #302's question and is not claimed here.

cards.headline: Phillips 2013: CPAP controlled the index better (AHI 4.5 vs 11.1/hour) but the device was worn longer — and sleepiness, driving and quality of life improved the same on both
cards.summary: CPAP vs mandibular device (2013): CPAP controlled the index better (AHI 4.5 vs 11.1/hour ) but the device was worn longer — sleepiness, driving and quality of life were equal.
cards.type: Randomised crossover trial (1 month of optimal CPAP and 1 month of mandibular advancement device, in random order)
cards.people: 126 patients with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (apnea–hypopnoea index 25.6 [SD 12.3]) randomised to a treatment order; 108 completed both treatments; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: CPAP was more efficacious at reducing the index (CPAP 4.5 ± 6.6 vs device 11.1 ± 12.1 events/hour; P<0.01) but reported compliance was higher with the device (6.50 ± 1.3 vs 5.20 ± 2 hours per night; P<0.00001). The 24-hour mean arterial pressure was not inferior on the device (CPAP-minus-device difference 0.2 mm Hg [95% CI −0.7 to 1.1]), although neither treatment improved blood pressure overall in this 1-month comparison. Sleepiness, driving simulator performance and disease-specific quality of life improved on both treatments by similar amounts, and the device was superior to CPAP on four general quality-of-life domains.
cards.watchOut: One month per treatment in a crossover: long-term adherence decay, dental and jaw effects of nightly device use, and any outcome beyond surrogate and symptom measures are outside this trial. Its blood-pressure neutrality also tempers CRESCENT's positive reading below — populations differed (CRESCENT required hypertension).
cards.source: Phillips CL et al. Health outcomes of continuous positive airway pressure versus oral appliance treatment for obstructive sleep apnea: a randomized controlled trial. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2013 Apr 15;187(8):879-87. PMID: 23413266. Registry ID: ACTRN12607000289415 (Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry), stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: CRESCENT 2024: a mandibular device was non-inferior to CPAP for 24-hour blood pressure at 6 months — pressure fell 2.5 mm Hg on the device and did not change on CPAP
cards.summary: CRESCENT (2024): a mandibular device was non-inferior to CPAP for 24-hour blood pressure at 6 months — pressure fell 2.5 mm Hg on the device.
cards.type: Investigator-initiated, randomised, non-inferiority trial (prespecified margin 1.5 mm Hg)
cards.people: 220 participants aged 40 years or older with hypertension, increased cardiovascular risk and moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (index 15 or more events/hour), randomised 1:1 to a mandibular advancement device or CPAP, from 321 recruited for polysomnography at 3 public hospitals; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 6 months, 24-hour mean arterial pressure had decreased by 2.5 mm Hg from baseline in the device group (P=0.003) and had not changed in the CPAP group (P=0.374); the between-group difference was −1.6 mm Hg (95% CI −3.51 to 0.24; non-inferiority P<0.001). The device group showed larger reductions in all secondary ambulatory pressure parameters, most pronounced during sleep. Daytime sleepiness improved on both treatments with a similar between-group difference, and there were no between-group differences in cardiovascular biomarkers.
cards.watchOut: Blood pressure is a surrogate: CRESCENT shows a dental device lowers pressure at least as much as CPAP in hypertensive patients over 6 months, not that either prevents heart attacks or strokes — that claim belongs to Shelf #302's event trials and is not made here. Non-inferiority also coexists with a point estimate favouring the device, which largely reflects CPAP adherence in practice.
cards.source: Ou YH et al. Mandibular Advancement vs CPAP for Blood Pressure Reduction in Patients With Obstructive Sleep Apnea. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2024 May 7;83(18):1760-1772. PMID: 38588926. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04119999, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: less index control, equal outcomes — the adherence trade is the mechanism, and it is now shown twice
cards.summary: Less index control, equal outcomes — the adherence trade is the mechanism, and it is now shown twice — LIKELY. BP surrogate only; no CV-event claim.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Phillips 2013 (126 randomised, 108 completing both arms) and CRESCENT (220 randomised, 6 months).
cards.result: Both trials tell the same story from different angles: CPAP is the stronger index-lowering machine, the device is the one patients wear longer, and measured health outcomes — sleepiness in both trials, quality of life in Phillips, ambulatory blood pressure in CRESCENT — end up similar or device-favouring. CRESCENT's 12-month final report (PMID 42013991, found in the currency sweep) sustained the blood-pressure non-inferiority at a year and is fenced here as a further report of the carded trial, not a third trial. The implanted stimulator (drafted #635) and tissue surgery (drafted #638) are different answers to CPAP intolerance and are not re-carded here; CPAP for cardiovascular-event prevention is Shelf #302.
cards.watchOut: Both trials recruited patients willing to try a device; in a patient who uses CPAP all night every night, CPAP's superior index control is unchallenged by anything on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Phillips CL et al. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2013;187(8):879-87. PMID: 23413266; Ou YH et al. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2024;83(18):1760-1772. PMID: 38588926. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Positional therapy for positional obstructive sleep apnea
shelves.question: In patients whose apnea is predominantly supine, does a vibrotactile sleep-position trainer reduce supine sleep and the apnea–hypopnoea index — against no treatment, head-to-head against an oral appliance, and against sham?
shelves.mesh: Patient Compliance · Polysomnography · Sleep Apnea Syndromes/metabolism,physiopathology,therapy · Sleep Stages · Vibration/therapeutic use · Mandibular Advancement/instrumentation · Mouth
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Three randomised trials now triangulate positional therapy. Laub 2017 (101 patients, open, against no treatment) halved supine sleep (47% to 17% of the night) and cut the total index from 18 to 10 events/hour while controls barely moved. Benoist 2017 (99 patients) found the trainer and an oral appliance equally effective head-to-head (median index 13.0 to 7.0 vs 11.7 to 9.1). And the sham-controlled, double-blind Thorax trial found in the currency sweep (120 patients, neck-worn device) beat sham by −4.41 events/hour (95% CI −7.77 to −1.06) over 3 months, improving sleep quality though not sleepiness. The honest price is persistence: discontinuation reached 28.8% by 2 months and 49.4% by 6 months in Laub's cohort. Three concordant randomised trials, one of them sham-blinded, carry LIKELY for patients whose apnea is genuinely positional.

cards.headline: Laub 2017: the sleep position trainer cut supine sleep from 47% to 17% of the night and the total index from 18 to 10 events/hour; controls did neither
cards.summary: Sleep position trainer (2017): cut supine sleep from 47% to 17% of the night and the total index from 18 to 10 events/hour; controls did not improve.
cards.type: Open, randomised, controlled trial (2 months) with a 6-month treated-cohort follow-up
cards.people: 101 patients with positional sleep apnea randomised to the Sleep Position Trainer (52) or a non-treatment control group (49) for 2 months, then all followed as a treated cohort to 6 months; mean supine index at entry was 35 per hour (SD 18) in the trainer group and 38 (SD 15) in controls; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the per-protocol analysis, mean total apnea–hypopnoea index went from 18 per hour (SD 10) at entry to 10 (SD 9; P<0.001) after 2 months with the trainer, vs 20 (SD 9) to 18 (SD 10; not significant) in controls. Mean supine sleep time fell from 47% (SD 22) to 17% (SD 18; P<0.001) with the trainer vs 48% (SD 20) to 39% (SD 21; not significant) in controls. The effect was maintained at 6 months and daytime sleepiness improved. Compliance (use over 4 hours per night on all weekdays) was 75.5% (SD 21.2) in the first 2 months; discontinuation was 28.8% at 2 months and 49.4% at 6 months.
cards.watchOut: Open-label against no treatment, with per-protocol headline numbers: expectation and selection both favour the device, which is why the sham-controlled trial below matters. The 49.4% six-month discontinuation is part of the result, not a footnote.
cards.source: Laub RR et al. A Sleep Position Trainer for positional sleep apnea: a randomized, controlled trial. J Sleep Res. 2017 Oct;26(5):641-650. PMID: 28370716. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the MEDLINE record carries no databank registry entry. (The topic draft attributed this trial to de Ruiter; the record's first author is Laub — de Ruiter is a co-author of the Benoist trial below.)

cards.headline: Benoist 2017: positional therapy and an oral appliance were equally effective in mild-to-moderate positional apnea (median index 13.0 to 7.0 vs 11.7 to 9.1)
cards.summary: Positional therapy vs oral appliance (2017): equally effective in mild-to-moderate positional apnea (median index 13.0 to 7.0 vs 11.7 to 9.1 ).
cards.type: Multicentre, prospective, randomised, controlled head-to-head trial (3 months)
cards.people: 99 patients with mild-to-moderate positional obstructive sleep apnea (index 5 to 30 events/hour) randomised to positional therapy with the sleep position trainer or oral appliance therapy; 81 completed the study; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat median index fell from 13.0 [IQR 9.7–18.5] to 7.0 [3.8–12.8] with positional therapy (p<0.001) and from 11.7 [9.0–16.2] to 9.1 [4.9–11.7] with the appliance (p<0.001) — equally effective, per the authors. Mean adherence (at least 4 hours per night, at least 5 days per week) was 89.3 ± 22.4% for the trainer vs 81.3 ± 30.0% for the appliance (p=0.208).
cards.watchOut: No untreated or sham arm: 'equally effective' compares two active therapies over 3 months in mild-to-moderate positional disease only, and 18 of 99 randomised patients did not complete the study.
cards.source: Benoist L et al. A randomized, controlled trial of positional therapy versus oral appliance therapy for position-dependent sleep apnea. Sleep Med. 2017 Jun;34:109-117. PMID: 28522078. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02045576, from the record's databank fields.
