cards.headline: Kelly 2026: against a sham device, neck-worn vibrotactile positional therapy cut the index by −4.41 events/hour over 3 months and improved sleep quality, not sleepiness
cards.summary: Sham-controlled vibrotactile therapy (2026): cut the index by −4.41 events/hour over 3 months versus sham and improved sleep quality.
cards.type: Randomised, parallel, double-blind, sham-controlled trial (3 months) — found in the currency sweep and carded
cards.people: 120 adults with positional obstructive sleep apnea (index over 5 events/hour, at least twice as high supine as non-supine; median baseline index 12.8 [IQR 9.2–18.5]) randomised 1:1 to a neck-worn positional therapy device (59) or sham positional therapy (61); 92 (77%) completed the trial; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Positional therapy reduced the apnea–hypopnoea index by −4.41 events/hour versus sham (95% CI −7.77 to −1.06; p=0.011), described by the authors as a 34% improvement (a relative figure, printed with the absolute difference beside it). Sleep quality improved (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index −1.0 [−2.1 to 0.0]; p=0.04) but sleepiness did not (Epworth −0.6 [−1.8 to 0.6]; p=0.3), against a low baseline Epworth of 8.8. Bed partners reported improved snoring and sleep quality, and over half of active-device users opted to continue it.
cards.watchOut: Mild average disease (median index 12.8) and a 23% non-completion rate: the sham-controlled win is real but modest in absolute events per hour, and this population's sleepiness was near-normal at entry, so the null sleepiness result cuts both ways.
cards.source: Kelly JL et al. Vibrotactile positional therapy for the treatment of positional obstructive sleep apnoea: a multicentre, randomised controlled trial. Thorax. 2026 Mar;81(4):370-379. PMID: 40992934. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04153240, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: change the position, change the index — shown against nothing, against an appliance, and against sham
cards.summary: Change the position, change the index — shown against nothing, against an appliance, and against sham — LIKELY.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Laub 2017 (101 randomised), Benoist 2017 (99 randomised) and Kelly 2026 (120 randomised) — 320 randomised patients in positional obstructive sleep apnea.
cards.result: The evidence ladder is complete for this niche: the trainer beats no treatment (index 18 to 10), matches the established dental device head-to-head (median 13.0 to 7.0 vs 11.7 to 9.1), and beats a sham device under double-blind conditions (−4.41 events/hour). What limits the therapy is not efficacy but staying with it — about half of Laub's cohort had stopped by 6 months. Mandibular devices for apnea in ANY position are Shelf #923; the trainer changes position itself and is a different intervention, fenced there and carded here.
cards.watchOut: Every trial required genuinely positional disease (supine index at least double the non-supine); nothing here supports positional therapy for non-positional apnea.

shelves.title: Central sleep apnea: transvenous phrenic nerve stimulation
shelves.question: Does transvenous phrenic nerve stimulation reduce central apnea events and improve sleep quality and quality of life in moderate-to-severe central sleep apnea — the pivotal randomised trial and its five-year follow-up? (No mortality claim is made on this shelf.)
shelves.mesh: Implantable Neurostimulators · Oxygen/blood · Polysomnography · Severity of Illness Index · Sleep Apnea, Central/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One pivotal randomised trial (151 implanted patients, stimulation on vs off for 6 months) found 51% of the treatment group vs 11% of controls achieved at least a 50% reduction in the apnea–hypopnoea index (difference 41%, 95% CI 25 to 54; p<0.0001), with concordant improvements in oxygenation, sleep metrics and quality of life, and 91% of patients free of serious procedure-, system- or therapy-related adverse events at 12 months. The five-year report is a follow-up of the same trial's remnant (52 completers of the original 151), showing sustained index improvements (median apnea–hypopnoea index 46 to 17 events/hour; central-apnea index 23 to 1) — supportive durability, not a second trial, so the shelf caps at POSSIBLE. Seven deaths occurred during the trial's first year, all judged unrelated to implant, system or therapy; no mortality benefit or harm claim is made or implied on this shelf.

cards.headline: Costanzo 2016: phrenic stimulation halved the index in 51% vs 11% of patients at 6 months (difference 41%) — the pivotal remedē trial
cards.summary: Pivotal phrenic-stimulation trial (2016): stimulation halved the index in 51% vs 11% of patients at 6 months (difference 41%).
cards.type: Prospective, multicentre, randomised controlled trial (implanted device, stimulation on vs off; polysomnography scored by masked core laboratory)
cards.people: 151 eligible patients with central sleep apnea (apnea–hypopnoea index at least 20 events/hour), medically stable and on guideline-recommended therapy, implanted at 31 centres in Germany, Poland and the USA and randomised to stimulation (73) or no stimulation (78) for 6 months; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Significantly more treatment patients achieved a 50% or greater index reduction at 6 months (35 of 68 [51%] vs 8 of 73 [11%]; difference 41%, 95% CI 25 to 54; p<0.0001). At 12 months, 138 of 151 patients (91%) had no serious adverse events related to the procedure, system or therapy; related serious events occurred in 7 control cases (9%) and 6 treatment cases (8%). Seven patients died, all unrelated to implant, system or therapy (four during the 6-month randomised period, three between 6 and 12 months). Non-serious therapy-related discomfort was reported by 27 of 73 treatment patients (37%) and was resolved with system reprogramming in 26 of them.
cards.watchOut: An on/off design in already-implanted patients: everyone bore the implant risk, the control group simply had therapy switched off, and the endpoint is a responder threshold on a sleep index — not symptoms alone, hospitalisation or survival. Industry-run (Respicardia), with about a third of treated patients feeling the therapy until reprogrammed.

shelves.title: Pharmacotherapy for obstructive sleep apnea: atomoxetine plus oxybutynin
shelves.question: Can a noradrenergic–antimuscarinic combination taken at night reduce obstructive sleep apnea severity pharmacologically — atomoxetine plus oxybutynin in the Taranto-Montemurro crossover trial, the MARIPOSA trial of the fixed combination, and the phase 3 SynAIRgy trial?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic Uptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Atomoxetine Hydrochloride/therapeutic use · Cross-Over Studies · Drug Combinations · Mandelic Acids/therapeutic use · Parasympatholytics/therapeutic use · Placebo Effect
shelves.balance: LIKELY — for reducing the apnea–hypopnoea index, with the effect shrinking as trials get longer and larger: the 1-night crossover (20 patients) cut the index by 63% (from a median 28.5 to 7.5 events/hour); the 4-week MARIPOSA trial (211 randomised) cut it by about 47% and 43% at the two fixed-combination doses against a smaller placebo fall; and the 26-week phase 3 SynAIRgy trial found in the currency sweep (646 patients unable to use PAP) showed a mean treatment difference of −4.0 events/hour (95% CI −6.4 to −1.6), a model-estimated 44.1% vs 17.6% fall from baseline (relative figures, with the absolute difference beside them). Three randomised blinded trials in sequence carry LIKELY for the index effect. The price also belongs on the face: in SynAIRgy 21.2% on the drug vs 3.1% on placebo stopped because of adverse events (dry mouth, nausea, insomnia, urinary hesitation the commonest), and no trial shows the combination improves sleepiness, fatigue (null in SynAIRgy) or any clinical outcome beyond the index and oxygenation.

cards.headline: Taranto-Montemurro 2019: one night of atomoxetine plus oxybutynin cut the index by 63% (median 28.5 to 7.5 events/hour) — and neither drug alone did anything
cards.summary: One-night crossover (2019): atomoxetine plus oxybutynin cut the index by 63% (median 28.5 to 7.5 events/hour) — and neither drug alone did.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind, crossover trial (single night per condition)
cards.people: 20 people with obstructive sleep apnea completing both conditions (median age 53 [IQR 46–58] years; median body mass index 34.8 [30.0–40.2] kg/m2), given 80 mg atomoxetine plus 5 mg oxybutynin or placebo before sleep, with in-laboratory polysomnography; a subgroup of 9 also received each drug separately.
cards.result: The combination lowered the apnea–hypopnoea index by 63% (IQR 34–86%), from 28.5 (10.9–51.6) to 7.5 (2.4–18.6) events/hour (P<0.001). Among the 15 patients with apnea on placebo (index over 10), the index fell by 74% (62–88%) and all 15 achieved at least a 50% reduction. Genioglossus responsiveness rose about threefold (from 2.2 [1.1–4.7] to 6.3 [3.0–18.3] %/cm H2O; P<0.001). Neither atomoxetine nor oxybutynin alone reduced the index in the 9-patient subgroup.
cards.watchOut: Twenty patients, one night: this is a mechanism proof, not a treatment trial — tolerance, sleep-quality effects and adherence over weeks cannot be read from it, which is exactly what the two later trials were for.
cards.source: Taranto-Montemurro L et al. The Combination of Atomoxetine and Oxybutynin Greatly Reduces Obstructive Sleep Apnea Severity. A Randomized, Placebo-controlled, Double-Blind Crossover Trial. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2019 May 15;199(10):1267-1276. PMID: 30395486. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02908529, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: MARIPOSA 2023: over 4 weeks the fixed combination cut the index by 47.1% and 42.9% at its two doses, against a smaller placebo fall
cards.summary: MARIPOSA (2023): over 4 weeks the fixed combination cut the index by 47.1% and 42.9% at its two doses, against a smaller placebo fall.
cards.type: Phase 2, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial (4 weeks)
cards.people: 211 patients with obstructive sleep apnea randomised to AD109 (aroxybutynin/atomoxetine) 2.5/75 mg, AD109 5/75 mg, atomoxetine 75 mg alone, or placebo; 181 were included in the prespecified efficacy analyses; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary index (4% desaturation criterion) fell from a median of 20.5 (IQR 12.3–27.2) to 10.8 (5.6–18.5) on AD109 2.5/75 mg (−47.1%), from 19.4 (13.7–26.4) to 9.5 (6.1–19.3) on 5/75 mg (−42.9%; both P<0.0001 vs placebo), and from 19.0 (11.8–28.8) to 11.8 (5.5–21.5) on atomoxetine alone (−38.8%; P<0.01 vs placebo), while placebo fell from 20.1 (11.9–25.9) to 16.3 (11.1–28.9). Fatigue improved with the 2.5/75 mg dose (P<0.05 vs placebo and atomoxetine); atomoxetine alone decreased total sleep time. The most common adverse events were dry mouth, insomnia and urinary hesitancy.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks, medians rather than means, and a surprisingly large atomoxetine-alone effect that the 1-night trial's subgroup did not show — the combination's margin over its own noradrenergic half is thinner than the placebo contrast suggests.

cards.headline: SynAIRgy 2026: at 26 weeks in 646 PAP-intolerant patients, AD109 beat placebo by −4.0 events/hour — and 21.2% vs 3.1% stopped for adverse events
cards.summary: SynAIRgy (2026): at 26 weeks in 646 PAP-intolerant patients, AD109 beat placebo by −4.0 events/hour — and 21.2% vs 3.1% stopped for adverse events.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-arm trial (26 weeks, 69 centres) — found in the currency sweep and carded
cards.people: 646 adults with mild-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea who were intolerant to or refused PAP therapy (median age 58 years; 49.3% female; median body mass index 32.4 kg/m2; median baseline index 19.6 events/hour — 35% mild, 42% moderate, 23% severe), randomised to AD109 2.5/75 mg or placebo.
cards.result: At week 26 the mean index treatment difference was −4.0 events/hour (95% CI −6.4 to −1.6; P=.001), representing a model-estimated 44.1% vs 17.6% decrease from baseline (P<.0001) — relative percentages printed with the absolute difference beside them. Oxygen desaturation index and hypoxic burden improved versus placebo; PROMIS-Fatigue did not differ significantly. Discontinuation due to adverse events was 21.2% on AD109 vs 3.1% on placebo; the most common adverse events were dry mouth, nausea, insomnia and urinary hesitation, with no serious treatment-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The phase 3 effect (−4.0 events/hour on a median baseline of 19.6) is materially smaller than the early trials' percentage headlines, one in five patients stopped the drug for adverse events, and fatigue — the patient-facing endpoint — was null. This is an index-lowering drug for PAP-intolerant patients, not yet a shown improver of how patients feel or fare.

shelves.title: Non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder in totally blind people: tasimelteon (SET and RESET)
shelves.question: Does tasimelteon entrain the circadian clock and improve night sleep in totally blind people with non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder — the SET entrainment trial and the RESET maintenance-withdrawal trial?
shelves.mesh: Benzofurans/therapeutic use · Blindness/complications · Circadian Rhythm/drug effects · Cyclopropanes/therapeutic use · Receptors, Melatonin/agonists · Sleep Disorders, Circadian Rhythm/drug therapy,etiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The twin phase 3 programme (two trials in one paper) shows a coherent entrainment story. In SET (84 randomised), tasimelteon entrained 20% of patients by month 1 vs 3% on placebo (difference 17%, 95% CI 3.2 to 31.6) and produced a clinical response in 24% vs none on placebo. In RESET (20 entrained patients randomised to continue or withdraw), 90% who continued stayed entrained vs 20% withdrawn to placebo (difference 70%, 26.4 to 100) — the drug works and stopping it loses the effect, which is strong causal evidence in a rare disorder. Two concordant blinded trials carry LIKELY, with the absolute scale on the face: most treated patients in SET did not entrain by the trial's strict definition (20% did), so this is a real effect for a minority-to-substantial fraction, not a universal fix. Melatonin itself for jet lag and insomnia in sighted people is Shelves #492 and #116 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: SET and RESET 2015: tasimelteon entrained 20% vs 3% at month 1, and 90% of continuers stayed entrained vs 20% after withdrawal
cards.summary: SET and RESET (2015): tasimelteon entrained 20% vs 3% at month 1, and 90% of continuers stayed entrained vs 20% after withdrawal.
cards.type: Two multicentre, randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (SET: 26-week entrainment; RESET: randomised withdrawal in entrained responders), reported in one paper
cards.people: Totally blind adults aged 18–75 years with a non-24-hour circadian period of 24.25 hours or longer: SET randomised 84 patients (tasimelteon 20 mg 42, placebo 42) at 27 US and 6 German centres; RESET randomised 20 patients who had entrained on open-label tasimelteon (10 continue, 10 withdraw to placebo); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In SET, circadian entrainment at month 1 occurred in 8 of 40 patients (20%) on tasimelteon vs 1 of 38 (3%) on placebo (difference 17%, 95% CI 3.2 to 31.6; p=0.0171), and a clinical response (entrainment plus clinical improvement on the Non-24 Clinical Response Scale) in 9 of 38 (24%) vs none of 34 on placebo (difference 24%, 8.4 to 39.0; p=0.0028). In RESET, 9 of 10 patients (90%) who continued tasimelteon remained entrained vs 2 of 10 (20%) withdrawn to placebo (difference 70%, 26.4 to 100; p=0.0026). No deaths were reported; discontinuation for adverse events was comparable (3 of 52 tasimelteon courses [6%] vs 2 of 52 placebo courses [4%]). The commonest tasimelteon side-effects in SET were headache (17% vs 7%), elevated liver enzymes (10% vs 5%), nightmares or abnormal dreams (10% vs none), upper respiratory infection (7% vs none) and urinary tract infection (7% vs 2%).
cards.watchOut: Small absolute numbers in a rare disorder: SET's entrainment difference rests on 8 patients vs 1, and its strict biochemical definition of entrainment (urinary metabolite rhythm) is a surrogate for the sleep and functioning outcomes patients feel — captured only in the composite clinical-response endpoint (24% vs 0%). RESET's 20 patients were pre-selected entrainment responders.
cards.source: Lockley SW et al. Tasimelteon for non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder in totally blind people (SET and RESET): two multicentre, randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials. cards.headline: Synthesis: entrainment shown, maintenance shown, effect confined to a responder fraction — LIKELY
cards.summary: Entrainment shown, maintenance shown, effect confined to a responder fraction — LIKELY.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: SET (84 randomised) and RESET (20 randomised from entrained responders), twin phase 3 trials in one report.
cards.result: The pair is stronger than either alone: SET shows the drug can entrain a clock that light cannot reach (20% vs 3% by the strict definition, 24% vs 0% on the clinical composite), and RESET's withdrawal design shows the effect is the drug's, not drift (90% vs 20% staying entrained). Continued treatment is necessary to hold the gain, per the trialists. The currency sweep's single hit — tasimelteon for primary insomnia in sighted people — does not touch this population and is not carded. Melatonin for jet lag (#492) and insomnia in sighted people (#116) is a different drug use in a different physiology and is fenced, not re-carded.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here supports tasimelteon for circadian problems in sighted people, whose clocks light can still reset; the shelf's population is total blindness with a measured long circadian period.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lockley SW et al. Lancet. 2015;386(10005):1754-64. PMID: 26466871. Registry IDs as on the card above.

shelves.title: Sleep problems in children with autism and neurodevelopmental disorders: melatonin
shelves.question: Does melatonin improve sleep onset and total sleep in children with autism spectrum disorder or neurodevelopmental disorders — prolonged-release melatonin in the Gringras autism trial, and immediate-release melatonin in the MENDS trial?
shelves.mesh: Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity/complications · Autism Spectrum Disorder/complications · Central Nervous System Depressants/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Delayed-Action Preparations · Melatonin/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/drug therapy,etiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY — for faster sleep onset and a modest gain in total sleep: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials, of two formulations, agree on the shape of the effect. Prolonged-release melatonin in the Gringras autism trial (125 children whose sleep had failed behavioural intervention) lengthened night sleep (a 57.5-minute within-group rise vs 9.14 minutes on placebo; p=.034 on the adjusted primary analysis) and shortened sleep latency (falls of 39.6 vs 12.5 minutes; adjusted difference −25.30 minutes), with 68.9% vs 39.3% achieving a clinically meaningful response. Immediate-release melatonin in MENDS (146 children) added 22.4 minutes of diary-measured total sleep (95% CI 0.5 to 44.3) and cut sleep onset latency by 37.5 minutes — but children also woke 29.9 minutes earlier, and the actigraphy total-sleep estimate was not significant (13.3 minutes, −15.5 to 42.2). Two concordant randomised trials carry LIKELY for onset and a small total-sleep gain; neither shows significant behaviour or family-functioning improvement, and MENDS's authors call the added sleep 'little' — that sizing is part of the stamp. Adult melatonin shelves (#116, #492) are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Gringras 2017: prolonged-release melatonin lengthened sleep and shortened latency in autistic children — responders 68.9% vs 39.3% (NNT 3.38)
cards.summary: Prolonged-release melatonin (2017): lengthened sleep and shortened latency in autistic children — responders 68.9% vs 39.3% (NNT 3.38).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (13 weeks) of paediatric prolonged-release melatonin minitablets
cards.people: 125 children and adolescents aged 2 to 17.5 years (96.8% autism spectrum disorder, 3.2% Smith-Magenis syndrome; some with ADHD comorbidity or neurogenetic disorders) whose sleep had failed to improve on behavioural intervention alone, randomised 1:1 to prolonged-release melatonin minitablets (PedPRM; 2 mg escalated to 5 mg) or placebo.
cards.result: After 13 weeks, participants slept on average 57.5 minutes longer at night on prolonged-release melatonin compared with 9.14 minutes on placebo (the trial met its primary endpoint; p=.034 for the adjusted treatment difference as reported). Sleep latency fell by 39.6 minutes on melatonin vs 12.5 on placebo (adjusted mean difference −25.30 minutes; p=.011), without earlier wake-up time. Clinically meaningful responses in total sleep time and/or latency occurred in 68.9% vs 39.3% (p=.001), corresponding to a number needed to treat of 3.38. Overall sleep disturbance tended to decrease; the formulation was generally safe, with somnolence more commonly reported on melatonin.
cards.watchOut: The abstract's printed adjusted difference for total sleep time carries a negative sign (−32.43 minutes) against the direction of the reported group changes (57.5 vs 9.14 minutes); this card therefore prints the group changes and the p-value exactly as reported and does not quote that signed figure. All outcomes are caregiver-diary based in a population pre-selected for behavioural-intervention failure.

cards.headline: MENDS 2012: immediate-release melatonin got children to sleep 37.5 minutes faster and added 22.4 minutes of sleep — but they woke 29.9 minutes earlier too
cards.summary: MENDS (2012): immediate-release melatonin got children to sleep 37.5 minutes faster and added 22.4 minutes of sleep — but they woke 29.9 minutes earlier.
cards.type: Randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled phase III trial (12 weeks)
cards.people: 146 children aged 3 years to 15 years 8 months with a range of neurological and developmental disorders and a severe sleep problem that had not responded to a standardised sleep-behaviour advice booklet, at 19 hospitals in England and Wales, randomised to immediate-release melatonin (0.5 mg escalated through 2, 6 and 12 mg by response) or placebo 45 minutes before bedtime.
cards.result: Melatonin increased total night sleep by 22.4 minutes (95% CI 0.5 to 44.3) on parent sleep diaries (n=110) and by 13.3 minutes (−15.5 to 42.2, not significant) on actigraphy (n=59). Sleep onset latency fell by 37.5 minutes on diaries (−55.3 to −19.7) and 45.3 minutes on actigraphy (−68.8 to −21.9), most strongly in children with the longest baseline latency (P=0.009). Children on melatonin also woke 29.9 minutes earlier than on placebo (13.6 to 46.3). Behaviour and family-functioning outcomes favoured melatonin but did not significantly improve, per the authors; adverse events were mild and similar between groups. The authors conclude children gained little additional sleep, though they fell asleep significantly faster.
cards.watchOut: Diary and actigraphy disagree on the headline (22.4 minutes significant vs 13.3 not), doses escalated as high as 12 mg, and the earlier waking claws back much of the latency gain — the honest summary is 'falls asleep faster, sleeps a little longer', not 'sleeps through'. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.summary: Onset is the reliable win; total-sleep gains are real but small, and waking shifts earlier — LIKELY.
cards.type: Synthesis

shelves.title: Restless legs syndrome: alpha-2-delta ligands against the dopamine standard
shelves.question: Do pregabalin and gabapentin enacarbil relieve restless legs symptoms without the augmentation that collects on dopamine agonists — pregabalin head-to-head against pramipexole over a year, and gabapentin enacarbil against placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anticonvulsants/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Benzothiazoles/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Dopamine Agonists/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Pramipexole · Pregabalin · Restless Legs Syndrome/drug therapy · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind randomised trials establish the non-dopaminergic class. Pregabalin beat placebo over 12 weeks in the year-long Allen trial (719 participants; symptom-score improvement greater by 4.5 points, responders 71.4% vs 46.8%) and — the shelf's key comparison — produced significantly less augmentation over 40–52 weeks than pramipexole 0.5 mg (2.1% vs 7.7%; p=0.001), though not significantly less than pramipexole 0.25 mg (2.1% vs 5.3%; p=0.08). Gabapentin enacarbil beat placebo in its own trial (222 patients; symptom change −13.2 vs −8.8, adjusted difference −4.0 [95% CI −6.2 to −1.9]; responders 76.1% vs 38.9%, adjusted odds ratio 5.1 — a relative measure, printed with the absolute responder rates beside it). The costs are sedation-class effects: somnolence 27% vs 7% and dizziness 20% vs 5% on gabapentin enacarbil, and six cases of suicidal ideation in the pregabalin arm of Allen's trial (vs three and two in the pramipexole arms) belong on the shelf face. Iron therapy and dopamine-agonist augmentation as a harm are home on Shelf #498 and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Allen 2014: pregabalin beat placebo at 12 weeks and caused less augmentation than pramipexole 0.5 mg over a year (2.1% vs 7.7%)
cards.summary: Pregabalin trial (2014): beat placebo at 12 weeks and caused less augmentation than pramipexole 0.5 mg over a year ( 2.1% vs 7.7% ).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trial (52 weeks; placebo comparison over the first 12 weeks, augmentation comparison over 40–52 weeks)
cards.people: 719 patients with restless legs syndrome randomised to pregabalin 300 mg daily (182), pramipexole 0.25 mg (178), pramipexole 0.5 mg (180), or placebo for 12 weeks followed by 40 weeks of randomly assigned active treatment (179); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Over 12 weeks, pregabalin improved the International RLS Study Group Rating Scale score by 4.5 points more than placebo (P<0.001), and 71.4% vs 46.8% were very much or much improved (P<0.001). Augmentation over 40 or 52 weeks was significantly lower on pregabalin than on pramipexole 0.5 mg (2.1% vs 7.7%; P=0.001) but not significantly lower than pramipexole 0.25 mg (2.1% vs 5.3%; P=0.08). Six cases of suicidal ideation occurred in the pregabalin group, three in the pramipexole 0.25 mg group and two in the 0.5 mg group.
cards.watchOut: The augmentation advantage is dose-specific: it is proven against the higher pramipexole dose and only numerically present against the lower one, so the card does not generalise it to all dopamine-agonist dosing. The suicidal-ideation counts are small numbers printed as reported, without a significance claim in the abstract.

cards.headline: Kushida 2009: gabapentin enacarbil 1,200 mg beat placebo — symptom change −13.2 vs −8.8, responders 76.1% vs 38.9%; somnolence 27% vs 7%
cards.summary: Gabapentin enacarbil (2009): 1,200 mg beat placebo — symptom change −13.2 vs −8.8 , responders 76.1% vs 38.9%; somnolence 27% vs 7%.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (12 weeks; PIVOT RLS I)
cards.people: 222 adults with moderate-to-severe primary restless legs syndrome randomised to gabapentin enacarbil (XP13512/GSK1838262) 1,200 mg once daily (114) or placebo (108); 192 completed the study; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 12 the mean change in International Restless Legs Scale score was −13.2 on gabapentin enacarbil vs −8.8 on placebo (adjusted treatment difference −4.0; 95% CI −6.2 to −1.9; p=0.0003). Investigator-rated responders were 76.1% vs 38.9% (adjusted odds ratio 5.1; 95% CI 2.8 to 9.2; p<0.0001 — a relative measure, printed with the absolute responder rates beside it). Significant effects on both coprimary measures were present from week 1. The commonest adverse events were somnolence (27% vs 7%) and dizziness (20% vs 5%), mild to moderate and generally remitting.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks and a single dose: the trial says nothing about augmentation — the very outcome that motivates the class — because that harm emerges over the year-plus horizon only Allen's trial reaches. Enacarbil is a gabapentin prodrug; its results should not be silently transferred to ordinary gabapentin dosing.

shelves.title: A tuberculosis vaccine that half-worked: M72/AS01E
shelves.question: Does M72/AS01E vaccination prevent progression to active pulmonary tuberculosis in already-infected (IGRA-positive) adults?
shelves.mesh: Africa · Latent Tuberculosis/therapy · Mycobacterium tuberculosis/immunology · Proportional Hazards Models · Tuberculosis/prevention & control · Tuberculosis Vaccines/adverse effects,immunology · Disease Progression
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One phase 2b trial in IGRA-positive, HIV-negative adults in Kenya, South Africa and Zambia, reported at two pre-specified horizons: vaccine efficacy against bacteriologically confirmed active pulmonary tuberculosis was 54.0% at the primary analysis (10 vs 22 cases; incidence 0.3 vs 0.6 per 100 person-years) and 49.7% in the final 3-year analysis (13 vs 26 cases) — roughly halving progression, with wide confidence intervals (final 95% CI 2.1 to 74.2) built on only 39 cases in total. Injection-site and influenza-like reactions were more common on vaccine (67.4% vs 45.4% reported unsolicited adverse events); serious adverse events, potential immune-mediated diseases and deaths were similar. A single trial with a surrogate-adjacent endpoint (progression in already-infected adults) and few events caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; the phase 3 test is the missing rung.

cards.headline: M72/AS01E primary analysis 2018: vaccine efficacy 54.0% against active pulmonary tuberculosis in IGRA-positive adults (10 vs 22 cases)
cards.summary: M72/AS01E 2018: vaccine efficacy 54.0% against active pulmonary tuberculosis in IGRA-positive adults (10 vs 22 cases).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2b trial (primary analysis at a mean of 2.3 years)
cards.people: HIV-negative adults aged 18–50 years with latent M. tuberculosis infection (positive interferon-γ release assay), most previously BCG-vaccinated, in Kenya, South Africa and Zambia, assigned to two doses of M72/AS01E (1,786) or placebo (1,787) one month apart; the according-to-protocol efficacy cohort numbered 1,623 and 1,660. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Ten participants in the vaccine group met the primary case definition (bacteriologically confirmed active pulmonary tuberculosis) vs 22 in the placebo group (incidence 0.3 vs 0.6 cases per 100 person-years); vaccine efficacy was 54.0% (90% CI 13.9 to 75.4; 95% CI 2.9 to 78.2; P=0.04) — a relative measure with its absolute incidence printed. Results in the total vaccinated cohort were similar (efficacy 57.0%; P=0.03). Unsolicited adverse events within 30 days were more frequent on vaccine (67.4% vs 45.4%), mainly injection-site reactions and influenza-like symptoms; serious adverse events, potential immune-mediated diseases and deaths occurred with similar frequency.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-two endpoint cases in total carry the headline: the confidence interval runs from almost nothing (2.9%) to 78.2%, so 'about half' is a point estimate on a small event base, in already-infected adults only — it says nothing about preventing infection itself (that question is Shelf #984's).

cards.summary: Final analysis 2019: efficacy held at 49.7% at 3 years (13 vs 26 cases).
cards.type: Final (3-year) analysis of the same randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2b trial
cards.people: 3,575 participants underwent randomisation (3,573 received at least one dose; 3,330 received both doses); the according-to-protocol efficacy cohort numbered 3,289, followed for 3 years after the second dose, in the same three African countries.
cards.result: Thirteen of 1,626 participants in the vaccine group and 26 of 1,663 in the placebo group met the first case definition of active pulmonary tuberculosis (incidence 0.3 vs 0.6 cases per 100 person-years); vaccine efficacy at month 36 was 49.7% (90% CI 12.1 to 71.2; 95% CI 2.1 to 74.2) — a relative measure. cards.watchOut: The same trial at a later horizon — durability evidence, not independent confirmation; the event count (39 cases) and interval width are unchanged in character from the primary analysis.

shelves.title: BCG revaccination to prevent tuberculosis infection
shelves.question: Does revaccinating BCG in adolescents prevent sustained M. tuberculosis infection?
shelves.mesh: BCG Vaccine/administration & dosage,adverse effects,immunology · Immunization, Secondary/adverse effects,methods · Intention to Treat Analysis · Interferon-gamma Release Tests · Mycobacterium tuberculosis/immunology · Tuberculosis/blood,diagnosis,immunology,prevention & control · Vaccine Efficacy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference, on the larger trial's primary endpoint): The 2025 phase 2b trial (1,836 QFT-negative adolescents) tested exactly the endpoint the earlier trial had suggested — sustained QuantiFERON conversion — as its PRIMARY endpoint, and found no protection: sustained conversion in 62 of 871 BCG-revaccinated vs 59 of 849 placebo participants (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.48; vaccine efficacy −3.8%). The 2018 trial (990 adolescents) had found revaccination did not prevent initial QFT conversion (efficacy 20.1%, P=0.29) but reduced sustained conversion on a SECONDARY endpoint (efficacy 45.4%, P=0.03). When the definitive test of a secondary-endpoint signal returns a null on that very endpoint, the signal is read as refuted; the stamp is POSSIBLE for the null rather than LIKELY because both trials are modest in size and the endpoint is a laboratory definition of infection, not disease. Injection-site reactions were more common with revaccination in both trials. Distinct from Shelf #982 (M72/AS01E against progression to disease in already-infected adults).

shelves.title: Albuterol–budesonide rescue inhaler for asthma (MANDALA, BATURA)
shelves.question: In asthma, does as-needed albuterol–budesonide fixed-dose rescue reduce severe exacerbations versus as-needed albuterol alone — in moderate-to-severe disease (MANDALA) and in mild disease (BATURA)?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Albuterol/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Asthma/drug therapy · Budesonide/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Drug Combinations · Ethanolamines/therapeutic use · Formoterol Fumarate/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two large double-blind event-driven trials agree across severity. In uncontrolled moderate-to-severe asthma (MANDALA, 3,132 patients), the higher-dose combination (albuterol 180 µg / budesonide 160 µg) lowered the risk of a first severe exacerbation versus albuterol alone (hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.89 — a relative measure; the abstract reports no absolute event rates for MANDALA); the lower-dose combination did not reach significance (HR 0.84, 0.71 to 1.00; P=0.052). In mild asthma (BATURA, 2,516 participants), a severe exacerbation occurred in 5.1% on the combination versus 9.1% on albuterol alone in the on-treatment population (HR 0.53, 0.39 to 0.73, relative). Both headline hazard ratios sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library treats cautiously on its own; the stamp rests on two concordant randomised trials, not on either ratio alone.

cards.headline: MANDALA 2022: higher-dose albuterol–budesonide rescue cut severe exacerbations versus albuterol alone — hazard ratio 0.74; the lower dose missed significance (0.84)
cards.summary: MANDALA 2022: higher-dose albuterol–budesonide rescue cut severe exacerbations vs albuterol alone (hazard ratio 0.74 , relative; the abstract reports no absolute rates and the card says so); the lower dose missed.
cards.type: Multinational, phase 3, double-blind, randomised, event-driven trial
cards.people: 3,132 patients with uncontrolled moderate-to-severe asthma receiving inhaled glucocorticoid-containing maintenance therapy, randomised 1:1:1 to albuterol–budesonide 180/160 µg, albuterol–budesonide 180/80 µg, or albuterol 180 µg alone, all as rescue medication; 97% were 12 years of age or older. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The risk of a first severe asthma exacerbation was significantly lower, by 26% (relative), in the higher-dose combination group than in the albuterol-alone group (hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.89; P=0.001). The hazard ratio in the lower-dose combination group versus albuterol alone was 0.84 (95% CI 0.71 to 1.00; P=0.052) — not significant. The abstract reports no absolute exacerbation rates, so no absolute difference is printed here. The incidence of adverse events was similar in the three trial groups.
cards.watchOut: The headline hazard ratio of 0.74 is a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, and the abstract gives no absolute rates: the size of the benefit for an individual patient cannot be read off this card. Only the higher budesonide dose met its endpoint.

cards.summary: BATURA 2025: in mild asthma, as-needed albuterol–budesonide halved severe exacerbations ( 5.1% vs 9.1% ; hazard ratio 0.53).
cards.type: Fully virtual, decentralised, phase 3b, multicentre, double-blind, event-driven trial

shelves.title: Dupilumab in uncontrolled asthma: exacerbations (QUEST) and steroid dependence (VENTURE)
shelves.question: Does dupilumab reduce severe exacerbations in moderate-to-severe uncontrolled asthma (LIBERTY ASTHMA QUEST) — and can it let glucocorticoid-dependent patients cut their oral steroid dose without losing control (VENTURE)?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Asthmatic Agents/adverse effects,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Asthma/classification,drug therapy · Bronchodilator Agents/therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Eosinophilia/chemically induced
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials answer the two halves of the question. QUEST (1,902 patients) found an annualized severe-exacerbation rate of 0.46 on dupilumab 200 mg every 2 weeks versus 0.87 on matched placebo (a 47.7% lower rate, relative), with the largest effect in patients with blood eosinophils ≥300 per cubic millimeter (0.37 versus 1.08; 65.8% lower, relative). VENTURE (210 glucocorticoid-dependent patients) found a mean glucocorticoid dose reduction of −70.1% on dupilumab versus −41.9% on placebo, with exacerbations 59% lower (relative) despite the taper. Dupilumab for atopic dermatitis, nasal polyps and eosinophilic oesophagitis is carded on Shelves #374, #375 and #396 — those trials are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: QUEST 2018: dupilumab cut the annualized severe-exacerbation rate from 0.87 to 0.46 (200 mg dose) — a 47.7% lower rate, relative
cards.summary: QUEST 2018: dupilumab cut the annualized severe-exacerbation rate from 0.87 to 0.46 at the 200 mg dose (a 47.7% lower rate, relative).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (52 weeks)
cards.people: 1,902 patients 12 years of age or older with uncontrolled asthma, randomised 2:2:1:1 to add-on subcutaneous dupilumab 200 or 300 mg every 2 weeks or matched-volume placebos for 52 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The annualized rate of severe asthma exacerbations was 0.46 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.53) on dupilumab 200 mg and 0.87 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.05) on matched placebo — a 47.7% lower rate with dupilumab (relative; P<0.001); similar results were seen with the 300 mg dose. At week 12, FEV1 had increased by 0.32 liters on the lower dose (difference versus matched placebo 0.14 liters; P<0.001). Among patients with a blood eosinophil count of 300 or more per cubic millimeter, the annualized exacerbation rate was 0.37 (0.29 to 0.48) on lower-dose dupilumab versus 1.08 (0.85 to 1.38) on placebo (65.8% lower, relative; 95% CI 52.0 to 75.6). Blood eosinophilia occurred in 52 patients (4.1%) on dupilumab versus 4 (0.6%) on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The overall-population relative reduction (47.7%) sits just inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band's edge when expressed as a rate ratio (~0.52); the eosinophil-high subgroup drives the large effect, so the stamp is for uncontrolled asthma as trialled, with benefit concentrated in type-2-high disease.

cards.headline: VENTURE 2018: dupilumab let steroid-dependent patients cut oral glucocorticoids by 70.1% versus 41.9% — and still had 59% fewer exacerbations, relative
cards.summary: VENTURE 2018: dupilumab let steroid-dependent patients cut oral glucocorticoids by 70.1% vs 41.9% — and still had 59% fewer exacerbations (relative).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (24 weeks)
cards.people: 210 patients with oral glucocorticoid-treated asthma, randomised to add-on dupilumab 300 mg or placebo every 2 weeks for 24 weeks, with glucocorticoid doses tapered from week 4 to week 20. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The percentage change in glucocorticoid dose at week 24 was −70.1% on dupilumab versus −41.9% on placebo (P<0.001); 80% versus 50% had a dose reduction of at least 50%, 69% versus 33% reduced to less than 5 mg per day, and 48% versus 25% completely discontinued oral glucocorticoids. shelves.title: Omalizumab for severe allergic asthma (Busse; INNOVATE)
shelves.question: Does anti-IgE omalizumab reduce exacerbations and steroid use in severe allergic asthma inadequately controlled on inhaled therapy — in Busse's pivotal trial and in the INNOVATE programme in the most severe patients?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Allergic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Anti-Idiotypic · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Asthma/drug therapy · Immunoglobulin E/blood,immunology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials, in progressively more severe populations, agree. Busse 2001 (525 patients with inhaled-corticosteroid-dependent severe allergic asthma) found fewer exacerbations per subject on omalizumab than placebo in both the stable-steroid phase (0.28 versus 0.54) and the steroid-reduction phase (0.39 versus 0.66), with greater inhaled-steroid reduction (median 75% versus 50%). INNOVATE (419 patients inadequately controlled despite high-dose ICS-LABA) found an adjusted clinically significant exacerbation rate of 0.68 versus 0.91 (a 26% relative reduction; P=0.042) and a severe-exacerbation rate of 0.24 versus 0.48 (P=0.002). Effects are modest in relative terms and sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band; the stamp rests on two concordant randomised trials. Omalizumab for chronic urticaria and food allergy is carded on Shelves #398 and #395 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Busse 2001: omalizumab halved exacerbations per subject — 0.28 vs 0.54 in the stable-steroid phase, 0.39 vs 0.66 while steroids were tapered
cards.summary: Busse 2001: omalizumab halved exacerbations per subject ( 0.28 vs 0.54 in the stable-steroid phase; 0.39 vs 0.66 while steroids were tapered).
cards.type: Phase III, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: 525 subjects with severe allergic asthma requiring daily inhaled corticosteroids, randomised to subcutaneous omalizumab (every 2 or 4 weeks by baseline IgE and weight) or placebo; inhaled steroid doses were held stable for 16 weeks, then tapered over 12 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Omalizumab produced significantly fewer asthma exacerbations per subject than placebo during the stable steroid phase (0.28 versus 0.54; P=.006) and during the steroid-reduction phase (0.39 versus 0.66; P=.003); the percentages of subjects experiencing an exacerbation were 14.6% versus 23.3% (P=.009) and 21.3% versus 32.3% (P=.004) respectively. Beclomethasone dipropionate reduction was greater with omalizumab (median 75% versus 50%; P<.001) and discontinuation more likely (39.6% versus 19.1%; P<.001). Adverse events were similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: A 2001-era trial against the background therapy of its day, with exacerbation counts as means per subject rather than time-to-event rates; the relative effect (~0.52 as a ratio) sits at the edge of the 0.5–2.0 caution band.

cards.summary: INNOVATE 2005: in the most severe patients, severe exacerbations fell from 0.48 to 0.24 per patient; the adjusted-versus-unadjusted primary discrepancy is disclosed on the card.
cards.type: Double-blind, parallel-group, multicentre randomised trial (28 weeks)
cards.people: 419 patients aged 12–75 years with severe persistent asthma inadequately controlled despite high-dose inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting β2-agonists (GINA 2002 step 4), with reduced lung function and a recent history of clinically significant exacerbations, randomised to omalizumab or placebo for 28 weeks; 419 were included in the efficacy analyses. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The adjusted rate of clinically significant asthma exacerbations (primary variable) was 0.68 on omalizumab versus 0.91 on placebo — a 26% relative reduction (P=0.042); unadjusted, the reduction was 19% and not significant. Omalizumab significantly reduced the severe exacerbation rate (0.24 versus 0.48; P=0.002) and the emergency visit rate (0.24 versus 0.43; P=0.038), and improved quality of life, morning peak flow and symptom scores. Adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint reached significance only after adjustment for a baseline imbalance in exacerbation history — the unadjusted comparison was not significant — so the severe-exacerbation result (0.24 versus 0.48) is the sturdier figure on this card.
cards.source: Humbert M et al. shelves.title: Single-inhaler triple therapy in uncontrolled asthma (TRIMARAN, TRIGGER, IRIDIUM)
shelves.question: In asthma uncontrolled on medium- or high-dose ICS-LABA, does adding a long-acting muscarinic antagonist in the same inhaler improve lung function and exacerbations — in the beclometasone–formoterol–glycopyrronium trials (TRIMARAN, TRIGGER) and the indacaterol-based IRIDIUM trial?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Asthma/drug therapy · Beclomethasone/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Combinations · Formoterol Fumarate/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Glycopyrrolate/administration & dosage,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY for lung-function benefit; POSSIBLE for exacerbation reduction. Three large double-blind trials consistently improved pre-dose/trough FEV1 when a LAMA was added in the same inhaler: by 57 mL (TRIMARAN) and 73 mL (TRIGGER) versus beclometasone–formoterol, and by 65–76 mL (IRIDIUM) versus matched mometasone–indacaterol. The exacerbation evidence is thinner: moderate/severe exacerbation rates fell by 15% in relative terms in TRIMARAN (rate ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.99) but by a non-significant 12% in TRIGGER (0.88, 0.75 to 1.03), and IRIDIUM's primary endpoint was lung function, not exacerbations. Relative ratios of 0.85–0.88 sit well inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid on their own — hence POSSIBLE for that half of the claim.

cards.headline: TRIMARAN/TRIGGER 2019: adding glycopyrronium improved FEV1 by 57 and 73 mL; exacerbations fell 15% (relative, significant) and 12% (not significant)
cards.summary: TRIMARAN/TRIGGER 2019: adding glycopyrronium improved FEV1 by 57 and 73 mL ; exacerbations fell 15% (relative, significant) and 12% (not significant) — two trials reported in one paper, carded as one record.
cards.type: Two parallel-group, double-blind, randomised, active-controlled phase 3 trials (52 weeks)
cards.people: Adults 18–75 years with uncontrolled asthma and at least one exacerbation in the previous year: TRIMARAN enrolled 1,155 patients previously on medium-dose ICS-LABA (579 triple versus 576 dual); TRIGGER enrolled 1,437 patients previously on high-dose ICS-LABA (573 single-inhaler triple, 576 dual, 288 dual plus separate tiotropium). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Versus beclometasone–formoterol, week-26 pre-dose FEV1 improved with the triple by 57 mL (95% CI 15 to 99; p=0.0080) in TRIMARAN and 73 mL (26 to 120; p=0.0025) in TRIGGER. Reductions in the rate of moderate and severe exacerbations over 52 weeks were 15% (rate ratio 0.85, 0.73 to 0.99; p=0.033) in TRIMARAN and 12% (0.88, 0.75 to 1.03; p=0.11) in TRIGGER — both relative measures, and the TRIGGER result was not significant. Four patients had treatment-related serious adverse events across the two trials; deaths with adverse events numbered 3 in TRIMARAN's triple group and 2 in TRIGGER (one triple, one dual), as reported in the abstract.
cards.watchOut: Two trials reported in one paper, with the exacerbation co-primary met in only one of them; the FEV1 gains (57–73 mL) are statistically clear but small in absolute terms, and no absolute exacerbation rates are given in the abstract.
cards.source: Virchow JC et al. Single inhaler extrafine triple therapy in uncontrolled asthma (TRIMARAN and TRIGGER): two double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, controlled phase 3 trials. Lancet. 2019;394(10210):1737-1749. PMID: 31582314. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02676076 (TRIMARAN) and NCT02676089 (TRIGGER), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: IRIDIUM 2020: once-daily mometasone–indacaterol–glycopyrronium improved trough FEV1 by 65–76 mL versus mometasone–indacaterol
cards.summary: IRIDIUM 2020: once-daily mometasone–indacaterol–glycopyrronium improved trough FEV1 by 65–76 mL vs dual therapy.
cards.type: 52-week, double-blind, double-dummy, parallel-group, active-controlled phase 3 trial
cards.people: 3,092 patients aged 18 to 75 years with symptomatic asthma despite medium- or high-dose ICS-LABA, at least one exacerbation in the previous year and FEV1 below 80% predicted, randomised across five arms (medium- and high-dose triple, medium- and high-dose dual, and high-dose fluticasone–salmeterol); 2,747 (88.8%) completed 52 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 26, trough FEV1 improved more with medium-dose triple than medium-dose dual (treatment difference 76 mL, 95% CI 41 to 111; p<0.001) and with high-dose triple than high-dose dual (65 mL, 31 to 99; p<0.001); both triple doses also beat high-dose fluticasone–salmeterol (99 mL and 119 mL). cards.watchOut: IRIDIUM's primary endpoint was lung function at week 26, not exacerbations: it supports the FEV1 half of this shelf and says nothing carded here about exacerbation prevention.

shelves.title: Bronchial thermoplasty for severe asthma (AIR2, RISA)
shelves.question: In severe asthma uncontrolled on ICS-LABA, does bronchial thermoplasty reduce severe exacerbations and emergency visits versus a sham bronchoscopy procedure (AIR2) — at what cost in peri-procedure hospitalisations?
shelves.mesh: Asthma/diagnosis,surgery · Bronchi/surgery · Bronchial Hyperreactivity/surgery · Bronchoscopy · Electrocoagulation · Patient Readmission/statistics & numerical data · Postoperative Complications/diagnosis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One sham-controlled trial with a modest quality-of-life primary, one small unblinded safety trial. AIR2 (288 adults) found a superior improvement in integrated Asthma Quality of Life Questionnaire score with thermoplasty versus sham (1.35 versus 1.16; posterior probability of superiority 96.0% in the intention-to-treat analysis), with fewer severe exacerbations, emergency department visits and days missed in the post-treatment period — but 6% more thermoplasty subjects were hospitalised during the treatment period (up to 6 weeks after the procedure). RISA (32 subjects) likewise found transient worsening and 7 hospitalisations in 4 of 15 treated subjects during treatment, against later improvements in rescue-medication use and asthma control. A single sham-controlled trial with Bayesian analysis and a peri-procedure harm signal caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: AIR2 2010: thermoplasty beat sham on quality of life (1.35 vs 1.16 AQLQ improvement) and later healthcare use — but hospitalised 6% more patients around the procedure
cards.summary: AIR2 2010: thermoplasty beat sham on quality of life (AQLQ improvement 1.35 vs 1.16) and later healthcare use — but hospitalised 6% more patients around the procedures.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled trial (three bronchoscopy procedures)
cards.people: 288 adult subjects with severe asthma remaining symptomatic despite high-dose inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting β2-agonists, randomised to bronchial thermoplasty or sham control (intention-to-treat). The abstract does not state the arm sizes, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The improvement in integrated Asthma Quality of Life Questionnaire score (average of 6, 9 and 12 months) was superior with thermoplasty (1.35 ± 1.10) versus sham (1.16 ± 1.23); posterior probability of superiority 96.0% (intention-to-treat) and 97.9% (per protocol); 79% of thermoplasty versus 64% of sham subjects achieved an AQLQ change of 0.5 or greater. Six percent more thermoplasty subjects were hospitalised in the treatment period (up to 6 weeks after the procedure). In the post-treatment period (6–52 weeks), the thermoplasty group experienced fewer severe exacerbations, emergency department visits and days missed from work/school (posterior probabilities of superiority 95.5, 99.9 and 99.3 respectively) — the abstract reports these as probabilities, without absolute event rates, so none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a quality-of-life score analysed with a Bayesian design, and the sham group itself improved by 1.16 points — a large sham effect. The exacerbation and emergency-visit benefits are reported without absolute rates in the abstract, and they were bought with more peri-procedure hospitalisations.
cards.source: Castro M et al. Effectiveness and safety of bronchial thermoplasty in the treatment of severe asthma: a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled clinical trial. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2010;181(2):116-124. PMID: 19815809. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00231114, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: RISA 2007: thermoplasty worsened asthma transiently (7 hospitalisations in 4 of 15 treated subjects), then improved control measures to 52 weeks
cards.summary: RISA 2007: transient worsening first (7 hospitalisations in 4 of 15 treated subjects), then improved control measures to 52 weeks.
cards.type: Randomised controlled safety and efficacy trial (unblinded control group)
cards.people: Adults symptomatic despite fluticasone (or equivalent) above 750 µg/day, a long-acting β2-agonist and other medications, randomised to bronchial thermoplasty (15 subjects) or control (17 subjects), followed through steroid-stable, steroid-wean and reduced-steroid phases to 52 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: During the treatment period, 7 hospitalisations for respiratory symptoms occurred in 4 of 15 thermoplasty subjects (5 within 3 days of treatment; 2 subjects had segmental collapse of the most recently treated lobe, one requiring bronchoscopy and aspiration of a mucus plug), versus no hospitalisations in the 17 control subjects; post-treatment hospitalisation rates were similar. At 22 weeks, thermoplasty subjects had significantly better rescue-medication use (−26.6 ± 40.1 versus −1.5 ± 11.7 puffs per 7 days; P<0.05), prebronchodilator FEV1% predicted (14.9 ± 17.4 versus −0.94 ± 22.3%; P=0.04) and Asthma Control Questionnaire scores (−1.04 ± 1.03 versus −0.13 ± 1.00; P=0.02), with rescue-medication and control-score differences maintained at 52 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-two subjects and no sham or blinding: RISA is a safety/feasibility signal, not efficacy proof, and its peri-procedure hospitalisation pattern (7 events in 15 treated subjects) is the harm half of this shelf.

shelves.title: Benralizumab for eosinophilic COPD exacerbations (GALATHEA, TERRANOVA, ABRA)
shelves.question: In COPD with eosinophilic inflammation and frequent exacerbations, does benralizumab prevent COPD exacerbations (the twin GALATHEA and TERRANOVA trials, both null) — and does a single dose help during an acute eosinophilic exacerbation (ABRA)?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Asthmatic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Eosinophils/metabolism · Injections, Subcutaneous · Leukocyte Count · Patient Acuity · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/drug therapy,immunology
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for maintenance prevention; POSSIBLE for acute treatment. GALATHEA and TERRANOVA — two parallel randomised trials of benralizumab added to inhaled therapy in frequent exacerbators with eosinophils ≥220 per cubic millimeter — found no significant reduction in the annualized exacerbation rate at any dose (rate ratios 0.83 to 1.04 across doses, all non-significant at week 56 in the primary population): two concordant nulls carry LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). ABRA, a single phase 2 trial (158 patients) of one 100 mg dose at an acute eosinophilic exacerbation of asthma or COPD, found treatment failure over 90 days in 45% of the pooled benralizumab groups versus 74% on prednisolone alone (odds ratio 0.26, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.56 — a relative measure) — promising, but one small mixed-disease trial, so POSSIBLE. Benralizumab for severe eosinophilic asthma is carded on Shelf #813 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: GALATHEA/TERRANOVA 2019: benralizumab did not significantly reduce COPD exacerbations at any dose — rate ratios 0.83 to 1.04, all non-significant
cards.summary: GALATHEA/TERRANOVA 2019: benralizumab did not significantly reduce COPD exacerbations at any dose (rate ratios 0.83–1.04, all non-significant) — twin trials in one report, carded as one record.
cards.type: Two parallel randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (56 weeks)
cards.people: Patients with moderate to very severe COPD and frequent exacerbations despite guideline-based inhaled treatment, enrolled at an approximately 2:1 ratio by eosinophil count (≥220 versus <220 per cubic millimeter); benralizumab doses were 30 or 100 mg (GALATHEA) and 10, 30 or 100 mg (TERRANOVA) every 8 weeks (every 4 weeks for the first three doses) versus placebo. The abstract does not state the total sample size, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the primary population (eosinophils ≥220 per cubic millimeter), annualized exacerbation rates in GALATHEA were 1.19 per year (30 mg), 1.03 (100 mg) and 1.24 (placebo), giving rate ratios versus placebo of 0.96 (P=0.65) and 0.83 (P=0.05); in TERRANOVA the rates were 0.99 (10 mg), 1.21 (30 mg), 1.09 (100 mg) and 1.17 (placebo), with rate ratios 0.85 (P=0.06), 1.04 (P=0.66) and 0.93 (P=0.40) — all relative measures. At 56 weeks, none of the rate ratios for any dose in either trial reached significance. Adverse events were similar between benralizumab and placebo.
cards.watchOut: The 100 mg GALATHEA result (rate ratio 0.83, P=0.05) is the closest approach to significance and it still does not cross it, in a programme with multiple doses and two trials — exactly the pattern this library reads as a null, not as a near-miss benefit.
cards.source: Criner GJ et al. Benralizumab for the Prevention of COPD Exacerbations. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(11):1023-1034. PMID: 31112385. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02138916 (GALATHEA) and NCT02155660 (TERRANOVA), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: ABRA 2025: one benralizumab injection at an acute eosinophilic exacerbation cut 90-day treatment failure to 45% vs 74% on prednisolone alone
cards.summary: ABRA 2025 (carded from the sweep): one benralizumab injection at an acute eosinophilic exacerbation cut 90-day treatment failure to 45% vs 74% on prednisolone alone.
cards.type: Multicentre, phase 2, double-blind, double-dummy, active placebo-controlled randomised trial
cards.people: 158 adults with blood eosinophils of 300 cells per microliter or more, recruited at the time of an acute exacerbation of asthma or COPD at two UK hospital groups, randomised 1:1:1 to benralizumab 100 mg once plus prednisolone 30 mg for 5 days (52), benralizumab alone (53), or prednisolone alone (53); 86 (54%) were female and 72 (46%) male, mean age 57 years (range 18–84).
cards.result: At 90 days, treatment failures occurred in 47 of 105 patients (45%) in the pooled benralizumab groups versus 39 of 53 (74%) on prednisolone alone (odds ratio 0.26, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.56; p=0.0005 — a relative measure, beside the absolute rates of 45% and 74%). The 28-day total visual-analogue-scale symptom difference was 49 mm (95% CI 14 to 84; p=0.0065) favouring pooled benralizumab. There were no fatal adverse events; hyperglycaemia and sinusitis/sinus infection adverse events were related to the prednisolone study drug only.
cards.watchOut: A single phase 2 trial mixing asthma and COPD exacerbations (no COPD-only result is given in the abstract), with an unusually high 74% failure rate in the prednisolone arm: the concept is promising, the COPD-specific claim is not yet isolated — hence POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.

shelves.title: Combination voriconazole plus anidulafungin for invasive aspergillosis (Marr)
shelves.question: In invasive aspergillosis, does adding anidulafungin to voriconazole improve survival versus voriconazole alone — overall, and in the galactomannan-diagnosed subgroup?
shelves.mesh: Anidulafungin · Antifungal Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Aspergillosis/complications,diagnosis,drug therapy,mortality · Drug Therapy, Combination · Echinocandins/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Galactose/analogs & derivatives · Hematologic Neoplasms/complications,therapy
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality outcome with a subgroup-driven reading): The single randomised trial (Marr 2015, 277 patients in the primary analysis) missed its primary outcome: 6-week mortality was 19.3% with combination therapy versus 27.5% with voriconazole alone (difference −8.2 percentage points, 95% CI −19.0 to 1.5; P=0.087 — not significant). The favourable reading rests on a POST HOC analysis of the dominant galactomannan-diagnosed subgroup (15.7% vs 27.3%; P=0.037). A non-significant primary outcome plus a post hoc subgroup is the definition of weak evidence on this library's scale: MAYBE (weak evidence) that combination therapy helps, and the trial was underpowered by its authors' own account.

cards.headline: Marr 2015: combination therapy did not significantly reduce 6-week mortality overall (19.3% vs 27.5%; P=0.087); the positive signal was confined to a post hoc galactomannan subgroup
cards.summary: Marr (2015): combination voriconazole + anidulafungin did not significantly reduce 6-week mortality overall ( 19.3% vs 27.5% ; P=0.087); the positive signal was confined to a post hoc subgroup.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial (93 international sites)
cards.people: 454 patients with haematological malignancy or haematopoietic cell transplantation and suspected or documented invasive aspergillosis, randomised to voriconazole plus anidulafungin or voriconazole plus placebo; the primary (modified intention-to-treat) analysis covered 277 patients with confirmed invasive aspergillosis, of whom 218 (78.7%) were diagnosed by radiographic findings and maximum galactomannan positivity. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mortality at 6 weeks was 19.3% (26 of 135) for combination therapy and 27.5% (39 of 142) for monotherapy (difference −8.2 percentage points, 95% CI −19.0 to 1.5; P=0.087 — not significant). Secondary mortality outcomes favoured combination therapy. In a post hoc analysis of the galactomannan-diagnosed subgroup, 6-week mortality was 15.7% (17 of 108) versus 27.3% (30 of 110) (difference −11.5 percentage points, 95% CI −22.7 to −0.4; P=0.037). Safety measures, including hepatotoxicity, did not differ. The authors state that mortality was higher than expected and the treatment difference lower than expected, reducing power, and that limitations in power preclude definitive conclusions about superiority.
cards.watchOut: The headline subgroup is explicitly post hoc — chosen after the data were seen — inside a trial that missed its primary endpoint; treating it as proven benefit would repeat the classic subgroup error. This is the card the Tier C flag exists for.

shelves.title: Cefiderocol for Gram-negative infection (APEKS-NP and CREDIBLE-CR)
shelves.question: Is cefiderocol non-inferior to high-dose extended-infusion meropenem for Gram-negative nosocomial pneumonia — and how does its mortality record in the CREDIBLE-CR trial of carbapenem-resistant infections read beside it?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Cephalosporins/therapeutic use · Gram-Negative Bacterial Infections/drug therapy · Healthcare-Associated Pneumonia/drug therapy · Meropenem/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Pneumonia, Bacterial/drug therapy,microbiology · Cefiderocol
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality outcomes on both cards): In APEKS-NP (300 randomised patients with Gram-negative nosocomial pneumonia), cefiderocol was non-inferior to high-dose extended-infusion meropenem on day-14 all-cause mortality (12.4% vs 11.6%; adjusted difference 0.8%, 95% CI −6.6 to 8.2, against a 12.5% margin). In CREDIBLE-CR — a descriptive, non-powered randomised trial in carbapenem-resistant infections — clinical cure was similar to best available therapy, but more patients died on cefiderocol (34% vs 18% by end of study), driven by the Acinetobacter subset, as the record itself reports. One non-inferiority trial plus an unresolved mortality imbalance caps at POSSIBLE, and the imbalance is why this shelf is Tier C.

cards.headline: APEKS-NP 2021: cefiderocol was non-inferior to meropenem for Gram-negative nosocomial pneumonia (day-14 mortality 12.4% vs 11.6%)
cards.summary: APEKS-NP (2021): cefiderocol non-inferior to meropenem for Gram-negative nosocomial pneumonia (day-14 mortality 12.4% vs 11.6% ).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, phase 3, non-inferiority trial (76 centres, 17 countries)
cards.people: 300 adults with hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated or healthcare-associated Gram-negative pneumonia randomised to cefiderocol 2 g (148) or meropenem 2 g (152), each as 3-hour infusions every 8 hours for 7–14 days, with open-label linezolid for at least 5 days in both arms; 292 patients formed the modified intention-to-treat population, of whom 251 (86%) had a qualifying Gram-negative pathogen (Klebsiella pneumoniae 32%, Pseudomonas aeruginosa 16%, Acinetobacter baumannii 16%, Escherichia coli 14%), 175 (60%) were mechanically ventilated and 199 (68%) were in intensive care. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: All-cause mortality at day 14 was 12.4% with cefiderocol (18 of 145) and 11.6% with meropenem (17 of 146) (adjusted treatment difference 0.8%, 95% CI −6.6 to 8.2; p=0.002 for the non-inferiority hypothesis against a 12.5% margin). Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported in 130 (88%) of 148 versus 129 (86%) of 150 patients; two participants (1%) in each group discontinued because of drug-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority on a 12.5% mortality margin in about 290 analysed patients is compatible with cefiderocol being several points worse; the comparator (high-dose extended-infusion meropenem) is also not the drug these resistant pathogens usually force clinicians to abandon.
cards.source: Wunderink RG et al. cards.headline: CREDIBLE-CR 2021: cure rates were similar to best available therapy, but deaths were numerically more frequent on cefiderocol (34% vs 18%), concentrated in Acinetobacter infections
cards.summary: CREDIBLE-CR (2021): cure rates similar to best available therapy, but deaths numerically more frequent on cefiderocol ( 34% vs 18% ), concentrated in Acinetobacter.
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, multicentre, pathogen-focused, DESCRIPTIVE phase 3 trial (95 hospitals, 16 countries) — not a powered non-inferiority test
cards.people: 152 adults with serious carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative infections (nosocomial pneumonia, bloodstream infection or sepsis, or complicated urinary tract infection) randomised 2:1 to cefiderocol (101) or best available therapy (51, pre-specified by the investigator, up to three drugs); 150 received treatment. In the carbapenem-resistant microbiological intention-to-treat population (118 patients), pathogens were Acinetobacter baumannii (46%), Klebsiella pneumoniae (33%) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (19%). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Clinical cure at test of cure for nosocomial pneumonia was 20 (50%, 95% CI 33.8 to 66.2) of 40 on cefiderocol versus 10 (53%, 28.9 to 75.6) of 19 on best available therapy; for bloodstream infection or sepsis, 10 (43%, 23.2 to 65.5) of 23 versus 6 (43%, 17.7 to 71.1) of 14; microbiological eradication in complicated UTI was 9 (53%, 27.8 to 77.0) of 17 versus 1 (20%, 0.5 to 71.6) of 5. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 91% (92 of 101) versus 96% (47 of 49). By the end of the study, 34 (34%) of 101 patients on cefiderocol and 9 (18%) of 49 on best available therapy had died; one death (in the best-therapy group) was considered related to study drug. The authors state the excess deaths occurred primarily in the subset with Acinetobacter spp infections.
cards.watchOut: Descriptive by design — no powered hypothesis, small pathogen subsets, and an open-label heterogeneous comparator — so the mortality imbalance is a warning signal, not a proven harm; but it has never been randomised away either, and it is the reason this shelf carries a Tier C flag.

cards.headline: Synthesis: non-inferior for pneumonia against meropenem; an unresolved Acinetobacter mortality warning from the carbapenem-resistant trial — POSSIBLE, Tier C
cards.summary: Synthesis: non-inferior for pneumonia against meropenem; an unresolved Acinetobacter mortality warning from the carbapenem-resistant trial — POSSIBLE (Tier C).
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: APEKS-NP 2021 (300 randomised, pneumonia) and CREDIBLE-CR 2021 (152 randomised, carbapenem-resistant infections).
cards.result: The two trials answer different halves of the cefiderocol question: APEKS-NP supports it as a meropenem-equivalent option for Gram-negative nosocomial pneumonia (day-14 mortality 12.4% vs 11.6%), while CREDIBLE-CR's similar cure rates came with 34% versus 18% mortality, concentrated in Acinetobacter. Sulbactam–durlobactam for that same Acinetobacter complex is Shelf #1082 — cross-referenced, not re-carded. The currency sweep's GAME CHANGER bloodstream-infection trial (PMID 41067237) is fenced here as the next test to watch. The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Do not average the two trials into reassurance: the population where cefiderocol is most needed (carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter) is exactly where its record is weakest.

shelves.title: Ensitrelvir for mild-to-moderate COVID-19 (SCORPIO-SR, SCORPIO-HR)
shelves.question: Does the oral 3CL-protease inhibitor ensitrelvir shorten symptom resolution in mild-to-moderate COVID-19 versus placebo — in the Japanese SCORPIO-SR trial and in the global SCORPIO-HR trial?
shelves.mesh: COVID-19 · Drugs, Chinese Herbal · Indazoles · SARS-CoV-2 · Triazines · Triazoles · Antiviral Agents/therapeutic use,adverse effects
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — symptom shortening in SCORPIO-SR · POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) in SCORPIO-HR. SCORPIO-SR (1,030 patients in the primary analysis population, treated within 72 hours of onset in Japan, Vietnam and South Korea) found 125-mg ensitrelvir shortened time to resolution of five characteristic Omicron symptoms by about 1 day of median time (167.9 vs 192.2 hours; P=0.04). SCORPIO-HR (2,093 non-hospitalised adults globally; 1,888 treated within 3 days) found NO significant difference in time to sustained resolution of 15 symptoms (12.5 vs 13.1 days; difference −0.6 days, 95% CI −1.38 to 0.19; P=0.14), despite clear antiviral activity (day-4 viral RNA reduced by 0.72 log10 more; negative cultures 95.5% vs 75.0%). Symptom-resolution outcomes only — no mortality claim, not Tier C. The split is the honest summary: a modest symptom benefit in one population and endpoint definition, not reproduced in the other.

cards.headline: SCORPIO-SR 2024: ensitrelvir 125 mg shortened time to resolution of five COVID-19 symptoms by about 1 day in patients treated within 72 hours
cards.summary: SCORPIO-SR (2024): ensitrelvir 125 mg shortened time to resolution of five COVID-19 symptoms by about 1 day when treated within 72 hours.
cards.type: Phase 3 part of a phase 2/3, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial (92 institutions, Japan, Vietnam, South Korea)
cards.people: 1,821 patients aged 12 to under 70 years with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 within 120 hours of a positive test were randomised to ensitrelvir 125 mg (375 mg day 1), ensitrelvir 250 mg (750 mg day 1) or placebo for 5 days; the primary analysis population (randomised within 72 hours of onset) comprised 1,030 patients (347, 340 and 343 per group; mean age 35.2 [SD 12.3] years; 552 [53.6%] men).
cards.result: A significant difference was observed between the 125-mg ensitrelvir group and placebo for time to resolution of the composite of five characteristic Omicron symptoms (P=0.04, Peto-Prentice generalised Wilcoxon test); the difference in median time was approximately 1 day (167.9 vs 192.2 hours; difference −24.3 hours, 95% CI −78.7 to 11.7 hours — the confidence interval for the median difference crosses zero despite the rank-test significance). Adverse events occurred in 267 of 604 (44.2%) on 125 mg, 321 of 599 (53.6%) on 250 mg and 150 of 605 (24.8%) on placebo, most visibly a decrease in high-density lipoprotein (31.1%, 38.6% and 3.8% respectively). No treatment-related serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: The headline significance comes from a rank test while the median-difference interval crosses zero; the population was young (mean age 35), Asian, and treated in the Omicron era — the authors themselves state generalisability outside Asia should be confirmed, which SCORPIO-HR then tested.
cards.source: Yotsuyanagi H et al. Efficacy and Safety of 5-Day Oral Ensitrelvir for Patients With Mild to Moderate COVID-19: The SCORPIO-SR Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Network Open. 2024 Feb 5;7(2):e2354991. PMID: 38335000. Registry ID: Japan Registry of Clinical Trials jRCT2031210350, stated in the record's abstract and databank fields.

cards.headline: SCORPIO-HR 2025: ensitrelvir did NOT significantly shorten sustained symptom resolution globally (12.5 vs 13.1 days; P=0.14), despite clear antiviral activity
cards.summary: SCORPIO-HR (2025): ensitrelvir did NOT significantly shorten sustained symptom resolution globally ( 12.5 vs 13.1 days ; P=0.14), despite clear antiviral activity.
cards.type: Global, phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: 2,093 non-hospitalised adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 and symptom onset within 5 days, randomised 1:1 to ensitrelvir (375 mg day 1, then 125 mg days 2–5) or placebo; 1,888 started treatment within 3 days of onset (the primary-endpoint population). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean time to sustained (at least 2 days) resolution of 15 COVID-19 symptoms was 12.5 days on ensitrelvir and 13.1 days on placebo (difference −0.6 days, 95% CI −1.38 to 0.19; P=0.14 — not significant). On day 4, ensitrelvir reduced viral RNA by 0.72 log10 copies/mL more than placebo (95% CI 0.55 to 0.90), and among culture-positive participants 274 of 287 (95.5%) on ensitrelvir versus 210 of 280 (75.0%) on placebo had negative cultures on day 4; RNA rebound was similar (under 1.5%). Adverse events were similar (61.5% vs 60.6%); no treatment-related serious adverse events or deaths occurred, and COVID-19 hospitalisations by day 29 were 3 (0.3%) versus 1 (0.1%).
cards.watchOut: A larger, global, null trial outweighs a smaller positive one on the same drug class question — but the endpoint definitions differed (5 symptoms vs sustained resolution of 15), so the split stamp, not a single verdict, is the accurate record.

shelves.title: Ramelteon for chronic insomnia
shelves.question: In adults with chronic primary insomnia, does ramelteon (4–16 mg) reduce latency to persistent sleep and improve total sleep time versus placebo?
