shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled five-period crossover trial (Erman 2006, 107 adults with chronic primary insomnia, each patient receiving placebo and ramelteon 4, 8, 16 and 32 mg in sequence) found every tested dose significantly reduced latency to persistent sleep and significantly increased total sleep time versus placebo, with no next-day residual effects and no excess adverse events. The stamp is POSSIBLE, not higher: this is a single crossover trial, the abstract prints no effect sizes in minutes for either outcome, and the topic question's dose range (4–16 mg) understates the range actually tested (4–32 mg) — the discrepancy is disclosed on the card. The Roth et al. ramelteon trials named in the topic draft were not pinned to verified records at build and are fenced without figures.

cards.headline: Erman 2006: ramelteon at 4–32 mg significantly shortened latency to persistent sleep and increased total sleep time versus placebo in a 107-patient crossover trial — with no effect sizes printed in the abstract
cards.summary: Erman 2006: ramelteon at 4–32 mg significantly shortened latency to persistent sleep and increased total sleep time versus placebo in a 107-patient crossover trial — with no effect sizes printed in the abstract
cards.type: Randomized, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled, five-period crossover study
cards.people: 107 patients aged 18–64 years with chronic primary insomnia, randomised to a dosing sequence comprising ramelteon 4, 8, 16 and 32 mg and placebo; every patient received all five treatments with a 5- to 12-day washout between treatments and served as their own control. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: All tested doses of ramelteon resulted in statistically significant reductions in latency to persistent sleep and increases in total sleep time versus placebo, measured polysomnographically; the abstract prints no numerical values for either outcome, so none are carded. No next-day residual effects were apparent at any dose on visual analog scales, digit symbol substitution, word-list memory or post-sleep questionnaire. There were no differences in the number or type of adverse events between any active treatment and placebo; the most common were headache, somnolence and sore throat.
cards.watchOut: A crossover design in 107 patients with significance claimed but no magnitudes printed: the size of the sleep-latency benefit cannot be judged from this record, and the shelf question's stated 4–16 mg range does not match the 4–32 mg range the trial actually tested.
cards.source: Erman M et al. An efficacy, safety, and dose-response study of Ramelteon in patients with chronic primary insomnia. Sleep medicine. 2006. PMID: 16309958. shelves.title: Low-dose doxepin for insomnia
shelves.question: In adults with chronic primary insomnia, does low-dose doxepin (3–6 mg) improve sleep maintenance (wake after sleep onset) versus placebo without next-day sedation?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Chronic Disease · Double-Blind Method · Doxepin · Female · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives · Male · Middle Aged · Polysomnography · Sleep · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders · Substance Withdrawal Syndrome · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 35-day sleep-laboratory trial (Krystal 2011, 221 adults with chronic primary insomnia) found doxepin 3 mg and 6 mg significantly improved wake after sleep onset on nights 1, 15 and 29, latency to persistent sleep on night 1, and total sleep time across the study, with no significant next-day residual effects, no rebound insomnia on discontinuation, and safety comparable to placebo. A single (well-conducted) trial earns POSSIBLE. The topic draft attributed this trial to Scharf et al.; the record's first author is Krystal AD — corrected on the card. The elderly doxepin programme named in the draft was not pinned to a verified record at build and is fenced without figures.

cards.headline: Krystal 2011: doxepin 3 mg and 6 mg significantly improved wake after sleep onset, latency to persistent sleep and total sleep time over 35 days, with no next-day residual effects
cards.summary: Krystal 2011: doxepin 3 mg and 6 mg significantly improved wake after sleep onset, latency to persistent sleep and total sleep time over 35 days, with no next-day residual effects
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled sleep laboratory trial (35 days, with 2 single-blind placebo discontinuation nights)
cards.people: 221 adults meeting DSM-IV-TR criteria for primary insomnia, randomised to nightly doxepin 3 mg (n=75), doxepin 6 mg (n=73) or placebo (n=73) for 35 days. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, doxepin 3 and 6 mg significantly improved wake time after sleep onset on night 1 (both P<0.0001), night 15 (3 mg P=0.0025; 6 mg P=0.0009) and night 29 (3 mg P=0.0248; 6 mg P=0.0009); latency to persistent sleep on night 1 (3 mg P=0.0047; 6 mg P=0.0007); and total sleep time on night 1 (both P<0.0001), night 15 (6 mg P=0.0035) and night 29 (3 mg P=0.0261; 6 mg P<0.0001). Sleep efficiency in the final quarter of the night improved significantly on nights 1, 15 and 29 except for 3 mg on night 29 (P=0.0691). The abstract prints P values rather than minute-level effect sizes, so no magnitudes are carded. Discontinuation rates were low, safety profiles were comparable across groups, there were no significant next-day residual effects, no spontaneous reports of memory impairment, complex sleep behaviours, anticholinergic effects, weight gain or increased appetite, and no rebound insomnia after discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: The topic draft named the wrong first author (Scharf); the verified record is Krystal et al. Efficacy is reported as significance levels without absolute minute differences in the abstract, and the population is adults — the separate elderly programme is not evidence on this shelf.
cards.source: Krystal AD et al. Efficacy and safety of doxepin 3 and 6 mg in a 35-day sleep laboratory trial in adults with chronic primary insomnia. Sleep. 2011. PMID: 21966075. shelves.title: Aerobic exercise for chronic primary insomnia
shelves.question: In adults with chronic primary insomnia, does a programme of moderate aerobic exercise improve sleep quality (PSQI), sleep latency and sleep efficiency versus a non-exercise control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Affect · Chronic Disease · Circadian Rhythm · Exercise · Exercise Therapy · Female · Health Status · Humans · Male · Medical Records · Middle Aged · Patient Dropouts · Polysomnography · Quality of Life · Sedentary Behavior · Sleep · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The pinned trial (Passos 2011) randomised only 19 sedentary adults with chronic primary insomnia — and it randomised them to morning versus late-afternoon exercise, NOT to exercise versus a non-exercise control; every sleep figure on the card is a before-and-after change pooled across the two timing groups. Polysomnography showed sleep onset latency falling from 17.1 to 8.7 minutes, wake after sleep onset from 63.2 to 40.1 minutes, and sleep efficiency rising from 79.8% to 87.2% after 6 months of moderate aerobic exercise, with no difference by time of day. A 19-person pre–post comparison inside a timing trial cannot answer the question as posed (exercise versus no exercise) at better than MAYBE (weak evidence). The Reid et al. 2010 trial named in the topic draft was not pinned to a verified record at build and is fenced without figures.

cards.headline: Passos 2011: after 6 months of aerobic exercise, polysomnographic sleep latency halved (17.1 to 8.7 min) — in 19 patients, with no non-exercise control group
cards.summary: Passos 2011: after 6 months of aerobic exercise, polysomnographic sleep latency halved (17.1 to 8.7 min) — in 19 patients, with no non-exercise control group
cards.type: Randomised trial of exercise TIMING (morning vs late afternoon) with pooled pre–post sleep outcomes — not an exercise-versus-control trial
cards.people: 19 sedentary individuals with chronic primary insomnia, mean age 45.0 (SE 1.9) years, who completed a 6-month moderate aerobic exercise training protocol, randomised to morning or late-afternoon exercise groups. The abstract does not state the sex mix or the numbers per timing group.
cards.result: Combining polysomnographic data across both timing groups, sleep onset latency fell from 17.1 (SE 2.6) min to 8.7 (SE 1.4) min (P<0.01), wake time after sleep onset fell from 63.2 (SE 12.8) min to 40.1 (SE 6.0) min, and sleep efficiency rose from 79.8 (SE 3.0)% to 87.2 (SE 1.6)% following exercise. Sleep diaries showed improved sleep quality (41.5% to 59.4%) and feeling rested in the morning (50.8% to 65.1%); the diary sleep-latency line is printed in the abstract as changing from 76.2 (SE 21.5) min to 80.3 (SE 7.4) min while being described as an improvement — an internal inconsistency in the record, carded as printed. Some quality-of-life measures improved and Profile of Mood States tension-anxiety, depression and total mood disturbance scores fell. There were generally no significant differences between morning and late-afternoon exercise.
cards.watchOut: The shelf question asks exercise versus a non-exercise control; this trial has no such arm — its randomisation was timing only, so the sleep gains are uncontrolled before-and-after changes vulnerable to time, expectation and regression to the mean. The diary-latency figures as printed (76.2 rising to 80.3 min, labelled an improvement) contradict themselves and should not be quoted.
cards.source: Passos GS et al. Effects of moderate aerobic exercise training on chronic primary insomnia. Sleep medicine. 2011. PMID: 22019457. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Valerian for insomnia
shelves.question: In adults with insomnia, does valerian extract improve self-rated sleep quality versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Humans · Internet · Middle Aged · Patient Education as Topic · Placebos · Plant Extracts · Plant Preparations · Research Design · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders · Television · Treatment Outcome · Valerian
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): One internet-based randomised double-blind trial (Oxman 2007, 405 adults with insomnia in Norway) MISSED its primary outcome: a minimally important improvement in self-reported sleep quality occurred in 29% on valerian versus 21% on placebo (difference 7.5%, 95% CI −0.9 to 15.9; P=0.08 — not significant). A secondary global self-assessment favoured valerian by 5.5 percentage points (P=0.04), with similar non-significant trends for night awakenings and sleep duration, and no important adverse-event differences. The topic draft's 'modest improvement' framing rests on the secondary outcomes; the primary-outcome null governs the stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Oxman 2007: valerian did not significantly improve sleep quality on the primary outcome (29% vs 21%; P=0.08); a secondary global rating favoured it (P=0.04)
cards.summary: Oxman 2007: valerian did not significantly improve sleep quality on the primary outcome (29% vs 21%; P=0.08); a secondary global rating favoured it (P=0.04)
cards.type: Televised, web-based randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Norway; 2-week run-in, 2 weeks of treatment)
cards.people: 405 participants aged 18 to 75 years with insomnia, recruited through a nationally televised health programme, who completed a 2-week diary run-in and were randomised and mailed valerian or placebo tablets for 2 weeks; all participants and investigators were blinded until after analysis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: For the primary outcome — a minimally important improvement in self-reported sleep quality (at least 0.5 units on a 7-point scale) — 29% of the valerian group versus 21% of the placebo group improved (difference 7.5%; 95% CI −0.9 to 15.9; P=0.08, not significant). On the end-of-treatment global self-assessment, 5.5% (95% CI 0.2 to 10.8) more valerian participants perceived their sleep as better or much better (P=0.04). Trends favouring valerian for night awakenings (difference 6.0%, 95% CI −0.5 to 12.5) and sleep duration (difference 7.5%, 95% CI −1.0 to 16.1) were not significant. There were no serious adverse events and no important or statistically significant differences in minor adverse events. The authors conclude valerian appears safe, with modest beneficial effects at most.
cards.watchOut: A primary-outcome null with a positive secondary global rating is the classic pattern that must not be upgraded: the shelf's stamp follows the prespecified primary outcome. Treatment lasted only 2 weeks and all outcomes were self-reported. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Oxman AD et al. A televised, web-based randomised trial of an herbal remedy (valerian) for insomnia. PloS one. 2007. PMID: 17940604. Registry ID: ISRCTN72748991, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Weighted blankets for insomnia
shelves.question: In adults with insomnia and psychiatric disorders, do weighted chain blankets improve insomnia severity (ISI) versus light control blankets over 4 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Actigraphy · Anxiety · Major Depressive Disorder · Humans · Sleep · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised controlled trial (Ekholm 2020, 120 outpatients with major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, generalised anxiety disorder or ADHD and insomnia) found a significant advantage for weighted metal chain blankets over light plastic chain blankets on the Insomnia Severity Index at 4 weeks (P<.001; large effect size, Cohen d 1.90), with better sleep maintenance, higher daytime activity, and reduced fatigue, depression and anxiety symptoms, and no serious adverse events. A single 4-week trial earns POSSIBLE. Note: the responder rates quoted in the topic draft (59.4% vs 5.4%) do NOT appear in the record's abstract and are not carded; the verified result is the ISI difference as printed.

cards.headline: Ekholm 2020: weighted chain blankets beat light blankets on the Insomnia Severity Index at 4 weeks (P<.001; effect size d=1.90) in 120 psychiatric outpatients
cards.summary: Ekholm 2020: weighted chain blankets beat light blankets on the Insomnia Severity Index at 4 weeks (P<.001; effect size d=1.90) in 120 psychiatric outpatients
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (1:1) with a 12-month open follow-up phase
cards.people: 120 patients with major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, generalized anxiety disorder or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, randomized to a weighted metal chain blanket or a light plastic chain blanket for 4 weeks; sleep and activity were also measured by wrist actigraphy. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 4 weeks there was a significant advantage in Insomnia Severity Index ratings for the weighted blanket over the light blanket (P<.001) with a large effect size (Cohen d 1.90). The weighted blanket also produced significantly better sleep maintenance, a higher daytime activity level, and reduced daytime symptoms of fatigue, depression and anxiety. No serious adverse events occurred. During the 12-month open follow-up, participants who continued weighted blankets maintained the sleep effect, and those switching from light to weighted blankets gained a similar ISI benefit. The abstract does not print ISI response or remission percentages, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks, one trial, and an effect size (d=1.90) that is unusually large for a sleep intervention — blinding a heavy blanket against a light one is inherently fragile, and the population is psychiatric outpatients, not primary insomnia. The responder rates in the topic draft could not be verified from the record and are excluded.
cards.source: Ekholm B et al. A randomized controlled study of weighted chain blankets for insomnia in psychiatric disorders. Journal of clinical sleep medicine : JCSM : official publication of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. 2020. PMID: 32536366. shelves.title: Adjunctive armodafinil/modafinil for residual sleepiness in CPAP-treated obstructive sleep apnea
shelves.question: In adults with obstructive sleep apnea who remain excessively sleepy despite adherent CPAP, does adjunctive armodafinil improve objective wakefulness (Maintenance of Wakefulness Test) versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Benzhydryl Compounds · Central Nervous System Stimulants · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Disorders of Excessive Somnolence · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Modafinil · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One 12-week multicentre double-blind randomised trial (Roth 2006, 395 enrolled patients with residual excessive sleepiness despite adherent nCPAP) found adjunctive armodafinil 150 or 250 mg significantly improved Maintenance of Wakefulness Test sleep latency at the final visit versus placebo, with more patients at least minimally improved on the Clinical Global Impression of Change (72% vs 37%), and larger improvements in Epworth Sleepiness Scale (−5.5 vs −3.3) and fatigue scores, with no effect on nighttime sleep or nCPAP use. A single trial earns POSSIBLE; the modafinil adjunct trials named in the topic draft were not pinned to verified records at build and are fenced without figures. The abstract's headline MWT figures (+1.9 vs +1.7 minutes, P<0.001) are internally awkward — a 0.2-minute difference carrying that P value — and are flagged on the card.

cards.headline: Roth 2006: adjunctive armodafinil improved wakefulness, global impression (72% vs 37% improved) and sleepiness scores in CPAP-adherent patients with residual sleepiness
cards.summary: Roth 2006: adjunctive armodafinil improved wakefulness, global impression (72% vs 37% improved) and sleepiness scores in CPAP-adherent patients with residual sleepiness
cards.type: 12-week, multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (37 centers, United States and Canada)
cards.people: 395 patients aged 18 to 65 years with residual excessive sleepiness associated with obstructive sleep apnea/hypopnea syndrome despite adherent nCPAP, enrolled and assigned to armodafinil 150 mg/day (133), armodafinil 250 mg/day (131) or placebo (131); 392 received at least one dose. Mean age was about 49–50 years and about 70% were men, as printed for the combined armodafinil and placebo groups.
cards.result: At the final visit, the mean (SD) change from baseline in Maintenance of Wakefulness Test sleep latency (averaged across morning and afternoon tests) was +1.9 (7.3) minutes in the combined armodafinil group versus +1.7 (8.6) minutes on placebo (P<0.001 as printed — a 0.2-minute mean difference with that P value is internally awkward and is carded exactly as the record prints it). The proportions at least minimally improved on the Clinical Global Impression of Change were 72% versus 37% (P<0.001); mean Epworth Sleepiness Scale changes were −5.5 (5.0) versus −3.3 (4.7) (P<0.001) and Brief Fatigue Inventory changes −1.2 (2.2) versus −0.6 (2.0) (P<0.01). No significant effects on nighttime sleep by polysomnography were found. Adverse events in the armodafinil group included headache, nausea, insomnia, anxiety and dizziness; serious adverse events occurred in 4 (1.5%) armodafinil patients and were judged not or unlikely drug-related.
cards.watchOut: Read the patient-level outcomes (CGI-C 72% vs 37%; ESS −5.5 vs −3.3) rather than the headline MWT line, whose printed means and P value do not sit comfortably together. The population was selected for nCPAP adherence — the result does not extend to patients whose sleepiness reflects untreated or undertreated apnea.

shelves.title: CPAP for blood pressure in resistant hypertension with obstructive sleep apnea (HIPARCO)
shelves.question: In patients with resistant hypertension and obstructive sleep apnea, does CPAP reduce 24-hour mean blood pressure versus no CPAP over 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antihypertensive Agents · Blood Pressure · Circadian Rhythm · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Drug Resistance · Female · Humans · Hypertension · Male · Middle Aged · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One open-label randomised trial with blinded endpoint assessment (HIPARCO, Martínez-García 2013, 194 patients with resistant hypertension and an apnea–hypopnea index of at least 15) found CPAP lowered 24-hour mean blood pressure by 3.1 mm Hg (95% CI 0.6 to 5.6; P=.02) and 24-hour diastolic pressure by 3.2 mm Hg (1.0 to 5.4; P=.005) more than control at 12 weeks, but NOT 24-hour systolic pressure (3.1 mm Hg, −0.6 to 6.7; P=.10), and increased the proportion with a nocturnal dipper pattern (35.9% vs 21.6%; adjusted odds ratio 2.4 relative, 1.2 to 5.1). This is a blood-pressure surrogate shelf over 12 weeks — it is not Tier C and borrows no cardiovascular-events claim (the events question is homed on Shelf #302). A single trial with a mixed systolic result earns POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: HIPARCO 2013: CPAP lowered 24-hour mean (−3.1 mm Hg) and diastolic pressure versus control at 12 weeks, but not systolic pressure (P=.10)
cards.summary: HIPARCO 2013: CPAP lowered 24-hour mean (−3.1 mm Hg) and diastolic pressure versus control at 12 weeks, but not systolic pressure (P=.10)
cards.type: Open-label, randomized, multicenter clinical trial of parallel groups with blinded end point design (24 teaching hospitals, Spain)
cards.people: 194 patients with resistant hypertension and an apnea-hypopnea index of 15 or higher (mean AHI 40.4 [SD 18.9]; an average of 3.8 antihypertensive drugs per patient), randomly assigned to CPAP (n=98) or no CPAP (n=96) for 12 weeks while continuing usual blood pressure medication; baseline 24-hour mean blood pressure was 103.4 mm Hg, systolic 144.2 mm Hg and diastolic 83 mm Hg; 72.4% of the CPAP group used it at least 4 hours per day. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: By intention to treat, the CPAP group achieved a greater decrease in 24-hour mean blood pressure (3.1 mm Hg [95% CI 0.6 to 5.6]; P=.02) and 24-hour diastolic blood pressure (3.2 mm Hg [1.0 to 5.4]; P=.005) than control, but not in 24-hour systolic blood pressure (3.1 mm Hg [−0.6 to 6.7]; P=.10). The proportion displaying a nocturnal dipper pattern at 12 weeks was greater with CPAP (35.9% vs 21.6%; adjusted odds ratio 2.4 — a relative measure — [1.2 to 5.1]; P=.02). Hours of CPAP use correlated positively with the decrease in 24-hour mean (r=0.29; P=.006), systolic (r=0.25; P=.02) and diastolic (r=0.30; P=.005) pressure.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks and a surrogate endpoint: the systolic result — the pressure most tied to events — was not significant, and no event outcomes were measured. Do not cite this shelf for cardiovascular-event reduction; that question lives on Shelf #302.

shelves.title: Oropharyngeal (myofunctional) exercises for obstructive sleep apnea
shelves.question: In adults with moderate obstructive sleep apnea, does a daily programme of oropharyngeal exercises reduce the apnea–hypopnoea index and neck circumference versus a control programme over 3 months?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Body Mass Index · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myofunctional Therapy · Polysomnography · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive · Snoring · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One small randomised trial (Guimarães 2009, 31 patients with moderate obstructive sleep apnea) found 3 months of daily oropharyngeal exercises reduced the apnea–hypopnea index within the exercise group from 22.4 to 13.7 events/h and neck circumference from 39.6 to 38.5 cm, with significant improvements in snoring, daytime sleepiness and sleep quality, while the sham-therapy control group showed no significant change in any variable. The stamp is POSSIBLE and no higher: 31 patients, and the abstract reports within-group changes and states the control group did not change, without printing a between-group P value for the AHI. The Ieto et al. trial named in the topic draft was not pinned to a verified record at build and is fenced without figures.

cards.headline: Guimarães 2009: oropharyngeal exercises cut AHI from 22.4 to 13.7 events/h and neck circumference in moderate OSA — a 31-patient trial
cards.summary: Guimarães 2009: oropharyngeal exercises cut AHI from 22.4 to 13.7 events/h and neck circumference in moderate OSA — a 31-patient trial
cards.type: Randomised trial (3 months of daily sham therapy vs oropharyngeal exercises)
cards.people: 31 patients with moderate obstructive sleep apnea syndrome, randomized to 3 months of daily (approximately 30 min) sham therapy (n=15, control) or a set of oropharyngeal exercises involving the tongue, soft palate and lateral pharyngeal wall (n=16); the whole group's body mass index was 30.3 (SD 3.4) kg/m2 and abdominal circumference 101.4 (SD 9.0) cm, unchanged over the study. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: No significant change occurred in the control group in any variable. In the exercise group, neck circumference fell significantly (39.6 [SD 3.6] vs 38.5 [SD 4.0] cm), as did snoring frequency (4 [4–4] vs 3 [1.5–3.5]), snoring intensity (3 [3–4] vs 1 [1–2]), daytime sleepiness (14 [SD 5] vs 8 [SD 6] on the Epworth scale), sleep quality score (10.2 [SD 3.7] vs 6.9 [SD 2.5]) and apnea–hypopnea index (22.4 [SD 4.8] vs 13.7 [SD 8.5] events/h) (all P<0.05, within-group). Changes in neck circumference correlated inversely with changes in AHI (r=0.59; P<0.001). Body mass index and abdominal circumference did not change significantly.
cards.watchOut: The AHI figures are before-and-after values inside the exercise group; the abstract does not print a direct between-group test for AHI, and with 16 treated patients the estimate is fragile. Moderate OSA only — nothing here addresses severe disease or CPAP replacement.

shelves.title: Nasal expiratory positive airway pressure (EPAP) for obstructive sleep apnea
shelves.question: In adults with obstructive sleep apnea, does a nasal EPAP device worn nightly reduce the apnea–hypopnoea index versus a sham device over 3 months?
shelves.mesh: Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Polysomnography · Positive-Pressure Respiration · Prospective Studies · Sleep · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One prospective multicentre sham-controlled double-blind randomised trial (Berry 2011, 250 randomised patients with obstructive sleep apnea and a pre-study AHI of at least 10/hour) found the nasal EPAP device reduced AHI far more than sham — median AHI on versus off device 5.0 versus 13.8 events/h at week 1, and a 42.7% median AHI decrease at month 3 versus 10.1% on sham (P<0.0001) — with Epworth Sleepiness Scale improving from 9.9 to 7.2 and median reported whole-night use on 88.2% of nights. A single device trial earns POSSIBLE. Shelf-face caveat from the topic draft stands: the device is no longer marketed in some regions, which limits the practical reach of the result.

cards.headline: Berry 2011: nasal EPAP reduced AHI by 42.7% at 3 months versus 10.1% on sham, with sleepiness improved and adherence high
cards.summary: Berry 2011: nasal EPAP reduced AHI by 42.7% at 3 months versus 10.1% on sham, with sleepiness improved and adherence high
cards.type: Prospective, multicenter, sham-controlled, parallel-group, randomized, double-blind clinical trial (19 sites; AERO study)
cards.people: 250 patients with obstructive sleep apnea (pre-study AHI at least 10/hour) treated with a nasal EPAP device (N=127) or a similar-appearing sham device (N=123) for 3 months; the intention-to-treat analysis (patients completing week 1 polysomnography) comprised EPAP N=119 and sham N=110, with polysomnography on device-on and device-off nights at week 1 and after 3 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 1, median AHI (device-on versus device-off) was significantly lower with EPAP (5.0 versus 13.8 events/h, P<0.0001) but not with sham (11.6 versus 11.1 events/h, not significant); the median AHI decrease was greater with EPAP (−52.7% vs −7.3%, P<0.0001). At month 3, the percentage decrease in AHI was 42.7% (EPAP) versus 10.1% (sham), P<0.0001. Over 3 months of EPAP treatment the Epworth Sleepiness Scale fell from 9.9 (SD 4.7) to 7.2 (SD 4.2) (P<0.0001), and the median percentage of reported nights used (entire night) was 88.2%.
cards.watchOut: AHI was measured on paired on/off nights — a device-effect design — and 21 of 250 randomised patients did not contribute to the intention-to-treat set. The result is a median percentage change; individual responses varied, and the device's later market withdrawal in some regions is a practical, not evidential, limit.
cards.source: Berry RB et al. A novel nasal expiratory positive airway pressure (EPAP) device for the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea: a randomized controlled trial. Sleep. 2011. PMID: 21461326. shelves.title: Melatonin for REM sleep behaviour disorder
shelves.question: In adults with REM sleep behaviour disorder, does melatonin (3–12 mg at bedtime) improve clinical global impression of RBD severity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Central Nervous System Depressants · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Male · Melatonin · Middle Aged · Polysomnography · REM Sleep Behavior Disorder · Sleep · Sleep, REM · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The entire randomised record pinned at build is one two-part double-blind placebo-controlled crossover study in EIGHT men (Kunz & Mahlberg 2010), using melatonin 3 mg only — not the 3–12 mg range in the shelf question, which no pinned trial tested. Melatonin significantly reduced the percentage of 30-second REM sleep epochs without muscle atonia (39% at baseline versus 27%; P=0.012) and improved clinical global impression (6.1 versus 4.6; P=0.024), with a carry-over pattern suggesting effects persisted into a subsequent placebo phase. Eight participants and a single low dose: MAYBE (weak evidence), and most clinical melatonin use in RBD rests on open-label experience outside this record.

cards.headline: Kunz 2010: melatonin 3 mg improved REM atonia and clinical global impression in REM sleep behaviour disorder — in a crossover study of 8 men
cards.summary: Kunz 2010: melatonin 3 mg improved REM atonia and clinical global impression in REM sleep behaviour disorder — in a crossover study of 8 men
cards.type: Two-part, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled cross-over study (4 weeks per part)
cards.people: Eight consecutively recruited males (mean age 54 years) with polysomnographically confirmed REM sleep behaviour disorder, receiving placebo and melatonin 3 mg daily in crossover, administered between 22:00 and 23:00 over 4 weeks per part, with polysomnography at baseline and at the end of each part. No women were studied.
cards.result: Compared with baseline, melatonin significantly reduced the number of 30-second REM sleep epochs without muscle atonia (39% versus 27%; P=0.012) and significantly improved clinical global impression (CGI: 6.1 versus 4.6; P=0.024). Patients who took placebo in Part II after melatonin in Part I kept a lower rate of atonia-free REM epochs (−16% compared with baseline; P=0.043), while patients on placebo in Part I improved only during Part II, on melatonin. The authors suggest melatonin might be a second useful agent besides clonazepam in RBD.
cards.watchOut: Eight men, one dose (3 mg), and a crossover whose carry-over effect contaminates the second period — the design that detected the signal also weakens it. The question's 3–12 mg range is not supported by any dose-ranging in this record. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Kunz D et al. A two-part, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of exogenous melatonin in REM sleep behaviour disorder. Journal of sleep research. 2010. PMID: 20561180. shelves.title: Baloxavir post-exposure prophylaxis in household contacts of influenza patients (BLOCKSTONE)
shelves.question: In household contacts of patients with influenza, does a single dose of baloxavir prevent clinical influenza confirmed by RT-PCR testing, compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antiviral Agents · Child · Child, Preschool · Dibenzothiepins · Disease Transmission, Infectious · Double-Blind Method · Endonucleases · Family · Female · Humans · Influenza A virus · Influenza, Human · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Morpholines · Oxazines · Pyridines · Pyridones · Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction · Thiepins · Triazines
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one pivotal trial. In BLOCKSTONE (752 household contacts of 545 index patients, Japan, 2018–19 season), clinical influenza confirmed by RT-PCR over 10 days developed in 1.9% of baloxavir recipients versus 13.6% on placebo (adjusted risk ratio 0.14 relative; 95% CI 0.06 to 0.30; P<0.001), and infection regardless of symptoms was also reduced (adjusted risk ratio 0.43 relative). Adverse events were similar (22.2% vs 20.5%). Two qualifications cap the stamp: this is a single trial, in one country and one season, with 95.6% influenza A among index cases; and reduced-susceptibility viral substitutions (PA I38T/M in 2.7%, E23K in 1.3% of the baloxavir group) emerged on treatment. Note for the developer: the drafting note names 'Iketani' as first author — the record's first author is Ikematsu; the card follows the record. (Treatment of influenza with baloxavir is homed on Shelf #727; this shelf is prophylaxis only.)

cards.headline: BLOCKSTONE 2020: single-dose baloxavir cut clinical influenza in household contacts to 1.9% versus 13.6% (adjusted risk ratio 0.14)
cards.summary: BLOCKSTONE 2020: single-dose baloxavir cut clinical influenza in household contacts to 1.9% versus 13.6% (adjusted risk ratio 0.14)
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: 752 household contacts of 545 index patients with confirmed influenza, randomised in Japan during the 2018–19 season to a single dose of baloxavir or placebo; 749 could be evaluated (374 baloxavir, 375 placebo). Among index patients, 95.6% had influenza A, 73.6% were younger than 12 years, and 52.7% themselves received baloxavir. The abstract does not state the contacts' mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Clinical influenza confirmed by RT-PCR over 10 days developed in 1.9% of the baloxavir group versus 13.6% of the placebo group (adjusted risk ratio 0.14 relative; 95% CI 0.06 to 0.30; P<0.001). Baloxavir was effective in high-risk, paediatric, and unvaccinated subgroups. Influenza infection regardless of symptoms was also less frequent (adjusted risk ratio 0.43 relative; 95% CI 0.32 to 0.58). Adverse events occurred in 22.2% versus 20.5%. Viral PA substitutions associated with reduced baloxavir susceptibility (I38T/M, E23K) were detected in 10 (2.7%) and 5 (1.3%) baloxavir-group participants; transmission of these variants from treated index patients to placebo-group contacts was not detected, though transmission to some baloxavir-group contacts could not be ruled out.
cards.watchOut: A single-season, single-country trial, conducted where index cases were mostly children with influenza A; effectiveness against influenza B and in other household structures is extrapolation. The emergence of reduced-susceptibility variants in roughly 4% of recipients is the standing pharmacological caveat for a single-dose agent used at population scale.

shelves.title: Upfront ambrisentan plus tadalafil in pulmonary arterial hypertension (AMBITION)
shelves.question: In treatment-naive pulmonary arterial hypertension, does initial combination therapy with ambrisentan plus tadalafil reduce clinical-failure events, compared with initial monotherapy with either agent?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Carbolines · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Hypertension, Pulmonary · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain · Peptide Fragments · Phenylpropionates · Pyridazines · Risk Factors · Tadalafil
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the clinical-failure composite includes death and hospitalisation for worsening pulmonary arterial hypertension). One pivotal trial (AMBITION, 500 treatment-naive patients with WHO functional class II or III symptoms): a first clinical-failure event occurred in 18% on initial combination therapy versus 31% on pooled monotherapy (hazard ratio 0.50 relative; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.72; P<0.001), with greater NT-proBNP reduction and more satisfactory clinical responses at week 24, and a longer 6-minute walk improvement. The abstract does not print the death component separately, so no mortality claim is made or supported — the composite is carded as the record gives it. Adverse events more frequent on combination therapy included peripheral oedema, headache, nasal congestion, and anaemia. One trial, however decisive its composite: POSSIBLE. Later combination trials tested other drug pairs and are separate shelves, not corroboration imported here.

cards.headline: AMBITION 2015: upfront ambrisentan plus tadalafil halved clinical failure (18% vs 31% pooled monotherapy; HR 0.50; P<0.001)
cards.summary: AMBITION 2015: upfront ambrisentan plus tadalafil halved clinical failure (18% vs 31% pooled monotherapy; HR 0.50; P<0.001)
cards.type: Event-driven, double-blind randomised trial
cards.people: 500 treatment-naive patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension and WHO functional class II or III symptoms, randomised 2:1:1 to initial combination therapy (ambrisentan 10 mg plus tadalafil 40 mg; 253 patients), ambrisentan monotherapy (126), or tadalafil monotherapy (121), all once daily; the primary analysis compared combination therapy against the pooled monotherapy groups. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A primary end-point event — the first occurrence of death, hospitalisation for worsening pulmonary arterial hypertension, disease progression, or unsatisfactory long-term clinical response — occurred in 18% of the combination group, 34% of the ambrisentan-monotherapy group, and 28% of the tadalafil-monotherapy group, and in 31% of the pooled-monotherapy group (hazard ratio for combination versus pooled monotherapy 0.50 relative; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.72; P<0.001). At week 24, NT-proBNP fell more with combination therapy (mean change −67.2% vs −50.4%; P<0.001), satisfactory clinical response was more frequent (39% vs 29%; odds ratio 1.56), and 6-minute walk distance improved more (median change 48.98 m vs 23.80 m; P<0.001). Peripheral oedema, headache, nasal congestion, and anaemia were more frequent on combination therapy.
cards.watchOut: The composite mixes death with a judgement-based component ('unsatisfactory long-term clinical response'), and the abstract does not decompose it — the card does not invent component rates. Two-drug-versus-one designs also cannot separate 'combination is better' from 'the better drug was in both arms of the pooled comparison'; the monotherapy arms' separate event rates (34% and 28%) are printed so the reader can see the spread.

shelves.title: Dupilumab for COPD with type 2 inflammation (BOREAS and NOTUS)
shelves.question: In COPD with type 2 inflammation (blood eosinophils at least 300 per microlitre) on standard inhaled therapy, does dupilumab reduce annualised moderate or severe exacerbations, compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Double-Blind Method · Eosinophils · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Quality of Life · Inflammation
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two phase 3 trials replicate the result. In BOREAS (939 patients on triple therapy), the annualised rate of moderate or severe exacerbations was 0.78 on dupilumab versus 1.10 on placebo (rate ratio 0.70 relative; 95% CI 0.58 to 0.86; P<0.001), with an 83 ml greater FEV1 improvement at week 12, sustained to week 52. NOTUS (935 patients) confirmed it: 0.86 versus 1.30 exacerbations per year (rate ratio 0.66 relative; 95% CI 0.54 to 0.82; P<0.001). The claim is bounded by the trials' borders: eosinophils at least 300 per microlitre, elevated exacerbation risk, background inhaled therapy. The primary outcome is exacerbation rate — not a mortality, infarction, or stroke claim — so this shelf is not Tier C, and no mortality claim is made. (Benralizumab in COPD is a separate question, homed on Shelf #1037.)

cards.headline: BOREAS 2023: dupilumab cut COPD exacerbations by 30% relative (0.78 vs 1.10 per year; rate ratio 0.70; P<0.001)
cards.summary: BOREAS 2023: dupilumab cut COPD exacerbations by 30% relative (0.78 vs 1.10 per year; rate ratio 0.70; P<0.001)
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind randomised trial
cards.people: 939 patients with COPD, a blood eosinophil count of at least 300 per microlitre, and elevated exacerbation risk despite standard triple therapy; 468 received dupilumab 300 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks and 471 placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The annualised rate of moderate or severe COPD exacerbations was 0.78 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.93) on dupilumab versus 1.10 (95% CI 0.93 to 1.30) on placebo (rate ratio 0.70 relative; 95% CI 0.58 to 0.86; P<0.001). Prebronchodilator FEV1 improved more with dupilumab by week 12 (least-squares mean difference 83 ml; 95% CI 42 to 125; P<0.001), sustained through week 52, and St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire scores improved more at week 52.
cards.watchOut: The relative reduction (30%) is the headline; the absolute rates (0.78 vs 1.10 per year) are printed beside it, per this library's wording rule — roughly one exacerbation avoided per three patient-years. The eosinophil threshold is an entry criterion, not a finding: nothing here speaks to COPD below 300 cells per microlitre.

cards.summary: NOTUS 2024: the replication — exacerbations 0.86 versus 1.30 per year (rate ratio 0.66; P<0.001)
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind randomised trial (confirmatory second trial)
cards.people: 935 patients with COPD and a blood eosinophil count of 300 cells per microlitre or higher; 470 received dupilumab 300 mg every 2 weeks and 465 placebo. cards.watchOut: An interim-analysis-triggered primary analysis is a design feature to notice, disclosed on the record itself; the effect estimate sits comfortably beside BOREAS's, which is what replication is for. shelves.title: Ensifentrine, dual PDE3/4 inhibitor, for COPD maintenance (ENHANCE-1 and ENHANCE-2)
shelves.question: In symptomatic moderate-to-severe COPD, does nebulised ensifentrine improve lung function (FEV1 area under the curve over 12 hours) and symptoms, compared with placebo, over 24 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Bronchodilator Agents · Double-Blind Method · Forced Expiratory Volume · Phosphoric Diester Hydrolases · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Quality of Life · Adult · Middle Aged · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Isoquinolines · Pyrimidinones
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — twin phase 3 trials, surrogate-led. The single programme report covers ENHANCE-1 (760 patients) and ENHANCE-2 (789): ensifentrine improved the primary lung-function end point in both (average FEV1 AUC over 12 hours: +87 ml [95% CI 55 to 119] and +94 ml [65 to 124] versus placebo; both P<0.001). Symptoms and quality of life improved significantly in ENHANCE-1 but NOT in ENHANCE-2 — a divergence printed on the card, not averaged away. Moderate or severe exacerbation rates over 24 weeks were lower (rate ratios 0.64 [P=0.050] and 0.57 [P=0.009]) as secondary end points. Most patients were on a background LAMA or LABA. A replicated bronchodilator effect of about 90 ml, inconsistent symptom benefit, and a 24-week horizon: POSSIBLE. No mortality or other event claim is made; none was an outcome.

cards.headline: ENHANCE-1 and ENHANCE-2 2023: ensifentrine improved FEV1 AUC in both trials (+87 ml and +94 ml); symptom benefit reached significance only in ENHANCE-1
cards.summary: ENHANCE-1 and ENHANCE-2 2023: ensifentrine improved FEV1 AUC in both trials (+87 ml and +94 ml); symptom benefit reached significance only in ENHANCE-1
cards.type: Two parallel phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, reported in a single programme paper
cards.people: ENHANCE-1: 760 patients randomised and treated; ENHANCE-2: 789. Patients were aged 40–80 years with moderate-to-severe symptomatic COPD (post-bronchodilator FEV1 52% and 51% of predicted), at 250 centres in 17 countries; 69% (ENHANCE-1) and 55% (ENHANCE-2) were receiving a concomitant long-acting muscarinic antagonist or long-acting beta-agonist. The report's abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Ensifentrine significantly improved average FEV1 area under the curve over 0–12 hours versus placebo in both trials (ENHANCE-1: 87 ml [95% CI 55 to 119]; ENHANCE-2: 94 ml [65 to 124]; both P<0.001). Symptoms (Evaluating Respiratory Symptoms) and quality of life (St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire) improved significantly versus placebo at week 24 in ENHANCE-1 but not in ENHANCE-2. Moderate or severe exacerbation rates over 24 weeks were reduced (ENHANCE-1: rate ratio 0.64 relative [95% CI 0.40 to 1.00]; P=0.050; ENHANCE-2: rate ratio 0.57 relative [0.38 to 0.87]; P=0.009), and time to first exacerbation was longer (hazard ratios 0.62 and 0.58).
cards.watchOut: The two trials are one programme with one report — they corroborate the lung-function result but share a sponsor, a protocol family, and a 24-week horizon. The symptom divergence between the twins is real and is the reason this shelf is POSSIBLE rather than higher: the patient-reported half of the claim replicated only once.

shelves.title: Withdrawing inhaled corticosteroids in severe COPD on triple therapy (WISDOM)
shelves.question: In patients with severe COPD on triple therapy, does stepwise withdrawal of the inhaled glucocorticoid increase exacerbations, compared with continued triple therapy?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Aged · Albuterol · Androstadienes · Bronchodilator Agents · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Fluticasone · Forced Expiratory Volume · Glucocorticoids · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Salmeterol Xinafoate · Scopolamine Derivatives · Spirometry · Tiotropium Bromide · Withholding Treatment
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one pivotal trial, a noninferiority result with a measurable lung-function cost. In WISDOM (2,485 patients with severe COPD and an exacerbation history, all run in on tiotropium plus salmeterol plus fluticasone), stepwise glucocorticoid withdrawal over 12 weeks met the prespecified noninferiority criterion for time to first moderate or severe exacerbation (hazard ratio 1.06 relative; 95% CI 0.94 to 1.19; prespecified criterion: upper limit under 1.20). The cost was trough FEV1: a 38 ml greater reduction from baseline at week 18 and 43 ml at week 52 in the withdrawal group (both significant), with no change in dyspnoea and minor health-status changes. So: withdrawal did not significantly increase exacerbations in this population, and it did give back some lung function. The population boundary matters — SUNSET later studied de-escalation in non-frequent exacerbators and is fenced in the synthesis as a different question. POSSIBLE, on one trial.

cards.headline: WISDOM 2014: ICS withdrawal was noninferior for exacerbations (HR 1.06; 95% CI 0.94 to 1.19) but cost 38–43 ml of FEV1
cards.summary: WISDOM 2014: ICS withdrawal was noninferior for exacerbations (HR 1.06; 95% CI 0.94 to 1.19) but cost 38–43 ml of FEV1
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, parallel-group noninferiority trial
cards.people: 2,485 patients with severe COPD and a history of exacerbation; all received triple therapy (tiotropium 18 µg daily, salmeterol 50 µg twice daily, fluticasone propionate 500 µg twice daily) during a 6-week run-in, then were randomised to continued triple therapy or stepwise withdrawal of fluticasone over 12 weeks, with 12 months of follow-up. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: For the primary end point (time to first moderate or severe exacerbation), glucocorticoid withdrawal met the prespecified noninferiority criterion (hazard ratio 1.06 relative; 95% CI 0.94 to 1.19; criterion: upper confidence limit below 1.20). At week 18, when withdrawal was complete, the adjusted mean reduction in trough FEV1 was 38 ml greater in the withdrawal group (P<0.001); at week 52 the difference was 43 ml (P=0.001). Dyspnoea did not change and health-status changes were minor in the withdrawal group.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority against a 1.20 margin means the data are compatible with up to a 19% relative increase in exacerbation hazard — 'no significant increase' and 'no increase' are different statements, and the card prints the interval so the reader can judge. The FEV1 cost, though small, was consistent and statistically firm: withdrawal is a trade, not a free de-prescription.

shelves.title: Indacaterol–glycopyrronium versus salmeterol–fluticasone in COPD (FLAME)
shelves.question: In patients with COPD and a history of exacerbations, does once-daily LAMA/LABA (indacaterol–glycopyrronium) prevent exacerbations better than LABA/ICS (salmeterol–fluticasone)?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adrenergic beta-2 Receptor Agonists · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Female · Fluticasone-Salmeterol Drug Combination · Glucocorticoids · Glycopyrrolate · Humans · Indans · Male · Middle Aged · Muscarinic Antagonists · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Quinolones
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one pivotal head-to-head trial. In FLAME (3,362 patients with COPD and at least one exacerbation in the previous year, 52 weeks), indacaterol–glycopyrronium was superior to salmeterol–fluticasone on the primary outcome, the annual rate of all exacerbations (3.59 vs 4.03; rate ratio 0.89 relative; 95% CI 0.83 to 0.96; P=0.003), and on moderate or severe exacerbations (0.98 vs 1.19; rate ratio 0.83 relative; P<0.001); time to first exacerbation was longer (hazard ratio 0.84 relative). Pneumonia was less frequent on the steroid-free regimen (3.2% vs 4.8%; P=0.02). The abstract states that adverse events and deaths were similar in the two groups without printing death rates, so no mortality claim is made or supported. The comparison is regimen against regimen — it does not isolate what dropping the steroid alone does (that is WISDOM's question, Shelf #1643). One large trial: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: FLAME 2016: LAMA/LABA beat LABA/ICS on exacerbations (rate ratio 0.89 for all; 0.83 for moderate or severe) with less pneumonia (3.2% vs 4.8%)
cards.summary: FLAME 2016: LAMA/LABA beat LABA/ICS on exacerbations (rate ratio 0.89 for all; 0.83 for moderate or severe) with less pneumonia (3.2% vs 4.8%)
cards.type: 52-week, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy noninferiority trial (superiority shown on the primary outcome)
cards.people: 3,362 patients with COPD and a history of at least one exacerbation during the previous year; 1,680 received indacaterol 110 µg plus glycopyrronium 50 µg once daily and 1,682 received salmeterol 50 µg plus fluticasone 500 µg twice daily. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Indacaterol–glycopyrronium was noninferior and then superior to salmeterol–fluticasone for the annual rate of all COPD exacerbations (3.59 vs 4.03; rate ratio 0.89 relative; 95% CI 0.83 to 0.96; P=0.003). Time to first exacerbation was longer (71 vs 51 days; hazard ratio 0.84 relative; P<0.001). The annual rate of moderate or severe exacerbations was lower (0.98 vs 1.19; rate ratio 0.83 relative; 95% CI 0.75 to 0.91; P<0.001), as was time to first severe exacerbation (hazard ratio 0.81). The treatment effect was independent of baseline blood eosinophil count. Pneumonia occurred in 3.2% versus 4.8% (P=0.02); the incidence of adverse events and deaths was similar in the two groups (rates not printed in the abstract).
cards.watchOut: A two-variable comparison: FLAME changes both the bronchodilator pairing and the steroid at once, so it ranks regimens rather than explaining mechanisms. Its pneumonia finding is the steroid-sparing dividend clinicians cite most; its exacerbation advantage, while real, is modest in absolute terms (about 0.4 fewer exacerbations per patient-year overall, 0.2 for moderate or severe).

shelves.title: Home non-invasive ventilation after hypercapnic COPD exacerbation (HOT-HMV)
shelves.question: In patients with persistent hypercapnia after an acute COPD exacerbation requiring non-invasive ventilation, does home mechanical ventilation plus oxygen prolong admission-free survival, compared with home oxygen alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Combined Modality Therapy · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Home Care Services · Humans · Hypercapnia · Male · Middle Aged · Noninvasive Ventilation · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy · Patient Readmission · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Quality of Life · Respiratory Insufficiency · Risk · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary composite is time to readmission or death). One small, heavily screened trial (HOT-HMV, 116 randomised of 2,021 screened patients with persistent hypercapnia, PaCO2 over 53 mm Hg, 2–4 weeks after an exacerbation): median time to readmission or death was 4.3 months with home ventilation plus oxygen versus 1.4 months with oxygen alone (adjusted hazard ratio 0.49 relative; 95% CI 0.31 to 0.77; P=0.002), and the 12-month readmission-or-death risk was 63.4% versus 80.4% (absolute reduction 17.0%). The composite was driven by readmission: deaths at 12 months were 16 versus 19 — no mortality claim is made or supported, and the balance says so explicitly. The eligible population is a narrow slice of post-exacerbation patients (obesity over BMI 35, obstructive sleep apnoea, and other respiratory-failure causes were excluded), and only 64 patients completed 12 months. A strong time-to-event signal in a small selected trial: POSSIBLE. (Non-invasive ventilation during the acute exacerbation itself is homed on Shelf #306; this shelf is the home-ventilation question.)

cards.headline: HOT-HMV 2017: home NIV plus oxygen delayed readmission or death (median 4.3 vs 1.4 months; adjusted HR 0.49); deaths alone were 16 versus 19
cards.summary: HOT-HMV 2017: home NIV plus oxygen delayed readmission or death (median 4.3 vs 1.4 months; adjusted HR 0.49); deaths alone were 16 versus 19
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (open-label)
cards.people: 116 patients with persistent hypercapnia (PaCO2 over 53 mm Hg) 2–4 weeks after resolution of respiratory acidaemia from an acute COPD exacerbation, recruited at 13 UK centres from 2,021 screened patients (mean age 67 years; 53% women; mean FEV1 0.6 L; mean PaCO2 59 mm Hg breathing air); 57 were randomised to home oxygen plus home non-invasive ventilation and 59 to home oxygen alone. Exclusions included BMI over 35, obstructive sleep apnoea, and other causes of respiratory failure. Sixty-four patients completed the 12-month study period.
cards.result: The median time to readmission or death was 4.3 months (IQR 1.3–13.8) in the home oxygen plus home NIV group versus 1.4 months (IQR 0.5–3.9) with home oxygen alone (adjusted hazard ratio 0.49 relative; 95% CI 0.31 to 0.77; P=0.002). The 12-month risk of readmission or death was 63.4% versus 80.4% (absolute risk reduction 17.0%; 95% CI 0.1% to 34.0%). At 12 months, 16 patients had died in the NIV group and 19 in the oxygen-alone group.
cards.watchOut: Read the composite by its parts: the trial was powered on time to readmission or death, and readmission supplies nearly all of the separation — deaths were numerically fewer by three, in 116 patients. The screening funnel (116 of 2,021) defines a very specific phenotype; results should not be extended to all post-exacerbation patients, and the open-label design matters for a readmission outcome that clinician behaviour can influence.

shelves.title: Endobronchial valves for severe emphysema (LIBERATE; EMPROVE)
shelves.question: In severe emphysema with heterogeneous disease and little or no collateral ventilation, do endobronchial valves improve FEV1 responder rates, compared with standard care, at one year — and at what pneumothorax cost?
shelves.mesh: Bronchi · Bronchoscopy · Equipment Design · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prostheses and Implants · Pulmonary Emphysema · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two randomised programmes, two different valve systems, the same direction. LIBERATE (Zephyr valve, 190 patients): at 12 months, 47.7% of valve patients versus 16.8% of controls achieved at least a 15% FEV1 improvement (P<0.001), with between-group differences of +0.106 L in FEV1, +39.31 m in 6-minute walk distance, and −7.05 points in St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire score; the price was pneumothorax in 26.6% of valve patients in the treatment period, and four deaths occurred in the valve group during that phase (plus one in each group later) — printed here beside the benefit, as the record gives them. EMPROVE (Spiration valve) corroborates: its 24-month follow-up report (147 patients) found the FEV1 and quality-of-life advantages maintained with significantly less dyspnoea, though that record's abstract states significance without printing FEV1 effect sizes, and none are supplied here. Benefit is real, mechanical, and bought with a one-in-four early pneumothorax rate in the pivotal Zephyr trial: LIKELY, in carefully selected patients with absent collateral ventilation. No mortality claim is made or supported.

cards.headline: LIBERATE 2018: Zephyr valves tripled FEV1 responders at 12 months (47.7% vs 16.8%); pneumothorax in 26.6% of treated patients
cards.summary: LIBERATE 2018: Zephyr valves tripled FEV1 responders at 12 months (47.7% vs 16.8%); pneumothorax in 26.6% of treated patients
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (2:1 allocation, unblinded)
cards.people: 190 patients with severe heterogeneous emphysema and little or no collateral ventilation in the target lobe, at 24 sites; 128 received Zephyr endobronchial valves and 62 received standard care. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 12 months, 47.7% of valve patients versus 16.8% of controls achieved a post-bronchodilator FEV1 improvement of at least 15% (P<0.001) — the primary outcome. Between-group differences favoured valves for FEV1 (+0.106 L; P<0.001), 6-minute walk distance (+39.31 m; P=0.002), St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire (−7.05 points; P=0.004), residual volume (−522 ml; P<0.001), dyspnoea score (−0.8 points), and BODE index (−1.2 points). Pneumothorax was the most common serious adverse event in the treatment period (procedure to day 45), occurring in 34 of 128 valve patients (26.6%). Four deaths occurred in the valve group during this phase, and one death in each group between day 46 and 12 months.
cards.watchOut: Patient selection is the intervention: benefit was shown only where collateral ventilation is absent, which requires pre-procedure fissure assessment most emphysema patients will not pass. The pneumothorax rate is the mechanism's shadow (rapid lobar collapse) and clusters in the first days. Mortality was not an outcome the trial could resolve — five deaths versus one are printed as the record gives them, without a claim in either direction.
cards.source: Criner GJ et al. A Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial of Zephyr Endobronchial Valve Treatment in Heterogeneous Emphysema (LIBERATE). cards.people: 147 patients with severe heterogeneous emphysema in the EMPROVE trial (102 treated with the Spiration Valve System, 45 controls), followed to 24 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.

shelves.title: Higher versus lower PEEP in ARDS (ALVEOLI, LOVS, EXPRESS)
shelves.question: In moderate-to-severe ARDS, does a higher-PEEP ventilation strategy reduce mortality, compared with a lower-PEEP strategy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Biomarkers · Female · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Intercellular Adhesion Molecule-1 · Interleukin-6 · Male · Middle Aged · Positive-Pressure Respiration · Pulmonary Surfactant-Associated Protein D · Respiratory Distress Syndrome · Respiratory Physiological Phenomena · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality is the primary outcome of all three trials). Three randomised trials tested higher-PEEP strategies against lower-PEEP strategies on a background of low-tidal-volume ventilation, and none reduced mortality. ALVEOLI (549 patients): death before discharge 27.5% with higher PEEP versus 24.9% with lower PEEP (P=0.48). LOVS (983 patients; higher PEEP plus recruitment manoeuvres): hospital mortality 36.4% versus 40.4% (relative risk 0.90 relative; P=0.19). EXPRESS (767 patients; PEEP set to a plateau-pressure target): 28-day mortality 27.8% versus 31.2% (P=0.31), with more ventilator-free and organ-failure-free days in the higher-PEEP group. Higher PEEP reliably improves oxygenation; across 2,299 patients it did not reliably keep anyone alive: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for an across-the-board higher-PEEP strategy. (Whether an individualised, recruitability-guided approach differs is a separate question, not tested by these three.)

cards.headline: ALVEOLI 2004: higher PEEP improved oxygenation settings separation but not survival (death before discharge 27.5% vs 24.9%; P=0.48)
cards.summary: ALVEOLI 2004: higher PEEP improved oxygenation settings separation but not survival (death before discharge 27.5% vs 24.9%; P=0.48)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (ARDS Network; pre-dates trial-registration norms — no registry ID appears in the record's databank fields, and none is invented)
cards.people: 549 patients with acute lung injury and ARDS, randomised to lower or higher PEEP set by PEEP/FiO2 tables, all with a tidal-volume goal of 6 ml/kg predicted body weight and a plateau-pressure limit of 30 cm H2O. Mean PEEP on days 1–4 was 8.3 cm H2O (lower group) versus 13.2 cm H2O (higher group). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Rates of death before hospital discharge were 24.9% in the lower-PEEP group and 27.5% in the higher-PEEP group (P=0.48; 95% CI for the difference −10.0 to 4.7 percentage points). Days of unassisted breathing to day 28 were 14.5 versus 13.8 (P=0.50). The authors concluded that clinical outcomes are similar whether lower or higher PEEP levels are used, on a background of low-tidal-volume ventilation.
cards.watchOut: ALVEOLI's achieved PEEP separation (about 5 cm H2O) was modest, the standing critique of the whole trio; but it is the critique of all three trials together, and three concordant nulls at increasing separation are what the shelf reports.
cards.source: Brower RG et al. Higher versus lower positive end-expiratory pressures in patients with the acute respiratory distress syndrome. The New England journal of medicine. 2004. shelves.title: High-frequency oscillatory ventilation in early severe ARDS (OSCILLATE and OSCAR)
shelves.question: In adults with early moderate-to-severe ARDS, does high-frequency oscillatory ventilation reduce mortality, compared with conventional lung-protective ventilation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · High-Frequency Ventilation · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives · Hypoxia · Male · Midazolam · Middle Aged · Positive-Pressure Respiration · Respiratory Distress Syndrome · Survival Analysis · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality is the primary outcome of both trials). The two 2013 trials diverge and the split is the honest summary. OSCILLATE (548 patients randomised of 1,200 planned; stopped early on the data monitoring committee's recommendation): in-hospital mortality was 47% on HFOV versus 35% on a control strategy of low tidal volumes with high PEEP (relative risk of death 1.33 relative; 95% CI 1.09 to 1.64; P=0.005), with more sedation, more neuromuscular blockade, and more vasoactive-drug exposure on HFOV — LIKELY (harm) for that aggressive recruitment-oriented HFOV protocol. OSCAR (795 patients): 30-day mortality was 41.7% versus 41.1% (P=0.85) — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for HFOV as practised in UK centres against usual care. Together they closed routine early HFOV in adult ARDS: no benefit anywhere, harm in the trial that pushed pressures hardest. Note for the developer: the drafting note pins PMID 23339638 as 'OSCILLATE (Ferguson)' — that record is in fact OSCAR (Young); OSCILLATE is PMID 23339639. Both trials are carded under their correct identities.

cards.headline: OSCILLATE 2013: HFOV increased in-hospital mortality (47% vs 35%; RR 1.33; P=0.005); stopped early for harm
cards.summary: OSCILLATE 2013: HFOV increased in-hospital mortality (47% vs 35%; RR 1.33; P=0.005); stopped early for harm
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial, stopped early on data-monitoring-committee recommendation
cards.people: 548 adults with new-onset moderate-to-severe ARDS, at 39 ICUs in five countries, randomised (of 1,200 planned) to HFOV targeting lung recruitment or to a control strategy of low tidal volumes and high PEEP targeting recruitment; 12% of the control group crossed over to HFOV for refractory hypoxaemia. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In-hospital mortality was 47% in the HFOV group versus 35% in the control group (relative risk of death with HFOV 1.33 relative; 95% CI 1.09 to 1.64; P=0.005), independent of baseline oxygenation or respiratory compliance. Patients on HFOV received higher midazolam doses (median 199 vs 141 mg per day; P<0.001), more neuromuscular blockers (83% vs 68%; P<0.001), and more vasoactive drugs (91% vs 84%; P=0.01), for longer (5 vs 3 days).
cards.watchOut: Early stopping for harm can exaggerate an effect, and OSCILLATE's HFOV protocol used high mean airway pressures with recruitment manoeuvres — the harm may belong to that protocol rather than to oscillation itself. The card therefore stamps the protocol, not the physics; OSCAR's more pragmatic application, on the next card, found no harm and no benefit.

cards.headline: Synthesis: no benefit in either trial; harm in the aggressive-protocol trial — a split verdict that closed routine HFOV
cards.summary: Synthesis: no benefit in either trial; harm in the aggressive-protocol trial — a split verdict that closed routine HFOV

shelves.title: Tiotropium in early-stage COPD (Tie-COPD)
shelves.question: In patients with mild-to-moderate (GOLD 1–2) COPD, does daily tiotropium improve FEV1 and slow its decline, compared with placebo, over two years?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Aged · Bronchodilator Agents · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Quality of Life · Tiotropium Bromide
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one pivotal trial, single-country (China). In Tie-COPD (841 patients with GOLD stage 1 or 2 COPD), tiotropium kept FEV1 higher than placebo throughout 2 years (mean differences of 127 to 169 ml before bronchodilator use, 71 to 133 ml after; all P<0.001). The decline story is split, and the card prints both halves: the annual decline in FEV1 BEFORE bronchodilator use was not significantly slowed (38 vs 53 ml per year; difference 15 ml per year; 95% CI −1 to 31; P=0.06), while the decline AFTER bronchodilator use was significantly less (29 vs 51 ml per year; difference 22 ml per year; P=0.006). The authors' conclusion — that tiotropium 'ameliorated the annual decline' — leans on the post-bronchodilator measure and is flagged on the card as an overstatement of the primary-frame result. The drafting note also says tiotropium 'reduced exacerbations'; the record's abstract prints no exacerbation rates, so none are carded. A real level effect on lung function, an unproven effect on pre-bronchodilator decline, one country: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Tie-COPD 2017: tiotropium held FEV1 higher for 2 years in early COPD; the pre-bronchodilator decline was not significantly slowed (P=0.06), the post-bronchodilator decline was (P=0.006)
cards.summary: Tie-COPD 2017: tiotropium held FEV1 higher for 2 years in early COPD; the pre-bronchodilator decline was not significantly slowed (P=0.06), the post-bronchodilator decline was (P=0.006)
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: 841 patients with GOLD stage 1 (mild) or 2 (moderate) COPD in China, randomised to tiotropium 18 µg once daily (419) or placebo (422) for 2 years; 388 and 383 patients respectively were in the full analysis set. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary end point — the between-group difference in change in FEV1 before bronchodilator use at 24 months — favoured tiotropium: FEV1 was higher on tiotropium throughout the trial (mean differences 127 to 169 ml before bronchodilator use and 71 to 133 ml after; P<0.001 for all comparisons). The annual decline in FEV1 before bronchodilator use was 38 ml per year on tiotropium versus 53 ml per year on placebo (difference 15 ml per year; 95% CI −1 to 31; P=0.06) — not significant. The annual decline after bronchodilator use was significantly less on tiotropium (29 vs 51 ml per year; difference 22 ml per year; 95% CI 6 to 37; P=0.006). Adverse events were generally similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The authors' conclusion states that tiotropium 'ameliorated the annual decline in the FEV1 after bronchodilator use' — accurate for that measure, but the before-bronchodilator decline, the frame of the primary end point, missed significance; readers should see both numbers, as carded. The drafting note's claim of reduced exacerbations is not supported by any figure in this record's abstract and is not carded.

shelves.title: Long-term inhaled hypertonic saline in cystic fibrosis (Elkins)
shelves.question: In patients with cystic fibrosis aged six years and older, does twice-daily inhaled hypertonic saline (7%) improve lung function and reduce pulmonary exacerbations over 48 weeks versus isotonic saline?
shelves.mesh: Absenteeism · Administration, Inhalation · Adolescent · Adult · Albuterol · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Bronchodilator Agents · Child · Cough · Cystic Fibrosis · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Isotonic Solutions · Male · Maximal Midexpiratory Flow Rate · Premedication · Saline Solution, Hypertonic · Sodium Chloride · Treatment Outcome · Vital Capacity
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single long-term double-blind trial (n=164) whose own primary endpoint was null: the rate of change (slope) in lung function over 48 weeks did not differ between groups (P=0.79). The positive findings are secondary framings of the same data — averaged across all post-randomisation visits, FEV1 was 68 mL higher (95% CI 3 to 132) and FVC 82 mL higher on hypertonic saline — plus fewer pulmonary exacerbations (a 56% relative reduction, P=0.02, labelled relative) and more exacerbation-free patients (76% versus 62%; P=0.03). The card leads with the null primary, as the record requires; the topic file's summary ('modestly improved FEV1 and cut exacerbation frequency') quotes only the favourable half. Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate for the long-term question in this age group. Adjacent to Shelf #811 (CFTR modulators) without overlap — a different therapy class.

cards.headline: Elkins: primary slope outcome null (P=0.79); averaged FEV1 +68 mL and 56% relative fewer exacerbations
cards.summary: Elkins: primary slope outcome null (P=0.79); averaged FEV1 +68 mL and 56% relative fewer exacerbations
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, parallel-group controlled trial (48 weeks)
cards.people: 164 patients with stable cystic fibrosis aged at least 6 years, randomised to inhale 4 mL of 7% hypertonic saline or 0.9% saline (control) twice daily for 48 weeks, with quinine sulfate added to both solutions to mask taste and a bronchodilator before each dose. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary outcome — rate of change (slope) in FVC, FEV1, and FEF25-75 over 48 weeks — did not differ significantly between groups (P=0.79). Averaged across all post-randomisation visits, absolute lung function was higher on hypertonic saline: FVC by 82 mL (95% CI 12 to 153) and FEV1 by 68 mL (3 to 132), with similar FEF25-75. Pulmonary exacerbations were fewer on hypertonic saline (relative reduction 56%; P=0.02), and 76% versus 62% of patients remained exacerbation-free (P=0.03). Hypertonic saline was not associated with worsening bacterial infection or inflammation.
cards.watchOut: The trial's headline therefore depends on which analysis is quoted: the prespecified slope analysis is null, while the averaged-level and exacerbation analyses favour treatment. The card prints the primary first. A single long-term trial in this age group; the infant and preschool saline trials address a different population and are fenced in the synthesis, not carded.
cards.source: Elkins MR et al. A controlled trial of long-term inhaled hypertonic saline in patients with cystic fibrosis. N Engl J Med. 2006. PMID: 16421364. shelves.title: Azithromycin for persistent uncontrolled asthma (AMAZES; AZISAST)
shelves.question: In adults with persistent uncontrolled asthma despite inhaled therapy, does azithromycin three times weekly for 48 weeks reduce severe exacerbations versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Administration, Oral · Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Anti-Asthmatic Agents · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Asthma · Azithromycin · Bronchodilator Agents · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two asthma macrolide trials answer differently in different populations, and the cards do not average them. AMAZES (n=420, persistent symptomatic asthma on inhaled corticosteroids plus a long-acting bronchodilator): azithromycin 500 mg three times weekly for 48 weeks reduced total exacerbations to 1.07 versus 1.86 per patient-year (IRR 0.59 relative, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.74) and improved quality of life, at the price of more diarrhoea (34% versus 19%) — LIKELY. AZISAST (n=109, severe exacerbation-prone asthma, 6 months): the primary endpoint rate was not significantly different overall (0.75 versus 0.81 per subject; p=0.682); a predefined subgroup analysis found benefit only in non-eosinophilic severe asthma (0.44 versus 1.03; p=0.013) — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) overall with a phenotype-specific signal. Correction: the topic file says AZISAST 'agrees in the eosinophilic subgroup' — the record shows the NON-eosinophilic subgroup; the card follows the record. Distinct from Shelf #817 (azithromycin in COPD) and Shelf #815 (macrolides in bronchiectasis) by disease.

cards.headline: AMAZES: exacerbations 1.07 versus 1.86 per patient-year (IRR 0.59 relative); diarrhoea 34% versus 19%
cards.summary: AMAZES: exacerbations 1.07 versus 1.86 per patient-year (IRR 0.59 relative); diarrhoea 34% versus 19%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled parallel-group trial (48 weeks)
cards.people: 420 adults (213 azithromycin, 207 placebo) with symptomatic asthma despite medium-to-high dose inhaled corticosteroids plus a long-acting bronchodilator, without hearing impairment or QT prolongation; azithromycin 500 mg three times weekly for 48 weeks. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Azithromycin reduced total (moderate and severe) exacerbations to 1.07 per patient-year (95% CI 0.85–1.29) versus 1.86 (1.54–2.18) on placebo (IRR 0.59 relative, 0.47–0.74; p<0.0001). The proportion with at least one exacerbation fell from 61% (placebo) to 44% (p<0.0001). Asthma-related quality of life improved (adjusted mean difference 0.36, 0.21–0.52; p=0.001). Diarrhoea was more common on azithromycin (34% versus 19%; p=0.001).
cards.watchOut: A rate-ratio (relative) result: the absolute saving is about 0.8 exacerbations per patient-year in a population exacerbating roughly twice a year. Macrolide resistance selection is the standing concern with long-term use and is not measured in this record.

cards.headline: AZISAST: primary endpoint null overall (0.75 versus 0.81); benefit only in the predefined non-eosinophilic subgroup
cards.summary: AZISAST: primary endpoint null overall (0.75 versus 0.81); benefit only in the predefined non-eosinophilic subgroup
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial (26 weeks)
cards.people: 109 patients with exacerbation-prone severe asthma on inhaled corticosteroids plus long-acting beta-agonists, randomised to low-dose azithromycin (55) or placebo (54) as add-on therapy for 6 months. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The rate of primary endpoints (severe exacerbations and lower respiratory tract infections requiring antibiotics) was 0.75 per subject on azithromycin (95% CI 0.55 to 1.01) versus 0.81 on placebo (0.61 to 1.09) — not significantly different (p=0.682). cards.watchOut: The topic file states AZISAST agrees with AMAZES 'in the eosinophilic subgroup' — the record shows the opposite phenotype (non-eosinophilic), and its overall primary was null; the card follows the record. The subgroup was predefined, which earns it more weight than a post-hoc split, but it remains a subgroup of a null trial.
