shelves.title: FeNO-guided asthma management in adolescents and young adults
shelves.question: In adolescents and young adults with asthma, does adding exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) measurements to guideline-based treatment decisions reduce exacerbations versus guideline-based care alone?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Adult · Androstadienes · Asthma · Breath Tests · Bronchodilator Agents · Child · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fluticasone · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Male · Nitric Oxide · Treatment Outcome · Urban Population
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one large randomised trial (546 patients aged 12–20) found that adding FeNO measurements to guideline-based management changed nothing clinical over 46 weeks: symptom days 1.93 versus 1.89 (difference 0.04, 95% CI −0.22 to 0.29; p=0.78), with no differences in other symptoms, pulmonary function, or exacerbations — while the FeNO group received significantly higher inhaled corticosteroid doses (+119 µg/day; p=0.001) to achieve the same control. The wider FeNO literature is fenced in the synthesis rather than carded: a pregnancy-population trial (a different question) and a 2016 Cochrane review of FeNO-guided treatment in children, which is a review and is named without figures. A single large, well-conducted null trial in exactly this population carries the stamp.

cards.headline: Szefler: symptom days 1.93 versus 1.89 (p=0.78); FeNO guidance raised steroid doses without improving control
cards.summary: Szefler: symptom days 1.93 versus 1.89 (p=0.78); FeNO guidance raised steroid doses without improving control
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, parallel-group trial (46 weeks after a 3-week run-in)
cards.people: 546 inner-city patients aged 12–20 years with persistent asthma, randomised at ten US centres after a 3-week guideline-based run-in (780 screened) to standard NAEPP-guideline treatment or the same treatment modified by fractional exhaled nitric oxide measurements.
cards.result: Mean days with asthma symptoms over 46 weeks were 1.93 (95% CI 1.74 to 2.11) in the FeNO-monitoring group versus 1.89 (1.71 to 2.07) in controls (difference 0.04 [−0.22 to 0.29]; p=0.78). Other symptoms, pulmonary function, and asthma exacerbations did not differ between groups. The FeNO group received higher inhaled corticosteroid doses (difference 119 µg per day [49 to 189]; p=0.001). Adverse events did not differ.
cards.watchOut: A null on every clinical endpoint with a real cost — more corticosteroid exposure for the same control. Both groups were well controlled on guideline care after the run-in, which may have left little room for any biomarker strategy to add value; that is a property of the studied setting, stated here rather than used to discount the result.
cards.source: Szefler SJ et al. Management of asthma based on exhaled nitric oxide in addition to guideline-based treatment for inner-city adolescents and young adults: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2008. PMID: 18805335. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00114413, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Antibiotic treatment strategies for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP-START)
shelves.question: In adults hospitalised with community-acquired pneumonia on non-ICU wards, is a default strategy of beta-lactam monotherapy non-inferior to beta-lactam plus macrolide, or to fluoroquinolone monotherapy, for 90-day mortality?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Community-Acquired Infections · Cross-Over Studies · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Fluoroquinolones · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Length of Stay · Macrolides · Male · Middle Aged · Pneumonia, Bacterial · beta-Lactams
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C), because the primary outcome is 90-day mortality. In CAP-START (2,283 patients on Dutch non-ICU wards, cluster-randomised crossover), crude 90-day mortality was 9.0% under the beta-lactam strategy, 11.1% under beta-lactam plus macrolide, and 8.8% under fluoroquinolone monotherapy; the authors concluded the beta-lactam strategy was non-inferior against a 3-percentage-point margin. The caveat printed on the card: in the intention-to-treat analysis as the abstract reports it, the risk difference for the combination strategy versus beta-lactam alone was +1.9 points with a 90% CI up to +4.4 — beyond the 3-point margin — so the non-inferiority conclusion rests on the trial's adjusted analyses rather than on the crude interval printed in the record. Single trial; hospital stay was a median of 6 days under all strategies.

cards.headline: CAP-START: 90-day mortality 9.0% (beta-lactam) versus 11.1% (combination) and 8.8% (fluoroquinolone); non-inferiority claimed
cards.summary: CAP-START: 90-day mortality 9.0% (beta-lactam) versus 11.1% (combination) and 8.8% (fluoroquinolone); non-inferiority claimed
cards.type: Cluster-randomised, crossover strategy trial (non-inferiority)
cards.people: 2,283 adults with clinically suspected community-acquired pneumonia admitted to non-ICU wards in the Netherlands, treated under rotating 4-month default strategies: 656 during beta-lactam periods, 739 during beta-lactam–macrolide periods, 888 during fluoroquinolone periods; median age 70 years; strategy adherence 93.0%, 88.0%, and 92.7% respectively (deviations allowed for medical reasons).
cards.result: Crude 90-day mortality was 9.0% (beta-lactam), 11.1% (beta-lactam–macrolide), and 8.8% (fluoroquinolone). In the intention-to-treat analysis, the risk of death was higher by 1.9 percentage points (90% CI −0.6 to 4.4) with the combination strategy than with beta-lactam alone, and lower by 0.6 points (−2.8 to 1.9) with the fluoroquinolone strategy; the authors concluded these results indicated non-inferiority of the beta-lactam strategy against the 3-point margin. Median hospital stay was 6 days for all strategies.
cards.watchOut: The margin caveat, printed rather than smoothed over: the crude intention-to-treat interval for the combination comparison reaches +4.4 points, beyond the trial's own 3-point non-inferiority margin — so the non-inferiority claim depends on the trial's adjusted analyses, which the abstract does not display. Cluster design and 7–12% strategy non-adherence further soften the comparison.
cards.source: Postma DF et al. Antibiotic treatment strategies for community-acquired pneumonia in adults. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID: 25830421. shelves.title: Primary insomnia: eszopiclone improved sleep onset, maintenance and total sleep time — objectively in elderly patients and sustained over 6 months in adults, with no tolerance
shelves.question: In adults and older adults with primary insomnia, does eszopiclone improve sleep onset and maintenance (polysomnographic and patient-reported) compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Azabicyclo Compounds · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Piperazines/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Placebos · Polysomnography/drug effects · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/drug therapy
shelves.balance: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials from eszopiclone's development programme support the claim. In 264 elderly patients (aged 64–86) studied with polysomnography, two weeks of eszopiclone 2 mg significantly shortened sleep onset, reduced wake after sleep onset, and increased sleep efficiency and total sleep time versus placebo, with unpleasant taste the commonest adverse effect (12.5% versus 0%). In 788 adults, six months of nightly eszopiclone 3 mg produced significant, sustained improvements in sleep latency, wake time after sleep onset, awakenings, total sleep time and sleep quality, with better next-day function ratings and no evidence of tolerance. Both trials come from the manufacturer's programme, and both measured sleep parameters and ratings rather than downstream health outcomes. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).

cards.headline: McCall 2006 (elderly, polysomnography): eszopiclone 2 mg beat placebo on sleep onset, wake after sleep onset, efficiency and total sleep time over 2 weeks
cards.summary: McCall 2006 (elderly, polysomnography): eszopiclone 2 mg beat placebo on sleep onset, wake after sleep onset, efficiency and total sleep time over 2 weeks
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial — polysomnography (McCall 2006)
cards.people: 264 elderly patients aged 64–86 years with chronic primary insomnia (DSM-IV) meeting polysomnographic entry criteria, randomised double-blind to eszopiclone 2 mg (n = 136) or placebo (n = 128) nightly for 2 weeks; sleep measured by polysomnography on nights 1, 2, 13 and 14 and by patient report throughout.
cards.result: Eszopiclone was associated with significantly shorter sleep onset, less wake after sleep onset, higher sleep efficiency, more total sleep time, and greater patient-reported quality and depth of sleep than placebo (p < 0.05 for all); daytime functioning measures did not differ significantly. Unpleasant taste (12.5% vs 0%), dry mouth (8.8%), somnolence (6.6%) and dizziness (6.6%) were commoner on eszopiclone.
cards.watchOut: Only two weeks long, and the abstract reports significance rather than the size of the sleep gains in minutes; the 6-month adult trial below carries the durability claim. (The slate draft named Scharf as this paper's author; the PubMed record's first author is McCall — Scharf is a co-author.)

cards.headline: Krystal 2003 (adults, 6 months): nightly eszopiclone 3 mg improved every sleep measure versus placebo, sustained, with no evidence of tolerance
cards.summary: Krystal 2003 (adults, 6 months): nightly eszopiclone 3 mg improved every sleep measure versus placebo, sustained, with no evidence of tolerance
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial — 6 months (Krystal 2003)
cards.people: 788 adults aged 21–69 with chronic primary insomnia (DSM-IV) reporting under 6.5 hours of sleep and/or sleep latency over 30 minutes, randomised double-blind to eszopiclone 3 mg (n = 593) or placebo (n = 195) nightly for 6 months, with weekly interactive voice-response sleep assessments and monthly visits.
cards.result: At the first week and at each month for the study duration, eszopiclone produced significant and sustained improvements versus placebo in sleep latency, wake time after sleep onset, number of awakenings, number of nights awakened per week, total sleep time and quality of sleep (P ≤ 0.003); monthly ratings of next-day function, alertness and sense of physical well-being were also significantly better (P ≤ 0.002). There was no evidence of tolerance; the most common adverse events were unpleasant taste and headache.
cards.watchOut: Patient-reported (voice-response) outcomes only — no polysomnography in this trial — and both carded trials come from the manufacturer's development programme; independent replication is absent from this record.

shelves.title: Insomnia in Alzheimer's dementia: suvorexant added about half an hour of sleep a night versus placebo over 4 weeks — one trial
shelves.question: In people with probable Alzheimer's dementia and insomnia, does suvorexant improve total sleep time compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Alzheimer Disease/psychology · Azepines/administration & dosage · Female · Humans · Male · Polysomnography · Sleep/drug effects · Sleep Aids, Pharmaceutical/administration & dosage · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/drug therapy · Triazoles/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: One phase 3 randomised trial answers this directly. In 285 people with mild-to-moderate probable Alzheimer's dementia and insomnia, four weeks of suvorexant (10 mg, increasable to 20 mg) improved polysomnographic total sleep time by 73 minutes from baseline versus 45 minutes on placebo — a treatment difference of 28 minutes (95% CI 11–45; p < 0.01). Somnolence was reported in 4.2% on suvorexant versus 1.4% on placebo. The trial measured sleep over four weeks only; it does not show longer-term safety in dementia, or effects on cognition, behaviour or falls. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single well-conducted trial with a modest gain. Flagged Tier C as a single-trial benefit shelf.

cards.headline: Herring 2020: suvorexant increased total sleep time 28 minutes more than placebo at 4 weeks in probable Alzheimer's dementia with insomnia
cards.summary: Herring 2020: suvorexant increased total sleep time 28 minutes more than placebo at 4 weeks in probable Alzheimer's dementia with insomnia
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Herring 2020)
cards.people: 285 participants with mild-to-moderate probable Alzheimer's disease dementia and insomnia meeting clinical criteria for both, randomised double-blind to suvorexant 10 mg (increasable to 20 mg based on clinical response; n = 142) or placebo (n = 143) for 4 weeks; sleep assessed by overnight polysomnography in a sleep laboratory; primary endpoint change from baseline in total sleep time at week 4. 277 participants (97%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Model-based least-squares mean improvement in total sleep time at week 4 was 73 minutes with suvorexant versus 45 minutes with placebo (difference 28 minutes, 95% CI 11–45; p < 0.01). Somnolence was reported in 4.2% of suvorexant-treated patients and 1.4% of placebo-treated patients.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks, one trial, a sleep-time endpoint only: nothing here addresses falls, cognition, behaviour or next-day function in dementia. The placebo group also gained 45 minutes — the drug's added value is the 28-minute difference.
cards.source: Herring WJ et al.. Polysomnographic assessment of suvorexant in patients with probable Alzheimer's disease dementia and insomnia: a randomized trial. Alzheimers Dement. 2020. shelves.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea with residual sleepiness: solriamfetol improved wakefulness dose-dependently — and blinded withdrawal lost the benefit within two weeks
shelves.question: In obstructive sleep apnoea with residual excessive daytime sleepiness, does solriamfetol improve wakefulness (maintenance of wakefulness test and Epworth score) compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Carbamates/therapeutic use · Disorders of Excessive Somnolence/drug therapy, etiology · Dopamine Uptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Norepinephrine Plasma Membrane Transport Proteins/drug effects · Phenylalanine/analogs & derivatives, therapeutic use · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive/complications
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials from the TONES programme support solriamfetol for excessive sleepiness in obstructive sleep apnoea despite current or prior sleep-apnoea treatment. In TONES 3 (476 participants, 12 weeks), solriamfetol 37.5–300 mg met both coprimary endpoints — maintenance of wakefulness test latency and Epworth score — at every dose, with dose-dependent effects from week 1; adverse events were commoner than on placebo (67.9% vs 47.9%), headache (10.1%) and nausea (7.9%) the most frequent. In TONES 4, responders stabilised on solriamfetol were re-randomised: those switched to placebo worsened sharply over two weeks (wakefulness −12.1 minutes; Epworth +4.5 points) while those continuing held their gains — between-group differences of 11.2 minutes and −4.6 points. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for wakefulness and sleepiness scores; the trials measured sleepiness, not accidents or cardiovascular outcomes.

cards.headline: Schweitzer 2019 (TONES 3): solriamfetol met both coprimary endpoints at every dose over 12 weeks, dose-dependently; adverse events 67.9% vs 47.9%
cards.summary: Schweitzer 2019 (TONES 3): solriamfetol met both coprimary endpoints at every dose over 12 weeks, dose-dependently; adverse events 67.9% vs 47.9%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Schweitzer 2019, TONES 3)
cards.people: 476 participants with obstructive sleep apnoea and excessive sleepiness, with current or prior sleep-apnoea treatment, randomised double-blind to solriamfetol 37.5, 75, 150 or 300 mg or placebo for 12 weeks; coprimary endpoints maintenance of wakefulness test sleep latency and Epworth Sleepiness Scale score (459 participants in the prespecified efficacy analyses).
cards.result: Both coprimary endpoints were met at all solriamfetol doses (P < 0.05), with dose-dependent effects observed at week 1 and maintained over the study duration. All doses except 37.5 mg produced higher percentages of participants reporting improvement on the Patient Global Impression of Change. Adverse events were reported by 67.9% of solriamfetol-treated versus 47.9% of placebo participants; the most common on solriamfetol were headache (10.1%), nausea (7.9%), decreased appetite (7.6%), anxiety (7.0%) and nasopharyngitis (5.1%). Five serious adverse events (three on solriamfetol) were judged unrelated to study drug.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports significance and dose-dependence rather than the size of the wakefulness gain at each dose; the withdrawal trial below supplies the concrete numbers. Blood-pressure and cardiovascular outcomes are not addressed in this record.
cards.source: Schweitzer PK et al.. Solriamfetol for Excessive Sleepiness in Obstructive Sleep Apnea (TONES 3). A Randomized Controlled Trial. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2019. PMID: 30521757. cards.headline: Strollo 2019 (TONES 4): switching responders to placebo lost 12.1 minutes of wakefulness in 2 weeks versus staying on solriamfetol (difference 11.2 minutes; Epworth difference −4.6)
cards.summary: Strollo 2019 (TONES 4): switching responders to placebo lost 12.1 minutes of wakefulness in 2 weeks versus staying on solriamfetol (difference 11.2 minutes; Epworth difference −4.6)
cards.type: Randomised withdrawal trial (Strollo 2019, TONES 4)
cards.people: Adults with obstructive sleep apnoea and excessive sleepiness who had improved during 2 weeks of open solriamfetol titration and 2 weeks of stable dosing (148 completers), then randomised double-blind to continue solriamfetol (n = 62) or switch to placebo (n = 62) for a further 2 weeks; coprimary endpoints change from week 4 to week 6 in maintenance of wakefulness test latency and Epworth score (modified intention-to-treat n = 122).
cards.result: Participants continuing solriamfetol maintained their improvement (least-squares mean change −1.0 minutes on the wakefulness test; −0.1 Epworth points), whereas those switched to placebo worsened (−12.1 minutes; +4.5 points): least-squares mean differences between treatments were 11.2 minutes (95% CI 7.8–14.6) and −4.6 points (95% CI −6.4 to −2.8). Worsening on the Patient Global Impression of Change was reported by 20% continuing versus 50% switched (P = .0005). Common adverse events included headache, dry mouth, nausea, dizziness and insomnia.
cards.watchOut: A withdrawal design proves the drug was doing the work in people who had already responded to and tolerated it — it does not estimate the effect of starting treatment in an unselected patient.
cards.source: Strollo PJ et al.. Solriamfetol for the Treatment of Excessive Sleepiness in OSA: A Placebo-Controlled Randomized Withdrawal Study. Chest. 2019. PMID: 30471270. shelves.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea with daytime sleepiness: pitolisant cut Epworth scores by about 2.6–2.8 points versus placebo — in patients refusing CPAP and in patients still sleepy on it
shelves.question: In obstructive sleep apnoea with excessive daytime sleepiness — in patients refusing CPAP or still sleepy on it — does pitolisant reduce sleepiness compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Disorders of Excessive Somnolence/drug therapy, etiology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Piperidines/therapeutic use · Receptors, Histamine H3/therapeutic use · Self Report · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive/complications, drug therapy · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The HAROSA programme ran the same 12-week design in the two populations that need an adjunct: patients refusing continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), and patients adherent to CPAP with residual sleepiness. In CPAP-refusers (268 randomised), pitolisant titrated to 20 mg daily reduced Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores by 2.8 points more than placebo (95% CI −4.0 to −1.5; P < 0.001), though objective wake-maintenance testing did not improve; adverse events were similar to placebo (29.5% vs 25.4%). In CPAP-adherent patients (244 randomised), the advantage was 2.6 points (95% CI −3.9 to −1.4; P < .001), with responder rates 71.0% versus 54.1% and adverse events commoner on pitolisant (47.0% vs 32.8%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent across two trials, but the effect is a few points on a self-reported sleepiness scale, with objective wakefulness unproven in the trial that measured it head-on.

cards.headline: Dauvilliers 2020 (HAROSA II, CPAP-refusers): pitolisant cut Epworth scores 2.8 points more than placebo — but wake-maintenance testing did not improve
cards.summary: Dauvilliers 2020 (HAROSA II, CPAP-refusers): pitolisant cut Epworth scores 2.8 points more than placebo — but wake-maintenance testing did not improve
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Dauvilliers 2020, HAROSA II)
cards.people: 268 patients with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnoea (mean apnoea–hypopnoea index 49/h; baseline Epworth score 15.7) who refused continuous positive airway pressure treatment, randomised double-blind 3:1 to pitolisant individually titrated up to 20 mg daily (n = 200) or placebo (n = 68) for 12 weeks; primary endpoint change in Epworth Sleepiness Scale score.
cards.result: Epworth scores were reduced 2.8 points more with pitolisant than with placebo (95% CI −4.0 to −1.5; P < 0.001), and the Pichot fatigue score was also reduced; however, wake maintenance on the Oxford Sleep Resistance test was not improved. Adverse events — mainly headache, insomnia, nausea and vertigo — occurred in 29.5% on pitolisant and 25.4% on placebo, with no cardiovascular or other significant safety concerns reported.
cards.watchOut: The win is on self-reported sleepiness; the objective wakefulness test in the same trial did not improve — calibrate the claim to feeling less sleepy, not to measured wakefulness or driving safety.

cards.headline: Pépin 2021 (HAROSA I, CPAP-adherent): pitolisant cut Epworth scores 2.6 points more than placebo; responders 71.0% vs 54.1%
cards.summary: Pépin 2021 (HAROSA I, CPAP-adherent): pitolisant cut Epworth scores 2.6 points more than placebo; responders 71.0% vs 54.1%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Pépin 2021, HAROSA I)
cards.people: 244 patients with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnoea adhering to continuous positive airway pressure (mean on-CPAP apnoea–hypopnoea index 4.2/h; baseline Epworth score 14.7) with residual excessive daytime sleepiness, randomised double-blind 3:1 to pitolisant individually titrated up to 20 mg daily (n = 183) or placebo (n = 61) for 12 weeks; primary endpoint change in Epworth Sleepiness Scale score.
cards.result: Epworth scores fell 2.6 points more with pitolisant than with placebo (95% CI −3.9 to −1.4; P < .001), and responders (Epworth ≤ 10 or a fall of ≥ 3 points) were 71.0% on pitolisant versus 54.1% on placebo (P = .013). Adverse events, mainly headache and insomnia, were commoner on pitolisant (47.0% vs 32.8%; P = .03); no cardiovascular or other significant safety concerns were reported.
cards.watchOut: The placebo responder rate was 54% — much of the improvement patients feel is context and expectation; the drug's attributable share is the 17-percentage-point responder gap and the 2.6-point Epworth difference.

shelves.title: Older adults with osteoarthritis pain and insomnia: CBT-I improved sleep in two trials — insomnia severity down 3.5 points versus control in the 327-patient COPE trial; pain relief was smaller and less durable
shelves.question: In older adults with osteoarthritis pain and insomnia, does cognitive-behavioural therapy for insomnia improve sleep — and does pain improve with it?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Comorbidity · Cross-Over Studies · Female · Humans · Male · Osteoarthritis/epidemiology, therapy · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/epidemiology, therapy
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials say CBT-I improves sleep in this population, with pain a secondary and less certain winner. The small first trial (51 patients; a secondary analysis) found self-reported sleep improved and pain reduced after CBT-I but not after an attention control, with gains maintained at one year — though its abstract reports directions rather than effect sizes. The definitive COPE trial (327 older adults with osteoarthritis pain; telephone CBT-I versus education-only control) cut Insomnia Severity Index scores by 3.5 points more than control at 2 months (95% CI −4.4 to −2.6; P < .001), sustained at 12 months (−3.0 points), with 56.3% versus 25.8% in insomnia remission at one year and significantly reduced fatigue; the pain advantage seen after treatment was not sustained at 12 months. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for sleep, with the pain claim kept modest on the shelf's face.

cards.headline: Vitiello 2009: CBT-I improved self-reported sleep and reduced pain versus attention control in 51 older adults with osteoarthritis and insomnia — maintained at 1 year
cards.summary: Vitiello 2009: CBT-I improved self-reported sleep and reduced pain versus attention control in 51 older adults with osteoarthritis and insomnia — maintained at 1 year
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial — secondary analysis (Vitiello 2009)
cards.people: 51 older adults (mean age about 67–69 years) with osteoarthritis and comorbid insomnia, randomised to CBT-I (n = 23) or an attention control (n = 28), neither treatment addressing pain directly; 12 control participants crossed over to CBT-I after the control phase. This card is a secondary analysis of the trial; sleep and pain were self-reported after treatment and, for the CBT-I groups, at 1-year follow-up.
cards.result: CBT-I participants reported significantly improved sleep and significantly reduced pain after treatment; control participants reported no significant improvements. At one-year follow-up, improved sleep and reduced pain were maintained both in the original CBT-I group and in those who had crossed over from control. The abstract reports directions and significance, not effect sizes.
cards.watchOut: Small (n = 51), a secondary analysis, with crossover after the control phase — supportive evidence for the COPE trial below, not stand-alone proof; the one-year pain claim rests on within-group follow-up, and no effect sizes are given in the record.
cards.source: Vitiello MV et al.. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia improves sleep and decreases pain in older adults with co-morbid insomnia and osteoarthritis. J Clin Sleep Med. 2009. PMID: 19968014. Registry ID: none — pre-modern-registration-era trial. cards.headline: McCurry 2021 (COPE, n = 327): telephone CBT-I beat education control on insomnia by 3.5 ISI points at 2 months and 3.0 at 12 months; remission 56.3% vs 25.8% at one year
cards.summary: McCurry 2021 (COPE, n = 327): telephone CBT-I beat education control on insomnia by 3.5 ISI points at 2 months and 3.0 at 12 months; remission 56.3% vs 25.8% at one year
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (McCurry 2021, COPE)
cards.people: 327 adults aged 60 years and over with moderate-to-severe insomnia and osteoarthritis pain, recruited statewide through Kaiser Permanente Washington, randomised to six 20- to 30-minute telephone CBT-I sessions over 8 weeks or an education-only control (information about sleep and osteoarthritis); blinded assessments at baseline, 2 months post-treatment and 12 months; primary outcome Insomnia Severity Index score.
cards.result: Insomnia Severity Index scores fell 8.1 points with CBT-I versus 4.8 with control at 2 months — an adjusted between-group difference of −3.5 points (95% CI −4.4 to −2.6; P < .001) — sustained at 12 months (−3.0 points, 95% CI −4.1 to −2.0; P < .001). At 12 months, 56.3% of the CBT-I group versus 25.8% of controls remained in insomnia remission (ISI ≤ 7). Fatigue was significantly reduced at both time points; pain differences favoured CBT-I after treatment but were not sustained at 12 months.
cards.watchOut: An education-only control cannot blind participants to a behavioural treatment, so expectation contributes to self-reported sleep gains; the strong feature is durability — the gap persisted a full year after treatment ended.
cards.source: McCurry SM et al.. Effect of Telephone Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia in Older Adults With Osteoarthritis Pain: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2021. PMID: 33616613. Registry ID: NCT02946957. shelves.title: Menopausal insomnia: telephone CBT-I beat menopause education — insomnia severity down 5.2 points more, with 70% versus 24% in the no-insomnia range at 8 weeks (MsFLASH) — one trial
shelves.question: In perimenopausal and postmenopausal women with vasomotor symptoms and insomnia, does telephone-delivered CBT-I improve insomnia severity compared with menopause education control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/instrumentation, methods · Female · Humans · Interview, Psychological/methods · Middle Aged · Patient Outcome Assessment · Perimenopause/physiology, psychology · Postmenopause/physiology, psychology · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/diagnosis, etiology, psychology, therapy · Teaching Materials · Telephone
shelves.balance: One well-run trial answers this. In the MsFLASH trial, 106 perimenopausal and postmenopausal women with moderate insomnia (Insomnia Severity Index ≥ 12) and at least two hot flashes daily received six telephone sessions of CBT-I or menopause education control over 8 weeks. Insomnia severity fell 9.9 points with CBT-I versus 4.7 with education (between-group difference 5.2 points; P < .001), sleep quality on the Pittsburgh index improved 2.7 points more, and at 8 weeks 70% of the CBT-I group versus 24% of controls scored in the no-insomnia range — differences sustained at 24 weeks. Hot-flash frequency did not differ between groups; hot-flash interference fell more with CBT-I. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single trial, but randomised with blinded assessment and a durable effect. Flagged Tier C as a single-trial benefit shelf.

cards.headline: McCurry 2016 (MsFLASH): telephone CBT-I beat menopause education — ISI difference 5.2 points at 8 weeks; no-insomnia range 70% vs 24%
cards.summary: McCurry 2016 (MsFLASH): telephone CBT-I beat menopause education — ISI difference 5.2 points at 8 weeks; no-insomnia range 70% vs 24%
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (McCurry 2016, MsFLASH)
cards.people: 106 perimenopausal or postmenopausal women aged 40–65 with moderate insomnia symptoms (Insomnia Severity Index ≥ 12) and two or more daily hot flashes, randomised single-site to six telephone CBT-I sessions (n = 53; sleep restriction, stimulus control, sleep hygiene, cognitive restructuring, homework) or menopause education control (n = 53) over 8 weeks, with blinded assessments at baseline, 8 and 24 weeks and intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: At 8 weeks, Insomnia Severity Index scores had decreased 9.9 points with CBT-I versus 4.7 with education (mean between-group difference 5.2 points, 95% CI −6.1 to −3.3; P < .001); Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores decreased 4.0 versus 1.4 points (difference 2.7 points, 95% CI −3.9 to −1.5; P < .001). At 8 and 24 weeks, 70% and 84% of the CBT-I group scored in the no-insomnia range versus 24% and 43% of controls, and diary sleep latency, wake time and sleep efficiency also improved more with CBT-I. Daily hot-flash frequency did not differ, but hot-flash interference decreased significantly more with CBT-I at 8 weeks (−15.7 vs −7.1; P = .03) and at 24 weeks (−22.8 vs −11.6; P = .003).
cards.watchOut: Single-site, 106 women, self-reported sleep outcomes against an education control — participants knew their treatment. The effect is large and durable, but a second trial in this exact population does not yet exist on this record.
cards.source: McCurry SM et al.. Telephone-Based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia in Perimenopausal and Postmenopausal Women With Vasomotor Symptoms: A MsFLASH Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2016. PMID: 27213646. Registry ID: NCT01936441. shelves.title: Delayed sleep-wake phase disorder: melatonin 0.5 mg an hour before the desired bedtime, plus scheduled sleep-wake times, advanced sleep onset by 34 minutes versus placebo — one trial
shelves.question: In delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, does low-dose melatonin timed before the desired bedtime, combined with behavioural sleep-wake scheduling, advance sleep and improve daytime function compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Actigraphy · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Melatonin/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · New South Wales · Sleep/drug effects · Sleep Aids, Pharmaceutical/therapeutic use · Sleep Wake Disorders/drug therapy · South Australia · Victoria · Young Adult
shelves.balance: One double-blind randomised trial — the first for this disorder on this record. In 116 clinically diagnosed patients whose endogenous melatonin rhythm was delayed relative to their desired bedtime, four weeks of fast-release melatonin 0.5 mg taken one hour before the desired bedtime, combined with behavioural sleep-wake scheduling (the placebo group received the scheduling too), brought actigraphic sleep onset 34 minutes earlier than placebo (95% CI −60 to −8). Sleep-related daytime impairment, sleep disturbance and insomnia severity also improved, and 52.8% versus 24.0% achieved more than minimal clinician-rated improvement; adverse events (light-headedness, daytime sleepiness, decreased libido) occurred at similar rates in both groups. Notably, melatonin onset time itself (DLMO) did not shift significantly in the subset tested — in this trial the benefit looks sleep-promoting rather than phase-shifting. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single trial, 4 weeks. Flagged Tier C as a single-trial benefit shelf.

cards.headline: Sletten 2018: melatonin 0.5 mg plus sleep-wake scheduling advanced sleep onset by 34 minutes versus placebo in delayed sleep-wake phase disorder
cards.summary: Sletten 2018: melatonin 0.5 mg plus sleep-wake scheduling advanced sleep onset by 34 minutes versus placebo in delayed sleep-wake phase disorder
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Sletten 2018)
cards.people: 116 patients with clinically diagnosed delayed sleep-wake phase disorder whose salivary dim-light melatonin onset was delayed relative to their desired (or required) bedtime, randomised double-blind at Australian outpatient clinics to fast-release melatonin 0.5 mg or placebo, taken 1 hour before the desired bedtime on at least 5 nights a week for 4 weeks; both groups received behavioural sleep-wake scheduling with bedtime fixed at the desired time. Primary outcome was actigraphic sleep onset time; intention-to-treat n = 116, mean age 29.0 years.
cards.result: Relative to baseline and compared with placebo, sleep onset occurred 34 minutes earlier in the melatonin group (95% CI −60 to −8). Sleep efficiency in the first third of time in bed increased; PROMIS sleep-related impairment and sleep disturbance, insomnia severity and functional disability decreased; and 52.8% on melatonin versus 24.0% on placebo showed more than minimal clinician-rated improvement (P < 0.05). Post-treatment melatonin onset (DLMO), assessed in a 43-patient subset, was not significantly different between groups. Adverse events — light-headedness, daytime sleepiness and decreased libido — occurred at similar rates in both groups; long-term benefit and safety were not assessed.
cards.watchOut: Only patients with a demonstrably delayed endogenous melatonin rhythm were enrolled, treatment lasted 4 weeks, and the circadian phase marker itself did not move significantly — benefit in unselected 'night owl' patients, and durability beyond 4 weeks, are unproven on this record. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Sletten TL et al.. Efficacy of melatonin with behavioural sleep-wake scheduling for delayed sleep-wake phase disorder: A double-blind, randomised clinical trial. PLoS Med. 2018. shelves.title: Oral mucolytics in COPD: twice-daily N-acetylcysteine and carbocisteine cut exacerbations by about a quarter in Chinese trials — the older 600 mg once-daily European trial found nothing
shelves.question: In people with COPD, do oral mucolytic antioxidants — N-acetylcysteine or carbocisteine — reduce exacerbations compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acetylcysteine/administration & dosage · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · China · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Free Radical Scavengers/administration & dosage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/complications, drug therapy, physiopathology · Treatment Outcome · Vital Capacity
shelves.balance: Mucolytic antioxidants are cheap, oral and widely used in COPD outside the English-speaking world, and the trial record splits by dose and place. PANTHEON (1,006 Chinese patients with moderate-to-severe COPD) found N-acetylcysteine 600 mg twice daily cut exacerbations from 1.49 to 1.16 per patient-year (risk ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.67–0.90). PEACE (709 Chinese patients) found carbocisteine 1,500 mg/day cut exacerbations from 1.35 to 1.01 per year (risk ratio 0.75, 0.62–0.92). The older European BRONCUS trial (523 patients, three years) used half the NAC dose — 600 mg once daily — and found nothing: 1.25 vs 1.29 exacerbations per year (HR 0.99) and no effect on lung-function decline. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real, modest effect at the higher dose in the populations studied, with the dose caveat on the shelf's face.

cards.headline: PANTHEON: N-acetylcysteine 600 mg twice daily — 1.16 vs 1.49 exacerbations per patient-year (risk ratio 0.78, 0.67–0.90)
cards.summary: PANTHEON: N-acetylcysteine 600 mg twice daily — 1.16 vs 1.49 exacerbations per patient-year (risk ratio 0.78, 0.67–0.90)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Zheng 2014, PANTHEON)
cards.people: 1,006 patients aged 40–80 with moderate-to-severe COPD (FEV1 30–70% predicted) at 34 Chinese hospitals, randomised to N-acetylcysteine 600 mg twice daily or placebo for 1 year, stratified by inhaled corticosteroid use.
cards.result: 497 exacerbations in the NAC group (1.16 per patient-year) vs 641 on placebo (1.49 per patient-year); risk ratio 0.78 (95% CI 0.67–0.90; p=0.0011). Adverse events 29% vs 26%, with acute exacerbation the commonest serious event in both groups (6% vs 7%) — the drug was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A Chinese population with relatively low inhaled-corticosteroid use by current Western standards; whether the effect adds to modern triple inhaled therapy is not what this trial tested. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Zheng JP et al.. Twice daily N-acetylcysteine 600 mg for exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (PANTHEON): a randomised, double-blind placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2014. PMID: 24621680. Registry ID: ChiCTR-TRC-09000460 (Chinese Clinical Trials Registry, as recorded in the record). cards.headline: PEACE: carbocisteine 1,500 mg/day cut exacerbations from 1.35 to 1.01 per year (risk ratio 0.75, 0.62–0.92)
cards.summary: PEACE: carbocisteine 1,500 mg/day cut exacerbations from 1.35 to 1.01 per year (risk ratio 0.75, 0.62–0.92)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Zheng 2008, PEACE)
cards.people: 709 patients with COPD (FEV1 25–79% predicted, at least two exacerbations in the previous 2 years) at 22 Chinese centres, randomised to carbocisteine 1,500 mg/day or placebo for 1 year; primary endpoint exacerbation rate.
cards.result: Exacerbations per patient per year: 1.01 (SE 0.06) on carbocisteine vs 1.35 (SE 0.06) on placebo; risk ratio 0.75 (95% CI 0.62–0.92; p=0.004). No significant interaction with COPD severity, smoking, or inhaled corticosteroid use. Carbocisteine was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Same geographic caveat as PANTHEON; carbocisteine is not marketed in all countries, so for many readers this is a class-evidence card rather than a purchasable option. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: BRONCUS: N-acetylcysteine 600 mg once daily for 3 years — no effect on exacerbations (HR 0.99) or FEV1 decline
cards.summary: BRONCUS: N-acetylcysteine 600 mg once daily for 3 years — no effect on exacerbations (HR 0.99) or FEV1 decline
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Decramer 2005, BRONCUS)
cards.people: 523 patients with COPD at 50 European centres, randomised to N-acetylcysteine 600 mg daily or placebo for 3 years; primary outcomes yearly FEV1 decline and exacerbation rate, analysed intention-to-treat.
cards.result: FEV1 decline: 54 mL/year on NAC vs 47 mL/year on placebo (difference in slope 8 mL, 95% CI −25 to 10). Exacerbations: 1.25 vs 1.29 per year (HR 0.99, 0.89–1.10; p=0.85). A subgroup analysis suggested possible benefit in patients not on inhaled corticosteroids, and a secondary analysis suggested an effect on hyperinflation.
cards.watchOut: Half the PANTHEON dose. The shelf reads the three trials together as a dose story, but that reconciliation is an interpretation across trials, not a tested comparison — a head-to-head dose trial does not exist. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Decramer M et al.. Effects of N-acetylcysteine on outcomes in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (Bronchitis Randomized on NAC Cost-Utility Study, BRONCUS): a randomised placebo-controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2005. PMID: 15866309. Registry ID: none recorded in the PubMed record. shelves.title: Does Mucinex thin mucus? Guaifenesin's own trials mostly say no
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with an acute respiratory infection and productive cough, does guaifenesin — the expectorant in Mucinex and Robitussin — thin mucus or relieve chest congestion compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Guaifenesin · Expectorants · Respiratory Tract Infections · Sputum · Mucociliary Clearance · Cough · Humans
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Guaifenesin — the expectorant in Mucinex and Robitussin — is supposed to thin mucus, and on the direct tests of that claim it does not: in the main trial (NCT01046136; 378 randomised, 295 completed), extended-release guaifenesin for 7 days changed neither sputum volume (P=.41) nor any sputum property (percent solids, tension, elasticity, viscosity, impedance; P=.45–.88) (Hoffer-Schaefer 2014), and a single 1,200 mg dose of Mucinex changed neither mucociliary nor cough clearance nor sputum properties in 38 adults (Bennett 2015). The one favourable signal comes from the same main trial's patient-reported report: the SUM8 diary score separated most at day 4 in favour of guaifenesin — in a pilot study whose stated purpose was validating that diary instrument (Albrecht 2012). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the objective expectorant claim fails its own trials, and the residual symptom signal is a single unvalidated-at-the-time diary score from a single trial counted once.

cards.headline: Hoffer-Schaefer 2014: extended-release guaifenesin changed no sputum measure at all — volume P=.41, and every sputum property P=.45 to .88
cards.summary: Hoffer-Schaefer 2014: extended-release guaifenesin changed no sputum measure at all — volume P=.41, and every sputum property P=.45 to .88
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Hoffer-Schaefer 2014)
cards.people: 378 adolescents and adults (188 guaifenesin, 190 placebo) who were otherwise healthy, with a productive cough from an acute respiratory tract infection of up to 5 days and at least 2 of cough, thickened mucus and chest congestion, at multiple centres; 295 completed the full protocol (151 guaifenesin, 144 placebo). The treatment was extended-release guaifenesin — two 600 mg tablets twice daily for 7 days — the Mucinex formulation named in the publication.
cards.result: Symptoms in both groups improved to a similar degree over time. There were no significant differences between guaifenesin and placebo for sputum volume (P=.41), percent solids (P=.69), interfacial tension (P=.88), elasticity (P=.71), viscosity (P=.45) or mechanical impedance (P=.75), measured on samples collected on days 1, 3, 4 and 8. The authors conclude the recommended dose had no measurable effect on sputum volume or properties and is unlikely to be an expectorant or mucolytic in acute respiratory infection. Registry ID: NCT01046136.
cards.watchOut: The null is on objective sputum measures; the trial's symptom outcomes are reported in the companion paper carded next — the two papers are one trial (NCT01046136), not two. 83 of 378 randomised subjects did not complete the full protocol.
cards.source: Hoffer-Schaefer A et al.. Guaifenesin has no effect on sputum volume or sputum properties in adolescents and adults with acute respiratory tract infections. Respiratory Care. 2014. PMID: 24003241. Registry ID: NCT01046136. cards.headline: Albrecht 2012: the SAME trial's symptom report (not a second trial) — the SUM8 diary score favoured guaifenesin at day 4, in a study whose stated purpose was validating the diary
cards.summary: Albrecht 2012: the SAME trial's symptom report (not a second trial) — the SUM8 diary score favoured guaifenesin at day 4, in a study whose stated purpose was validating the diary
cards.type: Patient-reported outcomes report of a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial (Albrecht 2012)
cards.people: The same pilot trial as the card above (NCT01046136): 378 patients randomised to 1,200 mg extended-release guaifenesin (n=188) or placebo (n=190) every 12 hours for 7 days for symptoms of upper respiratory tract infection, assessed with the Daily Cough and Phlegm Diary, the Spontaneous Symptom Severity Assessment and the Wisconsin Upper Respiratory Symptom Survey, followed by a two-phase validation study of those instruments.
cards.result: Subjective measures of efficacy at day 4 showed the most prominent difference between treatment groups, in favour of guaifenesin, and the 8-symptom (SUM8) questions in the Daily Cough and Phlegm Diary, analysed as a composite score, appeared to be the strongest candidate endpoint for further evaluation. Interviews supported the content of the assessments, which were validated in phase II; treatments were well tolerated. The abstract gives no numerical SUM8 treatment difference.
cards.watchOut: Count this trial once. The paper's stated purpose was to validate a symptom diary for future mucoactive-drug studies — a pilot and instrument-validation exercise — and its favourable day-4 signal is a patient-reported score in the same patients whose sputum measures were entirely null in the companion report. The authors include the product's manufacturer-side investigators.

cards.headline: Bennett 2015: a single 1,200 mg dose of Mucinex changed neither mucociliary nor cough clearance, nor any sputum property, in 38 adults
cards.summary: Bennett 2015: a single 1,200 mg dose of Mucinex changed neither mucociliary nor cough clearance, nor any sputum property, in 38 adults
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Bennett 2015)
cards.people: 38 non-smoking adults with an acute upper respiratory tract infection (19 guaifenesin, 19 placebo) in a randomised, parallel-group, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of a single dose of Mucinex 1,200 mg (2 × 600 mg extended-release tablets) versus placebo, with clearance of inhaled radioactive tracer measured in the morning and again 4 hours later, and sputum properties measured in the 8–12 subjects per cohort who expectorated during the cough period.
cards.result: There was no effect of extended-release guaifenesin on mucociliary or cough clearance compared with placebo: mucociliary clearance through 60 minutes was 8.3% versus 11.8% (period 1 versus 2) on placebo and 9.7% versus 11.1% on drug (not significant), and cough clearance was 9.9% versus 9.1% on placebo and 10.8% versus 5.6% on drug (not significant). There was no significant difference in sputum biophysical properties after drug or placebo. Registry ID: NCT01114581.
cards.watchOut: Very small (n=38), single-dose, and mechanistic — tracer clearance over hours, not days of illness. It tests whether one dose thins or clears mucus acutely and finds nothing; it cannot rule on multi-day symptom relief, which the larger trial above addresses.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the objective mucus measures are null everywhere; the only positive signal is one diary score in one pilot trial — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the objective mucus measures are null everywhere; the only positive signal is one diary score in one pilot trial — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Adolescents and adults with acute respiratory infection and productive cough across two distinct trials: NCT01046136 (378 randomised, reported twice) and Bennett 2015 (38, single dose).
cards.result: In NCT01046136, sputum volume and every measured sputum property were null (P=.41–.88) while its companion symptom report found the SUM8 diary score most separated at day 4; a single 1,200 mg dose changed neither mucociliary nor cough clearance nor sputum properties (Bennett 2015). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Two of the three cards are one trial — counting them as independent trials would double-count the only positive signal. The evidence base is manufacturer-programme research on a symptom-score instrument still being validated, in self-limiting infections that improve on their own.

shelves.title: Chronic cough that won't quit: gabapentin and gefapixant help some
shelves.question: In adults with refractory or unexplained chronic cough, do neuromodulators (gabapentin, pregabalin) or the P2X3 antagonist gefapixant reduce cough compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Cough · Chronic Disease · Gabapentin · Pregabalin · Pyrimidines · Sulfonamides · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: For a cough that has lasted years and resisted standard treatment, neuromodulators and the P2X3 antagonist gefapixant each beat placebo — modestly, and at a tolerability price. Gabapentin (maximum 1,800 mg/day for 10 weeks) improved cough-specific quality of life by 1.80 Leicester Cough Questionnaire points over placebo (95% CI 0.56–3.04; number needed to treat 3.58) in 62 patients, with side-effects in 31% versus 10%. Pregabalin 300 mg/day added to speech pathology improved LCQ by a further 3.5 points (95% CI 1.1–5.8) in 40 patients, though objective cough frequency did not differ. Gefapixant 45 mg twice daily reduced 24-hour cough frequency by a relative 18.5% in COUGH-1 and 14.6% in COUGH-2 beyond placebo, in over 2,000 participants whose cough had lasted on average more than 11 years; the 15 mg dose did not work, and taste disturbance was common (dysgeusia 16.2% and 21.1%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): placebo-controlled benefit is consistent across three agents, but the neuromodulator trials are small and the gefapixant effect is a modest relative reduction bought with taste side-effects.

cards.headline: Ryan 2012: gabapentin improved cough quality of life by 1.80 LCQ points over placebo (NNT 3.58) in 62 patients
cards.summary: Ryan 2012: gabapentin improved cough quality of life by 1.80 LCQ points over placebo (NNT 3.58) in 62 patients
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Ryan 2012)
cards.people: 62 adults with refractory chronic cough (more than 8 weeks, without active respiratory disease or infection) at an outpatient clinic in Australia, randomised to gabapentin (maximum tolerable daily dose 1,800 mg; n=32) or matching placebo (n=30) for 10 weeks.
cards.result: Gabapentin significantly improved cough-specific quality of life compared with placebo: between-group difference in Leicester Cough Questionnaire score during treatment 1.80 (95% CI 0.56–3.04), p=0.004, with a number needed to treat of 3.58. Side-effects occurred in 10 patients (31%) given gabapentin (the most common being nausea and fatigue) and 3 (10%) given placebo; 10 patients withdrew before the study end.
cards.watchOut: Small, single-clinic trial whose primary endpoint was a quality-of-life questionnaire rather than an objective cough count; funded by the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia and the Hunter Medical Research Institute.
cards.source: Ryan NM et al.. Gabapentin for refractory chronic cough: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. 2012. PMID: 22951084. Registry ID: ACTRN12608000248369. cards.headline: COUGH-1 and COUGH-2: gefapixant 45 mg cut 24-hour cough frequency by a relative 18.5% and 14.6% versus placebo; the 15 mg dose did not
cards.summary: COUGH-1 and COUGH-2: gefapixant 45 mg cut 24-hour cough frequency by a relative 18.5% and 14.6% versus placebo; the 15 mg dose did not
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trials (McGarvey 2022, COUGH-1 and COUGH-2)
cards.people: Adults aged 18 years or older with refractory chronic cough or unexplained chronic cough of at least 1 year (mean cough duration 11.6 years in COUGH-1 and 11.2 years in COUGH-2) and a cough severity visual analogue scale score of 40 mm or more: 730 participants treated in COUGH-1 (156 sites in 17 countries) and 1,314 in COUGH-2 (175 sites in 20 countries), randomised to placebo, gefapixant 15 mg twice per day, or gefapixant 45 mg twice per day.
cards.result: Gefapixant 45 mg twice per day showed significant reductions in 24-h cough frequency compared with placebo — a relative reduction of 18.5% at week 12 in COUGH-1 (p=0.041) and 14.6% at week 24 in COUGH-2 (p=0.031). Gefapixant 15 mg twice per day did not show a significant reduction in either study. The most common adverse events were taste-related: dysgeusia in 16.2% of participants in COUGH-1 and 21.1% in COUGH-2, and ageusia in 4.9% and 6.5% respectively.
cards.watchOut: Funded by Merck Sharp & Dohme, the manufacturer. The benefit is a modest relative reduction in cough frequency, seen only at the 45 mg dose, and taste disturbance was common.
cards.source: McGarvey LP et al.. Efficacy and safety of gefapixant, a P2X3 receptor antagonist, in refractory chronic cough and unexplained chronic cough (COUGH-1 and COUGH-2): results from two double-blind, randomised, parallel-group, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trials. The Lancet. 2022. PMID: 35248186. Registry ID: NCT03449134 and NCT03449147. cards.headline: Vertigan 2016: pregabalin plus speech pathology improved cough quality of life by 3.5 LCQ points — objective cough frequency did not differ
cards.summary: Vertigan 2016: pregabalin plus speech pathology improved cough quality of life by 3.5 LCQ points — objective cough frequency did not differ
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of combination therapy (Vertigan 2016)
cards.people: 40 patients with chronic refractory cough, randomly assigned to combined speech pathology treatment and pregabalin 300 mg daily, or combined speech pathology treatment and placebo, with outcomes at baseline, end of treatment, and 4 weeks after the end of treatment.
cards.result: Cough severity, cough frequency, and cough-related quality of life improved in both groups. The degree of improvement in the Leicester Cough Questionnaire and cough severity visual analogue scale was greater with pregabalin plus speech pathology: mean difference in LCQ 3.5 (95% CI 1.1 to 5.8) and in coughVAS 25.1 (95% CI 10.6 to 39.6). There was no significant difference in improvement in cough frequency between groups, and there was no deterioration in symptoms once pregabalin was withdrawn.
cards.watchOut: Only 40 patients, and both groups received speech pathology treatment — this tests pregabalin as an add-on, not on its own. The separation was on symptom and quality-of-life scores; the objective cough-frequency measure did not differ between groups.
cards.source: Vertigan AE et al.. Pregabalin and Speech Pathology Combination Therapy for Refractory Chronic Cough: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Chest. 2016. PMID: 26447687. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three agents beat placebo on cough symptoms, with modest effects and real tolerability costs — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: three agents beat placebo on cough symptoms, with modest effects and real tolerability costs — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Ryan 2012 (62 adults, gabapentin versus placebo), Vertigan 2016 (40 patients, pregabalin plus speech pathology versus placebo plus speech pathology), and McGarvey 2022 (2,044 treated participants across COUGH-1 and COUGH-2, gefapixant versus placebo).
cards.result: Gabapentin improved cough-specific quality of life by 1.80 LCQ points over placebo (number needed to treat 3.58); pregabalin added to speech pathology improved LCQ by a further 3.5 points without a significant difference in objective cough frequency; and gefapixant 45 mg twice daily reduced 24-h cough frequency by a relative 18.5% (COUGH-1) and 14.6% (COUGH-2) beyond placebo, with dysgeusia in 16.2% and 21.1% of participants. The direction of benefit is consistent across three different agents, but the sizes are moderate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The neuromodulator evidence rests on two small trials (n=62 and n=40) with questionnaire outcomes, and the large gefapixant trials were manufacturer-funded with a relative effect of under a fifth on cough frequency; none of these treatments abolishes the cough.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ryan NM et al. The Lancet. 2012 (PMID: 22951084); McGarvey LP et al. The Lancet. 2022 (PMID: 35248186); Vertigan AE et al. Chest. 2016 (PMID: 26447687).

shelves.title: Blue-light filtering glasses in the evening for better sleep
shelves.question: Do blue-light filtering (amber / blue-blocker) glasses worn in the evening improve sleep?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Attention · Circadian Rhythm · Computer Terminals · Cross-Over Studies · Eye Protective Devices · Humans · Lighting · Male · Melatonin · Photic Stimulation · Polysomnography · Sleep
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — three small randomised trials (n = 13–20) each found some benefit — less melatonin suppression, better self-rated sleep, more actigraphic sleep in insomnia — but the 2023 Cochrane review of 17 trials judged the sleep evidence very low certainty and indeterminate, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Blue-blocker glasses blunted evening melatonin suppression in teenagers, but measured sleep stages did not change
cards.summary: Blue-blocker glasses blunted evening melatonin suppression in teenagers, but measured sleep stages did not change
cards.type: Trial
cards.people: 13 healthy boys aged 15–17; crossover — one week of blue-blocker and one week of clear lenses while using LED screens in the evening, then a laboratory evening
cards.result: Compared with clear lenses, blue-blockers significantly attenuated LED-induced melatonin suppression and decreased vigilant attention and subjective alertness before bedtime. Polysomnography sleep stages and morning behavioural measures were not modified.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen participants and surrogate outcomes — the physiology moved, sleep itself did not measurably change.
cards.source: van der Lely S et al.. Blue blocker glasses as a countermeasure for alerting effects of evening light-emitting diode screen exposure in male teenagers. J Adolesc Health. 2015. PMID: 25287985. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Amber lenses improved self-rated sleep quality over two weeks in 20 adults
cards.summary: Amber lenses improved self-rated sleep quality over two weeks in 20 adults
cards.type: Trial
cards.people: 20 adult volunteers; amber (blue-blocking) vs yellow-tinted ultraviolet-only control glasses, worn for 3 hours before sleep; one baseline week, two treatment weeks
cards.result: Overall sleep quality improved significantly more in the amber-lens group than in controls (interaction P < 0.001), and positive affect also improved (P = 0.005). All outcomes were subjective diary ratings.
cards.watchOut: The amber group started with poorer sleep quality than controls, so part of the gain may be regression to the mean; no objective sleep recording.
cards.source: Burkhart K et al.. Amber lenses to block blue light and improve sleep: a randomized trial. Chronobiol Int. 2009. PMID: 20030543. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Amber lenses before bed improved sleep in 14 people with insomnia, on diaries and actigraphy
cards.summary: Amber lenses before bed improved sleep in 14 people with insomnia, on diaries and actigraphy
cards.type: Trial
cards.people: 14 adults (mean age 46.6) with insomnia symptoms; crossover — amber vs clear lenses for 2 hours before bedtime, 7 nights each, 4-week washout
cards.result: Insomnia rating scores, subjective total sleep time, sleep quality and soundness were all significantly better with amber lenses (P < 0.05), and actigraphic total sleep time was significantly higher (P = 0.035).
cards.watchOut: Fourteen people for one week per lens — a proof-of-concept trial, not a definitive one.

cards.headline: Cochrane review of 17 trials: the effect of blue-filtering lenses on sleep quality is indeterminate
cards.summary: Cochrane review of 17 trials: the effect of blue-filtering lenses on sleep quality is indeterminate
cards.type: Review
cards.people: 17 randomised trials, 5–156 participants each, follow-up from under a day to five weeks, in adults
cards.result: For sleep quality the review could not decide: across six trials (148 participants), three reported significant improvement with blue-filtering lenses and three reported no difference — very low-certainty evidence. It found probably little or no effect on best-corrected visual acuity, and no clear short-term effect on eye strain. Device-related adverse effects were infrequent (headache, discomfort, lower mood reported).
cards.watchOut: 65% of included trials were at high risk of bias from unmasked outcome assessment and only 35% were pre-registered.

cards.result: Small short trials lean positive — better subjective sleep and blunted melatonin suppression — but the largest synthesis of the same literature calls the sleep effect indeterminate, and objective sleep changes are inconsistent. shelves.title: Nirsevimab to prevent RSV infection and hospitalisation in infants
shelves.question: Does one injection of nirsevimab before the RSV season prevent respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) illness and hospitalisation in infants?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antiviral Agents · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Incidence · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Injections, Intramuscular · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, Tier C — three randomised trials (two placebo-controlled; one open-label pragmatic trial of 8,057 infants) consistently show large relative reductions in RSV illness and hospitalisation, with absolute hospitalisation rates of 0.3% vs 1.7% in HARMONIE. It is Tier C because hospitalisation is a hard outcome, every trial is one manufacturer's programme, and the term-infant hospitalisation result in MELODY was not itself significant.

cards.headline: In preterm infants, one dose cut medically attended RSV lung infections by 70% in relative terms
cards.summary: In preterm infants, one dose cut medically attended RSV lung infections by 70% in relative terms
cards.type: Trial
cards.people: 1,453 healthy preterm infants (29–34 weeks' gestation), randomised 2:1 to nirsevimab 50 mg once or placebo at the start of the RSV season
cards.result: Medically attended RSV lower respiratory tract infection through 150 days: 2.6% with nirsevimab vs 9.5% with placebo — 70.1% lower in relative terms (95% CI 52.3–81.2; P < 0.001). Hospitalisation for RSV infection: 0.8% vs 4.1% — 78.4% lower in relative terms (95% CI 51.9–90.3; P < 0.001). Adverse events were similar in the two groups, with no notable hypersensitivity reactions.
cards.watchOut: Funded by AstraZeneca and Sanofi Pasteur, the developers; this trial covers preterm infants only.

cards.headline: In term and late-preterm infants, RSV lung infections fell by three quarters in relative terms — but the hospitalisation difference was not significant (MELODY)
cards.summary: In term and late-preterm infants, RSV lung infections fell by three quarters in relative terms — but the hospitalisation difference was not significant (MELODY)
cards.type: Trial
cards.people: 1,490 infants born at ≥35 weeks' gestation, randomised 2:1 to one nirsevimab injection or placebo before the RSV season
cards.result: Medically attended RSV lower respiratory tract infection: 1.2% vs 5.0% — efficacy 74.5% in relative terms (95% CI 49.6–87.1; P < 0.001). Hospitalisation: 0.6% vs 1.6% — efficacy 62.1% in relative terms, but the confidence interval crosses zero (95% CI −8.6 to 86.8; P = 0.07). Serious adverse events: 6.8% vs 7.3%. Antidrug antibodies were detected in 6.1% of the nirsevimab group by day 361.
cards.watchOut: The headline hospitalisation benefit in healthy term infants was not statistically proven in this trial — the stronger hospitalisation evidence is the HARMONIE card below. Funded by MedImmune/AstraZeneca and Sanofi.

cards.headline: In 8,057 infants, RSV hospitalisations by 180 days were 0.3% with nirsevimab vs 1.7% with standard care (HARMONIE)
cards.summary: In 8,057 infants, RSV hospitalisations by 180 days were 0.3% with nirsevimab vs 1.7% with standard care (HARMONIE)
cards.type: Trial
cards.people: 8,057 infants aged ≤12 months in France, Germany and the UK, randomised to one nirsevimab dose (50 or 100 mg by weight) or standard care without RSV prophylaxis

cards.result: One injection before the season prevents roughly three quarters of medically attended RSV lung infections in relative terms, and in the large pragmatic trial cut RSV hospitalisations from 1.7% to 0.3%. shelves.title: North American ginseng extract (CVT-E002 / COLD-FX) to prevent colds and flu-like illness
shelves.question: Does the North American ginseng extract CVT-E002 (sold as COLD-FX) prevent colds and other respiratory infections?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adjuvants, Immunologic · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Chi-Square Distribution · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Institutionalization · Male · Panax · Plant Extracts · Respiratory Tract Infections
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — three double-blind trials of the same extract, CVT-E002 (n = 198, 279 analysed, and 43), all favour it for colds and respiratory symptoms, but all are one product from one research programme, event counts for laboratory-confirmed influenza are tiny, and the smallest trial's benefit appeared only in its second half.

cards.headline: In nursing-home residents, laboratory-confirmed influenza or RSV illness was 1 case on the extract vs 9 on placebo
cards.summary: In nursing-home residents, laboratory-confirmed influenza or RSV illness was 1 case on the extract vs 9 on placebo
cards.type: Trial
cards.people: 198 institutionalised older adults (average age 81 and 83.5 in the two seasons; about 90% influenza-vaccinated) in two pooled randomised trials; CVT-E002 200 mg twice daily or placebo for 8–12 weeks
cards.result: Laboratory-confirmed influenza illness: 1 of 97 on CVT-E002 vs 7 of 101 on placebo (odds ratio 7.73 for placebo vs extract; P = 0.033). Influenza and RSV combined: 1 of 97 vs 9 of 101 — absolute rates of about 1% vs 9%, an 89% relative reduction as the authors report it. The extract was safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Very few events — one or two cases either way would change the result. Two seasons pooled, and an industry-linked single-product programme.
cards.source: McElhaney JE et al.. A placebo-controlled trial of a proprietary extract of North American ginseng (CVT-E002) to prevent acute respiratory illness in institutionalized older adults. J Am Geriatr Soc. 2004. PMID: 14687309. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Adults taking the extract had fewer colds — and far fewer repeat colds — over one winter (the COLD-FX trial)
cards.summary: Adults taking the extract had fewer colds — and far fewer repeat colds — over one winter (the COLD-FX trial)
cards.type: Trial
cards.people: 323 adults aged 18–65 with at least two colds in the previous year, recruited in Edmonton, Canada; two capsules of North American ginseng extract or placebo daily for 4 months; 279 analysed
cards.result: Mean colds per person: 0.68 on the extract vs 0.93 on placebo (difference 0.25, 95% CI 0.04–0.45). Two or more colds: 10.0% vs 22.8%. Total symptom score and total days of symptoms were also lower (10.8 vs 16.5 days).
cards.watchOut: 44 randomised participants who never started treatment were excluded from the analysis, which can bias results; colds were self-scored. The extract is the programme's CVT-E002 preparation, though this abstract does not print the product code.

cards.headline: In 43 seniors, respiratory illness in the last two study months was 32% on COLD-FX vs 62% on placebo
cards.summary: In 43 seniors, respiratory illness in the last two study months was 32% on COLD-FX vs 62% on placebo
cards.type: Trial
cards.people: 43 community-dwelling adults aged 65 or older; COLD-FX (CVT-E002) 200 mg twice daily or placebo for 4 months, with influenza vaccination given after month one
cards.result: Frequency and duration of respiratory illness were similar in the first two months. In the last two months, 32% of the COLD-FX group vs 62% of the placebo group reported respiratory illness, and symptoms lasted 5.6 vs 12.6 days; the authors calculate relative reductions of 48% and 55%. No influenza circulated in the community during the study.
cards.watchOut: Tiny trial, and the positive window was the second half of the study — a pattern that can arise by chance. The record names the product (COLD-FX / CVT-E002) but no manufacturer.

shelves.title: Low-dose theophylline added to inhaled steroids to prevent COPD exacerbations (TWICS)
shelves.question: For people with COPD who keep having flare-ups despite inhaled corticosteroids, does adding low-dose theophylline reduce exacerbations?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Aged · Bronchodilator Agents · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C — a single large, well-run double-blind trial (TWICS, n = 1,578) found an exacerbation incidence rate ratio of 0.99 (95% CI 0.91–1.08) for low-dose theophylline added to inhaled corticosteroids. Tier C because the shelf rests on one trial; the null itself is precise enough to close the question for this dose range.

cards.headline: In 1,567 analysed patients, added theophylline changed exacerbations not at all: 2.24 vs 2.23 per year (TWICS)
cards.summary: In 1,567 analysed patients, added theophylline changed exacerbations not at all: 2.24 vs 2.23 per year (TWICS)
cards.type: Trial
cards.people: 1,578 patients with COPD (FEV1/FVC < 0.7) and at least two exacerbations in the previous year, all using inhaled corticosteroids, at 121 UK primary and secondary care sites; low-dose theophylline (200 mg once or twice daily, titrated to plasma levels of 1–5 mg/L) or placebo for one year, double-blind
cards.result: Moderate or severe exacerbations treated with antibiotics, oral corticosteroids or both: 1,727 in the theophylline group (mean 2.24 per year, 95% CI 2.10–2.38) vs 1,703 on placebo (mean 2.23, 95% CI 2.09–2.37) — adjusted incidence rate ratio 0.99 (95% CI 0.91–1.08), on primary-outcome data for 98% of participants. Serious adverse events included cardiac events in 2.4% vs 3.4% and gastrointestinal events in 2.7% vs 1.3%; nausea (10.9% vs 7.9%) and headache (9.0% vs 7.9%) were commoner on theophylline.
cards.watchOut: The trial's full report (the same TWICS trial, published in Health Technology Assessment 2019) found fewer COPD hospital admissions on theophylline (adjusted IRR 0.72, 95% CI 0.55–0.94) — but 39 of the 51 excess placebo admissions were accounted for by just 10 participants, so the authors did not rest any conclusion on it. One trial, however large, is one trial.
cards.source: Devereux G et al.. Effect of Theophylline as Adjunct to Inhaled Corticosteroids on Exacerbations in Patients With COPD: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 30326124. Registry ID: ISRCTN27066620. cards.type: Synthesis
cards.result: The laboratory idea — that low plasma concentrations of theophylline restore corticosteroid sensitivity in COPD — did not survive contact with a large pragmatic trial: exacerbation rates were identical. Adding low-dose theophylline to inhaled steroids to prevent flare-ups is not supported.
cards.watchOut: TWICS tested low anti-inflammatory doses (target plasma 1–5 mg/L), not the higher bronchodilator doses of older practice; this shelf answers the add-on prevention question only.

shelves.title: Andrographis (Kan Jang / KalmCold) for the common cold
shelves.question: Does Andrographis paniculata extract shorten or ease the common cold and other uncomplicated upper respiratory infections?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Diterpenes · Double-Blind Method · Drugs, Chinese Herbal · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Phytotherapy · Pilot Projects · Plants, Medicinal · Respiratory Tract Diseases
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — placebo-controlled trials of two standardised products (Kan Jang phase III, n = 179, symptom scores P ≤ 0.0006; KalmCold, n = 223) and a systematic review all favour Andrographis preparations for cold symptoms; small trials, score-based outcomes over 3–5 days, and product heterogeneity hold it at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Kan Jang — a fixed Andrographis combination — improved cold scores significantly in its phase III trial
cards.summary: Kan Jang — a fixed Andrographis combination — improved cold scores significantly in its phase III trial
cards.type: Trial
cards.people: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials of the standardised Andrographis paniculata extract fixed combination Kan Jang (extract SHA-10): a pilot (46 patients completing) and a phase III study (179 completing); medication three times daily — for exactly 3 days in phase III
cards.result: In the pilot, the total symptom score showed only a tendency to improvement (P = 0.08). In phase III, both the total symptom score and the physician's total diagnosis score improved highly significantly in the Kan Jang group vs placebo (P ≤ 0.0006 and P = 0.003); throat symptoms and signs improved most in both studies.
cards.watchOut: Kan Jang is a fixed combination — Andrographis with Eleutherococcus (Acanthopanax) senticosus — so credit cannot go to Andrographis alone. Outcomes are symptom and sign scores, not days of illness. The record names the product and its extract code (SHA-10) but no manufacturer.
cards.source: Melchior J et al.. cards.headline: KalmCold, a different manufacturer's Andrographis extract, beat placebo on symptom scores by day 5
cards.summary: KalmCold, a different manufacturer's Andrographis extract, beat placebo on symptom scores by day 5
cards.type: Trial
cards.people: 223 patients with uncomplicated upper respiratory tract infection; KalmCold (Andrographis paniculata extract) 200 mg/day or placebo for 5 days, double-blind; nine symptoms self-scored on visual analogue scales
cards.result: Symptoms fell in both groups over the first three days. From day 3 to day 5, most placebo-group symptoms plateaued or worsened while all KalmCold symptoms kept improving; at day 5 every symptom except earache was significantly better on KalmCold (P ≤ 0.05), as was the overall symptom score. The authors rate KalmCold's overall efficacy as 2.1 times — 52.7% — higher than placebo in relative terms. Adverse effects were few and did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: Self-scored symptoms with many simultaneous comparisons, in a single trial of this extract. The record names the product (KalmCold) but no manufacturer.

cards.headline: Systematic review: Andrographis, alone or in fixed combination, beat placebo on symptom severity
cards.summary: Systematic review: Andrographis, alone or in fixed combination, beat placebo on symptom severity
cards.type: Review
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials in uncomplicated upper respiratory tract infection; four trials met the inclusion criteria and 433 patients in three trials were pooled
cards.result: The Andrographis fixed combination with Acanthopanax senticosus was more effective than placebo by a mean difference of 2.13 points (95% CI 1.00–3.26; P = 0.0002) on its symptom severity score. Andrographis alone differed from placebo by 10.85 points (95% CI 10.36–11.34; P < 0.0001) on a different scale. The authors conclude the extract, alone or combined, may be an appropriate alternative treatment for uncomplicated acute URTI.
cards.watchOut: The two pooled estimates use different score scales and rest largely on the same small trial programme — this review summarises the Kan Jang-era evidence rather than adding independent proof.

cards.headline: What this means
cards.summary: What this means
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.result: Standardised Andrographis extracts probably ease cold symptoms somewhat over the worst days; the trials measure symptom scores over three to five days, not time back at work. Products differ — Kan Jang is a two-herb combination, KalmCold a single-herb extract — and evidence for one does not automatically cover the other, or any unstandardised andrographis product.
cards.watchOut: No trial used an objective outcome such as viral clearance or days absent from work; all are small and short.
cards.source: Synthesis of the references on this shelf.
