shelves.title: Steam inhalation for colds: feels like it should work — the blinded trials say it doesn't
shelves.question: Does inhaling steam (heated, humidified air) relieve the symptoms of the common cold?
shelves.mesh: Air · Common Cold · Heating · Humans · Humidity · Picornaviridae Infections · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Respiratory Therapy · Rhinovirus · Steam · Virus Shedding
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the Cochrane pooling of six trials (387 participants) is contradictory between statistical models and graded low quality, and the two double-blind device trials carded here are plainly negative: in one, the placebo group improved more than the steam group on several days. Breathing steam may feel soothing, but as a treatment for the common cold it has not beaten breathing room air.

cards.headline: Cochrane: six trials, 387 people — benefit uncertain between models, evidence graded low
cards.summary: Cochrane: six trials, 387 people — benefit uncertain between models, evidence graded low
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (Singh 2017)
cards.people: Six randomised trials (387 participants) of heated, humidified air (including the RhinoTherm device) for natural or experimentally induced common cold, pooled in the 2017 Cochrane review
cards.result: Symptom severity: fixed-effect analysis suggested benefit (OR 0.30, 95% CI 0.16–0.56) but the random-effects analysis did not (OR 0.22, 0.03–1.95). Resolution of symptoms was not significantly higher with heated air (OR 0.58, 0.28–1.18), nor was viral shedding different (OR 0.47, 0.04–5.19). Nasal resistance worsened in one US study and improved in an earlier Israeli one. Minor adverse events (discomfort, nasal irritation) were reported. The reviewers conclude the evidence shows neither benefit nor harm.
cards.watchOut: The two statistical models disagree, which is itself the finding: a handful of small, heterogeneous trials cannot settle the question — but the burden of proof sits with steam, and it has not been met.
cards.source: Singh M et al.. Heated, humidified air for the common cold. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017. PMID: 28849871. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Forstall 1994: a full hour of 43 °C steam changed no symptom score (P = .59 to .83)
cards.summary: Forstall 1994: a full hour of 43 °C steam changed no symptom score (P = .59 to .83)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Forstall 1994)
cards.people: 68 volunteers with natural colds at the Cleveland Clinic; a single 60-minute treatment of heated saturated air raising intranasal temperature to 43 °C (n = 32) vs ambient air at 20–24 °C (n = 36), double-blind, with 7 days of follow-up
cards.result: No significant differences in daily symptom scores for nasal congestion, drainage or sneezing between steam and placebo. The only significant objective difference favoured placebo: percentage improvement in nasal resistance on day 7 (P = .01). The authors conclude steam inhalation had no beneficial effect.
cards.watchOut: One intensive treatment session; a believer could argue for repeated daily steaming — but the second trial below used exactly that design and also failed.
cards.source: Forstall GJ et al.. Effect of inhaling heated vapor on symptoms of the common cold. JAMA. 1994. PMID: 8151854. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Macknin 1990: the placebo group improved MORE than the steam group on several days
cards.summary: Macknin 1990: the placebo group improved MORE than the steam group on several days
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Macknin 1990)
cards.people: 66 patients with natural colds; two 20-minute treatments with the Rhinotherm device (Netzer-Sereni, Beer Yaacov, Israel) delivering saturated air at 40–42 °C (n = 32) vs an identical device delivering ambient air (n = 34), double-blind
cards.result: Subjective improvement favoured placebo on isolated days: nasal congestion day 3 (40% vs 25%), drainage day 6 (71% vs 60%), sneezing day 7 (100% vs 67%). Nasal resistance improvement on day 7 was also better with placebo (11% vs −6%). The authors conclude steam inhalation showed no beneficial effects.
cards.watchOut: Small and old, but properly blinded with an identical sham device — the design most steam claims never face.

cards.headline: Synthesis: comfort ritual, not a treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: comfort ritual, not a treatment
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: 387 participants across six pooled trials; 134 patients in the two blinded device trials carded
cards.result: Heated, humidified air has not been shown to shorten or soften the common cold; in the best-blinded trials it performed no better than — and sometimes worse than — room air. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Steam carries a real-world scald risk, especially for children leaning over bowls of boiling water — a harm the trials (using controlled devices) understate. Nasal saline irrigation is a different intervention with its own shelf (#637).

shelves.title: Magnesium for sleep: two tiny trials in the elderly lean positive — the glycinate products everyone buys are untested
shelves.question: Do magnesium supplements improve sleep?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adrenocorticotropic Hormone · Aged · Aging · Aldosterone · Angiotensin II · Arginine Vasopressin · Cross-Over Studies · Dietary Supplements · Drug Administration Schedule · Electroencephalography · Female · Hormones · Humans · Hydrocortisone · Magnesium Compounds · Male · Middle Aged · Renin · Sleep · Sleep Stages · Sleep Wake Disorders · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two small trials in older adults point the same way (500 mg magnesium daily improved insomnia scores over 8 weeks in 46 elderly Iranians; a 12-person crossover found more slow-wave sleep on magnesium), but both are tiny, short, elderly-only, and neither tested the magnesium glycinate products most people now buy for sleep. The honest summary: plausible, unproven, and untested in the form and population doing the asking.

cards.headline: 500 mg magnesium daily for 8 weeks improved insomnia scores in 46 elderly adults
cards.summary: 500 mg magnesium daily for 8 weeks improved insomnia scores in 46 elderly adults
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Abbasi 2012)
cards.people: 46 elderly subjects with primary insomnia in Tehran; 500 mg magnesium daily or placebo for 8 weeks, double-blind; sleep measured by the Insomnia Severity Index, sleep logs and blood tests
cards.result: Versus placebo, magnesium significantly increased sleep time (P = 0.002), sleep efficiency (P = 0.03) and serum melatonin (P = 0.007), and decreased Insomnia Severity Index score (P = 0.006), sleep onset latency (P = 0.02) and serum cortisol (P = 0.008). Early-morning awakening improved marginally (P = 0.08). The record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.watchOut: 46 people, one centre, 8 weeks; the magnesium form is not specified in the abstract, and participants' baseline magnesium status is not established — supplementing the replete may do nothing.
cards.source: Abbasi B et al.. The effect of magnesium supplementation on primary insomnia in elderly: A double-blind placebo-controlled clinical trial. J Res Med Sci. 2012. PMID: 23853635. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: the record carries no MeSH terms

cards.headline: In 12 elderly subjects, magnesium increased slow-wave sleep (16.5 vs 10.1 minutes) in a crossover trial
cards.summary: In 12 elderly subjects, magnesium increased slow-wave sleep (16.5 vs 10.1 minutes) in a crossover trial
cards.type: Randomised crossover trial (Held 2002)
cards.people: 12 elderly subjects aged 60–80; placebo-controlled randomised crossover with two 20-day treatment periods (magnesium effervescent tablets rising to 30 mmol/day) separated by a 2-week washout; sleep EEG and overnight hormone sampling
cards.result: On magnesium, slow-wave sleep increased (16.5 ± 20.4 vs 10.1 ± 15.4 minutes, P ≤ 0.05), as did delta and sigma EEG power; overnight cortisol fell and renin and aldosterone rose. The authors conclude magnesium partially reversed age-related sleep EEG and neuroendocrine changes.
cards.watchOut: Twelve subjects and laboratory EEG endpoints — it shows magnesium can move sleep physiology in the elderly, not that it helps an ordinary insomniac sleep longer. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Held K et al.. Oral Mg(2+) supplementation reverses age-related neuroendocrine and sleep EEG changes in humans. Pharmacopsychiatry. 2002. PMID: 12163983. cards.headline: Synthesis: a reasonable, cheap experiment — not an established sleep aid
cards.summary: Synthesis: a reasonable, cheap experiment — not an established sleep aid
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: 58 older adults across the two randomised trials carded
cards.result: Both trials favour magnesium for sleep in older adults, on subjective scores in one and EEG architecture in the other; neither is large enough or long enough to establish benefit, and neither studied younger adults or magnesium glycinate. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Established insomnia treatments (CBT-I; melatonin and other agents on their own shelves) carry far more evidence. Magnesium can cause diarrhoea and accumulates dangerously in kidney failure.

shelves.title: Nasal strips for snoring and sleep apnoea: no measurable effect on apnoea — snoring evidence is one small open-label study
shelves.question: Do external nasal dilator strips (such as Breathe Right) reduce snoring or treat obstructive sleep apnoea?
shelves.mesh: Airway Management · Clinical Trials as Topic · Dilatation · Equipment Design · Humans · Severity of Illness Index · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive · Snoring · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — across 14 studies, nasal dilators (Breathe Right strips, NoZovent) did not significantly change the apnoea–hypopnoea index in sleep apnoea (28.7 to 27.4 events/hour, P = 0.64), oxygen saturation or snoring index. The only positive snoring evidence is a 35-person open-label study in non-apnoeic snorers, where partners graded snoring lower — the design most prone to expectation effects. For simple snoring the question stays open; for sleep apnoea, strips are not a treatment.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis of 14 studies: AHI 28.7 → 27.4 events/hour with nasal dilators (P = 0.64) — no effect on apnoea
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of 14 studies: AHI 28.7 → 27.4 events/hour with nasal dilators (P = 0.64) — no effect on apnoea
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Camacho 2016)
cards.people: 14 studies of internal (NoZovent) and external (Breathe Right) nasal dilators for snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea; apnoea–hypopnoea index reported in 147 patients
cards.result: AHI changed from 28.7 ± 24.0 to 27.4 ± 23.3 events/hour (P = 0.64). There was no significant change in AHI, lowest oxygen saturation, or snoring index in OSA patients. A subanalysis found a slight reduction in apnoea index with internal dilators (−4.87 events/hour) vs minimal change with external strips (+0.64).
cards.watchOut: The pooled studies are small and short; but the point estimate is essentially zero, so a large hidden benefit is unlikely.
cards.source: Camacho M et al.. Nasal Dilators (Breathe Right Strips and NoZovent) for Snoring and OSA: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Pulm Med. 2016. PMID: 28070421. cards.headline: The snoring study behind the marketing: 35 snorers, open-label, partners reported less snoring (P < 0.001)
cards.summary: The snoring study behind the marketing: 35 snorers, open-label, partners reported less snoring (P < 0.001)
cards.type: Open-label uncontrolled study (Ulfberg 1997)
cards.people: 35 habitual heavy snorers (18 women, 17 men) whose polysomnography confirmed apnoea index below 5 — i.e., not sleep apnoea; Breathe Right strips worn for 14 consecutive nights, no control group
cards.result: After 14 nights there were statistically significant decreases in partner-graded snoring (P < 0.001), patient-reported mouth dryness (P = 0.025) and Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores (P = 0.001).
cards.watchOut: No blinding, no control group, subjective partner ratings — this study cannot distinguish the strip's effect from expectation, and it deliberately excluded the apnoea patients the strips are often bought for.
cards.source: Ulfberg J et al.. Effect of Breathe Right nasal strip on snoring. Rhinology. 1997. PMID: 9299650. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: fine for a stuffy nose at night; not an apnoea treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: fine for a stuffy nose at night; not an apnoea treatment
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: 147 apnoea patients across 14 pooled studies; 35 non-apnoeic snorers in the only snoring-specific study
cards.result: Nasal dilators improve the feeling of nasal breathing without improving any measured apnoea outcome; the snoring claim rests on one small uncontrolled study. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for sleep apnoea; simple snoring remains genuinely untested by blinded trials.
cards.watchOut: Loud snoring with witnessed apnoeas or daytime sleepiness needs a sleep study and, if apnoea is confirmed, CPAP or another proven therapy — a strip must not delay that.
cards.source: Synthesis of Camacho M et al. Pulm Med. 2016 (PMID: 28070421); Ulfberg J et al. Rhinology. 1997 (PMID: 9299650).

shelves.title: Mepolizumab in eosinophilic COPD: exacerbations 0.80 vs 1.01 a year in MATINEE (rate ratio 0.79) — a real but modest effect, with no gain in symptoms or quality of life
shelves.question: In COPD with an eosinophilic phenotype despite triple inhaled therapy, does adding mepolizumab prevent exacerbations?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Administration, Inhalation · *Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · *Eosinophilia/blood/diagnosis/drug therapy/immunology · Eosinophils/drug effects/immunology · Injections, Subcutaneous · *Interleukin-5/antagonists & inhibitors · Phenotype · *Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/complications/diagnosis/drug therapy/immunology · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Yes, modestly, and only in the eosinophil-high phenotype. In MATINEE (Sciurba 2025), 804 patients with COPD, previous exacerbations and blood eosinophils of at least 300 cells/µL on triple inhaled therapy had an annualised rate of moderate or severe exacerbations of 0.80 on monthly mepolizumab versus 1.01 on placebo (rate ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.94; P = 0.01) — a 21% relative reduction, worth about one-fifth of an exacerbation per patient-year in absolute terms — and a longer time to first exacerbation (median 419 versus 321 days; hazard ratio 0.77, a relative measure). Quality of life and symptom scores did not differ, so patients had fewer events without feeling measurably better. The earlier METREX and METREO trials (Pavord 2017) point the same way at the higher eosinophil counts (rate ratio 0.82 in METREX's eosinophilic population) but were null in unselected patients (rate ratio 0.98) and not significant after multiplicity adjustment in METREO. Adverse events matched placebo in both programmes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a replicated, phenotype-bound, clinically modest effect. Dupilumab in type-2 COPD — the neighbouring biologic question — is on shelves #812 and #1641.

cards.headline: Sciurba 2025 (MATINEE): mepolizumab cut the annual exacerbation rate from 1.01 to 0.80 (rate ratio 0.79) in COPD with eosinophils at least 300 — quality of life and symptoms unchanged
cards.summary: Sciurba 2025 (MATINEE): mepolizumab cut the annual exacerbation rate from 1.01 to 0.80 (rate ratio 0.79) in COPD with eosinophils at least 300 — quality of life and symptoms unchanged
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial, 52–104 weeks (MATINEE) (Sciurba 2025)
cards.people: 804 patients with COPD, a history of exacerbations and a blood eosinophil count of at least 300 cells per microlitre, all receiving triple inhaled therapy, randomised 1:1 to mepolizumab 100 mg or placebo subcutaneously every 4 weeks. The primary endpoint was the annualised rate of moderate or severe exacerbations.
cards.result: The annualised exacerbation rate was 0.80 per year on mepolizumab versus 1.01 on placebo (rate ratio 0.79; 95% CI 0.66 to 0.94; P = 0.01) — a 21% relative reduction and an absolute difference of about 0.2 exacerbations per patient-year. Time to first moderate or severe exacerbation was longer on mepolizumab (Kaplan–Meier medians 419 versus 321 days; hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.93; P = 0.009 — a relative measure). Health-related quality of life and symptom measures did not differ significantly, which by the trial's hierarchy stopped formal testing of later secondary endpoints. Adverse-event incidence was similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The eosinophil threshold is doing the work: at 300 cells/µL and above the drug wins, and the 2017 trials (next card) show the effect fading as counts fall. An average 0.2 fewer exacerbations a year, bought with a monthly injection at biologic prices and no felt improvement in symptoms, is a judgement call about value that this shelf deliberately leaves visible.
cards.source: Sciurba FC et al. Mepolizumab to Prevent Exacerbations of COPD with an Eosinophilic Phenotype. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2025. PMID: 40305712. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04133909, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Pavord 2017 (METREX/METREO): rate ratio 0.82 in METREX's eosinophilic population, 0.98 in unselected patients — and METREO missed significance after adjustment
cards.summary: Pavord 2017 (METREX/METREO): rate ratio 0.82 in METREX's eosinophilic population, 0.98 in unselected patients — and METREO missed significance after adjustment
cards.type: Two phase 3 randomised placebo-controlled double-blind trials (METREX and METREO) (Pavord 2017)
cards.people: Patients with COPD and a history of moderate or severe exacerbations on inhaled glucocorticoid-based triple therapy received mepolizumab (100 mg in METREX; 100 or 300 mg in METREO) or placebo every 4 weeks for 52 weeks. METREX's eosinophilic-phenotype analysis population (462 patients) required blood eosinophils of at least 150 per cubic millimetre at screening or at least 300 in the previous year; its full modified intention-to-treat population was 836. METREO enrolled only eosinophilic-phenotype patients.
cards.result: In METREX's eosinophilic population the annual exacerbation rate was 1.40 per year on mepolizumab versus 1.71 on placebo (rate ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.68 to 0.98; adjusted P = 0.04) — an 18% relative reduction with absolute rates alongside — while the overall population showed no difference (rate ratio 0.98; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.12). In METREO the rates were 1.19 (100 mg) and 1.27 (300 mg) versus 1.49 per year on placebo, rate ratios 0.80 and 0.86, but adjusted P values were 0.07 and 0.14 — not significant. Effects grew with higher screening eosinophil counts. Safety matched placebo.
cards.watchOut: Two trials, three doses, and only one nominally significant comparison after adjustment: read alone in 2017 this programme looked like a near-miss. It took MATINEE's stricter eosinophil threshold (at least 300) and larger size to produce a clean positive — a reminder that the phenotype definition, not the molecule, was the moving part.
cards.source: Pavord ID et al. Mepolizumab for Eosinophilic Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28893134. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02105948 (METREX) and NCT02105961 (METREO), from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: the same modest effect twice, eight years apart — about one-fifth fewer exacerbations, confined to eosinophil-high COPD — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the same modest effect twice, eight years apart — about one-fifth fewer exacerbations, confined to eosinophil-high COPD — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Three phase 3 placebo-controlled trials of monthly mepolizumab added to triple inhaled therapy: METREX and METREO (2017; eosinophils at least 150/µL thresholds) and MATINEE (2025; at least 300/µL, 804 patients).
cards.result: Annualised moderate-or-severe exacerbation rate ratios of 0.79–0.82 in the eosinophilic populations (a 18–21% relative reduction; absolute differences about 0.2–0.3 exacerbations per patient-year), null in unselected COPD (0.98), with a dose–response by eosinophil count, longer time to first exacerbation in MATINEE, and no significant improvement in quality of life or symptoms anywhere. Safety was placebo-like throughout.
cards.watchOut: Exacerbation counts in COPD trials are sensitive to how events are captured and treated, and both programmes were run by the manufacturer; the replication across two eras and the internal eosinophil gradient are the counterweights. Nothing here speaks to mortality, lung-function decline, or patients below the eosinophil thresholds.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sciurba FC et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2025 (PMID: 40305712); Pavord ID et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2017 (PMID: 28893134).

shelves.title: Influenza vaccination in COPD: fewer influenza illnesses and fewer exacerbations in the randomised trials — but no trial shows fewer hospital admissions or deaths
shelves.question: In adults with COPD, does influenza vaccination reduce exacerbations and hospitalisation?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Aged · Comorbidity · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Incidence · Influenza Vaccines/*administration & dosage · Influenza, Human/epidemiology/*prevention & control · Male · Middle Aged · Poisson Distribution · Probability · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/*diagnosis/epidemiology · Reference Values · Respiratory Tract Infections/epidemiology/*prevention & control · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index · Sex Factors · Vaccination/*methods
shelves.balance: The randomised evidence says influenza vaccination protects people with COPD against influenza itself, and probably against exacerbations — but it has never been shown to keep them out of hospital or alive longer. In the only placebo-controlled trial in COPD (Wongsurakiat 2004, PMID: 15189916), influenza-related respiratory illness occurred at 6.8 versus 28.1 episodes per 100 person-years (relative risk 0.24 — a 76% relative reduction), while overall respiratory illness did not differ. The Cochrane pooling of the COPD trials (Kopsaftis 2018, PMID: 29943802) found inactivated vaccine reduced exacerbations by a mean of 0.37 per vaccinated person per season (95% CI −0.64 to −0.11), an estimate the reviewers graded low quality and based on just 180 participants; the mortality data were too small to show any effect. The hospitalisation half of the question is unanswered by vaccine-versus-placebo trials, and the one large dose-comparison trial (DANFLU-1 chronic lung disease analysis, Duus 2025, PMID: 41177098) found no extra benefit from high-dose over standard-dose vaccine in lung-disease patients (hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.28 to 3.30, for pneumonia or influenza hospitalisation). Local reactions are commoner with vaccine (27% versus 6%) but mild, and vaccination did not provoke early exacerbations. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — real protection against influenza illness, probable protection against exacerbations, unproven against hospitalisation and death. Tier C: taken to the developer personally, because the COPD-specific clinical benefit rests substantially on one small trial.

cards.headline: Wongsurakiat 2004: influenza-related respiratory illness 6.8 versus 28.1 per 100 person-years with vaccine versus placebo (relative risk 0.24) — but total respiratory illness unchanged
cards.summary: Wongsurakiat 2004: influenza-related respiratory illness 6.8 versus 28.1 per 100 person-years with vaccine versus placebo (relative risk 0.24) — but total respiratory illness unchanged
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 125 patients with COPD (Wongsurakiat 2004)
cards.people: 125 patients with COPD at a Bangkok university hospital, stratified by FEV1 into mild, moderate and severe obstruction and randomised to purified trivalent split-virus influenza vaccine (62 patients) or placebo (63), followed through the 1997–98 influenza seasons for influenza-related and overall acute respiratory illness (ARI), graded as outpatient treatment, hospitalisation or mechanical ventilation.
cards.result: Influenza-related ARI occurred at 6.8 per 100 person-years in the vaccine group versus 28.1 per 100 person-years on placebo (relative risk 0.24, p = 0.005 — a 76% relative reduction). Protection was seen across severity strata (relative risks 0.16 in mild, 0.55 in moderate [not significant] and 0.15 in severe COPD). There was no difference between groups in the incidence or severity of total ARI, most of which was not influenza.
cards.watchOut: A single small trial from one Thai centre in the 1990s, powered on influenza-related illness rather than on hospitalisation or death: the abstract reports no hospitalisation-specific effect, and the result depends on how much of a season's respiratory illness is truly influenza. It remains the only placebo-controlled trial of influenza vaccine conducted specifically in COPD.

cards.headline: Kopsaftis 2018 (Cochrane): inactivated influenza vaccine reduced COPD exacerbations by 0.37 per person per season — low-quality evidence from 180 participants; mortality untestable
cards.summary: Kopsaftis 2018 (Cochrane): inactivated influenza vaccine reduced COPD exacerbations by 0.37 per person per season — low-quality evidence from 180 participants; mortality untestable
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials in COPD (Cochrane, Kopsaftis 2018)
cards.people: 11 randomised trials with 6,750 participants, of which six were conducted in people with COPD (2,469 participants); the rest enrolled elderly or high-risk patients, some with chronic lung disease. Inactivated intramuscular vaccine and live attenuated intranasal vaccine were each compared with placebo.
cards.result: Inactivated vaccine reduced the total number of exacerbations per vaccinated participant compared with placebo (mean difference −0.37, 95% CI −0.64 to −0.11; p = 0.006; two RCTs, 180 participants; low quality evidence), driven by 'late' exacerbations occurring three or more weeks after vaccination (mean difference −0.39, 95% CI −0.61 to −0.18). Two studies reporting mortality were too small to detect any effect. Local adverse reactions were significantly commoner with vaccine but generally mild and transient; adding intranasal live attenuated vaccine to inactivated vaccine showed no additional benefit.
cards.watchOut: The headline exacerbation estimate rests on two small trials totalling 180 people, all of the included COPD trials were more than a decade old at the time of the review, and the review could not answer the hospitalisation or mortality questions at all. The much larger effects seen in observational studies of vaccinated COPD patients are not randomised evidence and are not carded here.
cards.source: Kopsaftis Z et al. Influenza vaccine for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018. PMID: 29943802. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Duus 2025 (DANFLU-1): in chronic lung disease, high-dose influenza vaccine showed no advantage over standard dose — pneumonia/influenza hospitalisation hazard ratio 0.95 (0.28 to 3.30)
cards.summary: Duus 2025 (DANFLU-1): in chronic lung disease, high-dose influenza vaccine showed no advantage over standard dose — pneumonia/influenza hospitalisation hazard ratio 0.95 (0.28 to 3.30)
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a pragmatic randomised trial (DANFLU-1, Duus 2025)
cards.people: 12,477 Danish adults aged 65–79 randomised open-label to high-dose or standard-dose inactivated influenza vaccine in the 2021/22 season, of whom 850 (6.8%) had chronic lung disease identified from diagnostic codes (the trial was not restricted to COPD, and this analysis compares vaccine doses, not vaccine against no vaccine).
cards.result: Participants with chronic lung disease had significantly higher hospitalisation rates for every outcome. Overall, high-dose vaccine was associated with a lower risk of hospitalisation for pneumonia or influenza (hazard ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.73), but within the chronic lung disease subgroup the estimate was 0.95 (95% CI 0.28 to 3.30), against 0.22 (0.08 to 0.57) in those without lung disease (p for interaction = 0.064); estimates for respiratory hospitalisation and all-cause mortality were likewise less favourable in the lung-disease subgroup. The authors call the subgroup findings hypothesis-generating.
cards.watchOut: Only 850 participants had lung disease, the confidence interval spans from large benefit to large harm, and 'chronic lung disease' here is a registry label, not spirometry-confirmed COPD. This card answers the dose question, not whether vaccination itself helps — it tempers any assumption that the high-dose advantage shown in general older populations (shelf #321) automatically extends to lung disease.
cards.source: Duus LS et al. Effects of high-dose versus standard-dose influenza vaccine among patients with chronic lung disease: A prespecified analysis of the DANFLU-1 trial. Respiratory Investigation. 2025. PMID: 41177098. Registry ID: NCT05048589, from the record. cards.headline: Wongsurakiat 2004 (safety companion report): local reactions 27% versus 6% with vaccine, no systemic excess, no early exacerbations and no loss of lung function
cards.summary: Wongsurakiat 2004 (safety companion report): local reactions 27% versus 6% with vaccine, no systemic excess, no early exacerbations and no loss of lung function
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled safety study — the same 125-patient cohort as the efficacy trial (Wongsurakiat 2004)
cards.people: The same 125 patients with COPD randomised to trivalent split-virus influenza vaccine (62) or placebo (63) in the Bangkok trial, assessed for local and systemic reactions in the week after injection and for respiratory illness, lung function, dyspnoea scores and 6-minute walk distance at 1 and 4 weeks.
cards.result: Local adverse reactions occurred in 27% of the vaccine group versus 6% on placebo (p = 0.002). Systemic reactions did not differ (76% versus 81%; p = 0.5). Respiratory illness in the first week (6.4% versus 6.3%) and first 4 weeks (24.2% versus 31.7%) did not differ, and there was no significant change in lung function, dyspnoea or exercise capacity in either group at any COPD severity.
cards.watchOut: This is a companion report on the identical cohort as the efficacy card above, not an independent trial — it adds safety detail, not a second efficacy result. Systemic symptom rates above 75% in both arms show how noisy background symptoms are in COPD, which is why the blinded comparison matters.
cards.source: Wongsurakiat P et al. Adverse effects associated with influenza vaccination in patients with COPD: a randomized controlled study. Respirology. 2004. PMID: 15612969. cards.headline: Synthesis: protection against influenza illness is real, exacerbation protection probable, hospitalisation and mortality unproven — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: protection against influenza illness is real, exacerbation protection probable, hospitalisation and mortality unproven — POSSIBLE
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Four records in COPD and chronic lung disease: one small placebo-controlled efficacy trial and its safety companion report (125 patients), the Cochrane pooling of the COPD randomised trials, and a prespecified lung-disease subgroup analysis (850 patients) of a 12,477-person dose-comparison trial.
cards.result: Influenza-related respiratory illness fell by about three quarters in relative terms in the placebo trial (relative risk 0.24); pooled trials show about 0.37 fewer exacerbations per vaccinated person per season (low-quality evidence); no randomised study shows fewer hospitalisations or deaths in COPD; and high-dose vaccine showed no measurable advantage over standard dose in lung-disease patients. Harm is limited to transient local reactions (27% versus 6%).
cards.watchOut: Almost everything rests on old, small trials plus one modern subgroup analysis that answered a different (dose) question. Large observational studies report hospitalisation and mortality benefits, but they are exactly the design most vulnerable to healthy-vaccinee bias, and this shelf cards only the randomised record.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wongsurakiat P et al. Chest. 2004 (PMID: 15189916); Wongsurakiat P et al. Respirology. 2004 (PMID: 15612969); Kopsaftis Z et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018 (PMID: 29943802); Duus LS et al. Respiratory Investigation. 2025 (PMID: 41177098).

shelves.title: Pneumococcal vaccination in COPD: fewer pneumonias and fewer exacerbations in the pooled trials — no difference in admissions or deaths
shelves.question: In adults with COPD, does pneumococcal vaccination reduce pneumonia and exacerbations?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Community-Acquired Infections/*prevention & control · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume/physiology · Humans · Immunocompetence/*physiology · Male · Middle Aged · Pneumococcal Infections/*prevention & control · *Pneumococcal Vaccines · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/*complications · Streptococcus pneumoniae · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The randomised trials in COPD point the same way for infection outcomes and nowhere for survival. The Cochrane pooling (Walters 2017, PMID: 28116747) found vaccination reduced community-acquired pneumonia (odds ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.89; six studies, 1,372 participants; moderate-quality evidence; number needed to vaccinate 21) and acute COPD exacerbations (odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.93; four studies, 446 participants; number needed to vaccinate 8), with no difference in hospital admissions, all-cause mortality (odds ratio 1.00) or cardiorespiratory mortality (1.07). The largest single trial (Alfageme 2006, PMID: 16227328) was null on its primary analysis (24% efficacy against pneumonia, 95% CI −24 to 54; p = 0.333) with benefit concentrated in patients under 65 and those with severe obstruction, and the oldest trial (Leech 1987, PMID: 3545418) found no difference in deaths, admissions or emergency visits despite a two- to three-fold antibody rise. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — moderate-quality pooled evidence for fewer pneumonias and exacerbations, no evidence for fewer admissions or deaths. Pneumococcal vaccination in older adults generally is covered on shelf #444; this shelf is the COPD-specific record.

cards.headline: Alfageme 2006: overall vaccine efficacy against pneumonia 24% (not significant); 76% in patients under 65 and 91% in younger patients with severe obstruction
cards.summary: Alfageme 2006: overall vaccine efficacy against pneumonia 24% (not significant); 76% in patients under 65 and 91% in younger patients with severe obstruction
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine, 596 patients with COPD (Alfageme 2006)
cards.people: 596 patients with COPD randomised to 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (298) or control, followed for a mean of 979 days for episodes of community-acquired pneumonia of pneumococcal or unknown cause, with prespecified analyses by age and airflow obstruction.
cards.result: There were 25 episodes of pneumococcal or unknown-cause pneumonia in the vaccinated group versus 33 in controls — an overall vaccine efficacy of 24% (95% CI −24 to 54; p = 0.333), not statistically significant. Efficacy was 76% (95% CI 20 to 93; p = 0.013) in patients younger than 65, 48% (−7 to 80; p = 0.076) in those with FEV1 below 40% predicted, and 91% (35 to 99; p = 0.002) in patients who were both younger and severely obstructed. All five cases of non-bacteraemic pneumococcal pneumonia occurred in the control group (p = 0.025).
cards.watchOut: The trial's own primary analysis is null, and the impressive subgroup figures come from small strata of a 596-patient trial — they generate hypotheses about who benefits most rather than proving them. The adjusted hazard ratio of 0.20 (0.06 to 0.68) quoted for the younger, severe subgroup should not be read alongside the null overall result as if both were primary findings.
cards.source: Alfageme I et al. Clinical efficacy of anti-pneumococcal vaccination in patients with COPD. Thorax. 2006. PMID: 16227328. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Leech 1987: no difference in deaths, hospital admissions, emergency visits or length of stay over two years — despite antibody levels rising two- to three-fold
cards.summary: Leech 1987: no difference in deaths, hospital admissions, emergency visits or length of stay over two years — despite antibody levels rising two- to three-fold
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial of 14-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine, 189 patients with severe COPD (Leech 1987)
cards.people: 189 patients with severe chronic airflow obstruction (FEV1 below 1.5 litres) randomised to a single injection of 14-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (92 patients) or saline placebo (97), followed for two years for mortality, hospital admissions, emergency department visits, length of stay and antibody response.
cards.result: There were no significant differences between the vaccine and placebo groups in mortality, number of hospital admissions, emergency department visits or length of stay in hospital. Antibody levels against the vaccine serotypes rose two- to three-fold in the vaccinated group, confirming the vaccine was immunogenic even though no clinical benefit was detected.
cards.watchOut: A small, old trial using the superseded 14-valent vaccine in the most severely obstructed patients — the group in whom polysaccharide vaccines work least well immunologically. Its null result on hard outcomes is consistent with the later Cochrane finding of no mortality or admission benefit, and it is a standing warning that antibody rises do not guarantee clinical protection.
cards.source: Leech JA et al. A prospective study of the efficacy of pneumococcal vaccines in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. CMAJ. 1987. PMID: 3545418. cards.headline: Walters 2017 (Cochrane): pneumonia odds ratio 0.62 and exacerbation odds ratio 0.60 with vaccination — mortality odds ratio 1.00 and no difference in admissions
cards.summary: Walters 2017 (Cochrane): pneumonia odds ratio 0.62 and exacerbation odds ratio 0.60 with vaccination — mortality odds ratio 1.00 and no difference in admissions
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials in COPD (Cochrane, Walters 2017)
cards.people: 12 randomised trials with 2,171 participants with COPD comparing injectable pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (with or without other vaccines) against control, assessing community-acquired pneumonia, pneumococcal pneumonia, exacerbations, hospital admissions and mortality.
cards.result: Vaccination reduced community-acquired pneumonia (odds ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.89; six studies, 1,372 participants; moderate-quality evidence; number needed to vaccinate 21, 95% CI 15 to 74) and pneumococcal pneumonia specifically (Peto odds ratio 0.26, 0.05 to 1.31; three studies, 476 participants; low-quality evidence). Acute exacerbations were reduced (odds ratio 0.60, 0.39 to 0.93; four studies, 446 participants; moderate-quality; number needed to vaccinate 8, 5 to 58). There was no significant difference in hospital admissions, all-cause mortality (odds ratio 1.00, 0.72 to 1.40; five studies, 1,053 participants) or cardiorespiratory mortality (1.07, 0.69 to 1.66).
cards.watchOut: The exacerbation estimate rests on only 446 participants and the pneumonia estimate on older polysaccharide-vaccine trials; conjugate pneumococcal vaccines, now standard in many programmes, have essentially no COPD-specific randomised outcome data. Odds ratios are relative measures — the absolute gains are the numbers needed to vaccinate (21 for one pneumonia prevented, 8 for one exacerbation).
cards.source: Walters JA et al. Pneumococcal vaccines for preventing pneumonia in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017. PMID: 28116747. cards.headline: Synthesis: fewer pneumonias and exacerbations on the pooled randomised evidence, no effect on admissions or death — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: fewer pneumonias and exacerbations on the pooled randomised evidence, no effect on admissions or death — POSSIBLE
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Three records in COPD: two randomised trials (596 and 189 patients) and the Cochrane pooling of 12 trials (2,171 participants), all of polysaccharide pneumococcal vaccines.
cards.result: Pooled, vaccination is associated with about a 38% relative reduction in the odds of community-acquired pneumonia (odds ratio 0.62; number needed to vaccinate 21) and a 40% relative reduction in the odds of an exacerbation (odds ratio 0.60; number needed to vaccinate 8), against a mortality odds ratio of exactly 1.00 and no reduction in hospital admissions. The largest trial was individually null overall, with benefit concentrated in younger and more severely obstructed patients.
cards.watchOut: Everything here is the older polysaccharide vaccine; whether modern conjugate vaccines do better in COPD is untested in randomised outcome trials. The exacerbation finding — the outcome that would matter most day to day — comes from just four small trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Alfageme I et al. Thorax. 2006 (PMID: 16227328); Leech JA et al. CMAJ. 1987 (PMID: 3545418); Walters JA et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017 (PMID: 28116747).

shelves.title: Benzonatate for cough: never shown to relieve cough in a clinical trial — its one controlled test measured a reflex and benzonatate alone failed it, while overdose data show real harm
shelves.question: In adults with acute or subacute cough, does benzonatate reduce cough versus placebo or other antitussives?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Administration, Oral · Adult · Antitussive Agents/therapeutic use · Butylamines/therapeutic use · Capsaicin · Common Cold/complications · Cough/chemically induced/drug therapy/virology · Cross-Over Studies · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Guaifenesin/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Reflex/drug effects · Sensory System Agents
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Benzonatate is one of the most prescribed cough suppressants in the United States, and there is no modern randomised trial showing it relieves anyone's cough. The only controlled trial of the drug itself (Dicpinigaitis 2009, PMID: 19121573) was a 30-person crossover study that measured capsaicin cough-reflex sensitivity — a laboratory reflex, not cough relief — in adults with acute viral cough: benzonatate 200 mg alone did not significantly suppress the reflex versus placebo, guaifenesin did, and only the benzonatate–guaifenesin combination beat either drug alone. The remaining efficacy record is a 3-patient case series in opioid-resistant cancer cough (Doona 1998, PMID: 9616460) and uncontrolled 1950s-era reports with no abstracted data. The harm record, by contrast, is modern and concrete: 4,689 paediatric exposure cases reported to US poison centres in 2010–2018, most of them unintentional ingestions by children aged 0–5 (Kim 2022, PMID: 36377394), and in a 20-year single-centre poison series, serious toxicity — seizures, ECG changes, coma — in 22% of intentional exposures, with 2 deaths among 265 exposures (Cicci 2025, PMID: 40511470). A drug can be widely used, genuinely unproven, and dangerous to toddlers who mistake the capsules for sweets; benzonatate is all three. The library's guaifenesin shelf (#2463) covers the expectorant tested alongside it. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (Tier C: a harm-bearing shelf resting on a single small surrogate-endpoint trial).

cards.headline: Dicpinigaitis 2009: in the only controlled trial, benzonatate alone did NOT suppress the cough reflex versus placebo — guaifenesin did, and the combination beat both
cards.summary: Dicpinigaitis 2009: in the only controlled trial, benzonatate alone did NOT suppress the cough reflex versus placebo — guaifenesin did, and the combination beat both
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover challenge study (Dicpinigaitis 2009)
cards.people: 30 adult nonsmokers with acute cough due to viral upper respiratory tract infection, in a double-blind crossover study. On 3 separate days within 7 days, each subject took benzonatate 200 mg, guaifenesin 600 mg, the combination, or placebo (each subject received 3 of the 4), and 1 hour later underwent capsaicin inhalation challenge to find the concentration provoking 5 or more coughs (C5) — a measure of cough-reflex sensitivity, not of the patient's actual cough.
cards.result: Guaifenesin significantly inhibited cough-reflex sensitivity versus placebo (p = 0.01); benzonatate alone did not (p = NS). The benzonatate–guaifenesin combination suppressed capsaicin-induced cough more than benzonatate alone (p < 0.001) or guaifenesin alone (p = 0.008). No outcome measured how much the subjects actually coughed or how they felt.
cards.watchOut: A surrogate endpoint in 30 people: cough-reflex sensitivity to inhaled capsaicin is not cough frequency, cough severity, or patient relief, and a drug can move one without the other. This single small study is the entire controlled efficacy record for benzonatate as an antitussive — there is no trial of benzonatate against placebo, codeine, or dextromethorphan measuring clinical cough outcomes.
cards.source: Dicpinigaitis PV et al. Inhibition of cough-reflex sensitivity by benzonatate and guaifenesin in acute viral cough. Respiratory Medicine. 2009. PMID: 19121573. cards.headline: Doona 1998: three patients with opioid-resistant cancer cough reported relief on benzonatate — a case series, no controls
cards.summary: Doona 1998: three patients with opioid-resistant cancer cough reported relief on benzonatate — a case series, no controls
cards.type: Case series, 3 patients (Doona 1998)
cards.people: Three patients with advanced cancer and chronic nonproductive cough that had not responded to opioids, treated with benzonatate as a peripherally acting non-opioid antitussive.
cards.result: All three patients were reported to achieve symptomatic relief. There was no comparator, no blinding, no cough measurement scale reported in the abstract, and no follow-up quantification — this is anecdote, recorded as such.
cards.watchOut: Cancer cough in three patients is not acute or subacute cough in the general adult population this shelf asks about; it is carded because it is the only other human efficacy report with an abstract in the modern record, and its presence shows how thin the file is. Uncontrolled symptom reports in palliative care overstate benefit as a rule.

cards.headline: Kim 2022: 4,689 paediatric benzonatate exposure cases reported to US poison centres, 2010–2018 — most were toddlers who got into the capsules
cards.summary: Kim 2022: 4,689 paediatric benzonatate exposure cases reported to US poison centres, 2010–2018 — most were toddlers who got into the capsules
cards.type: Retrospective multi-source exposure and adverse-event analysis (Kim 2022)
cards.people: All paediatric benzonatate exposure cases reported to US poison control centres from 2010 to 2018 (4,689 cases), analysed with pharmacy dispensing data, emergency-department surveillance, FDA adverse-event reports and the published literature. 3,727 cases (80%) were single-substance exposures; 3,590 (77%) were unintentional, and of the unintentional single-substance cases most involved children aged 0–5 years (2,718 cases, 83%).
cards.result: Paediatric benzonatate prescribing rose over the period while remaining below dextromethorphan-containing products. Intentional exposures rose among 10–16-year-olds, and most misuse/abuse cases were in that age band (59 cases, 61%). The proportion of cases with serious adverse effects was low and serious events were few each year — but the class of event includes death, and the exposure pattern (a sweet-looking capsule, a toddler, a handbag) is exactly the one regulators warned about.
cards.watchOut: Poison-centre data count exposures, not prescriptions, so no risk-per-prescription rate can be computed from this record; and the population is children, whereas the shelf's question is about adults — the card is here because household exposure of children is the dominant real-world harm of an adult's benzonatate prescription.
cards.source: Kim I et al. Benzonatate Exposure Trends and Adverse Events. Pediatrics. 2022. PMID: 36377394. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cicci 2025: in 265 poison-centre exposures over 20 years, 22% of intentional exposures had a serious effect and 2 patients died; unintentional exposures almost never did
cards.summary: Cicci 2025: in 265 poison-centre exposures over 20 years, 22% of intentional exposures had a serious effect and 2 patients died; unintentional exposures almost never did
cards.type: Retrospective poison-centre case series, 265 exposures (Cicci 2025)
cards.people: 265 benzonatate exposures reported to a single US regional poison centre, 2000–2019 (48 incomplete records excluded from 313 calls). Median age 19 years; 106 exposures (40%) were intentional and 143 (54%) unintentional, including 77 unintentional paediatric exposures. Serious adverse effects were defined as seizure, ECG changes, coma or CNS depression, or death.
cards.result: Of intentional exposures, 23 (22%) had at least one serious adverse effect and 40 (38%) were hospitalised. Of unintentional exposures, 1 (0.7%) had a serious adverse effect and 3 (2%) were hospitalised; none of the 77 unintentional paediatric exposures had a serious effect. Two deaths (0.8% of all exposures) occurred, both after intentional exposure. No treatment beyond supportive care was consistently used.
cards.watchOut: A single centre's call records over two decades, with incomplete records excluded: it describes what happens after exposure, not the risk faced by an adult taking prescribed doses for cough — at ordinary doses the drug's adverse effects are usually limited to sedation, dizziness and gastrointestinal upset. The overdose picture (a local-anaesthetic-like sodium-channel blocker) is nonetheless the reason a handful of capsules can kill.
cards.source: Cicci CD et al. Outcomes of benzonatate exposures reported to a single United States poison center: a 20-year review. Clinical Toxicology. 2025. PMID: 40511470. cards.headline: Synthesis: an unproven antitussive with a proven overdose hazard — MAYBE (weak evidence) for any benefit at all
cards.summary: Synthesis: an unproven antitussive with a proven overdose hazard — MAYBE (weak evidence) for any benefit at all
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The whole cardable record: one 30-person double-blind crossover challenge study in acute viral cough (2009), one 3-patient cancer-cough case series (1998), and two modern poison-data analyses covering 4,689 paediatric exposures (2010–2018) and 265 exposures at one centre (2000–2019). The 1950s–60s literature that supported the 1958 approval survives only as titles without abstracted data.
cards.result: Benzonatate alone failed the only controlled test it has ever been given (cough-reflex sensitivity, p = NS versus placebo); the combination with guaifenesin passed it, which is evidence about the combination, not about benzonatate. No trial measures benzonatate against placebo or another antitussive on actual cough. Meanwhile the harm data are quantitative and current: serious toxicity concentrated in intentional overdose (22% of intentional exposures in the single-centre series; 2 deaths) and a steady stream of unintentional toddler ingestions nationally.
cards.watchOut: Absence of evidence is the finding here, and it should be stated as precisely as that: not 'benzonatate does not work' — no adequate trial has tested whether it works — but 'benzonatate has never been shown to work, and its one controlled test was negative'. If a modern placebo-controlled trial of clinical cough outcomes is ever run, this shelf's stamp is the first thing to revisit.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dicpinigaitis PV et al. Respiratory Medicine. 2009 (PMID: 19121573); Doona M et al. Palliative Medicine. 1998 (PMID: 9616460); Kim I et al. Pediatrics. 2022 (PMID: 36377394); Cicci CD et al. Clinical Toxicology. 2025 (PMID: 40511470).

shelves.title: Daily toothbrushing in hospital: about a one-third relative reduction in hospital-acquired pneumonia across randomised trials
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults, does daily toothbrushing reduce hospital-acquired pneumonia?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Incidence · Intensive Care Units · Respiration, Artificial* · Toothbrushing*/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a consistent, moderate pooled effect for an intervention with no plausible downside at this scale. The 2024 synthesis of 15 randomised trials in 10,742 hospitalised adults found daily toothbrushing associated with lower hospital-acquired pneumonia (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.81 — a 33% relative reduction), with the effect clear in ventilated patients (RR 0.68) and imprecise outside the ICU (RR 0.32, CI 0.05 to 2.02); ICU mortality was also lower (RR 0.81, 0.69 to 0.95), with fewer ventilation and ICU days (Ehrenzeller 2024, PMID: 38109100). The Cochrane oral-care review's toothbrushing comparison agrees (VAP RR 0.61, 0.41 to 0.91; low-certainty, 5 trials, 910 patients; Zhao 2020, PMID: 33368159). Brushing cannot be blinded and pneumonia ascertainment is soft, which is why this is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY; the ICU mortality figure is a pooled secondary outcome and is flagged in the notes. Chlorhexidine oral care is a separate question, homed at shelf #469. Not Tier C: the claim rests on two concordant syntheses of randomised trials and is a pneumonia-prevention claim, not a mortality claim.

cards.headline: Ehrenzeller 2024: daily toothbrushing in hospital — hospital-acquired pneumonia RR 0.67, ICU mortality RR 0.81 across 15 randomised trials
cards.summary: Ehrenzeller 2024: daily toothbrushing in hospital — hospital-acquired pneumonia RR 0.67, ICU mortality RR 0.81 across 15 randomised trials
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 15 RCTs (Ehrenzeller 2024, JAMA Internal Medicine)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials of hospitalised adults comparing daily oral care with toothbrushing against regimens without toothbrushing: 15 trials, 10,742 patients (2,033 in intensive care and 8,709 in non-ICU departments; effective population 2,786 after adjustment for one large cluster-randomised trial).
cards.result: Toothbrushing was associated with lower hospital-acquired pneumonia (risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.81 — a 33% relative reduction) and lower ICU mortality (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.95). The pneumonia reduction was significant in patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.82) but not in non-ventilated patients (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.05 to 2.02). Toothbrushing in ICU patients was also associated with 1.24 fewer days of mechanical ventilation and 1.78 fewer ICU days.
cards.watchOut: Toothbrushing cannot be blinded, pneumonia diagnosis in these trials is partly judgement-based, and one large cluster trial dominates the non-ICU population — hence the shrunken effective sample. The ICU mortality signal (RR 0.81) is a secondary outcome of a pooled analysis, not the result of a trial powered for mortality; it should be read as supportive, not proven.
cards.source: Ehrenzeller S et al. Association Between Daily Toothbrushing and Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38109100. cards.headline: Zhao 2020 (Cochrane): in ventilated ICU patients, toothbrushing versus none cut ventilator-associated pneumonia (RR 0.61) — low-certainty evidence
cards.summary: Zhao 2020 (Cochrane): in ventilated ICU patients, toothbrushing versus none cut ventilator-associated pneumonia (RR 0.61) — low-certainty evidence
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 40 RCTs (Zhao 2020, Cochrane)
cards.people: Cochrane review of oral hygiene care in critically ill patients receiving mechanical ventilation for at least 48 hours: 40 randomised trials, 5,675 participants. The toothbrushing comparison pooled trials of toothbrushing (with or without antiseptics) versus no toothbrushing (with or without antiseptics).
cards.result: Toothbrushing was associated with reduced ventilator-associated pneumonia: RR 0.61 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.91), from 5 RCTs with 910 participants, assessed as low-certainty evidence. The same review's chlorhexidine mouthrinse/gel comparison reduced VAP from about 26% to about 18% (RR 0.67) without reducing mortality (RR 1.03) — chlorhexidine itself is homed at shelf #469 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-one of the 40 trials were at high risk of bias and only two at low risk; the toothbrushing estimate rests on five small trials. The direction agrees with the larger 2024 synthesis (Ehrenzeller), but neither source supports claims about how often, how long, or with what adjunct brushing should be done.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a cheap, unblindable intervention with a consistent one-third relative reduction in hospital pneumonia — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a cheap, unblindable intervention with a consistent one-third relative reduction in hospital pneumonia — POSSIBLE
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two syntheses of randomised trials: Ehrenzeller 2024 (15 trials, 10,742 hospitalised adults) and the Cochrane oral-hygiene review (Zhao 2020; toothbrushing comparison 5 trials, 910 ventilated patients).
cards.result: Hospital-acquired pneumonia: RR 0.67 (0.56–0.81) for daily toothbrushing versus no toothbrushing; ventilator-associated pneumonia in the Cochrane toothbrushing comparison: RR 0.61 (0.41–0.91). ICU mortality was lower in the 2024 synthesis (RR 0.81, 0.69–0.95), as were ventilation days and ICU stay. The non-ventilated subgroup estimate (RR 0.32, CI 0.05–2.02) is too imprecise to claim benefit outside the ICU on its own.
cards.watchOut: Neither synthesis can separate toothbrushing itself from the extra nursing attention that comes with a brushing protocol, and neither addresses dental harm, aspiration during brushing, or optimal frequency. The claim carded here is narrow: daily toothbrushing as part of hospital oral care, versus none.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ehrenzeller S et al. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 38109100); Zhao T et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020 (PMID: 33368159).

shelves.title: Over-the-counter cough suppressants in adults: codeine matched placebo exactly; dextromethorphan's pooled signal is small and contested
shelves.question: In adults with acute cough from a cold, do over-the-counter antitussives (dextromethorphan, codeine) reduce cough versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Adult · Ambulatory Care · Antitussive Agents/administration & dosage*, adverse effects · Child · Cough/drug therapy* · Drug Therapy, Combination/methods · Expectorants/administration & dosage*, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Histamine H1 Antagonists/administration & dosage* · Humans · Nonprescription Drugs/administration & dosage*, adverse effects · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the honest summary is that the standard suppressants have never clearly beaten placebo in the condition they are sold for. The Cochrane review of over-the-counter cough medicines (29 trials, 4,835 people) found the six adult antitussive trials variable and concluded there is no good evidence for or against these medicines (Smith 2014, PMID: 25420096). The direct tests explain why: codeine 50 mg was indistinguishable from placebo on sound-meter, frequency and subjective measures in 82 adults, while both groups improved dramatically on their own (Freestone 1997, PMID: 9364418); a single 30 mg dose of dextromethorphan gave 'very little if any support' for a clinically significant effect in 43 adults (Lee 2000, PMID: 11045895); yet pooling six single-dose dextromethorphan trials (710 patients) from the same measurement programme did find statistically significant reductions in sound-derived cough measures over 3 hours (Pavesi 2001, PMID: 11591548). A small, short-window, contested statistical signal is exactly what MAYBE (weak evidence) is for. Guaifenesin is homed at shelf #2463, sedating antihistamines at #2570, and benzonatate at #2566. Not Tier C: symptom claims only, resting on a Cochrane synthesis plus individual trials.

cards.headline: Smith 2014 (Cochrane): 29 trials of over-the-counter cough medicines — six adult antitussive trials with variable results; reviewers found no good evidence for or against
cards.summary: Smith 2014 (Cochrane): 29 trials of over-the-counter cough medicines — six adult antitussive trials with variable results; reviewers found no good evidence for or against
cards.type: Systematic review, 29 RCTs (Smith 2014, Cochrane)
cards.people: Cochrane review of over-the-counter cough medicines for acute cough in community settings: 29 placebo-controlled randomised trials, 4,835 people (3,799 adults, 1,036 children). In adults, six trials compared antitussives (including dextromethorphan and codeine) with placebo; three trials tested guaifenesin, three tested antihistamines as monotherapy, and others tested combinations and mucolytics.
cards.result: In adults, the six antitussive trials had variable results; the three antihistamine trials found antihistamines no more effective than placebo; guaifenesin trials conflicted (one positive, two not). In children, antitussives and antihistamines were no more effective than placebo. The reviewers' conclusion: there is no good evidence for or against the effectiveness of over-the-counter medicines in acute cough, and trial reporting was often poor.
cards.watchOut: An absence-of-evidence verdict built from small, old, heterogeneously measured trials: cough was scored by sound meters, counts, diaries and global impressions that cannot be pooled. Guaifenesin has its own shelf (#2463) and sedating antihistamines theirs (#2570); this shelf covers the antitussive ingredient itself.
cards.source: Smith SM et al. Over-the-counter (OTC) medications for acute cough in children and adults in community settings. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014. PMID: 25420096. cards.headline: Freestone 1997: codeine 50 mg versus placebo for cold cough — both groups improved markedly; codeine added nothing on any measure
cards.summary: Freestone 1997: codeine 50 mg versus placebo for cold cough — both groups improved markedly; codeine added nothing on any measure
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Freestone 1997)
cards.people: Double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 82 adults (mean age 23.5 years) with cough from an acute upper respiratory tract infection. A single dose of codeine 50 mg or matched placebo was assessed by three measures: cough sound-pressure levels on a sound meter, cough frequency by microphone recording, and subjective cough severity scores, on day 1 and again 2–5 days later.
cards.result: Cough fell highly significantly after both codeine and placebo on all three measures (P < 0.0001 within groups), with no significant difference between the treatment groups on any measure, and a further large fall between day 1 and day 2 in both groups. The authors conclude codeine is no more effective than placebo for cough associated with acute upper respiratory infection.
cards.watchOut: A single-dose laboratory study in young adults: it cannot exclude an effect of repeated dosing, but it is the direct test of the 'standard antitussive' claim, and its most useful lesson is the size of the placebo-plus-natural-history effect — most of what a cough medicine 'does' in the first 48 hours happens without it.
cards.source: Freestone C et al. Assessment of the antitussive efficacy of codeine in cough associated with common cold. Journal of Pharmacy and Pharmacology. 1997. PMID: 9364418. cards.headline: Lee 2000: dextromethorphan 30 mg single dose — 'very little if any support' for a clinically significant antitussive effect
cards.summary: Lee 2000: dextromethorphan 30 mg single dose — 'very little if any support' for a clinically significant antitussive effect
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Lee 2000)
cards.people: Double-blind randomised trial of 43 adults with acute dry or slightly productive cough from an upper respiratory tract infection, given a single dose of dextromethorphan 30 mg (21 patients) or placebo (22). Cough was recorded objectively (sound-pressure level, frequency) and subjectively before dosing and at 90, 135 and 180 minutes after.
cards.result: Both groups improved significantly within group on all measures; between groups there was little difference — the only statistically significant between-group result was mean cough sound-pressure change at 90 minutes (P = 0.019), one measure at one time point among many. The authors state the study provides 'very little if any support for clinically significant antitussive activity of a single 30 mg dose of dextromethorphan' in this setting.
cards.watchOut: Forty-three patients and a 3-hour window: this trial alone would be a footnote. Its weight comes from being the most careful single test in the exact population that buys the product — and from disagreeing with the pooled analysis carded next, which included trials from the same measurement programme.
cards.source: Lee PCL et al. Antitussive efficacy of dextromethorphan in cough associated with acute upper respiratory tract infection. Journal of Pharmacy and Pharmacology. 2000. PMID: 11045895. cards.headline: Pavesi 2001: pooling six single-dose dextromethorphan trials (710 patients) found statistically significant reductions in cough measures versus placebo
cards.summary: Pavesi 2001: pooling six single-dose dextromethorphan trials (710 patients) found statistically significant reductions in cough measures versus placebo
cards.type: Meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (Pavesi 2001, Chest)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of six randomised, double-blind, single-dose, placebo-controlled trials of dextromethorphan hydrobromide 30 mg in 710 adults with cough from uncomplicated upper respiratory tract infection (five studies in Bombay, India; one in Durban, South Africa), using a standardised computerised cough-sound acquisition system over 3 hours after dosing.
cards.result: The pooled analysis showed significantly greater reductions with dextromethorphan than placebo in cough bouts, cough components and cough effort, and an increase in cough latency, consistently across most studies. No absolute effect sizes are given in the abstract — the outcomes are composite sound-derived measures over a single 3-hour window.
cards.watchOut: This paper's stated purpose was partly to validate the measurement system, and its trials come from one research programme — the same programme whose best-known individual trial (Lee 2000) was essentially null. Statistical significance on sound composites over 3 hours is not the same as a patient feeling meaningfully less cough over a week of illness; no trial here measured that.
cards.source: Pavesi L et al. Application and validation of a computerized cough acquisition system for objective monitoring of acute cough: a meta-analysis. Chest. 2001. PMID: 11591548. cards.headline: Synthesis: codeine is a placebo-equal; dextromethorphan's signal is small, short-window and contested by its own programme's trial — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: codeine is a placebo-equal; dextromethorphan's signal is small, short-window and contested by its own programme's trial — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The Cochrane synthesis of over-the-counter cough medicines (29 trials, 4,835 people), the direct codeine trial (n = 82), the direct dextromethorphan trial (n = 43), and the six-trial dextromethorphan pooling (n = 710).
cards.result: Codeine 50 mg: no better than placebo on objective or subjective cough measures. Dextromethorphan 30 mg: statistically significant pooled reductions in sound-derived cough measures over 3 hours, against an essentially null result in the programme's own carefully measured individual trial. Cochrane's overall verdict stands over both: no good evidence for or against over-the-counter cough medicines in acute cough. Nothing in this record addresses cough lasting more than a few days, chronic cough, or children (where the trials are null).
cards.watchOut: Dextromethorphan and codeine both carry misuse and interaction burdens (serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs for dextromethorphan; opioid harms for codeine) that this efficacy record does not quantify — the absence of demonstrated benefit is what makes those burdens hard to justify, and that judgement belongs to the reader, stated here as context, not as a carded harm estimate.
cards.source: Synthesis of Smith SM et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014 (PMID: 25420096); Freestone C et al. Journal of Pharmacy and Pharmacology. 1997 (PMID: 9364418); Lee PCL et al. Journal of Pharmacy and Pharmacology. 2000 (PMID: 11045895); Pavesi L et al. Chest. 2001 (PMID: 11591548).

shelves.title: One inhaler for both jobs: maintenance-and-reliever therapy cut severe exacerbations by about a third relative versus fixed maintenance plus a separate reliever
shelves.question: In asthma, does single-inhaler maintenance-and-reliever therapy (MART) beat conventional maintenance plus a short-acting reliever?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/administration & dosage · Adrenergic beta-Agonists/administration & dosage · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/administration & dosage · Asthma/drug therapy · Bias · Budesonide/administration & dosage · Delayed-Action Preparations · Drug Therapy, Combination · Formoterol Fumarate/administration & dosage · Humans · Maintenance Chemotherapy · Risk Assessment
shelves.balance: The pooled evidence is consistent and clinically meaningful. Sobieraj's 2018 JAMA systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (22,748 patients) found that in patients aged 12 and over, single maintenance-and-reliever therapy (SMART/MART) with budesonide–formoterol reduced exacerbations versus the same dose of inhaled corticosteroid/LABA maintenance plus a short-acting reliever (risk ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.80; absolute risk difference −6.4 percentage points, 95% CI −10.2 to −2.6) and versus a higher maintenance dose (RR 0.77, 0.60 to 0.98) (PMID: 29554195). The largest constituent trial, Kuna 2007 (3,335 patients, 6 months), recorded severe exacerbation rates of 12 per 100 patients on MART versus 16 on fixed-dose budesonide–formoterol and 19 on salmeterol–fluticasone, both with terbutaline relief — rate ratios 0.72 and 0.61 — while MART patients used less inhaled corticosteroid overall (PMID: 17362472). The mechanism shows up in Buhl's 2012 pooled exploratory analysis: after a day of high reliever use, exacerbation treatment was needed within 21 days on only 2.5–3.4% of days with MART versus 6.0–10.1% with fixed-dose regimens — the extra reliever puffs deliver anti-inflammatory drug at exactly the moment of deterioration (PMID: 22816878). Caveats: every trial used budesonide–formoterol, because formoterol's rapid onset makes it usable as a reliever; the strategy cannot be assumed for salmeterol combinations. Data in children aged 4–11 rest on only 341 patients. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) (not Tier C: 16-trial meta-analysis with consistent direction). This is not shelf #308 — that asks about as-needed-only budesonide–formoterol in mild asthma with no daily maintenance; this shelf is for patients on daily maintenance treatment. Adding a long-acting muscarinic antagonist instead is shelf #1033.

cards.headline: Sobieraj 2018 (JAMA): across 16 trials and 22,748 patients, MART cut exacerbations by about a third relative versus the same maintenance dose plus a SABA reliever
cards.summary: Sobieraj 2018 (JAMA): across 16 trials and 22,748 patients, MART cut exacerbations by about a third relative versus the same maintenance dose plus a SABA reliever
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 16 RCTs (Sobieraj 2018, JAMA)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (N = 22,748) of single maintenance-and-reliever therapy — 15 of them budesonide–formoterol in a dry-powder inhaler — versus inhaled corticosteroid with or without LABA as controller plus a short-acting beta-agonist as reliever, in patients aged 5 and over with persistent asthma. Primary outcome: asthma exacerbations.
cards.result: Among patients aged 12 and over (n = 22,524), MART was associated with a reduced risk of exacerbations compared with the same dose of ICS/LABA controller therapy (risk ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.80; risk difference −6.4 percentage points, 95% CI −10.2 to −2.6) and compared with a higher dose of ICS/LABA controller therapy (RR 0.77, 0.60 to 0.98; RD −2.8 points, −5.2 to −0.3). Results were similar against ICS alone. Among children aged 4–11 (n = 341), MART also reduced exacerbations versus higher-dose ICS (RR 0.55, 0.32 to 0.94) and versus the same dose of ICS/LABA (RR 0.38, 0.23 to 0.63), on much thinner data.
cards.watchOut: A relative reduction of about a third (RR 0.68) is the headline; the absolute gain is about 6 fewer exacerbations per 100 patients over the trial periods against the same maintenance dose, and about 3 per 100 against a higher dose. Fifteen of 16 trials used one product combination (budesonide–formoterol) — the meta-analysis licenses no claim for MART with other ICS/LABA pairs.
cards.source: Sobieraj DM et al. Association of Inhaled Corticosteroids and Long-Acting β-Agonists as Controller and Quick Relief Therapy With Exacerbations and Symptom Control in Persistent Asthma: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. cards.headline: Kuna 2007: 3,335 patients — severe exacerbations 12 per 100 on MART versus 16 on fixed budesonide–formoterol and 19 on salmeterol–fluticasone over 6 months
cards.summary: Kuna 2007: 3,335 patients — severe exacerbations 12 per 100 on MART versus 16 on fixed budesonide–formoterol and 19 on salmeterol–fluticasone over 6 months
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial (Kuna 2007)
cards.people: Randomised double-blind 6-month trial in 3,335 symptomatic adults and adolescents (mean FEV1 73% predicted, mean inhaled corticosteroid dose 745 micrograms/day) comparing budesonide–formoterol 160/4.5 micrograms one inhalation twice daily plus as-needed inhalations (MART) against salmeterol–fluticasone 25/125 micrograms two inhalations twice daily plus terbutaline, and fixed-dose budesonide–formoterol 320/9 micrograms twice daily plus terbutaline.
cards.result: MART prolonged the time to first severe exacerbation (hospitalisation, emergency treatment or oral steroids) versus salmeterol–fluticasone (p = 0.0034) and versus fixed-dose budesonide–formoterol (p = 0.023). Severe exacerbation rates were 12, 16 and 19 events per 100 patients per 6 months for MART, fixed-dose budesonide–formoterol and salmeterol–fluticasone respectively — rate ratio 0.61 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.76) versus salmeterol–fluticasone and 0.72 (0.57 to 0.90) versus fixed-dose budesonide–formoterol, both relative measures. MART patients used less inhaled corticosteroid overall; lung function, asthma-control days and quality of life improved similarly in all groups.
cards.watchOut: The daily-control outcomes (symptoms, lung function, quality of life) were the same in all three arms — MART's advantage is specifically fewer severe exacerbations, bought by letting the reliever carry corticosteroid. Industry-conducted (the combination's manufacturer); the direction is corroborated by the independent meta-analysis above.
cards.source: Kuna P et al. Effect of budesonide/formoterol maintenance and reliever therapy on asthma exacerbations. International journal of clinical practice. 2007. PMID: 17362472. cards.headline: Buhl 2012: after a day of heavy reliever use, deterioration followed on 2.5–3.4% of days with MART versus 6.0–10.1% on fixed-dose regimens
cards.summary: Buhl 2012: after a day of heavy reliever use, deterioration followed on 2.5–3.4% of days with MART versus 6.0–10.1% on fixed-dose regimens
cards.type: Exploratory pooled analysis of two RCTs (Buhl 2012)
cards.people: Exploratory pooled post-hoc analysis of two randomised double-blind trials comparing budesonide–formoterol maintenance-and-reliever therapy (160/4.5 micrograms twice daily plus as needed) with similar or higher maintenance doses of ICS/LABA plus a short-acting reliever or formoterol. Episodes of high reliever use (more than 6 inhalations in a day) were identified, and severe exacerbations requiring treatment within the following 21 days counted.
cards.result: MART significantly reduced the risk of high-reliever-use episodes versus all alternative ICS/LABA regimens. After such an episode, exacerbation treatment was needed within 21 days on 6.0–10.1% of days across the fixed-dose regimens, compared with 2.5–3.4% of days with budesonide–formoterol maintenance-and-reliever therapy — consistent with the reliever doses themselves delivering corticosteroid during early deterioration.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and exploratory — it explains the mechanism behind the exacerbation reduction rather than proving a separate benefit, and its percentages are of days following high-use episodes, not of patients. Treat it as the 'why' card, not a third efficacy estimate.
cards.source: Buhl R et al. The effect of budesonide/formoterol maintenance and reliever therapy on the risk of severe asthma exacerbations following episodes of high reliever use: an exploratory analysis of two randomised, controlled studies with comparisons to standard therapy.
