cards.headline: Synthesis: MART prevents roughly one severe exacerbation in fifteen patients treated — by making the reliever an anti-inflammatory inhaler
cards.summary: Synthesis: MART prevents roughly one severe exacerbation in fifteen patients treated — by making the reliever an anti-inflammatory inhaler
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One JAMA meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (22,748 patients), its largest constituent double-blind trial (Kuna 2007, n = 3,335), and a pooled mechanistic analysis of two trials (Buhl 2012). All evidence is with budesonide–formoterol.
cards.result: Exacerbation risk ratio 0.68 (0.58–0.80) versus the same maintenance dose plus SABA — an absolute reduction of about 6.4 exacerbations per 100 patients — and 0.77 (0.60–0.98) versus a higher maintenance dose. In the largest trial, severe exacerbations ran at 12 versus 16–19 events per 100 patients per 6 months, with lower total inhaled-steroid exposure on MART and identical day-to-day control. Symptom control and lung function do not improve; severe attacks do fall.
cards.watchOut: The strategy is inseparable from the molecule: it works because formoterol acts within minutes. It must not be read across to salmeterol-containing combinations, whose reliever use would deliver a slow-onset LABA without extra steroid. Evidence in children under 12 is thin (341 patients in the meta-analysis), and none of this applies to mild asthma managed without daily maintenance — that is shelf #308.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sobieraj DM et al. JAMA. 2018 (PMID: 29554195); Kuna P et al. International Journal of Clinical Practice. 2007 (PMID: 17362472); Buhl R et al. Respiratory Research. 2012 (PMID: 22816878).

shelves.title: Pulmonary rehabilitation in stable COPD: breathlessness, quality of life and walking distance all improve beyond the clinically important margin — hospital days halve, though no fewer patients are admitted
shelves.question: In stable COPD, does pulmonary rehabilitation improve breathlessness, exercise capacity and hospital admissions?
shelves.mesh: Dyspnea/rehabilitation · *Exercise Tolerance · Female · *Health Status · Humans · Male · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/psychology/rehabilitation · *Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: For breathlessness, quality of life and exercise capacity this is among the best-supported interventions in COPD. McCarthy's 2015 Cochrane review pooled 65 randomised trials with 3,822 participants in stable disease: every Chronic Respiratory Questionnaire domain improved by more than its 0.5-unit minimal clinically important difference (dyspnoea mean difference 0.79, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.03; fatigue 0.68; emotional function 0.56; mastery 0.71), the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire total improved by −6.89 points (MCID 4), six-minute walk distance by 43.93 metres, and maximal exercise capacity by 6.77 watts (PMID: 25705944). The admissions part of the question needs care: the Cochrane review did not pool admission outcomes in stable COPD, and the largest single trial, Griffiths 2000 (200 patients followed for a year), found no difference in how many patients were admitted (40 versus 41) but half as many days in hospital among those admitted (10.4 versus 21.0 days, p = 0.022), alongside better walking ability and health status (PMID: 10665556). So: admissions prevented — not shown in stable disease; hospital burden reduced — suggested by one large trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) (not Tier C: 65-trial Cochrane synthesis). Rehabilitation started after a hospitalised exacerbation is a different question with its own readmission and mortality data — shelf #304; this shelf is the stable-disease programme.

cards.headline: McCarthy 2015 (Cochrane): 65 trials, 3,822 patients — every quality-of-life domain beat its clinically important threshold, and walking distance rose by 44 metres
cards.summary: McCarthy 2015 (Cochrane): 65 trials, 3,822 patients — every quality-of-life domain beat its clinically important threshold, and walking distance rose by 44 metres
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 65 RCTs (McCarthy 2015, Cochrane)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of 65 randomised trials (3,822 participants) of pulmonary rehabilitation — exercise training for at least 4 weeks, with or without education or psychological support — versus usual care in people with COPD (mean FEV1 about 38% predicted, mean age about 62). Most programmes lasted 8–12 weeks; 41 were hospital-based and 23 community-based.
cards.result: All outcomes improved significantly, and by clinically important margins. Chronic Respiratory Questionnaire (minimal clinically important difference 0.5 units): dyspnoea mean difference 0.79 (95% CI 0.56 to 1.03; 19 studies, 1,283 participants), fatigue 0.68 (0.45 to 0.92), emotional function 0.56 (0.34 to 0.78), mastery 0.71 (0.47 to 0.95). St George's Respiratory Questionnaire total score improved by −6.89 points (−9.26 to −4.52; MCID 4), and by −5.15 in the sensitivity analysis restricted to lower-risk-of-bias trials. Functional exercise capacity (six-minute walk distance) improved by 43.93 metres (32.64 to 55.21; 38 studies, 1,879 participants) and maximal exercise capacity by 6.77 watts (1.89 to 11.65). Hospital-based programmes showed larger CRQ effects than community-based ones in subgroup analysis.
cards.watchOut: Participants and therapists cannot be blinded in exercise trials, allocation concealment was often unclear, and attrition was high in several studies — the reviewers graded much of the evidence low to moderate quality, though the low-bias sensitivity analysis for SGRQ (−5.15 points) still exceeded the clinically important threshold. The review's outcomes are symptoms, quality of life and exercise capacity; it does not answer the admissions question.
cards.source: McCarthy B et al. Pulmonary rehabilitation for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015. PMID: 25705944. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Griffiths 2000: 200 patients followed for a year — no fewer admissions (40 vs 41 patients), but hospital days halved (10.4 vs 21.0) and walking and health status improved
cards.summary: Griffiths 2000: 200 patients followed for a year — no fewer admissions (40 vs 41 patients), but hospital days halved (10.4 vs 21.0) and walking and health status improved
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Griffiths 2000)
cards.people: Randomised controlled trial of 200 patients with disabling chronic lung disease (the majority with COPD) assigned to a 6-week multidisciplinary outpatient rehabilitation programme (18 visits: exercise, education, dietary and occupational therapy input) or standard medical management, with health-service use and wellbeing assessed over 1 year by intention to treat.
cards.result: There was no difference between the rehabilitation (n = 99) and control (n = 101) groups in the number of patients admitted to hospital (40 versus 41), but patients who were admitted spent significantly fewer days in hospital after rehabilitation (mean 10.4 days, SD 9.7, versus 21.0 days, SD 20.7; p = 0.022). The rehabilitation group had more general-practice surgery consultations (8.6 versus 7.3, p = 0.033) but fewer home visits (1.5 versus 2.8, p = 0.037), and showed greater improvements in walking ability and in general and disease-specific health status at 1 year.
cards.watchOut: The hospital-days figure is conditional on being admitted and comes from a single trial conducted in one UK centre in the 1990s; the population had 'disabling chronic lung disease', mostly but not exclusively COPD. It supports 'less time in hospital', not 'fewer admissions' — a distinction the post-exacerbation rehabilitation literature (shelf #304) does not have to make, because there admission outcomes were directly reduced.
cards.source: Griffiths TL et al. Results at 1 year of outpatient multidisciplinary pulmonary rehabilitation: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2000. PMID: 10665556. cards.headline: Synthesis: rehabilitation is the strongest non-drug treatment in stable COPD — for how patients feel and function; its admission benefit is in days, not events
cards.summary: Synthesis: rehabilitation is the strongest non-drug treatment in stable COPD — for how patients feel and function; its admission benefit is in days, not events
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One Cochrane meta-analysis of 65 randomised trials (3,822 participants; McCarthy 2015) and the largest long-follow-up trial of health-service use (Griffiths 2000, n = 200, 1 year).
cards.result: Breathlessness: CRQ dyspnoea +0.79 units against an MCID of 0.5. Quality of life: SGRQ −6.89 points against an MCID of 4, robust to restricting to low-bias trials (−5.15). Exercise: six-minute walk +43.93 metres; maximal capacity +6.77 watts. Admissions: number of patients admitted unchanged in the one large trial (40 versus 41), with hospital days among the admitted roughly halved (10.4 versus 21.0). No mortality claim can be made from this stable-disease evidence.
cards.watchOut: Programmes vary (4–52 weeks, hospital or community, exercise alone or multidisciplinary) and the pooled estimates average over that variety; benefits also fade without maintenance activity, which these trials largely did not test. Do not quote this shelf for rehabilitation begun during or immediately after a hospitalised exacerbation — timing changes both the benefits and the risks, and that question lives at shelf #304.
cards.source: Synthesis of McCarthy B et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015 (PMID: 25705944); Griffiths TL et al. Lancet. 2000 (PMID: 10665556).

shelves.title: Airway clearance in bronchiectasis: one small year-long placebo-controlled trial found fewer exacerbations and better quality of life — the rest of the evidence is short, tiny crossover studies
shelves.question: In bronchiectasis, do airway-clearance techniques (oscillatory PEP, ELTGOL) reduce exacerbations and improve quality of life?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Bronchiectasis/therapy · Cough · Exercise Therapy · Expectorants · Female · Glottis/pathology · Humans · Inflammation · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Respiration · Respiratory Function Tests · Respiratory Therapy/methods · Severity of Illness Index · Sputum/metabolism · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: Airway clearance is prescribed to almost everyone with bronchiectasis and chronic expectoration, yet the trial base is remarkably thin. The single long-term placebo-controlled trial, Muñoz 2018, randomised just 44 patients with chronic expectoration to twice-daily ELTGOL (slow expiration with the glottis open, in lateral posture) or placebo exercises for a year: the ELTGOL group cleared more sputum, had fewer exacerbations (p = 0.042) and clinically significant improvements in St George's Respiratory Questionnaire and Leicester Cough Questionnaire scores (both p < 0.001) (PMID: 29326318). Everything else is smaller and shorter: Lee's 2015 Cochrane review found only seven studies with 105 participants in total, six of them crossover designs, several testing a single treatment session; one oscillatory-device study (20 adults) found no significant difference in exacerbations at 12 weeks but a 7.5-unit SGRQ improvement, and short-term sputum expectoration rose by about 8.4 mL with oscillatory devices (PMID: 26591003). Heterogeneity precluded any meta-analysis. So the honest position: a plausible, low-harm intervention with one positive small trial on the outcomes that matter and a surrounding literature too small to confirm or refute it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) (Tier C: the exacerbation claim rests on a single 44-patient trial; the rest of the base is tiny short crossover studies). Drug treatments for bronchiectasis exacerbations (macrolides, brensocatib) are separate questions, homed elsewhere in this area.

cards.headline: Muñoz 2018: ELTGOL for a year in 44 patients — fewer exacerbations and clinically significant quality-of-life gains versus placebo exercises
cards.summary: Muñoz 2018: ELTGOL for a year in 44 patients — fewer exacerbations and clinically significant quality-of-life gains versus placebo exercises
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial (Muñoz 2018)
cards.people: Randomised placebo-controlled trial in 44 patients with bronchiectasis and chronic expectoration, allocated to the ELTGOL technique (slow expiration with the glottis opened in the lateral posture) twice daily (n = 22) or placebo exercises (n = 22) for 1 year. Primary outcome: sputum volume during the first intervention and 24 hours later; secondary outcomes included exacerbations, quality of life, sputum analyses, lung function, exercise capacity, inflammation, adherence and side effects.
cards.result: Sputum volume during the intervention and over the following 24 hours was higher in the ELTGOL group than the placebo group both at the start and at month 12. Over the year, the ELTGOL group had fewer exacerbations (p = 0.042) and a clinically significant improvement in St George's Respiratory Questionnaire score (p < 0.001) and Leicester Cough Questionnaire score (p < 0.001) compared with placebo. The authors conclude that twice-daily ELTGOL over 1 year facilitated secretion removal and was associated with fewer exacerbations, improved quality of life and reduced cough impact.
cards.watchOut: Forty-four patients from a single centre, and the abstract reports the exacerbation result as a p-value (0.042) without the event counts — a just-significant result in a small trial is fragile, and one or two events either way would move it. ELTGOL is also a specific taught technique with a trained-therapist learning curve; the result does not automatically transfer to every device or routine sold as 'airway clearance'.

cards.headline: Lee 2015 (Cochrane): the entire remaining trial base is 7 studies and 105 participants — too heterogeneous to pool, with quality-of-life signals but no exacerbation answer
cards.summary: Lee 2015 (Cochrane): the entire remaining trial base is 7 studies and 105 participants — too heterogeneous to pool, with quality-of-life signals but no exacerbation answer
cards.type: Systematic review, 7 RCTs (Lee 2015, Cochrane)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised parallel and crossover trials of airway clearance techniques versus no treatment, sham technique or directed coughing in bronchiectasis: seven studies, 105 participants, six of them crossover in design; six studied adults with stable bronchiectasis and one clinically stable children. Three studies were single treatment sessions; two lasted 15–21 days; two were longer-term.
cards.result: Heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis, so the review is narrative. One study of 20 adults comparing an oscillatory device with no treatment found no significant difference in the number of exacerbations at 12 weeks (low-quality evidence), but reported a clinically significant improvement in health-related quality of life: median difference in change in total St George's Respiratory Questionnaire score over 3 months of 7.5 units (p = 0.005). High-frequency chest wall oscillation or mixed techniques for 15 days also improved quality of life versus no treatment. Sputum expectoration increased with oscillatory devices by a mean of 8.4 mL (95% CI 3.4 to 13.4) in the short term and by 3 mL in the longer term (p = 0.02). Data were not available to assess time to exacerbation or hospitalisation. Most studies failed to use concealed allocation and could not blind participants or assessors.
cards.watchOut: A review whose included studies total 105 participants — fewer than a single modest drug trial — and which could not pool anything. Its quality-of-life findings come largely from single-session or 2–3-week crossover studies in which patients can feel the treatment working, so expectation effects on symptom scores cannot be excluded.
cards.source: Lee AL et al. Airway clearance techniques for bronchiectasis. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015. PMID: 26591003. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: probably helpful, certainly under-proven — one 44-patient trial carries the exacerbation claim for a near-universal prescription
cards.summary: Synthesis: probably helpful, certainly under-proven — one 44-patient trial carries the exacerbation claim for a near-universal prescription
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One 1-year randomised placebo-controlled trial of ELTGOL (Muñoz 2018, n = 44) and a Cochrane review of the other seven trials in the field (Lee 2015, 105 participants in total).
cards.result: Exacerbations: fewer with ELTGOL over 1 year (p = 0.042, counts not reported in the abstract); no difference at 12 weeks in the one oscillatory-device study (n = 20). Quality of life: improved in both sources (SGRQ p < 0.001 in Muñoz; median 7.5-unit SGRQ advantage in the device study). Sputum clearance: consistently increased (about +8.4 mL short-term with oscillatory devices). Hospitalisation and time to exacerbation: untested. The intervention is cheap and low-harm, which lowers the bar for adoption — but the evidence bar it has actually cleared is low too.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here compares one technique against another — ELTGOL, oscillatory PEP, active cycle of breathing and chest-wall oscillation are treated by the literature as near-interchangeable, on almost no comparative data. Nor does the evidence cover airway clearance during an acute exacerbation, or in cystic fibrosis, where the trial base and the questions differ.
cards.source: Synthesis of Muñoz G et al. The European Respiratory Journal. 2018 (PMID: 29326318); Lee AL et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015 (PMID: 26591003).

shelves.title: Oxygen at night for COPD patients who desaturate only in sleep: the one trial stopped at 243 of 600 planned patients and found nothing — too small to close the question
shelves.question: In COPD with isolated nocturnal desaturation, does nocturnal oxygen improve survival?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hypoxia/therapy · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Oximetry · Oxygen/blood · *Oxygen Inhalation Therapy · Patient Compliance · Patient Selection · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/mortality/physiopathology/therapy
shelves.balance: Long-term oxygen prolongs life in COPD with severe daytime hypoxaemia — that is shelf #305 and is not in doubt. This shelf asks the harder question: the patient whose oxygen saturation is acceptable by day but falls at night (below 90% for at least 30% of the recording time) and who therefore does not qualify for long-term oxygen. The only randomised trial, INOX (Lacasse 2020), was double-blind and placebo-controlled — nocturnal oxygen versus ambient air from a sham concentrator — over 3 to 4 years, with a primary composite of death or progression to meeting long-term oxygen criteria. It stopped early for recruitment and retention difficulties after randomising 243 of a projected 600 patients. At 3 years, 39.0% of the nocturnal-oxygen group and 42.0% of the placebo group had died or met the criteria (difference −3.0 percentage points, 95% CI −15.1 to 9.1) (PMID: 32937046). That interval is wide enough to contain a clinically important benefit and a clinically important harm; the authors' own conclusion is that the underpowered trial 'provides no indication' of effect in either direction. The honest stamp is therefore a weak no-difference: nothing here justifies prescribing nocturnal oxygen for isolated nocturnal desaturation, and nothing here proves it useless. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference — but the single trial was stopped early and underpowered, so a modest benefit or harm is not excluded) (Tier C: single trial, stopped early).

cards.headline: INOX (Lacasse 2020): nocturnal oxygen versus sham air — death or progression to long-term oxygen 39.0% versus 42.0% at 3 years, in a trial stopped at 40% of its planned size
cards.summary: INOX (Lacasse 2020): nocturnal oxygen versus sham air — death or progression to long-term oxygen 39.0% versus 42.0% at 3 years, in a trial stopped at 40% of its planned size
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Lacasse 2020, INOX)
cards.people: Double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (28 centres) in patients with COPD and isolated nocturnal desaturation — oxygen saturation below 90% for at least 30% of the nocturnal recording time — who did not qualify for long-term oxygen therapy. Patients were assigned 1:1 to nocturnal oxygen or ambient air delivered by a sham concentrator, for 3 to 4 years. Recruitment was stopped prematurely because of recruitment and retention difficulties after 243 of a projected 600 patients had been randomised. Primary outcome: composite of death from any cause or requirement for long-term oxygen therapy by NOTT criteria, intention to treat.
cards.result: At 3 years of follow-up, 39.0% of patients assigned to nocturnal oxygen (48 of 123) and 42.0% of those assigned to placebo (50 of 119) had died or met the criteria for long-term oxygen therapy — a difference of −3.0 percentage points (95% CI −15.1 to 9.1). The authors conclude that the underpowered trial provides no indication that nocturnal oxygen has a positive or negative effect on survival or progression to long-term oxygen therapy in this population.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval is the story: −15.1 to +9.1 percentage points spans effects any clinician would care about in both directions, because the trial recruited 243 of 600 planned patients. 'No indication of effect' is not evidence of no effect. The composite endpoint also mixes death with progression to oxygen criteria, and the trial says nothing about symptoms, sleep quality or exacerbations — outcomes on which nocturnal oxygen might still act and which were not its question.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one underpowered trial, one wide interval — nocturnal oxygen for isolated nocturnal desaturation remains unproven rather than disproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: one underpowered trial, one wide interval — nocturnal oxygen for isolated nocturnal desaturation remains unproven rather than disproven
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: A single double-blind sham-controlled randomised trial (INOX, Lacasse 2020), 243 patients randomised of 600 planned, 3-year follow-up.
cards.result: Death or progression to long-term oxygen therapy: 39.0% on nocturnal oxygen versus 42.0% on sham air (difference −3.0 percentage points, 95% CI −15.1 to 9.1). No significant difference, and no precision: the data are compatible with anything from a 15-point absolute benefit to a 9-point absolute harm. Pending a larger trial, the evidence supports not prescribing nocturnal oxygen for this indication on survival grounds — the burden of proof sits with the intervention — while honestly recording that the question is open.
cards.watchOut: Do not let this shelf bleed into shelf #305: patients with severe chronic daytime hypoxaemia were excluded here precisely because oxygen already has a proven survival benefit for them. Nor does INOX address nocturnal oxygen given for symptom relief, or desaturation driven by obstructive sleep apnoea, which has its own treatment pathway.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lacasse Y et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2020 (PMID: 32937046).

shelves.title: Oxygen for exertion in COPD: small gains in breathlessness scores straight after exercise in short studies, but the largest blinded trial found no benefit in daily breathlessness, quality of life or function
shelves.question: In COPD with exertional desaturation only, does ambulatory oxygen improve breathlessness and activity?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Ambulatory Care/methods · Dyspnea/etiology/physiopathology/therapy · Epidemiologic Methods · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Home Care Services · Humans · Hypoxia/etiology · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen/blood · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy/methods · Partial Pressure · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/complications/physiopathology/therapy · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The evidence splits cleanly by what is measured and when. Moore 2011, the largest and most rigorous trial — 143 breathless COPD patients without severe resting hypoxaemia, double-blind, randomised to domiciliary ambulatory oxygen or cylinder air at 6 L/min for any breathlessness-provoking activity over 12 weeks — found no significant difference in dyspnoea, health-related quality of life, mood or functional status, and exertional desaturation (present in 50 patients, to 88% or below) did not predict who benefited; both groups improved slightly, suggesting the gas flow itself, or trial participation, carries a placebo effect (PMID: 20880870). The Cochrane review by Ameer 2014 pooled four studies (331 participants) and did find statistically significant benefits in breathlessness measured immediately after exercise in two studies, and in the dyspnoea (mean difference 0.28, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.45) and fatigue (0.17, 0.04 to 0.31) domains of quality of life — while finding no evidence of effect on survival and limited, mostly null effects on exercise capacity (PMID: 24957353). Reconciling the two: oxygen can ease breathlessness during or just after a laboratory exercise test, in small short studies; prescribed for everyday use in the best blinded trial, it did not improve how patients felt or functioned day to day. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (small benefit on breathlessness measured immediately after exercise in short studies) / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference to day-to-day breathlessness, quality of life or function in the largest trial) (not Tier C: multiple RCTs and a Cochrane synthesis, though all trials are small). Oxygen for resting hypoxaemia is shelf #305; oxygen at night only is shelf #2670.

cards.headline: Moore 2011: 143 patients, double-blind oxygen versus air cylinders for 12 weeks — no benefit in breathlessness, quality of life or function, and exertional desaturation did not predict response
cards.summary: Moore 2011: 143 patients, double-blind oxygen versus air cylinders for 12 weeks — no benefit in breathlessness, quality of life or function, and exertional desaturation did not predict response
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Moore 2011)
cards.people: Parallel double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial of 143 patients with COPD (mean age 71.8 years, mean FEV1 1.16 litres, mean resting PaO2 9.5 kPa / 71.4 mm Hg) who were breathless on exertion but did not have severe resting hypoxaemia; 50 had exertional desaturation to 88% or below. Participants received cylinder oxygen or cylinder air at 6 L/min intranasally for use during any activity provoking breathlessness, for 12 weeks. Outcomes: dyspnoea, health-related quality of life, mood, functional status and cylinder use, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: No significant differences in any outcome were found between the oxygen and air groups. Statistically significant but clinically small improvements in dyspnoea and depression occurred across the whole study group over the 12 weeks regardless of allocation. Exertional desaturation was not predictive of outcome. The authors conclude that in breathless patients with COPD without severe resting hypoxaemia, domiciliary ambulatory oxygen confers no benefits in dyspnoea, quality of life or function, and that intranasal gas — air or oxygen — may itself provide a placebo benefit.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks is short, and the trial's null covers the outcomes it measured — daily dyspnoea, quality of life, mood, function — not breathlessness during a supervised exercise test, where other studies find an acute effect. A null in the group that desaturates on exertion (the 50-patient subgroup) is the finding that most directly contradicts the usual prescribing rationale, and it is a subgroup, with the imprecision that implies.
cards.source: Moore RP et al. A randomised trial of domiciliary, ambulatory oxygen in patients with COPD and dyspnoea but without resting hypoxaemia. Thorax. 2011. PMID: 20880870. cards.headline: Ameer 2014 (Cochrane): four small trials (331 patients) — breathlessness after exercise and two quality-of-life domains improved; survival and exercise capacity did not
cards.summary: Ameer 2014 (Cochrane): four small trials (331 patients) — breathlessness after exercise and two quality-of-life domains improved; survival and exercise capacity did not
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 4 RCTs (Ameer 2014, Cochrane)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of ambulatory oxygen (portable cylinders, battery devices or liquid oxygen) versus placebo air, usual care or co-intervention in patients with COPD who did not meet criteria for long-term oxygen therapy: four studies, 331 participants, searches current to November 2012.
cards.result: Two studies produced a statistically and clinically significant benefit for dyspnoea measured post-exercise. Across the four studies, quality-of-life domains improved significantly in favour of oxygen for dyspnoea (mean difference 0.28, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.45; p = 0.002) and fatigue (mean difference 0.17, 0.04 to 0.31; p = 0.009). No evidence of any effect was reported for survival, and benefits for exercise capacity were limited — one study showed a significant improvement in steps taken, in N-of-1 analyses only; other trials and N-of-1 studies showed no significant exercise-capacity benefit. The authors note the methodological rigour of the field was limited.
cards.watchOut: The pooled quality-of-life gains (0.28 and 0.17 points) are small fractions of their scales and come from four small, methodologically limited studies, several using laboratory exercise endpoints rather than daily-life measures. Set against Moore 2011's blinded null on everyday outcomes, the fairest reading is a real acute physiological effect that has not been shown to survive translation into daily life.

systematic review and meta-analysis, 4 rcts (ameer 2014, cochrane) cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of ambulatory oxygen (portable cylinders, battery devices or liquid oxygen) versus placebo air, usual care or co-intervention in patients with copd who did not meet criteria for long-term oxygen therapy: four studies, 331 participants, searches current to november 2012. two studies produced a statistically and clinically significant benefit for dyspnoea measured post-exercise. across the four studies, quality-of-life domains improved significantly in favour of oxygen for dyspnoea (mean difference 0.28, 95% ci 0.10 to 0.45; p = 0.002) and fatigue (mean difference 0.17, 0.04 to 0.31; p = 0.009). no evidence of any effect was reported for survival, and benefits for exercise capacity were limited — one study showed a significant improvement in steps taken, in n-of-1 analyses only; other trials and n-of-1 studies showed no significant exercise-capacity benefit. the authors note the methodological rigour of the field was limited. the pooled quality-of-life gains (0.28 and 0.17 points) are small fractions of their scales and come from four small, methodologically limited studies, several using laboratory exercise endpoints rather than daily-life measures. set against moore 2011's blinded null on everyday outcomes, the fairest reading is a real acute physiological effect that has not been shown to survive translation into daily life. ameer f et al. ambulatory oxygen for people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease who are not hypoxaemic at rest. the cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014. pmid: 24957353. registry id: none in the record. mesh: ambulatory care · exercise/physiology · humans · hypoxia/therapy · oxygen inhalation therapy/methods · pulmonary disease, chronic obstructive/blood/physiopathology/therapy · randomized controlled trials as topic · rest

cards.headline: Synthesis: oxygen relieves breathlessness in the exercise laboratory; prescribed for daily life, it has not been shown to
cards.summary: Synthesis: oxygen relieves breathlessness in the exercise laboratory; prescribed for daily life, it has not been shown to
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The largest double-blind domiciliary trial (Moore 2011, n = 143) and the Cochrane synthesis of the field (Ameer 2014, 4 trials, 331 participants).
cards.result: Post-exercise breathlessness: improved in two of the pooled small studies, with quality-of-life dyspnoea and fatigue domains favouring oxygen by 0.28 and 0.17 points. Day-to-day breathlessness, overall quality of life, mood and function over 12 weeks of real-world use: no significant difference between oxygen and air in the largest trial, including in patients who desaturated on exertion. Survival: no effect shown anywhere. Exercise capacity: mostly null. The prescription decision therefore turns on whether a patient values possible short-lived relief during exertion enough to carry the equipment — an individual trial of therapy, not an evidence-backed default.
cards.watchOut: This shelf covers patients who do not qualify for long-term oxygen at rest. It must not be quoted against oxygen in severe resting hypoxaemia (shelf #305, where survival benefit is proven), nor for nocturnal-only use (shelf #2670). Short-burst oxygen for breathlessness in palliative care is a separate question with its own shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Moore RP et al. Thorax. 2011 (PMID: 20880870); Ameer F et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014 (PMID: 24957353).

shelves.title: Inhaled liposomal amikacin for refractory MAC lung disease: culture conversion 29% versus 9% — real, but most patients still did not convert, and nearly nine in ten had respiratory side effects
shelves.question: In refractory Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease, does adding inhaled liposomal amikacin to guideline-based therapy improve culture conversion?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Amikacin/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Liposomes · Lung Diseases/drug therapy/microbiology · Male · Middle Aged · Mycobacterium avium Complex · Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare Infection/drug therapy · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: CONVERT (Griffith 2018) is the pivotal trial: 336 adults with amikacin-susceptible MAC lung disease whose sputum remained culture-positive despite at least 6 months of guideline-based therapy were randomised 2:1 to add daily amikacin liposome inhalation suspension (ALIS, 590 mg by nebuliser) to their regimen or continue guideline therapy alone. Culture conversion by month 6 — three consecutive monthly negative cultures — was achieved by 29.0% with ALIS versus 8.9% without (odds ratio 4.22, 95% CI 2.08 to 8.57; p < 0.001), an absolute gain of about 20 percentage points (PMID: 30216086). The follow-up report of the same trial (Griffith 2021) shows the conversions were meaningful: sustained and durable conversion (negative cultures through 12 months of further treatment and 3 months off it) in 16.1% of the ALIS group versus 0% on guideline therapy alone, intention to treat (PMID: 33887244). The price is tolerability: respiratory adverse events — mainly dysphonia, cough and dyspnoea — in 87.4% on ALIS versus 50.0% on guideline therapy alone, though serious treatment-emergent adverse events were comparable (20.2% versus 17.9%). Two framing points matter. First, 29% is a tripling of a low base: seven in ten patients on ALIS still had not converted by month 6, in a population defined by treatment failure. Second, the tested intervention is a specific manufactured liposomal formulation in 590 mg single-use vials; the record names the formulation and dose but no manufacturer, and nebulised intravenous amikacin or compounded preparations are not the tested intervention and may differ in delivery, safety and effect. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) (Tier C: a single randomised trial and its own follow-up report). Whether intermittent versus daily background regimens differ in nodular-bronchiectatic MAC is a separate question (slate topic 2962, not built in this batch).

cards.headline: CONVERT (Griffith 2018): culture conversion by month 6 in 29.0% with added ALIS versus 8.9% on guideline therapy alone — odds ratio 4.22
cards.summary: CONVERT (Griffith 2018): culture conversion by month 6 in 29.0% with added ALIS versus 8.9% on guideline therapy alone — odds ratio 4.22
cards.type: Randomised open-label trial, CONVERT (Griffith 2018)
cards.people: Prospective open-label randomised trial (CONVERT) in 336 adults with amikacin-susceptible Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease and MAC-positive sputum cultures despite at least 6 months of stable guideline-based therapy (GBT), randomised 2:1 to ALIS plus GBT (n = 224) or GBT alone (n = 112). Mean age 64.7 years, 69.3% female; most had underlying bronchiectasis (62.5%), COPD (14.3%) or both (11.9%). ALIS was given once daily from single-use vials delivering 590 mg amikacin to the nebuliser. Primary endpoint: culture conversion, defined as three consecutive monthly MAC-negative sputum cultures by month 6.
cards.result: Culture conversion was achieved by 65 of 224 patients (29.0%) with ALIS plus GBT and 10 of 112 (8.9%) with GBT alone (odds ratio 4.22, 95% confidence interval 2.08 to 8.57; p < 0.001); the hazard ratio for conversion was 3.90 (2.00 to 7.60). Respiratory adverse events (primarily dysphonia, cough and dyspnoea) were reported in 87.4% of patients receiving ALIS plus GBT and 50.0% receiving GBT alone; serious treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 20.2% and 17.9% respectively.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (patients knew whether they were inhaling the drug), though the endpoint — sputum culture — is a laboratory measurement resistant to expectation. The odds ratio of 4.22 is a relative measure: in absolute terms about 20 more conversions per 100 patients treated, meaning roughly five patients treated for one extra conversion, and 71% of the ALIS group had not converted by month 6. The abstract names the formulation and dose (590 mg liposomal suspension) but no manufacturer; the tested product is a specific manufactured liposomal preparation, and other nebulised amikacin preparations are not interchangeable with it.
cards.source: Griffith DE et al. Amikacin Liposome Inhalation Suspension for Treatment-Refractory Lung Disease Caused by Mycobacterium avium Complex (CONVERT). cards.headline: Griffith 2021 (follow-up report of the same CONVERT trial): conversions on ALIS were sustained and durable in 16.1% versus 0% — relapse 9.2% versus 30.0% among converters
cards.summary: Griffith 2021 (follow-up report of the same CONVERT trial): conversions on ALIS were sustained and durable in 16.1% versus 0% — relapse 9.2% versus 30.0% among converters
cards.type: Follow-up report of the CONVERT randomised trial (Griffith 2021) — a second report of the same trial as the card above, not an independent trial
cards.people: Pre-specified follow-up analysis of the CONVERT randomised trial (same population and randomisation as the 2018 report: ALIS plus guideline-based therapy, n = 224, versus guideline therapy alone, n = 112). Patients who achieved culture conversion by month 6 continued therapy for 12 months after conversion and were then observed off treatment; sustainability meant negative cultures throughout those 12 months, durability meant still negative 3 months after stopping.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat population, conversion that was both sustained and durable was achieved by 16.1% (36 of 224) on ALIS plus GBT versus 0% (0 of 112) on GBT alone (p < .0001). Among patients who had converted by month 6, 55.4% (36 of 65) in the ALIS arm versus none (0 of 10) in the GBT-alone arm achieved sustained and durable conversion (p = .0017). Relapse through 3 months after treatment was 9.2% (6 of 65) in the ALIS arm and 30.0% (3 of 10) in the GBT-alone arm. Common adverse events with ALIS (dysphonia, cough, dyspnoea, haemoptysis) occurred mainly within the first 8 months; no new safety signals emerged with 12 months of post-conversion treatment.
cards.watchOut: This is the same 336 patients as the CONVERT primary report, carded separately only because it answers the durability question the first report could not; it must never be counted as independent confirmation. The GBT-alone converter group it compares against is just 10 patients, so the 0% durable-conversion figure and the 30% relapse rate rest on very small denominators.
cards.source: Griffith DE et al. Amikacin Liposome Inhalation Suspension for Refractory Mycobacterium avium Complex Lung Disease: Sustainability and Durability of Culture Conversion and Safety of Long-term Exposure. Chest. 2021. PMID: 33887244. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02344004 (the same CONVERT trial as the 2018 report). cards.headline: Synthesis: ALIS triples conversion in refractory MAC and the conversions tend to last — at the cost of respiratory side effects in most patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: ALIS triples conversion in refractory MAC and the conversions tend to last — at the cost of respiratory side effects in most patients
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One randomised trial (CONVERT, n = 336) and its pre-specified durability follow-up, in adults with MAC lung disease still culture-positive after at least 6 months of guideline-based therapy.
cards.result: Culture conversion by month 6: 29.0% versus 8.9% (absolute difference about 20 percentage points; odds ratio 4.22, 2.08–8.57). Sustained and durable conversion: 16.1% versus 0% intention-to-treat. Respiratory adverse events: 87.4% versus 50.0%; serious adverse events similar (20.2% versus 17.9%). The benefit is genuine and the ceiling is plain: most refractory patients still do not convert, so ALIS is an addition to — not a replacement for — guideline-based multidrug therapy and specialist management.
cards.watchOut: A single-trial shelf (Tier C): no independent replication exists, the trial was open-label and manufacturer-sponsored in design, and the population was specifically amikacin-susceptible, treatment-refractory disease. Nothing here speaks to ALIS as initial therapy, in amikacin-resistant isolates, or in Mycobacterium abscessus disease.
cards.source: Synthesis of Griffith DE et al. American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine. 2018 (PMID: 30216086); Griffith DE et al. Chest. 2021 (PMID: 33887244) — two reports of the single CONVERT trial (NCT02344004).

shelves.title: Nintedanib for progressive fibrosing lung disease beyond IPF: decline slowed from 188 to 81 ml a year — a real surrogate win, bought with diarrhoea in two of three patients
shelves.question: In adults with progressive fibrosing interstitial lung diseases other than idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does nintedanib slow the annual decline in forced vital capacity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis/drug therapy, physiopathology · Indoles/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Vital Capacity/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — INBUILD is a well-run phase 3 trial with a clear result on its chosen outcome, and the outcome is a surrogate. Flaherty KR et al. (PMID: 31566307) randomised 663 patients with progressive fibrosing interstitial lung diseases other than IPF — fibrosing disease over more than 10% of lung volume, progression within 24 months despite treatment — to nintedanib 150 mg twice daily or placebo: over 52 weeks the adjusted annual FVC decline was −80.8 ml/year on nintedanib versus −187.8 ml/year on placebo, a difference of 107.0 ml/year (95% CI 65.4 to 148.5; P < 0.001), and in the UIP-like pattern subgroup the difference was 128.2 ml/year (95% CI 70.8 to 185.6). The cost is gastrointestinal: diarrhoea in 66.9% versus 23.9%, and more liver-function-test abnormalities. What the trial does not show is equally important: no mortality, exacerbation or quality-of-life benefit is reported in the record — the claim is slower loss of lung volume, extrapolated from the IPF experience where the same drug class earned its place on the same endpoint. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): nintedanib probably slows FVC decline across the progressive fibrosing phenotype, with diarrhoea in two of three patients as the standing price. Nintedanib in IPF itself is at shelf #810 and in systemic-sclerosis ILD at shelf #688; this shelf is the cross-diagnosis phenotype question.

cards.headline: INBUILD (Flaherty 2019): nintedanib slowed annual FVC decline by 107 ml/year versus placebo across progressive fibrosing ILDs — with diarrhoea in 66.9% versus 23.9%
cards.summary: INBUILD (Flaherty 2019): nintedanib slowed annual FVC decline by 107 ml/year versus placebo across progressive fibrosing ILDs — with diarrhoea in 66.9% versus 23.9%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, INBUILD (Flaherty 2019)
cards.people: 663 patients in 15 countries with fibrosing interstitial lung disease (other than IPF) affecting more than 10% of lung volume on high-resolution CT, who met criteria for ILD progression in the previous 24 months despite treatment, with FVC at least 45% predicted and diffusing capacity 30 to <80% predicted; randomised double-blind to nintedanib 150 mg twice daily or placebo, stratified by UIP-like versus other fibrotic pattern.
cards.result: In the overall population the adjusted annual rate of FVC decline over 52 weeks was −80.8 ml/year with nintedanib versus −187.8 ml/year with placebo — a between-group difference of 107.0 ml/year (95% CI 65.4 to 148.5; P < 0.001), i.e. decline slowed by more than half in relative terms (from 187.8 to 80.8 ml/year). In patients with a UIP-like fibrotic pattern, decline was −82.9 versus −211.1 ml/year, a difference of 128.2 ml/year (95% CI 70.8 to 185.6; P < 0.001). Diarrhoea was reported in 66.9% on nintedanib versus 23.9% on placebo, and liver-function-test abnormalities were more common with nintedanib.
cards.watchOut: FVC decline is a surrogate: the record reports no mortality, hospitalisation or quality-of-life outcome, and 52 weeks is short for diseases measured in years. The trial pools many different ILD diagnoses under one 'progressive fibrosing' banner — the average effect may not describe any single diagnosis well — and entry required documented recent progression, so the result does not extend to stable fibrotic ILD. Two-thirds of patients getting diarrhoea is not a footnote; it drives dose reductions and discontinuation in practice.
cards.source: Flaherty KR et al. Nintedanib in Progressive Fibrosing Interstitial Lung Diseases. New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31566307. Registry ID: NCT02999178. cards.headline: Synthesis: one definitive trial for the lung-function endpoint, silence on the outcomes patients feel — nintedanib slows the slope of decline in progressive fibrosing ILD
cards.summary: Synthesis: one definitive trial for the lung-function endpoint, silence on the outcomes patients feel — nintedanib slows the slope of decline in progressive fibrosing ILD
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One phase 3 randomised trial, 663 patients, 52 weeks (INBUILD, Flaherty 2019) — the entire randomised record for nintedanib in the cross-diagnosis progressive fibrosing phenotype.
cards.result: Annual FVC decline: −80.8 versus −187.8 ml/year (difference 107.0 ml/year, 95% CI 65.4 to 148.5) overall; −82.9 versus −211.1 ml/year (difference 128.2 ml/year) in the UIP-like subgroup. Harm: diarrhoea 66.9% versus 23.9%; more liver-test abnormalities. Mortality, exacerbations, quality of life: not reported in the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: A single-trial shelf: the stamp reflects a precise, clinically plausible surrogate effect in a well-conducted trial, discounted for the absence of patient-centred outcomes and for phenotype pooling. Whether 107 ml/year of preserved FVC converts into longer or better life is inferred from the IPF programme, not demonstrated here. Tier C is set because there is one trial and one outcome family.

shelves.title: Inhaled antibiotics for bronchiectasis: one RESPIRE trial positive, its twin negative, a pooled 19% relative cut in exacerbations — and resistance emerging at twice the rate
shelves.question: In adults with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis and frequent exacerbations, do inhaled antibiotics (ciprofloxacin dry-powder; inhaled colistin in chronic Pseudomonas infection) reduce exacerbations versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Bronchiectasis/drug therapy · Ciprofloxacin/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule* · Dry Powder Inhalers* · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Powders* · Proportional Hazards Models · Pseudomonas Infections/drug therapy · Pseudomonas aeruginosa/drug effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the pooled record says a small real effect; the individual phase 3 record says it is fragile. The largest meta-analysis (Laska IF et al., PMID: 31405826; 16 trials, 2,597 patients) found inhaled antibiotics reduced exacerbation frequency (rate ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.97 — a 19% relative reduction), prolonged time to first exacerbation (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.99), cut severe exacerbations (rate ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.78), and increased bacterial eradication (OR 3.36, 95% CI 1.63 to 6.91), without improving quality of life beyond the minimal important difference and with emergent bacterial resistance nearly doubled (risk ratio 1.91, 95% CI 1.46 to 2.49). The two RESPIRE trials of ciprofloxacin dry powder show why the pooled effect is modest: RESPIRE 1 (PMID: 29371383) met its endpoints on the 14-day on/off regimen (HR 0.53 for time to first exacerbation; 39% relative reduction in exacerbation frequency, from 1.0 to 0.6 mean exacerbations) but not the 28-day regimen, while RESPIRE 2 (PMID: 29371384) missed both primary endpoints. The colistin trial (Haworth CS et al., PMID: 24625200) likewise missed its primary endpoint overall (median time to exacerbation 165 versus 111 days; P = 0.11), reaching significance only in adherent patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): inhaled antibiotics probably reduce exacerbations modestly in frequently exacerbating bronchiectasis, with resistance emergence as the standing long-term concern. Macrolides for bronchiectasis are at shelf #815 and brensocatib at #818.

cards.headline: RESPIRE 1 (De Soyza 2018): ciprofloxacin dry powder on a 14-day on/off cycle prolonged time to first exacerbation (HR 0.53) and cut exacerbation frequency by 39% relative — the 28-day cycle did not
cards.summary: RESPIRE 1 (De Soyza 2018): ciprofloxacin dry powder on a 14-day on/off cycle prolonged time to first exacerbation (HR 0.53) and cut exacerbation frequency by 39% relative — the 28-day cycle did not
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, RESPIRE 1 (De Soyza 2018)
cards.people: 416 patients with non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis, at least two exacerbations in the previous year and pre-defined bacteria in sputum, randomised 2:1 to twice-daily ciprofloxacin dry-powder inhalation 32.5 mg or placebo in 14-day on/off cycles (137 active, 68 placebo) or 28-day on/off cycles (141 active, 70 placebo) for 48 weeks.
cards.result: The 14-day on/off regimen significantly prolonged time to first exacerbation versus pooled placebo (median >336 versus 186 days; HR 0.53, 97.5% CI 0.36 to 0.80; P = 0.0005) and reduced exacerbation frequency versus matching placebo by 39% in relative terms (mean exacerbations 0.6 versus 1.0; incidence rate ratio 0.61, 97.5% CI 0.40 to 0.91; P = 0.0061). Outcomes for the 28-day on/off regimen were not statistically significantly different from placebo. The safety profile was favourable.
cards.watchOut: A split result inside one trial: one of two regimens positive on both endpoints, the other null — exactly the pattern multiple comparisons produce, and the reason the near-identical RESPIRE 2 (next card) matters so much. Patients were selected for frequent exacerbations and culturable target bacteria; the result does not describe bronchiectasis generally.
cards.source: De Soyza A et al. RESPIRE 1: a phase III placebo-controlled randomised trial of ciprofloxacin dry powder for inhalation in non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis. cards.headline: RESPIRE 2 (Aksamit 2018): the twin trial missed both primary endpoints — trends favoured ciprofloxacin dry powder (HR 0.87 and 0.71) but neither regimen reached significance
cards.summary: RESPIRE 2 (Aksamit 2018): the twin trial missed both primary endpoints — trends favoured ciprofloxacin dry powder (HR 0.87 and 0.71) but neither regimen reached significance
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, RESPIRE 2 (Aksamit 2018)
cards.people: 521 patients with non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis, at least two exacerbations in the previous year and pre-defined sputum bacteria, randomised 2:1 to ciprofloxacin dry-powder inhalation (14-day on/off n = 176; 28-day on/off n = 171) or placebo (n = 88 and n = 86) for 48 weeks; enrolling countries and the alpha split differed from RESPIRE 1, and the exacerbation rate was low across all arms (mean 0.6 ± 0.9).
cards.result: Neither primary endpoint was met. Time to first exacerbation: HR 0.87 (95.1% CI 0.62 to 1.21; P = 0.3965) for the 14-day regimen and HR 0.71 (99.9% CI 0.39 to 1.27; P = 0.0511) for the 28-day regimen. Exacerbation frequency: incidence rate ratio 0.83 (95.1% CI 0.59 to 1.17; P = 0.2862) and 0.55 (99.9% CI 0.30 to 1.02; P = 0.0014 against a split alpha) respectively — reported by the authors as trends that did not achieve statistical significance on the primary endpoints. Ciprofloxacin dry powder was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Two near-identical phase 3 trials, one positive and one null, is the definition of an unstable evidence base — low event rates in RESPIRE 2 (mean 0.6 exacerbations) shrank its power, but that is an explanation, not a rescue. Any honest summary of inhaled ciprofloxacin in bronchiectasis has to carry both trials, which is why this shelf's stamp is POSSIBLE and not LIKELY.

cards.headline: Laska 2019 meta-analysis: pooling 16 trials (2,597 patients), inhaled antibiotics cut exacerbation frequency (rate ratio 0.81) and severe exacerbations (0.43) — but doubled emergent resistance (RR 1.91) and did not meaningfully improve quality of life
cards.summary: Laska 2019 meta-analysis: pooling 16 trials (2,597 patients), inhaled antibiotics cut exacerbation frequency (rate ratio 0.81) and severe exacerbations (0.43) — but doubled emergent resistance (RR 1.91) and did not meaningfully improve quality of life
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 16 RCTs (Laska 2019)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (2,597 patients) of inhaled antibiotics given for at least four weeks to adults with stable non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis and chronic respiratory tract infection, including the ciprofloxacin dry-powder and inhaled colistin programmes.
cards.result: Inhaled antibiotics reduced sputum bacterial load (mean reduction −2.32 log units, 95% CI −3.20 to −1.45) and increased bacterial eradication (OR 3.36, 95% CI 1.63 to 6.91). Exacerbation frequency fell (rate ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.97 — a 19% relative reduction), time to first exacerbation lengthened (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.99), the proportion with at least one exacerbation fell (risk ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.97), and severe exacerbations fell most (rate ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.78). Neither quality-of-life instrument improved beyond its minimal clinically important difference, and FEV1 change was a non-significant −0.87% predicted. Treatment-emergent adverse effects (OR 0.97) and bronchospasm (OR 0.99) did not differ, but emergence of bacterial resistance was significantly more frequent by the end of treatment (risk ratio 1.91, 95% CI 1.46 to 2.49).
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate averages different drugs (ciprofloxacin, colistin, aminoglycosides, aztreonam), devices and regimens whose individual trials are inconsistent — RESPIRE 2 and the colistin trial (Haworth 2014, PMID: 24625200; primary endpoint missed overall, P = 0.11, significant only in adherent patients) sit inside this average. The resistance signal (RR 1.91) is measured at treatment end; what it means for a patient's future exacerbations over years of cycling therapy is the open question the trials cannot answer.
cards.source: Laska IF et al. The efficacy and safety of inhaled antibiotics for the treatment of bronchiectasis in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The Lancet Respiratory Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31405826. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a modest pooled reduction in exacerbations, built from inconsistent trials — inhaled antibiotics help some frequently exacerbating patients, and breed resistance while doing it
cards.summary: Synthesis: a modest pooled reduction in exacerbations, built from inconsistent trials — inhaled antibiotics help some frequently exacerbating patients, and breed resistance while doing it
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two phase 3 ciprofloxacin dry-powder trials (416 and 521 patients), a 144-patient inhaled colistin trial in chronic Pseudomonas infection, and a 16-trial meta-analysis (2,597 patients).
cards.result: Pooled: exacerbation rate ratio 0.81 (95% CI 0.67 to 0.97), severe exacerbation rate ratio 0.43, eradication OR 3.36, resistance emergence RR 1.91 (Laska). Individually: RESPIRE 1 positive on one of two regimens (HR 0.53; frequency ratio 0.61); RESPIRE 2 null on both primary endpoints; colistin's primary endpoint missed overall (165 versus 111 days; P = 0.11) and met only in adherent patients (P = 0.038). Quality of life: no clinically important improvement in the pooled analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The fair clinical reading is narrower than the pooled headline: patients with frequent exacerbations and chronic Pseudomonas or other target organisms, who actually adhere to a demanding inhaled regimen, are the ones the positive results describe. Everyone else is extrapolation. Long-term resistance consequences remain genuinely unknown, and that unknown should be part of any shared decision about years of inhaled therapy.

shelves.title: Dornase alfa in non-CF bronchiectasis: the CF mucolytic that backfired — more exacerbations and faster FEV1 decline than placebo in the only trial
shelves.question: In adults with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, does aerosolised recombinant human DNase (dornase alfa) improve lung function or reduce exacerbations — or cause harm?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Aerosols · Bronchiectasis/drug therapy · Deoxyribonuclease I/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Expectorants/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Recombinant Proteins/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Spirometry · Time Factors · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — a cautionary shelf about borrowing a drug across diseases. Dornase alfa is established therapy in cystic fibrosis, but the one randomised trial in non-CF bronchiectasis (O'Donnell AE et al., PMID: 9596315; 349 stable adult outpatients with idiopathic bronchiectasis, aerosolised recombinant human DNase I twice daily versus placebo for 24 weeks) found the treatment worse on both primary endpoints: pulmonary exacerbations were more frequent and FEV1 decline was greater in the rhDNase group than on placebo, leading the investigators to conclude the drug was 'ineffective and potentially harmful' in this population. The record reports the direction of both effects without publishing the magnitudes in its abstract, so this shelf can state the harm direction but not size it — a real limitation, though for a harm verdict the direction plus a stopped-in-practice intervention is what matters. No later trial has rehabilitated the drug in non-CF bronchiectasis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): aerosolised DNase should not be used for non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis; its cystic fibrosis benefit does not transfer, and the one direct test pointed the other way.

cards.headline: O'Donnell 1998: in non-CF bronchiectasis, aerosolised rhDNase made both primary endpoints worse — exacerbations more frequent and FEV1 decline greater than placebo over 24 weeks
cards.summary: O'Donnell 1998: in non-CF bronchiectasis, aerosolised rhDNase made both primary endpoints worse — exacerbations more frequent and FEV1 decline greater than placebo over 24 weeks
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (O'Donnell 1998)
cards.people: 349 adult outpatients in stable condition with idiopathic bronchiectasis at 23 centres in North America, Great Britain and Ireland, randomised double-blind to aerosolised recombinant human DNase I or placebo twice daily for 24 weeks; primary endpoints were incidence of pulmonary exacerbations and mean percent change in FEV1 from baseline.
cards.result: Pulmonary exacerbations were more frequent and FEV1 decline was greater in patients who received rhDNase compared with placebo during the 24-week trial. The investigators conclude that rhDNase was ineffective and potentially harmful in adult outpatients in stable condition with idiopathic bronchiectasis, explicitly contrasting the result with the previously published efficacy of rhDNase in cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis. The record's abstract reports the direction of both primary-endpoint effects without numerical magnitudes.
cards.watchOut: The abstract gives no effect sizes, event counts or confidence intervals, so the size of the harm cannot be stated from the record — only its direction on both prespecified endpoints. The population was idiopathic bronchiectasis specifically (post-infective and other causes under-represented), and the trial predates modern bronchiectasis phenotyping; even so, it remains the only randomised test of the question and no subsequent evidence contradicts it.
cards.source: O'Donnell AE et al. Treatment of idiopathic bronchiectasis with aerosolized recombinant human DNase I. rhDNase Study Group. Chest. 1998. PMID: 9596315. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the cystic fibrosis success story does not cross over — the single direct trial in non-CF bronchiectasis found DNase ineffective and potentially harmful
cards.summary: Synthesis: the cystic fibrosis success story does not cross over — the single direct trial in non-CF bronchiectasis found DNase ineffective and potentially harmful
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One double-blind randomised trial, 349 patients, 24 weeks (O'Donnell 1998) — the entire randomised record for aerosolised DNase in non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis.
cards.result: Exacerbations: more frequent on rhDNase than placebo. FEV1: greater decline on rhDNase than placebo. Magnitudes: not reported in the record's abstract. Investigator conclusion: ineffective and potentially harmful. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm).
cards.watchOut: The stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because the harm is unquantified in the record and rests on one 1998 trial. But the practical asymmetry matters: there is no efficacy signal to weigh against the harm — both endpoints moved the wrong way — so the burden of proof now sits permanently on anyone proposing DNase outside cystic fibrosis. Tier C is set for the single-trial, unquantified base.

shelves.title: Inhaled mannitol for bronchiectasis: safe, plausible, and twice short of its primary endpoint — exacerbations not reduced, quality of life not clearly better
shelves.question: In adults with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, does inhaled dry-powder mannitol improve quality of life and reduce exacerbations versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bronchiectasis/diagnostic imaging, drug therapy, metabolism · Diuretics, Osmotic/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Dry Powder Inhalers* · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Humans · Lung/diagnostic imaging, metabolism · Male · Mannitol/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Respiratory Function Tests · Sputum/metabolism · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two trials of inhaled mannitol in non-CF bronchiectasis, and the endpoints that matter most did not move in either. In the 12-week phase 3 trial (Bilton D et al., PMID: 23429964; 343 patients), the primary quality-of-life endpoint was null — St George's Respiratory Questionnaire total score −3.4 points on mannitol versus −2.1 on placebo (P = 0.304) — and the significant sputum-weight difference (4.3 g; P = 0.002) was driven largely by a fall in the placebo group's sputum weight alongside its higher antibiotic use (45% versus 37%). In the 52-week trial (Bilton D et al., PMID: 25246664; 461 patients, against a low-dose mannitol control rather than true placebo), the exacerbation rate was not significantly reduced (rate ratio 0.92; P = 0.31), though time to first exacerbation lengthened (HR 0.78; P = 0.022) and SGRQ improved by −2.4 units (P = 0.046) — a difference below the instrument's usual clinically important threshold. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): mannitol is safe and may delay a first exacerbation, but neither trial showed it reduces exacerbation rates or delivers a clearly felt quality-of-life benefit. Airway clearance techniques for bronchiectasis are at shelf #2668.

cards.headline: Bilton 2013: over 12 weeks, inhaled mannitol did not improve quality of life versus placebo (SGRQ −3.4 vs −2.1 points; P = 0.304) — its one positive endpoint was confounded by antibiotic use
cards.summary: Bilton 2013: over 12 weeks, inhaled mannitol did not improve quality of life versus placebo (SGRQ −3.4 vs −2.1 points; P = 0.304) — its one positive endpoint was confounded by antibiotic use
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Bilton 2013)
cards.people: 343 patients aged 15–80 with high-resolution-CT-confirmed non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, FEV1 at least 50% predicted and at least 1 litre, who passed a negative mannitol provocation test, randomised double-blind to inhaled dry-powder mannitol 320 mg twice daily (n = 231) or placebo (n = 112) for 12 weeks; an open-label extension followed a subset for 52 weeks for safety.
cards.result: The primary quality-of-life endpoint did not differ: SGRQ total score changed by −3.4 points (95% CI −4.81 to −1.94) on mannitol versus −2.1 points (95% CI −4.12 to −0.09) on placebo (P = 0.304). The other primary endpoint, 24-hour sputum weight, differed by 4.3 g in mannitol's favour (95% CI 1.64 to 7.00; P = 0.002), but this was largely driven by a decrease in sputum weight in the placebo group, which in turn used more antibiotics (50 of 112, 45%) than the mannitol group (85 of 231, 37%). A subgroup (n = 82) showed less small-airway mucus plugging on CT at 12 weeks with mannitol (P = 0.048). Compliance was high and adverse events were similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: Patients who bronchoconstrict on a mannitol challenge were screened out before randomisation, so the tolerability picture applies to a pre-selected group. Twelve weeks is short for an exacerbation question — this trial was powered on symptoms and sputum — and its sputum-weight 'win' illustrates why surrogate endpoints mislead: the difference arose from the placebo arm's behaviour (more antibiotics, less sputum), not from mannitol clearing more mucus.
cards.source: Bilton D et al. Phase 3 randomized study of the efficacy and safety of inhaled dry powder mannitol for the symptomatic treatment of non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis. Chest. 2013. cards.headline: Bilton 2014: over 52 weeks, mannitol did not reduce the exacerbation rate (rate ratio 0.92; P = 0.31), though time to first exacerbation lengthened (HR 0.78) and SGRQ improved by 2.4 units
cards.summary: Bilton 2014: over 52 weeks, mannitol did not reduce the exacerbation rate (rate ratio 0.92; P = 0.31), though time to first exacerbation lengthened (HR 0.78) and SGRQ improved by 2.4 units
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Bilton 2014)
cards.people: 461 patients aged 18–85 with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, chronic excess sputum production and at least two pulmonary exacerbations in the previous 12 months, with FEV1 40–85% predicted and baseline SGRQ at least 30, randomised to inhaled mannitol 400 mg twice daily (n = 233) or low-dose mannitol control (n = 228) for 52 weeks.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was not met: the exacerbation rate was not significantly reduced on mannitol (rate ratio 0.92; P = 0.31). Time to first exacerbation was significantly longer on mannitol (HR 0.78; P = 0.022), and SGRQ score improved by −2.4 units versus control (P = 0.046). Adverse events were similar between groups, and the authors conclude mannitol was safe and well tolerated over 12 months.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was low-dose mannitol, not an inert placebo — if low-dose mannitol has any activity of its own, the trial underestimates the drug-versus-nothing effect; if it has none, the near-null rate ratio stands as the answer. Secondary endpoints (time to first exacerbation, SGRQ) turning positive when the primary rate endpoint fails is a familiar pattern that deserves a discount, and a 2.4-unit SGRQ difference is below the 4-unit change patients are generally taken to notice.
cards.source: Bilton D et al. Inhaled mannitol for non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis: a randomised, controlled trial. Thorax. 2014. PMID: 25246664. Registry ID: NCT00669331. cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, two missed primary endpoints — mannitol in bronchiectasis is safe, may delay a first exacerbation, and has not shown it reduces exacerbations or meaningfully improves quality of life
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, two missed primary endpoints — mannitol in bronchiectasis is safe, may delay a first exacerbation, and has not shown it reduces exacerbations or meaningfully improves quality of life
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two randomised trials (343 patients over 12 weeks against placebo; 461 patients over 52 weeks against low-dose mannitol control), both in non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis.
cards.result: Exacerbation rate: not significantly reduced in the year-long trial (rate ratio 0.92; P = 0.31). Time to first exacerbation: HR 0.78 (P = 0.022) favouring mannitol. Quality of life (SGRQ): null at 12 weeks (−3.4 versus −2.1; P = 0.304); −2.4 units at 52 weeks (P = 0.046), below the usual clinically important difference. Safety: adverse events similar to control in both trials. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Mannitol's cystic fibrosis evidence is a different population and does not rescue this shelf. What would change the verdict is a trial powered on exacerbations against a true placebo in an exacerbation-prone population; until then the honest summary is 'unproven, probably harmless'. Tier C is set because both trials missed their primary endpoints and the positive signals are secondary and small.

shelves.title: Breathing exercises for asthma: quality of life up a little, hyperventilation symptoms down — asthma control itself unmoved in 22 trials
shelves.question: In adults with asthma, do breathing exercises (including physiotherapist-led and Buteyko-style programmes) improve quality of life and asthma control versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Asthma/physiopathology, rehabilitation · Breathing Exercises/methods · Disease Progression · Health Education · Humans · Hyperventilation · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Respiratory Function Tests · Yoga*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but narrow benefit, on how patients feel rather than on the disease measures clinicians usually chase. The Cochrane review (Santino TA et al., PMID: 32212422; 22 studies, 2,880 participants with mostly mild-to-moderate asthma) found breathing exercises improved quality of life at three months versus inactive control (Asthma Quality of Life Questionnaire mean difference 0.42, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.68; moderate-certainty evidence) and reduced hyperventilation symptoms at four to six months (Nijmegen Questionnaire mean difference −3.22, 95% CI −6.31 to −0.13; moderate certainty), with FEV1 percent predicted higher (mean difference 6.88%, 95% CI 5.03 to 8.73) but absolute FEV1 inconclusive. Against that: asthma control scores were inconclusive at three months and essentially null at six months (ACQ mean difference −0.08, 95% CI −0.22 to 0.07), the AQLQ gain of 0.42 sits just below the 0.5-point change usually taken as the smallest patients notice, and certainty across outcomes ranged from moderate to very low with poor methods reporting in many trials — fourteen of the 22 studies were yoga trials, so 'breathing exercises' here is a bundle of unlike interventions. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): breathing retraining probably improves quality of life and breathlessness-pattern symptoms modestly as an adjunct; it is not a treatment for asthma control and must never displace inhaled therapy.

cards.headline: Santino 2020 (Cochrane): breathing exercises improved asthma quality of life at three months (AQLQ +0.42, moderate certainty) across 22 trials — but asthma control scores did not improve
cards.summary: Santino 2020 (Cochrane): breathing exercises improved asthma quality of life at three months (AQLQ +0.42, moderate certainty) across 22 trials — but asthma control scores did not improve
cards.type: Systematic review, 22 RCTs (Santino 2020, Cochrane)
cards.people: 22 randomised trials (2,880 participants) of breathing exercises in adults with asthma of mild-to-moderate severity, all outpatients: 14 trials of yoga, 4 of breathing retraining, and single trials or pairs of the Buteyko method, Buteyko plus pranayama, the Papworth method and deep diaphragmatic breathing; 20 trials compared against inactive control and 2 against asthma education. Searches ran to April 2019.
cards.result: Versus inactive control, quality of life (AQLQ) improved at three months (mean difference 0.42, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.68; 4 studies, 974 participants; moderate-certainty evidence); at six months the odds of at least a 0.5-unit AQLQ improvement were OR 1.34 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.86; 1 study, 655 participants). Hyperventilation symptoms (Nijmegen Questionnaire) were fewer at four to six months (mean difference −3.22, 95% CI −6.31 to −0.13; 2 studies, 118 participants; moderate certainty) but not at six months in a separate analysis (mean difference 0.63, 95% CI −0.90 to 2.17). Asthma symptoms (ACQ) were inconclusive up to three months (mean difference −0.15, 95% CI −2.32 to 2.02; low certainty) and null over six months (mean difference −0.08, 95% CI −0.22 to 0.07; 1 study, 449 participants). FEV1 in litres was inconclusive (mean difference −0.10 L, 95% CI −0.32 to 0.12; very low certainty), while FEV1 percent predicted favoured breathing exercises (mean difference 6.88%, 95% CI 5.03 to 8.73; 5 studies, 618 participants). Versus asthma education, quality of life favoured breathing exercises only at four to six months (mean difference 0.38, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.68; 1 study, 183 participants). The reviewers conclude breathing exercises may have some positive effects on quality of life, hyperventilation symptoms and lung function, with evidence certainty from moderate to very low.
cards.watchOut: Blinding a breathing intervention is near-impossible, so subjective outcomes (quality of life, symptom scores) are exactly where expectation bias lands — and those are the outcomes that improved, while the blinded-resistant outcome (asthma control) did not. The intervention label bundles yoga, Buteyko, Papworth and diaphragmatic breathing as if they were one treatment; adverse effects were not even an outcome in the review; and risk-of-bias assessment was hampered by incomplete reporting in most trials.

cards.headline: Synthesis: breathing exercises earn a place as an adjunct for quality of life and dysfunctional breathing symptoms — not as asthma treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: breathing exercises earn a place as an adjunct for quality of life and dysfunctional breathing symptoms — not as asthma treatment
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: 22 randomised trials, 2,880 adults with mostly mild-to-moderate asthma (Cochrane, Santino 2020) — the entire comparative record for breathing exercises in asthma.
cards.result: Quality of life: AQLQ mean difference +0.42 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.68) at three months, moderate certainty — just under the 0.5 minimal important difference. Hyperventilation symptoms: −3.22 points at four to six months, moderate certainty. Asthma control (ACQ): −0.08 (95% CI −0.22 to 0.07) at six months — no effect. Lung function: FEV1 percent predicted +6.88%, absolute FEV1 inconclusive. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The danger with this shelf is substitution, not the exercises themselves: patients who feel better on breathing retraining sometimes quietly stop their inhaled corticosteroids, and nothing in this record says the underlying airway inflammation is touched. The benefit is also an average across unlike techniques — a physiotherapist-led retraining programme and a yoga class are not interchangeable prescriptions, and the review cannot say which component, if any, carries the effect.
cards.source: Synthesis of Santino TA et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020 (PMID: 32212422).
