shelves.title: Montelukast for exercise-induced bronchoconstriction: the post-exercise lung-function fall cut nearly in half for a full 12 weeks — in one launch-era trial of mild asthma
shelves.question: In patients with exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, does daily montelukast attenuate the fall in FEV1 after exercise versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acetates/pharmacology, therapeutic use · Adolescent · Adrenergic beta-Agonists/therapeutic use · Adult · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/pharmacology, therapeutic use · Asthma, Exercise-Induced/drug therapy, physiopathology · Bronchial Provocation Tests · Bronchoconstriction/drug effects · Cyclopropanes · Double-Blind Method · Exercise · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume/drug effects · Humans · Leukotriene Antagonists* · Male · Methacholine Chloride · Middle Aged · Quinolines/pharmacology, therapeutic use · Sulfides
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-designed trial, a physiological endpoint, and a clear result. Leff JA et al. (PMID: 9664090) randomised 110 patients aged 15–45 with mild asthma and documented exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (FEV1 fall of at least 20% after exercise on two run-in occasions) to montelukast 10 mg at bedtime or placebo for 12 weeks: montelukast inhibited the post-exercise FEV1 area-under-the-curve endpoint by 47.4% relative to placebo (P = 0.002) — the protection was present at weeks 4, 8 and 12 with no sign of tolerance, the maximal post-exercise FEV1 fall was significantly smaller (P = 0.003), recovery to within 5% of pre-exercise values was faster (P = 0.04), and there was no rebound worsening during the two-week washout. Adverse event rates were similar. The discounts: the endpoint is a laboratory exercise challenge, not exacerbations or symptoms in daily life (though patients on montelukast did rate their asthma control better and used less rescue beta-agonist around challenges); the population had mild asthma; and a single 110-patient trial from the drug's launch era is the whole direct record for this exact question. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): daily montelukast probably attenuates exercise-induced bronchoconstriction substantially in mild asthma. Montelukast's other shelves — preschool viral wheeze #1426 and allergic rhinitis #2666 — are different questions, and its neuropsychiatric boxed warning belongs in any real prescribing conversation even though it postdates this trial.

cards.headline: Leff 1998: daily montelukast inhibited the post-exercise FEV1 fall by 47.4% versus placebo over 12 weeks in mild asthma with exercise-induced bronchoconstriction — no tolerance, no rebound
cards.summary: Leff 1998: daily montelukast inhibited the post-exercise FEV1 fall by 47.4% versus placebo over 12 weeks in mild asthma with exercise-induced bronchoconstriction — no tolerance, no rebound
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Leff 1998)
cards.people: 110 patients aged 15–45 with mild asthma and a fall in FEV1 of at least 20% after exercise on two occasions during a placebo run-in, randomised double-blind to montelukast 10 mg once daily at bedtime (n = 54) or placebo (n = 56) for 12 weeks, followed by a two-week single-blind placebo washout; exercise challenges were performed 20–24 hours after dosing at weeks 4, 8 and 12 and after washout.
cards.result: At 12 weeks montelukast gave significantly greater protection than placebo on the primary endpoint — the area under the FEV1 curve (percent change from baseline) in the first 60 minutes after exercise — expressed as 47.4% inhibition of the endpoint (P = 0.002). The maximal decrease in FEV1 after exercise was significantly smaller (P = 0.003) and the time to return to within 5% of pre-exercise lung function was significantly shorter (P = 0.04) with montelukast. Between-group differences were similar at weeks 4, 8 and 12, with no evidence of tolerance and no rebound worsening after washout. Patients on montelukast were more likely to rate their asthma control as better and less likely to need rescue beta-agonist during or after challenge; adverse event rates were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The headline 47.4% is a relative inhibition of a laboratory challenge endpoint, not a 47.4% reduction in real-world attacks — the trial reports no exacerbation or hospitalisation outcomes. Participants were selected for a reproducible large FEV1 fall, which enriches for responders to any protective therapy, and all had mild asthma; protection in moderate asthma or in pure exercise-induced bronchoconstriction without asthma is extrapolation. The trial also predates montelukast's boxed warning for serious neuropsychiatric events, which no reader in 1998 could weigh.

cards.headline: Synthesis: daily montelukast roughly halves the laboratory exercise response in mild asthma — a consistent, durable physiological effect from a single trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: daily montelukast roughly halves the laboratory exercise response in mild asthma — a consistent, durable physiological effect from a single trial
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One double-blind randomised trial, 110 patients aged 15–45, 12 weeks plus washout (Leff 1998) — the direct randomised record for montelukast in exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.
cards.result: Primary endpoint (post-exercise FEV1 area under the curve): 47.4% relative inhibition versus placebo (P = 0.002). Maximal FEV1 fall: significantly attenuated (P = 0.003). Recovery time: significantly faster (P = 0.04). Effect stable at 4, 8 and 12 weeks; no rebound on withdrawal; adverse events similar to placebo. Real-world exacerbation outcomes: not measured. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: A single-trial shelf on a surrogate challenge endpoint — the stamp credits the trial's internal consistency (three time points, three concordant measures, clean washout) and discounts for the absence of patient-centred outcomes and of any independent replication in this exact population. Tier C is set accordingly. The comparison that matters in clinic — daily montelukast versus pre-exercise inhaled beta-agonist or added inhaled corticosteroid — is not the comparison this trial made.

shelves.title: Erdosteine in COPD: fewer and shorter exacerbations overall — but read by severity, the benefit is mild events only and the serious ones did not budge
shelves.question: In adults with COPD and chronic bronchitis, does erdosteine reduce the rate and duration of exacerbations versus placebo on top of usual inhaled therapy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Monitoring/methods · Expectorants/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive*/diagnosis, drug therapy, physiopathology, psychology · Quality of Life* · Severity of Illness Index · Symptom Flare Up* · Thioglycolates*/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Thiophenes*/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with the benefit located precisely where it matters least. The RESTORE trial (Dal Negro RW et al., PMID: 29025888; 445 patients with GOLD stage II/III COPD on usual inhaled therapy) found erdosteine 300 mg twice daily for 12 months reduced the overall exacerbation rate by 19.4% in relative terms — 0.91 versus 1.13 exacerbations per patient-year (P = 0.01) — and shortened exacerbation duration by 24.6% in relative terms (9.55 versus 12.63 days; P = 0.023). But the rate reduction was driven entirely by mild events (0.23 versus 0.54 per patient-year; a 57.1% relative reduction; P = 0.002), while moderate and severe exacerbations — the ones that hospitalise and kill — were numerically more frequent on erdosteine (0.68 versus 0.59 per patient-year; P = 0.054), and neither quality of life (SGRQ) nor time to first exacerbation improved. The Cochrane mucolytic synthesis (Poole P et al., PMID: 31107966; 38 trials, 10,377 participants, erdosteine among the agents) supports a small class effect — mucolytic patients were more likely to stay exacerbation-free (Peto OR 1.73, 95% CI 1.56 to 1.91; number needed to treat 8 over about nine months) with 0.43 fewer disability days per month — while warning that recent trials show smaller effects than early ones and heterogeneity is high. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): erdosteine probably trims mild exacerbations and shortens episodes, with no demonstrated effect on the moderate-to-severe events that drive COPD outcomes. The N-acetylcysteine/carbocisteine mucolytic shelf is #2446; this is the erdosteine-specific question.

cards.headline: RESTORE (Dal Negro 2017): erdosteine cut the overall COPD exacerbation rate by 19.4% relative (0.91 vs 1.13/year) and duration by 24.6% — but the gain was all in mild events; moderate/severe exacerbations ran numerically higher (0.68 vs 0.59)
cards.summary: RESTORE (Dal Negro 2017): erdosteine cut the overall COPD exacerbation rate by 19.4% relative (0.91 vs 1.13/year) and duration by 24.6% — but the gain was all in mild events; moderate/severe exacerbations ran numerically higher (0.68 vs 0.59)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, RESTORE (Dal Negro 2017)
cards.people: 445 patients aged 40–80 with GOLD stage II/III COPD and chronic bronchitis (74% men; mean age 64.8 years; mean FEV1 51.8% predicted), randomised double-blind to erdosteine 300 mg twice daily or placebo added to usual COPD inhaled therapy for 12 months; results are the pre-specified intention-to-treat population.
cards.result: Erdosteine reduced the exacerbation rate by 19.4% in relative terms (0.91 versus 1.13 exacerbations per patient-year; P = 0.01). The effect was driven by mild exacerbations, whose rate fell by 57.1% in relative terms (0.23 versus 0.54 per patient-year; P = 0.002). Moderate and severe exacerbations did not fall — 0.68 versus 0.59 per patient-year, numerically favouring placebo (P = 0.054). Exacerbation duration fell by 24.6% in relative terms irrespective of severity (9.55 versus 12.63 days; P = 0.023). Subjective severity scores by patient (P = 0.022) and physician (P = 0.048) and reliever-medication use (P < 0.001) improved, but St George's Respiratory Questionnaire score and time to first exacerbation did not. Adverse event percentages were similar in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Read the primary result by severity before quoting it: a therapy that prevents mild, self-managed episodes while trending the wrong way on moderate/severe ones has a much smaller claim than its headline 19.4%. The moderate/severe difference is not significant, so harm is not shown either — but the burden of the trial is that the events patients fear most were untouched. Subjective severity scores improving while SGRQ does not is another internal inconsistency to weigh.
cards.source: Dal Negro RW et al. Effect of erdosteine on the rate and duration of COPD exacerbations: the RESTORE study. European Respiratory Journal. 2017. PMID: 29025888. Registry ID: NCT01032304 (also EudraCT 2008-008192-34). cards.headline: Poole 2019 (Cochrane): across 38 mucolytic trials (10,377 patients) the class modestly increased the chance of staying exacerbation-free (Peto OR 1.73; NNT 8) — with smaller effects in recent trials and high heterogeneity
cards.summary: Poole 2019 (Cochrane): across 38 mucolytic trials (10,377 patients) the class modestly increased the chance of staying exacerbation-free (Peto OR 1.73; NNT 8) — with smaller effects in recent trials and high heterogeneity
cards.type: Systematic review, 38 RCTs (Poole 2019, Cochrane)
cards.people: Cochrane review of 38 randomised trials (10,377 participants) of oral mucolytics — N-acetylcysteine, carbocisteine, erdosteine and ambroxol among them — versus placebo for at least two months in adults with chronic bronchitis or COPD, excluding asthma and cystic fibrosis; trial durations ran from two months to three years.
cards.result: Across 28 studies (6,723 participants), patients on mucolytics were more likely to be exacerbation-free during the study (Peto OR 1.73, 95% CI 1.56 to 1.91; moderate-certainty evidence), giving a number needed to treat of 8 (95% CI 7 to 10) over an average of nine months to keep one additional participant exacerbation-free; heterogeneity was high (I² = 62%). Disability days fell by 0.43 per participant per month (95% CI −0.56 to −0.30). Hospitalisation was reduced inconsistently (Peto OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.89; I² = 58%). Quality of life improved by a mean difference of −1.37 (95% CI −2.85 to 0.11), below the −4 minimal important difference and including no difference. Mortality was imprecise (Peto OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.87). The reviewers caution that more recent studies show less benefit than earlier ones, that the type or dose of mucolytic did not alter the effect size, and that selection or publication bias in early trials may inflate the class estimate.
cards.watchOut: This is a class-level card: erdosteine is one of several agents pooled, and the review found no basis to separate them — so it supports 'mucolytics do something small' rather than 'erdosteine specifically works'. The era effect the reviewers describe (early trials strongly positive, recent trials weaker) is the classic signature of a literature whose true effect is smaller than its average.
cards.source: Poole P et al. Mucolytic agents versus placebo for chronic bronchitis or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019. PMID: 31107966. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Vitamin D and COPD exacerbations: nothing for the average patient, a 45% relative rate cut for the profoundly deficient — the subgroup is the story
shelves.question: In adults with COPD, does vitamin D supplementation prevent moderate-to-severe exacerbations, particularly in those with baseline vitamin D deficiency?
shelves.mesh: Dietary Supplements* · Humans · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/blood, complications, prevention & control · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Vitamin D/analogs & derivatives, blood, therapeutic use · Vitamin D Deficiency/blood, drug therapy, etiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by baseline vitamin D level, and the split is the whole finding. The individual-participant-data meta-analysis (Jolliffe DA et al., PMID: 30630893) pooled the randomised trials of vitamin D for COPD exacerbation prevention (4 eligible trials, 560 participants; individual data for 469 of 472 participants in three trials) and found no overall effect on moderate/severe exacerbations (adjusted incidence rate ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.13). But the pre-specified subgroup analysis separated cleanly: in participants with baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 25 nmol/L, supplementation reduced the moderate/severe exacerbation rate (aIRR 0.55, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.84 — a 45% relative reduction), while in those at or above 25 nmol/L it did nothing (aIRR 1.04, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.27), with a significant interaction (P = 0.015). Serious adverse events did not differ (adjusted OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.75). PROPOSED SPLIT: vitamin D probably prevents COPD exacerbations only in patients with profound baseline deficiency (<25 nmol/L); supplementing the non-deficient is treating a number, not a risk. This is a different question from vitamin D for respiratory infection (shelf #4) and for asthma exacerbations (shelf #546).

cards.headline: Jolliffe 2019 (IPD meta-analysis): vitamin D did not prevent COPD exacerbations overall (aIRR 0.94) — but in patients with baseline 25(OH)D below 25 nmol/L the rate fell (aIRR 0.55), with a significant interaction (P = 0.015)
cards.summary: Jolliffe 2019 (IPD meta-analysis): vitamin D did not prevent COPD exacerbations overall (aIRR 0.94) — but in patients with baseline 25(OH)D below 25 nmol/L the rate fell (aIRR 0.55), with a significant interaction (P = 0.015)
cards.type: Individual-participant-data meta-analysis (Jolliffe 2019)
cards.people: Individual-participant-data meta-analysis of randomised trials of vitamin D supplementation in COPD reporting exacerbation incidence: 4 eligible trials (560 participants), with individual data obtained for 469 of 472 participants (99.4%) in three of them; analysis used fixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, GOLD spirometric grade and trial. Literature searched to October 2017.
cards.result: Overall, supplementation did not influence the rate of moderate/severe COPD exacerbations (adjusted incidence rate ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.13). In the pre-specified subgroup with baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 25 nmol/L, vitamin D reduced the moderate/severe exacerbation rate (aIRR 0.55, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.84 — a 45% relative reduction); in participants with baseline levels at or above 25 nmol/L there was no effect (aIRR 1.04, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.27). The test for interaction was significant (P = 0.015). Vitamin D did not influence the proportion experiencing at least one serious adverse event (adjusted OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.75).
cards.watchOut: Subgroup findings earn their keep only when pre-specified with a significant interaction — both hold here — but the deficient subgroup is still a subset of a 560-patient evidence base, so the 0.55 estimate carries real imprecision, and the threshold (25 nmol/L) marks profound deficiency, far below the levels most supplemented COPD patients have. The record reports relative rate ratios without the absolute exacerbation rates, so the absolute benefit in the deficient group cannot be sized from this record alone.
cards.source: Jolliffe DA et al. Vitamin D to prevent exacerbations of COPD: systematic review and meta-analysis of individual participant data from randomised controlled trials. Thorax. 2019. cards.summary: Synthesis: a null average concealing a deficient-only benefit — vitamin D for COPD exacerbations is a treat-the-deficiency intervention, not a general one
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Four randomised trials (560 participants; individual data for 469) pooled at participant level (Jolliffe 2019).
cards.result: All patients: aIRR 0.94 (95% CI 0.78 to 1.13) for moderate/severe exacerbations — no effect. Baseline 25(OH)D <25 nmol/L: aIRR 0.55 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.84). Baseline ≥25 nmol/L: aIRR 1.04 (95% CI 0.85 to 1.27). Interaction P = 0.015. Serious adverse events: adjusted OR 1.16 (95% CI 0.76 to 1.75). PROPOSED SPLIT — by baseline vitamin D status.
cards.watchOut: The practical consequence is a blood test before a prescription: without a baseline 25(OH)D below 25 nmol/L there is no evidence here for supplementing to prevent exacerbations (correcting deficiency for bone and general health is a separate matter, outside this question). The finding also needs a confirmatory trial randomised within the deficient stratum; until one exists, SPLIT with a pre-specified interaction is the honest grade, not proof.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jolliffe DA et al. Thorax. 2019 (PMID: 30630893).

shelves.title: Lung rehab by screen matches the rehab centre on walking distance — and far more people finish it (93% versus 70%)
shelves.question: In adults with chronic respiratory disease (mainly COPD), does telerehabilitation achieve exercise capacity and quality-of-life outcomes comparable to centre-based pulmonary rehabilitation?
shelves.mesh: Bias · Chronic Disease · Controlled Clinical Trials as Topic/statistics & numerical data · Dyspnea/rehabilitation · Exercise Tolerance/physiology · Humans · Internet/statistics & numerical data · Non-Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic/statistics & numerical data · Patient Compliance/statistics & numerical data · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/rehabilitation · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic/statistics & numerical data · Respiration Disorders/rehabilitation · Telephone/statistics & numerical data · Telerehabilitation/methods/statistics & numerical data · Videoconferencing/statistics & numerical data · Walk Test/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the outcome that matters most in pulmonary rehabilitation, getting people to finish a programme, telerehabilitation looks at least as good as the centre: in the Cochrane review (Cox NS et al., PMID: 33511633) 15 studies and 1,904 participants (99% with COPD) found probably little or no difference in 6-minute walk distance between telerehabilitation and in-person rehabilitation (mean difference 0.06 m, 95% CI −10.82 to 10.94; moderate-certainty evidence), little or no difference in quality of life or breathlessness, and a higher completion rate for telerehabilitation (93%, 95% CI 90% to 96%, versus 70% for in-person programmes). Against no rehabilitation, telerehabilitation may improve walk distance, and no safety signal appeared. The limits are real: five different telerehabilitation models, few participants per comparison, low certainty for several outcomes, and almost no evidence in chronic respiratory diseases other than COPD or beyond the programme period. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): telerehabilitation is a reasonable way to deliver pulmonary rehabilitation when travel or capacity blocks centre-based care — comparable outcomes, better completion — not a proven upgrade on the exercise benefit itself.

cards.headline: Cox 2021 (Cochrane): telerehabilitation matched centre-based pulmonary rehabilitation on walk distance (difference 0.06 m) — and 93% finished it versus 70% in person
cards.summary: Cox 2021 (Cochrane): telerehabilitation matched centre-based pulmonary rehabilitation on walk distance (difference 0.06 m) — and 93% finished it versus 70% in person
cards.type: Systematic review, 15 studies (Cox 2021, Cochrane)
cards.people: 15 studies (32 reports) with 1,904 participants with chronic respiratory disease, almost all (99%) with COPD, comparing telerehabilitation (five different models, at least 50% of the programme delivered remotely, exercise training required) with traditional in-person centre-based pulmonary rehabilitation, or with no rehabilitation; three included studies were controlled clinical trials rather than randomised trials.
cards.result: For primary pulmonary rehabilitation there was probably little or no difference between telerehabilitation and in-person rehabilitation in 6-minute walk distance (mean difference 0.06 m, 95% CI −10.82 to 10.94; 556 participants, four studies; moderate-certainty evidence). Quality of life on the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire total score may also differ little (mean difference −1.26, 95% CI −3.97 to 1.45; 274 participants, two studies; low-certainty evidence), as may breathlessness on the Chronic Respiratory Questionnaire dyspnoea domain (mean difference 0.13, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.40; 426 participants, three studies; low-certainty evidence). Completion favoured telerehabilitation: 93% (95% CI 90% to 96%) completed, versus 70% for in-person rehabilitation. Versus no rehabilitation, primary telerehabilitation may increase 6-minute walk distance (mean difference 22.17 m, 95% CI −38.89 to 83.23; 94 participants, two studies; low-certainty evidence), and as maintenance rehabilitation may increase it more (78.1 m, 95% CI 49.6 to 106.6; 209 participants, two studies; low-certainty evidence). No adverse effects of telerehabilitation were noted beyond those reported for in-person rehabilitation or no rehabilitation.
cards.watchOut: The equivalence rests on few studies per comparison and five quite different telerehabilitation models pooled together; certainty is only moderate for the headline walk-distance comparison and low for quality of life, breathlessness, and the no-rehabilitation comparisons. Almost everyone had COPD, so this says little about interstitial lung disease or bronchiectasis, and the review could not establish how long any benefit lasts after the programme ends or what telerehabilitation costs.
cards.source: Cox NS et al. Telerehabilitation for chronic respiratory disease. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021. PMID: 33511633. Registry ID: multiple included-trial registrations in the record (27 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers). cards.headline: Synthesis: remote delivery does not dilute the rehabilitation effect in COPD — the gain is access and completion, not a bigger exercise benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: remote delivery does not dilute the rehabilitation effect in COPD — the gain is access and completion, not a bigger exercise benefit
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: 15 studies, 1,904 participants (99% COPD) in the Cochrane review — the whole comparative record carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Exercise capacity: no meaningful difference versus centre-based rehabilitation (6-minute walk difference 0.06 m, 95% CI −10.82 to 10.94). Quality of life and breathlessness: little or no difference (low certainty). Completion: 93% telerehabilitation versus 70% in-person. Versus no rehabilitation: walk distance may improve (low certainty). Safety: no excess adverse effects reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority here is judged against confidence intervals from small pooled samples, not from a single large equivalence trial; a modest true disadvantage of remote delivery cannot be excluded, and programmes still need the staffing, monitoring, and escalation routes of the centre-based originals. The completion advantage is the most decision-relevant finding, because an unfinished centre programme delivers nothing at all.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cox NS et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021 (PMID: 33511633).

shelves.title: Breathing-muscle training strengthens the in-breath and eases breathlessness in COPD — but adds nothing on top of a full rehab programme
shelves.question: In adults with COPD, does inspiratory muscle training improve inspiratory muscle strength, dyspnoea and exercise capacity versus sham or no training?
shelves.mesh: Breathing Exercises/instrumentation/methods · Dyspnea/physiopathology/therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/radiotherapy/therapy · Quality of Life · Respiratory Muscles/physiopathology · Walk Test
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — inspiratory muscle training with threshold devices does what it mechanically promises in COPD: the systematic review and meta-analysis (Beaumont M et al., PMID: 29665262) pooled 43 studies (37 in the meta-analysis, 642 patients in the treatment groups) and found inspiratory muscle strength, exercise capacity, and quality of life increased and dyspnoea decreased after training. The important qualification sits in the same record: when inspiratory muscle training was added to a pulmonary rehabilitation programme, it produced no added effect on dyspnoea compared with pulmonary rehabilitation alone — so the benefit is clearest as a standalone intervention, not as an add-on to a programme that already trains the whole patient. The abstract reports directions of effect rather than pooled effect sizes, so the size of the gains cannot be graded from this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a reasonable standalone option for people with COPD who cannot access or complete full pulmonary rehabilitation; inside a rehabilitation programme, expect no extra breathlessness benefit.

cards.headline: Beaumont 2018: 43 studies — inspiratory muscle training improved strength, exercise capacity and quality of life and eased dyspnoea, but added nothing to dyspnoea inside pulmonary rehabilitation
cards.summary: Beaumont 2018: 43 studies — inspiratory muscle training improved strength, exercise capacity and quality of life and eased dyspnoea, but added nothing to dyspnoea inside pulmonary rehabilitation
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 43 studies (Beaumont 2018)
cards.people: 43 studies included in the systematic review and 37 in the meta-analysis, with 642 patients in the treatment groups overall; all studies used threshold-device inspiratory muscle training in patients with COPD, studied either on its own or added to a pulmonary rehabilitation programme.
cards.result: Dyspnoea measured by the Baseline Dyspnea Index decreased after inspiratory muscle training. Quality of life (St George's Respiratory Questionnaire), exercise capacity (6-minute walk test), and maximal inspiratory pressure were increased after inspiratory muscle training. During pulmonary rehabilitation, however, no added effect of inspiratory muscle training on dyspnoea was found compared with pulmonary rehabilitation alone. The review's abstract reports the direction and significance of these pooled effects without printing pooled effect sizes, so the magnitude of each gain cannot be stated from this record.
cards.watchOut: No pooled effect sizes appear in the record's abstract, so 'improved' cannot be converted into 'improved by how much' — a real limit when judging whether the gains clear minimal important differences. The component trials are small and use varying training loads and durations, and the null add-on result inside pulmonary rehabilitation warns against assuming the standalone benefit stacks on top of comprehensive rehabilitation.
cards.source: Beaumont M et al. Effects of inspiratory muscle training in COPD patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis. The clinical respiratory journal. 2018. PMID: 29665262. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: training the inspiratory muscles works as a standalone in COPD — strength, walking, quality of life up, breathlessness down — but it is not an add-on that deepens rehabilitation
cards.summary: Synthesis: training the inspiratory muscles works as a standalone in COPD — strength, walking, quality of life up, breathlessness down — but it is not an add-on that deepens rehabilitation
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: 43 studies (37 meta-analysed; 642 treated patients) of threshold-device inspiratory muscle training in COPD — the entire record carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Standalone inspiratory muscle training: maximal inspiratory pressure, 6-minute walk performance, and St George's Respiratory Questionnaire quality of life increased; Baseline Dyspnea Index dyspnoea decreased. Added to pulmonary rehabilitation: no added effect on dyspnoea versus rehabilitation alone. Pooled effect sizes are not reported in the record, so magnitudes are unquantified. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: This shelf should not be read as evidence that inspiratory muscle training substitutes for pulmonary rehabilitation, which trains exercise capacity, education, and self-management together; it is evidence for a narrower, device-based intervention whose clearest role is where full rehabilitation is unavailable or as targeted therapy for demonstrable inspiratory muscle weakness. Trials reporting clinical endpoints such as exacerbations or hospitalisations are not part of this record.
cards.source: Synthesis of Beaumont M et al. The clinical respiratory journal. 2018 (PMID: 29665262).

shelves.title: Oxygen at night is not CPAP: in HeartBEAT only CPAP lowered blood pressure — oxygen was no better than sleep-hygiene advice
shelves.question: In adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, how does nocturnal supplemental oxygen compare with CPAP for blood-pressure lowering and sleepiness?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Pressure · Cardiovascular Diseases/complications · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure* · Female · Humans · Hypoxia/etiology · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy* · Risk Factors · Sleep · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive/complications/physiopathology/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for CPAP, not for oxygen: the HeartBEAT trial (Gottlieb DJ et al., PMID: 24918372) randomised 318 patients with obstructive sleep apnoea and cardiovascular disease or multiple risk factors, and after 12 weeks CPAP lowered 24-hour mean arterial pressure versus control (−2.4 mm Hg, 95% CI −4.7 to −0.1) and versus supplemental oxygen (−2.8 mm Hg, 95% CI −5.1 to −0.5), while oxygen did not differ significantly from education alone. Correcting the low oxygen at night, by itself, did not reproduce CPAP's blood-pressure effect — the pressure problem in apnoea is apparently not only the oxygen dips. A 49-trial network meta-analysis of apnoea treatments and blood pressure (Kou C et al., PMID: 35703874) is consistent in kind: CPAP showed modest, stable blood-pressure lowering, while nocturnal supplemental oxygen was not among the treatments the authors identified as effective. Neither record reports a sleepiness advantage for oxygen. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): CPAP lowers blood pressure where nocturnal oxygen does not, so oxygen should not be substituted for CPAP when blood-pressure lowering is the goal.

cards.headline: Gottlieb 2014 (HeartBEAT): CPAP lowered 24-hour mean arterial pressure by 2.4–2.8 mm Hg versus control and versus oxygen — oxygen alone did not beat education
cards.summary: Gottlieb 2014 (HeartBEAT): CPAP lowered 24-hour mean arterial pressure by 2.4–2.8 mm Hg versus control and versus oxygen — oxygen alone did not beat education
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Gottlieb 2014, HeartBEAT)
cards.people: 318 patients recruited from cardiology practices with cardiovascular disease or multiple cardiovascular risk factors, screened with the Berlin questionnaire and home sleep testing, with an apnoea–hypopnoea index of 15 to 50 events per hour; randomised to sleep-hygiene and healthy-lifestyle education alone, education plus CPAP, or education plus nocturnal supplemental oxygen, for 12 weeks; 281 (88%) had ambulatory blood pressure at baseline and follow-up.
cards.result: At 12 weeks the 24-hour mean arterial pressure was lower with CPAP than with control (−2.4 mm Hg, 95% CI −4.7 to −0.1; P=0.04) and lower with CPAP than with supplemental oxygen (−2.8 mm Hg, 95% CI −5.1 to −0.5; P=0.02). There was no significant difference in 24-hour mean arterial pressure between the control group and the group receiving oxygen. A sensitivity analysis using multiple imputation for missing data did not change the results.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks and a blood-pressure endpoint: the trial says nothing about heart attacks, strokes, or death, and its abstract reports no sleepiness outcome, so this shelf cannot compare the two treatments for daytime sleepiness. Participants had moderate apnoea (AHI 15–50) plus cardiovascular disease or risk factors, recruited through cardiology practices — not a general sleep-clinic population — and CPAP's advantage was measured under trial adherence conditions.
cards.source: Gottlieb DJ et al. CPAP versus oxygen in obstructive sleep apnea. The New England journal of medicine. 2014. PMID: 24918372. Registry ID: NCT01086800. cards.headline: Kou 2022 network meta-analysis: across 49 apnoea trials, CPAP lowered blood pressure modestly — nocturnal oxygen was not among the effective treatments
cards.summary: Kou 2022 network meta-analysis: across 49 apnoea trials, CPAP lowered blood pressure modestly — nocturnal oxygen was not among the effective treatments
cards.type: Network meta-analysis, 49 RCTs (Kou 2022)
cards.people: 49 randomised controlled trials involving 4,893 patients with obstructive sleep apnoea, comparing CPAP, mandibular advancement devices, nocturnal supplemental oxygen, surgery, and several blood-pressure drug classes, with office, daytime, night-time, and 24-hour blood pressure outcomes; Bayesian network meta-analysis of trials to 1 June 2021.
cards.result: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists were significantly associated with blood pressure reduction, followed by ACE inhibitors/ARBs; renal sympathetic denervation reduced office, 24-hour, and daytime pressures; CPAP also demonstrated modest blood pressure lowering, described by the authors as mild but stable and potentially helpful as adjunctive therapy in apnoea patients with hypertension. Nocturnal supplemental oxygen was included as a treatment node but does not appear among the treatments the authors report as lowering blood pressure. The record's abstract does not print treatment-specific mean differences, so the size of CPAP's pooled effect cannot be stated from this record.
cards.watchOut: A network meta-analysis mixes direct and indirect comparisons across trials of differing populations and durations, and its abstract gives rankings and qualitative conclusions rather than the numeric effects — it corroborates HeartBEAT's direction (CPAP modestly effective; oxygen not credited) but cannot quantify how much worse oxygen is. Drug treatments for hypertension are ranked alongside apnoea treatments, which answers a different question from 'treat the apnoea'.
cards.source: Kou C et al. Effect of different treatments for obstructive sleep apnoea on blood pressure. Journal of hypertension. 2022. PMID: 35703874. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: on blood pressure the comparison is one-sided — CPAP lowers it a little, oxygen does not measurably lower it at all
cards.summary: Synthesis: on blood pressure the comparison is one-sided — CPAP lowers it a little, oxygen does not measurably lower it at all
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One 318-patient head-to-head randomised trial (HeartBEAT) plus a 49-trial, 4,893-patient network meta-analysis of apnoea treatments and blood pressure.
cards.result: Head-to-head at 12 weeks: CPAP −2.4 mm Hg versus control (95% CI −4.7 to −0.1) and −2.8 mm Hg versus oxygen (95% CI −5.1 to −0.5) in 24-hour mean arterial pressure; oxygen versus control: no significant difference. Network evidence: CPAP modest but stable blood-pressure lowering; oxygen not identified as effective. Sleepiness and cardiovascular events: not reported for this comparison in either record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — for CPAP over oxygen.
cards.watchOut: Do not over-read the null for oxygen: HeartBEAT was powered on blood pressure over 12 weeks in a cardiology population, and oxygen may still have roles in apnoea care outside this question (for example alongside CPAP for residual desaturation) that neither record tests. What the evidence does settle is narrower — as a stand-alone substitute for CPAP aimed at blood pressure, oxygen failed its head-to-head test. Tier C is set because the direct comparison rests on a single trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gottlieb DJ et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2014 (PMID: 24918372); Kou C et al. Journal of hypertension. 2022 (PMID: 35703874).

shelves.title: Servo-ventilation for central sleep apnoea in heart failure: the breathing normalised, and mortality rose by about a third
shelves.question: In patients with central sleep apnoea and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, does adaptive servo-ventilation improve survival or cardiovascular outcomes — or increase mortality?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases/etiology/mortality · Female · Heart Failure, Systolic/complications/physiopathology/therapy · Hospitalization · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Positive-Pressure Respiration/adverse effects/methods · Sleep Apnea, Central/complications/therapy · Stroke Volume · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — adaptive servo-ventilation suppresses central sleep apnoea beautifully and harms the patients it was meant to save: in SERVE-HF (Cowie MR et al., PMID: 26323938), 1,325 patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (≤45%) and predominantly central sleep apnoea had their apnoea–hypopnoea index driven down to a mean of 6.6 events per hour at 12 months, yet the primary composite endpoint did not improve (54.1% versus 50.8%; HR 1.13, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.31) and both all-cause mortality (HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.55) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.34, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.65) were significantly higher with the device. A later systematic review and meta-analysis (Wang J et al., PMID: 33524864) found no significant reduction in all-cause or cardiovascular mortality across eight studies, while reporting subgroup signals of fewer major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with less severe heart failure or profound nocturnal desaturation — signals built partly on observational studies that cannot overturn a large randomised mortality result in the population SERVE-HF actually studied. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and central sleep apnoea, adaptive servo-ventilation increases mortality and should not be used to improve survival in that population.

cards.headline: Cowie 2015 (SERVE-HF): the machine fixed the breathing (AHI 6.6/hour) and raised mortality — all-cause death HR 1.28, cardiovascular death HR 1.34
cards.summary: Cowie 2015 (SERVE-HF): the machine fixed the breathing (AHI 6.6/hour) and raised mortality — all-cause death HR 1.28, cardiovascular death HR 1.34
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Cowie 2015, SERVE-HF)
cards.people: 1,325 patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (left ventricular ejection fraction ≤45%), an apnoea–hypopnoea index of ≥15 events per hour, and predominantly central sleep apnoea, randomised to guideline-based medical treatment plus adaptive servo-ventilation or guideline-based medical treatment alone.
cards.result: In the adaptive servo-ventilation group the mean apnoea–hypopnoea index at 12 months was 6.6 events per hour, showing the device controlled the breathing disorder. The primary endpoint (first event of death from any cause, lifesaving cardiovascular intervention, or unplanned hospitalisation for worsening heart failure) did not differ significantly: 54.1% with servo-ventilation versus 50.8% with control (hazard ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.31; P=0.10). All-cause mortality was significantly higher with servo-ventilation (hazard ratio 1.28, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.55; P=0.01), as was cardiovascular mortality (hazard ratio 1.34, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.65; P=0.006).
cards.watchOut: The population is specific — ejection fraction ≤45% with predominantly central events — so the harm finding governs that group, not every patient with central sleep apnoea (for example preserved ejection fraction or opioid-related central apnoea, which SERVE-HF did not study). The trial also predates contemporary heart-failure drug therapy; whether the excess mortality would persist on modern background treatment is untested, but no trial has re-established safety, so the burden of proof sits with the device.
cards.source: Cowie MR et al. Adaptive Servo-Ventilation for Central Sleep Apnea in Systolic Heart Failure. The New England journal of medicine. 2015. PMID: 26323938. Registry ID: NCT00733343. cards.headline: Wang 2021 meta-analysis: no mortality reduction from servo-ventilation overall — claimed benefits appear only in subgroups drawn partly from observational studies
cards.summary: Wang 2021 meta-analysis: no mortality reduction from servo-ventilation overall — claimed benefits appear only in subgroups drawn partly from observational studies
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 8 studies (Wang 2021)
cards.people: Eight studies (three randomised controlled trials and five observational studies) including 2,208 participants with central sleep apnoea and heart failure, comparing adaptive servo-ventilation with usual care for all-cause and cardiovascular mortality and major adverse cardiovascular events.
cards.result: All-cause and cardiovascular mortality were not significantly reduced by adaptive servo-ventilation. In subgroup analyses, patients whose mean nadir nocturnal saturation was ≤80% had a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events with servo-ventilation (relative risk 0.18; P<0.001), as did patients with ejection fraction >33% (relative risk 0.35; P<0.001) or NYHA class I/II (relative risk 0.35; P<0.001); patients with ejection fraction ≤33% or NYHA class III/IV had no reduced risk. The authors conclude that patients with profound central-apnoea-associated hypoxaemia or less severe heart failure may still benefit.
cards.watchOut: Five of the eight studies are observational, where healthier patients are more likely to be offered and to tolerate a device — exactly the confounding that can manufacture subgroup 'benefits'. The subgroups are defined by study-level mean values (mean ejection fraction, mean nadir saturation), not by individual patients, and they sit against a 1,325-patient randomised trial showing increased mortality in the reduced-ejection-fraction population; treat the subgroup findings as hypotheses for future trials, not as a licence to use the device in SERVE-HF-type patients.
cards.source: Wang J et al. Therapeutic value of treating central sleep apnea by adaptive servo-ventilation in patients with heart failure: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Heart & lung : the journal of critical care. 2021. PMID: 33524864. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a treatment that normalises the breathing tracing while raising mortality — the randomised verdict in reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure is harm
cards.summary: Synthesis: a treatment that normalises the breathing tracing while raising mortality — the randomised verdict in reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure is harm
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One 1,325-patient randomised trial (SERVE-HF) plus an eight-study, 2,208-participant systematic review and meta-analysis dominated numerically by that trial and observational data.
cards.result: Breathing control: achieved (mean AHI 6.6 events/hour at 12 months on servo-ventilation). Primary composite outcome: no benefit (54.1% versus 50.8%; HR 1.13, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.31). Mortality: increased — all-cause HR 1.28 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.55), cardiovascular HR 1.34 (95% CI 1.09 to 1.65); meta-analysis confirms no mortality reduction overall. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm).
cards.watchOut: SERVE-HF is the cautionary tale this library keeps meeting: a surrogate endpoint (the apnoea–hypopnoea index) improved dramatically while the patient-centred outcome worsened, possibly because central apnoea in severe heart failure is partly compensatory. The finding should not be stretched to populations SERVE-HF excluded, but within its population — reduced ejection fraction, predominantly central apnoea — it is definitive enough that guidelines and regulators acted on it. Tier C is set because a single trial carries the mortality verdict, albeit a large and internally consistent one.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cowie MR et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2015 (PMID: 26323938); Wang J et al. Heart & lung : the journal of critical care. 2021 (PMID: 33524864).

shelves.title: The old IPF triple therapy harmed: 8 deaths versus 1 on placebo before the safety board stopped it (PANTHER-IPF)
shelves.question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does combination prednisone plus azathioprine plus N-acetylcysteine improve outcomes versus placebo — or increase death and hospitalisation?
shelves.mesh: Acetylcysteine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Aged · Azathioprine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Medication Adherence · Middle Aged · Prednisone/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pulmonary Fibrosis/drug therapy/mortality/physiopathology · Treatment Outcome · Vital Capacity
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — the long-standard triple therapy for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis was worse than doing nothing: in PANTHER-IPF (Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis Clinical Research Network, PMID: 22607134), patients with mild-to-moderate lung-function impairment randomised to prednisone plus azathioprine plus N-acetylcysteine had, at a planned interim analysis, eight deaths versus one on placebo (P=0.01) and 23 hospitalisations versus seven (P<0.001), with no evidence of physiological or clinical benefit — the data and safety monitoring board stopped the combination arm at a mean follow-up of 32 weeks. The wider drug-treatment landscape points the same way: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of 30 studies and 16 treatments (Canestaro WJ et al., PMID: 26836914) found no treatment better than placebo for respiratory-specific mortality, a reminder that for decades IPF pharmacotherapy produced activity without survival benefit — and in this case produced the opposite. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): the prednisone–azathioprine–N-acetylcysteine combination should not be used in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; this shelf answers the combination question only and does not judge N-acetylcysteine alone, whose separate comparison the trial continued.

cards.headline: PANTHER-IPF 2012: triple therapy stopped early — 8 deaths versus 1 and 23 hospitalisations versus 7 on placebo, with no sign of benefit
cards.summary: PANTHER-IPF 2012: triple therapy stopped early — 8 deaths versus 1 and 23 hospitalisations versus 7 on placebo, with no sign of benefit
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (PANTHER-IPF, 2012)
cards.people: Patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and mild-to-moderate lung-function impairment, randomised double-blind in a 1:1:1 ratio to prednisone plus azathioprine plus N-acetylcysteine, N-acetylcysteine alone, or placebo; the primary outcome was change in forced vital capacity over 60 weeks. At the planned interim analysis approximately 50% of data had been collected, with 77 patients in the combination group and 78 in the placebo group.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, the combination-therapy group had an increased rate of death (8 versus 1; P=0.01) and hospitalisation (23 versus 7; P<0.001). There was no evidence of physiological or clinical benefit for combination therapy. On these findings the independent data and safety monitoring board recommended termination of the combination-therapy group at a mean follow-up of 32 weeks; the N-acetylcysteine-only versus placebo comparison continued and is not reported in this record.
cards.watchOut: The harm verdict comes from an interim analysis with small absolute event counts (8 versus 1 deaths), so the size of the excess risk is imprecise even though the direction, the hospitalisation signal, and the absence of any offsetting benefit all align. The trial enrolled mild-to-moderate disease; it does not directly test the combination in advanced disease — but with harm shown where patients were healthiest, extrapolation offers no comfort. Which component (or interaction) caused the harm cannot be separated from this design.
cards.source: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis Clinical Research Network et al. Prednisone, azathioprine, and N-acetylcysteine for pulmonary fibrosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2012. cards.headline: Canestaro 2016 network meta-analysis: across 30 IPF drug studies and 16 treatments, none beat placebo on respiratory mortality — the era's pharmacotherapy was activity without survival benefit
cards.summary: Canestaro 2016 network meta-analysis: across 30 IPF drug studies and 16 treatments, none beat placebo on respiratory mortality — the era's pharmacotherapy was activity without survival benefit
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis, 30 studies (Canestaro 2016)
cards.people: 30 eligible randomised studies evaluating 16 unique non-steroid pharmacologic treatments for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, drawn from MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library to August 2014; outcomes were forced vital capacity and all-cause and respiratory-specific mortality, analysed in a Bayesian network framework.
cards.result: Under both fixed-effect and random-effect models, no treatment performed better than placebo for respiratory-specific mortality. For all-cause mortality, pirfenidone and nintedanib had effects approaching significance with credible intervals slightly crossing the null under a fixed-effect model. For respiratory-specific mortality, all-cause mortality, and decline in percent predicted forced vital capacity, nintedanib and pirfenidone were virtually indistinguishable, with no clear advantage detected for either; the authors note that although both were approved on reduced decline in pulmonary function, neither has a clear advantage on mortality outcomes.
cards.watchOut: This review explicitly did not evaluate steroid therapy, so it does not re-test the PANTHER combination itself; it is carded as landscape evidence — the surrounding generation of IPF drug trials found no mortality benefit for anything — not as a second verdict on triple therapy. Its search closed in August 2014, before the antifibrotic era matured, and network comparisons lean on indirect evidence across heterogeneous trials.
cards.source: Canestaro WJ et al. Drug Treatment of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis: Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis. Chest. 2016. PMID: 26836914. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: an entrenched standard of care, tested properly at last, killed and hospitalised more patients than placebo — the combination is contraindicated by its own trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: an entrenched standard of care, tested properly at last, killed and hospitalised more patients than placebo — the combination is contraindicated by its own trial
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One randomised trial stopped early for harm (77 combination versus 78 placebo patients at interim analysis) set against a 30-study network meta-analysis of the wider IPF drug landscape.
cards.result: Deaths: 8 on triple therapy versus 1 on placebo (P=0.01). Hospitalisations: 23 versus 7 (P<0.001). Lung-function or clinical benefit: none seen. Combination arm terminated at a mean of 32 weeks on the safety board's recommendation. Wider landscape: no IPF drug treatment of the era beat placebo on respiratory-specific mortality. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm).
cards.watchOut: Keep the claim precise: the verdict condemns the three-drug combination in mild-to-moderate IPF. It does not by itself condemn corticosteroids for acute exacerbations, immunosuppression for other interstitial lung diseases with inflammatory phenotypes, or N-acetylcysteine alone (whose PANTHER comparison continued separately). The historical lesson — that 'widely used' substituted for 'tested' for decades — is the part of this shelf most likely to recur elsewhere. Tier C is set because the verdict rests on a single, early-stopped trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis Clinical Research Network et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2012 (PMID: 22607134); Canestaro WJ et al. Chest. 2016 (PMID: 26836914).

shelves.title: Rehab works in lung scarring too: 44 extra metres on the walk test and less breathlessness — durability beyond the programme unproven
shelves.question: In adults with interstitial lung disease, does pulmonary rehabilitation improve exercise capacity, dyspnoea and quality of life versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Exercise* · Exercise Therapy · Exercise Tolerance · Humans · Lung Diseases, Interstitial/physiopathology/rehabilitation · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Walking
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pulmonary rehabilitation, proven in COPD, also works in interstitial lung disease on the outcomes measured immediately after the programme: the Cochrane review (Dowman L et al., PMID: 25284270) included nine studies and meta-analysed five (86 rehabilitation and 82 control participants), finding six-minute walk distance improved by a weighted mean difference of 44.34 m (95% CI 26.04 to 62.64) and peak oxygen consumption by 1.24 mL/kg/min (95% CI 0.46 to 2.03), with quality of life improved (standardised mean difference 0.59, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.98) and no adverse effects reported. The idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis subgroup showed the same pattern — walk distance up 35.63 m (95% CI 16.02 to 55.23) and dyspnoea reduced (standardised mean difference −0.68, 95% CI −1.12 to −0.25). What the record cannot show is durability: the only two studies with longer follow-up found no significant effects on clinical variables or survival at three or six months, and the reviewers graded the evidence low to moderate quality because six of nine studies existed only as abstracts. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): offer pulmonary rehabilitation in interstitial lung disease for near-term function, breathlessness, and quality of life — with honest uncertainty about how long the gains persist.

cards.headline: Dowman 2014 (Cochrane): rehabilitation in ILD added 44 m to the six-minute walk and improved quality of life — with the same pattern inside the IPF subgroup
cards.summary: Dowman 2014 (Cochrane): rehabilitation in ILD added 44 m to the six-minute walk and improved quality of life — with the same pattern inside the IPF subgroup
cards.type: Systematic review, 9 studies (Dowman 2014, Cochrane)
cards.people: Nine randomised and quasi-randomised studies of pulmonary rehabilitation versus no rehabilitation or other therapy in people with interstitial lung disease of any origin, searched to June 2014; five studies entered the meta-analysis (86 participants who undertook pulmonary rehabilitation and 82 control participants). Six of the nine studies were published only as abstracts, and only one study used a blinded assessor and intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: Pulmonary rehabilitation improved six-minute walk distance (weighted mean difference 44.34 m, 95% CI 26.04 to 62.64) and peak oxygen consumption (weighted mean difference 1.24 mL/kg/min, 95% CI 0.46 to 2.03). In the idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis subgroup, walk distance also improved (weighted mean difference 35.63 m, 95% CI 16.02 to 55.23), peak oxygen consumption improved (1.46 mL/kg/min, 95% CI 0.54 to 2.39), and dyspnoea was reduced (standardised mean difference −0.68, 95% CI −1.12 to −0.25); across all participants dyspnoea fell (standardised mean difference −0.66, 95% CI −1.05 to −0.28) and quality of life improved (standardised mean difference 0.59, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.98). No adverse effects of pulmonary rehabilitation were reported. Two studies reported longer-term outcomes, with no significant effects on clinical variables or survival at three or six months.
cards.watchOut: The pooled sample is tiny (168 participants in the meta-analysis), most studies were abstract-only reports with inadequate methods reporting, and the reviewers themselves graded the evidence low to moderate quality. The benefits are immediate post-programme measurements; the two studies that looked at three to six months found nothing significant, so durability and any effect on survival are unknown, and the data could not examine whether disease severity or training modality changes the result.
cards.source: Dowman L et al. Pulmonary rehabilitation for interstitial lung disease. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014. PMID: 25284270. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: short-term gains in walking, breathlessness, and quality of life are consistent in ILD including IPF — staying power is the unproven part
cards.summary: Synthesis: short-term gains in walking, breathlessness, and quality of life are consistent in ILD including IPF — staying power is the unproven part
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Nine studies (five meta-analysed; 86 rehabilitation versus 82 control participants) — the whole randomised record carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Six-minute walk distance: +44.34 m (95% CI 26.04 to 62.64) overall; +35.63 m in the IPF subgroup. Peak oxygen consumption: +1.24 mL/kg/min. Dyspnoea: standardised mean difference −0.66. Quality of life: standardised mean difference +0.59. Safety: no adverse effects reported. At three to six months: no significant effects on clinical variables or survival in the two studies reporting them. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the 44 m without its scaffolding: it comes from five small studies, several abstract-only, in mixed ILD populations whose programmes and comparators varied. The honest clinical statement is that rehabilitation in ILD behaves like rehabilitation in COPD in the short term and is safe in these trials — whether maintenance programmes can hold the gains in a progressive disease is a separate, unanswered question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dowman L et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014 (PMID: 25284270).

shelves.title: Infliximab for pulmonary sarcoidosis: a statistically real 2.5% FVC gain that patients could not feel on any other measure
shelves.question: In patients with chronic pulmonary sarcoidosis and disabling symptoms despite corticosteroids, does infliximab improve forced vital capacity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Chronic Disease · Female · Humans · Infliximab · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Peptidyl-Dipeptidase A/blood · Sarcoidosis, Pulmonary/drug therapy/physiopathology · Treatment Outcome · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha/antagonists & inhibitors · Vital Capacity/drug effects
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the only randomised trial of infliximab in chronic pulmonary sarcoidosis (Baughman RP et al., PMID: 16840744) hit its primary endpoint narrowly and nothing else: in 138 patients, combined infliximab (3 or 5 mg/kg) produced a mean increase of 2.5% in percent of predicted forced vital capacity at week 24 versus no change on placebo (P=0.038), while every major secondary endpoint — St George's Respiratory Questionnaire, 6-minute walk distance, and Borg dyspnoea score — showed no significant difference, and the authors themselves state that the clinical importance of the lung-function finding is not clear. Post hoc analyses suggested patients with more severe disease tended to benefit more, which is a hypothesis, not a result. A 2.5% predicted FVC shift that patients cannot feel on any symptom or walk measure, from a single phase 2 trial, is a signal worth the further evaluation the authors call for — not an established treatment effect. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): infliximab may nudge lung function in chronic pulmonary sarcoidosis, but symptomatic benefit is unproven and the case rests on one small trial.

cards.headline: Baughman 2006: infliximab raised percent predicted FVC by 2.5% versus no change on placebo (P=0.038) — and moved no symptom, walk, or quality-of-life measure
cards.summary: Baughman 2006: infliximab raised percent predicted FVC by 2.5% versus no change on placebo (P=0.038) — and moved no symptom, walk, or quality-of-life measure
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase 2 (Baughman 2006)
cards.people: 138 patients with chronic pulmonary sarcoidosis in a phase 2, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study; intravenous infliximab 3 or 5 mg/kg or placebo at weeks 0, 2, 6, 12, 18, and 24, with follow-up through week 52. The primary endpoint was change from baseline to week 24 in percent of predicted forced vital capacity.
cards.result: Patients in the combined infliximab groups (3 and 5 mg/kg) had a mean increase of 2.5% from baseline to week 24 in percent of predicted FVC, compared with no change in placebo-treated patients (P=0.038). No significant differences between treatment groups were observed for any of the major secondary endpoints at week 24 — St George's Respiratory Questionnaire, 6-minute walk distance, Borg's CR10 dyspnoea score, and the Lupus Pernio Physician's Global Assessment in patients with facial skin involvement. Post hoc exploratory analyses suggested patients with more severe disease tended to benefit more from infliximab. The authors conclude that the clinical importance of the FVC finding is not clear and that the results support further evaluation of anti-TNF therapy in severe, chronic, symptomatic sarcoidosis.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2 trial of 138 patients split across three arms, powered on a physiological endpoint: the 2.5% predicted FVC difference sits close to measurement variability for the test, and the complete absence of movement in dyspnoea, walk distance, and quality of life is the clinically relevant counterweight. The record's abstract reports no safety outcomes, so this card cannot weigh infliximab's known immunosuppression risks — a material omission when the demonstrated benefit is this small. The severe-disease signal is post hoc and exploratory.
cards.source: Baughman RP et al. Infliximab therapy in patients with chronic sarcoidosis and pulmonary involvement. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2006. PMID: 16840744. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one phase 2 trial, one borderline physiological endpoint, zero patient-felt outcomes — a lead for further trials, not a verdict
cards.summary: Synthesis: one phase 2 trial, one borderline physiological endpoint, zero patient-felt outcomes — a lead for further trials, not a verdict
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial, 138 patients with chronic pulmonary sarcoidosis — the entire randomised record carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Percent predicted FVC at week 24: +2.5% on combined infliximab versus no change on placebo (P=0.038). St George's Respiratory Questionnaire, 6-minute walk distance, Borg dyspnoea score: no significant differences. Safety: not reported in the record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: This shelf answers the randomised-evidence question only. Sarcoidosis care also draws on observational series and experience in refractory, organ-threatening disease, where the decision calculus differs from this trial's stable chronic pulmonary population; nothing here either licenses or forbids that use. What the trial does establish is the ceiling of the proven claim: a small lung-function effect of unclear clinical importance. Tier C is set because the evidence is a single phase 2 trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Baughman RP et al. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2006 (PMID: 16840744).

shelves.title: High-flow oxygen at home for high-CO2 COPD: exacerbations probably fall and CO2 holds steady — survival unproven
shelves.question: In patients with COPD and chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure, does long-term domiciliary high-flow nasal cannula therapy reduce exacerbations and improve carbon dioxide control versus long-term oxygen therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Cannula · Humans · Hypercapnia · Noninvasive Ventilation* · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive*/complications/therapy · Respiratory Insufficiency*/etiology/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — domiciliary high-flow nasal cannula therapy in COPD with persistent hypercapnic failure stabilised patients who otherwise deteriorated: in the 12-month randomised-trial cohort analysis (Storgaard LH et al., PMID: 33208303), 74 long-term-oxygen-treated patients completing the study (31 on high-flow, 43 controls) showed PaCO2 falling 1.3% on high-flow while rising 7% in controls (P=0.003), exacerbations rising by 2.2 per year in controls but only 0.15 per year on high-flow, and hospital admissions falling by 0.67 per year on high-flow (P=0.013) while rising in controls. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Pitre T et al., PMID: 37804997) — four randomised trials, 440 patients — found high-flow probably reduces acute exacerbations (relative risk 0.77, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.89; 69 fewer exacerbations per 1,000 patients; moderate certainty), may reduce hospital admissions (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.09; low certainty) and quality-of-life scores, but may have no effect on mortality (relative risk 1.22, 95% CI 0.64 to 2.35; low certainty). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): home high-flow therapy probably cuts exacerbations in chronic hypercapnic COPD; a survival benefit is unproven and the trial base is still small.

cards.headline: Storgaard 2020: over 12 months on home high-flow, PaCO2 and admissions fell while controls worsened — admissions down 0.67/year on high-flow, exacerbations nearly flat versus +2.2/year in controls
cards.summary: Storgaard 2020: over 12 months on home high-flow, PaCO2 and admissions fell while controls worsened — admissions down 0.67/year on high-flow, exacerbations nearly flat versus +2.2/year in controls
cards.type: Post hoc analysis of a randomised controlled trial (Storgaard 2020)
cards.people: Post hoc analysis of a randomised controlled trial cohort: 74 patients with COPD, persistent hypercapnic failure (PaCO2 >6 kPa) and hypoxic failure on long-term oxygen therapy who completed the 12-month study period — 31 treated with domiciliary high-flow nasal cannula and 43 controls — with blood gases at baseline, 6, and 12 months and exacerbation and admission counts compared with the prestudy year.
cards.result: After 12 months there was a 1.3% decrease in PaCO2 in patients using high-flow nasal cannula and a 7% increase in controls, measured before high-flow use on site (P=0.003); 30 minutes of high-flow at visits lowered PaCO2 significantly at 0, 6, and 12 months, including in controls who tried it at study end (P<0.001). The exacerbation rate increased versus the prestudy year by 2.2 per year in controls (P<0.001) and by 0.15 per year in high-flow-treated patients (P=0.661). Hospital admission rates increased in controls by 0.3 per year (P=0.180) and decreased by 0.67 per year on high-flow (P=0.013). The authors conclude high-flow stabilised PaCO2, exacerbations, and hospitalisations while untreated patients worsened.
cards.watchOut: A post hoc analysis of completers only (74 of the original trial population), unblinded by design — patients and clinicians knew who had the device, which can move admission decisions and exacerbation reporting. The comparisons lean on each group's own prestudy year, so regression to the mean and secular worsening are entangled with the treatment effect; the randomised contrast is the PaCO2 and event-rate divergence, not the within-group changes alone. Mortality is not reported in this record.
cards.source: Storgaard LH et al. Development in PaCO2 over 12 months in patients with COPD with persistent hypercapnic respiratory failure treated with high-flow nasal cannula-post-hoc analysis from a randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: Pitre 2023 meta-analysis: home high-flow probably reduces exacerbations (relative risk 0.77; 69 fewer per 1,000) — mortality effect uncertain (relative risk 1.22)
cards.summary: Pitre 2023 meta-analysis: home high-flow probably reduces exacerbations (relative risk 0.77; 69 fewer per 1,000) — mortality effect uncertain (relative risk 1.22)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 4 RCTs (Pitre 2023)
cards.people: Four randomised trials involving 440 adult patients with COPD and chronic hypercapnia initiated on home high-flow nasal cannula for at least one month, compared with standard care; risk of bias assessed with RoB 2.0 and evidence quality with GRADE.
cards.result: High-flow probably reduces acute exacerbations compared with standard care (relative risk 0.77, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.89; moderate certainty), corresponding to 69 fewer acute exacerbations per 1,000 patients. It may reduce hospital admissions (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.09; low certainty) and may lower the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire score (mean difference 8.12 units lower, 95% CI 13.30 to 2.95 lower; low certainty). It may have no effect on mortality (relative risk 1.22, 95% CI 0.64 to 2.35; low certainty). The authors call for larger randomised trials with longer follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Four trials and 440 patients is a thin base: the mortality confidence interval (0.64 to 2.35) is compatible with substantial benefit or substantial harm, and most outcomes are low certainty. Comparators were 'standard care' rather than home non-invasive ventilation, the established therapy for this population — so this record cannot say whether high-flow matches, beats, or should replace non-invasive ventilation, only that it beats usual care without it on exacerbations.
cards.source: Pitre T et al. Home high flow nasal cannula for chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure in COPD: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Respiratory medicine. 2023. PMID: 37804997. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: exacerbations probably fall and carbon dioxide stabilises on home high-flow — survival and the comparison with home ventilation remain open
cards.summary: Synthesis: exacerbations probably fall and carbon dioxide stabilises on home high-flow — survival and the comparison with home ventilation remain open
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One 12-month randomised-trial cohort (74 completers) plus a four-trial, 440-patient meta-analysis in COPD with chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure.
cards.result: Exacerbations: relative risk 0.77 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.89), 69 fewer per 1,000 patients, moderate certainty; in the cohort, exacerbations rose 0.15/year on high-flow versus 2.2/year in controls. Admissions: relative risk 0.87 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.09); cohort admissions fell 0.67/year on high-flow (P=0.013). PaCO2: −1.3% on high-flow versus +7% in controls over 12 months (P=0.003). Mortality: relative risk 1.22 (95% CI 0.64 to 2.35) — no demonstrated effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Position this therapy carefully: the evidence supports high-flow as an option in persistently hypercapnic COPD, particularly where non-invasive ventilation is not tolerated, but no carded trial pits high-flow head-to-head against home ventilation, and the mortality data are too imprecise to reassure. Tier C is set because the base is one small trial programme and a four-trial meta-analysis.
cards.source: Synthesis of Storgaard LH et al. BMJ open respiratory research. 2020 (PMID: 33208303); Pitre T et al. Respiratory medicine. 2023 (PMID: 37804997).

shelves.title: Varenicline plus bupropion quits more smokers at 3 and 6 months — by 12 months the edge is no longer significant
shelves.question: In cigarette smokers, does combining varenicline with bupropion increase prolonged abstinence versus varenicline alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Benzazepines/administration & dosage · Bupropion/administration & dosage · Delayed-Action Preparations · Dopamine Uptake Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nicotinic Agonists/administration & dosage · Quinoxalines/administration & dosage · Smoking Cessation/methods · Tobacco Use Disorder/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Varenicline
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adding bupropion sustained-release to varenicline helped smokers stay quit through the treatment period and six months, but the advantage had faded into non-significance by one year: in the randomised, blinded, placebo-controlled trial (Ebbert JO et al., PMID: 24399554), 506 cigarette smokers achieved prolonged abstinence at 12 weeks in 53.0% on combination therapy versus 43.2% on varenicline alone (odds ratio 1.49, 95% CI 1.05 to 2.12) and at 26 weeks in 36.6% versus 27.6% (odds ratio 1.52, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.22), while 7-day point-prevalence abstinence never differed significantly and at 52 weeks neither outcome did (prolonged abstinence 30.9% versus 24.5%; odds ratio 1.39, 95% CI 0.93 to 2.07). The combination also cost more anxiety (7.2% versus 3.1%) and depressive symptoms (3.6% versus 0.8%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but possibly temporary boost to quitting while both drugs are taken and shortly after — not a demonstrated improvement in one-year abstinence, and bought with more mood symptoms.

cards.headline: Ebbert 2014: varenicline plus bupropion beat varenicline alone on prolonged abstinence at 12 weeks (53.0% versus 43.2%) and 26 weeks — but not at 52 weeks
cards.summary: Ebbert 2014: varenicline plus bupropion beat varenicline alone on prolonged abstinence at 12 weeks (53.0% versus 43.2%) and 26 weeks — but not at 52 weeks
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Ebbert 2014)
cards.people: 506 adult cigarette smokers randomised at three midwestern clinical research sites to 12 weeks of varenicline plus bupropion sustained-release or varenicline plus placebo, with follow-up through week 52; 315 (62%) completed the study. Abstinence outcomes were biochemically confirmed; prolonged abstinence meant no smoking from two weeks after the target quit date.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, prolonged abstinence was 53.0% with combination therapy versus 43.2% with varenicline alone (odds ratio 1.49, 95% CI 1.05 to 2.12; P=.03), and 7-day point-prevalence abstinence was 56.2% versus 48.6% (odds ratio 1.36, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.93; P=.09). At 26 weeks, prolonged abstinence was 36.6% versus 27.6% (odds ratio 1.52, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.22; P=.03) and point-prevalence abstinence 38.2% versus 31.9% (odds ratio 1.32, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.91; P=.14). At 52 weeks neither outcome differed significantly: prolonged abstinence 30.9% versus 24.5% (odds ratio 1.39, 95% CI 0.93 to 2.07; P=.11) and point-prevalence abstinence 36.6% versus 29.2% (odds ratio 1.40, 95% CI 0.96 to 2.05; P=.08). Combination-therapy participants reported more anxiety (7.2% versus 3.1%; P=.04) and depressive symptoms (3.6% versus 0.8%; P=.03).
cards.watchOut: Only 62% completed the study, and the benefit pattern is endpoint-sensitive: the stricter prolonged-abstinence outcome reached significance at 12 and 26 weeks while point-prevalence abstinence never did, and by 52 weeks — the horizon that matters for health — nothing was significant. A single trial at three sites in one region, in smokers willing to take two drugs; whether the combination helps heavier or more dependent smokers specifically cannot be answered from this record. The excess anxiety and depressive symptoms are small in absolute terms but real, and matter in a population with high rates of mood disorder.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two quit drugs are better than one while treatment lasts — the one-year ledger shows a non-significant gap and more mood side effects
cards.summary: Synthesis: two quit drugs are better than one while treatment lasts — the one-year ledger shows a non-significant gap and more mood side effects
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One randomised, blinded, placebo-controlled trial, 506 cigarette smokers, 12 weeks of treatment and 52 weeks of follow-up — the entire record carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Prolonged abstinence: 53.0% versus 43.2% at 12 weeks (odds ratio 1.49, 95% CI 1.05 to 2.12); 36.6% versus 27.6% at 26 weeks (odds ratio 1.52, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.22); 30.9% versus 24.5% at 52 weeks (odds ratio 1.39, 95% CI 0.93 to 2.07; not significant). Point-prevalence abstinence: never significantly different. Harms: anxiety 7.2% versus 3.1%; depressive symptoms 3.6% versus 0.8%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Do not let the 12-week headline travel without its 52-week shadow: smoking-cessation pharmacotherapy is judged on sustained abstinence, and this trial's own authors conclude that further research is required to determine the role of combination therapy. The result also does not compare the combination against combination nicotine replacement or against varenicline with behavioural support intensified — only against varenicline plus placebo. Tier C is set because the evidence is a single trial.
