shelves.title: Warfarin for pulmonary fibrosis increased deaths 14 to 3 — ACE-IPF was stopped early, closing the anticoagulation hypothesis
shelves.question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does anticoagulation with warfarin improve survival or slow progression versus placebo — or increase mortality?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anticoagulants/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis/drug therapy/mortality/physiopathology · International Normalized Ratio · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Failure · Warfarin/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — anticoagulating the lung's clotting cascade was a biologically plausible idea that its randomised test refuted in the worst direction: in ACE-IPF (Noth I et al., PMID: 22561965), patients with progressive idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and no other indication for anticoagulation were randomised to warfarin (target INR 2.0 to 3.0) or placebo, and the data and safety monitoring board stopped the trial after 145 of the planned 256 subjects were enrolled because of low probability of benefit and an increase in mortality on warfarin — 14 deaths versus 3 on placebo (P=0.005) at a mean follow-up of 28 weeks. The primary composite of death, hospitalisation, or a ≥10% absolute decline in forced vital capacity showed no benefit. Together with PANTHER-IPF (shelf #2796), this closes the era in which plausible non-antifibrotic pharmacology was given to IPF patients untested: both landmark attempts increased mortality. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): warfarin should not be used to treat idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis in patients who lack another indication for anticoagulation.

cards.headline: Noth 2012 (ACE-IPF): warfarin trial stopped early — 14 deaths on warfarin versus 3 on placebo (P=0.005), no benefit on the composite outcome
cards.summary: Noth 2012 (ACE-IPF): warfarin trial stopped early — 14 deaths on warfarin versus 3 on placebo (P=0.005), no benefit on the composite outcome
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Noth 2012, ACE-IPF)
cards.people: Patients with progressive idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and no other indication for anticoagulation, randomised double-blind 1:1 to warfarin targeting an international normalised ratio of 2.0 to 3.0 or matching placebo for a planned 48 weeks, with INR monitored by encrypted home point-of-care devices to preserve blinding; 145 of the planned 256 subjects were enrolled (72 warfarin, 73 placebo) when the study was stopped, with a mean follow-up of 28 weeks.
cards.result: The primary outcome was the composite of time to death, nonbleeding nonelective hospitalisation, or a 10% or greater absolute decline in forced vital capacity. The study did not show a benefit for warfarin. Because of a low probability of benefit and an increase in mortality in the warfarin group (14 warfarin versus 3 placebo deaths; P=0.005), the independent data and safety monitoring board recommended stopping the study early. The authors conclude that treatment with warfarin was associated with an increased risk of mortality in an IPF population who lacked other indications for anticoagulation.
cards.watchOut: The trial stopped at just over half its planned enrolment, so the mortality estimate rests on 17 deaths in total — the direction is clear and the safety board acted on it, but the size of the excess risk is imprecise, and the record's abstract does not report the composite outcome's event rates numerically. The verdict applies to warfarin given for IPF itself in patients without another anticoagulation indication; it says nothing about anticoagulating an IPF patient who develops atrial fibrillation or venous thromboembolism, where the indication changes the balance entirely.
cards.source: Noth I et al. A placebo-controlled randomized trial of warfarin in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2012. PMID: 22561965. cards.headline: Synthesis: the coagulation hypothesis in IPF met its randomised test and patients died more often — warfarin for IPF itself is closed

cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial, 145 patients enrolled of 256 planned, stopped early by its safety board — the entire record carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Deaths: 14 on warfarin versus 3 on placebo (P=0.005) at a mean follow-up of 28 weeks. Primary composite (death, hospitalisation, or ≥10% absolute FVC decline): no benefit shown. shelves.title: One big dose of liposomal amphotericin B for disseminated histoplasmosis: response looked comparable in a 118-person trial, but the authors themselves say a confirmatory trial is needed
shelves.question: In people with HIV and disseminated histoplasmosis, does a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin B achieve clinical response comparable to standard daily dosing, with less toxicity?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Histoplasmosis*/drug therapy · Antifungal Agents/adverse effects · HIV · Prospective Studies · Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome*/drug therapy · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions* · Amphotericin B
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the modern randomised trial (118 people with AIDS-related disseminated histoplasmosis) found day-14 clinical response of 84% with a single 10 mg/kg dose of liposomal amphotericin B, 69% with a two-dose regimen, and 74% with standard daily dosing for 2 weeks, with no significant difference (P=0.69); day-14 survival was 89.0%, 78.0%, and 92.1% respectively (P=0.82), and infusion, kidney, and laboratory toxicities were similar across arms. The authors state response may be non-inferior but a confirmatory phase III trial is needed — this trial did not prove non-inferiority. Supporting biology comes from an older comparison across two separate trials (Wheat 2001): liposomal amphotericin B and itraconazole produced similar clinical response (86% vs 85%), but fungemia cleared faster with liposomal amphotericin B (over 85% vs 53% culture-negative at 2 weeks; P=0.0008), and the Cochrane review of disseminated histoplasmosis treatment in HIV found liposomal amphotericin B may raise clinical success versus the deoxycholate form (risk ratio 1.46, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.11; low certainty) with less nephrotoxicity. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): single-dose induction looks comparable and was no more toxic in a small trial, but equivalence is a hypothesis awaiting a confirmatory trial, not a result. Tier C is set for that reason.

cards.headline: Pasqualotto 2023: single-dose liposomal amphotericin B — day-14 response 84% vs 74% on standard daily dosing, survival 89.0% vs 92.1%, neither significant
cards.summary: Pasqualotto 2023: single-dose liposomal amphotericin B — day-14 response 84% vs 74% on standard daily dosing, survival 89.0% vs 92.1%, neither significant
cards.type: Randomised multicentre open-label trial (Pasqualotto 2023)
cards.people: 118 people with HIV/AIDS-related disseminated histoplasmosis in a prospective randomised multicentre open-label trial, assigned to (i) a single dose of liposomal amphotericin B 10 mg/kg, (ii) 10 mg/kg on day 1 plus 5 mg/kg on day 3, or (iii) 3 mg/kg daily for 2 weeks (control), all followed by oral itraconazole therapy. Median CD4 counts and clinical presentations were similar between arms. The primary outcome was clinical response (resolution of fever and signs/symptoms attributable to histoplasmosis) at day 14.
cards.result: Day-14 clinical response was 84% for single-dose liposomal amphotericin B, 69% for the 2-dose regimen, and 74% for the control arm (P=0.69). Overall survival at day 14 was 89.0% (34/38) for single-dose, 78.0% (29/37) for 2-dose, and 92.1% (35/38) for control (P=0.82). Infusion-related toxicity, kidney toxicity at multiple time points, and frequencies of anaemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and liver toxicity were similar across arms. The authors conclude one-day induction was safe and may be non-inferior, but that a confirmatory phase III trial is needed; a single dose would cut drug-acquisition costs more than fourfold.
cards.watchOut: With about 38 patients per arm, the confidence intervals around both response and survival are wide enough to include clinically important harm — 'no significant difference' here is absence of evidence, not evidence of equivalence, and the numerically lowest survival was in an experimental arm (2-dose, 78.0%).
cards.source: Pasqualotto AC et al. Single High Dose of Liposomal Amphotericin B in Human Immunodeficiency Virus/AIDS-Related Disseminated Histoplasmosis: A Randomized Trial. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2023. PMID: 37232940. Registry ID: NCT05814432. cards.headline: Wheat 2001: liposomal amphotericin B and itraconazole gave similar clinical response (86% vs 85%) but fungemia cleared far faster with liposomal amphotericin B
cards.summary: Wheat 2001: liposomal amphotericin B and itraconazole gave similar clinical response (86% vs 85%) but fungemia cleared far faster with liposomal amphotericin B
cards.type: Comparison across two closed clinical trials (Wheat 2001)
cards.people: Patients with disseminated histoplasmosis and AIDS treated in two separate closed clinical trials — 51 receiving liposomal amphotericin B and 59 receiving itraconazole — compared for clearance of fungal burden by blood culture and blood and urine Histoplasma antigen.
cards.result: Clinical response rates were similar: 86% with liposomal amphotericin B (n=51) versus 85% with itraconazole (n=59). Among patients with positive blood cultures at enrolment, cultures were negative at 2 weeks in over 85% of the liposomal amphotericin B group versus 53% of the itraconazole group (P=0.0008). Median antigen levels at 2 weeks fell by 1.6 U in serum with liposomal amphotericin B versus 0.1 U with itraconazole (P=0.02), and by 2.1 U versus 0.2 U in urine (P=0.0005). The authors conclude the more rapid clearance of fungemia supports liposomal amphotericin B rather than itraconazole for initial treatment of moderately severe or severe histoplasmosis.
cards.watchOut: This is a cross-trial comparison, not a randomised head-to-head: the two groups were enrolled in separate studies, so the faster clearance could reflect differences in patients or era as well as the drug. Fungal burden is also a surrogate — clinical response, the patient-level outcome, was identical.
cards.source: Wheat LJ et al. Clearance of fungal burden during treatment of disseminated histoplasmosis with liposomal amphotericin B versus itraconazole. cards.headline: Murray 2020 (Cochrane): liposomal amphotericin B may improve clinical success versus deoxycholate amphotericin B (RR 1.46) with less kidney toxicity — low-certainty evidence
cards.summary: Murray 2020 (Cochrane): liposomal amphotericin B may improve clinical success versus deoxycholate amphotericin B (RR 1.46) with less kidney toxicity — low-certainty evidence
cards.type: Systematic review (Cochrane, Murray 2020)
cards.people: Cochrane review of treatment for progressive disseminated histoplasmosis in people living with HIV, searching to 20 March 2020; 17 individual studies were identified, eight judged at critical risk of bias and removed from analysis. Questions covered induction therapy, maintenance duration, and timing of antiretroviral therapy.
cards.result: For induction, one randomised trial compared liposomal with deoxycholate amphotericin B: liposomal amphotericin B may have higher clinical success rates (risk ratio 1.46, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.11; 1 study, 80 participants; low-certainty evidence) and lower rates of nephrotoxicity (risk ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.67; 1 study, 77 participants; high-certainty evidence). Evidence comparing amphotericin B formulations with azoles for induction was very low certainty. No eligible study compared maintenance durations, fluconazole performed poorly compared with other azoles, and the single antiretroviral-timing study had one death in seven early-arm participants and none in three late-arm participants.
cards.watchOut: The Cochrane induction conclusion rests on the same single small randomised trial it summarises (80 participants) — it organises the evidence but does not multiply it, and most other treatment questions in this disease had no eligible comparative evidence at all.
cards.source: Murray et al. Treating progressive disseminated histoplasmosis in people living with HIV. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2020. PMID: 32343003. cards.headline: Synthesis: single-dose induction was statistically indistinguishable from standard dosing in a 118-person trial — promising, explicitly unconfirmed
cards.summary: Synthesis: single-dose induction was statistically indistinguishable from standard dosing in a 118-person trial — promising, explicitly unconfirmed
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One randomised trial of liposomal amphotericin B dosing strategies (118 participants), one cross-trial fungal-clearance comparison (110 participants), and a Cochrane review whose induction evidence is one 80-participant trial.
cards.result: Day-14 response: 84% (single dose), 69% (2-dose), 74% (standard) (P=0.69); day-14 survival 89.0%, 78.0%, 92.1% (P=0.82); toxicities similar. Fungemia clearance at 2 weeks favoured liposomal amphotericin B over itraconazole (over 85% vs 53%; P=0.0008) with equal clinical response (86% vs 85%). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: The cost and access argument for a single dose is powerful in the Latin American settings where this disease concentrates — which is exactly why the confirmatory trial matters: adopting an unproven induction regimen on cost grounds, in patients with 8–22% two-week mortality, risks trading survival for savings on the basis of a null result in 118 patients. Tier C is set because the dosing question rests on one small trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pasqualotto AC et al. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2023 (PMID: 37232940); Wheat LJ et al. Antimicrobial agents and chemotherapy. 2001 (PMID: 11451696); Murray et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2020 (PMID: 32343003).

shelves.title: Talaromycosis in HIV: amphotericin B and itraconazole tied at 2 weeks, but 6-month deaths were 11.3% versus 21.0% — induction choice decides survival
shelves.question: In HIV-associated talaromycosis, is amphotericin B deoxycholate induction superior to itraconazole for 6-month mortality?
shelves.mesh: AIDS-Related Opportunistic Infections/drug therapy*/mortality · Administration, Oral · Adult · Amphotericin B/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Antifungal Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Creatinine/metabolism · Deoxycholic Acid/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Drug Combinations · Female · Humans · Induction Chemotherapy/adverse effects · Infusions, Intravenous/adverse effects · Itraconazole/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Male · Mycoses/drug therapy*/mortality · Talaromyces*/isolation & purification
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in IVAP, an open-label trial of 440 adults with HIV-associated talaromycosis, amphotericin B deoxycholate and itraconazole looked equal at the 2-week primary endpoint (death 6.5% vs 7.4%; absolute difference 0.9 percentage points, 95% CI −3.9 to 5.6; non-inferiority met) but diverged by 6 months: death 11.3% versus 21.0% (absolute difference 9.7 percentage points, 95% CI 2.8 to 16.6; P=0.006), with faster clinical resolution and fungal clearance and lower relapse and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome rates on amphotericin. A meta-analysis of 975 patients (only one randomised trial among eight studies) found the same direction: initial amphotericin B was associated with lower mortality than initial itraconazole (risk ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.90). The price of amphotericin was significantly more infusion reactions, renal failure, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and anaemia. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): amphotericin B induction saves lives at 6 months compared with itraconazole induction, at a real toxicity cost — start with amphotericin where it can be given and monitored. Tier C is set because the randomised evidence is a single trial.

cards.headline: Le 2017 (IVAP): 6-month death 11.3% on amphotericin B vs 21.0% on itraconazole (difference 9.7 points; P=0.006), despite a tied 2-week result
cards.summary: Le 2017 (IVAP): 6-month death 11.3% on amphotericin B vs 21.0% on itraconazole (difference 9.7 points; P=0.006), despite a tied 2-week result
cards.type: Randomised open-label noninferiority trial (IVAP, Le 2017)
cards.people: 440 HIV-infected adults with talaromycosis confirmed by microscopy or culture, randomised in an open-label noninferiority trial to intravenous amphotericin B deoxycholate 0.7 to 1.0 mg/kg/day (219 patients) or itraconazole capsules 600 mg/day for 3 days then 400 mg/day for 11 days (221 patients); thereafter all patients received maintenance itraconazole. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality at week 2; secondary outcomes included mortality at week 24, time to clinical resolution, early fungicidal activity, relapse, immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, and side effects.
cards.result: Risk of death at week 2 was 6.5% in the amphotericin group and 7.4% in the itraconazole group (absolute risk difference 0.9 percentage points; 95% CI −3.9 to 5.6; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Risk of death at week 24 was 11.3% in the amphotericin group and 21.0% in the itraconazole group (absolute risk difference 9.7 percentage points; 95% CI 2.8 to 16.6; P=0.006). Amphotericin was associated with significantly faster clinical resolution and fungal clearance and significantly lower rates of relapse and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome. Patients receiving amphotericin had significantly higher rates of infusion-related reactions, renal failure, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and anaemia.
cards.watchOut: A noninferiority trial whose headline flips by time horizon: itraconazole passed the 2-week noninferiority test and then lost on the outcome that matters, 6-month mortality. The trial was open-label and conducted where amphotericin monitoring was available; its toxicity burden (renal failure, electrolyte losses) is the main barrier to applying the result where monitoring is scarce.
cards.source: Le T et al. A Trial of Itraconazole or Amphotericin B for HIV-Associated Talaromycosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2017. PMID: 28614691. Registry ID: ISRCTN59144167. cards.headline: Sheng 2021 (meta-analysis): initial amphotericin B associated with lower mortality than initial itraconazole — risk ratio 0.61 across 975 patients
cards.summary: Sheng 2021 (meta-analysis): initial amphotericin B associated with lower mortality than initial itraconazole — risk ratio 0.61 across 975 patients
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Sheng 2021)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of initial antifungal treatment for talaromycosis: 8 studies and 975 patients in total, of which one was a randomised controlled trial and the rest retrospective studies; 582 patients were initiated with amphotericin B and 393 with itraconazole. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality.
cards.result: Among patients initiated with amphotericin B, 31 died (9.28% as reported); among those initiated with itraconazole, 54 died (14.00% as reported). Initial amphotericin B was associated with significantly reduced mortality compared with itraconazole (risk ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.90; P=0.01; I²=4%) — a 39% relative risk reduction alongside the reported absolute rates of 9.28% and 14.00%. In subgroups by region and in studies with sample size below 100, the advantage was not significant; in studies with sample size at least 100 it was (risk ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.92; P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: Seven of the eight studies are retrospective, so treatment choice was confounded by severity and availability — sicker patients may have been channelled to either drug. The pooled result agrees with the one randomised trial, which is reassuring, but the meta-analysis adds breadth rather than independent randomised proof.
cards.source: Sheng et al. Efficacy of different antifungal drugs as initial treatment for patients with talaromycosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal de mycologie medicale. 2021. PMID: 33370708. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: amphotericin B induction wins on 6-month mortality in the trial (11.3% vs 21.0%) and in the pooled literature (risk ratio 0.61), at a higher toxicity price
cards.summary: Synthesis: amphotericin B induction wins on 6-month mortality in the trial (11.3% vs 21.0%) and in the pooled literature (risk ratio 0.61), at a higher toxicity price
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One randomised trial of 440 adults with HIV-associated talaromycosis (IVAP) plus a meta-analysis of 975 patients across eight studies.
cards.result: Week-2 death: 6.5% vs 7.4% (non-inferiority met for itraconazole). Week-24 death: 11.3% vs 21.0% (absolute difference 9.7 points, 95% CI 2.8 to 16.6; P=0.006). Meta-analysis mortality risk ratio 0.61 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.90) favouring initial amphotericin B. Toxicity (infusion reactions, renal failure, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, anaemia) significantly higher with amphotericin. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Judging induction therapy at 2 weeks would have produced the wrong answer in this disease — the mortality separation is late, driven by relapse and slower fungal clearance on itraconazole. Where amphotericin B deoxycholate cannot be monitored safely, the trial's net benefit may not transfer. Tier C is set because the randomised evidence is a single trial.

shelves.title: Steroids for moderate-to-severe Pneumocystis pneumonia in HIV: 31-day deaths 11% versus 23% in the 1990 trial that set the standard of care
shelves.question: In patients with moderate-to-severe Pneumocystis pneumonia and HIV, do adjunctive corticosteroids reduce mortality and respiratory failure versus antibiotics alone?
shelves.mesh: Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome/complications* · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/administration & dosage*/therapeutic use · Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Multivariate Analysis · Pneumonia, Pneumocystis/drug therapy*/mortality · Prednisone/administration & dosage · Prospective Studies · Random Allocation · Recurrence · Respiratory Insufficiency/drug therapy/etiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — in the California Collaborative Treatment Group trial (Bozzette 1990), 333 patients with AIDS and Pneumocystis pneumonia were randomised to early adjunctive corticosteroids or standard therapy alone. Among patients with confirmed or presumed pneumonia, cumulative risk at 31 days was lower with corticosteroids for respiratory failure (0.14 vs 0.30; P=0.004) and for death (0.11 vs 0.23; P=0.009) — absolute reductions of 16 and 12 percentage points — and death within 84 days was 0.16 versus 0.26 (P=0.026); intention-to-treat analysis of the entire cohort confirmed the findings. Benefit could not be demonstrated in mild disease (oxygenation ratio above 350, equivalent to arterial oxygen above 75 torr on room air), and corticosteroid patients had more localised herpetic lesions (26% vs 15%; P=0.04) without excess other infections or neoplasms. The NIH-University of California expert panel's consensus statement, published alongside, formalised corticosteroids as adjunctive therapy for this condition. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): early adjunctive corticosteroids reduce respiratory failure and death in moderate-to-severe Pneumocystis pneumonia in HIV — a foundational result that has structured practice since 1990, scoped to moderate-to-severe disease.

cards.headline: Bozzette 1990: early corticosteroids cut 31-day respiratory failure (0.14 vs 0.30) and death (0.11 vs 0.23) in AIDS-related Pneumocystis pneumonia
cards.summary: Bozzette 1990: early corticosteroids cut 31-day respiratory failure (0.14 vs 0.30) and death (0.11 vs 0.23) in AIDS-related Pneumocystis pneumonia
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Bozzette 1990, California Collaborative Treatment Group)
cards.people: 333 patients with AIDS and Pneumocystis pneumonia receiving standard treatment at multiple centres, randomly assigned to corticosteroids (beginning with the equivalent of prednisone 40 mg twice daily) or no additional therapy, in an unblinded prospective trial. Primary endpoints were respiratory failure (hypoxemia ratio below 75, intubation, or death), death, and dose-limiting toxicity of the initial standard therapy; the main analysis covered 225 patients with confirmed and 26 with presumed pneumocystis pneumonia.
cards.result: Patients assigned to corticosteroids had a lower cumulative risk at 31 days of respiratory failure (0.14 vs 0.30, P=0.004) and of death (0.11 vs 0.23, P=0.009), and a lower risk of death within 84 days (0.16 vs 0.26, P=0.026). The frequency of dose-limiting toxicity of standard therapy was similar in the two groups, and intention-to-treat analyses of the entire cohort confirmed the findings. Clinical benefit could not be demonstrated for patients with mild disease (hypoxemia ratio greater than 350, equivalent to a partial pressure of oxygen greater than 75 torr on room air). Corticosteroid patients had an excess of localised herpetic lesions (26% vs 15%, P=0.04) but not of other infections or neoplasms.
cards.watchOut: An unblinded 1990 trial from the pre-antiretroviral era, when baseline mortality was far higher than in treated HIV today — the absolute gains (12–16 points) belong to that risk context, even though the relative logic of blunting inflammatory lung injury still underpins practice. The mild-disease subgroup showed no demonstrable benefit, so the result must not be generalised to mild pneumonia.
cards.source: Bozzette SA et al. A controlled trial of early adjunctive treatment with corticosteroids for Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia in the acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. California Collaborative Treatment Group. The New England journal of medicine. 1990. PMID: 2233917. Registry ID: none in the record. the main analysis covered 225 patients with confirmed and 26 with presumed pneumocystis pneumonia. patients assigned to corticosteroids had a lower cumulative risk at 31 days of respiratory failure (0.14 vs 0.30, p=0.004) and of death (0.11 vs 0.23, p=0.009), and a lower risk of death within 84 days (0.16 vs 0.26, p=0.026). the frequency of dose-limiting toxicity of standard therapy was similar in the two groups, and intention-to-treat analyses of the entire cohort confirmed the findings. clinical benefit could not be demonstrated for patients with mild disease (hypoxemia ratio greater than 350, equivalent to a partial pressure of oxygen greater than 75 torr on room air). corticosteroid patients had an excess of localised herpetic lesions (26% vs 15%, p=0.04) but not of other infections or neoplasms. an unblinded 1990 trial from the pre-antiretroviral era, when baseline mortality was far higher than in treated hiv today — the absolute gains (12–16 points) belong to that risk context, even though the relative logic of blunting inflammatory lung injury still underpins practice. the mild-disease subgroup showed no demonstrable benefit, so the result must not be generalised to mild pneumonia. bozzette sa et al. a controlled trial of early adjunctive treatment with corticosteroids for pneumocystis carinii pneumonia in the acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. california collaborative treatment group. the new england journal of medicine. 1990. pmid: 2233917. registry id: none in the record. mesh: acquired immunodeficiency syndrome/complications* · adrenal cortex hormones/administration & dosage*/therapeutic use · adult · female · humans · male · multivariate analysis · pneumonia, pneumocystis/drug therapy*/mortality · prednisone/administration & dosage · prospective studies · random allocation · recurrence · respiratory insufficiency/drug therapy/etiology

cards.people: Consensus statement of the National Institutes of Health-University of California Expert Panel for Corticosteroids as Adjunctive Therapy for Pneumocystis Pneumonia, published in 1990 alongside the randomised evidence of that period. The PubMed record for this statement carries no abstract text.
cards.result: No abstract or numeric results are present in this record, so no figures are carded from it. Its role in this shelf is documentary: the contemporaneous expert consensus, issued by the NIH-University of California panel in the same journal issue period as the Bozzette trial, is the mechanism by which the trial evidence summarised by the panel was converted into a practice recommendation for adjunctive corticosteroid therapy in Pneumocystis pneumonia in the acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.
cards.watchOut: A consensus statement is expert synthesis, not primary evidence — it is carded here to document how the recommendation formed, and all numbers on this shelf come from the Bozzette trial record, not from this statement. Readers should not cite the panel as independent confirmation of the trial it was convened to evaluate.

shelves.title: Delamanid for multidrug-resistant TB: culture conversion at 2 months rose from 29.6% to 45.4% at the 100 mg dose — a surrogate gain with a QT-prolongation price
shelves.question: In multidrug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis, does adding delamanid to an optimised background regimen improve sputum culture conversion at 2 months?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antitubercular Agents/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mycobacterium tuberculosis/growth & development · Nitroimidazoles/adverse effects · Oxazoles/adverse effects · Sputum/microbiology · Survival Analysis · Tuberculosis, Multidrug-Resistant/drug therapy · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the multinational randomised trial (Gler MT et al., PMID: 22670901), 481 patients with pulmonary multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (nearly all HIV-negative) received delamanid 100 mg twice daily, delamanid 200 mg twice daily, or placebo for 2 months on top of a WHO-guideline background regimen. Sputum culture conversion in liquid broth at 2 months was 45.4 percent with 100 mg (P=0.008 versus placebo), 41.9 percent with 200 mg (P=0.04), and 29.6 percent with placebo — an absolute gain of about 16 and 12 percentage points respectively, with similar findings on solid medium. Most adverse events were mild to moderate and evenly distributed, but QT prolongation on electrocardiography was reported significantly more frequently with delamanid, though no clinical events due to QT prolongation were observed. A later systematic review and meta-analysis of bedaquiline and delamanid studies (Ahmed SH et al., PMID: 38296395) found a pooled 6-month culture conversion proportion of 0.849 in delamanid cohorts and a pooled QTc prolongation incidence of 0.344, but those pooled proportions come largely from non-randomised cohorts and cannot substitute for a mortality or cure end point. Two months of a surrogate marker, in one trial, is what this shelf has. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): delamanid plausibly improves early culture conversion as part of a multidrug regimen, with cardiac monitoring owed for the QT signal. Tier C is set because the evidence is a single trial on a surrogate outcome.

cards.headline: Gler 2012 (NEJM): delamanid 100 mg twice daily lifted 2-month culture conversion to 45.4% versus 29.6% on placebo (P=0.008); 200 mg gave 41.9% (P=0.04) — no dose advantage, more QT prolongation
cards.summary: Gler 2012 (NEJM): delamanid 100 mg twice daily lifted 2-month culture conversion to 45.4% versus 29.6% on placebo (P=0.008); 200 mg gave 41.9% (P=0.04) — no dose advantage, more QT prolongation
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Gler 2012)
cards.people: 481 patients with pulmonary multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, nearly all HIV-negative, in a multinational randomised placebo-controlled trial: delamanid 100 mg twice daily (161 patients), delamanid 200 mg twice daily (160), or placebo (160), each for 2 months added to a background regimen built to WHO guidelines. Conversion meant five or more consecutive negative cultures, assessed weekly in liquid broth and on solid medium.
cards.result: Sputum culture conversion in liquid broth at 2 months: 45.4 percent with delamanid 100 mg twice daily versus 29.6 percent with placebo (P=0.008), and 41.9 percent with 200 mg twice daily (P=0.04); results were similar on solid medium. Most adverse events were mild to moderate and evenly distributed across groups. QT prolongation was reported significantly more frequently in the delamanid groups, although no clinical events due to QT prolongation were observed.
cards.watchOut: Culture conversion at 2 months is a surrogate: the trial was not powered for cure, relapse, or mortality, treatment lasted only 2 months within much longer MDR regimens, and almost no participants had HIV — the population in whom MDR-TB is often deadliest. The flat dose-response (200 mg no better than 100 mg) and the QT signal both argue for the lower dose with monitoring.
cards.source: Gler MT et al. Delamanid for multidrug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22670901. Registry ID: NCT00685360. cards.headline: Ahmed 2024 (systematic review and meta-analysis): pooled 6-month culture conversion 0.849 in delamanid cohorts — but pooled QTc prolongation 0.344, from mostly non-randomised data
cards.summary: Ahmed 2024 (systematic review and meta-analysis): pooled 6-month culture conversion 0.849 in delamanid cohorts — but pooled QTc prolongation 0.344, from mostly non-randomised data
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Ahmed 2024)
cards.people: Twenty-one studies of bedaquiline, delamanid, or both in drug-resistant tuberculosis: 2,477 patients received bedaquiline, 937 delamanid, and 169 the combination; outcomes pooled with a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model.
cards.result: Pooled culture conversion at 6 months was 0.801 for bedaquiline, 0.849 for delamanid (p=0.059), and 0.823 for the combination. Pooled all-cause mortality at 6 months was 0.074 in the bedaquiline cohort, 0.031 in the delamanid cohort, and 0.172 in the combined cohort. QTc prolongation incidence was 0.163 with bedaquiline, 0.344 with delamanid, and 0.340 with the combination. Adverse event incidence in the delamanid cohort ranged from 13.2 percent to 86.2 percent across studies.
cards.watchOut: These are pooled single-arm proportions, not comparative effects — cohorts differ in background regimens, resistance patterns and severity, so the delamanid figures cannot be read as delamanid's causal contribution. The QTc figure (0.344) pools varying definitions and monitoring intensity; it confirms the signal from the trial rather than quantifying an individual's risk.
cards.source: Ahmed SH et al. Efficacy and safety of bedaquiline and delamanid in the treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis in adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Indian Journal of Tuberculosis. 2024. PMID: 38296395. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real surrogate benefit in one trial, a consistent QT warning across the literature, and no mortality evidence yet on this shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real surrogate benefit in one trial, a consistent QT warning across the literature, and no mortality evidence yet on this shelf
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One randomised trial of 481 patients (Gler 2012) plus a 21-study systematic review and meta-analysis of bedaquiline and delamanid in drug-resistant TB (Ahmed 2024).
cards.result: Two-month conversion (liquid broth): 45.4 percent (100 mg) and 41.9 percent (200 mg) versus 29.6 percent on placebo. Six-month pooled conversion in delamanid cohorts: 0.849. QT prolongation: significantly more frequent in the trial's delamanid arms; pooled QTc prolongation incidence 0.344 in the review. Mortality and cure: not established by the randomised record carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Delamanid is never used alone — every number here is for delamanid added to a multidrug background regimen, and the background regimen does most of the work. Do not let the 6-month pooled conversion proportion (0.849) be quoted as a trial result; it mixes cohorts without controls. Tier C is set for the single-trial, surrogate-end-point base.

shelves.title: Aspirin for tuberculous meningitis: infarct-or-death in 15.8% on high-dose aspirin versus 28.9% on placebo in a 120-patient phase 2 trial — a trend, with a significant signal only in confirmed cases
shelves.question: In tuberculous meningitis, does adjunctive aspirin reduce new cerebral infarction and mortality versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antitubercular Agents/administration & dosage · Aspirin/administration & dosage · Combined Modality Therapy/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions/epidemiology · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents/administration & dosage · HIV Infections/complications · Humans · Male · Mental Disorders/epidemiology · Middle Aged · Placebos/administration & dosage · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome · Tuberculosis, Meningeal/drug therapy
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the phase 2 trial (Mai NTH et al., PMID: 29482717) randomised 120 HIV-uninfected adults with tuberculous meningitis to aspirin 81 mg, aspirin 1000 mg, or placebo daily for the first 60 days, all with anti-tuberculosis drugs and dexamethasone. The primary efficacy outcome — new brain infarction on MRI or death by 60 days — occurred in 11 of 38 (28.9 percent) on placebo, 8 of 36 (22.2 percent) on aspirin 81 mg, and 6 of 38 (15.8 percent) on aspirin 1000 mg (p=0.40): a dose-ordered trend that is not significant. The safety outcome (gastrointestinal or cerebral bleeding by 60 days) occurred in 13.9 percent on placebo and 22.9 percent and 20.0 percent on the two aspirin doses (p=0.59). A pre-planned subgroup analysis found a significant interaction with diagnostic category, with a possible reduction in microbiologically confirmed disease (34.4 percent on placebo versus 14.8 percent and 10.7 percent on aspirin; p=0.06), and spinal-fluid analysis showed dose-dependent thromboxane suppression. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Rizvi I et al., PMID: 31512620; 4 trials, 546 patients) found aspirin did not significantly reduce mortality (risk ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.02; low-quality evidence) but did reduce new infarctions (risk ratio 0.52, 0.29 to 0.92; moderate-quality evidence). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): aspirin may prevent infarctions in tuberculous meningitis — the phase 3 trial the phase 2 authors call for is the test that matters. Tier C is set for the small phase 2 base.

cards.headline: Mai 2018 (phase 2 RCT): new infarction or death by 60 days in 28.9% on placebo, 22.2% on aspirin 81 mg, 15.8% on aspirin 1000 mg (p=0.40) — dose-ordered but not significant; bleeding numerically higher on aspirin
cards.summary: Mai 2018 (phase 2 RCT): new infarction or death by 60 days in 28.9% on placebo, 22.2% on aspirin 81 mg, 15.8% on aspirin 1000 mg (p=0.40) — dose-ordered but not significant; bleeding numerically higher on aspirin
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised placebo-controlled trial (Mai 2018)
cards.people: 120 HIV-uninfected adults with tuberculous meningitis in Vietnam, randomised to placebo (41), aspirin 81 mg/day (39), or aspirin 1000 mg/day (40) for the first 60 days, all receiving anti-tuberculosis drugs and dexamethasone. TBM was microbiologically proven in 92 of 120 (76.7 percent), and baseline imaging already showed at least one infarct in 40 of 114 (35.1 percent).
cards.result: Primary efficacy outcome (new MRI-confirmed brain infarction or death by 60 days): 11/38 (28.9 percent) on placebo, 8/36 (22.2 percent) on aspirin 81 mg, 6/38 (15.8 percent) on aspirin 1000 mg (p=0.40). Primary safety outcome (gastrointestinal or cerebral bleeding by 60 days): 5/36 (13.9 percent) on placebo, 8/35 (22.9 percent) on 81 mg, 8/40 (20.0 percent) on 1000 mg (p=0.59). In the planned subgroup of microbiologically confirmed TBM, events were 11/32 (34.4 percent) on placebo versus 4/27 (14.8 percent) on 81 mg and 3/28 (10.7 percent) on 1000 mg (p=0.06), with a significant treatment-by-diagnosis interaction (P for heterogeneity 0.01). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed aspirin dose-dependent inhibition of thromboxane A2 and upregulation of pro-resolving protectins.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2 trial of 120 patients with a composite imaging outcome: the denominators shift between analyses (missing MRI data), the headline comparison is non-significant, and the most encouraging result sits in a subgroup. HIV-infected patients — a large share of TBM worldwide — were excluded. The bleeding percentages, though non-significant, lean the wrong way and bound any enthusiasm until phase 3.

cards.summary: Rizvi 2019 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 4 trials, 546 patients): aspirin reduced new infarctions (risk ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.92) but not mortality (0.66, 0.42 to 1.02)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Rizvi 2019)
cards.people: Four randomised trials including 546 patients with tuberculous meningitis in whom aspirin was added to anti-tuberculosis regimens, identified from PubMed, the Cochrane Central Register and SCOPUS to September 2018; dichotomous outcomes pooled as risk ratios with a random-effects model and graded with GRADE.
cards.result: The addition of aspirin to anti-tuberculosis drug regimens did not significantly reduce mortality (risk ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.02; low-quality evidence) but significantly reduced the risk of new infarctions (risk ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.92; moderate-quality evidence). Aspirin did not differ from placebo on the adverse event outcome.
cards.watchOut: Four small trials with differing aspirin doses, populations and background steroid use; the mortality interval (0.42 to 1.02) sits just across no-effect, so a modest mortality benefit remains possible but unproven. Infarction ascertainment by imaging varies across trials and is vulnerable to who survived to be scanned.

cards.result: Infarction or death by 60 days: 28.9 percent (placebo) versus 22.2 percent (aspirin 81 mg) versus 15.8 percent (aspirin 1000 mg), p=0.40. shelves.title: Augmentation therapy in severe alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: lung density fell more slowly at total lung capacity (p=0.03) but the combined primary endpoint missed (p=0.06) — one trial, a CT surrogate, and density never regained
shelves.question: In adults with severe alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and emphysema, does weekly intravenous alpha-1 proteinase inhibitor (augmentation therapy) slow loss of lung density compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume/drug effects/physiology · Functional Residual Capacity/drug effects/physiology · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Lung/diagnostic imaging/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Pulmonary Emphysema/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy/etiology/physiopathology · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · Total Lung Capacity/drug effects/physiology · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult · alpha 1-Antitrypsin/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · alpha 1-Antitrypsin Deficiency/complications/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy/physiopathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — biologically coherent, directionally consistent, and statistically fragile. In RAPID (Chapman KR et al., PMID: 26026936), the combined primary endpoint — annual lung-density loss at total lung capacity (TLC) and functional residual capacity (FRC) together — did not reach significance: −1.50 versus −2.12 g/L per year, difference 0.62 g/L per year (95% CI −0.02 to 1.26), p=0.06. The TLC measure alone did: difference 0.74 (0.06 to 1.42), p=0.03; FRC alone did not (p=0.18). The open-label extension (McElvaney NG et al., PMID: 27916480) showed the delayed-start group's loss rate falling from −2.26 to −1.26 g/L per year once they switched to active treatment, while the early-start group's benefit persisted to 48 months — and lost density was never recovered, which argues for early treatment if treatment is given at all. The endpoint throughout is CT lung density, a surrogate: no trial here shows fewer exacerbations, better breathlessness, or longer life. Treatment-emergent adverse events were similar between groups in RAPID. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): augmentation probably slows emphysema progression on imaging; what that buys a patient, and at what point in the disease, remains inference. Tier C is set because the randomised base is a single trial.

cards.headline: Chapman 2015 (RAPID): combined density-loss endpoint missed (difference 0.62 g/L/yr, p=0.06); TLC alone positive (0.74, p=0.03), FRC alone null (p=0.18)
cards.summary: Chapman 2015 (RAPID): combined density-loss endpoint missed (difference 0.62 g/L/yr, p=0.06); TLC alone positive (0.74, p=0.03), FRC alone null (p=0.18)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial (Chapman 2015, RAPID)
cards.people: 180 non-smokers aged 18–65 with severe alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (serum <11 μM) and FEV1 35–70% predicted, at 28 centres in 13 countries, randomised to intravenous alpha-1 proteinase inhibitor 60 mg/kg weekly (n=93) or placebo (n=87) for 24 months; 92 and 85 were analysed.
cards.result: Annual lung-density loss at TLC and FRC combined: −1.50 g/L per year (SE 0.22) on treatment versus −2.12 (0.24) on placebo — difference 0.62 (95% CI −0.02 to 1.26), p=0.06. At TLC alone: −1.45 versus −2.19, difference 0.74 (0.06 to 1.42), p=0.03. At FRC alone: −1.54 versus −2.02, difference 0.48 (−0.22 to 1.18), p=0.18. Treatment-emergent adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The headline depends on which lung volume you read: the pre-specified combined primary endpoint was not significant, and a trial that needs its secondary decomposition to cross p=0.05 is a trial whose result is fragile. CT density is a validated progression marker in this disease but remains a surrogate for how a patient feels, functions, or survives.

cards.headline: McElvaney 2017 (RAPID-OLE): after switching from placebo, the delayed group's density loss slowed from −2.26 to −1.26 g/L/yr — but the two lost years were never recovered
cards.summary: McElvaney 2017 (RAPID-OLE): after switching from placebo, the delayed group's density loss slowed from −2.26 to −1.26 g/L/yr — but the two lost years were never recovered
cards.type: Open-label extension trial (McElvaney 2017, RAPID-OLE)
cards.people: 140 patients from RAPID who entered the 2-year open-label extension at 22 hospitals in 11 countries outside the USA — 76 early-start (active treatment throughout) and 64 delayed-start (placebo in RAPID, then active) — all receiving alpha-1 proteinase inhibitor 60 mg/kg weekly; the record names the products used as Zemaira or Respreeza (CSL Behring).
cards.result: During RAPID (months 0–24), density loss at TLC was −1.51 g/L per year in the early-start group versus −2.26 in the delayed-start group. During the extension (months 24–48), the delayed-start group's rate fell to −1.26 g/L per year on treatment, while the early-start group's rate was unchanged (−1.51 to −1.63), so efficacy was sustained to month 48. Lost lung density was never recovered in either group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, no placebo group, and extension populations are selected for tolerance and survival. The delayed-start 'catch-down in rate but never in level' pattern supports a real biological effect on progression; it is not randomised proof, and it still speaks only to CT density.
cards.source: McElvaney NG et al. Long-term efficacy and safety of α1 proteinase inhibitor treatment for emphysema caused by severe α1 antitrypsin deficiency: an open-label extension trial (RAPID-OLE). The Lancet Respiratory Medicine. 2017. PMID: 27916480. Registry ID: NCT00670007. cards.headline: Synthesis: imaging progression probably slowed; patient-important benefit inferred, not shown
cards.summary: Synthesis: imaging progression probably slowed; patient-important benefit inferred, not shown
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One 180-patient randomised trial over 24 months and its 140-patient open-label extension to 48 months — the controlled record for augmentation therapy in severe alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency emphysema.
cards.result: CT lung density: combined endpoint difference 0.62 g/L per year (p=0.06); TLC difference 0.74 (p=0.03); extension shows rate reduction on switching to treatment and no recovery of lost density. Symptoms, exacerbations, quality of life, mortality: no demonstrated differences in this record. Safety: treatment-emergent adverse events similar to placebo in the randomised phase. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Weekly intravenous therapy for years, at substantial cost, rests here on a single trial whose primary analysis landed at p=0.06. Clinicians who cite RAPID as proof should cite the whole result — including the miss — and patients should hear that the measured benefit is slower loss on a scan, with earlier starting favoured because lost lung does not come back. Tier C is set for the single-trial base.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chapman KR et al. The Lancet. 2015 (PMID: 26026936); McElvaney NG et al. The Lancet Respiratory Medicine. 2017 (PMID: 27916480).

shelves.title: Treating insomnia with digital CBT-I (Sleepio) also eases anxiety: effect g 0.39–0.44, with 84% of the anxiety gain mediated by better sleep
shelves.question: In people with insomnia and comorbid anxiety, does digital CBT-I (Sleepio) improve anxiety outcomes as well as sleep versus control?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/therapy · Anxiety/therapy · Anxiety Disorders/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Comorbidity · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooling individual data from 2,172 people with insomnia and clinically significant anxiety in two large Sleepio trials, digital CBT-I beat control on insomnia (Hedges' g 0.77–0.81) and on anxiety (g 0.39–0.44, both p<0.001) at post-treatment and follow-up, and 84% of the follow-up anxiety improvement was mediated by the earlier sleep improvement. The catch: participants had anxiety symptoms, not a formal anxiety disorder diagnosis, and the analysis was run by authors employed by or consulting for the company that sells Sleepio. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): digital CBT-I for insomnia produces a moderate knock-on reduction in anxiety symptoms, apparently by fixing sleep first.

cards.headline: Henry 2023: digital CBT-I beat control on anxiety (g 0.39–0.44) and insomnia (g 0.77–0.81); 84% of the anxiety effect mediated by sleep improvement
cards.summary: Henry 2023: digital CBT-I beat control on anxiety (g 0.39–0.44) and insomnia (g 0.77–0.81); 84% of the anxiety effect mediated by sleep improvement
cards.type: Individual-participant-data mediation analysis of two RCTs (Henry 2023, OASIS and DIALS)
cards.people: 2,172 participants with insomnia disorder and clinically significant anxiety symptoms from two randomised trials of digital CBT-I (Sleepio) versus usual care or sleep-hygiene education, assessed at baseline, post-intervention (week 8 or 10) and follow-up (week 22 or 24).
cards.result: Digital CBT-I was superior to control for insomnia (Hedges' g range 0.77–0.81; both p<0.001) and anxiety symptoms (g range 0.39–0.44; both p<0.001) at all time points. Reductions in anxiety at follow-up were mediated by post-intervention sleep improvement (% mediated = 84%). No variable moderated the treatment effect on anxiety.
cards.watchOut: This is a secondary mediation analysis, not a trial randomised for anxiety; participants had clinically significant anxiety symptoms without a formal anxiety disorder diagnosis, and most authors were employed by, shareholders in, or consultants to Big Health, the maker of Sleepio.
cards.source: Henry AL et al. Does treating insomnia with digital cognitive behavioural therapy (Sleepio) mediate improvements in anxiety for those with insomnia and comorbid anxiety? An analysis using individual participant data from two large randomised controlled trials. Journal of Affective Disorders. 2023. PMID: 37390923. Registry ID: ISRCTN60530898, ISRCTN61272251. shelves.title: Acupuncture for insomnia: better scores on subjective sleep scales in low-quality trials, objective sleep unproven — an umbrella review and an electroacupuncture meta-analysis agree on the caveats
shelves.question: In chronic insomnia, does acupuncture improve sleep quality versus sham acupuncture or no treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Melatonin/therapeutic use · Sleep · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/therapy · Systematic Reviews as Topic · Meta-Analysis as Topic · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — an umbrella review of 15 systematic reviews found acupuncture significantly improved subjective sleep quality and insomnia severity, but effects on objectively measured sleep were inconclusive and the quality of the underlying studies was rated low. A 2024 meta-analysis of electroacupuncture (31 trials, 2,226 subjects) found a higher clinical response rate than mixed controls (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.16–1.27) and a PSQI advantage of −3.23 points (−4.29 to −2.17), with no significant difference in adverse events (RR 1.48, 0.91–2.40) — but its trials were single-centre, small, and some of poor quality, and its controls mixed sham, no treatment, usual care and ordinary acupuncture. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): people report sleeping better after acupuncture; whether the needles beat a credible sham on objective sleep is not established.

cards.headline: Ell 2023 umbrella review: acupuncture improved subjective sleep quality and insomnia severity across 15 reviews; objective outcomes inconclusive, study quality low
cards.summary: Ell 2023 umbrella review: acupuncture improved subjective sleep quality and insomnia severity across 15 reviews; objective outcomes inconclusive, study quality low
cards.type: Systematic umbrella review (Ell 2023)
cards.people: 15 eligible systematic reviews and (network) meta-analyses of randomised trials of complementary and alternative treatments versus waiting-list or placebo in adults with insomnia disorder, from 391 records searched to December 2022.
cards.result: Acupuncture, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation and mind-body exercises significantly improved sleep quality and insomnia severity, but effects on objectively assessed outcomes were inconclusive. Melatonin reduced self-reported and objectively assessed sleep onset latency; light exposure and valerian did not significantly improve sleep outcomes. Overall, the quality of studies was rated as low, and results indicate alternative treatments are effective mostly on subjective outcomes.
cards.watchOut: An umbrella review inherits every weakness of the reviews beneath it: small, largely unblinded or sham-weak trials, mostly from one research tradition, with publication bias expected; subjective scales are exactly where expectancy effects land.

cards.search: ell 2023 umbrella review: acupuncture improved subjective sleep quality and insomnia severity across 15 reviews; objective outcomes inconclusive, study quality low ell 2023 umbrella review: acupuncture improved subjective sleep quality and insomnia severity across 15 reviews; objective outcomes inconclusive, study quality low in chronic insomnia, does acupuncture improve sleep quality versus sham acupuncture or no treatment? systematic umbrella review (ell 2023) 15 eligible systematic reviews and (network) meta-analyses of randomised trials of complementary and alternative treatments versus waiting-list or placebo in adults with insomnia disorder, from 391 records searched to december 2022. acupuncture, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation and mind-body exercises significantly improved sleep quality and insomnia severity, but effects on objectively assessed outcomes were inconclusive. melatonin reduced self-reported and objectively assessed sleep onset latency; light exposure and valerian did not significantly improve sleep outcomes. overall, the quality of studies was rated as low, and results indicate alternative treatments are effective mostly on subjective outcomes. an umbrella review inherits every weakness of the reviews beneath it: small, largely unblinded or sham-weak trials, mostly from one research tradition, with publication bias expected; subjective scales are exactly where expectancy effects land. ell j et al. complementary and alternative treatments for insomnia disorder: a systematic umbrella review. journal of sleep research. 2023. pmid: 37527850. mesh: adult · humans · cognitive behavioral therapy/methods · melatonin/therapeutic use · sleep · sleep initiation and maintenance disorders/therapy · systematic reviews as topic · meta-analysis as topic · randomized controlled trials as topic

cards.headline: Xu 2024: electroacupuncture response rate RR 1.21 and PSQI −3.23 versus mixed controls across 31 trials (2,226 patients) — small, single-centre, partly poor-quality trials
cards.summary: Xu 2024: electroacupuncture response rate RR 1.21 and PSQI −3.23 versus mixed controls across 31 trials (2,226 patients) — small, single-centre, partly poor-quality trials
cards.type: Meta-analysis (Xu 2024)
cards.people: 31 randomised trials with 2,226 subjects comparing electroacupuncture with sham acupuncture, no treatment, usual care or general acupuncture for insomnia, searched to January 2023.
cards.result: Electroacupuncture was more effective than the pooled control group (response rate RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.16–1.27), with PSQI reduced by a weighted mean difference of −3.23 points (−4.29 to −2.17; p<0.001) after treatment and at follow-up. Adverse events did not differ significantly (RR 1.48, 0.91–2.40; p=0.117). Seven to nine weeks of treatment showed the best efficacy in regression analysis (p<0.05).
cards.watchOut: Pooling sham-controlled trials with no-treatment and usual-care controls inflates the estimate — the sham-only contrast is the honest one and is not separated here; the authors themselves note single-centre, small, partly poor-quality trials.
cards.source: Xu HY et al. Efficacy and safety of electroacupuncture for insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Integrative Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38871592. shelves.title: Five days of prednisone matched 14 days in COPD exacerbations: re-exacerbation 37.2% versus 38.4% at six months — with less than half the steroid dose
shelves.question: In patients hospitalised with a COPD exacerbation, is a 5-day course of systemic glucocorticoids non-inferior to a conventional 14-day course for re-exacerbation within six months?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prednisone/administration & dosage · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/drug therapy/physiopathology · Respiratory Function Tests · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the shorter course is as effective and halves exposure. In the REDUCE trial (314 patients presenting to emergency departments with acute COPD exacerbation), 5 days of prednisone 40 mg was noninferior to 14 days for re-exacerbation within 180 days: hazard ratio 0.95 (90% CI 0.70 to 1.29), with estimated re-exacerbation rates of 37.2% on 5 days versus 38.4% on 14 days (difference −1.2%, 95% CI −12.2% to 9.8%), while mean cumulative prednisone dose was 379 mg versus 793 mg (p<0.001). A Cochrane review of eight trials (582 participants) likewise found no difference between courses of seven or fewer days and longer courses in treatment failure (odds ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.46), relapse (OR 1.04, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.56), adverse events, or hospital stay. The honest catch: adverse reactions such as hyperglycaemia and hypertension did not actually fall in REDUCE despite the halved dose, and the pooled evidence was graded moderate quality for imprecision — the gain proven is equal efficacy with less drug, not fewer side effects in the short term. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): five days of systemic glucocorticoid treats a hospitalised COPD exacerbation as well as 14 days, at roughly half the cumulative exposure.

cards.headline: Leuppi 2013 (REDUCE): re-exacerbation within 180 days in 35.9% on 5 days versus 36.8% on 14 days of prednisone — noninferior, at 379 mg versus 793 mg cumulative dose
cards.summary: Leuppi 2013 (REDUCE): re-exacerbation within 180 days in 35.9% on 5 days versus 36.8% on 14 days of prednisone — noninferior, at 379 mg versus 793 mg cumulative dose
cards.type: Randomised noninferiority trial (Leuppi 2013, REDUCE)
cards.people: 314 patients (311 in the intention-to-treat analysis) presenting to emergency departments at five Swiss teaching hospitals with acute COPD exacerbation, past or present smokers with at least 20 pack-years and no history of asthma; 92% were admitted. Prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days versus 14 days, double-blind and placebo-controlled, enrolled 2006–2011.
cards.result: Hazard ratio for time to next exacerbation, short versus conventional, was 0.95 (90% CI 0.70 to 1.29; p=0.006 for noninferiority) in intention-to-treat and 0.93 (90% CI 0.68 to 1.26) per protocol, meeting the predefined noninferiority criterion. Estimated re-exacerbation rates within 180 days were 37.2% (95% CI 29.5% to 44.9%) on 5 days versus 38.4% (95% CI 30.6% to 46.3%) on 14 days. There was no difference in time to death, the combined endpoint of exacerbation or death, or recovery of lung function. Mean cumulative prednisone dose was 379 mg versus 793 mg (p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Treatment-associated adverse reactions, including hyperglycaemia and hypertension, did not occur less frequently on the short course despite the halved dose — the trial proves equal efficacy with less exposure, not a measured short-term safety gain. Patients needing assisted ventilation and those with asthma were outside this record.
cards.source: Leuppi JD et al. Short-term vs conventional glucocorticoid therapy in acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: the REDUCE randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2013. PMID: 23695200. Registry ID: ISRCTN19646069. cards.headline: Walters 2018 (Cochrane): courses of seven days or fewer versus longer courses — treatment failure OR 0.72 (0.36 to 1.46), relapse OR 1.04 (0.70 to 1.56), no difference in adverse events or stay
cards.summary: Walters 2018 (Cochrane): courses of seven days or fewer versus longer courses — treatment failure OR 0.72 (0.36 to 1.46), relapse OR 1.04 (0.70 to 1.56), no difference in adverse events or stay
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Walters 2018, Cochrane)
cards.people: Eight randomised trials with 582 adults with acute COPD exacerbations (five hospital studies with 519 participants contributed to the meta-analysis); mean ages 65 to 73 years, COPD classified severe or very severe; short courses of three to seven days versus 10 to 15 days at equivalent daily doses, mostly oral prednisolone 30 mg. Patients requiring assisted ventilation were excluded.
cards.result: No difference between short and longer courses in treatment failure (n=457; OR 0.72, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.46), relapse (n=457; OR 1.04, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.56), likelihood of an adverse event (n=503; OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.69), length of hospital stay (mean difference −0.61 days, 95% CI −1.51 to 0.28), or lung function at end of treatment (FEV1 mean difference −0.04 L, 95% CI −0.19 to 0.10). The reviewers concluded five days of oral corticosteroids is likely sufficient for acute exacerbations of COPD.
cards.watchOut: Most pooled evidence was graded moderate quality because of imprecision — the confidence intervals around treatment failure are wide enough to hide a real difference in either direction, and people with mild or moderate COPD were not studied. The pool is dominated by one large noninferiority trial, so this review corroborates rather than independently replicates it.
cards.source: Walters JA et al. Different durations of corticosteroid therapy for exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018. PMID: 29553157. cards.headline: Synthesis: five days does the job of fourteen — equal re-exacerbation, half the drug, and no proven short-term safety dividend
cards.summary: Synthesis: five days does the job of fourteen — equal re-exacerbation, half the drug, and no proven short-term safety dividend
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One large double-blind noninferiority trial (314 patients, hospital-presenting COPD exacerbations) plus a Cochrane pool of eight trials (582 participants) comparing steroid courses of seven days or fewer with 10–15-day courses.
cards.result: Re-exacerbation within 180 days: 37.2% on 5 days versus 38.4% on 14 days (HR 0.95). Pooled treatment failure OR 0.72 (95% CI 0.36 to 1.46) and relapse OR 1.04 (0.70 to 1.56) for short versus long courses. Cumulative prednisone exposure roughly halved (379 mg versus 793 mg). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): the 5-day course is the adequately proven default for hospitalised exacerbations; longer courses add exposure without shown benefit.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority is not superiority: the margin accepted up to a 15% absolute increase in exacerbations in the trial design, and neither source studied ventilated patients or mild exacerbations managed entirely at home. Tier C is not set: a large randomised trial plus a concordant Cochrane review carry the shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Leuppi JD et al. JAMA. 2013 (PMID: 23695200); Walters JA et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018 (PMID: 29553157).

shelves.title: Eosinophil-guided steroids in COPD exacerbations: exposure cut from a median 5 days to 2 days, days alive and out of hospital unchanged — a small mortality imbalance keeps this at POSSIBLE
shelves.question: In patients hospitalised with a COPD exacerbation, can blood-eosinophil-guided prednisolone treatment safely reduce steroid exposure without increasing treatment failure compared with standard care?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Biomarkers/blood · Denmark · Eosinophils/drug effects · Female · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Methylprednisolone/therapeutic use · Prednisolone/therapeutic use · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the biomarker strategy spares steroids without a shown cost in the outcomes measured, in two randomised trials in different settings. In hospitalised patients (CORTICO-COP, 318 patients), giving prednisolone only on days when the blood eosinophil count was at least 0.3 × 10⁹ cells/L cut median systemic corticosteroid duration from 5 days to 2 days (p<0.0001), with days alive and out of hospital within 14 days of 8.9 versus 9.3 (difference −0.4, 95% CI −1.3 to 0.5) and treatment failure at 30 days of 26% in both groups — but deaths at 30 days were 6% guided versus 4% standard (difference 1.9%, 95% CI −2.8 to 6.5), a small imbalance the trial could not resolve. In UK primary care (STARR2), eosinophil-directed prednisolone was likewise non-inferior, with treatment failure at 30 days in 19% of guided versus 32% of standard-care exacerbations (relative risk 0.60, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.04). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): eosinophil guidance safely reduces steroid exposure in COPD exacerbations; a mortality cost has not been excluded, which is why this is not LIKELY.

cards.headline: Sivapalan 2019 (CORTICO-COP): steroid duration a median 2 days guided versus 5 days standard; days alive and out of hospital 8.9 versus 9.3; treatment failure 26% in both groups; deaths 6% versus 4%
cards.summary: Sivapalan 2019 (CORTICO-COP): steroid duration a median 2 days guided versus 5 days standard; days alive and out of hospital 8.9 versus 9.3; treatment failure 26% in both groups; deaths 6% versus 4%
cards.type: Randomised open-label non-inferiority trial (Sivapalan 2019, CORTICO-COP)
cards.people: 318 patients (159 per group) admitted within 24 hours to respiratory departments at three Danish university-affiliated hospitals with acute COPD exacerbation and specialist-verified COPD, all started on 80 mg intravenous methylprednisolone on day 1; from day 2 the guided group received prednisolone 37.5 mg only on days with blood eosinophils at least 0.3 × 10⁹ cells/L, while controls received it daily for four days.
cards.result: Days alive and out of hospital within 14 days: mean 8.9 days (95% CI 8.3 to 9.6) guided versus 9.3 days (8.7 to 9.9) standard (absolute difference −0.4, 95% CI −1.3 to 0.5; p=0.34), meeting non-inferiority. Treatment failure at 30 days occurred in 42 of 159 (26%) guided versus 41 of 159 (26%) standard patients (difference 0.6%, 95% CI −9.0 to 10.3). Deaths at 30 days: nine (6%) guided versus six (4%) standard (difference 1.9%, 95% CI −2.8 to 6.5; p=0.43). Median systemic corticosteroid duration was 2 days (IQR 1.0 to 3.0) versus 5 days (5.0 to 5.0), p<0.0001.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the authors state harm on some secondary measures could not be entirely excluded — the 30-day mortality point estimate favoured standard care. The trial was powered on days alive and out of hospital, not on death or failure, so its safety reassurance is bounded.

cards.headline: Ramakrishnan 2024 (STARR2): in primary care, treatment failure at 30 days in 19% of eosinophil-directed versus 32% of standard-care exacerbations (RR 0.60, 0.33 to 1.04) — non-inferior, no deaths
cards.summary: Ramakrishnan 2024 (STARR2): in primary care, treatment failure at 30 days in 19% of eosinophil-directed versus 32% of standard-care exacerbations (RR 0.60, 0.33 to 1.04) — non-inferior, no deaths
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Ramakrishnan 2024, STARR2)
cards.people: 308 participants recruited from 14 UK general practices; 144 exacerbations from 93 participants (mean age 70 years, mean FEV1 60.9% predicted, 56% male) with COPD and at least one prior exacerbation formed the modified intention-to-treat analysis. Eosinophil-directed treatment gave prednisolone 30 mg daily for 14 days only when the point-of-care eosinophil count was high (at least 2%), placebo when low; standard care gave prednisolone regardless. All patients also received antibiotics.
cards.result: Treatment failure at 30 days (re-treatment with antibiotics or steroids, hospitalisation for any cause, or death) occurred in 14 of 73 (19%) eosinophil-directed versus 23 of 71 (32%) standard-care exacerbations (relative risk 0.60, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.04; p=0.070), and the non-inferiority analysis supported eosinophil-directed treatment. Adverse events were similar between groups and no deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: The trial was designed for superiority but converted to a non-inferiority analysis after a randomisation-code error was found before data lock, and only 144 of the recruited exacerbations entered the primary analysis — a small, fragile evidence base. Its 2% eosinophil threshold and 14-day prescribed course also differ from the hospital trial's daily-count algorithm, so the two trials test a family of strategies, not one protocol.

144 exacerbations from 93 participants (mean age 70 years, mean fev1 60.9% predicted, 56% male) with copd and at least one prior exacerbation formed the modified intention-to-treat analysis. eosinophil-directed treatment gave prednisolone 30 mg daily for 14 days only when the point-of-care eosinophil count was high (at least 2%), placebo when low; standard care gave prednisolone regardless. all patients also received antibiotics. treatment failure at 30 days (re-treatment with antibiotics or steroids, hospitalisation for any cause, or death) occurred in 14 of 73 (19%) eosinophil-directed versus 23 of 71 (32%) standard-care exacerbations (relative risk 0.60, 95% ci 0.33 to 1.04; p=0.070), and the non-inferiority analysis supported eosinophil-directed treatment. adverse events were similar between groups and no deaths occurred. the trial was designed for superiority but converted to a non-inferiority analysis after a randomisation-code error was found before data lock, and only 144 of the recruited exacerbations entered the primary analysis — a small, fragile evidence base. its 2% eosinophil threshold and 14-day prescribed course also differ from the hospital trial's daily-count algorithm, so the two trials test a family of strategies, not one protocol. ramakrishnan s et al. blood eosinophil-guided oral prednisolone for copd exacerbations in primary care in the uk (starr2): a non-inferiority, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised controlled trial. the lancet. respiratory medicine. 2024. pmid: 37924830. registry id: eudract 2017-001586-24. mesh: aged · aged, 80 and over · female · humans · male · middle aged · anti-bacterial agents/therapeutic use · disease progression · double-blind method · eosinophils · glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · prednisolone/therapeutic use · primary health care · pulmonary disease, chronic obstructive/complications · united kingdom · adult

cards.headline: Synthesis: two settings, one direction — guidance spares steroids and short-term failure does not rise, but neither trial could exclude a small mortality cost
cards.summary: Synthesis: two settings, one direction — guidance spares steroids and short-term failure does not rise, but neither trial could exclude a small mortality cost
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two randomised non-inferiority trials of blood-eosinophil-guided systemic corticosteroid treatment in COPD exacerbations: 318 hospitalised patients in Denmark and 144 exacerbations in UK primary care.
cards.result: Steroid exposure fell sharply where measured (median 2 versus 5 days in hospital). Days alive and out of hospital differed by −0.4 days (95% CI −1.3 to 0.5); treatment failure was 26% versus 26% in hospital and 19% versus 32% (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.04) in primary care. Deaths in the hospital trial were 6% guided versus 4% standard. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the exposure saving is real and consistent; the safety margin on hard outcomes is not yet tight.
cards.watchOut: Thresholds, settings, and steroid regimens differ between the two trials, and both are non-inferiority designs with wide intervals on death. Tier C is not set: two randomised trials in concordant directions carry the shelf, but the stamp stays at POSSIBLE because of the unresolved mortality imbalance.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sivapalan P et al. The Lancet. Respiratory Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 31122894); Ramakrishnan S et al. The Lancet. Respiratory Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 37924830).

shelves.title: Tiotropium beat salmeterol head-to-head in COPD: first exacerbation at 187 versus 145 days, severe exacerbations 0.09 versus 0.13 a year — a modest, real edge
shelves.question: In patients with COPD at risk of exacerbations, does once-daily tiotropium prevent exacerbations better than twice-daily salmeterol?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adrenergic beta-2 Receptor Agonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Aged · Albuterol/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Bronchodilator Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Cholinergic Antagonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Pneumonia/epidemiology · Proportional Hazards Models · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/drug therapy/prevention & control · Salmeterol Xinafoate · Scopolamine Derivatives/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Tiotropium Bromide
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — in the one large direct comparison, tiotropium prevented exacerbations better than salmeterol, and a Cochrane pool of seven trials points the same way. In POET-COPD (7,376 patients with moderate-to-very-severe COPD and a prior exacerbation), tiotropium 18 µg once daily delayed the first exacerbation versus salmeterol 50 µg twice daily (187 versus 145 days; hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.90 — a 17% relative reduction in risk), cut the annual rate of moderate or severe exacerbations (0.64 versus 0.72; rate ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.96) and of severe exacerbations (0.09 versus 0.13; rate ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.82), with deaths of 1.7% versus 2.1% and similar serious adverse events. The Cochrane review of tiotropium versus long-acting beta-agonists (seven studies, 12,223 participants) found fewer patients experiencing one or more exacerbations on tiotropium (odds ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.93) and fewer exacerbations leading to hospitalisation (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.99), with no mortality difference. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): if a single long-acting bronchodilator is chosen for exacerbation prevention, tiotropium has the better of this direct evidence — by weeks of delay and fractions of an exacerbation a year, not by a transformation.

cards.headline: Vogelmeier 2011 (POET-COPD): time to first exacerbation 187 versus 145 days (HR 0.83); severe exacerbations 0.09 versus 0.13 per year; deaths 1.7% versus 2.1%
cards.summary: Vogelmeier 2011 (POET-COPD): time to first exacerbation 187 versus 145 days (HR 0.83); severe exacerbations 0.09 versus 0.13 per year; deaths 1.7% versus 2.1%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind double-dummy trial (Vogelmeier 2011, POET-COPD)
cards.people: 7,376 patients (3,707 tiotropium, 3,669 salmeterol) with moderate-to-very-severe COPD and a history of exacerbations in the preceding year, randomised for one year to tiotropium 18 µg once daily or salmeterol 50 µg twice daily.
cards.result: Tiotropium increased time to the first exacerbation (187 versus 145 days), a 17% relative reduction in risk (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.90; p<0.001), and increased time to the first severe exacerbation (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.85). Annual moderate or severe exacerbations were 0.64 versus 0.72 (rate ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.96) and severe exacerbations 0.09 versus 0.13 (rate ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.82), with the absolute rates printed alongside the relative effects. Serious adverse events and discontinuations were similar; deaths were 64 (1.7%) on tiotropium and 78 (2.1%) on salmeterol.
cards.watchOut: The absolute gains are small — about six fewer severe exacerbations per 100 patient-years — and the trial compared two single agents in patients not on the combination or triple therapy many now receive, so it ranks the two bronchodilators rather than settling modern inhaler strategy. It was funded by tiotropium's manufacturers.
cards.source: Vogelmeier C et al. Tiotropium versus salmeterol for the prevention of exacerbations of COPD. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2011. PMID: 21428765. Registry ID: NCT00563381.
