cards.headline: Chong 2012 (Cochrane): tiotropium versus long-acting beta-agonists — one or more exacerbations OR 0.86 (0.79 to 0.93), exacerbation hospitalisations OR 0.87 (0.77 to 0.99), no mortality difference
cards.summary: Chong 2012 (Cochrane): tiotropium versus long-acting beta-agonists — one or more exacerbations OR 0.86 (0.79 to 0.93), exacerbation hospitalisations OR 0.87 (0.77 to 0.99), no mortality difference
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Chong 2012, Cochrane)
cards.people: Seven randomised studies totalling 12,223 participants with stable COPD comparing tiotropium (HandiHaler) with salmeterol (four studies, 8,936 participants), formoterol (one study, 431), or indacaterol (two studies, 2,856), over three to 12 months; inhaled corticosteroids at a stable dose were allowed.
cards.result: Tiotropium reduced the number of participants experiencing one or more exacerbations compared with long-acting beta-agonists (odds ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.93) and reduced COPD exacerbations leading to hospitalisation (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.99), but not all-cause hospitalisations. There was no statistical difference in mortality, FEV1, or symptom scores. Non-fatal serious adverse events (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.78 to 0.99) and study withdrawals (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.99) were lower on tiotropium.
cards.watchOut: Quality-of-life results were too heterogeneous to pool and differed by which beta-agonist tiotropium faced, so the exacerbation edge does not come with a proven symptom edge. Most of the pooled weight is the single salmeterol comparison, so the review extends the head-to-head result to the class only thinly.
cards.source: Chong J et al. Tiotropium versus long-acting beta-agonists for stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012. PMID: 22972134. cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent, modest exacerbation advantage for tiotropium over salmeterol — symptoms and survival not separated
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent, modest exacerbation advantage for tiotropium over salmeterol — symptoms and survival not separated
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One 7,376-patient head-to-head randomised trial against salmeterol plus a Cochrane pool of seven trials (12,223 participants) against long-acting beta-agonists as a class, in moderate-to-very-severe COPD at exacerbation risk.
cards.result: First exacerbation delayed by about six weeks (187 versus 145 days; HR 0.83); severe exacerbations 0.09 versus 0.13 per year; pooled odds of one or more exacerbations OR 0.86 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.93). Mortality, lung function, and symptoms did not differ significantly in the pool. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): tiotropium is the better single bronchodilator for preventing exacerbations on this evidence.
cards.watchOut: Both sources predate widespread dual-bronchodilator and triple therapy, so the shelf ranks single agents only. Tier C is not set: a large randomised trial and a concordant systematic review carry the shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vogelmeier C et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2011 (PMID: 21428765); Chong J et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012 (PMID: 22972134).

shelves.title: Metoprolol did not prevent COPD exacerbations: first exacerbation at 202 versus 222 days, and hospitalised exacerbations nearly doubled (HR 1.91) — the observational promise failed its randomised test
shelves.question: In patients with moderate-to-very-severe COPD and no significant cardiac disease, does metoprolol prevent acute exacerbations compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-1 Receptor Antagonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Disease Progression · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Metoprolol/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/drug therapy · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — started purely to prevent exacerbations, metoprolol did not help and the severe end of the outcome worsened. In BLOCK COPD (532 patients with moderate-to-very-severe COPD, no established indication for a beta-blocker, and no significant cardiac disease), extended-release metoprolol did not change time to first exacerbation (median 202 versus 222 days on placebo; hazard ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.32), while exacerbations leading to hospitalisation were more frequent on metoprolol (HR 1.91, 95% CI 1.29 to 2.83); deaths were 11 versus 5, and the trial was stopped early for futility and safety concerns. The contrast matters: pooled observational data had associated beta-blocker therapy with fewer exacerbations (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.85) — an association inside the range that confounding by indication can manufacture, and one the randomised test did not confirm. This shelf is about starting a beta-blocker for COPD alone; it says nothing against beta-blockers given for a cardiac indication. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): no exacerbation benefit, with a hospitalisation signal, from the single randomised trial.

cards.headline: Dransfield 2019 (BLOCK COPD): time to first exacerbation 202 versus 222 days (HR 1.05, 0.84 to 1.32); exacerbation hospitalisation HR 1.91 (1.29 to 2.83); deaths 11 versus 5; trial stopped early
cards.summary: Dransfield 2019 (BLOCK COPD): time to first exacerbation 202 versus 222 days (HR 1.05, 0.84 to 1.32); exacerbation hospitalisation HR 1.91 (1.29 to 2.83); deaths 11 versus 5; trial stopped early
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial (Dransfield 2019, BLOCK COPD)
cards.people: 532 patients aged 40 to 85 with COPD, moderate airflow limitation (mean FEV1 41.1% predicted) and increased exacerbation risk (an exacerbation in the previous year or prescribed supplemental oxygen), randomised to extended-release metoprolol or placebo for roughly a year. Patients already taking a beta-blocker or with an established indication for one were excluded.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in median time to first exacerbation: 202 days on metoprolol versus 222 days on placebo (hazard ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.32; p=0.66). Metoprolol was associated with a higher risk of exacerbation leading to hospitalisation (HR 1.91, 95% CI 1.29 to 2.83). Side-effect frequency and nonrespiratory serious adverse events were similar; during treatment there were 11 deaths in the metoprolol group and five in the placebo group. The trial was stopped early because of futility for the primary endpoint and safety concerns.
cards.watchOut: Early stopping truncates the evidence: the hospitalisation and death imbalances rest on modest event counts in a trial that never reached its planned size, so the harm estimate is imprecise even though its direction is consistent. The population deliberately excluded anyone with a cardiac reason for a beta-blocker — the result must not be read onto patients who have one.
cards.source: Dransfield MT et al. Metoprolol for the Prevention of Acute Exacerbations of COPD. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31633896. Registry ID: NCT02587351. cards.headline: Gulea 2021: pooled observational data associated beta-blockers with fewer COPD exacerbations (HR 0.77, 0.70 to 0.85) — the association the randomised trial then failed to confirm
cards.summary: Gulea 2021: pooled observational data associated beta-blockers with fewer COPD exacerbations (HR 0.77, 0.70 to 0.85) — the association the randomised trial then failed to confirm
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Gulea 2021)
cards.people: 23 observational studies and 14 randomised trials of beta-blocker exposure versus no exposure or placebo in patients with COPD, with and without cardiovascular indications; the exacerbation meta-analysis pools the observational data, while randomised data were examined chiefly for lung function.
cards.result: In pooled observational data, beta-blocker therapy was associated with a reduced risk of acute COPD exacerbations versus no therapy (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.85). Among individual agents in randomised data, only propranolol was associated with a relative reduction in FEV1 versus placebo (199 patients evaluated). Narrative syntheses of mortality, hospitalisation, and quality of life were highly heterogeneous but suggested no detrimental effect of beta-blocker therapy on those outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The encouraging exacerbation figure is observational — patients prescribed beta-blockers differ systematically from those who are not, and an HR of 0.77 sits well inside the range confounding can produce; this card is the contrast that explains why a randomised trial was needed, not evidence of benefit. Its randomised component addresses lung function, not exacerbation prevention.

cards.headline: Synthesis: do not start metoprolol to prevent COPD exacerbations — the one randomised test was null on its primary outcome and adverse on hospitalised exacerbations
cards.summary: Synthesis: do not start metoprolol to prevent COPD exacerbations — the one randomised test was null on its primary outcome and adverse on hospitalised exacerbations
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One randomised placebo-controlled trial (532 patients with COPD and no beta-blocker indication), read against a systematic review whose observational pool (23 studies) had suggested protection.
cards.result: Time to first exacerbation: HR 1.05 (95% CI 0.84 to 1.32). Exacerbation leading to hospitalisation: HR 1.91 (95% CI 1.29 to 2.83). Deaths 11 versus 5 in a trial stopped early. Observational association for exacerbations: HR 0.77 (95% CI 0.70 to 0.85), not confirmed randomised. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C: a single early-stopped trial carries the harm claim, and the developer reviews single-trial harm shelves personally.
cards.watchOut: This shelf does not address continuing or starting beta-blockers for heart failure, post-infarction, or rate control — those indications were excluded by design. A second randomised trial could soften or sharpen the hospitalisation signal.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dransfield MT et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 31633896); Gulea C et al. Respiratory Research. 2021 (PMID: 33622362).

shelves.title: Simvastatin did not prevent COPD exacerbations: 1.36 versus 1.39 per person-year, first exacerbation at 223 versus 231 days, deaths 28 versus 30 — another retrospective statin promise that failed prospectively
shelves.question: In patients with COPD at risk of exacerbations, does daily simvastatin prevent exacerbations compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Lipids/blood · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/drug therapy/physiopathology · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Simvastatin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Treatment Failure · Vital Capacity
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the large prospective trial built to test the retrospective claims, simvastatin changed nothing it was asked to change. In STATCOPE (885 patients with moderate-to-severe COPD at high exacerbation risk, deliberately excluding anyone with a cardiovascular or diabetes indication for a statin), simvastatin 40 mg daily gave 1.36 exacerbations per person-year versus 1.39 on placebo (p=0.54), a median time to first exacerbation of 223 versus 231 days (p=0.34), and 28 versus 30 deaths (p=0.89), despite LDL cholesterol falling as expected. A 2026 meta-analysis of the three randomised trials (1,190 patients) likewise found no significant difference in annualised exacerbation rates (weighted mean difference −0.21 per person-year, 95% CI −0.61 to 0.20), though it reported lower exacerbation hospitalisation (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.97) at low GRADE certainty — a signal the largest trial's own event rates do not corroborate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): simvastatin should not be started to prevent COPD exacerbations; its proven uses remain cardiovascular.

cards.headline: Criner 2014 (STATCOPE): exacerbations 1.36 versus 1.39 per person-year (p=0.54); first exacerbation at a median 223 versus 231 days; deaths 28 versus 30
cards.summary: Criner 2014 (STATCOPE): exacerbations 1.36 versus 1.39 per person-year (p=0.54); first exacerbation at a median 223 versus 231 days; deaths 28 versus 30
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial (Criner 2014, STATCOPE)
cards.people: 885 participants aged 40 to 80 with COPD (mean FEV1 41.6% predicted, mean smoking history 50.6 pack-years, 44% women) at high exacerbation risk — supplemental oxygen, glucocorticoid or antibiotic treatment, or an emergency visit or hospitalisation for COPD in the past year — treated with simvastatin 40 mg daily or placebo for 12 to 36 months at 45 centres. Patients with diabetes or cardiovascular disease, or already needing a statin, were excluded.
cards.result: The mean number of exacerbations per person-year was 1.36 (±1.61) on simvastatin and 1.39 (±1.73) on placebo (p=0.54). Median days to first exacerbation were 223 (95% CI 195 to 275) versus 231 (95% CI 193 to 303) (p=0.34). Nonfatal serious adverse events per person-year were 0.63 versus 0.62. There were 28 deaths in the simvastatin group and 30 in the placebo group (p=0.89). LDL cholesterol was lower on simvastatin at closeout, confirming the drug was taken and active.
cards.watchOut: The exclusion of anyone with a statin indication is both the trial's strength and its boundary: it isolates the COPD claim, but says nothing about COPD patients who take statins for their hearts. Follow-up averaged about 641 days, long enough for the exacerbation claim being tested.
cards.source: Criner GJ et al. Simvastatin for the prevention of exacerbations in moderate-to-severe COPD. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2014. PMID: 24836125. Registry ID: NCT01061671. cards.headline: Wang 2026: three randomised trials pooled — annualised exacerbation rate no different (WMD −0.21, −0.61 to 0.20), but exacerbation hospitalisation lower on statins (RR 0.87, 0.77 to 0.97) at low certainty
cards.summary: Wang 2026: three randomised trials pooled — annualised exacerbation rate no different (WMD −0.21, −0.61 to 0.20), but exacerbation hospitalisation lower on statins (RR 0.87, 0.77 to 0.97) at low certainty
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Wang 2026)
cards.people: Three randomised placebo-controlled trials enrolling 1,190 patients with COPD treated with a statin for exacerbation prevention; certainty assessed with GRADE.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, statins were associated with a lower exacerbation-related hospitalisation rate (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.97; GRADE low) and severe exacerbation rate (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.78 to 0.99; low), but there was no statistically significant difference in the moderate exacerbation rate (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.04; very low), the annualised exacerbation rate (weighted mean difference −0.21 per person-year, 95% CI −0.61 to 0.20; very low), or the annualised moderate-to-severe exacerbation rate (WMD −0.21, 95% CI −0.57 to 0.15; very low), with the absolute pooled differences printed alongside the relative effects.
cards.watchOut: The pool contains only three trials and is dominated by one large null trial; the hospitalisation signal rests on low-certainty evidence and on outcome definitions that differ across the small trials, and the reviewers themselves call for further large high-quality studies. A low-GRADE secondary signal does not overturn a large trial's null primary outcome.
cards.source: Wang G et al. Statins for the prevention of exacerbations in COPD: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Systematic Reviews. 2026. PMID: 42157340. cards.headline: Synthesis: exacerbation rates are identical on simvastatin and placebo — the retrospective statin-in-COPD signal was confounding, not pharmacology
cards.summary: Synthesis: exacerbation rates are identical on simvastatin and placebo — the retrospective statin-in-COPD signal was confounding, not pharmacology
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One large randomised trial (885 patients, up to three years) plus a three-trial meta-analysis (1,190 patients) of statins versus placebo for COPD exacerbation prevention in patients without a cardiovascular statin indication.
cards.result: Exacerbations per person-year: 1.36 versus 1.39. Pooled annualised exacerbation difference: −0.21 per person-year (95% CI −0.61 to 0.20), not significant. Deaths in the large trial: 28 versus 30. The only positive pooled signal — exacerbation hospitalisation RR 0.87 — is low-certainty and uncorroborated by the dominant trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for exacerbation prevention.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here argues against statins for cardiovascular prevention in COPD patients who qualify on cardiac grounds — that population was excluded by design. Tier C is not set: the null rests on a large randomised trial with a concordant meta-analysis on its primary outcome.

shelves.title: Lung volume reduction surgery in severe emphysema: no overall survival advantage (0.11 deaths per person-year in both groups) — survival better with upper-lobe disease and low exercise capacity (RR 0.47), worse without them (RR 2.06)
shelves.question: In patients with severe emphysema, does lung volume reduction surgery improve survival, exercise capacity, and quality of life compared with medical therapy alone — and in which subgroups does it harm?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Pneumonectomy · Probability · Pulmonary Emphysema/drug therapy/mortality/physiopathology/surgery · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by anatomy and exercise capacity, and the split is the whole answer. In NETT (1,218 patients with severe emphysema, all after pulmonary rehabilitation), overall mortality was identical at 0.11 deaths per person-year in the surgery and medical groups (risk ratio 1.01), while exercise capacity improved by more than 10 W at 24 months in 15% of surgical versus 3% of medical patients (p<0.001). Within that null average, patients with predominantly upper-lobe emphysema and low baseline exercise capacity had lower mortality with surgery (risk ratio for death 0.47, p=0.005), while patients with non-upper-lobe emphysema and high exercise capacity had higher mortality with surgery (risk ratio 2.06, p=0.02). A prespecified high-risk subgroup of 140 patients (very low FEV1 with homogeneous disease or very low diffusion capacity) had such high early surgical mortality that enrolment of that subgroup was halted; over 15 years of follow-up their survival curves eventually crossed (log-rank p=0.95), but the high 30-day operative death risk remains the practical deterrent. PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit — exercise capacity for many, survival for the upper-lobe/low-exercise subgroup; harm — early death in high-risk and non-upper-lobe/high-exercise patients.

cards.headline: Fishman 2003 (NETT): overall mortality 0.11 per person-year in both groups (RR 1.01); exercise gain >10 W in 15% versus 3%; subgroup mortality RR 0.47 (upper-lobe, low exercise) versus RR 2.06 (non-upper-lobe, high exercise)
cards.summary: Fishman 2003 (NETT): overall mortality 0.11 per person-year in both groups (RR 1.01); exercise gain >10 W in 15% versus 3%; subgroup mortality RR 0.47 (upper-lobe, low exercise) versus RR 2.06 (non-upper-lobe, high exercise)
cards.type: Randomised trial (Fishman 2003, National Emphysema Treatment Trial)
cards.people: 1,218 patients with severe emphysema who completed pulmonary rehabilitation, randomised to lung-volume-reduction surgery or continued medical treatment, including a subgroup of 140 patients identified at interim analysis as at high risk of death from surgery.
cards.result: Overall mortality was 0.11 death per person-year in both groups (risk ratio for death with surgery 1.01; p=0.90). After 24 months, exercise capacity had improved by more than 10 W in 15% of the surgery group versus 3% of the medical group (p<0.001). Excluding the high-risk subgroup, mortality was 0.09 versus 0.10 deaths per person-year (RR 0.89; p=0.31) and exercise improvement 16% versus 3% (p<0.001). Among patients with predominantly upper-lobe emphysema and low exercise capacity, mortality was lower with surgery (RR 0.47; p=0.005); among those with non-upper-lobe emphysema and high exercise capacity, mortality was higher with surgery (RR 2.06; p=0.02), with the subgroup relative effects printed alongside the identical overall absolute mortality rates.
cards.watchOut: The survival split comes from subgroup analyses — prespecified in the trial's analytic framework but still subgroups — and the favourable subgroup is exactly the one later selection criteria adopted, so the trial is partly being read through its own conclusions. Surgery here was predominantly sternotomy-era technique in rehabilitation completers, a selected population.
cards.source: Fishman A et al. A randomized trial comparing lung-volume-reduction surgery with medical therapy for severe emphysema. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2003. PMID: 12759479. cards.headline: Kaplan 2014 (NETT high-risk follow-up): the halted high-risk subgroup died faster after surgery for three years, then the curves crossed — 15-year survival not significantly different (p=0.95), quality of life favouring surgery through five years
cards.summary: Kaplan 2014 (NETT high-risk follow-up): the halted high-risk subgroup died faster after surgery for three years, then the curves crossed — 15-year survival not significantly different (p=0.95), quality of life favouring surgery through five years
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised trial subgroup (Kaplan 2014, NETT)
cards.people: The 140 high-risk NETT patients with severe lung disease (the subgroup whose enrolment was halted early because of excess surgical mortality), randomised to lung-volume-reduction surgery plus maximal medical care or maximal medical care alone, followed prospectively for vital status over 15 years, with quality-of-life data through six years.
cards.result: Through the first three years, surgical patients in the high-risk subgroup had a significantly higher probability of death; the mortality curves then crossed, with a trend favouring surgery thereafter, and overall survival did not differ significantly between groups (log-rank p=0.95). Quality-of-life measures suggested an advantage for surgery through the first five years (p<0.01), and the combined quality-adjusted survival model favoured medical care for the first few years and surgery after four years.
cards.watchOut: This is a follow-up of 140 patients — survivors of an early-harm period dominate the later curves, so the late crossover cannot rehabilitate the procedure for high-risk patients, as the authors themselves note: the high 30-day mortality may discourage use despite potential long-term outcomes. Quality-of-life data were available only through six years and only in survivors.
cards.source: Kaplan RM et al. Long-term follow-up of high-risk patients in the National Emphysema Treatment Trial. The Annals of Thoracic Surgery. 2014. PMID: 25201722. shelves.title: Endobronchial coils for severe emphysema: walk distance improved by 14.6 m — below the 25 m threshold patients can feel — quality of life by 8.9 points, at a price of major complications in 34.8% versus 19.1%
shelves.question: In patients with severe heterogeneous emphysema, do endobronchial coils improve lung function, exercise capacity, and quality of life compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Bronchoscopy · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Hospitalization · Humans · Lung/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Pneumonia/etiology · Prostheses and Implants/adverse effects · Pulmonary Emphysema/physiopathology/therapy · Quality of Life · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — statistically real, clinically modest, and bought with complications. In RENEW (315 patients with severe emphysema and severe air trapping), bilateral endobronchial coils plus usual care beat usual care alone on the primary outcome by a median 14.6 m of six-minute walk distance at 12 months (10.3 m gained versus 7.6 m lost) — less than the 25 m difference prespecified as clinically important — although 40.0% versus 26.9% achieved at least a 25 m gain, the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire improved by 8.9 points more with coils, and the between-group FEV1 difference was 7.0%. Against that, major complications occurred in 34.8% of coil patients versus 19.1% on usual care (p=0.002), including pneumonia in 20% versus 4.5% and pneumothorax in 9.7% versus 0.6%. The earlier, smaller RESET trial (47 patients) found the same quality-of-life direction at 90 days (−8.36 points, 95% CI −16.24 to −0.47) with no difference in serious adverse events detected at that size. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): coils improve quality-of-life scores and lung function modestly in severe hyperinflation, with a complication burden that must be weighed patient by patient.

cards.headline: Sciurba 2016 (RENEW): six-minute walk difference 14.6 m favouring coils (MCID 25 m); responders 40.0% versus 26.9%; major complications 34.8% versus 19.1%, pneumonia 20% versus 4.5%
cards.summary: Sciurba 2016 (RENEW): six-minute walk difference 14.6 m favouring coils (MCID 25 m); responders 40.0% versus 26.9%; major complications 34.8% versus 19.1%, pneumonia 20% versus 4.5%
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (Sciurba 2016, RENEW)
cards.people: 315 patients (mean age 64 years, 52% women) with emphysema and severe air trapping at 26 North American and European sites, randomised to usual guideline care alone (157) or usual care plus bilateral coil treatment (158) — two bronchoscopic procedures four months apart placing 10 to 14 coils in one lobe of each lung; 90% completed 12-month follow-up.
cards.result: Median change in six-minute walk distance at 12 months was 10.3 m with coils versus −7.6 m with usual care, a between-group difference of 14.6 m (97.5% CI 0.4 to ∞; one-sided p=0.02), against a prespecified minimal clinically important difference of 25 m. Improvement of at least 25 m occurred in 40.0% versus 26.9% (odds ratio 1.8). The between-group difference in median FEV1 change was 7.0% and in St George's Respiratory Questionnaire −8.9 points, both favouring coils. Major complications occurred in 34.8% of coil participants versus 19.1% on usual care (p=0.002); pneumonia occurred in 20% versus 4.5% and pneumothorax in 9.7% versus 0.6%.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own authors call the exercise improvement 'modest and of uncertain clinical importance' — the average gain sits below the threshold patients are thought to feel, and the benefit is carried by a responder minority. Unblinded usual-care comparison, one-sided statistical testing, and only 12 months of follow-up further bound the claim; long-term health outcomes were not assessed.
cards.source: Sciurba FC et al. Effect of Endobronchial Coils vs Usual Care on Exercise Tolerance in Patients With Severe Emphysema: The RENEW Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27179849. cards.headline: Shah 2013 (RESET): quality of life improved by 8.36 SGRQ points more with coils at 90 days (95% CI −16.24 to −0.47; p=0.04) in 47 patients — no serious-adverse-event difference detected
cards.summary: Shah 2013 (RESET): quality of life improved by 8.36 SGRQ points more with coils at 90 days (95% CI −16.24 to −0.47; p=0.04) in 47 patients — no serious-adverse-event difference detected
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Shah 2013, RESET)
cards.people: 47 patients aged at least 35 with severe emphysema and hyperinflation at three UK centres, randomised to lung volume reduction coil treatment (23) or best medical care (24), with the primary endpoint 90 days after final treatment.
cards.result: The St George's Respiratory Questionnaire response at 90 days was greater with coils than with usual care: between-group difference in change from baseline −8.36 points (95% CI −16.24 to −0.47; p=0.04) — a difference exceeding the questionnaire's usual four-point clinically important threshold. No between-group difference in serious adverse events was detected.
cards.watchOut: Forty-seven patients and 90 days: this trial can show a short-term quality-of-life signal and nothing about durability, exacerbations, or the complication rates that only a larger trial could see — and the larger trial that followed found complications in a third of treated patients. Funded by the device manufacturer.

shelves.title: Hospital at home for COPD exacerbations: readmissions lower (RR 0.76) and mortality a non-significant trend (RR 0.65) — but only in the selected minority judged safe to send home
shelves.question: For acute COPD exacerbations, does hospital-at-home or early supported discharge give equivalent mortality and readmission outcomes to inpatient care in selected patients?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Disease Progression · Home Care Services, Hospital-Based/statistics & numerical data · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Patient Readmission/statistics & numerical data · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/mortality/therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for carefully selected patients, being treated at home did at least as well as a hospital bed, and readmissions fell. A Cochrane review of eight randomised trials (870 patients presenting to emergency departments with COPD exacerbations, excluding anyone with impaired consciousness, acute confusion, arterial pH below 7.35, or other features making home treatment irresponsible) found hospital at home reduced readmission compared with inpatient care (risk ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.99; p=0.04), with a trend toward lower mortality that did not reach significance (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.04; p=0.07), on evidence graded moderate quality; quality of life, lung function, and cost evidence was too weak for firm conclusions. In the largest early trial within that pool, only 192 of 583 patients referred for admission (33%) even met home-care criteria — the selection is the intervention's boundary. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): hospital at home is a safe, readmission-sparing alternative for the selected minority, not a substitute for admission in unselected exacerbations.

cards.headline: Jeppesen 2012 (Cochrane): eight trials, 870 patients — readmission RR 0.76 (0.59 to 0.99) favouring hospital at home; mortality RR 0.65 (0.40 to 1.04), not significant
cards.summary: Jeppesen 2012 (Cochrane): eight trials, 870 patients — readmission RR 0.76 (0.59 to 0.99) favouring hospital at home; mortality RR 0.65 (0.40 to 1.04), not significant
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Jeppesen 2012, Cochrane)
cards.people: Eight randomised trials with 870 patients who presented to emergency departments with acute COPD exacerbations and were selected as suitable for home treatment — trials excluded patients with impaired consciousness, acute confusion, acute radiograph or ECG changes, arterial pH below 7.35, or concomitant conditions making home care irresponsible. Hospital-at-home schemes provided respiratory-nurse support at home instead of inpatient admission.
cards.result: Hospital at home significantly reduced readmission rates compared with inpatient care (risk ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.99; p=0.04). Mortality showed a trend favouring hospital at home that did not reach statistical significance (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.04; p=0.07). Evidence for health-related quality of life, lung function (FEV1), and direct costs was in general too weak to support firm conclusions. The reviewers graded the readmission and mortality evidence as moderate quality and the remaining outcomes low or very low quality.
cards.watchOut: Every number applies only to patients already screened as home-safe — roughly a third of those referred for admission in the component trials — so the review cannot be extrapolated to unselected exacerbations. The mortality trend is a trend: its confidence interval includes meaningful harm as well as large benefit. This COPD-specific shelf is distinct from the library's general hospital-at-home shelf, which pools mixed diagnoses.
cards.source: Jeppesen E et al. Hospital at home for acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012. PMID: 22592692. cards.headline: Davies 2000: of 583 patients referred for admission, only 192 (33%) were eligible for home care — in those randomised, readmission at three months was 37% at home versus 34% in hospital, mortality 9% versus 8%
cards.summary: Davies 2000: of 583 patients referred for admission, only 192 (33%) were eligible for home care — in those randomised, readmission at three months was 37% at home versus 34% in hospital, mortality 9% versus 8%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Davies 2000)
cards.people: Patients with COPD exacerbations referred for admission to a UK university teaching hospital: 583 assessed, 192 meeting home-care criteria, 42 declining, and 150 randomised — 100 to nurse-administered hospital-at-home care and 50 to inpatient care — with three months of follow-up. Baseline post-bronchodilator FEV1 was about 36% predicted in the home group and 35% in the hospital group.
cards.result: No significant difference was found in FEV1 at two weeks (42.6% versus 42.1% predicted) or three months (41.5% versus 41.9%). Readmission at three months was 37% in the home-care group and 34% in the hospital group. Mortality at three months was 9% at home versus 8% in hospital, not significantly different.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 150 randomised patients from the year 2000 — far too small to exclude differences in mortality, and its readmission rates run higher than the later pooled estimate, a reminder that schemes and selection vary. Its enduring contribution is the denominator: two-thirds of referred patients were not candidates at all.
cards.source: Davies L et al. "Hospital at home" versus hospital care in patients with exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: prospective randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2000. PMID: 11082090. cards.headline: Synthesis: home treatment matches hospital outcomes in the screened third of exacerbations, and the pool suggests fewer readmissions — selection is doing much of the work
cards.summary: Synthesis: home treatment matches hospital outcomes in the screened third of exacerbations, and the pool suggests fewer readmissions — selection is doing much of the work
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: A Cochrane pool of eight randomised trials (870 selected patients) plus its early component trial documenting the selection funnel (192 of 583 referred patients eligible).
cards.result: Readmission: RR 0.76 (95% CI 0.59 to 0.99) favouring hospital at home. Mortality: RR 0.65 (95% CI 0.40 to 1.04), not significant; the component trial found 9% versus 8% at three months. Lung function recovered identically in both settings. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a readmission advantage with no shown mortality cost, in selected patients only.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials span different schemes and eras, and none can blind place of care. Tier C is not set: the shelf rests on a multi-trial systematic review, and no mortality benefit is claimed — only the absence of a shown mortality cost within wide intervals.

shelves.title: Intravenous magnesium in acute COPD exacerbations: peak flow better at 45 minutes and admission odds halved in pooled small trials (OR 0.45) — but no trial large enough to trust, and length of stay unmoved
shelves.question: In acute COPD exacerbations, does intravenous magnesium sulfate as an adjunct to standard therapy improve lung function and reduce admission or ventilation compared with placebo?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the pooled signal points one way, but it is built from small trials and a 45-minute flow measurement. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of nine studies (seven randomised trials and two observational studies) found adjunctive intravenous magnesium sulfate improved peak expiratory flow at 45 minutes (mean difference 18.50, 95% CI 6.36 to 30.65) and reduced hospital admission from the emergency department (odds ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.88), with no significant difference in length of stay (mean difference −0.83 days, 95% CI −2.99 to 1.33) or adverse events (OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.20 to 3.13). An earlier meta-analysis of seven studies found the same pattern — admission odds ratio 0.453 (95% CI 0.233 to 0.882) and small FEV1 gains during exacerbations but not in stable COPD. Neither pool reports a ventilation or mortality outcome, the two pools substantially overlap, and neither record carries MeSH indexing. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): a plausible, cheap adjunct with a consistent small-trial signal on admission — unproven where it matters most.

cards.headline: Farid 2025: nine studies pooled — peak flow at 45 minutes better by 18.50 (6.36 to 30.65), admission OR 0.45 (0.23 to 0.88), length of stay and adverse events not significantly different
cards.summary: Farid 2025: nine studies pooled — peak flow at 45 minutes better by 18.50 (6.36 to 30.65), admission OR 0.45 (0.23 to 0.88), length of stay and adverse events not significantly different
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Farid 2025)
cards.people: Nine studies (seven randomised trials and two observational studies) comparing intravenous magnesium sulfate plus standard treatment with standard treatment alone in acute exacerbations of COPD, searched to April 2025.
cards.result: Adjunctive intravenous magnesium significantly improved peak expiratory flow rate at 45 minutes (mean difference 18.50, 95% CI 6.36 to 30.65) and significantly reduced hospital admission rates from the emergency department (odds ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.88). No significant differences were observed in length of hospital stay (mean difference −0.83 days, 95% CI −2.99 to 1.33) or adverse events (OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.20 to 3.13). The authors conclude that large-scale multicentre randomised trials are needed to validate the findings.
cards.watchOut: Peak flow at 45 minutes is a surrogate measured before most admission decisions settle, and the admission outcome pools randomised with observational data from small single-centre studies — exactly the evidence tier where effects shrink when a large trial is done. No pooled ventilation or mortality outcome is reported, so the candidate question's hardest outcomes are simply unanswered here.

cards.headline: Jahangir 2022: seven studies — admission odds ratio 0.453 (0.233 to 0.882) and FEV1 higher during exacerbations, but no FEV1 effect in stable COPD
cards.summary: Jahangir 2022: seven studies — admission odds ratio 0.453 (0.233 to 0.882) and FEV1 higher during exacerbations, but no FEV1 effect in stable COPD
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Jahangir 2022)
cards.people: Seven studies of intravenous magnesium sulfate in COPD, covering both acute exacerbations and stable disease, identified from PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register; randomised trials formed the included evidence for the exacerbation analyses.
cards.result: In acute exacerbations, intravenous magnesium was associated with a significant increase in FEV1 (mean difference 2.537, 95% CI 0.717 to 4.357; p=0.006) and peak expiratory flow (standardised mean difference 1.073, 95% CI 0.748 to 1.397; p<0.001), a decrease in residual volume (mean difference −0.470, 95% CI −0.884 to −0.056; p=0.026), and a lower hospitalisation rate (odds ratio 0.453, 95% CI 0.233 to 0.882; p=0.020). In stable COPD there was no statistically significant FEV1 difference.
cards.watchOut: The FEV1 mean difference is reported without a clear unit context in the abstract and the standardised peak-flow effect is implausibly large for a bronchodilator adjunct — both are hallmarks of small-study effects. This pool overlaps heavily with the later 2025 pool, so the two reviews are one evidence base read twice, not two independent confirmations.

shelves.title: Supported self-management in COPD: hospitalisations fell 26.9% over two years in the Canadian programme trial, but the large European COMET trial missed its primary endpoint — and its startling mortality gap (1.9% versus 14.2%) is not credible at face value
shelves.question: In patients with COPD, does a supported self-management programme with an exacerbation action plan reduce hospital admissions and improve quality of life compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cause of Death · Disease Management · Disease Progression · Europe/epidemiology · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Home Care Services, Hospital-Based/organization & administration · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Lung/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/mortality/physiopathology/therapy · Quality of Life · Regression Analysis · Self Care/methods · Severity of Illness Index · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two big programme trials disagree on admissions, and the mortality number in one of them should not be believed as printed. In COMET (319 patients with severe COPD across Europe; self-management programme plus home telemonitoring, care coordination, and medical management versus usual care), the primary endpoint — unplanned all-cause hospitalisation days per year — was 17.4 versus 22.6 days, a difference that was not significant (mean difference −5.3, 95% CI −13.7 to −3.1 as printed; p=0.16), with no difference in exacerbation frequency; yet mortality was reported at 1.9% versus 14.2% (p<0.001), a gap far too large for the intervention and arising in a trial whose patient profiles and hospitalisation practices varied substantially across countries. In the Canadian multicentre trial of the named 'Living Well with COPD' self-management programme (191 patients with a prior hospitalisation), all-cause hospitalisations fell by a relative 26.9% and emergency visits by a relative 21.1% at two years compared with standard care. PROPOSED SPLIT: hospitalisation benefit shown for a supervised, action-plan programme in previously hospitalised patients; the broader multicomponent European programme missed its primary endpoint, and its mortality claim is flagged Tier C for personal review.

cards.headline: Kessler 2018 (COMET): hospitalisation days 17.4 versus 22.6 per year — primary endpoint not significant (p=0.16); exacerbations unchanged; mortality printed as 1.9% versus 14.2% (p<0.001)
cards.summary: Kessler 2018 (COMET): hospitalisation days 17.4 versus 22.6 per year — primary endpoint not significant (p=0.16); exacerbations unchanged; mortality printed as 1.9% versus 14.2% (p<0.001)
cards.type: Randomised open-label trial (Kessler 2018, COMET)
cards.people: 319 patients with severe COPD (FEV1 below 50% predicted) at European centres, randomised to a multicomponent home-based disease-management intervention — self-management programme, home telemonitoring, care coordination, and medical management — or to usual centre management (157 intervention, 162 usual care in the intention-to-treat analysis).
cards.result: Unplanned all-cause hospitalisation days per year were 17.4 (±35.4) on the intervention versus 22.6 (±41.8) on usual care (mean difference −5.3; p=0.16) — the primary endpoint was not significantly reduced. Per-protocol acute care hospitalisation days were fewer (p=0.047), the BODE index was lower (p=0.01), and there was no difference in exacerbation frequency. Mortality was 1.9% in the disease-management group versus 14.2% in the usual-care group (p<0.001). Patient profiles and hospitalisation practices varied substantially across countries.
cards.watchOut: A self-management and telemonitoring package cannot plausibly prevent seven of every eight deaths, and an open-label multinational trial with large cross-country practice variation is exactly where such an imbalance is manufactured — by case-mix and ascertainment, not by the programme. The mortality figure is reported here because the record prints it, but it should drive no decision until independently explained; the trial's trustworthy answer is its null primary endpoint.
cards.source: Kessler R et al. COMET: a multicomponent home-based disease-management programme versus routine care in severe COPD. The European Respiratory Journal. 2018. PMID: 29326333. cards.headline: Gadoury 2005 ('Living Well with COPD'): all-cause hospitalisations down a relative 26.9% and emergency visits down 21.1% at two years with a supervised self-management programme
cards.summary: Gadoury 2005 ('Living Well with COPD'): all-cause hospitalisations down a relative 26.9% and emergency visits down 21.1% at two years with a supervised self-management programme
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (Gadoury 2005)
cards.people: 191 patients with advanced COPD (mean FEV1 about 1 L; almost half reporting the worst dyspnoea grade) from seven Quebec hospitals, each with at least one hospitalisation in the preceding year, randomised to the named 'Living Well with COPD' disease-specific self-management programme — education with supervision and support, including exacerbation self-management — or to standard care, with outcomes taken from provincial hospitalisation and insurance databases over two years.
cards.result: At two years there was a statistically significant and clinically relevant relative reduction in all-cause hospitalisations of 26.9% and in all-cause emergency visits of 21.1% in the intervention group compared with standard care (relative effects as printed in the record; the abstract does not give the underlying absolute rates). After adjustment, younger age, female sex, higher education, better health status, and greater exercise capacity also predicted fewer hospitalisations.
cards.watchOut: The record reports relative reductions without the absolute hospitalisation rates alongside, so the size of the benefit in admissions per patient cannot be verified from the abstract — the wording standard for this library is why the relative figures are labelled relative here. The programme was intensive and supervised, in patients already hospitalised once; lighter-touch versions and lower-risk patients are outside this record. The programme name is given exactly as the publication prints it, per the naming rule for non-drug programmes.
cards.source: Gadoury MA et al. Self-management reduces both short- and long-term hospitalisation in COPD. The European Respiratory Journal. 2005. PMID: 16264046. shelves.title: Adding tiotropium to inhaled steroid plus LABA in uncontrolled asthma: severe exacerbations delayed (282 versus 226 days; HR 0.79) and FEV1 up by 86–154 mL in two replicate trials
shelves.question: In asthma uncontrolled on inhaled corticosteroid plus long-acting beta-agonist, does adding tiotropium improve lung function and reduce exacerbations compared with doubling the steroid or adding a leukotriene antagonist?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adrenergic beta-Agonists/therapeutic use · Adult · Aged · Asthma/drug therapy · Bronchodilator Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Scopolamine Derivatives/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Tiotropium Bromide
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two replicate trials agree, and a crossover trial answers the 'instead of what' question for the steroid-doubling option. In the PrimoTinA-asthma programme (two replicate randomised trials, 912 patients symptomatic on inhaled corticosteroid plus LABA with at least one severe exacerbation in the prior year), adding tiotropium 5 µg once daily improved peak FEV1 at 24 weeks by 86 mL (trial 1) and 154 mL (trial 2) over placebo, delayed the first severe exacerbation (282 versus 226 days), and reduced severe-exacerbation risk by a relative 21% (hazard ratio 0.79; p=0.03), with adverse events similar and no deaths. In the TALC crossover trial (210 patients uncontrolled on inhaled corticosteroid alone), tiotropium beat doubling the steroid dose on morning peak flow (difference 25.8 L/min; p<0.001), FEV1 (0.10 L; p=0.004), and symptom scores, and was non-inferior to adding salmeterol. The leukotriene-antagonist comparison in the candidate question was not tested in either record and is declared a gap, not answered here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): tiotropium is a proven add-on when steroid-plus-LABA asthma remains uncontrolled — with modest lung-function gains and a real, moderate exacerbation delay.

cards.headline: Kerstjens 2012 (PrimoTinA-asthma, two replicate trials): peak FEV1 up 86 and 154 mL over placebo; time to first severe exacerbation 282 versus 226 days (HR 0.79; p=0.03)
cards.summary: Kerstjens 2012 (PrimoTinA-asthma, two replicate trials): peak FEV1 up 86 and 154 mL over placebo; time to first severe exacerbation 282 versus 226 days (HR 0.79; p=0.03)
cards.type: Two replicate randomised controlled trials (Kerstjens 2012, PrimoTinA-asthma)
cards.people: 912 patients with asthma receiving inhaled glucocorticoids and long-acting beta-agonists who remained symptomatic, with post-bronchodilator FEV1 at or below 80% predicted (mean baseline 62% predicted, mean age 53 years) and at least one severe exacerbation in the previous year; tiotropium 5 µg or placebo by soft-mist inhaler once daily for 48 weeks.
cards.result: At 24 weeks the change in peak FEV1 favoured tiotropium by 86±34 mL in trial 1 (p=0.01) and 154±32 mL in trial 2 (p<0.001); trough FEV1 differences were 88±31 mL and 111±30 mL. Adding tiotropium increased time to the first severe exacerbation (282 versus 226 days), a 21% relative reduction in risk (hazard ratio 0.79; p=0.03), with the absolute times printed alongside. No deaths occurred and adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The exacerbation result is a pooled hazard ratio without the absolute exacerbation rates in the abstract, so the absolute benefit per patient-year cannot be computed from this record — the 56-day delay in first exacerbation is the tangible figure. Participants were selected for prior severe exacerbations and obstructed physiology; milder uncontrolled asthma is outside the record. Funded by the manufacturer.

cards.headline: Peters 2010 (TALC): tiotropium beat doubling the inhaled steroid — morning peak flow +25.8 L/min, FEV1 +0.10 L — and matched adding salmeterol on every outcome
cards.summary: Peters 2010 (TALC): tiotropium beat doubling the inhaled steroid — morning peak flow +25.8 L/min, FEV1 +0.10 L — and matched adding salmeterol on every outcome
cards.type: Randomised three-way crossover trial (Peters 2010, TALC)
cards.people: 210 adults with asthma inadequately controlled on an inhaled glucocorticoid alone, in a double-blind triple-dummy crossover comparing three step-ups: adding tiotropium, doubling the glucocorticoid dose, or adding the long-acting beta-agonist salmeterol.
cards.result: Tiotropium was superior to doubling the inhaled glucocorticoid on the primary outcome, morning peak expiratory flow (mean difference 25.8 L/min; p<0.001), and on evening peak flow (35.3 L/min; p<0.001), proportion of asthma-control days (difference 0.079; p=0.01), prebronchodilator FEV1 (0.10 L; p=0.004), and daily symptom scores (−0.11 points; p<0.001). Tiotropium was also non-inferior to adding salmeterol on all assessed outcomes and improved prebronchodilator FEV1 more than salmeterol (difference 0.11 L; p=0.003).
cards.watchOut: A crossover trial on inhaled steroid alone — one step earlier in the treatment ladder than the add-on trials — with short treatment periods and physiological primary outcomes; it ranks the step-up options for lung function and symptoms, not for exacerbations. It does not test a leukotriene antagonist, so that limb of the candidate question remains unanswered by the carded evidence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: tiotropium earns its place as the add-on — better than more steroid, equal to a LABA, and proven against placebo on exacerbations
cards.summary: Synthesis: tiotropium earns its place as the add-on — better than more steroid, equal to a LABA, and proven against placebo on exacerbations
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two replicate 48-week randomised trials (912 patients on ICS plus LABA) plus a 210-patient three-way crossover trial of step-up options on ICS alone, in uncontrolled asthma.
cards.result: Peak FEV1 advantage over placebo: 86 and 154 mL. First severe exacerbation: 282 versus 226 days (HR 0.79). Versus doubling the steroid: morning peak flow +25.8 L/min and FEV1 +0.10 L, both significant. Versus adding salmeterol: non-inferior on all outcomes. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit). Declared gap: no carded record compares tiotropium add-on with a leukotriene antagonist.

Tier C is not set: two concordant replicate randomised trials plus a supporting randomised comparison carry the shelf.

shelves.title: Heliox for acute severe asthma: no significant improvement in pulmonary function (SMD −0.28, −0.56 to 0.01) and no reduction in hospital admission (RR 0.83, 0.66 to 1.08) across ten small trials
shelves.question: In non-intubated patients with acute severe asthma, does heliox-driven nebulisation improve airflow and reduce admission compared with oxygen-driven nebulisation?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Asthma/therapy · Child · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Helium/therapeutic use · Humans · Oxygen/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for routine use in non-intubated acute asthma, the pooled trials show no benefit that reaches significance on either airflow or admission. The Cochrane review (ten randomised trials, 544 patients in emergency departments, seven adult and three paediatric) found no significant difference in pulmonary function between heliox and oxygen or air (standardised mean difference −0.28, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.01, with significant heterogeneity) and no significant difference in hospital admission (risk ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.08; p=0.17). An earlier systematic review of seven trials (392 patients) found the same: no significant pulmonary-function difference (SMD −0.20, 95% CI −0.91 to 0.51) and no admission difference in the nebuliser-driven subgroup (odds ratio 1.07, 95% CI 0.46 to 2.48). Both reviews note a possible signal confined to the subgroup with the most severe baseline obstruction — a hypothesis from a small number of studies, not a finding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): heliox has no established role in the initial treatment of acute asthma outside that unproven severe-obstruction niche.

cards.headline: Rodrigo 2006 (Cochrane): ten trials, 544 patients — pulmonary function SMD −0.28 (−0.56 to 0.01), admission RR 0.83 (0.66 to 1.08); benefit suggested only in the most obstructed subgroup
cards.summary: Rodrigo 2006 (Cochrane): ten trials, 544 patients — pulmonary function SMD −0.28 (−0.56 to 0.01), admission RR 0.83 (0.66 to 1.08); benefit suggested only in the most obstructed subgroup
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Rodrigo 2006, Cochrane)
cards.people: Ten randomised controlled trials involving 544 children and adults with acute asthma in emergency departments or equivalent acute care settings (seven adult studies, three paediatric; three assessed as high quality), comparing inhaled heliox with oxygen or air as placebo, on top of standard medical care; pulmonary function was recorded during 15 to 60 minutes of administration.
cards.result: Pooling the eight trials contributing data showed no significant group difference in pulmonary function (standardised mean difference −0.28, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.01), with significant heterogeneity among studies. At the end of treatment, heliox patients showed no significantly different risk of admission to hospital (risk ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.08; p=0.17). Heliox improved pulmonary function only in the subgroup with the most severe baseline impairment, a conclusion the reviewers base on a small number of studies. The reviewers conclude the evidence does not support heliox for all emergency-department patients with acute asthma.
cards.watchOut: The review is from 2006 and its trials are small and heterogeneous; the severe-obstruction subgroup signal is hypothesis-generating only. Intubated patients — where heliox's physics is most often invoked — were excluded by the question and by these trials, so nothing here speaks to ventilated asthma.

cards.headline: Rodrigo 2003: seven trials, 392 patients — no significant difference in spirometry (SMD −0.20, −0.91 to 0.51) or admissions (OR 1.07, 0.46 to 2.48); heart rate rose with heliox
cards.summary: Rodrigo 2003: seven trials, 392 patients — no significant difference in spirometry (SMD −0.20, −0.91 to 0.51) or admissions (OR 1.07, 0.46 to 2.48); heart rate rose with heliox
cards.type: Systematic review (Rodrigo 2003)
cards.people: Seven prospective controlled trials (randomised and nonrandomised) totalling 392 children and adults with acute asthma comparing heliox with placebo alongside standard acute treatments; six studies in adults and one in children, with spirometric measures as the main outcome in six trials.
cards.result: No significant differences were demonstrated between heliox and oxygen/air groups in pulmonary function (standardised mean difference −0.20, 95% CI −0.91 to 0.51; p=0.6). The four studies using heliox to drive nebulised therapy showed a nonsignificant pulmonary-function increase (SMD −0.21, 95% CI −0.43 to 0.01; p=0.06) and no significant admission difference (odds ratio 1.07, 95% CI 0.46 to 2.48; p=0.9). In two studies heliox produced a significantly greater heart-rate increase than oxygen/air (weighted mean difference 9.0 beats per minute, 95% CI 1.27 to 16.8; p=0.02). Heliox appeared safe and well tolerated overall.
cards.watchOut: This earlier review overlaps the later Cochrane pool and includes nonrandomised studies, so it corroborates weakly rather than independently. Its confidence intervals are wide enough to include a moderate benefit — the honest reading is 'no benefit shown', not 'benefit disproven', in very small trials.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two reviews, one answer — heliox does not measurably improve airflow or prevent admission in ordinary acute asthma care
cards.summary: Synthesis: two reviews, one answer — heliox does not measurably improve airflow or prevent admission in ordinary acute asthma care
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two systematic reviews (ten randomised trials, 544 patients; seven controlled trials, 392 patients — pools overlapping) of heliox versus oxygen or air in non-intubated acute asthma in emergency settings.
cards.result: Pulmonary function: SMD −0.28 (95% CI −0.56 to 0.01) and −0.20 (−0.91 to 0.51), neither significant. Admission: RR 0.83 (0.66 to 1.08) and OR 1.07 (0.46 to 2.48), neither significant. A severe-obstruction subgroup signal is noted but rests on few small studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for routine non-intubated use.
cards.watchOut: The evidence base is old and small; a modern large trial in the most severe stratum could reopen the subgroup question, but no such trial is in these records. Tier C is not set: the null is consistent across two systematic reviews.

shelves.title: Noninvasive ventilation in acute severe asthma: used widely, proven barely — the intubation data are two events in 86 patients (RR 4.48, CI 0.23 to 89.13), and the one positive pilot randomised 30 people
shelves.question: In acute severe asthma with respiratory failure, does noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation reduce intubation and mortality compared with standard therapy?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Asthma/complications · Disease Progression · Humans · Intubation, Intratracheal/statistics & numerical data · Positive-Pressure Respiration/methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Respiratory Insufficiency/etiology/therapy
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the honest summary is that the question is unanswered, with one small pilot leaning positive. The Cochrane review found six trials of noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (NPPV) in severe acute asthma, with five studies and 206 participants contributing data; for endotracheal intubation, the only outcome that matters most here, two studies contributed just two intubations among 45 NPPV patients and none among 41 controls (risk ratio 4.48, 95% CI 0.23 to 89.13) — a confidence interval that excludes nothing — and there were no deaths in either study. The single small hospitalisation result favoured NPPV (3 of 17 versus 10 of 16 admitted; RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.84). The pilot trial behind that signal randomised 30 emergency-department patients: 80% on bilevel ventilation reached a 50% FEV1 rise versus 20% on sham (p<0.004), with mean FEV1 rises of 53.5% versus 28.5%. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): lung function and admission lean NPPV's way in tiny trials; any claim about intubation or mortality is currently unfounded in either direction.

cards.headline: Lim 2012 (Cochrane): six trials, 206 participants with data — intubation 2 of 45 on NPPV versus 0 of 41 controls (RR 4.48, 0.23 to 89.13); no deaths; one small study showed fewer admissions (RR 0.28)
cards.summary: Lim 2012 (Cochrane): six trials, 206 participants with data — intubation 2 of 45 on NPPV versus 0 of 41 controls (RR 4.48, 0.23 to 89.13); no deaths; one small study showed fewer admissions (RR 0.28)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Lim 2012, Cochrane)
cards.people: Six randomised trials of adults with severe acute asthma presenting to emergency departments or admitted to hospital, comparing usual medical care plus NPPV by nasal or face mask with usual care alone; five studies on 206 participants contributed data and one was available only as an abstract. Studies mixing in COPD were excluded unless asthma data were separable.
cards.result: For endotracheal intubation, two studies contributed data: two intubations were needed among 45 participants on NPPV and none among 41 control patients (risk ratio 4.48, 95% CI 0.23 to 89.13). There were no deaths in either of these studies. Length of hospital stay was reported in two studies but could not be meta-analysed. Hospitalisation was reported in one small study: three admissions among 17 NPPV patients versus 10 among 16 controls (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.84). The reviewers conclude the data are too sparse to support NPPV in status asthmaticus and call for larger rigorous trials.
cards.watchOut: An RR of 4.48 built on two events is noise, not a harm signal — but it cuts both ways: there is equally no evidence NPPV prevents intubation, the outcome clinicians reach for it to achieve. Event rates this low mean even the pooled literature is effectively a case series with a control group.

cards.headline: Soroksky 2003: in 30 patients, 80% on bilevel ventilation versus 20% on sham reached a 50% FEV1 rise; hospitalisation 17.6% versus 62.5% (p=0.0134)
cards.summary: Soroksky 2003: in 30 patients, 80% on bilevel ventilation versus 20% on sham reached a 50% FEV1 rise; hospitalisation 17.6% versus 62.5% (p=0.0134)
cards.type: Randomised pilot trial (Soroksky 2003)
cards.people: Thirty patients with a severe asthma attack recruited from 124 asthmatic patients seen in a university-hospital emergency department (mean FEV1 about 37% predicted on bilevel ventilation and 34% on control), randomised to bilevel positive airway pressure plus conventional therapy for three hours or to a sham device at subtherapeutic pressures plus conventional therapy; the hospitalisation analysis included 33 patients by intention to treat.
cards.result: Eighty percent of the bilevel group reached the predetermined primary endpoint (an increase of at least 50% in FEV1 from baseline) versus 20% of controls (p<0.004). Mean FEV1 rise was 53.5% (±23.4%) with bilevel ventilation versus 28.5% (±22.6%) with conventional treatment (p=0.006). Hospitalisation was required for 3 of 17 patients (17.6%) in the bilevel group versus 10 of 16 (62.5%) in the control group (p=0.0134). The device used was a named commercial product (BiPAP; Respironics; Murrysville, PA, USA), printed here exactly as the publication gives it.
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients, three hours, one centre, and a sham that patients may have been able to distinguish — a pilot designed to detect a physiological signal, which it did, and incapable of saying anything about intubation or death. Its admission result is the same data that appears as the single hospitalisation study in the Cochrane pool, so the two cards are not independent evidence.
cards.source: Soroksky A et al. A pilot prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of bilevel positive airway pressure in acute asthmatic attack. Chest. 2003. PMID: 12684289. cards.summary: Synthesis: physiological promise, clinical silence — NPPV in severe asthma remains an unproven rescue, not an evidence-based one
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: A Cochrane pool of six small trials (206 participants with data) and the 30-patient sham-controlled pilot that supplies most of its positive signal, in adults with severe acute asthma.
cards.result: Intubation: 2 of 45 versus 0 of 41 (RR 4.48, 95% CI 0.23 to 89.13). Deaths: none recorded in the contributing studies. Admission in the pilot: 17.6% versus 62.5%. FEV1 recovery in the pilot: 80% versus 20% reaching a 50% rise. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: a single small trial carries the benefit lean, which the developer reviews personally.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here transfers from COPD exacerbations, where NPPV has large positive trials — asthma's reversible obstruction and younger population make it a different question, and this shelf is deliberately confined to asthma. A trial powered on intubation in severe asthma still does not exist in these records.

shelves.title: Adding clarithromycin to a beta-lactam in hospitalised pneumonia: the early combined response endpoint was met by 68% versus 38% at 72 hours — a single trial, on a composite of symptoms, organ score, and procalcitonin
shelves.question: In hospitalised patients with community-acquired pneumonia and a strong inflammatory response, does adding clarithromycin to standard beta-lactam therapy improve early clinical outcomes compared with beta-lactam alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Clarithromycin/therapeutic use · Greece · Prospective Studies · Procalcitonin · Pneumonia/drug therapy · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-blinded trial, on an early composite endpoint, in an inflammation-selected population. In ACCESS (278 adults hospitalised with community-acquired pneumonia who had systemic inflammatory response syndrome, a SOFA score of at least 2, and procalcitonin of at least 0.25 ng/mL), adding oral clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily for seven days to standard beta-lactam care met the primary composite endpoint — at least 50% improvement in respiratory symptom score plus at least 30% SOFA improvement or favourable procalcitonin kinetics at 72 hours — in 68% of patients versus 38% on placebo (difference 29.6%, 95% CI 17.7 to 40.3; odds ratio 3.40, 95% CI 2.06 to 5.63), with serious treatment-emergent adverse events in 43% versus 53% (p=0.14), none judged treatment-related. The supporting trial is a caution rather than a confirmation: in Garin's randomised comparison in moderately severe pneumonia, beta-lactam monotherapy failed to prove non-inferior to beta-lactam plus macrolide for clinical stability at day 7 (41.2% versus 33.6% not yet stable), with the combination's advantage concentrated in atypical-pathogen infection and the most severe stratum, and no mortality difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single trial carrying a benefit claim on a composite early-response endpoint — mortality and hospital stay benefits are not shown in either record.

cards.headline: Giamarellos-Bourboulis 2024 (ACCESS): primary composite endpoint met by 91 of 134 (68%) on clarithromycin versus 51 of 133 (38%) on placebo (OR 3.40, 2.06 to 5.63); serious adverse events 43% versus 53%
cards.summary: Giamarellos-Bourboulis 2024 (ACCESS): primary composite endpoint met by 91 of 134 (68%) on clarithromycin versus 51 of 133 (38%) on placebo (OR 3.40, 2.06 to 5.63); serious adverse events 43% versus 53%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Giamarellos-Bourboulis 2024, ACCESS)
cards.people: 278 adults in 18 internal-medicine departments of Greek public hospitals with community-acquired pneumonia, systemic inflammatory response syndrome, SOFA score of at least 2, and procalcitonin at least 0.25 ng/mL, randomised to standard care (intravenous third-generation cephalosporin or beta-lactam/beta-lactamase-inhibitor) plus oral clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily for seven days or matching placebo; 267 patients formed the primary analysis population.
cards.result: The primary composite endpoint — at least 50% decrease in respiratory symptom severity score plus at least 30% decrease in SOFA score or favourable procalcitonin kinetics (at least 80% fall, or below 0.25 ng/mL) after 72 hours — was met by 91 patients (68%) in the clarithromycin group and 51 (38%) in the placebo group (difference 29.6%, 95% CI 17.7 to 40.3; odds ratio 3.40, 95% CI 2.06 to 5.63; p<0.0001), with the absolute rates printed alongside the relative effect. Serious treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 58 patients (43%) on clarithromycin and 70 (53%) on placebo (difference 9.4%, 95% CI −2.6 to 20.9; p=0.14), none judged related to treatment assignment.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is a 72-hour composite in which a procalcitonin trajectory can carry the 'response' — it is the regulatory early-response endpoint, not recovery, discharge, or survival, and this record reports none of those harder outcomes. The population was deliberately inflammation-enriched (SIRS, SOFA at least 2, procalcitonin at least 0.25), so the result does not extend to ordinary ward pneumonia; the trial was part-funded by a manufacturer of the drug. cards.headline: Garin 2014: beta-lactam alone failed non-inferiority against beta-lactam plus macrolide — not stable at day 7 in 41.2% versus 33.6%; combination advantage confined to atypical infection and PSI class IV; mortality equal
cards.summary: Garin 2014: beta-lactam alone failed non-inferiority against beta-lactam plus macrolide — not stable at day 7 in 41.2% versus 33.6%; combination advantage confined to atypical infection and PSI class IV; mortality equal
cards.type: Randomised open-label noninferiority trial (Garin 2014)
cards.people: 580 immunocompetent adults hospitalised in six Swiss acute-care hospitals with moderately severe community-acquired pneumonia, randomised to a beta-lactam alone or a beta-lactam plus a macrolide, with follow-up to 90 days; Legionella was systematically sought and, if found, treated by adding a macrolide in the monotherapy arm.
cards.result: After seven days, 120 of 291 patients (41.2%) on monotherapy versus 97 of 289 (33.6%) on combination therapy had not reached clinical stability (difference 7.6%; p=0.07), and the upper limit of the one-sided 90% confidence interval (13.0%) exceeded the predefined 8% noninferiority boundary — noninferiority was not shown. Patients with atypical pathogens (hazard ratio 0.33, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.85) or PSI category IV pneumonia (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.10) reached stability more slowly on monotherapy, while those without atypical infection (HR 0.99) or with PSI I–III (HR 1.06) had equivalent outcomes. Thirty-day readmissions were higher on monotherapy (7.9% versus 3.1%; p=0.01); mortality, intensive care admission, complications, length of stay, and 90-day recurrence did not differ.
cards.watchOut: This trial's macrolide was given as antibacterial cover, not selected by inflammatory markers, and its population was moderately severe rather than inflammation-enriched — it bounds the general claim ('add a macrolide for everyone') rather than testing the ACCESS hypothesis. Its subgroup pattern (benefit where atypical cover matters) also offers a rival explanation for combination benefits that has nothing to do with anti-inflammation.

cards.headline: Synthesis: in inflammation-selected pneumonia, clarithromycin speeds the early response; in unselected pneumonia, the macrolide question remains a subgroup story — and neither trial shows a survival effect
cards.summary: Synthesis: in inflammation-selected pneumonia, clarithromycin speeds the early response; in unselected pneumonia, the macrolide question remains a subgroup story — and neither trial shows a survival effect
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One double-blind placebo-controlled trial (278 inflammation-selected patients) of clarithromycin added to beta-lactam care, read against one open-label noninferiority trial (580 patients with moderately severe pneumonia) of beta-lactam with versus without a macrolide.
cards.result: Early combined response at 72 hours: 68% versus 38% (OR 3.40, 95% CI 2.06 to 5.63). Clinical stability at day 7 in the unselected trial: not reached by 41.2% on monotherapy versus 33.6% on combination, noninferiority of monotherapy not shown; mortality did not differ in that trial and is not reported in the selected trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: single-trial benefit claim on a composite endpoint.
cards.watchOut: Two different macrolide rationales — anti-inflammatory modulation in selected patients versus atypical antibacterial cover in all-comers — are easy to conflate; this shelf keeps them separate and claims only the early-response result for the selected population. Macrolide resistance and QT effects are outside both records' reported outcomes.
cards.source: Synthesis of Giamarellos-Bourboulis EJ et al. The Lancet. Respiratory Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 38184008); Garin N et al. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2014 (PMID: 25286173).
