shelves.title: Adjunctive prednisone in hospitalised community-acquired pneumonia (STEP): clinical stability in 3.0 versus 4.4 days — faster stability with no survival claim, at a hyperglycaemia price of 19% versus 11%
shelves.question: In adults hospitalised with non-severe community-acquired pneumonia, does adjunctive prednisone shorten time to clinical stability and hospital stay compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage* · Community-Acquired Infections/drug therapy/microbiology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Pneumonia/drug therapy*/microbiology · Prednisone/administration & dosage* · Switzerland · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for speed to clinical stability, not for survival. In STEP (Blum CA et al., PMID: 25608756), 785 patients admitted to hospital with community-acquired pneumonia at seven tertiary care hospitals in Switzerland were randomly assigned within 24 hours of presentation to prednisone 50 mg daily for 7 days (n=392) or placebo (n=393). Median time to clinical stability — the primary endpoint, defined as time until stable vital signs for at least 24 hours — was shorter on prednisone: 3.0 days (IQR 2.5-3.4) versus 4.4 days (4.0-5.0) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.33, 95% CI 1.15-1.50, p<0.0001). Pneumonia-associated complications until day 30 did not differ significantly: 11 patients (3%) on prednisone versus 22 (6%) on placebo (odds ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.23-1.02; p=0.056). The price was glucose: in-hospital hyperglycaemia needing insulin treatment occurred in 76 patients (19%) on prednisone versus 43 (11%) on placebo (odds ratio 1.96, 95% CI 1.31-2.93, p=0.0010), while other adverse events compatible with corticosteroid use were rare and similar in both groups. The authors concluded that prednisone for 7 days in patients admitted to hospital with community-acquired pneumonia shortens time to clinical stability without an increase in complications. The fetched record reports no hospital length-of-stay figure and makes no survival claim, so this shelf claims neither: the proven gain is reaching stable vital signs about a day and a half sooner. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adjunctive prednisone 50 mg daily for 7 days shortened time to clinical stability in one large double-blind trial of hospitalised community-acquired pneumonia, with more insulin-treated hyperglycaemia and no demonstrated effect on complications or survival.

cards.headline: Blum 2015 (STEP): median time to clinical stability 3.0 days on prednisone versus 4.4 days on placebo (hazard ratio 1.33, p<0.0001) — complications 3% versus 6%, hyperglycaemia needing insulin 19% versus 11%
cards.summary: Blum 2015 (STEP): median time to clinical stability 3.0 days on prednisone versus 4.4 days on placebo (hazard ratio 1.33, p<0.0001) — complications 3% versus 6%, hyperglycaemia needing insulin 19% versus 11%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial (Blum 2015, STEP)
cards.people: 785 patients aged 18 years or older with community-acquired pneumonia, recruited from seven tertiary care hospitals in Switzerland within 24 hours of presentation and randomly assigned (1:1 ratio, computer-generated randomisation with variable block sizes of four to six, stratified by study centre) to prednisone 50 mg daily for 7 days (n=392) or placebo (n=393). From Dec 1, 2009, to May 21, 2014, 2911 patients were assessed for eligibility. The primary endpoint was time to clinical stability, defined as time (days) until stable vital signs for at least 24 hours, and analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Median time to clinical stability was shorter in the prednisone group (3.0 days, IQR 2.5-3.4) than in the placebo group (4.4 days, 4.0-5.0; hazard ratio 1.33, 95% CI 1.15-1.50, p<0.0001). Pneumonia-associated complications until day 30 did not differ between groups (11 [3%] in the prednisone group and 22 [6%] in the placebo group; odds ratio 0.49 [95% CI 0.23-1.02]; p=0.056), the absolute rates printed alongside the relative effects. The prednisone group had a higher incidence of in-hospital hyperglycaemia needing insulin treatment (76 [19%] vs 43 [11%]; odds ratio 1.96, 95% CI 1.31-2.93, p=0.0010). Other adverse events compatible with corticosteroid use were rare and similar in both groups. The authors concluded that prednisone treatment for 7 days in patients with community-acquired pneumonia admitted to hospital shortens time to clinical stability without an increase in complications, a finding they described as relevant from a patient perspective and an important determinant of hospital costs and efficiency.
cards.watchOut: One trial carries this shelf, and its primary endpoint is a process endpoint — days until vital signs are stable for 24 hours — not mortality or another hard outcome; the trial makes no survival claim, and the near-significant difference in pneumonia-associated complications (3% versus 6%, p=0.056) is not a demonstrated benefit. The question also asks about hospital stay, but the fetched record reports no length-of-stay figure, so no stay shortening is claimed here. The glucose price is real and immediate: nearly one in five patients on prednisone needed insulin for in-hospital hyperglycaemia, versus about one in nine on placebo.
cards.source: Blum CA et al. Adjunct prednisone therapy for patients with community-acquired pneumonia: a multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2015. PMID: 25608756. Registry ID: NCT00973154. cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial of 785 patients admitted to hospital with community-acquired pneumonia (STEP), testing prednisone 50 mg daily for 7 days against placebo, with 392 and 393 patients assigned.
cards.result: Time to clinical stability: median 3.0 days (IQR 2.5-3.4) on prednisone versus 4.4 days (4.0-5.0) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.33, 95% CI 1.15-1.50, p<0.0001). This shelf asks a genuinely different question: in adults hospitalised with non-severe community-acquired pneumonia, does adjunctive prednisone shorten time to clinical stability — STEP's own primary question, in the non-severe hospitalised population rather than the severe, life-or-death population of #159. shelves.title: Early switch from intravenous to oral antibiotics in severe pneumonia: cure 83% versus 85%, mortality 4% versus 6% — and two fewer days in hospital
shelves.question: In patients with severe community-acquired pneumonia who have stabilised, is an early switch from intravenous to oral antibiotics as effective as a full intravenous course?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Amoxicillin/therapeutic use · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Cephalosporins/therapeutic use · Clavulanic Acid/therapeutic use · Community-Acquired Infections/drug therapy · Drug Combinations · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Middle Aged · Pneumonia, Bacterial/drug therapy · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — switching stabilised patients to oral antibiotics after three intravenous days matched a full intravenous course on cure and mortality, and shortened both intravenous treatment and hospital stay, in a randomised trial and a concordant meta-analysis. In the Dutch multicentre trial (302 patients with severe community-acquired pneumonia on non-intensive-care wards; 265 in the intention-to-treat analysis), clinical cure was 83% with early switch versus 85% with seven intravenous days (difference 2%, 95% CI −7% to 10%) and day-28 mortality was 4% versus 6% (difference 2%, 95% CI −3% to 8%), while intravenous treatment was 3.4 days shorter (3.6 versus 7.0 days) and hospital stay 1.9 days shorter (9.6 versus 11.5 days). A meta-analysis of six randomised trials (1,219 patients with moderate-to-severe pneumonia) found treatment success, mortality (odds ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.33), and recurrence no different, hospitalisation 3.34 days shorter, and fewer drug-related adverse events with early switch (OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.89). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): for the patient who has stabilised, the oral switch is the adequately proven default — the benefit is time and freedom from the drip, at no shown clinical cost.

cards.headline: Oosterheert 2006: cure 83% early-switch versus 85% full-intravenous; mortality at day 28, 4% versus 6%; intravenous days 3.6 versus 7.0; hospital stay 9.6 versus 11.5 days
cards.summary: Oosterheert 2006: cure 83% early-switch versus 85% full-intravenous; mortality at day 28, 4% versus 6%; intravenous days 3.6 versus 7.0; hospital stay 9.6 versus 11.5 days
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Oosterheert 2006)
cards.people: 302 patients (mean age 69.5 years, mean pneumonia severity score 112.7) with severe community-acquired pneumonia on non-intensive-care wards at seven Dutch hospitals, randomised to three days of intravenous antibiotics followed — once clinically stable — by oral antibiotics, or to seven days of intravenous antibiotics; 265 patients formed the intention-to-treat analysis after early dropouts before day 3.
cards.result: Clinical cure was 83% in the intervention group and 85% in the control group (difference 2%, 95% CI −7% to 10%). Mortality at day 28 was 4% versus 6% (mean difference 2%, 95% CI −3% to 8%). Duration of intravenous treatment was reduced by a mean 3.4 days (3.6 versus 7.0 days) and length of hospital stay by 1.9 days (9.6 versus 11.5 days; 95% CI for the difference 0.6 to 3.2 days).
cards.watchOut: 'Severe' here means a high severity score on a general ward — patients in intensive care were not studied, and the switch was conditional on clinical stability, so the trial licenses switching the stabilised patient, not shortening intravenous therapy for the still-unstable one. Thirty-seven randomised patients dropped out before day 3 and were excluded, which slightly softens the intention-to-treat claim.
cards.source: Oosterheert JJ et al. Effectiveness of early switch from intravenous to oral antibiotics in severe community acquired pneumonia: multicentre randomised trial. BMJ. 2006. PMID: 17090560. 'severe' here means a high severity score on a general ward — patients in intensive care were not studied, and the switch was conditional on clinical stability, so the trial licenses switching the stabilised patient, not shortening intravenous therapy for the still-unstable one. thirty-seven randomised patients dropped out before day 3 and were excluded, which slightly softens the intention-to-treat claim. oosterheert jj et al. effectiveness of early switch from intravenous to oral antibiotics in severe community acquired pneumonia: multicentre randomised trial. bmj. 2006. pmid: 17090560. registry id: nct00273676. mesh: administration, oral · adolescent · adult · aged · amoxicillin/therapeutic use · anti-bacterial agents/administration & dosage · cephalosporins/therapeutic use · clavulanic acid/therapeutic use · community-acquired infections/drug therapy · drug combinations · humans · infusions, intravenous · middle aged · pneumonia, bacterial/drug therapy · time factors · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Athanassa 2008: six trials, 1,219 patients — treatment success and mortality no different (mortality OR 0.81, 0.49 to 1.33); hospitalisation 3.34 days shorter; drug-related adverse events fewer (OR 0.65)
cards.summary: Athanassa 2008: six trials, 1,219 patients — treatment success and mortality no different (mortality OR 0.81, 0.49 to 1.33); hospitalisation 3.34 days shorter; drug-related adverse events fewer (OR 0.65)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised trials (Athanassa 2008)
cards.people: Six randomised controlled trials including 1,219 hospitalised patients with moderate-to-severe community-acquired pneumonia, comparing early switch from intravenous to oral antibiotics with continuous intravenous treatment at the same total treatment duration; findings were similar in the severe-pneumonia subgroup.
cards.result: Treatment success did not differ between early switch and intravenous-only treatment in intention-to-treat (odds ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.59) or clinically evaluable patients (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.39). Mortality (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.33) and recurrence of pneumonia (OR 1.81, 95% CI 0.70 to 4.72) were not different, while duration of hospitalisation was shorter with early switch (weighted mean difference −3.34 days, 95% CI −4.42 to −2.25) and drug-related adverse events were fewer (OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.89).
cards.watchOut: The recurrence point estimate (OR 1.81) leans against switching, on a confidence interval too wide to read — the pool is reassuring on mortality and success, merely silent on recurrence. Trials span different antibiotics, switch criteria, and eras, and the largest contributing trial dominates the severe subgroup.
cards.source: Athanassa Z et al. Early switch to oral treatment in patients with moderate to severe community-acquired pneumonia: a meta-analysis. Drugs. 2008. PMID: 19016574. cards.headline: Synthesis: once a severe-pneumonia patient has stabilised, staying intravenous buys nothing measurable — the oral switch returns about two to three hospital days
cards.summary: Synthesis: once a severe-pneumonia patient has stabilised, staying intravenous buys nothing measurable — the oral switch returns about two to three hospital days
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One multicentre randomised trial (302 patients with severe pneumonia) plus a meta-analysis of six randomised trials (1,219 patients with moderate-to-severe pneumonia) of early intravenous-to-oral switch versus continued intravenous therapy.
cards.result: Cure: 83% versus 85%. Mortality: 4% versus 6% in the trial; pooled OR 0.81 (95% CI 0.49 to 1.33). Hospital stay: 1.9 days shorter in the trial, 3.34 days shorter pooled. Drug-related adverse events: fewer with switch (OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.89). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Every result is conditional on the switch being made after stabilisation — the trials' shared entry rule — and intensive-care patients are outside the evidence. Tier C is not set: a randomised trial and a concordant meta-analysis carry the shelf, and no mortality benefit is claimed.
cards.source: Synthesis of Oosterheert JJ et al. BMJ. 2006 (PMID: 17090560); Athanassa Z et al. Drugs. 2008 (PMID: 19016574).

shelves.title: A negative MRSA nasal PCR in pneumonia: vancomycin courses about a day shorter (−0.98 days) with no shown harm — and a negative predictive value of 96.5% at 10% prevalence, but only 94.8% in ventilator-associated pneumonia
shelves.question: In hospitalised patients with pneumonia, can a negative MRSA nasal PCR safely guide stopping or withholding anti-MRSA therapy, shortening vancomycin exposure without worse outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus/isolation & purification/genetics · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Antimicrobial Stewardship · Polymerase Chain Reaction/methods · Staphylococcal Infections/diagnosis/drug therapy/microbiology · Mass Screening/methods · Pneumonia, Staphylococcal/drug therapy/diagnosis/microbiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the diagnostic logic is strong and the stewardship outcomes point the right way, but every outcome study behind the practice is retrospective. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of six observational retrospective studies (1,649 hospitalised pneumonia patients) found MRSA nasal PCR screening was associated with vancomycin duration shorter by 0.98 days (95% CI −1.61 to −0.59), with no significant difference in acute kidney injury (odds ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.08), hospital stay (−0.20 days, 95% CI −0.85 to 0.45), or mortality (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.02) — the safety intervals are wide and all lean favourable without proving safety. The diagnostic foundation is a 2018 meta-analysis of 22 studies (5,163 patients): nasal screening had sensitivity 70.9% and specificity 90.3% for MRSA pneumonia, giving a negative predictive value of 96.5% at a 10% prevalence (98.1% in community- and healthcare-associated pneumonia) — but in ventilator-associated pneumonia sensitivity fell to 40.3% and the negative predictive value to 94.8%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a negative swab is a reasonable de-escalation prompt in non-ventilator pneumonia; the evidence is observational, and the ventilator-associated subgroup is exactly where the test is weakest.

cards.headline: Tanure 2026: six retrospective studies, 1,649 patients — vancomycin duration −0.98 days (−1.61 to −0.59) with screening; kidney injury OR 0.53 (0.26 to 1.08) and mortality OR 0.68 (0.45 to 1.02), neither significant
cards.summary: Tanure 2026: six retrospective studies, 1,649 patients — vancomycin duration −0.98 days (−1.61 to −0.59) with screening; kidney injury OR 0.53 (0.26 to 1.08) and mortality OR 0.68 (0.45 to 1.02), neither significant
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Tanure 2026)
cards.people: Six observational retrospective studies including 1,649 hospitalised patients with pneumonia, assessing the impact of nasal MRSA PCR screening on antibiotic de-escalation, therapy duration, acute kidney injury, hospital stay, and mortality.
cards.result: Random-effects models showed a significant reduction in vancomycin duration with screening (−0.98 days, 95% CI −1.61 to −0.59), greater in non-community-acquired pneumonia subgroups (−1.55 versus −0.68 days). Acute kidney injury was non-significantly lower (odds ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.08). No significant effect was observed for hospital stay (−0.20 days, 95% CI −0.85 to 0.45) or mortality (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.02). Most studies lacked consistent reporting on the timing of screening.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective before-and-after stewardship studies cannot separate the swab's effect from the stewardship programme wrapped around it, and 'no significant harm' in 1,649 observational patients is not proof of safety — the mortality interval still includes a small increase. Screening timing, the variable most likely to determine whether a negative result is trustworthy, was inconsistently reported.
cards.source: Tanure YCB et al. Impact of MRSA nasal swab screening and PCR in pneumonia treatment and antimicrobial stewardship: A systematic review and meta-analysis. cards.headline: Parente 2018: 22 studies, 5,163 patients — sensitivity 70.9%, specificity 90.3%; at 10% prevalence the negative predictive value is 96.5% overall and 98.1% in CAP/HCAP, but sensitivity is only 40.3% in ventilator-associated pneumonia
cards.summary: Parente 2018: 22 studies, 5,163 patients — sensitivity 70.9%, specificity 90.3%; at 10% prevalence the negative predictive value is 96.5% overall and 98.1% in CAP/HCAP, but sensitivity is only 40.3% in ventilator-associated pneumonia
cards.type: Diagnostic meta-analysis (Parente 2018)
cards.people: Twenty-two studies comprising 5,163 patients evaluating MRSA nasal screening against the development of MRSA pneumonia, across community-acquired, healthcare-associated, and ventilator-associated pneumonia.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity and specificity of the MRSA nares screen for all pneumonia types were 70.9% and 90.3%. At a 10% prevalence of MRSA pneumonia, the calculated positive predictive value was 44.8% and the negative predictive value 96.5%. For community-acquired and healthcare-associated pneumonia, sensitivity was 85% and specificity 92.1%, with positive and negative predictive values of 56.8% and 98.1%. For ventilator-associated pneumonia, sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values were 40.3%, 93.7%, 35.7%, and 94.8% respectively.
cards.watchOut: Negative predictive value is prevalence-dependent arithmetic, not a property of the swab: in a unit where MRSA causes a quarter of pneumonias, the same test misses far more. The ventilator-associated figures are the warning — a test that detects only 40% of MRSA VAP cases will falsely reassure in the highest-risk group, which is why this shelf's claim stops at non-ventilator pneumonia.
cards.source: Parente DM et al. The Clinical Utility of Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) Nasal Screening to Rule Out MRSA Pneumonia: A Diagnostic Meta-analysis With Antimicrobial Stewardship Implications. cards.headline: Synthesis: the swab rules out better than it rules in — a day of vancomycin saved per patient, on retrospective evidence, with the weakest performance where the stakes are highest
cards.summary: Synthesis: the swab rules out better than it rules in — a day of vancomycin saved per patient, on retrospective evidence, with the weakest performance where the stakes are highest
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: A six-study retrospective stewardship meta-analysis (1,649 patients) layered on a 22-study diagnostic meta-analysis (5,163 patients) of MRSA nasal screening in pneumonia.
cards.result: Vancomycin duration: −0.98 days (95% CI −1.61 to −0.59). Kidney injury OR 0.53 (0.26 to 1.08); mortality OR 0.68 (0.45 to 1.02) — neither significant. Negative predictive value at 10% prevalence: 96.5% overall, 98.1% in community/healthcare-associated pneumonia, 94.8% in ventilator-associated pneumonia with sensitivity of only 40.3%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the outcome evidence is observational, which the developer reviews personally.
cards.watchOut: A positive swab is a poor rule-in (positive predictive value 44.8% at 10% prevalence) — this shelf supports acting on negatives, not escalating on positives. No randomised trial of swab-guided de-escalation exists in these records.

shelves.title: Inhaled amikacin–fosfomycin added to intravenous therapy for Gram-negative ventilator pneumonia: bacterial counts fell, clinical outcomes did not — infection score change identical (p=0.70), deaths 24% versus 17%
shelves.question: In ventilator-associated pneumonia caused by Gram-negative bacilli, does adjunctive inhaled amikacin–fosfomycin improve clinical cure compared with standard intravenous therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: APACHE · Administration, Inhalation · Adult · Aged · Amikacin/administration & dosage · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fosfomycin/administration & dosage · Gram-Negative Bacterial Infections/drug therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pneumonia, Ventilator-Associated/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the one randomised trial of this specific inhalation system sterilised airways without helping patients. In the IASIS trial (143 patients with Gram-negative ventilator-associated pneumonia), the amikacin fosfomycin inhalation system (300 mg amikacin/120 mg fosfomycin aerosol twice daily for up to 10 days, added to standard intravenous care) did not differ from placebo aerosol on the primary endpoint of change in Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score (p=0.70), on the hierarchical endpoint of no mortality with clinical cure by day 14 (p=0.68), or on ventilator-free days (p=0.06); deaths were 17 of 71 (24%) on the system versus 12 of 72 (17%) on placebo (p=0.32), despite significantly fewer positive tracheal cultures on days 3 and 7. A broader meta-analysis of adjunctive inhaled antibiotics in ventilator-associated pneumonia (11 randomised trials, 1,210 patients, mostly other agents) found clinical cure modestly higher (relative risk 1.13, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.26) and microbiological eradication higher (RR 1.45, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.76) but mortality unchanged (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.21) and bronchospasm increased (RR 2.74, 95% CI 1.31 to 5.73) — its own authors do not support routine use. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for the amikacin–fosfomycin system the answer is a direct randomised no; for inhaled adjuncts as a class, cure-score gains have never converted into survival.

cards.headline: Kollef 2017 (IASIS): infection-score change no different (p=0.70); cure-with-survival endpoint p=0.68; deaths 24% on the inhalation system versus 17% on placebo (p=0.32)
cards.summary: Kollef 2017 (IASIS): infection-score change no different (p=0.70); cure-with-survival endpoint p=0.68; deaths 24% on the inhalation system versus 17% on placebo (p=0.32)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (Kollef 2017, IASIS)
cards.people: 143 patients with Gram-negative ventilator-associated pneumonia randomised between 2013 and 2016 to standard intravenous care plus the amikacin fosfomycin inhalation system (300 mg amikacin/120 mg fosfomycin by aerosol twice daily for 10 days or until extubation; 71 patients) or standard care plus placebo aerosol (72 patients); the primary endpoint was assessed in the subset with microbiologically proven Gram-negative infection at baseline. The delivery device was the investigational eFlow Inline System (PARI GmbH), named exactly as the publication gives it.
cards.result: Change from baseline in the Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score during treatment did not differ between groups (p=0.70). The secondary hierarchical endpoint of no mortality and clinical cure at day 14 or earlier was not significant (p=0.68), nor was the endpoint of no mortality and ventilator-free days (p=0.06). Deaths numbered 17 (24%) in the inhalation-system group and 12 (17%) in the placebo group (p=0.32). The inhalation group had significantly fewer positive tracheal cultures on days 3 and 7 than placebo — a microbiological effect without a clinical one.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2 trial of 143 patients cannot exclude a modest benefit or confirm the numerically higher mortality — but the burden of proof sits on the intervention, and every clinical endpoint here is flat or adverse-leaning while only cultures improved. The candidate list named this anchor 'INHALE'; the verified record is the IASIS trial of the amikacin fosfomycin inhalation system, and the shelf is built on that record (declared as a swap in the builder summary).

PMID: 27890714. Registry ID: NCT01969799. cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Tang 2021)
cards.people: Eleven randomised controlled trials including 1,210 patients with ventilator-associated pneumonia, comparing adjunctive inhaled antibiotic therapy plus intravenous treatment with intravenous treatment alone, across inhaled agents (predominantly aminoglycosides and colistin rather than the amikacin–fosfomycin system specifically).
cards.result: Adjunctive inhaled therapy improved clinical cure (relative risk 1.13, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.26) and microbiological eradication (RR 1.45, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.76) compared with intravenous therapy alone, but mortality was not reduced (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.21). Inhaled therapy was not associated with more renal impairment but was associated with increased bronchospasm during treatment (RR 2.74, 95% CI 1.31 to 5.73). The authors conclude that routine nebulised antibiotics for ventilator-associated pneumonia are not supported by the available evidence.
cards.watchOut: The class pool mixes agents, doses, and delivery devices, and its cure advantage is a relative 13% on a clinician-judged outcome in trials of varying blinding — while the one double-blind trial of a defined system found no cure advantage at all. Where the pooled and the specific disagree, the specific record governs this shelf's question.

cards.result: System-specific: infection-score change p=0.70; deaths 24% versus 17% (p=0.32); tracheal cultures improved. shelves.title: Vitamin D added to tuberculosis treatment does not speed sputum conversion: pooled trials show no significant difference in smear or culture conversion — symptoms scores improve slightly, bacteria clear at the same rate
shelves.question: In patients being treated for pulmonary tuberculosis, does adjunctive vitamin D accelerate sputum culture conversion or improve clinical outcomes compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Dietary Supplements · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Tuberculosis/diet therapy/drug therapy/prevention & control · Vitamin D/therapeutic use/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the outcome the question asks about, the pooled randomised answer is no. A 2025 meta-analysis of 26 randomised trials (19,586 participants, spanning prevention and treatment) found no significant differences between vitamin D and control in sputum smear conversion, sputum culture conversion, or time to sputum culture conversion during anti-tuberculosis treatment, although tuberculosis symptom scores were lower at eight weeks (mean difference −0.39, 95% CI −0.57 to −0.22) and 12 weeks (−0.53, 95% CI −0.84 to −0.22), safety profiles were similar, and a daily-dosing subgroup showed higher smear conversion at six and eight weeks. The best-known individual trial points the same way: in 146 London patients with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis, four 2.5 mg doses of vitamin D3 gave a median time to culture conversion of 36.0 versus 43.5 days (adjusted hazard ratio 1.39, 95% CI 0.90 to 2.16; p=0.14) — not significant — with a significant hastening only in the small subgroup carrying one vitamin-D-receptor genotype (HR 8.09, 95% CI 1.36 to 48.01), a subgroup finding with a confidence interval too wide to act on. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): vitamin D may ease symptom scores, but it does not clear sputum faster, and it is not a substitute for, or an accelerator of, standard therapy.

cards.headline: Meng 2025: 26 randomised trials, 19,586 participants — no significant difference in sputum smear conversion, culture conversion, or time to culture conversion; TB symptom scores lower by 0.39–0.53 points
cards.summary: Meng 2025: 26 randomised trials, 19,586 participants — no significant difference in sputum smear conversion, culture conversion, or time to culture conversion; TB symptom scores lower by 0.39–0.53 points
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Meng 2025)
cards.people: Twenty-six randomised trials involving 19,586 participants, comparing vitamin D supplementation with placebo or standard treatment for tuberculosis prevention (four trials) or as an adjunct to anti-tuberculosis treatment, searched to April 2024.
cards.result: For prevention, the pooled result was inconclusive (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.01). For treatment, there were no significant statistical differences between the vitamin D and non-vitamin D groups in sputum smear conversion, sputum culture conversion, or time to sputum culture conversion. Patients in the vitamin D group had significantly lower tuberculosis scores at eight weeks (mean difference −0.39, 95% CI −0.57 to −0.22) and 12 weeks (−0.53, 95% CI −0.84 to −0.22), with similar safety profiles. A subgroup analysis by dosing frequency found higher sputum smear conversion at six and eight weeks with daily supplementation. The authors conclude vitamin D does not accelerate clearance of tuberculosis bacteria but can improve symptoms.
cards.watchOut: The pool mixes prevention and treatment trials, doses, and routes, and its one positive treatment signal on conversion appears only in a dosing-frequency subgroup — the classic place for chance findings. The symptom-score differences (about half a point) are statistically firm but clinically small, and the record does not report mortality.
cards.source: Meng J et al. The role of vitamin D in the prevention and treatment of tuberculosis: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Infection. 2025. PMID: 39612153. MeSH: Humans · Dietary Supplements · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Tuberculosis/diet therapy/drug therapy/prevention & control · Vitamin D/therapeutic use/administration & dosage

cards.headline: Martineau 2011: median time to sputum culture conversion 36.0 versus 43.5 days (adjusted HR 1.39, 0.90 to 2.16; p=0.14) — not significant; a genotype subgroup (HR 8.09) rests on a handful of patients
cards.summary: Martineau 2011: median time to sputum culture conversion 36.0 versus 43.5 days (adjusted HR 1.39, 0.90 to 2.16; p=0.14) — not significant; a genotype subgroup (HR 8.09) rests on a handful of patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind controlled trial (Martineau 2011)
cards.people: 146 adults with sputum smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis in London, allocated to 2.5 mg vitamin D3 or placebo at baseline and at 14, 28, and 42 days after starting standard tuberculosis treatment; 126 patients (62 intervention, 64 placebo) formed the primary efficacy analysis, with genotyping for vitamin D receptor polymorphisms.
cards.result: Median time to sputum culture conversion was 36.0 days in the intervention group and 43.5 days in the placebo group (adjusted hazard ratio 1.39, 95% CI 0.90 to 2.16; p=0.14) — not statistically significant. The TaqI vitamin D receptor genotype modified the effect (p for interaction 0.03), with enhanced response only in patients with the tt genotype (HR 8.09, 95% CI 1.36 to 48.01; p=0.02); the FokI genotype did not modify the effect (p=0.85). Mean serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D at 56 days was 101.4 nmol/L on vitamin D versus 22.8 nmol/L on placebo, confirming the supplement was absorbed and active.
cards.watchOut: The genotype subgroup is tiny and its hazard ratio's confidence interval spans 1.36 to 48.01 — it is a hypothesis about pharmacogenetics, not a prescribing rule, and it has not been the basis of any replicated stratified trial in this evidence. Four bolus doses in a London population with profound baseline deficiency (22.8 nmol/L on placebo) may also not transfer to daily dosing or replete populations.
cards.source: Martineau AR et al. High-dose vitamin D(3) during intensive-phase antimicrobial treatment of pulmonary tuberculosis: a double-blind randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. 2011. PMID: 21215445. Registry ID: NCT00419068. shelves.title: Exercise rehabilitation after pulmonary embolism: early programmes after the clot show no clear between-group benefit in four small trials (250 patients) — but targeted rehabilitation for persistent breathlessness improved the shuttle walk by 53 m
shelves.question: After an acute pulmonary embolism, does a structured exercise and rehabilitation programme improve exercise capacity and quality of life compared with usual care?
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by timing and by who is enrolled. A 2026 systematic review of randomised trials of structured exercise training started within three months of acute venous thromboembolism found only four trials (250 patients in total; two after pulmonary embolism, one after deep vein thrombosis, one mixed): exercise capacity, cardiopulmonary function, or quality of life improved within the exercise groups in three studies, but differences between exercise and control groups were nonsignificant, limited by small samples and risk of bias — while no trial reported safety concerns from starting exercise within three months. The clearer positive result comes later and in a selected group: in a randomised trial of 211 survivors with persistent dyspnoea six to 72 months after pulmonary embolism, an eight-week programme of twice-weekly exercise plus one education session beat usual care on the incremental shuttle walk test by 53.0 m (95% CI 17.7 to 88.3; p=0.0035) and on the disease-specific quality-of-life questionnaire (mean difference −4%, 95% CI −0.09 to 0.00; p=0.041), with no differences in generic quality of life, dyspnoea scores, or endurance shuttle performance, and no adverse events. PROPOSED SPLIT: early routine rehabilitation after a clot — safe, benefit unproven; rehabilitation aimed at survivors still breathless months later — exercise capacity genuinely improved in one randomised trial.

cards.headline: Steiner 2026: four randomised trials, 250 patients — within-group improvements in three studies, but no significant exercise-versus-control differences; no safety concerns from early exercise
cards.summary: Steiner 2026: four randomised trials, 250 patients — within-group improvements in three studies, but no significant exercise-versus-control differences; no safety concerns from early exercise
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Steiner 2026)
cards.people: Four randomised trials (250 patients) of structured exercise training initiated within three months after acute venous thromboembolism — two after pulmonary embolism, one after deep vein thrombosis, one after either — including supervised aerobic or high-intensity interval training, home-based programmes, and combined behavioural counselling, each compared with standard anticoagulation-based care.
cards.result: Three studies demonstrated improvements in exercise capacity, cardiopulmonary function, or quality of life within the exercise groups; however, differences between exercise and control groups were nonsignificant and were limited by small sample sizes and risk of bias. No trial reported safety concerns regarding exercise initiated within three months after venous thromboembolism. The reviewers conclude that early structured exercise appears safe, that robust efficacy evidence is limited, and that large trials addressing prevention of post-thrombotic and post-PE syndromes are warranted.
cards.watchOut: Four trials and 250 patients across two different diseases (leg thrombosis and pulmonary embolism) cannot settle efficacy — 'nonsignificant' here means unmeasured, not disproven. The review's record carries no MeSH indexing, which is why this shelf's mesh field is empty. Programmes, intensities, and comparators differed across all four trials.
cards.source: Steiner D et al. Structured exercise training and rehabilitation in patients with acute venous thromboembolism: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials. European Journal of Preventive Cardiology. 2026. PMID: 41790033. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Jervan 2023: in 211 PE survivors with persistent dyspnoea, eight weeks of rehabilitation improved the incremental shuttle walk by 53.0 m (17.7 to 88.3; p=0.0035) and disease-specific quality of life — dyspnoea scores unchanged
cards.summary: Jervan 2023: in 211 PE survivors with persistent dyspnoea, eight weeks of rehabilitation improved the incremental shuttle walk by 53.0 m (17.7 to 88.3; p=0.0035) and disease-specific quality of life — dyspnoea scores unchanged
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Jervan 2023)
cards.people: 211 patients with persistent dyspnoea following pulmonary embolism diagnosed six to 72 months earlier, without cardiopulmonary comorbidities, at two hospitals; 108 randomised to a rehabilitation programme (two exercise sessions weekly for eight weeks plus one educational session) and 103 to usual care.
cards.result: At follow-up, the rehabilitation group performed better on the incremental shuttle walk test (mean difference 53.0 m, 95% CI 17.7 to 88.3; p=0.0035) and reported better scores on the Pulmonary Embolism quality-of-life questionnaire (mean difference −4%, 95% CI −0.09 to 0.00; p=0.041). There were no differences in generic quality of life, dyspnoea scores, or the endurance shuttle walk test. No adverse events occurred during the intervention.
cards.watchOut: This is rehabilitation for a chronic symptom months to years after the event — not the early post-discharge programme the systematic review examined — and it enrolled survivors without cardiopulmonary comorbidity, a favourable subset. Walking capacity improved while the symptom the patients enrolled for (dyspnoea scores) did not, a split worth stating plainly.
cards.source: Jervan Ø et al. The Effects of Exercise Training in Patients With Persistent Dyspnea Following Pulmonary Embolism: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Chest. 2023. PMID: 37149257. shelves.question: In connective-tissue-disease-associated interstitial lung disease that is progressing despite immunosuppression, is rituximab as effective as intravenous cyclophosphamide for lung function, with fewer adverse events?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — not because rituximab beat cyclophosphamide on the lung, but because it matched it while costing less harm. In RECITAL (101 patients with severe or progressive interstitial lung disease related to scleroderma, idiopathic inflammatory myositis, or mixed connective tissue disease), forced vital capacity improved from baseline at 24 weeks in both groups (+99 mL on cyclophosphamide, +97 mL on rituximab), and the adjusted difference of −40 mL (95% CI −153 to 74; p=0.49) showed rituximab was not superior; quality-of-life scores improved clinically importantly in both groups, survival, progression-free survival, and time to treatment failure did not differ, and deaths were three (6%) on rituximab versus two (4%) on cyclophosphamide, all from complications of the underlying diseases. The tolerability gap was real: 445 adverse events were reported on rituximab versus 646 on cyclophosphamide, serious adverse events numbered 29 versus 33, and corticosteroid exposure over 48 weeks was lower with rituximab. A 2025 meta-analysis of the head-to-head literature (six studies) likewise found no significant difference in FVC change (weighted mean difference 0.86, 95% CI −1.51 to 3.24), a possible DLCO advantage for rituximab (6.43, 95% CI 1.62 to 11.23) resting on only three studies, and fewer adverse events with rituximab. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single phase 2b trial carries the comparison — rituximab is a legitimate alternative where cyclophosphamide's toxicity is the deciding concern, not a more effective drug.

cards.headline: Maher 2023 (RECITAL): FVC change at 24 weeks +97 mL rituximab versus +99 mL cyclophosphamide (adjusted difference −40 mL, −153 to 74; p=0.49); adverse events 445 versus 646; deaths 3 versus 2
cards.summary: Maher 2023 (RECITAL): FVC change at 24 weeks +97 mL rituximab versus +99 mL cyclophosphamide (adjusted difference −40 mL, −153 to 74; p=0.49); adverse events 445 versus 646; deaths 3 versus 2
cards.type: Randomised double-blind double-dummy phase 2b trial (Maher 2023, RECITAL)
cards.people: 101 patients aged 18 to 80 with severe or progressive interstitial lung disease related to scleroderma, idiopathic inflammatory myositis, or mixed connective tissue disease at 11 UK specialist centres, randomised to rituximab 1,000 mg intravenously at weeks 0 and 2 (51 patients) or cyclophosphamide 600 mg/m² intravenously every four weeks for six doses (50 patients); 97 received at least one dose and formed the modified intention-to-treat population.
cards.result: At 24 weeks, FVC had improved from baseline in both groups (unadjusted mean increase 99 mL [SD 329] on cyclophosphamide and 97 mL [234] on rituximab); the adjusted primary-endpoint difference was −40 mL (95% CI −153 to 74; p=0.49) — rituximab was not superior. Quality-of-life (KBILD) scores improved by a mean 9.4 points on cyclophosphamide and 8.8 on rituximab. No significant differences were found in secondary endpoints except physician-assessed global disease activity at week 48, which favoured cyclophosphamide (difference 0.90, 95% CI 0.11 to 1.68). Corticosteroid exposure over 48 weeks was lower in the rituximab group. Two of 48 (4%) cyclophosphamide and three of 49 (6%) rituximab participants died, all from complications of connective tissue disease or interstitial lung disease; overall survival, progression-free survival, and time to treatment failure did not differ significantly. All participants reported at least one adverse event; events numbered 445 on rituximab versus 646 on cyclophosphamide, with 29 versus 33 serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2b superiority trial of 101 patients across three different connective tissue diseases: it can show 'not superior, similar trajectory' but cannot prove equivalence within a tight margin, and its FVC standard deviations (234–329 mL) dwarf the mean changes. Both groups improving may partly reflect regression to the mean and background care in a trial that enrolled patients at a progressive moment — there is no placebo or untreated arm to say either drug beat the disease's natural course here.
cards.source: Maher TM et al. Rituximab versus intravenous cyclophosphamide in patients with connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease in the UK (RECITAL): a double-blind, double-dummy, randomised, controlled, phase 2b trial. The Lancet. Respiratory Medicine. 2023. PMID: 36375479. Registry ID: NCT01862926. cards.headline: Liu 2025: six head-to-head studies — FVC change no different between rituximab and cyclophosphamide (WMD 0.86, −1.51 to 3.24); DLCO change favoured rituximab (6.43, 1.62 to 11.23) on only three studies; adverse events fewer with rituximab
cards.summary: Liu 2025: six head-to-head studies — FVC change no different between rituximab and cyclophosphamide (WMD 0.86, −1.51 to 3.24); DLCO change favoured rituximab (6.43, 1.62 to 11.23) on only three studies; adverse events fewer with rituximab
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Liu 2025)
cards.people: Six studies (two randomised trials and four retrospective observational studies) directly comparing rituximab with cyclophosphamide in connective-tissue-disease-related interstitial lung disease — four in systemic-sclerosis-related disease, one in anti-synthetase syndrome, and one mixed connective tissue disease population.
cards.result: The pooled weighted mean difference in percentage-predicted FVC change for rituximab versus cyclophosphamide was 0.86 (95% CI −1.51 to 3.24; p=0.48) — no significant difference. Percentage-predicted DLCO change favoured rituximab (weighted mean difference 6.43, 95% CI 1.62 to 11.23; p=0.009), but only three of the six studies reported DLCO change. Across the included studies, adverse events were fewer in the rituximab groups. The authors conclude rituximab shows similar lung-function efficacy to cyclophosphamide with a more favourable safety balance.
cards.watchOut: Four of six studies are retrospective, so the pooled tolerability advantage is exposed to the same confounding that governs which patients get which drug in practice; and the DLCO result — the pool's only significant efficacy difference — rests on half the studies. The randomised component of this pool overlaps the trial carded above, so this is corroboration of direction, not independent replication.
cards.source: Liu Y et al. Efficacy of rituximab versus cyclophosphamide in connective tissue disease-related interstitial lung disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Rheumatology. 2025. PMID: 40506621. cards.headline: Synthesis: equal lungs, unequal side-effect ledgers — rituximab is the tolerability choice in CTD-ILD, not the efficacy choice
cards.summary: Synthesis: equal lungs, unequal side-effect ledgers — rituximab is the tolerability choice in CTD-ILD, not the efficacy choice
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One double-blind double-dummy phase 2b trial (101 patients) plus a six-study head-to-head meta-analysis (two randomised, four retrospective) of rituximab versus intravenous cyclophosphamide in connective-tissue-disease-associated interstitial lung disease.
cards.result: FVC at 24 weeks: +97 versus +99 mL (adjusted difference −40 mL, 95% CI −153 to 74); pooled FVC% change difference 0.86 (−1.51 to 3.24), not significant. Adverse events in the trial: 445 versus 646; serious events 29 versus 33; steroid exposure lower with rituximab. Deaths in the trial: 3 versus 2, all from underlying disease. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: single-trial comparison.
cards.watchOut: Neither record can say whether either drug beats no treatment in this exact population — both arms improved, and the comparison is strictly relative. Fertility, malignancy, and cumulative-dose concerns that dominate real cyclophosphamide decisions accrue over years, beyond these records' 48-week horizon.
cards.source: Synthesis of Maher TM et al. The Lancet. Respiratory Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 36375479); Liu Y et al. Clinical Rheumatology. 2025 (PMID: 40506621).

shelves.title: Pirfenidone in progressive fibrotic lung disease beyond IPF (RELIEF): FVC decline slowed on a rank analysis in a trial stopped early for futility — median difference 1.69 points with an interval crossing zero
shelves.question: In patients with progressive fibrotic interstitial lung diseases other than idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis who are not responding to standard therapy, does pirfenidone slow forced vital capacity decline compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/pharmacology · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Monitoring/methods · Early Termination of Clinical Trials · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Lung Diseases, Interstitial/diagnosis/drug therapy/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Pulmonary Fibrosis/diagnosis/drug therapy/physiopathology · Pyridones/pharmacology · Respiratory Function Tests/methods · Symptom Assessment/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but fragile signal from one stopped-early trial. In RELIEF (Behr J et al., PMID: 33798455), 127 patients with progressive fibrotic ILD other than IPF were randomised to pirfenidone or placebo for 48 weeks before the trial was terminated early for futility at an interim analysis triggered by slow recruitment. The prespecified rank ANCOVA showed significantly less decline in FVC % predicted on pirfenidone (p=0.043), and the slope analysis estimated a difference of 3.53 FVC % predicted (95% CI 0.21 to 6.86) — yet the median difference for the primary endpoint was 1.69 FVC % predicted (95% CI -0.65 to 4.03), an interval that crosses zero. Deaths were 1 of 64 (2%) on pirfenidone versus 5 of 63 (8%) on placebo, far too few to read. A 2024 meta-analysis of antifibrotics in non-IPF progressive fibrosing ILD (Chong WH et al., PMID: 39089077) found less FVC decline with antifibrotics overall but substantially more gastrointestinal harm (nausea/vomiting 54.2% versus 20.3%; diarrhoea 65.2% versus 27.6%; discontinuation 18.4% versus 9.9%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pirfenidone probably attenuates FVC decline in progressive non-IPF fibrotic ILD, but the one pirfenidone trial was small, stopped early, and its headline interval includes no effect — Tier C.

cards.headline: Behr 2021 (RELIEF): rank ANCOVA favoured pirfenidone (p=0.043) but the median FVC difference was 1.69 points (95% CI -0.65 to 4.03) — and the trial was stopped early for futility
cards.summary: Behr 2021 (RELIEF): rank ANCOVA favoured pirfenidone (p=0.043) but the median FVC difference was 1.69 points (95% CI -0.65 to 4.03) — and the trial was stopped early for futility
cards.type: Randomised phase 2b trial (Behr 2021, RELIEF)
cards.people: 127 patients aged 18–80 years in 17 German centres with progressive fibrotic ILD due to connective tissue disease, fibrotic non-specific interstitial pneumonia, chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, or asbestos-induced fibrosis, with FVC 40–90% predicted and at least 5% predicted annual FVC decline despite conventional therapy, randomised to pirfenidone (titrated to 801 mg three times daily) or matched placebo added to ongoing medication for 48 weeks; 64 pirfenidone, 63 placebo.
cards.result: Rank ANCOVA of absolute change in FVC % predicted at week 48 showed significantly lower decline on pirfenidone (p=0.043; p=0.042 stratified by diagnosis). The median (Hodges–Lehmann) difference was 1.69 FVC % predicted (95% CI -0.65 to 4.03). The prespecified slope analysis estimated a difference of 3.53 FVC % predicted (95% CI 0.21 to 6.86) with deaths imputed as prespecified, or 2.79 (95% CI 0.03 to 5.54) without imputation. One death (2%, non-respiratory) occurred on pirfenidone and five deaths (8%, three respiratory) on placebo. Serious adverse events of infection occurred in 5 patients (8%) on pirfenidone versus 10 (16%) on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The trial was prematurely terminated after an interim futility analysis triggered by slow recruitment, and the authors themselves say results should be interpreted with care. The rank-based primary analysis is significant while the median-difference interval includes zero — the benefit estimate is method-sensitive and small in absolute terms.
cards.source: Behr J et al. Pirfenidone in patients with progressive fibrotic interstitial lung diseases other than idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (RELIEF): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2b trial. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2021. PMID: 33798455. Registry ID: EudraCT 2014-000861-32. cards.headline: Chong 2024 meta-analysis (7 RCTs, 1,816 patients): antifibrotics reduced FVC decline in non-IPF progressive fibrosing ILD, with nausea/vomiting 54.2% versus 20.3% and discontinuation 18.4% versus 9.9%
cards.summary: Chong 2024 meta-analysis (7 RCTs, 1,816 patients): antifibrotics reduced FVC decline in non-IPF progressive fibrosing ILD, with nausea/vomiting 54.2% versus 20.3% and discontinuation 18.4% versus 9.9%
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Chong 2024)
cards.people: Seven randomised trials totalling 1,816 adults with non-IPF progressive fibrosing ILD comparing an antifibrotic (pirfenidone or nintedanib) with placebo.
cards.result: Antifibrotics significantly reduced decline in FVC in millilitres (mean difference -66.80 mL; P<0.01) and in percent predicted (mean difference -1.80%; P<0.01) versus placebo. There was no significant difference in 6-minute walk decline overall (P=0.19), all-cause mortality (P=0.34), or all-cause hospitalisation (P=0.44). Adverse events were more frequent on antifibrotics: nausea/vomiting 54.2% versus 20.3% (P<0.01), diarrhoea 65.2% versus 27.6% (P=0.02), anorexia/weight loss 23.0% versus 7.7% (P<0.01), and events requiring discontinuation 18.4% versus 9.9% (P<0.01).
cards.watchOut: This pools two different drugs, so it supports the antifibrotic class in non-IPF disease rather than pirfenidone specifically; the pirfenidone-specific randomised base remains RELIEF alone. Gastrointestinal harm rates are high enough to shape real-world persistence.
cards.source: Chong WH et al. A systematic review and meta-analysis of the clinical benefits and adverse reactions of anti-fibrotics in non-IPF progressive fibrosing ILD. Heart & lung : the journal of critical care. 2024. PMID: 39089077. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small stopped-early pirfenidone trial plus a class-level meta-analysis — slower FVC decline, unproven patient-important benefit, heavy gastrointestinal cost
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small stopped-early pirfenidone trial plus a class-level meta-analysis — slower FVC decline, unproven patient-important benefit, heavy gastrointestinal cost
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: RELIEF (127 patients, pirfenidone versus placebo, 48 weeks, terminated early) read alongside a 7-trial, 1,816-patient meta-analysis of antifibrotics in non-IPF progressive fibrosing ILD.
cards.result: Pirfenidone: rank ANCOVA p=0.043 for FVC % predicted decline; median difference 1.69 points (95% CI -0.65 to 4.03); slope difference 3.53 points (95% CI 0.21 to 6.86); deaths 2% versus 8% (1 versus 5 patients). Class meta-analysis: FVC decline reduced (percent-predicted mean difference -1.80%; P<0.01) with no mortality or hospitalisation difference, and discontinuation 18.4% versus 9.9%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single pirfenidone trial carries this shelf.
cards.watchOut: FVC is a surrogate; no trial here shows pirfenidone improving breathlessness, exacerbations, or survival in non-IPF disease. The early termination and the interval crossing zero keep this at POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
cards.source: Synthesis of Behr J et al. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2021 (PMID: 33798455); Chong WH et al. Heart & lung : the journal of critical care. 2024 (PMID: 39089077).

shelves.question: In patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and chronic cough, does extended-release nalbuphine reduce cough frequency compared with placebo?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large, dose-ordered effect on objectively counted cough in a single phase 2b trial. In CORAL (Molyneaux PL et al., PMID: 41569557), 165 patients with IPF and chronic cough were randomised to nalbuphine extended-release 27 mg, 54 mg, or 108 mg twice daily or placebo for 6 weeks. Mean relative decreases in 24-hour cough frequency were 47.9% (27 mg, P=.008), 53.4% (54 mg, P<.001), and 60.2% (108 mg, P<.001), compared with 16.9% on placebo; in absolute terms cough fell from 24.6 to 11.9, 28.0 to 14.9, and 31.5 to 11.9 coughs per hour across the dose groups, versus 29.4 to 28.1 on placebo. Patient-reported cough frequency improved significantly at the two higher doses (-40.6% and -40.2% versus -21.9% on placebo) but not at 27 mg (-31.4%, P=.14). The published abstract reports no adverse-event rates, so the tolerability price of an opioid antitussive cannot be weighed from this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): nalbuphine ER substantially reduces objectively measured cough in IPF over six weeks; durability, safety rates, and any effect beyond cough counting are unshown — Tier C.

cards.headline: Molyneaux 2026 (CORAL): cough frequency fell 47.9%, 53.4% and 60.2% relative on 27, 54 and 108 mg nalbuphine ER versus 16.9% on placebo at week 6
cards.summary: Molyneaux 2026 (CORAL): cough frequency fell 47.9%, 53.4% and 60.2% relative on 27, 54 and 108 mg nalbuphine ER versus 16.9% on placebo at week 6
cards.type: Randomised phase 2b trial (Molyneaux 2026, CORAL)
cards.people: 165 patients with IPF, chronic cough for at least 8 weeks, and a Cough Severity Numerical Rating Scale score of 4 or higher, randomised at 52 sites in 10 countries to nalbuphine ER 27 mg (n=42), 54 mg (n=43), or 108 mg (n=40) twice daily, or placebo (n=40), for 6 weeks; 160 were included in the primary analysis (median age 71 years; 28.5% female); baseline mean cough count was 28.3 coughs per hour.
cards.result: The primary outcome — relative change in 24-hour cough frequency at week 6 — was -47.9% on 27 mg (from 24.6 to 11.9 coughs/h; P=.008), -53.4% on 54 mg (from 28.0 to 14.9 coughs/h; P<.001), and -60.2% on 108 mg (from 31.5 to 11.9 coughs/h; P<.001), compared with -16.9% on placebo (from 29.4 to 28.1 coughs/h); all reductions are relative changes as reported. Patient-reported cough frequency changed by -31.4% (P=.14), -40.6% (P=.004), and -40.2% (P<.005) across the doses versus -21.9% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks is short for a chronic symptom in a progressive disease, and the abstract reports no adverse-event rates for an opioid-class drug — the harm side of this shelf is a declared gap in the record fetched. Cough frequency is a symptom measure; no lung-function, exacerbation, or survival outcome was tested.
cards.source: Molyneaux PL et al. Oral Nalbuphine in Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis-Associated Cough: The CORAL Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2026. PMID: 41569557. Registry ID: NCT05964335. cards.headline: Synthesis: one well-executed phase 2b trial, a clear dose response on the objective endpoint, and an unpriced safety side
cards.summary: Synthesis: one well-executed phase 2b trial, a clear dose response on the objective endpoint, and an unpriced safety side
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: CORAL alone: 165 randomised patients with IPF-associated chronic cough, three nalbuphine ER doses versus placebo, 6 weeks, objective digital cough monitoring.
cards.result: Relative cough-frequency reductions of 47.9%, 53.4%, and 60.2% versus 16.9% on placebo, with patient-reported benefit significant only at 54 mg and 108 mg. No adverse-event rates appear in the published abstract. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single trial for a benefit claim, with the safety record incomplete in the abstract.
cards.watchOut: A second, larger or longer trial — and full adverse-event reporting — would be needed before this could rise above POSSIBLE. Opioid-class effects (sedation, nausea, constipation, dependence) are the obvious unmeasured price.
cards.source: Synthesis of Molyneaux PL et al. JAMA. 2026 (PMID: 41569557).

shelves.title: Sildenafil in advanced IPF (STEP-IPF): the walk-distance primary endpoint was missed — 10% versus 7% improved by 20% or more (P=0.39) — with small secondary gains in oxygenation, breathlessness and quality of life
shelves.question: In patients with advanced idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does sildenafil improve six-minute walk distance and breathlessness compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Dyspnea/drug therapy/etiology · Exercise Test · Female · Humans · Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis/drug therapy/mortality/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen/blood · Piperazines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pulmonary Diffusing Capacity · Purines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Quality of Life · Respiratory Function Tests · Sildenafil Citrate · Sulfones/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Vasodilator Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the outcome the trial was built around. In STEP-IPF (Zisman DA et al., PMID: 20484178), 180 patients with advanced IPF (diffusing capacity under 35% predicted) were randomised to sildenafil or placebo for 12 weeks. The primary outcome — an increase of 20% or more in 6-minute walk distance — occurred in 9 of 89 patients (10%) on sildenafil versus 6 of 91 (7%) on placebo (P=0.39). Small but significant differences favoured sildenafil for arterial oxygenation, diffusing capacity, degree of dyspnoea, and quality of life, and serious adverse events were similar between groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): sildenafil did not deliver the prespecified walk-distance benefit in advanced IPF; the secondary signals are hypothesis-generating only — Tier C, a single trial.

cards.headline: Zisman 2010 (STEP-IPF): 10% on sildenafil versus 7% on placebo achieved a 20% walk-distance gain (P=0.39) — primary endpoint not met
cards.summary: Zisman 2010 (STEP-IPF): 10% on sildenafil versus 7% on placebo achieved a 20% walk-distance gain (P=0.39) — primary endpoint not met
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Zisman 2010, STEP-IPF)
cards.people: 180 patients with advanced IPF, defined as a carbon monoxide diffusing capacity of less than 35% of the predicted value, randomised to oral sildenafil or placebo in a 12-week double-blind period (89 sildenafil, 91 placebo), followed by a 12-week open-label period.
cards.result: The proportion with an increase in 6-minute walk distance of 20% or more was 9 of 89 (10%) on sildenafil versus 6 of 91 (7%) on placebo (P=0.39) — not significant. Small but significant differences favoured sildenafil in arterial oxygenation, carbon monoxide diffusing capacity, degree of dyspnoea, and quality of life. Serious adverse events were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The abstract gives no absolute magnitudes for the secondary differences, so their clinical size cannot be judged from this record — a declared gap. Multiple secondary endpoints with a missed primary is the classic pattern for false-positive signals.
cards.source: Zisman DA et al. A controlled trial of sildenafil in advanced idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2010. PMID: 20484178. Registry ID: NCT00517933. cards.headline: Synthesis: a clean negative on walking capacity in advanced IPF, with equipoise-level secondary signals only
cards.summary: Synthesis: a clean negative on walking capacity in advanced IPF, with equipoise-level secondary signals only
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: STEP-IPF alone: 180 patients with advanced IPF (diffusing capacity <35% predicted), sildenafil versus placebo, 12 weeks.
cards.result: Primary endpoint: 10% versus 7% achieving a 20% or greater walk-distance improvement (P=0.39). shelves.title: High-dose N-acetylcysteine added to prednisone plus azathioprine in IPF (IFIGENIA): vital capacity decline slowed by 0.18 litres at one year — on a background regimen later abandoned, in a single trial
shelves.question: In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does high-dose N-acetylcysteine added to prednisone and azathioprine slow the decline in vital capacity compared with the same immunosuppression without N-acetylcysteine?
shelves.mesh: Acetylcysteine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/pharmacology · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/therapeutic use · Antioxidants/administration & dosage/adverse effects/pharmacology · Azathioprine/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Exercise Tolerance/drug effects · Female · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Prednisone/therapeutic use · Pulmonary Diffusing Capacity/drug effects · Pulmonary Fibrosis/drug therapy/mortality/physiopathology · Vital Capacity/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the lung-function measures, in a trial whose background therapy is no longer used. In IFIGENIA (Demedts M et al., PMID: 16306520), 182 patients with IPF were randomised to high-dose acetylcysteine 600 mg three times daily or placebo, each added to prednisone plus azathioprine, for one year. At 12 months the absolute differences in change from baseline favouring acetylcysteine were 0.18 litres (95% CI 0.03 to 0.32) for vital capacity — a 9% relative difference, P=0.02 — and 0.75 mmol/min/kPa (95% CI 0.27 to 1.23) for diffusing capacity — a 24% relative difference, P=0.003. Mortality was 9% on acetylcysteine versus 11% on placebo (P=0.69), and adverse events did not differ significantly except for fewer myelotoxic effects on acetylcysteine (P=0.03). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): acetylcysteine preserved vital capacity and diffusing capacity on top of immunosuppression in this single trial — Tier C, and the prednisone–azathioprine backbone it was added to has since been abandoned in IPF, which limits what the result can mean today.

cards.headline: Demedts 2005 (IFIGENIA): vital capacity difference 0.18 L (95% CI 0.03 to 0.32) and DLCO difference 0.75 (95% CI 0.27 to 1.23) favouring acetylcysteine at 12 months; mortality 9% versus 11%
cards.summary: Demedts 2005 (IFIGENIA): vital capacity difference 0.18 L (95% CI 0.03 to 0.32) and DLCO difference 0.75 (95% CI 0.27 to 1.23) favouring acetylcysteine at 12 months; mortality 9% versus 11%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Demedts 2005, IFIGENIA)
cards.people: 182 patients with IPF randomised to acetylcysteine 600 mg three times daily (n=92) or placebo (n=90), each added to standard therapy with prednisone plus azathioprine, for one year; 155 patients (80 acetylcysteine, 75 placebo) with confirmed usual interstitial pneumonia began treatment, and 71% versus 68% completed one year.
cards.result: At 12 months, absolute differences in change from baseline between acetylcysteine and placebo were 0.18 litres (95% CI 0.03 to 0.32) for vital capacity — a 9% relative difference (P=0.02) — and 0.75 mmol per minute per kilopascal (95% CI 0.27 to 1.23) for single-breath diffusing capacity — a 24% relative difference (P=0.003); relative differences are labelled relative as reported. Mortality during the study was 9% on acetylcysteine versus 11% on placebo (P=0.69). There were no significant differences in type or severity of adverse events except a significantly lower rate of myelotoxic effects on acetylcysteine (P=0.03).
cards.watchOut: A single trial, and its question is historically framed: the prednisone-plus-azathioprine backbone was later shown to be harmful in IPF and abandoned, so 'acetylcysteine on top of triple therapy' cannot be transplanted to modern antifibrotic-era care. Lung-function preservation without a mortality or symptom signal is a surrogate-level win.
cards.source: Demedts M et al. High-dose acetylcysteine in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2005. PMID: 16306520. shelves.title: Methotrexate in acute sarcoidosis: prednisone dose in months 7–12 was a median 8 versus 16 mg/day — in the 15 of 24 patients who stayed on therapy six months, with the all-patient analysis negative
shelves.question: In acute pulmonary sarcoidosis requiring treatment, is methotrexate steroid-sparing compared with prednisone alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Body Weight/drug effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Male · Methotrexate/therapeutic use · Prednisone/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Sarcoidosis/drug therapy · Sarcoidosis, Pulmonary/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a steroid-sparing signal that survives only in a completers analysis of a very small trial. Baughman RP et al. (PMID: 10746262) randomised 24 patients with new-onset symptomatic sarcoidosis starting prednisone to methotrexate or placebo for one year, with a predetermined prednisone taper. Only 15 patients received at least six months of therapy and were evaluated. Among them, median prednisone dose in the second six months was 8 mg/day (range 1–22) on methotrexate versus 16 mg/day (range 11–22) on placebo (p<0.01 between groups), with less weight gain on methotrexate and no difference in toxicity. Crucially, the difference was not seen when all patients including dropouts were analysed. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): methotrexate may halve the maintenance prednisone dose in acute sarcoidosis after six months, but the evidence is 15 analysed patients with a negative all-patient analysis — Tier C.

cards.headline: Baughman 2000: second-six-month median prednisone 8 mg/day on methotrexate versus 16 mg/day on placebo (p<0.01) — among 15 completers of 24 randomised, and not in the all-patient analysis
cards.summary: Baughman 2000: second-six-month median prednisone 8 mg/day on methotrexate versus 16 mg/day on placebo (p<0.01) — among 15 completers of 24 randomised, and not in the all-patient analysis
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial (Baughman 2000)
cards.people: 24 patients with new-onset symptomatic sarcoidosis within four weeks of starting prednisone, randomised to methotrexate or placebo for one year with monthly visits and a predetermined prednisone taper; only the 15 patients who received at least six months of therapy were evaluated in the main analysis.
cards.result: Prednisone dose fell in both groups. In the evaluated completers, median dose in the first six months was 26 mg/day (range 15–37) on methotrexate and 28 mg/day (range 24–33) on placebo; in the second six months it was 8 mg/day (range 1–22) on methotrexate versus 16 mg/day (range 11–22) on placebo, significantly less for methotrexate (p<0.01). Weight gain was less on methotrexate, and there was no difference in toxicity between groups. The between-group difference was not seen when all patients, including dropouts, were analysed.
cards.watchOut: Nine of 24 patients (38%) dropped out before the analysis population, and the headline result depends on excluding them — the all-patient analysis is negative. Ranges overlap widely (1–22 versus 11–22 mg/day), and disease outcomes (lung function, relapse) are not reported in the abstract.
cards.source: Baughman RP et al. Methotrexate is steroid sparing in acute sarcoidosis: results of a double blind, randomized trial. Sarcoidosis, vasculitis, and diffuse lung diseases : official journal of WASOG. 2000. PMID: 10746262. randomised double-blind trial (baughman 2000) 24 patients with new-onset symptomatic sarcoidosis within four weeks of starting prednisone, randomised to methotrexate or placebo for one year with monthly visits and a predetermined prednisone taper; only the 15 patients who received at least six months of therapy were evaluated in the main analysis. prednisone dose fell in both groups. in the evaluated completers, median dose in the first six months was 26 mg/day (range 15–37) on methotrexate and 28 mg/day (range 24–33) on placebo; in the second six months it was 8 mg/day (range 1–22) on methotrexate versus 16 mg/day (range 11–22) on placebo, significantly less for methotrexate (p<0.01). weight gain was less on methotrexate, and there was no difference in toxicity between groups. the between-group difference was not seen when all patients, including dropouts, were analysed. nine of 24 patients (38%) dropped out before the analysis population, and the headline result depends on excluding them — the all-patient analysis is negative. ranges overlap widely (1–22 versus 11–22 mg/day), and disease outcomes (lung function, relapse) are not reported in the abstract. baughman rp et al. methotrexate is steroid sparing in acute sarcoidosis: results of a double blind, randomized trial. sarcoidosis, vasculitis, and diffuse lung diseases : official journal of wasog. 2000. pmid: 10746262. mesh: adult · body weight/drug effects · double-blind method · female · glucocorticoids/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · humans · immunosuppressive agents/therapeutic use · male · methotrexate/therapeutic use · prednisone/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · sarcoidosis/drug therapy · sarcoidosis, pulmonary/drug therapy · treatment outcome

cards.summary: Synthesis: a plausible steroid-sparing effect resting on 15 patients and a completers-only analysis
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One double-blind trial: 24 randomised patients with acute sarcoidosis, 15 analysed, methotrexate versus placebo added to a prednisone taper over one year.
cards.result: Completers: median second-half prednisone 8 versus 16 mg/day (p<0.01); less weight gain on methotrexate; no toxicity difference. All-patient analysis: no significant difference. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: Steroid dose under a forced taper is partly a protocol artefact; without disease-control outcomes, a lower dose could mean undertreatment rather than sparing. A modern adequately powered trial would be needed to move this stamp.

shelves.title: Mucoactive agents including hypertonic saline in non-CF bronchiectasis: pooled exacerbations did not fall (mean difference -0.40/year, interval crossing zero) and FEV1 rose a small 3.23% predicted — at very low certainty
shelves.question: In non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, does inhaled hypertonic saline improve lung function, exacerbations, and quality of life compared with isotonic saline or usual care?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Expectorants/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Bronchiectasis/drug therapy/physiopathology/diagnosis · Mucociliary Clearance/drug effects · Lung/physiopathology/drug effects · Treatment Outcome · Quality of Life · Adult · Disease Progression · Recovery of Function
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the pooled record does not show the outcome patients care about most. The 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of mucoactive agents in bronchiectasis (McCullough B et al., PMID: 42342264) pooled seven randomised studies (n=1,259) reporting exacerbations and found no statistically significant difference in annualised exacerbation incidence (mean difference -0.40 per patient per year, 95% CI -1.04 to 0.24; p=0.22; I²=91%; very low certainty), while nine studies (n=767) showed a small increase in FEV1 % predicted of 3.23% (95% CI 0.31 to 6.15; p=0.03; very low certainty), with no significant differences in quality of life or adverse events. The earlier review of mucoactives in chronic non-CF lung disease (Tarrant BJ et al., PMID: 28397992) reported that normal and hypertonic saline improved spirometry, health-related quality of life, and sputum burden in non-CF bronchiectasis, while dornase alfa was detrimental there. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): hypertonic saline may give small lung-function and symptom gains in bronchiectasis, but an exacerbation benefit is unproven and the certainty is very low — Tier C.

cards.headline: McCullough 2026: exacerbations mean difference -0.40 per year (95% CI -1.04 to 0.24; p=0.22) — not significant; FEV1 % predicted +3.23% (95% CI 0.31 to 6.15) at very low certainty
cards.summary: McCullough 2026: exacerbations mean difference -0.40 per year (95% CI -1.04 to 0.24; p=0.22) — not significant; FEV1 % predicted +3.23% (95% CI 0.31 to 6.15) at very low certainty
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (McCullough 2026)
cards.people: 24 studies (20 randomised, 4 observational; n=7,051) of mucoactive agents in adults with bronchiectasis (cystic fibrosis and paediatric studies excluded), evaluating eight agents including hypertonic saline; seven randomised studies (n=1,259) reported exacerbations and nine studies (n=767) reported FEV1 % predicted. Most trials had high or some risk of bias.
cards.result: Pooled annualised exacerbation incidence did not differ significantly (mean difference -0.40 per patient per year, 95% CI -1.04 to 0.24; p=0.22; I²=91%; very low certainty). FEV1 % predicted increased by a mean of 3.23% (95% CI 0.31 to 6.15; p=0.03; I²=69.9%; very low certainty). Pooled analyses showed no significant differences for other spirometry measures, quality of life, or adverse events.
cards.watchOut: This pools eight different mucoactive agents, not hypertonic saline alone, and heterogeneity for exacerbations was extreme (I²=91%). The review's own conclusion is that overall clinical benefit remains uncertain.
cards.source: McCullough B et al. Mucoactive agents in bronchiectasis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. cards.headline: Tarrant 2017: saline (normal and hypertonic) improved spirometry, quality of life and sputum burden in non-CF bronchiectasis — while rhDNase worsened FEV1 by 1.9–4.3% and raised exacerbation risk (RR 1.35)
cards.summary: Tarrant 2017: saline (normal and hypertonic) improved spirometry, quality of life and sputum burden in non-CF bronchiectasis — while rhDNase worsened FEV1 by 1.9–4.3% and raised exacerbation risk (RR 1.35)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Tarrant 2017)
cards.people: Randomised trials of inhaled mucoactive agents (mannitol, dornase alfa, hypertonic or normal saline) in chronic lung diseases other than cystic fibrosis, including non-CF bronchiectasis; the dornase alfa bronchiectasis data cover 410 patients in two studies, with exacerbation risk from 349 patients in one study.
cards.result: In non-CF bronchiectasis, normal saline and hypertonic saline improved spirometry, health-related quality of life, and sputum burden (reported qualitatively in the review). By contrast, dornase alfa had detrimental effects in bronchiectasis: average FEV1 declines of 1.9–4.3% and FVC declines of 3.7–5.4% (n=410, two studies), and increased exacerbation risk (relative risk 1.35, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.79; n=349, one study). Some participants had FEV1 falls of 10–15% or more on screening with mucoactive agents (hypertonic saline: 3 of 80); most adverse events were mild and transient, including bronchospasm, cough, and breathlessness.
cards.watchOut: The saline findings are summarised qualitatively without pooled hypertonic-saline-specific effect sizes in the abstract — a declared gap. The dornase alfa harm is the standing warning against extrapolating cystic-fibrosis mucolytic results into bronchiectasis.
cards.source: Tarrant BJ et al. Mucoactive agents for chronic, non-cystic fibrosis lung disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Respirology (Carlton, Vic.). 2017. PMID: 28397992.
