cards.summary: Synthesis: small spirometric gains, no proven exacerbation benefit, very low certainty — and one mucolytic (dornase alfa) that harms in this disease
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two systematic reviews of mucoactive agents in non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis (2026: 24 studies, n=7,051; 2017: randomised trials across chronic non-CF lung disease).
cards.result: Exacerbations: mean difference -0.40 per year (95% CI -1.04 to 0.24), not significant, very low certainty. FEV1 % predicted: +3.23% (95% CI 0.31 to 6.15), very low certainty. shelves.title: Talc through an indwelling pleural catheter (IPC-PLUS): pleurodesis at day 35 in 43% versus 23% with the catheter alone (HR 2.20) — no difference in hospital days, mortality, or adverse events
shelves.question: In patients with malignant pleural effusion, does administering talc slurry through an indwelling pleural catheter increase pleurodesis success compared with the catheter alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Ambulatory Care · Catheters, Indwelling · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pleural Effusion, Malignant/mortality/therapy · Pleurodesis/adverse effects/methods · Quality of Life · Single-Blind Method · Survival Analysis · Talc/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a doubling of pleurodesis success in one well-run trial, on a procedural endpoint. In IPC-PLUS (Bhatnagar R et al., PMID: 29617585), patients with malignant pleural effusion and no substantial lung entrapment at 10 days after catheter insertion were randomised to 4 g talc slurry or placebo through the indwelling pleural catheter as outpatients. Successful pleurodesis at day 35 occurred in 30 of 69 patients (43%) on talc versus 16 of 70 (23%) on placebo (hazard ratio 2.20, 95% CI 1.23 to 3.92; P=0.008). There were no significant differences in effusion size or complexity, inpatient days, mortality, or adverse events, and no significant excess of catheter blockages with talc. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): talc via the catheter roughly doubles the chance of pleurodesis by day 35 without added harm in this trial — Tier C, a single trial, and pleurodesis is a mechanical endpoint rather than breathlessness or survival.

cards.headline: Bhatnagar 2018 (IPC-PLUS): pleurodesis at day 35 in 43% on talc versus 23% on placebo (HR 2.20, 95% CI 1.23 to 3.92; P=0.008)
cards.summary: Bhatnagar 2018 (IPC-PLUS): pleurodesis at day 35 in 43% on talc versus 23% on placebo (HR 2.20, 95% CI 1.23 to 3.92; P=0.008)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Bhatnagar 2018, IPC-PLUS)
cards.people: 154 patients with malignant pleural effusion at 18 UK centres who, 10 days after indwelling pleural catheter insertion with regular outpatient drainage, had no substantial lung entrapment; randomised single-blind to 4 g talc slurry (69 analysed) or placebo (70 analysed) through the catheter, with 70 days of follow-up; 584 patients were approached to reach the randomised target.
cards.result: Successful pleurodesis at day 35: 30 of 69 (43%) on talc versus 16 of 70 (23%) on placebo (hazard ratio 2.20, 95% CI 1.23 to 3.92; P=0.008) — absolute rates printed alongside the relative measure. No significant between-group differences in effusion size and complexity, number of inpatient days, mortality, or number of adverse events; no significant excess of catheter blockages in the talc group.
cards.watchOut: Only patients whose lung could re-expand (no substantial entrapment) were randomised — the group most likely to pleurodese anyway. Pleurodesis success is a procedural endpoint; the trial showed no gain in hospital days or survival, and follow-up was 70 days.

shelves.title: Surgery for pleural empyema (Cochrane): no mortality difference versus tube drainage in 8 small trials (391 patients) — hospital stay was shorter with VATS in adults, by a mean 5.90 days with thoracotomy in the one child trial
shelves.question: In pleural infection (empyema), does early video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery improve drainage, hospital stay, and mortality compared with chest-tube drainage with or without fibrinolytics?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Child · Drainage/adverse effects/methods/mortality · Empyema, Pleural/mortality/surgery/therapy · Humans · Length of Stay · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Selection Bias · Thoracic Surgery, Video-Assisted/adverse effects/mortality · Thoracostomy/adverse effects/mortality · Thrombolytic Therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for hospital stay only; survival was not shown to differ. The Cochrane review of surgical versus non-surgical management for pleural empyema (Redden MD et al., PMID: 28304084) included eight randomised trials with 391 participants — six in children and two in adults — comparing tube thoracostomy drainage, with or without intrapleural fibrinolytics, against video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) or thoracotomy. For VATS versus tube drainage (seven pooled studies) there was no statistically significant difference in mortality or procedural complications in adults or children; mortality data were sparse — one study reported one death in each arm and seven reported none. Hospital stay was significantly shorter with VATS, with the subgroup result clear in adults and insufficient evidence in children; the single thoracotomy-versus-drainage trial in children found a mean 5.90 days shorter stay and fewer procedural complications with thoracotomy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): early surgery shortens hospital stay in empyema without a demonstrated mortality advantage, on low-to-moderate quality evidence dominated by paediatric trials — Tier C.

cards.headline: Redden 2017 (Cochrane): VATS versus tube drainage — no significant difference in mortality or complications; hospital stay significantly shorter with VATS in adults; evidence low to moderate quality
cards.summary: Redden 2017 (Cochrane): VATS versus tube drainage — no significant difference in mortality or complications; hospital stay significantly shorter with VATS in adults; evidence low to moderate quality
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (Redden 2017)
cards.people: Eight randomised trials, 391 participants (six trials in children, two in adults), comparing tube thoracostomy drainage with or without intrapleural fibrinolytics against VATS or thoracotomy for pleural empyema; risk of bias was generally unclear for selection and blinding and low for attrition and reporting.
cards.result: VATS versus thoracostomy drainage (seven pooled studies): no statistically significant difference in mortality or procedural complications, in adults or children, with or without fibrinolysis; one study reported one death in each arm and seven studies reported no deaths. Length of hospital stay was significantly reduced with VATS overall and in the adult subgroup; evidence was insufficient to estimate the effect in children. Thoracotomy versus thoracostomy (one trial in children): no deaths in either arm, a statistically significant mean reduction in hospital stay of 5.90 days with thoracotomy, and significantly fewer procedural complications. Evidence quality was downgraded to low for mortality and moderate for other outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Only two of eight trials enrolled adults, deaths were almost absent (so a mortality effect is untestable here), and all non-surgical arms in the VATS comparison used fibrinolysis — the review could not separate the effect of fibrinolytic therapy itself.
cards.source: Redden MD et al. Surgical versus non-surgical management for pleural empyema. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. PMID: 28304084. cochrane systematic review (redden 2017) eight randomised trials, 391 participants (six trials in children, two in adults), comparing tube thoracostomy drainage with or without intrapleural fibrinolytics against vats or thoracotomy for pleural empyema; risk of bias was generally unclear for selection and blinding and low for attrition and reporting. vats versus thoracostomy drainage (seven pooled studies): no statistically significant difference in mortality or procedural complications, in adults or children, with or without fibrinolysis; one study reported one death in each arm and seven studies reported no deaths. length of hospital stay was significantly reduced with vats overall and in the adult subgroup; evidence was insufficient to estimate the effect in children. thoracotomy versus thoracostomy (one trial in children): no deaths in either arm, a statistically significant mean reduction in hospital stay of 5.90 days with thoracotomy, and significantly fewer procedural complications. evidence quality was downgraded to low for mortality and moderate for other outcomes. only two of eight trials enrolled adults, deaths were almost absent (so a mortality effect is untestable here), and all non-surgical arms in the vats comparison used fibrinolysis — the review could not separate the effect of fibrinolytic therapy itself. redden md et al. surgical versus non-surgical management for pleural empyema. the cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. pmid: 28304084. mesh: adult · child · drainage/adverse effects/methods/mortality · empyema, pleural/mortality/surgery/therapy · humans · length of stay · randomized controlled trials as topic · selection bias · thoracic surgery, video-assisted/adverse effects/mortality · thoracostomy/adverse effects/mortality · thrombolytic therapy

cards.headline: Synthesis: surgery buys days in hospital, not demonstrated survival — and the adult evidence base is two trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: surgery buys days in hospital, not demonstrated survival — and the adult evidence base is two trials
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One Cochrane review: 8 randomised trials, 391 participants, six paediatric and two adult, surgery (VATS or thoracotomy) versus tube drainage with or without fibrinolytics.
cards.result: Mortality: no significant difference (one death per arm in the only study reporting deaths). Hospital stay: significantly shorter with VATS (adult subgroup clear); 5.90 days shorter with thoracotomy in the single paediatric thoracotomy trial. Procedural complications: no difference for VATS; fewer with thoracotomy in that one trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: benefit rests on a length-of-stay outcome in a small, mostly paediatric, low-to-moderate quality base.
cards.watchOut: 'Early' surgery as modern pathways practise it was not isolated as a variable in these trials, and patient-centred outcomes (pain, function, treatment failure) were largely unreported — the review calls for trials measuring them.
cards.source: Synthesis of Redden MD et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017 (PMID: 28304084).

shelves.title: CPAP in older adults with sleep apnoea (PREDICT): sleepiness fell by 2.1 Epworth points at 3 months and 2.0 at 12 months — quality-adjusted life-years did not differ (0.01, interval crossing zero)
shelves.question: In older adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, does CPAP improve sleepiness, quality of life, and cognitive function compared with best supportive care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Comorbidity · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure/economics · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Female · Humans · Male · Quality of Life · Sleep · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive/therapy · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for sleepiness, the symptom CPAP is prescribed for, in the age group trials usually exclude. In PREDICT (McMillan A et al., PMID: 25172769), 278 patients aged 65 years or older with newly diagnosed obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome were randomised to CPAP plus best supportive care or best supportive care alone for 12 months. CPAP reduced the Epworth sleepiness score by 2.1 points (95% CI -3.0 to -1.3; p<0.0001) at 3 months and by 2.0 points (95% CI -2.8 to -1.2; p<0.0001) at 12 months, with larger effects in patients with higher CPAP use or higher baseline sleepiness. Quality-adjusted life-years were similar (treatment effect 0.01, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.04; p=0.787), mood, functionality, nocturia, accidents, cognitive function, and cardiovascular events were unchanged, and 37 serious adverse events occurred on CPAP versus 22 on supportive care — all classified as unrelated to the trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): CPAP durably reduces sleepiness in older patients with OSA; broader quality-of-life, cognitive, and cardiovascular gains were not shown — Tier C, a single trial.

cards.headline: McMillan 2014 (PREDICT): Epworth score -2.1 points at 3 months and -2.0 at 12 months with CPAP; QALYs 0.01 (95% CI -0.03 to 0.04) — no difference
cards.summary: McMillan 2014 (PREDICT): Epworth score -2.1 points at 3 months and -2.0 at 12 months with CPAP; QALYs 0.01 (95% CI -0.03 to 0.04) — no difference
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (McMillan 2014, PREDICT)
cards.people: 278 patients aged 65 years or older with newly diagnosed obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome at 14 UK sleep centres, randomised to CPAP plus best supportive care (n=140) or best supportive care alone (n=138) for 12 months; 231 (83%) completed the trial.
cards.result: CPAP reduced the Epworth sleepiness score by 2.1 points (95% CI -3.0 to -1.3; p<0.0001) at 3 months and by 2.0 points (95% CI -2.8 to -1.2; p<0.0001) at 12 months; the effect was greater with higher CPAP usage or higher baseline score. Quality-adjusted life-years were similar between groups (treatment effect 0.01, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.04; p=0.787) and health-care costs were marginally lower with CPAP (-£35, 95% CI -390 to 321; p=0.847). Objective sleepiness, mobility, total cholesterol, and LDL cholesterol improved at 3 months but were not sustained at 12 months; mood, functionality, nocturia, accidents, cognitive function, and cardiovascular events were unchanged. Serious adverse events: 37 on CPAP versus 22 on supportive care, all independently classified as unrelated to the trial.
cards.watchOut: An unblinded comparison against supportive care, so the subjective sleepiness endpoint is open to expectation effects; the objective sleepiness gain was not sustained. The serious-adverse-event imbalance (37 versus 22), though adjudicated unrelated, is part of the record.
cards.source: McMillan A et al. Continuous positive airway pressure in older people with obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome (PREDICT): a 12-month, multicentre, randomised trial. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2014. PMID: 25172769. Registry ID: ISRCTN90464927. shelves.title: Bariatric surgery for obstructive sleep apnoea: cohorts show apnoea remission in 65% — but the one randomised trial found no significant AHI advantage over conventional weight loss despite 27.8 kg versus 5.1 kg lost, so apnoea usually persists
shelves.question: In obese adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, does weight-loss (bariatric) surgery reduce apnoea severity compared with conservative weight management, and how often does apnoea persist after surgery?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Diet, Reducing · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity/complications/surgery · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive/complications · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the observational and randomised records point in different directions. In the only randomised trial (Dixon JB et al., PMID: 22990273), 60 obese patients with recently diagnosed OSA lost a mean of 27.8 kg (95% CI 20.9 to 34.7) with laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding versus 5.1 kg (95% CI 0.8 to 9.3) with a conventional weight-loss programme over two years — yet the apnoea–hypopnoea index fell by 25.5 events/hour with surgery versus 14.0 events/hour conventionally, a between-group difference of -11.5 events/hour (95% CI -28.3 to 5.3; P=.18), not significant. In the pooled cohort literature (Al Oweidat K et al., PMID: 37145243; 32 studies, 2,310 patients), bariatric surgery was associated with an AHI reduction of 19.3 events/hour (weighted mean difference -19.3, 95% CI -23.9 to -14.6) and an OSA remission rate of 65% (95% CI 54% to 76%) — meaning roughly a third of patients still had apnoea after surgery even in the favourable uncontrolled data. PROPOSED SPLIT: surgery produces large weight loss and lower AHI on average, apnoea persists in a substantial minority, and superiority over good conservative care for AHI itself is unproven by randomisation — Tier C.

cards.headline: Dixon 2012: weight loss 27.8 kg surgical versus 5.1 kg conventional, but AHI difference -11.5 events/hour (95% CI -28.3 to 5.3; P=.18) — not significant
cards.summary: Dixon 2012: weight loss 27.8 kg surgical versus 5.1 kg conventional, but AHI difference -11.5 events/hour (95% CI -28.3 to 5.3; P=.18) — not significant
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Dixon 2012)
cards.people: 60 obese patients (body mass index over 35 and under 55) with recently diagnosed OSA (apnoea–hypopnoea index 20 events/hour or more) prescribed CPAP, randomised in Melbourne to laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding (n=30) or a conventional weight-loss programme with dietitian and physician consultations and very-low-calorie diets as necessary (n=30), followed for two years; polysomnography was scored blinded to randomisation.
cards.result: Mean weight loss was 27.8 kg (95% CI 20.9 to 34.7) in the surgery group versus 5.1 kg (95% CI 0.8 to 9.3) conventionally (P<.001). AHI decreased by 25.5 events/hour (95% CI 14.2 to 36.7) with surgery and by 14.0 events/hour (95% CI 3.3 to 24.6) with conventional therapy; the between-group difference was -11.5 events/hour (95% CI -28.3 to 5.3; P=.18). CPAP adherence did not differ between groups. The Short Form 36 physical component summary improved more with surgery (mean difference 9.3, 95% CI 0.5 to 18.0; P=.04).
cards.watchOut: One small trial of one operation (adjustable gastric banding, now little used) with a wide interval — it excludes neither a large AHI benefit nor none. Conventional care here was an active, supported programme, not usual care, which narrows the contrast.
cards.source: Dixon JB et al. Surgical vs conventional therapy for weight loss treatment of obstructive sleep apnea: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2012. PMID: 22990273. cards.headline: Al Oweidat 2023 meta-analysis (32 cohort/case-control studies, 2,310 patients): AHI weighted mean difference -19.3 events/hour after bariatric surgery; OSA remission 65% (95% CI 54% to 76%)
cards.summary: Al Oweidat 2023 meta-analysis (32 cohort/case-control studies, 2,310 patients): AHI weighted mean difference -19.3 events/hour after bariatric surgery; OSA remission 65% (95% CI 54% to 76%)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies (Al Oweidat 2023)
cards.people: 32 cohort or case-control studies totalling 2,310 patients with diagnosed OSA who underwent any bariatric surgery and had postoperative polysomnography; no randomised trials were included by design.
cards.result: Bariatric surgery was associated with reductions in body mass index (weighted mean difference -11.9, 95% CI -13.4 to -10.4), apnoea–hypopnoea index (weighted mean difference -19.3, 95% CI -23.9 to -14.6), and respiratory disturbance index (weighted mean difference -33.9, 95% CI -42.1 to -25.7). The rate of OSA remission after surgery was 65% (95% CI 54% to 76%).
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled before–after data: regression to the mean, selection of surgical candidates, and variable remission definitions all inflate apparent benefit, and the review itself notes the incomplete remission rate implies non-weight drivers of OSA such as jaw anatomy. This card cannot establish superiority over conservative management — the randomised card above is the honest counterweight.
cards.source: Al Oweidat K et al. Bariatric surgery and obstructive sleep apnea: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep & breathing = Schlaf & Atmung. 2023. PMID: 37145243. shelves.title: Acetazolamide in sleep apnoea: apnoea–hypopnoea index fell clearly in central sleep apnoea (mean difference -22.60) but not significantly in obstructive sleep apnoea (mean difference -10.29, interval from -33.34 to +12.77)
shelves.question: In adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, does acetazolamide reduce the apnoea–hypopnoea index compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acetazolamide · Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors · Humans · Polysomnography · Sleep Apnea Syndromes · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by apnoea type, and the obstructive half of the split is the null. The systematic review and meta-analysis of acetazolamide in sleep apnoea at sea level (Ni YN et al., PMID: 33538687) pooled 15 controlled trials with only 256 patients in total. Acetazolamide reduced the apnoea–hypopnoea index overall (mean difference -15.82, 95% CI -21.91 to -9.74; P<.00001) and in central sleep apnoea (mean difference -22.60, 95% CI -29.11 to -16.09; P<.00001), but in obstructive sleep apnoea the reduction was not significant (mean difference -10.29, 95% CI -33.34 to 12.77; P=.38). It also improved arterial oxygen (mean difference 11.62, 95% CI 9.13 to 14.11), mean oxygen saturation (mean difference 1.78, 95% CI 0.53 to 3.04), and total sleep time (mean difference 25.74 minutes, 95% CI 4.10 to 47.38) across the pooled population, with high heterogeneity flagged by the authors. PROPOSED SPLIT: acetazolamide lowers AHI in central sleep apnoea; for obstructive sleep apnoea — the question on this shelf — a benefit is unproven on 256 pooled patients — Tier C.

cards.headline: Ni 2021: AHI mean difference -22.60 in central sleep apnoea (P<.00001) versus -10.29 in obstructive sleep apnoea (95% CI -33.34 to 12.77; P=.38) — 15 trials, 256 patients
cards.summary: Ni 2021: AHI mean difference -22.60 in central sleep apnoea (P<.00001) versus -10.29 in obstructive sleep apnoea (95% CI -33.34 to 12.77; P=.38) — 15 trials, 256 patients
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Ni 2021)
cards.people: 15 controlled trials totalling 256 patients with obstructive and/or central sleep apnoea at sea level, comparing acetazolamide with control; primary outcome was the apnoea–hypopnoea index.
cards.result: Acetazolamide reduced AHI overall (mean difference -15.82, 95% CI -21.91 to -9.74; P<.00001), in central sleep apnoea (mean difference -22.60, 95% CI -29.11 to -16.09; P<.00001), but not significantly in obstructive sleep apnoea (mean difference -10.29, 95% CI -33.34 to 12.77; P=.38). Across the pooled population it reduced the respiratory-related arousal index (mean difference -0.82, 95% CI -1.56 to -0.08; P=.03), improved partial pressure of arterial oxygen (mean difference 11.62, 95% CI 9.13 to 14.11; P<.00001), mean oxygen saturation (mean difference 1.78, 95% CI 0.53 to 3.04; P=.005), total sleep time (mean difference 25.74, 95% CI 4.10 to 47.38; P=.02), and sleep efficiency (mean difference 4.83, 95% CI 0.53 to 9.13; P=.03).
cards.watchOut: 256 patients across 15 trials is a very small base, heterogeneity was high (the authors call it an important limitation), and the oxygenation and sleep-architecture gains are pooled across apnoea types, so they cannot be credited to obstructive disease specifically. Adverse effects of acetazolamide are not quantified in the abstract — a declared gap.

systematic review and meta-analysis (ni 2021) 15 controlled trials totalling 256 patients with obstructive and/or central sleep apnoea at sea level, comparing acetazolamide with control; primary outcome was the apnoea–hypopnoea index. acetazolamide reduced ahi overall (mean difference -15.82, 95% ci -21.91 to -9.74; p<.00001), in central sleep apnoea (mean difference -22.60, 95% ci -29.11 to -16.09; p<.00001), but not significantly in obstructive sleep apnoea (mean difference -10.29, 95% ci -33.34 to 12.77; p=.38). across the pooled population it reduced the respiratory-related arousal index (mean difference -0.82, 95% ci -1.56 to -0.08; p=.03), improved partial pressure of arterial oxygen (mean difference 11.62, 95% ci 9.13 to 14.11; p<.00001), mean oxygen saturation (mean difference 1.78, 95% ci 0.53 to 3.04; p=.005), total sleep time (mean difference 25.74, 95% ci 4.10 to 47.38; p=.02), and sleep efficiency (mean difference 4.83, 95% ci 0.53 to 9.13; p=.03). 256 patients across 15 trials is a very small base, heterogeneity was high (the authors call it an important limitation), and the oxygenation and sleep-architecture gains are pooled across apnoea types, so they cannot be credited to obstructive disease specifically. adverse effects of acetazolamide are not quantified in the abstract — a declared gap. ni yn et al. the role of acetazolamide in sleep apnea at sea level: a systematic review and meta-analysis. journal of clinical sleep medicine : jcsm : official publication of the american academy of sleep medicine. 2021. pmid: 33538687. mesh: acetazolamide · carbonic anhydrase inhibitors · humans · polysomnography · sleep apnea syndromes · sleep apnea, obstructive

shelves.title: Sulthiame in obstructive sleep apnoea: AHI fell 41% relative on 400 mg and 32% relative on 200 mg versus 5% on placebo in four weeks — with paraesthesia in 79% and 67% versus 18%, in one small dose-guiding trial
shelves.question: In adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, does the carbonic anhydrase inhibitor sulthiame reduce apnoea severity and improve oxygenation compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Sleep Apnea Syndromes/drug therapy · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive/therapy · Thiazines/therapeutic use · Benzenesulfonamides
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one of the largest drug effects on AHI reported, from one small four-week trial with a heavy side-effect signature. Hedner J et al. (PMID: 35202553) randomised patients with moderate-to-severe OSA who did not tolerate positive airway pressure to sulthiame 400 mg (n=34), sulthiame 200 mg (n=12), or placebo (n=22) for four weeks. The apnoea–hypopnoea index fell from 55.2 to 33.0 events/hour on 400 mg (a 41.0% relative reduction) and from 61.1 to 40.6 events/hour on 200 mg (a 32.1% relative reduction), versus 53.9 to 50.9 events/hour on placebo (a 5.4% relative reduction; P<0.001 for both dose comparisons); relative reductions are labelled relative as reported. Mean overnight oxygen saturation improved by 1.1% at both doses. But intermittent paraesthesia was reported by 79% on 400 mg, 67% on 200 mg, and 18% on placebo; dyspnoea occurred in 18% on 400 mg; and six patients in the higher-dose group withdrew because of adverse events. A prespecified endotypic analysis of the same trial programme (Hoff E et al., PMID: 37776971) showed sulthiame reduced loop gain and improved ventilation measures that correlated with the AHI fall. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): sulthiame substantially reduces AHI and improves oxygenation over four weeks, at a paraesthesia cost most patients will feel — Tier C, a single trial programme.

cards.headline: Hedner 2022: AHI 55.2 to 33.0 events/h on sulthiame 400 mg and 61.1 to 40.6 on 200 mg versus 53.9 to 50.9 on placebo (P<0.001 both doses); paraesthesia 79%, 67% and 18%
cards.summary: Hedner 2022: AHI 55.2 to 33.0 events/h on sulthiame 400 mg and 61.1 to 40.6 on 200 mg versus 53.9 to 50.9 on placebo (P<0.001 both doses); paraesthesia 79%, 67% and 18%
cards.type: Randomised dose-guiding trial (Hedner 2022)
cards.people: Patients with moderate and/or severe OSA not tolerating positive airway pressure therapy, randomised double-blind to sulthiame 400 mg (n=34), sulthiame 200 mg (n=12), or placebo (n=22) for 4 weeks; the trial's primary purpose was safety and tolerability.
cards.result: AHI fell from 55.2 to 33.0 events/h on 400 mg (a 41.0% relative reduction) and from 61.1 to 40.6 events/h on 200 mg (a 32.1% relative reduction), versus 53.9 to 50.9 events/h on placebo (a 5.4% relative reduction); P<0.001 for both dose comparisons, with relative reductions labelled relative as reported. An AHI reduction of 50% or more was reached by 40% on 400 mg, 25% on 200 mg, and 5% on placebo. Mean overnight oxygen saturation improved by 1.1% at both doses (P<0.001 and P=0.034). Intermittent paraesthesia was reported by 79% (400 mg), 67% (200 mg), and 18% (placebo); dyspnoea by 18% on 400 mg; six patients in the higher-dose group withdrew because of adverse events; there were no serious adverse events. Patient-related outcomes were unchanged.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks, 68 patients, and a 200 mg arm of only 12 patients; the trial was designed for safety and dose guidance, not clinical outcomes. Paraesthesia in four of five patients at the effective dose is a tolerability ceiling, and sleepiness did not improve.

cards.headline: Hoff 2024 (endotypic analysis of the same trial programme): sulthiame reduced loop gain by a mean 0.16 and raised lowest-decile ventilation — changes that correlated with the AHI fall
cards.summary: Hoff 2024 (endotypic analysis of the same trial programme): sulthiame reduced loop gain by a mean 0.16 and raised lowest-decile ventilation — changes that correlated with the AHI fall
cards.type: Randomised trial tertiary analysis (Hoff 2024)
cards.people: Per-protocol tertiary analysis of a randomised trial in patients aged 18–75 years with body mass index 20–35, AHI of 15 events/h or more, Epworth score of 6 or more, and non-acceptance or non-tolerance of positive airway pressure, randomised to placebo (n=22), sulthiame 200 mg (n=12), or sulthiame 400 mg (n=24) for 4 weeks, with polysomnography at baseline and follow-up and endotypic traits derived from the tracings.
cards.result: Sulthiame (200 mg and 400 mg groups) consistently reduced loop gain (response to a 1-cycle/min disturbance; mean -0.16, 95% CI -0.18 to -0.13; P<.05) and increased ventilation at the lowest decile of ventilatory drive (median +12, 95% CI 4 to 20; P<.05) and median ventilation at eupneic drive (median +4, 95% CI 0 to 5; P<.05). The loop-gain change correlated with the percentage AHI change at 200 mg (r=0.65; P<.05), and the ventilation changes correlated with AHI change across all sulthiame patients (rs=-0.59 and rs=-0.65; P<.05 for all).
cards.watchOut: This is a mechanistic re-analysis of the same small trial population as the primary card, not independent confirmation — it explains the effect rather than replicating it. Per-protocol analysis of a tertiary endpoint in 58 patients is hypothesis-generating.
cards.source: Hoff E et al. Modification of Endotypic Traits in OSA by the Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitor Sulthiame. Chest. 2024. PMID: 37776971. Registry ID: EudraCT 2017-004767-13. shelves.title: Dornase alfa in cystic fibrosis (Fuchs): exacerbations needing intravenous antibiotics occurred in 27% on placebo versus 22% once daily and 19% twice daily over 24 weeks, with FEV1 up about 5.8%
shelves.question: In cystic fibrosis, does daily inhaled recombinant human DNase (dornase alfa) reduce pulmonary exacerbations and slow lung-function decline compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aerosols · Airway Obstruction/therapy · Child · Child, Preschool · Cystic Fibrosis/complications/physiopathology/therapy · Deoxyribonuclease I/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Expectorants/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Lung/physiopathology · Male · Recombinant Proteins/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Vital Capacity
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the founding trial of a now-standard therapy, still a single trial on this shelf. Fuchs HJ et al. (PMID: 7503821) randomised 968 adults and children with cystic fibrosis to recombinant human DNase once daily, twice daily, or placebo for 24 weeks as outpatients. One or more exacerbations of respiratory symptoms requiring parenteral antibiotics occurred in 27% of patients on placebo, 22% on once-daily DNase, and 19% on twice-daily DNase — age-adjusted relative risk reductions of 28% (P=0.04) and 37% (P<0.01) respectively, relative reductions labelled relative with the absolute rates alongside. FEV1 improved during the study by a mean of 5.8% with once-daily and 5.6% with twice-daily dosing. No patient had anaphylaxis; voice alteration and laryngitis were more frequent on DNase but rarely severe and resolved within 21 days. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): daily dornase alfa modestly reduces exacerbations and improves lung function over 24 weeks — Tier C by the single-trial rule, despite the therapy's later standard-of-care status.

cards.headline: Fuchs 1994: exacerbations in 27% on placebo versus 22% once daily and 19% twice daily — 28% and 37% relative risk reductions; FEV1 improved 5.8% and 5.6%
cards.summary: Fuchs 1994: exacerbations in 27% on placebo versus 22% once daily and 19% twice daily — 28% and 37% relative risk reductions; FEV1 improved 5.8% and 5.6%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Fuchs 1994, Pulmozyme Study Group)
cards.people: 968 adults and children with cystic fibrosis treated as outpatients for 24 weeks, randomised double-blind to recombinant human DNase once daily, twice daily, or placebo; the endpoint was exacerbations of respiratory symptoms requiring parenteral antibiotics, plus pulmonary function.
cards.result: One or more exacerbations occurred in 27% of patients given placebo, 22% of those treated once daily, and 19% of those treated twice daily. Compared with placebo, once-daily and twice-daily DNase reduced the age-adjusted risk of respiratory exacerbations by 28% (P=0.04) and 37% (P<0.01) respectively — relative reductions, with the absolute rates printed alongside. FEV1 improved during the study by a mean (±SD) of 5.8±0.7% once daily and 5.6±0.7% twice daily. None of the patients had anaphylaxis; voice alteration and laryngitis were more frequent in DNase-treated patients but rarely severe and resolved within 21 days of onset.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-four weeks in a lifelong disease, from 1994 — before modern CFTR modulator therapy changed the exacerbation baseline entirely. The twice-daily regimen's extra benefit over once daily is small (19% versus 22% absolute), and the trial predates current background care.
cards.source: Fuchs HJ et al. Effect of aerosolized recombinant human DNase on exacerbations of respiratory symptoms and on pulmonary function in patients with cystic fibrosis. shelves.title: Intermittent inhaled tobramycin in cystic fibrosis (Ramsey): FEV1 rose 10% versus a 2% fall on placebo across two concordant trials, and hospitalisation risk fell 26% relative over 24 weeks
shelves.question: In cystic fibrosis patients chronically infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, does intermittent inhaled tobramycin improve lung function and reduce exacerbations and hospitalisation compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adolescent · Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Bronchial Diseases/complications/drug therapy/microbiology · Child · Cystic Fibrosis/complications/drug therapy/physiopathology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume/drug effects · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Nebulizers and Vaporizers · Pseudomonas Infections/complications/drug therapy/microbiology · Pseudomonas aeruginosa/drug effects/isolation & purification · Sputum/microbiology · Tobramycin/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant double-blind trials reported in a single record. Ramsey BW et al. (PMID: 9878641) conducted two multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials totalling 520 patients with cystic fibrosis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, using 300 mg inhaled tobramycin or placebo twice daily in three four-weeks-on, four-weeks-off cycles over 24 weeks. FEV1 rose by an average of 10% at week 20 from week 0 on tobramycin versus a 2% decline on placebo (P<0.001). Sputum Pseudomonas density fell by 0.8 log10 colony-forming units per gram on tobramycin versus a rise of 0.3 on placebo (P<0.001), and patients on tobramycin were 26% less likely to be hospitalised (95% CI 2 to 43) — a relative reduction, reported without absolute hospitalisation rates in the abstract. No detectable ototoxic or nephrotoxic effects and no serum accumulation were seen, though the proportion of isolates with a tobramycin minimum inhibitory concentration of 8 µg/mL or higher rose from 25% to 32% on tobramycin versus falling from 20% to 17% on placebo. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): intermittent inhaled tobramycin improves lung function, lowers bacterial density, and reduces hospitalisation in chronically infected cystic fibrosis, with a measurable resistance drift as the price to watch.

cards.headline: Ramsey 1999 (two trials): FEV1 +10% on tobramycin versus -2% on placebo at week 20 (P<0.001); hospitalisation risk 26% lower relative (95% CI 2 to 43)
cards.summary: Ramsey 1999 (two trials): FEV1 +10% on tobramycin versus -2% on placebo at week 20 (P<0.001); hospitalisation risk 26% lower relative (95% CI 2 to 43)
cards.type: Two randomised double-blind trials (Ramsey 1999, Cystic Fibrosis Inhaled Tobramycin Study Group)
cards.people: 520 patients with cystic fibrosis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection (mean age 21 years) across two multicentre trials, randomised to 300 mg inhaled tobramycin or placebo twice daily for four weeks, followed by four weeks off, in three on–off cycles over 24 weeks.
cards.result: FEV1 increased by an average of 10% at week 20 compared with week 0 on tobramycin, versus a 2% decline on placebo (P<0.001). Pseudomonas density in sputum fell by an average of 0.8 log10 CFU per gram from week 0 to week 20 on tobramycin versus an increase of 0.3 log10 CFU per gram on placebo (P<0.001). Patients in the tobramycin group were 26% less likely to be hospitalised than those on placebo (95% CI 2 to 43) — a relative reduction; absolute hospitalisation rates are not given in the abstract, a declared gap. Inhaled tobramycin was not associated with detectable ototoxic or nephrotoxic effects or with accumulation of the drug in serum. The proportion of patients whose isolates had a tobramycin minimum inhibitory concentration of 8 µg/mL or higher rose from 25% at week 0 to 32% at week 24 on tobramycin, versus a fall from 20% to 17% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-four weeks only; the resistance drift (25% to 32% of isolates at higher minimum inhibitory concentration) is the long-term concern the trial was too short to price. Hospitalisation is reported only as a relative effect in the abstract.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two concordant trials, a double-digit lung-function swing, and a resistance signal that argues for the intermittent design itself
cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant trials, a double-digit lung-function swing, and a resistance signal that argues for the intermittent design itself
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials reported together: 520 patients with cystic fibrosis chronically infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, intermittent inhaled tobramycin versus placebo, 24 weeks.
cards.result: FEV1: +10% versus -2% at week 20 (P<0.001). Sputum bacterial density: -0.8 versus +0.3 log10 CFU/g (P<0.001). Hospitalisation: 26% relative reduction (95% CI 2 to 43). Resistance marker: isolates at minimum inhibitory concentration 8 µg/mL or higher rose 25% to 32% on tobramycin versus 20% to 17% on placebo. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit); Tier C is not set — two concordant randomised blinded trials carry the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Like the other cystic-fibrosis shelves of its era, this predates CFTR modulators; the size of the added benefit on modern background therapy is not estimated here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ramsey BW et al. The New England journal of medicine. 1999 (PMID: 9878641).

shelves.title: Lumacaftor–ivacaftor in Phe508del-homozygous cystic fibrosis (TRAFFIC/TRANSPORT): FEV1 improved by 2.6–4.0 percentage points and pulmonary exacerbations ran 30–39% lower relative across two phase 3 trials
shelves.question: In cystic fibrosis patients homozygous for Phe508del, does lumacaftor–ivacaftor improve lung function and reduce exacerbations compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aminophenols/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Aminopyridines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Benzodioxoles/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Child · Cystic Fibrosis/drug therapy/genetics · Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator/genetics · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume/drug effects · Homozygote · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mutation · Quinolones/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 trials with a modest lung-function gain and a clearer exacerbation gain. Wainwright CE et al. (PMID: 25981758) report TRAFFIC and TRANSPORT, two randomised double-blind trials totalling 1,108 patients aged 12 years or older with cystic fibrosis homozygous for Phe508del, comparing lumacaftor (600 mg once daily or 400 mg every 12 hours) plus ivacaftor 250 mg every 12 hours against placebo for 24 weeks, from a mean baseline FEV1 of 61% predicted. The mean absolute improvement in FEV1 % predicted differed from placebo by 2.6 to 4.0 percentage points across the dose groups in both studies (P<0.001) — a 4.3 to 6.7% mean relative treatment difference, labelled relative. Pooled pulmonary exacerbation rates were 30 to 39% lower in the lumacaftor–ivacaftor groups than on placebo (relative reductions), and rates of events leading to hospitalisation or intravenous antibiotics were also lower. Adverse events were generally similar between groups, but discontinuation due to an adverse event was 4.2% on lumacaftor–ivacaftor versus 1.6% on placebo. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): the first CFTR corrector–potentiator combination delivered a small FEV1 gain and a substantial relative reduction in exacerbations for Phe508del-homozygous patients.

cards.headline: Wainwright 2015 (TRAFFIC and TRANSPORT): FEV1 difference 2.6 to 4.0 percentage points (P<0.001 in both studies); pooled exacerbation rate 30 to 39% lower relative on active treatment
cards.summary: Wainwright 2015 (TRAFFIC and TRANSPORT): FEV1 difference 2.6 to 4.0 percentage points (P<0.001 in both studies); pooled exacerbation rate 30 to 39% lower relative on active treatment
cards.type: Two randomised phase 3 trials (Wainwright 2015, TRAFFIC and TRANSPORT)
cards.people: 1,108 patients aged 12 years or older with cystic fibrosis homozygous for the Phe508del CFTR mutation (mean baseline FEV1 61% of predicted), randomised across two identically designed trials to lumacaftor 600 mg once daily or 400 mg every 12 hours, each combined with ivacaftor 250 mg every 12 hours, or matched placebo, for 24 weeks.
cards.result: In both studies the primary endpoint — absolute change in FEV1 % predicted at week 24 — significantly favoured lumacaftor–ivacaftor, with mean differences from placebo of 2.6 to 4.0 percentage points across dose groups (P<0.001), corresponding to a mean relative treatment difference of 4.3 to 6.7% (P<0.001), labelled relative as reported. Pooled analyses showed pulmonary exacerbation rates 30 to 39% lower in the lumacaftor–ivacaftor groups than on placebo (relative reductions; absolute rates are not given in the abstract, a declared gap), and lower rates of events leading to hospitalisation or intravenous antibiotics. Adverse-event incidence was generally similar between groups; discontinuation due to an adverse event was 4.2% on lumacaftor–ivacaftor versus 1.6% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The FEV1 gain (under 4 percentage points) is modest — the clinical weight of this combination sits in the exacerbation reduction, which the abstract reports only in relative terms. Twenty-four weeks, in patients 12 and older with one genotype only.

shelves.title: Azithromycin in cystic fibrosis with chronic Pseudomonas (Saiman): FEV1 rose 0.097 L versus 0.003 L on placebo and exacerbation hazard fell (HR 0.65) over 24 weeks — with nausea, diarrhoea and wheeze each 13–17% more common
shelves.question: In cystic fibrosis patients chronically infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, does thrice-weekly azithromycin improve lung function and reduce exacerbations compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Azithromycin/therapeutic use · Child · Chronic Disease · Cystic Fibrosis/complications/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Forced Expiratory Flow Rates · Hospitalization · Humans · Interleukin-8/blood · Male · Pancreatic Elastase/blood · Proportional Hazards Models · Pseudomonas Infections/complications/drug therapy · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single well-conducted trial with a small lung-function gain, a clearer exacerbation signal, and a noticeable gastrointestinal price. Saiman L et al. (PMID: 14519709) randomised 185 patients aged 6 years or older with cystic fibrosis and at least one year of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection to azithromycin 250 mg or 500 mg by weight, three days a week, or placebo, for 168 days. FEV1 rose by a mean of 0.097 L on azithromycin versus 0.003 L on placebo (mean difference 0.094 L, 95% CI 0.023 to 0.165; P=.009). The hazard of a pulmonary exacerbation was lower on azithromycin (hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.95; P=.03), and patients gained an average of 0.7 kg more weight (95% CI 0.1 to 1.4; P=.02). Against that, nausea occurred in 17% more participants on azithromycin (P=.01), diarrhoea in 15% more (P=.009), and wheezing in 13% more (P=.007). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): thrice-weekly azithromycin modestly improves lung function and reduces exacerbation hazard in chronically infected cystic fibrosis — Tier C, a single trial.

cards.headline: Saiman 2003: FEV1 mean difference 0.094 L (95% CI 0.023 to 0.165; P=.009); exacerbation hazard ratio 0.65 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.95); nausea +17%, diarrhoea +15%, wheeze +13%
cards.summary: Saiman 2003: FEV1 mean difference 0.094 L (95% CI 0.023 to 0.165; P=.009); exacerbation hazard ratio 0.65 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.95); nausea +17%, diarrhoea +15%, wheeze +13%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Saiman 2003)
cards.people: 185 patients aged 6 years or older with cystic fibrosis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection for one or more years and FEV1 of 30% or more, at 23 US cystic fibrosis centres, randomised to oral azithromycin 250 mg (under 40 kg) or 500 mg (40 kg or more) three days a week (n=87) or identically packaged placebo (n=98) for 168 days.
cards.result: At day 168 the azithromycin group had a mean FEV1 increase of 0.097 L (SD 0.26) versus 0.003 L (SD 0.23) on placebo (mean difference 0.094 L, 95% CI 0.023 to 0.165; P=.009). Exacerbation risk was lower on azithromycin (hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.95; P=.03), and end-of-study weight was an average of 0.7 kg higher (95% CI 0.1 to 1.4; P=.02). Nausea occurred in 17% more participants in the azithromycin group (P=.01), diarrhoea in 15% more (P=.009), and wheezing in 13% more (P=.007).
cards.watchOut: A single 24-week trial from 2003, before CFTR modulators; long-term macrolide resistance and non-tuberculous mycobacteria concerns with chronic azithromycin are outside this record's window and are not quantified in the abstract.
cards.source: Saiman L et al. Azithromycin in patients with cystic fibrosis chronically infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2003. PMID: 14519709. shelves.title: Physiotherapy and speech-therapy cough suppression (PSALTI): cough quality of life improved by 1.53 Leicester points and objective cough frequency fell 41% relative versus lifestyle advice in refractory chronic cough
shelves.question: In adults with refractory chronic cough, does physiotherapy and speech-and-language-therapy cough-suppression treatment reduce cough frequency and improve quality of life compared with healthy-lifestyle advice?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Chronic Disease · Cough/therapy · Counseling · Female · Humans · Language Therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Physical Therapy Modalities · Quality of Life · Single-Blind Method · Speech Therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a non-drug treatment that beat an active control on both quality of life and objectively counted cough, in one small trial. Chamberlain Mitchell SA et al. (PMID: 27682331) randomised 75 patients with refractory chronic cough to four weekly one-to-one sessions of a physiotherapy and speech-and-language-therapy intervention (education, laryngeal hygiene and hydration, cough-suppression techniques, breathing exercises, and psychoeducational counselling) or to healthy-lifestyle advice. Health-related quality of life on the Leicester Cough Questionnaire improved by 1.53 points more with the intervention (95% CI 0.21 to 2.85; p=0.024) at week 4, and 24-hour cough frequency decreased by 41% relative to control (p=0.030) — a relative reduction as reported, with the confidence interval printed in the record as 36% to 95%. Improvements within the intervention group were sustained to three months, and capsaicin cough-reflex sensitivity did not differ between groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): PSALTI improves cough quality of life and reduces objective cough frequency in refractory chronic cough — Tier C, a single small trial with an assessor-blinded (single-blind) design.

cards.headline: Chamberlain Mitchell 2017 (PSALTI): Leicester score +1.53 points versus control (95% CI 0.21 to 2.85; p=0.024); cough frequency -41% relative (p=0.030), sustained to 3 months
cards.summary: Chamberlain Mitchell 2017 (PSALTI): Leicester score +1.53 points versus control (95% CI 0.21 to 2.85; p=0.024); cough frequency -41% relative (p=0.030), sustained to 3 months
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Chamberlain Mitchell 2017, PSALTI)
cards.people: 75 patients with refractory chronic cough randomised across multiple centres to four weekly one-to-one PSALTI sessions (n=34) — education, laryngeal hygiene and hydration, cough-suppression techniques, breathing exercises, and psychoeducational counselling — or a control intervention of healthy-lifestyle advice (n=41); primary outcome was change in Leicester Cough Questionnaire at week 4, with 24-hour objective cough frequency (Leicester Cough Monitor) and capsaicin cough-reflex sensitivity as secondary outcomes.
cards.result: In the observed-case analysis, health-related quality of life improved on average by 1.53 points (95% CI 0.21 to 2.85) more in the PSALTI group than control (p=0.024). Cough frequency decreased by 41% (95% CI 36% to 95%) in the PSALTI group relative to control (p=0.030) — a relative reduction as reported in the record. Improvements within the PSALTI group were sustained up to 3 months. There was no significant between-group difference in the capsaicin concentration causing five or more coughs.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind (patients cannot be blinded to therapy), 75 patients, and an observed-case primary analysis — attrition and expectation effects can both inflate a quality-of-life endpoint, though the objective cough monitor moved in the same direction. The record's confidence interval for the cough-frequency reduction (36% to 95%) is unusually wide and is quoted as printed.
cards.source: Chamberlain Mitchell SA et al. Physiotherapy, and speech and language therapy intervention for patients with refractory chronic cough: a multicentre randomised control trial. Thorax. 2017. PMID: 27682331. Registry ID: ISRCTN73039760. cards.headline: Synthesis: the best-tested non-drug option for refractory cough rests on one 75-patient trial — enough for POSSIBLE, not more
cards.summary: Synthesis: the best-tested non-drug option for refractory cough rests on one 75-patient trial — enough for POSSIBLE, not more
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: PSALTI trial alone: 75 patients with refractory chronic cough, four sessions of physiotherapy/speech-therapy cough suppression versus healthy-lifestyle advice, outcomes at 4 weeks and 3 months.

shelves.title: Home treatment triage for low-risk pulmonary embolism (HOME-PE): Hestia was non-inferior to sPESI — 30-day adverse outcomes 3.82% versus 3.57% per protocol, with about 37–38% of patients treated at home under either rule
shelves.question: In low-risk acute pulmonary embolism, does a Hestia-based home-treatment strategy perform as well as a simplified (sPESI-based) strategy for safe outpatient care?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Humans · Patient Discharge · Prognosis · Pulmonary Embolism/drug therapy · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a large strategy trial that found the two triage rules interchangeable in practice. In HOME-PE (Roy PM et al., PMID: 34363386), 1,975 normotensive patients with acute pulmonary embolism at 26 hospitals in four European countries were randomised to triage by the Hestia rule or by the simplified Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (sPESI), with discharge home if the tool was negative and the responsible physician agreed. In the per-protocol population, the 30-day composite of recurrent venous thromboembolism, major bleeding, or all-cause death occurred in 3.82% (34 of 891) in the Hestia arm versus 3.57% (32 of 896) in the sPESI arm (P=0.004 for non-inferiority against a 2.5% absolute margin). In intention-to-treat, 38.4% of Hestia patients (378 of 984) versus 36.6% of sPESI patients (361 of 986) were treated at home (P=0.41), with 30-day composite rates among home-treated patients of 1.33% (5 of 375) and 1.11% (4 of 359); no recurrent or fatal pulmonary embolism occurred in either home-treatment arm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): Hestia and sPESI triage are equally safe routes to home treatment for roughly a third of normotensive PE patients — Tier C, a single (large) strategy trial.

cards.result: Per protocol, the 30-day composite of recurrent venous thromboembolism, major bleeding, or all-cause death occurred in 3.82% (34 of 891) in the Hestia arm and 3.57% (32 of 896) in the sPESI arm (P=0.004 for non-inferiority, margin 2.5% absolute). shelves.title: Nintedanib plus add-on pirfenidone in IPF (INJOURNEY): tolerable over 12 weeks — gastrointestinal events 69.8% versus 52.9% on nintedanib alone — with only an exploratory FVC signal (-13.3 versus -40.9 mL)
shelves.question: In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, is combining nintedanib with pirfenidone safe and does it slow lung-function decline more than either drug alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Disease Progression · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis/diagnosis/drug therapy/mortality · Indoles/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Safety · Pyridones/therapeutic use · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index · Survival Rate · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — safety was the question this trial could answer, and efficacy it could not. In INJOURNEY (Vancheri C et al., PMID: 28889759), 104 patients with IPF who had tolerated a 4–5-week nintedanib run-in were randomised open-label to nintedanib 150 mg twice daily with add-on pirfenidone (titrated to 801 mg three times daily) or nintedanib alone for 12 weeks. The primary endpoint — on-treatment gastrointestinal adverse events — occurred in 37 of 53 patients (69.8%) on the combination versus 27 of 51 (52.9%) on nintedanib alone, a profile the authors describe as manageable and in line with each drug's known effects; nintedanib plasma concentrations were similar with and without pirfenidone. The exploratory efficacy readout was a mean FVC change at week 12 of -13.3 mL (SE 17.4) on the combination versus -40.9 mL (SE 31.4) on nintedanib alone — descriptive only, from 48 and 44 patients, in an open-label 12-week window far too short and small to establish added benefit. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): the combination is tolerable in run-in-selected patients; whether it slows decline more than a single antifibrotic is unproven — Tier C.

cards.headline: Vancheri 2018 (INJOURNEY): gastrointestinal adverse events 69.8% on nintedanib plus pirfenidone versus 52.9% on nintedanib alone; exploratory FVC change -13.3 versus -40.9 mL at 12 weeks
cards.summary: Vancheri 2018 (INJOURNEY): gastrointestinal adverse events 69.8% on nintedanib plus pirfenidone versus 52.9% on nintedanib alone; exploratory FVC change -13.3 versus -40.9 mL at 12 weeks
cards.type: Randomised open-label safety trial (Vancheri 2018, INJOURNEY)
cards.people: Patients with IPF and FVC of 50% predicted or more who completed a 4- to 5-week run-in on nintedanib 150 mg twice daily without dose reduction or interruption, randomised to nintedanib with add-on pirfenidone titrated to 801 mg three times daily (n=53) or nintedanib alone (n=51) for 12 weeks; the primary endpoint was the percentage of patients with on-treatment gastrointestinal adverse events.
cards.result: On-treatment gastrointestinal adverse events were reported in 37 of 53 patients (69.8%) on the combination versus 27 of 51 (52.9%) on nintedanib alone. Predose plasma trough concentrations of nintedanib were similar alone or with pirfenidone. Mean (SE) change from baseline in FVC at week 12 was -13.3 (17.4) mL on the combination (n=48) versus -40.9 (31.4) mL on nintedanib alone (n=44). Analyses were descriptive and exploratory, and the authors concluded the combination had a manageable safety and tolerability profile in line with each drug's adverse-event profile.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 12 weeks, run-in survivors only — patients who could not tolerate nintedanib alone never entered randomisation, so tolerability is overstated for an unselected clinic population. The FVC difference has no inferential testing and a standard error larger than the combination arm's mean change; it cannot support an efficacy claim.
cards.source: Vancheri C et al. Nintedanib with Add-on Pirfenidone in Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis. Results of the INJOURNEY Trial. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2018. PMID: 28889759. Registry ID: NCT02579603. shelves.title: Continuous alternating inhaled antibiotics in cystic fibrosis: the one head-to-head trial (90 patients) found no difference from intermittent tobramycin on any outcome — while inhaled antibiotics versus placebo do cut exacerbations (RR 0.66)
shelves.question: In cystic fibrosis with chronic Pseudomonas infection, do continuous alternating inhaled antibiotic regimens suppress infection better than intermittent single-agent therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Child, Preschool · Humans · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Aztreonam/therapeutic use · Cystic Fibrosis/complications/drug therapy/microbiology · Lysine/therapeutic use · Quality of Life · Tobramycin/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the alternating-versus-intermittent comparison specifically. The Cochrane review of inhaled anti-pseudomonal antibiotics for long-term therapy in cystic fibrosis (Smith S et al., PMID: 36373968) included 18 trials with 3,042 participants; exactly one trial (90 participants) compared intermittent tobramycin with continuous tobramycin alternating with aztreonam, and it found no differences between groups in any outcome. The wider review found inhaled antibiotics may improve lung function versus placebo (4 trials, 814 participants) and may reduce exacerbation frequency (risk ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.93; 3 trials, 946 participants; low-certainty evidence) — so suppressive inhaled therapy itself has support, but intensifying it into a continuous alternating regimen showed no added benefit in the only direct test. Other single-trial comparisons in the review: aztreonam lysine probably improved FEV1 % predicted versus tobramycin by a mean difference of -3.40% as printed (95% CI -6.63 to -0.17; 1 trial, 273 participants; moderate-certainty evidence, with endpoint-definition caveats), and levofloxacin produced fewer hospitalisations for respiratory exacerbations than tobramycin (risk ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.98; 1 trial, 282 participants). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): continuous alternating regimens have not beaten intermittent single-agent therapy where directly compared — Tier C, resting on one 90-patient comparison inside a low-certainty review.

cards.headline: Smith 2022 (Cochrane): one trial (90 patients) of intermittent versus continuous alternating tobramycin–aztreonam found no differences; inhaled antibiotics versus placebo reduced exacerbations (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.93)
cards.summary: Smith 2022 (Cochrane): one trial (90 patients) of intermittent versus continuous alternating tobramycin–aztreonam found no differences; inhaled antibiotics versus placebo reduced exacerbations (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.93)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (Smith 2022)
cards.people: 18 randomised or quasi-randomised trials, 3,042 participants aged 5 to 45 years with cystic fibrosis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection receiving inhaled anti-pseudomonal antibiotics for at least three months: 11 trials (1,130 participants) versus placebo or usual treatment, five trials (1,255) comparing different antibiotics, two trials (585) comparing tobramycin regimens, and one trial (90) comparing intermittent tobramycin with continuous tobramycin alternating with aztreonam.
cards.result: For the alternating-versus-intermittent comparison, the single trial found no differences between groups for any outcomes. Across the review, inhaled antibiotics may improve lung function versus placebo (4 trials, 814 participants) and may reduce exacerbation frequency (risk ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.93; 3 trials, 946 participants; low-certainty evidence), and may reduce days off school or work (mean difference -5.30 days, 95% CI -8.59 to -2.01; 1 trial, 245 participants; low-certainty evidence). There was no effect on survival and no effect on antibiotic resistance in the two meta-analysed trials; tinnitus and voice alteration occurred more often with inhaled antibiotics. Certainty was low for most outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The shelf's headline comparison rests on one 90-patient trial with no effect sizes given in the abstract — a declared gap. Most comparisons in this review are single trials with differing outcome definitions, which is why the authors call the pooled benefit estimates very limited.
cards.source: Smith S et al. Inhaled anti-pseudomonal antibiotics for long-term therapy in cystic fibrosis. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2022. PMID: 36373968. shelves.title: Mucolytics for children with chronic suppurative lung disease (Cochrane): one small crossover trial of 3% hypertonic saline reported 2.50 versus 7.80 exacerbations per child-year — at very low certainty and high risk of bias
shelves.question: In children with chronic suppurative lung disease and bronchiectasis, do mucolytic therapies improve lung function or reduce exacerbations?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Child · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Chronic Disease · Expectorants/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Quality of Life · Bronchiectasis/drug therapy · Lung Diseases/drug therapy · Adolescent · Suppuration/drug therapy · Bias · Child, Preschool · Bronchitis/drug therapy
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a strikingly large effect from exactly the kind of trial that most often misleads. The Cochrane review of mucolytics for children with chronic suppurative lung disease (O'Farrell HE et al., PMID: 40152354) found only one eligible randomised trial: a crossover study of nebulised 3% hypertonic saline before chest physiotherapy versus physiotherapy alone, each phase eight weeks, with analysable first-phase data for 52 children (26 per arm) with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis. The mean number of exacerbations per child-year was 2.50 (SD 0.64) on hypertonic saline versus 7.80 (SD 1.05) on control (mean difference -5.30, 95% CI -5.77 to -4.83), and improvement in FEV1 % predicted was greater on saline (mean difference 9.11%, 95% CI 6.11 to 12.11), as was FVC improvement (mean difference 6.23%, 95% CI 3.33 to 9.13) — all graded very low-certainty evidence from a study the reviewers judged at high risk of bias (unblinding, missing data, deviations, and reporting bias). No quality-of-life data existed, no studies covered exacerbation-state treatment, oral mucolytics, or protracted bacterial bronchitis, and no dropouts due to adverse events were reported. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): hypertonic saline may help children with bronchiectasis, but the entire evidence base is one small high-bias crossover trial — Tier C.

cards.people: One included randomised crossover trial: 63 children in the total cohort with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, with reported first-phase data for 52 children (26 per arm; intervention-arm mean age 9.80 years, 42.3% male; control-arm mean age 9.10 years, 38.4% male), comparing nebulised 3% hypertonic saline before chest physiotherapy with physiotherapy alone, each phase lasting eight weeks, during a stable state.
cards.result: Mean exacerbations per child-year were 2.50 (SD 0.64) on hypertonic saline versus 7.80 (SD 1.05) on control (mean difference -5.30, 95% CI -5.77 to -4.83; 52 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Mean improvement in FEV1 % predicted was 14.15% (SD 5.50) versus 5.04% (SD 5.55) (mean difference 9.11%, 95% CI 6.11 to 12.11), and in FVC 13.77% (SD 5.73) versus 7.54% (SD 4.90) (mean difference 6.23%, 95% CI 3.33 to 9.13) — both very low-certainty. Quality of life was not measured. The authors reported no dropouts due to adverse events. The study was judged at high risk of bias due to unblinding, missing data, deviation from the intended intervention, and reporting bias.
cards.watchOut: An eight-week first phase annualised into 'per child-year' exacerbation rates produces the dramatic -5.30 figure; seasonal and regression effects in an unblinded crossover can manufacture exactly this pattern. No other mucolytic, setting, or disease subgroup (including protracted bacterial bronchitis) has any randomised data in children.

shelves.title: Targeted lung denervation in severe COPD (AIRFLOW-2): respiratory adverse events 32% versus 71% with sham in the 3–6.5-month window (OR 0.19) — but 83% versus 90% over the full 12.5 months, with symptoms and lung function unchanged
shelves.question: In patients with severe COPD, does targeted lung denervation reduce exacerbations and improve quality of life compared with sham bronchoscopy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Bronchodilator Agents/therapeutic use · Bronchoscopy · Denervation · Double-Blind Method · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/complications/physiopathology/surgery · Radiofrequency Ablation · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real reduction in a prespecified safety-window event rate, which fades when the whole follow-up is counted. In AIRFLOW-2 (Slebos DJ et al., PMID: 31404499), 82 patients with symptomatic moderate-to-severe COPD (FEV1 30–60% predicted) were randomised double-blind to targeted lung denervation (bronchoscopic radiofrequency ablation of parasympathetic nerves) plus optimal pharmacotherapy or sham bronchoscopy. During the predefined 3- to 6.5-month window, respiratory adverse events (a composite including exacerbation, wheeze, bronchitis, dyspnoea, pneumonia, and respiratory failure) occurred in 32% on denervation versus 71% on sham (P=0.008; odds ratio 0.19, 95% CI 0.0750 to 0.4923; P=0.0006). Over 0 to 12.5 months, however, the rates were 83% versus 90% (P=0.52). The risk of COPD exacerbation requiring hospitalisation over 0–12.5 months was lower with denervation (hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.99; P=0.039), but there was no statistical difference in time to first moderate or severe exacerbation, patient-reported symptoms, or other physiological measures. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): denervation reduced hospitalised exacerbations in this small sham-controlled trial, without improving symptoms or lung function — Tier C, a single trial, and the quality-of-life half of the question is answered negatively by this record.

cards.headline: Slebos 2019 (AIRFLOW-2): respiratory adverse events 32% versus 71% at 3–6.5 months (OR 0.19, 95% CI 0.0750 to 0.4923) but 83% versus 90% over 12.5 months; hospitalised-exacerbation HR 0.35 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.99)
cards.summary: Slebos 2019 (AIRFLOW-2): respiratory adverse events 32% versus 71% at 3–6.5 months (OR 0.19, 95% CI 0.0750 to 0.4923) but 83% versus 90% over 12.5 months; hospitalised-exacerbation HR 0.35 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.99)
cards.type: Randomised sham-controlled trial (Slebos 2019, AIRFLOW-2)
cards.people: 82 patients (50% female; mean age 63.7 years; mean FEV1 41.6% predicted) with symptomatic COPD (modified Medical Research Council dyspnoea score 2 or more, or COPD Assessment Test score 10 or more; FEV1 30–60% predicted), randomised 1:1 to targeted lung denervation plus optimal pharmacotherapy or sham bronchoscopy, double-blind, with blinding maintained through 12.5 months; the primary endpoint was the rate of defined respiratory adverse events between 3 and 6.5 months.
cards.result: In the 3- to 6.5-month window, respiratory adverse events occurred in 32% of the denervation group versus 71% of the sham group (P=0.008; odds ratio 0.19, 95% CI 0.0750 to 0.4923; P=0.0006). Between 0 and 12.5 months the rates were 83% versus 90% (P=0.52). The risk of COPD exacerbation requiring hospitalisation over 0–12.5 months was lower with denervation (hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.99; P=0.039). There was no statistical difference in time to first moderate or severe COPD exacerbation, patient-reported symptoms, or other physiological measures over 12.5 months.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint was a safety endpoint (respiratory adverse events in a chosen window), not efficacy; the window-specific win disappears over full follow-up, and the hospitalisation hazard ratio's interval (0.13 to 0.99) nearly touches 1 in an 82-patient trial. Symptoms and quality of life — half the shelf's question — did not improve.

cards.headline: Synthesis: fewer hospitalised exacerbations on a borderline interval, no symptomatic gain — a pivotal-trial question, not a settled therapy
cards.summary: Synthesis: fewer hospitalised exacerbations on a borderline interval, no symptomatic gain — a pivotal-trial question, not a settled therapy
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: AIRFLOW-2 alone: 82 patients with symptomatic moderate-to-severe COPD, targeted lung denervation versus sham bronchoscopy, both with optimal pharmacotherapy, 12.5 months blinded follow-up.
cards.result: Respiratory adverse events (3–6.5 months): 32% versus 71% (OR 0.19). Full-period events: 83% versus 90% (P=0.52). Hospitalised exacerbation: HR 0.35 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.99). Symptoms and physiology: no difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: single small trial, benefit claim on a secondary hospitalisation endpoint.
cards.watchOut: A larger pivotal sham-controlled trial was designed to test exacerbation reduction as a primary endpoint; until such a trial reports, denervation's place in COPD care is investigational and this stamp should not rise.

shelves.title: Isolated subsegmental pulmonary embolism: anticoagulation has never been shown to cut recurrence (RR 0.61, interval crossing 1) but triples bleeding (RR 3.10) in pooled observational data — while surveillance itself carried a 3.1% 90-day recurrence in a prospective cohort
shelves.question: In patients with isolated subsegmental pulmonary embolism and no deep-vein thrombosis, does anticoagulation improve outcomes compared with clinical surveillance alone?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Pulmonary Embolism/drug therapy · Anticoagulants/therapeutic use/pharmacology · Hemorrhage/chemically induced
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — for routine anticoagulation: the pooled record shows a bleeding price without a proven recurrence benefit, though surveillance is not free either. The 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis (Nicoletto M et al., PMID: 41962426) pooled observational comparisons of anticoagulation versus clinical surveillance in isolated subsegmental pulmonary embolism: venous thromboembolism recurrence did not differ significantly (risk ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.35; 8 studies, 674 patients), all-cause mortality did not differ (risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.12), but any bleeding was significantly more frequent with anticoagulation (risk ratio 3.10, 95% CI 1.39 to 6.88; 9 studies, 862 patients), with a similar association for major bleeding. The surveillance side's own risk is quantified by the prospective cohort of Le Gal G et al. (PMID: 34807722): among 266 low-risk patients with isolated subsegmental PE and no deep-vein thrombosis managed without anticoagulation, recurrent venous thromboembolism occurred in 3.1% (95% CI 1.6% to 6.1%) over 90 days — 2.1% (95% CI 0.8% to 5.5%) for a single subsegmental embolism and 5.7% (95% CI 2.2% to 14.4%) for multiple — with no fatal recurrent pulmonary embolism; recruitment was stopped early because the predefined stopping rule was met. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): on current observational evidence, routine anticoagulation for isolated subsegmental PE buys bleeding without demonstrated protection — Tier C, observational evidence throughout, and a randomised trial is still owed.

cards.headline: Nicoletto 2026 meta-analysis: recurrence RR 0.61 (95% CI 0.28 to 1.35) — not significant; any bleeding RR 3.10 (95% CI 1.39 to 6.88) with anticoagulation
cards.summary: Nicoletto 2026 meta-analysis: recurrence RR 0.61 (95% CI 0.28 to 1.35) — not significant; any bleeding RR 3.10 (95% CI 1.39 to 6.88) with anticoagulation
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Nicoletto 2026)
cards.people: Observational studies comparing anticoagulation with clinical surveillance in isolated subsegmental pulmonary embolism: eight studies (674 patients) reporting venous thromboembolism recurrence and nine studies (862 patients) reporting safety outcomes, searched to April 2025.
cards.result: Recurrence of venous thromboembolism did not differ significantly between anticoagulated and non-anticoagulated patients (risk ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.35; I²=0%). Any bleeding complication was more frequent with anticoagulation (risk ratio 3.10, 95% CI 1.39 to 6.88; I²=0%), with a similar association when restricted to major bleeding. All-cause mortality did not differ significantly (risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.12; I²=45%). The authors conclude the available evidence does not support a net clinical benefit from routine anticoagulation in isolated subsegmental pulmonary embolism.
cards.watchOut: Entirely observational: clinicians anticoagulate the patients they judge higher-risk, so confounding by indication runs through every pooled estimate — it could hide a real recurrence benefit or exaggerate the bleeding gap. Absolute event rates are not pooled in the abstract, a declared gap. The recurrence point estimate (0.61) lies in the zone this library treats as too weak to carry a benefit claim on its own.
cards.source: Nicoletto M et al. Anticoagulation therapy vs clinical surveillance in isolated subsegmental pulmonary embolism: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Thrombosis research. 2026. cards.headline: Le Gal 2022 prospective cohort: without anticoagulation, 90-day recurrence was 3.1% (95% CI 1.6% to 6.1%) — 2.1% for single and 5.7% for multiple subsegmental emboli, with no fatal recurrence
cards.summary: Le Gal 2022 prospective cohort: without anticoagulation, 90-day recurrence was 3.1% (95% CI 1.6% to 6.1%) — 2.1% for single and 5.7% for multiple subsegmental emboli, with no fatal recurrence
cards.type: Prospective cohort study (Le Gal 2022)
cards.people: 266 patients in the primary analysis (292 enrolled of a projected 300, at 18 sites) with isolated subsegmental pulmonary embolism, bilateral leg ultrasound at diagnosis (repeated at one week if negative), who received no anticoagulant therapy because no deep venous thrombosis was found; primary outcome was recurrent venous thromboembolism over 90 days. Recruitment was stopped prematurely because the predefined stopping rule was met.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 8 patients, a cumulative incidence of 3.1% (95% CI 1.6% to 6.1%) over 90 days. Incidence was 2.1% (95% CI 0.8% to 5.5%) in patients with a single isolated subsegmental embolism and 5.7% (95% CI 2.2% to 14.4%) in those with multiple. No patient had a fatal recurrent pulmonary embolism. The authors note the recurrence rate was higher than expected and that the study was restricted to low-risk subsegmental embolism.
cards.watchOut: This is the surveillance arm's risk with no comparator — it cannot by itself say whether anticoagulation would have prevented those recurrences. Early stopping on a predefined rule and the single-versus-multiple split (wide intervals) both counsel care; patients with proximal deep-vein thrombosis were excluded by design.
cards.source: Le Gal G et al. Risk for Recurrent Venous Thromboembolism in Patients With Subsegmental Pulmonary Embolism Managed Without Anticoagulation : A Multicenter Prospective Cohort Study. Annals of internal medicine. 2022. PMID: 34807722. Registry ID: NCT01455818. cards.headline: Synthesis: surveillance is defensible but not harmless (3.1% recurrence); anticoagulation is unproven and measurably bloody — single versus multiple emboli may be the decision that matters
cards.summary: Synthesis: surveillance is defensible but not harmless (3.1% recurrence); anticoagulation is unproven and measurably bloody — single versus multiple emboli may be the decision that matters
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: A 2026 observational meta-analysis (674–862 patients across comparisons) read with a 266-patient prospective surveillance cohort with protocol ultrasound exclusion of deep-vein thrombosis.
cards.result: Anticoagulation versus surveillance: recurrence risk ratio 0.61 (95% CI 0.28 to 1.35, not significant); bleeding risk ratio 3.10 (95% CI 1.39 to 6.88); mortality risk ratio 0.70 (95% CI 0.44 to 1.12, not significant). Surveillance alone: 90-day recurrence 3.1% overall, 2.1% single, 5.7% multiple, no fatal recurrence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) for routine anticoagulation, Tier C: observational evidence, personal-review territory.
cards.watchOut: A randomised placebo-controlled trial of anticoagulation in low-risk subsegmental embolism has been designed but had not reported in this record; its result could overturn this shelf, and patients with cancer, prior venous thromboembolism, or multiple emboli may sit on the other side of the balance.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nicoletto M et al. Thrombosis research. 2026 (PMID: 41962426); Le Gal G et al. Annals of internal medicine. 2022 (PMID: 34807722).
