shelves.title: House dust mite avoidance for asthma: 49 trials and 2,733 patients — no effect on peak flow, symptoms, medication use or the number improved (Cochrane)
shelves.question: In people with mite-sensitive asthma, do chemical, physical or combined house dust mite control measures improve asthma outcomes compared with placebo or no treatment?
shelves.mesh: Allergens/immunology · Animals · Asthma/immunology/prevention & control · Dust · Environment, Controlled · Humans · Insecticides · Mites/immunology · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one of the most thoroughly negative records in the library, and it concerns advice still routinely given. The Cochrane review (Gøtzsche PC et al., PMID: 15495009) assembled 49 randomised trials with 2,733 patients with mite-sensitive asthma: 31 trials of physical methods (such as allergen-impermeable covers), 10 of chemical methods (acaricides) and 8 of combined methods. Despite many trials being of poor quality — which would be expected to exaggerate effects — there was no effect on the most reported outcome, morning peak flow (standardised mean difference -0.02, 95% CI -0.13 to 0.08; 1,339 patients), and no significant differences in patients improved (relative risk 1.01, 0.80 to 1.27), symptom scores (SMD -0.01) or medication use (SMD -0.05). The reviewers concluded such methods cannot be recommended. Later versions of this review have not reversed the finding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): mite allergen can be reduced in the mattress while asthma, measurably, does not care.

cards.headline: Cochrane (Gøtzsche 2004): 49 trials, 2,733 patients — morning peak flow SMD -0.02 (CI -0.13 to 0.08); patients improved RR 1.01; symptoms and medication use unchanged
cards.summary: Cochrane (Gøtzsche 2004): 49 trials, 2,733 patients — morning peak flow SMD -0.02 (CI -0.13 to 0.08); patients improved RR 1.01; symptoms and medication use unchanged
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Gøtzsche 2004, Cochrane)
cards.people: 49 randomised trials with 2,733 people with asthma known to be sensitive to house dust mites, testing chemical methods (10 trials), physical methods (31) or combined methods (8) to reduce mite allergen exposure in the home, versus placebo or no treatment.
cards.result: For morning peak flow (1,339 patients), the standardised mean difference was -0.02 (95% CI -0.13 to 0.08). There were no statistically significant differences in the number of patients improved (relative risk 1.01, 0.80 to 1.27), asthma symptom scores (SMD -0.01, -0.10 to 0.13) or medication usage (SMD -0.05, -0.18 to 0.09). The reviewers note that many trials were of poor quality and would be expected to exaggerate reported effects — yet still found none — and conclude that chemical and physical mite control methods cannot be recommended.
cards.watchOut: This is the 2004 version of the review (the record fetched for this shelf); the trials largely did not verify that allergen exposure actually fell, so the null convicts the interventions as delivered in trials, not the biological hypothesis that mite allergen matters. Multi-component environmental programmes for inner-city children are a different intervention and a different question.

shelves.title: Inhaled aztreonam for bronchiectasis: two phase 3 trials missed their quality-of-life endpoint — one nominal 'win' was judged not clinically significant, and airway side effects rose
shelves.question: In adults with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis colonised with Gram-negative bacteria, does aztreonam for inhalation solution improve respiratory-symptom quality of life compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects · Aztreonam/administration & dosage · Aztreonam/adverse effects · Bronchiectasis/drug therapy · Bronchiectasis/etiology · Cough/chemically induced · Double-Blind Method · Dyspnea/chemically induced · Female · Gram-Negative Bacteria/drug effects · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Sputum/drug effects · Sputum/microbiology · Time · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two large phase 3 trials of the same regimen failed to show clinical benefit. AIR-BX1 (266 randomised) and AIR-BX2 (274 randomised) tested aztreonam for inhalation solution 75 mg three times daily, in two 4-week courses, against placebo in bronchiectasis with Gram-negative colonisation; the primary endpoint was change in Quality of Life-Bronchiectasis Respiratory Symptoms score at 4 weeks. The adjusted difference was 0.8 points (95% CI -3.1 to 4.7; p=0.68) in AIR-BX1 and 4.6 points (1.1 to 8.2; p=0.011) in AIR-BX2 — the second result statistically significant but explicitly judged not clinically significant by the trialists (the scale's minimal important difference is 8.0 points). Treatment-related adverse events and discontinuations were more common on aztreonam in both trials, with dyspnoea, cough and increased sputum each more frequent than on placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): inhaled aztreonam does not provide clinically significant symptom benefit in non-CF bronchiectasis and adds airway side effects.

cards.headline: Barker 2014 (AIR-BX1 and AIR-BX2): quality-of-life differences 0.8 points (p=0.68) and 4.6 points (p=0.011, below the 8-point minimal important difference) — more adverse events and discontinuations on aztreonam
cards.summary: Barker 2014 (AIR-BX1 and AIR-BX2): quality-of-life differences 0.8 points (p=0.68) and 4.6 points (p=0.011, below the 8-point minimal important difference) — more adverse events and discontinuations on aztreonam
cards.type: Two randomised phase 3 trials reported in one paper (Barker 2014, AIR-BX1 and AIR-BX2)
cards.people: Adults (18 years or older) with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis and a history of positive sputum or bronchoscopic culture for target Gram-negative organisms: AIR-BX1 randomised 266 patients (134 aztreonam, 132 placebo) at 47 clinics; AIR-BX2 randomised 274 (136 aztreonam, 138 placebo) at 65 clinics. Treatment was aztreonam for inhalation solution 75 mg or placebo three times daily by eFlow nebuliser, in two 4-week courses each followed by 4 weeks off treatment.
cards.result: The adjusted mean difference versus placebo in Quality of Life-Bronchiectasis Respiratory Symptoms score change at 4 weeks was 0.8 (95% CI -3.1 to 4.7; p=0.68) in AIR-BX1 and 4.6 (1.1 to 8.2; p=0.011) in AIR-BX2; the trialists state the 4.6-point difference was not deemed clinically significant. In both studies, treatment-related adverse events were more common in the aztreonam group, as were discontinuations from adverse events; dyspnoea, cough and increased sputum were each more common on aztreonam than placebo.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a symptom score at 4 weeks, not exacerbations or hospitalisations — the trials cannot exclude an exacerbation effect in either direction, and they enrolled only Gram-negative-colonised patients. The companion validation paper for the QOL-B instrument (Quittner 2015) puts the Respiratory Symptoms minimal important difference at 8.0 points, which is the yardstick that makes AIR-BX2's 4.6-point result clinically insignificant; that paper is discussed here but not carded, as it is an instrument study of the same two trials.

shelves.title: Itraconazole for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis: responses in 46% versus 19% on placebo in the one steroid-dependent trial — exacerbations cut from 1.3 to 0.4 per patient in the pooled record
shelves.question: In patients with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, does adding itraconazole to corticosteroid-based care improve response, reduce exacerbations and lower IgE compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/therapeutic use · Antifungal Agents/adverse effects · Antifungal Agents/therapeutic use · Aspergillosis, Allergic Bronchopulmonary/drug therapy · Aspergillosis, Allergic Bronchopulmonary/immunology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Immunoglobulin E/blood · Itraconazole/adverse effects · Itraconazole/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small, old, but genuinely randomised evidence base. In the double-blind trial in corticosteroid-dependent ABPA, a composite response (at least 50% steroid-dose reduction, at least 25% IgE fall, plus improvement in exercise tolerance, lung function or infiltrates) occurred in 13 of 28 patients (46%) on itraconazole 200 mg twice daily for 16 weeks versus 5 of 27 (19%) on placebo (P=0.04), with similar adverse-event rates. The Cochrane review of azoles in ABPA (three randomised trials, 94 participants) found itraconazole-treated patients more likely to achieve a decline in serum IgE of 25% or more (Peto odds ratio 3.30; 95% CI 1.30 to 8.15), and in one trial exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids numbered 0.4 per patient on itraconazole versus 1.3 on placebo (p<0.03), with sputum eosinophils down 35% versus 19% (p<0.01). The caveat is scale and era: fewer than 100 randomised patients, 16-week horizons, and a flagged interaction concern — adrenal suppression when itraconazole is combined with inhaled corticosteroids. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): itraconazole improves immunologic and clinical response in ABPA over 16 weeks, on small-trial evidence.

cards.headline: Stevens 2000: composite response in 13 of 28 (46%) on itraconazole versus 5 of 27 (19%) on placebo over 16 weeks (P=0.04)
cards.summary: Stevens 2000: composite response in 13 of 28 (46%) on itraconazole versus 5 of 27 (19%) on placebo over 16 weeks (P=0.04)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial (Stevens 2000)
cards.people: 55 patients meeting immunologic and pulmonary-function criteria for corticosteroid-dependent allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, randomised to itraconazole 200 mg twice daily (n=28) or placebo (n=27) for 16 weeks, followed by an open-label phase in which all patients received itraconazole 200 mg daily for 16 weeks. Response required at least a 50% reduction in corticosteroid dose, at least a 25% fall in serum IgE, and at least one of: 25% improvement in exercise tolerance or pulmonary function, or resolution/absence of pulmonary infiltrates.
cards.result: Responses occurred in 13 of 28 patients (46%) on itraconazole versus 5 of 27 (19%) on placebo (P=0.04), with absolute rates printed alongside. Adverse-event rates were similar in the two groups. In the open-label phase, 12 of 33 previous non-responders (36%) responded, and no double-blind responder relapsed.
cards.watchOut: A 55-patient trial from 2000 with a composite response definition that mixes steroid-sparing, a biomarker (IgE) and clinical measures; the open-label second phase has no control group and cannot confirm durability. Patients had corticosteroid-dependent disease, so the result does not cover milder ABPA.
cards.source: Stevens DA et al. A randomized trial of itraconazole in allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2000. PMID: 10717010. cards.headline: Wark 2004 (Cochrane): across the itraconazole trials, IgE fell by ≥25% more often on treatment (Peto odds ratio 3.30); exacerbations 0.4 versus 1.3 per patient in one trial

cards.type: Meta-analysis (Wark 2004, Cochrane systematic review)
cards.people: Systematic review of controlled trials of azole antifungals in allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis associated with asthma (patients with cystic fibrosis excluded): 12 trials identified, of which 3 were prospective, randomised and controlled, totalling 94 participants — two itraconazole trials (16 weeks) and one ketoconazole trial (400 mg daily for 12 months).
cards.result: Meta-analysis of the two itraconazole trials showed treated patients were more likely to have a decline in serum IgE of 25% or more (Peto odds ratio 3.30; 95% CI 1.30 to 8.15). In one itraconazole trial, exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids numbered 0.4 per patient on itraconazole versus 1.3 per patient on placebo (p<0.03), and sputum eosinophils fell 35% versus 19% (p<0.01). The ketoconazole trial reduced immunological markers and symptom scores without significant lung-function improvement. The reviewers flag adrenal suppression with combined inhaled corticosteroids and itraconazole as a potential concern.
cards.watchOut: The whole randomised base is 94 participants, and the review's search closed in January 2003 — it pools the same small trials, including Stevens 2000 carded above, so it corroborates rather than independently replicates them. IgE decline is a biomarker, not a patient outcome.
cards.source: Wark PA et al. Azoles for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis associated with asthma. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2004. PMID: 15266440. shelves.title: Tezepelumab for COPD (COURSE): the primary endpoint missed — exacerbations 1.75 versus 2.11 a year (rate ratio 0.83, not significant), with the signal confined to higher-eosinophil subgroups
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-very-severe COPD on triple inhaled therapy who keep exacerbating, does tezepelumab reduce the annualised rate of moderate or severe exacerbations compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/drug therapy · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Placebos
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the overall trial population. COURSE randomised 333 patients with moderate-to-very-severe COPD on triple therapy and at least two exacerbations in the prior year to tezepelumab 420 mg every 4 weeks or placebo for 52 weeks. The annualised rate of moderate or severe exacerbations was 1.75 on tezepelumab versus 2.11 on placebo (rate ratio 0.83 [90% CI 0.64-1.06]; p=0.10 one-sided) — the primary endpoint was not met. Prespecified eosinophil subgroups leaned favourable at higher counts (rate ratio 0.66 [95% CI 0.42-1.04] at 150 to <300 cells/µL and 0.54 [0.25-1.15] at ≥300 cells/µL) but harmful-leaning below 150 cells/µL (1.19 [0.75-1.90]), and every subgroup interval crosses 1. Adverse events occurred in 81% versus 75% and serious adverse events in 30% in both groups; five patients died on treatment (two tezepelumab, three placebo), none judged treatment-related. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): tezepelumab did not significantly reduce COPD exacerbations overall in its phase 2a trial; the eosinophil-high hypothesis is unproven and is being tested further.

cards.headline: Singh 2025 (COURSE): exacerbation rate ratio 0.83 (90% CI 0.64-1.06; p=0.10) — primary endpoint not met; subgroup ratios 1.19, 0.66 and 0.54 across rising eosinophil bands, all crossing 1
cards.summary: Singh 2025 (COURSE): exacerbation rate ratio 0.83 (90% CI 0.64-1.06; p=0.10) — primary endpoint not met; subgroup ratios 1.19, 0.66 and 0.54 across rising eosinophil bands, all crossing 1
cards.type: Randomised phase 2a trial (Singh 2025, COURSE)
cards.people: 333 patients aged 40-80 years with moderate-to-very-severe COPD on triple inhaled maintenance therapy and at least two moderate-to-severe exacerbations in the prior 12 months, at 90 sites in ten countries, randomised to tezepelumab 420 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks (n=165) or placebo (n=168) for up to 52 weeks.
cards.result: The annualised rate of moderate or severe COPD exacerbations over 52 weeks was 1.75 on tezepelumab versus 2.11 on placebo (rate ratio 0.83 [90% CI 0.64-1.06]; p=0.10 one-sided) — a relative effect that was not statistically significant. Prespecified subgroups by baseline blood eosinophil count: rate ratio 1.19 (95% CI 0.75-1.90) below 150 cells/µL, 0.66 (0.42-1.04) at 150 to <300 cells/µL, and 0.54 (0.25-1.15) at 300 cells/µL or higher. Adverse events occurred in 133 (81%) of 165 tezepelumab patients and 126 (75%) of 168 on placebo; serious adverse events in 49 (30%) and 50 (30%); five on-treatment deaths (two tezepelumab, three placebo), none judged causally related to treatment.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2a trial sized for signal-finding, analysed with a one-sided p-value and 90% intervals for the primary endpoint; the eosinophil gradient is a subgroup pattern within a negative trial — the classic setup for a hypothesis that later trials may or may not confirm. The rate ratio of 0.83 is a relative effect from a randomised trial, reported here with its absolute rates (1.75 versus 2.11 per year).

shelves.title: Montelukast for chronic asthma: morning FEV1 improved about 7-10% more than placebo in its 1998 dose-ranging trials — symptom and reliever-use gains were fractions of a point and a puff
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with chronic persistent asthma, does oral montelukast improve lung function, symptoms and reliever use compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acetates/administration & dosage · Acetates/adverse effects · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Asthma/drug therapy · Asthma/physiopathology · Chronic Disease · Cyclopropanes · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume/drug effects · Humans · Leukotriene Antagonists · Male · Middle Aged · Peak Expiratory Flow Rate/drug effects · Quality of Life · Quinolines/administration & dosage · Quinolines/adverse effects · Spirometry · Sulfides
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real but modest, from the drug's original dose-ranging trials. In a 343-patient 6-week trial, pooled montelukast doses beat placebo on morning FEV1 percentage change by 10.30% (95% CI 5.56 to 15.04), with as-needed beta-agonist use down 0.98 puffs (95% CI -1.53 to -0.44) and morning peak flow up 18.80 L/min (8.62 to 28.98). In a second, 3-week trial, pooled 10 and 50 mg doses beat placebo on FEV1 change by 7.1%, morning peak flow by 19.23 L/min, daytime symptom score by -0.29 points and beta-agonist use by -0.82 puffs/day. Adverse experiences were similar to placebo and not dose-related in both trials, and doses above 10 mg once daily added nothing — the 10 mg evening dose is where the effect plateaus. These are short trials in mild-to-moderate asthma using lung function and symptom scores, not exacerbations or hospitalisations. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): montelukast improves asthma control measures modestly over 3-6 weeks in chronic asthma, at the 10 mg dose.

cards.headline: Altman 1998: pooled montelukast beat placebo on morning FEV1 by 10.30% (95% CI 5.56 to 15.04), reliever use by -0.98 puffs and morning peak flow by 18.80 L/min over 6 weeks
cards.summary: Altman 1998: pooled montelukast beat placebo on morning FEV1 by 10.30% (95% CI 5.56 to 15.04), reliever use by -0.98 puffs and morning peak flow by 18.80 L/min over 6 weeks
cards.type: Randomised dose-ranging trial (Altman 1998, Montelukast Asthma Study Group)
cards.people: 343 asthmatic patients with FEV1 40-80% of predicted and at least 15% reversibility after inhaled beta-agonist, randomised after a 3-week single-blind placebo run-in to placebo or montelukast 10, 100 or 200 mg once daily in the evening, or 10 or 50 mg twice daily, for a 6-week double-blind period; all used inhaled short-acting beta-agonists as needed.
cards.result: All montelukast doses produced similar, significant differences versus placebo. Least-square mean differences for pooled montelukast versus placebo: morning FEV1 percentage change from baseline 10.30% (95% CI 5.56 to 15.04); as-needed beta-agonist use -0.98 puffs (95% CI -1.53 to -0.44); morning peak expiratory flow 18.80 L/min (95% CI 8.62 to 28.98); physicians' and patients' global evaluations and asthma quality-of-life scores also significant (p≤0.050). Adverse experiences were not dose-related and were similar between montelukast and placebo.
cards.watchOut: A dose-ranging registration trial of 6 weeks in patients not on inhaled corticosteroids by modern standards — it establishes pharmacologic activity and the flat dose-response, not montelukast's place against or alongside inhaled steroids, and not exacerbation prevention. Several tested doses (up to 200 mg) far exceed the marketed 10 mg dose.
cards.source: Altman LC et al. A placebo-controlled, dose-ranging study of montelukast, a cysteinyl leukotriene-receptor antagonist. Montelukast Asthma Study Group. The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology. 1998. PMID: 9679847. cards.headline: Noonan 1998: pooled 10 and 50 mg montelukast beat placebo on FEV1 change by 7.1%, symptoms by -0.29 points and reliever use by -0.82 puffs/day over 3 weeks
cards.summary: Noonan 1998: pooled 10 and 50 mg montelukast beat placebo on FEV1 change by 7.1%, symptoms by -0.29 points and reliever use by -0.82 puffs/day over 3 weeks
cards.type: Randomised dose-ranging trial (Noonan 1998, Montelukast Asthma Study Group)
cards.people: Patients with chronic asthma (FEV1 40-80% predicted, at least 15% reversibility) randomised after a 2-week placebo run-in to placebo or montelukast 2, 10 or 50 mg once daily in the evening for a 3-week double-blind period.
cards.result: Montelukast 10 and 50 mg caused similar responses, superior to 2 mg and significantly different from placebo (p<0.05, linear trend test) on daytime symptom score, as-needed beta-agonist use, quality of life and exacerbation frequency. Differences (least-square mean) between pooled 10 and 50 mg groups and placebo: 7.1% change from baseline in FEV1, 19.23 L/min in morning peak flow, -0.29 in daytime asthma symptom score (absolute value) and -0.82 in beta-agonist use (puffs/day). Adverse experiences were neither dose-related nor different from placebo.
cards.watchOut: Three weeks is very short, exacerbation 'frequency' over 3 weeks is a fragile endpoint, and the record does not print the trial's total sample size in its abstract. Both carded trials predate modern controller therapy, so effect sizes against today's inhaled-steroid background are unknown from this record.
cards.source: Noonan MJ et al. Montelukast, a potent leukotriene receptor antagonist, causes dose-related improvements in chronic asthma. Montelukast Asthma Study Group. The European respiratory journal. 1998. PMID: 9657560. cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant dose-ranging trials — a real, small, plateauing effect on control measures

shelves.title: Buteyko breathing for asthma: reliever use fell (by 904 µg/day in one trial, two puffs/day in another) and symptoms improved — lung function and airway responsiveness never moved
shelves.question: In people with asthma, does the Buteyko breathing technique reduce symptoms and medication use compared with control classes or placebo devices, and does it change lung function or bronchial responsiveness?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Agonists/therapeutic use · Adult · Algorithms · Asthma/therapy · Breathing Exercises · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume/physiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Satisfaction · Steroids/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Vital Capacity/physiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for symptoms and reliever use only; the objective measures are null in both trials. In Bowler's blinded trial (39 subjects), the Buteyko group cut daily beta-agonist dose by a median 904 µg at 3 months versus 57 µg in controls (P=0.002), with inhaled steroid dose falling 49% versus 0 (P=0.06) and a trend to better quality of life (P=0.09) — but no change in daily peak flow or FEV1 in either group. In Cooper's 6-month three-arm trial (90 patients on inhaled corticosteroids), symptom scores improved most with Buteyko (median change -3 versus 0 on placebo device; p=0.003 between groups) and bronchodilator use fell by two puffs/day (p=0.005), while methacholine responsiveness (PD20), FEV1, exacerbations and ability to reduce inhaled steroids did not differ between groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Buteyko training reduces reliever use and symptoms in asthma without changing the underlying airway physiology — patients should not read it as a substitute for controller therapy, which neither trial showed could be safely withdrawn.

cards.headline: Bowler 1998: median daily beta-agonist dose fell 904 µg on Buteyko versus 57 µg on control classes at 3 months (P=0.002); peak flow and FEV1 unchanged
cards.summary: Bowler 1998: median daily beta-agonist dose fell 904 µg on Buteyko versus 57 µg on control classes at 3 months (P=0.002); peak flow and FEV1 unchanged
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Bowler 1998)
cards.people: 39 community-recruited subjects aged 12-70 years with asthma and substantial medication use, randomised to Buteyko breathing technique classes or control classes, with medication use, peak flow, FEV1, end-tidal CO2, minute volume and quality of life measured at 3 months; assessors blinded.
cards.result: At 3 months the Buteyko group had a median reduction in daily beta-agonist dose of 904 µg (range 29 to 3129 µg) versus 57 µg (range -2343 to 1143 µg) in controls (P=0.002). Daily inhaled steroid dose fell 49% (range -100% to 150%) versus 0 (range -82% to +100%) (P=0.06). Quality-of-life improvement trended greater with Buteyko (P=0.09). No change in daily peak expiratory flow or FEV1 occurred in either group; minute volume was lower in the Buteyko group at 3 months (P=0.004) and end-tidal CO2 did not change.
cards.watchOut: Only 39 subjects, and participants cannot be blinded to a breathing technique — reliever use and symptoms are exactly the outcomes expectation can move, while the blinded-proof outcomes (FEV1, peak flow) were null. The steroid-dose fall was not significant (P=0.06) and was not tested as a safety outcome.
cards.source: Bowler SD et al. Buteyko breathing techniques in asthma: a blinded randomised controlled trial. The Medical journal of Australia. 1998. PMID: 9887897. cards.headline: Cooper 2003: symptom scores improved most on Buteyko (median -3 versus 0 on placebo device; p=0.003) and reliever use fell two puffs/day — PD20, FEV1 and steroid reduction all null
cards.summary: Cooper 2003: symptom scores improved most on Buteyko (median -3 versus 0 on placebo device; p=0.003) and reliever use fell two puffs/day — PD20, FEV1 and steroid reduction all null
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Cooper 2003)
cards.people: 90 patients with asthma taking an inhaled corticosteroid, randomised after a 2-week run-in to Eucapnic Buteyko breathing, a Pink City Lung Exerciser mimicking pranayama, or a placebo lung-exerciser device, practised twice daily at home for 6 months, followed by an optional steroid-reduction phase; 69 patients (78%) completed.
cards.result: There was no significant difference between groups in methacholine PD20 at 3 or 6 months. Median symptom-score change at 6 months was 0 (interquartile range -1 to 1) on placebo device, -1 (-2 to 0.75) with the lung exerciser, and -3 (-4 to 0) with Buteyko (p=0.003 for the between-group difference). Bronchodilator use fell by two puffs/day in the Buteyko group with no change in the other groups (p=0.005). No between-group differences were seen in FEV1, exacerbations, or ability to reduce inhaled corticosteroids.
cards.watchOut: A 22% dropout rate and an unblindable intervention; the placebo device controlled for attention and gadget use but not for the specific expectation attached to a named breathing method. Steroid reduction — the outcome that would matter most and could harm — showed no benefit.

cards.people: Two randomised trials of Buteyko breathing in asthma (39 subjects over 3 months against control classes; 90 patients over 6 months against active and placebo breathing devices).
cards.result: Reliever use: median beta-agonist dose -904 µg/day versus -57 µg (P=0.002); bronchodilator use -2 puffs/day versus no change (p=0.005). Symptoms: median score change -3 versus 0 (p=0.003) in the larger trial. Lung function (FEV1, peak flow) and bronchial responsiveness (PD20): no change in either trial. shelves.title: Doxycycline for community COVID-19: recovery half a day sooner at most and hospitalisation 5.3% versus 4.5% in PRINCIPLE — the trial was stopped for futility
shelves.question: In adults with COVID-19 in the community, does doxycycline improve recovery and reduce hospitalisation compared with usual care alone?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · COVID-19/diagnosis/mortality/virology · Doxycycline/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Female · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Minimal Clinically Important Difference · Risk Factors · SARS-CoV-2/isolation & purification · Self Report/statistics & numerical data · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom/epidemiology · COVID-19 Drug Treatment
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — from a single large open-label community trial, stopped for futility. In PRINCIPLE, median time to first self-reported recovery was 9.6 days on doxycycline versus 10.1 days on usual care (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.93–1.17), an estimated benefit of 0.5 days with a probability of only 0.10 that the benefit reached the 1.5-day threshold for clinical meaningfulness. Hospitalisation or death related to COVID-19 occurred in 5.3% of the doxycycline group and 4.5% of the usual care group (estimated absolute difference −0.5%, 95% Bayesian credible interval −2.6 to 1.4), and there were five deaths (0.6%) on doxycycline versus two (0.2%) on usual care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): doxycycline should not be used as a routine community treatment for COVID-19. Single-trial shelf — flagged in the summary.

cards.headline: Butler 2021 (PRINCIPLE doxycycline): median recovery 9.6 vs 10.1 days (hazard ratio 1.04); hospitalisation or death 5.3% vs 4.5% — randomisation stopped when the futility criterion was met
cards.summary: Butler 2021 (PRINCIPLE doxycycline): median recovery 9.6 vs 10.1 days (hazard ratio 1.04); hospitalisation or death 5.3% vs 4.5% — randomisation stopped when the futility criterion was met
cards.type: Randomised open-label adaptive platform trial (Butler 2021, PRINCIPLE)
cards.people: 2,689 people in UK primary care aged 65 years or older, or 50 years or older with comorbidities, unwell for 14 days or less with suspected COVID-19 or a positive PCR test; 2,508 contributed follow-up data to the primary analysis, including 780 allocated usual care plus oral doxycycline (200 mg on day 1, then 100 mg daily for 6 days) and 948 allocated usual care only, between July and December 2020.
cards.result: There was little evidence of a difference in median time to first self-reported recovery: 9.6 days (95% Bayesian credible interval 8.3–11.0) on doxycycline versus 10.1 days (8.7–11.7) on usual care (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% BCI 0.93–1.17); the estimated benefit was 0.5 days (95% BCI −0.99 to 2.04) and the probability of a clinically meaningful benefit of at least 1.5 days was 0.10. Hospitalisation or death related to COVID-19 occurred in 41 participants (5.3%) in the doxycycline group and 43 (4.5%) in the usual care group (estimated absolute percentage difference −0.5%, 95% BCI −2.6 to 1.4); there were five deaths (0.6%) in the doxycycline group and two (0.2%) in the usual care group.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf: PRINCIPLE is the only large randomised test of doxycycline for community COVID-19, and it was open-label with a self-reported recovery endpoint — but the futility stop, the near-unity hazard ratio, and the numerically higher hospitalisation rate on doxycycline all point the same way. Many participants had suspected rather than PCR-confirmed COVID-19, as was unavoidable in community testing conditions in 2020.

shelves.title: Azithromycin for community COVID-19: recovery no faster and hospitalisation 3% in both groups in PRINCIPLE — and 28-day mortality 22% versus 22% when RECOVERY tested it in hospital
shelves.question: In patients with suspected COVID-19 in the community, does azithromycin improve recovery and reduce hospitalisation compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antimicrobial Stewardship · Azithromycin/pharmacology/therapeutic use · COVID-19/complications/diagnosis/immunology · Cytokine Release Syndrome/immunology/prevention & control/virology · Drug Resistance, Bacterial · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Admission/statistics & numerical data · Risk Factors · SARS-CoV-2/drug effects/isolation & purification · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom · COVID-19 Drug Treatment
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — in the community and in hospital alike. In PRINCIPLE, among people at increased risk of an adverse course with suspected COVID-19 in the community, 80% on azithromycin 500 mg daily for 3 days and 77% on usual care reported feeling recovered within 28 days, with little evidence of a meaningful benefit in time to first reported recovery (hazard ratio 1.08, 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.95–1.23; estimated benefit in median time to recovery 0.94 days, 95% BCI −0.56 to 2.43; probability of a clinically meaningful benefit of at least 1.5 days was 0.23). Hospitalisation was 3% in both groups (16 of 500 vs 28 of 823; absolute benefit 0.3%, 95% BCI −1.7 to 2.2), and there were no deaths in either group. In hospital, RECOVERY found 28-day mortality of 22% in both groups (rate ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.87–1.07; p=0.50). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): azithromycin does not speed recovery or reduce hospitalisation in community COVID-19, and its routine use carries an antibiotic-stewardship cost the PRINCIPLE authors state plainly.

cards.headline: PRINCIPLE azithromycin: time to recovery hazard ratio 1.08 with only a 0.23 probability of a clinically meaningful benefit; hospitalisation 3% vs 3%, no deaths in either group
cards.summary: PRINCIPLE azithromycin: time to recovery hazard ratio 1.08 with only a 0.23 probability of a clinically meaningful benefit; hospitalisation 3% vs 3%, no deaths in either group
cards.type: Randomised open-label adaptive platform trial (PRINCIPLE Trial Collaborative Group 2021)
cards.people: People in UK primary care aged 65 years or older, or 50 years or older with at least one comorbidity, unwell for 14 days or less with suspected COVID-19; 2,265 were randomly assigned in the azithromycin evaluation period (May to November 2020), and 2,120 (94%) provided follow-up data for the primary analysis — 500 in the azithromycin plus usual care group (azithromycin 500 mg daily for 3 days), 823 in usual care alone, and 797 in other intervention groups.
cards.result: Within 28 days, 402 (80%) of 500 participants in the azithromycin group and 631 (77%) of 823 in the usual care group reported feeling recovered. There was little evidence of a meaningful benefit in time to first reported recovery (hazard ratio 1.08, 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.95–1.23), equating to an estimated benefit in median time to first recovery of 0.94 days (95% BCI −0.56 to 2.43); the probability of a clinically meaningful benefit of at least 1.5 days was 0.23. Hospitalisation occurred in 16 (3%) of 500 azithromycin participants and 28 (3%) of 823 usual care participants (absolute benefit 0.3%, 95% BCI −1.7 to 2.2). There were no deaths in either group, and safety outcomes were similar.
cards.watchOut: Suspected rather than confirmed COVID-19 in many participants, and an open-label design with self-reported recovery — but the hospitalisation endpoint is objective and equally null, and the authors' stewardship point stands on the record: routine azithromycin for community COVID-19 spends antibiotic effectiveness for no measured gain.

cards.headline: RECOVERY azithromycin (hospital): 28-day mortality 22% vs 22% (rate ratio 0.97, p=0.50) in 7,763 patients — the same null at the severe end of the illness
cards.summary: RECOVERY azithromycin (hospital): 28-day mortality 22% vs 22% (rate ratio 0.97, p=0.50) in 7,763 patients — the same null at the severe end of the illness
cards.type: Randomised open-label platform trial (RECOVERY Collaborative Group 2021)
cards.people: 7,763 adults admitted to 176 UK hospitals with COVID-19 (mean age 65.3 years, 38% women), randomised to usual care plus azithromycin 500 mg once daily by mouth or intravenously for 10 days or until discharge (2,582) or usual care alone (5,181), between April and November 2020.
cards.result: Overall, 561 (22%) patients allocated azithromycin and 1,162 (22%) allocated usual care died within 28 days (rate ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.87–1.07; p=0.50). There was no significant difference in duration of hospital stay (median 10 days vs 11 days) or in the proportion discharged alive within 28 days (rate ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.98–1.10; p=0.19), and among those not ventilated at baseline, no difference in progression to invasive mechanical ventilation or death (risk ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.87–1.03; p=0.24).
cards.watchOut: This card answers the hospital version of the question, not the community one on the shelf's face — it is included because it removes the 'too mild to show an effect' reading of PRINCIPLE: azithromycin was equally null where event rates were high and the endpoint was mortality.

shelves.title: Stimulus control alone for insomnia: small-to-large gains against passive controls (g 0.38–0.85) that shrink to negligible (g 0.06–0.30) against active treatments — in 11 mostly decades-old trials a modern meta-analysis calls uncertain
shelves.question: In adults with insomnia, does stimulus-control therapy alone improve sleep compared with control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Sleep Latency · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the component works against doing nothing and adds little against anything active. Jansson-Fröjmark M et al. (PMID: 37496454) meta-analysed 11 randomised and experimental studies of stimulus control for insomnia, the majority published between 1978 and 1998: against passive comparators, stimulus control produced small-to-large improvements in sleep onset latency and total sleep time (Hedges g = 0.38–0.85), but against active comparators the improvements were negligible (g = 0.06–0.30), with methodological uncertainties throughout. Verreault MD et al. (PMID: 37586843) included 23 randomised studies in a network meta-analysis and likewise found stimulus control effective against control conditions, while rating the included studies generally poor quality with inconsistencies in the network. The one modern primary trial verified, Goodhines PA et al. (PMID: 35943968), was a pilot in 82 college students in which a single-session peer-led stimulus-control arm (n=14) improved within-group insomnia severity (d = 1.66) — a feasibility signal, not a confirmatory test. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): stimulus control alone probably improves sleep versus passive control, on old, small, low-quality trials.

cards.headline: Jansson-Fröjmark 2024: 11 trials — stimulus control beat passive controls on sleep onset latency and total sleep time (g 0.38–0.85) but not active comparators (g 0.06–0.30)
cards.summary: Jansson-Fröjmark 2024: 11 trials — stimulus control beat passive controls on sleep onset latency and total sleep time (g 0.38–0.85) but not active comparators (g 0.06–0.30)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled and experimental studies (Jansson-Fröjmark 2024)
cards.people: 11 included studies in adults with insomnia, the majority published between 1978 and 1998, comparing stimulus control against passive and active comparators, with sleep-diary outcomes (number of awakenings, sleep onset latency, total sleep time) at post-treatment and follow-up.
cards.result: Against passive comparators, stimulus control resulted in small-to-large improvements on sleep onset latency and total sleep time (standardised mean difference, Hedges g = 0.38–0.85). Against active comparators, the improvements were negligible (g = 0.06–0.30). The authors note methodological uncertainties in the included trials and call for more robust studies before stronger conclusions.
cards.watchOut: Most of the underlying trials predate modern trial conduct by decades; a pooled effect assembled from 1978–1998 studies of a behavioural technique is exactly the evidence grade MAYBE (weak evidence) exists for.

cards.headline: Verreault 2024: 23 randomised studies in a network meta-analysis — stimulus control effective versus control, but study quality generally poor and the network inconsistent
cards.summary: Verreault 2024: 23 randomised studies in a network meta-analysis — stimulus control effective versus control, but study quality generally poor and the network inconsistent
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis (Verreault 2024)
cards.people: 23 randomised studies (1972 to June 2022) in adults with a diagnosis of insomnia including at least one stimulus-control instruction in a treatment group, comparing stimulus control alone, full CBT-I and other components; risk of bias assessed with the Quality Assessment of Controlled Intervention Studies.
cards.result: Stimulus control was an effective intervention to improve insomnia compared with control conditions, and not all stimulus-control instructions appeared essential — particularly those intended to recondition the bedroom for sleep. The authors caution that the included studies were generally of poor quality, with a small number of studies and inconsistencies in the network meta-analysis, so results should be interpreted cautiously.
cards.watchOut: A network built largely from the same old, small trials as the pairwise meta-analysis is corroboration of direction, not independent confirmation of size.

cards.headline: Goodhines 2024 (pilot): single-session peer-led stimulus control in 14 college students improved insomnia severity within-group (d = 1.66) at 1 month — feasibility, not proof
cards.summary: Goodhines 2024 (pilot): single-session peer-led stimulus control in 14 college students improved insomnia severity within-group (d = 1.66) at 1 month — feasibility, not proof
cards.type: Randomised pilot feasibility trial (Goodhines 2024)
cards.people: 82 college students with insomnia symptoms (mean age 18.6 years, 58% female): randomised to single-session electronic peer-led cognitive refocusing (n=12), stimulus control (n=14) or awareness control (n=14), with a further non-randomly recruited no-treatment group (n=42); outcomes at 1 month.
cards.result: Within-group effects showed greater improvements in insomnia symptom severity for stimulus control (d = 1.66) and cognitive refocusing (d = 1.13) relative to awareness control (d = 0.90), and in pre-sleep cognitive arousal for stimulus control (d = 1.42) relative to awareness control (d = 0.75). Feasibility ratings were comparable across conditions; the authors frame both brief interventions as feasible and potentially efficacious.
cards.watchOut: Fourteen students in the stimulus-control arm, within-group effect sizes, and a non-randomised fourth arm: this card shows the intervention can be delivered in modern form, not that it works. Single-session college insomnia also generalises poorly to chronic insomnia disorder in clinic patients.

cards.headline: Synthesis: an old, small, low-quality trial base that consistently beats passive control and consistently fails to beat active treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: an old, small, low-quality trial base that consistently beats passive control and consistently fails to beat active treatment
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two 2024 systematic reviews (11 and 23 included studies, overlapping trial bases, mostly small and decades old) plus one modern pilot randomised trial (n=82, stimulus-control arm n=14).
cards.result: Versus passive comparators: Hedges g 0.38–0.85 for sleep onset latency and total sleep time. Versus active comparators: g 0.06–0.30. Quality: generally poor, with methodological uncertainties and network inconsistencies declared by both reviews. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) for stimulus control alone versus passive control.
cards.watchOut: Full CBT-I packages are homed elsewhere in the library; this shelf answers only the component question, and its honest answer is that the component has never been tested in a large modern trial of its own.

shelves.title: Adding baloxavir to a neuraminidase inhibitor in hospitalised severe influenza: no faster recovery — 97.5 versus 100.2 hours to clinical improvement in the one double-blind trial (FLAGSTONE)
shelves.question: In hospitalised patients with influenza, does oseltamivir plus baloxavir combination therapy beat monotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents · Dibenzothiepins/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Humans · Influenza, Human/drug therapy · Morpholines · Neuraminidase/therapeutic use · Pyridones · Treatment Outcome · Triazines
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one large double-blind trial, a clean null on its primary endpoint. In FLAGSTONE (Kumar D et al., PMID: 35085510), 366 hospitalised patients aged 12 years or older with severe influenza were randomised to baloxavir plus a standard-of-care neuraminidase inhibitor or placebo plus a neuraminidase inhibitor. Median time to clinical improvement was 97.5 hours on the combination versus 100.2 hours on neuraminidase inhibitor alone (median difference −2.7 hours, 95% CI −53.4 to 25.9; p=0.467). The combination was well tolerated: serious adverse events occurred in 12% versus 15%, and deaths in 2% (4 patients) versus 6% (7 patients), none considered treatment-related — but the trial was not powered to settle mortality, so the death gap is a numerically favourable wobble, not a finding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): adding baloxavir to a neuraminidase inhibitor does not speed clinical improvement in hospitalised severe influenza; single-trial shelf, held for the developer's verdict.

cards.headline: Kumar 2022 (FLAGSTONE): time to clinical improvement 97.5 hours with baloxavir added versus 100.2 hours without (p=0.467) — combination therapy did not beat neuraminidase inhibitor alone
cards.summary: Kumar 2022 (FLAGSTONE): time to clinical improvement 97.5 hours with baloxavir added versus 100.2 hours without (p=0.467) — combination therapy did not beat neuraminidase inhibitor alone
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Kumar 2022, FLAGSTONE)
cards.people: 366 patients aged 12 years or older, hospitalised with laboratory-confirmed influenza and a National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2) of 4 or greater, recruited at 124 centres in 25 countries and randomised 2:1 to baloxavir plus standard-of-care neuraminidase inhibitor (241 patients) or placebo plus neuraminidase inhibitor (125 patients). The neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir, zanamivir or peramivir) were chosen and given per local practice; baloxavir was dosed by weight on day 1 and day 4, and on day 7 if there had been no clinical improvement by day 5. The modified intention-to-treat infected population comprised 322 patients (208 combination, 114 control), 87% with influenza A.
cards.result: Median time to clinical improvement (NEWS2 of 2 or lower for 24 hours, or hospital discharge) was 97.5 hours (95% CI 75.9 to 117.2) in the baloxavir group and 100.2 hours (75.9 to 144.4) in the control group — a median difference of −2.7 hours (95% CI −53.4 to 25.9; p=0.467), not significant. Serious adverse events occurred in 29 of 239 patients (12%) on the combination versus 19 of 124 (15%) on neuraminidase inhibitor alone, with no new safety signals. Four deaths (2%) occurred in the baloxavir group and seven (6%) in the control group; none were considered related to treatment.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf. The comparator backbone was 'a neuraminidase inhibitor per local practice', not oseltamivir for every patient, so the trial answers the combination question for the drug class rather than for one named pairing. The mortality difference (2% versus 6%) comes from 11 deaths in total in a trial powered on time to improvement — it must not be read as a survival benefit.
cards.source: Kumar D et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: one well-run trial, one clear answer — routine combination antiviral therapy for hospitalised influenza is not supported
cards.summary: Synthesis: one well-run trial, one clear answer — routine combination antiviral therapy for hospitalised influenza is not supported
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (FLAGSTONE) of 366 hospitalised patients with severe influenza (NEWS2 ≥4), testing baloxavir added to standard-of-care neuraminidase inhibitor therapy.
cards.result: Time to clinical improvement: 97.5 versus 100.2 hours (difference −2.7 hours, 95% CI −53.4 to 25.9; p=0.467). Serious adverse events: 12% versus 15%. Deaths: 2% versus 6% (4 versus 7 patients; none treatment-related; not a powered endpoint). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), single-trial flag: the combination was safe but not superior, and the trial's own conclusion was that combination antivirals would not be routinely indicated for hospitalised influenza.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf (flagged per the relaxed intake rules): one randomised blinded trial alone carries this shelf. Outpatient baloxavir questions are homed elsewhere (live #727, #1630); this shelf is only the hospitalised combination question.

shelves.title: Wildfire smoke and health: in a meta-analysis of over 124 million people, each extra 10 μg/m³ of wildfire PM2.5 came with a 2% relative rise in all-cause mortality and a 4% relative rise in respiratory hospital admissions and emergency visits — all of it observational
shelves.question: What does wildfire smoke do to your health? When wildfire smoke raises fine particulate matter (PM2.5) in the air, what happens to deaths, hospital admissions and emergency department visits — especially for lung and heart disease?
shelves.mesh: Air Pollutants/adverse effects · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality · Emergency Room Visits · Emergency Service, Hospital/statistics & numerical data · Environmental Exposure/adverse effects · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Particulate Matter/adverse effects · Particulate Matter/analysis · Respiratory Tract Diseases/epidemiology · Respiratory Tract Diseases/mortality · Smoke/adverse effects · Wildfires
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm — observational only). Nobody can ethically randomise people to breathe wildfire smoke, so this entire shelf is observational epidemiology, and it should be read that way. In the largest synthesis (Wang 2025: 45 studies, a meta-analysis of over 124 million patients), each 10 μg/m³ rise in wildfire PM2.5 was associated with a relative risk of 1.02 (95% CI 1.01–1.03) for all-cause mortality, 1.04 (1.02–1.05) for respiratory hospital admission and 1.04 (1.02–1.06) for respiratory emergency department visits. A global time-series study of 749 cities (Chen 2021) found nearly identical relative risks for death (1.019 per 10 μg/m³) and estimated that 0.62% of all deaths each year are attributable to wildfire PM2.5. The cardiovascular signal is weaker and inconsistent between studies. The per-person relative risks are small, but smoke exposes whole populations at once, so the absolute number of extra deaths and admissions is large. These studies measure outdoor particle levels, not what any one person breathed, and smoke days differ from ordinary days in heat and behaviour, so residual confounding cannot be excluded.

cards.headline: Wang 2025 (meta-analysis, 45 studies, over 124 million patients): per 10 μg/m³ of wildfire PM2.5 — relative risk 1.02 for death, 1.04 for respiratory admission, 1.04 for respiratory emergency visits
cards.summary: Wang 2025 (meta-analysis, 45 studies, over 124 million patients): per 10 μg/m³ of wildfire PM2.5 — relative risk 1.02 for death, 1.04 for respiratory admission, 1.04 for respiratory emergency visits
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Wang 2025)
cards.people: People living in wildfire-affected regions, mostly North America (21 of 45 studies) and Australia (11 of 45); the meta-analysis pooled over 124 million patients from studies of wildfire particles and cardiorespiratory disease published between 1 January 2000 and 1 August 2024.
cards.result: Per 10 μg/m³ increase in wildfire PM2.5: all-cause mortality relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 1.01–1.03) — a 2% relative increase; respiratory hospital admission 1.04 (1.02–1.05); respiratory emergency department visits 1.04 (1.02–1.06). For wildfire PM10, respiratory hospital admission was 1.01 (1.00–1.02). Associations with cardiovascular disease were inconclusive: mortality 1.02 (1.01–1.03), hospital admission 1.01 (1.00–1.02), emergency visits 1.01 (0.98–1.04).
cards.watchOut: Every number here is a relative measure from observational studies: a relative risk of 1.02 is a 2% relative rise, not 2 extra deaths per 100 people — the absolute risk to any one person on a smoke day is small, and it is the population-wide exposure that makes the totals large. Exposure was estimated from outdoor monitors and models, not from what individuals actually breathed.
cards.source: Wang Y, Chen J, Huang Y, Wang J, Xiong Y, Xue T, Yue X, Qian F, Wang M. Associations of wildfire-derived particulate matter with hospitalization, emergency department visits and mortality: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Environmental Research. 2025. cards.headline: Chen 2021 (749 cities, 43 countries, 65.6 million deaths): wildfire PM2.5 relative risk 1.019 for all-cause death per 10 μg/m³; an estimated 0.62% of all deaths each year attributable to wildfire PM2.5
cards.summary: Chen 2021 (749 cities, 43 countries, 65.6 million deaths): wildfire PM2.5 relative risk 1.019 for all-cause death per 10 μg/m³; an estimated 0.62% of all deaths each year attributable to wildfire PM2.5
cards.type: Global multi-city time-series study (Chen 2021)
cards.people: Whole populations of 749 cities in 43 countries and regions, 2000–2016: the underlying death registries recorded 65.6 million all-cause deaths, 15.1 million cardiovascular deaths and 6.8 million respiratory deaths.
cards.result: Per 10 μg/m³ increase in the 3-day moving average (lag 0–2 days) of wildfire-related PM2.5, the pooled relative risk of death was 1.019 (95% CI 1.016–1.022) for all causes, 1.017 (1.012–1.021) for cardiovascular causes and 1.019 (1.013–1.025) for respiratory causes — relative increases of about 2% per 10 μg/m³. The authors estimated the fractions of annual deaths attributable to wildfire PM2.5 at 0.62% of all-cause deaths, 0.55% of cardiovascular deaths and 0.64% of respiratory deaths.
cards.watchOut: A time-series design compares deaths on smokier versus less smoky days within each city, which controls for fixed differences between cities but cannot fully separate smoke from the heat and fire weather that come with it, and it captures short-term (same-week) effects only. The attributable fractions are model-based estimates, not counted deaths.
cards.source: Chen G, Guo Y, Yue X, Tong S, Gasparrini A, Bell ML, Armstrong B, Schwartz J, Jaakkola JJK, Zanobetti A, et al. Mortality risk attributable to wildfire-related PM2·5 pollution: a global time series study in 749 locations. The Lancet Planetary Health. 2021. PMID: 34508679. cards.type: Narrative review with systematic review and meta-analysis (Gould 2024)
cards.people: A review of the worldwide literature on wildfire smoke exposure and health, including the methodological literature on how smoke exposure is measured and modelled.
cards.result: The authors' systematic review and meta-analysis found positive impacts of wildfire smoke exposure on all-cause mortality and respiratory hospitalizations, but less consistent evidence on cardiovascular morbidity. The abstract reports no pooled numerical effect sizes, so this card contributes direction and consistency of the literature, not new numbers.
cards.watchOut: This is a review's conclusion, not a new dataset, and its own meta-analysis is reported in the paper's figures rather than its abstract. The authors emphasise that estimates are sensitive to how nonlinear and lagged smoke effects are modelled — one reason the cardiovascular findings differ between studies.

cards.headline: Synthesis: wildfire smoke is consistently associated with more deaths and more respiratory care — small relative risks, whole-population exposure, observational evidence only
cards.summary: Synthesis: wildfire smoke is consistently associated with more deaths and more respiratory care — small relative risks, whole-population exposure, observational evidence only
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: People exposed to wildfire smoke, including the general population of smoke-affected regions and people with lung and heart disease within them.
cards.result: Two large independent syntheses agree closely: per 10 μg/m³ of wildfire PM2.5, all-cause mortality rises by about 2% in relative terms (RR 1.02 in Wang 2025; 1.019 in Chen 2021), respiratory hospital admissions and emergency visits rise by about 4% in relative terms, and roughly 0.6% of all deaths worldwide each year are statistically attributable to wildfire PM2.5. The respiratory signal is the most consistent; the cardiovascular signal is positive for mortality but inconclusive for admissions and emergency care.
cards.watchOut: Nothing on this shelf is randomised, and nothing can be: the honest reading is a consistent, dose-scaled association across designs and continents, with confounding (heat, behaviour, exposure mismeasurement) still possible. The numbers describe populations, not a prediction for any one person's smoke day.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wang Y et al. Environmental Research. 2025 (PMID: 40020860); Chen G et al. The Lancet Planetary Health. 2021 (PMID: 34508679); Gould CF et al. Annual Review of Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 37738508).

shelves.title: Stopping simple snoring (no sleep apnoea): a jaw-advancement device beat a combined nasal/positional bundle in the one head-to-head pilot trial (partner-rated response 91% versus 58%) — and palatal radiofrequency beat sham in one small trial, modestly
shelves.question: How do I stop snoring? In adults who snore without obstructive sleep apnoea (primary/simple snoring), do mandibular advancement devices, combined nasal and positional measures, or soft-palate radiofrequency surgery reduce snoring?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Mandibular Advancement/instrumentation · Middle Aged · Pilot Projects · Snoring/therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the trial record for simple snoring is thin: one small pilot randomised trial and one small sham-controlled surgical trial, with no large or long-term study. In the pilot randomised trial in primary snoring (Ioerger 2024, PMID: 38780959; 50 couples randomised, 42 dyads completed, 4 weeks), a mandibular advancement device (MAD) was rated a responder by the sleeping partner in 21 of 23 snorers (91%) versus 11 of 19 (58%) on combined airway and positional therapy (CAPT — external nasal dilator, nasal saline lavage with mometasone, mouth taping, and lateral positional therapy): a difference of 33 percentage points (95% CI 8–58), number needed to treat 3; both options reduced snoring, and adverse-effect withdrawals were 2 in each group. For surgery, the only placebo-controlled trial of soft-palate radiofrequency in primary snoring (Stuck 2005, PMID: 16124664; 26 patients, 23 completed) found partner-rated snoring scores improving from 8.1 to 5.2 on a 10 cm scale with radiofrequency versus 8.4 to 8.0 with sham needle insertion (P < 0.05) — a real but moderate effect, in the authors' own words. The systematic review of palatal radiofrequency (Bäck 2009, PMID: 19365852; 30 studies, only 2 randomised) confirms that this single sham-controlled trial is the controlled core of the surgical literature, that radiofrequency causes less postoperative pain than other procedures, and that most studies were uncontrolled with short follow-up, precluding solid conclusions. BOUNDARY: this shelf is simple snoring only. External nasal dilator strips used alone are homed on Shelf #2530 and are not re-carded here (the dilator appears here only as one component of the CAPT bundle); mandibular advancement devices versus CPAP for obstructive sleep apnoea are homed on Shelf #923, and oropharyngeal exercises for OSA on Shelf #1507 — different questions, not re-carded. Anyone whose snoring comes with witnessed apnoeas or daytime sleepiness needs an apnoea evaluation, not this shelf. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a MAD is the best-tested option on a small evidence base; the combined nasal/positional bundle also helped most users in the same small trial; palatal radiofrequency has one small positive sham-controlled trial and a mostly uncontrolled literature behind it.

cards.headline: Ioerger 2024 (the head-to-head pilot trial in primary snoring): partner-rated response in 91% on a mandibular advancement device versus 58% on combined nasal/positional therapy — difference 33 points, NNT 3
cards.summary: Ioerger 2024 (the head-to-head pilot trial in primary snoring): partner-rated response in 91% on a mandibular advancement device versus 58% on combined nasal/positional therapy — difference 33 points, NNT 3
cards.type: Pilot randomised clinical trial in primary snoring (Ioerger 2024)
cards.people: People who snore without sleep apnoea and their sleeping partners at a US academic medical centre: 50 couples randomised to a mandibular advancement device (MAD) or to combined airway and positional therapy (CAPT: external nasal dilator, nasal saline lavage with mometasone, mouth taping, and lateral positional therapy) for 4 weeks; 42 dyads completed the study (23 MAD, 19 CAPT). Among the snorers, 26 (62%) were female and mean age was 48 (SD 14) years. The outcome was the partner's rating on the Clinical Global Impression of Improvement scale (very much or much improved = responder).
cards.result: Of 23 dyads randomised to MAD, 21 snorers (91%) were rated responders by their sleeping partner, versus 11 of 19 dyads (58%) on CAPT — a difference of 33 percentage points (95% CI 8–58) and a number needed to treat of 3. Both treatments reduced primary snoring. Of 10 participants withdrawn, 4 were withdrawn for adverse effects, evenly split (2 MAD, 2 CAPT). The authors concluded the MAD may be more effective than CAPT for primary snoring, and that choice should weigh convenience, adverse effects, and cost.
cards.watchOut: A pilot trial: 42 completing couples, 4 weeks, a convenience sample, and a subjective partner-rated outcome with no sham device — expectation effects cannot be excluded, and the 95% CI on the difference (8–58 points) is wide. It compares two active bundles, so it cannot say how much of either effect exceeds placebo; and CAPT bundles four measures at once, so no single component (dilator, steroid lavage, mouth taping, position) can be credited or blamed separately.
cards.source: Ioerger P, Afshari A, Hentati F, Strober W, Kallogjeri D, Ju YE, Piccirillo JF. Mandibular Advancement vs Combined Airway and Positional Therapy for Snoring: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery. 2024. PMID: 38780959. Registry ID: NCT05756647. cards.headline: Stuck 2005 (the sham-controlled surgical trial): soft-palate radiofrequency cut partner-rated snoring from 8.1 to 5.2 on a 10-point scale versus 8.4 to 8.0 on sham (P < 0.05) — significant, but 'only moderate'
cards.summary: Stuck 2005 (the sham-controlled surgical trial): soft-palate radiofrequency cut partner-rated snoring from 8.1 to 5.2 on a 10-point scale versus 8.4 to 8.0 on sham (P < 0.05) — significant, but 'only moderate'
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial of radiofrequency surgery for primary snoring (Stuck 2005)
cards.people: 26 outpatients with primary snoring (apnoea–hypopnoea index < 15, body mass index < 35) at a German university ENT department, randomised to two sessions of temperature-controlled radiofrequency surgery of the soft palate under local anaesthesia (total energy 3,300 Joule) or placebo (insertion of the device needle without energy delivery); 23 completed (12 radiofrequency, 11 placebo). Snoring was rated by the bed partner on 10 cm visual analogue scales.
cards.result: Snoring scores did not change in the placebo group (8.4 ± 1.6 to 8.0 ± 2.3) while improving in the radiofrequency group (8.1 ± 1.3 to 5.2 ± 2.4); the between-group difference was statistically significant (P < 0.05). The authors concluded radiofrequency surgery was significantly better than placebo, although the reduction in snoring was only moderate in their group of patients, and that the study underlines the necessity for well-controlled trials in snoring treatment.
cards.watchOut: Very small (23 completers) and short-term, with a partner-rated subjective score and no objective snoring measurement; a post-treatment score of 5.2 out of 10 means substantial snoring remained. It tested two treatment sessions of one radiofrequency protocol in people with AHI < 15 — it says nothing about single-session treatment, other palatal operations, or people with sleep apnoea.
cards.source: Stuck BA, Sauter A, Hörmann K, Verse T, Maurer JT. Radiofrequency surgery of the soft palate in the treatment of snoring. A placebo-controlled trial. Sleep. 2005. PMID: 16124664. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Bäck 2009 (systematic review of palatal radiofrequency for snoring): 30 studies but only 2 randomised — the one placebo-controlled trial was positive; the rest is mostly uncontrolled, short-follow-up observation
cards.summary: Bäck 2009 (systematic review of palatal radiofrequency for snoring): 30 studies but only 2 randomised — the one placebo-controlled trial was positive; the rest is mostly uncontrolled, short-follow-up observation
cards.type: Systematic review of radiofrequency ablation of the soft palate for snoring (Bäck 2009)
cards.people: Controlled or prospective studies of soft-palate radiofrequency ablation in at least 10 adults (≥18 years) without moderate/severe obstructive sleep apnoea: of 159 articles identified, 30 met the criteria — 2 randomised controlled trials, 4 clinical controlled trials, and 24 prospective uncontrolled studies.
cards.result: The only placebo-controlled RCT indicated soft-palate radiofrequency to be superior to placebo (the Stuck 2005 trial carded above). The other RCT, comparing different radiofrequency generators, showed no evidence of a difference in snoring efficacy and only minor differences in discomfort. In two controlled trials snoring relief with radiofrequency was comparable to other interventions, and in three it came with less postoperative pain. Radiologic results were contradictory. Neither long-term side effects nor major adverse events were reported. The authors concluded radiofrequency may reduce snoring symptoms at least in the short term and carries a small risk of adverse effects, but that most of the literature is observational with short follow-up, which precludes solid conclusions about effectiveness.
cards.watchOut: This review is carded as the shelf's map of the surgical evidence, not as an effect estimate: it pools nothing, and its positive controlled core is the single small Stuck trial. 'No major adverse events reported' in mostly small uncontrolled series is weaker reassurance than the same words from large trials, and short follow-up cannot speak to relapse, which is the known failure mode of palatal procedures.
cards.source: Bäck LJJ, Hytönen ML, Roine RP, Malmivaara AOV. Radiofrequency ablation treatment of soft palate for patients with snoring: a systematic review of effectiveness and adverse effects. cards.headline: Synthesis: for simple snoring, a jaw device has the best (still small) trial support, a combined nasal/positional bundle helped most users, and palatal radiofrequency has exactly one small positive sham-controlled trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: for simple snoring, a jaw device has the best (still small) trial support, a combined nasal/positional bundle helped most users, and palatal radiofrequency has exactly one small positive sham-controlled trial
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Three sources: the pilot randomised trial of MAD versus combined airway/positional therapy in primary snoring (Ioerger 2024; 50 couples randomised, 42 completing; NCT05756647), the randomised placebo-controlled trial of soft-palate radiofrequency (Stuck 2005; 26 patients), and the systematic review of palatal radiofrequency (Bäck 2009; 30 studies, 2 randomised).
cards.result: Partner-rated response at 4 weeks: 91% (21/23) on MAD versus 58% (11/19) on the combined nasal/positional bundle (difference 33 percentage points, 95% CI 8–58; NNT 3), with both arms improving (Ioerger 2024). Partner-rated snoring score after palatal radiofrequency: 8.1 → 5.2 versus 8.4 → 8.0 on sham (P < 0.05), a moderate reduction with snoring persisting (Stuck 2005); the wider radiofrequency literature is 24 uncontrolled series out of 30 studies, with less postoperative pain than comparator procedures and no major adverse events reported (Bäck 2009). No trial on this shelf exceeds 4 weeks of randomised follow-up for the device/bundle comparison, and none measures objective snoring sound. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — real signals, small and short trials; nothing here supports a stronger stamp.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. This shelf covers snoring WITHOUT obstructive sleep apnoea only. Nasal strips alone are Shelf #2530; MAD versus CPAP for OSA is Shelf #923; oropharyngeal exercises for OSA are Shelf #1507. Snoring with witnessed apnoeas, gasping, or daytime sleepiness is an apnoea presentation until tested, and none of these treatments is a substitute for that evaluation.

shelves.title: Antibiotics for acute bronchitis: no difference in overall clinical improvement (relative risk 1.07), cough shorter by about half a day on average — and adverse effects more common (relative risk 1.20; one extra person harmed per 24 treated)
shelves.question: Do antibiotics help bronchitis? In people with acute bronchitis (an acute chesty cough, without pneumonia and without underlying lung disease), do antibiotics shorten the cough or speed recovery — and what harms do they cause?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Bronchitis/drug therapy · Cough/drug therapy · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the outcome patients care about — getting better. The Cochrane review of 17 trials (Smith 2017) found no difference in the proportion clinically improved (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.99–1.15), with small average gains on some cough measures (mean cough duration 0.46 days shorter; cough still present at follow-up RR 0.64, NNTB 6) set against more adverse effects (RR 1.20; NNTH 24). The largest placebo-controlled trial, GRACE (Little 2013; 2,061 adults with acute lower-respiratory-tract infection, pneumonia not suspected), found amoxicillin did not shorten moderately-bad symptoms (HR 1.06, P=0.229), caused nausea, rash or diarrhoea in one extra patient per 21 treated, and produced one case of anaphylaxis; its one positive finding — fewer new or worsening symptoms (15.9% versus 19.3%; NNT 30) — is a secondary outcome. If a prescription feels hard to withhold, delayed prescribing is the evidence-based compromise: in the Cochrane prescribing review (Spurling 2023), cough outcomes did not differ between delayed, immediate and no antibiotics in any study, while delaying cut antibiotic use from 93% to 30% with similar satisfaction (86% versus 91%).

cards.headline: Smith 2017 (Cochrane review, 17 trials, 5,099 participants): no difference in clinical improvement (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.99–1.15); mean cough 0.46 days shorter; adverse effects RR 1.20, one extra harm per 24 treated
cards.summary: Smith 2017 (Cochrane review, 17 trials, 5,099 participants): no difference in clinical improvement (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.99–1.15); mean cough 0.46 days shorter; adverse effects RR 1.20, one extra harm per 24 treated
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis (Smith 2017)
cards.people: 5,099 participants in 17 randomised trials of antibiotics versus placebo or no treatment for acute bronchitis or acute productive cough, in people without underlying pulmonary disease.
cards.result: At follow-up there was no difference in participants described as clinically improved (11 studies, 3,841 participants; RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.99–1.15). Participants given antibiotics were less likely to have a cough at follow-up (4 studies, 275 participants; RR 0.64, 0.49–0.85; NNTB 6) or a night cough (4 studies, 538; RR 0.67, 0.54–0.83; NNTB 7), and mean cough duration was shorter (7 studies, 2,776; mean difference −0.46 days, −0.87 to −0.04). Days feeling ill were reduced by 0.64 days (5 studies, 809) and days with impaired activity by 0.49 days (6 studies, 767). Adverse effects were more common on antibiotics (12 studies, 3,496; RR 1.20, 1.05–1.36; number needed to harm 24).
cards.watchOut: The cough-at-follow-up result rests on only 275 participants, and the half-day average shortening is of a cough that typically lasts weeks — the review's authors conclude there is limited evidence of clinical benefit, while noting frail elderly people with multimorbidity were largely excluded from the trials and might differ.
cards.source: Smith SM, Fahey T, Smucny J, Becker LA. Antibiotics for acute bronchitis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017. PMID: 28626858. cards.headline: Little 2013 — the GRACE trial (2,061 adults, 12 countries): amoxicillin did not shorten 'moderately bad or worse' symptoms (HR 1.06, P=0.229); nausea, rash or diarrhoea in one extra patient per 21 treated; one anaphylaxis
cards.summary: Little 2013 — the GRACE trial (2,061 adults, 12 countries): amoxicillin did not shorten 'moderately bad or worse' symptoms (HR 1.06, P=0.229); nausea, rash or diarrhoea in one extra patient per 21 treated; one anaphylaxis
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial (Little 2013, GRACE consortium)
cards.people: Adults over 18 in primary care in 12 European countries with acute lower-respiratory-tract infection (cough of up to 28 days) in whom pneumonia was not suspected: 1,038 assigned to amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 7 days and 1,023 to placebo.
cards.result: Neither the duration of symptoms rated 'moderately bad' or worse (hazard ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.96–1.18; P=0.229) nor mean symptom severity on days 2–4 (1.69 with placebo versus 1.62 with amoxicillin; difference −0.07, −0.15 to 0.007; P=0.074) differed significantly. New or worsening symptoms were less common on amoxicillin (162 of 1,021, 15.9%, versus 194 of 1,006, 19.3%; P=0.043; number needed to treat 30). Nausea, rash or diarrhoea were significantly more common on amoxicillin (number needed to harm 21, 95% CI 11–174; P=0.025), and one case of anaphylaxis was noted with amoxicillin. Hospital admissions: 2 on placebo, 1 on amoxicillin. There was no evidence of selective benefit in patients aged 60 years or older (n=595).
cards.watchOut: This trial enrolled acute lower-respiratory-tract infection, a slightly broader group than bronchitis alone, though pneumonia was excluded clinically. The one significant benefit (new or worsening symptoms) is a secondary outcome among several, and it is smaller than the harm rate on the trial's own numbers (NNT 30 versus NNH 21).

cards.headline: Spurling 2023 (Cochrane prescribing review, 12 studies, 3,968 participants): for cough, no difference between delayed, immediate and no antibiotics in any study — delayed prescriptions cut antibiotic use from 93% to 30%
cards.summary: Spurling 2023 (Cochrane prescribing review, 12 studies, 3,968 participants): for cough, no difference between delayed, immediate and no antibiotics in any study — delayed prescriptions cut antibiotic use from 93% to 30%
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of prescribing strategies (Spurling 2023)
cards.people: 3,968 participants (data from 3,750 available for analysis) in 12 randomised trials of delayed versus immediate versus no antibiotic prescribing for acute respiratory tract infections, including cough and bronchitis presentations; six studies were in children only, two in adults only and four in both.
cards.result: For cough (four studies), there were no differences among delayed, immediate and no prescribed antibiotics for clinical outcomes in any of the four studies. Delayed antibiotics probably reduced antibiotic use compared with immediate antibiotics (OR 0.03, 95% CI 0.01–0.07; 8 studies, 2,257 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) — the authors summarise use as 30% with delayed versus 93% with immediate prescribing, and 13% with no antibiotics versus 27% with delayed. Patient satisfaction probably did not differ between delayed and immediate antibiotics (OR 0.77, 0.45–1.29; 7 studies, 1,927 participants; satisfaction 86% versus 91%), and there were no differences in complication rates.
cards.watchOut: Most included infections were not bronchitis specifically (otitis media, sore throat and colds are pooled in several analyses), so the cough-specific finding rests on four studies. Satisfaction slightly favoured immediate antibiotics in absolute terms (91% versus 86%) even though the pooled odds ratio was not significant.
cards.source: Spurling GKP, Dooley L, Clark J, Askew DA. Immediate versus delayed versus no antibiotics for respiratory infections. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2023. PMID: 37791590. Registry ID: none in the record (Cochrane review).
