cards.headline: Synthesis: antibiotics do not speed overall recovery from acute bronchitis; they trim about half a day of cough for some and harm about 1 in 21–24 treated
cards.summary: Synthesis: antibiotics do not speed overall recovery from acute bronchitis; they trim about half a day of cough for some and harm about 1 in 21–24 treated
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Adults and children with acute bronchitis or acute lower-respiratory-tract infection without suspected pneumonia and without underlying lung disease.
cards.result: Across 17 placebo-controlled trials there is no significant difference in overall clinical improvement (RR 1.07, CI crossing 1), and the largest trial found no shortening of moderately-bad symptoms at all. The measurable gains are small averages: cough shorter by 0.46 days, about 0.5–0.6 fewer days feeling ill or impaired. The measurable harms are of similar size: adverse effects RR 1.20 (NNTH 24 in the review; NNH 21 for nausea/rash/diarrhoea in GRACE, plus one anaphylaxis). Delayed prescribing achieves the same cough outcomes with a third of the antibiotic use.
cards.watchOut: These trials largely excluded frail, multimorbid and very elderly patients, and none of this applies where pneumonia is suspected — that is a different question with a different evidence base. Population-level antibiotic resistance, a real cost of prescribing, is not captured in any of these per-patient numbers.
cards.source: Synthesis of Smith SM et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017 (PMID: 28626858); Little P et al. The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 2013 (PMID: 23265995); Spurling GKP et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2023 (PMID: 37791590).

shelves.title: Home treatment of pulmonary embolism by the Hestia criteria: recurrence 2.0%, death 1.0% and major bleeding 0.7% at 3 months in the original 297-patient study — prospective management evidence, not a randomised comparison
shelves.question: In patients with acute pulmonary embolism who meet Hestia criteria, is outpatient (home) treatment as safe as hospital treatment for recurrent clots, bleeding, and death?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Aged · Ambulatory Care · Anticoagulants/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nadroparin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Netherlands · Patient Selection · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Embolism/diagnosis/etiology/mortality/prevention & control · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Secondary Prevention · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Venous Thrombosis/complications/diagnosis/drug therapy/mortality · Vitamin K/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — management-study and cohort evidence only; no randomised home-versus-hospital comparison in Hestia-selected patients is carded. In the original Hestia Study (Zondag 2011, PMID: 21645235), 297 patients with acute pulmonary embolism who met the Hestia criteria were treated entirely as outpatients: recurrent venous thromboembolism 2.0%, death 1.0% (none from fatal pulmonary embolism), and major bleeding 0.7% over 3 months. Two later Hestia-based programmes agree at smaller scale — a United States protocol cohort (Kline 2016, PMID: 27143861; 253 patients, 67 with pulmonary embolism) recorded no recurrence or major haemorrhage among its pulmonary embolism patients at 30 days, and a French programme adding sPESI, biomarker and imaging requirements (Assayag 2022, PMID: 35940966; 43 outpatients) recorded no death or recurrence at 3 months. The randomised low-risk pulmonary embolism home-treatment question is homed at pack #3373 and is not re-carded here; this shelf is specifically about Hestia-criteria selection. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Hestia-selected patients treated at home have low absolute event rates, on prospective management and cohort evidence.

cards.headline: Zondag 2011 (Hestia Study): of 297 patients with acute pulmonary embolism selected by the Hestia criteria and treated entirely as outpatients, 2.0% had recurrent venous thromboembolism, 1.0% died, and 0.7% had major bleeding within 3 months
cards.summary: Zondag 2011 (Hestia Study): of 297 patients with acute pulmonary embolism selected by the Hestia criteria and treated entirely as outpatients, 2.0% had recurrent venous thromboembolism, 1.0% died, and 0.7% had major bleeding within 3 months
cards.type: Prospective management (cohort) study (Zondag 2011, Hestia Study)
cards.people: 297 patients with objectively proven acute pulmonary embolism at 12 hospitals in the Netherlands (2008–2010), triaged with the predefined Hestia criteria for outpatient eligibility and treated at home (sent home immediately or within 24 hours) with nadroparin followed by vitamin K antagonists; all completed 3 months of follow-up.
cards.result: Recurrent venous thromboembolism occurred in 6 patients (2.0%, 95% CI 0.8 to 4.3) — five pulmonary embolism (1.7%) and one deep vein thrombosis (0.3%). Three patients (1.0%, 95% CI 0.2 to 2.9) died during follow-up, none of fatal pulmonary embolism. Two patients had a major bleeding event (0.7%, 95% CI 0.08 to 2.4), one of which was a fatal intracranial bleed.
cards.watchOut: A single-arm management study: there is no hospital-treated comparison group, so 'as safe as hospital treatment' is inferred from low absolute event rates in a criteria-selected group, not measured against admitted patients.
cards.source: Zondag W et al. Outpatient treatment in patients with acute pulmonary embolism: the Hestia Study. Journal of Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 2011. PMID: 21645235. Registry ID: Dutch Trial Register No 1319, as printed in the record. cards.headline: Kline 2016: 253 Hestia-negative venous thromboembolism patients (67 with pulmonary embolism) treated at home on oral monotherapy had 2 recurrences and 2 major haemorrhages in 30 days — all four events in patients enrolled with deep vein thrombosis
cards.summary: Kline 2016: 253 Hestia-negative venous thromboembolism patients (67 with pulmonary embolism) treated at home on oral monotherapy had 2 recurrences and 2 major haemorrhages in 30 days — all four events in patients enrolled with deep vein thrombosis
cards.type: Prospective cohort study within a home-treatment protocol (Kline 2016)
cards.people: 253 patients with venous thromboembolism selected as low-risk by the Hestia criteria and treated at home with oral factor Xa antagonist monotherapy in a United States emergency-department protocol (2013–2015), including 67 with pulmonary embolism; primary outcomes were recurrence and haemorrhage at 30 days.
cards.result: Within 30 days, 2 of 253 patients had recurrent deep vein thrombosis and 2 of 253 had major haemorrhage; all four had deep vein thrombosis at enrolment, so no recurrence or major haemorrhage was recorded among the 67 pulmonary embolism patients in this record. Quality-of-life scores improved over treatment similarly for deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism patients, and physician comfort with home treatment of pulmonary embolism rose after the protocol.
cards.watchOut: Only 67 of the 253 patients had pulmonary embolism, and the record does not report a pulmonary-embolism-only event rate — the reassuring zeros in that subgroup rest on a small denominator.
cards.source: Kline JA et al. Outpatient treatment of low-risk venous thromboembolism with monotherapy oral anticoagulation: patient quality of life outcomes and clinician acceptance. Patient Preference and Adherence. 2016. PMID: 27143861. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Assayag 2022: in a French programme requiring both Hestia and sPESI scores of 0, 43 patients treated as outpatients had no death and no thromboembolic recurrence at 3 months
cards.summary: Assayag 2022: in a French programme requiring both Hestia and sPESI scores of 0, 43 patients treated as outpatients had no death and no thromboembolic recurrence at 3 months
cards.type: Prospective programme cohort study (Assayag 2022)
cards.people: 313 consecutive emergency-department patients with confirmed pulmonary embolism (2019–2021) screened for a general-practitioner-inclusive outpatient programme requiring sPESI and Hestia scores of 0, normal troponin and NT-pro-BNP, and no right-ventricular dilation; 66 (21%) were eligible and 43 received outpatient treatment.
cards.result: At 3-month follow-up among the outpatients there were no deaths and no recurrence of thromboembolism; one patient was hospitalised early for COVID-19, and 3 women treated with rivaroxaban had minor bleeding (heavy menstrual bleeding). A preceding retrospective cohort found 19% of 138 pulmonary embolism patients eligible, with no complication at day 90.
cards.watchOut: The programme layered biomarker and imaging requirements on top of the Hestia criteria and treated only 43 patients — it supports Hestia-based selection inside a structured programme, not Hestia alone in unselected practice.
cards.source: Assayag F et al. Home treatment of low-risk pulmonary embolism patients: Efficacy and safety of an outpatient program including the general practitioner. cards.headline: Synthesis: Hestia-selected outpatients have consistently low event rates (recurrence 2.0%, death 1.0%, major bleeding 0.7% in the original study) — from management studies and cohorts, not from a randomised comparison
cards.summary: Synthesis: Hestia-selected outpatients have consistently low event rates (recurrence 2.0%, death 1.0%, major bleeding 0.7% in the original study) — from management studies and cohorts, not from a randomised comparison
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: the original Hestia prospective management study (297 patients), a United States Hestia-protocol cohort (253 patients, 67 with pulmonary embolism), and a French Hestia-plus-sPESI programme cohort (43 outpatients). The broader randomised question of home treatment for low-risk pulmonary embolism is homed at pack #3373 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: In the Hestia Study, outpatient treatment of criteria-selected patients gave recurrent venous thromboembolism in 2.0%, death in 1.0% (none from fatal pulmonary embolism), and major bleeding in 0.7% over 3 months (Zondag 2011). Later Hestia-based programmes report the same pattern at smaller scale: no recurrence or major haemorrhage among pulmonary embolism patients at 30 days (Kline 2016) and no death or recurrence at 3 months (Assayag 2022). No carded study randomised Hestia-selected patients to home versus hospital care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — management-study and cohort evidence only.
cards.watchOut: The Hestia criteria are a selection rule, and selection rules fail silently when applied loosely: the low event rates belong to patients who passed every criterion and entered a follow-up programme.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zondag W et al. Journal of Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 2011 (PMID: 21645235); Kline JA et al. Patient Preference and Adherence. 2016 (PMID: 27143861); Assayag F et al. Annales de Cardiologie et d'Angéiologie. 2022 (PMID: 35940966).

shelves.title: Eradicating a new Pseudomonas isolate in bronchiectasis: about 40% clear at 12 months on observational evidence — 48% with combined systemic plus inhaled antibiotics — with no randomised test of eradication versus no eradication
shelves.question: In bronchiectasis with a first or new Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate, does eradication therapy clear the organism and reduce exacerbations compared with no eradication treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Pseudomonas Infections/diagnosis/drug therapy/chemically induced · Administration, Inhalation · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects · Bronchiectasis/diagnosis/drug therapy · Cystic Fibrosis/complications/diagnosis/drug therapy · Pseudomonas aeruginosa
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the eradication question, printed on the face: no randomised trial compares eradication with no eradication in the carded records. Conceição 2024 (PMID: 38296344), a systematic review of 6 observational studies in 289 patients, found a pooled 12-month eradication rate of 40%, higher with combined systemic plus inhaled antibiotics (48%) than with systemic antibiotics alone (27%). White 2012 (PMID: 22204744), a retrospective cohort of 30 patients treated after a first isolate, found initial clearance in 80.0% and exacerbations falling from 3.93 to 2.09 per year, though 11 of 24 clearers were later reinfected. Tejada 2021 (PMID: 33947626), a trial meta-analysis of inhaled antibiotics in chronic infection (not first isolation), supports sputum clearance (odds ratio 3.19–7.22) with a 10% relative reduction in exacerbations and doubled antimicrobial resistance. Whether eradication itself improves long-term outcomes versus no eradication is untested in the carded evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.

cards.headline: Conceição 2024: across 6 observational studies of 289 patients, eradication therapy cleared Pseudomonas aeruginosa at 12 months in about 40% — 48% with combined systemic plus inhaled antibiotics versus 27% with systemic antibiotics alone
cards.summary: Conceição 2024: across 6 observational studies of 289 patients, eradication therapy cleared Pseudomonas aeruginosa at 12 months in about 40% — 48% with combined systemic plus inhaled antibiotics versus 27% with systemic antibiotics alone
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Conceição 2024)
cards.people: 6 observational studies including 289 adults with bronchiectasis (cystic fibrosis excluded) treated with systemic or inhaled antibiotics to eradicate Pseudomonas aeruginosa, pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis conducted to MOOSE guidelines; primary outcome was the percentage negative for P. aeruginosa at 12 months.
cards.result: The pooled 12-month eradication rate was 40% (95% CI 34 to 45; p < 0.00001; I2 = 0%). Combined systemic and inhaled antibiotic treatment was associated with a higher eradication rate (48%, 95% CI 41 to 55) than systemic antibiotics alone (27%, 95% CI 13 to 45). The authors note eradication is recommended by guidelines but the evidence base is limited. The record reports no pooled exacerbation or mortality effect size for eradication versus no eradication.
cards.watchOut: There is no untreated comparison group anywhere in this evidence: 40% clearance at 12 months mixes true drug effect with spontaneous clearance and reinfection, and none of the included studies was randomised.
cards.source: Conceição M et al. Eradication treatment for Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection in adults with bronchiectasis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. European Respiratory Review. 2024. PMID: 38296344. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: White 2012: in 30 patients receiving eradication therapy after a first Pseudomonas isolate, 80.0% initially cleared the organism and exacerbation frequency fell from 3.93 to 2.09 per year
cards.summary: White 2012: in 30 patients receiving eradication therapy after a first Pseudomonas isolate, 80.0% initially cleared the organism and exacerbation frequency fell from 3.93 to 2.09 per year
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study (White 2012)
cards.people: 30 patients with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis undergoing Pseudomonas eradication therapy after initial Pseudomonas infection (2004–2010), identified retrospectively with median follow-up of 26.4 months (N = 30 printed here as the record reports it); regimens were intravenous antibiotics (n = 12), intravenous antibiotics followed by oral ciprofloxacin (n = 13), or ciprofloxacin alone (n = 5), combined with 3 months of nebulised colistin.
cards.result: Pseudomonas was initially eradicated from sputum in 24 patients (80.0%); 13 of the 24 remained Pseudomonas-free and 11 were subsequently reinfected (median time 6.2 months). Exacerbation frequency fell from 3.93 per year before eradication to 2.09 per year after (p = 0.002); admission rates were similar (0.39 versus 0.29 per year, not significant) and lung function was unchanged. Twenty of 30 patients reported initial clinical improvement.
cards.watchOut: A before-and-after comparison in 30 patients with no control group: exacerbation rates often fall after any index event (regression to the mean), and over half of those who cleared were reinfected or lost clearance over follow-up.
cards.source: White L et al. Outcomes of Pseudomonas eradication therapy in patients with non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis. Respiratory Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22204744. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tejada 2021: inhaled antibiotics increased sputum eradication of Pseudomonas (odds ratio 3.19 in exacerbations, 7.22 in stable patients) and reduced exacerbations by a relative 10% — while doubling antimicrobial resistance
cards.summary: Tejada 2021: inhaled antibiotics increased sputum eradication of Pseudomonas (odds ratio 3.19 in exacerbations, 7.22 in stable patients) and reduced exacerbations by a relative 10% — while doubling antimicrobial resistance
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of trials of inhaled antibiotics (Tejada 2021)
cards.people: 12 trials (2,476 participants) of inhaled antibiotics in adults with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa chronic bronchial infection, in stable or exacerbated states, pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42019136154).
cards.result: Inhaled antibiotics increased P. aeruginosa eradication from sputum in patients with exacerbations (odds ratio 3.19, 95% CI 1.70 to 5.99) and in stable patients (odds ratio 7.22, 95% CI 2.81 to 18.59). In stable patients they reduced exacerbation rates (relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.82 to 0.98 — a 10% relative reduction; number needed to treat 59) but increased antimicrobial resistance at the end of therapy (relative risk 2.10, 95% CI 1.35 to 3.27). No significant effect was found on lung function, mortality, hospitalisations or quality of life.
cards.watchOut: These trials treated chronic Pseudomonas infection, not a first or new isolate — they support the inhaled component's ability to clear sputum, but they do not directly test an eradication strategy at first isolation, and the resistance cost is real.
cards.source: Tejada S et al. Inhaled antibiotics for treatment of adults with non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis: A systematic review and meta-analysis. European Journal of Internal Medicine. 2021. PMID: 33947626. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42019136154, from the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: eradication therapy clears a new Pseudomonas isolate in roughly 40% at a year on observational evidence, with combined systemic plus inhaled treatment doing best — and no randomised eradication trial is carded (observational only for the eradication question)
cards.summary: Synthesis: eradication therapy clears a new Pseudomonas isolate in roughly 40% at a year on observational evidence, with combined systemic plus inhaled treatment doing best — and no randomised eradication trial is carded (observational only for the eradication question)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence for the eradication question itself: one systematic review of 6 observational studies (289 patients) and one retrospective first-isolate cohort (30 patients), plus one trial meta-analysis of inhaled antibiotics in chronic infection (2,476 participants) carded as supporting evidence for the inhaled component only.
cards.result: Pooled 12-month eradication was 40%, higher with combined systemic and inhaled antibiotics (48%) than systemic antibiotics alone (27%) (Conceição 2024). In the first-isolate cohort, initial clearance was 80.0% and exacerbations fell from 3.93 to 2.09 per year, but 11 of 24 clearers were reinfected (White 2012). Inhaled antibiotics clear sputum and modestly reduce exacerbations in chronic infection while doubling resistance emergence (Tejada 2021). No carded study compares eradication with no eradication in a randomised design, and no pooled exacerbation or mortality effect for eradication itself is reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for eradication at first/new isolation.
cards.watchOut: Guidelines recommend eradication, but the carded evidence can show clearance rates, not that eradication causes better long-term outcomes — that comparison has never been randomised in the records carded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Conceição M et al. European Respiratory Review. 2024 (PMID: 38296344); White L et al. Respiratory Medicine. 2012 (PMID: 22204744); Tejada S et al. European Journal of Internal Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 33947626).

shelves.title: Pancreatic enzymes in cystic fibrosis: dosing by fat intake is the convention and the regimen behind a positive trial — but it has never been tested against fixed dosing, and the Cochrane review says meal-size dose variation is an unanswered question
shelves.question: Should adults with cystic fibrosis have pancreatic enzyme doses adjusted based on fat intake?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain · Adult · Age Factors · Capsules · Child · Cystic Fibrosis · Delayed-Action Preparations · Enzyme Replacement Therapy · Gastrointestinal Agents · Humans · Microspheres · Nutritional Status · Pancreas · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Weight Gain
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for the comparative question itself. Dosing pancreatic enzymes in proportion to fat eaten is how the therapy is described and how the positive placebo-controlled trials dosed it: Trapnell 2009 targeted 4,000 lipase units per gram of fat and achieved a coefficient of fat absorption of 88.6% versus 49.6% on placebo. But a fixed-dose regimen also beat placebo withdrawal in Borowitz 2011 (overall adjusted difference in fat absorption 10.6 percentage points), and the Cochrane review of 14 trials and 641 participants states plainly that there is no evidence on the relative dosages of enzymes needed or on variations based on differences in meals and meal sizes, and calls for a properly designed trial. No trial has ever randomised adults to fat-adjusted versus fixed dosing, so the adjustment strategy itself is untested even though enzyme therapy dosed that way works. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): fat-intake-based dosing is the conventional framework and the regimen used in the successful trials, but its superiority over fixed dosing has never been tested head-to-head.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2020: across 14 trials and 641 people with cystic fibrosis, there is no evidence on the relative dosages of enzymes needed or on variations based on differences in meals and meal sizes
cards.summary: Cochrane 2020: across 14 trials and 641 people with cystic fibrosis, there is no evidence on the relative dosages of enzymes needed or on variations based on differences in meals and meal sizes
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane, Somaraju 2020)
cards.people: Systematic review of 14 randomised and quasi-randomised trials (641 children and adults with cystic fibrosis receiving pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy for at least four weeks, versus placebo or other enzyme preparations); individual trials enrolled 14 to 129 participants, 13 lasted four weeks and one lasted seven weeks.
cards.result: The review could mostly not combine data because trials compared different formulations, and the findings provided insufficient evidence to determine the size and precision of the effects of different formulations; the quality of evidence ranged from moderate to very low, with a high risk of attrition and reporting bias. There was limited evidence of benefit from enteric-coated microspheres over non-enteric-coated preparations up to one month. The authors state there is no evidence on the long-term effectiveness and risks of enzyme replacement, on the relative dosages needed for people with different severity of pancreatic insufficiency, on the optimum time to start, or on variations based on differences in meals and meal sizes — and that a properly designed trial is needed to answer these questions. The review's background nonetheless describes standard practice as: enzyme preparations need to be taken whenever food is taken, and the dose needs to be adjusted according to the food consumed.
cards.watchOut: This review answers the shelf's question directly — and its answer is that the meal-size/dose question has not been trialled. The fat-adjusted dosing described in its background is practice convention, not a tested comparison.
cards.source: Somaraju URR et al. Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy for people with cystic fibrosis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020. PMID: 32761612. cards.headline: Trapnell 2009: dosed by fat intake (target 4,000 lipase units per gram of fat), pancrelipase gave a coefficient of fat absorption of 88.6% versus 49.6% on placebo — in 32 subjects
cards.summary: Trapnell 2009: dosed by fat intake (target 4,000 lipase units per gram of fat), pancrelipase gave a coefficient of fat absorption of 88.6% versus 49.6% on placebo — in 32 subjects
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled crossover trial (Trapnell 2009)
cards.people: 32 subjects aged 12 years or older with cystic fibrosis and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, in a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, two-period crossover study of a 24,000-unit pancrelipase preparation (5-day treatment sequences). Single-study N = 32, printed here.
cards.result: Mean coefficient of fat absorption was 88.6% on pancrelipase versus 49.6% on placebo, and coefficient of nitrogen absorption was 85.1% versus 49.9% (P < 0.001 for both). Symptoms were improved and fewer treatment-emergent adverse events were reported on pancrelipase than placebo; one patient discontinued for weight loss unrelated to study drug. The dose in this trial was prescribed in proportion to fat eaten (target 4,000 lipase units/g fat) — so this is evidence that a fat-adjusted regimen works against placebo, not evidence that fat adjustment beats any other dosing scheme.
cards.watchOut: A 5-day crossover in 32 adolescents and adults: it validates enzyme therapy dosed per gram of fat against no therapy. It randomised nobody to a fixed dose, so it cannot show that adjusting for fat intake is better than not adjusting.
cards.source: Trapnell BC et al. Efficacy and safety of Creon 24,000 in subjects with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency due to cystic fibrosis. Journal of Cystic Fibrosis. 2009. PMID: 19815466. cards.headline: Borowitz 2011: a FIXED dose (one capsule with each meal and snack, increases not allowed) also beat placebo — fat absorption improved by an adjusted 10.6 percentage points overall
cards.summary: Borowitz 2011: a FIXED dose (one capsule with each meal and snack, increases not allowed) also beat placebo — fat absorption improved by an adjusted 10.6 percentage points overall
cards.type: Phase III randomised-withdrawal placebo-controlled trial (Borowitz 2011)
cards.people: 138 subjects aged 7 years or older with cystic fibrosis and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency in an international phase III parallel-group randomised-withdrawal, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of liprotamase, a non-porcine enzyme preparation; after an open-label treatment period, subjects were randomised 1:1 to liprotamase or placebo, one capsule with 3 meals and 2 snacks per day at a fixed dose.
cards.result: The adjusted least-squares mean difference between liprotamase and placebo for change in coefficient of fat absorption was 15.1% (P = 0.001) in the subgroup with baseline fat absorption under 40%, 8.6% (P = 0.006) in those with baseline 40% or above, and 10.6% (P < 0.001) in the overall intent-to-treat population; nitrogen absorption results were similar, stool weight fell significantly (stool frequency did not), and the preparation was well tolerated with no safety concerns identified. A fixed per-meal dose — explicitly not adjusted to the fat content of each meal — was therefore also effective against placebo.
cards.watchOut: Liprotamase is a non-porcine, biotechnology-derived preparation (named here because the tested product is not a standard approved pancrelipase product), and this was a withdrawal design in patients already stabilised on enzymes — it shows fixed dosing can work, not that fixed dosing equals fat-adjusted dosing.
cards.source: Borowitz D et al. International phase III trial of liprotamase efficacy and safety in pancreatic-insufficient cystic fibrosis patients. Journal of Cystic Fibrosis. 2011. PMID: 21831726. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: enzyme therapy works, and the trials that prove it used both fat-adjusted and fixed dosing — no trial has compared the two strategies, and the Cochrane review says the meal-size dosing question is unanswered
cards.summary: Synthesis: enzyme therapy works, and the trials that prove it used both fat-adjusted and fixed dosing — no trial has compared the two strategies, and the Cochrane review says the meal-size dosing question is unanswered
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review of 14 trials (641 children and adults), one 32-subject crossover trial dosed at a target of 4,000 lipase units per gram of fat, and one 138-subject randomised-withdrawal trial at a fixed dose. The review's population overlaps the individual trials, so participant numbers are not simply additive; the evidence base is well over 30 people, and no small-N stamp labelling applies — the limitation is the missing comparison, not the size.
cards.result: Fat-adjusted dosing beat placebo on fat absorption (88.6% vs 49.6%, Trapnell 2009); fixed dosing also beat placebo (adjusted difference 10.6 percentage points overall, Borowitz 2011); and the systematic review of the whole field concludes there is no evidence on relative dosages or on variations based on differences in meals and meal sizes (Cochrane 2020). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for fat-intake-based adjustment as a tested strategy: it is the conventional framework and the regimen behind one positive trial, but it has never been randomised against fixed dosing in adults.
cards.watchOut: Do not read this shelf as evidence against fat-based dosing: nothing here shows it is worse. The honest statement is narrower — the comparison that would prove it better has never been run.
cards.source: Synthesis of Somaraju URR et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020 (PMID: 32761612); Trapnell BC et al. Journal of Cystic Fibrosis. 2009 (PMID: 19815466); Borowitz D et al. Journal of Cystic Fibrosis. 2011 (PMID: 21831726).

shelves.title: An inhaled corticosteroid with every reliever use in asthma (LIKELY benefit): severe exacerbations fall versus reliever alone across three large trial designs, matching daily maintenance in mild asthma at a fraction of the steroid dose
shelves.question: Should adults with asthma use an inhaled corticosteroid whenever they use a short-acting bronchodilator?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adult · Black or African American · Anti-Asthmatic Agents · Asthma · Beclomethasone · Glucocorticoids · Hispanic or Latino · Humans · Quality of Life · Surveys and Questionnaires · Symptom Flare Up
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). The strategy named in the question has been tested three ways, and each large trial points the same direction. In PREPARE (PARTICS), Black and Latinx adults with moderate-to-severe asthma who took beclomethasone 80 µg every time they used their reliever had a lower annualised rate of severe exacerbations than usual care (0.69 vs 0.82 per year; HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.999). In mild asthma, an inhaled corticosteroid carried in the reliever itself (budesonide–formoterol) halved the exacerbation rate versus albuterol alone in Novel START (0.195 vs 0.400 per year; relative rate 0.49) and was noninferior to daily maintenance budesonide in SYGMA 2 (0.11 vs 0.12 per year) at about a quarter of the steroid dose — with slightly worse day-to-day symptom scores than daily maintenance. The fixed albuterol–budesonide rescue inhaler's own exacerbation trials (MANDALA and BATURA) are homed on live shelf #1030 and are cross-pointed, not re-carded here; DENALI is carded here only for its component-contribution lung-function results. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): taking an inhaled corticosteroid with every reliever use reduces severe exacerbations versus reliever alone and matches daily maintenance for exacerbations in mild asthma.

cards.headline: Israel 2022 (PREPARE/PARTICS): taking beclomethasone 80 µg every time the reliever was used cut severe exacerbations — 0.69 vs 0.82 per year (HR 0.85) in 1,201 Black and Latinx adults
cards.summary: Israel 2022 (PREPARE/PARTICS): taking beclomethasone 80 µg every time the reliever was used cut severe exacerbations — 0.69 vs 0.82 per year (HR 0.85) in 1,201 Black and Latinx adults
cards.type: Pragmatic open-label randomised trial (PREPARE/PARTICS, Israel 2022)
cards.people: 1,201 Black (603) and Latinx (598) adults with moderate-to-severe asthma in a pragmatic, open-label trial (PCORI-funded PREPARE): 600 were assigned to a patient-activated, reliever-triggered inhaled glucocorticoid strategy (beclomethasone dipropionate 80 µg taken with reliever use) plus usual care, and 601 to usual care alone, after one instructional visit, with 15 monthly questionnaires.
cards.result: The annualised rate of severe asthma exacerbations was 0.69 (95% CI 0.61 to 0.78) in the intervention group and 0.82 (95% CI 0.73 to 0.92) with usual care (hazard ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.999; P = 0.048 — a relative measure, with the absolute rates printed beside it). Asthma Control Test scores rose by 3.4 vs 2.5 points (difference 0.9, 95% CI 0.5 to 1.2), Asthma Symptom Utility Index by 0.12 vs 0.08 (difference 0.04), and missed days of work, school or usual activities were 13.4 vs 16.8 per year (rate ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.95). Serious adverse events occurred in 12.2% of participants, evenly distributed between groups.
cards.watchOut: This is the one card that tests the shelf's exact strategy — a separate steroid inhaler fired by each reliever use — and its effect is real but modest and borderline (upper confidence limit 0.999), in an open-label design where the intervention group also received instruction and attention.
cards.source: Israel E et al. Reliever-Triggered Inhaled Glucocorticoid in Black and Latinx Adults with Asthma. New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 35213105. Registry ID: NCT02995733. cards.headline: Beasley 2019 (Novel START): reliever-carried budesonide–formoterol halved exacerbations versus albuterol alone (0.195 vs 0.400 per year; relative rate 0.49) in mild asthma
cards.summary: Beasley 2019 (Novel START): reliever-carried budesonide–formoterol halved exacerbations versus albuterol alone (0.195 vs 0.400 per year; relative rate 0.49) in mild asthma
cards.type: Open-label randomised controlled trial (Novel START, Beasley 2019)
cards.people: 675 adults with mild asthma randomised in a 52-week, open-label, parallel-group trial (668 analysed) to as-needed albuterol (100 µg, two inhalations), twice-daily budesonide 200 µg plus as-needed albuterol, or as-needed budesonide–formoterol (200/6 µg, one inhalation); inhaler use was electronically monitored.
cards.result: The annualised exacerbation rate with as-needed budesonide–formoterol was lower than with albuterol alone (absolute rate 0.195 vs 0.400; relative rate 0.49, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.72; P < 0.001) and did not differ significantly from budesonide maintenance (0.195 vs 0.175; relative rate 1.12, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.79; P = 0.65). Severe exacerbations numbered 9 with budesonide–formoterol versus 23 with albuterol (relative risk 0.40, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.86) and 21 with maintenance (relative risk 0.44, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.96) — relative measures, with the counts printed beside them. Mean daily inhaled budesonide dose was 107 ± 109 µg in the reliever group versus 222 ± 113 µg with maintenance.
cards.watchOut: Here the corticosteroid rides in a combination reliever whose bronchodilator is formoterol (a long-acting agent), not a short-acting one — it tests the same 'steroid with every relief' principle, delivered differently from the separate-inhaler strategy in the PREPARE card.
cards.source: Beasley R et al. Controlled Trial of Budesonide-Formoterol as Needed for Mild Asthma. New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31112386. Registry ID: ACTRN12615000999538. cards.headline: Bateman 2018 (SYGMA 2): as-needed budesonide–formoterol was noninferior to daily budesonide maintenance for severe exacerbations (0.11 vs 0.12 per year) at about a quarter of the steroid dose — but symptom control was slightly worse
cards.summary: Bateman 2018 (SYGMA 2): as-needed budesonide–formoterol was noninferior to daily budesonide maintenance for severe exacerbations (0.11 vs 0.12 per year) at about a quarter of the steroid dose — but symptom control was slightly worse
cards.type: Double-blind randomised noninferiority trial (SYGMA 2, Bateman 2018)
cards.people: 4,215 patients aged 12 years or older with mild asthma eligible for regular inhaled glucocorticoids, randomised in a 52-week double-blind multicentre trial (4,176 in the full analysis set: 2,089 as-needed budesonide–formoterol 200/6 µg, 2,087 twice-daily budesonide 200 µg maintenance plus as-needed terbutaline 0.5 mg).
cards.result: As-needed budesonide–formoterol was noninferior to maintenance budesonide for severe exacerbations (prespecified noninferiority limit 1.2): annualised rates 0.11 (95% CI 0.10 to 0.13) vs 0.12 (95% CI 0.10 to 0.14); rate ratio 0.97 (upper one-sided 95% confidence limit 1.16). Median daily inhaled glucocorticoid dose was 66 µg in the reliever group versus 267 µg with maintenance. Time to first exacerbation was similar (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.17). The change in ACQ-5 symptom score differed by 0.11 units (95% CI 0.07 to 0.15) in favour of maintenance therapy — the reliever strategy protected against exacerbations as well as daily treatment while controlling daily symptoms slightly less well.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority for exacerbations is not superiority, and the comparison is against daily maintenance — not against the SABA-alone habit this shelf's question starts from; adolescents aged 12 and over are included alongside adults.
cards.source: Bateman ED et al. As-Needed Budesonide-Formoterol versus Maintenance Budesonide in Mild Asthma. New England Journal of Medicine. 2018. PMID: 29768147. Registry ID: NCT02224157. cards.headline: Chipps 2023 (DENALI): both components of the albuterol–budesonide rescue inhaler contributed to lung function — trough FEV1 at 12 weeks was 132.8 mL better than albuterol alone for the 180/160 µg dose
cards.summary: Chipps 2023 (DENALI): both components of the albuterol–budesonide rescue inhaler contributed to lung function — trough FEV1 at 12 weeks was 132.8 mL better than albuterol alone for the 180/160 µg dose
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind randomised component-contribution trial (DENALI, Chipps 2023)
cards.people: 1,001 patients randomised in a phase 3 double-blind trial (989 aged 12 years or older evaluable for efficacy) with mild-to-moderate asthma, assigned 1:1:1:1:1 to four-times-daily albuterol–budesonide 180/160 µg or 180/80 µg, albuterol 180 µg, budesonide 160 µg, or placebo for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Change in FEV1 area under the curve over 12 weeks was greater with albuterol–budesonide 180/160 µg than with budesonide alone (least-squares mean difference 80.7 mL, 95% CI 28.4–132.9; P = .003), and trough FEV1 at week 12 was greater with albuterol–budesonide 180/160 µg and 180/80 µg than with albuterol alone (differences 132.8 mL, 95% CI 63.6–201.9, and 120.8 mL, 95% CI 51.5–190.1; both P < .001). Onset and duration of bronchodilation matched albuterol, and the adverse-event profile matched the monocomponents. DENALI was a component-contribution (combination-rule) trial with lung-function endpoints, conducted four-times-daily rather than as needed.
cards.watchOut: DENALI proves the budesonide in the rescue inhaler does measurable work on lung function; it does not itself measure exacerbations. The exacerbation trials of this exact inhaler (MANDALA and BATURA) are homed on live shelf #1030 and are not re-carded here.
cards.source: Chipps BE et al. Albuterol-Budesonide Pressurized Metered Dose Inhaler in Patients With Mild-to-Moderate Asthma: Results of the DENALI Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial. cards.summary: Synthesis: every large trial of 'steroid with every relief' beats reliever alone or matches daily maintenance for severe exacerbations — the corticosteroid-with-reliever strategy is supported across three different delivery designs
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: 1,201 adults in the reliever-triggered separate-inhaler trial, 668 analysed in the open-label mild-asthma trial, 4,176 in the double-blind noninferiority trial, and 989 evaluable in the component-contribution trial — over 7,000 participants in total, so no small-N stamp labelling applies. The fixed albuterol–budesonide exacerbation trials are homed on live shelf #1030 and are cross-pointed, not counted here.
cards.result: Severe exacerbations: 0.69 vs 0.82 per year with reliever-triggered beclomethasone (HR 0.85; PREPARE); 0.195 vs 0.400 per year for reliever-carried budesonide–formoterol versus albuterol alone (relative rate 0.49; Novel START); and noninferiority to daily maintenance at a quarter of the steroid dose (SYGMA 2), with slightly worse daily symptom scores than maintenance. DENALI confirms the steroid component contributes independently to lung function. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The designs differ — separate triggered inhaler, combination reliever with a long-acting bronchodilator, fixed combination rescue — and the shelf's LIKELY rests on their concordance for the underlying strategy, not on any single product; daily symptom control remains slightly better on scheduled maintenance in the one trial that measured it head-to-head.
cards.source: Synthesis of Israel E et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35213105); Beasley R et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 31112386); Bateman ED et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2018 (PMID: 29768147); Chipps BE et al. Chest. 2023 (PMID: 37003355). The albuterol–budesonide exacerbation trials (MANDALA, BATURA) are homed on live shelf #1030.

shelves.title: Nebuliser versus inhaler in severe COPD: not shown to be better — trials totalling 250 patients found no difference on the primary outcome, and the poor-technique patients this question is about have never been randomised
shelves.question: Is nebulized therapy better than inhaler therapy for adults with severe COPD and poor inhaler technique?
shelves.mesh: Bronchodilator Agents · Disease Progression · Dry Powder Inhalers · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Inhalation Spacers · Metered Dose Inhalers · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Time Factors
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — nebulised therapy has not been shown to be better. The direct trial evidence is eight small randomised studies totalling 250 participants in COPD exacerbations (Cochrane 2016): on the primary outcome, FEV1 one hour after dosing, nebuliser and metered-dose inhaler plus spacer made no difference (the treatment made no difference), with similar serious adverse events; a secondary timing of the same measurement favoured the nebuliser by 83 mL. In stable COPD the device literature is smaller still (three studies, 61 patients). Crucially, no trial has randomised the population this question is actually about — patients whose inhaler technique is poor: the one severe-COPD hospital trial (Berry 1989, n = 20, mean FEV1 0.69 L) concluded the inhaler-plus-spacer worked 'provided patients are able to master the technique', which is precisely the condition these patients fail. The practical case for a nebuliser in a patient who cannot use an inhaler is a delivery argument, not a demonstrated outcome advantage. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): no demonstrated superiority of nebulised over inhaler therapy; the poor-technique subgroup is untested.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2016: eight trials, 250 participants — on the primary outcome (FEV1 at one hour) nebuliser versus inhaler plus spacer made no difference in COPD exacerbations
cards.summary: Cochrane 2016: eight trials, 250 participants — on the primary outcome (FEV1 at one hour) nebuliser versus inhaler plus spacer made no difference in COPD exacerbations
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane, van Geffen 2016)
cards.people: Systematic review of eight randomised controlled trials (parallel and crossover) totalling 250 participants, comparing nebuliser delivery of bronchodilators with pressurised metered-dose inhaler plus spacer during exacerbations of COPD, in hospital or outpatient settings; mechanically ventilated patients were excluded, and no study comparing dry-powder inhalers with nebulisers was found.
cards.result: Two studies assessed the primary outcome, change in FEV1 one hour after dosing; they could not be pooled, but both showed a non-significant difference in favour of the nebuliser, with similar frequencies of serious adverse events. For the secondary outcome 'change in FEV1 closest to one hour after dosing', there was a significant difference of 83 mL (95% CI 10 to 156; P = 0.03) in favour of nebuliser treatment. For adverse events, the odds ratio was 1.65 (95% CI 0.42 to 6.48) — non-significant, in favour of the inhaler-plus-spacer group (a relative measure). The reviewers conclude there is a lack of evidence in favour of one mode of delivery over another: the studies were few, difficult to pool and of low quality.
cards.watchOut: These were exacerbation trials in patients able to use both devices in a supervised setting — they do not enrol, stratify by, or even report inhaler technique, so they cannot answer whether a nebuliser wins in the patient who cannot use an inhaler.
cards.source: van Geffen WH et al. Bronchodilators delivered by nebuliser versus pMDI with spacer or DPI for exacerbations of COPD. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016. PMID: 27569680. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Berry 1989: in 20 hospitalised patients with severe COPD (mean FEV1 0.69 L), nebuliser and inhaler-plus-spacer improved FEV1 and breathlessness by statistically indistinguishable amounts
cards.summary: Berry 1989: in 20 hospitalised patients with severe COPD (mean FEV1 0.69 L), nebuliser and inhaler-plus-spacer improved FEV1 and breathlessness by statistically indistinguishable amounts
cards.type: Double-blind randomised crossover trial (Berry 1989)
cards.people: 20 subjects (mean age 69 years) with severe airflow obstruction (mean FEV1 0.69 L) hospitalised for an acute exacerbation of COPD, in a double-blind crossover study within 24 hours of admission: each patient received albuterol by metered-dose inhaler plus spacer (0.36 mg) and by nebuliser (2.5 mg), with active drug given by only one device at a time in random order, the sequence repeated after 4 hours with the alternate device. Single-study N = 20, printed here.
cards.result: Both delivery methods produced significant improvements in FEV1, FVC and Borg dyspnoea score. The percent improvement in FEV1 was slightly larger after the nebuliser (16.7% vs 13.4%) and the Borg score improvement slightly larger after the inhaler plus spacer (−1.08 vs −0.73), but these differences were not statistically significant — the devices made no demonstrable difference. The authors' conclusion carries the caveat this shelf turns on: the inhaler-plus-spacer system is effective in this setting 'provided patients are able to master the technique'.
cards.watchOut: Twenty patients, one centre, 1989 device technology, and a crossover of single doses — and its equivalence conclusion is explicitly conditional on mastering inhaler technique, the very thing the shelf's population cannot do. This trial is also one of the eight inside the Cochrane review's 250 participants, so the two cards' numbers overlap.
cards.source: Berry RB et al. Nebulizer vs spacer for bronchodilator delivery in patients hospitalized for acute exacerbations of COPD. Chest. 1989. PMID: 2582828. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ram 2002 (Cochrane, stable COPD): only three studies and 61 patients compared inhaler devices head-to-head — too little evidence for firm conclusions in non-acute COPD either
cards.summary: Ram 2002 (Cochrane, stable COPD): only three studies and 61 patients compared inhaler devices head-to-head — too little evidence for firm conclusions in non-acute COPD either
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane, Ram 2002)
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised trials of pressurised metered-dose inhalers versus any other hand-held inhaler device for bronchodilators in non-acute (stable) COPD: fourteen studies appeared potentially relevant but only three (61 patients) met the entry criteria — two comparing dry-powder devices with a metered-dose inhaler for beta2-agonist delivery, and one 36-patient crossover comparing a soft-mist device with a metered-dose inhaler for ipratropium.
cards.result: For the dry-powder comparisons, none of the reported outcome measures differed significantly between devices. The single soft-mist study showed a significant increase in FEV1 versus the metered-dose inhaler (difference in change from baseline 70 mL, 95% CI 10 to 130 mL), with a similar-sized effect on FVC and no differences on other outcomes. The reviewers conclude the very small number of studies and patients does not permit firm conclusions. Notably, no included study required prior ability to use the inhalers, and it was assumed all randomised patients had been trained on and were capable of using the study devices.
cards.watchOut: This review compares hand-held devices with each other in stable disease — nebulisers enter it only through its search scope — and its trials assumed trained, capable users. It is carded to show how thin the maintenance-setting device evidence is, not as a nebuliser trial.
cards.source: Ram FSF et al. Pressurised metered-dose inhalers versus all other hand-held inhalers devices to deliver bronchodilators for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2002. PMID: 11869627. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: nebulised therapy is not shown to be better than inhaler therapy in COPD — and in the specific situation this shelf asks about, severe disease with poor inhaler technique, no comparative trial exists at all
cards.summary: Synthesis: nebulised therapy is not shown to be better than inhaler therapy in COPD — and in the specific situation this shelf asks about, severe disease with poor inhaler technique, no comparative trial exists at all
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review of exacerbation trials (8 studies, 250 participants, including the 20-patient severe-COPD crossover carded separately), and one Cochrane review of stable-COPD device trials (3 studies, 61 patients). Unique participants total roughly 300 across both reviews — over the small-N threshold, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the gap is that none of these patients was enrolled for poor inhaler technique.
cards.result: Primary outcome, FEV1 at one hour in exacerbations: no difference between nebuliser and inhaler plus spacer (the treatment made no difference); a secondary timing favoured the nebuliser by 83 mL (95% CI 10 to 156). In severe hospitalised COPD, single-dose FEV1 gains were 16.7% (nebuliser) vs 13.4% (inhaler plus spacer), not significant. No trial in any carded record selected patients for poor inhaler technique. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for nebuliser superiority: unproven in general, and untested in the poor-technique population.
cards.watchOut: 'Not shown to be better' is not 'shown to be worse': for an individual patient who genuinely cannot master any hand-held device, a nebuliser may be the only way the drug gets in at all — a delivery necessity this evidence neither confirms nor refutes.
cards.source: Synthesis of van Geffen WH et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016 (PMID: 27569680); Berry RB et al. Chest. 1989 (PMID: 2582828); Ram FSF et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2002 (PMID: 11869627).

shelves.title: Sedating antihistamines for sleep in insomnia with depression: avoid — benefit is thin and tolerance rapid, harms are documented in older adults, and the depression population itself has never been trialled
shelves.question: Should adults with insomnia and depression avoid sedating antihistamines for sleep?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cross-Over Studies · Diphenhydramine · Dizziness · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives · Male · Nausea · Patient Dropouts · Placebos · Sleep · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders · Temazepam · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm/avoid) — with the central gap printed on the face: no carded trial has tested sedating antihistamines in adults who have insomnia AND depression. The harm/benefit case is assembled from adjacent populations. For benefit, the direct diphenhydramine trials are weak: in elderly insomniacs, 50 mg improved only the number of awakenings versus placebo (1.7 vs 2.0) while a benzodiazepine improved four sleep measures (Glass 2008); in mild insomnia, 50 mg modestly improved subjective measures and sleep efficiency over 14 days with no polysomnographic difference (Morin 2005); and the class review concludes trial results are mixed, large controlled trials are lacking, and tolerance to over-the-counter antihistamines develops rapidly (Vande Griend 2012). For harm, the sedative-hypnotic meta-analysis in older people — which explicitly excluded people with psychiatric disorders — found small sleep gains (25.2 extra minutes) against adverse cognitive events 4.78 times and daytime fatigue 3.82 times more common than placebo (Glass 2005). In a depressed population, none of this has been measured directly; the shelf's advice to avoid rests on thin benefit plus class harm signals, not on depression-specific evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): avoid as a sleep strategy — benefit is small and tolerance rapid, harms are documented in older adults, and the insomnia-with-depression population is untested.

cards.headline: Glass 2008: in elderly insomniacs, diphenhydramine 50 mg beat placebo on exactly one sleep measure (awakenings 1.7 vs 2.0) while temazepam improved four — and neither drug was tested in depression
cards.summary: Glass 2008: in elderly insomniacs, diphenhydramine 50 mg beat placebo on exactly one sleep measure (awakenings 1.7 vs 2.0) while temazepam improved four — and neither drug was tested in depression
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled crossover trial (Glass 2008)
cards.people: Elderly individuals with insomnia (mean age 73.9 years, range 70–89) in a randomised, controlled, crossover trial of 14-night treatment periods with temazepam 15 mg, diphenhydramine 50 mg and placebo, with sleep-diary outcomes and morning-after psychomotor and memory testing; the participant N is not documented in the record.
cards.result: Temazepam improved sleep quality (3.3 ± 0.9 vs 2.9 ± 0.8; P = 0.03), total sleep time (6.9 ± 1.0 vs 6.3 ± 1.3 hours; P = 0.02), number of awakenings (1.5 ± 1.3 vs 2.0 ± 1.2; P < 0.001) and sleep-onset latency (25 ± 22 vs 37 ± 25 minutes; P = 0.03) versus placebo. Diphenhydramine improved only the number of awakenings versus placebo (1.7 ± 1.1 vs 2.0 ± 1.2; P < 0.05) — the treatment made no significant difference on the other subjective sleep measures at the dose tested. Adverse-event counts were similar across treatments, although there was one fall, on temazepam. The authors conclude temazepam is more effective than diphenhydramine at these doses, with the choice in the elderly weighing relative benefits and risks.
cards.watchOut: Two weeks, subjective diary outcomes, an N the record does not state, and a non-depressed elderly sample: this is the strongest direct diphenhydramine trial carded, and it still cannot speak to adults with depression, to longer use, or to next-day function beyond its brief morning-after tests.
cards.source: Glass JR et al. Effects of 2-week treatment with temazepam and diphenhydramine in elderly insomniacs: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Journal of Clinical Psychopharmacology. 2008. PMID: 18344728. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Morin 2005: in 184 adults with mild insomnia, diphenhydramine 50 mg for 14 days modestly improved subjective sleep and sleep efficiency — with no difference on any polysomnographic sleep-continuity variable
cards.summary: Morin 2005: in 184 adults with mild insomnia, diphenhydramine 50 mg for 14 days modestly improved subjective sleep and sleep efficiency — with no difference on any polysomnographic sleep-continuity variable
cards.type: Multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial (Morin 2005)
cards.people: 184 adults (110 women, 74 men; mean age 44.3 years) with mild insomnia in a multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled parallel-group trial at nine US sleep centres: a valerian–hops combination for 28 days (n = 59), placebo for 28 days (n = 65), or diphenhydramine (two 25 mg tablets) for 14 days followed by placebo for 14 days (n = 60).
cards.result: Both active treatments produced modest improvements in subjective sleep parameters, but few comparisons with placebo reached statistical significance. Diphenhydramine produced significantly greater increases in sleep efficiency and a trend for increased total sleep time versus placebo during the first 14 days; patients rated their insomnia severity lower than placebo at day 14. There was no significant group difference on any sleep-continuity variable measured by polysomnography, and no alteration of sleep stages 3–4 or REM sleep with any treatment. There were no significant residual effects, no serious adverse events, and no rebound insomnia on discontinuation in this short trial.
cards.watchOut: Mild insomnia, 14 days of drug, and a subjective-objective split (diaries improved, polysomnography did not): nothing here addresses chronic nightly use, tolerance beyond two weeks, or patients whose insomnia rides on depression.
cards.source: Morin CM et al. Valerian-hops combination and diphenhydramine for treating insomnia: a randomized placebo-controlled clinical trial. Sleep. 2005. PMID: 16335333. Registry ID: none in the record. multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial (morin 2005) 184 adults (110 women, 74 men; mean age 44.3 years) with mild insomnia in a multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled parallel-group trial at nine us sleep centres: a valerian–hops combination for 28 days (n = 59), placebo for 28 days (n = 65), or diphenhydramine (two 25 mg tablets) for 14 days followed by placebo for 14 days (n = 60). both active treatments produced modest improvements in subjective sleep parameters, but few comparisons with placebo reached statistical significance. diphenhydramine produced significantly greater increases in sleep efficiency and a trend for increased total sleep time versus placebo during the first 14 days; patients rated their insomnia severity lower than placebo at day 14. there was no significant group difference on any sleep-continuity variable measured by polysomnography, and no alteration of sleep stages 3–4 or rem sleep with any treatment. there were no significant residual effects, no serious adverse events, and no rebound insomnia on discontinuation in this short trial. mild insomnia, 14 days of drug, and a subjective-objective split (diaries improved, polysomnography did not): nothing here addresses chronic nightly use, tolerance beyond two weeks, or patients whose insomnia rides on depression. morin cm et al. valerian-hops combination and diphenhydramine for treating insomnia: a randomized placebo-controlled clinical trial. sleep. 2005. pmid: 16335333. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aged · diphenhydramine · female · humans · humulus · hypnotics and sedatives · male · middle aged · phytotherapy · plant extracts · quality of life · severity of illness index · sleep initiation and maintenance disorders · sleep stages · surveys and questionnaires · valerian

cards.headline: Vande Griend 2012: reviewing the H1-antihistamine insomnia literature — 16 qualifying trials, mixed results, large controlled trials lacking, and tolerance to over-the-counter antihistamines develops rapidly
cards.summary: Vande Griend 2012: reviewing the H1-antihistamine insomnia literature — 16 qualifying trials, mixed results, large controlled trials lacking, and tolerance to over-the-counter antihistamines develops rapidly
cards.type: Systematic literature review (Vande Griend 2012)
cards.people: Literature review of randomised double-blind trials of histamine-1 receptor antagonists for insomnia in adults (including the elderly), evaluating sleep latency, wake after sleep onset, total sleep time, awakenings and sleep efficiency against placebo or an approved insomnia treatment: 65 trials were evaluated and 16 met the inclusion criteria.
cards.result: With the exception of low-dose doxepin (a tricyclic at hypnotic micro-doses, not an over-the-counter antihistamine), trials of H1 antagonists show mixed results and are limited by sample size and generalisability; large, randomised, appropriately controlled trials are lacking, making safety and efficacy difficult to define. The reviewers state over-the-counter antihistamines may have a role for short-term insomnia treatment in younger adults, but tolerance develops rapidly; that mirtazapine should not be used solely for insomnia; and that patients taking these agents chronically should be evaluated for continued efficacy and potential harm. No effect size for diphenhydramine or doxylamine is reported in the record — that absence is printed here plainly.
cards.watchOut: A narrative-systematic review without pooled numbers: its value on this shelf is the tolerance finding and the explicit statement that the large trials do not exist — it cannot quantify how much harm or benefit a depressed insomniac should expect.
cards.source: Vande Griend JP et al. Histamine-1 receptor antagonism for treatment of insomnia. Journal of the American Pharmacists Association. 2012. PMID: 23229983. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Glass 2005 (BMJ meta-analysis): in 2,417 older insomniacs WITHOUT psychiatric disorders, sedative hypnotics added 25.2 minutes of sleep but made adverse cognitive events 4.78 times and daytime fatigue 3.82 times more common
cards.summary: Glass 2005 (BMJ meta-analysis): in 2,417 older insomniacs WITHOUT psychiatric disorders, sedative hypnotics added 25.2 minutes of sleep but made adverse cognitive events 4.78 times and daytime fatigue 3.82 times more common
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised trials (Glass 2005)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 24 randomised trials (2,417 participants) of any pharmacological sedative treatment for at least five nights in people aged 60 or over with insomnia who were otherwise free of psychiatric or psychological disorders — the exclusion that matters most for this shelf's question.
cards.result: Sleep quality improved (effect size 0.14; P < 0.05), total sleep time increased by a mean of 25.2 minutes (P < 0.001) and night-time awakenings fell by 0.63 (P < 0.001) with sedatives versus placebo — statistically significant but small. Adverse events were more common with sedatives: adverse cognitive events 4.78 times more common (95% CI 1.47 to 15.47; P < 0.01), adverse psychomotor events 2.61 times more common (95% CI 1.12 to 6.09), and daytime fatigue 3.82 times more common (95% CI 1.88 to 7.80; P < 0.001) — relative measures, as printed in the record. The authors conclude that in people over 60 the benefits may not justify the increased risk, particularly with additional risk factors for cognitive or psychomotor adverse events.
cards.watchOut: This is a class-level analysis (mostly benzodiazepines and Z-drugs, not antihistamines specifically) in people screened free of psychiatric illness — it supplies the harm context for sedative sleep aids in older adults, and by its own design it says nothing directly about patients with depression.
cards.source: Glass J et al. Sedative hypnotics in older people with insomnia: meta-analysis of risks and benefits. BMJ. 2005. PMID: 16284208. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the honest answer is 'avoid' on indirect evidence — benefit is one-measure thin and tolerance is rapid, harms are documented in older adults, and the insomnia-with-depression population has never been trialled
cards.summary: Synthesis: the honest answer is 'avoid' on indirect evidence — benefit is one-measure thin and tolerance is rapid, harms are documented in older adults, and the insomnia-with-depression population has never been trialled
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one elderly crossover trial of diphenhydramine (N not documented in the record), one 184-patient mild-insomnia trial, one class review of 16 qualifying trials, and one meta-analysis of 24 trials and 2,417 older participants that excluded psychiatric disorders. Summed where numbers exist, the evidence base exceeds 30 participants, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the disqualifying gap is population, not size — zero participants were enrolled for insomnia with depression.
cards.result: Diphenhydramine's demonstrated benefit is a single improved diary measure in the elderly trial and a modest sleep-efficiency gain over 14 days in mild insomnia, with polysomnography null; the class review finds mixed results and rapid tolerance; the older-adult meta-analysis finds small gains against roughly 3.8–4.8-fold relative increases in fatigue and cognitive adverse events for sedatives as a class. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): sedating antihistamines are a poor sleep strategy for adults with insomnia and depression — on evidence that is honestly indirect for that exact population.
cards.watchOut: Do not over-read this shelf in either direction: nothing here shows antihistamines worsen depression itself, and nothing shows they are dangerous for every short-term user — the case is thin benefit, rapid tolerance, and documented class harms in older adults, extrapolated to a population no trial has studied.
cards.source: Synthesis of Glass JR et al. Journal of Clinical Psychopharmacology. 2008 (PMID: 18344728); Morin CM et al. Sleep. 2005 (PMID: 16335333); Vande Griend JP et al. Journal of the American Pharmacists Association. 2012 (PMID: 23229983); Glass J et al. BMJ. 2005 (PMID: 16284208).

shelves.title: Tapering Z-drugs in older adults: stopping is achievable and often durable, but improved long-term sleep quality has never been measured — the one Z-drug trial counted discontinuation, not sleep
shelves.question: Does tapering Z-drugs improve sleep quality long term in older adults with insomnia?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Community Pharmacy Services · Comorbidity · Deprescriptions · Female · Health Services · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives · Male · Middle Aged · Odds Ratio · Patient Education as Topic · Polypharmacy · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — because the question's exact outcome, long-term sleep quality after tapering Z-drugs, has never been measured in a trial. What exists: one randomised trial in older adults shows Z-drugs can be stopped — patient education, with or without a pharmacist call, roughly doubled 6-month discontinuation versus usual care (56% and 55% vs 26%; adjusted odds ratios about 4.0 and 4.1, relative measures) — but it reported no sleep-quality outcome (Kuntz 2019). The long-term data come from benzodiazepine (not Z-drug) cohorts: among 47 older adults who had successfully stopped after taper-based programmes, 42.6% had resumed benzodiazepines by 24 months, with the taper-containing groups relapsing least (Morin 2005, the long-term follow-up of the supervised-taper programme homed on pack #3829, cross-pointed and not re-carded); and a secondary analysis found patients who stayed medication-free had less severe insomnia over the following six months (Belleville 2008) — an association that may run from better sleep to successful stopping rather than the reverse. A non-randomised primary-care protocol (which excluded zolpidem users) kept 85% of dose-reducers off benzodiazepines at 12 months (Fernandes 2022). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): tapering gets many older adults off Z-drugs, but whether their sleep is better long term is untested — the honest expectation from adjacent evidence is substantial relapse and no measured sleep-quality gain.

cards.headline: Kuntz 2019: education (with or without a pharmacist call) roughly doubled Z-drug discontinuation at 6 months in 150 older adults — 56% and 55% vs 26% on usual care — but sleep quality was not an outcome
cards.summary: Kuntz 2019: education (with or without a pharmacist call) roughly doubled Z-drug discontinuation at 6 months in 150 older adults — 56% and 55% vs 26% on usual care — but sleep quality was not an outcome
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Kuntz 2019)
cards.people: 150 Kaiser Permanente Northwest members aged 64 years or older who had received 2 to 3 fills of a Z-drug (eszopiclone, zolpidem or zaleplon) in 2016, randomised to usual care, educational information only, or educational information plus a pharmacist consultation; analysed groups were 50, 50 and 49 patients.
cards.result: Discontinuation at 6 months: 28 of 50 (56%) with education only and 27 of 49 (55%) with education plus pharmacist consultation versus 13 of 50 (26%) with usual care — absolute rates as printed in the record. After adjustment for demographics, comorbidity and anxiolytic/antidepressant use, the odds of discontinuation were about four times higher with education only (adjusted OR 4.02, 95% CI 1.66–9.77) and with education plus consultation (adjusted OR 4.10, 95% CI 1.65–10.19) than with usual care — relative measures, with the absolute rates beside them. The record reports no sleep-quality, insomnia-severity or daytime-function outcome: this trial shows older adults can be helped off Z-drugs, not that their sleep improves afterwards.
cards.watchOut: The intervention was education-driven deprescribing rather than a pharmacologic taper schedule, follow-up was 6 months, and 'discontinued' is a prescription-record outcome — a patient can be off the drug and sleeping worse, which this design cannot detect.
cards.source: Kuntz JL et al. Patient Education and Pharmacist Consultation Influence on Nonbenzodiazepine Sedative Medication Deprescribing Success for Older Adults. Permanente Journal. 2019. PMID: 30624198. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Morin 2005 (2-year follow-up): of 47 older adults who had stopped benzodiazepines after taper-based treatment, 42.6% had relapsed by 24 months — taper groups relapsed least (about 31–33% vs 69% with CBT alone)
cards.summary: Morin 2005 (2-year follow-up): of 47 older adults who had stopped benzodiazepines after taper-based treatment, 42.6% had relapsed by 24 months — taper groups relapsed least (about 31–33% vs 69% with CBT alone)
cards.type: Long-term follow-up / survival analysis of a randomised discontinuation trial (Morin 2005)
cards.people: 47 older adults (mean age 62.1 years) with persistent insomnia and prolonged benzodiazepine use (average 18.9 years) who had successfully discontinued following cognitive-behaviour therapy for insomnia, a supervised medication taper, or the combined approach, followed for 24 months for medication-free survival (relapse = resumed benzodiazepine hypnotics). This is the long-term follow-up report of the supervised-taper trial programme homed on pack #3829; that programme's own trial records are cross-pointed there and are not re-carded here.
cards.result: By 24 months, 42.6% of the sample had resumed benzodiazepine use. Relapse was significantly lower in the combined (33.3%) and taper (30.8%) groups than in the CBT-only group (69.2%). Medication-free survival at 12 months was 83.3% (taper), 70.8% (combined) and 38.5% (CBT); at 24 months, 64.8%, 64.9% and 28.9%. Mean survival time was 18.6 months (taper) and 12.6 months (combined) versus 8.5 months (CBT alone). Predictors of relapse included treatment condition, end-of-treatment insomnia severity and psychological distress. The outcome is staying off the drug — long-term sleep quality itself was not the endpoint of this follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Benzodiazepines, not Z-drugs; a completer cohort (only people who had already succeeded in stopping were followed), so its relapse rates flatter any real-world taper; and relapse is a medication outcome, not a sleep-quality measurement.
cards.source: Morin CM et al. Long-term outcome after discontinuation of benzodiazepines for insomnia: a survival analysis of relapse. Behaviour Research and Therapy. 2005. PMID: 15531349. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Belleville 2008: patients who stayed medication-free for six months after a taper had less severe insomnia and anxiety than those who did not — an association that cannot show the taper improved their sleep
cards.summary: Belleville 2008: patients who stayed medication-free for six months after a taper had less severe insomnia and anxiety than those who did not — an association that cannot show the taper improved their sleep
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised taper trial (Belleville 2008)
cards.people: Secondary analysis of a randomised clinical trial comparing a hypnotic taper intervention with or without self-help treatment for insomnia in chronic hypnotic users (benzodiazepines and Z-drugs, per the record's indexing), comparing participants who were medication-free at follow-up with those still using sleep medication on insomnia severity, withdrawal symptoms, psychological symptoms, perceived health, readiness to change and self-efficacy; the participant N is not documented in the record.
cards.result: There were no significant baseline differences between those who would remain medication-free and those still using medication at the end of the taper intervention. Differences emerged midway through the 8-week withdrawal programme and were accentuated afterwards: participants medication-free over the next six months had less severe insomnia and anxiety symptoms, a more positive perception of their health, and higher self-efficacy to refrain from hypnotic use. There were no group differences in readiness to change or stages of change. The authors conclude successful discontinuation was associated with overall improvement of insomnia, anxiety and distress symptoms, perceived health and self-efficacy.
cards.watchOut: Reverse causation is built into this design: people whose sleep held up are the people who stayed off the drug, so 'medication-free patients slept better' may describe who succeeds rather than what tapering does. The record also does not state the analysed N.
cards.source: Belleville G et al. Hypnotic discontinuation in chronic insomnia: impact of psychological distress, readiness to change, and self-efficacy. Health Psychology. 2008. PMID: 18377143. cards.headline: Fernandes 2022: a non-randomised primary-care taper protocol stopped benzodiazepines in 59.4% and kept 85% of dose-reducers off at 12 months — but zolpidem users were excluded from it
cards.summary: Fernandes 2022: a non-randomised primary-care taper protocol stopped benzodiazepines in 59.4% and kept 85% of dose-reducers off at 12 months — but zolpidem users were excluded from it
cards.type: Non-randomised single-arm intervention study (Fernandes 2022)
cards.people: 66 patients (74% female; 66.7% aged over 64; median benzodiazepine use 120 months) with benzodiazepine dependence and chronic daily use of at least 3 months, recruited by family physicians in primary care for a standardised protocol (switch to diazepam, then gradual taper); patients taking zolpidem, those on at least 30 mg diazepam-equivalent daily, and those with other substance abuse or major psychiatric disease were excluded.
cards.result: Overall, 59.4% of participants successfully stopped benzodiazepines by the last intervention visit (60.7% excluding protocol deviations); 31 patients reported at least one withdrawal symptom, most frequently insomnia and anxiety. Among patients who reduced dosage, 85% remained without benzodiazepines after 12 months, and 77% of protocol completers were satisfied. Men had a higher probability of success (relative risk 0.51 as printed in the record; P = 0.001). No sleep-quality endpoint is reported — and by design the study says nothing about Z-drugs, whose users were excluded.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and non-randomised, in benzodiazepine users selected to exclude the highest doses and psychiatric comorbidity — its 12-month durability figure describes protocol completers and dose-reducers, not everyone who starts a taper, and not Z-drug users at all.
cards.source: Fernandes M et al. Discontinuation of chronic benzodiazepine use in primary care: a nonrandomized intervention. Family Practice. 2022. PMID: 35196378. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: tapering can get older adults off Z-drugs (about 55% vs 26% at 6 months with education support), but long-term sleep quality after tapering has never been a trial outcome — adjacent benzodiazepine data show about 43% relapse by two years
cards.summary: Synthesis: tapering can get older adults off Z-drugs (about 55% vs 26% at 6 months with education support), but long-term sleep quality after tapering has never been a trial outcome — adjacent benzodiazepine data show about 43% relapse by two years
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised Z-drug deprescribing trial (150 older adults, 6 months), one 24-month follow-up of 47 older benzodiazepine discontinuers, one secondary taper-trial analysis (N not documented in the record), and one non-randomised 66-patient benzodiazepine protocol. Countable participants total 263 — over the small-N threshold — but only the first card's participants took Z-drugs, and none of the four records reports long-term sleep quality as an endpoint. The supervised-taper-plus-CBT trials themselves are homed on pack #3829 and the masked-taper trial on pack #3816; both are cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: Discontinuation is achievable and durable for many (56%/55% vs 26% at 6 months, Kuntz 2019; 85% of dose-reducers still off at 12 months, Fernandes 2022), but relapse is substantial (42.6% by 24 months, Morin 2005) and the only sleep finding is associational (successful discontinuers had less severe insomnia, Belleville 2008). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for improved long-term sleep quality from tapering Z-drugs: plausible, unmeasured, and not what the trials tested.
cards.watchOut: This shelf must not be read as 'tapering does not help': stopping Z-drugs has its own safety rationale in older adults. The narrow, honest point is that the sleep-quality dividend patients are usually promised has never been measured long term.
