shelves.title: Caffeine after midday and sleep: the timing evidence is real (45 minutes of sleep lost; coffee's modelled cutoff 8.8 hours before bed) — but a midday rule has never been trialled, and never in people with insomnia
shelves.question: For adults with insomnia, does limiting caffeine after midday improve sleep quality in a trial setting?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analysis of Variance · Caffeine · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Polysomnography · Sleep · Time Factors · Wakefulness
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the direction is well supported and the specific intervention is untested. No carded trial has randomised adults with insomnia to a midday caffeine cutoff. What the trial literature shows is timing- and dose-dependent harm from caffeine near bedtime: 400 mg of caffeine disrupted sleep versus placebo even when taken 6 hours before bed (Drake 2013); and a meta-analysis of 24 studies found caffeine cut total sleep time by 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7%, and calculated that a standard coffee (107 mg caffeine) should be finished at least 8.8 hours before bedtime and a high-dose pre-workout drink (217.5 mg) at least 13.2 hours before (Gardiner 2023). A midday cutoff for a typical late-evening bedtime lands between those two lines — about 10–11 hours before bed — so it covers ordinary coffee on the meta-analysis's arithmetic but not high-dose products. The systematic review evidence (Clark 2017) adds that dose- and timing-response relationships are established, that older adults' sleep may be more sensitive, and that most studies were in young healthy men — not in people with insomnia. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): limiting caffeine after midday is consistent with the trial evidence on caffeine timing, but the cutoff itself, in insomnia patients, has never been trialled.

cards.headline: Drake 2013: caffeine 400 mg significantly disrupted sleep versus placebo at every timing tested — at bedtime, 3 hours before, and even 6 hours before bed
cards.summary: Drake 2013: caffeine 400 mg significantly disrupted sleep versus placebo at every timing tested — at bedtime, 3 hours before, and even 6 hours before bed
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled timing study (Drake 2013)
cards.people: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in the home environment comparing a fixed 400 mg dose of caffeine administered at 0, 3 or 6 hours before habitual bedtime against placebo, with sleep disturbance measured by self-report and by a validated portable sleep monitor (objective monitoring); the participant N is not documented in the record.
cards.result: Caffeine at bedtime, 3 hours prior and 6 hours prior each had significant effects on sleep disturbance relative to placebo (P < 0.05 for all). The authors report that the magnitude of reduction in total sleep time indicates caffeine taken 6 hours before bedtime has important disruptive effects on sleep, and that the study provides empirical support for sleep-hygiene recommendations to refrain from substantial caffeine use for a minimum of 6 hours before bedtime. The record reports significance and this qualitative magnitude statement; it does not print the per-timing total-sleep-time values, and none are invented here.
cards.watchOut: A single fixed 400 mg dose — roughly four standard coffees at once — in volunteers studied at home, not a trial of a midday cutoff and not in insomnia patients: it proves late caffeine harms sleep, and bounds the problem, but a noon rule for ordinary coffee doses is an extrapolation from it.
cards.source: Drake C et al. Caffeine effects on sleep taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before going to bed. Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine. 2013. PMID: 24235903. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gardiner 2023 (meta-analysis, 24 studies): caffeine cut total sleep time by 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7% — a standard coffee should be finished at least 8.8 hours before bed, a pre-workout drink 13.2 hours before
cards.summary: Gardiner 2023 (meta-analysis, 24 studies): caffeine cut total sleep time by 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7% — a standard coffee should be finished at least 8.8 hours before bed, a pre-workout drink 13.2 hours before
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Gardiner 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 24 studies of caffeine consumption and the characteristics of subsequent night-time sleep, undertaken to identify the time after which caffeine should not be consumed before bedtime; the total participant number across the 24 studies is not documented in the record.
cards.result: Caffeine consumption reduced total sleep time by 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7%, increased sleep-onset latency by 9 minutes and wake after sleep onset by 12 minutes, increased light sleep (duration +6.1 minutes; proportion +1.7%) and decreased deep sleep (duration −11.4 minutes; proportion −1.4%). To avoid reductions in total sleep time, the authors calculate that coffee (107 mg caffeine per 250 mL) should be consumed at least 8.8 hours before bedtime and a standard pre-workout supplement serve (217.5 mg) at least 13.2 hours before bedtime. For a person sleeping at 23:00, those lines fall at about 14:12 and 09:48 respectively — so a midday cutoff satisfies the coffee line but not the high-dose line.
cards.watchOut: The 8.8- and 13.2-hour cutoffs are modelled from dose–timing data across heterogeneous studies, mostly in healthy sleepers: they are the best quantitative guide available, but they were not themselves tested as advice given to insomnia patients.
cards.source: Gardiner C et al. The effect of caffeine on subsequent sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep Medicine Reviews. 2023. PMID: 36870101. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Caffeine · Sleep · Polysomnography · Coffee · Sleep Deprivation

cards.headline: Clark 2017: across epidemiological studies and randomised trials, caffeine typically prolonged sleep latency, reduced total sleep time and efficiency and worsened perceived quality — with dose- and timing-response established and older adults possibly more sensitive
cards.summary: Clark 2017: across epidemiological studies and randomised trials, caffeine typically prolonged sleep latency, reduced total sleep time and efficiency and worsened perceived quality — with dose- and timing-response established and older adults possibly more sensitive
cards.type: Systematic review of epidemiological studies and randomised trials (Clark 2017)
cards.people: Systematic review of epidemiological studies and randomised controlled trials of coffee and caffeine effects on sleep, covering sleep latency, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, perceived sleep quality, sleep stages and EEG slow-wave activity, and individual differences including age and genetic polymorphisms of adenosine neurotransmission and metabolism.
cards.result: Caffeine typically prolonged sleep latency, reduced total sleep time and sleep efficiency, and worsened perceived sleep quality; slow-wave sleep and EEG slow-wave activity were typically reduced, while stage-1 sleep, wakefulness and arousals increased. Dose- and timing-response relationships were established. The sleep of older adults may be more sensitive to caffeine than that of younger adults, and pronounced individual differences exist in young people as well. The reviewers note most studies were conducted in male adults of Western countries, limiting generalisability, and call for longitudinal studies of causal relationships between caffeine-induced sleep changes and health. The record reports no single pooled effect size — that absence is printed here plainly.
cards.watchOut: A qualitative synthesis spanning epidemiology (confounded by why people drink caffeine) and small trials: it establishes consistency and dose–timing response, but it cannot certify that advising a midday cutoff will improve any given insomnia patient's sleep.
cards.source: Clark I et al. Coffee, caffeine, and sleep: A systematic review of epidemiological studies and randomized controlled trials. Sleep Medicine Reviews. 2017. PMID: 26899133. cards.headline: Synthesis: caffeine's sleep harm is dose- and timing-dependent and real (45 minutes of sleep lost on average) — a midday cutoff fits the evidence for ordinary coffee, but no trial has tested the cutoff, or enrolled insomnia patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: caffeine's sleep harm is dose- and timing-dependent and real (45 minutes of sleep lost on average) — a midday cutoff fits the evidence for ordinary coffee, but no trial has tested the cutoff, or enrolled insomnia patients
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised timing study (400 mg caffeine at 0/3/6 hours before bed; N not documented in the record), one meta-analysis of 24 studies (total participant N not documented in the record), and one systematic review of epidemiological studies and trials. Because neither quantitative record prints a participant total, a summed evidence-base N cannot be computed from the fetched records, and no small-N stamp label is applied on numbers the records do not give; the limitation printed instead is the population and intervention gap.
cards.result: Caffeine disrupted sleep even 6 hours before bedtime at 400 mg (Drake 2013); across 24 studies it cost 45 minutes of total sleep and 7% of sleep efficiency, with modelled no-later-than times of 8.8 hours before bed for a standard coffee and 13.2 hours for a high-dose pre-workout drink (Gardiner 2023); dose- and timing-response are established and older adults may be more sensitive (Clark 2017). A midday cutoff is roughly 10–11 hours before a typical bedtime — inside the coffee line, outside the high-dose line. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for the midday-cutoff intervention in insomnia: directionally supported, never directly trialled.
cards.watchOut: Sleep-hygiene advice is usually given as if trialled; on this shelf it is not. The evidence supports 'earlier and less caffeine, better sleep' — the noon line is a practical reading of the dose–timing data, not a tested prescription.

shelves.title: Procalcitonin guidance in pneumonia: LIKELY to safely shorten antibiotic courses — median 12 to 5 days in the pneumonia-only trial and 10.7 to 7.2 days in the large trial's pneumonia subgroup, with no worse outcomes
shelves.question: Does procalcitonin guidance safely reduce antibiotic duration in adults with pneumonia?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Algorithms · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Calcitonin · Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide · Decision Support Techniques · Drug Utilization · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Humans · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Practice Guidelines as Topic · Protein Precursors · Respiratory Tract Infections · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for safely shortening antibiotic courses in pneumonia, on concordant randomised evidence — with the library cross-point printed here: the broader question of procalcitonin guidance across all acute respiratory infections is homed on live shelf #314, which cards the intensive-care and US emergency-department trials (including a large US trial that found no reduction in antibiotic use); those records are NOT re-carded here. This shelf asks the narrower pneumonia question, and its anchor trial was never carded. In pneumonia specifically: the pneumonia-only randomised trial cut median duration from 12 to 5 days with similar outcomes; the large Swiss trial's pneumonia subgroup (925 patients) cut mean duration from 10.7 to 7.2 days with a similar adverse-outcome rate; and the patient-level meta-analysis of 26 trials found 2.4 fewer antibiotic days, fewer antibiotic side-effects, and lower 30-day mortality with guidance (adjusted OR 0.83). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): procalcitonin guidance safely reduces antibiotic duration in adults with pneumonia.

cards.headline: Christ-Crain 2006 (ProCAP): in the pneumonia-only randomised trial, procalcitonin guidance cut median antibiotic duration from 12 to 5 days and total antibiotic exposure by about half (relative risk 0.52), with a similar outcome success rate of 83% in both groups
cards.summary: Christ-Crain 2006 (ProCAP): in the pneumonia-only randomised trial, procalcitonin guidance cut median antibiotic duration from 12 to 5 days and total antibiotic exposure by about half (relative risk 0.52), with a similar outcome success rate of 83% in both groups
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Christ-Crain 2006, ProCAP)
cards.people: 302 consecutive patients with suspected community-acquired pneumonia randomised to antibiotic treatment by usual practice (control, n = 151) or by a procalcitonin algorithm (n = 151) — antibiotics strongly discouraged below 0.1 µg/L, discouraged below 0.25 µg/L, encouraged above 0.25 µg/L and strongly encouraged above 0.5 µg/L. Groups were similar at baseline, including Pneumonia Severity Index.
cards.result: Procalcitonin guidance reduced total antibiotic exposure (relative risk, 0.52; 95% CI 0.48 to 0.55; P < 0.001), antibiotic prescriptions on admission (85% vs 99%; P < 0.001) and antibiotic treatment duration (median 5 vs 12 days; P < 0.001). After adjustment for Pneumonia Severity Index, the hazard ratio for antibiotic discontinuation was 3.2 (95% CI 2.5 to 4.2) in the procalcitonin group. Outcome was similar in both groups, with an overall success rate of 83%.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre-era trial of 302 patients from 2006, when usual-practice pneumonia courses ran to a median of 12 days; against a modern 5-day standard course the achievable saving would be smaller. The 83% success rate is the trial's overall figure, printed as the record gives it.
cards.source: Christ-Crain M et al. Procalcitonin guidance of antibiotic therapy in community-acquired pneumonia: a randomized trial. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2006. cards.headline: Schuetz 2009 (ProHOSP): in 1,359 patients with lower respiratory infection, procalcitonin guidance cut mean antibiotic duration from 8.7 to 5.7 days overall — and in the community-acquired pneumonia subgroup (925 patients) from 10.7 to 7.2 days — with a similar adverse-outcome rate (15.4% vs 18.9%) and fewer antibiotic side-effects
cards.summary: Schuetz 2009 (ProHOSP): in 1,359 patients with lower respiratory infection, procalcitonin guidance cut mean antibiotic duration from 8.7 to 5.7 days overall — and in the community-acquired pneumonia subgroup (925 patients) from 10.7 to 7.2 days — with a similar adverse-outcome rate (15.4% vs 18.9%) and fewer antibiotic side-effects
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Schuetz 2009, ProHOSP)
cards.people: 1,359 patients with mostly severe lower respiratory tract infections randomised in the emergency departments of 6 Swiss tertiary hospitals to a procalcitonin algorithm with predefined cut-offs for starting and stopping antibiotics, or to standard guidelines; a noninferiority trial with a 7.5% boundary for the composite of death, intensive-care admission, disease-specific complications or recurrent infection within 30 days. The pneumonia subgroup numbered 925 patients.
cards.result: Overall adverse outcomes were similar (15.4% [n = 103] with procalcitonin guidance vs 18.9% [n = 130] with standard care; difference −3.5%, 95% CI −7.6% to 0.4%). Mean antibiotic duration was 5.7 vs 8.7 days (relative change −34.8%, 95% CI −40.3% to −28.7%); in community-acquired pneumonia, 7.2 vs 10.7 days (relative change −32.4%, 95% CI −37.6% to −26.9%). Antibiotic-associated adverse effects were less frequent with guidance (19.8% [n = 133] vs 28.1% [n = 193]; difference −8.2%, 95% CI −12.7% to −3.7%).
cards.watchOut: The trial randomised all lower respiratory infections, not pneumonia alone — the pneumonia figures are its prespecified disease subgroup (925 of 1,359 patients), and the safety composite is the whole-trial result. The intervention was open-label.

cards.headline: Schuetz 2018 (patient-level meta-analysis, 26 trials, 6,708 patients): procalcitonin guidance was associated with 2.4 fewer antibiotic days (5.7 vs 8.1), fewer antibiotic side-effects (16% vs 22%) and lower 30-day mortality (9% vs 10%; adjusted OR 0.83)
cards.summary: Schuetz 2018 (patient-level meta-analysis, 26 trials, 6,708 patients): procalcitonin guidance was associated with 2.4 fewer antibiotic days (5.7 vs 8.1), fewer antibiotic side-effects (16% vs 22%) and lower 30-day mortality (9% vs 10%; adjusted OR 0.83)
cards.type: Patient-level meta-analysis of randomised trials (Schuetz 2018)
cards.people: 6,708 patients with acute respiratory infections from 26 randomised trials in 12 countries, pooled at individual-patient level: 3,336 allocated to procalcitonin-guided treatment and 3,372 to control. Settings ranged from primary care to intensive care; the analysis was conducted to a prespecified Cochrane protocol after US approval of procalcitonin for guiding antibiotic therapy in acute respiratory infections.
cards.result: 30-day mortality was lower with procalcitonin guidance (286 [9%] deaths in 3,336 patients vs 336 [10%] in 3,372 controls; adjusted odds ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.99; P = 0.037), with a similar benefit across subgroups by setting and type of infection. Guidance was associated with a 2.4-day reduction in antibiotic exposure (5.7 vs 8.1 days; 95% CI for the difference −2.71 to −2.15; P < 0.0001) and fewer antibiotic-related side-effects (16% vs 22%; adjusted OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.82; P < 0.0001). Absolute mortality rates (9% vs 10%) are printed beside the relative odds ratio, as reported.
cards.watchOut: This pools all acute respiratory infections, not pneumonia alone, and the mortality difference is small in absolute terms (about 1 percentage point) with an upper confidence limit close to 1 — it supports safety of shorter courses; it should not be quoted as proof that procalcitonin itself saves lives in pneumonia.
cards.source: Schuetz P et al. Effect of procalcitonin-guided antibiotic treatment on mortality in acute respiratory infections: a patient level meta-analysis. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2018. PMID: 29037960. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: for pneumonia specifically, procalcitonin guidance shortened antibiotic courses in every carded randomised comparison — median 12 to 5 days in the pneumonia-only trial, 10.7 to 7.2 days in the large trial's pneumonia subgroup — without a worse outcome rate, and with fewer antibiotic side-effects
cards.summary: Synthesis: for pneumonia specifically, procalcitonin guidance shortened antibiotic courses in every carded randomised comparison — median 12 to 5 days in the pneumonia-only trial, 10.7 to 7.2 days in the large trial's pneumonia subgroup — without a worse outcome rate, and with fewer antibiotic side-effects
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one pneumonia-only randomised trial (302 patients), one large randomised trial with a 925-patient pneumonia subgroup (1,359 randomised in total), and a patient-level meta-analysis of 26 trials (6,708 patients). Total carded participants exceed 8,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies. Cross-point (not re-carded): live shelf #314 homes procalcitonin guidance across all acute respiratory infections, including the intensive-care trial and a large US emergency-department trial that found no reduction in antibiotic use — the discordant result that keeps this shelf's claim pneumonia-specific.
cards.result: Duration: median 5 vs 12 days (Christ-Crain 2006); pneumonia subgroup mean 7.2 vs 10.7 days with adverse outcomes 15.4% vs 18.9% overall (Schuetz 2009); pooled exposure 5.7 vs 8.1 days with side-effects 16% vs 22% and 30-day mortality 9% vs 10%, adjusted OR 0.83 (Schuetz 2018). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): procalcitonin guidance safely reduces antibiotic duration in adults with pneumonia.
cards.watchOut: Control-arm durations in these trials (10–12 days) are longer than modern standard pneumonia courses, so the absolute days saved today would be fewer; and the broader respiratory-infection literature carded on shelf #314 contains a large null US trial — the LIKELY stamp here is for pneumonia, where the randomised evidence is concordant.
cards.source: Synthesis of Christ-Crain M et al. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2006 (PMID: 16603606); Schuetz P et al. JAMA. 2009 (PMID: 19738090); Schuetz P et al. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2018 (PMID: 29037960).

shelves.title: Dupilumab in severe eosinophilic asthma (partial completion of #1031): exacerbation benefit is real and concentrates at eosinophil counts of 300/µL or above — though anti-IL-5 drugs may beat it in that stratum
shelves.question: Does dupilumab reduce exacerbations in adults with severe eosinophilic asthma?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Eosinophils · Anti-Asthmatic Agents · Biological Products · Asthma · Leukocyte Count · Eosinophilia · Double-Blind Method
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion, built under the one-home precedent for homed anchors: the primary QUEST and VENTURE trial reports are already carded on live shelf #1031 (dupilumab in moderate-to-severe asthma), so they are cross-pointed here by shelf number only and are NOT re-carded; this shelf is built entirely on free reports that cut the evidence the way #1031 does not — by severity and by eosinophil count. A systematic review of placebo-controlled biologic trials found exacerbation reduction with all biologics, dupilumab included, in patients with baseline blood eosinophil count 300 cells/µL or above, and consistent dupilumab reduction (300 mg dose) in the 150 to under 300 band (Korn 2023). In oral-corticosteroid-dependent severe asthma, dupilumab reduced the severe exacerbation rate by 71% (relative) in patients on under 10 mg/day baseline steroid and by 48% (relative) in those on 10 mg/day or more, while freeing 72% and 37% respectively from steroids entirely (Domingo 2022, a VENTURE post hoc analysis). In allergic and nonallergic asthma alike, exacerbation rates fell by 60%-72% (relative) across the phase 2b and VENTURE populations (Brusselle 2023). One cautionary comparative cohort found that, in patients with eosinophils 300/µL or above, dupilumab users had more exacerbations than anti-IL-5 users (weighted rate ratio 2.85) — a between-biologic comparison without a placebo arm, not a failure of dupilumab against no treatment (Kimura 2025). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme (post hoc and review evidence): dupilumab reduces exacerbations in severe eosinophilic asthma, with the effect concentrated at higher eosinophil counts; the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because the primary trials are homed on #1031 and the slice-specific evidence here is post hoc, review-level and observational.

cards.headline: Korn 2023: across placebo-controlled trials, dupilumab reduced exacerbations in severe asthma at eosinophil counts of 300/µL and above, and (300 mg dose) at 150 to under 300/µL — but not below 150/µL
cards.summary: Korn 2023: across placebo-controlled trials, dupilumab reduced exacerbations in severe asthma at eosinophil counts of 300/µL and above, and (300 mg dose) at 150 to under 300/µL — but not below 150/µL
cards.type: Systematic review (Korn 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials of US Food and Drug Administration-approved biologics in severe, uncontrolled asthma with annualised asthma exacerbation rate reduction as a primary or secondary endpoint, comparing exacerbation-rate ratios and other outcomes versus placebo across baseline blood eosinophil count (BEC) subgroups. The record does not state a total participant count for the review.
cards.result: In patients with baseline BEC of 300 cells/µL or above, exacerbation reduction was demonstrated with all biologics, and other outcomes were generally improved. In patients with BEC from 0 to under 300 cells/µL, consistent exacerbation reduction was demonstrated only with tezepelumab; in the 150 to under 300 cells/µL band, consistent reduction was demonstrated with tezepelumab and with dupilumab (300 mg dose only); in the 0 to under 150 cells/µL band, reduction was demonstrated only with tezepelumab. The authors conclude that the efficacy of all biologics in reducing exacerbations in severe asthma increases with higher baseline eosinophil count. The record reports the pattern qualitatively, without printing dupilumab's stratum-specific rate ratios.
cards.watchOut: A cross-trial descriptive review without head-to-head trials and without stratum-specific numbers in the record: it establishes where dupilumab's benefit concentrates (higher eosinophil counts), not its exact size in the eosinophilic stratum.
cards.source: Korn S et al. Efficacy of Biologics in Severe, Uncontrolled Asthma Stratified by Blood Eosinophil Count: A Systematic Review. Advances in therapy. 2023. PMID: 37233876. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Eosinophils · Anti-Asthmatic Agents · Biological Products · Asthma · Leukocyte Count · Eosinophilia · Double-Blind Method

cards.headline: Domingo 2022: in steroid-dependent severe asthma, dupilumab cut the severe exacerbation rate by 71% (relative) at lower baseline steroid doses and 48% (relative) at higher doses, and stopped steroids in 72% and 37%
cards.summary: Domingo 2022: in steroid-dependent severe asthma, dupilumab cut the severe exacerbation rate by 71% (relative) at lower baseline steroid doses and 48% (relative) at higher doses, and stopped steroids in 72% and 37%
cards.type: Post hoc analysis of a randomised controlled trial, VENTURE (Domingo 2022)
cards.people: Post hoc analysis of the phase 3 LIBERTY ASTHMA VENTURE trial (NCT02528214) in patients with oral-corticosteroid-dependent severe asthma receiving dupilumab 300 mg every 2 weeks versus placebo, categorised by baseline oral corticosteroid dose (under 10 mg/day versus 10 mg/day or more). The record does not state the subgroup participant counts.
cards.result: Dupilumab reduced daily oral corticosteroid dose from baseline at week 24 in both dose groups. The proportions who stopped corticosteroids by week 24 were 72% on dupilumab versus 42% on placebo in the under-10 mg/day group and 37% versus 23% in the 10 mg/day-or-more group (P<.01 and P<.05 respectively). Dupilumab significantly reduced the annualised severe exacerbation rate by 71% and 48% in relative terms (P<.01 and P<.05) in the two groups, and improved pre- and post-bronchodilator FEV1 at week 24 in both. The authors conclude dupilumab reduces steroid dose and exacerbations across baseline steroid-dose strata in steroid-dependent severe asthma.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc subgrouping of a single trial whose primary report is homed on live shelf #1031; the exacerbation figures are relative reductions without the absolute annualised rates printed in this record, and steroid-dependent severe asthma is a severity cut, not an eosinophil cut.
cards.source: Domingo C et al. Dupilumab Efficacy in Steroid-Dependent Severe Asthma by Baseline Oral Corticosteroid Dose. The journal of allergy and clinical immunology. In practice. 2022. PMID: 35398549. Registry ID: NCT02528214. cards.headline: Brusselle 2023: dupilumab reduced exacerbation rates by 60% (relative) in phase 2b and 72% (relative) in VENTURE in allergic asthma, with similar benefits in nonallergic asthma
cards.summary: Brusselle 2023: dupilumab reduced exacerbation rates by 60% (relative) in phase 2b and 72% (relative) in VENTURE in allergic asthma, with similar benefits in nonallergic asthma
cards.type: Post hoc analysis of randomised controlled trials, phase 2b and VENTURE (Brusselle 2023)
cards.people: Post hoc assessment of dupilumab versus placebo in the phase 2b study (NCT01854047) and phase 3 VENTURE (NCT02528214), in patients with uncontrolled moderate-to-severe or oral-corticosteroid-dependent severe asthma, stratified by allergic status (total serum IgE 30 IU/mL or above plus at least one perennial aeroallergen-specific IgE 0.35 kU/L or above). The record does not state the stratum participant counts.
cards.result: In patients with allergic asthma, dupilumab (phase 2b pooled 200/300 mg; VENTURE 300 mg) every 2 weeks versus placebo reduced the annualised severe exacerbation rate (phase 2b: -60%, P<.01; VENTURE: -72%, P<.001), and in phase 2b increased pre-bronchodilator FEV1 (P<.01) and FEV1/FVC ratio (P<.05). Dupilumab significantly improved asthma control and quality of life and reduced most type 2 biomarkers in both studies, and significantly reduced oral corticosteroid use in VENTURE. Similar benefits were observed in patients without evidence of allergic asthma. The authors conclude dupilumab reduces exacerbations and improves lung function, control and quality of life with or without allergic asthma.
cards.watchOut: Allergic status is a type-2 marker, not an eosinophil count: this card supports dupilumab's effect across type-2 phenotypes in severe asthma, while the eosinophil-specific gradient is carried by the Korn 2023 review card.
cards.source: Brusselle G et al. Dupilumab Efficacy in Patients With Uncontrolled or Oral Corticosteroid-Dependent Allergic and Nonallergic Asthma. The journal of allergy and clinical immunology. In practice. 2023. PMID: 36572184. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kimura 2025: in a Japanese cohort, patients with eosinophils of 300/µL or above on dupilumab had more exacerbations than those on anti-IL-5 biologics (weighted rate ratio 2.85) — a between-drug signal, not a placebo comparison
cards.summary: Kimura 2025: in a Japanese cohort, patients with eosinophils of 300/µL or above on dupilumab had more exacerbations than those on anti-IL-5 biologics (weighted rate ratio 2.85) — a between-drug signal, not a placebo comparison
cards.type: Retrospective cohort, comparative effectiveness (Kimura 2025)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort study using Japan's National Hospital Organization database (2016-2020) of 320 patients with asthma using biologics — 205 (64.1%) on anti-IL-5 agents (mepolizumab, benralizumab), 75 (23.4%) on omalizumab and 40 (12.5%) on dupilumab — with baseline backgrounds balanced by inverse probability treatment weighting; outcomes were asthma hospitalisations and exacerbations, overall and in eosinophil-stratified subgroups.
cards.result: After weighting, exacerbations per 100 person-years were 117.0 (anti-IL-5), 134.6 (omalizumab) and 287.3 (dupilumab); dupilumab versus anti-IL-5 weighted rate ratio 2.69 (95% CI 1.91-3.78). In patients with eosinophil counts of 300/µL or above, the dupilumab group had more exacerbations than the anti-IL-5 group (weighted rate ratio 2.85, 95% CI 1.82-4.46). In patients below 300/µL, the omalizumab group had fewer hospitalisations than the anti-IL-5 group (weighted rate ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.13-0.51). Hospitalisation rates did not significantly differ between dupilumab and anti-IL-5 overall (weighted rate ratio 1.48, 95% CI 0.81-2.72). The authors conclude anti-IL-5 biologics may be more effective than dupilumab at high eosinophil counts.
cards.watchOut: Only 40 dupilumab patients, no placebo or untreated group, and channeling bias is likely (dupilumab is often chosen for patients with nasal polyps or atopic dermatitis, or after other biologics): this card qualifies which biologic may be strongest at very high eosinophil counts; it does not show dupilumab fails against no treatment.
cards.source: Kimura Y et al. Differences in asthma-related outcomes by anti-IL-5 biologics, omalizumab, and dupilumab based on blood eosinophil counts. cards.headline: Synthesis: dupilumab reduces exacerbations in severe eosinophilic asthma — the benefit is clearest at eosinophil counts of 300/µL and above, and one comparative cohort favours anti-IL-5 drugs in exactly that stratum
cards.summary: Synthesis: dupilumab reduces exacerbations in severe eosinophilic asthma — the benefit is clearest at eosinophil counts of 300/µL and above, and one comparative cohort favours anti-IL-5 drugs in exactly that stratum
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one systematic review of placebo-controlled biologic trials stratified by eosinophil count (total N not documented in the record), two post hoc analyses of the dupilumab trial programme in severe and steroid-dependent asthma (subgroup Ns not documented in the records), and one eosinophil-stratified comparative cohort (320 patients, 40 on dupilumab). Because several records do not document participant counts, a summed total N cannot be honestly printed; the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE for a single trial programme instead.
cards.result: Exacerbation reduction with dupilumab was demonstrated at baseline eosinophil counts of 300 cells/µL or above and, at the 300 mg dose, at 150 to under 300 cells/µL, but not below 150 cells/µL (Korn 2023). In steroid-dependent severe asthma, relative exacerbation reductions were 71% and 48% by baseline steroid-dose stratum (Domingo 2022), and 60%-72% (relative) in allergic asthma across phase 2b and VENTURE (Brusselle 2023). Against anti-IL-5 biologics rather than placebo, dupilumab users with eosinophils of 300/µL or above had a higher exacerbation rate (weighted rate ratio 2.85; Kimura 2025). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme, as a partial completion of live shelf #1031, whose cards home the primary QUEST and VENTURE reports including the QUEST eosinophil strata.
cards.watchOut: FLAG for the developer: this pack is built under the one-home precedent for homed anchors — the QUEST/VENTURE primary reports stay homed on #1031 and are cross-pointed in prose only; if the developer prefers the eosinophil strata to live only on #1031, this pack should be dropped rather than re-carded.

shelves.title: FeNO-guided asthma treatment in adults (partial completion of #1728): pooled trials show fewer exacerbations (odds ratio about 0.6) and no other benefit — useful for frequent exacerbators, not a universal guide
shelves.question: Should fractional exhaled nitric oxide guide asthma treatment adjustments in adults?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Pregnancy · Asthma · Inflammation · Nitric Oxide · Fractional Exhaled Nitric Oxide Testing
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1728 covers FeNO-guided treatment in adolescents and young adults; this shelf answers the same question for adults generally. Two meta-analytic generations agree on a narrow benefit: the Cochrane adult review found fewer patients with one or more exacerbations on FeNO-guided care (odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.43-0.84; number needed to treat 12 over 52 weeks) but no difference in hospitalisation, rescue steroid courses, symptoms, lung function or final inhaled steroid dose — and its authors state the universal use of FeNO to guide therapy in adults cannot be advocated (Petsky 2016). The 2023 update, pooling 12 adult trials and 2,116 patients, found the same pattern (odds ratio 0.61 for having an exacerbation; rate ratio 0.67) with no demonstrable effect on severe exacerbations, quality of life, FEV1 or treatment dose (Korevaar 2023). The two landmark single trials are individually null on exacerbations: Smith 2005 achieved a much lower final steroid dose on FeNO guidance (370 vs 641 µg/day) with a non-significant 45.6% relative exacerbation reduction, and Shaw 2007 found no significant difference in severe exacerbations (-21%, 95% CI -57% to 43%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): FeNO-guided adjustment probably prevents some exacerbations in adults — most plausibly in those with frequent exacerbations — without improving day-to-day control, and the evidence does not support it as a universal routine.

cards.headline: Petsky 2016 (Cochrane, adults): FeNO-guided treatment cut the odds of having one or more exacerbations (odds ratio 0.60; NNT 12 over 52 weeks) but changed nothing else — the authors say universal use cannot be advocated
cards.summary: Petsky 2016 (Cochrane, adults): FeNO-guided treatment cut the odds of having one or more exacerbations (odds ratio 0.60; NNT 12 over 52 weeks) but changed nothing else — the authors say universal use cannot be advocated
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, Cochrane (Petsky 2016)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials comparing adjustment of asthma medication based on exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) against management based on clinical symptoms (with or without spirometry/peak flow) or guidelines, in adults. Seven adult studies were included; of 1,700 randomised participants, 1,546 completed the trials; mean ages ranged from 28 to 54 years; FeNO cut-offs used ranged from 15 to 35 ppb and study duration from 4 to 12 months.
cards.result: The number of people having one or more asthma exacerbations was significantly lower in the FeNO group (odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.84), with a number needed to treat to benefit of 12 (95% CI 8 to 32) over 52 weeks; the exacerbation rate was also lower (rate ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.77). There was no difference for exacerbations requiring hospitalisation (odds ratio 0.14, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.67) or rescue oral corticosteroids (odds ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.48), and no significant difference in FEV1, FeNO levels, symptom scores or inhaled corticosteroid dose at final visit. Evidence quality ranged from moderate (exacerbations) to very low. The authors conclude FeNO tailoring decreased exacerbation frequency but did not affect symptoms, FeNO levels or steroid dose, so universal use in adults cannot be advocated; the intervention may be most useful in adults with frequent exacerbations.
cards.watchOut: The included trials differed in exacerbation definitions, FeNO cut-offs (15-35 ppb) and adjustment algorithms, three had inadequate blinding, and six of seven were industry supported — the pooled exacerbation benefit is real but its size depends on protocol choices no consensus has settled.
cards.source: Petsky HL et al. Exhaled nitric oxide levels to guide treatment for adults with asthma. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016. PMID: 27580628. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Korevaar 2023: updating Cochrane with 12 adult trials (2,116 patients), FeNO guidance probably reduces exacerbations (odds ratio 0.61; rate ratio 0.67) with no demonstrable effect on severe exacerbations or lung function
cards.summary: Korevaar 2023: updating Cochrane with 12 adult trials (2,116 patients), FeNO guidance probably reduces exacerbations (odds ratio 0.61; rate ratio 0.67) with no demonstrable effect on severe exacerbations or lung function
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Korevaar 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis updating the 2016 Cochrane review (search to 9 May 2023), including 12 randomised controlled trials (2,116 patients) comparing FeNO-guided treatment with usual symptom-guided treatment in adult asthma patients. All trials showed high or unclear risk of bias in at least one domain; five reported support from a FeNO manufacturer.
cards.result: FeNO-guided treatment probably reduces the number of patients having one or more exacerbations (odds ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.83; six trials; GRADE moderate certainty) and the exacerbation rate (rate ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.82; six trials; moderate certainty), and may slightly improve Asthma Control Questionnaire score (mean difference -0.10, 95% CI -0.18 to -0.02; six trials; low certainty) — a change the authors judge unlikely to be clinically important. An effect on severe exacerbations, quality of life, FEV1, treatment dosage and FeNO values could not be demonstrated. Subgroup analyses (severity, control, atopy, pregnancy, obesity) showed no clear differences, though subgroup evidence was limited.
cards.watchOut: An update of the same trial pool as the Cochrane card (the two reviews overlap and must not be summed): its value is showing the exacerbation signal survived seven more years of trials while every other outcome stayed null.
cards.source: Korevaar DA et al. Effectiveness of FeNO-guided treatment in adult asthma patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical and experimental allergy : journal of the British Society for Allergy and Clinical Immunology. 2023. PMID: 37293870. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Smith 2005: FeNO guidance let patients finish on 270 µg/day less inhaled steroid (370 vs 641 µg/day, P=0.003) with a non-significant 45.6% relative reduction in exacerbations
cards.summary: Smith 2005: FeNO guidance let patients finish on 270 µg/day less inhaled steroid (370 vs 641 µg/day, P=0.003) with a non-significant 45.6% relative reduction in exacerbations
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Smith 2005)
cards.people: Single-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial of 97 patients with asthma regularly receiving inhaled corticosteroids, assigned to stepwise corticosteroid dose adjustment based on FeNO measurements or on a conventional-guidelines algorithm; after dose optimisation, patients were followed for 12 months. Forty-six FeNO-group and 48 control-group patients completed the study. Primary outcome: frequency of asthma exacerbations.
cards.result: Final mean daily fluticasone doses were 370 µg/day (95% CI 263 to 477) in the FeNO group and 641 µg/day (95% CI 526 to 756) in the control group (P=0.003) — a difference of 270 µg/day (95% CI 112 to 430). Exacerbation rates were 0.49 episodes per patient per year (95% CI 0.20 to 0.78) in the FeNO group and 0.90 (95% CI 0.31 to 1.49) in the control group, a non-significant reduction of 45.6% (95% CI for the difference -78.6% to 54.5%). There were no significant differences in other markers of asthma control, oral prednisone use, pulmonary function or sputum eosinophils. The authors conclude FeNO measurements allow maintenance inhaled steroid doses to be significantly reduced without compromising asthma control.
cards.watchOut: The trial's win was steroid sparing at equal control, not fewer exacerbations — its confidence interval for exacerbations spans from a 78.6% reduction to a 54.5% increase, so it cannot carry an exacerbation claim on its own.
cards.source: Smith AD et al. Use of exhaled nitric oxide measurements to guide treatment in chronic asthma. The New England journal of medicine. 2005. PMID: 15914548. cards.headline: Shaw 2007: FeNO-based titration made no significant difference to severe exacerbations (-21%, 95% CI -57% to 43%) or total steroid use over 12 months in primary care
cards.summary: Shaw 2007: FeNO-based titration made no significant difference to severe exacerbations (-21%, 95% CI -57% to 43%) or total steroid use over 12 months in primary care
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Shaw 2007)
cards.people: Single-blind randomised controlled trial of 118 participants with a primary care diagnosis of asthma, randomised to corticosteroid therapy titrated on FeNO measurements (n=58) or on British Thoracic Society guidelines (n=60), assessed monthly for 4 months then every 2 months for 8 months. Primary outcome: number of severe asthma exacerbations; analysis by intention to treat. Trial registration ISRCTN08067387.
cards.result: Mean exacerbation frequency was 0.33 per patient per year (SD 0.69) in the FeNO group and 0.42 (SD 0.79) in the control group (mean difference -21%; 95% CI -57% to 43%; P=0.43) — the treatment made no significant difference. Overall the FeNO group used 11% more inhaled corticosteroid (95% CI -17% to 42%; P=0.40), although the final daily dose was lower in the FeNO group (557 vs 895 µg; mean difference 338 µg, 95% CI -640 to -37; P=0.028). The authors conclude a FeNO-based strategy did not produce a large reduction in exacerbations or in total inhaled corticosteroid use compared with guideline management.
cards.watchOut: A null single trial does not erase the pooled result — but it shows the pooled benefit is an average of small, protocol-dependent effects, and in this primary-care population with few severe exacerbations there was little room to show one.
cards.source: Shaw DE et al. The use of exhaled nitric oxide to guide asthma management: a randomized controlled trial. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2007. PMID: 17496226. Registry ID: ISRCTN08067387. cards.headline: Synthesis: pooled adult evidence says FeNO guidance prevents some exacerbations (odds ratio about 0.6) and nothing else — a targeted tool for frequent exacerbators, not a universal guide
cards.summary: Synthesis: pooled adult evidence says FeNO guidance prevents some exacerbations (odds ratio about 0.6) and nothing else — a targeted tool for frequent exacerbators, not a universal guide
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: two overlapping meta-analyses of adult randomised trials (7 trials/1,700 randomised in 2016; 12 trials/2,116 patients in 2023 — overlapping pools, not additive) and the two landmark single trials (97 and 118 randomised patients). Total unique randomised participants are those of the 2023 pool, 2,116, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: FeNO-guided care reduced the odds of one or more exacerbations (odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.43-0.84, Cochrane 2016; 0.61, 95% CI 0.44-0.83, Korevaar 2023) and the exacerbation rate (rate ratios 0.59 and 0.67), with no demonstrated effect on severe exacerbations, hospitalisation, symptoms, FEV1 or final steroid dose. Individually, Smith 2005 traded a significantly lower final steroid dose for a non-significant exacerbation reduction, and Shaw 2007 found no significant difference on either. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), as a partial completion of live shelf #1728 (adolescents and young adults).
cards.watchOut: FeNO cut-offs and adjustment algorithms varied across every trial (15-35 ppb): 'FeNO-guided' is a family of protocols, and the pooled benefit cannot tell a clinician which cut-off to use.

shelves.question: Is bronchial thermoplasty effective for severe asthma that does not respond to biologics?

shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion, built honestly on the evidence status: live shelf #1036 covers bronchial thermoplasty (BT) in severe asthma on inhaled therapy; this shelf asks about the population #1036 does not — patients whose severe asthma has not responded to biologics. The desk-check finding, stated plainly: no randomised trial, and no study of any design carded here, has enrolled patients specifically because they failed a biologic and then tested BT in them. What exists is observational evidence in refractory populations where biologic exposure was common. In the Australian BT Registry, 43% of 77 severe patients had already been treated with a monoclonal antibody before BT, and the cohort as a whole improved markedly (Asthma Control Questionnaire 3.2 to 1.6 at 6 months; exacerbations in the prior 6 months 3.7 to 0.7; 48.8% of steroid-dependent patients weaned off oral steroids entirely) — but outcomes were not reported separately for the post-biologic subgroup (Langton 2020). In an Italian real-world series, the 30 BT patients — who started worse than the biologic groups — achieved reductions in hospitalisations (93.7%) and exacerbations (73.5%) comparable to the biologic arms over 12 months (Menzella 2021). A 15-patient Japanese cohort (N on the face) found BT improved symptoms even in refractory asthma with severe airflow limitation (Inoue 2024). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: BT can help selected patients with refractory severe asthma, many of them biologic-experienced, but its effectiveness specifically after biologic failure has never been directly tested, and this shelf must not be read as if it has.

cards.headline: Langton 2020: in a 77-patient severe-asthma registry where 43% had already received a monoclonal antibody, bronchial thermoplasty halved symptom scores and cut exacerbations from 3.7 to 0.7 per 6 months
cards.summary: Langton 2020: in a 77-patient severe-asthma registry where 43% had already received a monoclonal antibody, bronchial thermoplasty halved symptom scores and cut exacerbations from 3.7 to 0.7 per 6 months
cards.type: Registry cohort, before-and-after outcomes (Langton 2020)
cards.people: Seventy-seven consecutive patients in the Australian Bronchial Thermoplasty Registry with severe asthma (mean age 57.7 ± 11.4 years, 57.1% female, 53.2% taking maintenance oral steroids, 43% previously treated with a monoclonal antibody, mean FEV1 55.8% ± 19.8% predicted). Outcomes were measured at 6 and 12 months after bronchial thermoplasty: Asthma Control Questionnaire (ACQ) score, exacerbation frequency, short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) requirement, oral corticosteroid use and spirometry.
cards.result: Asthma Control Questionnaire score improved from 3.2 ± 1.0 at baseline to 1.6 ± 1.1 at 6 months (P<.001). Exacerbation frequency in the previous 6 months fell from 3.7 ± 3.3 to 0.7 ± 1.2 (P<.001). SABA requirement fell from 9.3 ± 7.1 to 3.5 ± 6.0 puffs/day (P<.001), 48.8% of patients were weaned completely off oral steroids, and FEV1 improved significantly. Baseline ACQ score strongly predicted improvement; patients with more than two exacerbations in the previous 6 months showed the greatest exacerbation reduction (-5.3 ± 2.8; P<.001). Outcomes for the 43% with prior monoclonal-antibody treatment were not reported separately in the record.
cards.watchOut: A before-and-after registry analysis with no control group: regression to the mean and concurrent care changes inflate apparent benefit, and — critically for this shelf — the post-biologic patients are inside the cohort but their separate results are not in the record.
cards.source: Langton D et al. Predicting the Response to Bronchial Thermoplasty. The journal of allergy and clinical immunology. In practice. 2020. PMID: 31712191. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Menzella 2021 (BIOTERM): 30 bronchial-thermoplasty patients who started worse than the biologic groups still cut hospitalisations by 93.7% and exacerbations by 73.5% over 12 months
cards.summary: Menzella 2021 (BIOTERM): 30 bronchial-thermoplasty patients who started worse than the biologic groups still cut hospitalisations by 93.7% and exacerbations by 73.5% over 12 months
cards.type: Real-world comparative cohort (Menzella 2021, BIOTERM)
cards.people: Real-world Italian evaluation of 199 consecutive patients with severe refractory asthma, selected by eligibility criteria for all available biologics and bronchial thermoplasty (BT), treated with omalizumab (54 patients), mepolizumab (83), benralizumab (32) or BT (30), and observed for 12 months. The BT group's starting point was worse than the biologic groups for hospitalisations, exacerbations and oral corticosteroid use.
cards.result: In the BT subgroup (30 patients), hospitalisations fell by 93.7% (P=0.001) and exacerbations by 73.5% (P<0.0001) over 12 months, and BT achieved the second-largest oral-steroid-sparing effect (-76%, P<0.0001, versus -90.2% for mepolizumab). For comparison, exacerbation reductions were 66.6% with benralizumab, 88.8% with omalizumab and 92.1% with mepolizumab. The authors conclude that all biologics reduced hospitalisations, exacerbations and steroid use to varying degrees, and that BT — despite its group starting worse — obtained positive results comparable to biologics.
cards.watchOut: Non-randomised, with treatment chosen clinically and groups differing at baseline; the BT patients were biologic-eligible refractory patients, not documented biologic failures — this is evidence about refractory asthma broadly, not about the post-failure sequence.
cards.source: Menzella F et al. A Real-World Evaluation of Clinical Outcomes of Biologicals and Bronchial Thermoplasty for Severe Refractory Asthma (BIOTERM). Journal of asthma and allergy. 2021. PMID: 34413654. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Inoue 2024: in 15 patients with refractory asthma (N on the face), bronchial thermoplasty improved symptoms and quality of life even when FEV1 was under 60% predicted
cards.summary: Inoue 2024: in 15 patients with refractory asthma (N on the face), bronchial thermoplasty improved symptoms and quality of life even when FEV1 was under 60% predicted
cards.type: Retrospective observational cohort (Inoue 2024)
cards.people: Single-centre retrospective observational cohort of 15 patients with refractory asthma (Global Initiative for Asthma step 4 or 5) who underwent bronchial thermoplasty between June 2016 and January 2022, including patients with severely impaired airflow limitation (pre-bronchodilator FEV1 under 60% predicted; group 1, n=6) versus FEV1 of 60% or above (group 2, n=9). Clinical characteristics, type-2 inflammation and concurrent treatment were equivalent between groups. Total N = 15.
cards.result: Bronchial thermoplasty significantly improved asthma-related symptoms (Asthma Control Test and Asthma Quality of Life Questionnaire scores) in both groups. FEV1 improved significantly in group 1 (severe obstruction) but not group 2. Four patients in group 2, and none in group 1, had an exacerbation requiring additional systemic corticosteroids after treatment, including two requiring prolonged hospitalisation. Long-term responders (reduced systemic or inhaled corticosteroid without newly adding biologics over more than 2 years of follow-up) were 2 of 6 (33.3%) in group 1 and 4 of 9 (44.4%) in group 2. The authors conclude BT in refractory asthma with severe airflow limitation is as safe and efficacious as in moderate airflow limitation.
cards.watchOut: Fifteen patients from one centre, retrospectively reviewed, with no comparator: this card shows BT is feasible and can coincide with improvement in very obstructed refractory patients; it cannot estimate an effect size for anyone, let alone for post-biologic patients.
cards.source: Inoue T et al. Safety and efficacy of bronchial thermoplasty in refractory asthma with severe obstructive respiratory dysfunction. Therapeutic advances in respiratory disease. 2024. PMID: 38804685. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: no study has tested bronchial thermoplasty specifically after biologic failure — the honest answer is 'untested in that exact population, with supportive observational evidence in refractory asthma'
cards.summary: Synthesis: no study has tested bronchial thermoplasty specifically after biologic failure — the honest answer is 'untested in that exact population, with supportive observational evidence in refractory asthma'
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: a 77-patient national registry cohort (43% monoclonal-antibody-experienced), a 199-patient real-world comparative cohort (30 bronchial thermoplasty patients), and a 15-patient single-centre cohort — 291 unique participants in total, so no small-N stamp labelling applies, though every design is observational and none isolates post-biologic-failure patients.
cards.result: After bronchial thermoplasty, registry patients' symptom scores improved from 3.2 to 1.6 and exacerbations fell from 3.7 to 0.7 per 6 months, with 48.8% of steroid-dependent patients weaned off oral steroids (Langton 2020); real-world thermoplasty patients cut hospitalisations by 93.7% and exacerbations by 73.5% (Menzella 2021); symptom benefit extended to patients with FEV1 under 60% predicted (Inoue 2024). No carded record enrolled patients on the basis of biologic non-response or reported that subgroup's outcomes separately. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, as a partial completion of live shelf #1036.
cards.watchOut: FLAG for the developer: the brief anticipated this gap ('build the shelf honestly on that evidence status') — the shelf is an evidence-status shelf. If a trial or cohort in documented biologic non-responders appears, this pack should be re-cut around it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Langton D et al. The journal of allergy and clinical immunology. In practice. 2020 (PMID: 31712191); Menzella F et al. Journal of asthma and allergy. 2021 (PMID: 34413654); Inoue T et al. Therapeutic advances in respiratory disease. 2024 (PMID: 38804685).

shelves.title: Prednisone duration for a home-treated COPD exacerbation (partial completion of #3926): 5 vs 14 days has never been tested at home — and the one home trial of 5 days found no benefit over placebo
shelves.question: How many days of prednisone are needed for a COPD exacerbation treated at home, 5 days or 14 days?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Aged · Ambulatory Care · Double-Blind Method · Emergency Treatment · Female · Glucocorticoids · Humans · Male · Prednisone · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Quality of Life · Secondary Prevention · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion, built honestly on the evidence status: live shelf #3926 homes REDUCE, the hospital trial that found 5 days of glucocorticoid non-inferior to 14 days in hospitalised exacerbations; this shelf asks whether that answer transfers to exacerbations treated at home — and the desk-check finding is that the 5-versus-14-day comparison has never been run in home-treated patients in any record fetched this session. The home evidence that exists cuts at a more basic question. A 10-day course of prednisone after emergency-department discharge modestly reduced 30-day relapse versus placebo (27% vs 43%, P=0.05; Aaron 2003, 147 patients). But the only primary-care trial of a 5-day course found prednisone no better than placebo — treatment failure was 42.0% versus 34.5% (relative risk 1.22, P=0.25), with respiratory-related failure significantly higher on prednisone (27.6% vs 13.6%; relative risk 2.00) — in a trial that reached only 43% of its planned sample (Thebault 2023, 175 patients). The one trial designed to optimise duration at home compares 3 days against 5, not 5 against 14, and its record is a protocol with no results (Urwyler 2019, RECUT, NCT02386735). So the honest answer to '5 or 14?' at home is: 14 days has no supporting evidence in this setting at all, 5 days is the longest course with any home-trial pedigree — and whether even 5 days helps a mild primary-care exacerbation is genuinely in doubt. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): no home-treated trial compares 5 with 14 days; practice extrapolates the hospital answer, while the one home trial of 5 days found no benefit over placebo.

cards.headline: Thebault 2023: at home in primary care, 5 days of prednisone was no better than placebo — treatment failure 42.0% vs 34.5% (the treatment made no difference), with respiratory failure significantly worse on prednisone
cards.summary: Thebault 2023: at home in primary care, 5 days of prednisone was no better than placebo — treatment failure 42.0% vs 34.5% (the treatment made no difference), with respiratory failure significantly worse on prednisone
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, primary care outpatients (Thebault 2023)
cards.people: Multicentre, parallel, double-blind, pragmatic randomised controlled trial in France: 66 general practitioners enrolled patients aged 40 years or older with at least 10 pack-years of smoking and a diagnosis of certain or likely acute COPD exacerbation treated as outpatients. Oral prednisone 40 mg or placebo was given daily for 5 days. The main outcome was treatment failure at 8 weeks (unplanned emergency or ambulatory visit, hospital admission, or death). A total of 175 patients were included — 43% of the planned sample size of 202 per group.
cards.result: The all-cause 8-week treatment failure rate was 42.0% in the prednisone group and 34.5% in the placebo group (relative risk 1.22, 95% CI 0.87-1.69, P=0.25) — the treatment made no difference. The respiratory-related 8-week treatment failure rate was 27.6% on prednisone versus 13.6% on placebo (relative risk 2.00, 95% CI 1.15-3.57, P=0.015). The authors conclude that, although the planned sample size was not achieved, the study does not suggest oral corticosteroids are more effective than placebo for an acute COPD exacerbation treated in primary care.
cards.watchOut: Underpowered (43% of planned recruitment) and in milder, GP-diagnosed exacerbations ('certain or likely'), so it does not prove steroids useless at home — but it removes any assumption that the hospital steroid benefit automatically transfers to the home setting on which a 5-vs-14 choice would rest.
cards.source: Thebault JL et al. Efficacy and safety of oral corticosteroids to treat outpatients with acute exacerbations of COPD in primary care: a multicentre pragmatic randomised controlled study. ERJ open research. 2023. PMID: 37701369. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Aaron 2003: after emergency-department discharge, 10 days of prednisone cut 30-day relapse from 43% to 27% (P=0.05) — the only positive home-course trial, and it tested 10 days, not 5 or 14
cards.summary: Aaron 2003: after emergency-department discharge, 10 days of prednisone cut 30-day relapse from 43% to 27% (P=0.05) — the only positive home-course trial, and it tested 10 days, not 5 or 14
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, emergency-department outpatients (Aaron 2003)
cards.people: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial of 147 patients discharged from the emergency department after a COPD exacerbation, assigned to 10 days of oral prednisone 40 mg once daily or identical placebo. All patients received oral antibiotics for 10 days plus inhaled bronchodilators. The primary endpoint was relapse — an unscheduled office visit or return to the emergency department for worsening dyspnoea — within 30 days.
cards.result: The overall 30-day relapse rate was lower on prednisone than placebo (27% vs 43%, P=0.05), and time to relapse was prolonged (P=0.04). After 10 days, the prednisone group had greater improvement in FEV1 (mean increase from baseline 34% ± 42% vs 15% ± 31%, P=0.007) and significant improvements in dyspnoea scores (P=0.04 and P=0.02), but not in health-related quality of life (P=0.14). The authors conclude outpatient prednisone offers a small advantage over placebo after emergency treatment of a COPD exacerbation.
cards.watchOut: These patients had exacerbations severe enough to reach an emergency department — a step up from the purely home-managed exacerbation — and the tested course was 10 days against placebo, so the trial supports 'some steroid versus none' in that setting, not any particular duration.
cards.source: Aaron SD et al. Outpatient oral prednisone after emergency treatment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2003. PMID: 12826636. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Urwyler 2019 (RECUT): the only trial designed to optimise steroid duration in outpatients compares 3 days with 5 — and its record is a protocol with no results, so the home duration question is still open
cards.summary: Urwyler 2019 (RECUT): the only trial designed to optimise steroid duration in outpatients compares 3 days with 5 — and its record is a protocol with no results, so the home duration question is still open
cards.type: Study protocol, no results (Urwyler 2019, RECUT)
cards.people: Protocol for a prospective double-blind randomised non-inferiority trial in Swiss primary care (RECUT, NCT02386735), planning to recruit 470 patients with acutely exacerbated COPD, randomised to prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days (conventional arm, n=235) or for 3 days followed by 2 days of placebo (experimental arm, n=235). The primary endpoint is time to next exacerbation during 6 months of follow-up. The protocol states that no data are available on the optimum duration of corticosteroid treatment in primary-care patients with acute COPD exacerbations.
cards.result: No outcome results are reported — this is a study protocol. Its stated rationale is that the additional benefit of corticosteroids appears most apparent in the first 3 to 5 days, that inpatient guidelines recommend 5 to 7 days, and that the optimum duration in outpatients is unknown; the trial is designed to test whether 3 days is non-inferior to the conventional 5 days in outpatients. Even when it reports, it will compare 3 against 5 days — the 14-day course of the hospital era is not under test in the home setting in any record fetched this session.
cards.watchOut: A protocol card is evidence about the state of the science, not about prednisone: it is carded so the shelf does not pretend the 5-versus-14-day home question has been tested, and it must never be cited as a trial result.
cards.source: Urwyler P et al. Reduction of corticosteroid use in outpatient treatment of exacerbated COPD - Study protocol for a randomized, double-blind, non-inferiority study, (The RECUT-trial). Trials. 2019. PMID: 31842993. Registry ID: NCT02386735. study protocol, no results (urwyler 2019, recut) protocol for a prospective double-blind randomised non-inferiority trial in swiss primary care (recut, nct02386735), planning to recruit 470 patients with acutely exacerbated copd, randomised to prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days (conventional arm, n=235) or for 3 days followed by 2 days of placebo (experimental arm, n=235). the primary endpoint is time to next exacerbation during 6 months of follow-up. the protocol states that no data are available on the optimum duration of corticosteroid treatment in primary-care patients with acute copd exacerbations. no outcome results are reported — this is a study protocol. its stated rationale is that the additional benefit of corticosteroids appears most apparent in the first 3 to 5 days, that inpatient guidelines recommend 5 to 7 days, and that the optimum duration in outpatients is unknown; the trial is designed to test whether 3 days is non-inferior to the conventional 5 days in outpatients. even when it reports, it will compare 3 against 5 days — the 14-day course of the hospital era is not under test in the home setting in any record fetched this session. a protocol card is evidence about the state of the science, not about prednisone: it is carded so the shelf does not pretend the 5-versus-14-day home question has been tested, and it must never be cited as a trial result. urwyler p et al. reduction of corticosteroid use in outpatient treatment of exacerbated copd - study protocol for a randomized, double-blind, non-inferiority study, (the recut-trial). trials. 2019. pmid: 31842993. registry id: nct02386735. mesh: administration, oral · adrenal cortex hormones · ambulatory care · disease progression · double-blind method · drug administration schedule · equivalence trials as topic · female · forced expiratory volume · humans · lung · male · prednisone · prospective studies · pulmonary disease, chronic obstructive · switzerland · time factors · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: nobody has randomised home-treated patients to 5 versus 14 days — the home literature tests steroids against placebo (one positive 10-day trial, one null 5-day trial) and is now testing 3 versus 5
cards.summary: Synthesis: nobody has randomised home-treated patients to 5 versus 14 days — the home literature tests steroids against placebo (one positive 10-day trial, one null 5-day trial) and is now testing 3 versus 5
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: two home/outpatient randomised trials against placebo (175 primary-care patients on a 5-day course; 147 emergency-department discharges on a 10-day course) and one duration-trial protocol (470 planned, 3 vs 5 days, no results). Total randomised participants across the two completed trials = 322, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is the missing comparison, not sample size.
cards.result: Five days of prednisone at home made no difference to 8-week treatment failure versus placebo (42.0% vs 34.5%; relative risk 1.22; Thebault 2023), while 10 days after emergency discharge reduced 30-day relapse (27% vs 43%; Aaron 2003). No record fetched this session compares any two durations in home-treated patients, and the one duration trial in progress compares 3 with 5 days (Urwyler 2019). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence), as a partial completion of live shelf #3926 (which homes the 5-vs-14-day answer for hospitalised exacerbations only).
cards.watchOut: FLAG for the developer: this is an evidence-absence shelf by design — the brief's slice (home-treated 5 vs 14 days) has no direct trial. If the developer prefers not to shelve untested comparisons, this is the pack to drop; if shelved, its MAYBE stamp and this flag are the honest labelling.
cards.source: Synthesis of Thebault JL et al. ERJ open research. 2023 (PMID: 37701369); Aaron SD et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2003 (PMID: 12826636); Urwyler P et al. Trials. 2019 (PMID: 31842993).

shelves.title: Home ventilation in stable hypercapnic COPD (partial completion of #1645): SPLIT — targeted high-intensity ventilation cut 1-year mortality from 33% to 12%, while unselected stable-patient trials showed no survival benefit
shelves.question: Does home noninvasive ventilation improve survival in adults with stable hypercapnic COPD?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Austria · Blood Gas Monitoring, Transcutaneous · Female · Germany · Humans · Hypercapnia · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Noninvasive Ventilation · Positive-Pressure Respiration · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Severity of Illness Index · Survival Rate · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1645 covers home ventilation started after an exacerbation in patients with persistent post-exacerbation hypercapnia; this shelf answers the different population #1645 does not — patients with stable hypercapnic COPD and no recent exacerbation. The evidence genuinely divides, and the dividing line is how the ventilation is delivered. The one large targeted trial, which set ventilators to reduce PaCO2 by at least 20%, found a striking survival benefit in stable stage IV disease: 1-year mortality 12% versus 33% (hazard ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.11-0.49; Köhnlein 2014, 195 patients). But the earlier meta-analysis that separated stable from post-hospital patients found no survival benefit in the stable subgroup (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.55-1.43 across 7 trials; Dretzke 2016) — its included trials largely predated high-intensity, CO2-targeted ventilation. The most recent meta-analysis (19 trials, 1,482 patients) finds an overall mortality reduction (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.61-0.95) that concentrates exactly where Köhnlein aimed: baseline PaCO2 of 55 mmHg or above (relative risk 0.69) and larger achieved PaCO2 reductions (relative risk 0.42), with no significant benefit below those marks (Wu 2022). PROPOSED SPLIT — survival benefit is demonstrated when home ventilation is high-intensity and targeted at marked hypercapnia (one definitive trial plus the PaCO2-defined subgroups of the latest meta-analysis), while unselected stable-hypercapnia trials pooled in 2016 showed no benefit (the treatment made no difference): patient selection and ventilator targeting, not the machine alone, decide the answer.

cards.headline: Köhnlein 2014: home ventilation targeted to cut PaCO2 by at least 20% reduced 1-year mortality from 33% to 12% in stable hypercapnic COPD (hazard ratio 0.24)
cards.summary: Köhnlein 2014: home ventilation targeted to cut PaCO2 by at least 20% reduced 1-year mortality from 33% to 12% in stable hypercapnic COPD (hazard ratio 0.24)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Köhnlein 2014)
cards.people: Investigator-initiated, prospective, multicentre, randomised, controlled trial (NCT00710541) in 36 respiratory units in Germany and Austria, enrolling 195 patients with stable GOLD stage IV COPD, PaCO2 of 7 kPa (51.9 mmHg) or higher and pH above 7.35. Patients were randomised 1:1 to optimised standard treatment alone (n=93) or with additional long-term non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NPPV) for at least 12 months (n=102), with NPPV targeted to reduce baseline PaCO2 by at least 20% or to below 6.5 kPa (48.1 mmHg). The primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality, analysed by intention to treat; the intervention was unblinded but outcome assessment was blinded.
cards.result: One-year mortality was 12% (12 of 102 patients) in the NPPV group and 33% (31 of 93 patients) in the control group (hazard ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.11-0.49, P=0.0004). Fourteen patients (14%) reported facial skin rash, managed by changing mask type; no other intervention-related adverse events were reported. The authors conclude that adding long-term NPPV to standard treatment improves survival in hypercapnic stable COPD when NPPV is targeted to greatly reduce hypercapnia.
cards.watchOut: A single trial with an unusually large effect (hazard ratio 0.24) in very severe (stage IV) disease, using high-intensity settings most earlier trials did not use: the result supports targeted ventilation in markedly hypercapnic patients, not any home ventilator for any stable patient.
cards.source: Köhnlein T et al. Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation for the treatment of severe stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a prospective, multicentre, randomised, controlled clinical trial. The Lancet. cards.headline: Dretzke 2016: in stable patients specifically, domiciliary ventilation showed no survival benefit (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.55-1.43, 7 trials) — the post-hospital signal came from non-randomised studies
cards.summary: Dretzke 2016: in stable patients specifically, domiciliary ventilation showed no survival benefit (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.55-1.43, 7 trials) — the post-hospital signal came from non-randomised studies
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Dretzke 2016)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis (search to September 2014) of 31 randomised and non-randomised studies of domiciliary noninvasive ventilation versus usual care in COPD, stratified by a proxy for exacerbation risk: patients in a stable state versus patients immediately post-exacerbation hospitalisation. Outcomes were hospital admissions, mortality and health-related quality of life.
cards.result: For stable patients, there was no evidence of a survival benefit from noninvasive ventilation (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.55-1.43, I2=60.4%, 7 randomised trials) — the treatment made no difference — though there was a possible trend toward fewer hospitalisations (weighted mean difference -0.46, 95% CI -1.02 to 0.09, 5 trials) and improved quality of life. For post-hospital patients, survival benefit could not be demonstrated in the three randomised trials (relative risk 0.89, 95% CI 0.53-1.49) but appeared in four non-randomised studies (relative risk 0.45, 95% CI 0.32-0.65). Post hoc analyses suggested improvements in hypercapnia were associated with reduced admissions across both populations. The authors conclude the effectiveness of domiciliary ventilation remains uncertain and that optimum settings and timing need to be established.
cards.watchOut: This review's stable-patient pool largely predates CO2-targeted high-intensity ventilation and mixes settings and severities (heterogeneity I2=60.4%): its null is a fair summary of the older, untargeted literature, not a refutation of the targeted approach tested by Köhnlein.
cards.source: Dretzke J et al. The effect of domiciliary noninvasive ventilation on clinical outcomes in stable and recently hospitalized patients with COPD: a systematic review and meta-analysis. International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. 2016. PMID: 27698560. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wu 2022: pooling 19 trials (1,482 patients), home ventilation reduced mortality (relative risk 0.76) — but the benefit tracked baseline PaCO2 of 55 mmHg or above and the size of the PaCO2 fall
cards.summary: Wu 2022: pooling 19 trials (1,482 patients), home ventilation reduced mortality (relative risk 0.76) — but the benefit tracked baseline PaCO2 of 55 mmHg or above and the size of the PaCO2 fall
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Wu 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis (search January 1980 to June 2020) of 19 randomised clinical trials involving 1,482 patients with stable hypercapnic COPD (730 receiving long-term home noninvasive positive pressure ventilation, 752 controls), comparing home ventilation with control treatment; the main outcome was mortality, with evidence quality assessed by GRADE.
cards.result: Long-term home ventilation significantly reduced mortality (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.61-0.95, P=0.02, I2=14%), hospital admissions and PaCO2, and improved PaO2, dyspnoea, exercise capacity and quality of life, with no significant benefit for FEV1 percent predicted. In subgroup analysis, the mortality benefit was associated with baseline PaCO2 of 55 mmHg or above (relative risk 0.69, P=0.02) versus below 55 mmHg (relative risk 0.87, P=0.32), and with a larger achieved PaCO2 reduction (relative risk 0.42, P<0.0001) versus a smaller reduction (relative risk 0.91, P=0.38). The authors conclude large multicentre randomised trials are still needed to confirm the findings.
cards.watchOut: The PaCO2 subgroups are trial-level (ecological) comparisons, so 'benefit only above 55 mmHg' is a hypothesis about targeting, strongly concordant with Köhnlein's design but not a patient-level proof; the pool also includes the Köhnlein trial itself.
cards.source: Wu Z et al. International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. 2022. PMID: 35418751. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: survival benefit in stable hypercapnic COPD is real only where ventilation is targeted at substantial hypercapnia — unselected stable-patient trials pooled to no benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: survival benefit in stable hypercapnic COPD is real only where ventilation is targeted at substantial hypercapnia — unselected stable-patient trials pooled to no benefit
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one targeted randomised trial in stable stage IV hypercapnic COPD (195 patients) and two meta-analyses that bracket it (31 studies stratified by stability, 2016; 19 randomised trials/1,482 stable hypercapnic patients, 2022 — the later pool includes the targeted trial, so Ns are not additive). No small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Targeted high-intensity home ventilation reduced 1-year mortality from 33% to 12% (hazard ratio 0.24; Köhnlein 2014). Pooled across older, largely untargeted trials, stable patients showed no survival benefit (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.55-1.43; Dretzke 2016). Pooling all randomised stable-hypercapnia trials, mortality fell (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.61-0.95), concentrated at baseline PaCO2 of 55 mmHg or above and with larger PaCO2 reductions (Wu 2022). PROPOSED SPLIT, as a partial completion of live shelf #1645 (which homes the post-exacerbation population, not stable disease).
cards.watchOut: Do not prescribe from the pooled relative risk alone: the entire disagreement in this literature is about who is ventilated and how hard — a stable patient with modest hypercapnia on low settings matches the null trials, not Köhnlein.
cards.source: Synthesis of Köhnlein T et al. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2014 (PMID: 25066329); Dretzke J et al. International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. 2016 (PMID: 27698560); Wu Z et al. International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. 2022 (PMID: 35418751).
