shelves.title: Antifibrotics and survival in progressive fibrosis other than IPF (weak evidence): modelled survival favours nintedanib and small observed counts point the same way — but no trial has shown a mortality benefit
shelves.question: Does antifibrotic therapy improve survival in adults with progressive pulmonary fibrosis other than idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
shelves.mesh: Bayes Theorem · Clinical Trials as Topic · Humans · Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis · Lung Diseases, Interstitial · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2783, which answers the lung-function half of this question: on #2783 nintedanib slowed the annual FVC decline in progressive fibrosing ILD (INBUILD, difference 107.0 mL/year) — but the INBUILD record reports no mortality comparison, so survival was left uncovered there and is the whole subject here. The survival evidence is indirect and thin. A Bayesian modelling analysis (Langford 2022, PMID: 34957531) matched 654 INBUILD patients to IPF trial patients and estimated median overall survival of 6.34–6.50 years on nintedanib versus 3.42–3.76 years on control — modelled, not observed, survival. In the Japanese INBUILD population (108 patients), mortality hazard ratios favoured nintedanib at both reported horizons — 0.54 (95% CI 0.14–2.11) at 52 weeks (Inoue 2021, PMID: 34564020) and 0.41 (95% CI 0.11–1.51) over the whole trial (Ogura 2022, PMID: 35927208) — with every interval crossing no effect. The only other randomised antifibrotic trial in this population, RELIEF (pirfenidone), is homed on pack #3951 and is not re-carded here; its death counts (1 of 64 versus 5 of 63) are printed on that shelf and are far too few to read. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): every estimate points toward longer survival, but none is a powered, observed mortality result, so a survival benefit is unproven.

cards.headline: Langford 2022: modelled — not observed — median survival of 6.34–6.50 years on nintedanib versus 3.42–3.76 years on control in progressive fibrosis other than IPF (Bayesian estimate borrowed from IPF trials)
cards.summary: Langford 2022: modelled — not observed — median survival of 6.34–6.50 years on nintedanib versus 3.42–3.76 years on control in progressive fibrosis other than IPF (Bayesian estimate borrowed from IPF trials)
cards.type: Bayesian survival modelling analysis (Langford 2022)
cards.people: Propensity-matched analysis: 1,099 patients with IPF from the TOMORROW, INPULSIS-1, INPULSIS-2 and INPULSIS-ON trials (640 nintedanib, 459 placebo) matched to 654 patients with progressive fibrosing ILDs other than IPF in INBUILD (326 nintedanib, 328 placebo). Seven survival models were fitted to the IPF data; the three best-fitting (gamma, log-logistic, Weibull) generated informative priors to extrapolate INBUILD survival.
cards.result: All three models gave consistent Bayesian estimates for the matched non-IPF population: median overall survival ranging from 6.34 to 6.50 years after starting nintedanib, versus 3.42 to 3.76 years for the control group. The authors present this as the first estimate of long-term overall survival in PF-ILDs other than IPF and state the analysis suggests nintedanib may prolong survival — an extrapolation from IPF trial survival, not deaths observed in the non-IPF population itself.
cards.watchOut: The survival gap is generated by a model that assumes non-IPF fibrosis behaves like IPF; it is not a mortality result measured in these patients, and it must never be quoted as a trial finding.
cards.source: Langford B et al. bayesian survival modelling analysis (langford 2022) propensity-matched analysis: 1,099 patients with ipf from the tomorrow, inpulsis-1, inpulsis-2 and inpulsis-on trials (640 nintedanib, 459 placebo) matched to 654 patients with progressive fibrosing ilds other than ipf in inbuild (326 nintedanib, 328 placebo). seven survival models were fitted to the ipf data; the three best-fitting (gamma, log-logistic, weibull) generated informative priors to extrapolate inbuild survival. all three models gave consistent bayesian estimates for the matched non-ipf population: median overall survival ranging from 6.34 to 6.50 years after starting nintedanib, versus 3.42 to 3.76 years for the control group. the authors present this as the first estimate of long-term overall survival in pf-ilds other than ipf and state the analysis suggests nintedanib may prolong survival — an extrapolation from ipf trial survival, not deaths observed in the non-ipf population itself. the survival gap is generated by a model that assumes non-ipf fibrosis behaves like ipf; it is not a mortality result measured in these patients, and it must never be quoted as a trial finding. langford b et al. using data on survival with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis to estimate survival with other types of progressive fibrosis interstitial lung disease: a bayesian framework. advances in therapy. 2022. pmid: 34957531. registry id: none in the record. mesh: bayes theorem · clinical trials as topic · humans · idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis · lung diseases, interstitial · survival analysis

cards.headline: Inoue 2021: in the 108-patient Japanese INBUILD subgroup, mortality hazard ratio 0.54 for nintedanib versus placebo — but the 95% CI (0.14–2.11) crosses no effect (subgroup N on the face)
cards.summary: Inoue 2021: in the 108-patient Japanese INBUILD subgroup, mortality hazard ratio 0.54 for nintedanib versus placebo — but the 95% CI (0.14–2.11) crosses no effect (subgroup N on the face)
cards.type: Randomised trial subgroup analysis (Inoue 2021, INBUILD)
cards.people: 108 Japanese patients with progressive fibrosing ILDs randomised in INBUILD to nintedanib 150 mg twice daily or placebo, treatment continued until the last patient completed 52 weeks; time to death was evaluated up to the last patient's week-52 visit. Subgroup N = 108.
cards.result: Adjusted annual FVC decline was −148.31 mL/year on nintedanib versus −240.36 mL/year on placebo (adjusted difference 92.05 mL/year, 95% CI −10.69 to 194.80), with no heterogeneity versus non-Japanese patients (interaction P = 0.75). The risk of acute exacerbation or death was lower on nintedanib (hazard ratio 0.30, 95% CI 0.10–0.91) and mortality was numerically lower (hazard ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.14–2.11) — a relative measure whose interval includes both large benefit and harm. No new safety findings were reported.
cards.watchOut: A 108-patient subgroup of a trial powered on FVC, not death: the mortality interval (0.14–2.11) is compatible with almost anything, and subgroup findings are hypothesis-generating.
cards.source: Inoue Y et al. Efficacy and safety of nintedanib in Japanese patients with progressive fibrosing interstitial lung diseases: Subgroup analysis of the randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 INBUILD trial. Respiratory medicine. 2021. PMID: 34564020. Registry ID: NCT02999178. cards.headline: Ogura 2022: over the whole INBUILD trial, the same 108 Japanese patients showed a death hazard ratio of 0.41 for nintedanib versus placebo (95% CI 0.11–1.51) — again crossing no effect
cards.summary: Ogura 2022: over the whole INBUILD trial, the same 108 Japanese patients showed a death hazard ratio of 0.41 for nintedanib versus placebo (95% CI 0.11–1.51) — again crossing no effect
cards.type: Randomised trial subset analysis, whole-trial follow-up (Ogura 2022, INBUILD)
cards.people: Further subset analysis of the same 108 Japanese patients with progressive fibrosing ILDs who received at least one dose of study medication in INBUILD (the population of the Inoue 2021 card above), followed over the whole trial period — longer than the 52-week analysis — comparing nintedanib 150 mg twice daily with placebo on ILD progression (absolute FVC decline of at least 10% predicted), acute exacerbation, and death.
cards.result: Over the whole trial, nintedanib numerically lowered the risk of ILD progression or death (hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.37–1.16), acute exacerbation of ILD or death (HR 0.28, 95% CI 0.09–0.83), and death alone (HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.11–1.51) — all relative measures; only the exacerbation-or-death composite excludes no effect. The most common adverse event was diarrhoea, manageable for most patients by dose reduction and interruption, and the safety profile was consistent with the earlier report. The authors describe the outcome reductions as nominal.
cards.watchOut: This is the same 108 patients as the Inoue card followed longer — not independent confirmation — and a national subset of a trial powered on FVC; 'nominally reduced' is the authors' own wording.
cards.source: Ogura T et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: survival in non-IPF progressive fibrosis is suggested by a model and by one small subgroup followed two ways — it has never been shown by a powered mortality result
cards.summary: Synthesis: survival in non-IPF progressive fibrosis is suggested by a model and by one small subgroup followed two ways — it has never been shown by a powered mortality result
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Bayesian survival extrapolation (654 matched non-IPF INBUILD patients) and two analyses of a single 108-patient national subgroup of INBUILD (52-week and whole-trial horizons; the same patients, counted once). No carded study was designed or powered to measure survival in this population. RELIEF, the pirfenidone trial in the same population, is homed on pack #3951 and cross-pointed in the balance, not re-carded.
cards.result: Modelled median survival favoured nintedanib by roughly 3 years (6.34–6.50 versus 3.42–3.76 years; Langford 2022). Observed subgroup data are consistent in direction but inconclusive: mortality HR 0.54 (95% CI 0.14–2.11) at 52 weeks (Inoue 2021) and HR 0.41 (95% CI 0.11–1.51) over the whole trial (Ogura 2022). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for a survival benefit.
cards.watchOut: Slowing FVC decline (the covered slice on shelf #2783) is not the same as living longer; this shelf exists precisely because that step has not been demonstrated with observed mortality data.
cards.source: Synthesis of Langford B et al. Advances in therapy. 2022 (PMID: 34957531); Inoue Y et al. Respiratory medicine. 2021 (PMID: 34564020); Ogura T et al. Respiratory investigation. 2022 (PMID: 35927208).

shelves.title: Ramelteon for sleep-onset insomnia in older adults (SPLIT): measured sleep latency shortens by about 8–10 minutes in both elderly trials — a meta-analysis subgroup found no subjective benefit over 65
shelves.question: Is ramelteon effective for sleep-onset insomnia in older adults?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Indenes · Male · Mental Recall · Placebos · Receptors, Melatonin · Sleep · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1500, which covers ramelteon in general adults with chronic primary insomnia (its carded trial enrolled ages 18–64) — the older-adult slice was uncovered there and is the whole subject here. The slice genuinely divides. Two randomised trials in patients aged 65 and over are positive: a 2-night crossover study (Roth 2007, PMID: 17519067, N = 100, mean age 70.7) found latency to persistent sleep of 28.7 minutes on ramelteon 4 mg and 30.8 minutes on 8 mg versus 38.4 minutes on placebo, with total sleep time and sleep efficiency also improved and no next-day residual effects; and a 35-night outpatient trial (Roth 2006, PMID: 16709464, N = 829) found patient-reported sleep latency of 70.2 minutes on either dose versus 78.5 minutes on placebo at week 1 (P = .008), sustained at weeks 3 and 5, with no rebound or withdrawal on discontinuation. Against that, the subgroup analysis of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 trials (Liu 2012, PMID: 22897464) found subjective sleep latency was reduced only in patients aged 18–64 — not in patients over 65. PROPOSED SPLIT — objective sleep latency improves in older adults in both elderly trials, while the meta-analytic subgroup found no subjective latency benefit over 65: ramelteon shortens measured sleep onset in older adults by roughly 8–10 minutes, but whether older patients themselves feel they fall asleep faster is unproven.

cards.headline: Roth 2007: in 100 older adults, ramelteon cut latency to persistent sleep to 28.7 minutes (4 mg) and 30.8 minutes (8 mg) versus 38.4 minutes on placebo over 2 nights
cards.summary: Roth 2007: in 100 older adults, ramelteon cut latency to persistent sleep to 28.7 minutes (4 mg) and 30.8 minutes (8 mg) versus 38.4 minutes on placebo over 2 nights
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial (Roth 2007)
cards.people: 100 older adults (37 men, 63 women; mean age 70.7 years, range 65–83) with chronic primary insomnia in a randomised, 9-week, 3-period crossover trial at 17 sleep centres; each participant received placebo, ramelteon 4 mg and ramelteon 8 mg for two consecutive nights per phase, separated by 5- to 12-day washouts. Sleep was measured by polysomnography, with a post-sleep questionnaire and next-day residual-effect testing.
cards.result: Latency to persistent sleep was significantly shorter on ramelteon 4 mg (28.7 min versus 38.4 min, P < 0.001) and 8 mg (30.8 min versus 38.4 min, P = 0.005) than placebo. Total sleep time (P = 0.036 and P = 0.007) and sleep efficiency (P = 0.037 and P = 0.007) were also significantly improved at both doses. Subjective sleep latency improved significantly only at 4 mg (P = 0.037), not 8 mg (P = 0.120). Treatment-related adverse-event incidence was 7% on placebo, 11% on 4 mg and 5% on 8 mg, and no residual pharmacologic effects were observed on digit-symbol substitution, memory recall, visual analogue scales or the post-sleep questionnaire.
cards.watchOut: Two nights per dose in a crossover: this measures an immediate laboratory effect on sleep onset, not whether weeks of treatment help an older person at home.
cards.source: Roth T et al. A 2-night, 3-period, crossover study of ramelteon's efficacy and safety in older adults with chronic insomnia. Current medical research and opinion. 2007. PMID: 17519067. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Roth 2006: in 829 older adults over 35 nights, patient-reported sleep latency was 70.2 minutes on ramelteon (either dose) versus 78.5 minutes on placebo at week 1, sustained to week 5, with no rebound or withdrawal
cards.summary: Roth 2006: in 829 older adults over 35 nights, patient-reported sleep latency was 70.2 minutes on ramelteon (either dose) versus 78.5 minutes on placebo at week 1, sustained to week 5, with no rebound or withdrawal
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Roth 2006)
cards.people: 829 older adults (aged 65 years or over) with chronic insomnia in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 35-night outpatient trial at multiple centres, taking placebo, ramelteon 4 mg or ramelteon 8 mg nightly for 5 weeks, with sleep diaries, weekly clinic visits, and a 7-day placebo run-out to assess rebound insomnia and withdrawal.
cards.result: Both doses significantly reduced patient-reported sleep latency at week 1 (4 mg: 70.2 versus 78.5 min, P = .008; 8 mg: 70.2 versus 78.5 min, P = .008). Reductions persisted at week 3 on 8 mg (60.3 versus 69.3 min, P = .003) and at week 5 on 4 mg (63.4 versus 70.6 min, P = .028) and 8 mg (57.7 versus 70.6 min, P < .001). Total sleep time was significantly increased on 4 mg at week 1 (324.6 versus 313.9 min, P = .004) and week 3 (336.0 versus 324.3 min, P = .007). There was no significant rebound insomnia or withdrawal after discontinuation, and adverse-event incidence was similar across groups, mostly mild or moderate.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is real but modest — about 8 minutes of self-reported latency at week 1 — and the identical 70.2-minute figure printed for both doses means there is no dose-response to exploit by choosing 8 mg over 4 mg.
cards.source: Roth T et al. Effects of ramelteon on patient-reported sleep latency in older adults with chronic insomnia. Sleep medicine. 2006. PMID: 16709464. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Liu 2012: meta-analysis subgroup — subjective sleep latency fell only in patients aged 18–64, not in patients over 65 (the split in this shelf)
cards.summary: Liu 2012: meta-analysis subgroup — subjective sleep latency fell only in patients aged 18–64, not in patients over 65 (the split in this shelf)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis with age subgroup analysis (Liu 2012)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 randomised controlled trials of ramelteon versus placebo or other treatment in chronic insomnia, identified from 175 references across Medline, Embase, PsycINFO and the Cochrane Library to September 2011; efficacy was pooled overall and by age subgroup (18–64 years versus over 65 years).
cards.result: Across all ages there were significant improvements in subjective and polysomnographic sleep latency, total sleep time and latency to REM, but not in the percentage of REM sleep. By subgroup analysis, however, subjective sleep latency was reduced only in patients aged 18–64 years, and not in patients over 65 years. Ramelteon was not associated with a higher risk ratio for any frequent adverse event versus control. The authors conclude efficacy and safety are promising and that more research is required — the record prints no pooled effect size for the over-65 subgroup, so none is carded.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup null in a meta-analysis can reflect fewer, smaller older-adult trials rather than a true absence of effect — but it directly contradicts the patient-reported outcome of the largest elderly trial carded here, and readers deserve both.
cards.source: Liu J et al. Ramelteon in the treatment of chronic insomnia: systematic review and meta-analysis. International journal of clinical practice. 2012. PMID: 22897464. cards.headline: Synthesis: ramelteon shortens measured sleep onset in older adults in both elderly trials — the disagreement is over whether patients over 65 feel it
cards.summary: Synthesis: ramelteon shortens measured sleep onset in older adults in both elderly trials — the disagreement is over whether patients over 65 feel it
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised trials conducted specifically in patients aged 65 and over (N = 100 crossover, 2 nights per dose; N = 829 parallel-group, 35 nights) and one 8-trial meta-analysis whose age subgroup analysis cuts the other way on the subjective outcome. cards.result: Objective latency to persistent sleep fell by about 8–10 minutes versus placebo in the crossover trial (Roth 2007), and diary-reported latency fell by about 8 minutes at week 1, sustained to week 5, in the large outpatient trial (Roth 2006), with no rebound or withdrawal in either. cards.watchOut: General-adult ramelteon evidence lives on shelf #1500 and is not re-carded here; this shelf's narrower claim is only about patients aged 65 and over, where the effect is about 8–10 minutes of sleep latency.

shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #920, which covers pitolisant's efficacy against placebo and modafinil (and its cataplexy trial) — those efficacy records are homed there and are not re-carded here. This shelf covers the slice #920 leaves open: dependence. The direct test is a formal human abuse-potential study (Setnik 2020, PMID: 31626696, NCT03152123): in 38 completers — nondependent recreational stimulant users, not narcolepsy patients — Drug Liking scores for pitolisant at the therapeutic dose (35.6 mg) and at six times that dose (213.6 mg) were similar to placebo and significantly lower than for phentermine 60 mg (mean differences 21.4 and 19.7 points, P < 0.0001). Longer exposure data point the same way without measuring dependence directly: in the 1-year open-label Harmony III study (Dauvilliers 2019, PMID: 31529094, n = 102), sleepiness fell (ESS −4.6 points) and the record reports no dependence or withdrawal outcome; and in the European post-authorisation safety study (Plazzi 2025, PMID: 39978240, 364 patients dosed, interim at 42.6 months), discontinuation was mainly for safety reasons (14.3%), lack of response (8.7%) and patient decision (7.6%) — the record reports no abuse or dependence signal, and also reports no dedicated dependence endpoint, which is printed plainly on its card. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — low dependence potential: a single dedicated abuse-potential trial in non-patients, supported by up to 42.6 months of uneventful real-world exposure, supports 'no dependence signal'; it cannot prove zero dependence risk in patients taking the drug for years.

cards.headline: Setnik 2020: pitolisant's Drug Liking scores matched placebo at both the therapeutic dose (35.6 mg) and six times it (213.6 mg) — and were significantly below phentermine (differences 21.4 and 19.7 points, P < 0.0001) in 38 completers
cards.summary: Setnik 2020: pitolisant's Drug Liking scores matched placebo at both the therapeutic dose (35.6 mg) and six times it (213.6 mg) — and were significantly below phentermine (differences 21.4 and 19.7 points, P < 0.0001) in 38 completers
cards.type: Randomised double-blind crossover human abuse-potential study (Setnik 2020)
cards.people: Nondependent, recreational stimulant users who could distinguish phentermine 60 mg from placebo in a drug-discrimination qualification phase, randomised in a four-period, double-blind crossover study to single doses of pitolisant 35.6 mg (therapeutic), pitolisant 213.6 mg (supratherapeutic), phentermine HCl 60 mg and placebo. 38 participants completed (73.7% male, 65.8% white, mean age 33.3 years). These were healthy volunteers, not patients with narcolepsy — printed on the face because it bounds what the study can show.
cards.result: Mean maximum Drug Liking ('at this moment', 100-point scale) was significantly greater for phentermine than for pitolisant 35.6 mg (mean difference 21.4, P < 0.0001) and pitolisant 213.6 mg (mean difference 19.7, P < 0.0001), while pitolisant at both doses was similar to placebo; Overall Drug Liking and Take Drug Again scores showed the same pattern. Adverse-event incidence was 82.1% after phentermine, 72.5% after pitolisant 213.6 mg, 47.5% after pitolisant 35.6 mg and 48.8% after placebo. The authors conclude pitolisant showed significantly lower abuse potential than phentermine and a profile similar to placebo, suggesting a low risk of abuse.
cards.watchOut: Single doses in 38 recreational stimulant users measure liking, not dependence after months of daily dosing in patients — the design is the regulatory standard for abuse potential, but it is a proxy, and the N is printed on the face.
cards.source: Setnik B et al. Evaluation of the abuse potential of pitolisant, a selective H3-receptor antagonist/inverse agonist, for the treatment of adult patients with narcolepsy with or without cataplexy. Sleep. 2020. PMID: 31626696. Registry ID: NCT03152123. MeSH: Adult · Cataplexy · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Female · Histamine Agonists · Humans · Male · Narcolepsy · Piperidines

cards.headline: Dauvilliers 2019 (Harmony III): over up to 1 year of open-label pitolisant in 102 patients, sleepiness fell by 4.6 ESS points and the record reports no dependence or withdrawal outcome
cards.summary: Dauvilliers 2019 (Harmony III): over up to 1 year of open-label pitolisant in 102 patients, sleepiness fell by 4.6 ESS points and the record reports no dependence or withdrawal outcome
cards.type: Open-label single-arm long-term study (Dauvilliers 2019, Harmony III)
cards.people: 102 adult patients with narcolepsy (75 with cataplexy) and Epworth Sleepiness Scale score of at least 12, in an open-label, single-arm, pragmatic study; after titration, pitolisant once daily at up to 40 mg for up to 1 year (first pitolisant exposure for 73 patients); concomitant stimulants and anti-cataplectic agents were allowed. 68 patients (51 with cataplexy) completed 12 months.
cards.result: ESS score decreased by 4.6 ± 0.6 points; two-thirds of completers were responders (ESS ≤ 10 or a fall of at least 3) and one-third normalised (ESS ≤ 10). Complete and partial cataplexy fell by 76% and 65%, hallucinations by 54%, sleep paralysis by 63% and sleep attacks by 27%. Common treatment-emergent adverse events were headache (11.8%), insomnia (8.8%), weight gain (7.8%), anxiety (6.9%), depressive symptoms (4.9%) and nausea (4.9%); 7 patients had a serious adverse effect, unrelated to pitolisant except a possibly related miscarriage. About one-third stopped pitolisant, mostly (19.6%) for insufficient benefit. The record reports no dependence, abuse or withdrawal outcome — an absence printed plainly, not evidence the outcome was measured.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no comparator and a third of patients stopping (mostly for insufficient benefit): it shows sustained effect and tolerability over a year, but dependence was not a measured endpoint.
cards.source: Dauvilliers Y et al. Long-term use of pitolisant to treat patients with narcolepsy: Harmony III Study. Sleep. 2019. PMID: 31529094. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Anxiety · Central Nervous System Stimulants · Depression · Female · Headache · Histamine H3 Antagonists · Humans · Male · Narcolepsy · Piperidines · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Plazzi 2025: in 364 dosed patients followed in routine European practice (interim at 42.6 months), discontinuation was for safety reasons (14.3%), lack of response (8.7%) or patient decision (7.6%) — the record reports no abuse or dependence signal, and no dependence endpoint
cards.summary: Plazzi 2025: in 364 dosed patients followed in routine European practice (interim at 42.6 months), discontinuation was for safety reasons (14.3%), lack of response (8.7%) or patient decision (7.6%) — the record reports no abuse or dependence signal, and no dependence endpoint
cards.type: Prospective non-interventional safety study, interim analysis (Plazzi 2025)
cards.people: Prospective, non-interventional 5-year post-authorisation safety study of adults with narcolepsy type 1 (71.4%) or type 2 (28.6%) receiving pitolisant in routine care: 370 patients enrolled (mean age 40 ± 15 years, 51.4% women), 364 received at least one dose, data available for 356 (97.8%); 68.4% had at least one comorbidity. Interim analysis after 42.6 months.
cards.result: 355 treatment-emergent adverse events (3 serious) were reported by 156 patients (42.9% of the safety population), 218 possibly treatment-related in 109 patients (29.9%). Pitolisant was discontinued by 131 patients (35.4%), mainly for safety reasons (14.3%), lack of response (8.7%) and patient decision (7.6%). Improvements were observed in excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy and quality of life, with good adherence and satisfaction reported. The record reports no abuse, misuse or dependence event — and, printed plainly, the study's stated objectives were long-term safety and utilisation patterns, not a dedicated dependence assessment.
cards.watchOut: 'No signal reported' in a study not designed to detect dependence is weaker than a negative dedicated study; this card supports, and cannot substitute for, the abuse-potential trial above.
cards.source: Plazzi G et al. Interim analysis of a post-authorization safety study of pitolisant in treating narcolepsy: A real-world European study. Sleep medicine. 2025. PMID: 39978240. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: pitolisant reduces sleepiness (efficacy homed on shelf #920) and shows a placebo-like abuse profile in its one dedicated study, with no dependence signal in up to 42.6 months of follow-up
cards.summary: Synthesis: pitolisant reduces sleepiness (efficacy homed on shelf #920) and shows a placebo-like abuse profile in its one dedicated study, with no dependence signal in up to 42.6 months of follow-up
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one dedicated human abuse-potential crossover study (38 completers, non-patients), one 1-year open-label treatment study (n = 102), and one real-world safety cohort (364 dosed, interim at 42.6 months). Efficacy trials themselves are homed on shelf #920 and are not re-carded here.
cards.result: Drug Liking for pitolisant matched placebo at therapeutic and supratherapeutic doses and was significantly below phentermine (Setnik 2020). Sleepiness improved over 1 year of treatment (ESS −4.6; Dauvilliers 2019), and no abuse or dependence event is reported in the real-world interim analysis (Plazzi 2025) — though neither follow-up study measured dependence as an endpoint. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — low dependence potential on current evidence.
cards.watchOut: The honest bound: dependence has been tested directly only as single-dose liking in volunteers; long-term patient data are reassuring by absence of signal, not by measurement.
cards.source: Synthesis of Setnik B et al. Sleep. 2020 (PMID: 31626696); Dauvilliers Y et al. Sleep. 2019 (PMID: 31529094); Plazzi G et al. Sleep medicine. 2025 (PMID: 39978240).

shelves.title: MAD versus CPAP in mild-to-moderate OSA (SPLIT): CPAP normalises breathing more, sleepiness improves the same — and patients adhere better to the device
shelves.question: Is a mandibular advancement device as effective as CPAP for mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnea?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases · Comorbidity · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Cross-Over Studies · Disorders of Excessive Somnolence · England · Female · Humans · Male · Mandibular Advancement · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Quality-Adjusted Life Years · Regression Analysis · Risk Assessment · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive · State Medicine
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #923, which compares a mandibular advancement device (MAD) with CPAP in OSA generally — its carded trials (a general-population crossover trial and the CRESCENT blood-pressure trial) are homed there and are not re-carded here. This shelf covers only the mild-to-moderate slice, and the answer is consistent across all three slice-specific sources: CPAP lowers the apnoea–hypopnoea index (AHI) more, while sleepiness improves about the same. In TOMADO and its updated systematic review (Sharples 2014, PMID: 25359435), pooled AHI fell by 25.4 events/hour on CPAP versus 9.3/hour on MADs (between-treatment difference 7.0/hour favouring CPAP, P < 0.001), while the Epworth Sleepiness Scale fell by 1.6 points on both; the review notes no trial compared CPAP with a MAD in mild OSAH specifically. In the 1-year randomised trial in mild/moderate OSA (Aarab 2011, PMID: 21454959, n = 43, mean AHI 20.8/hour), CPAP improved AHI by 4.1 events/hour more than the MAD (P = 0.000 as printed), sleepiness improved similarly in both groups (P = 0.367), and more CPAP patients withdrew for side effects. In the mild-OSA-only randomised trial (E Silva 2021, PMID: 33394328, n = 79, AHI 9.5/hour), both devices reduced AHI versus control at 6 and 12 months and MAD adherence was higher, but CPAP was superior on total and LDL cholesterol at 12 months. PROPOSED SPLIT — on the breathing index CPAP wins (AHI), on sleepiness the devices tie (sleepiness): a MAD is a reasonable, often better-tolerated alternative in mild-to-moderate OSA, but it is not as effective as CPAP at normalising breathing.

cards.headline: Sharples 2014 (TOMADO + updated review): CPAP lowered AHI by 25.4 events/hour versus 9.3/hour for MADs (difference 7.0/hour favouring CPAP) — while sleepiness fell by 1.6 points on both
cards.summary: Sharples 2014 (TOMADO + updated review): CPAP lowered AHI by 25.4 events/hour versus 9.3/hour for MADs (difference 7.0/hour favouring CPAP) — while sleepiness fell by 1.6 points on both
cards.type: Randomised crossover trial with updated systematic review and economic model (Sharples 2014, TOMADO)
cards.people: Health Technology Assessment report combining (1) the TOMADO crossover randomised trial of three mandibular advancement devices (self-moulded, semibespoke, fully bespoke) versus no treatment in 90 adults with mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnoea-hypopnoea, and (2) an updated systematic review (77 randomised trials in adult OSAH) comparing MADs with conservative management, MADs with CPAP, and CPAP with conservative management, feeding a lifetime cost-utility model for mild to moderate OSAH.
cards.result: In TOMADO, all three devices improved AHI versus no treatment (relative risks 0.74, 0.67 and 0.64) and lowered Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores by 1.51 to 2.37 points; differences between devices were not significant. In the updated meta-analysis, MADs and CPAP both significantly improved AHI (MAD −9.3/hour; CPAP −25.4/hour, both P < 0.001), with an effect difference of 7.0/hour (P < 0.001) favouring CPAP; MAD and CPAP reduced the ESS score similarly (1.6 points each, P < 0.001). The review states plainly that no trials compared CPAP with MADs in mild OSAH. All devices were cost-effective at £20,000 per quality-adjusted life-year at 4 weeks in the trial analysis.
cards.watchOut: The head-to-head AHI and ESS figures come from the pooled review across OSA severities, not from mild-to-moderate patients alone — the report itself notes the mild-OSA head-to-head trial did not exist; the two trials below supply the slice-specific data.
cards.source: Sharples L et al. Clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness results from the randomised controlled Trial of Oral Mandibular Advancement Devices for Obstructive sleep apnoea-hypopnoea (TOMADO) and long-term economic analysis of oral devices and continuous positive airway pressure. Health technology assessment (Winchester, England). 2014. PMID: 25359435. Registry ID: ISRCTN02309506. cards.headline: Aarab 2011: over 1 year in 43 patients with mild/moderate OSA, CPAP improved AHI by 4.1 events/hour more than a MAD — sleepiness improved similarly in both groups, and more CPAP patients withdrew for side effects (N on the face)
cards.summary: Aarab 2011: over 1 year in 43 patients with mild/moderate OSA, CPAP improved AHI by 4.1 events/hour more than a MAD — sleepiness improved similarly in both groups, and more CPAP patients withdrew for side effects (N on the face)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with 1-year follow-up (Aarab 2011)
cards.people: 43 patients with mild/moderate obstructive sleep apnea (mean age 52.2 ± 9.6 years; mean AHI 20.8 ± 9.9 events/hour) randomly assigned to a mandibular advancement device (n = 21) or nasal CPAP (n = 22), with polysomnography before treatment, at short-term evaluation, and at 6 and 12 months, and excessive daytime sleepiness assessed at each recording. Trial N = 43.
cards.result: The AHI improvements achieved initially remained stable over 1 year in both groups (P = 0.650 for change over time). AHI improved 4.1 events/hour more in the CPAP group than the MAD group (P = 0.000 as printed in the record). Daytime sleepiness values improved gradually over time (P = 0.000) and the improvements were similar for both groups (P = 0.367). More patients withdrew from CPAP than from the MAD because of side effects. The authors suggest the larger AHI improvement with CPAP may not be clinically relevant, given the equal sleepiness benefit.
cards.watchOut: Only 43 patients: the trial can show the direction of the AHI gap and the sleepiness tie, but its small size means rarer outcomes (cardiovascular events, accidents) are entirely unaddressed.
cards.source: Aarab G et al. Long-term follow-up of a randomized controlled trial of oral appliance therapy in obstructive sleep apnea. Respiration; international review of thoracic diseases. 2011. PMID: 21454959. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Mandibular Advancement · Middle Aged · Polysomnography · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: E Silva 2021: in mild OSA only (79 patients), both MAD and CPAP reduced AHI versus no treatment and MAD adherence was higher — but CPAP was superior on cholesterol at 12 months
cards.summary: E Silva 2021: in mild OSA only (79 patients), both MAD and CPAP reduced AHI versus no treatment and MAD adherence was higher — but CPAP was superior on cholesterol at 12 months
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial in mild OSA (E Silva 2021)
cards.people: 79 patients with mild OSA (both sexes, ages 18–65, BMI under 35 kg/m²; mean age 47 ± 9 years, 54% men, AHI 9.5 ± 2.9 events/hour) randomised to CPAP, a mandibular advancement device, or no-treatment control, with physical examination, metabolic profile and full polysomnography at baseline, 6 and 12 months.
cards.result: MAD and CPAP both reduced AHI at 6 and 12 months compared with the control group, and MAD adherence was higher than CPAP adherence at 6 and 12 months (the record prints no AHI values or adherence percentages, so none are carded). Despite lower adherence, CPAP was more effective over 12 months at reducing total cholesterol (189.3 ± 60.2 mg/dL at baseline to 173.4 ± 74.3 mg/dL) and LDL cholesterol (112.8 ± 54.9 mg/dL to 94.5 ± 67.4 mg/dL), and was superior to the MAD on both lipid measures after 1 year.

cards.headline: Synthesis: in mild-to-moderate OSA the MAD matches CPAP on sleepiness but not on the breathing index — and it is the device patients stay on
cards.summary: Synthesis: in mild-to-moderate OSA the MAD matches CPAP on sleepiness but not on the breathing index — and it is the device patients stay on
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one HTA report (90-patient mild-to-moderate crossover trial plus a 77-trial updated review), one 1-year randomised trial in mild/moderate OSA (n = 43), and one randomised trial in mild OSA only (n = 79). General-severity MAD-versus-CPAP trials are homed on shelf #923 and are not re-carded here.
cards.result: CPAP reduces AHI substantially more (pooled −25.4 versus −9.3 events/hour; 4.1 events/hour more in the 1-year mild/moderate trial), sleepiness improves equally (ESS −1.6 on both in the pooled review; similar improvement, P = 0.367, in the 1-year trial), and adherence and tolerability favour the MAD (higher adherence in mild OSA; more side-effect withdrawals on CPAP). PROPOSED SPLIT — AHI: CPAP better; sleepiness: equal.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial in this severity band measures hard outcomes (cardiovascular events, mortality, accidents): 'as effective' can only be answered here for AHI, sleepiness and metabolic markers.

shelves.title: Timed light and circadian adaptation in night work (POSSIBLE): melatonin onset moves hours in the intended direction in every simulation study — full adaptation remains the exception
shelves.question: Does timed light therapy help night shift workers adapt their circadian rhythm?
shelves.mesh: Adaptation, Physiological · Adult · Analysis of Variance · Chronobiology Disorders · Circadian Rhythm · Darkness · Female · Humans · Light · Male · Melatonin · Sleep · Treatment Outcome · Wakefulness · Work Schedule Tolerance
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of pack #5050, which covers scheduled bright light and melatonin for alertness and sleep in night-shift workers — its carded studies are homed there and are not re-carded here (one of them also measured adaptation, which is why this shelf is scoped strictly to the circadian-phase outcome and cards three different studies). On the phase outcome itself, timed light works as chronobiology predicts. In a simulated-night-work study (Horowitz 2001, PMID: 11440916, n = 54), both 2,500-lux bright light during the night shift and a fixed 08:00–16:00 sleep/darkness schedule significantly delayed dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO), their effects combined additively, and light produced the larger shifts — though neither consistently shifted the rhythm fully into the sleep episode. A compromise-phase protocol (Smith 2008, PMID: 19090319, n = 24) — five 15-minute bright-light pulses during shifts, dark sunglasses outdoors, scheduled dark sleep and afternoon light as a 'brake' — moved final DLMO to about 04:30 versus about 00:30 in controls, with better night performance and near-complete allotted sleep. And daytime light control alone (Dumont 2009, PMID: 19755587, n = 38) shifted DLMO by +2.3 hours (advance profile) or −4.1 hours (delay profile) by design, with shifts differing between groups by the third night. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): timed light — during the shift, and controlled across the day — reliably moves circadian phase in the intended direction in simulation studies; complete adaptation is uncommon, the studies are small laboratory simulations rather than trials in working shift workers, and real-world adherence is untested in these records.

cards.headline: Horowitz 2001: bright light (2,500 lux) during night shifts and fixed sleep in darkness each significantly delayed melatonin onset, combined additively — light shifted phase more (n = 54)
cards.summary: Horowitz 2001: bright light (2,500 lux) during night shifts and fixed sleep in darkness each significantly delayed melatonin onset, combined additively — light shifted phase more (n = 54)
cards.type: Controlled laboratory simulation study (Horowitz 2001)
cards.people: 54 healthy subjects in a shift-work simulation of 4 day shifts and 3 night shifts followed by a 38-hour constant routine, allocated to bright light (2,500 lux) or room light (150 lux) during night shifts, crossed with scheduled sleep at home in darkened bedrooms from 08:00 to 16:00 (fixed sleep) or ad libitum sleep (free sleep). Dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO) was measured before and after the night shifts.
cards.result: Both the fixed-sleep condition and the bright-light condition significantly phase-delayed DLMO; the treatments combined additively, with light leading to larger phase shifts. Free-sleep subjects who spontaneously adopted consistent sleep schedules adapted better than those who did not. Neither properly timed bright light nor fixed sleep schedules were consistently sufficient to shift the melatonin rhythm completely into the sleep episode. The record prints no numerical DLMO shift in hours, so none is carded. The authors conclude scheduling of sleep/darkness should play a major role in prescriptions for shift-work phase misalignment.
cards.watchOut: A 3-night simulation in healthy volunteers, not working shift workers on real rosters: it proves phase can be moved, not that a workforce programme sustains adaptation.
cards.source: Horowitz TS et al. Efficacy of bright light and sleep/darkness scheduling in alleviating circadian maladaptation to night work. American journal of physiology. Endocrinology and metabolism. 2001. PMID: 11440916. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Smith 2008: a compromise-phase light protocol moved melatonin onset to about 04:30 versus about 00:30 in controls after 7 simulated night shifts — with near-daytime performance by the last shift (n = 24)
cards.summary: Smith 2008: a compromise-phase light protocol moved melatonin onset to about 04:30 versus about 00:30 in controls after 7 simulated night shifts — with near-daytime performance by the last shift (n = 24)
cards.type: Controlled between-subjects simulation study (Smith 2008)
cards.people: 24 healthy subjects in a home-and-laboratory study of 3 simulated night shifts, 2 days off, then 4 more night shifts. The experimental group received five 15-minute bright-light pulses from light boxes during night shifts, wore dark sunglasses when outside, slept in dark bedrooms at scheduled times after shifts and on days off, and received outdoor afternoon light exposure (the 'light brake'); controls had normal room light during shifts, lighter sunglasses, and unrestricted sleep and outdoor light.
cards.result: Final dim-light melatonin onset in the experimental group was approximately 04:30 — close to the target compromise phase position — and significantly later than the control group's approximately 00:30. Experimental subjects performed better than controls and slept for nearly all the allotted time in bed; by the last night shift they performed almost as well during the night as during daytime baseline. Controls showed pronounced performance impairment late in night shifts and large individual differences in sleep duration. The authors conclude relatively inexpensive, feasible interventions can produce adaptation to night work while still allowing adequate night sleep on days off.
cards.watchOut: The intervention is a package — light pulses, sunglasses, scheduled dark sleep and an afternoon light brake — so the phase shift cannot be credited to timed light alone; and 24 simulated-shift volunteers are not a permanent night workforce.
cards.source: Smith MR et al. Night shift performance is improved by a compromise circadian phase position: study 3. Circadian phase after 7 night shifts with an intervening weekend off. Sleep. 2008. PMID: 19090319. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dumont 2009: controlling daytime light exposure alone shifted melatonin onset by +2.3 hours (advance profile) or −4.1 hours (delay profile) in simulated night work (n = 38)
cards.summary: Dumont 2009: controlling daytime light exposure alone shifted melatonin onset by +2.3 hours (advance profile) or −4.1 hours (delay profile) in simulated night work (n = 38)
cards.type: Controlled laboratory simulation study (Dumont 2009)
cards.people: 38 healthy subjects (15 men, 23 women, aged 20–35) in a laboratory simulation of 2 day shifts followed by 4 consecutive night shifts (00:00–08:00), divided into 3 groups given daytime light-exposure profiles designed to delay phase (n = 12), advance phase (n = 13) or hold phase stable (n = 13); night-time light intensity was set at 50 lux in all groups. Circadian phase was tracked by salivary DLMO and urinary 6-sulfatoxymelatonin acrophase.
cards.result: Salivary DLMO showed a significant phase advance of 2.3 hours (±1.3) in the advance group and a significant phase delay of 4.1 hours (±1.3) in the delay group; the stable group showed a smaller but significant delay of 1.7 hours (±1.6). Urinary acrophases were highly correlated with salivary DLMO and showed phase shifts occurring rapidly, differing between groups by the third night shift. The authors conclude significant phase shifts can be achieved in night workers by controlling daytime light exposure, with no night-time intervention.
cards.watchOut: Even the 'stable' profile drifted 1.7 hours — uncontrolled everyday light is itself a phase-shifting exposure, which is exactly why real-world shift workers so rarely stay adapted.
cards.source: Dumont M et al. Controlled patterns of daytime light exposure improve circadian adjustment in simulated night work. Journal of biological rhythms. 2009. PMID: 19755587. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: timed light moves circadian phase in the intended direction in every carded study — partially, in simulations, with sleep/darkness scheduling as a co-intervention
cards.summary: Synthesis: timed light moves circadian phase in the intended direction in every carded study — partially, in simulations, with sleep/darkness scheduling as a co-intervention
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: three controlled laboratory simulation studies in healthy volunteers (n = 54, 24 and 38; 116 participants in total), all measuring dim-light melatonin onset as the adaptation outcome. Alertness and sleep outcomes for scheduled light in shift workers are homed in pack #5050 and are not re-carded here.
cards.result: Bright light during the shift and fixed sleep/darkness each delayed DLMO and combined additively (Horowitz 2001); a compromise-phase light package delayed DLMO by about 4 hours versus control (about 04:30 versus about 00:30; Smith 2008); and daytime light profiles alone advanced phase by 2.3 hours or delayed it by 4.1 hours (Dumont 2009). No study achieved complete, consistent re-entrainment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for circadian adaptation.
cards.watchOut: All three studies are short simulations in young healthy volunteers; none tests a sustained programme in actual night-shift workers, where days off, commuting light and family schedules work against adaptation.

shelves.title: Melatonin in delayed sleep-wake phase disorder (POSSIBLE): timing beats dose — 0.5 mg and 3.0 mg shift the clock equally at their optimal times, and phase can be estimated from a sleep diary
shelves.question: Is melatonin timing more important than dose for adults with delayed sleep-wake phase disorder?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Central Nervous System Depressants · Drug Administration Schedule · Humans · Melatonin · Sleep Disorders, Circadian Rhythm · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2429, which answers whether timed low-dose melatonin (0.5 mg, 1 hour before the desired bedtime) plus behavioural scheduling beats placebo in delayed sleep-wake phase disorder (DSWPD) — that trial is homed there and is not re-carded here. This shelf covers the comparison #2429 does not make: timing versus dose. No trial in DSWPD patients has randomised timing against dose directly; the answer is assembled from three directions. First, melatonin timed to circadian phase works in this disorder: a meta-analysis of 5 adult trials (van Geijlswijk 2010, PMID: 21120122) found melatonin advanced endogenous melatonin onset by 1.18 hours (95% CI 0.89–1.48) and sleep onset by 0.67 hours (95% CI 0.45–0.89), and cut sleep-onset latency by 23.27 minutes (95% CI 4.83–41.72). Second, the only head-to-head dose comparison using one protocol (Burgess 2010, PMID: 20410229, phase response curves in 34 healthy adults) found the optimal administration time differs by dose — maximum advances with 0.5 mg taken 2–4 hours before DLMO — but that when each dose is given at its own optimal time, 0.5 mg and 3.0 mg yield similarly sized advances and delays: timing, not milligrams, sets the shift. Third, timing can only be got right if phase is known, and in 24 DSWPD patients self-reported sleep timing estimated DLMO within ±1.5 hours in up to 88% of the sample (Lovato 2016, PMID: 27611743) — the practical route to timing treatment without a laboratory. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — timing over dose: within the studied range, when melatonin is taken relative to the circadian clock matters more than whether the dose is 0.5 or 3 mg; the dose-comparison evidence is from healthy volunteers, not DSWPD patients, and that indirectness is printed on the face. The record for the meta-analysis names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: van Geijlswijk 2010: in delayed sleep phase disorder, melatonin advanced endogenous melatonin onset by 1.18 hours and sleep onset by 0.67 hours, and cut sleep-onset latency by 23.27 minutes (meta-analysis of 5 adult trials, 91 adults)
cards.summary: van Geijlswijk 2010: in delayed sleep phase disorder, melatonin advanced endogenous melatonin onset by 1.18 hours and sleep onset by 0.67 hours, and cut sleep-onset latency by 23.27 minutes (meta-analysis of 5 adult trials, 91 adults)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (van Geijlswijk 2010)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of exogenous melatonin versus placebo in delayed sleep phase disorder (published 1990–2009, indexed in PubMed, Embase and sleep/chronobiology society abstracts) reporting endogenous melatonin onset, clock hour of sleep onset, wake-up time, sleep-onset latency or total sleep time: 5 trials including 91 adults, and 4 trials including 226 children (children's data are background only on this adult shelf; the adult figures are the carded result).
cards.result: In adults, melatonin treatment advanced mean endogenous melatonin onset by 1.18 hours (95% CI 0.89–1.48) and the clock hour of sleep onset by 0.67 hours (95% CI 0.45–0.89), and decreased sleep-onset latency by 23.27 minutes (95% CI 4.83–41.72). Wake-up time and total sleep time did not change significantly. The authors conclude melatonin is effective in advancing the sleep-wake rhythm and the endogenous melatonin rhythm in delayed sleep phase disorder. The record does not report a dose-response analysis, so none is carded — that absence is part of this shelf's point. The record names no specific product or brand; products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.watchOut: The pooled adult base is 91 patients across 5 small trials, and the trials dosed by clock schedule rather than testing dose against timing — this card establishes that phase-timed melatonin works, not which dose is best.
cards.source: van Geijlswijk IM et al. The use of exogenous melatonin in delayed sleep phase disorder: a meta-analysis. Sleep. 2010. PMID: 21120122. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Burgess 2010: 0.5 mg versus 3.0 mg melatonin phase response curves — the optimal clock time differs by dose, but at its optimal time each dose yields similarly sized phase advances and delays (n = 34, healthy adults)
cards.summary: Burgess 2010: 0.5 mg versus 3.0 mg melatonin phase response curves — the optimal clock time differs by dose, but at its optimal time each dose yields similarly sized phase advances and delays (n = 34, healthy adults)
cards.type: Double-blind placebo-controlled phase-response-curve study (Burgess 2010)
cards.people: 34 healthy adults (16 men, 18 women, aged 18–42) in two 5-day laboratory sessions, each preceded by 7–9 days of fixed sleep times; during 3 days of an ultradian dim-light/dark cycle in each session, participants took one pill daily at the same clock time — 0.5 mg melatonin or placebo, double-blind and counterbalanced — and phase shifts were derived against placebo and plotted against baseline dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO); the resulting 0.5 mg phase response curve was compared with the group's previously published 3.0 mg curve from the same protocol. These were healthy volunteers, not DSWPD patients — printed on the face.
cards.result: Maximum advances occurred when 0.5 mg melatonin was taken in the afternoon, 2–4 hours before the DLMO (or 9–11 hours before sleep midpoint); the time for maximum delays was less distinct, peaking soon after wake time on the fitted curve. The optimal administration time for advances and delays is later for the lower dose than for 3.0 mg. Critically, when each dose is given at its optimal time, both yield similarly sized advances and delays — a sixfold dose difference did not buy a bigger shift. The record prints no single numerical shift size for either dose, so none is carded.
cards.watchOut: Healthy young volunteers over 3 days of dosing: this is the mechanistic dose-versus-timing evidence, and applying it to DSWPD patients assumes their phase response behaves the same way — an assumption the DSWPD meta-analysis above is consistent with but does not test.

cards.headline: Lovato 2016: in 24 patients with delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, self-reported sleep timing estimated circadian phase (DLMO) within ±1.5 hours in up to 88% — making correct timing feasible without a laboratory (N on the face)
cards.summary: Lovato 2016: in 24 patients with delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, self-reported sleep timing estimated circadian phase (DLMO) within ±1.5 hours in up to 88% — making correct timing feasible without a laboratory (N on the face)
cards.type: Diagnostic estimation study in DSWPD patients (Lovato 2016)
cards.people: 24 individuals (17 male; mean age 21.96 ± 5.11 years) meeting ICSD-3 criteria for delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, selected from a community-based sample; circadian phase (DLMO, core body temperature minimum, melatonin-secretion midpoint) was measured during the first 24 hours of an 80-hour laboratory ultradian routine, and compared with 7-day sleep/wake diaries, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and a disorder-specific sleep-timing questionnaire completed beforehand. Study N = 24.
cards.result: Self-reported sleep-timing variables correlated moderately to strongly (positively) with DLMO, temperature minimum and melatonin midpoint. Regression equations estimated circadian phase within ±1.5 hours of the measured phase most accurately for a combination of sleep-timing measures (88% of the sample), followed by diary-reported midsleep (83%) and sleep onset time (79%). The authors suggest self-reported sleep timing may be useful clinically to predict a therapeutically relevant circadian phase in DSWPD — the prerequisite for timing melatonin correctly. This study tested no treatment; it is carded as evidence about the timing half of the timing-versus-dose question.
cards.watchOut: 24 young, mostly male patients and a ±1.5-hour tolerance: good enough to place a dose in the advance zone of the phase response curve, not a substitute for measured DLMO where precision matters.

cards.headline: Synthesis: no DSWPD trial has randomised timing against dose — but phase-timed melatonin works in the disorder, and the dose comparison shows timing, not milligrams, sets the shift
cards.summary: Synthesis: no DSWPD trial has randomised timing against dose — but phase-timed melatonin works in the disorder, and the dose comparison shows timing, not milligrams, sets the shift
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: a meta-analysis in the target disorder (5 adult trials, 91 adults), one same-protocol dose-comparison phase-response study (34 healthy adults), and one phase-estimation study in DSWPD patients (n = 24). The placebo-controlled efficacy trial of timed 0.5 mg melatonin in DSWPD is homed on shelf #2429 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Melatonin advanced melatonin onset by 1.18 hours and sleep onset by 0.67 hours in DSWPD (van Geijlswijk 2010). Given at their respective optimal times, 0.5 mg and 3.0 mg produced similarly sized advances and delays, while the optimal time itself shifted with dose (Burgess 2010). Patients' own sleep timing can locate their phase within ±1.5 hours in most cases, making timed dosing practical (Lovato 2016). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — timing over dose, on indirect dose-comparison evidence.
cards.watchOut: The headline comparison has never been run as a trial in the disorder itself: anyone needing a precise prescription still needs the patient's phase, and a wrongly timed larger dose can shift the clock the wrong way.
cards.source: Synthesis of van Geijlswijk IM et al. Sleep. 2010 (PMID: 21120122); Burgess HJ et al. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2010 (PMID: 20410229); Lovato N et al. Chronobiology international. 2016 (PMID: 27611743).

shelves.title: Clonazepam or melatonin for REM sleep behavior disorder — a split choice: clonazepam improved the polysomnography in the only head-to-head trial, melatonin was gentler (less sleepiness, no rise in depressive symptoms), and neither has been tested for falls or injuries
shelves.question: Should adults with REM sleep behavior disorder take clonazepam or melatonin for safety?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Clonazepam · Melatonin · Prospective Studies · REM Sleep Behavior Disorder · Polysomnography
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1509, which covers melatonin versus placebo in REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) — this pack covers the slice #1509 does not: the clonazepam comparison and the safety choice between the two first-line drugs. In the only head-to-head randomised trial (Byun 2023, PMID: 35141811; 34 patients with isolated RBD), 4 weeks of clonazepam 0.5 mg — but not prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg — improved REM sleep without atonia on polysomnography, and clinical global improvement tended to favour clonazepam (P = 0.068); but depressive symptoms increased on clonazepam, while daytime sleepiness and insomnia symptoms improved on melatonin and not on clonazepam, and mild-to-moderate adverse events were reported by 4 patients (13.3%), similar between groups. A meta-analysis of polysomnography studies (Que 2022, PMID: 36387478) found drug-specific objective effects for both agents without a direct safety verdict, and a 2026 systematic review of 18 video-polysomnography-confirmed studies in synucleinopathies (Byun 2026, PMID: 42623795) concluded clonazepam shows possible benefit but raises important safety concerns in vulnerable populations, while melatonin appears better tolerated with inconsistent efficacy. No trial is powered for falls, fractures or injuries — the outcomes the safety question most cares about. PROPOSED SPLIT (clonazepam: better objective efficacy on polysomnography; melatonin: better tolerated) — on the narrow safety-and-tolerability evidence available, melatonin is the gentler drug and clonazepam the more effective one, and the choice turns on which of those the individual patient needs.

cards.headline: Byun 2023: in the only head-to-head randomised trial, clonazepam 0.5 mg improved REM sleep without atonia and melatonin 2 mg did not — but depressive symptoms rose on clonazepam while sleepiness and insomnia improved on melatonin (34 patients randomised; N on the face)
cards.summary: Byun 2023: in the only head-to-head randomised trial, clonazepam 0.5 mg improved REM sleep without atonia and melatonin 2 mg did not — but depressive symptoms rose on clonazepam while sleepiness and insomnia improved on melatonin (34 patients randomised; N on the face)
cards.type: Randomised, open-label head-to-head trial (Byun 2023)
cards.people: Patients with video-polysomnography-confirmed isolated REM sleep behavior disorder; of 40 patients with probable RBD considered, 34 were enrolled and randomised to clonazepam 0.5 mg or prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg, taken 30 minutes before bedtime for 4 weeks, in a prospective, open-label, randomised trial. Randomised N = 34.
cards.result: Visual scoring parameters of REM sleep without atonia (RWA) indices were reduced, and automatic scoring parameters tended to be improved, after clonazepam treatment but not after prolonged-release melatonin. The proportion of N2 sleep increased, and N3 and REM sleep decreased, only in the clonazepam group. The clonazepam group tended to answer 'much or very much improvement' on the clinical global impression more frequently than the melatonin group (P = 0.068). Daytime sleepiness and insomnia symptoms were reduced after prolonged-release melatonin but not after clonazepam. Depressive symptoms increased after clonazepam. Four patients (13.3%) reported mild-to-moderate adverse events, which were similar between the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 4 weeks, and only 34 patients: this trial can compare short-term polysomnography and symptom signals, but it cannot measure the harms that drive the safety choice in older adults — falls, fractures, cognitive effects and dependence — and its melatonin arm used a 2 mg prolonged-release dose, lower than the 3–12 mg range on home shelf #1509.
cards.source: Byun JI et al. Comparative efficacy of prolonged-release melatonin versus clonazepam for isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder. Sleep and Breathing. 2023. PMID: 35141811. cards.headline: Que 2022: across 13 polysomnography studies, clonazepam and melatonin each moved different objective measures — clonazepam reduced stage 2 sleep percentage; melatonin improved sleep efficiency and reduced phasic and tonic muscle activity — with no direct safety comparison
cards.summary: Que 2022: across 13 polysomnography studies, clonazepam and melatonin each moved different objective measures — clonazepam reduced stage 2 sleep percentage; melatonin improved sleep efficiency and reduced phasic and tonic muscle activity — with no direct safety comparison
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled trials (Que 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised and non-randomised controlled trials of pharmacotherapies (clonazepam, melatonin, pramipexole, ramelteon, rotigotine) in patients with REM sleep behavior disorder assessed by polysomnography; of 454 studies identified, 13 were eligible. Total participant N is not documented as a single figure in the record.
cards.result: Compared with baseline, clonazepam significantly decreased the percentage of stage 2 sleep [4.00 (95% CI 0.90 to 7.10)]. Melatonin significantly improved sleep efficiency [2.51 (95% CI 0.75 to 4.28)], significantly reduced time spent in bed [-11.71 (95% CI -23.05 to -0.37)], phasic activity [-25.79 (95% CI -42.13 to -9.46)] and tonic activity [-10.44 (95% CI -12.24 to -8.64)]. The record reports no pooled adverse-event or safety effect size for either drug — that absence is printed plainly here rather than filled in.
cards.watchOut: Most comparisons here are against baseline, not against the other drug or placebo, so pre–post improvements absorb placebo effects, regression to the mean and night-to-night variability in RBD severity.

cards.headline: Byun 2026: across 18 video-polysomnography-confirmed studies in synucleinopathies, clonazepam showed possible benefit but raised important safety concerns in vulnerable populations, while melatonin appeared better tolerated with inconsistent efficacy
cards.summary: Byun 2026: across 18 video-polysomnography-confirmed studies in synucleinopathies, clonazepam showed possible benefit but raised important safety concerns in vulnerable populations, while melatonin appeared better tolerated with inconsistent efficacy
cards.type: Systematic review, narrative synthesis (Byun 2026)
cards.people: Systematic review (PRISMA; PROSPERO CRD420261340322) of randomised, crossover, open-label and observational studies of pharmacological treatments for RBD in synucleinopathies — Parkinson's disease, Parkinson's disease dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies, multiple system atrophy, and isolated RBD — requiring video-polysomnography-confirmed RBD; 18 studies met the inclusion criteria. Total participant N is not documented as a single figure in the record.
cards.result: Subjective clinical improvement was reported more often than objective video-polysomnography improvement. Clonazepam and melatonin remain the principal treatments in practice, but the evidence was limited and inconsistent: clonazepam showed possible benefit but raised important safety concerns in vulnerable synucleinopathy populations; melatonin appeared better tolerated, but its efficacy was inconsistent across synucleinopathy phenotypes and the evidence remains insufficient for definitive subgroup conclusions. The authors call for larger randomised trials using standardised clinical and video-polysomnography outcomes. No pooled effect size is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: A narrative synthesis of small, heterogeneous studies: 'safety concerns' for clonazepam here are a qualitative judgement across vulnerable populations, not a measured excess of falls or fractures in any single study.
cards.source: Byun JJ et al. Pharmacological treatments of REM sleep behaviour disorder in synucleinopathies: a systematic review of effectiveness and safety. Sleep Medicine. 2026. PMID: 42623795. cards.headline: Synthesis: clonazepam wins the polysomnography comparison and melatonin wins tolerability — the safety choice is a trade-off, not a verdict for either drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: clonazepam wins the polysomnography comparison and melatonin wins tolerability — the safety choice is a trade-off, not a verdict for either drug
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one head-to-head randomised trial in isolated RBD (34 patients randomised; clonazepam 0.5 mg vs prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg for 4 weeks), one meta-analysis of 13 polysomnography studies, and one systematic review of 18 studies in synucleinopathies. The only directly comparative randomised evidence is the 34-patient trial, whose N is printed on its face; the reviews overlap with it and with each other, so no summed total N is claimed.
cards.result: Four weeks of clonazepam, but not prolonged-release melatonin, improved REM sleep without atonia, with a trend to better clinical global improvement (P = 0.068), at the cost of increased depressive symptoms; melatonin reduced daytime sleepiness and insomnia symptoms, and mild-to-moderate adverse events were similar between groups (13.3% of patients) (Byun 2023). Across the wider literature both drugs move objective sleep measures (Que 2022), and the 2026 synucleinopathy review judges clonazepam possibly beneficial but safety-concerning in vulnerable patients, and melatonin better tolerated but inconsistently effective (Byun 2026). No carded study measures falls, fractures or dream-enactment injuries head-to-head. PROPOSED SPLIT (clonazepam: better objective efficacy; melatonin: better tolerated).
cards.watchOut: Home shelf #1509 covers melatonin versus placebo; this shelf must not be read as re-judging that question. The head-to-head trial's melatonin dose (2 mg prolonged-release) is at the bottom of the range used in practice, so 'clonazepam beat melatonin' here means 'beat 2 mg prolonged-release melatonin over 4 weeks in 34 patients'.
cards.source: Synthesis of Byun JI et al. Sleep and Breathing. 2023 (PMID: 35141811); Que Z et al. Heliyon. 2022 (PMID: 36387478); Byun JJ et al. Sleep Medicine. 2026 (PMID: 42623795).

shelves.title: Trazodone for sleep in Alzheimer's dementia: one small trial found 42.5 more minutes of night-time sleep on 50 mg versus placebo — promising, low-certainty, and never replicated
shelves.question: Does trazodone help sleep in Alzheimer's dementia better than placebo?
shelves.mesh: Actigraphy · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alzheimer Disease · Cognition Disorders · Comorbidity · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors · Sleep Wake Disorders · Trazodone · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3683, which covers trazodone in general chronic insomnia — this pack covers the slice #3683 does not: Alzheimer's dementia specifically. The entire randomised evidence is one small trial (Camargos 2014, PMID: 24495406): in 30 community-dwelling patients with probable Alzheimer's disease and sleep disturbance, trazodone 50 mg at night for 2 weeks increased actigraphic night-time sleep by 42.5 minutes and night-time percent sleep by 8.5 percentage points versus placebo, with no effect on cognition or function and no difference in adverse events. The Cochrane review of pharmacotherapies for sleep disturbances in dementia (McCleery 2020, PMID: 33189083) graded that same trial as low-certainty evidence (total nocturnal sleep time mean difference 42.46 minutes, 95% CI 0.9 to 84.0), and a 2024 meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials of sleep drugs in Alzheimer's disease (Bedward 2024, PMID: 38597219) likewise called trazodone promising while requiring more trials. One small, short, single-centre trial programme therefore caps this shelf at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): trazodone 50 mg probably buys roughly three-quarters of an hour more night-time sleep over 2 weeks in Alzheimer's dementia — a real but thinly evidenced gain, from a single trial of 30 patients.

cards.summary: Camargos 2014: trazodone 50 mg gave Alzheimer's patients 42.5 more minutes of night-time sleep and 8.5 percentage points more night-time percent sleep than placebo over 2 weeks — in the only randomised trial, of 30 patients (N on the face)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Camargos 2014)
cards.people: Community-dwelling individuals with probable Alzheimer's disease and sleep disturbance at a university geriatric medical centre; the complete analysis comprised 30 patients assigned to trazodone (N = 15) or placebo (N = 15), receiving 50 mg of trazodone once daily at 10:00 P.M. or placebo for 2 weeks, after 7–9 days of baseline evaluation, assessed by actigraphy and structured scales. Trial N = 30.
cards.result: Compared with the placebo group, trazodone users slept 42.5 more minutes per night and had their night-time percent sleep increased by 8.5 percentage points according to actigraphic data post-treatment. Neither trazodone nor placebo induced significant daytime sleepiness or naps. Neither treatment showed any effect on cognition (Mini-Mental State Examination and five further cognitive tests) or functionality (Katz index). There were no differences in frequency or severity rating of adverse events between the groups.
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients, 2 weeks, one centre: the confidence interval around the sleep gain is wide, actigraphy infers sleep from movement (it can score quiet wakefulness as sleep, a particular risk with a sedating drug), and 2 weeks says nothing about tolerance, falls or longer-term safety in dementia.
cards.source: Camargos EF et al. Trazodone improves sleep parameters in Alzheimer disease patients: a randomized, double-blind, and placebo-controlled study. The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry. 2014. PMID: 24495406. Registry ID: NCT01142258. cards.headline: Cochrane 2020: the same single trazodone trial is low-certainty evidence — total nocturnal sleep time mean difference 42.46 minutes (95% CI 0.9 to 84.0), sleep efficiency +8.53%, with several secondary outcomes uncertain or showing no difference (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Cochrane 2020: the same single trazodone trial is low-certainty evidence — total nocturnal sleep time mean difference 42.46 minutes (95% CI 0.9 to 84.0), sleep efficiency +8.53%, with several secondary outcomes uncertain or showing no difference (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (McCleery 2020)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials comparing any drug with placebo for sleep disorders in people with dementia who had an identified sleep disturbance at baseline; nine eligible trials covered melatonin (5 studies, n = 222), trazodone (1 study, n = 30), ramelteon (1 study, n = 74) and orexin antagonists (2 studies, n = 323). Participants in the trazodone study had moderate-to-severe dementia due to Alzheimer's disease.
cards.result: For trazodone 50 mg for 2 weeks, the review found low-certainty evidence that it may improve total nocturnal sleep time (mean difference 42.46 minutes, 95% CI 0.9 to 84.0; 1 study, n = 30) and sleep efficiency (mean difference 8.53%, 95% CI 1.9 to 15.1; 1 study, n = 30) in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease. The effect on time awake after sleep onset was uncertain (mean difference -20.41 minutes, 95% CI -60.4 to 19.6). There may be little or no effect on number of night-time awakenings (mean difference -3.71, 95% CI -8.2 to 0.8) or time asleep in the day (mean difference 5.12 minutes, 95% CI -28.2 to 38.4) — for those outcomes the treatment made no difference the review could detect. No serious adverse effects of trazodone were reported.
cards.watchOut: This card re-analyses the Camargos trial on the card above — it is a certainty grading of the same 30 patients, not independent confirmation, and the shelf's evidence base must not be double-counted.
cards.source: McCleery J et al. Pharmacotherapies for sleep disturbances in dementia. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020. PMID: 33189083. Registry ID: NCT01142258 (the trazodone trial included in the review; from the record). cards.headline: Bedward 2024: across 14 randomised trials of sleep drugs in Alzheimer's disease, trazodone and orexin antagonists 'showed promising results' while melatonin showed no difference — but more trials are needed for definite answers
cards.summary: Bedward 2024: across 14 randomised trials of sleep drugs in Alzheimer's disease, trazodone and orexin antagonists 'showed promising results' while melatonin showed no difference — but more trials are needed for definite answers
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Bedward 2024)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (January 2000 to July 2023; eight databases) comparing a pharmacological intervention with placebo for improving sleep in people with Alzheimer's disease; 14 randomised trials examining eight different interventions and 29 different sleep outcomes were included. Total participant N is not documented as a single figure in the record.
cards.result: Eszopiclone positively affected sleep efficiency, as did orexin antagonists; there was no difference when melatonin was used (the treatment made no difference). The interventions demonstrated low discontinuation rates and few adverse drug reactions. Although melatonin was the most investigated intervention, the evidence for its efficacy is inconclusive; trazodone and orexin receptor antagonists showed promising results, however more randomised trials are needed for definite answers. The record reports no trazodone-specific pooled effect size — that absence is printed plainly here.
cards.watchOut: 'Promising' here rests on the same single 30-patient trazodone trial carded above; a meta-analysis cannot manufacture replication, and pooling across eight different drugs and 29 outcomes invites selective emphasis.
cards.source: Bedward A et al. Pharmacological interventions to improve sleep in people with Alzheimer's disease: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Expert Review of Neurotherapeutics. 2024. PMID: 38597219. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Alzheimer Disease · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Melatonin · Orexin Receptor Antagonists · Sleep Wake Disorders · Sleep · Trazodone · Eszopiclone · Hypnotics and Sedatives
