cards.headline: Synthesis: one 30-patient trial says trazodone 50 mg adds about 42 minutes of night sleep in Alzheimer's dementia; two reviews grade that same trial as low-certainty and promising-but-unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: one 30-patient trial says trazodone 50 mg adds about 42 minutes of night sleep in Alzheimer's dementia; two reviews grade that same trial as low-certainty and promising-but-unproven
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence for the trazodone question is a single randomised trial of 30 patients (15 trazodone, 15 placebo; 2 weeks; actigraphy), re-graded by a Cochrane review and included in a 14-trial meta-analysis of sleep drugs in Alzheimer's disease. Unique participants randomised to trazodone or placebo for this question: 30 — printed here because the shelf's total evidence base for trazodone is that one small trial.
cards.result: Trazodone users slept 42.5 more minutes per night than placebo users, with night-time percent sleep up 8.5 percentage points, no cognitive or functional effect, and no difference in adverse events (Camargos 2014). Cochrane expresses the same result as a mean difference of 42.46 minutes (95% CI 0.9 to 84.0) at low certainty, with wake-after-sleep-onset uncertain and awakenings and daytime sleep showing no difference (McCleery 2020). The 2024 meta-analysis calls trazodone promising and notes melatonin showed no difference in the same population (Bedward 2024). A larger trial targeting sleep and cognition with trazodone in early Alzheimer's disease / amnestic mild cognitive impairment (REST, NCT05282550, planned n = 100) is described in the literature as a design paper with no results in the records fetched this session, so the gap may narrow. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme, total N = 30.
cards.watchOut: Home shelf #3683 covers trazodone in general chronic insomnia and reaches a cooler verdict there; this shelf is narrower (Alzheimer's dementia, actigraphy, 50 mg, 2 weeks) and its warmer point estimate comes from far fewer patients — the two shelves are consistent once the populations are kept separate.
cards.source: Synthesis of Camargos EF et al. The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry. 2014 (PMID: 24495406); McCleery J et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020 (PMID: 33189083); Bedward A et al. Expert Review of Neurotherapeutics. 2024 (PMID: 38597219).

shelves.title: Extending sleep in short sleepers: feasible and metabolically promising in small short trials (less eating, lower blood pressure in some) — but the mortality question behind the 7-hour U-curve has never been trial-tested
shelves.question: How much sleep duration is associated with lowest mortality in adults, and does extending sleep in short sleepers help?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Body Mass Index · Energy Intake · Humans · Male · Obesity · Overweight · Sleep · Young Adult
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #493, which covers the observational duration–mortality association (the U-curve, lowest risk at about 7 hours) — this pack covers the slice #493 cannot answer from cohorts: whether deliberately extending sleep in habitual short sleepers improves health. No trial has tested sleep extension against mortality or cardiovascular events; the carded trials are small, short and surrogate-outcome. In the largest (Tasali 2022, PMID: 35129580; 80 adults with overweight sleeping under 6.5 hours), a single sleep-hygiene counselling session extended sleep by about 1.2 hours per night and cut objectively measured energy intake by 270 kcal/day (95% CI -393 to -147) versus control, with weight reduction. A 6-week cognitive-behavioural extension programme in 18 men (Hartescu 2022, PMID: 34459060) added 79 minutes of sleep and improved blood pressure and insulin-resistance markers. A meta-analysis of 13 experimental studies (Zhu 2022, PMID: 34279625) found extension feasible (+51 minutes of total sleep time), no overall blood-pressure effect, a blood-pressure reduction only in the pre-hypertension/hypertension subgroup, and no significant pooled effect on fasting glucose or insulin resistance (the treatment made no difference on those pooled outcomes). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): extending sleep in short sleepers is achievable and improves some short-term metabolic measures, but whether it moves the mortality curve that home shelf #493 describes is untested.

cards.headline: Tasali 2022: one counselling session extended sleep by about 1.2 hours a night and cut objectively measured energy intake by 270 kcal/day in 80 adults with overweight who habitually slept under 6.5 hours
cards.summary: Tasali 2022: one counselling session extended sleep by about 1.2 hours a night and cut objectively measured energy intake by 270 kcal/day in 80 adults with overweight who habitually slept under 6.5 hours
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (Tasali 2022)
cards.people: Adults aged 21 to 40 years with body mass index 25.0 to 29.9 and habitual sleep duration under 6.5 hours per night, in a single-centre randomised clinical trial (2014–2020); after a 2-week habitual-sleep baseline, participants were randomised to an individualised sleep-hygiene counselling session aiming to extend bedtime to 8.5 hours, or to continue habitual sleep, with no prescribed diet or physical activity. Data from 80 randomised participants (mean age 29.8 years; 41 men) were analysed.
cards.result: Sleep duration increased by approximately 1.2 hours per night (95% CI 1.0 to 1.4; P < 0.001) in the sleep-extension group versus control, measured by actigraphy. The extension group had a significant decrease in objectively assessed energy intake compared with control (-270 kcal/day; 95% CI -393 to -147; P < 0.001), and change in sleep duration was inversely correlated with change in energy intake (r = -0.41; 95% CI -0.59 to -0.20; P < 0.001). No significant treatment effect on total energy expenditure was found, resulting in weight reduction in the sleep-extension group versus control (the record reports the direction, not a kilogram figure).
cards.watchOut: Two weeks of intervention in 80 young adults with overweight: energy intake over a fortnight is a mechanism, not a health outcome, and nothing here shows the effect persists, that weight stays off, or that any clinical event is prevented.
cards.source: Tasali E et al. Effect of Sleep Extension on Objectively Assessed Energy Intake Among Adults With Overweight in Real-life Settings: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2022. PMID: 35129580. Registry ID: NCT02253368. MeSH: Adult · Body Mass Index · Energy Intake · Humans · Male · Obesity · Overweight · Sleep · Young Adult

cards.headline: Hartescu 2022: a 6-week extension programme added 79 minutes of sleep and lowered systolic blood pressure by about 11 mmHg versus control — in 18 men at increased diabetes risk (small N on the face)
cards.summary: Hartescu 2022: a 6-week extension programme added 79 minutes of sleep and lowered systolic blood pressure by about 11 mmHg versus control — in 18 men at increased diabetes risk (small N on the face)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Hartescu 2022)
cards.people: 18 men (mean age 41 years) who were overweight/obese (mean body mass index 30 kg/m2), habitual short sleepers at increased risk of type 2 diabetes, randomised to a 6-week sleep-extension programme based on cognitive behavioural principles (n = 10) or a control group (n = 8). Trial N = 18.
cards.result: Baseline-to-6-week change in actigraphic total sleep time was greater in the extension group: 79 minutes (95% CI 68.90 to 88.05) versus 6 minutes (95% CI -4.43 to 16.99). Changes in the extension versus control groups respectively also showed lower fasting insulin (-11.03 [95% CI -22.70 to 0.65] versus 7.07 [95% CI -4.60 to 18.74] pmol/L), lower systolic blood pressure (-11.09 [95% CI -17.49 to -4.69] versus 0.76 [95% CI -5.64 to 7.15] mmHg), lower diastolic blood pressure (-12.16 [95% CI -17.74 to -6.59] versus 1.38 [95% CI -4.19 to 6.96] mmHg), and improved insulin resistance (HOMA-IR -0.51 [95% CI -0.98 to -0.03] versus 0.28 [95% CI -0.20 to 0.76]).
cards.watchOut: Eighteen men, 6 weeks, surrogate endpoints: blood-pressure falls of this size in a sample this small are exactly the results small trials produce by chance and selection, and the trial enrolled men only despite the record's MeSH listing both sexes.
cards.source: Hartescu I et al. Sleep extension and metabolic health in male overweight/obese short sleepers: A randomised controlled trial. Journal of Sleep Research. 2022. PMID: 34459060. Registry ID: NCT04467268. MeSH: Adult · Blood Glucose · Body Mass Index · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Female · Glucose · Humans · Insulin · Insulin Resistance · Male · Obesity · Overweight · Sleep

cards.headline: Zhu 2022: across 13 experimental studies, sleep extension added 51 minutes of sleep and lowered 24-hour blood pressure only in people with pre-hypertension or stage 1 hypertension (systolic -7.8 mmHg); pooled glucose and insulin-resistance effects showed no difference (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Zhu 2022: across 13 experimental studies, sleep extension added 51 minutes of sleep and lowered 24-hour blood pressure only in people with pre-hypertension or stage 1 hypertension (systolic -7.8 mmHg); pooled glucose and insulin-resistance effects showed no difference (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of experimental studies (Zhu 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42019146174) of experimental sleep-extension studies in adults without a diagnosed sleep disorder in free-living settings; 13 studies from 11 trials were included, with interventions ranging from 3 days to 6 weeks. Total participant N is not documented as a single figure in the record.
cards.result: Sleep extension increased total sleep time by 51 minutes [95% CI 39 to 63]. Overall, sleep extension did not result in significant changes in blood pressure; however, subgroup analysis found that when 24-hour mean blood pressure was obtained among those with pre-hypertension or stage 1 hypertension, sleep extension reduced systolic blood pressure (weighted mean difference -7.8 mmHg; 95% CI -10.6 to -4.9) and diastolic blood pressure (weighted mean difference -4.2 mmHg; 95% CI -6.7 to -1.8). The pooled effects on fasting glucose and insulin resistance were not significant (the treatment made no difference on those pooled outcomes), and the effect on other parameters such as heart rate was not consistent.
cards.watchOut: Interventions as short as 3 days are pooled with 6-week programmes, and the headline blood-pressure benefit comes from a subgroup defined by how blood pressure was measured and who had it — a hypothesis-generating cut, not a demonstrated indication.
cards.source: Zhu B et al. Feasibility of sleep extension and its effect on cardiometabolic parameters in free-living settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis of experimental studies. European Journal of Cardiovascular Nursing. 2022. PMID: 34279625. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: short sleepers can be taught to sleep about an hour longer, and short-term metabolic measures improve — but no trial connects extending sleep to the mortality benefit the observational U-curve implies
cards.summary: Synthesis: short sleepers can be taught to sleep about an hour longer, and short-term metabolic measures improve — but no trial connects extending sleep to the mortality benefit the observational U-curve implies
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised trials (80 adults with overweight sleeping under 6.5 hours; 18 men at increased diabetes risk — its N printed on its face) and one meta-analysis of 13 experimental studies whose interventions lasted 3 days to 6 weeks. Unique randomised participants on the two trial cards total 98, so no small-N stamp applies to the shelf as a whole; no carded study measured mortality, cardiovascular events or diabetes incidence.
cards.result: Extension raised sleep by about 1.2 hours/night (Tasali 2022) and 79 minutes/night (Hartescu 2022), and by 51 minutes pooled (Zhu 2022). Energy intake fell by 270 kcal/day with weight reduction (Tasali 2022); blood pressure and HOMA-IR improved in the 18-man trial (Hartescu 2022); pooled across studies, blood pressure fell only in the pre-hypertension/hypertension subgroup (systolic -7.8 mmHg) and pooled glucose and insulin-resistance effects were not significant (Zhu 2022). Home shelf #493's lowest-mortality duration (about 7 hours) comes from cohorts; whether moving a short sleeper toward it changes their risk is precisely what these short surrogate-outcome trials cannot show. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — short-term surrogate outcomes only.
cards.watchOut: Do not let this shelf upgrade home shelf #493: the association there is observational, and a 2-week calorie effect plus small-trial blood-pressure changes are not evidence that sleep extension reduces mortality — that trial has never been run.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tasali E et al. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35129580); Hartescu I et al. Journal of Sleep Research. 2022 (PMID: 34459060); Zhu B et al. European Journal of Cardiovascular Nursing. 2022 (PMID: 34279625).

shelves.title: Corticosteroids in all community-acquired pneumonia (PARTIAL completion of #159, which covers severe pneumonia only): no demonstrated mortality reduction across all severities — about a day faster recovery instead
shelves.question: Should adults with community-acquired pneumonia receive corticosteroids to reduce mortality?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Age Factors · Community-Acquired Infections/*drug therapy/mortality · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Hyperglycemia/etiology · Length of Stay/*statistics & numerical data · Odds Ratio · Pneumonia/*drug therapy/mortality · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Regression Analysis · Risk Factors · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #159 covers corticosteroids in severe community-acquired pneumonia only (its mortality signal rests on the ICU-severe CAPE COD trial) and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded; this shelf asks the slice #159 does not: all adults with community-acquired pneumonia, most of them not severely ill. Across all severities, a mortality reduction is not demonstrated. The individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 6 placebo-controlled trials (Briel 2018, 1,506 patients) found 30-day mortality of 5.0% on corticosteroids vs 5.9% on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.21 — the treatment made no significant difference), with no effect modification by severity or inflammation. An earlier aggregate meta-analysis (Siemieniuk 2015) was more favourable on its face (risk ratio 0.67 relative, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.01; risk difference 2.8%) but its interval also crosses no effect and its certainty was rated moderate. The two all-comer/non-ICU randomised trials carded here agree on the pattern: steroids shorten time to stability and hospital stay by about a day (Wittermans 2021: stay 4.5 vs 5.0 days; 30-day mortality did not differ) and in one trial bought nothing at all while increasing late failure (Snijders 2010). The consistent price is hyperglycaemia (22.1% vs 12.0% in the individual-patient analysis) and more pneumonia-related rehospitalisation (5.0% vs 2.7%). One carded trial (STEP) already sits on home #159 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — unproven for mortality in all-comer pneumonia: the demonstrated gain is about a day faster recovery, not fewer deaths, outside the severe subgroup homed at #159.

cards.headline: Briel 2018 individual-patient meta-analysis (1,506 patients, 6 trials): 30-day mortality 5.0% vs 5.9% — adjusted odds ratio 0.75 (0.46–1.21), no significant mortality effect and no modification by severity
cards.summary: Briel 2018 individual-patient meta-analysis (1,506 patients, 6 trials): 30-day mortality 5.0% vs 5.9% — adjusted odds ratio 0.75 (0.46–1.21), no significant mortality effect and no modification by severity
cards.type: Individual patient data meta-analysis (Briel 2018)
cards.people: Individual patient data from 1,506 patients in 6 randomised, placebo-controlled trials of adjunctive corticosteroids in adults hospitalised with community-acquired pneumonia, analysed with uniform outcome definitions and adjustment for pneumonia severity, age and clustering.
cards.result: Within 30 days of randomisation, 37 of 748 patients (5.0%) assigned to corticosteroids and 45 of 758 patients (5.9%) assigned to placebo died (adjusted odds ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.21; P = .24, relative measure) — the treatment made no significant difference to mortality. Time to clinical stability and length of hospital stay were each reduced by approximately 1 day (−1.03 days, 95% CI −1.62 to −0.43; and −1.15 days, 95% CI −1.75 to −0.55). More patients on corticosteroids had hyperglycemia (22.1% vs 12.0%; adjusted odds ratio 2.15, 95% CI 1.60 to 2.90) and pneumonia-related rehospitalisation (5.0% vs 2.7%; adjusted odds ratio 1.85, 95% CI 1.03 to 3.32). No significant effect modification by pneumonia severity or degree of inflammation was found.
cards.watchOut: These 6 trials predate the severe-pneumonia hydrocortisone trial homed at #159, so this analysis answers the all-comer question as it stood in the earlier trials; its confidence interval (0.46–1.21) excludes neither a worthwhile benefit nor slight harm, which is why the stamp says unproven rather than disproven.
cards.source: Briel M et al. Corticosteroids in Patients Hospitalized With Community-Acquired Pneumonia: Systematic Review and Individual Patient Data Metaanalysis. cards.headline: Siemieniuk 2015 meta-analysis: a possible mortality reduction (risk ratio 0.67 relative, 0.45–1.01; risk difference 2.8%, moderate certainty) with clearer reductions in ventilation and ARDS — and more hyperglycaemia
cards.summary: Siemieniuk 2015 meta-analysis: a possible mortality reduction (risk ratio 0.67 relative, 0.45–1.01; risk difference 2.8%, moderate certainty) with clearer reductions in ventilation and ARDS — and more hyperglycaemia
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Siemieniuk 2015)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of systemic corticosteroids in hospitalised adults with community-acquired pneumonia (through May 2015); the mortality analysis pooled 12 trials and 1,974 patients. Median age in the trials was typically in the 60s and approximately 60% of patients were male.
cards.result: Adjunctive corticosteroids were associated with possible reductions in all-cause mortality (12 trials; 1,974 patients; risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.01, relative measure; risk difference 2.8%; moderate certainty), need for mechanical ventilation (5 trials; 1,060 patients; risk ratio 0.45 relative; risk difference 5.0%; moderate certainty) and acute respiratory distress syndrome (4 trials; 945 patients; risk ratio 0.24 relative; risk difference 6.2%; moderate certainty). Time to clinical stability fell by 1.22 days and hospitalisation by 1.00 day (high certainty). Hyperglycemia requiring treatment increased (risk ratio 1.49 relative; risk difference 3.5%; high certainty), with no increase in gastrointestinal hemorrhage.
cards.watchOut: The mortality interval just crosses 1.0 and the pooled trials mix severities and steroid regimens; the ventilation and ARDS reductions come from few events in sicker subsets and should not be read as all-comer effects.
cards.source: Siemieniuk RAC et al. Corticosteroid Therapy for Patients Hospitalized With Community-Acquired Pneumonia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2015. PMID: 26258555. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wittermans 2021 (Santeon-CAP): in non-ICU hospitalised pneumonia, oral dexamethasone shortened stay (4.5 vs 5.0 days) and ICU admissions (3% vs 7%) — 30-day mortality did not differ
cards.summary: Wittermans 2021 (Santeon-CAP): in non-ICU hospitalised pneumonia, oral dexamethasone shortened stay (4.5 vs 5.0 days) and ICU admissions (3% vs 7%) — 30-day mortality did not differ
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Wittermans 2021)
cards.people: Multicentre, stratified, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial in four Dutch teaching hospitals: 401 immunocompetent adults hospitalised with community-acquired pneumonia outside the ICU, assigned to oral dexamethasone 6 mg once daily (n = 203) or placebo (n = 198) for 4 days, stratified by pneumonia severity index class I–III and IV–V.
cards.result: Median length of stay was shorter on dexamethasone (4.5 days, 95% CI 4.0–5.0) than placebo (5.0 days, 95% CI 4.6–5.4; p = 0.033), with no statistically significant stay difference within either severity subgroup. The ICU admission rate was lower in the dexamethasone arm (5 patients, 3%, vs 14 patients, 7%; p = 0.030). Thirty-day mortality did not differ between groups (the record does not print the mortality rates). Readmission tended to be higher on dexamethasone (20 patients, 10%, vs 9 patients, 5%; p = 0.051) and hyperglycaemia was more prevalent (14 patients, 7%, vs 1 patient, 1%; p = 0.001).
cards.watchOut: A non-ICU population has low baseline mortality, so a 401-patient trial cannot settle the mortality question; its mortality statement is 'did not differ' without printed rates, and the readmission trend runs against the stay benefit.
cards.source: Wittermans E et al. Adjunctive treatment with oral dexamethasone in non-ICU patients hospitalised with community-acquired pneumonia: a randomised clinical trial. European Respiratory Journal. 2021. PMID: 33446608. Registry ID: NCT01743755. cards.headline: Snijders 2010: prednisolone 40 mg for 7 days did not improve cure at day 7 or 30 in hospitalised pneumonia — and late failure was more common (19.2% vs 6.4% as printed)
cards.summary: Snijders 2010: prednisolone 40 mg for 7 days did not improve cure at day 7 or 30 in hospitalised pneumonia — and late failure was more common (19.2% vs 6.4% as printed)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Snijders 2010)
cards.people: Randomised, double-blind trial of 213 patients hospitalised with clinically and radiologically diagnosed community-acquired pneumonia, assigned to prednisolone 40 mg daily for 7 days or placebo alongside antibiotics; 25.4% had a CURB-65 score above 2 and 43.7% were in Pneumonia Severity Index class IV–V.
cards.result: Clinical cure at day 7 was 80.8% (84/104) on prednisolone vs 85.3% (93/109) on placebo (P = 0.38), and at day 30 was 66.3% (69/104) vs 77.1% (84/109) (P = 0.08) — the treatment made no difference to cure. Patients on prednisolone had faster defervescence and faster C-reactive protein decline. A subanalysis of patients with severe pneumonia showed no differences in clinical outcome. Late failure (beyond 72 hours after admission) was more common in the prednisolone group (20 patients, 19.2%) than in the placebo group (10 patients, 6.4% as printed in the record; P = 0.04). Adverse events were few and did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: The authors themselves conclude prednisolone should not be recommended as routine adjunctive treatment in pneumonia on this evidence, while noting a benefit in more severely ill patients could not be excluded — the severe end of that question is the one homed at #159.
cards.source: Snijders D et al. Efficacy of corticosteroids in community-acquired pneumonia: a randomized double-blinded clinical trial. American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine. 2010. PMID: 20133929. Registry ID: NCT00170196. cards.headline: Synthesis: across all adults with community-acquired pneumonia, corticosteroids have not been shown to reduce mortality — the reproducible gains are about a day faster stability and discharge, paid for in hyperglycaemia and readmissions
cards.summary: Synthesis: across all adults with community-acquired pneumonia, corticosteroids have not been shown to reduce mortality — the reproducible gains are about a day faster stability and discharge, paid for in hyperglycaemia and readmissions
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: an individual-patient meta-analysis (1,506 patients, 6 trials), an aggregate meta-analysis (mortality pool 1,974 patients, 12 trials) and two all-comer/non-ICU randomised trials (401 and 213 patients). shelves.question: Is RSV vaccination effective at preventing hospitalization in older adults with chronic lung disease?

shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #320 covers RSV vaccines in adults 60 and older generally (lower respiratory tract disease efficacy and its waning) and home live #5203 covers the mRNA vaccine trial; both are cross-pointed here, not re-carded. This shelf asks the slice neither isolates: older adults with chronic lung disease, and the hospitalisation outcome. Two honest gaps frame the answer. First, no carded record reports a vaccine effectiveness figure for chronic lung disease alone: the pivotal trial's prespecified subgroup analysis (Feldman 2024, an AReSVi-006 report) groups lung with cardiac conditions as 'cardiorespiratory' and found efficacy against lower respiratory tract disease of 92.1% relative in that combined group (94.6% relative with any condition of interest), and hospitalisation was not an outcome in that record. Second, the hospitalisation evidence is real-world and all-older-adult: the US IVY test-negative study (Surie 2025) estimated effectiveness against RSV-associated hospitalisation at 58% relative over two seasons (69% relative same-season, 48% relative prior-season), and a 2026 meta-analysis of 8 real-world studies pooled an odds ratio of 0.23 for hospitalisation; neither reports a chronic-lung-disease subgroup in its record, and both found effectiveness lower in immunocompromised patients. So the lung-specific hospitalisation number a reader wants does not exist in the carded records; what exists is high trial efficacy in the broader cardiorespiratory group plus substantial real-world protection against hospitalisation in older adults generally. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — the hospitalisation evidence is observational and the chronic-lung-disease-specific hospitalisation estimate is not separately reported in any carded record.

cards.headline: Feldman 2024 (AReSVi-006 subgroup analysis): efficacy against RSV lower respiratory tract disease was 92.1% relative in participants with cardiorespiratory conditions — but lung disease is not separated from cardiac disease, and hospitalisation was not an outcome
cards.summary: Feldman 2024 (AReSVi-006 subgroup analysis): efficacy against RSV lower respiratory tract disease was 92.1% relative in participants with cardiorespiratory conditions — but lung disease is not separated from cardiac disease, and hospitalisation was not an outcome
cards.type: Randomised trial subgroup analysis (Feldman 2024, AReSVi-006)
cards.people: Prespecified subgroup analysis of the randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 AReSVi-006 trial in adults 60 years and older: 12,467 participants received the adjuvanted RSV prefusion F vaccine and 12,499 received placebo; 39.6% (vaccine) and 38.9% (placebo) had at least one coexisting cardiorespiratory or endocrine/metabolic condition of interest. Median efficacy follow-up was 6.7 months.
cards.result: Efficacy against first RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease was 94.6% relative in participants with at least one condition of interest, 92.1% relative in those with at least one cardiorespiratory condition, 100% relative in those with at least one endocrine/metabolic condition, and 92.0% relative in those with at least two conditions of interest. Efficacy against RSV-related acute respiratory illness was 81.0% relative with at least one condition (88.1% relative for cardiorespiratory). Postvaccination neutralising titres were at least as high in participants with conditions of interest as in those without. The record does not report chronic lung disease separately from cardiac conditions, and does not report hospitalisation as an outcome.
cards.watchOut: 'Cardiorespiratory' bundles chronic lung disease with heart conditions, so the 92.1% figure cannot be quoted as the lung-disease estimate; subgroup efficacies from a single season with few events carry wide uncertainty the record's summary does not print.
cards.source: Feldman RG et al. Respiratory Syncytial Virus Prefusion F Protein Vaccine Is Efficacious in Older Adults With Underlying Medical Conditions. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2024. PMID: 37698366. Registry ID: NCT04886596. cards.headline: Surie 2025 (IVY Network): real-world effectiveness against RSV hospitalisation was 58% relative over two seasons (69% same-season, 48% prior-season) in 6,958 hospitalised adults 60+ — no lung-disease subgroup in the record
cards.summary: Surie 2025 (IVY Network): real-world effectiveness against RSV hospitalisation was 58% relative over two seasons (69% same-season, 48% prior-season) in 6,958 hospitalised adults 60+ — no lung-disease subgroup in the record
cards.type: Test-negative case-control study (Surie 2025)
cards.people: Test-negative, case-control study of 6,958 adults aged 60 years or older hospitalised with acute respiratory illness at 26 hospitals in 20 US states during the 2023–24 and 2024–25 RSV seasons: 821 RSV case patients and 6,137 controls; median age 72 years; 26.3% were immunocompromised. A total of 63 cases (7.7%) and 966 controls (15.7%) were vaccinated.
cards.result: Estimated vaccine effectiveness against RSV-associated hospitalisation was 58% (95% CI 45%–68%) across the two seasons, 69% (95% CI 52%–81%) for same-season vaccination versus 48% (95% CI 27%–63%) for prior-season vaccination (relative measures). Effectiveness was significantly lower in immunocompromised adults (30%, 95% CI −9% to 55%) than immunocompetent adults (67%, 95% CI 53%–77%), and lower in those with cardiovascular disease (56%, 95% CI 32%–72%) than without (80%, 95% CI 62%–90%). The record does not report a chronic lung disease subgroup estimate.
cards.watchOut: Test-negative observational estimates can be biased by who gets vaccinated and who gets tested; the fall from 69% to 48% by season also means a single 'effectiveness' number hides waning that matters for patients with lung disease, who are vaccinated earliest.
cards.source: Surie D et al. RSV Vaccine Effectiveness Against Hospitalization Among US Adults Aged 60 Years or Older During 2 Seasons. JAMA. 2025. PMID: 40884491. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sumsuzzman 2026 meta-analysis: across 8 real-world studies, vaccination was associated with lower odds of RSV hospitalisation (odds ratio 0.23, 0.20–0.27) — subgroups were reported by age and immune status, not by lung disease
cards.summary: Sumsuzzman 2026 meta-analysis: across 8 real-world studies, vaccination was associated with lower odds of RSV hospitalisation (odds ratio 0.23, 0.20–0.27) — subgroups were reported by age and immune status, not by lung disease
cards.type: Meta-analysis of real-world effectiveness studies (Sumsuzzman 2026)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 8 cohort and case-control studies (from 4,925 records screened) reporting real-world effectiveness of the bivalent RSVpreF and adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccines against RSV-related hospitalisation and emergency department visits in adults aged 60 years or older, using studies published January 2023 to December 2025.
cards.result: Vaccination was associated with lower odds of RSV-related hospitalisation (odds ratio 0.23, 95% CI 0.20–0.27, relative measure) and emergency department visits (odds ratio 0.23, 95% CI 0.21–0.27, relative measure). Effectiveness against hospitalisation was lower in immunocompromised adults (odds ratio 0.31, 95% CI 0.27–0.34) than in immunocompetent individuals (odds ratio 0.20, 95% CI 0.11–0.35). Effectiveness did not differ by age group (60–74 vs 75 years or older) or vaccine product. No chronic lung disease subgroup is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: A pooled odds ratio of 0.23 is a relative association across observational designs, not a trial efficacy; heterogeneity was low as printed (I² = 6.5%), but the underlying studies share the same confounding risks.
cards.source: Sumsuzzman DM et al. Real-World Effectiveness of RSVpreF and RSVpreF3 Vaccines in Preventing Hospitalization and Emergency Department Visits Associated With Respiratory Syncytial Virus in Older Adults: A Meta-analysis. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2026. PMID: 41705791. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD420251021777 (from the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: vaccination very likely protects older adults with chronic lung disease against RSV hospitalisation, but the exact lung-specific hospitalisation figure has never been reported — the trial number is for a combined cardiorespiratory group and the hospitalisation numbers are for older adults generally
cards.summary: Synthesis: vaccination very likely protects older adults with chronic lung disease against RSV hospitalisation, but the exact lung-specific hospitalisation figure has never been reported — the trial number is for a combined cardiorespiratory group and the hospitalisation numbers are for older adults generally
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised-trial subgroup analysis (24,966 participants; cardiorespiratory subgroup), one large US test-negative hospitalisation study (6,958 hospitalised adults) and one meta-analysis of 8 real-world studies. The general older-adult efficacy shelves are live #320 and #5203, cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: Trial efficacy against lower respiratory tract disease in the cardiorespiratory subgroup was 92.1% relative (Feldman 2024). Real-world effectiveness against RSV hospitalisation was 58% relative over two seasons (Surie 2025) and the pooled real-world odds ratio for hospitalisation was 0.23 (Sumsuzzman 2026). No carded record separates chronic lung disease for the hospitalisation outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — hospitalisation evidence observational, lung-specific estimate not separately reported, as stated.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the numbers: 92.1% is trial efficacy against lower respiratory illness in a combined cardiac-plus-lung group, while 58% and odds ratio 0.23 are real-world hospitalisation associations in all older adults — three different quantities that happen to point the same way.
cards.source: Synthesis of Feldman RG et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2024 (PMID: 37698366); Surie D et al. JAMA. 2025 (PMID: 40884491); Sumsuzzman DM et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2026 (PMID: 41705791).

shelves.title: RSV vaccination over age 75 (PARTIAL completion of #5203 and #320): effectiveness does not drop off at 75+ in real-world data, but no trial reports an over-75-only efficacy estimate
shelves.question: Does RSV vaccination prevent lower respiratory illness in adults over 75?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Aged · Female · Male · Middle Aged · *Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections/prevention & control/epidemiology · *Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccines/adverse effects/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · United States/epidemiology · Case-Control Studies · *Vaccine Efficacy · Aged, 80 and over · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #5203 is the older-adult mRNA RSV vaccine shelf (one trial, all older adults) and home live #320 covers RSV vaccines in adults 60 and older generally; both are cross-pointed here, not re-carded. This shelf asks the slice neither isolates: adults over 75, across RSV vaccine types. The central fact is a reporting gap: no carded trial record publishes an efficacy estimate for the over-75 group alone — the trials enrolled 60+ populations and their records report pooled estimates (the pooled randomised efficacy against lower respiratory tract disease was 81.38% relative in the first season across five vaccines, Riccò 2024; one vaccine's two-season efficacy was 67.2% relative, Ison 2024 — neither record separates the over-75s). What does speak directly to age is real-world: in a US test-negative study of 787,822 tested adults (Fry 2025), vaccine effectiveness against RSV acute respiratory illness was 75.1% relative overall and was similar in the 60–74 and 75-and-older groups, including in immunocompromised patients (73.1% relative at 75+); the same record quantifies the Guillain-Barré ledger (excess 5.2 cases per million doses for the adjuvanted vaccine and 18.2 per million for the bivalent vaccine). So protection in the over-75s is supported by age-stratified real-world data showing no drop-off, resting on trial efficacy proven only for the pooled 60+ population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — no over-75-only trial estimate exists in the carded records; the age-specific support is observational.

cards.headline: Fry 2025: in 787,822 tested US adults, vaccine effectiveness was 75.1% relative against RSV illness and was similar at 75+ and 60–74 — the only carded record that stratifies effectiveness at age 75
cards.summary: Fry 2025: in 787,822 tested US adults, vaccine effectiveness was 75.1% relative against RSV illness and was similar at 75+ and 60–74 — the only carded record that stratifies effectiveness at age 75
cards.type: Test-negative case-control study with self-controlled safety series (Fry 2025)
cards.people: Test-negative case-control study using a US electronic-health-record platform (over 270 million patients): 787,822 adults aged 60 years or older tested for RSV between October 2023 and April 2024, of whom 53,963 tested positive (1,318 cases, 2.4%, and 66,928 controls, 9.1%, were vaccinated). A self-controlled case series among 4,746,518 vaccine recipients assessed adverse events.
cards.result: Overall vaccine effectiveness was 75.1% (95% CI 73.6%–76.4%, relative measure) against RSV-associated acute respiratory infection and was similar for age groups 60 to 74 years and 75 years or older, and against urgent care visits or hospitalisations (the record does not print a separate percentage for the 75-and-older group). In immunocompromised patients, effectiveness ranged from 67.0% (95% CI 62.6%–70.9%) at ages 60–74 to 73.1% (95% CI 69.9%–76.0%) at 75 years or older; the lowest effectiveness was in stem-cell transplant recipients (29.4% at 60–74; 44.4% at 75+). No excess risk of immune thrombocytopenic purpura was detected; excess Guillain-Barré syndrome was 5.2 cases per 1,000,000 doses (adjuvanted RSVPreF3+AS01 vaccine) and 18.2 per 1,000,000 doses (bivalent RSVpreF vaccine).
cards.watchOut: 'Similar' across age groups is the record's wording — it prints no 75-and-older point estimate, so this card supports 'no evident drop-off with age' and cannot support a precise over-75 effectiveness figure.
cards.source: Fry SE et al. Effectiveness and Safety of Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine for US Adults Aged 60 Years or Older. JAMA Network Open. 2025. PMID: 40343698. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Riccò 2024 meta-analysis: pooled randomised efficacy against lower respiratory tract disease was 81.38% relative in the first season across five RSV vaccines — in 60+ populations, with the over-75s not separated
cards.summary: Riccò 2024 meta-analysis: pooled randomised efficacy against lower respiratory tract disease was 81.38% relative in the first season across five RSV vaccines — in 60+ populations, with the over-75s not separated
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Riccò 2024)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of RSV vaccination in older adults (age 60 years and older), searching PubMed, Embase, Scopus and medRxiv to March 2024: nine studies included, five randomised trials of five vaccines (bivalent RSVpreF, adjuvanted RSVPreF3, Ad26.RSV.preF, MEDI7510 and mRNA-1345).
cards.result: The pooled vaccine efficacy for prevention of lower respiratory tract disease with three or more signs/symptoms during the first RSV season was 81.38% (95% CI 70.94 to 88.06, relative measure). In follow-up data (two seasons for RSVPreF3, mid-second-season for RSVpreF, 12 months for mRNA-1345) the pooled efficacy was 61.15% (95% CI 45.29 to 72.40, relative measure). Estimates were affected by substantial heterogeneity, attributed partly to inconsistent case definitions across the parent trials. The record reports no age subgroup analysis and no estimate for adults over 75.
cards.watchOut: Pooling five different vaccine platforms with different case definitions produced substantial heterogeneity; the pooled figure is context for the 60+ trial evidence (homed at #320/#5203), not an over-75 estimate, and two of the five products were experimental vaccines never marketed.
cards.source: Riccò M et al. Efficacy of Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccination to Prevent Lower Respiratory Tract Illness in Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Vaccines. 2024. PMID: 38793751. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Ison 2024 (AReSVi-006, two seasons): one dose held 67.2% relative efficacy against lower respiratory tract disease over two seasons and a second dose added nothing — again in a 60+ population with no over-75 cut in the record
cards.summary: Ison 2024 (AReSVi-006, two seasons): one dose held 67.2% relative efficacy against lower respiratory tract disease over two seasons and a second dose added nothing — again in a 60+ population with no over-75 cut in the record
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial, two-season report (Ison 2024)
cards.people: Phase 3 blinded trial report of the adjuvanted RSV prefusion F vaccine over two RSV seasons: efficacy analysis comprised 24,967 participants aged 60 years or older (one-dose group 6,227; revaccination group 6,242; placebo 12,498), with median efficacy follow-up of 17.8 months.
cards.result: Efficacy over two seasons of one vaccine dose was 67.2% (97.5% CI 48.2–80.0, relative measure) against RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease and 78.8% (95% CI 52.6–92.0, relative measure) against severe disease. A first dose followed by revaccination one year later gave 67.1% (97.5% CI 48.1–80.0) against lower respiratory tract disease and 78.8% against severe disease — revaccination was well tolerated but did not seem to provide additional efficacy benefit. The record does not report efficacy separately for participants over 75.

cards.headline: Synthesis: RSV vaccination prevents lower respiratory illness in the over-75s on the best available reading — real-world effectiveness does not fall at 75+, but no trial has ever published an over-75-only efficacy estimate
cards.summary: Synthesis: RSV vaccination prevents lower respiratory illness in the over-75s on the best available reading — real-world effectiveness does not fall at 75+, but no trial has ever published an over-75-only efficacy estimate
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one US test-negative study that stratifies at age 75 (787,822 tested adults), one meta-analysis of the five randomised vaccine trials in 60+ adults, and one two-season randomised trial report (24,967 participants). The primary trial shelves are live #320 and #5203, cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: Real-world effectiveness against RSV illness was 75.1% relative overall and similar at 75+ and 60–74, including 73.1% relative in immunocompromised patients aged 75+ (Fry 2025). Pooled randomised efficacy against lower respiratory tract disease in 60+ populations was 81.38% relative in season one, falling to 61.15% relative with longer follow-up (Riccò 2024), and one vaccine held 67.2% relative over two seasons with no gain from revaccination (Ison 2024). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — age-specific support observational; no over-75-only trial estimate in the carded records, as stated.
cards.watchOut: Guideline recommendations that single out age 75+ rest on risk (older age, more severe disease) plus this absence of an effectiveness drop-off — not on a dedicated over-75 trial; the shelf should be quoted that way.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fry SE et al. JAMA Network Open. 2025 (PMID: 40343698); Riccò M et al. Vaccines. 2024 (PMID: 38793751); Ison MG et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2024 (PMID: 38253338).

shelves.title: Pneumococcal vaccination in diabetes (PARTIAL completion of #444, older adults generally): fewer pneumonia hospitalisations in observational diabetes data, and the highest trial efficacy in the diabetes subgroup
shelves.question: In adults with diabetes, does pneumococcal vaccination reduce pneumonia hospitalizations?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Community-Acquired Infections/immunology/prevention & control · Comorbidity · Diabetes Complications/*immunology · Diabetes Mellitus/*immunology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Immunization/adverse effects · Male · Pneumococcal Infections/immunology/microbiology/*prevention & control · Pneumococcal Vaccines/administration & dosage/*immunology · Pneumonia, Pneumococcal/immunology/prevention & control · *Vaccine Potency · Vaccines, Conjugate/administration & dosage/immunology
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #444 covers pneumococcal vaccines in older adults generally (vaccine-type disease prevented; all-cause pneumonia and mortality not shown) and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded; this shelf asks only the diabetes-specific slice. The diabetes evidence is thinner and mostly observational, but it points the same way and one randomised-trial cut is striking. A post-hoc analysis of the CAPiTA trial (Huijts 2017) found the conjugate vaccine's efficacy against vaccine-type pneumonia was modified by diabetes: 89.5% relative in participants with diabetes vs 24.7% relative in those without — but that rests on only 139 vaccine-type pneumonia cases, with wide intervals, and the outcome is vaccine-type pneumonia, not hospitalisation. For hospitalisation itself, the evidence is observational: a 2024 meta-analysis of diabetes-specific studies (Silverii 2024) found hospitalisation for overall pneumonia in the year after polysaccharide vaccination lower in vaccinated diabetic patients (odds ratio 0.63, unadjusted, relative measure) with no significant differences for other outcomes, and a Taiwanese population cohort in diabetic elderly (Kuo 2016) found less invasive pneumococcal disease (adjusted odds ratio 0.86 relative) and less respiratory failure with the polysaccharide vaccine, with shorter hospital stays. People with diabetes are also at higher pneumococcal risk to begin with (invasive disease odds ratio 2.42 in the same meta-analysis), so even a modest relative effect acts on a higher baseline. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the hospitalisation outcome: pneumococcal vaccination is associated with fewer pneumonia hospitalisations in adults with diabetes, and the one randomised dataset shows high vaccine-type efficacy in the diabetes subgroup, but no trial has tested hospitalisation in diabetic patients directly.

cards.headline: Huijts 2017 (CAPiTA post-hoc): conjugate vaccine efficacy against vaccine-type pneumonia was 89.5% relative in elderly participants with diabetes vs 24.7% without — diabetes significantly modified efficacy, on only 139 cases
cards.summary: Huijts 2017 (CAPiTA post-hoc): conjugate vaccine efficacy against vaccine-type pneumonia was 89.5% relative in elderly participants with diabetes vs 24.7% without — diabetes significantly modified efficacy, on only 139 cases
cards.type: Post-hoc subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (Huijts 2017)
cards.people: Post-hoc analysis of the CAPiTA double-blind randomised trial (84,496 immunocompetent participants aged 65 years or older receiving the 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine or placebo). Comorbidity status was verified on medical records in the 139 subjects who developed the primary endpoint of vaccine-type community-acquired pneumonia; diabetes status by primary-care coding was also determined in 40,427 subjects.
cards.result: Diabetes caused significant effect modification (p = 0.002), yielding vaccine efficacy against vaccine-type pneumonia of 89.5% (95% CI 65.5–96.8, relative measure) in participants with diabetes and 24.7% (95% CI −10.4 to 48.7, relative measure) in those without. In the 40,427 subjects with primary-care-coded diabetes status, efficacy was 85.6% (95% CI 36.7–96.7, relative measure) with diabetes and 7.0% (95% CI −58.5 to 45.5, relative measure) without (effect modification p = 0.020). No effect modification was seen for heart disease, respiratory disease, smoking or any comorbidity. The outcome is vaccine-type pneumonia, not pneumonia hospitalisation.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and built on 139 endpoint cases: the diabetes subgroup interval is wide (65.5–96.8) and the non-diabetes estimate straddles no effect, so the honest claim is 'efficacy was at least as high, and nominally much higher, in diabetes' — not a precise 89.5% promise. The parent CAPiTA trial itself is homed at #444; only this diabetes-cut report is carded here.
cards.source: Huijts SM et al. Post-hoc analysis of a randomized controlled trial: Diabetes mellitus modifies the efficacy of the 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine in elderly. Vaccine. 2017. PMID: 28410813. Registry ID: NCT00744263. cards.headline: Silverii 2024 meta-analysis (diabetes-specific): hospitalisation for overall pneumonia in the year after polysaccharide vaccination was lower in vaccinated diabetic patients (odds ratio 0.63, unadjusted) — other outcomes not significant
cards.summary: Silverii 2024 meta-analysis (diabetes-specific): hospitalisation for overall pneumonia in the year after polysaccharide vaccination was lower in vaccinated diabetic patients (odds ratio 0.63, unadjusted) — other outcomes not significant
cards.type: Meta-analysis of observational studies in diabetes (Silverii 2024)
cards.people: Meta-analysis restricted to people with diabetes mellitus: 36 observational studies of diabetes as a risk factor for pneumococcal disease, and 11 studies (1 randomised trial and 10 observational studies) assessing conjugate and polysaccharide vaccine efficacy/effectiveness in diabetic patients, from searches to June 2023.
cards.result: People with diabetes were at higher risk of invasive pneumococcal disease (unadjusted odds ratio 2.42, 95% CI 2.00–2.92, relative measure), pneumococcal pneumonia (unadjusted odds ratio 2.98, 95% CI 2.76–3.22) and intensive care admission for pneumococcal disease (unadjusted odds ratio 2.09, 95% CI 1.20–3.66). In vaccinated diabetic individuals, vaccine-type pneumonia incidence in the one clinical trial was lower (odds ratio 0.237, 95% CI 0.008–0.704, relative measure), and hospitalisation for overall pneumonia during the year following polysaccharide vaccination was significantly lower in observational studies (unadjusted odds ratio 0.63, 95% CI 0.45–0.89, relative measure), with no significant differences for other outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The hospitalisation figure is an unadjusted odds ratio pooled from observational studies, so healthy-vaccinee bias can manufacture exactly this kind of association; the trial-derived vaccine-type estimate (0.237) has an extremely wide interval from very few events.
cards.source: Silverii GA et al. Diabetes as a risk factor for pneumococcal disease and severe related outcomes and efficacy/effectiveness of vaccination in diabetic population. Results from meta-analysis of observational studies. Acta Diabetologica. 2024. PMID: 38684540. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kuo 2016: in diabetic elderly in Taiwan's national insurance data, polysaccharide vaccination was associated with less invasive pneumococcal disease (adjusted odds ratio 0.86) and respiratory failure, and shorter hospital stays
cards.summary: Kuo 2016: in diabetic elderly in Taiwan's national insurance data, polysaccharide vaccination was associated with less invasive pneumococcal disease (adjusted odds ratio 0.86) and respiratory failure, and shorter hospital stays
cards.type: Retrospective population cohort study (Kuo 2016)
cards.people: Population-based retrospective cohort from the Taiwanese National Health Insurance Research Database (2000–2009), comparing pneumococcal-disease incidence in 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine recipients with propensity-score matched unvaccinated patients, all with diabetes in old age (the record's conclusion specifies diabetic elderly aged 75 and more). The cohort size is not documented in the record.
cards.result: The vaccinated group had reduced risks of invasive pneumococcal disease (adjusted odds ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.78–0.94, relative measure), respiratory failure (adjusted odds ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.77–0.93, relative measure) and a shorter length of hospitalisation (−1.27 days, P = 0.0012). In the influenza-vaccinated subgroup, those who also received the pneumococcal vaccine had reduced risks of invasive disease, hospitalisation and respiratory failure, shorter stays and lower medical costs than those without it; receiving both vaccines gave better protection than pneumococcal vaccination alone. The record does not print a separate effect size for pneumonia hospitalisation in the whole cohort.
cards.watchOut: Administrative-data cohort: vaccinated diabetic elderly differ from unvaccinated ones in care-seeking and comorbidity management despite propensity matching, and the headline outcomes are invasive disease and respiratory failure rather than pneumonia hospitalisation itself.
cards.source: Kuo CS et al. Effectiveness of 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine on diabetic elderly. Medicine. 2016. PMID: 27368047. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: in diabetes, pneumococcal vaccination is associated with fewer pneumonia hospitalisations in observational data and showed its highest vaccine-type efficacy in the diabetes subgroup of the one big trial — but the hospitalisation claim itself has never been randomised
cards.summary: Synthesis: in diabetes, pneumococcal vaccination is associated with fewer pneumonia hospitalisations in observational data and showed its highest vaccine-type efficacy in the diabetes subgroup of the one big trial — but the hospitalisation claim itself has never been randomised
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: a post-hoc diabetes analysis of an 84,496-participant randomised trial (139 vaccine-type pneumonia cases), a diabetes-specific meta-analysis (11 vaccine studies, 1 randomised and 10 observational), and a national-insurance cohort in diabetic elderly (size not documented in the record). The general older-adult shelf is live #444, cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: Vaccine-type pneumonia efficacy was 89.5% relative with diabetes vs 24.7% relative without in the trial's post-hoc cut (Huijts 2017). Hospitalisation for overall pneumonia after polysaccharide vaccination was lower in vaccinated diabetic patients (unadjusted odds ratio 0.63 relative) (Silverii 2024), and invasive disease and respiratory failure were lower in the vaccinated diabetic-elderly cohort (adjusted odds ratios 0.86 and 0.84 relative) (Kuo 2016). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the hospitalisation outcome, as stated.
cards.watchOut: Diabetes raises pneumococcal risk roughly two- to three-fold in these records, so relative benefits translate into larger absolute benefits than in the general older-adult population of #444 — but every hospitalisation number here remains vulnerable to healthy-vaccinee bias.
cards.source: Synthesis of Huijts SM et al. Vaccine. 2017 (PMID: 28410813); Silverii GA et al. Acta Diabetologica. 2024 (PMID: 38684540); Kuo CS et al. Medicine. 2016 (PMID: 27368047).

shelves.title: Sleep gets lighter and more broken with adult ageing: slow-wave and REM shares fall, stage 1/2 and wake after sleep onset rise — and the spindles and REM that remain track next-morning cognition
shelves.question: How does human sleep architecture (slow-wave and REM proportions, sleep continuity) change across adult ageing, and how do those changes relate to next-day cognition?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aging/psychology · Child · Child, Preschool · Humans · Middle Aged · Polysomnography · Reference Values · Sleep · Sleep Stages · Sleep Wake Disorders/diagnosis,etiology · Time Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Kryger-era sleep-medicine texts). The textbooks describe adult sleep as organised in nonREM–REM cycles in which slow-wave sleep predominates early and REM later, and describe ageing sleep as lighter and more fragmented. The carded human polysomnography data confirm that account quantitatively in direction: the Ohayon 2004 meta-analysis of 65 studies (3,577 subjects) found that in adults total sleep time, sleep efficiency, slow-wave %, REM % and REM latency decreased with age while sleep latency, stage 1 %, stage 2 % and wake after sleep onset increased, with only sleep efficiency continuing to decrease after 60. Primary studies agree (Landolt 1996: less slow-wave sleep, more stage 1 and wake after sleep onset in middle-aged versus young men). For cognition, the evidence is observational only and is labelled as such: spindle density and REM duration predicted next-morning performance in 58 older adults (Lafortune 2014), and short NREM/REM cycles predicted 4-year cognitive decline in 235 older adults (Suh 2019, 14 events). No intervention evidence is carded. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the architecture changes, with the cognition relation stated as association.

cards.headline: Ohayon 2004 meta-analysis (65 studies, 3,577 subjects): in adults, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, slow-wave sleep %, REM % and REM latency all fell with age, while sleep latency, stage 1 %, stage 2 % and wake after sleep onset rose — but only sleep efficiency kept falling after age 60
cards.summary: Ohayon 2004 meta-analysis (65 studies, 3,577 subjects): in adults, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, slow-wave sleep %, REM % and REM latency all fell with age, while sleep latency, stage 1 %, stage 2 % and wake after sleep onset rose — but only sleep efficiency kept falling after age 60
cards.type: Meta-analysis of quantitative sleep parameters (Ohayon 2004) — 65 studies, 3,577 subjects
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 65 polysomnography/actigraphy studies representing 3,577 healthy subjects aged 5 to 102 years, published 1960–2003, with numeric sleep-stage data.
cards.result: In adults, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, percentage of slow-wave sleep, percentage of REM sleep, and REM latency all significantly decreased with age, while sleep latency, percentage of stage 1 sleep, percentage of stage 2 sleep, and wake after sleep onset significantly increased with age. However, only sleep efficiency continued to significantly decrease after 60 years of age. Effect sizes were greatly modified by how rigorously participants were screened for mental disorders, organic disease, drug/alcohol use and sleep apnoea — screening could diminish or even mask age associations.
cards.watchOut: This is a meta-analysis of mostly cross-sectional studies, not a longitudinal cohort: age differences between people are not the same as change within a person, and the authors themselves warn that screening quality changes the apparent size of every age effect. No percentage-point values are printed here because the fetched record reports directions and significance, not the pooled stage percentages.
cards.source: Ohayon MM et al. Meta-analysis of quantitative sleep parameters from childhood to old age in healthy individuals: developing normative sleep values across the human lifespan. Sleep. 2004. PMID: 15586779. Registry ID: none in the record. meta-analysis of quantitative sleep parameters (ohayon 2004) — 65 studies, 3,577 subjects meta-analysis of 65 polysomnography/actigraphy studies representing 3,577 healthy subjects aged 5 to 102 years, published 1960–2003, with numeric sleep-stage data. in adults, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, percentage of slow-wave sleep, percentage of rem sleep, and rem latency all significantly decreased with age, while sleep latency, percentage of stage 1 sleep, percentage of stage 2 sleep, and wake after sleep onset significantly increased with age. however, only sleep efficiency continued to significantly decrease after 60 years of age. effect sizes were greatly modified by how rigorously participants were screened for mental disorders, organic disease, drug/alcohol use and sleep apnoea — screening could diminish or even mask age associations. this is a meta-analysis of mostly cross-sectional studies, not a longitudinal cohort: age differences between people are not the same as change within a person, and the authors themselves warn that screening quality changes the apparent size of every age effect. no percentage-point values are printed here because the fetched record reports directions and significance, not the pooled stage percentages. ohayon mm et al. meta-analysis of quantitative sleep parameters from childhood to old age in healthy individuals: developing normative sleep values across the human lifespan. sleep. 2004. pmid: 15586779. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · aging/psychology · child · child, preschool · humans · middle aged · polysomnography · reference values · sleep · sleep stages · sleep wake disorders/diagnosis,etiology · time factors

cards.headline: Landolt 1996: middle-aged men (mean 62 years) had less total sleep, lower sleep efficiency and less slow-wave sleep than young men (mean 22.4 years), with more stage 1 and more wake after sleep onset — N not documented in the record
cards.summary: Landolt 1996: middle-aged men (mean 62 years) had less total sleep, lower sleep efficiency and less slow-wave sleep than young men (mean 22.4 years), with more stage 1 and more wake after sleep onset — N not documented in the record
cards.type: Primary human polysomnography/EEG comparison, young vs middle-aged men (Landolt 1996) — N not documented in the record
cards.people: Middle-aged men (mean age 62.0 years) compared with young men (mean age 22.4 years) in a controlled sleep-EEG study; the fetched record does not print the number of men in each group (N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Even though the older men reported more nocturnal awakenings, subjective sleep quality did not differ. Total sleep time, sleep efficiency and slow-wave sleep were lower in the middle-aged men, while stage 1 and wakefulness after sleep onset were higher; the wakefulness difference was most pronounced in the third and fourth nonREM–REM cycles. EEG power density in nonREM sleep was reduced below 14 Hz in the older men, slow-wave activity declined across the night in both groups, and the age-related attenuation of the sleep-dependent decline in slow-wave activity and rise in spindle activity was a central finding.
cards.watchOut: Men only, two age groups only, and N not documented in the fetched record — printed on the face as the labelling rule requires. A two-group cross-section cannot show when in adult life the changes occur; the Ohayon meta-analysis card above supplies the lifespan pattern.
cards.source: Landolt HP et al. Effect of age on the sleep EEG: slow-wave activity and spindle frequency activity in young and middle-aged men. Brain research. 1996. PMID: 8955514. cards.headline: Lafortune 2014: in 58 healthy adults aged 50–91, higher N2 spindle density predicted better next-morning verbal learning, visual attention and verbal fluency, and longer REM sleep predicted better verbal learning
cards.summary: Lafortune 2014: in 58 healthy adults aged 50–91, higher N2 spindle density predicted better next-morning verbal learning, visual attention and verbal fluency, and longer REM sleep predicted better verbal learning
cards.type: Primary human polysomnography cohort with next-morning cognition (Lafortune 2014) — N = 58
cards.people: 58 healthy middle-aged and older adults (aged 50–91 years) without sleep disorders who underwent a baseline polysomnography night followed by neuropsychological testing the next morning (selective/sustained visual attention, declarative verbal memory, working memory, verbal fluency).
cards.result: Higher all-night stage N2 spindle density predicted better performance on verbal learning, visual attention and verbal fluency; spindle frequency and slow-wave density/slope predicted fewer cognitive variables. Rapid eye movement sleep duration was associated with better verbal learning potential. The authors conclude spindle density is a marker of cognitive functioning in older adults and may reflect neuroanatomic integrity, and that REM sleep may mark age-related changes in acetylcholine transmission involved in encoding new information.
cards.watchOut: Observational and cross-sectional: spindle density predicting next-morning scores is an association, not proof that restoring spindles or slow waves would restore cognition — this leg is labelled observational and is why the cognition half of this shelf is stated as association, not causation.
cards.source: Lafortune M et al. Sleep spindles and rapid eye movement sleep as predictors of next morning cognitive performance in healthy middle-aged and older participants. Journal of sleep research. 2014. PMID: 24245769. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Suh 2019: in 235 cognitively normal older adults followed 4 years, a shorter average NREM/REM cycle — and especially shorter REM duration per cycle — was associated with developing mild cognitive impairment or dementia (14 of 235, 5.9%)
cards.summary: Suh 2019: in 235 cognitively normal older adults followed 4 years, a shorter average NREM/REM cycle — and especially shorter REM duration per cycle — was associated with developing mild cognitive impairment or dementia (14 of 235, 5.9%)
cards.type: Prospective polysomnography cohort, 4-year cognitive follow-up (Suh 2019) — N = 235, observational
cards.people: 235 community-dwelling cognitively normal Korean elderly (mean age 68 years, 60% female) with baseline overnight polysomnography, followed for 4 years for incident mild cognitive impairment or dementia in the Korean Longitudinal Study on Cognitive Aging and Dementia.
cards.result: 14 participants (5.9%) developed mild cognitive impairment or dementia. A short average NREM/REM cycle length was significantly associated with cognitive decline (OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.94–0.99; p = 0.02), and when substructure was considered, the average REM sleep duration per cycle was significantly related to the outcome (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.76–0.98; p = 0.03). The authors propose short cycle duration, especially REM per cycle, as a possible early marker of cognitive decline.
cards.watchOut: Only 14 outcome events in an exploratory analysis — the confidence intervals are wide in practical terms and multiple architecture measures were examined, so this is a marker signal, not a validated predictor. Observational: it does not show that lengthening cycles would prevent decline.
cards.source: Suh SW et al. Short Average Duration of NREM/REM Cycle Is Related to Cognitive Decline in an Elderly Cohort: An Exploratory Investigation. Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD. 2019. PMID: 31322573. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the textbook ageing pattern is confirmed in human polysomnography — lighter, more broken sleep with less slow-wave and REM sleep — and the architecture that remains tracks next-day and longer-term cognition, observationally
cards.summary: Synthesis: the textbook ageing pattern is confirmed in human polysomnography — lighter, more broken sleep with less slow-wave and REM sleep — and the architecture that remains tracks next-day and longer-term cognition, observationally
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: the Ohayon 2004 meta-analysis (65 studies, 3,577 subjects), a young-versus-middle-aged men's EEG study (Landolt 1996, N not documented in the record), a 58-person next-morning cognition study (Lafortune 2014), and a 235-person 4-year prospective cohort (Suh 2019). Textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Kryger-era sleep-medicine texts, named as framing, not as evidence cards.
cards.result: Direction of adult ageing is concordant across all sources: slow-wave sleep and REM percentages fall, stage 1 and stage 2 percentages rise, sleep latency and wake after sleep onset rise, total sleep time and efficiency fall — with sleep efficiency the one measure that kept falling after 60 in the meta-analysis. For cognition, the human data are associational: spindle density and REM duration relate to next-morning performance, and short NREM/REM cycles relate to later decline. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the architecture changes; the cognition link is presented as observational association within that stamp.
cards.watchOut: No carded study intervenes on sleep architecture and measures cognition, so nothing here licenses a claim that increasing slow-wave sleep improves cognition in older adults — that would be an intervention question for a different shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ohayon MM et al. Sleep. 2004 (PMID: 15586779); Landolt HP et al. Brain research. 1996 (PMID: 8955514); Lafortune M et al. Journal of sleep research. 2014 (PMID: 24245769); Suh SW et al. Journal of Alzheimer's disease. 2019 (PMID: 31322573). Textbook framing: Ganong; Kryger-era sleep texts.

shelves.title: Glymphatic clearance in human sleep: consistent proxy evidence (CSF waves, tracer clearance, amyloid-beta shifts) but no direct human demonstration — an emerging physiology
shelves.question: In humans, does slow-wave sleep enhance glymphatic clearance of interstitial solutes including amyloid-beta, and what direct human evidence exists?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Brain/blood supply,physiology · Brain Waves/physiology · Cerebrospinal Fluid/physiology · Cerebrovascular Circulation · Delta Rhythm · Electroencephalography · Female · Hemodynamics · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Sleep/physiology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology for CSF physiology; the glymphatic pathway was defined in animal experiments and is presented in textbooks as the proposed route — animal mechanism is context here, never a card). Graded honestly: the direct human evidence is thin. What exists in humans is four proxy legs, each concordant and each indirect. Fultz 2019 imaged waves of CSF flow coupled to neural slow waves and haemodynamics in human nonREM sleep, but measured no solute. Eide 2021 gave humans an intrathecal MRI tracer and found one night of total sleep deprivation impaired its clearance from most brain regions, unrecovered the next night — the closest human analogue of a clearance experiment, with a deprivation arm of only n = 7. Ju 2017 disrupted slow-wave activity experimentally and saw next-morning CSF amyloid-beta40 rise (N = 17), an effect the authors attribute at least partly to neuronal activity rather than clearance alone. Shokri-Kojori 2018 found PET amyloid burden higher after one deprived night in 20 controls — a net-balance signal that cannot separate production from clearance. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the hypothesis is supported by consistent human proxies; it is not established human physiology.

cards.headline: Fultz 2019: during human nonREM sleep, neural slow waves were followed by haemodynamic oscillations coupled to waves of cerebrospinal fluid flow — macroscopic CSF waves in the sleeping human brain (participant number not documented in the record)
cards.summary: Fultz 2019: during human nonREM sleep, neural slow waves were followed by haemodynamic oscillations coupled to waves of cerebrospinal fluid flow — macroscopic CSF waves in the sleeping human brain (participant number not documented in the record)
cards.type: Primary human sleep neuroimaging study (Fultz 2019) — N not documented in the record
cards.people: Humans studied during sleep with accelerated neuroimaging measuring electrophysiological, haemodynamic and cerebrospinal fluid dynamics simultaneously; the fetched record does not print the participant number (N not documented in the record).
cards.result: A coherent pattern of oscillating electrophysiological, haemodynamic and CSF dynamics appeared during non-rapid eye movement sleep: neural slow waves were followed by haemodynamic oscillations, which in turn were coupled to CSF flow. The authors conclude the sleeping brain exhibits waves of CSF flow on a macroscopic scale, interlinked with neural and haemodynamic rhythms — the human imaging counterpart of the clearance physiology described in textbooks.
cards.watchOut: This study shows CSF flow coupling, not clearance of any named solute: no amyloid-beta, tau or other waste product was measured entering or leaving the brain. N not documented in the fetched record, printed on the face. Treating coupled CSF waves as proof of glymphatic solute clearance is the inference this shelf refuses to make.
cards.source: Fultz NE et al. Coupled electrophysiological, hemodynamic, and cerebrospinal fluid oscillations in human sleep. Science (New York, N.Y.). 2019. PMID: 31672896. Registry ID: none in the record (figshare data deposit only). cards.headline: Eide 2021: one night of total sleep deprivation impaired clearance of an intrathecally injected MRI tracer from most brain regions — and the lost clearance was not recovered by the next night's sleep (tracer cohort 24: 7 sleep-deprived, 17 controls)
cards.summary: Eide 2021: one night of total sleep deprivation impaired clearance of an intrathecally injected MRI tracer from most brain regions — and the lost clearance was not recovered by the next night's sleep (tracer cohort 24: 7 sleep-deprived, 17 controls)
cards.type: Primary human tracer-clearance study (Eide 2021) — n = 24 total (7 sleep-deprived, 17 controls)
cards.people: Two cohorts given intrathecal gadobutrol (0.5 ml of 1 mmol/ml) as a tracer molecule with multiphase MRI up to 48 hours: a sleep-deprivation cohort (n = 7, total sleep deprivation from Day 1 to Day 2 — a small group, printed on the face) and an age- and gender-matched control cohort allowed free sleep (n = 17). All were allowed free sleep from Day 2 to 3.
cards.result: Tracer enrichment of the brain was similar between groups at baseline, but one night of sleep deprivation impaired clearance of the tracer from most brain regions, including cerebral cortex, white matter and limbic structures, on the morning of Day 2. The impaired clearance in the sleep-deprivation group was not compensated by subsequent sleep from Day 2 to 3. The authors present this as in vivo human evidence that one night of total sleep deprivation impairs molecular clearance from the human brain.
cards.watchOut: The sleep-deprived group is n = 7, below the usual 10-human floor — carded under the physiology labelling rule with the number on the face, because it is one of the only direct human clearance experiments. The tracer is gadobutrol, a contrast molecule, not amyloid-beta; impaired tracer clearance supports, but does not directly demonstrate, impaired amyloid clearance. Participants were patients undergoing this intrathecal procedure, not a general-population sample.
cards.source: Eide PK et al. Sleep deprivation impairs molecular clearance from the human brain. Brain : a journal of neurology. 2021. PMID: 33829232. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ju 2017: experimentally disrupting slow-wave activity for one night raised next-morning cerebrospinal fluid amyloid-beta40 in 17 healthy adults (r = 0.610, p = 0.009) — an effect specific to slow-wave disruption, not to sleep duration or efficiency
cards.summary: Ju 2017: experimentally disrupting slow-wave activity for one night raised next-morning cerebrospinal fluid amyloid-beta40 in 17 healthy adults (r = 0.610, p = 0.009) — an effect specific to slow-wave disruption, not to sleep duration or efficiency
cards.type: Primary human experimental slow-wave disruption study with CSF sampling (Ju 2017) — N = 17
cards.people: 17 healthy adults aged 35–65 years without sleep disorders who underwent 5–14 days of actigraphy, then slow-wave activity disruption during polysomnography with cerebrospinal fluid collection the following morning, compared with an identical sham-condition protocol; CSF amyloid-beta, tau, total protein, YKL-40 and hypocretin were measured.
cards.result: Specific disruption of slow-wave activity correlated with an increase in amyloid-beta40 (r = 0.610, P = 0.009). The effect was specific for slow-wave activity and not for sleep duration or efficiency, and specific to amyloid-beta rather than total protein, tau, YKL-40 or hypocretin. Separately, worse home sleep quality (actigraphy sleep efficiency over the preceding six nights) was associated with higher tau (r = 0.543, P = 0.045).
cards.watchOut: A rise in CSF amyloid-beta after slow-wave disruption can reflect increased neuronal production/release as well as reduced clearance — the authors themselves frame the likely driver as neuronal activity. This card therefore shows slow-wave sleep modulates CSF amyloid-beta levels; it does not by itself prove the route is glymphatic clearance.
cards.source: Ju YS et al. Slow wave sleep disruption increases cerebrospinal fluid amyloid-β levels. Brain : a journal of neurology. 2017. PMID: 28899014. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Shokri-Kojori 2018: one night of sleep deprivation increased PET-measured brain amyloid-beta burden in the right hippocampus and thalamus of 20 healthy controls, versus a rested night
cards.summary: Shokri-Kojori 2018: one night of sleep deprivation increased PET-measured brain amyloid-beta burden in the right hippocampus and thalamus of 20 healthy controls, versus a rested night
cards.type: Primary human sleep-deprivation PET study (Shokri-Kojori 2018) — N = 20
cards.people: 20 healthy controls tested with 18F-florbetaben PET after a night of rested sleep (baseline) and after a night of sleep deprivation, measuring brain amyloid-beta burden.
cards.result: One night of sleep deprivation, relative to baseline, resulted in a significant increase in amyloid-beta burden in the right hippocampus and thalamus. The increases were associated with mood worsening after sleep deprivation but were not related to APOE genotype. Baseline amyloid burden in subcortical regions and precuneus was inversely associated with reported night sleep hours.
cards.watchOut: PET burden rising overnight is a net-balance measure: it cannot distinguish reduced clearance from increased production, and a single night in 20 healthy controls says nothing about whether chronic sleep loss raises plaque burden over years. Regional (right hippocampus/thalamus) rather than global effects, in a small sample, argue for caution.
cards.source: Shokri-Kojori E et al. β-Amyloid accumulation in the human brain after one night of sleep deprivation. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. 2018. PMID: 29632177. Registry ID: none in the record.
