cards.headline: Synthesis: direct human evidence is thin and indirect — CSF flow couples to slow waves, tracer clearance falls after sleep deprivation, and CSF/PET amyloid-beta rises when slow-wave sleep is disrupted — but no human study has directly shown slow-wave sleep clearing amyloid-beta via the glymphatic pathway
cards.summary: Synthesis: direct human evidence is thin and indirect — CSF flow couples to slow waves, tracer clearance falls after sleep deprivation, and CSF/PET amyloid-beta rises when slow-wave sleep is disrupted — but no human study has directly shown slow-wave sleep clearing amyloid-beta via the glymphatic pathway
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded human evidence: Fultz 2019 (CSF-flow imaging during nonREM sleep, N not documented in the record), Eide 2021 (intrathecal tracer clearance, 24 participants of whom 7 were sleep-deprived), Ju 2017 (slow-wave disruption with CSF sampling, N = 17), and Shokri-Kojori 2018 (amyloid PET after sleep deprivation, N = 20). Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology for cerebrospinal fluid formation and circulation; the glymphatic (glial-lymphatic) pathway itself was defined in animal work and is named here as textbook/animal context only — no animal study is carded as evidence.
cards.result: Each human leg measures a proxy: coupled CSF waves (no solute measured), clearance of an injected contrast tracer (not amyloid), CSF amyloid-beta concentration (production and clearance confounded), and PET amyloid burden after one night (net balance only). Together they are consistent with the hypothesis that slow-wave sleep enhances clearance of interstitial solutes including amyloid-beta, and inconsistent with no effect — but the direct demonstration in humans does not yet exist. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING, graded honestly for that reason.
cards.watchOut: Total carded human participants across the three studies that report numbers: 61, with the key deprivation arm only n = 7. Any stamp stronger than EMERGING would claim a human demonstration that the literature does not contain.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fultz NE et al. Science. 2019 (PMID: 31672896); Eide PK et al. Brain. 2021 (PMID: 33829232); Ju YS et al. Brain. 2017 (PMID: 28899014); Shokri-Kojori E et al. shelves.title: Benralizumab and steroid tapering in severe asthma: 75% median dose reduction versus 25% on placebo (ZONDA), and 63% eliminated steroids under a monitored taper (PONENTE)
shelves.question: In adults with severe asthma who depend on daily oral corticosteroids, does benralizumab allow the steroid dose to be tapered or stopped versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Asthma/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous · Interleukin-5 Receptor alpha Subunit/antagonists & inhibitors · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: Premise verified: steroid-sparing is homed for dupilumab on live shelf #1031 (VENTURE) — a different drug; no benralizumab steroid-sparing home exists (live #813 covers benralizumab exacerbations in SIROCCO, not tapering), so this is the uncovered question. The placebo-controlled leg is ZONDA 2017: median oral glucocorticoid dose down 75% on benralizumab versus 25% on placebo (P<0.001), odds of reduction more than 4-fold, exacerbation rates relatively 55–70% lower with absolute rates printed on the card, and no FEV1 effect. PONENTE 2021/2022 is the practical leg — open-label and single-arm, labelled as such: a personalised rapid taper with adrenal monitoring eliminated oral corticosteroids in 376/598 (62.9%) and got 81.9% to elimination or 5 mg/day or less, with reductions largely maintained for 6 further months; adrenal insufficiency was found in 60% at first assessment, which is why the algorithm monitors it. A 2024 network meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (1,052 patients) places benralizumab's steroid-sparing odds (OR about 4.1 for both regimens) alongside dupilumab and mepolizumab, at low-to-moderate confidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single drug programme (one RCT plus its single-arm taper study) caps the stamp despite the large randomised effect.

cards.headline: ZONDA 2017: benralizumab cut the median oral glucocorticoid dose by 75% versus 25% on placebo at 28 weeks (220 randomised), with exacerbation rates 55–70% relatively lower — and no significant FEV1 effect
cards.summary: ZONDA 2017: benralizumab cut the median oral glucocorticoid dose by 75% versus 25% on placebo at 28 weeks (220 randomised), with exacerbation rates 55–70% relatively lower — and no significant FEV1 effect
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial — ZONDA (Nair 2017) — 220 randomised
cards.people: Adults with severe asthma associated with eosinophilia who relied on oral glucocorticoids, in a 28-week randomised controlled trial of benralizumab 30 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks, or every 8 weeks (first three doses every 4 weeks), versus placebo; 369 enrolled, 220 underwent randomisation and started treatment. Primary endpoint: percentage change in oral glucocorticoid dose from baseline to week 28 while asthma control was maintained.
cards.result: Both benralizumab regimens significantly reduced the median final oral glucocorticoid dose from baseline by 75%, compared with a 25% reduction on placebo (P<0.001 for both comparisons); the odds of a dose reduction were more than 4 times as high with benralizumab as with placebo. Annual exacerbation rates were lower in relative terms: 0.83 versus 1.83 with every-4-week dosing (a 55% relatively lower rate, P=0.003) and 0.54 versus 1.83 with every-8-week dosing (a 70% relatively lower rate, P<0.001) — absolute rates are printed beside the relative figures. There was no significant effect of either regimen on FEV1 at 28 weeks, symptom measures were mixed, and adverse-event frequencies were similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: Steroid reduction was protocol-driven while control was maintained, in an eosinophilic, steroid-dependent population — the result does not extend to non-eosinophilic asthma. The exacerbation figures are marginal (modelled) annual rates; FEV1 did not improve, so the benefit is steroid sparing and exacerbations, not lung function.
cards.source: Nair P et al. Oral Glucocorticoid-Sparing Effect of Benralizumab in Severe Asthma. The New England journal of medicine. 2017. PMID: 28530840. Registry ID: NCT02075255 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: PONENTE 2022: with a personalised rapid tapering algorithm after starting benralizumab, 62.9% of 598 steroid-dependent patients eliminated oral corticosteroids entirely and 81.9% eliminated them or reached 5 mg/day or less — single-arm, no placebo group
cards.summary: PONENTE 2022: with a personalised rapid tapering algorithm after starting benralizumab, 62.9% of 598 steroid-dependent patients eliminated oral corticosteroids entirely and 81.9% eliminated them or reached 5 mg/day or less — single-arm, no placebo group
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, single-arm study — PONENTE (Menzies-Gow 2022) — N = 598, uncontrolled (labelled)
cards.people: 598 adults with severe eosinophilic asthma (blood eosinophils at least 150 cells per microlitre at enrolment or at least 300 in the previous year) requiring maintenance oral corticosteroids for at least 3 months, at 138 centres in 17 countries; benralizumab 30 mg every 4 weeks for three doses then every 8 weeks, with oral corticosteroid reduction from week 4 by 1–5 mg every 1–4 weeks depending on starting dose, asthma control and adrenal function (morning cortisol, then ACTH stimulation when required, at 5 mg/day).
cards.result: 376 of 598 patients (62.88%, 95% CI 58.86–66.76) eliminated oral corticosteroids sustained for at least 4 weeks, and 490 (81.94%, 78.62–84.94) eliminated use or achieved 5 mg/day or less where adrenal insufficiency was the reason for stopping further reduction. Reductions were achieved irrespective of baseline eosinophil count, baseline steroid dose or treatment duration. Adrenal insufficiency was detected in 321 of 533 patients (60%) at first assessment and 205 (38%) 2–3 months later. 75% of patients had no exacerbation during the reduction phase (annualised rate 0.63); 38 patients (6%) had 46 exacerbations leading to emergency or urgent care or hospitalisation.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and open-label: with no placebo or usual-care taper group, PONENTE cannot show how much of the elimination exceeds what a structured taper alone would achieve — ZONDA supplies the placebo-controlled leg. The 60% adrenal-insufficiency rate at first testing is the safety core of this study: tapering this fast requires adrenal monitoring, which the algorithm built in.
cards.source: Menzies-Gow A et al. Oral corticosteroid elimination via a personalised reduction algorithm in adults with severe, eosinophilic asthma treated with benralizumab (PONENTE): a multicentre, open-label, single-arm study. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2022. PMID: 34619104. Registry ID: NCT03557307 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: PONENTE maintenance phase 2022: the steroid reduction held for about 6 further months — median dose stayed 0.0 mg, only 3.2% increased their daily dose, 84.5% stayed exacerbation-free, and a third of those with adrenal insufficiency improved their adrenal function
cards.summary: PONENTE maintenance phase 2022: the steroid reduction held for about 6 further months — median dose stayed 0.0 mg, only 3.2% increased their daily dose, 84.5% stayed exacerbation-free, and a third of those with adrenal insufficiency improved their adrenal function
cards.type: Open-label maintenance-phase report of PONENTE (Menzies-Gow 2022) — N = 563, uncontrolled (labelled)
cards.people: 563 of the 598 PONENTE patients (94.1%) who completed the reduction phase and entered a maintenance phase of about 6 months, continuing benralizumab 30 mg every 8 weeks at their final oral corticosteroid dose (investigators could prescribe steroids for exacerbations or increase doses for loss of control).
cards.result: From the end of reduction to the end of maintenance the median oral corticosteroid dose was unchanged (0.0 mg, range 0.0–40.0); 18 of 563 patients (3.2%) had daily dose increases; mean ACQ-6 improved from 1.26 to 1.18; 476 patients (84.5%) were exacerbation-free; mean SGRQ improved by 19.65 points from baseline. Of patients entering maintenance with adrenal insufficiency, 104 of 321 (32.4%) showed improvement in adrenal function. Adverse events were consistent with previous reports; the maintenance-phase report also states 91.5% of patients had eliminated steroids or reached 5 mg/day or less by the end of the reduction phase on its accounting.
cards.watchOut: Still uncontrolled — durability in a single arm shows reductions can persist on benralizumab, not that benralizumab caused the persistence. The 91.5% figure here uses a broader end-of-reduction accounting than the primary endpoint's 81.94%; both are printed with their sources rather than blended.
cards.source: Menzies-Gow A et al. Adrenal function recovery after durable oral corticosteroid sparing with benralizumab in the PONENTE study. The European respiratory journal. 2022. PMID: 35896216. Registry ID: NCT03557307 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: Phinyo 2024 network meta-analysis (7 RCTs, 1,052 steroid-dependent patients): benralizumab every 8 weeks (OR 4.12, 95% CI 2.22–7.64) and every 4 weeks (OR 4.09, 2.22–7.55) were efficacious versus placebo for oral corticosteroid dose reduction, with low-to-moderate confidence
cards.summary: Phinyo 2024 network meta-analysis (7 RCTs, 1,052 steroid-dependent patients): benralizumab every 8 weeks (OR 4.12, 95% CI 2.22–7.64) and every 4 weeks (OR 4.09, 2.22–7.55) were efficacious versus placebo for oral corticosteroid dose reduction, with low-to-moderate confidence
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (Phinyo 2024) — 1,052 patients
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials of biologics versus placebo in oral-corticosteroid-dependent asthma, searching PubMed, Scopus, Embase, CENTRAL and Google Scholar to July 2023; 7 RCTs involving 1,052 patients. Primary outcome: overall reduction in oral corticosteroid dose while asthma control was maintained.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, benralizumab every 8 weeks (odds ratio 4.12, 95% CI 2.22–7.64), benralizumab every 4 weeks (4.09, 2.22–7.55), dupilumab (3.25, 1.90–5.55) and mepolizumab (2.39, 1.25–4.57) were efficacious in reducing the oral corticosteroid dose, with low-to-moderate confidence, whereas tralokinumab, tezepelumab and subcutaneous reslizumab were not. Indirect comparison found no significant differences among benralizumab, dupilumab and mepolizumab; exacerbation results were consistent with the primary analysis; adverse events were comparable to placebo except eosinophilia with dupilumab.
cards.watchOut: Network estimates for benralizumab rest substantially on ZONDA itself, so this card corroborates the trial's place in the class rather than adding an independent benralizumab trial; confidence is rated low to moderate by the authors, and indirect (cross-trial) comparisons are not head-to-head evidence.
cards.source: Phinyo P et al. Efficacy and Safety of Biologics for Oral Corticosteroid-Dependent Asthma: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis. The journal of allergy and clinical immunology. In practice. 2024. PMID: 37972921. Registry ID: none in the record. systematic review and network meta-analysis of 7 rcts (phinyo 2024) — 1,052 patients systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials of biologics versus placebo in oral-corticosteroid-dependent asthma, searching pubmed, scopus, embase, central and google scholar to july 2023; 7 rcts involving 1,052 patients. primary outcome: overall reduction in oral corticosteroid dose while asthma control was maintained. compared with placebo, benralizumab every 8 weeks (odds ratio 4.12, 95% ci 2.22–7.64), benralizumab every 4 weeks (4.09, 2.22–7.55), dupilumab (3.25, 1.90–5.55) and mepolizumab (2.39, 1.25–4.57) were efficacious in reducing the oral corticosteroid dose, with low-to-moderate confidence, whereas tralokinumab, tezepelumab and subcutaneous reslizumab were not. indirect comparison found no significant differences among benralizumab, dupilumab and mepolizumab; exacerbation results were consistent with the primary analysis; adverse events were comparable to placebo except eosinophilia with dupilumab. network estimates for benralizumab rest substantially on zonda itself, so this card corroborates the trial's place in the class rather than adding an independent benralizumab trial; confidence is rated low to moderate by the authors, and indirect (cross-trial) comparisons are not head-to-head evidence. phinyo p et al. efficacy and safety of biologics for oral corticosteroid-dependent asthma: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. the journal of allergy and clinical immunology. in practice. 2024. pmid: 37972921. registry id: none in the record. mesh: humans · anti-asthmatic agents/therapeutic use · biological products/therapeutic use · asthma/drug therapy · adrenal cortex hormones/therapeutic use · eosinophilia/drug therapy

cards.headline: Synthesis: benralizumab does allow tapering — a 75% median dose reduction versus 25% on placebo in the one placebo-controlled trial, with about 63% eliminating steroids under a monitored taper algorithm in the large single-arm study
cards.summary: Synthesis: benralizumab does allow tapering — a 75% median dose reduction versus 25% on placebo in the one placebo-controlled trial, with about 63% eliminating steroids under a monitored taper algorithm in the large single-arm study
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: ZONDA (randomised, placebo-controlled, 220 randomised), PONENTE (single-arm, N = 598, plus its 563-patient maintenance report), and a network meta-analysis of 7 steroid-sparing RCTs (1,052 patients). Steroid-sparing for dupilumab is a different drug's question, homed on live shelf #1031 (VENTURE) and cross-pointed here, not re-carded.
cards.result: Placebo-controlled: median oral glucocorticoid dose fell 75% on benralizumab versus 25% on placebo, with more than 4-fold odds of a reduction and relatively lower exacerbation rates (absolute rates 0.54–0.83 versus 1.83 per year). Uncontrolled but practical: under PONENTE's personalised algorithm with adrenal monitoring, 62.9% eliminated steroids and 81.9% eliminated or reached 5 mg/day or less, and reductions largely held for 6 more months — against a 60% initial adrenal-insufficiency detection rate that makes monitoring non-optional. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one placebo-controlled trial plus a large single-arm programme is a single development programme, which caps the stamp.
cards.watchOut: No head-to-head trial compares benralizumab tapering against another biologic's tapering; the network comparison is indirect. Nothing here applies to steroid-dependent asthma without an eosinophilic phenotype, which ZONDA and PONENTE required.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nair P et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2017 (PMID: 28530840); Menzies-Gow A et al. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2022 (PMID: 34619104); Menzies-Gow A et al. shelves.title: Dupilumab in 6–11-year-olds (VOYAGE): exacerbations 0.31 versus 0.75 per year on placebo, with better lung function, control and quality of life
shelves.question: In children aged 6–11 years with moderate-to-severe asthma, does dupilumab reduce exacerbations versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Asthmatic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Asthma/drug therapy,physiopathology · Biomarkers/analysis · Breath Tests · Child · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous · Lung/physiopathology · Male · Nitric Oxide/administration & dosage · Patient Acuity · Symptom Flare Up
shelves.balance: Premise verified against the files themselves: live #1031 (QUEST/VENTURE) and pack #5903 (adults with severe eosinophilic asthma) are adult/adolescent only — the 6–11 population was uncovered. The evidence is one programme. VOYAGE 2021 randomised 408 children aged 6–11 with uncontrolled moderate-to-severe asthma to weight-banded dupilumab or placebo every 2 weeks for 52 weeks on background therapy: in the type 2 phenotype, annualised severe exacerbations were 0.31 versus 0.75 — a 59.3% relative risk reduction with the absolute rates printed beside it — predicted FEV1 improved 5.2 percentage points more, and asthma control was significantly better. A VOYAGE analysis (Fiocchi 2023, same children, not an independent trial) adds control and quality-of-life detail: 70% versus 46% well-controlled at week 52, with child and caregiver quality of life improved. EXCURSION (365 children, open-label, labelled) extends tolerability to 2 years with a profile consistent with the parent trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — the single-programme cap applies.

cards.headline: VOYAGE 2021: in children 6–11 with type 2 asthma, dupilumab cut the annualised severe exacerbation rate to 0.31 versus 0.75 on placebo — a 59.3% relative risk reduction (408 children, 52 weeks)
cards.summary: VOYAGE 2021: in children 6–11 with type 2 asthma, dupilumab cut the annualised severe exacerbation rate to 0.31 versus 0.75 on placebo — a 59.3% relative risk reduction (408 children, 52 weeks)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial — VOYAGE (Bacharier 2021) — N = 408
cards.people: 408 children aged 6–11 years with uncontrolled moderate-to-severe asthma, randomised to subcutaneous dupilumab (100 mg if 30 kg or less, 200 mg if over 30 kg) or matched placebo every 2 weeks for 52 weeks, all continuing stable standard background therapy. Primary endpoint: annualised rate of severe asthma exacerbations, evaluated in the type 2 inflammatory phenotype population (blood eosinophils at least 150 per cubic millimetre or fractional exhaled nitric oxide at least 20 ppb) and in those with eosinophils at least 300.
cards.result: In the type 2 phenotype, the annualised rate of severe exacerbations was 0.31 (95% CI 0.22–0.42) with dupilumab and 0.75 (95% CI 0.54–1.03) with placebo — a 59.3% relative risk reduction (95% CI 39.5–72.6; P<0.001), with the absolute rates printed here beside the relative figure. The change in percentage of predicted FEV1 at week 12 was 10.5 versus 5.3 percentage points (mean difference 5.2, 95% CI 2.1–8.3; P<0.001), asthma control was significantly better (P<0.001), results were similar in the eosinophils-at-least-300 population, and serious adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The headline efficacy populations are biomarker-defined (type 2 phenotype / higher eosinophils); the record's primary results are for those populations, not for all 408 children regardless of biomarkers. Weight-banded dosing (100/200 mg) is the tested regimen — results do not automatically transfer to other doses.
cards.source: Bacharier LB et al. Dupilumab in Children with Uncontrolled Moderate-to-Severe Asthma. The New England journal of medicine. 2021. PMID: 34879449. Registry ID: NCT02948959 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: VOYAGE control and quality-of-life analysis 2023: dupilumab improved ACQ-7-IA by a least-squares mean difference of −0.44 at week 52, with 70% versus 46% achieving well-controlled asthma, and improved quality of life for children and caregivers
cards.summary: VOYAGE control and quality-of-life analysis 2023: dupilumab improved ACQ-7-IA by a least-squares mean difference of −0.44 at week 52, with 70% versus 46% achieving well-controlled asthma, and improved quality of life for children and caregivers
cards.type: Secondary analysis of the VOYAGE trial (Fiocchi 2023) — n = 350 type 2 children
cards.people: The 350 children aged 6–11 years with uncontrolled moderate-to-severe type 2 asthma (eosinophils at least 150 cells per microlitre or fractional exhaled nitric oxide at least 20 ppb) from VOYAGE, treated with dupilumab or placebo for 52 weeks; outcomes were asthma control (ACQ-7-IA change and clinically meaningful response of at least 0.5 points, and well-controlled asthma at 0.75 points or less), children's quality of life (PAQLQ(S)-IA) and caregivers' quality of life (PACQLQ).
cards.result: Dupilumab significantly improved ACQ-7-IA by week 4 with sustained improvement through week 52 (least-squares mean difference at week 52: −0.44, 95% CI −0.59 to −0.30; p<0.0001); a clinically meaningful response was achieved by 86% versus 75% at week 52 (p=0.0051). Well-controlled asthma was achieved by 61% versus 43% at week 24 (p=0.0001) and 70% versus 46% at week 52 (p<0.0001). Children's and caregivers' quality-of-life scores were significantly improved by week 52.
cards.watchOut: This is a further analysis of the same VOYAGE children, not an independent trial — it deepens the control/quality-of-life picture for the one randomised programme and must not be counted as a second trial. Several outcomes are questionnaire scores reported by interviewers and caregivers in a trial where injection-site and other cues can partly unblind.
cards.source: Fiocchi AG et al. Dupilumab leads to better-controlled asthma and quality of life in children: the VOYAGE study. The European respiratory journal. 2023. PMID: 37734856. Registry ID: NCT02948959 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: EXCURSION 2024: in the 52-week open-label extension (365 children from VOYAGE), dupilumab's safety profile stayed consistent with the parent trial — 63.6% had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event, most often nasopharyngitis, pharyngitis and upper respiratory infections
cards.summary: EXCURSION 2024: in the 52-week open-label extension (365 children from VOYAGE), dupilumab's safety profile stayed consistent with the parent trial — 63.6% had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event, most often nasopharyngitis, pharyngitis and upper respiratory infections
cards.type: Open-label extension study — EXCURSION (Bacharier 2024) — N = 365, uncontrolled (labelled)
cards.people: 365 of the 408 VOYAGE children enrolled in EXCURSION, a 52-week open-label extension at 70 centres in 17 countries: 240 continued dupilumab (100 mg at 30 kg or less, 200 mg above, every 2 weeks; a subset at 30 kg or less later switched to 300 mg every 4 weeks after a protocol amendment) and 125 who had received placebo in VOYAGE started dupilumab. Primary endpoint: number and proportion with any treatment-emergent adverse event; analyses descriptive.
cards.result: During EXCURSION, 232 of 365 children (63.6%) experienced at least one treatment-emergent adverse event (61.3% in the continued-dupilumab group, 68.0% in the placebo-to-dupilumab group), most frequently nasopharyngitis, pharyngitis and upper respiratory tract infections. The authors conclude long-term dupilumab was well tolerated with an acceptable safety profile consistent with the parent study.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no comparator: EXCURSION addresses longer-term tolerability in children who already completed (and mostly tolerated) a year of trial treatment — a survivor population. It cannot re-establish efficacy, and event rates without a placebo arm cannot be attributed to the drug versus childhood background rates.
cards.source: Bacharier LB et al. Assessment of long-term safety and efficacy of dupilumab in children with asthma (LIBERTY ASTHMA EXCURSION): an open-label extension study. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2024. PMID: 37956679. Registry ID: NCT03560466 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: one randomised trial in 6–11-year-olds shows fewer exacerbations, better lung function and better control on dupilumab — a single programme, so POSSIBLE, with extension data supporting tolerability only
cards.summary: Synthesis: one randomised trial in 6–11-year-olds shows fewer exacerbations, better lung function and better control on dupilumab — a single programme, so POSSIBLE, with extension data supporting tolerability only
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence is one programme: VOYAGE (phase 3 RCT, 408 children, 52 weeks), its control/quality-of-life analysis (350 type 2 children), and the EXCURSION open-label extension (365 children, 52 further weeks). Adult/adolescent dupilumab asthma is homed elsewhere (live #1031; pack #5903, adults with severe eosinophilic asthma) and is not re-carded here — this shelf is the 6–11 population only.
cards.result: In type 2 children, exacerbations ran at 0.31 versus 0.75 per year (a 59.3% relative risk reduction, absolute rates beside it), predicted FEV1 improved by 5.2 percentage points more than placebo, and 70% versus 46% reached well-controlled asthma at 52 weeks. shelves.title: Varenicline plus a nicotine patch: one positive trial, one null trial, and a fragile pooled benefit — a split, and not a COPD-specific evidence base
shelves.question: In adults who smoke, does adding a nicotine patch to varenicline improve quit rates versus varenicline alone? (Assigned as a COPD question — see the premise correction: the trials did not require COPD.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Benzazepines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Breath Tests · Carbon Monoxide/analysis · Cholinergic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nicotine/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Quinoxalines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Smoking Cessation/methods · Tobacco Use Cessation Devices · Tobacco Use Disorder/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Varenicline
shelves.balance: PREMISE CORRECTION (prominent): this question was assigned as 'in adults with COPD'. The fetched records do not support that framing — Koegelenberg 2014 enrolled 'generally healthy smokers' and Ramon 2014 enrolled clinic smokers of 20 or more cigarettes a day; neither required COPD, and no COPD-specific varenicline-plus-patch trial was found this session. The shelf is therefore built for adults who smoke, with the COPD application stated as extrapolation. Premise verified against neighbouring homes: combination NRT (pack #2608) and varenicline plus bupropion (pack #2800) are different questions. The evidence splits. Koegelenberg (446 randomised, patch pre-loaded 2 weeks before quit day): continuous abstinence 55.4% versus 40.9% at 12 weeks and 49.0% versus 32.6% at 24 weeks. Ramon (341 heavy smokers): 39.1% versus 31.8% at 12 weeks, not significant — the treatment made no difference overall, with only a post hoc heavier-smoker subgroup signal. Zhou 2026 (7 trials, 2,631 participants): relative abstinence 1.33 (1.04–1.69) versus varenicline alone, rated low-certainty, and not significant (1.26, 0.94–1.68) after excluding the high-risk-of-bias trial; skin reactions are increased (relative rate 1.67 for patch combinations). PROPOSED SPLIT.

cards.headline: Koegelenberg 2014: adding a nicotine patch to varenicline raised continuous abstinence to 55.4% versus 40.9% at 12 weeks and 49.0% versus 32.6% at 24 weeks (446 generally healthy smokers randomised; 435 analysed)
cards.summary: Koegelenberg 2014: adding a nicotine patch to varenicline raised continuous abstinence to 55.4% versus 40.9% at 12 weeks and 49.0% versus 32.6% at 24 weeks (446 generally healthy smokers randomised; 435 analysed)
cards.type: Randomised, blinded, placebo-patch-controlled trial (Koegelenberg 2014) — 446 randomised
cards.people: 446 generally healthy smokers randomised (435 in the efficacy and safety analyses) at 7 centres in South Africa, 2011–2012: nicotine patch or placebo patch started 2 weeks before the target quit date and continued 12 weeks, with varenicline started 1 week before the quit date, continued 12 weeks and tapered in week 13. Abstinence was confirmed by exhaled carbon monoxide. NOTE: this trial did not require COPD — participants were generally healthy smokers (see the premise correction in the balance).
cards.result: The combination was associated with a higher continuous abstinence rate at 12 weeks (55.4% versus 40.9%; odds ratio 1.85, 95% CI 1.19–2.89; P = .007) and at 24 weeks (49.0% versus 32.6%; OR 1.98, 95% CI 1.25–3.14; P = .004), and higher point-prevalence abstinence at 6 months (65.1% versus 46.7%; OR 2.13, 95% CI 1.32–3.43; P = .002). Nausea, sleep disturbance, skin reactions, constipation and depression were numerically more frequent with the combination, with only skin reactions statistically significant (14.4% versus 7.8%; P = .03); the varenicline-alone group had more abnormal dreams and headaches.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one country, patch started 2 weeks before the quit date — a pre-loading design that may not match starting patch and varenicline together on the quit day. 'Generally healthy smokers' means smokers with COPD were not the studied population; applying this to COPD is extrapolation.

cards.headline: Ramon 2014: adding a 21 mg nicotine patch to varenicline made no difference to continuous abstinence overall — 39.1% versus 31.8% at 12 weeks (OR 1.24, 95% CI 0.8–2.6) in 341 heavy smokers (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Ramon 2014: adding a 21 mg nicotine patch to varenicline made no difference to continuous abstinence overall — 39.1% versus 31.8% at 12 weeks (OR 1.24, 95% CI 0.8–2.6) in 341 heavy smokers (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Ramon 2014) — N = 341
cards.people: 341 smokers who smoked 20 or more cigarettes per day, recruited from a smoking cessation clinic in Spain (2012–2013), randomised to varenicline plus a 21 mg/24-hour nicotine patch (n = 170) or varenicline plus a placebo patch (n = 171) for 11 weeks after the target quit day, with a standard 12-week varenicline course and behavioural support in both groups. Primary outcome: continuous abstinence for weeks 2–12 confirmed by exhaled carbon monoxide.
cards.result: The combination was not associated with higher continuous abstinence at 12 weeks (39.1% versus 31.8%; OR 1.24, 95% CI 0.8–2.6) or at 24 weeks (32.8% versus 28.2%; OR 1.17, 95% CI 0.4–1.9) when all smokers were analysed — the treatment made no difference overall. In post hoc subgroup analysis, smokers of more than 29 cigarettes per day had higher abstinence with the combination at 12 weeks (OR 1.39, 95% CI 1.2–2.5) and 24 weeks (OR 1.46, 95% CI 1.2–2.8); subgroups by dependence level and previous quit attempts showed no differences. Reported adverse events did not differ between groups (P = 0.79).
cards.watchOut: The heavy-smoker subgroup finding is post hoc — hypothesis-generating, not a basis for a claim. The confidence interval for the main result (0.8–2.6) is wide: this trial excludes neither a useful benefit nor none, which is precisely why the shelf is a split rather than a null.

cards.headline: Zhou 2026 meta-analysis (7 trials, 2,631 participants): combination varenicline plus nicotine replacement gave a relative abstinence rate of 1.33 (95% CI 1.04–1.69) versus varenicline alone at 6 months or more — but excluding the high-risk-of-bias trial, the result was not significant (RR 1.26, 0.94–1.68)
cards.summary: Zhou 2026 meta-analysis (7 trials, 2,631 participants): combination varenicline plus nicotine replacement gave a relative abstinence rate of 1.33 (95% CI 1.04–1.69) versus varenicline alone at 6 months or more — but excluding the high-risk-of-bias trial, the result was not significant (RR 1.26, 0.94–1.68)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (Zhou 2026) — 2,631 participants
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA, GRADE, Cochrane RoB 2.0; PROSPERO CRD42024600510) of randomised or quasi-randomised trials of varenicline combined with nicotine replacement versus varenicline alone or NRT alone, searched to June 2025; 7 trials including 2,631 participants. Primary outcome: smoking abstinence at the longest follow-up (at least 6 months).
cards.result: Compared with varenicline alone, combination therapy was associated with higher abstinence at the longest follow-up (risk ratio 1.33, 95% CI 1.04–1.69; 5 studies; I2 = 51%) — a relative measure; the review does not print a single pooled absolute rate pair on the fetched record. A sensitivity analysis at 3 months or more was similar (RR 1.31, 1.06–1.62; 6 studies), but excluding the trial at high risk of bias the result was not statistically significant (RR 1.26, 0.94–1.68). Versus NRT alone, only one trial was included and the combination effect was not significant (RR 0.94, 0.51–1.72). Adverse events were more common with the combination (RR 1.11, 1.02–1.20), especially skin reactions with patch plus varenicline (RR 1.67, 1.29–2.16); serious adverse events were infrequent and generally unrelated. The authors rate this low-certainty evidence.
cards.watchOut: Low-certainty by the authors' own GRADE assessment, with moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 51%) and a headline result that depends on including a high-risk-of-bias trial. The combination in the pooled trials is not always a patch (NRT forms vary), so this card supports the combination class, with the two patch-specific trials carded above carrying the patch question itself.
cards.source: Zhou X et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: a genuine split — the largest patch trial is positive, the second patch trial is null overall, and the pooled estimate is positive but fragile and low-certainty
cards.summary: Synthesis: a genuine split — the largest patch trial is positive, the second patch trial is null overall, and the pooled estimate is positive but fragile and low-certainty
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: two patch-specific randomised trials (Koegelenberg 2014, 446 randomised, patch pre-loading, positive at 12 and 24 weeks; Ramon 2014, 341 heavy smokers, null overall with a post hoc heavy-smoker subgroup signal) and a 7-trial meta-analysis of varenicline plus NRT (Zhou 2026, 2,631 participants, low certainty). Combination NRT without varenicline (pack #2608) and varenicline plus bupropion (pack #2800) are different questions, homed on those packs and not re-carded here.
cards.result: Absolute abstinence differences in the positive trial were about 14–16 percentage points at 12–24 weeks; in the null trial about 5–7 points and not significant. Pooled, the relative rate is 1.33 (1.04–1.69) versus varenicline alone, losing significance when the high-bias-risk trial is removed. Skin reactions are the consistent added harm. PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit is plausible, especially in heavier smokers, but it is not established — and none of the carded trials required COPD, so for COPD specifically the evidence is extrapolation from general smoker populations.
cards.watchOut: A 2024 hospital trial of varenicline plus NRT lozenges (not patch) is deliberately not carded: lozenges are a different NRT form from the patch this shelf asks about, and borrowing it would blur the question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Koegelenberg CF et al. JAMA. 2014 (PMID: 25005652); Ramon JM et al. BMC medicine. 2014 (PMID: 25296623); Zhou X et al. Addiction. 2026 (PMID: 41208435).

shelves.title: Depemokimab every 6 months (SWIFT-1/-2): exacerbations roughly halved versus placebo in two replicate trials, with no significant quality-of-life difference
shelves.question: In adults with severe asthma, does depemokimab given every 6 months reduce exacerbations versus placebo? (Trials enrolled from age 12 — see cards.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Asthma/blood,diagnosis,drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Eosinophilia/blood,diagnosis,drug therapy · Eosinophils · Forced Expiratory Volume · Injections, Subcutaneous · Interleukin-5/antagonists & inhibitors · Leukocyte Count · Severity of Illness Index · Disease Progression · Adolescent · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Premise verified: live #813 homes mepolizumab (MENSA) and benralizumab (SIROCCO) exacerbations only — depemokimab was uncovered. Two wording corrections from the fetched records: SWIFT-1/-2 enrolled patients aged 12 and over, so 'adults' in the assigned question is answered for a mixed adolescent/adult population (no adults-only estimate is printed in the record); and the benefit is specific — exacerbations fell (0.46 vs 1.11 and 0.56 vs 1.08 per year; relative rate reductions 58% and 48% with absolute rates beside them) while St George's Respiratory Questionnaire quality of life did not differ significantly in either trial, halting the secondary hierarchy. The AGILE open-label extension (629 patients, labelled uncontrolled) shows the reduced rate sustained over a second year (0.56) with 9% serious adverse events and none treatment-related; a pre-specified subgroup analysis suggests larger benefit with comorbid nasal polyps (rate ratio 0.31, n = 113). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant replicate trials, but one development programme, which caps the stamp.

cards.headline: SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 2024: depemokimab 100 mg every 6 months cut annualised exacerbations to 0.46 versus 1.11 (rate ratio 0.42) and 0.56 versus 1.08 (rate ratio 0.52) versus placebo — but made no significant difference to quality-of-life (SGRQ) scores in either trial
cards.summary: SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 2024: depemokimab 100 mg every 6 months cut annualised exacerbations to 0.46 versus 1.11 (rate ratio 0.42) and 0.56 versus 1.08 (rate ratio 0.52) versus placebo — but made no significant difference to quality-of-life (SGRQ) scores in either trial
cards.type: Two replicate phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials — SWIFT-1/-2 (Jackson 2024) — 792 randomised
cards.people: Patients aged 12 years and over (the trials included adolescents — see watchOut) with severe asthma and an eosinophilic phenotype (eosinophils at least 300 cells per microlitre in the previous 12 months or at least 150 at screening) and a history of exacerbations despite medium- or high-dose inhaled glucocorticoids, in two replicate phase 3A randomised placebo-controlled trials: depemokimab 100 mg subcutaneously or placebo at weeks 0 and 26, plus standard care. Across both trials 792 underwent randomisation and 762 were in the full analysis (502 depemokimab, 260 placebo). Primary endpoint: annualised exacerbation rate at 52 weeks.
cards.result: SWIFT-1: annualised exacerbations 0.46 (95% CI 0.36–0.58) with depemokimab versus 1.11 (0.86–1.43) with placebo (rate ratio 0.42, 95% CI 0.30–0.59; P<0.001) — a 58% relative rate reduction, with the absolute rates printed beside it. SWIFT-2: 0.56 (0.44–0.70) versus 1.08 (0.83–1.41) (rate ratio 0.52, 0.36–0.73; P<0.001) — a 48% relative rate reduction. No significant between-group difference in change in St George's Respiratory Questionnaire score was observed in either trial, so no statistical inference was drawn on subsequent secondary endpoints. The proportion with any adverse event was similar between groups in both trials.
cards.watchOut: The assigned question says 'adults', but SWIFT enrolled patients aged 12 and over — results are for a mixed adolescent/adult severe eosinophilic population, and the record does not print an adults-only estimate. The exacerbation benefit did not carry through to a significant quality-of-life difference, and the hierarchical testing stopped there — lung-function and symptom claims beyond exacerbations are not established by these trials.
cards.source: Jackson DJ et al. Twice-Yearly Depemokimab in Severe Asthma with an Eosinophilic Phenotype. The New England journal of medicine. 2024. PMID: 39248309. Registry ID: NCT04719832 and NCT04718103 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: AGILE integrated analysis 2026: over 2 years, twice-yearly depemokimab's reduced exacerbation rate was sustained (0.51 in the SWIFT year, 0.56 in the extension year) with adverse events in about 71% and serious adverse events in 9% — open-label extension, no placebo arm
cards.summary: AGILE integrated analysis 2026: over 2 years, twice-yearly depemokimab's reduced exacerbation rate was sustained (0.51 in the SWIFT year, 0.56 in the extension year) with adverse events in about 71% and serious adverse events in 9% — open-label extension, no placebo arm
cards.type: Open-label extension with integrated post hoc analysis — AGILE (Wechsler 2026) — N = 629, uncontrolled (labelled)
cards.people: 629 patients who completed SWIFT-1 or SWIFT-2 and joined AGILE, a 52-week single-arm open-label extension at 156 centres in 14 countries: 419 continued depemokimab and 210 switched from placebo to depemokimab (100 mg every 26 weeks). Primary endpoints were adverse events, serious adverse events and immunogenicity; exacerbation rate, SGRQ, ACQ-5 and FEV1 were secondary, with a post hoc integrated 104-week analysis.
cards.result: During the extension year, adverse events occurred in 297 of 419 (71%) continuing patients and 146 of 210 (70%) switchers; serious adverse events were infrequent (9% in each group), with no treatment-related or fatal serious adverse events reported. In the continuing group the annualised exacerbation rate was sustained over 2 years (0.51, 95% CI 0.43–0.61 in the SWIFT period; 0.56, 0.47–0.66 in AGILE), and SGRQ, ACQ-5 and FEV1 improvements were maintained; switchers improved after starting depemokimab. The authors conclude twice-yearly depemokimab was well tolerated with sustained efficacy over 2 years.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and limited to SWIFT completers — a population that already tolerated and mostly responded to a year of therapy; sustained rates without a control arm cannot exclude regression to the mean or survivor effects. MeSH debt: this record carried no MeSH list as fetched this session, so the fallback text is used (see summary).
cards.source: Wechsler ME et al. Long-term safety and efficacy of twice-yearly depemokimab in type 2 asthma with an eosinophilic phenotype: 2-year integrated analysis of the phase 3a SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 studies and AGILE open-label extension. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2026. PMID: 42956801. Registry ID: NCT05243680 (AGILE), with NCT04719832 and NCT04718103 (SWIFT-1/-2) (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: SWIFT CRSwNP subgroup analysis 2026: in patients with comorbid chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, depemokimab's exacerbation rate was 0.51 versus 1.61 on placebo (rate ratio 0.31) — a small pre-specified subgroup (80 versus 33 patients)

cards.type: Pre-specified subgroup analysis of SWIFT-1/-2 (Heffler 2026) — CRSwNP subgroup n = 113
cards.people: Pre-specified subgroup analysis of pooled SWIFT-1/-2 data in patients with type 2 asthma and comorbid chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP): depemokimab 100 mg or placebo every 26 weeks for 52 weeks plus standard care; outcomes were annualised exacerbation rate, SGRQ and ACQ-5 by baseline CRSwNP subgroup. In the CRSwNP subgroup, 80 patients received depemokimab and 33 placebo.
cards.result: In the asthma-with-CRSwNP subgroup the annualised exacerbation rate was 0.51 (95% CI 0.34–0.75) with depemokimab versus 1.61 (0.99–2.60) with placebo (rate ratio 0.31, 0.17–0.58) — a 69% relative rate reduction, with absolute rates beside it. SGRQ improved more with depemokimab (difference −7.12 points at 4 weeks, −8.32 at 52 weeks) and ACQ-5 likewise (−0.40 at 2 weeks, −0.76 at 52 weeks) in this subgroup — improvements the authors note were greater than in the overall SWIFT population, identifying CRSwNP comorbidity as a phenotype with enhanced benefit.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup of 113 patients from the same two trials — it refines who may benefit most; it is not independent confirmation of the main result, and subgroup quality-of-life findings sit downstream of the main trials' non-significant SGRQ result, so they should be read as phenotype signals, not as overturning it. cards.people: The carded evidence is one programme: SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 (two replicate randomised trials reported in one 2024 paper, 792 randomised), the AGILE open-label extension integrated analysis (629 patients, 2 years), and a pre-specified CRSwNP subgroup analysis of the same trials. shelves.title: Auto-titrating versus fixed CPAP: clinically interchangeable — 11 minutes more use and half an Epworth point for APAP, 1.3% minimum saturation for fixed, and no blood-pressure difference
shelves.question: In adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, is auto-titrating CPAP as effective as fixed-pressure CPAP for sleepiness, apnoea control and blood pressure?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Humans · Positive-Pressure Respiration/methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive/therapy
shelves.balance: Desk-check: no APAP-versus-fixed home exists; CPAP shelves in the library cover other comparators. The answer to 'as effective?' is yes, clinically — and the wording follows the house null convention because the comparison, not either treatment, is what shows no difference (both modes work versus no treatment: Patil 2019 found PAP itself reduces disease severity, sleepiness and blood pressure). Ip 2012 pooled 24 RCTs: similar AHI, sleep measures and quality of life; APAP ahead by 11 minutes of use per night and 0.5 Epworth points, fixed CPAP ahead by 1.3% on minimum oxygen saturation — statistically real, clinically marginal, and in opposing directions. Patil 2019 (336 studies) concluded auto-adjusting PAP produced no clinically significant difference in patient outcomes versus standard CPAP. The Hukins 2004 crossover shows the same pattern at trial level (compliance 5.05 vs 4.86 h/night, Epworth 7.9 vs 8.4; N not documented in the record), with APAP's real advantages being lower pressures, fewer leaks and fewer side effects (15 vs 28 reports). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — for the modality comparison, on two independent syntheses.

cards.headline: Ip 2012 meta-analysis (24 RCTs): APAP and fixed CPAP produced similar changes in apnoea–hypopnoea index, sleep measures and quality of life — APAP's statistical edges were 11 extra minutes of use per night and 0.5 Epworth points, while fixed CPAP improved minimum oxygen saturation by 1.3% more
cards.summary: Ip 2012 meta-analysis (24 RCTs): APAP and fixed CPAP produced similar changes in apnoea–hypopnoea index, sleep measures and quality of life — APAP's statistical edges were 11 extra minutes of use per night and 0.5 Epworth points, while fixed CPAP improved minimum oxygen saturation by 1.3% more
cards.type: Systematic review with meta-analyses of 24 RCTs (Ip 2012)
cards.people: Systematic review with meta-analyses of English-language randomised controlled trials comparing auto-titrating positive airway pressure (APAP) with fixed continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) in adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, searched to September 2010; 24 RCTs met the inclusion criteria, with data extracted and confirmed by paired reviewers and random-effects meta-analyses.
cards.result: In individual studies, APAP and fixed CPAP resulted in similar changes from baseline in the apnoea–hypopnoea index, most other sleep study measures and quality of life. By meta-analysis, APAP improved compliance by 11 minutes per night (95% CI 3–19) and reduced sleepiness on the Epworth Sleepiness Scale by 0.5 points (95% CI 0.2–0.8 point reduction) compared with fixed CPAP, while fixed CPAP improved minimum oxygen saturation by 1.3% more than APAP (95% CI 0.4–2.2%). The authors conclude the differences are statistically significant but of unclear clinical importance, that treatment effects are similar, and that choice may depend on preference, reasons for non-compliance and cost. Studies had relatively short follow-up, generally excluded significant comorbidities, and no study reported objective clinical outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Blood pressure — one of the three outcomes in the assigned question — is not among the pooled results reported in this record; the blood-pressure leg rests on the Patil 2019 card below, which found no clinically significant modality difference. 'Similar in trials that excluded comorbid patients' may not transfer to complex patients, who were largely excluded.

cards.headline: Patil 2019 AASM systematic review (336 studies; 184 in meta-analyses): auto-adjusting PAP did not result in clinically significant differences in patient outcomes compared with standard CPAP, while PAP versus no treatment did reduce disease severity, sleepiness and blood pressure
cards.summary: Patil 2019 AASM systematic review (336 studies; 184 in meta-analyses): auto-adjusting PAP did not result in clinically significant differences in patient outcomes compared with standard CPAP, while PAP versus no treatment did reduce disease severity, sleepiness and blood pressure
cards.type: Systematic review, meta-analysis and GRADE assessment (Patil 2019) — 336 studies, 184 meta-analysed
cards.people: American Academy of Sleep Medicine systematic review and GRADE assessment supporting its positive airway pressure guideline: studies comparing PAP with no treatment and studies comparing PAP modalities (continuous, auto-adjusting, bilevel) in adults with obstructive sleep apnoea; 336 studies met inclusion criteria and 184 provided data suitable for meta-analyses, covering disease severity, sleepiness, blood pressure, motor vehicle accidents, sleep-related quality of life, initiation strategies, interfaces, humidification and adherence interventions.
cards.result: PAP compared with no treatment produced a clinically significant reduction in disease severity, sleepiness and blood pressure, and improvement in sleep-related quality of life. Home initiation was equivalent to in-laboratory titration. Critically for this shelf: the use of auto-adjusting or bilevel PAP did not result in clinically significant differences in patient outcomes compared with standard continuous PAP — so the blood-pressure and sleepiness benefits of PAP are benefits of PAP itself, not of the auto-titrating mode. Educational, behavioural, troubleshooting and telemonitoring interventions did improve adherence.
cards.watchOut: A guideline evidence review, not a single head-to-head meta-analysis with one pooled APAP-versus-fixed number for each outcome — its conclusion is a GRADE-level judgement of 'no clinically significant difference' across outcomes. It does not mean every individual trial was null on every measure (see the Hukins card for the pattern at trial level).

cards.headline: Hukins 2004 crossover trial: 2 months each of APAP and fixed CPAP gave no difference in compliance (5.05 vs 4.86 hours/night, P = .14) or sleepiness (Epworth 7.9 vs 8.4, both improved from 12.4 at baseline) — but APAP used lower pressures, leaked less and caused fewer side effects (15 vs 28 reports, P = .02); participant number not documented in the record
cards.summary: Hukins 2004 crossover trial: 2 months each of APAP and fixed CPAP gave no difference in compliance (5.05 vs 4.86 hours/night, P = .14) or sleepiness (Epworth 7.9 vs 8.4, both improved from 12.4 at baseline) — but APAP used lower pressures, leaked less and caused fewer side effects (15 vs 28 reports, P = .02); participant number not documented in the record
cards.type: Randomised, single-blind crossover trial (Hukins 2004) — N not documented in the record
cards.people: Consecutive patients with obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome requiring CPAP at a tertiary sleep centre, in a randomised, single-blind crossover study of 2 months each of conventional fixed CPAP and auto-titrating APAP in random order at home; outcomes were objective compliance, Epworth Sleepiness Score, SF-36, ease/attitude measures, side effects, and device pressures and leaks. The fetched record does not print the participant number (N not documented in the record).
cards.result: There were no differences between modes in overall compliance (CPAP 4.86 ± 2.65, APAP 5.05 ± 2.38 hours per night, P = .14) or Epworth scores (baseline 12.4 ± 5.1; CPAP 8.4 ± 5.2; APAP 7.9 ± 4.8 — improved versus baseline, not significant between modes), and SF-36 Role Physical and Vitality improved versus baseline with no between-mode difference. APAP delivered significantly lower median and 95th-centile pressures and fewer system leaks, with fewer reported side effects (CPAP 28, APAP 15 reports, P = .02), and compliance was greater with APAP in patients reporting any side effect. The author concludes APAP may be indicated in patients reporting side effects with conventional CPAP.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the fetched record, printed on the face. A single-centre crossover from 2004 (Autoset T-era device): modern APAP algorithms differ, and crossover designs can carry period effects. It is carded as the trial-level illustration of the meta-analytic pattern, not as stand-alone proof.

cards.headline: Synthesis: for sleepiness, apnoea control and blood pressure, auto-titrating and fixed CPAP are clinically interchangeable — the differences found are minutes of use and fractions of a point, in both directions
cards.summary: Synthesis: for sleepiness, apnoea control and blood pressure, auto-titrating and fixed CPAP are clinically interchangeable — the differences found are minutes of use and fractions of a point, in both directions
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: a 24-RCT meta-analysis (Ip 2012), the AASM systematic review and GRADE assessment (Patil 2019; 336 studies, 184 meta-analysed), and a randomised crossover trial (Hukins 2004, N not documented in the record). Desk-check: no APAP-versus-fixed home exists — other CPAP shelves cover different comparators (oxygen, mandibular devices, residual-sleepiness drugs) and are not re-carded.
cards.result: Apnoea–hypopnoea index and most sleep measures: similar. Sleepiness: a 0.5-point Epworth edge to APAP in meta-analysis, below clinical importance, and no between-mode difference in the crossover trial (7.9 vs 8.4). Blood pressure: PAP lowers it versus no treatment, with no clinically significant difference between auto-adjusting and standard CPAP (Patil). Adherence: 11 minutes per night in APAP's favour; minimum oxygen saturation 1.3% in fixed CPAP's favour — small, opposing, and clinically marginal. APAP's practical advantages are lower delivered pressures, fewer leaks and fewer side effects. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the clinical outcomes asked about, across two independent syntheses.
cards.watchOut: The underlying trials were short and excluded many comorbid patients, and none reported hard clinical outcomes — 'no clinically significant difference' is a statement about sleepiness, AHI, blood pressure and quality of life over weeks to months, not about long-term cardiovascular events.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ip S et al. Systematic reviews. 2012 (PMID: 22587875); Patil SP et al. Journal of clinical sleep medicine. 2019 (PMID: 30736888); Hukins C. Sleep. 2004 (PMID: 15683142).

synthesis the carded evidence: a 24-rct meta-analysis (ip 2012), the aasm systematic review and grade assessment (patil 2019; 336 studies, 184 meta-analysed), and a randomised crossover trial (hukins 2004, n not documented in the record). desk-check: no apap-versus-fixed home exists — other cpap shelves cover different comparators (oxygen, mandibular devices, residual-sleepiness drugs) and are not re-carded. apnoea–hypopnoea index and most sleep measures: similar. sleepiness: a 0.5-point epworth edge to apap in meta-analysis, below clinical importance, and no between-mode difference in the crossover trial (7.9 vs 8.4). blood pressure: pap lowers it versus no treatment, with no clinically significant difference between auto-adjusting and standard cpap (patil). adherence: 11 minutes per night in apap's favour; minimum oxygen saturation 1.3% in fixed cpap's favour — small, opposing, and clinically marginal. apap's practical advantages are lower delivered pressures, fewer leaks and fewer side effects. proposed likely (the treatment made no difference) for the clinical outcomes asked about, across two independent syntheses. the underlying trials were short and excluded many comorbid patients, and none reported hard clinical outcomes — 'no clinically significant difference' is a statement about sleepiness, ahi, blood pressure and quality of life over weeks to months, not about long-term cardiovascular events. synthesis of ip s et al. systematic reviews. 2012 (pmid: 22587875); patil sp et al. journal of clinical sleep medicine. 2019 (pmid: 30736888); hukins c. sleep. 2004 (pmid: 15683142).

shelves.title: Mepolizumab in younger children: the one placebo-controlled trial (ages 6–17) cut exacerbations by a relative 27% (0.96 versus 1.30 per year); the 6–11 study itself was a 36-child dosing study with no placebo arm
shelves.question: In children aged 6–11 years with severe eosinophilic asthma, does mepolizumab reduce exacerbations versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Asthma/drug therapy · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Pulmonary Eosinophilia · Child · Humans · Disease Progression · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #813 homes mepolizumab and benralizumab in adult severe eosinophilic asthma (MENSA, SIROCCO) and is not re-carded here; the uncovered slice is the 6–11 age band. The placebo-controlled evidence touching that band is one trial: MUPPITS-2 randomised 290 urban US children and adolescents aged 6–17 with exacerbation-prone eosinophilic asthma (blood eosinophils ≥150 cells/µL) to mepolizumab (40 mg at ages 6–11; 100 mg at 12–17) or placebo for 52 weeks, and exacerbations averaged 0.96 versus 1.30 (rate ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.96 — a 27% relative reduction, printed beside the absolute rates); treatment-emergent adverse events were reported in 29% on mepolizumab versus 11% on placebo, with no deaths attributed to the drug. The record prints no separate result for the 6–11 subgroup, so the trial supports the band only as part of its wider age range. The one study confined to ages 6–11 (Gupta 2019; 36 children) was open-label and non-randomised, designed for pharmacokinetics: weight-banded dosing (40 mg under 40 kg; 100 mg at or above) produced exposures within twofold of the adult target and cut blood eosinophils by 83–89% at 12 weeks, with no new safety signals — it establishes that the dose reaches children, not that it prevents attacks. The Cochrane anti-IL-5 review (17 studies, about 7,600 participants) found exacerbation rates roughly halved across the class in severe eosinophilic asthma (mepolizumab subcutaneous rate ratio 0.45), but only one of its studies was in children and its pooled estimate is adult-driven context, not child evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): direction and biology align from trial, dosing study and class review, but a dedicated placebo-controlled efficacy result for ages 6–11 alone does not exist in these records.

cards.headline: MUPPITS-2 2022: mepolizumab cut exacerbations over 52 weeks — 0.96 versus 1.30 per year (rate ratio 0.73) in 290 children and adolescents aged 6–17
cards.summary: MUPPITS-2 2022: mepolizumab cut exacerbations over 52 weeks — 0.96 versus 1.30 per year (rate ratio 0.73) in 290 children and adolescents aged 6–17
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (MUPPITS-2)
cards.people: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at nine urban US medical centres: 290 children and adolescents aged 6–17 from socioeconomically disadvantaged neighbourhoods with exacerbation-prone eosinophilic asthma (≥2 exacerbations in the previous year; blood eosinophils ≥150 cells/µL), assigned to mepolizumab (146; 40 mg at ages 6–11, 100 mg at 12–17) or placebo (144) every 4 weeks plus guideline-based care for 52 weeks; 248 completed the study.
cards.result: The mean number of asthma exacerbations treated with systemic corticosteroids over 52 weeks was 0.96 (95% CI 0.78 to 1.17) on mepolizumab versus 1.30 (1.08 to 1.57) on placebo (rate ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.96; p = 0.027 — a 27% relative reduction, printed beside the absolute rates). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 42/146 (29%) on mepolizumab versus 16/144 (11%) on placebo, as reported; no deaths were attributed to mepolizumab.
cards.watchOut: The trial spans ages 6–17 and the record prints no 6–11-only result: the younger band contributed participants and received the 40 mg dose, but the 0.73 rate ratio is the whole-cohort figure. The population was specifically urban, disadvantaged and exacerbation-prone — generalising to all children with severe eosinophilic asthma goes beyond the record.
cards.source: Jackson DJ et al. Mepolizumab for urban children with exacerbation-prone eosinophilic asthma in the USA (MUPPITS-2): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial. Lancet (London, England). 2022. PMID: 35964610. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03292588. cards.headline: Gupta 2019: in the only study confined to ages 6–11 (36 children, open-label), weight-banded mepolizumab cut blood eosinophils by 83–89% — a dosing study, not an efficacy trial
cards.summary: Gupta 2019: in the only study confined to ages 6–11 (36 children, open-label), weight-banded mepolizumab cut blood eosinophils by 83–89% — a dosing study, not an efficacy trial
cards.type: Open-label, non-randomised pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic study in children 6–11 (Gupta 2019)
cards.people: Multinational, non-randomised, open-label pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic study in 36 children aged 6–11 with severe eosinophilic asthma (eosinophils ≥150 cells/µL at screening or ≥300 cells/µL in the prior year, and ≥2 prior-year exacerbations): mepolizumab 40 mg if under 40 kg (n = 26) or 100 mg if 40 kg or more (n = 10), subcutaneously every 4 weeks for 12 weeks. No placebo or comparator group.
cards.result: Bodyweight-adjusted mepolizumab exposures were within twofold of the target adult exposure. At week 12, blood eosinophils had fallen by 89% (40 mg group, to 42 cells/µL) and 83% (100 mg group, to 55 cells/µL) from baseline — relative reductions printed beside the absolute counts. Mepolizumab was well tolerated with no new safety signals compared with adult and adolescent studies. The authors state the study was not designed to evaluate efficacy outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Carded as dosing and target-engagement evidence only: with no placebo arm and 36 children, it cannot show fewer exacerbations, and its eosinophil falls are a biomarker, not a clinical outcome. Do not cite this card as efficacy evidence for the 6–11 band.
cards.source: Gupta A et al. Subcutaneous mepolizumab in children aged 6 to 11 years with severe eosinophilic asthma. Pediatric pulmonology. 2019. PMID: 31502421. cards.headline: Cochrane 2022 (Farne): anti-IL-5 therapies roughly halved exacerbation rates in severe eosinophilic asthma (mepolizumab rate ratio 0.45) — but only 1 of 17 studies was in children
cards.summary: Cochrane 2022 (Farne): anti-IL-5 therapies roughly halved exacerbation rates in severe eosinophilic asthma (mepolizumab rate ratio 0.45) — but only 1 of 17 studies was in children
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Farne 2022)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of anti-IL-5 or anti-IL-5-receptor therapies (mepolizumab, reslizumab, benralizumab) versus placebo in adults and children with asthma: 17 studies, about 7,600 participants, predominantly severe eosinophilic asthma; one study was in children aged 6–17 and nine others included children over 12 without separate age reporting. Overall certainty was graded high for the main comparisons.
cards.result: In severe eosinophilic asthma on standard care, clinically significant exacerbations were reduced with rate ratios of 0.45 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.55, high-certainty) for subcutaneous mepolizumab, 0.53 for intravenous mepolizumab, 0.43 for intravenous reslizumab and 0.59 for subcutaneous benralizumab — relative measures; the abstract prints no pooled absolute rates, so none are printed here. Health-related quality of life improved with all anti-IL-5 agents in severe eosinophilic asthma.
cards.watchOut: The pooled 0.45 rate ratio is overwhelmingly adult evidence — the same adult programme homed on live shelf #813. It is carded here as class context showing the child trial's direction is biologically consistent, and must not be quoted as the expected effect size in 6–11-year-olds, for whom the only randomised figure is MUPPITS-2's 0.73.
cards.source: Farne HA et al. Anti-IL-5 therapies for asthma. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2022. PMID: 35838542. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — systematic review, not a single trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: one child-inclusive trial shows fewer exacerbations; the 6–11-only evidence is a dosing study — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one child-inclusive trial shows fewer exacerbations; the 6–11-only evidence is a dosing study — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: MUPPITS-2 (290 children and adolescents aged 6–17, placebo-controlled), the Gupta pharmacokinetic study (36 children aged 6–11, open-label) and the Cochrane anti-IL-5 review (17 studies, about 7,600 participants, one in children). Adult mepolizumab evidence is homed on live shelf #813 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Versus placebo, mepolizumab reduced exacerbations in the only randomised trial enrolling 6–11-year-olds (0.96 versus 1.30 over 52 weeks; rate ratio 0.73, a 27% relative reduction); weight-banded dosing in 6–11-year-olds achieved adult-range exposure and 83–89% eosinophil reductions; and the class effect in (mostly adult) severe eosinophilic asthma is larger (rate ratio 0.45). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): benefit in this age band is supported but rests on one trial's wider-age result — a dedicated 6–11 efficacy readout would be needed for more.
cards.watchOut: Quote the child figure (rate ratio 0.73; 0.96 versus 1.30 exacerbations a year), not the adult 0.45, when counselling about ages 6–11 — and note the trial's higher reported treatment-emergent adverse-event rate on mepolizumab (29% versus 11%) when weighing the benefit.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jackson DJ et al. Lancet (London, England). 2022 (PMID: 35964610); Gupta A et al. Pediatric pulmonology. 2019 (PMID: 31502421); Farne HA et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2022 (PMID: 35838542). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Reflux treatment in IPF: SPLIT — an early cohort linked reflux medication to longer survival, but the largest pooled analysis and the one small surgical trial found no benefit
shelves.question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does treating gastro-oesophageal reflux (antacid therapy or fundoplication) slow progression or improve survival?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Case-Control Studies · Comorbidity · Female · Fundoplication · Gastroesophageal Reflux/epidemiology,therapy · Histamine H2 Antagonists/therapeutic use · Humans · Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis/diagnostic imaging,epidemiology,therapy · Male · Proportional Hazards Models · Proton Pump Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Radiography · Retrospective Studies · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: SPLIT — grade with care: the evidence is observational plus one small surgical trial. Lee 2011 (retrospective cohort, 204 patients) found reported reflux-medication use was an independent predictor of longer survival with a lower fibrosis score. Kreuter 2016 (post-hoc pooled analysis of 624 placebo-arm patients from the three pirfenidone trials) found the opposite pattern: disease progression 39% versus 42%, mortality 7% versus 7% — antacid therapy made no difference (the treatment made no difference) — with more infections in advanced disease. WRAP-IPF (Raghu 2018; 58 randomised patients with IPF and proven abnormal acid reflux) found laparoscopic anti-reflux surgery did not significantly change 48-week FVC decline (−0.05 L vs −0.13 L; P = .28). The IPF family homes (live #810 antifibrotics; packs #2783, #2801) do not cover reflux treatment.

cards.headline: Lee 2011 (observational): in a 204-patient IPF cohort, reported use of reflux medication was an independent predictor of longer survival and was associated with a lower radiologic fibrosis score
cards.summary: Lee 2011 (observational): in a 204-patient IPF cohort, reported use of reflux medication was an independent predictor of longer survival and was associated with a lower radiologic fibrosis score
cards.type: Retrospective observational cohort (Lee 2011) — N = 204
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of 204 patients with well-characterised idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis from two academic medical centres. Reflux-related variables were common: reflux symptoms in 34%, a history of reflux disease in 45%, reported use of reflux medication in 47%, and Nissen fundoplication in 5%. Survival was analysed with regression adjustment.
cards.result: On unadjusted analysis all reflux-related variables were associated with longer survival; after adjustment, use of gastro-oesophageal reflux medication remained an independent predictor of longer survival time, and reflux-medication use was associated with a lower radiologic fibrosis score, consistently across both centres. The authors interpret this as supporting a role for reflux and chronic microaspiration in the pathobiology of IPF.
cards.watchOut: Observational and retrospective: patients prescribed reflux medication differ from those who are not (access, comorbidity, clinician behaviour), and 'reported use' is not randomised treatment — a survival association of this shape is exactly what confounding by indication and immortal-time effects produce. No hazard ratio is printed because the record's abstract does not report one.
cards.source: Lee JS et al. Gastroesophageal reflux therapy is associated with longer survival in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2011. PMID: 21700909. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kreuter 2016 (pooled trial-placebo analysis): among 624 placebo-arm patients from three pirfenidone trials, antacid therapy made no difference to disease progression, mortality or lung-function decline at 52 weeks (the treatment made no difference) — with more infections in advanced disease
cards.summary: Kreuter 2016 (pooled trial-placebo analysis): among 624 placebo-arm patients from three pirfenidone trials, antacid therapy made no difference to disease progression, mortality or lung-function decline at 52 weeks (the treatment made no difference) — with more infections in advanced disease
cards.type: Post-hoc pooled analysis of randomised-trial placebo arms (Kreuter 2016) — N = 624 (291 antacid, 333 not)
cards.people: Post-hoc pooled analysis of the placebo groups of three phase 3 pirfenidone trials in IPF (CAPACITY 004, CAPACITY 006, ASCEND): 624 patients, of whom 291 (47%) received antacid therapy and 333 (53%) did not. Disease progression at 1 year was defined as a 10% or greater fall in predicted FVC, a 50 m or greater fall in 6-minute walk distance, or death.
cards.result: Disease progression occurred in 39% on antacid therapy versus 42% without (P = .4844) — the treatment made no difference. All-cause mortality (7% vs 7%), IPF-related mortality (4% vs 5%), FVC decline of 10% or more (17% vs 19%) and mean FVC change (−4.9% vs −5.5% predicted) likewise did not differ, and hospital admission was non-significantly higher with antacids (22% vs 16%; P = .0522). In advanced IPF (FVC under 70%), overall infections (74% vs 62%; P = .0174) and pulmonary infections (14% vs 6%; P = .0214) were higher in antacid-treated patients. The authors conclude antacid therapy did not improve outcomes and might increase infection risk in advanced disease.
cards.watchOut: Antacid use was not randomised even here — this is an observational comparison nested in trial populations, so confounding by indication survives; but it is the largest, best-characterised dataset on the question and it flatly contradicts the earlier cohort's survival signal.
cards.source: Kreuter M et al. Antacid therapy and disease outcomes in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: a pooled analysis. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2016. PMID: 27050871. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: WRAP-IPF (Raghu 2018): the one randomised trial — laparoscopic anti-reflux surgery in IPF with abnormal acid reflux — found no significant difference in 48-week FVC change (adjusted difference favouring surgery, P = .28), in 58 patients
cards.summary: WRAP-IPF (Raghu 2018): the one randomised trial — laparoscopic anti-reflux surgery in IPF with abnormal acid reflux — found no significant difference in 48-week FVC change (adjusted difference favouring surgery, P = .28), in 58 patients
cards.type: Randomised controlled phase 2 trial, WRAP-IPF (Raghu 2018) — N = 58; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01982968
cards.people: Multicentre randomised controlled phase 2 trial at six US academic centres: patients with IPF, abnormal acid gastro-oesophageal reflux on 24-hour pH monitoring (DeMeester score 14.7 or more) and preserved FVC were randomised to laparoscopic anti-reflux surgery (29 patients) or no surgery (29 patients). Primary endpoint: change in FVC from randomisation to week 48. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01982968.
cards.result: The adjusted rate of FVC change over 48 weeks was −0.05 L with surgery versus −0.13 L without (P = .28) — no significant difference. Acute exacerbation, respiratory hospitalisation and death were less common in the surgery group without statistical significance (1 death with surgery versus 4 without). Surgery was safe and well tolerated; dysphagia (29%) and abdominal distension (14%) were the commonest adverse events. The authors call for a larger, well-powered randomised study.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-eight patients cannot exclude a real benefit — the point estimate favours surgery and the confidence intervals are wide — and differential missing FVC data at 48 weeks (27 surgery vs 20 no-surgery patients measured) weakens the comparison further. A null in a trial this size is 'unproven', not 'disproven'.
cards.source: Raghu G et al. Laparoscopic anti-reflux surgery for the treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (WRAP-IPF): a multicentre, randomised, controlled phase 2 trial. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2018. PMID: 30100404. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01982968. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — an early observational survival signal for reflux treatment in IPF was not confirmed by the largest pooled analysis or by the one small randomised surgical trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — an early observational survival signal for reflux treatment in IPF was not confirmed by the largest pooled analysis or by the one small randomised surgical trial
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: a 204-patient retrospective cohort (Lee 2011), a 624-patient pooled post-hoc analysis of trial placebo arms (Kreuter 2016), and the 58-patient WRAP-IPF randomised surgical trial (Raghu 2018). The IPF family homes — live shelf #810 (antifibrotics) and packs #2783/#2801 (nintedanib beyond IPF; warfarin in IPF) — cover other drug questions, not reflux treatment.
cards.result: Lee 2011 found reflux-medication use independently associated with longer survival; Kreuter 2016 found antacid therapy made no difference to progression, mortality or FVC decline (the treatment made no difference), with an infection signal in advanced disease; WRAP-IPF found no significant FVC benefit from fundoplication in a trial too small to settle the question. The honest summary is a split: the hypothesis remains biologically live, the best current data show no demonstrated benefit, and no carded evidence supports starting antacid therapy or referring for fundoplication to slow IPF itself (as distinct from treating reflux symptoms on their own merits).
cards.watchOut: Everything except WRAP-IPF is observational or post-hoc, and WRAP-IPF is small: this shelf grades the claim 'treating reflux slows IPF' as unproven with a negative lean, and a future adequately powered trial could move it in either direction.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lee JS et al. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2011 (PMID: 21700909); Kreuter M et al. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2016 (PMID: 27050871); Raghu G et al. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2018 (PMID: 30100404). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.
