shelves.title: Fluticasone versus budesonide inhalers in COPD (observational only): pneumonia rates consistently higher on fluticasone — 11.0 versus 6.4 per 100 patient-years in PATHOS
shelves.question: In adults with COPD, do fluticasone-containing inhalers carry a higher pneumonia risk than budesonide-containing inhalers?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-2 Receptor Agonists/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Albuterol/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Androstadienes/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Budesonide/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Cohort Studies · Ethanolamines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Fluticasone · Formoterol Fumarate · Glucocorticoids/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Humans · Pneumonia/chemically induced,mortality · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/drug therapy,mortality · Salmeterol Xinafoate
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, graded with care. PATHOS (Janson 2013; 2,734 propensity-matched patients per cohort) found pneumonia at 11.0 versus 6.4 events per 100 patient-years on fluticasone/salmeterol versus budesonide/formoterol (rate ratio 1.73, a relative figure), with higher pneumonia mortality (hazard ratio 1.76, a relative figure; 97 vs 52 deaths) but no difference in all-cause mortality. Suissa 2013 (163,514-patient Quebec cohort) found serious-pneumonia rate ratios versus non-use of 2.01 for fluticasone (dose-related) versus 1.17 for budesonide (relative figures). Choi 2021 (Korean nationwide matched cohort, 14,518 per group) found pneumonia in 14.22% versus 10.66% (hazard ratio 1.34, a relative figure), rising with cumulative dose. No randomised molecule head-to-head exists; severity confounding in records data is the standing caveat, printed on the face.

cards.headline: PATHOS (Janson 2013, observational matched cohort): pneumonia rates were 73% higher on fluticasone/salmeterol than on budesonide/formoterol (rate ratio 1.73, a relative figure) — 11.0 versus 6.4 events per 100 patient-years — and pneumonia mortality was higher (hazard ratio 1.76, a relative figure)
cards.summary: PATHOS (Janson 2013, observational matched cohort): pneumonia rates were 73% higher on fluticasone/salmeterol than on budesonide/formoterol (rate ratio 1.73, a relative figure) — 11.0 versus 6.4 events per 100 patient-years — and pneumonia mortality was higher (hazard ratio 1.76, a relative figure)
cards.type: Observational propensity-matched cohort study, PATHOS (Janson 2013) — 2,734 matched patients per cohort; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01146392
cards.people: Observational retrospective pairwise cohort study (PATHOS) linking Swedish primary-care records to hospital, drug and death registries, 1999–2009: patients with physician-diagnosed COPD prescribed budesonide/formoterol or fluticasone/salmeterol were propensity-matched 1:1, yielding 2,734 patients in each cohort. Outcomes: pneumonia events, pneumonia hospital admission and pneumonia-related mortality. Registered as ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01146392.
cards.result: There were 2,746 pneumonia episodes over 19,170 patient-years. Compared with budesonide/formoterol, fluticasone/salmeterol carried a higher pneumonia rate (rate ratio 1.73, 95% CI 1.57 to 1.90; absolute rates 11.0 vs 6.4 per 100 patient-years) and a higher admission rate (rate ratio 1.74, 95% CI 1.56 to 1.94; 7.4 vs 4.3 per 100 patient-years). Pneumonia-related mortality was higher on fluticasone/salmeterol (97 vs 52 deaths; hazard ratio 1.76, 95% CI 1.22 to 2.53), while all-cause mortality did not differ (hazard ratio 1.08). Relative ratios are labelled relative, with the absolute rates printed beside them.
cards.watchOut: Observational: propensity matching balances measured factors only — COPD severity, prior pneumonia and smoking intensity are imperfectly captured in records, and the comparison is between fixed combinations (fluticasone/salmeterol versus budesonide/formoterol), so molecule, dose and partner bronchodilator are entangled.
cards.source: Janson C et al. Pneumonia and pneumonia related mortality in patients with COPD treated with fixed combinations of inhaled corticosteroid and long acting β2 agonist: observational matched cohort study (PATHOS). BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2013. PMID: 23719639. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01146392. cards.headline: Suissa 2013 (observational cohort with nested case-control): serious pneumonia risk was markedly higher with fluticasone (rate ratio 2.01, a relative figure) than with budesonide (rate ratio 1.17, a relative figure), each versus non-use, and rose with fluticasone dose
cards.summary: Suissa 2013 (observational cohort with nested case-control): serious pneumonia risk was markedly higher with fluticasone (rate ratio 2.01, a relative figure) than with budesonide (rate ratio 1.17, a relative figure), each versus non-use, and rose with fluticasone dose
cards.type: Observational cohort with nested case-control analysis (Suissa 2013) — cohort N = 163,514; 20,344 serious pneumonia events
cards.people: New-user cohort of 163,514 patients with COPD identified in Quebec health insurance databases (treated 1990–2005, followed to 2007), with a nested case-control analysis of 20,344 serious pneumonia events (first hospitalisation for, or death from, pneumonia). Current inhaled corticosteroid use was compared by molecule and dose, adjusted for age, sex, respiratory disease severity and comorbidity.
cards.result: Current inhaled corticosteroid use overall was associated with a 69% relative increase in serious pneumonia (rate ratio 1.69, 95% CI 1.63 to 1.75). The rate was higher with fluticasone (rate ratio 2.01, 95% CI 1.93 to 2.10, increasing with daily dose) and much lower with budesonide (rate ratio 1.17, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.26). Risk was sustained with long-term use, declined after stopping, and had disappeared by 6 months after discontinuation (rate ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.17). The authors note residual confounding cannot be ruled out.
cards.watchOut: The fluticasone-versus-budesonide contrast here is indirect — each molecule is compared with non-use, not head-to-head — and fluticasone users may have had more severe disease; the dose gradient and the disappearance of risk after stopping strengthen, but cannot prove, a causal reading.
cards.source: Suissa S et al. Inhaled corticosteroids in COPD and the risk of serious pneumonia. Thorax. 2013. PMID: 24130228. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Choi 2021 (observational nationwide cohort): after propensity matching (14,518 patients per group), pneumonia developed in 14.22% on fluticasone propionate versus 10.66% on budesonide (hazard ratio 1.34, a relative figure), rising with cumulative dose
cards.summary: Choi 2021 (observational nationwide cohort): after propensity matching (14,518 patients per group), pneumonia developed in 14.22% on fluticasone propionate versus 10.66% on budesonide (hazard ratio 1.34, a relative figure), rising with cumulative dose
cards.type: Observational propensity-matched nationwide cohort (Choi 2021) — 14,518 matched patients per group
cards.people: Retrospective cohort using Korean National Health Insurance Service claims for the entire population: patients newly diagnosed with COPD and prescribed fluticasone propionate or budesonide were propensity-matched 1:1 (14,518 in each group). Pneumonia risk was analysed overall and by cumulative inhaled corticosteroid dose quartile.
cards.result: Pneumonia was more likely in fluticasone propionate users than budesonide users (14.22% vs 10.66%; P < .0001), with incidence rates of 2,914.77 versus 2,102.90 per 100,000 person-years and a hazard ratio of 1.34 (95% CI 1.26 to 1.43) — a relative figure, with the absolute percentages printed beside it. The relative risk rose with cumulative dose, from 1.06 (95% CI 0.93 to 1.21) in the lowest quartile to 1.49 (95% CI 1.33 to 1.66) in the highest. The authors conclude inhaler type and dose need careful consideration in COPD.
cards.watchOut: Claims data carry no lung-function or smoking measurements, so matched groups can still differ in the severity that drives both inhaler choice and pneumonia; the null result in the lowest-dose quartile is a reminder that the excess is dose-concentrated, not uniform.

International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. 2021. PMID: 34858023. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three independent observational programmes agree — fluticasone-containing regimens carry a higher pneumonia risk than budesonide-containing regimens in COPD; observational evidence caps the stamp at POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: three independent observational programmes agree — fluticasone-containing regimens carry a higher pneumonia risk than budesonide-containing regimens in COPD; observational evidence caps the stamp at POSSIBLE
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence is entirely observational: the PATHOS propensity-matched cohort (2,734 patients per arm), the Quebec new-user cohort of 163,514 patients with nested case-control analysis, and the Korean nationwide matched cohort (14,518 per arm). No randomised head-to-head trial of the two molecules exists in the carded set.
cards.result: The direction is consistent and dose-related: PATHOS found pneumonia rates of 11.0 versus 6.4 per 100 patient-years (rate ratio 1.73, relative) with higher pneumonia mortality on fluticasone/salmeterol; Suissa found serious-pneumonia rate ratios versus non-use of 2.01 for fluticasone against 1.17 for budesonide; Choi found 14.22% versus 10.66% cumulative pneumonia (hazard ratio 1.34, relative). Absolute excesses are material (roughly 3.5–4.6 extra events per 100 patient-years in PATHOS terms), but every estimate comes from records data where severity confounding is the standing alternative explanation.
cards.watchOut: Observational cap applies: this shelf cannot exclude that fluticasone is preferentially prescribed to sicker patients in ways registries do not capture. The claim is graded POSSIBLE (harm), observational — concordant, dose-related, and unproven by randomisation.
cards.source: Synthesis of Janson C et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2013 (PMID: 23719639); Suissa S et al. Thorax. 2013 (PMID: 24130228); Choi JH et al. International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. 2021 (PMID: 34858023). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: How fast PaCO2 rises during apnoea: a fast first minute, then about 3–6 mm Hg per minute depending on state — the Frumin and Stock measurements
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how fast does arterial carbon dioxide rise during apnoea, and what determines the rate?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Apnea/blood · Carbon Dioxide/analysis,blood · Consciousness · Functional Residual Capacity/physiology · Humans · Hypercapnia/blood · Lung Volume Measurements · Models, Biological · Tidal Volume/physiology · Time Factors · Total Lung Capacity/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong (textbook framing, not evidence). The human measurements are concordant: PaCO2 rise in apnoea is logarithmic — fast at first as arterial blood equilibrates toward mixed venous PCO2 (Stock 1988, awake: 7 mm Hg in the first 10 seconds; Stock 1989, anaesthetised and obstructed: 12 mm Hg in the first minute), then roughly linear at about 6 mm Hg/minute awake (Stock 1988, 20 volunteers) and 3.4 mm Hg/minute anaesthetised (Stock 1989, 14 adults). Frumin 1959 established that apnoeic oxygenation keeps oxygen flowing while CO2 accumulates; Stock 1989 showed the oxygen flow does not meaningfully eliminate CO2, so the steady rate is set by CO2 production and body stores. Classic small studies; Ns are printed on the card faces.

cards.headline: Stock 1988 (awake volunteers): PaCO2 rose fastest at the very start of apnoea — about 7 mm Hg in the first 10 seconds — then settled to about 6 mm Hg per minute
cards.summary: Stock 1988 (awake volunteers): PaCO2 rose fastest at the very start of apnoea — about 7 mm Hg in the first 10 seconds — then settled to about 6 mm Hg per minute
cards.type: Primary human physiology study
cards.people: 20 awake volunteers who held their breath at functional residual capacity with FiO2 1.0, for 0, 10 and 20 seconds and then as long as possible, exhaling through an infrared CO2 analyser after each interval to estimate the arterial CO2 rise.
cards.result: The estimated PaCO2 rise was logarithmic: 7 mm Hg during the first 10 seconds (43 mm Hg/minute), 2 mm Hg during the next 10 seconds (13 mm Hg/minute), and 6 mm Hg/minute thereafter. The authors conclude PaCO2 rises more rapidly in awake apnoeic humans than earlier (anaesthesia-based) estimates suggested, and that these values are better for estimating safe apnoea duration in conscious, critically ill patients.
cards.watchOut: Breath-holding at functional residual capacity with FiO2 1.0 in 20 volunteers; end-tidal CO2 was used to estimate the arterial rise, and rates differ with starting lung volume, starting CO2 and metabolic rate.

cards.headline: Stock 1989 (anaesthetised, obstructed airway): PaCO2 rose 12 mm Hg in the first minute of apnoea, then 3.4 mm Hg per minute — slower than in awake subjects, and apnoeic oxygenation flows did not wash out meaningful CO2
cards.summary: Stock 1989 (anaesthetised, obstructed airway): PaCO2 rose 12 mm Hg in the first minute of apnoea, then 3.4 mm Hg per minute — slower than in awake subjects, and apnoeic oxygenation flows did not wash out meaningful CO2
cards.type: Primary human physiology study
cards.people: 14 consenting healthy adults under enflurane–oxygen anaesthesia (deep enough to prevent spontaneous ventilation, no neuromuscular blockade), whose tracheal tubes were clamped; arterial blood sampled before and at intervals to 300 seconds while oxygen saturation stayed above 0.92.
cards.result: The PaCO2 rise was best described by a logarithmic function; piecewise linear approximation gave a rise of 12 mm Hg during the first minute of apnoea and 3.4 mm Hg/minute thereafter. The authors state these values should be used when estimating apnoea duration from PaCO2 change in anaesthetised patients without ventilatory support, and that the oxygen flows used in earlier apnoeic-oxygenation work probably did not eliminate significant quantities of CO2 — that is, the rate is set by CO2 production and body CO2 stores, not by the oxygen flow.
cards.watchOut: Anaesthetised patients with a clamped tube are not awake apnoeic patients — the two Stock cards deliberately bracket the states, and neither rate should be applied to the other population.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Stock MC et al. The PaCO2 rate of rise in anesthetized patients with airway obstruction. J Clin Anesth. 1989. PMID: 2516732. cards.headline: Synthesis: arterial CO2 rises logarithmically in apnoea — a fast first phase as arterial blood equilibrates with mixed venous CO2, then a steady climb set by metabolic CO2 production
cards.summary: Synthesis: arterial CO2 rises logarithmically in apnoea — a fast first phase as arterial blood equilibrates with mixed venous CO2, then a steady climb set by metabolic CO2 production
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of Frumin 1959, Stock 1988 and Stock 1989, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology (textbook framing, not evidence cards).
cards.result: The carded human measurements agree on the shape: a rapid initial rise (Stock awake: 7 mm Hg in the first 10 seconds; Stock anaesthetised: 12 mm Hg in the first minute) reflecting equilibration of arterial with venous CO2, followed by a roughly linear rise — about 6 mm Hg/minute in awake apnoeic volunteers and 3.4 mm Hg/minute in anaesthetised patients with an obstructed airway. What determines the rate, on the carded evidence and the textbook account: metabolic CO2 production, the size and filling of body CO2 stores (hence the logarithmic shape), starting lung volume and CO2 level, and whether any CO2 is being eliminated — the oxygen flow of apnoeic oxygenation maintains oxygenation (Frumin) but does not meaningfully remove CO2 (Stock 1989). Textbook values for the steady phase (about 3–4 mm Hg/minute after the first minute in anaesthetised apnoea) are the textbook's account and match the anaesthetised measurement carded here; the awake rate measured by Stock is faster.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: the steady-phase rate varies with CO2 production and stores, so the quoted rates are for resting humans at resting lung volume, not for sepsis, exercise or children.
cards.source: Synthesis of Frumin MJ et al. Anesthesiology. 1959 (PMID: 13825447); Stock MC et al. J Clin Anesth. 1988 (PMID: 3152423); Stock MC et al. J Clin Anesth. 1989 (PMID: 2516732). Registry IDs: none in the records (classic physiology).

shelves.title: The ventilatory response to CO2: measured by rebreathing as a threshold and a slope — Read's method and the Duffin programme's human values
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how large is the ventilatory response to inhaled carbon dioxide, and how is it normally measured and distributed?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Blood Gas Analysis · Chemoreceptor Cells/physiology · Female · Humans · Male · Models, Biological · Respiratory Mechanics/physiology · Tidal Volume
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Ganong and Boron & Boulpaep (textbook framing, not evidence). The measurement is Read's 1967 rebreathing method and its modern Duffin modification: ventilation is plotted against rising PCO2 and the response is a threshold plus a slope. Duffin's 22-subject programme formalised the shape (basal ventilation below threshold, linear rise above, tidal volume dominant). The carded Duffin-programme measurement of central sensitivity is 1.87 ± 0.66 L/min per mm Hg under control conditions (Vovk 2000, N=7, printed on the face); textbook values for the overall response (roughly 2–3 L/min per mm Hg, widely distributed) are given as the textbook's account in the Synthesis. Classic small studies; Ns printed on the faces.

cards.headline: Duffin 2000: in 22 subjects the rebreathing response has a clear shape — ventilation flat at a basal level until PCO2 crosses a threshold, then rising linearly, tidal volume contributing more than frequency
cards.summary: Duffin 2000: in 22 subjects the rebreathing response has a clear shape — ventilation flat at a basal level until PCO2 crosses a threshold, then rising linearly, tidal volume contributing more than frequency
cards.type: Primary human physiology study
cards.people: 22 healthy subjects studied with a modified Read rebreathing technique: prior hyperventilation so rebreathing began hypocapnic, with oxygen added under control to hold iso-oxia, allowing the response to be measured at several iso-oxic PO2 levels.
cards.result: As PCO2 rose, ventilation was first steady at a basal value, then increased once PCO2 exceeded a breakpoint — interpreted as the threshold of the combined central and peripheral chemoreflex responses. Above threshold, ventilation rose linearly with PCO2, tidal volume usually contributing more than frequency. Under strong drive (such as hypoxia) a second breakpoint often appeared, beyond which ventilation rose at a different slope with frequency contributing more. The authors fitted a three-segment model and derived parameters for an 'average subject' for the chemoreflex control system — that is, the response is characterised by a threshold and a slope (sensitivity), and both vary between people.
cards.watchOut: A modelling paper built on 22 subjects' rebreathing data: the 'average subject' parameters smooth over the wide real inter-individual spread that is itself part of this shelf's answer.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Duffin J et al. A model of the chemoreflex control of breathing in humans: model parameters measurement. Respir Physiol. 2000. PMID: 10786641. cards.headline: Vovk & Duffin 2000 (N=7, small classic study): central CO2 sensitivity averaged 1.87 L/min per mm Hg before acetazolamide — and the drug raised the central slope while blunting the peripheral one
cards.summary: Vovk & Duffin 2000 (N=7, small classic study): central CO2 sensitivity averaged 1.87 L/min per mm Hg before acetazolamide — and the drug raised the central slope while blunting the peripheral one
cards.type: Primary human physiology study
cards.people: 7 healthy adults (four women and three men, aged 25 ± 3 years) studied at rest with a modified Read rebreathing technique in hypoxic and hyperoxic backgrounds, before and after intravenous acetazolamide 10 mg/kg. N=7 printed here per the small-N labelling rule.
cards.result: Central chemoreflex sensitivity (the slope of the ventilatory response to CO2 in hyperoxia) was 1.87 ± 0.66 L/min per mm Hg CO2 under control conditions and rose to 4.07 ± 1.03 after acetazolamide (P<0.05), with a leftward shift of the ventilation–PCO2 curve in hyperoxia. Peripheral chemosensitivity, isolated by subtracting the hyperoxic from the hypoxic slope, was 3.66 ± 0.92 L/min per mm Hg under control conditions and was blunted to 1.33 ± 0.46 after acetazolamide (P<0.05). The control values give a directly measured human central sensitivity from the Duffin programme; the drug contrast shows the measured slope is a property of the chemoreflex state, not a fixed constant.
cards.watchOut: Very small study (N=7, printed on the face) and an acetazolamide experiment: the control slope is the usable normative value; the drug values show state-dependence, not a treatment recommendation.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the hypercapnic ventilatory response is a threshold-plus-slope measurement — typically a few litres per minute per mm Hg, widely distributed between healthy people
cards.summary: Synthesis: the hypercapnic ventilatory response is a threshold-plus-slope measurement — typically a few litres per minute per mm Hg, widely distributed between healthy people
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of Read 1967, Duffin 2000 and Vovk & Duffin 2000, framed by Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (textbook framing, not evidence cards).
cards.result: How it is measured: by rebreathing (Read's method and its Duffin modification), plotting ventilation against rising end-tidal PCO2 under controlled oxygen. How it is described: a threshold PCO2 below which ventilation stays basal, and a slope above it — Duffin's 22-subject fits formalise exactly this, with tidal volume carrying most of the rise until drive is strong. How large: the directly measured central slope in the carded Duffin-programme study was 1.87 ± 0.66 L/min per mm Hg (control, hyperoxic), with peripheral contribution on top of that in hypoxia; the textbook account (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) puts the overall response in the range of roughly 2–3 L/min per mm Hg in healthy adults with wide inter-individual spread — presented here as the textbook's account, consistent with the carded measurements. The response is a distribution, not a constant: it varies with chemoreflex state (acetazolamide card), oxygen background and the person measured.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: response slopes vary with method (rebreathing vs steady-state), oxygen background and the person — quote a range and a method, never a single 'normal' number.

shelves.title: Ventilatory acclimatisation to altitude: CO2 falls about 10 Torr and the hypoxic response roughly doubles over the first 1–2 weeks — the Severinghaus and Birmingham programme measurements
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how do ventilation and arterial gases change over the first days of ascent to high altitude (ventilatory acclimatisation)?
shelves.mesh: Acclimatization/physiology · Adult · Altitude · Atmospheric Pressure · Carbon Dioxide/blood · Chemoreceptor Cells/physiology · Humans · Hypoxia/physiopathology · Male · Oxygen/blood · Respiratory Mechanics/physiology · Time Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall (textbook framing, not evidence). The Severinghaus programme's chamber studies at 3,810 m (N=6, printed on the faces) show the time course directly: hypoxic ventilatory response unchanged in the first day or so, then rising — 0.91 to 1.46 L/min per % fall in SaO2 by about day 5 (+60%, confirmed independently in the parallel cerebral blood-flow study) and still rising at day 12 — while resting end-tidal CO2 falls from 42.3 to 30.8 Torr and early hypoxic ventilatory depression (set point +9.2 Torr on day 2) recedes (+4.5 Torr by day 12). The Birmingham expedition cohort (Milledge 1988, N=32) adds that the rate of acclimatisation, not the sea-level response size, is what tracks symptoms.

cards.headline: Sato & Severinghaus 1992: the hypoxic ventilatory response rose over the first days at 3,810 m — from 0.91 at sea level to 1.46 L/min per % fall in saturation by about day 5 — while resting end-tidal CO2 fell from 42.3 to 30.8 Torr
cards.summary: Sato & Severinghaus 1992: the hypoxic ventilatory response rose over the first days at 3,810 m — from 0.91 at sea level to 1.46 L/min per % fall in saturation by about day 5 — while resting end-tidal CO2 fell from 42.3 to 30.8 Torr
cards.type: Primary human physiology study
cards.people: Six normal men tested at sea level, after 1–5 days at 3,810 m altitude, and three times over a week after return. Isocapnic 5-minute step hypoxic ventilatory response (HVR) measured after hyperoxia to remove hypoxic ventilatory depression, at an end-tidal PCO2 set to hold hyperoxic ventilation at 140 mL/kg/min.
cards.result: Sea-level HVR of 0.91 ± 0.38 L/min per % fall in SaO2 was unchanged after 30 ± 18 hours at altitude (1.04 ± 0.37) but rose significantly to 1.27 ± 0.57 by day 3.2 ± 0.8 and 1.46 ± 0.59 by day 4.8 ± 0.4, remaining high for the first days back at sea level before normalising by days 4–7. The isocapnic test PCO2 needed fell from 45.4 ± 1.7 Torr at sea level to 33.3 ± 1.8 at altitude, against resting end-tidal PCO2 of 42.3 ± 2.0 and 30.8 ± 2.6 Torr respectively — that is, over the first days the men hyperventilated progressively and their CO2 set point dropped by roughly 10 Torr. Arterial pH at matched saturation rose from 7.378 at sea level to 7.44 by day 2.
cards.watchOut: Classic small chamber study (N=6, printed on the face) at one altitude (3,810 m); individual time courses vary and higher or faster ascents may differ.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Sato M et al. Augmented hypoxic ventilatory response in men at altitude. J Appl Physiol. 1992. PMID: 1506356. cards.headline: Sato & Severinghaus 1994: over 12 days at 3,810 m the hypoxic response kept rising without reaching a plateau, and the central chemoreceptor CO2 set point was estimated up 9.2 Torr on day 2, easing to 4.5 Torr by day 12
cards.summary: Sato & Severinghaus 1994: over 12 days at 3,810 m the hypoxic response kept rising without reaching a plateau, and the central chemoreceptor CO2 set point was estimated up 9.2 Torr on day 2, easing to 4.5 Torr by day 12
cards.type: Primary human physiology study
cards.people: Six subjects studied before, during and after 12 days at 3,810 m (barometric pressure about 488 Torr), with hypoxic ventilatory response and hypoxic ventilatory depression measured with and without 15 minutes of preoxygenation, and hypercapnic ventilatory response tested at ambient and high saturation.
cards.result: Preoxygenated HVR rose from −1.13 ± 0.23 L/min per %SpO2 at sea level to −2.17 ± 0.13 by altitude day 12, without reaching a plateau, and returned to control after 4 days back at sea level. At matched saturation and PCO2, ambient ventilation was lower by 13.3 ± 2.4 L/min on day 2 and by 5.9 ± 3.5 L/min on day 12 — estimated from the hypercapnic response to equal a rise in the central chemoreceptor PCO2 set point of 9.2 ± 2.1 Torr on day 2 and 4.5 ± 1.3 Torr on day 12, the signature of hypoxic ventilatory depression early on being progressively overcome. Hypercapnic response itself was not significantly increased at altitude when corrected appropriately.
cards.watchOut: Same six-subject programme as the previous card (a companion study, not an independent replication); the set-point figures are model estimates derived from the hypercapnic response, not direct CSF measurements.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Sato M et al. Time course of augmentation and depression of hypoxic ventilatory responses at altitude. J Appl Physiol. 1994. PMID: 7961252. cards.headline: Jensen & Severinghaus 1996: in the same 5-day, 3,810 m sojourn, cerebral blood-flow sensitivity to hypoxia also rose — and the paper confirms the ventilatory response rose 60% in those 5 days
cards.summary: Jensen & Severinghaus 1996: in the same 5-day, 3,810 m sojourn, cerebral blood-flow sensitivity to hypoxia also rose — and the paper confirms the ventilatory response rose 60% in those 5 days
cards.type: Primary human physiology study
cards.people: Six sea-level native men studied before and during a 5-day sojourn at 3,810 m, with transcranial Doppler cerebral blood-flow velocity responses to 5-minute isocapnic hypoxia and hyperoxic hypercapnia steps, run in parallel with the hypoxic ventilatory response study.
cards.result: The fractional cerebral blood-flow response to hypoxia rose from 0.346 ± 0.104 at sea level to 0.463 ± 0.084 on altitude day 5 (P<0.05); estimated CBF rise per 1% fall in SaO2 at 80% saturation rose from 1.30% to 1.74%. CBF sensitivity to CO2 rose from 4.01 ± 0.62%/Torr to 5.12 ± 0.79%/Torr by day 5 (not significant after correction to log PCO2). The authors note the parallel carotid chemosensitisation in the same subjects increased the hypoxic ventilatory response by 60% over the same 5 days, from 0.91 ± 0.38 to 1.46 ± 0.59 L/min per % fall in SaO2 — an independent report of the Sato 1992 ventilatory time course.
cards.watchOut: Same six subjects again — this card corroborates the ventilatory time course from within the same programme, so the shelf's independent human cohorts are the chamber group and the expedition group.

cards.headline: Milledge 1988 (Birmingham expedition programme): in 32 expedition members, sea-level hypoxic and CO2 responses did not predict acute mountain sickness — the rate of respiratory acclimatisation mattered more
cards.summary: Milledge 1988 (Birmingham expedition programme): in 32 expedition members, sea-level hypoxic and CO2 responses did not predict acute mountain sickness — the rate of respiratory acclimatisation mattered more
cards.type: Primary human physiology study
cards.people: 32 members of two mountaineering expeditions (the Birmingham Medical Research Expeditionary Society programme) whose hypoxic ventilatory response and CO2 ventilatory response were measured before departure; both teams ascended rapidly to base camps at 5,200 m and 4,300 m and stayed at least four days, with daily acute mountain sickness symptom scores.
cards.result: Acute mountain sickness ranged from unaffected to severe enough to require evacuation, but there was no correlation between sickness scores and pre-expedition hypoxic ventilatory response or CO2 response. The authors conclude that when ascent takes a day or more, sea-level HVR is probably not the major determinant of ventilation at altitude and does not predict susceptibility to acute mountain sickness; the rate of respiratory acclimatization is probably more important.
cards.watchOut: Pre-expedition responses were measured at sea level; the null prediction finding applies to ascents taking a day or more, as the authors state, not to abrupt altitude exposure.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (expedition cohort) | Milledge JS et al. Hypoxic ventilatory response and acute mountain sickness. Eur Respir J. 1988. PMID: 3224691. Registry ID: none in the record (physiology study). cards.headline: Synthesis: ventilatory acclimatisation is a days-long process — progressive hyperventilation, a CO2 set point falling by about 10 Torr, and a hypoxic response that roughly doubles over 1–2 weeks
cards.summary: Synthesis: ventilatory acclimatisation is a days-long process — progressive hyperventilation, a CO2 set point falling by about 10 Torr, and a hypoxic response that roughly doubles over 1–2 weeks
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of Sato 1992, Sato 1994, Jensen 1996 and Milledge 1988, framed by Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology and Guyton & Hall (textbook framing, not evidence cards).
cards.result: The carded human time courses agree: on arrival at about 3,800 m the hypoxic ventilatory response is initially unchanged and partly offset by hypoxic ventilatory depression (an estimated central set-point rise of 9.2 Torr on day 2); over the following days carotid chemosensitisation raises the hypoxic response — +60% by day 5 (0.91 to 1.46 L/min per % fall in SaO2) and still rising at day 12 in the 12-day study — resting CO2 falls by roughly 10 Torr (end-tidal 42.3 to 30.8 Torr), arterial pH rises early (7.378 to 7.44 at matched saturation) and is then partly corrected as the textbook account describes (renal bicarbonate excretion and cerebrospinal-fluid pH normalisation — the acid–base mechanism is the textbook's account; the carded Milledge acid–base record was not used for numbers). The expedition data add the practical corollary: how fast a person acclimatises matters more than their sea-level response size. Classic small chamber studies (N=6, printed on the faces); the expedition cohort is N=32.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: the day-by-day numbers come from small chamber studies at 3,810 m; the acid–base mechanism is textbook framing, and rates at other altitudes are extrapolations.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sato M et al. J Appl Physiol. 1992 (PMID: 1506356); Sato M et al. J Appl Physiol. 1994 (PMID: 7961252); Jensen JB et al. J Appl Physiol. 1996 (PMID: 8926248); Milledge JS et al. Eur Respir J. 1988 (PMID: 3224691). Registry IDs: none in the records (physiology studies).

shelves.title: The intrinsic circadian period is 24.18 hours — the Czeisler forced-desynchrony measurement and the Duffy & Wright programme
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the endogenous period of the circadian clock when measured under forced desynchrony?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aging/physiology · Biological Clocks/genetics,physiology · Body Temperature · Circadian Rhythm/genetics,physiology · Darkness · Female · Humans · Hydrocortisone/blood · Light · Male · Melatonin/blood · Middle Aged · Sleep
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Boron & Boulpaep (textbook framing, not evidence). Czeisler 1999 measured the intrinsic period under forced desynchrony in controlled dim light at 24.18 hours on average, in young and older adults alike — replacing the light-confounded 25-hour figure. The Duffy & Wright programme cards show the period determining the phase angle of entrainment (Wright 2005), organising sleep propensity (Dijk & Duffy 1999, N=24), and adapting modestly after entrainment to non-24-hour days (Scheer 2007). Live shelf #927 is tasimelteon treatment in blind people — a different question, verified in its file.

cards.headline: Czeisler 1999: under forced desynchrony in carefully controlled light, the intrinsic period of the human circadian pacemaker averages 24.18 hours — in both young and older people, with a tight distribution
cards.summary: Czeisler 1999: under forced desynchrony in carefully controlled light, the intrinsic period of the human circadian pacemaker averages 24.18 hours — in both young and older people, with a tight distribution
cards.type: Primary human physiology study
cards.people: Healthy young and older individuals living in carefully controlled lighting conditions under a forced desynchrony protocol, with precise estimation of the endogenous periods of the melatonin, core body temperature and cortisol rhythms. N not documented in the fetched record's abstract (groups described as healthy young and older individuals).
cards.result: The intrinsic period averaged 24.18 hours in both age groups, with a tight distribution consistent with other species. The authors contrast this with earlier reports (activity-rhythm periods of 13–65 hours, median 25.2; temperature-rhythm average 25 hours) that were confounded by light levels sufficient to distort period estimation. The near-24-hour value — not 25 hours — is the corrected measurement on which modern circadian physiology rests.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract does not print the group sizes, so the face says 'N not documented' for this card; the 24.18-hour value is the record's own reported average for both age groups.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (forced desynchrony) | Czeisler CA et al. Stability, precision, and near-24-hour period of the human circadian pacemaker. Science. 1999. PMID: 10381883. cards.headline: Dijk & Duffy 1999: forced desynchrony of sleep itself — 482 sleep episodes in 13 older and 11 young subjects show sleep propensity locked to the melatonin and temperature rhythms
cards.summary: Dijk & Duffy 1999: forced desynchrony of sleep itself — 482 sleep episodes in 13 older and 11 young subjects show sleep propensity locked to the melatonin and temperature rhythms
cards.type: Primary human physiology study
cards.people: 13 older men and women and 11 young men studied by forced desynchrony of polysomnographically recorded sleep episodes (482 episodes in total, 9 hours 20 minutes each) against the circadian rhythms of plasma melatonin and core body temperature.
cards.result: Sleep propensity co-varied with the circadian rhythms of body temperature and melatonin in both age groups: sleep latencies were longest just before melatonin secretion onset and short close to the temperature nadir. Older people had reduced stage 4 sleep, shorter REM latencies when sleep coincided with the melatonin rhythm, reduced sleep duration at all circadian phases and faster deterioration of sleep consolidation — interpreted as a reduced homeostatic drive interacting with a weaker circadian sleep-promoting signal in the early morning. The study is carded as the forced-desynchrony programme's sleep-side measurement: the protocol that yields the 24.18-hour period also maps what the clock does to sleep at every phase.
cards.watchOut: Sleep-architecture findings, not a period measurement — carded to show what the forced-desynchrony protocol measures besides tau; Ns (13 older, 11 young) are printed on the face.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (forced desynchrony) | Dijk DJ, Duffy JF et al. Ageing and the circadian and homeostatic regulation of human sleep during forced desynchrony of rest, melatonin and temperature rhythms. J Physiol. 1999. PMID: 10087357. cards.headline: Wright & Duffy 2005: the measured intrinsic period predicts how a person entrains — shorter-period people fall asleep and wake at a later biological time, and light history moves the phase angle
cards.summary: Wright & Duffy 2005: the measured intrinsic period predicts how a person entrains — shorter-period people fall asleep and wake at a later biological time, and light history moves the phase angle
cards.type: Primary human physiology study
cards.people: Humans whose circadian period was estimated during a forced desynchrony protocol (melatonin as the marker of internal biological time), with the phase angle of entrainment observed under scheduled sleep–wake/light–dark conditions inside and outside the laboratory, including 5 days at about 450 lux versus 2 days at about 150 lux daytime light.
cards.result: The phase relationship between the internal clock, sleep–wake homeostasis and the light–dark cycle (the phase angle of entrainment) was strongly determined by intrinsic period and by the strength of the synchronizer: individuals with shorter circadian periods initiated sleep and awakened at a later biological time than those with longer periods, and the phase angle was shorter after the moderate bright-light schedule than after the indoor-light schedule. The period measured under forced desynchrony is therefore not an abstraction — it determines everyday entrainment behaviour.
cards.watchOut: Phase-angle relationships are correlational across individuals; light history was partly observational (inside vs outside the laboratory conditions differed in duration as well as intensity).
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (forced desynchrony) | Wright KP Jr et al. Intrinsic period and light intensity determine the phase relationship between melatonin and sleep in humans. cards.headline: Scheer, Wright & Czeisler 2007: the period is plastic — after entrainment to the 24.65-hour Martian sol, the intrinsic period measured by forced desynchrony was significantly longer than after entrainment to a 23.5-hour day
cards.summary: Scheer, Wright & Czeisler 2007: the period is plastic — after entrainment to the 24.65-hour Martian sol, the intrinsic period measured by forced desynchrony was significantly longer than after entrainment to a 23.5-hour day
cards.type: Primary human physiology study
cards.people: Healthy adults entrained with a model-based lighting regimen (moderately bright light, about 450 lux) to the 24.65-hour Martian sol and to a 23.5-hour day, with circadian periods of plasma melatonin, plasma cortisol and core body temperature estimated under forced desynchrony protocols before/after.
cards.result: Moderately bright light timed to the second or first half of the wake episode entrained individuals to the 24.65-hour sol and the 23.5-hour day respectively. The intrinsic period of the circadian pacemaker was significantly longer following entrainment to the Martian sol than following entrainment to the 23.5-hour day — after-effects of entrainment demonstrating, for the first time in this programme, plasticity of the human circadian period. The 24.18-hour average is thus a population mean of a period that itself adapts modestly to the day it has been living on.
cards.watchOut: After-effect sizes are described qualitatively in the record ('significantly longer'); no exact post-entrainment period value is printed in the abstract, so none is quoted on the face.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the endogenous circadian period is 24.18 hours on average — measured only when the imposed day is set far from 24 hours so the clock runs free (forced desynchrony)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the endogenous circadian period is 24.18 hours on average — measured only when the imposed day is set far from 24 hours so the clock runs free (forced desynchrony)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of Czeisler 1999, Dijk & Duffy 1999, Wright 2005 and Scheer 2007, framed by Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (textbook framing, not an evidence card). Live shelf #927 covers tasimelteon entrainment in totally blind people with non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder — a treatment question, not this measurement question.
cards.result: Forced desynchrony imposes a day length (for example 28 hours) outside the range of entrainment, so the pacemaker expresses its own period while sleep and meals are spread across all circadian phases. Measured that way, in dim controlled light, the human intrinsic period averages 24.18 hours with a tight distribution, the same in young and older adults (Czeisler 1999) — correcting the older 25-hour textbook figure, which came from light-confounded free-run studies. The Duffy & Wright programme adds what the number does: it sets each person's phase angle of entrainment (Wright 2005), it organises sleep propensity across the cycle (Dijk & Duffy 1999), and it is itself modestly plastic, lengthening after entrainment to a longer-than-24-hour day (Scheer 2007).
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: the 24.18-hour figure is a mean under dim-light forced desynchrony; individual periods vary around it and the period itself is modestly plastic, per the carded Scheer study.

shelves.title: Physiological dead space: an anatomic part that scales with height (~150 mL in adults) plus an alveolar part set by ventilation–perfusion matching — the fraction of each breath wasted falls from roughly a third at rest toward a tenth as tidal volume rises in exercise
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what determines physiological dead space, and how does the dead-space fraction of each breath change from rest to exercise?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Physiological dead space is the sum of anatomic dead space (the conducting airways, measured by Fowler's single-breath nitrogen method and scaling with height — Hart 1963, 73 normal subjects) and alveolar dead space (ventilated but under-perfused alveoli, the ventilation–perfusion matching term). What changes from rest to exercise is chiefly the denominator and the matching: tidal volume rises severalfold while anatomic volume changes little, and perfusion of the upper lung improves, so the dead-space fraction (VD/VT, by the Bohr equation in its Enghoff form) falls from roughly 0.3 at rest toward 0.1–0.15 in healthy exercise — the Sun 2002 Wasserman-group reference study of 474 healthy adults formalises VD/VT as the determinant, with arterial CO₂, of ventilatory efficiency; Balmain's healthy controls show the alveolar component staying near zero at rest and low workloads; and Weisman's healthy recruits measured 0.11–0.12 at steady-state strenuous exercise. Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall, named as textbook framing. Where a carded record does not print a resting healthy VD/VT, the resting figure is carried as the textbook's account and labelled as such in the Synthesis.

cards.headline: Hart 1963: anatomic dead space by Fowler's single-breath nitrogen method scales with height in 73 normal subjects aged 4–42 — no sex difference on any size basis
cards.summary: Hart 1963: anatomic dead space by Fowler's single-breath nitrogen method scales with height in 73 normal subjects aged 4–42 — no sex difference on any size basis
cards.type: Human physiological study (Fowler single-breath nitrogen method), J Appl Physiol 1963
cards.people: Seventy-three normal subjects aged 4 to 42 years, anatomic respiratory dead space measured by Fowler's single-breath nitrogen washout method.
cards.result: Anatomic dead space correlated closely with height (Vd (mL) = 7.585 × height (cm)^2.363 × 10⁻⁴; r = .917) and also with body weight, surface area and functional residual capacity; compared on any of these bases there was no significant sex difference. The relation to height appeared constant from birth to adulthood, and dead space increases more rapidly than weight, surface area or functional residual capacity during early growth. The anatomic component of dead space is thus a size variable — in adults, the classic ~150 mL of the textbook account (Boron & Boulpaep), presented as the textbook figure consistent with this height relationship.
cards.watchOut: The record carries no MeSH list, so the source line uses the exact fallback text. Children are included (ages 4–42); the adult ~150 mL value is the textbook's summary of this relationship, labelled as such, not a number printed in this record.
cards.source: Hart MC et al. Relation between anatomic respiratory dead space and body size and lung volume. J Appl Physiol. 1963. PMID: 31094493. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Sun 2002 (Wasserman group): in 474 healthy adults, ventilatory efficiency is mathematically determined by arterial CO₂ and the physiological dead-space fraction — the reference frame for VD/VT in exercise
cards.summary: Sun 2002 (Wasserman group): in 474 healthy adults, ventilatory efficiency is mathematically determined by arterial CO₂ and the physiological dead-space fraction — the reference frame for VD/VT in exercise
cards.type: Human physiological study (cardiopulmonary exercise testing reference study), Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2002
cards.people: Four hundred seventy-four healthy adults aged 17–78 years performing incremental cycle and treadmill cardiopulmonary exercise tests at three test sites, with total ventilation corrected for equipment dead space.
cards.result: The relationship between ventilation and CO₂ output — ventilatory efficiency — is determined by the arterial CO₂ pressure and the physiological dead space–tidal volume ratio (VD/VT). Of three expressions compared, the lowest ventilation-to-CO₂-output ratio during exercise was the least variable and was unaffected by site, ergometer or measurement system; its regression on age, sex and height was: lowest VE/VCO₂ = 27.94 + 0.108 × age + (0.97 if female, 0.0 if male) − 0.0376 × height (cm). Ageing raises the ventilatory requirement for a given CO₂ output — the population-level signature of a dead-space fraction that falls less completely with exercise as age advances.
cards.watchOut: The record frames VD/VT as the determinant of ventilatory efficiency but does not print the cohort's resting and exercise VD/VT values themselves; the rest-to-exercise fall in the fraction is quantified by the Weisman and Balmain cards and the textbook account, not by this record.
cards.source: Sun XG et al. Ventilatory efficiency during exercise in healthy subjects. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2002. PMID: 12450934. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Balmain 2022: in 12 healthy controls, alveolar dead space was ~0.01 L at rest, 0.06 L at 20 W and 0.19 L at peak exercise — versus 0.12, 0.22 and 0.37 L in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
cards.summary: Balmain 2022: in 12 healthy controls, alveolar dead space was ~0.01 L at rest, 0.06 L at 20 W and 0.19 L at peak exercise — versus 0.12, 0.22 and 0.37 L in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
cards.type: Human physiological study (exercise gas exchange with arterial sampling), Chest 2022
cards.people: Twelve healthy control participants (and 23 patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction), with gas exchange and arterial blood gases at rest, 20 W and peak exercise; physiological dead space by the Enghoff modification of the Bohr equation, and alveolar dead space computed as total physiological dead space minus anatomic dead space.
cards.result: In healthy controls, alveolar dead space barely rose from rest (0.01 ± 0.06 L/breath) to 20 W (0.06 ± 0.13 L/breath, P = .19) and reached only 0.19 ± 0.17 L/breath at peak exercise — small against tidal volumes that rise severalfold, so the alveolar fraction of each breath stays low in health. In the heart-failure patients, alveolar dead space was significantly higher at every stage (0.12 ± 0.07 at rest, 0.22 ± 0.08 at 20 W, 0.37 ± 0.16 L at peak) and its rise correlated with ventilatory inefficiency (VE/VCO₂ slope, r = 0.69). Health keeps alveolar dead space near zero; disease is what fills it.
cards.watchOut: The healthy leg is a 12-person control group within a heart-failure study; alveolar dead space is a derived difference (physiological minus anatomic), so its near-zero resting value carries the measurement error of both terms.
cards.source: Balmain BN et al. Alveolar Dead Space Is Augmented During Exercise in Patients With Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction. Chest. 2022. PMID: 35753384. cards.headline: Weisman 1988: healthy young recruits at steady-state strenuous exercise had a physiological dead-space fraction of 0.11–0.12 — a third of the textbook resting value
cards.summary: Weisman 1988: healthy young recruits at steady-state strenuous exercise had a physiological dead-space fraction of 0.11–0.12 — a third of the textbook resting value
cards.type: Human physiological study (exercise with arterial blood gases), Am J Med 1988
cards.people: Twenty-two healthy black male basic recruits — 11 with sickle cell trait and 11 controls — performing incremental exercise to exhaustion and a steady-state exercise test with radial arterial sampling, at simulated sea level and simulated 2,300 m altitude.
cards.result: At the simulated 2,300 m condition, steady-state exercise physiological dead space to tidal volume ratio was 0.12 in the sickle-cell-trait group and 0.11 in controls, with arterial oxygen tension 64 versus 65 mmHg and alveolar–arterial oxygen difference 22 versus 21 mmHg — the two groups indistinguishable, as they were at sea level. A VD/VT of ~0.11–0.12 during strenuous steady-state exercise in healthy young men is the direct measured counterpart of the textbook resting fraction of ~0.3 (Boron & Boulpaep account): the fraction falls by roughly two thirds as tidal volume rises and perfusion matching improves.
cards.watchOut: The quoted VD/VT values are from the simulated-altitude steady-state test (the sea-level values are described as similar between groups without separate printing); young male military recruits only.
cards.source: Weisman IM et al. Effect of moderate inspiratory hypoxia on exercise performance in sickle cell trait. Am J Med. 1988. PMID: 3132039. cards.headline: Synthesis: dead space is a fixed-ish anatomic volume plus a matching-dependent alveolar volume — exercise shrinks the fraction mainly by growing the breath, secondarily by perfusing the apex
cards.summary: Synthesis: dead space is a fixed-ish anatomic volume plus a matching-dependent alveolar volume — exercise shrinks the fraction mainly by growing the breath, secondarily by perfusing the apex
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (Hart 1963; Sun 2002; Balmain 2022; Weisman 1988), framed by Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall.
cards.result: The determinants are separable and each is carded: anatomic dead space is set by body size (height, r = .917 — Hart) and changes little breath-to-breath; alveolar dead space is set by ventilation–perfusion matching and is near zero in health at rest and low workloads (Balmain controls), rising when perfusion fails to follow ventilation (the heart-failure contrast). The fraction VD/VT — the quantity the Bohr/Enghoff equation yields and the quantity that, with arterial CO₂, sets ventilatory efficiency (Sun) — therefore falls from the textbook resting value of roughly 0.3 (Boron & Boulpaep account) to a measured ~0.11–0.12 at strenuous steady-state exercise in healthy young men (Weisman), chiefly because tidal volume rises severalfold against a near-constant anatomic volume. Ageing blunts the fall (Sun's age term), and added external dead space is compensated by larger tidal volumes in health — the system's reserve is ventilatory, not structural.
cards.watchOut: Fowler's own 1948 method paper predates abstract-indexed records and is not carded; the method reaches this shelf through Hart's 1963 application of it, and the resting VD/VT of ~0.3 is carried as the textbook's account because no carded healthy-cohort record prints a resting VD/VT directly — the exercise values, by contrast, are measured and carded.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hart MC et al., J Appl Physiol 1963 (PMID: 31094493); Sun XG et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2002 (PMID: 12450934); Balmain BN et al., Chest 2022 (PMID: 35753384); Weisman IM et al., Am J Med 1988 (PMID: 3132039). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Diffusing capacity rises ~26% from sitting to supine and rises linearly with pulmonary blood flow in exercise without reaching a plateau — capillary recruitment and distension, not the membrane, do the work
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how does lung diffusing capacity (DLCO) change with posture and exercise, and what drives the change?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Carbon Monoxide/physiology · Female · Humans · Male · Oxygen Consumption · Physical Exertion · Posture · Pulmonary Diffusing Capacity
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Three human studies, three complementary legs. Posture: DLCO measured during exhalation was 26.3% higher supine than sitting in 8 healthy subjects, and the two postures converged at maximal exercise (Stokes 1981). Exercise: in 44 healthy non-smokers aged 17–68 from the Johnson programme's laboratory tradition (Hsia 1995), DLCO, membrane diffusing capacity and capillary blood volume all rose linearly with pulmonary blood flow from rest to 80% of maximal workload with no plateau — pulmonary blood flow was the dominant determinant of recruitment. Mechanism: the Roughton-Forster partition shows both components rising with flow, and the post-exercise study (Johns 2004, 9 women) shows the components moving in opposite directions when flow falls — capillary blood volume down 21.2% while membrane capacity rose 14.7% — proving the flow/volume term, not membrane injury, drives short-term DLCO change. Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep (recruitment and distension of pulmonary capillaries raising surface area and capillary blood volume), named as textbook framing.

cards.headline: Stokes 1981: DLCO was 26.3% higher supine than sitting at rest in 8 healthy subjects, rose curvilinearly with exercise in both postures, and converged at maximal exercise
cards.summary: Stokes 1981: DLCO was 26.3% higher supine than sitting at rest in 8 healthy subjects, rose curvilinearly with exercise in both postures, and converged at maximal exercise
cards.type: Human physiological study (DLCO by posture and exercise), J Appl Physiol 1981
cards.people: Eight healthy subjects with DLCO measured during exhalation (from 30% to 45% of exhaled vital capacity) at rest and during exercise, both sitting and supine. N = 8 — a small classic physiology study, printed plainly under the physiology small-N labelling rule.
cards.result: At the lung volumes studied, resting DLCO was 26.3 ± 3.2% higher (mean ± SE, relative figure) in the supine than in the sitting position (P < 0.001). In both positions DLCO rose significantly with increasing exercise (P < 0.001) and approached similar values at maximal exercise; the rise was curvilinear — faster during mild exercise than during heavy exercise (P = 0.02) — and in the supine position DLCO appeared to reach a physiological maximum during exercise. Lying down recruits the same capillary volume that mild exercise does, which is why posture stops mattering at maximal work.
cards.watchOut: N = 8; DLCO was measured over a mid-exhalation volume window rather than by the standard single-breath total-lung-capacity method, so the 26.3% is a within-method posture contrast, labelled relative, not an absolute DLCO value.
cards.source: Stokes DL et al. Nonlinear increases in diffusing capacity during exercise by seated and supine subjects. J Appl Physiol Respir Environ Exerc Physiol. 1981. PMID: 7298429. cards.headline: Hsia 1995: in 44 healthy non-smokers, DLCO, membrane capacity and capillary blood volume all rose linearly with pulmonary blood flow to 80% of maximal workload — no plateau, and flow was the main determinant
cards.summary: Hsia 1995: in 44 healthy non-smokers, DLCO, membrane capacity and capillary blood volume all rose linearly with pulmonary blood flow to 80% of maximal workload — no plateau, and flow was the main determinant
cards.type: Human physiological study (rebreathing DLCO reference values, rest and exercise), Am J Respir Crit Care Med 1995
cards.people: Forty-four normal, healthy, non-smoking individuals aged 17–68 years, with DLCO, lung volumes, pulmonary blood flow and septal tissue volume measured simultaneously at rest and during steady-state exercise at 25%, 50% and 80% of maximal workload, at two alveolar oxygen tensions, by a rebreathing technique; membrane diffusing capacity (DMCO) and capillary blood volume (VC) derived by the Roughton-Forster relationship.
cards.result: DLCO and DMCO were significantly related to pulmonary blood flow (Qc), age and body surface area, and VC to Qc and surface area; normalising for these variables largely eliminated male–female differences. From rest to near-maximal exercise, DLCO, DMCO and VC increased linearly with Qc without evidence of reaching a plateau, and the authors concluded that pulmonary blood flow is the most important determinant of the recruitment of diffusing capacity.
cards.watchOut: Rebreathing-technique values are not interchangeable with single-breath clinical DLCO; the record reports relationships and determinants rather than a single rest-to-exercise percentage, so none is claimed from this card.

cards.headline: Johns 2004: after maximal exercise in 9 healthy women, DLCO fell up to 8.9% below baseline for 3 hours — driven by a 21.2% fall in capillary blood volume while membrane capacity rose 14.7%
cards.summary: Johns 2004: after maximal exercise in 9 healthy women, DLCO fell up to 8.9% below baseline for 3 hours — driven by a 21.2% fall in capillary blood volume while membrane capacity rose 14.7%
cards.type: Human physiological study (rebreathing DLCO components after exercise), Eur J Appl Physiol 2004
cards.people: Nine healthy females with DLCO, capillary blood volume (Vc) and membrane diffusing capacity (Dm) measured by a rebreathing method before and 1, 2, 3, 16 and 24 hours after maximal treadmill exercise.
cards.result: DLCO was depressed by up to 8.9 ± 3.0% (relative) for the first 3 hours after exercise and had returned to baseline by 16 hours. Vc fell 21.2 ± 4.1% at 3 hours post-exercise while Dm simultaneously increased 14.7 ± 9.1% — the reciprocal movement rules out interstitial oedema or blood-gas-barrier injury as the cause and identifies redistribution of blood away from the lungs (a fall in pulmonary capillary blood volume) as the driver of the DLCO fall. The same volume term that raises DLCO during exercise lowers it afterwards.
cards.watchOut: N = 9, women only, and the measurements are post-exercise recovery, not during exercise; the red-cell-reorientation explanation for the Dm rise is the authors' hypothesis, flagged as such in the report and not treated here as measured fact.
cards.source: Johns DP et al. Decreased lung capillary blood volume post-exercise is compensated by increased membrane diffusing capacity. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2004. PMID: 15278353. cards.headline: Synthesis: DLCO is a flow-recruited variable — posture and exercise both act by filling more pulmonary capillaries, and the ceiling, if any, lies beyond ordinary maximal exercise in the upright posture
cards.summary: Synthesis: DLCO is a flow-recruited variable — posture and exercise both act by filling more pulmonary capillaries, and the ceiling, if any, lies beyond ordinary maximal exercise in the upright posture
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human studies above (Stokes 1981; Hsia 1995; Johns 2004), framed by Boron & Boulpaep's account of capillary recruitment and distension.
cards.result: The three legs triangulate one mechanism. Supine posture raises resting DLCO by about a quarter (Stokes, +26.3% relative) by perfusing the upper lung; exercise raises DLCO in either posture, fastest at low workloads, until posture no longer matters at maximal work (Stokes) — and across a 44-person reference cohort the rise is linear in pulmonary blood flow with no plateau to 80% of maximum, with both the membrane component and capillary blood volume recruited (Hsia). When flow is withdrawn after exercise, DLCO falls through the volume component alone while the membrane component compensates upward (Johns). The Boron & Boulpaep framing — recruitment and distension of the pulmonary capillary bed increasing both surface area and the volume of blood available for gas exchange — is the textbook statement of exactly this evidence, presented as framing. Agostoni's posture/exercise programme is consistent with this account in the wider literature but no Agostoni record with extractable numbers was fetched this session, so none is carded.
cards.watchOut: Methods differ across cards (exhalation-window, rebreathing, single-breath traditions), so percentages are within-study contrasts, not interchangeable absolute values; two of three cohorts are small (N = 8 and N = 9) and are labelled on their faces. Haemoglobin, carboxyhaemoglobin and altitude all shift DLCO independently and are outside this question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Stokes DL et al., J Appl Physiol 1981 (PMID: 7298429); Hsia CC et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 1995 (PMID: 7633723); Johns DP et al., Eur J Appl Physiol 2004 (PMID: 15278353). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Growth hormone and slow-wave sleep (physiology): the night's largest GH pulse rides the first slow-wave episode, smaller pulses follow later slow-wave phases, and the coupling tracks sleep — not the clock — across the night
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how are growth-hormone pulses coupled to slow-wave sleep across the night?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose/analysis · Chlordiazepoxide/pharmacology · Chlorpromazine/pharmacology · Electroencephalography · Eye Movements · Female · Growth Hormone/blood,metabolism · Humans · Hydrocortisone/blood · Imipramine/pharmacology · Insulin/blood · Isocarboxazid/pharmacology · Male · Phenobarbital/pharmacology · Phenytoin/pharmacology · Secretory Rate/drug effects · Sleep/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron and Boulpaep Medical Physiology): most daily growth-hormone (GH) secretion in healthy adults is sleep-related, released in pulses entrained to slow-wave sleep (SWS) — the textbooks' account, and the carded human studies agree in detail. Takahashi 1968 found a major GH peak (13–72 mµg/mL, lasting 1.5–3.5 hours) appearing with the onset of deep sleep in 7 of 8 young adults, smaller peaks (6–14 mµg/mL) with later deep-sleep phases, the peak delayed when sleep onset was delayed, and a fresh peak (14–46 mµg/mL) when subjects returned to sleep after 2–3 hours awake. Sassin 1969 showed the release reverses when the sleep–wake cycle is reversed by 12 hours — coupling to sleep, not circadian time. The Van Cauter programme quantified it: about 70% of sleep GH pulses coincide with SWS and pulse size correlates with concurrent SWS (Van Cauter and Plat 1996), across 149 healthy men GH secretion fell by 372 µg per decade from early adulthood to midlife in parallel with SWS falling from 18.9% to 3.4% of sleep, with GH amount associated with SWS independently of age (Van Cauter 2000). Under chronic partial sleep loss the pattern adapts rather than simply shrinking — a presleep pulse appears alongside the postsleep-onset pulse (Spiegel 2000). Live shelf #47 asks a different question — what tracks GH pulses after weight loss (insulin versus leptin) — and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Takahashi 1968: a major GH peak (13–72 mµg/mL) appeared with the onset of deep sleep in 7 of 8 young adults, and moved when sleep moved
cards.summary: Takahashi 1968: a major GH peak (13–72 mµg/mL) appeared with the onset of deep sleep in 7 of 8 young adults, and moved when sleep moved
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (overnight sampling with EEG sleep staging)
cards.people: 8 young adults (ages 20–30) studied over 38 nights with blood drawn every 30 minutes through an indwelling catheter and continuous EEG/electrooculogram sleep staging; N = 8 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: In seven subjects a plasma GH peak of 13–72 mµg/mL lasting 1.5–3.5 hours appeared with the onset of deep sleep; smaller peaks of 6–14 mµg/mL occasionally appeared during subsequent deep-sleep phases. Peak secretion was delayed if sleep onset was delayed, and subjects awakened for 2–3 hours and allowed to return to sleep showed another GH peak of 14–46 mµg/mL. Peaks were not correlated with changes in plasma glucose, insulin or cortisol. The authors conclude that altered hypothalamic activity associated with sleep initiation produces the major GH peak, unrelated to hypoglycaemia or to cortisol and insulin changes.
cards.watchOut: Classic small study (N = 8) with 30-minute sampling, so pulse timing is resolved to about half an hour; GH values are in the era's assay units (mµg/mL, equivalent to ng/mL) and are not directly interchangeable with modern assay numbers.
cards.source: Takahashi Y et al. Growth hormone secretion during sleep. J Clin Invest. 1968. PMID: 5675428. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sassin 1969: reversing the sleep–wake cycle by 12 hours reversed GH release with it — the coupling is to slow-wave sleep, not to an independent clock
cards.summary: Sassin 1969: reversing the sleep–wake cycle by 12 hours reversed GH release with it — the coupling is to slow-wave sleep, not to an independent clock
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (sleep-cycle reversal experiment)
cards.people: Healthy adult men studied with EEG sleep staging and GH sampling across normal and 12-hour-reversed sleep–waking cycles; N not documented in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Release of human growth hormone during sleep was significantly related to the slow, synchronised stages of sleep. When sleep–waking cycles were reversed by 12 hours, the release of growth hormone with sleep was reversed as well; the authors conclude GH release does not follow an inherent circadian rhythm independent of sleep, and would seem to be controlled by neural mechanisms related to slow-wave sleep.
cards.watchOut: A short Science report whose abstract gives the qualitative reversal finding without pulse sizes or subject numbers (N not documented in the record); it establishes what the coupling follows, not how large the pulses are.
cards.source: Sassin JF et al. Human growth hormone release: relation to slow-wave sleep and sleep-walking cycles. Science. 1969. PMID: 4307378. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Van Cauter and Plat 1996: in men about 70% of GH pulses during sleep coincide with slow-wave sleep, and the amount secreted in those pulses correlates with the amount of SWS
cards.summary: Van Cauter and Plat 1996: in men about 70% of GH pulses during sleep coincide with slow-wave sleep, and the amount secreted in those pulses correlates with the amount of SWS
cards.type: Programme synthesis / review of primary human sleep–GH studies (Van Cauter programme)
cards.people: A synthesis of the Van Cauter programme's human sleep–GH studies in normal persons of both sexes from childhood to late adulthood, including the programme's GHRH and ageing data; a review of primary human work, carded as the programme synthesis.
cards.result: In adults the most reproducible GH pulse occurs shortly after sleep onset in association with the first phase of slow-wave sleep (stages III and IV). In men approximately 70% of GH pulses during sleep coincide with SWS, and the amount of GH secreted during these pulses correlates with the concurrent amount of SWS. Sleep-related GH secretion appears primarily dependent on growth-hormone-releasing hormone release. During the fourth decade (ages 30–40) total 24-hour GH secretion falls two- to threefold, over the same narrow age range in which SWS decreases dramatically.
cards.watchOut: A review, not a single experiment: its 70% figure summarises the programme's primary studies (two of which are carded separately on this shelf). Its record's MeSH includes animal terms because the review also discusses rodent GHRH work — no animal data are carded here.
cards.source: Van Cauter E et al. Physiology of growth hormone secretion during sleep. J Pediatr. 1996. PMID: 8627466. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Van Cauter 2000: across 149 healthy men, GH secretion fell 372 µg per decade as slow-wave sleep fell from 18.9% to 3.4% of the night — and GH amount tracked SWS independently of age
cards.summary: Van Cauter 2000: across 149 healthy men, GH secretion fell 372 µg per decade as slow-wave sleep fell from 18.9% to 3.4% of the night — and GH amount tracked SWS independently of age
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (pooled 24-hour GH profiles with polysomnography, ages 16–83)
cards.people: 149 healthy men aged 16–83 years (mean BMI 24.1) without sleep complaints, pooled from studies at four laboratories between 1985 and 1999, with 24-hour plasma GH and cortisol profiles and polygraphic sleep recording; N = 149 printed on the face of this physiology card.
cards.result: Mean slow-wave sleep fell from 18.9% (SEM 1.3%) in early adulthood (16–25 years) to 3.4% (1.0%) in midlife (36–50 years), replaced by lighter sleep. The SWS decline was paralleled by a major decline in GH secretion (−372 µg per decade; p < 0.001) to midlife, then a slower further decline (−43 µg per decade; p < 0.02). Independently of age, the amount of GH secretion was significantly associated with slow-wave sleep (p < 0.001). Evening cortisol rose by 19.3 nmol/L per decade (about 0.70 µg/dL per decade), significant only after age 50.
cards.watchOut: Men only, and a pooled cross-sectional age comparison rather than the same men followed for decades; it quantifies the SWS–GH association across the lifespan, while the within-night coupling itself rests on Takahashi 1968 and Sassin 1969.

cards.headline: Spiegel 2000: under chronic partial sleep loss the GH pattern adapted — a presleep pulse appeared beside the postsleep-onset pulse, which still tracked slow-wave activity
cards.summary: Spiegel 2000: under chronic partial sleep loss the GH pattern adapted — a presleep pulse appeared beside the postsleep-onset pulse, which still tracked slow-wave activity
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (sleep-restriction and sleep-extension protocol)
cards.people: 11 young men studied after 6 nights of restricted bedtimes (01:00–05:00) and after 7 nights of extended bedtimes (21:00–09:00), with 24-hour GH profiles and EEG slow-wave activity measurement; N = 11 printed on the face of this physiology card.
cards.result: In normal men the majority of GH secretion occurs in a single large postsleep-onset pulse, suppressed during total sleep deprivation. During sleep debt the pattern became biphasic, with both a presleep-onset 'circadian' pulse and a postsleep-onset pulse; postsleep-onset secretion was negatively related to presleep secretion and tended to correlate positively with concomitant slow-wave activity. When sleep was restricted, slow-wave sleep and slow-wave activity increased during early sleep, but in the second rather than the first slow-wave cycle. The authors conclude adaptation mechanisms operate during chronic partial sleep loss.
cards.watchOut: A sleep-debt adaptation study in 11 young men: it shows the coupling bends under chronic restriction rather than breaking, but its presleep pulse should not be read as the normal pattern in rested sleep.
cards.source: Spiegel K et al. Adaptation of the 24-h growth hormone profile to a state of sleep debt. Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol. 2000. PMID: 10956244. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the first slow-wave episode carries the night's major GH pulse, later slow-wave phases carry smaller ones, and the whole pattern follows sleep rather than clock time — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: the first slow-wave episode carries the night's major GH pulse, later slow-wave phases carry smaller ones, and the whole pattern follows sleep rather than clock time — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Carded human data: 8 young adults over 38 nights (Takahashi 1968), a cycle-reversal experiment (Sassin 1969; N not documented in the record), the Van Cauter programme synthesis, 149 healthy men aged 16–83 (Van Cauter 2000) and 11 young men under sleep restriction/extension (Spiegel 2000).
cards.result: Five concordant legs: a major sleep-onset pulse tied to deep sleep (13–72 mµg/mL) with smaller pulses at later deep-sleep phases; reversal of release when sleep is reversed; about 70% of sleep pulses coinciding with SWS with size tracking SWS amount; a lifespan association between SWS loss and GH loss independent of age; and adaptation — not abolition — of the postsleep pulse under sleep debt. This matches the textbook account in Ganong and in Boron and Boulpaep, which frame this shelf. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. What tracks GH pulses after weight loss is a different question, homed at live shelf #47.
cards.watchOut: Physiology of healthy sleep: GH pulse patterns in acromegaly, GH deficiency, critical illness or with GH therapy are different questions on their own shelves.

shelves.title: Nerandomilast in IPF and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: two phase 3 trials slow FVC decline by about 45–80 mL over 52 weeks, with diarrhoea in a third or more
shelves.question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or progressive pulmonary fibrosis, does the oral PDE4B inhibitor nerandomilast slow the decline in forced vital capacity compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Double-Blind Method · Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis/diagnosis,drug therapy,physiopathology · Lung/physiopathology · Phosphodiesterase 4 Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Vital Capacity/drug effects · Antifibrotic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Disease Progression · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Tablets · Administration, Oral · Cyclobutanes · Indoles · Pyridones · Organic Chemicals · Piperidines
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for the forced-vital-capacity claim. Two independent phase 3, double-blind trials (FIBRONEER-IPF, n = 1,177; FIBRONEER-ILD, n = 1,176) each found both doses of the oral preferential PDE4B inhibitor nerandomilast slowed 52-week FVC decline versus placebo (adjusted differences 44.9–81.1 mL), building on a 12-week phase 2 stabilisation signal, and the FIBRONEER-ILD whole-follow-up report is directionally concordant on exacerbation, respiratory hospitalisation or death. The claim is a lung-function slope, not a proven symptom or survival benefit in the primary reports; diarrhoea (roughly 30–41% on drug vs 16–25% on placebo) is the consistent cost. The carded records present nerandomilast as an investigational agent; no regulatory status beyond what the records state is claimed.

cards.headline: Phase 2 (Richeldi 2022): over 12 weeks, nerandomilast (BI 1015550) held FVC at +5.7 mL while placebo fell −81.7 mL in patients not on background antifibrotics
cards.summary: Phase 2 (Richeldi 2022): over 12 weeks, nerandomilast (BI 1015550) held FVC at +5.7 mL while placebo fell −81.7 mL in patients not on background antifibrotics
cards.type: Phase 2, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2022
cards.people: 147 adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis randomly assigned 2:1 to oral nerandomilast 18 mg twice daily or placebo for 12 weeks, analysed separately by background antifibrotic use (Bayesian primary analysis).
cards.result: Among patients without background antifibrotic therapy, the median change in forced vital capacity at 12 weeks was +5.7 mL (95% credible interval −39.1 to 50.5) on nerandomilast and −81.7 mL (−133.5 to −44.8) on placebo — a median difference of 88.4 mL (29.5 to 154.2), with a 0.998 probability that nerandomilast was superior. The record's abstract reports the no-background stratum in full; the trial was short and small, and it is carded as the phase 2 signal the phase 3 programme was built on.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks and 147 patients with a Bayesian analysis: a stabilisation signal, not proof of slowed decline — the 52-week phase 3 trials below are the test.
cards.source: Richeldi L et al. Trial of a Preferential Phosphodiesterase 4B Inhibitor for Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2022. PMID: 35569036. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04419506, from the record's databank fields.
