cards.headline: FIBRONEER-IPF (2025): nerandomilast slowed 52-week FVC decline by 68.8 mL (18 mg) and 44.9 mL (9 mg) versus placebo in 1,177 patients
cards.summary: FIBRONEER-IPF (2025): nerandomilast slowed 52-week FVC decline by 68.8 mL (18 mg) and 44.9 mL (9 mg) versus placebo in 1,177 patients
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (FIBRONEER-IPF), N Engl J Med 2025
cards.people: 1,177 adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis randomly assigned 1:1:1 to nerandomilast 18 mg twice daily, nerandomilast 9 mg twice daily, or placebo, stratified by background antifibrotic therapy (77.7% were taking nintedanib or pirfenidone at enrolment).
cards.result: Adjusted mean change in forced vital capacity at week 52 was −114.7 mL (95% CI −141.8 to −87.5) on nerandomilast 18 mg, −138.6 mL (−165.6 to −111.6) on 9 mg, and −183.5 mL (−210.9 to −156.1) on placebo. The adjusted differences versus placebo were 68.8 mL (95% CI 30.3 to 107.4; P < 0.001) for 18 mg and 44.9 mL (6.4 to 83.3; P = 0.02) for 9 mg. Diarrhoea was the most frequent adverse event (41.3% on 18 mg, 31.1% on 9 mg, 16.0% on placebo); serious adverse events were balanced across groups.
cards.watchOut: Most patients were already on an antifibrotic, so this is largely add-on evidence; the endpoint is the FVC slope, a surrogate — the abstract reports no mortality result, and none is claimed here.
cards.source: Richeldi L et al. Nerandomilast in Patients with Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40387033. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05321069, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: FIBRONEER-ILD (2025): in progressive pulmonary fibrosis beyond IPF, nerandomilast slowed FVC decline by 67.2 mL (18 mg) and 81.1 mL (9 mg) versus placebo in 1,176 patients
cards.summary: FIBRONEER-ILD (2025): in progressive pulmonary fibrosis beyond IPF, nerandomilast slowed FVC decline by 67.2 mL (18 mg) and 81.1 mL (9 mg) versus placebo in 1,176 patients
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (FIBRONEER-ILD), N Engl J Med 2025
cards.people: 1,176 adults with progressive pulmonary fibrosis (non-IPF) who received at least one dose, randomly assigned 1:1:1 to nerandomilast 18 mg twice daily, 9 mg twice daily, or placebo, stratified by background nintedanib (43.5% taking it at baseline) and by fibrotic pattern on high-resolution CT.
cards.result: Adjusted mean change in forced vital capacity at week 52 was −98.6 mL (95% CI −123.7 to −73.4) on nerandomilast 18 mg, −84.6 mL (−109.6 to −59.7) on 9 mg, and −165.8 mL (−190.5 to −141.0) on placebo. Adjusted differences versus placebo were 67.2 mL (95% CI 31.9 to 102.5; P < 0.001) for 18 mg and 81.1 mL (46.0 to 116.3; P < 0.001) for 9 mg — note the 9-mg difference is numerically the larger here, so no dose ordering is claimed. Diarrhoea was again most frequent (36.6%, 29.5% and 24.7% respectively).
cards.watchOut: A mixed progressive-fibrosis population (autoimmune, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and other fibrosing diseases pooled), so the result is a class-level PPF finding, not a verdict for any single diagnosis within it.
cards.source: Maher TM et al. Nerandomilast in Patients with Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40388329. cards.headline: FIBRONEER-ILD whole follow-up (2026): over the full trial, the composite of exacerbation, respiratory hospitalisation or death favoured nerandomilast (relative HR 0.77–0.78), and death itself had a relative HR of 0.51 at both doses
cards.summary: FIBRONEER-ILD whole follow-up (2026): over the full trial, the composite of exacerbation, respiratory hospitalisation or death favoured nerandomilast (relative HR 0.77–0.78), and death itself had a relative HR of 0.51 at both doses
cards.type: Whole-follow-up report of a phase 3 randomised trial (FIBRONEER-ILD), Eur Respir J 2026
cards.people: The same 1,176 FIBRONEER-ILD patients (512 taking background nintedanib) followed to the final database lock: mean exposure 15.1 ± 5.7 months, mean observation 17.0 ± 4.1 months.
cards.result: For the key secondary composite — first acute exacerbation of interstitial lung disease, hospitalisation for a respiratory cause, or death — the relative hazard ratio versus placebo was 0.78 (95% CI 0.61 to 1.00) for nerandomilast 9 mg and 0.77 (0.60 to 0.99) for 18 mg; for death alone the relative hazard ratio was 0.51 (95% CI 0.34 to 0.78) at both doses. The composite benefit was smaller in patients taking background nintedanib (relative HR 0.90 and 0.93) than in those not taking it (0.69 and 0.65). Adverse events led to discontinuation in 12.5% (placebo), 12.0% (9 mg) and 12.3% (18 mg). Absolute event rates are not printed in the record's abstract, so the relative figures stand with that caveat on the face.
cards.watchOut: A secondary-endpoint analysis of one trial, with the 9-mg composite interval touching 1.00 and no absolute rates in the abstract: supportive of the FVC finding, not an independent mortality trial.
cards.source: Wijsenbeek MS et al. Nerandomilast in progressive pulmonary fibrosis: data from the whole follow-up period of the FIBRONEER-ILD trial. The European respiratory journal. 2026. PMID: 41887669. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant phase 3 trials slow FVC decline by roughly 45–80 mL over a year — LIKELY for the lung-function claim, with diarrhoea the price
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded reports above: phase 2 in IPF (147 patients), FIBRONEER-IPF (1,177), FIBRONEER-ILD (1,176) and its whole-follow-up report.
cards.result: The programme is unusually coherent: a 12-week phase 2 stabilisation signal, then two independent 52-week phase 3 trials — one in IPF, one in progressive pulmonary fibrosis beyond IPF — each showing both nerandomilast doses slowing forced vital capacity decline versus placebo by about 45–81 mL, mostly on top of background antifibrotic therapy. The whole-follow-up FIBRONEER-ILD report adds a concordant direction on exacerbation/hospitalisation/death (relative HR 0.77–0.78) and death (relative HR 0.51), printed as secondary-endpoint, relative-only evidence. Diarrhoea in roughly a third to two-fifths of treated patients is the consistent price; serious adverse events were balanced. The carded records describe nerandomilast as an investigational oral preferential PDE4B inhibitor studied in these trials; no carded record states a regulatory approval, and none is claimed on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: FVC decline is a surrogate: patients were not shown in the primary reports to feel better, and the mortality signal rests on one trial's secondary analysis with relative figures only. Both phase 3 trials were industry programme trials of the same drug — concordant, but a single programme.
cards.source: Synthesis of Richeldi L et al., N Engl J Med 2022 (PMID: 35569036); Richeldi L et al., N Engl J Med 2025 (PMID: 40387033); Maher TM et al., N Engl J Med 2025 (PMID: 40388329); Wijsenbeek MS et al., Eur Respir J 2026 (PMID: 41887669). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: STOP2: 10 days of IV antibiotics was non-inferior to 14 in early responders with a CF exacerbation — and 21 days beat 14 in nobody
shelves.question: In adults with cystic fibrosis having a pulmonary exacerbation with early treatment improvement, is 10 days of intravenous antibiotics non-inferior to 14 days for recovery of lung function?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Cystic Fibrosis/complications,drug therapy · Disease Progression · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Respiratory Function Tests · Respiratory Tract Infections/drug therapy,etiology · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised programme caps the stamp. STOP2 (982 adults with cystic fibrosis) randomised by early treatment response: in the 277 early responders, 10 days of intravenous antibiotics was non-inferior to 14 days for percent predicted FEV1 recovery (difference −0.65 points, 95% CI −3.3 to 2.0, excluding the non-inferiority margin); in the 705 non-early responders, extending to 21 days made no difference versus 14 days (difference −0.10 points). Two STOP2 secondary analyses are carded as labelled context (home-only treatment recovered less; 39.5% of exacerbations were virus-positive). The 10-day answer applies only to adults already improving by day 7–10.

cards.headline: STOP2 (Goss 2021): in early responders, 10 days of IV antibiotics was non-inferior to 14 days for lung-function recovery (difference −0.65 points, 95% CI −3.3 to 2.0); in non-early responders, 21 days was no better than 14
cards.summary: STOP2 (Goss 2021): in early responders, 10 days of IV antibiotics was non-inferior to 14 days for lung-function recovery (difference −0.65 points, 95% CI −3.3 to 2.0); in non-early responders, 21 days was no better than 14
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, controlled trial (STOP2), Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2021
cards.people: 982 adults with cystic fibrosis treated with intravenous antimicrobials for a pulmonary exacerbation in a multicentre randomised trial. After 7–10 days, 277 participants meeting predefined lung-function and symptom improvement criteria (early responders) were randomised to 10 or 14 days' total duration; the remaining 705 were randomised to 14 or 21 days.
cards.result: The primary outcome was change in percent predicted FEV1 from treatment initiation to 2 weeks after stopping antibiotics. In early responders, mean change was 12.8 points on 10 days and 13.4 on 14 days — a difference of −0.65 points (95% CI −3.3 to 2.0), which excluded the predefined non-inferiority margin, so 10 days was non-inferior to 14. In non-early responders, mean change was 3.3 points on 21 days and 3.4 on 14 days (difference −0.10, 95% CI −1.3 to 1.1), so prolonging to 21 days bought nothing (the treatment made no difference). Symptoms, weight and adverse events were supportive as secondary endpoints.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority applies only to patients who have already improved early on treatment — the trial's own design makes that restriction, and the shorter course was not tested in people who were not improving. One trial programme: the stamp is capped accordingly.
cards.source: Goss CH et al. A Randomized Clinical Trial of Antimicrobial Duration for Cystic Fibrosis Pulmonary Exacerbation Treatment. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2021. PMID: 34469706. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02781610, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: STOP2 site-of-treatment analysis (2022): participants treated only at home recovered less lung function (5.0 points) than those treated only in hospital (8.0 points) — recovery context for the duration verdict
cards.summary: STOP2 site-of-treatment analysis (2022): participants treated only at home recovered less lung function (5.0 points) than those treated only in hospital (8.0 points) — recovery context for the duration verdict
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised trial (STOP2), J Cyst Fibros 2022
cards.people: STOP2 participants analysed by where their intravenous antimicrobials were given — a clinician-chosen, non-randomised stratification factor: 33% hospital only, 46% hospital and home, 21% home only — with propensity-score weighting used to compare responses. This is a secondary analysis of the STOP2 trial carded above, not an independent trial.
cards.result: Mean percent predicted FEV1 improvement was significantly lower (P < 0.05) in the home-only group, 5.0 points (95% CI 3.5 to 6.5), than in the hospital-and-home group, 7.0 (5.9 to 8.1), and the hospital-only group, 8.0 (6.7 to 9.4); weight recovery showed the same direction. The analysis does not change the duration result, but it warns that measured 'recovery' in exacerbation trials depends on where and how completely treatment is delivered.
cards.watchOut: Treatment location was chosen by clinicians, not randomised, so confounding by severity and support at home is expected despite propensity weighting; carded as context for interpreting recovery, not as evidence about duration.
cards.source: Sanders DB et al. Association of site of treatment with clinical outcomes following intravenous antimicrobial treatment of a pulmonary exacerbation. Journal of cystic fibrosis : official journal of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society. 2022. PMID: 34857494. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: STOP2 viral ancillary study (2024): a respiratory virus was found in 39.5% of exacerbations, and virus-positive participants had a lower risk of a future exacerbation (relative HR 0.82) — exacerbations are not one uniform event
cards.summary: STOP2 viral ancillary study (2024): a respiratory virus was found in 39.5% of exacerbations, and virus-positive participants had a lower risk of a future exacerbation (relative HR 0.82) — exacerbations are not one uniform event
cards.type: Ancillary study of a randomised trial (STOP2), Ann Am Thorac Soc 2024
cards.people: 621 STOP2 participants contributing 1,254 sputum samples tested by multiplex PCR for respiratory viruses across up to three study visits — an ancillary study of the STOP2 trial carded above, not an independent duration trial.
cards.result: One or more respiratory viruses were detected in samples from 245 participants (39.5%). Virus-positive participants were more symptomatic at presentation (mean symptom score 53.8 vs 51.1) with a greater drop in percent predicted FEV1 from their prior 6-month baseline (5.8 vs 3.6 points), yet virus positivity was associated with a reduced risk of future exacerbation (relative hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.99; P = 0.034) and a longer median time to the next exacerbation (255 vs 172 days; P = 0.021). Exacerbation biology varies within the trial population the duration verdict rests on.
cards.watchOut: An observational comparison inside a trial (virus status was not assigned), carded to characterise the exacerbation population — it neither strengthens nor weakens the randomised duration comparison itself.
cards.source: Thornton CS et al. Prevalence and Clinical Impact of Respiratory Viral Infections from the STOP2 Study of Cystic Fibrosis Pulmonary Exacerbations. Annals of the American Thoracic Society. 2024. PMID: 37963297. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02781610, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: for the adult with CF who is already improving by day 7–10, 10 days is enough — one large randomised programme, graded POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: for the adult with CF who is already improving by day 7–10, 10 days is enough — one large randomised programme, graded POSSIBLE
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the STOP2 primary report (982 randomised adults) and its two carded secondary/ancillary analyses above.
cards.result: STOP2 is the only randomised duration trial of its size in cystic fibrosis exacerbations, and its answer is two-sided in a clinically useful way: early responders lose nothing by stopping at 10 days instead of 14 (difference −0.65 FEV1 points, interval excluding the non-inferiority margin), and non-early responders gain nothing from extending to 21 days instead of 14 (the treatment made no difference, −0.10 points). The secondary analyses counsel humility about the setting — home-only treatment recovered less lung function, and two-fifths of exacerbations carried a respiratory virus — but they do not disturb the randomised comparison. Because the whole verdict rests on a single trial programme, the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE despite the trial's size and clean non-inferiority result.
cards.watchOut: Adults only, intravenous treatment only, and 'early responder' is a defined trial category (predefined lung-function and symptom improvement by day 7–10) — the 10-day course should not be generalised to patients who are not improving or to children.
cards.source: Synthesis of Goss CH et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2021 (PMID: 34469706); STOP2 site-of-treatment analysis, J Cyst Fibros 2022 (PMID: 34857494); Thornton CS et al., Ann Am Thorac Soc 2024 (PMID: 37963297). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: MAC lung disease, first treatment: thrice-weekly triple therapy converts sputum as often as daily therapy in noncavitary disease — and patients stay on it more easily
shelves.question: In adults with newly diagnosed Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease, is intermittent (thrice-weekly) triple therapy as effective as daily triple therapy for sputum culture conversion and relapse?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antitubercular Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Azithromycin/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Clarithromycin/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Comorbidity · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Ethambutol/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Logistic Models · Macrolides/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Mycobacterium avium Complex/drug effects · Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare Infection/drug therapy · Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care · Practice Guidelines as Topic · Republic of Korea · Retrospective Studies · Rifampin/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Sputum/microbiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). In treatment-naive noncavitary nodular bronchiectatic MAC lung disease, intermittent three-times-weekly macrolide–rifampin–ethambutol therapy achieved sputum culture conversion statistically indistinguishable from daily therapy in both a 217-patient retrospective cohort (adjusted 73.6% vs 71.3%; Jeong 2015 — a cohort, not an RCT, a premise correction to the slate) and the 2025 iREC randomised trial (70.3% vs 80.0%, P = 0.53; Nakagawa), with better tolerability on intermittent dosing in both. The trial's wide intervals and the cohort's retrospective design cap the stamp at POSSIBLE. Cavitary disease is excluded from every card — daily therapy remains its standard — and refractory MAC add-on therapy is home on #2673, not here.

cards.headline: Jeong 2015: in a 217-patient retrospective cohort, thrice-weekly therapy converted sputum as often as daily therapy (adjusted 73.6% vs 71.3%) with far fewer regimen changes (21% vs 46%)
cards.summary: Jeong 2015: in a 217-patient retrospective cohort, thrice-weekly therapy converted sputum as often as daily therapy (adjusted 73.6% vs 71.3%) with far fewer regimen changes (21% vs 46%)
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study (registered cohort, NCT00970801), Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2015
cards.people: 217 treatment-naive patients with noncavitary nodular bronchiectatic Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease at a Korean referral centre: 99 received daily and 118 received intermittent (three-times-weekly) therapy, each a macrolide (clarithromycin or azithromycin) plus rifampin and ethambutol. Retrospective cohort — not the randomised trial it is sometimes cited as; the design is printed on the face.
cards.result: Sputum culture conversion did not differ: 76% on daily versus 67% on intermittent therapy unadjusted (P = 0.154), and adjusted proportions of 71.3% (95% CI 59.1 to 81.1) versus 73.6% (62.9 to 82.2; P = 0.785) — effectively identical. Symptomatic improvement (75% vs 82%) and radiographic improvement (68% vs 73%) also did not differ. The practical difference was tolerability: the initial regimen had to be modified in 46% of the daily group versus 21% of the intermittent group (P < 0.001), driven by ethambutol discontinuation (24% vs 1%).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and single-centre: who got daily versus intermittent therapy was a clinical choice, so sicker patients may sit in the daily arm. It covers noncavitary nodular bronchiectatic disease only — cavitary disease is a different, daily-therapy question.
cards.source: Jeong BH et al. Intermittent antibiotic therapy for nodular bronchiectatic Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2015. PMID: 25393520. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00970801, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Nakagawa 2025 (iREC): the randomised trial — culture conversion 70.3% intermittent vs 80.0% daily (P = 0.53), with significantly fewer liver-enzyme elevations on intermittent therapy
cards.summary: Nakagawa 2025 (iREC): the randomised trial — culture conversion 70.3% intermittent vs 80.0% daily (P = 0.53), with significantly fewer liver-enzyme elevations on intermittent therapy
cards.type: Open-label, multicentre, randomised trial (iREC), Ann Am Thorac Soc 2025
cards.people: 141 patients with previously untreated noncavitary nodular bronchiectatic MAC pulmonary disease randomised at 21 Japanese hospitals (full analysis set 138: 70 intermittent, 68 daily) to clarithromycin, rifampicin and ethambutol either three days per week (higher per-dose amounts) or daily, for 1 year. Open-label randomised trial.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — proportion requiring modification of the initial regimen — was 20.0% (14/70) on intermittent versus 33.8% (23/68) on daily therapy (adjusted odds ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.22 to 1.05; P = 0.06), not statistically significant. Culture conversion was 70.3% versus 80.0% (P = 0.53), time to conversion 28.0 versus 28.5 days, CT improvement 60.9% versus 71.0%, and clarithromycin resistance developed in 1.4% versus 0% — none significantly different. Liver injury markers clearly favoured intermittent dosing: elevated aspartate aminotransferase 16.9% versus 41.2% (P = 0.003) and alanine aminotransferase 18.3% versus 44.1% (P = 0.002). Point estimates for conversion actually favour daily therapy numerically, so equivalence is 'no shown difference', not proven sameness.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 138 analysed patients, and powered on regimen modification rather than conversion: the conversion interval is wide enough to hide a real difference in either direction. Noncavitary disease only.
cards.source: Nakagawa T et al. Intermittent versus Daily Therapy for Noncavitary Mycobacterium avium Complex Pulmonary Disease: An Open-Label Randomized Trial. cards.headline: Lam 2006: a prospective thrice-weekly treatment cohort — 44% culture response overall, fourfold higher in noncavitary than cavitary disease
cards.summary: Lam 2006: a prospective thrice-weekly treatment cohort — 44% culture response overall, fourfold higher in noncavitary than cavitary disease
cards.type: Prospective single-arm treatment trial, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2006
cards.people: 91 HIV-negative adults with moderate-to-severe MAC lung disease treated prospectively for 1 year with three-times-weekly clarithromycin, ethambutol and rifampin in a 17-city US trial cohort (participants originally enrolled in an inhaled interferon-gamma trial). Single-arm prospective study — no daily-therapy comparator.
cards.result: Treatment response rates were 44% for sputum culture (response sustained 2 months or longer), 60% for high-resolution CT and 53% for symptoms. Noncavitary disease predicted a 4.0-times higher culture response (95% CI 1.7 to 9.2) and 4.9-times higher CT response than cavitary disease; previously untreated patients responded 2.2 times as often for culture. This cohort is why the intermittent question is confined to noncavitary disease: the same regimen performs far worse once cavities are present.
cards.watchOut: No comparator arm and a moderate-to-severe, partly pre-treated population, so its 44% conversion should not be compared directly with the treatment-naive cohorts above; carded for the cavitary/noncavitary split and as the prospective base under the guideline recommendation.
cards.source: Lam PK et al. Factors related to response to intermittent treatment of Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2006. PMID: 16514112. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Synthesis: for noncavitary nodular bronchiectatic MAC, thrice-weekly therapy converts sputum about as often as daily therapy and is easier to stay on — POSSIBLE, and noncavitary only
cards.summary: Synthesis: for noncavitary nodular bronchiectatic MAC, thrice-weekly therapy converts sputum about as often as daily therapy and is easier to stay on — POSSIBLE, and noncavitary only
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports above: Jeong 2015 retrospective cohort (217 patients), Nakagawa 2025 randomised trial (138 analysed), Lam 2006 prospective intermittent cohort (91).
cards.result: The comparison the guidelines (ATS/ERS/ESCMID/IDSA 2020) rest on is consistent across designs: culture conversion on intermittent therapy is statistically indistinguishable from daily therapy (adjusted 73.6% vs 71.3% in the cohort; 70.3% vs 80.0% in the trial), while tolerability favours intermittent dosing — regimen modification 21% vs 46% in the cohort and significantly fewer liver-enzyme elevations in the trial. The randomised trial's conversion point estimate numerically favours daily therapy and its intervals are wide, and the largest comparative dataset is retrospective, so the stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. The boundary is firm: every carded report is noncavitary nodular bronchiectatic disease, and Lam's cohort shows conversion collapsing in cavitary disease — daily therapy remains the cavitary standard, and refractory disease after initial therapy is a different question, home on shelf #2673 (inhaled liposomal amikacin add-on), which is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Relapse after conversion is thinly reported in the carded records (the trial followed patients for the 1-year treatment period), so the verdict is about conversion and tolerability during therapy, not long-term relapse.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jeong BH et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2015 (PMID: 25393520); Nakagawa T et al., Ann Am Thorac Soc 2025 (PMID: 40153596); Lam PK et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2006 (PMID: 16514112). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis treatment: an observational, near-null base — steroids made no difference in fibrotic disease, mycophenolate moves DLCO only, avoidance unproven
shelves.question: In adults with fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, do antigen avoidance, corticosteroids or mycophenolate slow lung-function decline and improve survival?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Alveolitis, Extrinsic Allergic/drug therapy,physiopathology · Azathioprine/therapeutic use · Carbon Monoxide · Chronic Disease · Female · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Linear Models · Male · Middle Aged · Mycophenolic Acid/therapeutic use · Prednisone/therapeutic use · Pulmonary Diffusing Capacity · Retrospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Vital Capacity
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational evidence only, labelled as such, with no dedicated randomised trial in existence. In the largest fibrotic-phenotype cohort (De Sadeleer 2018; 109 fibrotic patients), corticosteroids made no difference to survival or lung function and antigen avoidance showed only a non-significant trend (P = 0.15). Mycophenolate/azathioprine initiation was followed by a DLCO improvement (+4.2% at 1 year) but no significant FVC change (Morisset 2017), and registry immunosuppression in 344 fibrotic patients changed neither lung function nor symptoms, with worse survival in the unknown-antigen subgroup (Mullin 2024). Nothing carded shows a treatment slowing decline in fibrotic HP; the guideline-era practice rests on non-fibrotic disease and mechanism, not on fibrotic-phenotype outcomes.

cards.headline: De Sadeleer 2018: in 109 patients with fibrotic HP, corticosteroids made no difference to survival or lung function, and antigen avoidance showed only a non-significant trend (P = 0.15)
cards.summary: De Sadeleer 2018: in 109 patients with fibrotic HP, corticosteroids made no difference to survival or lung function, and antigen avoidance showed only a non-significant trend (P = 0.15)
cards.type: Retrospective single-centre cohort study, J Clin Med 2018
cards.people: 202 patients with hypersensitivity pneumonitis followed at a single centre (2005–2016): 93 non-fibrotic and 109 fibrotic on chest CT, analysed for the effects of corticosteroid treatment and exposure (antigen) avoidance on survival and lung-function trajectories. Retrospective cohort — observational evidence, labelled as such.
cards.result: Fibrotic patients were declining before treatment (forced vital capacity falling 0.56% predicted per month) and had a median survival of 9.2 years. Corticosteroid treatment and exposure avoidance did not result in survival differences in fibrotic disease, and corticosteroids produced no therapeutic effect on FVC or DLCO in the fibrotic group — (the treatment made no difference) — while in non-fibrotic patients both corticosteroids and avoidance were followed by FVC and DLCO increases. For antigen avoidance in fibrotic disease there was only a positive numerical trend for FVC (P = 0.15), which the authors leave as unresolved.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, single-centre, and treatment was not randomised — patients given steroids may have been declining faster to begin with (confounding by indication). Its record carries no MeSH list, so the fallback line is used and the debt is declared in the part summary.
cards.source: De Sadeleer LJ et al. Effects of Corticosteroid Treatment and Antigen Avoidance in a Large Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis Cohort: A Single-Centre Cohort Study. Journal of clinical medicine. 2018. PMID: 30577667. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Morisset 2017: starting mycophenolate or azathioprine in chronic HP was followed by a 4.2-point DLCO improvement at 1 year, but FVC did not significantly improve (+0.5%, P = 0.46)
cards.summary: Morisset 2017: starting mycophenolate or azathioprine in chronic HP was followed by a 4.2-point DLCO improvement at 1 year, but FVC did not significantly improve (+0.5%, P = 0.46)
cards.type: Retrospective multicentre cohort study, Chest 2017
cards.people: 70 patients with chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis treated with mycophenolate mofetil (51) or azathioprine (19) at four interstitial lung disease centres, with lung-function trajectories before and after treatment initiation modelled over a median 11 months of follow-up. Retrospective cohort — observational evidence, labelled as such.
cards.result: Before treatment, FVC and DLCO percent predicted were declining at 0.12% and 0.10% per month respectively. After starting mycophenolate or azathioprine, FVC change at 1 year was +0.5% (P = 0.46 — no significant change), while DLCO improved by 4.2% at 1 year (P < 0.001); in the mycophenolate-only subgroup, FVC rose a non-significant 1.3% (P = 0.103) and DLCO 3.9% (P < 0.001). A gas-transfer signal without an FVC effect, in a before–after design with no untreated comparison group.
cards.watchOut: Before–after comparisons invite regression to the mean and survivor bias (patients must live and stay on drug to be measured at 1 year); concurrent prednisone use was adjusted for but not randomised. The slate dated this paper 2018; the record is Chest 2017 — corrected on the face.
cards.source: Morisset J et al. Use of Mycophenolate Mofetil or Azathioprine for the Management of Chronic Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis. Chest. 2017. PMID: 27816444. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mullin 2024: in 344 patients with fibrotic HP, immunosuppression did not change lung function or symptoms, and was associated with worse survival when the antigen was unknown (relative HR 2.65)
cards.summary: Mullin 2024: in 344 patients with fibrotic HP, immunosuppression did not change lung function or symptoms, and was associated with worse survival when the antigen was unknown (relative HR 2.65)
cards.type: Retrospective multicentre registry cohort study, Chest 2024
cards.people: 344 patients with fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis in the Canadian Registry for Pulmonary Fibrosis, by causative antigen (avian 93, mold 88, other 15, unknown 148); treatment defined as mycophenolate at least 1,000 mg/day or azathioprine at least 75 mg/day for at least 30 days, taken by 58%. Retrospective registry cohort — observational evidence, labelled as such.
cards.result: There was no change in lung function or symptom scores with initiation of immunosuppression in the full cohort. Immunosuppression was not associated with a survival change in avian-antigen disease (relative hazard ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.11 to 1.59; P = 0.20) or mold-antigen disease (1.13, 0.26 to 4.97; P = 0.88), but in patients whose causative antigen was unknown, survival was worse on immunosuppression (relative hazard ratio 2.65, 95% CI 1.01 to 6.92; P = 0.047). Absolute survival rates are not printed in the record's abstract, so the relative figure stands with that caveat.
cards.watchOut: The unknown-antigen harm signal is one subgroup among several with a lower interval bound of 1.01 — hypothesis-generating, and confounded if patients with unidentified antigen were also those still being exposed. It argues for antigen hunting before immunosuppression, not for a proven drug harm.
cards.source: Mullin ML et al. Impact of Antigen Exposure on Outcomes and Treatment Response in Fibrotic Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis. Chest. 2024. PMID: 38128609. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: in fibrotic HP no drug has been shown to slow decline — steroids made no difference in the fibrotic cohort, mycophenolate shows a DLCO-only signal, and antigen avoidance remains unproven (weak, observational evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: in fibrotic HP no drug has been shown to slow decline — steroids made no difference in the fibrotic cohort, mycophenolate shows a DLCO-only signal, and antigen avoidance remains unproven (weak, observational evidence)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded observational cohorts above (De Sadeleer 2018, n = 202 with 109 fibrotic; Morisset 2017, n = 70; Mullin 2024, n = 344) — the evidence base the ATS/JRS/ALAT 2020 hypersensitivity pneumonitis guideline also rests on; no dedicated randomised trial of any of these treatments in fibrotic HP exists.
cards.result: Read together, the cohorts are close to null for the fibrotic phenotype: corticosteroids made no difference to survival or lung function in fibrotic patients (De Sadeleer), though they helped non-fibrotic disease in the same cohort; mycophenolate/azathioprine was followed by a statistically significant DLCO improvement but no significant FVC change (Morisset); and registry immunosuppression changed neither lung function nor symptoms, with a possible survival penalty when the antigen was never identified (Mullin). Antigen avoidance — the one intervention every guideline puts first — has only a non-significant FVC trend (P = 0.15) in fibrotic disease in these data; its support is mechanistic and from non-fibrotic disease, and it is printed here as unproven rather than effective. Antifibrotic therapy for the progressive phenotype is a separate question (INBUILD subgroup context; nintedanib in progressive fibrosis is home on #2783 and pirfenidone on #3951) and is not re-carded here. The stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence) because the base is entirely observational and the fibrotic-phenotype results are null-to-mixed.
cards.watchOut: All three cohorts are retrospective with treatment chosen clinically; none can exclude confounding by indication, and none randomised antigen avoidance — the honest summary is an evidence absence for fibrotic HP treatment, not proof that nothing works.
cards.source: Synthesis of De Sadeleer LJ et al., J Clin Med 2018 (PMID: 30577667); Morisset J et al., Chest 2017 (PMID: 27816444); Mullin ML et al., Chest 2024 (PMID: 38128609). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: PREDMETH: first-line methotrexate was non-inferior to prednisone for FVC change at 24 weeks in new pulmonary sarcoidosis — with a different, not smaller, side-effect burden
shelves.question: In adults with newly diagnosed pulmonary sarcoidosis requiring treatment, is first-line methotrexate non-inferior to prednisone for lung-function change, with fewer glucocorticoid side effects?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Methotrexate/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Netherlands · Prednisone/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Sarcoidosis, Pulmonary/diagnosis,drug therapy,physiopathology · Vital Capacity/drug effects,physiology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial caps the stamp. PREDMETH (138 treatment-naive adults, open-label non-inferiority) found first-line methotrexate non-inferior to prednisone for the 24-week change in percent predicted FVC (adjusted difference −1.17 points, 95% CI −4.27 to 1.93; margin 5 points), with similar overall adverse-event rates but a different profile — less weight gain, insomnia and appetite increase; more nausea, fatigue and liver-test abnormality. Two second-line methotrexate cohorts are carded as labelled context only. The slice is genuinely unhomed: #3955 is methotrexate as steroid-sparer and #2798 is infliximab in refractory disease; neither is re-carded.

cards.headline: PREDMETH (2025): first-line methotrexate was non-inferior to prednisone for 24-week FVC change in new pulmonary sarcoidosis (adjusted difference −1.17 points, 95% CI −4.27 to 1.93; margin 5)
cards.summary: PREDMETH (2025): first-line methotrexate was non-inferior to prednisone for 24-week FVC change in new pulmonary sarcoidosis (adjusted difference −1.17 points, 95% CI −4.27 to 1.93; margin 5)
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomised non-inferiority trial (PREDMETH), N Engl J Med 2025
cards.people: 138 treatment-naive adults with pulmonary sarcoidosis requiring treatment, randomised 1:1 at multiple centres to prednisone (70) or methotrexate (68) on prespecified schedules, in an open-label non-inferiority trial. Primary endpoint: mean change in percent predicted forced vital capacity from baseline to week 24.
cards.result: Unadjusted mean FVC change at week 24 was +6.75 percentage points (95% CI 4.50 to 8.99) on prednisone and +6.11 points (3.72 to 8.50) on methotrexate. The adjusted between-group difference was −1.17 percentage points (95% CI −4.27 to 1.93), inside the 5-point non-inferiority margin — methotrexate was non-inferior. Adverse events occurred in a similar percentage in both groups, but their character differed as expected: weight gain, insomnia and increased appetite were most common with prednisone; nausea, fatigue and abnormal liver-function tests were among the most common with methotrexate. The record notes methotrexate's slower onset of action as its known trade-off.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and 24 weeks: non-inferiority on a lung-function endpoint at 6 months does not settle relapse after stopping, extrapulmonary disease, or long-term toxicity — and the interval (−4.27 to 1.93) still allows methotrexate to be up to about 4 points worse.
cards.source: Kahlmann V et al. First-Line Treatment of Pulmonary Sarcoidosis with Prednisone or Methotrexate. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40387020. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04314193, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Vorselaars 2013 (second-line context): in 200 patients needing second-line therapy, methotrexate spared prednisone as well as azathioprine did, with fewer infections (18.1% vs 34.6%)
cards.summary: Vorselaars 2013 (second-line context): in 200 patients needing second-line therapy, methotrexate spared prednisone as well as azathioprine did, with fewer infections (18.1% vs 34.6%)
cards.type: Retrospective multicentre cohort study (second-line therapy), Chest 2013
cards.people: 200 patients with sarcoidosis starting second-line therapy at international centres — 145 methotrexate, 55 azathioprine — followed retrospectively for up to 2 years. This is second-line, steroid-sparing context for methotrexate's efficacy and side-effect profile, NOT first-line head-to-head evidence; the distinction is printed on the face.
cards.result: Prednisone daily dose fell by a mean of 6.32 mg/year on therapy, with similar steroid-sparing capacity for methotrexate and azathioprine; 70% of patients completing 1 year reduced prednisone by at least 10 mg/day. FEV1 rose a mean of 52 mL/year (P = 0.006) and vital capacity 95 mL/year (P = 0.001) across both groups. Infections were commoner on azathioprine (34.6% vs 18.1%, P = 0.01); other side effects did not differ. Methotrexate's ability to hold lung function while prednisone is withdrawn — the property PREDMETH later tested head-to-head — is visible here a decade earlier.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, no untreated or prednisone-only comparator, and a second-line population (patients who had already failed or not tolerated steroids) — it supports methotrexate's plausibility and tolerability, not the first-line claim itself.
cards.source: Vorselaars ADM et al. Methotrexate vs azathioprine in second-line therapy of sarcoidosis. Chest. 2013. PMID: 23538719. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Fang 2019 (second-line real-world context): 81.7% of 60 pulmonary sarcoidosis patients responded to methotrexate on imaging, with prednisone sparing in responders
cards.summary: Fang 2019 (second-line real-world context): 81.7% of 60 pulmonary sarcoidosis patients responded to methotrexate on imaging, with prednisone sparing in responders
cards.type: Retrospective single-centre real-world study, Sarcoidosis Vasc Diffuse Lung Dis 2020
cards.people: 60 patients with pulmonary sarcoidosis treated with methotrexate (various doses, at least 3 months, without folic-acid supplementation) at a single centre after progression despite corticosteroids or corticosteroid intolerance, assessed retrospectively by high-resolution CT response, symptom scores and prednisone dose. Second-line context only, like the card above.
cards.result: 49 patients (81.7%) were assessed as methotrexate responders by CT, with no significant difference in response rate across dose groups; responders' quality-of-life score (St George's Respiratory Questionnaire) improved from a median 16.7 to 10.7 (P = 0.029), and the corticosteroid-sparing effect was confirmed in responders (P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, uncontrolled and responder-defined: patients who did not respond or stopped early shape the denominator less visibly, and 'response' here is imaging-based. Carded only as supporting real-world tolerability/efficacy context for methotrexate in lung disease.
cards.source: Fang et al. Effectiveness and tolerability of methotrexate in pulmonary sarcoidosis: A single center real-world study. Sarcoidosis, vasculitis, and diffuse lung diseases : official journal of WASOG. 2019. PMID: 32476957. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one non-inferiority trial makes first-line methotrexate a legitimate alternative to prednisone for lung function — POSSIBLE, resting on PREDMETH alone
cards.summary: Synthesis: one non-inferiority trial makes first-line methotrexate a legitimate alternative to prednisone for lung function — POSSIBLE, resting on PREDMETH alone
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports above: PREDMETH (138 randomised, first-line head-to-head) plus two second-line context cohorts (Vorselaars 2013, n = 200; Fang 2019, n = 60) that are labelled as context and do not answer the first-line question themselves.
cards.result: The first-line slice was genuinely unhomed: shelf #3955 covers methotrexate only as a steroid-sparing add-on in acute sarcoidosis (Baughman 2000) and #2798 covers infliximab in refractory disease — neither is re-carded here. PREDMETH answers the new question directly: at 24 weeks, methotrexate's FVC improvement (+6.11 points) was non-inferior to prednisone's (+6.75), with an adjusted difference of −1.17 points whose interval stays inside the 5-point margin, and with the expected side-effect trade — prednisone's weight gain, insomnia and appetite increase against methotrexate's nausea, fatigue and liver-test abnormalities, at similar overall adverse-event rates. The second-line cohorts show the same drug holding lung function while prednisone is tapered, which supports plausibility but adds no first-line weight. A single open-label trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE: relapse after treatment ends, slower onset in patients who need rapid control, and long-term methotrexate monitoring all remain open.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority is not equality: the confidence interval allows a real, smaller benefit for prednisone, and 24 weeks says nothing about the relapses that define sarcoidosis over years.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kahlmann V et al., N Engl J Med 2025 (PMID: 40387020); Vorselaars ADM et al., Chest 2013 (PMID: 23538719); Fang et al., Sarcoidosis Vasc Diffuse Lung Dis 2019 (PMID: 32476957). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: ABPA: medium-dose prednisolone matched high-dose, and adding itraconazole has not been shown to prevent relapse
shelves.question: In adults with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, what glucocorticoid regimen (dose and duration, with or without an azole) best achieves remission without relapse?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Aspergillosis, Allergic Bronchopulmonary/complications,diagnostic imaging,drug therapy,physiopathology · Asthma/complications,diagnostic imaging,drug therapy,physiopathology · Bronchiectasis/complications,diagnostic imaging,drug therapy,physiopathology · Disease Progression · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Humans · Male · Prednisolone/administration & dosage · Severity of Illness Index · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · Treatment Outcome · Vital Capacity · Young Adult · Administration, Oral · Antifungal Agents/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Aspergillosis, Allergic Bronchopulmonary/complications,drug therapy · Asthma/complications · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Itraconazole/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Prednisolone/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Respiratory Function Tests · Antifungal Agents/therapeutic use · Asthma/complications,drug therapy · Glucocorticoids · Immunoglobulin E · Itraconazole · Prednisolone
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised trials from one specialist programme, capped at POSSIBLE for that single-programme base. On dose: medium-dose prednisolone matched high-dose on exacerbations at 1 year (50% vs 40.9%) and glucocorticoid dependence at 2 years (14.6% vs 11.4%), with a significantly lower cumulative dose and fewer side effects — so more steroid bought no protection against relapse. On drug choice: prednisolone alone produced a composite response in 100% vs 88% on itraconazole alone at 6 weeks, with similar IgE falls, exacerbations and time to first exacerbation, but significantly more side effects. Adding itraconazole to prednisolone showed only a trend to fewer 1-year exacerbations (20.6% vs 33%, P=.054). The regimen the record supports is a medium-dose glucocorticoid course, with an azole as an alternative or adjunct rather than a proven relapse-sparer. Itraconazole added to steroids in glucocorticoid-dependent ABPA is a different question, homed on Shelf #4255, and its trials are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Agarwal 2016: medium-dose prednisolone matched high-dose in ABPA — exacerbations 50% vs 40.9% at 1 year, glucocorticoid dependence 14.6% vs 11.4% at 2 years — with significantly less cumulative steroid and fewer side effects
cards.summary: Agarwal 2016: medium-dose prednisolone matched high-dose in ABPA — exacerbations 50% vs 40.9% at 1 year, glucocorticoid dependence 14.6% vs 11.4% at 2 years — with significantly less cumulative steroid and fewer side effects
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, Eur Respir J 2016
cards.people: 92 treatment-naive adults with acute-stage allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis complicating asthma, randomised to high-dose (n=44) or medium-dose (n=48) oral prednisolone in a single-centre randomised trial. The record's abstract does not state the milligram doses of the two protocols.
cards.result: Primary outcomes did not differ: exacerbation after 1 year occurred in 40.9% on high-dose vs 50% on medium-dose (P=.59), and glucocorticoid-dependent ABPA after 2 years in 11.4% vs 14.6% (P=.88). Composite response rates at 6 weeks were significantly higher in the high-dose group, but improvement in lung function and time to first exacerbation were similar. Cumulative glucocorticoid dose and side effects were significantly higher in the high-dose group. The authors conclude medium-dose glucocorticoids are as effective and safer than high-dose in ABPA.
cards.watchOut: The early composite-response advantage for high-dose did not translate into fewer exacerbations or less steroid dependence — the outcomes that define 'remission without relapse' — while its harms were significantly greater. Single-centre trial from the programme that produced all three cards on this shelf.

cards.headline: Agarwal 2018: prednisolone beat itraconazole for early response in acute ABPA (composite response 100% vs 88%, P=.007), but exacerbations, IgE fall and time to first exacerbation were similar — and side effects were significantly fewer on itraconazole
cards.summary: Agarwal 2018: prednisolone beat itraconazole for early response in acute ABPA (composite response 100% vs 88%, P=.007), but exacerbations, IgE fall and time to first exacerbation were similar — and side effects were significantly fewer on itraconazole
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (unblinded), Chest 2018
cards.people: 131 treatment-naive adults with acute-stage allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis complicating asthma, randomised unblinded to oral prednisolone (n=63) or itraconazole (n=68), each for 4 months.
cards.result: Composite response at 6 weeks was significantly higher on prednisolone (100% vs 88%; P=.007). The percent decline in IgE after 6 weeks and 3 months, the numbers with exacerbations after 1 and 2 years, time to first exacerbation (mean 437 vs 442 days) and improvement in lung function after 6 weeks were all similar between groups. Treatment side effects were significantly higher in the glucocorticoid arm (P<.001). The authors conclude prednisolone is more effective at inducing response, while itraconazole remains an attractive alternative with fewer side effects.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded, and the steroid's win is on a 6-week composite response — by 1–2 years the relapse outcomes the question asks about were indistinguishable, so this card supports prednisolone for induction speed, not for relapse prevention.
cards.source: Agarwal R et al. A Randomized Trial of Itraconazole vs Prednisolone in Acute-Stage Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis Complicating Asthma. Chest. 2018. PMID: 29331473. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01321827, stated in the record's abstract. cards.headline: Agarwal 2022: adding itraconazole to prednisolone only trended to fewer 1-year exacerbations in ABPA (20.6% vs 33%, P=.054); no one in either arm became glucocorticoid-dependent
cards.summary: Agarwal 2022: adding itraconazole to prednisolone only trended to fewer 1-year exacerbations in ABPA (20.6% vs 33%, P=.054); no one in either arm became glucocorticoid-dependent
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, Eur Respir J 2022
cards.people: 191 treatment-naive adults with acute-stage allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis complicating asthma, randomised to prednisolone alone for 4 months (n=94) or prednisolone for 4 months plus itraconazole for 6 months (n=97).
cards.result: The 1-year exacerbation rate was 33% on prednisolone alone vs 20.6% on the combination (P=.054) — a trend, not a significant difference. No participant in either group progressed to glucocorticoid-dependent ABPA within 24 months. All subjects in both groups had a composite response at 6 weeks, with similar IgE declines (mean 47.6% vs 45.5%) and similar mean time to first exacerbation (417 days overall). No participant required therapy modification for treatment-emergent adverse events. The authors call for a three-arm multicentre trial to define the best strategy.
cards.watchOut: P=.054 is not a demonstrated benefit: the combination's relapse advantage remains a trend in a single-centre trial, and printing it as proven would overstate the record. All three trials come from the same investigator programme, which is why the stamp is capped.
cards.source: Agarwal R et al. A randomised trial of prednisolone versus prednisolone and itraconazole in acute-stage allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis complicating asthma. cards.headline: Synthesis: a medium-dose glucocorticoid course is the regimen the randomised record supports for acute ABPA — higher doses and routine azole addition have not been shown to prevent relapse
cards.summary: Synthesis: a medium-dose glucocorticoid course is the regimen the randomised record supports for acute ABPA — higher doses and routine azole addition have not been shown to prevent relapse
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three randomised trials carded above (92, 131 and 191 adults with acute-stage ABPA complicating asthma; 414 randomised in total), all from the Agarwal programme.
cards.result: Read together: dose escalation fails (medium-dose tied high-dose on exacerbations and steroid dependence, with fewer harms); prednisolone induces response more reliably than itraconazole alone (100% vs 88%) but at significantly greater side-effect cost, with relapse outcomes tied; and adding itraconazole to prednisolone has not significantly reduced exacerbations (P=.054). So the best-supported answer to 'which regimen achieves remission without relapse' is a medium-dose prednisolone course, with itraconazole reserved as an alternative for patients who cannot take steroids or as an adjunct of unproven relapse benefit. The itraconazole-in-steroid-dependent-ABPA question lives on Shelf #4255 and is not re-carded here. One programme, no multicentre confirmation: POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
cards.watchOut: Every card is from a single centre and a single investigator group; an independent multicentre replication could move this stamp in either direction, and the trialists themselves call for one.
cards.source: Synthesis of Agarwal R et al. The European respiratory journal. 2016 (PMID: 26585431); Agarwal R et al. Chest. 2018 (PMID: 29331473); Agarwal R et al. The European respiratory journal. 2022 (PMID: 34503983). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: CENTERSTONE: treating the index patient with baloxavir reduced household influenza transmission (9.5% vs 13.4%)
shelves.question: In households with an influenza index case, does treating the index patient with single-dose baloxavir reduce laboratory-confirmed transmission to household contacts compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Antiviral Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Dibenzothiepins/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Drug Resistance, Viral · Family Characteristics · Incidence · Influenza, Human/drug therapy,epidemiology,prevention & control,transmission · Morpholines/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Pyridones/therapeutic use,adverse effects · Triazines/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Virus Shedding/drug effects · Administration, Oral · Influenza A virus/drug effects,isolation & purification · Influenza B virus/drug effects,isolation & purification · Antiviral Agents/therapeutic use · Dibenzothiepins/therapeutic use · Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Influenza, Human/drug therapy · Insurance, Health · Morpholines/therapeutic use · Neuraminidase · Orthomyxoviridae · Oseltamivir/therapeutic use · Pyridones/therapeutic use · Triazines
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised trial programme caps the stamp. In CENTERSTONE (1,457 index patients aged 5–64 treated within 48 hours of symptom onset), single-dose baloxavir given to the index patient reduced laboratory-confirmed transmission to household contacts by day 5: adjusted incidence 9.5% vs 13.4% on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 0.68; adjusted relative risk reduction 29% relative, beside the absolute incidences printed here). Transmission that produced symptoms was not significantly reduced (5.8% vs 7.6%; P=.16). A whole-genome-sequencing re-analysis confirmed the result was not an artefact of community-acquired infections misread as household spread (adjusted OR 0.69 after the most stringent pairing cutoff), and a large Japanese claims study found less household transmission from baloxavir-treated index patients than from oseltamivir-treated ones (observational). The counterweight: drug-resistant viruses emerged in 7.2% of baloxavir-treated index patients. This shelf is about treating the index case to protect contacts — post-exposure prophylaxis of contacts themselves is homed on Shelf #1630 (BLOCKSTONE) and treatment efficacy on Shelf #727, and neither is re-carded here.

cards.headline: CENTERSTONE (Monto 2025): treating the index patient with single-dose baloxavir cut laboratory-confirmed household transmission by day 5 (adjusted incidence 9.5% vs 13.4%; adjusted OR 0.68) — but transmission causing symptoms was not significantly reduced (5.8% vs 7.6%)
cards.summary: CENTERSTONE (Monto 2025): treating the index patient with single-dose baloxavir cut laboratory-confirmed household transmission by day 5 (adjusted incidence 9.5% vs 13.4%; adjusted OR 0.68) — but transmission causing symptoms was not significantly reduced (5.8% vs 7.6%)
cards.type: Phase 3b randomised placebo-controlled trial (CENTERSTONE), N Engl J Med 2025
cards.people: 1,457 influenza-positive index patients aged 5 to 64 years (726 baloxavir, 731 placebo) and 2,681 household contacts, enrolled across the 2019–2024 influenza seasons in a multicountry phase 3b trial; index patients received single-dose baloxavir or placebo within 48 hours of symptom onset.
cards.result: By day 5, transmission of laboratory-confirmed influenza from index patient to household contact was significantly lower on baloxavir (adjusted incidence 9.5% vs 13.4%; adjusted odds ratio 0.68, 95.38% CI 0.50 to 0.93; P=.01), an adjusted relative risk reduction of 29% relative (95.38% CI 12 to 45) beside the absolute incidences above. The first secondary endpoint — transmission by day 5 that resulted in symptoms — was 5.8% vs 7.6% and not significant (adjusted OR 0.75, 95.38% CI 0.50 to 1.12; P=.16). Drug-resistant viruses emerged during follow-up in 7.2% (95% CI 4.1 to 11.6) of baloxavir-group index patients; no resistant viruses were detected in household contacts. No new safety signals were identified.
cards.watchOut: The significant endpoint counts infections detected by testing, including asymptomatic ones; the endpoint patients feel — a contact becoming ill — did not reach significance. A single trial: the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE, and the 7.2% resistance-emergence figure is the standing cost of treating index cases at scale.
cards.source: Monto AS et al. Efficacy of Baloxavir Treatment in Preventing Transmission of Influenza. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40267424. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03969212, stated in the record's abstract. cards.headline: CENTERSTONE sequencing analysis (Lauring 2026): whole-genome sequencing confirmed the transmission pairs were real household spread, and the baloxavir effect survived the most stringent pairing cutoff (adjusted incidence 9.2% vs 12.9%; adjusted OR 0.69)
cards.summary: CENTERSTONE sequencing analysis (Lauring 2026): whole-genome sequencing confirmed the transmission pairs were real household spread, and the baloxavir effect survived the most stringent pairing cutoff (adjusted incidence 9.2% vs 12.9%; adjusted OR 0.69)
cards.type: Secondary genomic analysis of a randomised trial (CENTERSTONE), Clin Infect Dis 2026
cards.people: Households from the CENTERSTONE trial (carded above) with two or more influenza-positive individuals; 259 putative transmission pairs were analysed, with reliable viral sequence data from both members of 145 pairs. This is a secondary analysis of the same trial, not an independent trial.
cards.result: Depending on the sequence-distance cutoff, 10.4% to 14.5% of putative pairs were reclassified as not household transmission (community infection with a matching subtype). Excluding pairs by the most stringent cutoff (0.0002), adjusted transmission incidence was 9.2% (95.38% CI 7.2 to 11.8) on baloxavir vs 12.9% (10.2 to 16.2) on placebo (adjusted OR 0.69, 95.38% CI 0.50 to 0.95). The authors conclude the sequence-based definition supports the trial's primary endpoint.
cards.watchOut: This card strengthens confidence in the trial's internal validity; it adds no new randomised evidence, so it does not lift the single-trial cap on the stamp.
cards.source: Lauring AS et al. Whole genome sequencing of influenza virus transmission pairs confirms the efficacy of baloxavir in reducing household transmission. cards.headline: Komeda 2021 (observational): in Japanese claims data, household transmission followed 18.0% of baloxavir-treated index cases vs 24.2% of oseltamivir-treated ones (adjusted OR for oseltamivir vs baloxavir 1.09) — but baloxavir did not beat the inhaled neuraminidase inhibitors
cards.summary: Komeda 2021 (observational): in Japanese claims data, household transmission followed 18.0% of baloxavir-treated index cases vs 24.2% of oseltamivir-treated ones (adjusted OR for oseltamivir vs baloxavir 1.09) — but baloxavir did not beat the inhaled neuraminidase inhibitors
cards.type: Observational claims-database study, Clin Infect Dis 2021
cards.people: Index patients identified in a Japanese health-insurance claims database for the 2018–2019 season — 84,672 families in the oral baloxavir group and 62,004 in the oral oseltamivir group, with inhaled zanamivir and laninamivir groups as further controls. Household transmission was an influenza diagnosis in a non-index family member on days 3–8. Observational — treatment was not randomised.
cards.result: Household transmission occurred in 17.98% of baloxavir families vs 24.16% of oseltamivir families; the covariate-adjusted odds ratio (oseltamivir/baloxavir) was 1.09 (95% CI 1.05 to 1.12), indicating significantly lower transmission with baloxavir than oseltamivir. Against the inhaled agents the direction reversed or vanished (adjusted OR 0.93 for zanamivir vs baloxavir; 0.99 for laninamivir vs baloxavir), which the authors attribute in part to unmeasured confounding by route of administration.
cards.watchOut: Observational and claims-based: who received baloxavir was chosen, not randomised, household infection was a diagnosis code rather than a laboratory endpoint, and the inhaled-drug comparisons cut against a simple class story. Carded as real-world context for the trial, labelled observational.
cards.source: Komeda T et al. Comparison of Household Transmission of Influenza Virus From Index Patients Treated With Baloxavir Marboxil or Neuraminidase Inhibitors: A Health Insurance Claims Database Study. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2021. PMID: 33103200. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: treating the index case with baloxavir reduces laboratory-confirmed household transmission — one placebo-controlled trial, genomically confirmed, with the symptomatic-transmission endpoint still unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: treating the index case with baloxavir reduces laboratory-confirmed household transmission — one placebo-controlled trial, genomically confirmed, with the symptomatic-transmission endpoint still unproven
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of CENTERSTONE (1,457 index patients, 2,681 household contacts), its whole-genome-sequencing secondary analysis, and one large observational claims comparison (about 147,000 families in the two main groups).
cards.result: The randomised evidence answers the question as posed: yes for laboratory-confirmed transmission by day 5 (9.5% vs 13.4%, adjusted OR 0.68 — a 29% relative risk reduction beside a 3.9-percentage-point absolute difference), not yet for transmission that makes contacts ill (P=.16). The sequencing analysis removes the main measurement objection to the trial, and the claims data are directionally consistent against oseltamivir. What keeps this at POSSIBLE is the single-trial base, the asymptomatic-inclusive primary endpoint, and resistance emerging in 7.2% of treated index patients. Giving baloxavir to the contacts themselves (BLOCKSTONE) is Shelf #1630, and baloxavir's effect on the treated patient's own illness is Shelf #727; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Households, seasons and circulating strains in one trial programme (2019–2024) may not transfer to a season dominated by a different subtype; the trial enrolled index patients aged 5–64, so transmission effects from treating younger children or older adults are extrapolation.
cards.source: Synthesis of Monto AS et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2025 (PMID: 40267424); Lauring AS et al. Clinical infectious diseases. 2026 (PMID: 42592831); Komeda T et al. Clinical infectious diseases. 2021 (PMID: 33103200). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Early oseltamivir in hospitalised influenza: observational data link starting within 2 days to about half the mortality odds — no randomised trial exists
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults with influenza, is early oseltamivir associated with lower mortality than late or no oseltamivir? (Observational evidence only.)
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antiviral Agents/therapeutic use · Child · Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Influenza A Virus, H1N1 Subtype · Influenza, Human/drug therapy,mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Neuraminidase/antagonists & inhibitors · Oseltamivir/therapeutic use · Pandemics · Proportional Hazards Models · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult · Zanamivir/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: All of the evidence on this shelf is observational — there is no randomised trial of oseltamivir timing in hospitalised influenza — so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and the observational label is carried on the stamp line. The direction is consistent across three different designs and eras: the PRIDE individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 29,234 hospitalised patients with 2009 pandemic H1N1 (early treatment within 2 days of symptom onset versus later treatment: adjusted odds ratio for death 0.48, 95% CI 0.41–0.56; each day of delay up to day 5 raised the mortality hazard, adjusted HR 1.23 per day); a Spanish ICU cohort in ventilated pandemic patients (ICU mortality 21.5% with early versus 34.3% with late treatment); and a 2022–23 US sentinel cohort of 840 hospitalised adults (treatment on the admission day versus late or none: adjusted OR for in-hospital death 0.36, 95% CI 0.18–0.72). These are adjusted associations, not proven effects: patients treated early differ from patients treated late, and confounding by indication and immortal-time bias can manufacture exactly this pattern. The neighbouring questions are homed elsewhere: oseltamivir for outpatient illness is live shelf #583, combination baloxavir–oseltamivir in hospital is pack #4799, and avian influenza is pack #5312.

cards.headline: PRIDE individual-patient-data meta-analysis (Muthuri 2014): early neuraminidase inhibitor treatment versus later treatment was associated with half the mortality odds (adjusted OR 0.48, 95% CI 0.41–0.56) in 29,234 hospitalised patients with pandemic H1N1 influenza
cards.summary: PRIDE individual-patient-data meta-analysis (Muthuri 2014): early neuraminidase inhibitor treatment versus later treatment was associated with half the mortality odds (adjusted OR 0.48, 95% CI 0.41–0.56) in 29,234 hospitalised patients with pandemic H1N1 influenza
cards.type: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis of observational studies (PRIDE, Muthuri 2014) — 29,234 patients, observational
cards.people: 29,234 patients of all ages admitted to hospital worldwide with laboratory-confirmed or clinically diagnosed influenza A H1N1pdm09 infection, from 78 studies (January 2009–March 2011). Neuraminidase inhibitor treatment (predominantly oseltamivir) was classified by timing from symptom onset; analyses adjusted for treatment propensity and confounders.
cards.result: Any neuraminidase inhibitor treatment versus none was associated with lower mortality (adjusted OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.70–0.93; p=0.0024). Early treatment (within 2 days of symptom onset) versus later treatment was associated with a reduction in mortality risk (adjusted OR 0.48, 95% CI 0.41–0.56; p<0.0001), and early versus no treatment likewise (adjusted OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.37–0.67). The mortality hazard rose with each day's delay in starting treatment up to day 5 (adjusted HR 1.23 per day, 95% CI 1.18–1.28). The associations were less pronounced and not significant in children. All measures are relative (odds/hazard ratios); the record does not print a single pooled absolute mortality pair.
cards.watchOut: Observational throughout: propensity adjustment cannot remove confounding by indication (clinicians treat deteriorating patients later, and patients must survive long enough to be treated late — immortal-time bias). The population is pandemic H1N1 from 2009–11, all ages; extrapolation to seasonal influenza in older adults is indirect. The study was funded by F Hoffmann-La Roche, the manufacturer of oseltamivir, as stated on the record.
cards.source: Muthuri SG et al. Effectiveness of neuraminidase inhibitors in reducing mortality in patients admitted to hospital with influenza A H1N1pdm09 virus infection: a meta-analysis of individual participant data. Lancet Respir Med. 2014. PMID: 24815805. Registry ID: none in the record. analyses adjusted for treatment propensity and confounders. any neuraminidase inhibitor treatment versus none was associated with lower mortality (adjusted or 0.81, 95% ci 0.70–0.93; p=0.0024). early treatment (within 2 days of symptom onset) versus later treatment was associated with a reduction in mortality risk (adjusted or 0.48, 95% ci 0.41–0.56; p<0.0001), and early versus no treatment likewise (adjusted or 0.50, 95% ci 0.37–0.67). the mortality hazard rose with each day's delay in starting treatment up to day 5 (adjusted hr 1.23 per day, 95% ci 1.18–1.28). the associations were less pronounced and not significant in children. all measures are relative (odds/hazard ratios); cards.headline: Lewis 2025 US sentinel cohort (840 hospitalised adults, 2022–23 season): oseltamivir started on the admission day versus late or never was associated with lower odds of in-hospital death (adjusted OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.18–0.72) and ICU admission (adjusted OR 0.24)
cards.summary: Lewis 2025 US sentinel cohort (840 hospitalised adults, 2022–23 season): oseltamivir started on the admission day versus late or never was associated with lower odds of in-hospital death (adjusted OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.18–0.72) and ICU admission (adjusted OR 0.24)
cards.type: Prospective observational cohort (Lewis 2025) — N = 840, observational
cards.people: 840 adults (aged 18 years or older) hospitalised with laboratory-confirmed influenza A at 24 US hospitals, prospectively enrolled 1 October 2022–21 July 2023: 415 (49%) started oseltamivir on the day of admission (early) and 425 (51%) started later or were not treated. Models adjusted for admission-day severity, age, sex, site and vaccination status.
cards.result: Early treatment was associated with lower peak pulmonary disease severity (proportional adjusted OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.49–0.72) and lower odds of ICU admission (adjusted OR 0.24, 95% CI 0.13–0.47), acute kidney replacement therapy or vasopressor use (adjusted OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.22–0.67), and in-hospital death (adjusted OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.18–0.72). All are relative (adjusted odds) measures from an observational comparison; absolute event rates by group are not printed on the fetched record.
cards.watchOut: 'Early' here means the admission day, not within 2 days of symptom onset — a different clock from PRIDE. Patients not treated at all are pooled with late-treated patients, and untreated patients in routine care are often those judged least ill or, conversely, those in whom influenza was recognised late; either way the comparison is not randomised.
cards.source: Lewis NM et al. Benefit of Early Oseltamivir Therapy for Adults Hospitalized With Influenza A: An Observational Study. Clin Infect Dis. 2025. PMID: 39607747. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rodríguez 2011 Spanish ICU cohort: among 385 ventilated patients with pandemic H1N1 who received oseltamivir, ICU mortality was 21.5% with early (within 2 days) versus 34.3% with late treatment (multivariable OR for early treatment 0.44, 95% CI 0.21–0.87)
cards.summary: Rodríguez 2011 Spanish ICU cohort: among 385 ventilated patients with pandemic H1N1 who received oseltamivir, ICU mortality was 21.5% with early (within 2 days) versus 34.3% with late treatment (multivariable OR for early treatment 0.44, 95% CI 0.21–0.87)
cards.type: Prospective observational ICU cohort (Rodríguez 2011) — 385 treated ventilated patients, observational
cards.people: Prospective observational cohort of ICU patients with confirmed 2009 pandemic influenza A in Spain; 657 enrolled, 404 (61.5%) mechanically ventilated, and 385 ventilated patients who received oseltamivir formed the study group: 79 (20.5%) treated early (within 2 days) and 306 treated later. All received oseltamivir for a median of 10 days.
cards.result: ICU mortality was 34.3% in the late-treatment group versus 21.5% in the early-treatment group (OR 1.9, 95% CI 1.06–3.41) — an absolute difference of about 13 percentage points. Multivariable and propensity-score analyses both identified early treatment as independently associated with reduced ICU mortality (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.21–0.87; propensity OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.22–0.90). ICU stay, hospital stay and ventilator days were all longer in the late group.
cards.watchOut: Only 79 patients were treated early, and 'within 2 days' is timed from a start point the abstract does not fully specify in the fetched record. Sicker patients presenting later in their illness dominate the late group — the classic confounding this design cannot fully remove. Pandemic H1N1 ICU patients are younger and different from typical seasonal-influenza ICU populations.
cards.source: Rodríguez A et al. Impact of early oseltamivir treatment on outcome in critically ill patients with 2009 pandemic influenza A. J Antimicrob Chemother. 2011. PMID: 21385717. cards.headline: Synthesis: three observational designs point the same way — earlier is associated with less death — but no randomised evidence exists, so this stays POSSIBLE and labelled observational
cards.summary: Synthesis: three observational designs point the same way — earlier is associated with less death — but no randomised evidence exists, so this stays POSSIBLE and labelled observational
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: PRIDE individual-patient-data meta-analysis (29,234 hospitalised pandemic-H1N1 patients, 78 studies), a 2022–23 US prospective cohort (840 adults), and a Spanish ICU cohort (385 ventilated treated patients). Outpatient oseltamivir efficacy is homed on live shelf #583, hospital combination therapy on pack #4799, and avian influenza on pack #5312; none is re-carded here.
cards.result: Early versus late treatment: adjusted OR 0.48 (PRIDE) and ICU mortality 21.5% versus 34.3% (Spanish cohort, about 13 percentage points absolute). Admission-day versus late/none: adjusted OR 0.36 for death (US cohort). The consistency across eras (pandemic and seasonal), settings (ward and ICU) and analytic methods (propensity, multivariable, time-dependent models) strengthens the association, but every design shares the same vulnerability — treatment timing is chosen by clinicians and by how ill the patient already is — so a causal mortality claim is not warranted on this record.
cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade this shelf on the basis of guideline recommendations: guidelines rest on this same observational record. A randomised trial of timing in hospitalised influenza has never been done and is unlikely now that early treatment is standard advice.
cards.source: Synthesis of Muthuri SG et al. Lancet Respir Med. 2014 (PMID: 24815805); Lewis NM et al. Clin Infect Dis. 2025 (PMID: 39607747); Rodríguez A et al. J Antimicrob Chemother. 2011 (PMID: 21385717).
