shelves.title: Non-HIV Pneumocystis pneumonia: steroid evidence splits by severity — possible benefit only in respiratory failure, possible harm when given unselectively; no study ranks the TMP-SMX alternatives
shelves.question: In non-HIV immunocompromised adults with Pneumocystis pneumonia, do adjunctive corticosteroids improve survival in hypoxaemic disease, and which alternative to trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole is best when it cannot be used? (Observational evidence.)
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · HIV Seronegativity · Humans · Hypoxia/etiology,therapy · Immunocompetence · Immunocompromised Host · Intubation, Intratracheal/statistics & numerical data · Observational Studies as Topic · Pneumonia, Pneumocystis/drug therapy,mortality,therapy · Respiration, Artificial/statistics & numerical data · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: This is an observational-evidence shelf (the HIV Pneumocystis questions are homed separately on packs #2965 and #2966) and the steroid evidence genuinely splits by severity. Two meta-analyses of overlapping retrospective studies disagree in emphasis: Fujikura 2017 (7 studies) found no mortality benefit overall (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.60–2.67) and none in severe hypoxaemia (OR 0.90, 0.44–1.83); Ding 2020 (16 studies, 2,518 cases) found steroids associated with higher mortality in unselected patients (OR 1.37, 1.07–1.75) but lower mortality in the respiratory-failure subgroup (OR 0.63, 0.41–0.95). The one primary cohort (Pareja 1998, n=30, all with PO2 <65 mm Hg) found faster recovery with high-dose steroids but no mortality difference (44% vs 36%; the treatment made no difference to survival). On the second half of the question the record is thin: no carded study compares atovaquone, pentamidine or clindamycin–primaquine head-to-head in non-HIV disease, so no 'best alternative' can be named; the one comparative treatment study found (Nagai 2024) addresses trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole dose, not alternatives — low dose performed similarly to conventional dose with fewer adverse events. PROPOSED SPLIT for steroids; the alternatives question is an evidence gap, stated as such.

cards.headline: Pareja 1998 (30 patients, all hypoxaemic): high-dose adjunctive steroids shortened ventilation, ICU stay and oxygen use, but in-hospital mortality was 44% versus 36% — the treatment made no difference to survival
cards.summary: Pareja 1998 (30 patients, all hypoxaemic): high-dose adjunctive steroids shortened ventilation, ICU stay and oxygen use, but in-hospital mortality was 44% versus 36% — the treatment made no difference to survival
cards.type: Retrospective cohort (Pareja 1998) — N = 30, observational
cards.people: Retrospective review of 30 adults with histologically confirmed non-HIV Pneumocystis pneumonia at one US tertiary hospital (transplantation 13, long-term immunosuppression 9, chemotherapy for malignancy 8); all had PO2 <65 mm Hg or oxygen saturation <90% on room air. Sixteen received increased high-dose steroids (60 mg or more prednisone-equivalent daily) alongside trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole or pentamidine; 14 stayed on low-dose (30 mg or less) or tapering steroids.
cards.result: The high-dose group needed mechanical ventilation for fewer days (6.3 vs 18.0 days; p=0.047), had shorter ICU stays (8.5 vs 15.8 days; p=0.025) and shorter supplemental-oxygen use (10.0 vs 32.2 days; p=0.05). Intubation rates (75% vs 57%; p=0.442) and in-hospital mortality (44% vs 36%; p=0.722) did not differ — the treatment made no difference to survival in this small cohort.
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients, one centre, 1998 — steroid allocation was the treating team's choice, so sicker or slower-to-improve patients may have been selected for high-dose steroids (or the reverse). Recovery-time endpoints favour steroids but are exactly the endpoints most open to that bias; mortality, the endpoint that matters most, was null.
cards.source: Pareja JG et al. Use of adjunctive corticosteroids in severe adult non-HIV Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia. Chest. 1998. PMID: 9596297. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Fujikura 2017 meta-analysis of 7 observational studies: adjunctive corticosteroids did not affect mortality in non-HIV Pneumocystis pneumonia (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.60–2.67), including in severe hypoxaemia (OR 0.90, 0.44–1.83) — the treatment made no difference
cards.summary: Fujikura 2017 meta-analysis of 7 observational studies: adjunctive corticosteroids did not affect mortality in non-HIV Pneumocystis pneumonia (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.60–2.67), including in severe hypoxaemia (OR 0.90, 0.44–1.83) — the treatment made no difference
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Fujikura 2017) — 7 studies, observational
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis (random-effects) of observational studies of adjunctive corticosteroids in non-HIV Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia; 7 studies eligible. Primary outcome mortality; secondary outcome intubation or mechanical ventilation.
cards.result: Adjunctive corticosteroids were not associated with mortality (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.60–2.67) and showed no benefit in the severe-hypoxaemia subgroup (PaO2 <70 mm Hg; OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.44–1.83) or for intubation/mechanical ventilation (OR 1.34, 95% CI 0.44–4.11) — the treatment made no difference on any pooled outcome. The authors conclude the results warrant a randomised trial.
cards.watchOut: Confidence intervals are wide — this analysis excludes neither moderate benefit nor moderate harm. It pools only 7 of the studies the later Ding analysis includes, and neither meta-analysis can undo the confounding by indication inside every contributing retrospective study.
cards.source: Fujikura Y et al. Adjunctive Corticosteroids for Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia in Non-HIV-infected Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Observational Studies. Arch Bronconeumol. 2017. PMID: 27616706. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ding 2020 meta-analysis of 16 observational studies (2,518 cases): steroids were associated with higher mortality in unselected non-HIV Pneumocystis pneumonia (OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.07–1.75) but lower mortality in respiratory failure (OR 0.63, 0.41–0.95)
cards.summary: Ding 2020 meta-analysis of 16 observational studies (2,518 cases): steroids were associated with higher mortality in unselected non-HIV Pneumocystis pneumonia (OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.07–1.75) but lower mortality in respiratory failure (OR 0.63, 0.41–0.95)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Ding 2020) — 16 studies, 2,518 cases, observational
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis (fixed-effects) of retrospective observational studies of adjunctive corticosteroid treatment in non-HIV Pneumocystis pneumonia, searched 1989–2019; 2,518 cases from 16 studies. Subgroups: all cases, hypoxaemia (PaO2 <70 mm Hg), and respiratory failure (PaO2 <60 mm Hg).
cards.result: In all cases pooled, corticosteroids were associated with increased mortality (OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.07–1.75; p=0.01). In hypoxaemic patients the association pointed to benefit without reaching significance (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.47–1.01; p=0.05), and in respiratory failure it was significant (OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.41–0.95; p=0.03). The authors advise withholding steroids in patients without hypoxaemia and call for a randomised trial in respiratory failure.
cards.watchOut: The harm signal in unselected patients and the benefit signal in respiratory failure come from the same confounded retrospective base: clinicians give steroids to the sickest patients, which can produce apparent harm overall and apparent benefit within the sickest stratum. The severity gradient is biologically plausible (it mirrors the proven HIV pattern) but it is not trial evidence.
cards.source: Ding L et al. Adjunctive corticosteroids may be associated with better outcome for non-HIV Pneumocystis pneumonia with respiratory failure: a systemic review and meta-analysis of observational studies. cards.headline: Nagai 2024 (136 patients): low-dose trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole had similar 30-day mortality to conventional dose (6.7% vs 18.4% adjusted comparison, p=0.080) with far fewer grade 3+ adverse events (29.8% vs 59.0%) — a dosing answer, not an alternatives ranking
cards.summary: Nagai 2024 (136 patients): low-dose trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole had similar 30-day mortality to conventional dose (6.7% vs 18.4% adjusted comparison, p=0.080) with far fewer grade 3+ adverse events (29.8% vs 59.0%) — a dosing answer, not an alternatives ranking
cards.type: Retrospective observational cohort (Nagai 2024) — N = 136, observational
cards.people: Multicentre retrospective cohort (3 Japanese institutions, 2006–2021) of 136 patients with non-HIV Pneumocystis pneumonia treated with trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole: low dose (trimethoprim <12.5 mg/kg/day; n=55) versus conventional dose (12.5–20 mg/kg/day; n=81), adjusted by propensity overlap weighting. Mean age 70.7 years; 55.1% women.
cards.result: After adjustment there was no significant difference in 30-day mortality (6.7% vs 18.4%; p=0.080) or 180-day mortality (14.6% vs 26.1%; p=0.141). Grade 3 or higher adverse events were significantly less frequent with low dose (29.8% vs 59.0%; p=0.005), especially nausea and hyponatraemia; initial treatment completion was 43.3% versus 29.6% (p=0.158).
cards.watchOut: This card answers 'how much trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole', not 'what instead of it'. No carded study compares atovaquone, pentamidine or clindamycin–primaquine against each other or against trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole in non-HIV disease; any ranking of alternatives would be invention, and this shelf does not offer one.

cards.headline: Synthesis: steroids split by severity in confounded data; the alternatives half of the question has no comparative evidence to synthesise
cards.summary: Synthesis: steroids split by severity in confounded data; the alternatives half of the question has no comparative evidence to synthesise
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one small hypoxaemic cohort (Pareja 1998, n=30), two overlapping meta-analyses of retrospective studies (Fujikura 2017, 7 studies; Ding 2020, 16 studies and 2,518 cases), and one dosing cohort (Nagai 2024, n=136). HIV-associated Pneumocystis steroid and prophylaxis questions are homed on packs #2965 and #2966 and are not re-carded here.
cards.result: Steroids: null overall in one meta-analysis, harmful-looking overall but beneficial-looking in respiratory failure in the other, and faster recovery without a survival difference in the only primary cohort. The defensible reading mirrors Ding's own advice — reserve adjunctive steroids for hypoxaemic/respiratory-failure disease, do not give them to non-hypoxaemic patients — while grading the whole claim as observational and split. Alternatives to trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole: no head-to-head comparative evidence in non-HIV disease was found this session; choice among atovaquone, pentamidine and clindamycin–primaquine rests on toxicity, route and severity conventions, not on carded comparative data.
cards.watchOut: MeSH debt: the Ding 2020 record carried no MeSH terms in the fetched record, so its card uses the exact fallback wording; the pack-level MeSH is Fujikura 2017's. A randomised steroid trial in non-HIV Pneumocystis pneumonia remains the missing study both meta-analyses call for.

shelves.title: The alveolar gas equation and the A–a gradient: alveolar PO2 is set by inspired oxygen, barometric pressure and the PaCO2/respiratory-quotient term; the gradient across to arterial blood is small at rest in health, widens with age and at high exercise intensity, and widens early in lung disease through V/Q mismatch
shelves.question: How does the alveolar gas equation determine alveolar oxygen tension, and what determines the size of the alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient in health and disease?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Carbon Dioxide/blood · Female · Humans · Japan · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen/blood · Partial Pressure · Reference Standards · Reference Values
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, gas-exchange chapters). The textbook account: alveolar oxygen tension is given by the alveolar gas equation — PAO2 = FiO2 × (barometric pressure − water-vapour pressure) − PaCO2/R, where R is the respiratory exchange ratio — so alveolar PO2 rises with inspired oxygen and falls as PaCO2 rises. Arterial PO2 sits below alveolar PO2 by the alveolar–arterial (A–a) gradient, whose textbook determinants are ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) inequality (the dominant term even in health), anatomical shunt/venous admixture, and, at high cardiac outputs or in disease, alveolar–capillary diffusion limitation; mixed venous oxygen content modulates the effect of any given mismatch. The carded human studies fit that frame. In 78 healthy elderly subjects the A–a difference stayed within a maximum of 20.2 Torr while PaO2 fell only slowly with age (regression slope −0.126 Torr per year) (Yamasawa 1992). During incremental exercise in 6 healthy men the gradient barely moved at low work rates and then rose rapidly past a threshold at high metabolic rates (Powers 1991; N=6, labelled). In mild COPD — FEV1 still 94% predicted — the gradient was already elevated at rest and throughout exercise, alongside higher dead-space fraction (Elbehairy 2015). Note: the classic Mellemgaard 1966 components study was located by title search this session but its PubMed record carries no abstract, so no numbers could be sourced from a fetched record and it is NOT carded, per the standing rule. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Yamasawa 1992: in 78 healthy elderly subjects PaO2 averaged 89.8 Torr and the A–a oxygen difference never exceeded 20.2 Torr
cards.summary: Yamasawa 1992: in 78 healthy elderly subjects PaO2 averaged 89.8 Torr and the A–a oxygen difference never exceeded 20.2 Torr
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (reference values in healthy elderly) — N = 78
cards.people: 78 healthy Japanese subjects older than 60 years (oldest a 96-year-old woman), all non-smokers, independently ambulant, with no respiratory symptoms, chest disease, cardiac disease or obesity; arterial puncture performed recumbent.
cards.result: PaO2 ranged from 79 to 106 Torr with a mean of 89.8 Torr; PaCO2 ranged from 32 to 48 Torr (mean 39.6 Torr). The maximum alveolar–arterial O2 tension difference was 20.2 Torr (and the maximum arterial–alveolar N2 difference 11.6 Torr). The age regression was PaO2 = 99.32 − 0.126 × age, with a residual standard deviation of 6.06 Torr — arterial oxygen tension declines only slowly with age in health, and the gradient remains modest.
cards.watchOut: Recumbent, resting measurements in one ethnic cohort; posture and altitude change the numbers. The record reports the maximum gradient, not a mean gradient, and it is presented as such.

cards.headline: Powers 1991: the A–a gradient stayed nearly flat at low exercise intensities, then rose rapidly past a threshold at high work rates (N=6, labelled)
cards.summary: Powers 1991: the A–a gradient stayed nearly flat at low exercise intensities, then rose rapidly past a threshold at high work rates (N=6, labelled)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (incremental exercise) — N = 6 (small N, labelled on the face)
cards.people: Six healthy male subjects performing incremental exercise at sea level (inspired PO2 149 Torr), with alveolar–arterial PO2 difference measured across metabolic rates.
cards.result: An alinear (threshold) model best described the relationship between the A–a PO2 difference and metabolic rate: only small increases occurred at low work rates, followed by a rapid increase at higher work rates, with the inflection point confirmed mathematically. The authors concluded that gas-exchange efficiency is unaltered from rest during low-to-moderate exercise, but high-intensity exercise compromises it, as shown by significant widening of the A–a PO2 difference.
cards.watchOut: Classic small study: N=6 is printed on the face per the labelling rule for sub-10 physiology studies. It establishes the shape of the exercise response, not a population value.
cards.source: Powers SK et al. Evidence for an alveolar-arterial PO2 gradient threshold during incremental exercise. International journal of sports medicine. 1991. PMID: 1889942. cards.headline: Elbehairy 2015: even in mild COPD (FEV1 94% predicted) the A–a gradient was elevated at rest and throughout exercise, with higher dead-space fraction
cards.summary: Elbehairy 2015: even in mild COPD (FEV1 94% predicted) the A–a gradient was elevated at rest and throughout exercise, with higher dead-space fraction
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (case–control exercise study) — N = 22 (11 COPD, 11 controls)
cards.people: 22 subjects — 11 patients with GOLD grade 1B COPD and 11 age-matched healthy controls — undergoing physiological testing and a symptom-limited incremental cycle exercise test with arterial blood-gas collection; patients' post-bronchodilator FEV1 was 94 ± 10% predicted.
cards.result: Arterial blood gases stayed within the normal range and effective alveolar ventilation did not differ from controls, but the alveolar–arterial O2 tension gradient was elevated at rest and throughout exercise in COPD (P<0.05), and the ventilatory equivalent for CO2, dead-space/tidal-volume ratio and arterial-to-end-tidal CO2 difference were all higher during exercise (P<0.05). Peak oxygen uptake was reduced (80 ± 18 vs 113 ± 24% predicted). Within all subjects, dead-space fraction correlated with the ventilatory equivalent for CO2 during submaximal exercise (r=0.780, P<0.001) — V/Q inequality widens the gradient before spirometry or resting gases become frankly abnormal.
cards.watchOut: The record states the gradient was elevated (P<0.05) without printing its absolute values in the abstract, so none are claimed here; the card is used for the direction and the mechanism (V/Q inequality/dead space), which the record does support.
cards.source: Elbehairy AF et al. Pulmonary Gas Exchange Abnormalities in Mild Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease. Implications for Dyspnea and Exercise Intolerance. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2015. PMID: 25826478. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the equation sets alveolar PO2 from inspired gas and PaCO2; the gradient then reports V/Q inequality, shunt and diffusion — small at rest, wider with age, heavy exercise and early disease
cards.summary: Synthesis: the equation sets alveolar PO2 from inspired gas and PaCO2; the gradient then reports V/Q inequality, shunt and diffusion — small at rest, wider with age, heavy exercise and early disease
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology. No new data.
cards.result: Alveolar PO2 is an input-side quantity: it is fixed by the alveolar gas equation once inspired oxygen, barometric pressure, PaCO2 and the exchange ratio are known (textbook account). The A–a gradient is the output-side check on transfer: at most 20.2 Torr in healthy elderly subjects at rest (PMID 1569721), nearly unchanged through moderate exercise but widening rapidly at high work rates (PMID 1889942), and already widened at rest in mild COPD through V/Q inequality (PMID 25826478). A widened gradient therefore localises the problem to the lung (mismatch, shunt or diffusion), whereas hypoxaemia with a normal gradient points back to the equation's inputs — hypoventilation or low inspired oxygen. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Scope: the equation and the gradient in health and disease. The shunt fraction itself — the gradient's zero-ventilation extreme — is the next shelf (#6350), and V/Q distributions measured by inert-gas techniques are folded into #6351.

shelves.title: Shunt and venous admixture: the shunt equation divides the flow that bypasses ventilated alveoli by total flow using oxygen contents; 100% oxygen can fully oxygenate blood passing even poorly ventilated units, but blood that never sees an alveolus stays venous — so shunt hypoxaemia is oxygen-refractory, and inert-gas studies show healthy lungs have essentially no shunt on air
shelves.question: What is intrapulmonary shunt and venous admixture, how is the shunt fraction calculated, and why does breathing 100% oxygen correct hypoxaemia from ventilation–perfusion mismatch but not from true shunt?
shelves.mesh: Acetone/blood · Adult · Age Factors · *Air · Carbon Dioxide/blood · Cardiac Output · Chromatography, Gas · Clinical Trials as Topic · Computers · Cyclopropanes/blood · Ethane/blood · Ethyl Ethers/blood · Halothane/blood · Hematocrit · Hemoglobins · Humans · Hydrogen-Ion Concentration · Male · Middle Aged · *Oxygen/blood · Posture · Regional Blood Flow · *Respiration · *Ventilation-Perfusion Ratio
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, pulmonary circulation/gas-exchange chapters). The textbook account: venous admixture is the amount of mixed venous blood that must be added to fully oxygenated end-capillary blood to produce the observed arterial oxygen content, and the shunt fraction follows the shunt equation — Qs/Qt = (Cc′O2 − CaO2)/(Cc′O2 − CvO2), using end-capillary, arterial and mixed venous oxygen contents. True shunt is blood traversing unventilated units (V/Q = 0); low-V/Q units are not shunt, because raising inspired oxygen raises their alveolar PO2 until their end-capillary blood is fully saturated — which is why 100% oxygen corrects V/Q hypoxaemia but cannot correct the shunted fraction, whose blood never contacts alveolar gas. The carded human studies anchor each limb. In 12 normal subjects the inert-gas method found no intrapulmonary shunt breathing air at any age; on 100% oxygen a small shunt appeared (mean 0.5% of cardiac output in the young, 3.2% in older subjects) — absorption collapse of low-V/Q units, exactly as the textbook predicts (Wagner 1974). In 20 patients with acute respiratory failure, venous admixture was 12–63% and fell from 29% to 24% when FiO2 was raised to 1.0 while the inert-gas (true) shunt was unchanged (Lemaire 1985). And the shunt equation works in reverse at the bedside: assuming constant venous admixture, PaO2 at lower FiO2 was predicted from 100%-oxygen data with a regression coefficient of 0.97 in 19 ventilated patients (Ogawa 1989). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Wagner 1974: 12 normal subjects had no intrapulmonary shunt breathing air; on 100% oxygen a small shunt appeared (0.5% young, 3.2% older) — collapse of low-V/Q units
cards.summary: Wagner 1974: 12 normal subjects had no intrapulmonary shunt breathing air; on 100% oxygen a small shunt appeared (0.5% young, 3.2% older) — collapse of low-V/Q units
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (multiple inert gas elimination technique) — N = 12
cards.people: 12 normal subjects aged 21–60 studied with the multiple inert gas elimination technique (six infused inert gases); in 9 the ventilation–perfusion distributions were compared breathing air and 100% oxygen, and in 3 the effects of posture were examined.
cards.result: In four young semirecumbent subjects (21–24 years) the blood-flow and ventilation distributions were near log-normal (95.5% range of V/Q 0.3–2.1) with no intrapulmonary shunt (V/Q of 0) breathing air; on oxygen a shunt developed in three of them, mean 0.5% of cardiac output. The five older subjects (39–60 years) had broader distributions with low-V/Q areas (0.01–0.1) in three, still no shunt on air, but all five developed a shunt on oxygen (mean 3.2%, one reaching 10.7%). Shunt measured on oxygen, Bohr dead space and the alveolar–arterial oxygen difference were all consistent with the distributions.

cards.headline: Lemaire 1985: in 20 patients with acute respiratory failure, venous admixture fell from 29% to 24% on 100% oxygen while true (inert-gas) shunt was unchanged
cards.summary: Lemaire 1985: in 20 patients with acute respiratory failure, venous admixture fell from 29% to 24% on 100% oxygen while true (inert-gas) shunt was unchanged
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (dual-method shunt measurement in respiratory failure) — N = 20
cards.people: 20 patients with acute respiratory failure spanning a wide range of venous admixture (12–63%), studied as FiO2 was increased from their maintenance level to 1.0; intrapulmonary shunt measured both by the conventional oxygen method and by the multiple inert gas elimination technique; 11 had bacterial pneumonia with a low-V/Q mode.
cards.result: Mean venous admixture decreased from 29% to 24% when FiO2 was increased to 1.0, while the inert-gas shunt measurement remained unaltered and the pattern of blood-flow distribution stayed similar in both conditions — even in the pneumonia patients whose low-V/Q units were considered liable to collapse on pure oxygen. No increase in shunt was documented, and the authors concluded that reluctance to measure shunt during 100% oxygen breathing should be re-evaluated.
cards.watchOut: The fall in calculated venous admixture on oxygen is the V/Q component being corrected — the oxygen method counts low-V/Q blood as admixture at low FiO2 — while the inert-gas shunt is the anatomical/true component. Short oxygen exposures; prolonged 100% oxygen can still cause absorption atelectasis, as the Wagner card shows in normals.
cards.source: Lemaire F et al. Intrapulmonary shunt is not increased by 100% oxygen ventilation in acute respiratory failure. Bulletin europeen de physiopathologie respiratoire. 1985. PMID: 2988676. cards.headline: Ogawa 1989: solving the shunt equation in reverse predicted PaO2 at lower FiO2 with a regression coefficient of 0.97 in 19 ventilated patients
cards.summary: Ogawa 1989: solving the shunt equation in reverse predicted PaO2 at lower FiO2 with a regression coefficient of 0.97 in 19 ventilated patients
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (shunt-equation prediction in ventilated patients) — N = 19
cards.people: 19 intubated, mechanically ventilated patients with respiratory failure; arterial and mixed venous blood gases obtained at FiO2 1.0 were used to predict PaO2 at other FiO2 values (23 comparisons), assuming intrapulmonary venous admixture and the arteriovenous oxygen content difference remain constant.
cards.result: PaO2 values predicted by the program (which resolves Adair's equation and the shunt equation inversely) matched measured PaO2 with a regression coefficient of 0.97, more accurate than prediction from the arterial/alveolar oxygen tension ratio (0.91). The authors concluded the approach may help bedside decisions about lowering FiO2 in patients needing high FiO2 — a direct demonstration that a fixed shunt fraction determines how PaO2 responds to inspired oxygen.
cards.watchOut: The prediction rests on the stated assumptions (constant admixture and constant arteriovenous content difference); when cardiac output or oxygen consumption changes, mixed venous content changes and the prediction drifts — the equation's inputs, not the equation, are the limit.

cards.headline: Synthesis: contents, not tensions, define shunt — oxygen saturates every ventilated unit, so only the never-ventilated fraction keeps arterial oxygen down
cards.summary: Synthesis: contents, not tensions, define shunt — oxygen saturates every ventilated unit, so only the never-ventilated fraction keeps arterial oxygen down
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology. No new data.
cards.result: The shunt equation (textbook account) mixes three oxygen contents — end-capillary, arterial and mixed venous — to give the fraction of cardiac output bypassing ventilated alveoli. Human data show each behaviour the equation predicts: no shunt in healthy lungs on air, with a small shunt appearing on 100% oxygen as low-V/Q units collapse (PMID 4601004); a large venous admixture in respiratory failure that partly corrects on oxygen while true shunt does not move (PMID 2988676); and PaO2 across FiO2 values predictable from a single assumed admixture (PMID 2791599). That is the whole clinical test: hypoxaemia that corrects on 100% oxygen is V/Q mismatch; hypoxaemia that does not is true shunt. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Scope: intrapulmonary shunt and venous admixture. Cardiac right-to-left shunts and hepatopulmonary vascular dilatation are disease shelves, not this physiology; the A–a gradient that shunt widens is shelf #6349.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 4601004, 2988676, 2791599), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology. No additional source.

shelves.title: West's zones plus hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction: gravity stacks alveolar, arterial and venous pressures into flow zones from apex to base, imaging confirms posture redistributes flow — but lung structure outweighs gravity — and alveolar hypoxia constricts the feeding vessels within minutes, a response reversed by inhaled nitric oxide and blunted by volatile anaesthetics
shelves.question: How do West's zones of the lung and hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction together determine pulmonary vascular pressures and blood-flow distribution, and what inhibits hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adult · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Carbon Dioxide/blood · Endothelins/blood,metabolism · Female · Humans · Hypoxia/physiopathology · Lung/blood supply,drug effects,metabolism · Male · Methemoglobin/analysis · Nitric Oxide/administration & dosage,pharmacology · Oxygen/blood · Pulmonary Artery/drug effects · Pulmonary Circulation/drug effects · Pulmonary Gas Exchange/drug effects · Stroke Volume/drug effects · Vascular Resistance/drug effects · Vasoconstriction/drug effects · Vasodilation/drug effects · Ventricular Function, Right/drug effects
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, pulmonary circulation chapters). The textbook account of West's zones: in the upright lung, alveolar pressure is roughly uniform while pulmonary arterial and venous pressures rise down the lung under gravity, so flow is set zone by zone — zone 1 (alveolar pressure exceeds arterial: no flow, normally absent), zone 2 (arterial exceeds alveolar exceeds venous: flow set by the arterial–alveolar difference), zone 3 (venous exceeds alveolar: flow set by the arterial–venous difference), with a zone 4 at the base from interstitial pressure. Superimposed on gravity, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (the Euler–Liljestrand mechanism) constricts vessels feeding hypoxic alveoli and diverts blood to ventilated units. The carded human studies support both layers — and qualify the first: perfusion per unit volume rose from upper to lower regions in upright and most other postures in 14 normal volunteers (Amis 1984), and flipping volunteers from upright to head-down clearly redistributed flow from base to apex, yet the authors concluded lung structure is the main determinant and gravity secondary (Ax 2017; N=8, labelled). HPV is directly demonstrable in humans: breathing 12% oxygen raised mean pulmonary artery pressure from 14.7 to 19.8 mmHg in 9 healthy adults, and inhaled nitric oxide (40 ppm) reversed it selectively, with no systemic effect (Frostell 1993; N=9, labelled). What inhibits HPV in practice: volatile anaesthetics — during one-lung ventilation, shunt fraction fell significantly when patients were switched from isoflurane or sevoflurane to propofol, which does not share the inhibition (Abe 1998). The MIGET anchors folded into this row (Wagner's inert-gas distributions) are carded on shelf #6350 for the shunt measurement and are the same dataset that mapped these V/Q distributions. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Amis 1984: in 14 normal volunteers, perfusion per unit alveolar volume increased from upper to lower lung in the upright posture and V/Q fell down the lung
cards.summary: Amis 1984: in 14 normal volunteers, perfusion per unit alveolar volume increased from upper to lower lung in the upright posture and V/Q fell down the lung
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (regional perfusion across postures) — N = 14
cards.people: 14 normal male volunteers studied with a gamma camera in upright, supine, lateral decubitus, prone and prone-suspended postures, using inhaled and infused radioactive krypton isotopes to measure regional perfusion per unit alveolar volume (Q/VA) and ventilation–perfusion ratios.
cards.result: In the vertical axis, Q/VA increased from upper to lower lung regions in the upright, lateral decubitus, prone and prone-suspended postures, but was uniform in the supine posture and within the dependent lung in decubitus. Vertically, V/Q decreased from upper to lower regions in all postures except supine and the dependent decubitus lung. The authors noted that gravity's effects on the vertical distributions are modified when functional residual capacity is low, because perfusion is then more uniformly distributed — the zonal gradient is real in the upright lung and posture-dependent, as the zone model requires.
cards.watchOut: Regional (lobar-scale) measurements, not a direct test of zone boundaries within a lung at one moment; carded for the vertical perfusion gradient and its posture dependence, which the record directly measures.
cards.source: Amis TC et al. Effect of posture on inter-regional distribution of pulmonary perfusion and VA/Q ratios in man. Respiration physiology. 1984. PMID: 6463424. cards.headline: Ax 2017: flipping 8 volunteers from upright to head-down redistributed flow from base to apex — but lung structure, not gravity, was the main determinant (N=8, labelled)
cards.summary: Ax 2017: flipping 8 volunteers from upright to head-down redistributed flow from base to apex — but lung structure, not gravity, was the main determinant (N=8, labelled)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (dual-isotope SPECT perfusion imaging) — N = 8 (small N, labelled on the face)
cards.people: 8 healthy volunteers imaged with quantitative SPECT after intravenous injection of labelled macroaggregated albumin in the upright posture (one tracer) and the head-down posture (a second tracer) on a tilt table, both during tidal breathing; all images acquired supine.
cards.result: The shift from upright to head-down posture caused a clear redistribution of blood flow from basal to apical regions. The authors concluded that posture — and thereby gravity — has a much greater influence between upright and head-down positions than between horizontal postures, but that the results are also consistent with lung structure being the main determinant of regional blood flow and gravity a secondary contributor.
cards.watchOut: Small N, printed on the face per the labelling rule. This card is the modern qualification of the zone model: zones describe the gravitational component correctly, but they are not the whole distribution — a correction to any purely gravity-based reading, stated in the balance.
cards.source: Ax M et al. The influence of gravity on regional lung blood flow in humans: SPECT in the upright and head-down posture. Journal of applied physiology. 2017. PMID: 28336539. cards.headline: Frostell 1993: breathing 12% oxygen raised mean pulmonary artery pressure from 14.7 to 19.8 mmHg in 9 healthy adults, and inhaled nitric oxide reversed it with no systemic effect (N=9, labelled)
cards.summary: Frostell 1993: breathing 12% oxygen raised mean pulmonary artery pressure from 14.7 to 19.8 mmHg in 9 healthy adults, and inhaled nitric oxide reversed it with no systemic effect (N=9, labelled)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (hypoxia challenge with inhaled nitric oxide) — N = 9 (small N, labelled on the face)
cards.people: Nine healthy adults studied awake with pulmonary and radial artery catheters while breathing air, then 12% oxygen in nitrogen, then the same hypoxic mixture containing 40 ppm nitric oxide; a separate phase tested nitric oxide while breathing air.
cards.result: On 12% oxygen, PaO2 fell from 106 ± 4 to 47 ± 2 mmHg, mean pulmonary artery pressure rose from 14.7 ± 0.8 to 19.8 ± 0.9 mmHg, and cardiac output rose from 6.1 ± 0.4 to 7.7 ± 0.6 L/min. Adding 40 ppm nitric oxide at the same FiO2 brought pulmonary artery pressure back down to the air-breathing level (P<0.01) while PaO2 and PaCO2 were unchanged, with no alteration in systemic vascular resistance or mean arterial pressure. Nitric oxide in air changed nothing. The authors concluded inhaled nitric oxide selectively reverses human hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction without systemic vasodilation.
cards.watchOut: Whole-lung hypoxia in volunteers demonstrates the pressor response and its pharmacological reversal; the textbook's regional diversion claim (blood redirected from hypoxic to ventilated units) is the same mechanism read at segmental scale, and the one-lung-ventilation card shows it operating regionally in patients.
cards.source: Frostell CG et al. Inhaled nitric oxide selectively reverses human hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction without causing systemic vasodilation. Anesthesiology. 1993. PMID: 8457043. cards.headline: Abe 1998 randomised trial (n=20): during one-lung ventilation, shunt fraction fell significantly after switching from a volatile anaesthetic to propofol — volatile agents inhibit HPV
cards.summary: Abe 1998 randomised trial (n=20): during one-lung ventilation, shunt fraction fell significantly after switching from a volatile anaesthetic to propofol — volatile agents inhibit HPV
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (crossover anaesthetic comparison during one-lung ventilation) — N = 20
cards.people: 20 patients undergoing prolonged one-lung ventilation for oesophageal surgery, allocated to sequences in which isoflurane or sevoflurane preceded propofol, with arterial and mixed venous sampling and haemodynamics measured before, during and after one-lung ventilation, with and without 4 cm H2O PEEP.
cards.result: Shunt fraction (Qs/Qt) increased significantly after one-lung ventilation began in both groups and decreased significantly after conversion from the volatile anaesthetic to propofol in both groups; after PEEP was applied during propofol anaesthesia, PaO2 increased significantly. Arterial oxygen values with propofol were greater than with isoflurane or sevoflurane, and shunt fractions lower. The clinical reading is the physiology: volatile anaesthetics blunt hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction in the non-ventilated lung, so more blood keeps flowing through it as shunt; removing them restores the diversion.
cards.watchOut: HPV inhibition is inferred from shunt fraction and oxygenation, not measured at the vessel — the standard human readout, and concordant with the Frostell card's direct pressure measurements. Other HPV inhibitors named in textbooks (vasodilators, high cardiac output, hypocapnia) are presented as the textbook account in the balance/synthesis framing, not as carded numbers.

cards.headline: Synthesis: zones stack the pressures, gravity moves the flow, and HPV patrols the match — nitric oxide and volatile anaesthetics turn it down
cards.summary: Synthesis: zones stack the pressures, gravity moves the flow, and HPV patrols the match — nitric oxide and volatile anaesthetics turn it down
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology. No new data.
cards.result: West's zones (textbook account) follow from one fact: alveolar pressure is uniform while vascular pressures climb down the upright lung, so the flow rule changes from apex to base. Human imaging confirms the resulting gradient and its posture dependence (PMIDs 6463424, 28336539), with the modern correction that lung structure outweighs gravity. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is the active layer: demonstrable within minutes in healthy humans (mean pulmonary artery pressure 14.7 → 19.8 mmHg on 12% oxygen, PMID 8457043), selectively reversed by inhaled nitric oxide, and clinically blunted by volatile anaesthetics, whose removal lowers shunt during one-lung ventilation (PMID 9806702). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Scope: pressure/flow distribution and HPV in the normal and anaesthetised lung. Pulmonary hypertension as a disease, and inhaled nitric oxide as a therapy, are treatment shelves, not this physiology.

shelves.title: CO2 transport: most CO2 travels as bicarbonate made inside the red cell by carbonic anhydrase, with chloride shifting in as bicarbonate leaves (the chloride shift); deoxygenated haemoglobin carries more CO2 and buffers the protons (the Haldane effect — 78% of the PaCO2 rise when hypoxic patients breathe oxygen), while CO2 and protons lower oxygen affinity in the tissues (the Bohr effect)
shelves.question: How is carbon dioxide transported in blood — as bicarbonate, carbamino compounds and dissolved gas — and how do the chloride shift, the Bohr effect and the Haldane effect link oxygen and carbon dioxide carriage?
shelves.mesh: Blood Circulation/physiology · Carbon Dioxide/blood · Humans · Middle Aged · Oxygen/blood · Oxyhemoglobins/metabolism · Partial Pressure · Regression Analysis
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, respiratory chapters). The textbook account: CO2 leaves the tissues in three forms — dissolved, as carbamino compounds with haemoglobin and plasma proteins, and, for the bulk of the load, as bicarbonate: inside the red cell, carbonic anhydrase hydrates CO2 to carbonic acid, the proton is buffered by haemoglobin, bicarbonate exits to plasma on the band-3 exchanger, and chloride enters in its place (the chloride shift, or Hamburger phenomenon), reversing in the lungs. Two linkages couple the gases: the Bohr effect — CO2 and protons reduce haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, unloading oxygen where CO2 is produced — and its reciprocal, the Haldane effect — deoxygenated haemoglobin binds more CO2 and more protons, so oxygen unloading in the tissues promotes CO2 loading, and oxygenation in the lungs promotes CO2 release. The carded human studies quantify the linkages in people. In 20 severely hypoxic, hypercapnic patients, the Haldane shift accounted for 78% of the PaCO2 rise seen when they breathed 100% oxygen (Luft 1981). A regression built from 247 patient measurements expresses the Haldane contribution to venous PCO2 as a function of the arteriovenous HbO2 difference and haematocrit with r²=0.99 (Giovannini 1999). In human whole blood exposed to CO2-rich gas, plasma bicarbonate rose as plasma chloride fell — the chloride shift measured directly (Hirakawa 1993; human component n=9, labelled). And blocking the enzyme that starts the bicarbonate limb has the predicted in-vivo consequence: acetazolamide in 10 ventilated patients retained CO2 and shifted the oxygen dissociation curve rightward by the Bohr mechanism, as the authors describe (Berthelsen 1987). The textbook's percentage split between the three carriage forms is presented as the textbook's account; no carded record in this session prints that split, so it is not claimed as a carded number. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Luft 1981: in 20 hypoxic, hypercapnic patients, the Haldane effect accounted for 78% of the PaCO2 rise on breathing 100% oxygen
cards.summary: Luft 1981: in 20 hypoxic, hypercapnic patients, the Haldane effect accounted for 78% of the PaCO2 rise on breathing 100% oxygen
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (air vs 100% oxygen in hypoxic patients) — N = 20
cards.people: 20 severely hypoxic and hypercapnic patients studied breathing air and then 100% oxygen, with arterial, alveolar and mixed expired CO2 pressures, CO2 production and arterial oxygen saturation measured in both conditions.
cards.result: On 100% oxygen, mean PaCO2 rose from 50.8 to 56.6 Torr while alveolar PCO2 was unchanged (38.3 vs 38.6 Torr), so the arterial–alveolar CO2 gradient widened from 12.5 to 18.0 Torr. The rise in PaCO2 correlated significantly with arterial unsaturation on air. When the investigators estimated the rise expected purely from the shift of the CO2 dissociation curve on complete oxygenation of haemoglobin (the Haldane effect), it accounted for 78% of the observed PaCO2 change and 87% of the dead-space/tidal-volume change (0.59 to 0.64). Oxygenating haemoglobin unloads CO2 — measured in patients, not just in vitro.
cards.watchOut: The 78% figure is the authors' modelled attribution of the PaCO2 rise to the Haldane shift, printed as such; ventilation changes on oxygen may contribute to the remainder. Patients had severe lung disease — the effect size in health is the Giovannini card's business.
cards.source: Luft UC et al. Contribution of the Haldane effect to the rise of arterial Pco2 in hypoxic patients breathing oxygen. Critical care medicine. 1981. PMID: 6780265. cards.headline: Giovannini 1999: from 247 patient measurements, the Haldane effect's contribution to venous PCO2 is a tight function of the arteriovenous HbO2 difference and haematocrit (r²=0.99)
cards.summary: Giovannini 1999: from 247 patient measurements, the Haldane effect's contribution to venous PCO2 is a tight function of the arteriovenous HbO2 difference and haematocrit (r²=0.99)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (quantitative Haldane-effect model from patient measurements) — 247 measurements
cards.people: A large series of measurements in patients (n=247 measurements) processed by regression analysis to quantify how much of the venous–arterial PCO2 difference is mediated by oxygen-linked CO2 binding (the Haldane effect).
cards.result: The fitted expression estimates the Haldane-mediated reduction in venous PCO2 from the arteriovenous difference in haemoglobin-bound oxygen and the haematocrit, with r²=0.99 (P<<0.001), and its estimates compared well with previously published experiments. The authors present it as a way to assess the Haldane effect's impact on venous PCO2 and the venoarterial PCO2 gradient in investigative and clinical settings — the reciprocal linkage between oxygen saturation and CO2 carriage, quantified for human blood in vivo.
cards.watchOut: The record counts measurements (n=247), not distinct patients, and it is printed that way on this card. A fitted equation is a quantification tool, not a new mechanism; the mechanism's in-vivo demonstration is the Luft card.
cards.source: Giovannini I et al. Quantitative assessment of changes in blood CO(2) tension mediated by the haldane effect. Journal of applied physiology. 1999. PMID: 10444650. cards.headline: Hirakawa 1993: in human whole blood loaded with CO2, plasma bicarbonate rose as plasma chloride fell — the chloride shift, measured directly (human blood n=9, labelled)
cards.summary: Hirakawa 1993: in human whole blood loaded with CO2, plasma bicarbonate rose as plasma chloride fell — the chloride shift, measured directly (human blood n=9, labelled)
cards.type: Primary human study (human whole-blood CO2 loading experiment) — human component N = 9 (labelled); canine component not used
cards.people: Human venous blood from 9 donors (a parallel canine series, n=8 dogs, is part of the same paper and is NOT used as evidence here) aerated with a CO2-rich gas mixture (15% CO2, 25% O2, 60% N2), with blood gases, haematocrit and plasma sodium, chloride and bicarbonate measured, including runs with acetazolamide and anion-exchange blockers.
cards.result: When CO2-rich gas was passed through human whole blood, PCO2 and plasma sodium and bicarbonate contents per ml of blood increased, while pH and plasma chloride content per ml of whole blood decreased — bicarbonate leaving the red cell for plasma as chloride moves in, the chloride shift. The ion changes were related by simple stoichiometric equations (the bicarbonate change approximately equalling the sodium plus chloride changes), and the authors describe sodium and bicarbonate release from erythrocytes occurring simultaneously with the chloride shift.
cards.watchOut: Mixed-species paper: only the human whole-blood experiments are carded, per the no-animal-evidence rule, and the dog series is flagged here rather than silently included. An in-vitro blood experiment demonstrates the shift's stoichiometry; the in-vivo human demonstrations are the Luft and Berthelsen cards.
cards.source: Hirakawa S et al. Transport of Na+ and HCO3- out of red blood cells is simultaneous with a chloride shift in canine and human whole blood exposed to CO2-rich gas. cards.headline: Berthelsen 1987: blocking carbonic anhydrase with acetazolamide in 10 ventilated patients retained CO2 and right-shifted the oxygen curve — the bicarbonate limb and the Bohr effect in vivo
cards.summary: Berthelsen 1987: blocking carbonic anhydrase with acetazolamide in 10 ventilated patients retained CO2 and right-shifted the oxygen curve — the bicarbonate limb and the Bohr effect in vivo
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (carbonic anhydrase inhibition in ventilated patients) — N = 10
cards.people: 10 critically ill, mechanically ventilated patients given acetazolamide 15 mg/kg (carbonic anhydrase inhibition), with pulmonary gas exchange, arterial and central venous oxygen tensions and contents measured.
cards.result: Median arterial oxygen tension rose by 0.9 kPa and central venous oxygen tension and content rose by 16–18% and 6–8% respectively, while pulmonary venous admixture and physiological dead-space ventilation both increased — so the oxygenation change was not better lung exchange. The authors explain the arterial rise by a rightward shift of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve from the increased blood acidity during carbonic anhydrase inhibition (the Bohr effect), and the venous rise by improved cardiac performance, possibly sympathetic activation in response to acetazolamide-induced CO2 retention. Inhibiting the enzyme that hydrates CO2 slows the bicarbonate limb of CO2 carriage, exactly as the transport model predicts.
cards.watchOut: The Bohr-shift explanation is the authors' interpretation of an oxygenation change in a small, uncontrolled study — carded for the direction of the perturbation (enzyme blockade → CO2 retention → acid shift of the curve), not as a measurement of the Bohr coefficient.
cards.source: Berthelsen PG et al. Respiratory function and carbonic anhydrase inhibition. Intensive care medicine. 1987. PMID: 3116060. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: bicarbonate is the bulk carrier, the red cell is where it is made, and oxygen and CO2 carriage are geared together by Bohr and Haldane
cards.summary: Synthesis: bicarbonate is the bulk carrier, the red cell is where it is made, and oxygen and CO2 carriage are geared together by Bohr and Haldane
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology. No new data.
cards.result: CO2 produced in the tissues is hydrated inside the red cell and leaves it as plasma bicarbonate, chloride shifting in to balance charge — measured directly in human blood (PMID 8336423) and functionally confirmed when carbonic anhydrase blockade retains CO2 in patients (PMID 3116060). The two reciprocal effects gear the gases together: protons and CO2 unload oxygen in the tissues (Bohr), and deoxygenated haemoglobin takes up more CO2 (Haldane) — the latter large enough to explain 78% of the PaCO2 rise when hypoxic patients are oxygenated (PMID 6780265) and tight enough to model from 247 patient measurements (PMID 10444650). The textbook's form-by-form percentage split of CO2 carriage is its own account; the carded human record establishes the mechanisms and their magnitudes in vivo. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Scope: CO2 carriage in blood. Ventilatory control of PaCO2 and acid–base compensation are separate shelves; the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve and 2,3-BPG are folded into the slate's oxygen-affinity row, not this one.

shelves.title: Oxygen delivery, the Fick principle and DO2crit: above a critical delivery, consumption is set by metabolic demand and extraction rises as delivery falls; below it, consumption falls with delivery and lactate rises — the biphasic relation is demonstrated in humans, with the threshold near 330 mL/min/m² in anaesthetised surgical patients but only 3.8–4.5 mL/min/kg in dying critically ill patients, and sepsis did not move it
shelves.question: What are oxygen delivery and oxygen consumption, what determines critical oxygen delivery (DO2crit), and when does oxygen consumption become supply-dependent?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Bacterial Infections/complications,metabolism,physiopathology,therapy · Calorimetry, Indirect · Cell Hypoxia · Cohort Studies · Critical Illness · Female · Humans · Lactates/blood · Lactic Acid · Male · Middle Aged · Models, Biological · Multiple Organ Failure/etiology,prevention & control · *Oxygen Consumption · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy/standards · Reference Values
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, circulation/tissue-oxygen chapters). The textbook account: oxygen delivery (DO2) is cardiac output multiplied by arterial oxygen content, and oxygen consumption (VO2) follows from the Fick principle — VO2 = cardiac output × (arterial − mixed venous oxygen content). As delivery falls, tissues first compensate by extracting a larger fraction of the delivered oxygen, so consumption stays constant (supply independence); below a critical delivery (DO2crit), extraction can rise no further, consumption falls in proportion to delivery (supply dependence), and anaerobic metabolism with lactate production begins. The carded human studies demonstrate the biphasic curve directly and show the threshold is context-dependent, not a universal constant. In 58 anaesthetised surgical patients the critical value was 330 mL/min/m² (8.2 mL/min/kg), with consumption plateauing at 109 ± 16 mL/min/m² above it (Shibutani 1983). In 18 critically ill patients studied as life support was withdrawn, the biphasic relation appeared in every individual, with DO2crit of 3.8 ± 1.5 (septic) vs 4.5 ± 1.3 mL/min/kg (nonseptic) — no significant difference, and considerably lower than older pooled-group estimates (Ronco 1993). And supply dependence is a state, not a trait: the same 10 septic patients showed VO2 tracking DO2 during shock (extraction fixed) but not after recovery, when extraction adjusted and VO2 stayed constant (Friedman 1998). Any single textbook DO2crit number is therefore the textbook's simplification; the carded human values are the two measured settings above. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Shibutani 1983: in 58 anaesthetised patients the critical oxygen delivery was 330 mL/min/m² (8.2 mL/min/kg) — below it VO2 fell in proportion to DO2, above it VO2 plateaued at 109 ± 16
cards.summary: Shibutani 1983: in 58 anaesthetised patients the critical oxygen delivery was 330 mL/min/m² (8.2 mL/min/kg) — below it VO2 fell in proportion to DO2, above it VO2 plateaued at 109 ± 16
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (DO2/VO2 relation under anaesthesia) — N = 58 patients, 99 measurement sets
cards.people: 58 patients anaesthetised (diazepam, pancuronium, fentanyl) for cardiac surgery, with 99 sets of haemodynamic measurements taken after sternotomy and before cardiopulmonary bypass, spanning a range of oxygen deliveries.
cards.result: Regression analysis identified a critical DO2 of 330 mL/min/m², or 8.2 mL/min/kg. Below it, VO2 decreased in proportion to DO2 (VO2 = 0.36 × DO2 − 11.20; n=30, r=0.77, P<10⁻⁶). Above it, VO2 plateaued at 109 ± 16 mL/min/m² (n=69, r=−0.02), while mixed venous oxygen tension kept falling as DO2 fell — compensatory extraction rising until it could rise no more. The authors concluded that a fall in VO2 below the critical delivery signals tissue oxygen deprivation.

cards.headline: Ronco 1993: measured individually as support was withdrawn, DO2crit was 3.8 ± 1.5 mL/min/kg in septic and 4.5 ± 1.3 in nonseptic patients — sepsis did not alter the threshold or extraction ability
cards.summary: Ronco 1993: measured individually as support was withdrawn, DO2crit was 3.8 ± 1.5 mL/min/kg in septic and 4.5 ± 1.3 in nonseptic patients — sepsis did not alter the threshold or extraction ability
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (individual biphasic DO2/VO2 curves, calorimetry) — N = 18 (9 septic, 9 nonseptic)
cards.people: 18 critically ill patients (9 septic, 9 nonseptic) in two university intensive care units, studied with simultaneous indirect calorimetry (VO2), Fick-calculated DO2 and arterial lactate measured every 5–20 minutes while life support was discontinued; sepsis was confirmed by cultures and autopsy evidence of a source.
cards.result: In all septic and eight nonseptic patients, DO2 and VO2 showed a biphasic relationship. There were no differences between septic and nonseptic patients in critical DO2 (3.8 ± 1.5 vs 4.5 ± 1.3 mL/min/kg; P>.28), critical oxygen extraction ratio (0.61 ± 0.05 vs 0.59 ± 0.16; P>.64) or maximal extraction ratio (0.74 ± 0.08 vs 0.80 ± 0.11; P>.29), with over 90% power to detect a 2 mL/min/kg difference in critical DO2. The authors concluded the individually measured critical delivery is considerably lower than previously reported from pooled group data, that sepsis does not alter DO2crit or tissue extraction ability, and that pushing DO2 to supranormal levels hoping to raise VO2 may be inappropriate.
cards.watchOut: Measurements were made during withdrawal of life support in dying patients — the only setting in which the full curve to very low delivery can be observed in humans, and the reason the values sit far below the anaesthetised-surgical threshold. VO2 by calorimetry is independent of the Fick calculation, answering the coupling criticism of earlier pooled studies.
cards.source: Ronco JJ et al. Identification of the critical oxygen delivery for anaerobic metabolism in critically ill septic and nonseptic humans. JAMA. 1993. PMID: 8411504. cards.headline: Friedman 1998: the same 10 septic patients were supply-dependent during shock (VO2 121 → 165 as DO2 rose, extraction fixed) and supply-independent after recovery (VO2 unchanged, extraction adjusted)
cards.summary: Friedman 1998: the same 10 septic patients were supply-dependent during shock (VO2 121 → 165 as DO2 rose, extraction fixed) and supply-independent after recovery (VO2 unchanged, extraction adjusted)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (within-patient shock vs recovery comparison) — N = 10
cards.people: 10 critically ill adults (55 ± 19 years) whose haemodynamic and blood-gas data were reviewed retrospectively in two phases: during an episode of septic shock (phase A), when DO2 was acutely altered by fluids, vasoactive drugs or PEEP, and after recovery from the episode (phase B).
cards.result: In phase A, changes in VO2 (121 ± 32 vs 165 ± 36 mL/min/m², P<0.001) paralleled changes in DO2 (415 ± 153 vs 607 ± 217 mL/min/m², P<0.001) while oxygen extraction stayed stable (31.9 ± 11.2 vs 30.2 ± 8.9%). In phase B, DO2 changes (412 ± 118 vs 526 ± 152, P<0.001) were met by opposite changes in extraction (36.1 ± 4.2 vs 28.9 ± 4.9%, P<0.001) and VO2 was unchanged (147 ± 35 vs 149 ± 33). The VO2/DO2 slope was greater in phase A than phase B (0.26 ± 0.09 vs 0.08 ± 0.08, P<0.004), and lactate was higher in phase A (3.3 ± 1.8 vs 1.6 ± 0.6 mEq/L, P<0.05). Supply dependency characterised the shock state in the same patients who later showed independence.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, and DO2/VO2 share measured variables here, so the phase contrast (same patients, same methods, opposite pattern) carries the inference rather than either phase alone. Carded for that within-patient demonstration that supply dependence comes and goes with the shock state.
cards.source: Friedman G et al. Oxygen supply dependency can characterize septic shock. Intensive care medicine. 1998. PMID: 9539067. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one biphasic curve, two regimes — extraction compensates until DO2crit, then consumption is delivery's prisoner and lactate testifies
cards.summary: Synthesis: one biphasic curve, two regimes — extraction compensates until DO2crit, then consumption is delivery's prisoner and lactate testifies
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology. No new data.
cards.result: The Fick framework (textbook account) predicts exactly what human studies show: a plateau where VO2 is demand-set and extraction absorbs delivery changes, and a slope where VO2 tracks DO2. The threshold was 330 mL/min/m² in anaesthetised surgical patients (PMID 6409505) and roughly half that per kilogram in dying critically ill patients, with sepsis making no difference to the threshold or to maximal extraction (PMID 8411504) — yet supply dependence itself is a reversible feature of the shock state (PMID 9539067). DO2crit is therefore a property of the patient's metabolic state, not a universal constant, and any single quoted number should be read with its setting attached. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Scope: whole-body delivery/consumption physiology. What limits maximal oxygen uptake in exercise (cardiac output vs extraction) is pack #6248, and supranormal-delivery resuscitation trials are treatment shelves, not this physiology.

shelves.title: Surfactant, Laplace's law and interdependence: Laplace's law says a smaller alveolus needs a higher collapsing pressure unless surface tension falls as it shrinks — surfactant does exactly that, and human material proves the point in reverse: lungs low in lecithin could not lower surface tension and developed hyaline membranes, and lavage surfactant from diseased human lungs bottoms out at 15–20 mN/m instead of near zero
shelves.question: How does surfactant lower alveolar surface tension (Laplace's law), stabilise alveoli of different sizes, and what is alveolar interdependence?
shelves.mesh: Female · Fetal Death · Gestational Age · Hemorrhage/complications · Humans · Hyaline Membrane Disease/etiology,metabolism,pathology · Infant Mortality · Infant, Newborn · Lipoproteins · Lung/analysis,pathology · Phosphatidylcholines/analysis · Pregnancy · Pregnancy in Diabetics/complications · Pulmonary Alveoli/metabolism,pathology · Pulmonary Edema/etiology · Respiration · Surface Tension · Surface-Active Agents
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, respiratory mechanics chapters). The textbook account: the pressure tending to collapse a spherical alveolus follows Laplace's law, P = 2T/r — at equal surface tension a smaller alveolus would need the higher pressure and would empty into its larger neighbour. Surfactant breaks that instability because its surface tension is area-dependent: as an alveolus shrinks, the surfactant film compresses and tension falls steeply, so small alveoli are not squeezed out; as it expands, tension rises, checking overdistension. Alveolar interdependence is the mechanical complement — alveoli share walls, so surrounding parenchyma tethers any unit that starts to collapse and pulls it back open. The carded human studies are the deficiency and dysfunction experiments nature and disease provide. In 95 stillbirths and neonatal deaths, lung lecithin content was negatively correlated with the minimum surface tension of lung extract, and lungs with hyaline membranes sat in the low-lecithin range (Boughton 1970). Healthy human lavage surfactant reaches a minimum surface tension of about 0–3.4 mN/m on a pulsating bubble surfactometer; after lung transplantation it could only reach 15.8 ± 1.1 mN/m (Hohlfeld 1998), and in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis about 15–20 mN/m versus ~0 in controls (Günther 1999) — when the film cannot lower tension, the Laplace instability the textbook describes is what the lung lives with. Note: the founding Avery & Mead 1959 study was located by title search this session, but its PubMed record carries no abstract, so no numbers could be sourced from a fetched record and it is NOT carded, per the standing rule; Boughton 1970 supplies the carded human lecithin–tension relation. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Boughton 1970: in 95 stillbirths and neonatal deaths, lung lecithin was negatively correlated with minimum surface tension — hyaline-membrane lungs were the low-lecithin, high-tension ones
cards.summary: Boughton 1970: in 95 stillbirths and neonatal deaths, lung lecithin was negatively correlated with minimum surface tension — hyaline-membrane lungs were the low-lecithin, high-tension ones
cards.type: Primary human study (lung lecithin vs surface tension in perinatal deaths) — N = 95 (34 stillbirths, 61 neonatal deaths)
cards.people: 34 stillbirths and 61 neonatal deaths in which lung lecithin content and the surface-tension properties of lung tissue were both determined; in 24 cases the palmitic-lecithin fraction was also measured (44–79% of total lecithins).
cards.result: Lecithin content ranged from 1.5 to 18.6% of dry lung tissue and was negatively correlated with the minimum surface tension of lung extract in both fresh stillbirths and neonatal deaths. Cases with hyaline membranes had lung lecithin in the lower range (<8% of dry tissue). After 29 weeks' gestation, fresh stillbirths and neonatal deaths other than hyaline-membrane cases had normal lung surfactant, apart from a small group of very immature infants lacking surfactant who survived less than 2.5 hours. The authors present lung lecithin as a measure of surfactant reserve and surfactant deficiency — by promoting interstitial pulmonary oedema — as the immediate cause of hyaline membrane disease.
cards.watchOut: Post-mortem tissue measurements, not in-vivo alveolar mechanics — carded because it is a direct human measurement of the surfactant-amount/surface-tension relation at the heart of this shelf, in the population (newborns) where deficiency declares itself.
cards.source: Boughton K et al. Hyaline membrane disease. II. Lung lecithin. Archives of disease in childhood. 1970. PMID: 5464063. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hohlfeld 1998: healthy human lavage surfactant reached a minimum surface tension of 3.4 ± 1.9 mN/m; after lung transplantation only 15.8 ± 1.1 mN/m
cards.summary: Hohlfeld 1998: healthy human lavage surfactant reached a minimum surface tension of 3.4 ± 1.9 mN/m; after lung transplantation only 15.8 ± 1.1 mN/m
cards.type: Primary human study (lavage surfactant biophysics, patients vs healthy controls) — N = 70 (60 recipients, 10 controls)
cards.people: Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid from 60 lung transplant recipients compared with 10 healthy subjects; phospholipid concentrations, surfactant subfractions and total protein measured, and surface activity measured with a pulsating bubble surfactometer.
cards.result: Minimum surface tension was 15.8 ± 1.1 mN/m in transplant recipients versus 3.4 ± 1.9 mN/m in healthy subjects (P=0.0004). The ratio of small to large surfactant aggregates was increased in transplant patients (P=0.043), while protein-to-phospholipid ratios did not differ significantly. Episodes of infection or rejection did not change surface activity, and surface tension did not correlate with time after transplantation or pulmonary function — a persistent impairment of the film's ability to lower tension, attributed by the authors to type-II-cell malfunction.
cards.watchOut: The healthy-control arm (n=10) is the card's normal anchor and is small; the patient arm shows dysfunction, not the stabilising mechanism itself — the mechanism is the textbook frame, and this card quantifies what its failure looks like in human material.
cards.source: Hohlfeld JM et al. Pulmonary surfactant activity is impaired in lung transplant recipients. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 1998. PMID: 9730994. cards.headline: Günther 1999: control human surfactant reached ~0 mN/m, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and sarcoidosis ~5, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis 15–20 mN/m
cards.summary: Günther 1999: control human surfactant reached ~0 mN/m, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and sarcoidosis ~5, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis 15–20 mN/m
cards.type: Primary human study (lavage surfactant biophysics across diseases vs controls) — N = 141 (112 patients, 29 controls)
cards.people: Bronchoalveolar lavage fluids from patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (n=36), hypersensitivity pneumonitis (n=32) and sarcoidosis (n=44), compared with 29 healthy control subjects; surfactant phospholipids, proteins and apoproteins quantified, and large-aggregate surface activity assayed on the pulsating bubble surfactometer.
cards.result: Surface activity was severely impaired in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (minimum surface tension approximately 15–20 mN/m), only modestly affected in hypersensitivity pneumonitis and sarcoidosis (approximately 5 mN/m), and essentially complete in controls (approximately 0 mN/m). Surfactant protein A concentrations, large-aggregate content and phospholipid:protein ratios were significantly decreased in all patient groups versus controls, and adding soluble lavage proteins back to pelleted surfactant raised minimum tension further — protein inhibition of the film, graded with disease severity.
cards.watchOut: Lavage dilutes and samples the alveolar film indirectly, and values are surfactometer readings on recovered material — the standard human method, concordant across both lavage cards on this shelf. Disease severity and surfactant failure travel together here; causation in either direction is not what this card claims.
cards.source: Günther A et al. Surfactant abnormalities in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and sarcoidosis. The European respiratory journal. 1999. PMID: 10543276. cards.headline: Synthesis: Laplace sets the trap, surfactant's area-dependent tension springs it shut, and interdependence tethers the walls — human deficiency states show the trap working
cards.summary: Synthesis: Laplace sets the trap, surfactant's area-dependent tension springs it shut, and interdependence tethers the walls — human deficiency states show the trap working
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology. No new data.
cards.result: Laplace's law (textbook account: P = 2T/r) makes unequal alveoli unstable at fixed tension; surfactant's falling tension on compression is the stabiliser, and shared alveolar walls (interdependence) add mechanical tethering. The human record shows the system and its failure quantitatively: the less lecithin a newborn lung contained, the higher its extract's minimum surface tension, with hyaline membranes in the low-lecithin range (PMID 5464063); functioning human surfactant reaches ~0–3.4 mN/m, while diseased lungs' surfactant stalls at 5 to 20 mN/m depending on the disease (PMIDs 9730994, 10543276). A film that cannot lower tension at small radius leaves Laplace's law in charge — collapse of small units and the clinical picture that follows. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Scope: the physiology of surface tension and alveolar stability. Exogenous surfactant as a treatment (neonatal and ARDS shelves #871 and #1324 in the live library) is therapy, not this physiology, and is cross-pointed rather than re-carded.

shelves.title: Diaphragm fatigue and the tension–time index: TTdi multiplies the pressure load (mean Pdi as a fraction of maximum) by the duty cycle (Ti/Ttot); above a critical TTdi of about 0.15–0.18 the human diaphragm cannot sustain the pattern — endurance falls below an hour and the EMG fatigue signature appears — while resting breathing, even in COPD, normally sits well below the threshold
shelves.question: What is diaphragm fatigue, how is it quantified by the tension–time index of the diaphragm, and at what threshold does the diaphragm fatigue?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Airway Resistance · Carbon Dioxide/blood · Diaphragm/physiopathology · Electromyography · Female · Functional Residual Capacity · Humans · Lung Diseases, Obstructive/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle Contraction · Oxygen/blood · Pressure · Time Factors · Vital Capacity
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, respiratory-muscle chapters; the tension–time framework is Bellemare & Grassino's). The textbook account: a rhythmically contracting muscle fatigues when the product of its relative force and its duty cycle exceeds what its blood supply can service. For the diaphragm that product is the tension–time index, TTdi = (mean transdiaphragmatic pressure / maximal transdiaphragmatic pressure) × (inspiratory time / total breath time). The carded human studies fix the threshold. Bellemare & Grassino's programme found the fatigue threshold in normal subjects at a TTdi of about 15% of maximum: in their COPD study, resting TTdi ran 1–12% (mean 5%), but when 5 patients raised their TTdi to an imposed 17%, the diaphragm's EMG developed the fatigue pattern seen in normals at similar levels (Bellemare 1983). The companion EMG study in 5 normal subjects showed the high/low-frequency power ratio decaying at a rate monotonically (hyperbolically) related to Pdi × Ti/Ttot, with the decay rate predicting how long the pattern could be sustained (Bellemare 1982; N=5, labelled). Zocchi 1993 independently reproduced the diaphragm figure — above a critical TTdi of 0.15–0.18, endurance is under an hour and falls as TTdi rises — and showed the rib-cage muscles have their own, higher critical index (0.30) when they are the predominantly recruited group (N=4, labelled). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Bellemare & Grassino 1983: the human diaphragm's fatigue threshold is a TTdi of about 15% of maximum — COPD patients rest at 1–12%, but imposing 17% produced the fatigue EMG pattern
cards.summary: Bellemare & Grassino 1983: the human diaphragm's fatigue threshold is a TTdi of about 15% of maximum — COPD patients rest at 1–12%, but imposing 17% produced the fatigue EMG pattern
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (tension–time index at rest and under imposed load) — N = 20 patients (5 in the imposed-pattern phase)
cards.people: 20 patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in whom the tension–time index of resting ventilation was measured; 5 of them then voluntarily changed their breathing pattern (Ti/Ttot from 0.33 to 0.49) to raise TTdi from a control 8% to an imposed 17% of maximum, with diaphragm EMG recorded. The normal-subject threshold referenced is from the authors' programme in healthy volunteers.
cards.result: The fatigue threshold of the human diaphragm in normal subjects corresponds to a TTdi of about 15% of Pdimax. In the COPD patients, resting TTdi ranged from 1 to 12% of Pdimax (mean 5%) and was significantly related to total airway resistance (r=0.57, P<0.05). At the imposed 17% TTdi, the high-frequency/low-frequency power ratio of the diaphragm EMG declined progressively — a fatigue pattern quantitatively similar to that in normal subjects at similar TTdi — followed by a progressive fall in mean transdiaphragmatic pressure. The authors concluded the COPD diaphragm's force reserve is reduced (lower Pdimax) and can be exhausted by even minor changes in breathing pattern: at a Ti/Ttot of 0.40, COPD patients could raise mean Pdi only 3-fold before reaching a fatiguing pattern, versus 8-fold in normal subjects.
cards.watchOut: The 15% normal threshold is stated in this record as the programme's established value in normal subjects; the imposed-load experiment that displays it was performed in 5 COPD patients. Both facts are printed on the card rather than blended.
cards.source: Bellemare F et al. Force reserve of the diaphragm in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Journal of applied physiology. 1983. PMID: 6411667. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bellemare & Grassino 1982: the diaphragm EMG fatigue signature decays at a rate set by Pdi × Ti/Ttot, and that rate predicts endurance time (N=5, labelled)
cards.summary: Bellemare & Grassino 1982: the diaphragm EMG fatigue signature decays at a rate set by Pdi × Ti/Ttot, and that rate predicts endurance time (N=5, labelled)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (EMG fatigue quantification in normal subjects) — N = 5 (small N, labelled on the face)
cards.people: Five normal subjects breathing through high inspiratory resistance at sustained combinations of transdiaphragmatic pressure (0.1–0.8 of Pdimax) and duty cycle (Ti/Ttot 0.2–1.0), with the diaphragm EMG's high-frequency (150–350 Hz) to low-frequency (20–40 Hz) power ratio tracked breath by breath.
cards.result: Where decay occurred it was exponential, and its time constant was monotonically related to Pdi × Ti/Ttot — the tension–time product — following a hyperbolic relationship. The EMG decay measure followed the same trends as myopotential conduction velocity and the centre frequency of the EMG spectrum, and its values were directly related to the time a given pattern could be sustained (Tlim). The authors concluded EMG changes and endurance time are related expressions of the metabolic changes induced by the contraction pattern — the measurement basis on which the tension–time threshold rests.
cards.watchOut: Classic small study: N=5 is printed on the face per the labelling rule. EMG spectral shift is a fatigue signature, not force failure itself; its link to endurance time within the same experiments is what qualifies it as the threshold's measuring instrument.
cards.source: Bellemare F et al. Evaluation of human diaphragm fatigue. Journal of applied physiology. 1982. PMID: 7174414. Registry ID: none in the record.
