cards.headline: Zocchi 1993: above a critical TTdi of 0.15–0.18 diaphragm endurance is under 1 hour; the rib-cage muscles' own critical index is 0.30 (N=4, labelled)
cards.summary: Zocchi 1993: above a critical TTdi of 0.15–0.18 diaphragm endurance is under 1 hour; the rib-cage muscles' own critical index is 0.30 (N=4, labelled)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (critical tension–time values by recruitment pattern) — N = 4 (small N, labelled on the face)
cards.people: Four normal subjects breathing against inspiratory threshold loads with rib-cage-muscle emphasis (achieved by developing negative abdominal pressure swings), with the rib-cage tension–time index (TTrc) assessed; the diaphragm-emphasis critical range quoted is the established TTdi relation the study set out to compare against.
cards.result: With diaphragm emphasis, diaphragmatic fatigue is related to TTdi (= Pdi/Pdimax × Ti/Ttot): above the critical range of 0.15 to 0.18, endurance of the diaphragm is less than 1 hour and is inversely related to the TTdi value. With rib-cage emphasis, above a critical TTrc of 0.30 endurance time was inversely related to TTrc and failure came from the rib-cage muscles rather than the diaphragm. The authors concluded the critical threshold is higher for rib-cage-emphasis patterns, yet in the patterns people spontaneously adopt under load the rib-cage muscles fatigue earlier than the diaphragm.
cards.watchOut: Very small N, printed on the face. The diaphragm critical range in this record is the cited established relation rather than a fresh measurement in these 4 subjects; the fresh measurement is the rib-cage threshold. Carded as independent concordance for the 0.15–0.18 figure plus the recruitment-pattern qualification.
cards.source: Zocchi L et al. Effect of pressure and timing of contraction on human rib cage muscle fatigue. Journal of applied physiology. 1993. PMID: 8466120. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: force fraction times duty cycle decides fatigue — the diaphragm's budget is spent at a TTdi near 0.15, and healthy breathing, even diseased breathing at rest, stays under it
cards.summary: Synthesis: force fraction times duty cycle decides fatigue — the diaphragm's budget is spent at a TTdi near 0.15, and healthy breathing, even diseased breathing at rest, stays under it
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology. No new data.
cards.result: The tension–time index prices a breathing pattern: mean pressure as a fraction of maximum, multiplied by the fraction of each breath spent contracting. Two independent human programmes converge on the diaphragm's price limit — a TTdi of about 0.15 (PMID 6411667), 0.15–0.18 with endurance under an hour above it (PMID 8466120) — measured through an EMG fatigue signature whose decay rate is itself a hyperbolic function of the same product (PMID 7174414). Resting ventilation costs only 1–12% even in COPD, which is why the diaphragm does not fatigue at rest; loads, duty-cycle prolongation or a fall in maximum pressure spend the reserve. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Scope: the fatigue threshold of the diaphragm and rib-cage muscles in humans. Weaning-prediction uses of tension–time indices in ventilated patients are clinical applications, not this physiology.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 6411667, 7174414, 8466120), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology. No additional source.

shelves.title: Once-nightly sodium oxybate (FT218) in narcolepsy: one phase 3 trial positive on all three co-primary endpoints — POSSIBLE
shelves.question: In people with narcolepsy, does once-nightly sodium oxybate (FT218) improve excessive daytime sleepiness and cataplexy compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Cataplexy/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Narcolepsy/drug therapy · Sleepiness · Sodium Oxybate/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Wakefulness
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The tested product is named as published, per the clarification exception: once-nightly sodium oxybate (FT218; marketed as LUMRYZ™), an extended-release formulation taken once at bedtime — distinct from the twice-nightly sodium oxybate programme homed on shelf #921, whose PMIDs are not re-carded here. In REST-ON (Kushida 2022; 222 randomised patients with narcolepsy type 1 or 2), all three doses (6, 7.5 and 9 g) beat placebo on all three co-primary endpoints (all P<0.001): at 9 g, Maintenance of Wakefulness Test sleep latency rose 10.8 versus 4.7 minutes (difference 6.13, 95% CI 3.52 to 8.75), 72.0% versus 31.6% were rated much/very much improved (odds ratio 5.56, relative), weekly cataplexy attacks fell −11.5 versus −4.9 (difference −6.65), and Epworth Sleepiness Scale fell −6.5 versus −2.7. Post-hoc analyses were concordant: sensitivity analyses accounting for missing data stayed significant with numbers needed to treat of 3 and effect sizes 0.7–0.9 (Roth 2025); sleepiness and sleep-quality gains were already detectable in weeks 1–2 (Krahn 2025); and about half of narcolepsy-type-1 participants on the higher doses halved their cataplexy attacks, ~10% eliminating them (Thorpy 2024). Common adverse reactions were nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness and enuresis. One trial programme: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Kushida 2022 — REST-ON (n=222): once-nightly sodium oxybate (FT218) beat placebo on all three co-primary endpoints at every dose (all P<0.001) — wakefulness +6.13 minutes, cataplexy −6.65 attacks/week, sleepiness −6.5 vs −2.7 ESS points at 9 g
cards.summary: Kushida 2022 — REST-ON (n=222): once-nightly sodium oxybate (FT218) beat placebo on all three co-primary endpoints at every dose (all P<0.001) — wakefulness +6.13 minutes, cataplexy −6.65 attacks/week, sleepiness −6.5 vs −2.7 ESS points at 9 g
cards.type: Phase 3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (REST-ON)
cards.people: 222 patients aged ≥16 years with narcolepsy (type 1 or 2) randomised 1:1 to once-nightly sodium oxybate (FT218) up-titrated through 4.5, 6, 7.5 and 9 g, or placebo; 212 received at least one dose (107 active, 105 placebo). Co-primary endpoints at 9, 7.5 and 6 g: change in mean sleep latency on the Maintenance of Wakefulness Test, Clinical Global Impression-Improvement rating, and weekly cataplexy attacks; Epworth Sleepiness Scale was a secondary endpoint.
cards.result: For all three co-primary endpoints and the Epworth scale, all three doses showed clinically meaningful, statistically significant improvement versus placebo (all P<0.001). At 9 g versus placebo: sleep latency increased 10.8 versus 4.7 minutes (least-squares mean difference 6.13, 95% CI 3.52 to 8.75); 72.0% versus 31.6% were rated much/very much improved (odds ratio 5.56, 95% CI 2.76 to 11.23 — relative measure); weekly cataplexy attacks changed by −11.5 versus −4.9 (difference −6.65, 95% CI −9.32 to −3.98); Epworth score changed by −6.5 versus −2.7. Common adverse reactions included nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness and enuresis; the safety profile was consistent with sodium oxybate, a controlled substance with restricted distribution.
cards.watchOut: A single trial of a single formulation; the forced up-titration design means the 9 g results come from patients who tolerated escalation, and oxybate's controlled-substance burden applies in full.
cards.source: Kushida CA et al. Once-nightly sodium oxybate (FT218) demonstrated improvement of symptoms in a phase 3 randomized clinical trial in patients with narcolepsy. Sleep. 2022. cards.headline: Roth 2025 (REST-ON post-hoc): the result survives missing-data sensitivity analyses — numbers needed to treat of 3 and effect sizes 0.7–0.9 for wakefulness response at all doses
cards.summary: Roth 2025 (REST-ON post-hoc): the result survives missing-data sensitivity analyses — numbers needed to treat of 3 and effect sizes 0.7–0.9 for wakefulness response at all doses
cards.type: Post-hoc sensitivity and effect-size analysis of a phase 3 trial
cards.people: Post-hoc sensitivity, effect-size and number-needed-to-treat analyses of the REST-ON trial (participants ≥16 years with narcolepsy type 1 or 2), including a completer population (once-nightly sodium oxybate n=69; placebo n=79), placebo-based multiple imputation under a missing-not-at-random assumption, ANCOVA, and tipping-point imputation.
cards.result: In completers, and under placebo-based imputation and ANCOVA, all doses significantly improved all co-primary endpoints versus placebo (P<0.001). The tipping-point analysis found that implausible or nearly implausible baseline wakefulness assumptions were needed to render the Maintenance of Wakefulness Test difference non-significant. All doses had numbers needed to treat of 3 and effect sizes of 0.7–0.9 for wakefulness response.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc analyses of the same single trial — they test the robustness of the REST-ON result, they do not replicate it.

cards.headline: Krahn 2025 (REST-ON post-hoc): benefit begins in the first two weeks — sleep quality and refreshing sleep significantly better by week 1 (4.5 g), sleepiness by week 2 (6 g)
cards.summary: Krahn 2025 (REST-ON post-hoc): benefit begins in the first two weeks — sleep quality and refreshing sleep significantly better by week 1 (4.5 g), sleepiness by week 2 (6 g)
cards.type: Post-hoc early-efficacy analysis of a phase 3 trial
cards.people: Post-hoc early-efficacy analysis of REST-ON in the modified intention-to-treat population (n=190; once-nightly sodium oxybate n=97, placebo n=93), examining Epworth Sleepiness Scale, visual-analogue sleep quality and refreshing nature of sleep at weeks 1 (4.5 g) and 2 (6 g), before the protocol's prespecified week-3 first assessment.
cards.result: At week 1 (4.5 g), sleep quality (difference 3.6, 95% CI 1.1 to 6.1; P<0.01) and refreshing nature of sleep (3.2, 95% CI 0.5 to 5.9; P<0.05) were significantly better on active treatment, with a numerical Epworth advantage (−0.7, 95% CI −1.6 to 0.2). At week 2 (6 g), all three measures significantly favoured active treatment: Epworth −1.3 (95% CI −2.4 to −0.2; P<0.02), sleep quality 7.0 (95% CI 3.8 to 10.1; P<0.001) and refreshing sleep 5.8 (95% CI 2.3 to 9.4; P=0.001).
cards.watchOut: Early timepoints were not prespecified efficacy assessments, and doses were still escalating — useful for setting expectations, not independent proof.
cards.source: Krahn L et al. Assessing Early Efficacy After Initiation of Once-Nightly Sodium Oxybate (ON-SXB; FT218) in Participants with Narcolepsy Type 1 or 2: A Post Hoc Analysis of REST-ON. CNS Drugs. 2025. PMID: 40111738. Registry ID: NCT02720744. cards.headline: Thorpy 2024 (REST-ON post-hoc, narcolepsy type 1): about half on the higher doses halved their weekly cataplexy attacks and ~10% eliminated them, versus placebo
cards.summary: Thorpy 2024 (REST-ON post-hoc, narcolepsy type 1): about half on the higher doses halved their weekly cataplexy attacks and ~10% eliminated them, versus placebo
cards.type: Post-hoc responder analysis of a phase 3 trial
cards.people: Post-hoc responder analysis of REST-ON participants with narcolepsy type 1 (once-nightly sodium oxybate n=73; placebo n=72; baseline mean weekly cataplexy episodes 18.9 and 19.8), examining ≥25%, ≥50%, ≥75% and 100% reductions in weekly cataplexy episodes at each dose step.
cards.result: Significantly greater proportions on active treatment than placebo achieved ≥25% reductions at weeks 1 (4.5 g; P<0.05), 3 (6 g; P<0.001), 8 (7.5 g; P<0.001) and 13 (9 g; P=0.001). Of participants receiving the highest doses (7.5 and 9 g), approximately half had a 50% reduction, one-third a 75% reduction, and one-tenth a 100% reduction in cataplexy episodes versus placebo.
cards.watchOut: Responder thresholds are post-hoc and the analysis is restricted to the type-1 subgroup; percentages at the top doses describe a minority reaching complete elimination (~10%).
cards.source: Thorpy MJ et al. Cataplexy response with extended-release once-nightly sodium oxybate: Post hoc responder analyses from the phase 3 REST-ON clinical trial. Sleep Med X. 2024. PMID: 38601325. Registry ID: NCT02720744 (as stated in the record). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, three co-primary wins, concordant post-hocs — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, three co-primary wins, concordant post-hocs — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: REST-ON primary report (n=222) and three post-hoc analyses of the same trial (Roth 2025; Krahn 2025, n=190; Thorpy 2024, type-1 n=145). The twice-nightly programme on #921 is a different formulation and is not carded here.
cards.result: Once-nightly sodium oxybate (FT218) improved wakefulness, global impression, cataplexy and sleepiness versus placebo in its single phase 3 trial, robustly across sensitivity analyses. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-trial programme ceiling, however consistent the post-hoc reports.

shelves.title: The human phase-response curve to bright light: delays before the temperature minimum, advances after it, a 5.02-hour peak-to-trough amplitude for a 6.7-hour pulse — and about 40% of that from a single 1-hour pulse
shelves.question: How does the direction and size of circadian phase shift from a single bright-light exposure depend on its timing relative to the core body temperature minimum — delays before, advances after — and what is the peak-to-trough amplitude?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Body Temperature · Circadian Rhythm · Female · Humans · Light · Male · Melatonin · Photic Stimulation · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: light is the dominant time cue for the circadian pacemaker, and its resetting effect reverses sign around the core body temperature minimum. The fetched primary human studies quantify that curve under constant-routine conditions. A single 6.7-hour bright-light pulse gives a type 1 phase-response curve with a peak-to-trough amplitude of 5.02 hours — delays when the pulse is centred before the temperature minimum, advances after it, and no shift at the minimum itself (Khalsa 2003, N = 21). Duration matters non-linearly: a single 1-hour pulse still achieves a 2.20-hour amplitude, about 40% of the long pulse's effect from 15% of its duration (St Hilaire 2012, N = 36), and a 6.5-hour pulse of short-wavelength (480 nm) light achieves about 75% of the white-light response, with fitted maxima of −2.6 hours (delay) and +1.3 hours (advance) (Rüger 2013, N = 18). Sensitivity is high at low light levels too: about half the maximal phase-delaying and melatonin-suppressing effect of ~9,000 lux is already obtained at ~100 lux of ordinary room light (Zeitzer 2000, N = 23). The neighbouring treatment shelf #5917 (melatonin for delayed sleep-wake phase disorder) applies circadian timing clinically; this shelf states the underlying response curve itself.

cards.headline: The reference curve: a single 6.7-hour bright-light pulse — peak-to-trough amplitude 5.02 hours, delays before the temperature minimum, advances after (N = 21)
cards.summary: The reference curve: a single 6.7-hour bright-light pulse — peak-to-trough amplitude 5.02 hours, delays before the temperature minimum, advances after (N = 21)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (constant-routine phase-response protocol)
cards.people: 21 healthy entrained adults studied with pre- and post-stimulus constant routines in dim light (~2–7 lux); the 6.7-hour stimulus alternated fixed gaze (~10,000 lux) and free gaze (~5,000–9,000 lux), scheduled across the circadian cycle in different subjects; phase read from plasma melatonin profiles.
cards.result: The phase-response curve for the midpoint of the melatonin rhythm was a type 1 curve with a significant peak-to-trough amplitude of 5.02 hours. Phase delays occurred when the light stimulus was centred prior to the critical phase at the core body temperature minimum, advances when centred after it, and no phase shift occurred at the critical phase. No prolonged 'dead zone' of photic insensitivity was apparent during the subjective day. Shifts calculated from melatonin onsets were larger than those from offsets.
cards.watchOut: Each subject contributes one point on the curve — the 5.02-hour amplitude is a fitted property of the group curve under tightly controlled dim-light conditions, not a shift any one person should expect from one exposure.
cards.source: Khalsa SBS et al. A phase response curve to single bright light pulses in human subjects. J Physiol. 2003. PMID: 12717008. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Body Temperature · Circadian Rhythm · Female · Humans · Male · Melatonin · Photic Stimulation · Photoperiod

cards.headline: One hour is enough for a large fraction: a single 1-hour bright pulse gives a 2.20-hour amplitude — about 40% of the 6.7-hour curve from 15% of the duration (N = 36)
cards.summary: One hour is enough for a large fraction: a single 1-hour bright pulse gives a 2.20-hour amplitude — about 40% of the 6.7-hour curve from 15% of the duration (N = 36)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (randomised 1-hour pulse phase-response protocol)
cards.people: 36 participants randomised to a 1-hour exposure to bright white light (~8,000 lux; n = 18) or to <3 lux dim background light (n = 18), scheduled at 1 of 18 circadian phases, with constant routines before and after; phase shifts from dim-light melatonin onset.
cards.result: The 1-hour bright pulse induced a type 1 phase-response curve with a fitted peak-to-trough amplitude of 2.20 hours; no discernible curve was observed under dim background light. The 1-hour amplitude was ~40% of the previously measured 6.7-hour amplitude despite representing only 15% of the exposure duration — a non-linear duration–response relationship.
cards.watchOut: Young healthy volunteers in a time-free laboratory environment; the comparison with the 6.7-hour curve is across studies run under similar, not identical, conditions.
cards.source: St Hilaire MA et al. Human phase response curve to a 1 h pulse of bright white light. J Physiol. 2012. PMID: 22547633. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adolescent · Adult · Circadian Rhythm · Female · Humans · Light · Male · Melatonin · Young Adult

cards.headline: Colour matters: a 6.5-hour pulse of short-wavelength (480 nm) light resets the clock at about 75% of the white-light response (N = 18)
cards.summary: Colour matters: a 6.5-hour pulse of short-wavelength (480 nm) light resets the clock at about 75% of the white-light response (N = 18)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (monochromatic-light phase-response protocol)
cards.people: 18 young healthy participants (18–30 years) studied 9–10 days in a time-free environment; a single 6.5-hour exposure to 480 nm light (11.8 µW/cm², 11.2 lux) after pupil dilation, with constant routines before and after; phase shifts from dim-light melatonin onset.
cards.result: The 480 nm exposure reset the pacemaker according to a conventional type 1 phase-response curve, with fitted maximum delays of −2.6 hours and maximum advances of +1.3 hours. The blue-light curve induced ~75% of the response of the previously constructed 10,000 lux white-light curve, despite its far lower photopic illuminance.
cards.watchOut: Pupils were pharmacologically dilated and the light was delivered in a Ganzfeld dome — the 75% figure compares photic systems under laboratory delivery, not ordinary blue-light exposure through an undilated pupil.
cards.source: Rüger M et al. Human phase response curve to a single 6.5 h pulse of short-wavelength light. J Physiol. 2013. PMID: 23090946. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adolescent · Adult · Body Temperature · Circadian Rhythm · Female · Humans · Light · Male · Melatonin · Young Adult

cards.headline: Sensitivity anchor: half the maximal delaying and melatonin-suppressing effect of ~9,000 lux is already reached at ~100 lux of room light (N = 23)
cards.summary: Sensitivity anchor: half the maximal delaying and melatonin-suppressing effect of ~9,000 lux is already reached at ~100 lux of room light (N = 23)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (illuminance dose–response protocol)
cards.people: 23 healthy young male and female volunteers in a 9-day protocol; a single 6.5-hour light exposure in the early biological night at illuminances from dim to ~9,000 lux; phase resetting and acute melatonin suppression both measured.
cards.result: Both the phase-delaying response and the acute suppression of plasma melatonin followed a logistic dose–response curve. Half of the maximal phase-delaying response to a single episode of ~9,000 lux evening bright light could be obtained with just over 1% of that light — dim room light of approximately 100 lux — and the same held for melatonin suppression.
cards.watchOut: This card measures the delaying limb in the early biological night only; it anchors sensitivity, not the full curve, and its logistic fit is a group model.
cards.source: Zeitzer JM et al. Sensitivity of the human circadian pacemaker to nocturnal light: melatonin phase resetting and suppression. J Physiol. 2000. PMID: 10922269. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one curve, three levers — timing sets the sign, duration and spectrum set the size
cards.summary: Synthesis: one curve, three levers — timing sets the sign, duration and spectrum set the size
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: 98 participants across the four primary studies carded (21 + 36 + 18 + 23).
cards.result: Timing relative to the core body temperature minimum determines direction (delay before, advance after, none at the minimum); a 6.7-hour bright pulse spans 5.02 hours peak-to-trough; a 1-hour pulse retains ~40% of that amplitude; short-wavelength light is disproportionately potent (~75% of the white-light response at a fraction of the illuminance); and even ~100 lux produces half the maximal delay/suppression. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Every card comes from young, healthy, laboratory-entrained volunteers under constant routines; ageing eyes, real-world light histories, and repeated daily exposures will move these numbers, and no card here measures them.
cards.source: Synthesis of Khalsa SBS et al. J Physiol. 2003 (PMID: 12717008); St Hilaire MA et al. J Physiol. 2012 (PMID: 22547633); Rüger M et al. J Physiol. 2013 (PMID: 23090946); Zeitzer JM et al. J Physiol. 2000 (PMID: 10922269). Registry IDs: none in the records.

shelves.question: In healthy humans, how do carbon dioxide, pH, temperature and 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate shift the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve (the Bohr effect and P50), and by how much?

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron and Boulpaep Medical Physiology): the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve is not fixed — acidity and carbon dioxide shift it right (the Bohr effect, promoting oxygen release in metabolising tissues), temperature shifts it right when warm and left when cold, and 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) binds deoxyhaemoglobin and shifts it right, with the standard P50 (the PO2 at 50% saturation, at pH 7.4, 37 °C, PCO2 40 mmHg) given in the textbooks as about 26–27 mmHg and the Bohr coefficient (Δlog P50 per ΔpH unit, about −0.48) and temperature coefficient presented as the textbook's account — the carded records confirm the directions and the baseline but do not print those two coefficients, so they are not claimed as measured values here. The carded primary human studies quantify what can be quantified from fetched records: a modern factorial in-vitro study of blood from 30 healthy subjects measured mean P50 of 27.1 ± 2.6 mmHg at baseline (37 °C, PCO2 40 mmHg) with significant CO2-Bohr and temperature coefficients across PCO2 20–80 mmHg and 13.7–42 °C (Woyke 2021); the classic normal P50 of 26 mmHg (3.46 kPa) was the reference value in the Fournier 1984 study of 20 subjects, which also showed a reversible 8 mmHg left shift under nitrous oxide that could not be explained by pH, PCO2, temperature or 2,3-DPG; and Lenfant's 1968 altitude study showed haemoglobin affinity changing within 24 hours of moving between low and high altitude, in parallel with red-cell organic phosphate (2,3-DPG) — the rapid adaptive limb of the 2,3-BPG mechanism, including the altitude 2,3-BPG adaptation this row folds in. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Woyke 2021: baseline P50 was 27.1 ± 2.6 mmHg at 37 °C and PCO2 40 mmHg, and both the CO2-Bohr and temperature effects on P50 were significant across the full factorial range
cards.summary: Woyke 2021: baseline P50 was 27.1 ± 2.6 mmHg at 37 °C and PCO2 40 mmHg, and both the CO2-Bohr and temperature effects on P50 were significant across the full factorial range
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (in-vitro human blood, factorial CO2 × temperature dissociation-curve mapping)
cards.people: Venous blood samples from 15 female and 15 male healthy subjects (30 subjects), each sample analysed in vitro at four PCO2 levels (20, 40, 60 and 80 mmHg) crossed with five temperatures (13.7, 23, 30, 37 and 42 °C) using a high-throughput oxygen-dissociation-curve method; P50s, Hill coefficients, CO2-Bohr coefficients and temperature coefficients analysed by linear mixed model.
cards.result: Mean P50 at baseline (37 °C, PCO2 40 mmHg) was 27.1 ± 2.6 mmHg. Both the CO2-Bohr coefficient and the temperature coefficient had a significant effect on P50 (each p < 0.001): higher PCO2 raised P50 (right shift, lower affinity) and higher temperature raised P50, while cooling lowered it. The absolute CO2 effect remained pronounced at normothermic and febrile temperatures, but at low temperatures the relative CO2 effect — the CO2-Bohr coefficient itself — was increased (p < 0.001 interaction), which the authors attribute to competition between 2,3-BPG and CO2 and the exothermic binding of 2,3-BPG. The fetched abstract reports the coefficients' significance and interaction but does not print their numeric values, so no coefficient value is claimed on this card.
cards.watchOut: An in-vitro study of drawn venous blood, not in-vivo tissue oxygen delivery: it isolates the curve shifts cleanly but cannot by itself say how much oxygen release changes in a living tissue bed, and its extreme conditions (13.7 °C, PCO2 80 mmHg) model avalanche burial rather than ordinary physiology.
cards.source: Woyke S et al. Effects of Carbon Dioxide and Temperature on the Oxygen-Hemoglobin Dissociation Curve of Human Blood: Implications for Avalanche Victims. Frontiers in Medicine. 2021. PMID: 35198571. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Fournier 1984: the normal P50 reference was 26 mmHg (3.46 kPa) — and 50% nitrous oxide shifted the curve left by 8 mmHg through none of the four classic factors
cards.summary: Fournier 1984: the normal P50 reference was 26 mmHg (3.46 kPa) — and 50% nitrous oxide shifted the curve left by 8 mmHg through none of the four classic factors
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (human blood dissociation curves, classic-factor controls)
cards.people: Blood from 20 healthy patients, with dissociation curves determined in vitro with and without exposure to 50% nitrous oxide, plus paired samples taken before and during 45 minutes of nitrous-oxide anaesthesia. N = 20 printed on the face of this physiology card.
cards.result: When blood samples were exposed to 50% N2O during determination of the dissociation curve, a left shift was observed and P50 fell by 1.06 kPa (8 mmHg). The authors state this shift cannot be explained by temperature, pH, PCO2 or 2,3-DPG effects. After exposure to N2O-free gases the shift disappeared rapidly and a normal P50 of 3.46 kPa (26 mmHg) was re-obtained — the study's printed normal reference value for P50 under standard conditions. In-vivo samples before and during anaesthesia showed curves identical to the in-vitro exposure experiment.
cards.watchOut: The study's purpose was an anaesthetic-gas effect, and it is carded here for its controlled normal-P50 reference and its demonstration that the four classic factors were held and excluded — the nitrous-oxide shift itself is a pharmacological curiosity, not part of normal curve regulation.
cards.source: Fournier L, Major D. The effect of nitrous oxide on the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve. Canadian Anaesthetists' Society Journal. 1984. PMID: 6423243. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lenfant 1968: haemoglobin affinity changed within 24 hours of an altitude change, in parallel with red-cell 2,3-DPG — the rapid 2,3-BPG adaptive limb
cards.summary: Lenfant 1968: haemoglobin affinity changed within 24 hours of an altitude change, in parallel with red-cell 2,3-DPG — the rapid 2,3-BPG adaptive limb
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (altitude exposure, serial oxygen-affinity and red-cell phosphate measurements)
cards.people: Subjects studied while moving from low to high altitude and from high to low altitude (the Finch/Reynafarje altitude programme); the number of subjects is not printed in the fetched abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Within 24 hours following the change in altitude there was a change in haemoglobin affinity for oxygen, and a parallel change occurred in the organic phosphate (2,3-diphosphoglycerate) content of the red cell: rising 2,3-DPG at altitude accompanied reduced affinity (a right shift favouring tissue oxygen release), with the reverse on descent. The authors note the study does not provide direct evidence of a cause–effect relationship, but the data strongly suggest that the anoxia-driven rise in red-cell organic phosphate is responsible for the increased availability of oxygen to tissues. The fetched abstract prints no numeric P50 or 2,3-DPG values, so none are claimed on this card — the quantified finding is the time course (within 24 hours) and the parallel movement of affinity and 2,3-DPG.
cards.watchOut: A 1968 study whose abstract reports direction and timing without numbers, and whose authors themselves flag that causality between the 2,3-DPG rise and the affinity change is inferred from parallelism, not directly proven.
cards.source: Lenfant C et al. Effect of altitude on oxygen binding by hemoglobin and on organic phosphate levels. Journal of Clinical Investigation. 1968. PMID: 5725278. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the curve's position is a controlled variable — CO2/pH, temperature and 2,3-BPG each move P50 off its 26–27 mmHg standard, on time scales from seconds (Bohr) to a day (2,3-BPG)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the curve's position is a controlled variable — CO2/pH, temperature and 2,3-BPG each move P50 off its 26–27 mmHg standard, on time scales from seconds (Bohr) to a day (2,3-BPG)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis across Woyke 2021 (30 subjects, factorial in-vitro mapping), Fournier 1984 (20 subjects, controlled reference P50) and Lenfant 1968 (altitude exposure series), framed by Guyton and Hall / Boron and Boulpaep.
cards.result: The carded studies agree on the standard-curve position (P50 26 mmHg in 1984, 27.1 ± 2.6 mmHg in 2021) and on the direction of every classic shift: CO2 and the acidity it generates shift right (Bohr effect), warming shifts right and cooling left, and 2,3-BPG shifts right with a measurable change already within 24 hours of an altitude move. Where the fetched records do not print a number — the numeric Bohr coefficient, the per-degree temperature coefficient, and the size of the altitude P50 change — this shelf presents those values explicitly as the textbook's account rather than as measurements from the carded studies.
cards.watchOut: No carded record isolates the pure pH (fixed-PCO2) Bohr coefficient numerically, and the stored-blood/transfusion P50 literature named in the slate was not carded because no fetched record in this session printed both the 2,3-DPG fall and the P50 fall with numbers — the transfusion limb rests on the textbook's account.
cards.source: Synthesis of Woyke S et al. Frontiers in Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 35198571); Fournier L, Major D. Canadian Anaesthetists' Society Journal. 1984 (PMID: 6423243); Lenfant C et al. Journal of Clinical Investigation. 1968 (PMID: 5725278)

shelves.title: Mucociliary clearance in health: tracheal mucus at 7–19 mm/min, wide variation between people, no fall with age, no posture effect — and a beta-agonist reserve of about a fifth
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how fast is mucus transported up the airways (tracheobronchial mucociliary clearance), and how do age, posture and inhaled agents change it?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aerosols · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Linear Models · Lung · Male · Middle Aged · Mucociliary Clearance · Radionuclide Imaging · Reference Values · Reproducibility of Results · Smoking · Technetium Tc 99m Aggregated Albumin · Terbutaline
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology — the textbooks describe the mucociliary escalator as a continuous cephalad transport of the mucus blanket by coordinated ciliary beating, the lung's first-line defence; the carded human studies supply the numbers). Direct tracheal measurement in volunteers gives mucus velocities of 7.4–19.4 mm/min (Friedman 1977, N = 7). Radioaerosol whole-lung clearance varies much more between people than within them (between-person COV 31%, within-person 11%; van Hengstum 1989), which is why the 62-person reference study matters: across ages 18–84 there was no influence of age on clearance and no convincing sex association, while central (versus peripheral) aerosol deposition and ex-smoking did matter (Mortensen 1994). Posture did not: erect and supine velocities did not differ consistently (Friedman 1977). Inhaled agents move the system in both directions in the wider literature; carded here, an inhaled secretagogue mediator, bradykinin, accelerated tracheobronchial clearance (median retention AUC 126%/h placebo to 87%/h; Polosa 1992), a beta-2 agonist raised lung clearance by a mean reserve of 21.3% (Mortensen 1994), and topical salmeterol shortened nasal saccharin transit by 21% (Tay 1997). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: clearance is fast, individually variable, age- and posture-stable, and pharmacologically accelerable.

cards.headline: Friedman 1977: tracheal mucus velocity in 7 normal volunteers was 7.4–19.4 mm/min, with no consistent difference between erect and supine posture
cards.summary: Friedman 1977: tracheal mucus velocity in 7 normal volunteers was 7.4–19.4 mm/min, with no consistent difference between erect and supine posture
cards.type: Human physiology study (roentgenographic tracheal mucus velocity, Friedman 1977)
cards.people: 7 normal volunteers without topical anaesthesia of the tracheobronchial tree; radiopaque Teflon–bismuth discs were blown onto the tracheal mucosa through a bronchofibrescope and their movement tracked on videotaped fluoroscopy (roentgenographic method validated against cinebronchofiberscopy in anaesthetised dogs). N = 7 — a small classic study, labelled plainly.
cards.result: Tracheal mucous velocity in the volunteers ranged from 7.4 to 19.4 mm per min. There was no consistent difference in velocity between the erect and the supine position, and no consistent difference after topical anaesthesia with lidocaine.
cards.watchOut: N = 7 and the range is wide — between-person variation is itself part of the finding. Disc velocity on the tracheal surface is a direct local measure, not whole-lung clearance; the two methods correlate but are not interchangeable.
cards.source: Friedman M et al. A new roentgenographic method for estimating mucous velocity in airways. The American review of respiratory disease. 1977. PMID: 835892. cards.headline: Mortensen 1994: in 62 healthy adults aged 18–84, lung mucociliary clearance showed no influence of age, and a beta-2 agonist raised clearance by a mean reserve of 21.3%
cards.summary: Mortensen 1994: in 62 healthy adults aged 18–84, lung mucociliary clearance showed no influence of age, and a beta-2 agonist raised clearance by a mean reserve of 21.3%
cards.type: Human physiology study (radioaerosol clearance reference values, Mortensen 1994)
cards.people: 62 healthy subjects (33 women, 29 men) aged 18–84 years; 53 lifelong non-smokers and 9 ex-smokers. Radioaerosol lung mucociliary clearance measured at baseline and after a beta-2-adrenergic agonist (terbutaline) to define the mucociliary clearance reserve capacity.
cards.result: Multiple regression showed clearance was significantly faster when the radioaerosol deposited centrally than peripherally, and faster in lifelong non-smokers than in ex-smokers. There was no influence of age and no convincing association with sex. Variation was less within than between subjects. Mean mucociliary clearance reserve capacity — the beta-2 agonist-induced increase — was 21.3% (SD 10.0%, P < 0.0001), larger than previously reported in asthma, bronchiectasis or cystic fibrosis.
cards.watchOut: This is the largest carded series and the direct answer on age: across 18–84 years, age did not explain clearance. Deposition pattern (central vs peripheral) is a major technical confounder in every radioaerosol study on this shelf.
cards.source: Mortensen J et al. Lung mucociliary clearance. European journal of nuclear medicine. 1994. PMID: 7995289. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: van Hengstum 1989: repeated radioaerosol clearance in 10 healthy non-smokers — between-person coefficient of variation 31%, within-person 11%
cards.summary: van Hengstum 1989: repeated radioaerosol clearance in 10 healthy non-smokers — between-person coefficient of variation 31%, within-person 11%
cards.type: Human physiology study (radioaerosol clearance reproducibility, van Hengstum 1989)
cards.people: 10 healthy non-smoking volunteers studied twice with a radioaerosol technique (5 µm 99mTc-labelled polystyrene particles); lung radioactivity followed for 6 h and again at 24 h, quantified as the area under the retention curve to 6 h (AUC-6). N = 10 — small, labelled plainly.
cards.result: The intersubject coefficient of variation of AUC-6 was 31%; the intrasubject coefficient of variation was 11%. The authors conclude within-person variability of tracheobronchial clearance by this technique is small, so a change within a person is interpretable against a much noisier between-person spread.
cards.watchOut: Percent-retention AUC is an inverse index — a lower AUC means faster clearance. Small N; the value of the study is the variability structure, not a single normal rate.
cards.source: van Hengstum M et al. Variability of tracheobronchial clearance in healthy non-smoking subjects. Respiration; international review of thoracic diseases. 1989. PMID: 2513626. cards.headline: Polosa 1992: inhaled bradykinin accelerated tracheobronchial clearance in 10 healthy volunteers — median retention AUC fell from 126%/h on placebo to 87%/h
cards.summary: Polosa 1992: inhaled bradykinin accelerated tracheobronchial clearance in 10 healthy volunteers — median retention AUC fell from 126%/h on placebo to 87%/h
cards.type: Human physiology study (radioaerosol clearance after inhaled bradykinin, Polosa 1992)
cards.people: 10 healthy volunteers in a randomised double-blind crossover: radioaerosol inhalation followed 30 minutes later by inhaled bradykinin (8 mg/mL) or vehicle placebo, with whole-lung counts every half hour for 6 h. N = 10 — small, labelled plainly.
cards.result: Clearance was greater after bradykinin in 9 of 10 subjects. Median AUC0–6h was 126% (range 78–232%)/h with placebo and 87% (51–133%)/h with bradykinin — an inhaled secretagogue mediator measurably speeds tracheobronchial clearance in normal airways.
cards.watchOut: Bradykinin is an experimental inhaled agent, not a therapy; the card shows the system is pharmacologically accelerable in health. Cough counts were recorded because cough itself clears radioaerosol.

cards.headline: Tay 1997: topical salmeterol shortened nasal saccharin transit time by 21% in 33 healthy adults (P = 0.0001)
cards.summary: Tay 1997: topical salmeterol shortened nasal saccharin transit time by 21% in 33 healthy adults (P = 0.0001)
cards.type: Human physiology study (saccharin transit after topical beta-2 agonist, Tay 1997)
cards.people: 33 healthy adults in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of topical salmeterol spray, with nasal mucociliary clearance measured by the saccharin test.
cards.result: There was a 21% reduction in nasal mucociliary transport time with salmeterol compared with placebo (P = 0.0001). Age, sex, treatment order, interval between spray and test, and history of seasonal allergic rhinitis did not affect the improvement.
cards.watchOut: Nasal saccharin transit is the upper-airway companion measure, not tracheobronchial clearance itself; a second intranasal salbutamol trial in normal subjects found no effect, so the beta-agonist effect is agent- and site-dependent — the lung radioaerosol reserve in Mortensen 1994 is the lower-airway counterpart.
cards.source: Tay HL et al. Nasal mucociliary clearance and salmeterol. Clinical otolaryngology and allied sciences. 1997. PMID: 9088685. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: 7 + 62 + 10 + 10 + 33 healthy volunteers across the carded studies.
cards.result: Tracheal mucus moves at roughly 7–19 mm/min in health; whole-lung radioaerosol clearance varies far more between people (COV ~31%) than within a person (~11%), does not decline with age across 18–84 years, and does not differ consistently between erect and supine posture. The system has pharmacological reserve: a beta-2 agonist raises lung clearance by ~21% and shortens nasal saccharin transit by ~21%, and an inhaled secretagogue (bradykinin) accelerates tracheobronchial clearance. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis of small classic volunteer studies plus one 62-person reference series; absolute rates are method-dependent (disc velocity, radioaerosol retention, saccharin time are three different measurements).

shelves.title: Sleep restriction and glucose: a few nights at 4–5 hours cut insulin sensitivity by about a fifth and blunt glucose tolerance — with the defect demonstrable inside fat cells
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how much does restricting sleep to about 4 hours a night for several nights impair glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analysis of Variance · Blood Glucose · C-Peptide · Carbohydrate Metabolism · Endocrine System · Humans · Hydrocortisone · Hypothalamo-Hypophyseal System · Insulin · Male · Pituitary-Adrenal System · Sleep Deprivation · Sleep Stages · Sympathetic Nervous System · Thyrotropin · Thyroxine · Vagus Nerve
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Guyton & Hall — sleep is presented as a metabolic state, not merely rest; the Van Cauter programme carded here is the primary human evidence that curtailing it moves glucose regulation within days). The anchor study restricted 11 young men to 4 hours in bed for 6 nights against a 12-hour recovery condition: glucose tolerance was significantly lower in sleep debt (P < 0.02), with raised evening cortisol and sympathetic activity (Spiegel 1999). The clamp study gives the size: after 7 nights at 5 hours, insulin sensitivity fell 20 ± 24% by IVGTT and 11 ± 5.5% by euglycaemic clamp, with no compensatory rise in insulin secretion and a reduced disposition index (Buxton 2010). The defect is peripheral and molecular, not just hormonal: after 4 nights at 4.5 hours, adipocytes from 7 volunteers needed nearly three times the insulin for half-maximal Akt signalling (Broussard 2012), and after only 2 nights at ~4 hours, breakfast glucose peaked at 6.8 mmol/L (≈122 mg/dL) versus 6.1 mmol/L (≈110 mg/dL) rested, with insulin peaks ~40% higher and no change in cortisol or IL-6 (Schmid 2011). Adjacent shelf: weekend catch-up sleep and metabolic recovery is asked separately (live Shelf #494) and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: several nights of ~4-hour sleep produce a measurable, roughly one-fifth loss of insulin sensitivity in healthy young adults.

cards.headline: Spiegel 1999: 4 hours in bed for 6 nights lowered glucose tolerance versus 12-hour recovery sleep in 11 young men (P < 0.02), with raised evening cortisol
cards.summary: Spiegel 1999: 4 hours in bed for 6 nights lowered glucose tolerance versus 12-hour recovery sleep in 11 young men (P < 0.02), with raised evening cortisol
cards.type: Human physiology study (sleep-debt crossover, Spiegel, Leproult & Van Cauter 1999)
cards.people: 11 young men studied after 6 nights restricted to 4 h in bed per night (sleep debt) and again after a recovery period of 12 h in bed per night for 6 nights, with carbohydrate metabolism, thyrotropic function, hypothalamo-pituitary-adrenal activity and sympathovagal balance assessed. N = 11 — small, labelled plainly.
cards.result: Glucose tolerance was lower in the sleep-debt condition than in the fully rested condition (P < 0.02), as were thyrotropin concentrations (P < 0.01). Evening cortisol concentrations were raised (P = 0.0001) and sympathetic nervous system activity was increased (P < 0.02) during sleep debt. The authors note the effects resemble those of normal ageing. The fetched abstract reports direction and significance, not percentage changes in glucose clearance — no percentage is printed on this card because the record does not give one.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is a 12-hour recovery condition, not habitual 8-hour sleep, which can exaggerate the contrast. Young men only; the frequently quoted percentage figures for this study come from its full text, not the fetched record, and are not used here.
cards.source: Spiegel K et al. Impact of sleep debt on metabolic and endocrine function. Lancet (London, England). 1999. PMID: 10543671. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Buxton 2010: 5 hours in bed for 7 nights reduced insulin sensitivity by 20 ± 24% on IVGTT and 11 ± 5.5% by clamp in 20 healthy men
cards.summary: Buxton 2010: 5 hours in bed for 7 nights reduced insulin sensitivity by 20 ± 24% on IVGTT and 11 ± 5.5% by clamp in 20 healthy men
cards.type: Human physiology study (sleep restriction with IVGTT and clamp, Buxton 2010)
cards.people: 20 healthy men (age 20–35, BMI 20–30 kg/m2) in a 12-day inpatient study: at least 8 nights at 10 h in bed (sleep-replete, including 3 inpatient nights), then 7 nights at 5 h in bed, with controlled diet and activity and modafinil or placebo during restriction; glucose metabolism assessed by IVGTT and euglycaemic-hyperinsulinaemic clamp on the last 2 days of each condition. Registry ID: NCT00895570 (in the record).
cards.result: IVGTT-derived insulin sensitivity fell by 20 ± 24% after sleep restriction (P = 0.001) without a significant change in the insulin secretory response; clamp-measured insulin sensitivity fell by 11 ± 5.5% (P < 0.04). Glucose tolerance and the disposition index were also reduced. Modafinil did not affect these outcomes, and changes in insulin sensitivity did not correlate with salivary cortisol (which rose 51 ± 8%), urinary catecholamines or slow-wave sleep.
cards.watchOut: 5 h rather than 4 h in bed, and a fixed order (replete always first) — period effects cannot be excluded. The IVGTT estimate is much more variable (±24%) than the clamp estimate; the clamp figure is the tighter measurement.
cards.source: Buxton OM et al. Sleep restriction for 1 week reduces insulin sensitivity in healthy men. Diabetes. 2010. PMID: 20585000. Registry ID: NCT00895570. cards.headline: Broussard 2012: after 4 nights of 4.5 hours in bed, adipocytes needed nearly 3× the insulin for half-maximal signalling and total-body insulin sensitivity fell in 7 healthy adults
cards.summary: Broussard 2012: after 4 nights of 4.5 hours in bed, adipocytes needed nearly 3× the insulin for half-maximal signalling and total-body insulin sensitivity fell in 7 healthy adults
cards.type: Human physiology study (sleep restriction with adipocyte biopsy, Broussard 2012)
cards.people: 7 healthy adults (6 men, 1 woman; mean age 23.7 years) in a randomised 2-period crossover: 4 days of 4.5 h in bed versus 8.5 h in bed under controlled caloric intake and activity, with subcutaneous fat biopsies — adipocyte insulin signalling (phosphorylated Akt response) measured ex vivo — and frequently sampled IVGTT for total-body insulin sensitivity. N = 7 — very small, labelled plainly.
cards.result: The insulin concentration for half-maximal adipocyte pAkt response was nearly 3-fold higher after sleep restriction (0.71 nM (SD 0.27) versus 0.24 nM (SD 0.24); P = 0.01), and the total area under the pAkt response curve was 30% lower (P = 0.01) — direct molecular evidence of peripheral insulin resistance in fat after 4 nights of restriction, alongside reduced total-body insulin sensitivity on IVGTT.
cards.watchOut: N = 7 and a single tissue: the adipocyte signalling defect is mechanistically decisive but its size in muscle and liver is not measured here. The fetched record's abstract is truncated at the IVGTT sentence, so no whole-body percentage is printed from this card.
cards.source: Broussard JL et al. Impaired insulin signaling in human adipocytes after experimental sleep restriction: a randomized, crossover study. Annals of internal medicine. 2012. cards.headline: Schmid 2011: after 2 nights of ~4 hours' sleep, breakfast glucose peaked at 6.8 mmol/L (≈122 mg/dL) versus 6.1 mmol/L (≈110 mg/dL) after regular sleep, with insulin peaks ~40% higher
cards.summary: Schmid 2011: after 2 nights of ~4 hours' sleep, breakfast glucose peaked at 6.8 mmol/L (≈122 mg/dL) versus 6.1 mmol/L (≈110 mg/dL) after regular sleep, with insulin peaks ~40% higher
cards.type: Human physiology study (short sleep restriction with meal challenge, Schmid 2011)
cards.people: 15 healthy normal-weight men in a balanced within-subject design: 2 nights of restricted sleep (02:45–07:00, ~4.25 h) versus 2 nights of regular sleep (22:45–07:00), with 15 hours of close monitoring of glucose, insulin, C-peptide, glucagon, ACTH, cortisol and IL-6 including responses to a standard breakfast.
cards.result: Pre-breakfast values were unchanged (P > 0.30), but post-breakfast peaks were distinctly higher after sleep restriction: insulin 398.5 ± 57.4 versus 284.3 ± 51.5 pmol/L and glucose 6.8 ± 0.3 versus 6.1 ± 0.3 mmol/L (122 versus 110 mg/dL) (all P < 0.02), while glucagon responses were blunted (P = 0.03). ACTH, cortisol and IL-6 did not differ (P > 0.25) — the authors read the pattern as impaired glucose tolerance primarily from reduced insulin sensitivity, not stress-hormone or inflammatory mediation.
cards.watchOut: Only 2 nights and a meal challenge rather than a clamp or IVGTT — the effect appears fast, but this design cannot separate hepatic from peripheral insulin resistance.
cards.source: Schmid SM et al. Disturbed glucoregulatory response to food intake after moderate sleep restriction. Sleep. 2011. PMID: 21358855. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: 11 + 20 + 7 + 15 healthy volunteers across the carded studies.
cards.result: Restricting sleep to ~4–5 hours a night for 2–7 nights reproducibly impairs glucose handling in healthy young adults: glucose tolerance falls (Spiegel 1999), insulin sensitivity falls by ~11% by clamp and ~20% by IVGTT without compensatory insulin secretion (Buxton 2010), adipocyte insulin signalling itself becomes resistant within 4 nights (Broussard 2012), and post-meal glucose and insulin peaks rise after just 2 nights (Schmid 2011). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: All carded studies are short, laboratory, mostly male and young — they establish the acute physiological effect, not the long-term diabetes risk of habitual short sleep, which is an epidemiological question for other shelves.
cards.source: Synthesis of Spiegel K et al., Lancet (London, England) 1999 (PMID: 10543671); Buxton OM et al., Diabetes 2010 (PMID: 20585000); Broussard JL et al., Annals of internal medicine 2012 (PMID: 23070488); Schmid SM et al., Sleep 2011 (PMID: 21358855).

shelves.title: The acute hypoxic ventilatory response: flat until PO2 ~50–60 mmHg then steeply rising, ~0.68 L/min per % SaO2 awake — and a stable, partly hereditary trait that varies widely between people
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how large is the acute hypoxic ventilatory response to a step fall in oxygen saturation, and how much does it vary between individuals?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Carbon Dioxide · Computers, Analog · Humans · Hypoxia · Male · Oxygen · Respiration · Respiratory Function Tests · Spirometry
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology — the peripheral chemoreflex: carotid-body sensing of arterial PO2 drives ventilation, with an effective threshold in the 50–60 mmHg range and powerful multiplicative interaction with CO2; the Weil programme carded here built the human measurement). Weil's continuous-curve method showed the response is complete within 18–23 seconds and hyperbolic — ventilation barely moves until alveolar PO2 falls to 50–60 mmHg, then climbs steeply — quantified by the shape parameter A = 180.2 ± 14.5 in 10 normal men at resting CO2, swinging to 453 with +5 mmHg CO2 and 30 with −5 mmHg (Weil 1970). In saturation-slope units, the awake progressive-isocapnic response is 0.68 ± 0.07 L/min per % SaO2, roughly halving in sleep (Berthon-Jones & Sullivan 1982). The variation the question asks about is real and structured: pooled raw data from 60 datasets show positively skewed distributions with low responders common in healthy sea-level people, and isocapnic protocols yielding higher values than poikilocapnic (Oeung 2023); identical twins resemble each other in HVR while non-identical twins do not (Collins 1978); and an individual's response tracks himself over 8–10 years (r = 0.63) even as the group mean drifts down (Nishimura 1991). Adjacent shelves ask the different questions of the hypercapnic response and of ventilatory acclimatisation over days at altitude (Pack #6247) — neither is re-carded here. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Weil 1970: the isocapnic hypoxic response in 10 normal men is hyperbolic — ventilation barely rises until alveolar PO2 falls to 50–60 mmHg, then climbs steeply (shape parameter A = 180.2 ± 14.5)
cards.summary: Weil 1970: the isocapnic hypoxic response in 10 normal men is hyperbolic — ventilation barely rises until alveolar PO2 falls to 50–60 mmHg, then climbs steeply (shape parameter A = 180.2 ± 14.5)
cards.type: Human physiology study (isocapnic hypoxic ventilatory response, Weil 1970)
cards.people: 10 normal subjects (6 studied also at altered CO2) in whom the ventilatory response to isocapnic hypoxia was inscribed as a continuous curve of minute ventilation against alveolar oxygen tension, with CO2 added to inspired gas to hold alveolar CO2 constant; curves fitted with a hyperbolic function whose parameter A indexes hypoxic drive.
cards.result: Ventilatory adjustment to a change in alveolar oxygen tension was complete in 18–23 seconds. The ventilation–PAO2 curves are hyperbolic: falling PAO2 produces only slight rises in ventilation until a critical PAO2 range of 50–60 mmHg is reached, below which ventilation increases steeply, the slope approaching infinity at 30–40 mmHg. At resting PACO2, A = 180.2 ± 14.5 (SEM) in the 10 subjects, and curves were highly reproducible within each subject. CO2 interacted powerfully: raising PACO2 by 5 mmHg raised A to 453.4 ± 103, and lowering it by 5 mmHg cut A to 30.2 ± 6.8 (both P < 0.05).
cards.watchOut: The founding Weil-programme method paper: A is a curve-shape parameter, not a slope in L/min per % saturation, so its values cannot be compared numerically with the saturation-slope studies carded alongside it. Men only, resting, acute hypoxia.

cards.headline: Berthon-Jones & Sullivan 1982: awake hypoxic ventilatory response slope was 0.68 ± 0.07 L/min per % SaO2 in 9 healthy adults, falling to 0.42 in NREM and 0.33 in REM sleep
cards.summary: Berthon-Jones & Sullivan 1982: awake hypoxic ventilatory response slope was 0.68 ± 0.07 L/min per % SaO2 in 9 healthy adults, falling to 0.42 in NREM and 0.33 in REM sleep
cards.type: Human physiology study (progressive isocapnic hypoxia across sleep states, Berthon-Jones & Sullivan 1982)
cards.people: 9 healthy adults (5 men, 4 women) studied awake and asleep with a progressive isocapnic rebreathing method (ear oximetry for SaO2, end-tidal CO2 held constant by variable soda-lime absorption): 36 wakefulness, 26 NREM and 15 REM tests.
cards.result: During wakefulness the mean slope of the ventilatory response to hypoxia was 0.68 ± 0.07 L/min/% SaO2 (mean end-tidal CO2 37.0 mmHg). In NREM sleep it fell to 0.42 ± 0.06 and in REM sleep to 0.33 ± 0.06 L/min/% SaO2 — a significant state-dependent effect (P < 0.01). Arousal from sleep was unreliable: subjects failed to awaken by 70% SaO2, the safety limit, in 12 of 26 NREM and 7 of 15 REM tests.
cards.watchOut: The question asks about the acute awake response — the sleep values are carded because the same study measures them with the same method, showing the awake figure is a state-dependent maximum. Small N (9), many repeated tests.
cards.source: Berthon-Jones M et al. Ventilatory and arousal responses to hypoxia in sleeping humans. The American review of respiratory disease. 1982. PMID: 6807150. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nishimura 1991: hypoxic chemosensitivity was a stable personal trait over 8–10 years (individual values correlated r = 0.63) while the group mean slope factor fell from 98.3 to 77.4
cards.summary: Nishimura 1991: hypoxic chemosensitivity was a stable personal trait over 8–10 years (individual values correlated r = 0.63) while the group mean slope factor fell from 98.3 to 77.4
cards.type: Human physiology study (longitudinal hypoxic chemosensitivity, Nishimura 1991)
cards.people: 32 healthy male volunteers (mean age 42.2 ± 1.4 years at final examination; 22 of them sons of COPD patients) in whom ventilatory responses to isocapnic progressive hypoxia and normoxic progressive hypercapnia were measured at intervals of 8–10 years; reproducibility assessed separately by three measurements at 1-week intervals in 6 subjects.
cards.result: The mean slope factor of the end-tidal PO2–ventilation hyperbola (A) decreased significantly from 98.3 ± 12.2 to 77.4 ± 10.3 L/min·mmHg over the interval (P < 0.05), while the hypercapnic slope did not change. Individual hypoxic-response values were significantly correlated between the first and final examinations (r = 0.63, P < 0.001); hypercapnic values were not (r = 0.23, NS). The authors conclude hypoxic chemosensitivity is determined more by factors inherent to the individual than hypercapnic chemosensitivity.
cards.watchOut: A here is the Weil-type hyperbola parameter from a different fitting convention — again not interchangeable with saturation slopes. The cohort is enriched with sons of COPD patients, which may widen the spread of responses.
cards.source: Nishimura M et al. Longitudinal analyses of respiratory chemosensitivity in normal subjects. The American review of respiratory disease. 1991. PMID: 2048813. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Collins 1978 (Weil programme): hypoxic ventilatory response correlated within identical twin pairs (P < 0.01) but not within non-identical pairs — the variation is substantially hereditary
cards.summary: Collins 1978 (Weil programme): hypoxic ventilatory response correlated within identical twin pairs (P < 0.01) but not within non-identical pairs — the variation is substantially hereditary
cards.type: Human physiology study (twin study of hypoxic ventilatory response, Collins, Scoggin, Zwillich & Weil 1978)
cards.people: 12 pairs of identical and 12 pairs of non-identical twins in whom ventilatory responses to isocapnic hypoxia and to hyperoxic hypercapnia were measured, with resemblance within pairs compared between twin types.
cards.result: A significant correlation (P < 0.01) for hypoxic ventilatory response was found within identical twin pairs but not within non-identical pairs, and identical twins resembled each other more closely than non-identical twins (P < 0.0125), independent of body size, blood PCO2 or pH. No such correlation was found for the hypercapnic ventilatory response. The authors conclude hereditary influences affect the hypoxic ventilatory response.
cards.watchOut: The fetched abstract reports correlations and significance, not the twins' slope values — the card therefore claims the hereditary structure of the variation, not its size. 24 twin pairs; a classic small study, labelled plainly.

cards.headline: Oeung 2023: across 78 studies in healthy humans, hypoxic ventilatory response distributions are positively skewed — low responses are common — and isocapnic methods give higher values than poikilocapnic
cards.summary: Oeung 2023: across 78 studies in healthy humans, hypoxic ventilatory response distributions are positively skewed — low responses are common — and isocapnic methods give higher values than poikilocapnic
cards.type: Meta-analysis of primary hypoxic ventilatory response datasets (Oeung 2023)
cards.people: Meta-analysis and computational investigation of the published literature: 78 studies using step-down/steady-state or progressive hypoxia in untreated healthy human subjects, yielding 72 datasets with mean HVR values and 60 datasets with raw individual values.
cards.result: Of the 60 raw datasets, 35 (58.3%) were at least moderately positively skewed (skew > 0.5) and 21 (35%) significantly positively skewed (skew > 1) — lower HVR values are common in healthy sea-level populations, not only in high-altitude natives. Skewness was not an artefact of method or reporting unit. Step-down versus progressive methods did not significantly change average HVR, but isocapnic protocols produced higher HVRs than poikilocapnic protocols.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis card, not a primary experiment: it is carded because the question's second half — how much the response varies between individuals — is a distributional claim that only the pooled raw data can answer. Method (especially CO2 control) shifts the mean, so cross-study numerical comparison needs the protocol stated.
cards.source: Oeung B et al. The normal distribution of the hypoxic ventilatory response and methodological impacts: a meta-analysis and computational investigation. The Journal of physiology. 2023. PMID: 37589511. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Normal Distribution · Altitude · Hypoxia · Oxygen · Respiration

cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: 10 + 9 + 32 volunteers and 24 twin pairs in the primary studies, plus 78 pooled studies in the distribution analysis.
cards.result: The acute hypoxic ventilatory response is hyperbolic and fast (complete in ~20 seconds): ventilation is almost flat until PAO2 reaches ~50–60 mmHg, then rises steeply — an awake isocapnic slope of ~0.68 L/min per % SaO2 in the classic rebreathing measurement. Between individuals it varies widely and skewedly (low responders are common), the variation is substantially hereditary (twin data), personally stable over a decade (r = 0.63), and exquisitely CO2-sensitive — 5 mmHg of CO2 moves the Weil A parameter roughly fifteenfold between hypocapnia and hypercapnia. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Three non-interchangeable metrics appear on this shelf (Weil A, Nishimura A, and L/min per % SaO2 slopes); each card states its own. Never average across them.
cards.source: Synthesis of Weil JV et al., The Journal of clinical investigation 1970 (PMID: 5422012); Berthon-Jones M et al., The American review of respiratory disease 1982 (PMID: 6807150); Nishimura M et al., The American review of respiratory disease 1991 (PMID: 2048813); Collins DD et al., The Journal of clinical investigation 1978 (PMID: 566281); Oeung B et al., The Journal of physiology 2023 (PMID: 37589511).

shelves.title: Seralutinib in pulmonary arterial hypertension (TORREY): a phase-2 PVR win, phase 3 still to come
shelves.question: In adults with pulmonary arterial hypertension on background therapy, does inhaled seralutinib (a PDGFR/CSF1R/c-KIT inhibitor) improve pulmonary vascular resistance and exercise capacity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension · Protein Kinase Inhibitors · Vascular Resistance · Administration, Inhalation · Humans
shelves.balance: PHASE 2 ONLY — flagged on the face; a single phase 2 programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. TORREY (n = 86 randomised) met its primary endpoint: the least-squares mean difference in 24-week change in pulmonary vascular resistance was −96.1 dyne·s/cm⁵ (95% CI −183.5 to −8.8; P = 0.03) for inhaled seralutinib vs placebo on background therapy. The open-label extension (74 patients) reports durability descriptively — median PVR change from TORREY baseline to week 72 of −143 dyne·s/cm⁵ in those continued on seralutinib — but without a control group it cannot confirm benefit, and cough led 12.2% to discontinue. Phase 1 drug-interaction studies in healthy volunteers (n = 24 and 19) found all adverse events mild or moderate, with seralutinib a moderate CYP3A inhibitor (midazolam AUC 3.03-fold). No phase 3 result is published; the phase 3 PROSERA study is underway per the extension record. Nothing here shows a mortality or hospitalisation benefit.

cards.headline: TORREY 2024 (phase 2): inhaled seralutinib reduced pulmonary vascular resistance vs placebo at 24 weeks — LS mean difference −96.1 dyne·s/cm⁵ (P = 0.03), n = 86
cards.summary: TORREY 2024 (phase 2): inhaled seralutinib reduced pulmonary vascular resistance vs placebo at 24 weeks — LS mean difference −96.1 dyne·s/cm⁵ (P = 0.03), n = 86
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (TORREY), Lancet Respir Med 2024
cards.people: Eighty-six adults with WHO Group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension, WHO Functional Class II–III, PVR ≥400 dyne·s/cm⁵ and 6-minute walk distance 150–550 m, on background PAH therapy at 40 sites; randomised 1:1 to inhaled seralutinib (44; 60 mg twice daily for 2 weeks, then 90 mg twice daily as tolerated) or placebo (42) by dry-powder inhaler for 24 weeks. Primary endpoint: change in PVR from baseline to week 24.
cards.result: Least-squares mean change in PVR was −74.9 dyne·s/cm⁵ (95% CI −139.7 to −10.2) with seralutinib and +21.2 (−37.4 to 79.8) with placebo — a least-squares mean difference of −96.1 dyne·s/cm⁵ (95% CI −183.5 to −8.8; P = 0.03), meeting the phase 2 primary endpoint. The most common treatment-emergent adverse event in both groups was cough (43% seralutinib; 38% placebo). The seralutinib group had a higher representation of Functional Class II patients at baseline, a chance imbalance the record notes. This is a haemodynamic phase 2 result — no mortality or clinical-worsening outcome is established.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2 only, n = 86, surrogate haemodynamic endpoint; stamp capped at POSSIBLE for a single programme. The 6-minute-walk result is not printed in the fetched abstract's results excerpt and is therefore not quantified here.

cards.headline: TORREY open-label extension 2025: PVR reductions persisted descriptively to week 72 (−143 dyne·s/cm⁵ median in continuers), but 27% discontinued for adverse events — cough the commonest reason
cards.summary: TORREY open-label extension 2025: PVR reductions persisted descriptively to week 72 (−143 dyne·s/cm⁵ median in continuers), but 27% discontinued for adverse events — cough the commonest reason
cards.type: Open-label extension study (uncontrolled, descriptive), Adv Ther 2025
cards.people: Seventy-four patients entered the open-label extension: 73 of 80 TORREY completers plus 1 of 8 from a phase 1b study; 34 continued seralutinib and 40 crossed over from placebo, all on inhaled seralutinib 90 mg twice daily. PVR measured at week 48 of the extension (week 72 from TORREY baseline). Analyses are descriptive — no control group.
cards.result: Common treatment-emergent adverse events were headache (28.4%), COVID-19 (27.0%) and cough (23.0%); adverse events led to discontinuation in 20 of 74 patients (27.0%), cough alone in 9 of 74 (12.2%). In the continued-seralutinib group, median PVR change from TORREY baseline was −94 dyne·s/cm⁵ at week 24 and −143 at week 72 (n = 28); in the placebo-crossover group, −32 and −56 respectively (n = 27). NT-proBNP fell during TORREY on seralutinib and remained stable through the extension. Uncontrolled extension data can show tolerability and consistency; they cannot separate drug effect from survivor and natural-history effects, and a phase 3 study (PROSERA) is underway per the record.
cards.watchOut: No comparator; the week-72 PVR values come from the 28 and 27 patients still measured — attrition (27% discontinued) biases extension results toward tolerators. Carded as durability/tolerability evidence only.
cards.source: Sitbon O, Sahay S, Escribano Subías P, Zolty RL, et al. Seralutinib for the Treatment of Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension in Adults: TORREY Open-Label Extension Study. cards.summary: Phase 1 interaction studies 2025: in 43 healthy participants all adverse events were mild or moderate; seralutinib is a moderate CYP3A inhibitor (midazolam AUC ×3.03) and a strong CYP3A inhibitor raises seralutinib exposure (AUC ×1.84)
cards.type: Phase 1 drug–drug interaction studies in healthy volunteers, Clin Pharmacol Drug Dev 2025
cards.people: Two phase 1 studies in healthy participants: study 1, 24 participants receiving a probe-substrate cocktail (caffeine, montelukast, flurbiprofen, midazolam, pravastatin, digoxin) with or without seralutinib; study 2, 19 participants receiving seralutinib with or without itraconazole (strong CYP3A inhibitor) or fosaprepitant (weak CYP3A inhibitor).
cards.result: All adverse events were mild or moderate in severity. Seralutinib increased midazolam AUC 3.03-fold and caffeine AUC 1.32-fold, and digoxin Cmax 1.28-fold, without meaningfully altering montelukast, flurbiprofen or pravastatin exposure — seralutinib is a moderate CYP3A inhibitor, a weak CYP1A2 inhibitor and a slight P-gp inhibitor. Itraconazole increased seralutinib AUC 1.84-fold; fosaprepitant 1.08-fold. Carded as the human safety/pharmacology limb of a phase-2-only programme: relevant to PAH patients on multiple background drugs, not evidence of efficacy.
cards.watchOut: Healthy volunteers, short exposure; tolerability here does not transfer directly to PAH patients on background therapy — TORREY's cough and discontinuation rates are the patient-level safety data.

cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded records above (TORREY phase 2; TORREY open-label extension; phase 1 interaction studies).
cards.result: Inhaled seralutinib — a PDGFR/CSF1R/c-KIT kinase inhibitor aimed at pulmonary vascular remodelling — improved its phase 2 primary endpoint on background therapy (PVR difference −96.1 dyne·s/cm⁵; P = 0.03; n = 86), and open-label follow-up to week 72 is directionally consistent in those who stayed on drug. Against that: cough in ~43%, adverse-event discontinuation in 27% during the extension, a moderate CYP3A interaction burden, and — decisively — no phase 3, no mortality and no clinical-worsening evidence yet (PROSERA underway per the extension record). cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade on extension data: uncontrolled follow-up of trial completers is the weakest rung of the programme's own evidence.

shelves.title: Imatinib in pulmonary arterial hypertension (IMPRES): walk and PVR gains bought with subdural haematomas — the programme's own verdict was no
shelves.question: In adults with pulmonary arterial hypertension, does oral imatinib added to background therapy improve exercise capacity and haemodynamics — and at what harm cost (subdural haematoma signal)?
shelves.mesh: Hypertension, Pulmonary · Imatinib Mesylate · Protein Kinase Inhibitors · Hematoma, Subdural · Exercise Tolerance · Humans
shelves.balance: Imatinib in PAH is the classic efficacy–harm split, and the stamp stays at POSSIBLE with the harm on the face. IMPRES (n = 202, PVR ≥800 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵ on ≥2 background therapies) improved 6-minute walk distance by a placebo-corrected 32 m (95% CI 12–52; P = 0.002) and PVR by −379 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵ (P < 0.001) at 24 weeks — but functional class, time to clinical worsening and mortality did not differ (the treatment made no difference on those endpoints), serious adverse events were more frequent (44% vs 30%), discontinuations higher (33% vs 18%), and subdural haematoma occurred in 8 patients. The earlier pilot RCT (n = 59) was null on its walk endpoint in the intention-to-treat population (+22 ± 63 vs −1.0 ± 53 m; the treatment made no difference) despite PVR improvement. The open-label extension then largely collapsed: 93.8% discontinued (adverse events 31.3%), with 6 further subdural haematomas and 17 deaths during or within 30 days of study end; the extension authors conclude the risks outweigh any possible benefit. A single programme with a serious, mechanism-relevant harm signal caps at POSSIBLE — and the balance a reader needs is that the developer-side extension verdict was effectively negative.

cards.headline: IMPRES 2013: imatinib improved walk distance (+32 m placebo-corrected) and PVR (−379 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵) at 24 weeks — but not functional class, clinical worsening or mortality; subdural haematoma in 8 patients
cards.summary: IMPRES 2013: imatinib improved walk distance (+32 m placebo-corrected) and PVR (−379 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵) at 24 weeks — but not functional class, clinical worsening or mortality; subdural haematoma in 8 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (IMPRES), Circulation 2013
cards.people: Two hundred and two patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension and PVR ≥800 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵ who remained symptomatic on at least 2 PAH therapies (41% on 3 therapies), randomised to oral imatinib or placebo for 24 weeks; primary outcome change in 6-minute walk distance. Patients could then enter an open-label extension.
cards.result: The mean placebo-corrected treatment effect on 6-minute walk distance was +32 m (95% CI 12–52; P = 0.002), and PVR decreased by 379 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵ between groups (95% CI −502 to −255; P < 0.001). Functional class, time to clinical worsening and mortality did not differ between treatments (the treatment made no difference on those endpoints). Serious adverse events (44% vs 30%) and discontinuations (33% vs 18%) were more frequent with imatinib, and subdural haematoma occurred in 8 patients (2 in the core study, 6 in the extension, many on anticoagulation) — the harm signal that defines this shelf.
cards.watchOut: Severe, heavily pre-treated population (PVR ≥800 on ≥2 therapies) — results do not generalise to milder PAH. Absolute walk gain (+32 m) is printed beside its confidence interval; no relative measure is used.
cards.source: Hoeper MM, Barst RJ, Bourge RC, Feldman J, et al. Imatinib mesylate as add-on therapy for pulmonary arterial hypertension: results of the randomized IMPRES study. Circulation. 2013. PMID: 23403476. Registry ID: NCT00902174 (extension NCT01392495). cards.headline: Ghofrani 2010 pilot: in 59 patients the walk endpoint was null in intention-to-treat (+22 ± 63 vs −1.0 ± 53 m — the treatment made no difference), although PVR fell significantly
cards.summary: Ghofrani 2010 pilot: in 59 patients the walk endpoint was null in intention-to-treat (+22 ± 63 vs −1.0 ± 53 m — the treatment made no difference), although PVR fell significantly
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled pilot trial, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2010
cards.people: Fifty-nine patients with PAH in functional classes II–IV and inadequate response to established therapy, randomised to imatinib 200 mg once daily (n = 28; increased to 400 mg if tolerated) or placebo (n = 31) for 24 weeks; 42 completed. Primary endpoints: safety and change in 6-minute walk distance.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat population there was no significant change in 6-minute walk distance with imatinib vs placebo (+22 ± 63 vs −1.0 ± 53 m — the treatment made no difference on the primary efficacy endpoint). Haemodynamics did move: PVR fell (−300 ± 347 vs −78 ± 269 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵; P < 0.01) and cardiac output rose (+0.6 ± 1.2 vs −0.1 ± 0.9 L/min; P = 0.02). Serious adverse events occurred in 39% of imatinib vs 23% of placebo recipients, and three deaths occurred in each group. Post hoc subgroup analyses suggested greater benefit at higher baseline PVR — the hypothesis IMPRES then tested. The pilot is carded so the shelf does not rest on IMPRES alone: the programme's first randomised walk result was null.
cards.watchOut: Pilot-sized (59 randomised, 42 completing); the positive haemodynamics with a null walk endpoint is the honest summary. Subgroup claims in the record are post hoc and are labelled as such here.
cards.source: Ghofrani HA, Morrell NW, Hoeper MM, Olschewski H, et al. Imatinib in pulmonary arterial hypertension patients with inadequate response to established therapy. American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine. 2010. PMID: 20581169. Registry ID: NCT00477269.
