cards.headline: IMPRES extension 2015: 93.8% discontinued the open-label extension, with 6 more subdural haematomas and 17 deaths — the authors conclude risks outweigh any possible benefit
cards.summary: IMPRES extension 2015: 93.8% discontinued the open-label extension, with 6 more subdural haematomas and 17 deaths — the authors conclude risks outweigh any possible benefit
cards.type: Open-label long-term extension study of IMPRES, J Heart Lung Transplant 2015
cards.people: One hundred and forty-four of the 202 IMPRES patients (66 imatinib, 78 placebo) entered the open-label imatinib extension, followed for up to 204 weeks until early sponsor termination on April 16, 2014; only 9 patients completed the extension before termination.
cards.result: Overall 93.8% (135 of 144) discontinued: administrative reasons (sponsor termination) 32.6% and adverse events 31.3% were the primary reasons. Serious and unexpected adverse events were frequent, including 6 subdural haematomas in the extension and 17 deaths during or within 30 days of study end. Patients who tolerated imatinib and stayed in longer did improve in functional class and walk distance — a tolerator-selected subgroup. The authors' conclusion is printed on this card's face because it is the programme's own verdict: severe adverse events, significant side effects and a high discontinuation rate limit imatinib's utility in PAH, and these risks outweigh any possible benefit.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled extension terminated early by the sponsor; deaths in an uncontrolled extension of severely ill patients cannot be attributed to the drug individually — the card reports the counts as the record gives them, alongside the discontinuation and haematoma pattern that drove the authors' conclusion.
cards.source: Frost AE, Barst RJ, Hoeper MM, Chang HJ, et al. Long-term safety and efficacy of imatinib in pulmonary arterial hypertension. The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation. 2015. PMID: 26210752. Registry ID: NCT01392495. cards.headline: Synthesis: real haemodynamic and walk gains in one trial, a null pilot before it, and a harm profile that ended the programme — POSSIBLE with the harm on the face
cards.summary: Synthesis: real haemodynamic and walk gains in one trial, a null pilot before it, and a harm profile that ended the programme — POSSIBLE with the harm on the face
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded records above (Ghofrani 2010 pilot; IMPRES 2013; IMPRES extension 2015).
cards.result: The imatinib-in-PAH programme shows a consistent haemodynamic effect (PVR −300 in the pilot, −379 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵ placebo-corrected in IMPRES) and one positive walk result (+32 m in IMPRES) against a null walk result in the pilot's intention-to-treat analysis. It shows no difference in functional class, clinical worsening or mortality in the only adequately sized trial. And it shows a distinctive, repeated harm: subdural haematoma (8 patients across core + extension in the IMPRES report; 6 more counted in the extension report), serious adverse events in 44% vs 30%, and an extension that 93.8% of patients left. Development in PAH stopped. The stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit) only in the narrow sense that a randomised trial met walk and haemodynamic endpoints; any clinical use of this shelf's content must carry the extension authors' conclusion that risks outweigh any possible benefit.
cards.watchOut: Subdural-haematoma counts overlap between the IMPRES core report (8 total incl. extension at that time) and the extension report (6 in the extension); the cards keep each record's own count and wording rather than summing them.

shelves.title: Intravenous reslizumab in severe eosinophilic asthma: exacerbations roughly halved in two duplicate phase 3 trials
shelves.question: In adults with severe eosinophilic asthma uncontrolled on high-dose inhaled therapy, does intravenous reslizumab reduce exacerbations and improve lung function versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Asthma · Double-Blind Method · Eosinophils · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the trials agree, but they are one sponsor programme, so the stamp is capped. In two duplicate 52-week phase 3 trials (953 patients with eosinophils 400 cells per microlitre or higher and at least one prior exacerbation), intravenous reslizumab 3.0 mg/kg every 4 weeks cut the annual exacerbation rate to a rate ratio of 0.50 and 0.41 versus placebo — roughly a 50-59% relative reduction. A separate 16-week phase 3 trial showed the lung-function side: FEV1 improved by 160 mL more than placebo at the 3.0 mg/kg dose. The anti-IL-5 family home (live #813) covers mepolizumab and benralizumab only; reslizumab is the intravenous member of the family and is carded here on its own trials.

cards.headline: Castro 2015 (two duplicate phase 3 trials): reslizumab cut exacerbation frequency to rate ratios of 0.50 and 0.41 versus placebo
cards.summary: Castro 2015 (two duplicate phase 3 trials): reslizumab cut exacerbation frequency to rate ratios of 0.50 and 0.41 versus placebo
cards.type: Two duplicate multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials, 52 weeks each.
cards.people: 953 patients aged 12-75 years (477 reslizumab, 476 placebo) whose asthma was inadequately controlled on medium-to-high-dose inhaled corticosteroid therapy, with blood eosinophils of 400 cells per microlitre or higher and one or more exacerbations in the previous year; intravenous reslizumab 3.0 mg/kg or placebo every 4 weeks for 1 year.
cards.result: Asthma exacerbation frequency fell significantly on reslizumab in both trials: rate ratio 0.50 (95% CI 0.37 to 0.67) in study 1 and 0.41 (0.28 to 0.59) in study 2, both p<0.0001 — a 50% and 59% relative reduction in exacerbation rate. Common adverse events were similar to placebo; the most common were worsening asthma, upper respiratory tract infection and nasopharyngitis.
cards.watchOut: The rate ratios are relative measures: the record does not print the absolute annual exacerbation rates alongside them, so the absolute gain for an individual patient cannot be stated from this card. Entry required eosinophils of at least 400 cells per microlitre — the result does not extend to non-eosinophilic asthma.
cards.source: Castro M et al. Reslizumab for inadequately controlled asthma with elevated blood eosinophil counts: results from two multicentre, parallel, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trials. Lancet Respir Med. 2015;3:355-366. PMID: 25736990 · NCT01287039 · NCT01285323 (registry IDs stated in the record). cards.headline: Bjermer 2016 (phase 3, 16 weeks): reslizumab 3.0 mg/kg improved FEV1 by 160 mL more than placebo
cards.summary: Bjermer 2016 (phase 3, 16 weeks): reslizumab 3.0 mg/kg improved FEV1 by 160 mL more than placebo
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, 16 weeks.
cards.people: Patients aged 12-75 years with asthma inadequately controlled on at least a medium-dose inhaled corticosteroid and a blood eosinophil count of 400 cells per microlitre or higher, randomised to reslizumab 0.3 mg/kg, 3.0 mg/kg or placebo every 4 weeks for 16 weeks (four doses). The record's abstract does not state the total number randomised.
cards.result: Pre-bronchodilator FEV1 improved versus placebo by 115 mL (95% CI 16 to 215; P=.0237) at 0.3 mg/kg and 160 mL (60 to 259; P=.0018) at 3.0 mg/kg. cards.headline: Open-label extension (Murphy 2017): benefit was maintained for up to 24 months, with no new safety signal
cards.summary: Open-label extension (Murphy 2017): benefit was maintained for up to 24 months, with no new safety signal
cards.type: Open-label extension study of the phase 3 programme (no comparator).
cards.people: 1,051 patients who had completed one of three placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in moderate-to-severe eosinophilic asthma received open-label reslizumab 3.0 mg/kg intravenously every 4 weeks for up to 24 months (571 previously on reslizumab, 480 reslizumab-naive).
cards.result: Serious adverse events affected 78 of 1,051 patients (7%); 18 (2%) discontinued because of adverse events and there were 3 deaths, all judged non-treatment-related. shelves.title: Vanzacaftor triple in cystic fibrosis (SKYLINE): non-inferior to the elexacaftor triple on lung function, once daily instead of twice
shelves.question: In people with cystic fibrosis aged 6 years and older with at least one F508del allele, does once-daily vanzacaftor-tezacaftor-deutivacaftor improve lung function and sweat chloride versus placebo — and how does it compare with elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Cystic Fibrosis · Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Female · Humans · Male · Sweat · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — with the comparison stated plainly: the SKYLINE trials were active-controlled, not placebo-controlled. After a 4-week run-in on elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor, 971 people aged 12 years and older were randomised to switch to once-daily vanzacaftor-tezacaftor-deutivacaftor or stay on the elexacaftor triple; lung function (FEV1 percent predicted) was non-inferior in both trials (treatment difference +0.2 percentage points in each). So the honest claim is 'as good as the current standard on lung function, with once-daily dosing', not 'better'. The paediatric card (RIDGELINE, ages 6-11) is single-arm and safety-led. These SKYLINE trials are the cystic fibrosis programme — not the unrelated soticlestat epilepsy programme of the same name (pack #6166). Live #811 homes the older modulators only.

cards.headline: SKYLINE-102 and SKYLINE-103 (Keating 2025): vanzacaftor triple was non-inferior to the elexacaftor triple on FEV1 (difference +0.2 points in both trials)
cards.summary: SKYLINE-102 and SKYLINE-103 (Keating 2025): vanzacaftor triple was non-inferior to the elexacaftor triple on FEV1 (difference +0.2 points in both trials)
cards.type: Two randomised, active-controlled, double-blind phase 3 non-inferiority trials, 52 weeks.
cards.people: 971 people aged 12 years and older with stable cystic fibrosis — 398 in Trial 102 (F508del-minimal function genotypes) and 573 in Trial 103 (F508del-F508del, F508del-residual function, F508del-gating or other responsive genotypes) — all after a 4-week run-in on elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor, then randomised 1:1 for 52 weeks.
cards.result: Absolute change in FEV1 percent predicted through week 24: Trial 102, +0.5 points on vanzacaftor-tezacaftor-deutivacaftor versus +0.3 on elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (least-squares mean difference 0.2, 95% CI -0.7 to 1.1; p<0.0001 for non-inferiority); Trial 103, +0.2 versus 0.0 (difference 0.2, -0.5 to 0.9; p<0.0001). Non-inferiority was met in both trials (lower bound above the -3.0 margin). Most adverse events were mild or moderate; infective pulmonary exacerbation occurred in 28% on the vanzacaftor triple versus 32% on the elexacaftor triple in pooled data.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against an effective standard is not superiority, and there is no placebo arm: everyone entered already on the elexacaftor triple, so these trials cannot say what the vanzacaftor triple does in modulator-naive patients. The practical gain is once-daily dosing.
cards.source: Keating C et al. Vanzacaftor-tezacaftor-deutivacaftor versus elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor in individuals with cystic fibrosis aged 12 years and older (SKYLINE Trials VX20-121-102 and VX20-121-103). cards.headline: RIDGELINE (Hoppe 2025): in children aged 6-11 the vanzacaftor triple was tolerated, with adverse events consistent with cystic fibrosis itself
cards.summary: RIDGELINE (Hoppe 2025): in children aged 6-11 the vanzacaftor triple was tolerated, with adverse events consistent with cystic fibrosis itself
cards.type: Single-arm, open-label phase 3 trial in children (design printed on the face: no comparator).
cards.people: 78 children aged 6-11 years (median age 9.3 years; 44% female) with at least one elexacaftor-responsive CFTR variant and FEV1 of 60% predicted or higher, treated open-label for 24 weeks after prior or run-in elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor.
cards.result: 75 of 78 children (96%) had adverse events, all mild or moderate; the most common were cough (46%), pyrexia (21%), headache (18%), infective pulmonary exacerbation (17%) and oropharyngeal pain (17%). Serious adverse events occurred in 6 children (8%). The primary endpoint was safety and tolerability.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm paediatric data support tolerability only; efficacy in children is extrapolated from the randomised trials in people aged 12 and older. The shelf question's 'versus placebo' framing has no placebo-controlled trial behind it for this drug — the comparison that exists is against the active standard.

cards.headline: Quality-of-life analysis (Wainwright 2026): CFQ-R utility scores slightly favoured the vanzacaftor triple (pooled difference 0.017)
cards.summary: Quality-of-life analysis (Wainwright 2026): CFQ-R utility scores slightly favoured the vanzacaftor triple (pooled difference 0.017)
cards.type: Post hoc analysis of the phase 3 programme's quality-of-life data.
cards.people: Post hoc pooled analysis of the SKYLINE-102, SKYLINE-103 and RIDGELINE phase 3 populations (people aged 6 years and older on the vanzacaftor triple or the elexacaftor triple), using Cystic Fibrosis Questionnaire-Revised scores through week 52 (ages 14 and older) and week 24 (children 6-11).
cards.result: CFQ-R-8D utility scores were higher on vanzacaftor-tezacaftor-deutivacaftor than on elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (pooled difference 0.017; nominal P=0.01), driven by the F508del/minimal-function subgroup (0.031; nominal P=0.004) rather than other genotypes (0.008; nominal P=0.35). Children aged 6-11 improved in 6 of 7 non-respiratory CFQ-R domains, from 3.7 points (emotional functioning) to 7.2 points (social functioning).
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and nominally significant only — a small utility difference (0.017) of uncertain clinical importance. It supports tolerability and lived experience; it does not change the headline, which is lung-function equivalence.

cards.summary: Synthesis: a once-daily triple that matches the standard on lung function in two trials — LIKELY as an equivalent, not an advance in efficacy
cards.type: Synthesis card.
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised active-controlled phase 3 trials in 971 people aged 12 years and older (SKYLINE-102/103), one single-arm paediatric trial (RIDGELINE, 78 children), and a post hoc quality-of-life analysis of the same programme.

shelves.title: Pamrevlumab in IPF (ZEPHYRUS-1): FVC fell in both groups and the treatment made no difference
shelves.question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does pamrevlumab (anti-CTGF antibody) slow forced vital capacity decline versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Connective Tissue Growth Factor · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis · Male · Middle Aged · Vital Capacity
shelves.balance: UNLIKELY — the phase 2 trial (PRAISE, 103 patients) reported slower FVC decline on pamrevlumab, but ZEPHYRUS-1, the phase 3 test of that promise, was negative: FVC fell by 260 mL on pamrevlumab and 330 mL on placebo over 48 weeks, a between-group difference of 70 mL that was not significant (P=.29), and no secondary or patient-reported outcome separated either (the treatment made no difference). Deaths were identical (23 in each group). Phase 2 hope does not survive its own phase 3 trial.

cards.headline: PRAISE phase 2 (Richeldi 2020): pamrevlumab slowed FVC percent-predicted decline over 48 weeks (difference 4.3 points, p=0.033) — the signal phase 3 then tested
cards.summary: PRAISE phase 2 (Richeldi 2020): pamrevlumab slowed FVC percent-predicted decline over 48 weeks (difference 4.3 points, p=0.033) — the signal phase 3 then tested
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 48 weeks.
cards.people: 103 patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and FVC of 55% predicted or greater (50 pamrevlumab, 53 placebo) at 39 centres in 7 countries; pamrevlumab 30 mg/kg intravenously or placebo every 3 weeks for 48 weeks.
cards.result: Mean change in percent predicted FVC at week 48 was -2.9% on pamrevlumab versus -7.2% on placebo (between-group difference 4.3%, 95% CI 0.4 to 8.3; p=0.033) — described by the authors as a 60.3% relative reduction in decline (a relative measure; the absolute difference was 4.3 percentage points). Disease progression occurred in 10.0% versus 31.4% (p=0.013). Treatment-emergent serious adverse events occurred in 24% on pamrevlumab versus 15% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Carded as background, not support: this 103-patient phase 2 result is exactly what ZEPHYRUS-1 (Card 2) was designed to confirm, and it did not. A phase 2 positive followed by a phase 3 negative is read on this shelf by the phase 3 result.

cards.headline: ZEPHYRUS-1 (Raghu/Richeldi 2024): no significant FVC difference — pamrevlumab -260 mL versus placebo -330 mL at 48 weeks (difference 70 mL, P=.29)
cards.summary: ZEPHYRUS-1 (Raghu/Richeldi 2024): no significant FVC difference — pamrevlumab -260 mL versus placebo -330 mL at 48 weeks (difference 70 mL, P=.29)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 48 weeks.
cards.people: 356 patients aged 40-85 years with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis not receiving nintedanib or pirfenidone at enrolment (181 pamrevlumab, 175 placebo), at 117 sites in 9 countries; pamrevlumab 30 mg/kg intravenously every 3 weeks or placebo for 48 weeks.
cards.result: Absolute change in FVC from baseline to week 48: least-squares mean -260 mL (95% CI -350 to -170) on pamrevlumab versus -330 mL (-430 to -230) on placebo; between-group difference 70 mL (-60 to 190), P=.29 — not significant. There were no significant between-group differences in any secondary outcome (including disease progression) or in patient-reported outcomes. Deaths: 23 patients in each group (12.7% versus 13.1%). Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 88.4% versus 86.3% and serious adverse events in 28.2% versus 34.3%.
cards.watchOut: Null wording is deliberate: the point estimate (70 mL) favoured pamrevlumab but the confidence interval crosses no effect and the trial's own conclusion is no significant difference — this must not be summarised as a 'trend to benefit'. Patients were not on background antifibrotics at enrolment, so the trial also says nothing about pamrevlumab added to nintedanib or pirfenidone.

cards.headline: Pre-phase 3 meta-analysis (Di Martino 2021): pooling the phase 2 data made pamrevlumab look the strongest of the three IPF drugs — a reading ZEPHYRUS-1 then overturned
cards.summary: Pre-phase 3 meta-analysis (Di Martino 2021): pooling the phase 2 data made pamrevlumab look the strongest of the three IPF drugs — a reading ZEPHYRUS-1 then overturned
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (evidence available to March 2020).
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of six phase 2/3 randomised trials of pirfenidone, nintedanib and pamrevlumab in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, searched to March 2020 — before ZEPHYRUS-1 reported, so its pamrevlumab estimate rests on the phase 2 PRAISE trial alone.
cards.result: For change in percent predicted FVC, all three drugs beat placebo (pamrevlumab effect 4.30%, 95% CI 0.45 to 8.15 — the largest point estimate of the three, on the widest interval). Pamrevlumab also showed a positive effect on avoiding a 10% FVC reduction (OR 0.24, 0.08 to 0.73) but no effect on all-cause mortality; only pirfenidone showed a mortality effect (OR 0.50, 0.31 to 0.83). The authors called the pamrevlumab results encouraging ahead of phase 3.
cards.watchOut: Dated by design: this card is kept so the shelf shows what the evidence looked like before phase 3 — and why a meta-analysis of one small phase 2 trial inherits that trial's fragility. It must never be quoted without Card 2 (ZEPHYRUS-1).

cards.headline: Synthesis: phase 2 said yes, phase 3 said no — the adequately powered answer stands (UNLIKELY)
cards.summary: Synthesis: phase 2 said yes, phase 3 said no — the adequately powered answer stands (UNLIKELY)
cards.type: Synthesis card.
cards.people: The carded evidence: the phase 2 PRAISE trial (103 patients, positive), a pre-phase 3 meta-analysis resting on it (positive), and the phase 3 ZEPHYRUS-1 trial (356 patients, negative).
cards.result: Pamrevlumab made no difference to FVC decline, disease progression, patient-reported outcomes or mortality versus placebo over 48 weeks (the treatment made no difference). On this evidence there is no demonstrated benefit to weigh against the burden of 3-weekly intravenous infusions.
cards.watchOut: A single negative phase 3 trial earns UNLIKELY rather than a stronger negative stamp: one trial can miss a small effect, but the burden of proof now sits with anyone proposing further use.
cards.source: Synthesis of Card 1. No new data.

shelves.title: Zinpentraxin alfa in IPF: a positive phase 2 was not confirmed — phase 3 STARSCAPE stopped for futility and showed no benefit
shelves.question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does zinpentraxin alfa (recombinant pentraxin-2) slow lung-function decline versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Vital Capacity
shelves.balance: UNLIKELY — and the programme's history is the lesson. The phase 2 trial (117 patients) reported slower FVC decline on recombinant human pentraxin 2; the phase 3 STARSCAPE trial (664 patients) was terminated early after a prespecified futility analysis showed no treatment benefit, and its final analysis found FVC change essentially identical between groups (the treatment made no difference). A post hoc analysis traced the phase 2 signal to extreme FVC decline in two placebo patients. The programme is finished; both published reports are carded so the reversal is visible on the shelf.

cards.headline: Phase 2 (Raghu 2018): pentraxin 2 slowed FVC percent-predicted decline over 28 weeks (difference +2.3 points, P=.001) — the signal phase 3 then tested
cards.summary: Phase 2 (Raghu 2018): pentraxin 2 slowed FVC percent-predicted decline over 28 weeks (difference +2.3 points, P=.001) — the signal phase 3 then tested
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 28 weeks.
cards.people: 117 patients aged 40-80 years with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (77 pentraxin 2, 39 placebo; one randomised patient never dosed) at 18 sites in 7 countries; recombinant human pentraxin 2 (the drug later named zinpentraxin alfa) 10 mg/kg intravenously every 4 weeks or placebo for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Least-squares mean change in FVC percent predicted to week 28: -2.5 on pentraxin 2 versus -4.8 on placebo (difference +2.3, 90% CI 1.1 to 3.5; P=.001). Six-minute walk distance changed by -0.5 m versus -31.8 m (difference +31.3 m, 90% CI 17.4 to 45.1; P<.001). The most common adverse events were cough (18% versus 5%), fatigue (17% versus 10%) and nasopharyngitis (16% versus 23%).
cards.watchOut: Carded as background, not as support: the phase 3 post hoc analysis (Card 2) found this result was driven by extreme FVC decline in two placebo patients. A 117-patient phase 2 with a 2:1 randomisation is exactly the setting where two outliers can manufacture a signal.

cards.headline: STARSCAPE phase 3 (Richeldi 2024): terminated early for futility — FVC change -235.7 mL on zinpentraxin versus -214.9 mL on placebo (P=.54)
cards.summary: STARSCAPE phase 3 (Richeldi 2024): terminated early for futility — FVC change -235.7 mL on zinpentraxin versus -214.9 mL on placebo (P=.54)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled pivotal trial, terminated early for futility; results published in full.
cards.people: 664 randomised patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (331 zinpentraxin alfa, 333 placebo) at 275 sites in 29 countries; zinpentraxin alfa 10 mg/kg intravenously every 4 weeks or placebo, planned for 52 weeks.
cards.result: The trial was terminated early after a prespecified futility analysis demonstrated no treatment benefit. In the final analysis, absolute change in FVC to week 52 was -235.72 mL on zinpentraxin alfa versus -214.89 mL on placebo (P=.5420), with no apparent treatment effects on secondary endpoints (percent predicted FVC, 6-minute walk distance). One or more adverse events occurred in 74.6% on zinpentraxin and 72.3% on placebo. Post hoc analysis revealed that extreme FVC decline in two placebo-treated patients produced the clinical benefit reported by phase 2.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is built only on the two published reports (phase 2 and phase 3). The termination is stated plainly because it is part of the evidence: the programme did not fail to report — it reported, and the answer was no benefit.

cards.headline: Open-label extension (Raghu 2019): pentraxin 2 looked sustained to week 76 in uncontrolled follow-up — the kind of evidence phase 3 exists to test
cards.summary: Open-label extension (Raghu 2019): pentraxin 2 looked sustained to week 76 in uncontrolled follow-up — the kind of evidence phase 3 exists to test
cards.type: Open-label extension study (no comparator) — design labelled on the face.
cards.people: 111 of the 116 patients who completed the phase 2 double-blind period entered the open-label extension, all receiving recombinant human pentraxin 2 (the zinpentraxin alfa programme) in 28-week cycles; patients previously on placebo crossed over to active treatment, so there was no control group.
cards.result: The extension's primary objective was long-term safety and tolerability, assessed from adverse events to week 76 in all patients who received at least one extension dose; efficacy (percent predicted FVC and 6-minute walk distance) was exploratory and descriptive only, with no placebo comparison possible after crossover.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled extension data cannot confirm efficacy: everyone knew they were on the drug, the frailest patients drop out, and there is no placebo arm. Its apparent durability is part of why the STARSCAPE futility result (Card 2) surprised the field.
cards.source: Raghu G et al. Long-term treatment with recombinant human pentraxin 2 protein in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: an open-label extension study. Lancet Respir Med. 2019. cards.summary: Synthesis: phase 2 said yes, the adequately powered phase 3 said no — the phase 3 answer stands (UNLIKELY)

cards.people: The carded evidence: one phase 2 trial (117 patients, positive), its open-label extension (111 patients, uncontrolled), and one phase 3 trial (664 patients, terminated for futility, negative) — all published.

shelves.title: Co-trimoxazole in IPF: two randomised trials, both negative — no gain in survival, hospitalisation, lung function or quality of life
shelves.question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does co-trimoxazole improve quality of life, lung function or survival versus placebo/usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole Drug Combination
shelves.balance: UNLIKELY — three randomised trials asked the question and none found benefit on its primary analysis. The earliest (Shulgina 2013, 181 patients) found no intention-to-treat effect on lung function, with quality-of-life and mortality signals only in a per-protocol subgroup. EME-TIPAC (342 patients, double-blind, placebo-controlled) found co-trimoxazole did not reduce death, transplant or hospital admission (hazard ratio 1.2, P=.32), with no difference in lung function or patient-reported outcomes. CleanUP-IPF (513 patients, pragmatic) tested co-trimoxazole or doxycycline added to usual care and was itself stopped for futility: no improvement in respiratory hospitalisation or death (adjusted HR 1.04, P=.83), and no interaction favouring co-trimoxazole over doxycycline. Gastrointestinal and skin adverse events were commoner on co-trimoxazole across the trials.

cards.headline: EME-TIPAC (Wilson 2020): co-trimoxazole did not reduce death, transplant or hospital admission versus placebo (HR 1.2, P=.32)
cards.summary: EME-TIPAC (Wilson 2020): co-trimoxazole did not reduce death, transplant or hospital admission versus placebo (HR 1.2, P=.32)
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial (phase 3), 12-42 months.
cards.people: 342 patients with moderate or severe idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (breathlessness score above 1 and FVC 75% predicted or less) at 39 UK specialist centres; oral co-trimoxazole 960 mg twice daily (170 patients) or matched placebo (172) for 12-42 months, all with folic acid 5 mg daily.
cards.result: Events per person-year were 0.45 on co-trimoxazole versus 0.38 on placebo for the composite of death, lung transplant or first nonelective hospital admission (hazard ratio 1.2, 95% CI 0.9 to 1.6; P=.32). There were no statistically significant differences in other event outcomes, lung function, or patient-reported outcomes (dyspnoea, quality of life, cough measures). Adverse events numbered 696 on co-trimoxazole versus 640 on placebo, including more nausea (89 versus 67) and rash (31 versus 20).
cards.watchOut: This is the direct placebo-controlled test of co-trimoxazole itself, and it is negative on the primary composite and on every lung-function and patient-reported secondary outcome — the shelf question's quality-of-life and lung-function limbs are answered here, not just survival.

cards.headline: CleanUP-IPF (Martinez 2021): adding co-trimoxazole or doxycycline to usual care did not improve respiratory hospitalisation or death (adjusted HR 1.04, P=.83); trial stopped for futility
cards.summary: CleanUP-IPF (Martinez 2021): adding co-trimoxazole or doxycycline to usual care did not improve respiratory hospitalisation or death (adjusted HR 1.04, P=.83); trial stopped for futility
cards.type: Pragmatic, randomised, unblinded clinical trial; stopped for futility.
cards.people: 513 patients older than 40 years with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis at 35 US sites, randomised to usual care plus antimicrobial therapy (254) or usual care alone (259); the antimicrobial was co-trimoxazole (128 patients) or doxycycline (126), chosen by the site investigator before randomisation. The trial was unblinded and pragmatic, with no placebo.
cards.result: After mean follow-up of 13.1 months, 108 primary events occurred: 20.4 events per 100 patient-years on antimicrobials versus 18.4 on usual care (adjusted HR 1.04, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.53; P=.83). There was no significant interaction by agent (adjusted HR 1.15 [0.68 to 1.95] for co-trimoxazole versus 0.82 [0.46 to 1.47] for doxycycline; P=.66). The study was terminated for futility in December 2019. Diarrhoea (10.2% versus 3.1%) and rash (6.7% versus 0%) were commoner on antimicrobials.
cards.watchOut: CleanUP-IPF randomised the antimicrobial strategy, not co-trimoxazole alone — half its treatment arm received doxycycline. It corroborates EME-TIPAC rather than independently testing co-trimoxazole, and the prespecified interaction analysis gives no reason to think co-trimoxazole was the exception.

cards.headline: Shulgina 2013 (earlier RCT): no effect on lung function by intention-to-treat; quality-of-life and mortality signals appeared only in the per-protocol analysis
cards.summary: Shulgina 2013 (earlier RCT): no effect on lung function by intention-to-treat; quality-of-life and mortality signals appeared only in the per-protocol analysis
cards.type: Double-blind, multicentre, placebo-controlled randomised trial, 12 months.
cards.people: 181 patients with fibrotic idiopathic interstitial pneumonia (89% definite or probable IPF) at UK centres, randomised to co-trimoxazole 960 mg twice daily (the record also describes the dose as 960 mg daily in its companion economic report) or placebo for 12 months in addition to usual care.
cards.result: By intention-to-treat, co-trimoxazole had no effect on FVC (mean difference 15.5 mL, 95% CI -93.6 to 124.6), diffusing capacity, 6-minute walk or dyspnoea score (the treatment made no difference). In the per-protocol analysis only, quality-of-life utility improved (mean difference 0.12, 0.01 to 0.22), fewer patients needed increased oxygen (OR 0.05, 0.00 to 0.61), and all-cause mortality was lower (3 of 53 versus 14 of 65; HR 0.21, 0.06 to 0.78; p=0.02). Respiratory infections fell, but nausea and rash increased.
cards.watchOut: Per-protocol mortality findings in a trial whose intention-to-treat primary endpoint was null are hypothesis-generating at best — patients who adhere differ from those who do not. The two larger, later trials (Cards 1-2), analysed by intention-to-treat, found no mortality benefit, which is why this card does not lift the stamp.
cards.source: Shulgina L et al. Treating idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with the addition of co-trimoxazole: a randomised controlled trial. Thorax. 2013. cards.headline: Synthesis: the lung-microbiome hypothesis was tested twice and failed twice — co-trimoxazole in IPF is UNLIKELY to help
cards.summary: Synthesis: the lung-microbiome hypothesis was tested twice and failed twice — co-trimoxazole in IPF is UNLIKELY to help
cards.type: Synthesis card.
cards.people: The carded evidence: Shulgina 2013 (181 patients), EME-TIPAC (342 patients, placebo-controlled, co-trimoxazole alone) and CleanUP-IPF (513 patients, pragmatic, co-trimoxazole or doxycycline) — 1,036 randomised patients in total.
cards.result: No trial found benefit on its intention-to-treat primary endpoint (the treatment made no difference); the only positive signals are per-protocol findings in the smallest, earliest trial, which the two larger trials did not reproduce. Co-trimoxazole brought more nausea, diarrhoea and rash. Three randomised trials support UNLIKELY.
cards.watchOut: These trials tested co-trimoxazole as disease-modifying therapy for IPF itself. They say nothing about treating a documented infection in a patient who happens to have IPF, which remains ordinary clinical care.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1-2. No new data.

shelves.title: Nebulised tranexamic acid for non-massive haemoptysis: one small trial — bleeding resolved within 5 days in 96% versus 50%
shelves.question: In adults with non-massive haemoptysis, does nebulised tranexamic acid shorten bleeding duration and hospital stay versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adult · Antifibrinolytic Agents · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hemoptysis · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Tranexamic Acid · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, with the size printed in the stamp: the entire randomised evidence is one double-blind trial of 47 patients (Wand 2018). Nebulised tranexamic acid 500 mg three times daily resolved haemoptysis within 5 days in 96% versus 50% on saline placebo, shortened hospital stay by about 2 days, and no patient on tranexamic acid needed an invasive procedure to control bleeding versus 18.2% on placebo. The direction is encouraging and the drug was well tolerated, but a single 47-patient, single-centre trial cannot carry more than POSSIBLE. Massive haemoptysis was excluded — nothing here applies to it.

cards.headline: Wand 2018: nebulised tranexamic acid resolved haemoptysis within 5 days in 96% versus 50% on placebo, in 47 patients
cards.summary: Wand 2018: nebulised tranexamic acid resolved haemoptysis within 5 days in 96% versus 50% on placebo, in 47 patients
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial — the only randomised trial carded for this question (N = 47).
cards.people: 47 hospitalised adults with non-massive haemoptysis of various causes (25 nebulised tranexamic acid, 22 saline placebo). Patients with massive haemoptysis (more than 200 mL expectorated blood in 24 hours) or haemodynamic or respiratory instability were excluded.
cards.result: Resolution of haemoptysis within 5 days: 96% on tranexamic acid versus 50% on placebo (P<.0005). Mean hospital stay was 5.7 days (SD 2.5) versus 7.8 days (SD 4.6) (P=.046). No tranexamic-acid patient required interventional bronchoscopy or angiographic embolisation versus 18.2% on placebo (P=.041), expectorated blood volume fell significantly from day 2, the 1-year recurrence rate was lower (P=.009), and no side effects were noted in either group.
cards.watchOut: Small-N warning, on the face: with 47 patients, the 96% versus 50% contrast rests on a handful of events, and a single-centre result this large usually shrinks on replication. The stamp carries the total N for exactly this reason.
cards.source: Wand O et al. Inhaled Tranexamic Acid for Hemoptysis Treatment: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Chest. 2018;154:1379-1384. PMID: 30321510 · NCT01496196 (registry ID stated in the record). cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Mahalingam 2025): across 3 small RCTs and 2 observational studies (351 patients), nebulised tranexamic acid was associated with higher odds of bleeding cessation
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Mahalingam 2025): across 3 small RCTs and 2 observational studies (351 patients), nebulised tranexamic acid was associated with higher odds of bleeding cessation
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 3 randomised trials and 2 observational studies.
cards.people: 351 patients with nonmassive haemoptysis across three randomised trials and two observational studies (192 treated, 159 controls), pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis; the Wand 2018 trial (Card 1) is one of the three randomised trials, so this card overlaps it and is not independent evidence.
cards.result: Nebulised tranexamic acid was 3.85 times more likely to achieve haemoptysis cessation than alternative treatments across the randomised trials (pooled odds ratio), and treated patients required 43% fewer pulmonary interventional procedures (a relative measure). The pooled difference in post-therapy bleeding volume (about 20 mL less) was inconclusive, with wide confidence intervals. The reviewers rated the evidence limited by risk of bias and study limitations and called for larger randomised trials.
cards.watchOut: A meta-analysis of tiny trials does not manufacture a large evidence base: the randomised total behind it remains a few hundred patients at most, dominated by the same small trials. It corroborates Wand's direction; it does not upgrade the stamp.
cards.source: Mahalingam S et al. Effectiveness of Inhalational Tranexamic Acid in Patients with Nonmassive Hemoptysis — A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Lung. 2025. PMID: 39751689. cards.headline: Retrospective matched cohort (Alkazemi 2023): in moderate-to-massive haemoptysis, nebulised tranexamic acid showed no significant difference in invasive interventions
cards.summary: Retrospective matched cohort (Alkazemi 2023): in moderate-to-massive haemoptysis, nebulised tranexamic acid showed no significant difference in invasive interventions
cards.type: Retrospective matched cohort study (observational) — design labelled on the face.
cards.people: 72 hospitalised adults with haemoptysis at a single tertiary centre, 2018-2021: 14 patients who received at least one dose of nebulised tranexamic acid, matched to 58 controls on severity criteria (median age 65.5 years; 59.7% male). This cohort included moderate-to-massive haemoptysis — a sicker population than Wand's non-massive trial.
cards.result: There was no difference in the proportion requiring an invasive intervention (35.7% on tranexamic acid versus 56.9% on control; p=0.344), nor in time to resolution (p=0.050), duration of mechanical ventilation (p=0.128), recurrence (p=1.000) or hospital length of stay (p=0.139) (the treatment made no difference in this small observational cohort).
cards.watchOut: Only 14 treated patients and a different (more severe) population: this null cohort neither confirms nor refutes Wand, but it is a reminder that the positive randomised result has not been reproduced at scale or in massive haemoptysis.
cards.source: Alkazemi A et al. Effectiveness of Nebulized Tranexamic Acid in Patients with Moderate-to-Massive Hemoptysis at a Tertiary Academic Medical Center. J Aerosol Med Pulm Drug Deliv. 2023. PMID: 37962861. Registry ID: none in the record (observational study). cards.summary: Synthesis: a positive small trial, a corroborating meta-analysis of small studies, and one null cohort — POSSIBLE, awaiting a larger trial
cards.type: Synthesis card.
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial of 47 patients (Wand 2018), a meta-analysis of 3 small randomised trials and 2 observational studies (351 patients, overlapping Wand), and one retrospective matched cohort of 72 patients in more severe haemoptysis (null).
cards.result: The randomised and pooled evidence favours nebulised tranexamic acid for non-massive haemoptysis — resolution, stay, procedures — while the one observational cohort in moderate-to-massive bleeding found no difference. The claim stays at POSSIBLE, with the anchor trial's N printed in the stamp line, until a larger randomised trial reports.
cards.watchOut: The systemic tranexamic acid shelves (trauma, gastrointestinal bleeding) are different questions with different routes and risks; they neither support nor undermine this inhaled, local use.

shelves.title: Ketamine as a bronchodilator in acute severe asthma: the small randomised trials found no added benefit
shelves.question: In adults with acute severe asthma not responding to standard bronchodilators, does ketamine improve airflow and avert intubation versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anesthetics, Dissociative · Asthma · Bronchodilator Agents · Double-Blind Method · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Ketamine · Male · Middle Aged · Peak Expiratory Flow Rate
shelves.balance: UNLIKELY — ketamine's bronchodilator reputation rests on physiology and case series; the randomised trials do not confirm it. The adult emergency-department trial (Howton 1996, 44 analysed patients) found both groups improved on standard therapy with no detectable difference from adding ketamine, and no difference in admission. A 2020 trial in ventilated adults with severe bronchospasm found ketamine no better than fentanyl on airway resistance at 3 or 24 hours. The one paediatric randomised trial (Allen 2005) is carded and labelled as paediatric — it too was negative. A 2022 systematic review of the prospective studies concluded the data do not support ketamine for refractory severe asthma exacerbations.

cards.headline: Howton 1996 (adults, emergency department): ketamine added to standard therapy produced no detectable bronchodilator advantage over placebo
cards.summary: Howton 1996 (adults, emergency department): ketamine added to standard therapy produced no detectable bronchodilator advantage over placebo
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adults, 1996 (N = 44 analysed).
cards.people: 53 consecutive adults aged 18-65 with acute asthma and peak flow below 40% predicted after three albuterol nebulisers; the first 9 were excluded from analysis after the ketamine bolus dose was lowered for dysphoric reactions, leaving 44 analysed. All received oxygen, continuous nebulised albuterol and methylprednisolone, then ketamine (0.1-0.2 mg/kg bolus, then 0.5 mg/kg per hour for 3 hours) or placebo.
cards.result: Peak flow, Borg dyspnoea score, respiratory rate and FEV1 all improved significantly over time within each group, but no difference could be detected between ketamine and placebo (the treatment made no difference), and the hospital admission rate did not differ between groups (P=.1088). Patients rated ketamine slightly more satisfying (4.3 versus 3.7 on a 1-5 scale; P=.0285).
cards.watchOut: Small and old: 44 analysed patients give limited power to exclude a modest effect, and dosing was constrained by dysphoric reactions. The trial is carded because it remains the direct adult placebo-controlled test — and it was negative.
cards.source: Howton JC et al. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of intravenous ketamine in acute asthma. Ann Emerg Med. 1996;27:170-175. PMID: 8629747. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era trial). cards.headline: Nedel 2020 (ventilated adults): ketamine infusion did not improve airway resistance versus fentanyl at 3 or 24 hours
cards.summary: Nedel 2020 (ventilated adults): ketamine infusion did not improve airway resistance versus fentanyl at 3 or 24 hours
cards.type: Single-centre, evaluator-blinded randomised trial in ventilated adults (mixed asthma and COPD bronchospasm).
cards.people: Adults on invasive mechanical ventilation with acute severe bronchospasm due to status asthmaticus or COPD exacerbation, randomised to ketamine or fentanyl, each as bolus plus continuous infusion, at a single centre. The record's abstract does not state the number randomised — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Change in maximal airway resistance at 3 hours: 0 (SD 6) on ketamine versus -3 (SD 7.7) on fentanyl (P=.16); at 24 hours, -3 (SD 17) versus -3.5 (SD 13.7) (P=.73). Intrinsic PEEP changes also did not differ at 3 hours (P=.77) or 24 hours (P=.72) — ketamine was not associated with improvement in ventilatory variables (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: The population mixes status asthmaticus with COPD exacerbation and the comparator is fentanyl sedation, not placebo — it tests ketamine as a ventilator adjunct, a narrower question than the shelf's. Its null result agrees with, but does not duplicate, Howton.
cards.source: Nedel W et al. Negative results for ketamine use in severe acute bronchospasm: a randomised controlled trial. Anaesthesiol Intensive Ther. 2020;52:215-218. PMID: 32876408. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Allen & Macias 2005 (PAEDIATRIC trial — children, not adults): ketamine infusion gave no incremental benefit in 68 children with acute severe asthma
cards.summary: Allen & Macias 2005 (PAEDIATRIC trial — children, not adults): ketamine infusion gave no incremental benefit in 68 children with acute severe asthma
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial — IN CHILDREN (ages 2-18), carded as supporting evidence for an adult question and labelled as such on the face.
cards.people: PAEDIATRIC POPULATION, labelled plainly: 68 children aged 2-18 years presenting to a paediatric emergency department with a moderately severe acute asthma exacerbation (Pulmonary Index score 8-14 after albuterol, ipratropium and glucocorticoids); 33 received ketamine (0.2 mg/kg bolus, then 0.5 mg/kg per hour for 2 hours) and 35 placebo, all on continuous nebulised albuterol.
cards.result: Mean decrease in Pulmonary Index score at the end of the infusion was 3.2 (SD 2.0) on ketamine versus 3.6 (SD 1.3) on placebo (difference 0.4, 95% CI -0.4 to 1.3) — no significant difference and no incremental benefit over standard therapy (the treatment made no difference). No short-term adverse effects required stopping the infusion.
cards.watchOut: This card must not be quoted as adult evidence: it is a paediatric trial. It is included because the adult literature is so thin, and because its negative result in children removes the 'it works in kids' argument sometimes used to justify adult use.

cards.headline: La Via 2022 (systematic review of prospective studies): no clear benefit from ketamine in refractory severe asthma exacerbations
cards.summary: La Via 2022 (systematic review of prospective studies): no clear benefit from ketamine in refractory severe asthma exacerbations
cards.type: Systematic review of prospective studies (search to August 2021).
cards.people: Seven prospective studies (five randomised trials, population range 44-92 patients; four adult studies and three paediatric), with two additional small uncontrolled prospective studies of 10 and 11 patients. Comparators across the randomised trials were placebo (three trials), fentanyl and aminophylline.
cards.result: Despite wide heterogeneity in dosing, severity scores and outcomes, the overview found an absence of clear benefit from ketamine in refractory severe asthma exacerbations, with some signals towards side effects; the reviewers concluded their systematic review does not support the use of ketamine in refractory severe exacerbations and called for well-designed multicentre trials.
cards.watchOut: A review of small, heterogeneous trials inherits their weakness — but here the review and each individually carded trial point the same way, which is what supports the UNLIKELY stamp rather than a shrug.

cards.headline: Synthesis: every randomised test is negative — ketamine as an asthma bronchodilator is UNLIKELY to add benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: every randomised test is negative — ketamine as an asthma bronchodilator is UNLIKELY to add benefit
cards.type: Synthesis card.
cards.people: The carded evidence: two small adult randomised trials (Howton 1996; Nedel 2020, N not documented in its record), one paediatric randomised trial (Allen 2005, 68 children, labelled paediatric), and a systematic review of all seven prospective studies.
cards.result: No randomised trial in any age group found ketamine improved airflow, admission or ventilator mechanics beyond standard care (the treatment made no difference). shelves.title: Inhaled treprostinil in IPF without pulmonary hypertension (TETON-1 and TETON-2): FVC decline roughly halved in two phase 3 trials
shelves.question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (without pulmonary hypertension), does inhaled treprostinil slow FVC decline versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Administration, Inhalation · Antifibrotic Agents · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Vital Capacity
shelves.balance: LIKELY — this shelf is built on the two peer-reviewed phase 3 reports (New England Journal of Medicine, 2026), not on the earlier topline press announcements. TETON-2 (593 patients): median FVC change at 52 weeks was -49.9 mL on inhaled treprostinil versus -136.4 mL on placebo (difference 95.6 mL, P<0.001). TETON-1 (598 patients) found the same pattern (difference 130.1 mL, P<0.001), and clinical worsening was less frequent in both trials (hazard ratios 0.71 and 0.67). Three quarters of patients were already on background antifibrotic therapy, so this is largely add-on evidence. Cough was the commonest adverse event (about half of treprostinil patients) and discontinuation was higher on treprostinil. This is a different population from live #1109, which homes inhaled treprostinil for pulmonary hypertension with interstitial lung disease (INCREASE).

cards.headline: TETON-2 (Nathan 2026): inhaled treprostinil slowed FVC decline — median change -49.9 mL versus -136.4 mL on placebo (difference 95.6 mL, P<0.001)
cards.summary: TETON-2 (Nathan 2026): inhaled treprostinil slowed FVC decline — median change -49.9 mL versus -136.4 mL on placebo (difference 95.6 mL, P<0.001)
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (TETON-2), 52 weeks; peer-reviewed full report.
cards.people: 593 patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (298 treprostinil, 295 placebo); mean age 71.7 years, 80.1% men, mean baseline FVC 76.8% predicted, and 75.4% receiving background antifibrotic therapy. Inhaled treprostinil or placebo, 12 breaths four times daily, for 52 weeks.
cards.result: Median change in FVC at week 52: -49.9 mL (95% CI -79.2 to -19.5) on treprostinil versus -136.4 mL (-172.5 to -104.0) on placebo; between-group difference 95.6 mL (52.2 to 139.0; P<0.001). Clinical worsening occurred in 27.2% versus 39.0% (hazard ratio 0.71, 0.53 to 0.95; P=.02). There was no substantial difference in time to acute exacerbation, so later secondary endpoints were not formally inferred. Cough occurred in 48.3% versus 24.1%; discontinuation was 33.6% versus 24.7%.
cards.watchOut: The absolute FVC sparing (about 96 mL over a year) is modest next to the cough burden and a one-in-three discontinuation rate — LIKELY describes the direction of benefit, not its size. Most patients were already on antifibrotics, so the cleanest reading is add-on benefit.
cards.source: Nathan SD et al. Inhaled Treprostinil for Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis. N Engl J Med. 2026;395:127-137. PMID: 41812190 · NCT05255991 (registry ID stated in the record; TETON-2). cards.headline: TETON-1 (Nathan 2026): the second trial agreed — FVC difference 130.1 mL (P<0.001) and less clinical worsening (HR 0.67)
cards.summary: TETON-1 (Nathan 2026): the second trial agreed — FVC difference 130.1 mL (P<0.001) and less clinical worsening (HR 0.67)
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (TETON-1), 52 weeks; peer-reviewed full report including combined TETON-1/TETON-2 analyses.
cards.people: 598 patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (299 treprostinil, 299 placebo); mean age 73.0 years, 77.3% men, baseline FVC 74.6% predicted, and 77.6% receiving background antifibrotic therapy. Inhaled treprostinil or placebo, 12 breaths four times daily, for 52 weeks.
cards.result: Median change in FVC at week 52: -43.3 mL (95% CI -92.1 to -9.1) on treprostinil versus -196.2 mL (-227.1 to -155.6) on placebo; difference 130.1 mL (82.2 to 178.1; P<0.001). Clinical worsening occurred in 31.8% versus 44.5% (hazard ratio 0.67, 0.52 to 0.88; P=.003). No significant difference in time to acute exacerbation. Cough occurred in 54.8% versus 33.1%; discontinuation was 40.5% versus 32.8%, with adverse events the primary reason in 20.7% versus 14.7%. Combined analyses of both trials were similar.
cards.watchOut: Two trials from one sponsor programme pointing the same way is strong concordance, but both share the same design, the same sponsor and the same tolerability problem (cough in roughly half, discontinuation in a third or more) — real-world persistence may be lower than trial persistence.

cards.headline: Combined TETON-1 + TETON-2 analysis (Nathan 2026): pooled FVC difference 111.8 mL (P<0.0001); deaths 6.9% versus 9.4%
cards.summary: Combined TETON-1 + TETON-2 analysis (Nathan 2026): pooled FVC difference 111.8 mL (P<0.0001); deaths 6.9% versus 9.4%
cards.type: Prespecified combined (integrated) analysis of the two phase 3 trials.
cards.people: All 1,191 patients randomised across TETON-1 and TETON-2 who received at least one dose (597 inhaled treprostinil, 594 placebo) — the fully integrated dataset of Cards 1 and 2, not a new population.
cards.result: Median FVC change at week 52 was -45.4 mL (95% CI -73.8 to -23.1) on treprostinil versus -161.7 mL (-194.5 to -134.1) on placebo (difference 111.8 mL, 79.7 to 144.0; P<0.0001). Treprostinil was superior on five of six secondary endpoints, including time to first clinical worsening, time to first IPF exacerbation, quality of life (K-BILD), percent predicted diffusing capacity and percent predicted FVC. Deaths occurred in 41 patients (6.9%) on treprostinil versus 56 (9.4%) on placebo. Cough was the most common adverse event.
cards.watchOut: A pooled analysis sharpens the estimate but adds no independent patients — the LIKELY stamp rests on the two trials themselves. Note the pooled exacerbation endpoint reached significance here even though neither trial's hierarchical testing did individually; the mortality counts (6.9% versus 9.4%) are descriptive, not a powered mortality result.

cards.type: Synthesis card.
cards.people: The carded evidence: TETON-2 (593 patients) and TETON-1 (598 patients), totalling 1,191 randomised patients, both published in full in a peer-reviewed journal. No press-release data are carded.

shelves.title: Clofazimine in refractory MAC lung disease: observational cohorts only — about half convert, relapse is common, no randomised trial exists
shelves.question: In adults with refractory Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease, does adding clofazimine to a multidrug regimen improve culture conversion and survival?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Clofazimine · Drug Therapy, Combination · Ethambutol · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Macrolides · Male · Middle Aged · Mycobacterium avium Complex · Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare Infection · Retrospective Studies · Rifampin
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, observational only — every card on this shelf is a cohort or case series; there is no randomised trial of clofazimine in MAC lung disease, so the stamp is capped and the design is labelled on each card. The largest MAC-specific cohort (Jarand 2016, 107 patients) found 95% eventually converted to negative cultures on clofazimine- or rifampin-based regimens, with conversion commoner on clofazimine (100% versus 71%) — but half relapsed microbiologically. A severe-disease cohort (170 patients) found 45.3% converted within 6 months, and a refractory-NTM series found 50% of pulmonary patients converted within 12 months. No carded study isolates a survival effect of clofazimine itself. Adjacent homes: pack #2673 (liposomal amikacin, CONVERT) and pack #6313 (first-line MAC regimens) ask different questions.

cards.headline: Jarand 2016 (retrospective cohort): 95% of 107 MAC patients converted on clofazimine- or rifampin-based regimens; conversion was 100% with clofazimine versus 71% with rifampin
cards.summary: Jarand 2016 (retrospective cohort): 95% of 107 MAC patients converted on clofazimine- or rifampin-based regimens; conversion was 100% with clofazimine versus 71% with rifampin
cards.type: Retrospective observational cohort (no randomisation) — design labelled on the face.
cards.people: 107 adults with MAC lung disease treated and monitored for at least 6 months after treatment (79% female, mean age 67 years; sputum smear-positive in 54%). Most (84%) received clofazimine with a macrolide and ethambutol; 14 patients (13%) received rifampin, a macrolide and ethambutol.
cards.result: 95% of patients converted from positive to negative sputum cultures, in a mean of 4.5 months. A significantly greater proportion converted on clofazimine-containing regimens than on rifampin-containing regimens (100% versus 71%; P=.0002). Microbiologic relapse occurred in 52 of 107 patients (49%) and 36% required retreatment, with no difference in relapse or retreatment between the two regimen groups.
cards.watchOut: Observational warning: regimen choice was the clinician's, not random — patients given clofazimine instead of rifampin likely differed (intolerance, interactions, severity), so the 100% versus 71% contrast cannot be read as clofazimine's causal effect. The 49% relapse rate is the sobering half of this card.
cards.source: Jarand J et al. Long-term Follow-up of Mycobacterium avium Complex Lung Disease in Patients Treated With Regimens Including Clofazimine and/or Rifampin. Chest. 2016. PMID: 26513209. cards.headline: Martiniano 2017 (observational cohort, mostly refractory NTM): 50% of pulmonary patients converted within 12 months on clofazimine regimens; 14% stopped for adverse reactions
cards.summary: Martiniano 2017 (observational cohort, mostly refractory NTM): 50% of pulmonary patients converted within 12 months on clofazimine regimens; 14% stopped for adverse reactions
cards.type: Observational cohort study (no comparator, no randomisation) — design labelled on the face.
cards.people: 112 patients with nontuberculous mycobacterial infection treated with clofazimine as part of a multidrug regimen, 2006-2014 (median age 62 years; 21% with cystic fibrosis; 78% with refractory disease after previous therapy failure). Mycobacterium abscessus complex accounted for 48%, MAC for 37%, and two species for 14% — a mixed-NTM cohort, not MAC alone.
cards.result: 41 of 82 patients (50%) with pulmonary disease converted to negative cultures within 12 months. Median clofazimine duration was 383 days; 16 patients (14%) stopped clofazimine because of an adverse drug reaction, after a median of 101 days. The authors judged clofazimine safe, reasonably tolerated and active in this heterogeneous population.
cards.watchOut: Only 37% of this cohort had MAC — the rest were largely M. abscessus — so its 50% conversion figure supports clofazimine's general activity in refractory NTM rather than answering the MAC question directly. It is carded for its refractory population and its tolerability data, with that limit stated.

cards.headline: Lee 2024 (retrospective cohort, severe MAC): 45.3% converted within 6 months on clofazimine-containing regimens; longer courses did better
cards.summary: Lee 2024 (retrospective cohort, severe MAC): 45.3% converted within 6 months on clofazimine-containing regimens; longer courses did better
cards.type: Retrospective observational cohort (no comparator) — design labelled on the face.
cards.people: 170 patients with severe MAC pulmonary disease at a single Korean university hospital, treated 2011-2022 with clofazimine-containing regimens (median age 68 years; 67.1% female; cavities in 71.2%). There was no non-clofazimine comparator group.
cards.result: 77 patients (45.3%) achieved culture conversion within 6 months, and 84 of 154 patients (54.6%) attained microbiological cure. Clofazimine dose (100 mg versus 50 mg) was not associated with conversion (adjusted OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.29 to 1.42) or cure (adjusted OR 1.21, 0.52 to 2.81). Microbiological cure reached 71.0% when clofazimine was given for 6-12 months versus 23.1% when given for under 6 months.
cards.watchOut: Without a comparator, the 45.3% conversion rate cannot be separated from the companion drugs in the regimen or from natural history; the duration gradient (better cure with 6-12 months) may simply reflect that patients who are doing well stay on treatment longer.
cards.source: Lee I et al. Treatment Outcomes of Clofazimine-Containing Regimens in Severe Mycobacterium avium Complex Pulmonary Disease. Open Forum Infect Dis. 2024. PMID: 38328494. Registry ID: none in the record (observational study). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent observational activity, no randomised proof and no isolated survival data — POSSIBLE (observational)
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent observational activity, no randomised proof and no isolated survival data — POSSIBLE (observational)
cards.type: Synthesis card.
cards.people: The carded evidence: three observational cohorts totalling 389 patients (Jarand 107 MAC; Martiniano 112 mixed NTM, 78% refractory; Lee 170 severe MAC). No randomised trial and no survival comparison isolating clofazimine was fetched.
cards.result: Across cohorts, roughly half to nearly all patients converted on clofazimine-containing regimens, relapse after conversion was common (49% in the longest follow-up), and about 1 in 7 stopped the drug for adverse reactions. That pattern supports POSSIBLE benefit as a salvage component of multidrug therapy — and nothing stronger, because confounding by indication runs through every card.
cards.watchOut: The shelf question asks about survival as well as conversion: no carded study answers the survival limb. That gap is stated, not filled — a guideline recommendation to use clofazimine in refractory MAC rests on this same observational base.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1-3. No new data.

shelves.title: Alveolar dead space in ARDS: about 0.58 of each breath is wasted early on, and the fraction independently predicts death
shelves.question: In ARDS, what fraction of tidal volume is wasted as alveolar dead space, why does it rise, and how strongly does the dead-space fraction predict mortality in humans?
shelves.mesh: Respiratory Dead Space · Respiratory Distress Syndrome · Capnography · Tidal Volume · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. In ARDS the alveolar dead-space fraction is roughly double the healthy resting value: Nuckton 2002 measured a mean of 0.58 ± 0.09 within hours of onset in 179 patients — about three-fifths of every tidal volume ventilating alveoli too poorly perfused to exchange gas. The fraction independently predicted death (odds ratio 1.45 per 0.05 increase, 95% CI 1.15–1.83), while hypoxaemia severity did not. Three further human cohorts agree: a sustained 0.63–0.66 trajectory in nonsurvivors over 6 days (n = 59), significant survivor separation by days 1–2 in trial-enrolled patients (n = 126), and the strongest adjusted mortality association in 685 patients measured by volumetric capnography (+22% per 0.05 rise; not discriminatory in mild ARDS). Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Bohr–Enghoff): dead space is ventilation that does not exchange — in health mostly anatomic, in ARDS mostly alveolar, from microvascular injury and thrombosis in ventilated units. All evidence is observational: the fraction is an established prognostic marker of lung injury severity, not a proven treatment target.

cards.headline: Nuckton 2002: early in ARDS the dead-space fraction averaged 0.58 — and each 0.05 rise carried 45% higher odds of death (n = 179)
cards.summary: Nuckton 2002: early in ARDS the dead-space fraction averaged 0.58 — and each 0.05 rise carried 45% higher odds of death (n = 179)
cards.type: Human prospective observational study in ARDS, N Engl J Med 2002
cards.people: 179 intubated patients with ARDS at multiple centres; dead-space fraction measured prospectively a mean of 10.9 hours after ARDS developed; outcome was mortality before hospital discharge, analysed by multiple logistic regression.
cards.result: The mean dead-space fraction was markedly elevated at 0.58 ± 0.09 early in ARDS, and was higher in patients who died than in survivors (0.63 ± 0.10 vs 0.54 ± 0.09; P < 0.001). It independently predicted death: for every 0.05 increase in dead-space fraction, the odds of death rose 45% (OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.15–1.83; P = 0.002). The only other independent predictors were SAPS II and quasistatic respiratory-system compliance — hypoxaemia severity itself did not independently predict death.
cards.watchOut: Association, not a treatment target: nothing in this study shows that lowering dead space (rather than the lung injury it reflects) improves survival. Measurement was a single early time point.
cards.source: Nuckton TJ, Alonso JA, Kallet RH, Daniel BM, Pittet JF, Eisner MD, et al. Pulmonary dead-space fraction as a risk factor for death in the acute respiratory distress syndrome. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2002. PMID: 11973365. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Kallet 2004: over the first 6 days of ARDS, dead-space fraction stayed high in nonsurvivors (0.66 by day 6) and fell in survivors (0.51) — n = 59
cards.summary: Kallet 2004: over the first 6 days of ARDS, dead-space fraction stayed high in nonsurvivors (0.66 by day 6) and fell in survivors (0.51) — n = 59
cards.type: Human prospective observational cohort (serial measurements), Respir Care 2004
cards.people: 59 patients ventilated for at least 6 days with ARDS; serial VD/VT measured with a bedside metabolic monitor within 24 hours of meeting ARDS criteria and again on days 2, 3 and 6 during volume-regulated ventilation.
cards.result: VD/VT was higher in nonsurvivors at every time point: day 1, 0.61 ± 0.09 vs 0.54 ± 0.08 (P < 0.05); day 2, 0.63 ± 0.09 vs 0.53 ± 0.09 (P < 0.001); day 3, 0.64 ± 0.09 vs 0.53 ± 0.09 (P < 0.001); day 6, 0.66 ± 0.09 vs 0.51 ± 0.08 (P < 0.001). A sustained elevation, rather than the admission value alone, characterised patients who went on to die.
cards.watchOut: Only patients who remained ventilated for 6 days could be measured serially — a survivor-selection structure; 59 patients at one centre group. The trajectory is prognostic information, not evidence that manipulating VD/VT changes fate.
cards.source: Kallet RH, Alonso JA, Pittet JF, Matthay MA. Prognostic value of the pulmonary dead-space fraction during the first 6 days of acute respiratory distress syndrome. Respiratory Care. 2004. PMID: 15329171. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Kallet 2014: in 126 trial-enrolled ARDS patients, VD/VT separated survivors from nonsurvivors by day 1–2 (odds ratio 6.84 per 0.10 on day 1)
cards.summary: Kallet 2014: in 126 trial-enrolled ARDS patients, VD/VT separated survivors from nonsurvivors by day 1–2 (odds ratio 6.84 per 0.10 on day 1)
cards.type: Human prospective observational study nested in a multicentre trial, Respir Care 2014
cards.people: 126 subjects with acute lung injury/ARDS (Berlin definition) enrolled in a multicentre phase 3 trial of aerosolised albuterol; VD/VT and mechanics measured within 4 hours of enrolment and on days 1 and 2 in those needing arterial blood gases.
cards.result: At baseline, nonsurvivors had only a trend to higher VD/VT (0.62 ± 0.11 vs 0.56 ± 0.11; P = .08). By study day 1 the separation was significant (0.64 ± 0.12 vs 0.55 ± 0.11; P = .01) and day 2 (0.67 ± 0.12 vs 0.56 ± 0.11; P = .004). Adjusted odds ratios for mortality per 0.10 change in VD/VT were 6.84 (95% CI 1.62–28.84) on day 1 and 4.90 (1.28–18.73) on day 2. Markedly elevated VD/VT (≥ 0.60) in early ARDS was associated with higher mortality.
cards.watchOut: Wide confidence intervals (day-1 OR 6.84 spans 1.62–28.84) and measurements only in patients who had arterial lines sampled — the day-1/2 signal is real but imprecise, and the baseline value alone did not significantly separate the groups.
cards.source: Kallet RH, Zhuo H, Liu KD, Calfee CS, Matthay MA. The association between physiologic dead-space fraction and mortality in subjects with ARDS enrolled in a prospective multi-center clinical trial. Respiratory Care. 2014. PMID: 24381187. cards.headline: Kallet 2017: in 685 ARDS patients measured by volumetric capnography, dead-space fraction was the strongest adjusted mortality predictor (+22% per 0.05)
cards.summary: Kallet 2017: in 685 ARDS patients measured by volumetric capnography, dead-space fraction was the strongest adjusted mortality predictor (+22% per 0.05)
cards.type: Human retrospective observational study (volumetric capnography), Respir Care 2017
cards.people: 685 subjects with ARDS at a single centre (2010–2016), VD/VT measured by volumetric capnography as part of clinical management with lung-protective ventilation, 99% within 48 hours of ARDS onset; retrospective observational analysis with multivariable logistic regression.
cards.result: VD/VT was elevated across all ARDS etiologies — highest with aspiration and pneumonia, lower with non-pulmonary sepsis and trauma — yet within every etiology group it was significantly higher in nonsurvivors than survivors, and in both moderate and severe (but not mild) Berlin-definition ARDS. In the final adjusted model VD/VT carried the strongest mortality association: risk of death rose 22% for every 0.05 increase in VD/VT.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and single-centre; in mild ARDS the fraction did not distinguish survivors from nonsurvivors, so its prognostic value is a moderate-to-severe ARDS finding. Etiology shifts the level, so a single cut-off does not travel across causes.
cards.source: Kallet RH, Zhuo H, Ho K, Lipnick MS, Gomez A, Matthay MA. Lung Injury Etiology and Other Factors Influencing the Relationship Between Dead-Space Fraction and Mortality in ARDS. cards.headline: Synthesis: in ARDS roughly three-fifths of each breath is wasted — and the wasted fraction is among the strongest bedside predictors of death
cards.summary: Synthesis: in ARDS roughly three-fifths of each breath is wasted — and the wasted fraction is among the strongest bedside predictors of death
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Ventilated adults with ARDS across four human studies carded above (n = 179, 59, 126 and 685), read with the textbook framing: dead space is the part of each breath that does not take part in gas exchange (Guyton & Hall's account, quantified by the Bohr equation in its Enghoff form), normally roughly a third of a resting tidal volume — the textbook's figure, with the healthy-lung question homed separately.
cards.result: In ARDS the alveolar component explodes: ventilated alveoli lose their perfusion to microvascular injury and thrombosis, and the measured fraction rises to a mean of about 0.58 within hours of onset (Nuckton 2002). Four cohorts over 15 years agree that the fraction independently predicts mortality — OR 1.45 per 0.05 rise in Nuckton, a sustained 0.63–0.66 trajectory in nonsurvivors in the serial study, and the strongest adjusted predictor in the 685-patient capnography cohort (+22% relative increase in mortality risk per 0.05 — a relative measure, from an observational model). PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the elevation and its prognostic association. Not established: any ventilator strategy chosen to lower dead space itself improving survival.
cards.watchOut: Dead-space fraction is a severity readout of the injured pulmonary circulation. Treating the number (for example with higher pressures to recruit) can worsen the lung injury that produced it — the association does not license targeting VD/VT directly.

shelves.title: Prolonged-release oxycodone–naloxone for severe refractory restless legs syndrome: IRLS severity fell 8.15 points more than placebo over 12 weeks (n=306) — with treatment-related adverse events in 73% and constipation among the serious harms
shelves.question: In adults with severe restless legs syndrome refractory to first-line (dopaminergic/gabapentinoid) therapy, does prolonged-release oxycodone–naloxone improve IRLS severity versus placebo over 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Delayed-Action Preparations · Disorders of Excessive Somnolence/etiology · Dopamine Agonists/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Flank Pain/chemically induced · Gastrointestinal Diseases/chemically induced · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Naloxone/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Oxycodone/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Patient Selection · Quality of Life · Restless Legs Syndrome/drug therapy · Salvage Therapy · Severity of Illness Index · Sleep · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One large, well-conducted trial answers this question, supported by its own secondary-endpoint analysis and by current guideline positioning. In Trenkwalder 2013 (306 randomised; severe restless legs syndrome, mean IRLS score 31.6, inadequately controlled on mainly dopaminergic therapy), prolonged-release oxycodone–naloxone titrated from 5/2.5 mg twice daily to a maximum of 40/20 mg twice daily reduced IRLS severity by −16.5 points versus −9.4 on placebo at 12 weeks (between-group difference 8.15 points, 95% CI 5.46–10.85; p<0.0001), and the benefit persisted through a 40-week open-label extension (mean score 9.7). The secondary analysis (Oertel 2016) found sleep disturbance, sleep adequacy, sleep quantity (+0.77 hours) and quality of life all significantly better on drug. The harm side is substantial and belongs on the face: treatment-related adverse events in 73% on drug versus 43% on placebo during the blinded phase, and five serious treatment-related events on drug, including constipation, subileus and ileus — constipation is this combination's dominant clinical problem despite the naloxone component. The 2025 American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline suggests extended-release oxycodone and other opioids over no opioids in adults with RLS (conditional recommendation, moderate certainty) — a second-line, refractory-disease position, not a first-line one. A single randomised programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Trenkwalder 2013 (306 randomised): IRLS severity fell −16.5 on oxycodone–naloxone vs −9.4 on placebo (difference 8.15 points, p<0.0001); treatment-related adverse events 73% vs 43%
cards.summary: Trenkwalder 2013 (306 randomised): IRLS severity fell −16.5 on oxycodone–naloxone vs −9.4 on placebo (difference 8.15 points, p<0.0001); treatment-related adverse events 73% vs 43%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with open-label extension (Trenkwalder 2013)
cards.people: 306 patients at 55 sites in Austria, Germany, Spain and Sweden with severe restless legs syndrome (symptoms ≥6 months, IRLS sum score ≥15; mean 31.6) inadequately controlled by previous, mainly dopaminergic, treatment; patients with severe COPD or a history of sleep apnoea were excluded. Randomised 1:1 to prolonged-release oxycodone–naloxone (starting 5.0/2.5 mg twice daily, titrated to a maximum 40/20 mg twice daily) or placebo for 12 weeks; 276 were in the primary analysis (132 drug, 144 placebo) and 197 entered the 40-week open-label extension.
cards.result: Mean IRLS change at 12 weeks was −16.5 (SD 11.3) on drug versus −9.4 (SD 10.9) on placebo (mean difference 8.15 points, 95% CI 5.46–10.85; p<0.0001). After the extension phase, the mean sum score was 9.7 (SD 7.8) on open-label drug. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 109 of 150 (73%) on drug versus 66 of 154 (43%) on placebo in the blinded phase and in 57% during the extension; five of 306 patients (2%) had serious treatment-related events while taking the drug — vomiting with concurrent duodenal ulcer, constipation, subileus, ileus and acute flank pain.
cards.watchOut: The placebo group also improved by 9.4 points, so the drug's added value is the 8.15-point difference, not the headline −16.5. Patients with sleep apnoea or severe lung disease were excluded — precisely the patients in whom opioid respiratory risk matters most — and 12 blinded weeks cannot speak to dependence or augmentation over years.

cards.headline: Oertel 2016 secondary analysis (same 306-patient programme): sleep disturbance, adequacy, quantity (+0.77 h) and quality of life all significantly better on drug
cards.summary: Oertel 2016 secondary analysis (same 306-patient programme): sleep disturbance, adequacy, quantity (+0.77 h) and quality of life all significantly better on drug
cards.type: Secondary-endpoint analysis of the randomised trial (Oertel 2016)
cards.people: The full analysis population of the Trenkwalder trial (132 on prolonged-release oxycodone–naloxone, 144 on placebo), analysed for Medical Outcomes Study sleep scale domains, the RLS-6 scale and the RLS quality-of-life questionnaire over the 12-week blinded phase and the 40-week extension.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, improvements on drug versus placebo were significantly greater for sleep disturbance (−18.6; 95% CI −24.4 to −12.9; p<0.0001), sleep adequacy (+14.9; 95% CI 7.9–21.9; p<0.0001) and sleep quantity (+0.77 hours; 95% CI 0.43–1.11; p<0.0001); drug also reduced symptom severity when falling asleep and during the night and daytime tiredness (RLS-6, all p<0.001), and quality of life improved more on drug (difference −9.02; 95% CI −12.85 to −5.19; p<0.001). All sleep and quality-of-life measures also improved during open-label treatment.
cards.watchOut: Secondary endpoints from the same single trial — they deepen the one programme's answer (the benefit is felt in sleep, the outcome patients care about) but they are not independent replication, and the extension phase is uncontrolled.
cards.source: Oertel WH et al. Sleep and Quality of Life Under Prolonged Release Oxycodone/Naloxone for Severe Restless Legs Syndrome: An Analysis of Secondary Efficacy Variables of a Double-Blind, Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Study with an Open-Label Extension.
