cards.headline: Winkelman 2025 AASM guideline: extended-release oxycodone and other opioids suggested over no opioids in adults with RLS — conditional recommendation, moderate certainty
cards.summary: Winkelman 2025 AASM guideline: extended-release oxycodone and other opioids suggested over no opioids in adults with RLS — conditional recommendation, moderate certainty
cards.type: Clinical practice guideline (American Academy of Sleep Medicine, 2025)
cards.people: Adults (and, for other recommendations, children) with restless legs syndrome or periodic limb movement disorder; recommendations were graded from a systematic review using GRADE, with iron studies as a good-practice statement for all patients with clinically significant RLS.
cards.result: Recommendation 9 states that in adults with RLS, the Academy suggests the use of extended-release oxycodone and other opioids over no opioids (conditional recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence). The same guideline suggests against the standard use of levodopa and positions iron assessment and repletion first — opioids sit in the refractory, later-line position that the Trenkwalder trial studied.
cards.watchOut: A conditional (weak) recommendation resting substantially on the single trial carded above: the guideline endorses a place in therapy for refractory disease, not routine use, and says nothing that softens the constipation and long-term opioid cautions on this shelf's face.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a large severity win in truly refractory disease, bought with a 73% adverse-event rate and a real bowel price
cards.summary: Synthesis: a large severity win in truly refractory disease, bought with a 73% adverse-event rate and a real bowel price
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One randomised programme (306 randomised, 276 analysed) with its secondary analysis, positioned by the 2025 AASM guideline — all in severe restless legs syndrome that had failed mainly dopaminergic therapy.
cards.result: An 8.15-point IRLS advantage over placebo at 12 weeks, maintained open-label to a mean score of 9.7, with concordant sleep and quality-of-life gains — against treatment-related adverse events in 73% versus 43% and serious constipation-spectrum events (constipation, subileus, ileus) on drug. POSSIBLE (benefit) for the refractory population studied; not evidence for earlier-line use.
cards.watchOut: No second randomised trial exists, long-term dependence, tolerance and augmentation on opioids in RLS are unanswered by this programme, and the trial excluded sleep apnoea and severe lung disease.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Oveporexton (tested product: Takeda TAK-861) for narcolepsy type 1: wakefulness latency up 14.3–19.8 minutes vs ~0 on placebo across two phase 3 trials (n=273), cataplexy down 79–89% median — with urinary frequency and insomnia in a majority
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with narcolepsy type 1, does twice-daily oveporexton (tested product — Takeda TAK-861) improve wakefulness (MWT), daytime sleepiness (ESS) and weekly cataplexy rate versus placebo over 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Double-Blind Method · Narcolepsy/drug therapy · Orexin Receptors/agonists · Sleep/drug effects · Sleep Latency/drug effects · Wakefulness/drug effects · Treatment Outcome · Urination/drug effects · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/chemically induced,epidemiology
shelves.balance: The tested product is Takeda's oveporexton (TAK-861), an oral orexin receptor 2-selective agonist, named under the tested-product clarification exception. The evidence is unusually concordant: a phase 2 trial (112 randomised) and two phase 3 trials (FirstLight, 168 enrolled; RadiantLight, 105 enrolled — 273 in total) all show large, dose-related gains on every core measure. In the phase 3 pair, Maintenance of Wakefulness Test latency rose by 14.3–19.8 minutes on oveporexton versus −0.4 to −0.8 minutes on placebo (all adjusted p<0.001), Epworth scores fell by 9.7–11.8 points versus 1.5–1.7, and median weekly cataplexy reductions were 79.0–88.8% versus 27.7–39.1%. A secondary analysis found attention, memory and executive-function measures also improved. The harms are frequent and belong on the face: adverse events in 86–89% on drug versus 43–54% on placebo, with increased urinary frequency and transient insomnia each occurring in a majority of oveporexton participants in the phase 3 trials (phase 2: insomnia 48%, urinary urgency 33%, urinary frequency 32%, with no hepatotoxicity — the class's earlier compound, TAK-994, was stopped for liver injury, and a 2026 class meta-analysis keeps that history visible). Twelve weeks is the longest blinded frame; durability and long-term safety are unproven. Two concordant phase 3 trials on top of a concordant phase 2 carry LIKELY (benefit) for the 12-week outcomes. The mechanism this drug replaces — cerebrospinal-fluid hypocretin-1 deficiency — is shelved as the hypocretin physiology pack #6599, built in this same wave.

cards.headline: Dauvilliers & Mignot 2026 — FirstLight and RadiantLight phase 3 (273 enrolled): MWT latency +14.3 to +19.8 min on oveporexton vs −0.4 to −0.8 on placebo; ESS −9.7 to −11.8 vs −1.5 to −1.7; median cataplexy reductions 79.0–88.8% vs 27.7–39.1%
cards.summary: Dauvilliers & Mignot 2026 — FirstLight and RadiantLight phase 3 (273 enrolled): MWT latency +14.3 to +19.8 min on oveporexton vs −0.4 to −0.8 on placebo; ESS −9.7 to −11.8 vs −1.5 to −1.7; median cataplexy reductions 79.0–88.8% vs 27.7–39.1%
cards.type: Two randomised controlled trials reported together (Dauvilliers 2026, FirstLight & RadiantLight)
cards.people: Participants aged 16–70 with narcolepsy type 1: 168 enrolled in FirstLight (randomised 3:3:2 to oveporexton 1 mg twice daily, 2 mg twice daily or placebo) and 105 in RadiantLight (2:1 to oveporexton 2 mg twice daily or placebo), treated for 12 weeks. Primary endpoint: change in mean sleep latency on the Maintenance of Wakefulness Test (MWT; 0–40 minutes, normal ≥20); key secondaries: Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS; 0–24, normal ≤10) and weekly cataplexy rate.
cards.result: Mean MWT latency changes ranged from +14.3 to +19.8 minutes across the oveporexton arms versus −0.4 to −0.8 minutes on placebo (adjusted p<0.001 for all comparisons); ESS changes ranged from −9.7 to −11.8 versus −1.5 to −1.7 (adjusted p<0.001); median percent reductions in weekly cataplexy rate ranged from 79.0% to 88.8% versus 27.7% to 39.1% (adjusted p<0.001). Adverse events occurred in 86–89% on oveporexton versus 43–54% on placebo; the most common were increased urinary frequency and transient insomnia, each occurring in a majority of participants receiving oveporexton.
cards.watchOut: Effects this large in 12-week trials still leave open durability, and the ranges pool two trials and two doses rather than reporting one arm's exact figure. A majority-rate urinary and insomnia burden is a real adherence question for a lifelong twice-daily drug, and adolescents are represented from age 16 only.
cards.source: Dauvilliers Y et al. Oveporexton for Narcolepsy Type 1 - Results from Two Phase 3 Trials. The New England journal of medicine. 2026. PMID: 42714024. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06470828, NCT06505031. cards.headline: Dauvilliers 2025 phase 2 (112 randomised): MWT latency +12.5 to +25.4 min across dose regimens vs −1.2 on placebo at 8 weeks; insomnia 48%, urinary urgency 33%, urinary frequency 32%; no hepatotoxic effects
cards.summary: Dauvilliers 2025 phase 2 (112 randomised): MWT latency +12.5 to +25.4 min across dose regimens vs −1.2 on placebo at 8 weeks; insomnia 48%, urinary urgency 33%, urinary frequency 32%; no hepatotoxic effects
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Dauvilliers 2025, phase 2)
cards.people: 112 participants with narcolepsy type 1 randomised to oveporexton regimens (0.5 mg twice daily, n=23; 2 mg twice daily, n=21; 2 mg followed by 5 mg daily, n=23; 7 mg once daily, n=23) or placebo (n=22) for 8 weeks. Primary endpoint: change in average sleep latency on the Maintenance of Wakefulness Test.
cards.result: MWT latency changes were +12.5, +23.5, +25.4 and +15.0 minutes across the four regimens versus −1.2 on placebo (adjusted p≤0.001 for all); ESS changes were −8.9, −13.8, −12.8 and −11.3 versus −2.5 (adjusted p≤0.004); weekly cataplexy incidence at week 8 was 4.24, 3.14, 2.48 and 5.89 versus 8.76 on placebo (significant for the 2 mg twice-daily and 2 mg/5 mg regimens). The commonest adverse events were insomnia (48%, most resolving within a week), urinary urgency (33%) and urinary frequency (32%), with no hepatotoxic effects observed.
cards.watchOut: A dose-ranging phase 2 with ~22 patients per arm: it picked the phase 3 doses and previewed the harm profile, but its per-arm estimates are imprecise; the absence of liver signal in 90 exposed patients does not settle class hepatotoxicity (see the synthesis card).

cards.headline: Lammers 2026 cognition secondary analysis (same phase 2 trial, 112 randomised): attention, memory and executive-function measures improved vs placebo over 8 weeks
cards.summary: Lammers 2026 cognition secondary analysis (same phase 2 trial, 112 randomised): attention, memory and executive-function measures improved vs placebo over 8 weeks
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised trial (Lammers 2026)
cards.people: The 112 randomised participants of the phase 2 TAK-861-2001 trial (aged 18–70 with narcolepsy type 1), assessed with the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (attention), Continuous Paired Associate Learning test (memory) and One Back / digit-symbol tests (executive function) over 8 weeks.
cards.result: Oveporexton improved attention, memory and executive function versus placebo: placebo-adjusted least-squares mean changes in Psychomotor Vigilance Task lapses ranged from −8.60 to −10.77 across dose groups (all 95% CIs excluding zero), and Continuous Paired Associate Learning errors from −15.51 to −22.52, with executive-function measures also favouring drug. The authors frame these as exploratory effects on the cognitive symptoms of narcolepsy type 1.
cards.watchOut: A secondary, exploratory analysis of a small phase 2 trial with many correlated outcomes: hypothesis-generating for cognition, not a basis for prescribing — the wakefulness and cataplexy cards above carry this shelf's claim.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the first orexin-replacement drug works on every core narcolepsy measure at 12 weeks — the open questions are durability and the urinary/insomnia burden
cards.summary: Synthesis: the first orexin-replacement drug works on every core narcolepsy measure at 12 weeks — the open questions are durability and the urinary/insomnia burden
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two phase 3 trials (273 enrolled), one phase 2 trial (112 randomised) and its cognition analysis — all of Takeda oveporexton (TAK-861) in narcolepsy type 1. The physiology it targets — loss of hypocretin (orexin) neurons and low cerebrospinal-fluid hypocretin-1 — is shelved separately as pack #6599.
cards.result: Wakefulness latency gains of roughly 14–20 minutes, Epworth falls of roughly 10–12 points and median cataplexy reductions of 79–89% versus 28–39% on placebo, consistent from phase 2 to phase 3: LIKELY (benefit) at 12 weeks. Against the benefit: adverse events in 86–89%, urinary frequency and transient insomnia in a majority, no blinded data beyond 12 weeks, and a class history (the earlier agonist TAK-994 was terminated after hepatotoxicity, noted in the 2026 class meta-analysis) that makes long-term liver surveillance part of this drug's story even though no hepatotoxicity appeared in oveporexton's own trials.
cards.watchOut: No trial compares oveporexton with oxybates, pitolisant or solriamfetol head-to-head, and none runs long enough to judge years of twice-daily use in adolescents and adults with a lifelong disease.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Lower-sodium (mixed-salt) oxybate in narcolepsy (PARTIAL — the slice live #921 sodium oxybate and live #922 idiopathic hypersomnia do not cover): under randomised withdrawal, placebo patients' cataplexy rose (median +2.35 attacks/week) while continuers held at 0.00; 92% less sodium than sodium oxybate
shelves.question: In people with narcolepsy, does lower-sodium oxybate (calcium/magnesium/potassium/sodium oxybates; tested product — Jazz lower-sodium oxybate, LXB/JZP-258) maintain control of cataplexy and daytime sleepiness under randomised withdrawal, and how does its sodium load compare with sodium oxybate?

shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of two verified homes: live #921 cards the twice-nightly SODIUM oxybate programme in narcolepsy, and live #922 cards lower-sodium oxybate only in IDIOPATHIC HYPERSOMNIA. This shelf builds only the mixed-salt formulation IN NARCOLEPSY, and re-cards no PMID homed on either. The tested product is Jazz's lower-sodium oxybate (LXB; JZP-258) — a calcium/magnesium/potassium/sodium oxybate mixture with the same active moiety as sodium oxybate and, per the trial record's pharmacology reporting, 92% less sodium (labelled here as a formulation/pharmacology fact, not a clinical-outcome finding: no trial shows the sodium reduction itself improves cardiovascular outcomes). The single phase 3 trial (Bogan 2021) used randomised withdrawal: 201 adults with narcolepsy with cataplexy enrolled and entered open-label titration/transition; 134 were randomised to continue LXB or switch to placebo for 2 weeks — the denominator for every efficacy number is those 134 withdrawal-randomised patients, not all-comers with narcolepsy. Placebo patients worsened significantly (median weekly cataplexy change +2.35 attacks versus 0.00 on continued LXB, p<0.0001; Epworth median change +2.0 versus 0.0, p<0.0001), and a companion analysis (Dauvilliers 2022) documents the transition course, including a transient cataplexy rise while other anticataplectics were tapered. Commonest events on LXB were headache (20.4%), nausea (12.9%) and dizziness (10.4%). A withdrawal design in stabilised patients caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Bogan 2021 randomised withdrawal (201 enrolled, 134 randomised): placebo switchers' cataplexy rose by a median 2.35 attacks/week vs 0.00 in continuers (p<0.0001); Epworth +2.0 vs 0.0 (p<0.0001)
cards.summary: Bogan 2021 randomised withdrawal (201 enrolled, 134 randomised): placebo switchers' cataplexy rose by a median 2.35 attacks/week vs 0.00 in continuers (p<0.0001); Epworth +2.0 vs 0.0 (p<0.0001)
cards.type: Randomised-withdrawal phase 3 trial (Bogan 2021)
cards.people: 201 adults aged 18–70 with narcolepsy with cataplexy enrolled into a 12-week open-label optimised-treatment and titration period (transitioning to lower-sodium oxybate [LXB] from prior cataplexy medications), a 2-week stable-dose period, then a 2-week double-blind randomised-withdrawal period in which 134 participants were randomised 1:1 to continue LXB or switch to placebo. Efficacy was assessed in the 134 randomised; safety in all 201 enrolled. The randomised denominator — stabilised open-label completers — is stated here because every efficacy figure below rests on it.
cards.result: During withdrawal, symptoms worsened significantly on placebo: median change in weekly cataplexy attacks from the stable-dose period was +2.35 (Q1 0.00, Q3 11.61) on placebo versus 0.00 (−0.49, 1.75) on continued LXB (p<0.0001; mean changes 11.46 [SD 24.75] vs 0.12 [5.77]), and median Epworth change was +2.0 (0.0, 5.0) versus 0.0 (−1.0, 1.0) (p<0.0001; mean 3.0 [4.68] vs 0.0 [2.90]). The commonest treatment-emergent adverse events with LXB were headache (20.4%), nausea (12.9%) and dizziness (10.4%). The record states LXB contains 92% less sodium than sodium oxybate — a formulation comparison from the product's pharmacology reporting, labelled as such.
cards.watchOut: A withdrawal trial proves the drug was holding symptoms down in people who had already transitioned onto and tolerated it; it cannot estimate the benefit of starting LXB in an untreated patient, the blinded phase lasted 2 weeks, and the sodium-load advantage has never been tied to a clinical outcome in a trial.
cards.source: Bogan RK et al. Efficacy and safety of calcium, magnesium, potassium, and sodium oxybates (lower-sodium oxybate [LXB]; JZP-258) in a placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomized withdrawal study in adults with narcolepsy with cataplexy. Sleep. 2021. PMID: 33184650. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03030599. cards.headline: Dauvilliers 2022 transition analysis (same trial): cataplexy-free days converged to ~6 per week in all entry groups by the stable-dose period; tapering other anticataplectics transiently raised cataplexy
cards.summary: Dauvilliers 2022 transition analysis (same trial): cataplexy-free days converged to ~6 per week in all entry groups by the stable-dose period; tapering other anticataplectics transiently raised cataplexy
cards.type: Secondary analysis of the randomised-withdrawal trial (Dauvilliers 2022)
cards.people: The same trial's participants, grouped by entry treatment: sodium oxybate only (group A), sodium oxybate plus other anticataplectics (B), other anticataplectics without sodium oxybate (C), and anticataplectic-naive (D), followed through the 12-week open-label LXB initiation/optimisation period (with taper of other anticataplectics in weeks 3–10), the stable-dose period and the withdrawal period.
cards.result: At entry, median weekly cataplexy attacks were lowest in those already on sodium oxybate (2.00 alone; 0.58 with other anticataplectics) versus 3.50 on other anticataplectics and 5.83 in naive patients. Attacks fell in weeks 1–2 of LXB treatment in all groups, rose transiently in groups tapering other anticataplectics during weeks 3–10 (most prominently in group C), and fell throughout initiation in naive patients; by the end of the stable-dose period, median cataplexy-free days per week were similar across groups (6.0, 6.1, 6.0 and 6.2).
cards.watchOut: An open-label transition analysis without a parallel control: it shows switching to LXB monotherapy is feasible and where the bumpy weeks fall, but the improvements during initiation cannot be separated from expectancy and regression to the mean — the blinded withdrawal card above is the efficacy evidence.
cards.source: Dauvilliers Y et al. Changes in Cataplexy Frequency in a Clinical Trial of Lower-Sodium Oxybate with Taper and Discontinuation of Other Anticataplectic Medications. CNS drugs. 2022. cards.headline: Bogan 2023 long-term safety analysis (same programme; 201 in the main study, 74 in the 24-week extension): headache 21%, nausea 13%, dizziness 10% during titration/stable-dose; no new safety pattern vs sodium oxybate
cards.summary: Bogan 2023 long-term safety analysis (same programme; 201 in the main study, 74 in the 24-week extension): headache 21%, nausea 13%, dizziness 10% during titration/stable-dose; no new safety pattern vs sodium oxybate
cards.type: Long-term safety analysis of the trial and its open-label extension (Bogan 2023)
cards.people: The 201-participant safety population of the Bogan 2021 programme (52 entering on sodium oxybate alone, 23 on sodium oxybate plus other anticataplectics, 36 on other anticataplectics alone, 90 anticataplectic-naive), followed through the 12-week open-label titration period, the 2-week stable-dose period and a subsequent 24-week open-label extension entered by 74 participants.
cards.result: During titration and stable-dose periods the commonest treatment-emergent events were headache (42 participants, 21%; median duration 1 day), nausea (26, 13%; median 9 days) and dizziness (21, 10%; median 7 days). In the extension, headache (9%), nasopharyngitis (8%) and dizziness (7%) led, and the authors conclude the long-term safety and tolerability profile of lower-sodium oxybate was generally consistent with the known profile of sodium oxybate. Discontinuations attributed to adverse events were 21 of 65 discontinuations (32%) in the main study periods and 3 of 7 (43%) in the extension.
cards.watchOut: Open-label safety follow-up of trial survivors: it extends the tolerability picture to ~9 months but cannot add efficacy evidence, and patients who could not tolerate the drug largely left before the extension began.
cards.source: Bogan RK et al. Long-Term Safety and Tolerability During a Clinical Trial and Open-Label Extension of Low-Sodium Oxybate in Participants with Narcolepsy with Cataplexy. CNS drugs. 2023. PMID: 36947322. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03030599, from the record's databank fields. cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One phase 3 randomised-withdrawal trial in narcolepsy with cataplexy (201 enrolled, 134 randomised), its transition analysis and its long-term safety analysis — the mixed-salt slice that live #921 (sodium oxybate in narcolepsy) and live #922 (lower-sodium oxybate in idiopathic hypersomnia) leave uncovered.

shelves.title: PHYSIOLOGY — CSF hypocretin-1 deficiency as the mechanism of narcolepsy type 1: undetectable in 7 of 9 patients in the founding report, <100 pg/mL in 32 of 38 cases versus all controls measurable, hypocretin neurons reduced 85–95% at autopsy, and ≤110 pg/mL validated as diagnostic in 570 subjects
shelves.question: In human narcolepsy type 1, is cerebrospinal-fluid hypocretin-1 absent or very low, are hypocretin-producing neurons lost at autopsy, and how specific is the deficiency for the cataplexy phenotype?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Animals · Carrier Proteins · Dogs · Female · Humans · Intracellular Signaling Peptides and Proteins · Male · Mice · Mice, Knockout · Middle Aged · Narcolepsy/cerebrospinal fluid,genetics,metabolism · Neuropeptides · Neurotransmitter Agents/cerebrospinal fluid,deficiency,genetics · Orexins
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Kryger's Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine): narcolepsy type 1 is the human hypocretin (orexin) deficiency syndrome — loss of the hypothalamic hypocretin neurons that stabilise wakefulness. The carded primary human data are concordant across three methods. Cerebrospinal fluid: hypocretin was undetectable in 7 of 9 narcolepsy patients in the founding report (Nishino 2000; N=9 printed plainly); in the larger series, hypocretin-1 was <100 pg/mL in 32 of 38 narcolepsy–cataplexy cases while all 34 controls were measurable at 169–376 pg/mL (Nishino 2001). Anatomy: post-mortem hypocretin neuron numbers were reduced by 85–95%, with intermixed melanin-concentrating hormone neurons preserved and gliosis in the region (Thannickal 2000; N not documented in the record). Accuracy: in 274 patients and 296 controls, cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1 below 110 pg/mL was diagnostic for narcolepsy, values above 200 pg/mL were normal, and low levels clustered in HLA-DQB1*0602-positive cataplexy (Mignot 2002). No animal studies are carded. This is the mechanism shelf for the orexin-agonist treatment shelf, pack #6579 (oveporexton), built this wave.

cards.headline: Nishino 2000: hypocretin was undetectable in the cerebrospinal fluid of 7 of 9 people with narcolepsy — the founding human observation (N=9, printed plainly)
cards.summary: Nishino 2000: hypocretin was undetectable in the cerebrospinal fluid of 7 of 9 people with narcolepsy — the founding human observation (N=9, printed plainly)
cards.type: Primary human cerebrospinal fluid study (Nishino 2000)
cards.people: 9 people with narcolepsy whose cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin was measured, reported in a brief Lancet report; N=9 printed plainly on the face of this physiology card — a sub-10 sample, labelled as such per the floor's labelling rule.
cards.result: Hypocretin was undetectable in seven out of nine people with narcolepsy, indicating abnormal hypocretin transmission. The authors frame the finding against animal models in which alterations in the hypocretin receptor 2 and preprohypocretin genes produce narcolepsy.
cards.watchOut: The fetched record's abstract is three sentences long: it gives no control values and no concentrations, so this card claims only what it states — undetectable in 7 of 9. The quantitative picture comes from the larger cohorts carded below, not from this founding report.

cards.headline: Thannickal 2000: post-mortem brains of people with narcolepsy had an 85–95% reduction in hypocretin neurons, with neighbouring melanin-concentrating hormone neurons preserved and gliosis in the hypocretin cell region
cards.summary: Thannickal 2000: post-mortem brains of people with narcolepsy had an 85–95% reduction in hypocretin neurons, with neighbouring melanin-concentrating hormone neurons preserved and gliosis in the hypocretin cell region
cards.type: Primary human post-mortem neuropathology study (Thannickal 2000)
cards.people: Post-mortem hypothalamic tissue from people with narcolepsy and controls, counting hypocretin (Hcrt) neurons and intermixed melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH) neurons; the fetched record does not state the number of brains, so this card prints N not documented for its groups.
cards.result: Human narcoleptics had an 85%–95% reduction in the number of Hcrt neurons. MCH neurons, which are intermixed with Hcrt cells in the normal brain, were not reduced in number, indicating the cell loss is relatively specific for Hcrt neurons. Gliosis was present in the hypocretin cell region, consistent with a degenerative process causing the loss. The authors note that, unlike canine and murine narcolepsy, most human narcolepsy is not familial and has not been linked to mutations of the Hcrt system.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the fetched record, and post-mortem counting cannot by itself prove the cell loss caused the symptoms rather than followed them — but the specificity (Hcrt neurons lost, intermixed MCH neurons spared) and the gliosis are the anatomical core of the deficiency mechanism.
cards.source: Thannickal TC et al. Reduced number of hypocretin neurons in human narcolepsy. Neuron. 2000. PMID: 11055430. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nishino 2001: cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1 was dramatically decreased (<100 pg/mL) in 32 of 38 narcolepsy–cataplexy cases, and measurable (169–376 pg/mL) in all 34 controls
cards.summary: Nishino 2001: cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1 was dramatically decreased (<100 pg/mL) in 32 of 38 narcolepsy–cataplexy cases, and measurable (169–376 pg/mL) in all 34 controls
cards.type: Primary human cerebrospinal fluid case-control study (Nishino 2001)
cards.people: 38 successive narcolepsy–cataplexy cases (36 HLA-DQB1*0602-positive) and 34 matched controls (15 healthy and 19 neurological patients); cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1, leptin and body mass index were measured.
cards.result: Hypocretin-1 was measurable in all controls (169–376 pg/mL), was unaffected by freezing/thawing or prolonged storage, and showed no concentration gradient. It was dramatically decreased (<100 pg/mL) in 32 of 38 patients, all of them HLA-positive; four patients had normal levels (2 HLA-negative) and two HLA-positive patients had high levels (609 and 637 pg/mL). Cerebrospinal fluid leptin and adjusted body mass index were significantly higher in patients than controls, which the authors read as altered energy homeostasis connected to the hypocretin system.
cards.watchOut: Six of 38 cases did not show the deficiency — hypocretin deficiency is the mechanism of most, not all, narcolepsy–cataplexy, and the two high values are unexplained in the record. Sensitivity in this series is about 84%, so a normal level does not exclude the diagnosis.
cards.source: Nishino S et al. Low cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin (Orexin) and altered energy homeostasis in human narcolepsy. Annals of neurology. 2001. PMID: 11558795. cards.headline: Mignot 2002 (274 patients, 296 controls): cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1 below 110 pg/mL was diagnostic for narcolepsy; values above 200 pg/mL were normal; most low-level subjects were HLA-DQB1*0602-positive narcolepsy–cataplexy patients
cards.summary: Mignot 2002 (274 patients, 296 controls): cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1 below 110 pg/mL was diagnostic for narcolepsy; values above 200 pg/mL were normal; most low-level subjects were HLA-DQB1*0602-positive narcolepsy–cataplexy patients
cards.type: Primary human diagnostic-accuracy case series (Mignot 2002)
cards.people: 570 subjects studied at US and European sleep and neurology clinics, 1999–2002: 274 patients with narcolepsy, hypersomnia, sleep apnoea, restless legs, insomnia and atypical hypersomnias, plus 296 controls (healthy and with neurological disorders). Signal detection analysis set the diagnostic threshold against International Classification of Sleep Disorders diagnoses, blinded.
cards.result: Hypocretin-1 levels below 110 pg/mL were diagnostic for narcolepsy; values above 200 pg/mL were considered normal. Most subjects with low levels were HLA-DQB1*0602-positive narcolepsy–cataplexy patients (HLA frequency 93% in typical cataplexy versus 17% in controls), and these patients did not always have abnormal multiple sleep latency tests. Rare subjects without cataplexy, without DQB1*0602, or with secondary narcolepsy had low levels; ten hypersomnia subjects had intermediate levels. Healthy controls and subjects with other sleep disorders all had normal levels; neurological subjects (n=194) were generally normal, with intermediate or low levels in a few acute neuropathological conditions. The authors conclude narcolepsy–cataplexy with hypocretin deficiency is a genuine disease entity and cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1 measurement is a definitive diagnostic test when interpreted in clinical context.
cards.watchOut: Accuracy was established against a clinical criterion standard in referral-clinic populations — spectrum effects mean the 110 pg/mL threshold performs best exactly where it was derived (suspected narcolepsy with cataplexy), and intermediate values (110–200 pg/mL) remain a grey zone the authors themselves flag.
cards.source: Mignot E et al. The role of cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin measurement in the diagnosis of narcolepsy and other hypersomnias. Archives of neurology. 2002. PMID: 12374492. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: cerebrospinal fluid deficiency, selective neuron loss and a validated diagnostic threshold converge — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: cerebrospinal fluid deficiency, selective neuron loss and a validated diagnostic threshold converge — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded primary human studies. Textbook framing (Kryger's Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine): narcolepsy type 1 is the human hypocretin-deficiency syndrome, defined by loss of the hypothalamic hypocretin (orexin) neurons that stabilise wakefulness and gate REM sleep phenomena such as cataplexy. Treatment partner: pack #6579 (oveporexton, the orexin receptor 2 agonist built this wave) cross-points here for the mechanism its drug replaces.
cards.result: Three independent human methods converge on one mechanism: cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1 is undetectable or very low in most narcolepsy–cataplexy patients and normal in controls and other sleep disorders (Nishino 2000, 7 of 9; Nishino 2001, 32 of 38 below 100 pg/mL versus all controls measurable); the hypocretin neurons themselves are 85–95% lost at autopsy with neighbouring neurons spared (Thannickal 2000); and a ≤110 pg/mL threshold was validated as diagnostic across 570 subjects (Mignot 2002). No animal studies are carded; animal genetics appear only as the textbook framing above. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: The deficiency is not universal (roughly one in six narcolepsy–cataplexy cases in the 2001 series had normal or high levels) and its cause — the degenerative process behind the gliosis — is not established by any carded record; what is established is the deficiency and the neuron loss, not why they happen.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nishino S et al. Lancet (London, England). 2000 (PMID: 10615891); Thannickal TC et al. Neuron. 2000 (PMID: 11055430); Nishino S et al. Annals of neurology. 2001 (PMID: 11558795); Mignot E et al. Archives of neurology. 2002 (PMID: 12374492).

shelves.title: PHYSIOLOGY — Closed-loop acoustic stimulation, slow-wave sleep and memory: in-phase stimulation enhances slow oscillations in anchor studies of N=11–13 and improved word retention in both, but a double-blind replication enhanced oscillations with no memory benefit, and the pooled memory effect is small and non-significant (g=0.25, p=0.07)
shelves.question: In humans, does phase-locked acoustic stimulation delivered during slow-wave sleep enhance slow-wave activity and improve overnight declarative-memory retention versus sham stimulation?
shelves.mesh: Acoustic Stimulation · Adult · Brain/physiology · Brain Waves/physiology · Electroencephalography · Female · Humans · Male · Memory/physiology · Neurons/physiology · Neuropsychological Tests · Periodicity · Polysomnography · Sleep/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Textbook framing (Kryger's Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine): the <1 Hz slow oscillation of non-REM sleep and its coupled spindles are the textbook substrate of declarative-memory consolidation, so entraining them is physiologically plausible. The human record splits by outcome type. Oscillations: in-phase closed-loop acoustic stimulation enhanced slow oscillations and spindle coupling in young adults (Ngo 2013; N=11, printed plainly) and increased slow-wave activity during stimulation intervals in older adults (Papalambros 2017; N=13), though whole-night slow-wave activity was unchanged in the latter. Memory: retention improved in both founding studies, but a double-blind replication that enhanced the same oscillations found no memory benefit in either of two experiments (Henin 2019; n=12 and n=19 — the treatment made no difference to behaviour), and the meta-analysis of 10 studies / 177 participants pools a small, non-significant effect (Hedges g=0.25, p=0.07), significant only in the phase-locked subgroup (g=0.36, p=0.047). No animal studies are carded. EMERGING, not ESTABLISHED, because the behavioural half of the claim remains unreplicated at anchor samples of n=11–13.

cards.headline: Ngo 2013: auditory stimulation in phase with slow-oscillation up states enhanced slow oscillations and spindle coupling and improved declarative memory retention — in N=11 participants (printed plainly)
cards.summary: Ngo 2013: auditory stimulation in phase with slow-oscillation up states enhanced slow oscillations and spindle coupling and improved declarative memory retention — in N=11 participants (printed plainly)
cards.type: Primary human closed-loop stimulation study (Ngo 2013)
cards.people: 11 healthy adults, each tested on two experimental nights (in-phase auditory stimulation versus no-stimulation control, order balanced), learning 120 word pairs in the evening and tested on retention the next morning; a separate out-of-phase stimulation condition was also examined. N=11 printed plainly — the sample size and word counts below are from the paper's full text, retrieved this session; the PubMed abstract does not state them.
cards.result: Auditory stimulation in phase with the ongoing slow-oscillation rhythm profoundly enhanced the slow oscillation, phase-coupled spindle activity and, consequently, consolidation of declarative memory; stimulation out of phase with the slow-oscillation rhythm remained ineffective. In the full text, the overnight memory-retention gain was 22.2 ± 2.3 words after in-phase stimulation versus 13.0 ± 2.5 words in the control condition (p<0.001, paired t test).
cards.watchOut: Eleven participants, one laboratory, one word-pair task: this is the founding demonstration, and its effect size should be read against the replication record carded below, where the same oscillation enhancement repeatedly occurred without the memory effect.
cards.source: Ngo HV et al. Auditory closed-loop stimulation of the sleep slow oscillation enhances memory. Neuron. 2013. PMID: 23583623. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Papalambros 2017: phase-locked acoustic stimulation in 13 older adults increased slow-wave and spindle activity during stimulation intervals and improved overnight word recall versus sham — while whole-night slow-wave activity was similar between conditions (N=13, printed plainly)
cards.summary: Papalambros 2017: phase-locked acoustic stimulation in 13 older adults increased slow-wave and spindle activity during stimulation intervals and improved overnight word recall versus sham — while whole-night slow-wave activity was similar between conditions (N=13, printed plainly)
cards.type: Primary human closed-loop stimulation crossover study (Papalambros 2017)
cards.people: 13 healthy participants aged 60–84 years, each completing one night of acoustic stimulation and one night of sham in random order. A real-time adaptive phase-locked-loop algorithm predicted slow-wave upstates from frontopolar EEG and delivered pulses of pink noise in trains of five pulses (ON intervals) separated by pauses of similar length (OFF intervals). Verbal paired-associate memory was tested before and after sleep.
cards.result: Slow-wave activity (SWA) over the entire sleep period was similar between stimulation and sham conditions, but SWA and spindle activity were increased during ON intervals compared with matched sham periods, sustained across almost the entire five-pulse interval. Overnight improvement in word recall was significantly greater with acoustic stimulation than sham, and correlated with the ON-versus-OFF change in SWA. The authors conclude phase-targeted acoustic stimulation can enhance SWA and improve sleep-dependent memory storage in older adults.
cards.watchOut: The whole-night SWA null beside the ON-interval increase matters: the stimulation amplified oscillations while it was on, in trains, rather than transforming the night's sleep — and the memory correlation is within-subject and correlational. N=13, single centre.
cards.source: Papalambros NA et al. Acoustic Enhancement of Sleep Slow Oscillations and Concomitant Memory Improvement in Older Adults. Frontiers in human neuroscience. 2017. PMID: 28337134. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Henin 2019: closed-loop acoustic stimulation robustly enhanced slow oscillations and spindles in two experiments (n=12 nap study; n=19 double-blind word-pair replication) — but produced NO memory benefit in either (the treatment made no difference to behaviour)
cards.summary: Henin 2019: closed-loop acoustic stimulation robustly enhanced slow oscillations and spindles in two experiments (n=12 nap study; n=19 double-blind word-pair replication) — but produced NO memory benefit in either (the treatment made no difference to behaviour)
cards.type: Primary human closed-loop stimulation replication studies (Henin 2019)
cards.people: Experiment 1: 12 healthy subjects in a randomised within-subject crossover, receiving closed-loop acoustic stimulation or sham during a daytime nap, tested on a virtual-reality spatial navigation task. Experiment 2: 19 healthy subjects in a double-blind replication of the word-pair design used by Ngo 2013, with closed-loop stimulation during nocturnal sleep.
cards.result: In both experiments, stimulation successfully enhanced slow-oscillation and spindle activity/power during sleep. However, no effects on behavioural performance were observed for spatial navigation (experiment 1), and associative memory performance was not strengthened by stimulation in the double-blind word-pair replication (experiment 2) — on behaviour, the treatment made no difference in either experiment. The authors conclude that enhancement of sleep oscillations may be insufficient to enhance memory performance in spatial navigation or verbal association tasks.
cards.watchOut: This is the balance card the founding papers require: the electrophysiological effect replicates reliably while the memory effect does not, under a double-blind protocol closer to the original methods than most replications manage. Task, nap-versus-night and population differences remain possible explanations, as the authors note.
cards.source: Henin S et al. Closed-Loop Acoustic Stimulation Enhances Sleep Oscillations But Not Memory Performance. eNeuro. 2019. PMID: 31604814. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Meta-analysis — Wunderlin 2021 (10 studies, 11 experiments, 177 participants): acoustic slow-wave enhancement showed a small, non-significant overall memory effect (Hedges g=0.25, p=0.07); the phase-locked subgroup reached significance (g=0.36, p=0.047)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis — Wunderlin 2021 (10 studies, 11 experiments, 177 participants): acoustic slow-wave enhancement showed a small, non-significant overall memory effect (Hedges g=0.25, p=0.07); the phase-locked subgroup reached significance (g=0.36, p=0.047)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of human acoustic-stimulation studies (Wunderlin 2021)
cards.people: 10 primary studies with 11 experiments and 177 healthy participants in total, applying acoustic slow-wave enhancement during sleep with pre- and post-sleep episodic memory testing; literature searched to October 2020 across PubMed, Web of Science and PsycInfo; effect sizes pooled with a random-effects model.
cards.result: The combined effect on overnight episodic-memory consolidation was small and not significant overall (Hedges g=0.25, p=0.07). Subgroup models gave g=0.31 (p=0.051) in young adults, g=0.36 (p=0.047) for phase-locked stimulation approaches, and g=0.44 (p=0.01) for their combination. There was no indication of publication bias. The authors conclude acoustic enhancement of slow-wave sleep tends to increase overnight consolidation but effects remain small and — outside subgroups — at trend level, and that the evidence is not sufficient to recommend commercially available devices.
cards.watchOut: A second meta-analysis on this question (2022) was identified this session but is a retracted publication and is therefore not carded, per standing rule. This card's pooled N of 177 across 11 experiments is itself the headline: the entire literature is smaller than a single modest trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: oscillations reliably enhanced, memory effect small and inconsistently replicated — PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING
cards.summary: Synthesis: oscillations reliably enhanced, memory effect small and inconsistently replicated — PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human records. Textbook framing (Kryger's Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine): the <1 Hz slow oscillation of non-REM sleep, with its coupled spindles, is the textbook mechanism for consolidating declarative memory during sleep — which is why entraining it acoustically is a plausible intervention on a settled physiological substrate, even though the intervention's behavioural payoff is not settled.
cards.result: The electrophysiology is consistent: in-phase closed-loop acoustic stimulation enhances slow oscillations and spindle coupling in young adults (Ngo 2013, n=11) and in older adults during stimulation intervals (Papalambros 2017, n=13). The memory claim is where the record splits: positive in both founding studies, absent in a double-blind replication that enhanced the same oscillations (Henin 2019, n=12 and n=19), and small and non-significant when pooled (g=0.25, p=0.07; Wunderlin 2021). Anchor samples of n=11–13 are printed on the cards' faces. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
cards.watchOut: Commercial sleep devices already market this effect; the carded evidence — 177 participants across the whole meta-analysed literature — does not support recommending them, which is the meta-analysis authors' own conclusion.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ngo HV et al. Neuron. 2013 (PMID: 23583623); Papalambros NA et al. Frontiers in human neuroscience. 2017 (PMID: 28337134); Henin S et al. eNeuro. 2019 (PMID: 31604814); Wunderlin M et al. Sleep. 2021 (PMID: 33406249).

shelves.title: The breath-hold breaking point: involuntary inspiratory contractions build through the hold and drive its dyspnoea; larger starting lung volume delays them, CO₂ accumulation sets the main timetable, and manoeuvres that slow the CO₂ rise lengthen the hold at an unchanged breakpoint CO₂ tension
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what sets the breath-hold breaking point — how much do starting lung volume, arterial CO₂ and O₂ each contribute, and how much can involuntary breathing movements be tolerated before the hold breaks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Apnea/physiopathology · Carbon Dioxide/blood,metabolism · Diaphragm/innervation,physiology · Dyspnea/etiology · Fasting/physiology · Functional Residual Capacity · Humans · Immersion · Lung/physiology · Lung Volume Measurements · Male · Muscle Contraction · Oxygen/blood · Pulmonary Gas Exchange · Respiration/physiology · Respiratory Muscles/physiology · Total Lung Capacity
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbook account: a breath hold ends not at a fixed blood-gas value but when the involuntary respiratory drive — driven mainly by rising CO₂, amplified by falling O₂, and expressed as involuntary inspiratory contractions and air hunger — overcomes voluntary suppression; starting lung volume, metabolic rate and CO₂ storage all move the timing. The carded human studies support each limb: contractions in almost all of 52 subjects, growing to the breakpoint (Whitelaw 1981); larger lung volume delaying them (Whitelaw 1987); fasting slowing CO₂ production, lengthening the hold and lowering the breakpoint oxygen level (Lindholm 2007); immersion enlarging CO₂ storage and lengthening the hold at unchanged breakpoint CO₂ (Chang 1996). Parkes' 2006 review (PMID 16272264, fetched this session) is the standing caution: no single mechanism yet encompasses all the breakpoint's properties — that limit is printed in the Synthesis. Refusals: Fowler 1954 (PMID 13152037), Godfrey & Campbell 1968 (PMID 5684100) and 1969 (PMID 5193728) and Hill 1973 (PMID 4763084) were all verified by title search but their PubMed records carry empty abstracts, so under the standing rule they are NOT carded and no numbers are attributed to them. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Whitelaw 1981: involuntary respiratory-muscle contractions appeared in almost all of 52 breath-holding subjects and grew in amplitude and frequency to the breakpoint
cards.summary: Whitelaw 1981: involuntary respiratory-muscle contractions appeared in almost all of 52 breath-holding subjects and grew in amplitude and frequency to the breakpoint
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (breath-hold neuromuscular recording) — N = 52
cards.people: 52 subjects; in detailed studies subjects rebreathed a mixture of 8% CO₂ in O₂, then held the breath on an occluded mouthpiece with the glottis open at functional residual capacity, contractions monitored as waves of negative (pleural/gastric) pressure.
cards.result: The involuntary contractions occurred in almost all subjects and were regular in a majority. They were reproducible and increased in amplitude and frequency through the breath hold, but the breakpoint did not always correspond to the same pressure or frequency. Contraction frequency and dP/dt were much higher during breath holding than during occluded breathing at the same gas tensions while rebreathing, and taking three breaths reduced contraction amplitude without altering gas tensions — consistent with the contractions contributing to the dyspnoea of breath holding, without a simple magnitude–dyspnoea correlation.
cards.watchOut: Breath holds began from a hypercapnic rebreathing plateau (8% CO₂), not from room air: the design isolates the contraction phenomenon at matched gas tensions, and durations from this protocol are not comparable to ordinary breath-hold times.
cards.source: Whitelaw WA et al. Respiratory neuromuscular output during breath holding. Journal of applied physiology: respiratory, environmental and exercise physiology. 1981. PMID: 6451605. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Whitelaw 1987: holding at a larger lung volume delayed the onset and reduced the frequency of the involuntary contractions that build to the breakpoint
cards.summary: Whitelaw 1987: holding at a larger lung volume delayed the onset and reduced the frequency of the involuntary contractions that build to the breakpoint
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (breath holds at varied lung volume) — N not stated in the fetched record
cards.people: Healthy subjects (number not stated in the fetched record) who rebreathed 8% CO₂–92% O₂ to an alveolar plateau and then breath-held at various lung volumes, with diaphragm contraction pressure waves followed by gastric and pleural pressures.
cards.result: At all volumes, regular rhythmic inspiratory-muscle contractions increased in amplitude and frequency until the breakpoint, with expiratory muscle activity more prominent in some subjects. Increasing lung volume caused a delay in onset and a decrease in frequency of contractions, with no consistent change in duty cycle; the fall in oesophageal pressure swings was accountable by force–length and geometric properties. The volume effect on contraction timing most resembled a chest-wall reflex — the record's evidence that starting lung volume acts on the breakpoint through the involuntary-contraction/dyspnoea pathway, not only through gas stores.
cards.watchOut: N is not documented in the fetched abstract and is printed as such, per the labelling rule. As with the companion study, holds started from a CO₂-loaded plateau at each volume, so volume was varied at matched starting gas tensions.
cards.source: Whitelaw WA et al. Effect of lung volume on breath holding. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 1987. PMID: 3110125. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lindholm 2007: in 10 men, 18 hours of fasting lengthened the breath hold to first diaphragmatic contraction (148 vs 129 s) but the breakpoint came at a lower oxygen level
cards.summary: Lindholm 2007: in 10 men, 18 hours of fasting lengthened the breath hold to first diaphragmatic contraction (148 vs 129 s) but the breakpoint came at a lower oxygen level
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (diet-manipulation breath-hold protocol) — N = 10
cards.people: 10 male non-divers performing repeated breath holds to the first diaphragmatic contraction (physiological breakpoint) and to maximal breakpoint, under normal diet, after 14 and 18 hours of fasting, and after post-fast carbohydrate consumption; duration, respiratory exchange ratio, end-tidal PO₂/PCO₂, SaO₂ and glucose measured.
cards.result: Duration to the first diaphragmatic contraction rose from 129 ± 34 s on the control diet to 148 ± 33 s after 18 h fasting, and fell to 122 ± 30 s after carbohydrate (P<0.001); similar trends held for maximal holds. End-tidal PO₂ at the breakpoint was higher after carbohydrate than after fasting (10.4 ± 1.2 vs 9.5 ± 1.2 kPa, P<0.05) — fasting slows CO₂ production (lower respiratory exchange ratio), so the CO₂-driven urge arrives later, but at a lower, less safe oxygen level. The record frames the urge to breathe, and hence the breakpoint, as mainly CO₂-driven.
cards.watchOut: Small study in non-divers at rest; the manipulation is metabolic rate/CO₂ production, so this card speaks to the CO₂ contribution and its O₂ trade-off, not to trained divers' maximal performance.
cards.source: Lindholm P et al. Effects of fasting and carbohydrate consumption on voluntary resting apnea duration. European journal of applied physiology. 2007. PMID: 17406888. cards.headline: Chang 1996: head-out immersion prolonged maximal breath-hold time by 20% and slowed the rise of end-tidal CO₂ by 31%, while the CO₂ level at the breakpoint did not change
cards.summary: Chang 1996: head-out immersion prolonged maximal breath-hold time by 20% and slowed the rise of end-tidal CO₂ by 31%, while the CO₂ level at the breakpoint did not change
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (immersion breath-hold and CO₂-storage protocol) — N = 13 for breath holds (sub-protocols n = 5 and n = 9)
cards.people: Healthy humans studied in air and during head-out immersion in 35 °C water: maximal breath holds (n = 13), air-breathing measurements (n = 5) and 4-minute CO₂ rebreathing (n = 9).
cards.result: Immersed maximal breath-hold time was prolonged by 20.3% (P<0.05) and the rate of rise of end-tidal PCO₂ was 31% slower (P<0.05), but breaking-point PETCO₂ (CO₂ sensitivity) and the rate of fall of end-tidal PO₂ (metabolism) were unchanged. Estimated immediate tissue CO₂ storage capacity rose from 0.52 ± 0.03 (control) to 0.66 ± 0.04 ml·kg⁻¹·mmHg⁻¹ on immersion — the hold lengthens because CO₂ accumulates more slowly into a larger effective store, reaching the same breakpoint tension later.
cards.watchOut: The prolonged immersed hold did not itself correlate with the measured storage-capacity increase in the record's own analysis, and the authors leave that mechanism open — printed here as the record states it, not smoothed over.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the breakpoint is where a rising CO₂ drive, sensed through involuntary respiratory contractions and dyspnoea, overcomes voluntary suppression — lung volume, CO₂ stores and O₂ each move the timing
cards.summary: Synthesis: the breakpoint is where a rising CO₂ drive, sensed through involuntary respiratory contractions and dyspnoea, overcomes voluntary suppression — lung volume, CO₂ stores and O₂ each move the timing
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (respiratory control chapters), with Parkes 2006 (PMID 16272264) as the field's review synthesis. No new data.
cards.result: Involuntary inspiratory contractions build through every hold and contribute to its dyspnoea (PMID 6451605); a larger starting lung volume delays and slows them (PMID 3110125); slowing CO₂ production lengthens the hold but lets oxygen fall lower before the break (PMID 17406888); and enlarging the effective CO₂ store slows the CO₂ rise and lengthens the hold at an unchanged breakpoint CO₂ tension (PMID 8781848). Parkes' review, cited in the balance, adds the honest limit: no single mechanism — lung shrinkage, blood gases or carotid chemoreceptors alone — explains the breakpoint breath. The classic Fowler (1954) and Godfrey & Campbell (1968/1969) experiments were verified by title search this session but their PubMed records carry no abstracts, so no numbers are sourced from them and they are not carded. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

shelves.title: Closing capacity with age: closing volume and closing capacity rise steadily with age in every population regression, while FRC does not — so dependent airways close during tidal breathing (supine first, then upright), and when lung volume falls below closing capacity, shunt rises roughly fivefold
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how does closing capacity change with age — at about what age does closing capacity exceed functional residual capacity upright and supine, and what does that imply for dependent airway closure and the age-related widening of the alveolar–arterial gradient?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aging · Anesthesia, Inhalation · Closing Volume · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Functional Residual Capacity · Humans · Lung/physiology · Lung Volume Measurements · Male · Middle Aged · Nitrogen · Reference Values · Respiratory Function Tests · Smoking/complications · Vital Capacity
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbook account: small dependent airways close at low lung volumes because local pleural pressure exceeds airway pressure; the lung volume at which this begins (closing volume, and closing capacity = closing volume + residual volume) rises with age as elastic recoil is lost, while functional residual capacity changes little — so closing capacity comes to exceed FRC first supine (textbook account: roughly the mid-40s) and then upright (roughly the mid-60s), producing dependent closure during tidal breathing, V/Q mismatch and the age-related widening of the A–a gradient. Those crossing ages are labelled here as the textbook's account: no record fetched this session prints them. The carded human evidence carries the age rise itself, three independent ways (Buist 1979 three-city regressions; Teculescu 1996, N=158; Sixt 1984, N=178), and the gas-exchange consequence of the crossed state (Dueck 1988: shunt 11.4% when FRC < closing capacity vs 2.4% when above). Refusals: Leblanc, Ruff & Milic-Emili 1970 (PMID 5437433), Buist & Ross 1973 (PMID 4695626) and McCarthy et al. 1972 (PMID 5030172) were verified by title search but their PubMed records carry empty abstracts, so they are NOT carded and no numbers are attributed to them. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Buist 1979: in three North American cities, closing volume and closing capacity rose with age in nonsmokers with near-identical regression slopes — and the age effect was considerably greater than the smoking effect
cards.summary: Buist 1979: in three North American cities, closing volume and closing capacity rose with age in nonsmokers with near-identical regression slopes — and the age effect was considerably greater than the smoking effect
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population single-breath nitrogen regressions) — total N not stated in the fetched record
cards.people: Population samples in Montreal, Portland and Winnipeg studied with the single-breath nitrogen test (closing volume, closing capacity, slope of phase III) alongside spirometry, analysed by age, sex and smoking habit in nonsmokers and smokers. (Total N not stated in the fetched record.)
cards.result: In nonsmokers, the age-related regressions for closing volume, closing capacity and the phase III slope (and for the FEV₁/FVC ratio) had very similar slopes in all three cities, suggesting geography, climate, air pollution and occupation had no detectable effect on these tests. Closing capacity as a percentage of total lung capacity was the most frequently abnormal measure in men. Although cigarettes smoked significantly affected every test except FEV₁/FVC in men, the effect of age was considerably greater than the effect of smoking, and the smoking dose–response was weak.
cards.watchOut: N is not documented in the fetched abstract and is printed as such. The record reports the age regressions qualitatively (similar slopes; age >> smoking) without printing the slope coefficients, so none are claimed here.
cards.source: Buist AS et al. Relationship between the single-breath N test and age, sex, and smoking habit in three North American cities. The American review of respiratory disease. 1979. cards.headline: Teculescu 1996: in 158 healthy adults aged 21–64, the closing-volume/vital-capacity and closing-capacity/total-lung-capacity ratios depended on age
cards.summary: Teculescu 1996: in 158 healthy adults aged 21–64, the closing-volume/vital-capacity and closing-capacity/total-lung-capacity ratios depended on age
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (reference-value regression cohort) — N = 158
cards.people: 158 healthy subjects (68 women), ages 21 to 64, from a rural community in a non-polluted area of northeast France, measured with a computerised single-breath nitrogen washout: alveolar nitrogen slope (phase III), closing volume and closing capacity, regressed against age, height, weight and BMI with 95% confidence intervals.
cards.result: Phase III slope increased with age in both sexes. The closing volume to vital capacity ratio and the closing capacity to total lung capacity ratio depended on age and, in males, increased with BMI. A practical limit is printed in the record: even accepting a 15% difference between test and spirometric vital capacity, only 46.3% of asymptomatic nonsmokers produced a valid single-breath nitrogen test — a high failure rate that limits field use in older, test-naive populations.
cards.watchOut: Reference equations are for the computerised system used; the record notes manual and computer measurements differ systematically, so values are method-specific. Ages stop at 64 — the oldest decades are carried by the other cards and the textbook account.
cards.source: Teculescu DB et al. Computerized single-breath nitrogen washout: predicted values in a rural French community. Lung. 1996. PMID: 8747001. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sixt 1984: in 178 healthy never-smoking men aged 30–70, closing volume was predicted by a simple regression on age, and the alveolar-plateau slope rose at an accelerating rate after age 50
cards.summary: Sixt 1984: in 178 healthy never-smoking men aged 30–70, closing volume was predicted by a simple regression on age, and the alveolar-plateau slope rose at an accelerating rate after age 50
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (reference-value regression cohort, men) — N = 178
cards.people: 178 healthy never-smoking men aged 30–70, selected by systematic sampling from an urban population, studied with the single-breath nitrogen washout (closing volume and slope of the alveolar plateau, delta N₂) and spirometry.
cards.result: A prediction equation for closing volume was produced by simple regression on age alone. Delta N₂ showed an accelerated increase with age above 50, described by a curvilinear (exponential-in-age) equation in the record, and its distribution was not homogeneous across the age range; the authors propose 180% of predicted as the upper reference limit for delta N₂. Reference equations for vital capacity, FEV₁ and FEV₁% were built on age and height.
cards.watchOut: Men only, never-smokers: the cleanest age signal, but not directly a women's reference. The exponential delta-N₂ equation is quoted in the record in a form tied to its own units; this card carries its shape (accelerating after 50), not a re-derived coefficient.
cards.source: Sixt R et al. The single-breath N2-test and spirometry in healthy non-smoking males. European journal of respiratory diseases. 1984. PMID: 6723839. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dueck 1988: when anaesthesia dropped functional residual capacity below closing capacity, shunt rose to 11.4% — versus 2.4% when FRC stayed above closing capacity
cards.summary: Dueck 1988: when anaesthesia dropped functional residual capacity below closing capacity, shunt rose to 11.4% — versus 2.4% when FRC stayed above closing capacity
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (FRC–closing-capacity–shunt relation under anaesthesia) — N = 18
cards.people: 18 non-obese surgical patients aged 21–34 under halothane anaesthesia; FRC by helium dilution, closing capacity measured awake, and intrapulmonary shunt distinguished from V/Q inequality by multiple inert-gas elimination analysis, awake and anaesthetised, supine.
cards.result: Awake supine FRC was 34.6 ± 6.6% of total lung capacity and closing capacity 29.8 ± 5.3% of TLC. Anaesthesia with paralysis and mechanical ventilation reduced FRC by 14.6 ± 13.3% to 29.8% of TLC (P = 0.002), and shunt rose from 1.2 ± 1.5% awake to 8.6 ± 8.3% (P = 0.005). Anaesthetised subjects whose FRC fell below their awake closing capacity had an average shunt of 11.4 ± 8.3%, versus 2.4 ± 2.8% in those whose FRC stayed above closing capacity (P = 0.025); nonsmokers developed shunt only if FRC fell below closing capacity.
cards.watchOut: Young surgical patients under anaesthesia, not healthy ageing volunteers: this card carries the consequence of the FRC-below-closing-capacity state (dependent closure and shunt), which is the same state ageing produces at rest — the age crossing itself is carried by the regression cards and the textbook account.
cards.source: Dueck R et al. The lung volume at which shunting occurs with inhalation anesthesia. Anesthesiology. 1988. PMID: 3195757. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: closing capacity climbs steadily with age while FRC does not — so dependent airways begin to close during ordinary tidal breathing, first supine and then upright, widening V/Q mismatch with age
cards.summary: Synthesis: closing capacity climbs steadily with age while FRC does not — so dependent airways begin to close during ordinary tidal breathing, first supine and then upright, widening V/Q mismatch with age
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (respiratory mechanics chapters). No new data.
cards.result: Single-breath nitrogen regressions in three independent populations agree that closing volume and closing capacity rise with age — age dominating smoking as a determinant (PMIDs 475152, 8747001, 6723839), with the alveolar-plateau slope accelerating after 50 (PMID 6723839). The textbook account puts the crossing ages at roughly the mid-40s supine and the mid-60s upright for closing capacity exceeding FRC; those specific ages are presented here as the textbook's account, because no carded record in this session prints them. What a carded record does show is the consequence when the crossing occurs: FRC below closing capacity produced an ~11% shunt versus ~2% above it (PMID 3195757). Dependent closure during tidal breathing is thus the mechanical link between ageing and the widening alveolar–arterial gradient. The classic Leblanc/Ruff/Milic-Emili 1970, Buist & Ross 1973 and McCarthy 1972 records were verified by title search but carry empty abstracts, so they are not carded and no numbers are attributed to them. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Scope: closing capacity and ageing in health, and its gas-exchange consequence. The alveolar gas equation and the A–a gradient itself are pack #6349, whose gradient discussion presupposes this physiology — cross-point, do not duplicate.

shelves.title: A DUE: one Opsynvi tablet (macitentan + tadalafil) cut pulmonary vascular resistance 29% relative vs macitentan and 28% relative vs tadalafil at 16 weeks — a haemodynamic surrogate endpoint
shelves.question: In adults with pulmonary arterial hypertension on background therapy, does a single-tablet combination of macitentan 10 mg + tadalafil 40 mg, compared with either agent alone, improve pulmonary vascular resistance and clinical outcomes?
shelves.balance: The tested product is the single tablet Opsynvi (macitentan/tadalafil, Janssen/Johnson & Johnson), named per the clarification exception because the question is about this fixed combination. In the single phase 3 programme (A DUE, n=187), the single tablet reduced pulmonary vascular resistance at week 16 by 29% relative versus macitentan alone (geometric mean ratio 0.71) and 28% relative versus tadalafil alone (geometric mean ratio 0.72) (PMID 38267108). FLAG: the primary endpoint is a haemodynamic surrogate (PVR) — the trial was not powered for, and does not report, a clinical-worsening or mortality benefit. In the open-label extension, 91% of patients who started on the single tablet were alive at end of study and walk distance and NT-proBNP gains were sustained to week 120, uncontrolled (PMID 41820779, a second report of the same A DUE programme). A Chinese subgroup (n=23) showed larger relative PVR reductions (PMID 41250682) — a subgroup, not independent confirmation. Anaemia, hypotension and oedema were more frequent on the combination. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one programme, surrogate primary endpoint — the stamp cannot be LIKELY on this base.

cards.headline: A DUE (Grünig 2024): single-tablet macitentan/tadalafil cut PVR 29% relative vs macitentan and 28% relative vs tadalafil at week 16
cards.summary: A DUE (Grünig 2024): single-tablet macitentan/tadalafil cut PVR 29% relative vs macitentan and 28% relative vs tadalafil at week 16
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase 3 — A DUE (Grünig 2024)
cards.people: 187 patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension, WHO functional class II–III (treatment-naïve or on prior endothelin-receptor-antagonist or PDE5-inhibitor monotherapy), randomised to single-tablet macitentan 10 mg/tadalafil 40 mg (n=108), macitentan (n=35) or tadalafil (n=44) for 16 weeks.
cards.result: Primary endpoint — change in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) at week 16, a haemodynamic surrogate: reduction with the single tablet was significantly greater than with macitentan (29% relative; geometric mean ratio 0.71, 95% CL 0.61–0.82, P<0.0001) and than with tadalafil (28% relative; geometric mean ratio 0.72, 95% CL 0.64–0.80, P<0.0001). Three patients died in the single-tablet arm, judged unrelated to treatment. Adverse events leading to discontinuation, serious adverse events, and events of special interest (anaemia, hypotension, oedema) were more frequent with the single tablet.
cards.watchOut: PVR is a surrogate: a 29% relative PVR reduction is not a 29% reduction in death or clinical worsening, and this 16-week trial does not measure those outcomes. The comparison also builds in the expected effect of taking two active drugs instead of one — the open question the tablet answers is convenience/adherence, which the trial design cannot isolate.
cards.source: Grünig E et al. A DUE: Randomized Trial of Macitentan/Tadalafil Single-Tablet Combination Therapy for Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2024. PMID: 38267108. Registry ID: NCT03904693. cards.headline: A DUE open-label period (Ford 2026): gains held to 2 years and 91% of the original single-tablet group were alive — uncontrolled follow-up of the same programme
cards.summary: A DUE open-label period (Ford 2026): gains held to 2 years and 91% of the original single-tablet group were alive — uncontrolled follow-up of the same programme
cards.type: Open-label extension report — A DUE programme (Ford 2026)
cards.people: 185 patients received the single tablet at some point across the double-blind and open-label periods (median exposure 105.1 weeks); the efficacy set is the 107–108 patients randomised to the single tablet from the start of A DUE. Explicitly labelled: second report of the A DUE programme (PMID 38267108), not an independent trial.
cards.result: In the efficacy set, 91% of patients were alive at end of study. Mean change in 6-minute walk distance from single-tablet initiation to open-label week 120 was +60.5 m (SD 84.2), and NT-proBNP geometric mean was 50.2% of baseline at week 120. In the safety set, adverse events occurred in 94.1% and serious adverse events in 33.5%; 10.3% discontinued for an adverse event; 7 on-treatment deaths were all judged unrelated to treatment.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, no comparator, and survivors stay in: sustained walk distance in patients who remained on treatment for 2 years cannot be read as a treatment effect. It answers tolerability over time, not efficacy.
cards.source: Ford HJ et al. Long-Term Treatment with Single-Tablet Combination of Macitentan and Tadalafil in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension: Results from A DUE and Its Open-Label Period. Advances in Therapy. 2026. PMID: 41820779. Registry ID: NCT03904693. cards.headline: A DUE Chinese subgroup (Fan 2025): in 23 patients, PVR fell 50% relative vs macitentan and 41% relative vs tadalafil
cards.summary: A DUE Chinese subgroup (Fan 2025): in 23 patients, PVR fell 50% relative vs macitentan and 41% relative vs tadalafil
cards.type: Subgroup analysis — A DUE programme (Fan 2025)
cards.people: 23 participants from China within the 187-patient A DUE trial (subgroup analysis; N = 23, printed plainly), randomised by their baseline treatment stratum to the single tablet or monotherapy.
cards.result: PVR reduction was greater with the single tablet than with macitentan (adjusted geometric mean ratio 0.50, 95% CL 0.35–0.72, p=0.0017 — a 50% relative reduction) and than with tadalafil (ratio 0.59, 95% CL 0.43–0.80, p=0.0040 — a 41% relative reduction). Safety was consistent with the overall population; the authors state the data should be interpreted with caution due to the small sample size.
cards.watchOut: A 23-patient subgroup of the same single trial: it adds no independent evidence, and larger relative effects in small subgroups are the expected direction of noise. Carded to show the programme's full published record, not as confirmation.

cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial programme shows the single tablet lowers PVR more than either drug alone — clinical-outcome benefit is untested
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One phase 3 programme: A DUE (187 patients, 16-week double-blind), its open-label period (185 exposed), and a 23-patient Chinese subgroup of the same trial.
cards.result: PVR at 16 weeks: 29% relative reduction vs macitentan and 28% relative vs tadalafil (geometric mean ratios 0.71 and 0.72). shelves.title: IMPALA-2: inhaled molgramostim improved DLCO by 6.0 percentage points over placebo in autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (n=164) — a physiological surrogate; whole-lung lavage remains the practical standard
shelves.question: In adults with autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, does inhaled molgramostim, compared with placebo, improve gas exchange?
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials of one programme (Savara) point the same way. IMPALA (n=138): continuous daily inhaled molgramostim improved the alveolar-arterial oxygen difference by 6.2 mm Hg more than placebo at 24 weeks (PMID 32897035). IMPALA-2 (n=164 — large for this rare disease but small in absolute terms; N printed on the face): DLCO rose 9.8 vs 3.8 percentage points at week 24 (difference 6.0 points, P<0.001) and the gap persisted at week 48 (PMID 40834301). A 2026 meta-analysis of 4 inhaled GM-CSF RCTs (402 patients) found the same direction (DLCO mean difference 5.09 points) (PMID 42045620). FLAGS: DLCO and A-aDo2 are physiological surrogates, not lavage avoided, hospitalisation or survival; whole-lung lavage is the practical standard of care and was NOT the trial comparator — the trials compare molgramostim with placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): concordant randomised evidence from a single sponsor programme, on surrogate endpoints.

cards.headline: IMPALA (Trapnell 2020): daily inhaled molgramostim improved the alveolar-arterial oxygen difference by 6.2 mm Hg more than placebo at 24 weeks
cards.summary: IMPALA (Trapnell 2020): daily inhaled molgramostim improved the alveolar-arterial oxygen difference by 6.2 mm Hg more than placebo at 24 weeks
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial — IMPALA (Trapnell 2020)
cards.people: 138 patients with autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis randomised to continuous inhaled molgramostim 300 micrograms once daily (n=46), intermittent molgramostim every other week (n=45), or placebo (n=47), for 24 weeks followed by an open-label extension.
cards.result: Primary endpoint — change in alveolar-arterial difference in oxygen concentration (A-aDo2) at week 24: improvement was greater with continuous molgramostim than placebo (−12.8 vs −6.6 mm Hg; estimated treatment difference −6.2 mm Hg, P=0.03). St George's Respiratory Questionnaire total score also improved more (−12.4 vs −5.1 points; difference −7.4, P=0.01), and continuous dosing beat intermittent dosing on multiple endpoints. Adverse and serious adverse event rates were similar across groups, except chest pain, which was more frequent with continuous molgramostim.
cards.watchOut: A-aDo2 is a gas-exchange surrogate measured under trial conditions (data for 4 patients on nasal oxygen had to be imputed). The trial does not show fewer whole-lung lavages, and intermittent dosing — the regimen many patients would prefer — was weaker.
cards.source: Trapnell BC et al. IMPALA: Inhaled Molgramostim Therapy in Autoimmune Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2020. PMID: 32897035. Registry ID: NCT02702180. cards.headline: IMPALA-2 (Trapnell 2025): DLCO rose 9.8 vs 3.8 percentage points at week 24 (difference 6.0, P<0.001) in 164 patients
cards.summary: IMPALA-2 (Trapnell 2025): DLCO rose 9.8 vs 3.8 percentage points at week 24 (difference 6.0, P<0.001) in 164 patients
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase 3 — IMPALA-2 (Trapnell 2025)
cards.people: 164 patients with autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (N = 164, printed plainly — large for this rare disease, small in absolute terms) randomised to inhaled molgramostim 300 micrograms once daily (n=81) or placebo (n=83) for 48 weeks.
cards.result: Primary endpoint — change in DLCO (% predicted, haemoglobin-adjusted) at week 24: +9.8 percentage points with molgramostim vs +3.8 with placebo (estimated difference 6.0 points, 95% CI 2.5 to 9.4, P<0.001). At week 48 the difference persisted (+11.6 vs +4.7 points, P<0.001). SGRQ total score improved more at week 24 (−11.5 vs −4.9 points, P=0.007); the SGRQ activity score did not differ significantly, so later secondary endpoints carry no statistical inference. Adverse and serious adverse event percentages were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: DLCO is a physiological surrogate: patients' placebo-group DLCO also rose 3.8 points, and the trial was not designed to show lavage avoided or lives saved. Whole-lung lavage remains the practical standard treatment; it was not the comparator in this trial.
cards.source: Trapnell BC et al. IMPALA-2: Phase 3 Trial of Inhaled Molgramostim in Autoimmune Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2025. PMID: 40834301. cards.headline: Meta-analysis 2026: pooling 4 inhaled GM-CSF RCTs (402 patients), DLCO improved by 5.09 percentage points and the A-a gradient fell by 4.25 mm Hg
cards.summary: Meta-analysis 2026: pooling 4 inhaled GM-CSF RCTs (402 patients), DLCO improved by 5.09 percentage points and the A-a gradient fell by 4.25 mm Hg
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 4 RCTs (2026)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 4 randomised trials of inhaled GM-CSF (the molgramostim programme and other inhaled GM-CSF trials) in autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, 402 patients (224 inhaled GM-CSF, 178 control) with at least 25 weeks of follow-up.
cards.result: Inhaled GM-CSF improved DLCO % predicted (mean difference 5.09, 95% CI 2.05 to 8.13, p=0.001, I2=0%) and reduced the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient (mean difference −4.25 mm Hg, 95% CI −6.62 to −1.88, p=0.0004, I2=0%), with corresponding rises in arterial oxygen; dyspnea scores improved (standardised mean difference −0.49).
cards.watchOut: The pool mixes GM-CSF formulations and is dominated by the same sponsor programme as the two trial cards — it summarises the evidence rather than adding an independent replication. All pooled endpoints remain physiological surrogates.
cards.source: Efficacy and Safety of Inhaled GM-CSF in Autoimmune Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Lung. 2026. PMID: 42045620.
