shelves.title: PROMIS colistin trials in bronchiectasis: PROMIS-I cut exacerbations (rate ratio 0.61), PROMIS-II found nothing (rate ratio 1.00) — a split programme
shelves.question: In adults with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, does inhaled colistin (colistimethate sodium), compared with placebo, reduce exacerbations?
shelves.balance: Standalone pack cross-pointed to home pack #2784 (inhaled antibiotics in bronchiectasis), which cards the RESPIRE ciprofloxacin trials and the Laska meta-analysis; the PROMIS colistin programme is not carded there, and the Haworth 2014 colistin trial named in #2784's prose is homed there and deliberately NOT re-carded here. PREMISE CORRECTION: the slate described the PROMIS product as a dry-powder inhalation; the publication itself reports colistimethate sodium delivered via the I-neb nebuliser system (Zambon) — the face follows the publication. The two phase 3 trials disagree: PROMIS-I (n=377) found an annual exacerbation rate of 0.58 vs 0.95 (rate ratio 0.61, a 39% relative reduction) (PMID 39270696); PROMIS-II (n=287), terminated prematurely because of the COVID-19 pandemic, found 0.89 vs 0.89 (rate ratio 1.00). An earlier class-level systematic review found inhaled antibiotics reduced exacerbation risk (risk ratio 0.72, relative) at the cost of more bronchospasm (PMID 24925920). PROPOSED SPLIT: one positive and one null phase 3 trial of the same product — placement (sibling shelf vs added cards under #2784's question) is the developer's ruling at serve time.

cards.headline: PROMIS-I: inhaled colistimethate sodium cut the annual exacerbation rate to 0.58 vs 0.95 (rate ratio 0.61)
cards.summary: PROMIS-I: inhaled colistimethate sodium cut the annual exacerbation rate to 0.58 vs 0.95 (rate ratio 0.61)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase 3 — PROMIS-I (Haworth 2024)
cards.people: 377 patients with bronchiectasis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection and at least two exacerbations requiring oral antibiotics (or one requiring intravenous antibiotics) in the previous year, randomised to twice-daily inhaled colistimethate sodium via the I-neb system (n=177) or placebo (n=200) for 12 months, across 17 countries. Explicitly labelled: PROMIS-I is trial 1 of 2 reported in this single publication (PMID 39270696).
cards.result: Annual exacerbation rate 0.58 on colistimethate sodium vs 0.95 on placebo (rate ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.46–0.82, p=0.0010 — a 39% relative reduction). Adverse events occurred in 81% of patients in both groups; no deaths were related to study treatment and no major safety issues were identified.
cards.watchOut: The tested delivery is nebulised colistimethate sodium via the I-neb adaptive aerosol system (Zambon), not a dry powder — results should not be transferred to other colistin formulations or devices without thought. The twin trial (next card) did not replicate this result.

cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase 3 — PROMIS-II (Haworth 2024)
cards.people: 287 patients with bronchiectasis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, same eligibility as PROMIS-I, randomised to twice-daily inhaled colistimethate sodium via I-neb (n=152) or placebo (n=135) for 12 months. Explicitly labelled: PROMIS-II is trial 2 of 2 reported in the same publication as PROMIS-I (PMID 39270696) — a distinct randomised trial, not a second report of PROMIS-I.
cards.result: No significant difference in the annual exacerbation rate: 0.89 vs 0.89 (rate ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.75–1.35, p=0.98). The trial was prematurely terminated because of the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic. Adverse events occurred in 81% (colistimethate) vs 77% (placebo); no deaths were related to study treatment.
cards.watchOut: Early termination and pandemic-era exacerbation patterns (fewer circulating respiratory viruses, disrupted follow-up) are real explanations for a null result — but they are explanations offered after the fact. A stopped, null twin trial halves the confidence PROMIS-I alone would justify, which is why this pack's stamp is SPLIT.
cards.source: Haworth CS et al. PROMIS-II (trial 2 of 2 in this publication): Inhaled colistimethate sodium in patients with bronchiectasis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection: results of PROMIS-I and PROMIS-II. The Lancet Respiratory Medicine. 2024. PMID: 39270696. Registry ID: EudraCT 2016-004558-13. cards.headline: Brodt 2014 systematic review: inhaled antibiotics as a class cut exacerbation risk (risk ratio 0.72, relative) — and tripled bronchospasm
cards.summary: Brodt 2014 systematic review: inhaled antibiotics as a class cut exacerbation risk (risk ratio 0.72, relative) — and tripled bronchospasm
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Brodt 2014)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials (1,264 adults) of inhaled antibiotics in stable non-CF bronchiectasis, 8 trials (590 patients) contributing to the meta-analysis; drugs included amikacin, aztreonam, ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, colistin and tobramycin, given for 4 weeks to 12 months. This review predates PROMIS and does not include it.
cards.result: Inhaled antibiotics reduced sputum bacterial load (weighted mean difference −2.65 log10 CFU/g), increased bacterial eradication (risk ratio 4.2, 95% CI 1.66–10.64) and reduced the risk of acute exacerbations (risk ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.55–0.94 — a 28% relative reduction). Bronchospasm occurred in 10% on inhaled antibiotics vs 2.3% on control (risk ratio 2.96, 95% CI 1.30–6.73); withdrawal rates for adverse events were the same (12.2%).
cards.watchOut: Class-level pooling across six different antibiotics, five of the 12 trials unpublished, and the colistin-specific trials inside it are the older nebulised studies — not the PROMIS I-neb programme. It supports biological plausibility for inhaled suppression, not the PROMIS result itself. The later Laska 2019 meta-analysis is carded at home pack #2784 and is not repeated here.
cards.source: Brodt AM et al. Inhaled antibiotics for stable non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis: a systematic review. The European Respiratory Journal. 2014. PMID: 24925920. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — PROMIS-I says inhaled colistimethate sodium prevents exacerbations; its twin, stopped early in the pandemic, says it does not
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — PROMIS-I says inhaled colistimethate sodium prevents exacerbations; its twin, stopped early in the pandemic, says it does not
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: PROMIS-I (377 patients) and PROMIS-II (287 patients), two phase 3 trials reported in one publication, plus a pre-PROMIS class-level systematic review (12 trials, 1,264 patients).
cards.result: PROMIS-I: annual exacerbation rate ratio 0.61 (0.58 vs 0.95). PROMIS-II: rate ratio 1.00 (0.89 vs 0.89), trial terminated early for COVID-19. Class-level data (pre-PROMIS) favour inhaled antibiotics for exacerbation risk (risk ratio 0.72, relative) with more bronchospasm (10% vs 2.3%). PROPOSED SPLIT. Cross-point: home pack #2784 cards RESPIRE ciprofloxacin and the Laska 2019 meta-analysis under the broader inhaled-antibiotics question; the Haworth 2014 colistin trial is homed in #2784's prose and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: One PMID (39270696) appears on two cards because the journal published both phase 3 trials in a single paper; the cards are explicitly labelled as two distinct trials (PROMIS-I and PROMIS-II), not two reports of one trial. Flagged for the coordinator as a schema-rule judgement call. Product correction vs the slate: I-neb nebulised colistimethate sodium (Zambon), not dry powder.
cards.source: Synthesis of Haworth CS et al. The Lancet Respiratory Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 39270696, PROMIS-I and PROMIS-II); Brodt AM et al. The European Respiratory Journal. 2014 (PMID: 24925920).

shelves.title: Ralinepag in PAH: phase 2 cut PVR; the ADVANCE OUTCOMES phase 3 (2026) cut first clinical worsening (hazard ratio 0.45, relative) — one programme, with 19% stopping for adverse events
shelves.question: In adults with pulmonary arterial hypertension, does oral ralinepag, compared with placebo on background therapy, improve exercise capacity and haemodynamics?
shelves.balance: PREMISE CORRECTION at build: the slate was mined as PHASE-2 ONLY, but re-checking at build found the phase 3 ADVANCE OUTCOMES trial published in The Lancet in 2026 — it is carded here, and the pack is built on phase 2 + phase 3, not phase 2 alone. Phase 2 (n=61): ralinepag reduced pulmonary vascular resistance vs placebo (least-squares mean −29.8% relative, p=0.03) with no significant walk-distance difference (PMID 31391223). Its open-label extension (45 patients) showed durable PVR reduction and +36.3 m walk distance at 24 months, uncontrolled (PMID 38198043). ADVANCE OUTCOMES (687 patients analysed): first clinical worsening in 18% on ralinepag vs 36% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.45 — a 55% relative reduction) (PMID 42520828). The cost: 19% discontinued ralinepag for adverse events vs 3% on placebo, and 41 randomised patients from sites in China were excluded from the analysis sets for data-integrity concerns — both printed on the face. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single sponsor programme (United Therapeutics) with one phase 3 — positive, but the stamp must not imply an established, broadly replicated therapy.

cards.headline: Phase 2 (Torres 2019): ralinepag cut PVR by 163.9 dyn·s·cm−5 vs a 0.7 rise on placebo (p=0.02); walk distance did not differ
cards.summary: Phase 2 (Torres 2019): ralinepag cut PVR by 163.9 dyn·s·cm−5 vs a 0.7 rise on placebo (p=0.02); walk distance did not differ
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase 2 (Torres 2019)
cards.people: 61 adults with symptomatic pulmonary arterial hypertension on mono or dual background therapy, randomised 2:1 to immediate-release ralinepag (n=40, titrated over 9 weeks to a maximum 300 micrograms twice daily) or placebo (n=21) for 22 weeks.
cards.result: Primary endpoint — absolute change in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) at week 22: −163.9 dyn·s·cm−5 on ralinepag vs +0.7 on placebo (p=0.02); least-squares mean percentage change in PVR was −29.8% relative to placebo (p=0.03). Six-minute walk distance rose 36.2 m vs 29.4 m (p=0.90 — no significant difference). Serious adverse events occurred in 10% on ralinepag vs 29% on placebo; discontinuations 13% vs 10%.
cards.watchOut: PVR is a haemodynamic surrogate and the trial's functional endpoint (walk distance) was null. Note for the record: a separate PubMed entry (PMID 38636973) is only a published erratum to this paper and is not carded. The phase 2 formulation was twice-daily immediate-release; the phase 3 used a once-daily formulation.
cards.source: Torres F et al. Efficacy and safety of ralinepag, a novel oral IP agonist, in PAH patients on mono or dual background therapy: results from a phase 2 randomised, parallel group, placebo-controlled trial. The European Respiratory Journal. 2019. PMID: 31391223. Registry ID: NCT02279160. cards.headline: Phase 2 open-label extension (Barberà 2024): at 24 months walk distance was up 36.3 m and PVR stayed down — in the 45 of 61 patients who continued
cards.summary: Phase 2 open-label extension (Barberà 2024): at 24 months walk distance was up 36.3 m and PVR stayed down — in the 45 of 61 patients who continued
cards.type: Open-label extension — phase 2 programme (Barberà 2024)
cards.people: 45 of the 61 phase 2 participants (30 previously on ralinepag, 15 previously on placebo) enrolled in the open-label extension, all receiving ralinepag, later transitioned to an extended-release formulation. Explicitly labelled: extension report of the phase 2 programme (PMID 31391223), not an independent trial.
cards.result: Most common adverse events were prostacyclin-class effects: headache 64.4%, diarrhoea 37.8%, jaw pain 33.3%, declining after a stable dose was reached. At month 24, 6-minute walk distance had increased by a mean of 36.3 m from extension baseline (P=0.004); 84.8% remained stable in functional class. Post-baseline PVR at 1 or 2 years had fallen by a median of 52.2 dyn·s/cm5 and median pulmonary artery pressure by 2.0 mmHg (P=0.05).
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled and survivor-selected: the 45 who continued are those who tolerated and stayed on the drug. Durability in continuers is not evidence of efficacy — the randomised phase 3 (next card) is.
cards.source: Barberà J et al. Ralinepag Phase II Open-Label Extension Study in Patients with Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension. Advances in Therapy. 2024. PMID: 38198043. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ADVANCE OUTCOMES (McLaughlin 2026): first clinical worsening 18% vs 36% (hazard ratio 0.45, relative) — but 19% stopped ralinepag for adverse events vs 3%
cards.summary: ADVANCE OUTCOMES (McLaughlin 2026): first clinical worsening 18% vs 36% (hazard ratio 0.45, relative) — but 19% stopped ralinepag for adverse events vs 3%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase 3 — ADVANCE OUTCOMES (McLaughlin 2026)
cards.people: 687 patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension in the full analysis and safety sets (350 ralinepag, 337 placebo), on contemporary background therapy (80% on dual therapy); ralinepag started at 50 micrograms once daily and titrated weekly to the highest tolerated dose. 728 patients were randomised and dosed; 41 treated patients from sites in China were excluded from the analysis sets because of regulatory challenges and data integrity concerns — stated here as the paper states it.
cards.result: Primary outcome — time to first clinical worsening (death, hospitalisation for worsening PAH or right heart failure, starting parenteral or inhaled prostacyclin-pathway therapy, disease progression, or unsatisfactory long-term response): 64 of 350 (18%) on ralinepag vs 121 of 337 (36%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.33–0.62, p<0.0001 — a 55% relative reduction). The largest component differences were disease progression, prostacyclin initiation and unsatisfactory response. Adverse events were the primary reason for discontinuation in 19% on ralinepag vs 3% on placebo; serious adverse events 28% vs 31%; adverse events leading to death 4% in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The composite leans on softer components (disease progression, unsatisfactory long-term response, starting another prostacyclin) rather than death, and the exclusion of 41 randomised patients for data-integrity concerns is unusual and belongs in any reading of the result. One in five patients could not stay on the drug because of adverse events.
cards.source: McLaughlin VV et al. Ralinepag for the treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension (ADVANCE OUTCOMES): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 study. The Lancet. 2026. PMID: 42520828. Registry ID: NCT03626688. cards.headline: Synthesis: one programme, now with a positive phase 3 — ralinepag delays clinical worsening, at a high intolerance cost
cards.summary: Synthesis: one programme, now with a positive phase 3 — ralinepag delays clinical worsening, at a high intolerance cost
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Phase 2 RCT (61 patients), its open-label extension (45 patients), and the ADVANCE OUTCOMES phase 3 (687 patients analysed).
cards.result: Haemodynamics: PVR −29.8% relative vs placebo in phase 2. Clinical worsening in phase 3: 18% vs 36% (hazard ratio 0.45, relative). Tolerability: prostacyclin-class adverse events in most patients and 19% vs 3% adverse-event discontinuation in phase 3. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): single-programme evidence caps the stamp; the phase 3 result postdates the slate's phase-2-only premise and is flagged as a premise correction.
cards.watchOut: Do not read this shelf as 'an established PAH therapy': at build there is one sponsor programme, one phase 3 trial, and no independent replication or long-term mortality data. Regulatory status is not asserted anywhere on this pack — the cards report trial results only.

shelves.title: Anaesthesia-induced atelectasis: within 5 minutes of induction, dependent lung collapses in nearly everyone — and the size of the collapse tracks the shunt (r = 0.93–0.99)
shelves.question: In patients under general anaesthesia, what is the physiological basis, extent and time course of anaesthesia-induced atelectasis and the resulting shunt?
shelves.balance: Framing (textbook account, Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology — respiratory mechanics and ventilation-perfusion matching, cited as framing, not as evidence cards): induction of general anaesthesia drops functional residual capacity, the dependent lung is compressed, and collapsed but perfused alveoli create shunt. The Uppsala human CT programme measured every element of that account. The densities appear within 5 minutes of induction in all 20 patients studied, occupy about 4.8% of the transverse lung area in the most caudal slice, and do not grow over the next 20 minutes (PMID 3885791). Their extent correlates with shunt at r=0.93 and with impaired arterial oxygenation at r=0.99 (PMID 3085429); shunt after 15 minutes of anaesthesia ranged from 1% to 17% of cardiac output (PMID 3813078). Pooled CT data in 243 subjects found atelectasis in 90% of anaesthetised patients, larger with 100% inspired oxygen than with 30–50% (12.8 vs 8.1 cm2) (PMID 31918847). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: a single research group's classic programme, replicated internally across four decades of human studies and concordant with the textbook account; no animal study is carded (animal work appears nowhere in this pack's evidence).

cards.headline: Brismar 1985: within 5 minutes of induction, every one of 20 patients developed dependent lung densities — 4.8% of the caudal lung area — and PEEP abolished them
cards.summary: Brismar 1985: within 5 minutes of induction, every one of 20 patients developed dependent lung densities — 4.8% of the caudal lung area — and PEEP abolished them
cards.type: Primary human study — CT before/after induction (Brismar 1985)
cards.people: 20 patients (aged 23–76) studied by computed tomography before and after induction of general anaesthesia with muscular relaxation, plus 4 subjects studied awake over a longer period (N = 20 anaesthetised, printed plainly — a classic small physiology study).
cards.result: No lung-tissue abnormality was present before anaesthesia. Within 5 minutes of induction, all subjects developed crest-shaped densities of increased density in the dependent regions of both lungs: largest in the most caudal segment (4.8 ± 0.8% of the transverse lung area, mean ± SE), smaller cephalad (3.4 ± 0.7%). The densities did not increase over a further 20 minutes and were not affected by inspired oxygen fraction. Moving to the lateral position cleared them from the non-dependent lung; PEEP of 10 cmH2O eliminated or reduced them. The 4 awake subjects showed no densities after 90 minutes supine. The authors proposed these densities are atelectasis formed by compression of lung tissue rather than by gas resorption.
cards.watchOut: N = 20, and the identification of the densities as atelectasis was, in 1985, a proposal — the title says so. The two following cards are the same programme's tests of that proposal against gas exchange. Compression vs absorption as the mechanism is revisited by the 2020 pooled data (card 4): high inspired oxygen enlarged the atelectasis, which pure compression would not predict.
cards.source: Brismar B et al. Pulmonary densities during anesthesia with muscular relaxation — a proposal of atelectasis. Anesthesiology. 1985. PMID: 3885791. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hedenstierna 1986: the bigger the atelectasis, the bigger the shunt — correlation r = 0.93 with shunt and r = 0.99 with oxygenation impairment (n=8)
cards.summary: Hedenstierna 1986: the bigger the atelectasis, the bigger the shunt — correlation r = 0.93 with shunt and r = 0.99 with oxygenation impairment (n=8)
cards.type: Primary human study — CT plus inert-gas elimination (Hedenstierna 1986)
cards.people: 8 essentially lung-healthy patients (N = 8, printed plainly — sub-10 N labelled per the physiology floor rule) studied awake and during halothane anaesthesia with mechanical ventilation; gas exchange by multiple inert gas elimination and blood gases, atelectasis by CT.
cards.result: Awake, ventilation and perfusion were well matched in most patients and no patient had CT signs of atelectasis. After 15 minutes of anaesthesia, shunt had appeared in all patients, ranging from 1% (unchanged from awake, in two patients) to 17% of cardiac output; the major ventilation-perfusion mode widened. Dependent densities (interpreted as atelectasis) appeared in 6 of 8 patients, and their extent correlated significantly with shunt magnitude (r=0.93, P<0.01) and with impairment of arterial oxygenation (r=0.99, P<0.001). The authors concluded atelectasis is the major or sole cause of impaired gas exchange in the lung-healthy anaesthetised subject.
cards.watchOut: N = 8: correlations of 0.93–0.99 in 8 subjects are striking but rest on few points, and correlation inside one programme's measurements is not independent proof of causation. Halothane-era anaesthesia; the direction of the physiology, not the exact shunt range, is what later work confirms.
cards.source: Hedenstierna G et al. Correlation of gas exchange impairment to development of atelectasis during anaesthesia and muscle paralysis. Acta Anaesthesiologica Scandinavica. 1986. PMID: 3085429. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tokics 1987: densities in 11 of 13 patients and shunt in all after 15 minutes — present even with spontaneous breathing, worse after paralysis
cards.summary: Tokics 1987: densities in 11 of 13 patients and shunt in all after 15 minutes — present even with spontaneous breathing, worse after paralysis
cards.type: Primary human study — breathing mode and paralysis (Tokics 1987)
cards.people: 13 supine patients with no apparent lung disease (N = 13), studied awake and during halothane anaesthesia by CT and multiple inert gas elimination; 5 were also studied during spontaneous breathing under anaesthesia before muscle paralysis.
cards.result: Awake, no patient had clear CT atelectasis. After 15 minutes of anaesthesia with mechanical ventilation, 11 of 13 had dependent densities and all had a shunt (1% to 17% of cardiac output); shunt magnitude correlated with density size (r=0.84, P<0.001). During spontaneous breathing under anaesthesia, densities and shunt were both present but small (1.8% and 3.7% respectively, as reported); both increased after muscle paralysis. PEEP reduced the density area in all patients but did not consistently reduce the shunt.
cards.watchOut: The PEEP dissociation — less atelectasis on CT without a consistent fall in shunt — is a standing caution against treating the CT picture and the gas-exchange defect as interchangeable measures. N = 13, single programme.
cards.source: Tokics L et al. Lung collapse and gas exchange during general anesthesia: effects of spontaneous breathing, muscle paralysis, and positive end-expiratory pressure. Anesthesiology. 1987. PMID: 3813078. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hedenstierna 2020: pooled CT data in 243 subjects — atelectasis in 90% under anaesthesia, larger on 100% oxygen (12.8 vs 8.1 cm2)
cards.summary: Hedenstierna 2020: pooled CT data in 243 subjects — atelectasis in 90% under anaesthesia, larger on 100% oxygen (12.8 vs 8.1 cm2)
cards.type: Primary human study — pooled CT analysis, 243 subjects (Hedenstierna 2020)
cards.people: Pooled primary analysis of previously published CT studies: 243 subjects aged 18–78, BMI 18–52 kg/m2, without clinical cardiopulmonary disease, scanned awake and during anaesthesia before surgery after preoxygenation with inspired oxygen fraction above 0.8, then ventilated with FIO2 0.3 or higher and no PEEP.
cards.result: Atelectasis of up to 39 cm2 in a transverse scan near the diaphragm was seen in 90% of subjects during anaesthesia. Atelectasis area rose with age to about 50 years and fell beyond it, and rose with BMI up to 30 kg/m2 with no further increase in obesity — greater age and obesity limited, rather than increased, atelectasis formation. Subjects receiving FIO2 1.0 had more atelectasis than those on FIO2 0.3–0.5 (12.8 vs 8.1 cm2, P<0.001), supporting an absorption component alongside compression. Arterial oxygen fell with both age and BMI.
cards.watchOut: A pooled re-analysis of the same research programme's earlier studies (publication type includes meta-analysis) — it extends the classic findings to age, BMI and oxygen fraction but is not an independent group's replication. Ventilation here used no PEEP, so areas are larger than in modern PEEP-managed practice.
cards.source: Hedenstierna G et al. Higher age and obesity limit atelectasis formation during anaesthesia: an analysis of computed tomography data in 243 subjects. British Journal of Anaesthesia. 2020. PMID: 31918847. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: anaesthesia collapses dependent lung within minutes in almost everyone, and the collapse — not a primary perfusion change — accounts for the shunt
cards.summary: Synthesis: anaesthesia collapses dependent lung within minutes in almost everyone, and the collapse — not a primary perfusion change — accounts for the shunt
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Four primary human CT/gas-exchange studies from the Uppsala programme: 20 patients (1985), 8 patients (1986), 13 patients (1987), and a pooled 243 subjects (2020).
cards.result: Time course: densities appear within 5 minutes of induction and do not grow over the next 20 minutes. Extent: about 3–5% of transverse lung area on single slices, up to 39 cm2 near the diaphragm in pooled data, present in 90% of anaesthetised subjects. Mechanism: compression of dependent lung (posture-dependent, PEEP-reversible) with an absorption contribution at high inspired oxygen. Consequence: shunt of 1–17% of cardiac output whose size tracks atelectasis extent (r=0.84–0.99 across studies). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Ganong (ventilation-perfusion matching and the effects of anaesthesia on lung volumes) — cited as framing, not as evidence cards. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Single-programme provenance is the honest caveat: one research group generated nearly all the primary human data, using halothane-era techniques in the classic studies. The findings are textbook-settled and internally replicated over 35 years, which is why the stamp is ESTABLISHED — but independent-group CT replication is thin, and modern anaesthetic practice (PEEP, recruitment, lower FIO2) modifies the magnitudes.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brismar B et al. Anesthesiology. 1985 (PMID: 3885791); Hedenstierna G et al. Acta Anaesthesiologica Scandinavica. 1986 (PMID: 3085429); Tokics L et al. Anesthesiology. 1987 (PMID: 3813078); Hedenstierna G et al. British Journal of Anaesthesia. 2020 (PMID: 31918847).

shelves.title: PHYSIOLOGY — Homeostatic sleep pressure (Process S): NREM slow-wave activity rises with prior wakefulness, rebounds after deprivation, and declines exponentially across sleep
shelves.question: In healthy humans, does NREM EEG slow-wave activity behave as a homeostatic marker of sleep need — rising with duration of prior wakefulness, rebounding after sleep deprivation, and declining exponentially across sleep?
shelves.balance: Framing (textbook account, named as such): the two-process model — presented in Kryger's Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine and in the standard physiology texts (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) as framing, not as an evidence card — holds that sleep timing and depth are governed by a homeostatic Process S, which builds during wakefulness and dissipates during sleep, interacting with a circadian Process C. What the human studies carded here directly show is the EEG behaviour: slow-wave activity (SWA; spectral power 0.75–4.5 Hz in NREM sleep) is enhanced after prolonged wakefulness, increases by roughly 20% after partial sleep restriction and falls immediately after recovery sleep, declines monotonically and exponentially across successive NREM–REM cycles, and can be quantitatively simulated from prior wake/sleep history alone (Achermann's model fit). Forced desynchrony separates the two processes: SWA's circadian modulation is low-amplitude and does not parallel the circadian rhythm of sleep propensity, which is dominated by Process C — the circadian half of the model is homed separately at pack #6250, and closed-loop acoustic stimulation exploiting SWA physiology is pack #6601; both are cross-pointed, neither is carded here. What human data do NOT establish is what S is made of: adenosine is the best-characterised candidate substrate signal (caffeine's antagonism of adenosine receptors is the everyday pharmacological probe), but equating Process S with adenosine outright goes beyond the human evidence, and this entry does not do so.

cards.headline: Dijk & Czeisler 1995 (forced desynchrony, N = 8): slow-wave activity declined across every sleep episode and showed only low-amplitude circadian modulation
cards.summary: Dijk & Czeisler 1995 (forced desynchrony, N = 8): slow-wave activity declined across every sleep episode and showed only low-amplitude circadian modulation
cards.type: Primary human forced-desynchrony physiology study, Journal of Neuroscience 1995
cards.people: 8 healthy men (N = 8, printed on the face) lived 33–36 days in a time-cue-free environment on a 28-hour rest–activity cycle, so sleep episodes (9.33 hours each) occurred at all circadian phases with preceding wakefulness held near-constant — separating homeostatic from circadian contributions.
cards.result: Slow-wave activity (0.75–4.5 Hz) decreased in the course of all sleep episodes, regardless of circadian phase. Its circadian modulation was low-amplitude and did not parallel the circadian rhythm of sleep propensity; by contrast, REM sleep and sleep-spindle activity showed marked circadian rhythms (spindle crest at the beginning of the habitual sleep episode), and sleep propensity reflected a nonadditive interaction of the circadian and sleep-dependent components.
cards.watchOut: Classic small-N physiology (N = 8, all men): the claim rests on convergence across the carded studies and decades of replication, not on this sample size alone. Sub-10 N labelled plainly per the physiology rule.
cards.source: Dijk DJ, Czeisler CA. Contribution of the circadian pacemaker and the sleep homeostat to sleep propensity, sleep structure, electroencephalographic slow waves, and sleep spindle activity in humans. J Neurosci. 1995. PMID 7751928. cards.headline: Dijk, Brunner & Borbély 1990 (N = 9): after 36 hours awake, SWA was significantly enhanced in the first two NREM–REM cycles, then declined exponentially
cards.summary: Dijk, Brunner & Borbély 1990 (N = 9): after 36 hours awake, SWA was significantly enhanced in the first two NREM–REM cycles, then declined exponentially
cards.type: Primary human sleep-deprivation physiology study, American Journal of Physiology 1990
cards.people: 9 healthy subjects (N = 9, printed on the face) recorded at baseline (habitual bedtime after 16 hours awake) and during recovery sleep with a phase-advanced bedtime after 36 hours of wakefulness, with recovery sleep lasting more than 12 hours in all subjects.
cards.result: SWA in NREM sleep was significantly enhanced during the first two NREM–REM cycles of recovery sleep after 36 hours awake. Slow-wave sleep and SWA decreased monotonically over the first three (baseline) and four (recovery) cycles, and the time course in both conditions was adequately described by an exponentially declining function with a horizontal asymptote — as the two-process model predicts if SWA rises with prior wakefulness and falls exponentially with sleep.
cards.watchOut: N = 9, printed on the face. A within-subject laboratory study: the exponential decline is a description of EEG power, and the inference that it indexes a homeostatic 'need' is the model's interpretation, supported by the deprivation contrast in this same study.
cards.source: Dijk DJ, Brunner DP, Borbély AA. Time course of EEG power density during long sleep in humans. Am J Physiol. 1990. PMID 2316712. MeSH: Adult; Analysis of Variance; Computer Simulation; Electroencephalography; Humans; Male; Models, Biological; Sleep/physiology; Sleep Stages/physiology; Time Factors

cards.headline: Brunner, Dijk & Borbély 1993 (N = 9): four nights of 4-hour sleep raised SWA by ~20%, which fell immediately after the first recovery night
cards.summary: Brunner, Dijk & Borbély 1993 (N = 9): four nights of 4-hour sleep raised SWA by ~20%, which fell immediately after the first recovery night
cards.type: Primary human repeated partial sleep-deprivation study, Sleep 1993
cards.people: 9 healthy young subjects (N = 9, printed on the face): three baseline nights of 8 hours, four nights restricted to 4 hours of sleep (2300–0300), then three recovery nights of 8 hours, with EEG power spectra measured in sleep and wakefulness.
cards.result: Sleep restriction curtailed stages 1–2 and REM sleep but left slow-wave sleep largely unaffected. In accordance with the two-process model, SWA in NREM sleep increased by approximately 20% in the first night after restriction began, stayed at that level through the restriction nights, and decreased immediately after the first recovery night — the signature of a homeostat that accumulates with sleep loss and discharges with sleep. Higher-frequency EEG changes followed a different, progressive time course paralleling the cumulative REM deficit.
cards.watchOut: N = 9, printed on the face. Partial (not total) deprivation: the ~20% SWA rise is the response to a 4-hour nightly restriction, and should not be quoted as the response to total deprivation.

cards.headline: Achermann 1993: a quantitative Process S model fit baseline SWA (16 subjects, 26 nights) and predicted SWA under three other protocols (n = 8–9 each)
cards.summary: Achermann 1993: a quantitative Process S model fit baseline SWA (16 subjects, 26 nights) and predicted SWA under three other protocols (n = 8–9 each)
cards.type: Quantitative model fit to primary human EEG data, Brain Research Bulletin 1993
cards.people: Model parameters were estimated against empirical SWA from baseline nights of 16 subjects (26 nights), then tested by simulating three independent experimental protocols — evening sleep, morning sleep after prolonged waking, and extended sleep from habitual bedtime — with n = 8 or 9 subjects each.
cards.result: A close fit was obtained between simulated and empirical SWA in all three protocols, including occasional late SWA peaks during extended sleep; minor discrepancies suggested indirect or direct circadian influences on SWA. The authors conclude the two-process homeostasis concept can be refined to account quantitatively for the data and to predict changes induced by prolonging waking or sleep.
cards.watchOut: A modelling paper built on the small human datasets carded above — its strength is predictive fit across protocols, not a large new sample. Values no carded record confirms are presented in this pack's balance explicitly as the textbook's account, per the physiology rule.

cards.summary: Synthesis: SWA behaves as the homeostat's readout in humans — ESTABLISHED for the EEG behaviour, unsettled for the molecule

cards.result: Across protocols, human NREM slow-wave activity rises with the duration of prior wakefulness, rebounds after deprivation, and declines exponentially across sleep, and a single homeostatic variable quantitatively predicts those changes — the defining behaviour of Process S. shelves.title: The daily melatonin rhythm as a circadian phase marker: DLMO timing, reliability, and suppression by evening light
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what does the daily melatonin rhythm look like as a circadian phase marker — dim-light melatonin onset timing relative to sleep, peak amplitude, and suppression by evening light — measured under controlled dim-light protocols?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Ganong and Boron & Boulpaep (textbook framing, not evidence). Home pack #6250 measures the clock's endogenous period (24.18 h) under forced desynchrony — verified by reading its file: it cards Czeisler 1999, Dijk & Duffy 1999, Wright 2005 and Scheer 2007 (PMIDs 10381883, 10087357, 15834113, 17684566), none of which is carded here, and it does not card DLMO timing, reliability or light-suppression figures. This pack cards that uncovered slice: melatonin is light-suppressible in humans (Lewy, PMID 7434030, N = 6); its phase markers are more stable than the temperature nadir and track sleep offset best (Benloucif, PMID 15834114, N = 42); the calculated DLMO moves ~22–24 minutes with threshold choice (Molina & Burgess, PMID 21823817, N = 122); and ordinary room light before bedtime delays onset in 99% and shortens duration by ~90 minutes (Gooley, PMID 21193540, N = 116).

cards.headline: Lewy 1980: bright light acutely suppresses nocturnal melatonin in humans — ordinary room light did not (N = 6)
cards.summary: Lewy 1980: bright light acutely suppresses nocturnal melatonin in humans — ordinary room light did not (N = 6)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study
cards.people: Six normal human subjects whose nocturnal melatonin secretion was measured under bright artificial light and under room light of lesser intensity. N = 6, printed on the face.
cards.result: Bright artificial light suppressed nocturnal secretion of melatonin in all six subjects. Room light of less intensity — sufficient to suppress melatonin in other mammals — failed to do so in humans. The record establishes the founding fact of the phase-marker literature: human melatonin is light-suppressible, but only above a higher intensity threshold than in other mammals, which is why phase must be measured under dim light.
cards.watchOut: Very small classic study (N = 6) with acute night-time exposures; the room-light null is a short-exposure result — compare the Gooley card, where 8 hours of room light before bedtime did suppress onset. Intensity and duration both matter.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Lewy AJ et al. Light suppresses melatonin secretion in humans. Science. 1980. PMID: 7434030. Registry ID: none in the record (physiology study). cards.headline: Benloucif 2005: in 42 healthy adults on regular schedules, melatonin phase markers were more stable than the temperature nadir — and melatonin offset tracked sleep best
cards.summary: Benloucif 2005: in 42 healthy adults on regular schedules, melatonin phase markers were more stable than the temperature nadir — and melatonin offset tracked sleep best
cards.type: Primary human physiology study
cards.people: 42 healthy young subjects studied on at least two hospital admissions separated by at least 3 weeks, after a week of monitored regular sleep at home, with melatonin phase estimated by 9 methods and temperature nadir by curve-fitting procedures.
cards.result: Melatonin phase markers were more stable across admissions and more highly correlated with sleep timing than estimates of the temperature minimum. Of the temperature methods, simple cosine analysis was least variable. Sleep offset was more strongly correlated with the phase markers than sleep onset, and the relative measures of melatonin offset had the highest correlations, the lowest study-to-study variability, and the strongest association with sleep timing — the declining phase of the melatonin profile was the most stable and reliable phase reference in this dataset. This is the reliability evidence for using dim-light melatonin onset/offset as the circadian phase marker in free-living schedules.
cards.watchOut: Measured in people keeping regular schedules in their natural environment, not under forced desynchrony: it validates melatonin as a phase marker for entrained life, and its onset-versus-offset comparison is method-dependent (9 onset/offset definitions were compared).
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Benloucif S et al. Stability of melatonin and temperature as circadian phase markers and their relation to sleep times in humans. J Biol Rhythms. 2005. cards.headline: Molina & Burgess 2011: how a DLMO is calculated moves it by ~25 minutes — hourly sampling is adequate, but the 3 pg/mL and 3k thresholds give systematically different onsets (N = 122)
cards.summary: Molina & Burgess 2011: how a DLMO is calculated moves it by ~25 minutes — hourly sampling is adequate, but the 3 pg/mL and 3k thresholds give systematically different onsets (N = 122)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (methods re-analysis of human DLMO profiles)
cards.people: 122 individuals (64 women) whose salivary dim-light melatonin profiles, collected at baseline, were re-analysed with hourly versus half-hourly sampling and with a fixed 3 pg/mL threshold versus a variable '3k' threshold (mean plus two standard deviations of the first three low daytime points).
cards.result: DLMOs from hourly sampling occurred on average only 6–8 minutes earlier than from half-hourly sampling and correlated at r ≥ 0.89, so hourly sampling is adequate for a reasonable phase estimate — though in up to 19% of cases the hourly DLMO differed from the half-hourly DLMO by more than 30 minutes. The 3k threshold was significantly lower than 3 pg/mL and produced DLMOs 22–24 minutes earlier, while the fixed 3 pg/mL threshold produced significantly less variable DLMOs. A quoted DLMO therefore carries its method with it: threshold choice alone shifts the 'onset' by roughly a quarter of an hour.
cards.watchOut: A re-analysis of collected profiles, not a new physiology experiment: it quantifies measurement error in the marker, and its 19% tail of >30-minute discrepancies is the caution for single-sample clinical timing.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Molina TA, Burgess HJ. Calculating the dim light melatonin onset: the impact of threshold and sampling rate. Chronobiol Int. 2011. PMID: 21823817. cards.headline: Gooley 2011: room light before bedtime delayed melatonin onset in 99% of 116 volunteers and shortened melatonin duration by about 90 minutes
cards.summary: Gooley 2011: room light before bedtime delayed melatonin onset in 99% of 116 volunteers and shortened melatonin duration by about 90 minutes
cards.type: Primary human physiology study
cards.people: 116 healthy volunteers aged 18–30 years who lived in a clinical research centre for at least 5 consecutive days, exposed to room light (<200 lux) or dim light (<3 lux) in the 8 hours preceding bedtime, with daily melatonin profiles (retrospective pooled analysis of two studies).
cards.result: Compared with dim light, room light before bedtime suppressed melatonin, producing a later melatonin onset in 99.0% of individuals and shortening melatonin duration by about 90 minutes. Room light during the usual hours of sleep suppressed melatonin by more than 50% in most (85%) trials. Evening light therefore does not merely shift the phase marker — it truncates the measured rhythm itself, which is why DLMO protocols specify dim light (<3 lux in this programme) for the hours before sampling.
cards.watchOut: Pooled retrospective analysis of two inpatient studies in young adults (18–30 years); the 99% figure is for onset delay under an 8-hour pre-bedtime exposure — not a claim about brief or low-intensity exposures.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Gooley JJ et al. Exposure to room light before bedtime suppresses melatonin onset and shortens melatonin duration in humans. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2011. PMID: 21193540. Registry ID: none in the record (physiology study). cards.headline: Synthesis: The daily melatonin rhythm as a circadian phase marker: DLMO timing, reliability, and suppression by evening light
cards.summary: Synthesis: The daily melatonin rhythm as a circadian phase marker: DLMO timing, reliability, and suppression by evening light
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of Lewy 1980, Benloucif 2005, Molina & Burgess 2011 and Gooley 2011, framed by Ganong Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (textbook framing, not evidence cards). Home pack #6250 (endogenous circadian period under forced desynchrony) is cross-pointed; its four carded PMIDs are deliberately not re-carded here.
cards.result: Under dim light, melatonin rises in the evening, and the dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO) is the standard human circadian phase marker because the rhythm is stable within a person and tightly related to sleep timing — more stable than the core-temperature nadir, with melatonin offset the single most reliable anchor in the Benloucif dataset. Two measurement facts travel with every DLMO: the threshold definition moves it (a fixed 3 pg/mL salivary threshold gives later, less variable onsets than the lower 3k threshold, by ~22–24 minutes), and light destroys the measurement — bright light suppresses secretion acutely (Lewy, N = 6), and even room light (<200 lux) across the evening delays onset in 99% of people and shortens the melatonin episode by ~90 minutes (Gooley, N = 116). The carded records quantify onset, offset, reliability and suppression; no carded record prints a single normative peak-amplitude value, so none is quoted — amplitude is presented in teaching as assay- and matrix-dependent (plasma versus saliva), which is the textbook's account.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: DLMO clock times vary with the population's habitual sleep schedule, so this pack reports timing relative to sleep and method, not a universal clock hour; amplitude norms are not carded because the fetched records do not print them.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID: 7434030; PMID: 15834114; PMID: 21823817; PMID: 21193540. Registry IDs: none in the records (physiology studies).

shelves.title: Cough-reflex calibration (physiology): capsaicin and citric-acid thresholds (C2/C5) are reproducible within a person but vary widely between people — women need 3–5-fold less capsaicin than men, and an ACE inhibitor can shift the threshold within a week
shelves.question: In humans, how is the cough reflex calibrated — what are capsaicin and citric-acid cough thresholds (C2/C5) in healthy volunteers, how reproducible are they, and how do sex, smoking and ACE inhibition shift sensitivity in the challenge studies?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology — respiratory-reflex sections): cough is a vagal airway reflex whose afferent limb runs through capsaicin-sensitive (TRPV1-bearing) sensory nerves, and inhaled tussigen challenge is how its sensitivity is calibrated in humans. The carded primary studies quantify that calibration. Thresholds are defined by the concentration provoking 2 (C2) or 5 (C5) coughs. Between people they span orders of magnitude (C5 from 0.95 to 1000 µM capsaicin in one volunteer series), but within a person the single-breath capsaicin method is reproducible over repeated tests, with a first-test effect that can overestimate sensitivity (Hoffmeyer 2013; N = 16). Sex is the largest ordinary determinant: women had 3–5-fold lower capsaicin thresholds than men at both young and middle age (Fujimura 1996; N = 160), confirmed across three ethnic groups with no ethnic difference once sex was accounted for (Dicpinigaitis 2001; N = 182). Citric-acid thresholds by a portable hand-held method correlate tightly with the hospital dosimeter method (r = 0.95) but read 2–3 times higher — thresholds are method-specific and must be carded per method (Barber 2005; N = 25). One week of the ACE inhibitor ramipril measurably increased cough sensitivity to both capsaicin and citric acid in healthy volunteers, while zofenopril did not on the C2 endpoint (Lavorini 2014; N = 40) — the challenge-study demonstration behind ACE-inhibitor cough. Smoking effects named in the row question were not carded: the fetched smoking literature was preclinical or paediatric, so no smoking number is printed. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Fujimura 1996: capsaicin cough threshold was 3–5-fold lower in women than in men, in both young and middle-aged healthy subjects (N = 160)
cards.summary: Fujimura 1996: capsaicin cough threshold was 3–5-fold lower in women than in men, in both young and middle-aged healthy subjects (N = 160)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (capsaicin cough challenge, sex and age groups)
cards.people: 160 nonsmoking, nonatopic healthy subjects: 40 young men (24 ± 2 years), 40 young women (22 ± 2 years), 40 middle-aged men (48 ± 5 years) and 40 middle-aged women (50 ± 7 years). Cough threshold was the lowest inhaled capsaicin concentration causing five or more coughs (C5).
cards.result: The cough threshold was 3–5 fold lower in females than in males both in the young group (p < 0.001) and in the middle-aged group (p < 0.005). Threshold correlated weakly with height, weight, FVC and FEV1 when all subjects were pooled, but not within any group, and multiple regression identified sex as the significant predictive factor in either age group — the apparent size/lung-function correlations were the sex difference in disguise.
cards.watchOut: A threshold ratio (3–5 fold), not an absolute concentration, is what this record prints; absolute C5 values differ between laboratories and delivery methods, which is why this shelf cards each method separately.
cards.source: Fujimura M et al. Female gender as a determinant of cough threshold to inhaled capsaicin. The European respiratory journal. 1996. PMID: 8866583. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dicpinigaitis 2001: women were more cough-sensitive than men in every ethnic group tested, and there was no ethnic difference once sex was accounted for (N = 182)
cards.summary: Dicpinigaitis 2001: women were more cough-sensitive than men in every ethnic group tested, and there was no ethnic difference once sex was accounted for (N = 182)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (capsaicin cough challenge across ethnic groups)
cards.people: 182 healthy volunteers from three ethnic groups — Caucasian (white, non-Hispanic, of European origin), Indian (from the Indian subcontinent) and Chinese — undergoing capsaicin cough challenge with C2 (concentration inducing ≥2 coughs) and C5 (≥5 coughs) determined in each subject.
cards.result: Within each ethnic group, log C5 showed the cough reflex was more sensitive in women than in men (p = 0.00002 in Caucasian subjects; p = 0.003 in Indian volunteers; p = 0.002 in Chinese subjects), and C2 data gave similar results. When subjects were evaluated by gender, multivariate analysis of variance demonstrated no ethnic differences in sensitivity to capsaicin.
cards.watchOut: Group labels are the record's own 2001 categories, printed as published. The study confirms the sex effect independently of the Fujimura programme; it does not print a pooled absolute threshold usable across methods.
cards.source: Dicpinigaitis PV et al. Ethnic and gender differences in cough reflex sensitivity. Respiration; international review of thoracic diseases. 2001. PMID: 11694809. cards.headline: Hoffmeyer 2013: single-breath capsaicin C5 was reproducible within a person over four tests in 3 weeks, but the first test read low — and between people C5 spanned 0.95 to 1000 µM (N = 16)
cards.summary: Hoffmeyer 2013: single-breath capsaicin C5 was reproducible within a person over four tests in 3 weeks, but the first test read low — and between people C5 spanned 0.95 to 1000 µM (N = 16)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (capsaicin challenge reproducibility)
cards.people: 16 healthy volunteers in a repeated-measures crossover exposure study (clean air and CO2 up to 2.0 vol% for 4 h), with capsaicin cough reflex assessed after each exposure by the single-breath dose-response method per ERS 2007 guidelines: 12 doubling doses from 0.49 to 1000 µM, endpoint C5. Small classic-style study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: Inter-individual C5 responsiveness spanned a representative range of 0.95–1000 µM — three orders of magnitude between healthy people. On an intra-individual basis, reproducibility across the four tests within 3 weeks was good. CO2 exposure had no influence on the cough reflex. The first capsaicin test demonstrated a lower C5 threshold independent of the CO2 concentration applied, so sensitivity may be overestimated at the first test occasion.
cards.watchOut: N = 16 and the study's primary purpose was a CO2-exposure question; the reproducibility and first-test findings are the physiology carried here, and the wide inter-individual range is itself the finding — there is no single 'normal' C5.
cards.source: Hoffmeyer F et al. Reproducibility of sensitivity to capsaicin assessed by single breath inhalation methodology. Advances in experimental medicine and biology. 2013. PMID: 22826051. cards.headline: Barber 2005: a portable hand-held citric-acid challenge was reproducible and correlated r = 0.95 with the hospital dosimeter method — but its thresholds read 2–3 times higher (N = 25)
cards.summary: Barber 2005: a portable hand-held citric-acid challenge was reproducible and correlated r = 0.95 with the hospital dosimeter method — but its thresholds read 2–3 times higher (N = 25)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (citric-acid challenge method comparison)
cards.people: 25 healthy volunteers performing citric-acid cough challenges by an established hospital dosimeter protocol and, on a separate occasion, by inhaling citric acid (10–3000 mM) from DeVilbiss 40 hand-held nebulisers; reproducibility of the hand-held method was assessed in 11 of the volunteers.
cards.result: Cough thresholds were consistently higher by the hand-held method: geometric mean concentrations causing two coughs (D2) were 3.14 log mM (hand-held) versus 2.77 log mM (dosimeter) (p < 0.001), a geometric mean difference of 0.51 log mM (95% CI 0.18–0.83). The two techniques nevertheless correlated strongly (r = 0.95, p < 0.0001), and the coefficient of repeatability for the hand-held method was 0.40 log mM — a rapid, portable, reproducible challenge whose absolute values are method-bound.
cards.watchOut: Citric-acid and capsaicin thresholds are not interchangeable, and neither are two citric-acid delivery methods: this card is the shelf's warning that every threshold number belongs to its protocol.
cards.source: Barber CM et al. Reproducibility and validity of a Yan-style portable citric acid cough challenge. Pulmonary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2005. PMID: 15707851. cards.headline: Lavorini 2014: one week of ramipril increased cough sensitivity to both capsaicin and citric acid in healthy volunteers; zofenopril did not on C2 (N = 40, crossover)
cards.summary: Lavorini 2014: one week of ramipril increased cough sensitivity to both capsaicin and citric acid in healthy volunteers; zofenopril did not on C2 (N = 40, crossover)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (ACE-inhibitor crossover, capsaicin and citric-acid challenge)
cards.people: 40 healthy volunteers in a randomised crossover study of zofenopril 30 mg daily versus ramipril 10 mg daily, each for 7 consecutive days separated by a 21-day washout. Cough sensitivity to capsaicin and citric acid was measured as C2 and C5 for each agent, with spontaneous cough, exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) and bradykinin also measured.
cards.result: Ramipril, but not zofenopril, increased (p < 0.01) cough sensitivity to both tussigenic agents as assessed by C2. With citric acid, C5 values after both ramipril and zofenopril were significantly lower than control values (p < 0.05 and p < 0.01 respectively). Spontaneous cough was infrequently reported with either drug. Ramipril also raised FeNO from 24 ± 9.6 to 33 ± 16 parts per billion (p < 0.01); neither drug changed plasma bradykinin. The authors conclude zofenopril has less impact on the cough reflex — an agent difference within the ACE-inhibitor class, demonstrated in healthy volunteers.
cards.watchOut: Seven days of drug in healthy volunteers, not chronic therapy in patients: it demonstrates that ACE inhibition can shift the calibrated threshold within a week, and that the shift differs between two agents of the same class — it does not estimate clinical cough incidence.
cards.source: Lavorini F et al. A crossover randomized comparative study of zofenopril and ramipril on cough reflex and airway inflammation in healthy volunteers. Cough (London, England). 2014. PMID: 25632296. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: the cough reflex is a calibrated, individually variable reflex — reproducible in a person, 3–5-fold more sensitive in women, method-bound in its numbers, and shifted within days by an ACE inhibitor
cards.summary: Synthesis: the cough reflex is a calibrated, individually variable reflex — reproducible in a person, 3–5-fold more sensitive in women, method-bound in its numbers, and shifted within days by an ACE inhibitor
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Carded human data: 160 + 182 healthy volunteers in the sex/ethnicity threshold studies, 16 in the reproducibility study, 25 in the citric-acid method study and 40 in the ACE-inhibitor crossover (423 participants in total, with the 11-person reproducibility subset inside the 25).
cards.result: Capsaicin C5 and citric-acid D2/C2 thresholds measure the same vagal reflex through different tussigens and devices, and the numbers travel only with their method (hand-held citric acid reads 2–3× the dosimeter value at r = 0.95 correlation). Within a method, a person's threshold is stable over weeks (with a lower first test), while between healthy people capsaicin C5 spans ~0.95–1000 µM. Sex is the dominant ordinary determinant (3–5-fold lower thresholds in women, replicated across three ethnic groups with no ethnic effect), and pharmacology moves the set-point quickly: ramipril increased sensitivity to both agents within 7 days. Textbook framing (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) supplies the reflex arc; every number here is from a fetched primary record. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: No smoking-effect number is carded: the fetched smoking-and-cough-sensitivity literature was preclinical or in children of smokers, so the row's smoking slice is reported as uncarded in the builder summary rather than filled from animal data. Challenge thresholds in chronic-cough patients are a clinical question with its own shelves.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fujimura M et al. Eur Respir J. 1996 (PMID: 8866583); Dicpinigaitis PV et al. Respiration. 2001 (PMID: 11694809); Hoffmeyer F et al. Adv Exp Med Biol. 2013 (PMID: 22826051); Barber CM et al. Pulm Pharmacol Ther. 2005 (PMID: 15707851); Lavorini F et al. Cough. 2014 (PMID: 25632296). Textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology — framing, not evidence cards.

shelves.title: Astegolimab in COPD (ALIENTO and ARNASA): a split result — each dose regimen missed significance in one of the two trials; the prespecified pooled analysis shows a 15% relative reduction with every-2-week dosing
shelves.question: In adults with COPD and a history of exacerbations despite inhaled maintenance therapy, does astegolimab (anti-ST2 monoclonal antibody) versus placebo reduce the rate of moderate-to-severe exacerbations?
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the split is between the two trials and the two dose regimens, and it is printed here rather than pooled away. ALIENTO (phase 2b, n=1,301) and ARNASA (phase 3, n=1,375) randomised current or former smokers with COPD and frequent exacerbations, irrespective of blood eosinophil count, to astegolimab 476 mg every 2 weeks, every 4 weeks, or placebo for 52 weeks on top of optimised inhaled therapy. In ALIENTO, the adjusted exacerbation rate ratio vs placebo was 0.85 (95% CI 0.72–1.00; p=0.049) for every-2-week dosing but 0.93 (0.79–1.10; p=0.38) for every-4-week dosing. In ARNASA the pattern reversed: 0.85 (0.72–1.01; p=0.068) every 2 weeks and 0.82 (0.70–0.98; p=0.024) every 4 weeks. Rate ratios are relative measures. The prespecified pooled analysis (2,682 participants) was significant for both regimens — a 15% relative reduction in the annualised rate of moderate/severe exacerbations with every-2-week dosing (rate ratio 0.85; 95% CI 0.76–0.96; p=0.0077) and 12% relative with every-4-week dosing (0.88; 0.78–0.99; p=0.0265) — and a nominally significant reduction in severe exacerbations with every-2-week dosing (rate ratio 0.68). Adverse events and deaths (3.1–3.2%) were balanced. Phase 1 studies (152 participants) established tolerability and pharmacokinetics but contain no COPD efficacy data. SPLIT: a real pooled signal whose individual trials do not each confirm it.

cards.headline: ALIENTO and ARNASA (phase 2b and phase 3, reported together): rate ratios 0.85 (p=0.049) and 0.93 (p=0.38) in ALIENTO; 0.85 (p=0.068) and 0.82 (p=0.024) in ARNASA — each regimen significant in only one trial
cards.summary: ALIENTO and ARNASA (phase 2b and phase 3, reported together): rate ratios 0.85 (p=0.049) and 0.93 (p=0.38) in ALIENTO; 0.85 (p=0.068) and 0.82 (p=0.024) in ARNASA — each regimen significant in only one trial
cards.type: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials (phase 2b ALIENTO; phase 3 ARNASA), reported in one publication
cards.people: ALIENTO: 1,301 participants (astegolimab every 2 weeks n=433, every 4 weeks n=437, placebo n=431), treated October 2021 to February 2024. ARNASA: 1,375 participants (459, 459 and 457), treated January 2023 to June 2024. All were current or former smokers with COPD and a history of frequent exacerbations, enrolled irrespective of baseline blood eosinophils, receiving subcutaneous astegolimab 476 mg or placebo alongside optimised inhaled maintenance therapy for 52 weeks; the primary endpoint was the annualised rate of moderate or severe exacerbations.
cards.result: Adjusted rate ratios vs placebo (relative measures) in ALIENTO were 0.85 (95% CI 0.72–1.00; p=0.049) for every-2-week astegolimab and 0.93 (0.79–1.10; p=0.38) for every-4-week dosing. In ARNASA they were 0.85 (0.72–1.01; p=0.068) every 2 weeks and 0.82 (0.70–0.98; p=0.024) every 4 weeks. Adverse events were balanced: 84.0% of ALIENTO and 85.5% of ARNASA participants had one or more adverse event; the most common non-COPD events were nasopharyngitis (ALIENTO) and upper respiratory chest infection (ARNASA); deaths occurred in 3.1% and 3.2% of participants respectively and were balanced across groups.
cards.watchOut: Two trials in one publication, counted here as one report with both trials labelled. The discordance is by regimen within each trial — quoting either trial alone, for either dose, misstates the programme.
cards.source: Papi A et al. Safety and efficacy of astegolimab for COPD with frequent exacerbations regardless of baseline blood eosinophil counts (ALIENTO and ARNASA): randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2b and 3 trials. Lancet. 2026. PMID: 42150581. Registry ID: NCT05037929 and NCT05595642 (ClinicalTrials.gov, as listed in the record). cards.headline: Prespecified pooled analysis of ALIENTO + ARNASA (2,682 participants): annualised moderate/severe exacerbation rate reduced by 15% relative with every-2-week dosing (rate ratio 0.85; p=0.0077) and 12% relative every 4 weeks (0.88; p=0.0265)
cards.summary: Prespecified pooled analysis of ALIENTO + ARNASA (2,682 participants): annualised moderate/severe exacerbation rate reduced by 15% relative with every-2-week dosing (rate ratio 0.85; p=0.0077) and 12% relative every 4 weeks (0.88; p=0.0265)
cards.type: Prespecified pooled analysis of two randomised trials
cards.people: The pooled intention-to-treat population of ALIENTO and ARNASA: 2,682 participants with COPD, a history of frequent exacerbations and current/former smoking status, irrespective of blood eosinophil count and chronic bronchitis, randomised 1:1:1 to astegolimab 476 mg every 2 weeks, every 4 weeks, or placebo for 52 weeks plus optimised maintenance therapy.
cards.result: Astegolimab reduced the annualised rate of moderate/severe exacerbations by 15% relative in the every-2-week arm (adjusted rate ratio 0.85; 95% CI 0.76–0.96; p=0.0077) and by 12% relative in the every-4-week arm (rate ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.78–0.99; p=0.0265) — rate ratios are relative measures. A nominally significant reduction in the annualised rate of severe exacerbations was seen with every-2-week dosing (rate ratio 0.68; 95% CI 0.52–0.87; p=0.0028). Astegolimab was well tolerated. A hierarchical testing plan gated secondary-endpoint testing on primary-endpoint success.
cards.watchOut: A pooled analysis of the same two trials in Card 1 — it adds statistical precision, not new patients; the per-trial discordance in Card 1 is the reason the stamp is SPLIT rather than positive.
cards.source: Wedzicha JA et al. Astegolimab for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with frequent exacerbations: pooled analysis of the ALIENTO and ARNASA trials. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2026. PMID: 42148875. Registry ID: NCT05037929 and NCT05595642 (ClinicalTrials.gov, as listed in the record). cards.headline: Phase 1 programme (152 participants, three randomised studies): astegolimab was well tolerated with no deaths, serious adverse events or discontinuations for adverse events — safety and pharmacokinetics only, no COPD efficacy data
cards.summary: Phase 1 programme (152 participants, three randomised studies): astegolimab was well tolerated with no deaths, serious adverse events or discontinuations for adverse events — safety and pharmacokinetics only, no COPD efficacy data
cards.type: Three randomised phase 1 studies (safety, pharmacokinetics, immunogenicity)
cards.people: 152 participants enrolled, randomised and treated across three randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 1 studies: single-ascending doses in healthy participants and patients with mild atopic asthma, multiple-ascending doses in healthy participants, and single-ascending doses in healthy Japanese and White adults; astegolimab n=112, placebo n=40, subcutaneous (2.1–560 mg) or intravenous (210 or 700 mg).
cards.result: No deaths, serious adverse events, or discontinuations due to adverse events occurred, and no clinically meaningful differences in treatment-emergent adverse-event incidence were seen between arms. Exposure rose more than dose-proportionally over 2.1–420 mg for single doses and was approximately dose-proportional at ≥70 mg subcutaneously; no pharmacokinetic differences by ethnicity were seen after body-weight adjustment. Antidrug antibodies occurred in 14–23% (subcutaneous) and 33–50% (intravenous) of healthy participants in the single- and multiple-dose studies.
cards.watchOut: Healthy volunteers and mild asthma patients, single or short dosing: this card supports tolerability of the molecule, not efficacy or long-term safety in COPD.

shelves.title: Tozorakimab in COPD (OBERON and TITANIA): exacerbation rates about 30% relatively lower than placebo in two replicate phase 3 trials — the primary endpoint was defined in former smokers
shelves.question: In adults with COPD (current or former smokers) with exacerbations despite standard inhaled therapy, does tozorakimab (anti-IL-33 monoclonal antibody) 300 mg every 4 weeks versus placebo reduce moderate-to-severe exacerbations?
mesh: Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/diagnosis,drug therapy,prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY. Two replicate phase 3 trials — OBERON (877 patients) and TITANIA (873 patients) — randomised adults with COPD who were current or former smokers, with exacerbations in the previous year despite stable standard inhaled therapy and no eosinophil-count eligibility criterion, to tozorakimab 300 mg or placebo every 4 weeks for 52 weeks. The primary endpoint was defined in former smokers: annualised moderate/severe exacerbation rates were 1.34 vs 1.90 events (rate ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.57–0.88; p=0.002) in OBERON and 1.37 vs 2.07 (rate ratio 0.66; 0.55–0.80; p<0.001) in TITANIA. In the overall population the rate ratios were 0.70 and 0.71 (both p<0.001) — all rate ratios are relative measures, printed beside the absolute rates. Because the primary population was former smokers, benefit in current smokers is established within the combined population rather than independently — as the slate flagged. The phase 2a FRONTIER-4 trial (135 patients, 600 mg dose) missed its primary lung-function endpoint (pre-bronchodilator FEV1 difference 24 mL, p=0.216) while showing exacerbation signals in patients with ≥2 prior exacerbations. The pooled FRONTIER phase 2 safety analysis (1,076 patients across four diseases) found tolerability similar to placebo apart from more injection-site reactions. The slate noted a long-term extension (PROSPERO) that missed its primary endpoint exists only as congress data — it is fenced here, not carded. LIKELY on the two concordant phase 3 trials.

cards.headline: OBERON and TITANIA (replicate phase 3): former-smoker exacerbation rates 1.34 vs 1.90 (rate ratio 0.71) and 1.37 vs 2.07 (rate ratio 0.66); overall-population rate ratios 0.70 and 0.71 — all relative measures
cards.summary: OBERON and TITANIA (replicate phase 3): former-smoker exacerbation rates 1.34 vs 1.90 (rate ratio 0.71) and 1.37 vs 2.07 (rate ratio 0.66); overall-population rate ratios 0.70 and 0.71 — all relative measures
cards.type: Two replicate randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (OBERON and TITANIA), reported in one publication
cards.people: OBERON overall population: 877 patients (tozorakimab 446, placebo 431). TITANIA: 873 patients (438, 435). Adults with COPD, current or former smokers, with a history of exacerbations in the previous year despite stable standard-of-care inhaled maintenance therapy; no blood-eosinophil eligibility criterion. Add-on subcutaneous tozorakimab 300 mg or placebo every 4 weeks for 52 weeks; the primary endpoint was the annualised rate of moderate or severe exacerbations among former smokers, with the overall population as the first key secondary endpoint.
cards.result: Among former smokers, annualised moderate/severe exacerbation rates were 1.34 (tozorakimab) vs 1.90 (placebo) events in OBERON (rate ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.57–0.88; p=0.002) and 1.37 vs 2.07 in TITANIA (rate ratio 0.66; 95% CI 0.55–0.80; p<0.001). In the overall population, rates were 1.41 vs 2.00 in OBERON (rate ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.58–0.85; p<0.001) and 1.44 vs 2.03 in TITANIA (rate ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.59–0.84; p<0.001). Adverse events occurred in 70.4% (tozorakimab) vs 77.2% (placebo) in OBERON and 80.1% vs 79.8% in TITANIA.
cards.watchOut: Two trials in one publication, counted here as one report with both trials labelled. The primary endpoint population was former smokers; the current-smoker claim rests on the overall-population analysis, not on a separately powered current-smoker endpoint.
cards.source: Sciurba FC et al. Tozorakimab to prevent COPD exacerbations. N Engl J Med. 2026. PMID: 42708515. Registry ID: NCT05166889 and NCT05158387 (ClinicalTrials.gov, as listed in the record). cards.headline: FRONTIER-4 (phase 2a, 135 patients, 600 mg dose): primary lung-function endpoint missed (pre-bronchodilator FEV1 difference 24 mL, p=0.216); exacerbation signal concentrated in patients with ≥2 prior exacerbations (hazard ratio 0.61, an 80%-CI estimate)
cards.summary: FRONTIER-4 (phase 2a, 135 patients, 600 mg dose): primary lung-function endpoint missed (pre-bronchodilator FEV1 difference 24 mL, p=0.216); exacerbation signal concentrated in patients with ≥2 prior exacerbations (hazard ratio 0.61, an 80%-CI estimate)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2a trial (FRONTIER-4)
cards.people: 135 patients (tozorakimab 67, placebo 68) with moderate-to-severe COPD with chronic bronchitis receiving dual or triple inhaled therapy; tozorakimab 600 mg or placebo subcutaneously every 4 weeks for 24 weeks; the primary endpoint was change in pre-bronchodilator FEV1 at week 12.
cards.result: Pre-bronchodilator FEV1 improved non-significantly more on tozorakimab (least-squares mean difference 24 mL; 80% CI −15 to 63; p=0.216), while post-bronchodilator FEV1 differed significantly (67 mL; 80% CI 17–116; p=0.044). Tozorakimab did not significantly reduce COPD composite exacerbation events overall (hazard ratio 0.79; 80% CI 0.57–1.11; p=0.186 — a relative measure), with larger effects in the prespecified subgroup with ≥2 prior exacerbations (hazard ratio 0.61; 80% CI 0.37–1.00; pre-bronchodilator FEV1 difference 69 mL, p=0.072). Tozorakimab was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A missed primary endpoint at twice the phase 3 dose, reported with 80% confidence intervals: FRONTIER-4 is hypothesis-generating support for the phase 3 exacerbation question, not independent confirmation.
cards.source: Singh D et al. A phase 2a trial of the IL-33 monoclonal antibody tozorakimab in patients with COPD: FRONTIER-4. Eur Respir J. 2025. PMID: 40154559. Registry ID: NCT04631016 (as listed in the record's abstract; no databank entry in the record). cards.headline: FRONTIER phase 2 safety programme (1,076 patients across diabetic kidney disease, atopic dermatitis, asthma and COPD): adverse-event profile similar to placebo except injection-site reactions (1.2–20.9% vs 0.0–4.9%)
cards.summary: FRONTIER phase 2 safety programme (1,076 patients across diabetic kidney disease, atopic dermatitis, asthma and COPD): adverse-event profile similar to placebo except injection-site reactions (1.2–20.9% vs 0.0–4.9%)
cards.type: Pooled safety analysis of four phase 2 trials
cards.people: 1,076 participants (tozorakimab 738, placebo 338) across the four randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled FRONTIER phase 2 studies (FRONTIER-1 diabetic kidney disease; FRONTIER-2 atopic dermatitis; FRONTIER-3 asthma; FRONTIER-4 COPD with chronic bronchitis), receiving subcutaneous tozorakimab 30–600 mg or placebo every 4 weeks for 4–7 doses, with 24–36 weeks of follow-up from the first dose.
cards.result: The proportions with at least one treatment-emergent or serious treatment-emergent adverse event were generally similar between tozorakimab and placebo. Deaths occurred only in FRONTIER-1, in similar proportions (0.9% vs 0.8%) and were unrelated to tozorakimab. Adverse events of special interest, including heart-failure progression events, were infrequent (0.0–1.5% vs 0.0–0.8%); injection-site reactions were more frequent on tozorakimab (1.2–20.9% vs 0.0–4.9%). No clinically significant laboratory or vital-sign trends were seen and immunogenicity was low.
cards.watchOut: Pools four different diseases and doses; it characterises the molecule's tolerability, not COPD-specific long-term safety, which rests on the 52-week phase 3 trials in Card 1.
cards.source: Patel R et al. Safety profile of tozorakimab (an anti-IL-33 monoclonal antibody): data from the FRONTIER phase 2 program. Biologics. 2026. PMID: 42540646. Registry ID: none listed in the record.

shelves.title: Fevipiprant in asthma: a failed programme — the phase 2 sputum-eosinophil signal did not replicate; LUSTER-1/2 missed on exacerbations after multiplicity adjustment and ZEAL-1/2 were null on lung function (the treatment made no difference)
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with uncontrolled asthma, does fevipiprant (oral CRTh2/DP2 antagonist) versus placebo improve lung function and reduce exacerbations?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the honest answer is that the phase 3 programme failed. Fevipiprant (QAW039, Novartis) reduced sputum eosinophils in a 61-patient single-centre phase 2 trial (sputum eosinophil percentage fell 4.5-fold vs 1.3-fold on placebo; between-group difference 3.5-fold, p=0.0014), but that biomarker signal did not convert: in LUSTER-1 and LUSTER-2 (1,771 patients with severe asthma), neither trial showed a statistically significant reduction in moderate-to-severe exacerbations after adjusting for multiple testing — high-eosinophil rate ratios ranged from 1.04 (150 mg, LUSTER-1) to 0.69 (150 mg, LUSTER-2), with only modest, inconsistent reductions at 450 mg. In ZEAL-1 and ZEAL-2 (1,347 patients completing treatment), the primary lung-function endpoint was null in both — FEV1 differences of +41 mL (p=0.088) and −31 mL (p=0.214); the ZEAL authors conclude DP2 inhibition with fevipiprant is not effective in the studied population (the treatment made no difference). The SPIRIT long-term safety study (2,538 randomised) found a placebo-like safety profile, with exploratory, multiplicity-unadjusted efficacy signals the authors say should be interpreted with caution; SPIRIT was terminated early by the sponsor. Per the slate, Novartis stopped development after the phase 3 results. This shelf is kept for completeness of a guideline-era question: a real phase 2 biomarker effect, no demonstrated clinical benefit at phase 3.

cards.headline: LUSTER-1 and LUSTER-2 (phase 3, severe asthma): neither trial significantly reduced exacerbations after multiplicity adjustment — high-eosinophil rate ratios 1.04 and 0.83 (LUSTER-1) and 0.69 and 0.72 (LUSTER-2)
cards.summary: LUSTER-1 and LUSTER-2 (phase 3, severe asthma): neither trial significantly reduced exacerbations after multiplicity adjustment — high-eosinophil rate ratios 1.04 and 0.83 (LUSTER-1) and 0.69 and 0.72 (LUSTER-2)
cards.type: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (LUSTER-1 and LUSTER-2), reported in one publication
cards.people: LUSTER-1: 894 patients randomised (fevipiprant 150 mg n=301, 450 mg n=295, placebo n=298) at 174 sites in 25 countries. LUSTER-2: 877 patients (296, 294, 287) at 169 sites in 19 countries. Adolescents and adults (≥12 years) with severe, uncontrolled asthma on GINA Steps 4–5 dual or triple therapy received once-daily fevipiprant or placebo for 52 weeks; the primary endpoint was the annualised rate of moderate-to-severe exacerbations, analysed in patients with high blood eosinophils (≥250 cells/µL) and in the overall population.
cards.result: In the high-eosinophil population, annualised exacerbation rate ratios vs placebo (relative measures) were 1.04 (95% CI 0.77–1.41) for 150 mg and 0.83 (0.61–1.14) for 450 mg in LUSTER-1, and 0.69 (0.50–0.96) for 150 mg and 0.72 (0.52–1.01) for 450 mg in LUSTER-2. In the overall population, rate ratios were 0.96 and 0.78 (LUSTER-1) and 0.82 and 0.76 (LUSTER-2). The authors state that neither trial showed a statistically significant reduction in exacerbations after adjusting for multiple testing, while noting consistent modest reductions at the 450 mg dose. In the pooled population, serious adverse events occurred in 9% of each group; deaths occurred in two patients on fevipiprant 450 mg and three on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Two trials in one publication, counted here as one report with both trials labelled. Individual nominal confidence intervals that exclude 1.0 (e.g. 0.69 in LUSTER-2) do not survive the trials' own multiplicity adjustment — the authors' conclusion governs.
cards.source: Brightling CE et al. Effectiveness of fevipiprant in reducing exacerbations in patients with severe asthma (LUSTER-1 and LUSTER-2): two phase 3 randomised controlled trials. Lancet Respir Med. 2021. PMID: 32979986. Registry ID: NCT02563067 and NCT02555683 (ClinicalTrials.gov, as listed in the record).
