cards.headline: ZEAL-1 and ZEAL-2 (phase 3): primary lung-function endpoint null in both trials — FEV1 differences +41 mL (p=0.088) and −31 mL (p=0.214); the authors conclude fevipiprant is not effective in this population (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: ZEAL-1 and ZEAL-2 (phase 3): primary lung-function endpoint null in both trials — FEV1 differences +41 mL (p=0.088) and −31 mL (p=0.214); the authors conclude fevipiprant is not effective in this population (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Two replicate randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (ZEAL-1 and ZEAL-2), reported in one publication
cards.people: Patients aged ≥12 years with uncontrolled asthma on standard-of-care therapy received fevipiprant 150 mg once daily or placebo for 12 weeks; 662 patients in ZEAL-1 and 685 in ZEAL-2 completed the treatment period. The primary endpoint was change from baseline in pre-dose FEV1 at 12 weeks; key secondaries were daytime symptom score, reliever use and Asthma Quality-of-Life Questionnaire score.
cards.result: In ZEAL-1, least-squares mean FEV1 change was 112 mL on fevipiprant vs 71 mL on placebo (difference +41 mL; 95% CI −6 to 88; adjusted p=0.088). In ZEAL-2, change was 126 mL vs 157 mL (difference −31 mL; 95% CI −80 to 18; adjusted p=0.214) — numerically favouring placebo. There were no statistically significant differences in any key secondary outcome in either study. The authors conclude the ZEAL studies did not demonstrate significant improvement in lung function or other clinical outcomes and that DP2 receptor inhibition with fevipiprant is not effective in the studied patient population.
cards.watchOut: Two trials in one publication, counted here as one report with both trials labelled. ZEAL tested the 150 mg dose only and a 12-week horizon — a fair test of lung function, not of the 450 mg exacerbation hypothesis, which LUSTER tested and also failed to confirm.
cards.source: Castro M et al. Efficacy and safety of fevipiprant in patients with uncontrolled asthma: two replicate, phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (ZEAL-1 and ZEAL-2). EClinicalMedicine. 2021. PMID: 33997741. Registry ID: NCT03215758 (ZEAL-1) and NCT03226392 (ZEAL-2), as listed in the record's abstract.

cards.headline: Phase 2 (Gonem et al., 61 patients): sputum eosinophil percentage fell 4.5-fold on fevipiprant vs 1.3-fold on placebo (between-group difference 3.5-fold, p=0.0014) — the biomarker signal the phase 3 programme could not convert
cards.summary: Phase 2 (Gonem et al., 61 patients): sputum eosinophil percentage fell 4.5-fold on fevipiprant vs 1.3-fold on placebo (between-group difference 3.5-fold, p=0.0014) — the biomarker signal the phase 3 programme could not convert
cards.type: Single-centre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 trial
cards.people: 61 patients with persistent moderate-to-severe asthma and a sputum eosinophil count ≥2% despite inhaled corticosteroids, at a single centre (Glenfield Hospital, Leicester, UK), randomised to fevipiprant 225 mg twice daily (n=30) or placebo (n=31) for 12 weeks after a 2-week single-blind placebo run-in, followed by a 6-week washout; the primary outcome was change in sputum eosinophil percentage.
cards.result: Sputum eosinophil percentage fell from a geometric mean of 5.4% to 1.1% on fevipiprant and from 4.6% to 3.9% on placebo — a 4.5-fold vs 1.3-fold reduction from baseline (difference between groups 3.5-fold; 95% CI 1.7–7.0; p=0.0014). Fevipiprant had a favourable safety profile, with no deaths or serious adverse events and no withdrawals judged related to the study drug; three fevipiprant and four placebo patients withdrew because of asthma exacerbations.
cards.watchOut: A 61-patient biomarker trial at a different dose (225 mg twice daily): it proves target engagement in sputum, not clinical benefit — LUSTER and ZEAL are what happened when the clinical endpoints were tested at scale.
cards.source: Gonem S et al. cards.headline: SPIRIT (long-term safety, 2,538 randomised): safety profile similar to placebo over ≥52 weeks; exploratory efficacy signals were multiplicity-unadjusted, and the sponsor terminated the study early
cards.summary: SPIRIT (long-term safety, 2,538 randomised): safety profile similar to placebo over ≥52 weeks; exploratory efficacy signals were multiplicity-unadjusted, and the sponsor terminated the study early
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled long-term safety trial (SPIRIT)
cards.people: 2,538 patients aged ≥12 years with uncontrolled asthma randomised approximately 3:3:1 to fevipiprant 150 mg (n=1,093), fevipiprant 450 mg (n=1,085) or placebo (n=360), newly enrolled or rolled over from previous fevipiprant phase 3 trials; 1,184 patients received ≥52 weeks and 163 received ≥104 weeks of treatment across a 52-week double-blind period and an optional 104-week single-blind period.
cards.result: Primary endpoints were time to first treatment-emergent adverse event, serious adverse event, and adverse event leading to discontinuation. Both doses were well tolerated, with a safety profile similar to placebo in both new and roll-over patients. In exploratory analyses, reduced moderate-to-severe exacerbation rates, longer time to first exacerbation and improved FEV1 were observed for both doses vs placebo — without multiplicity adjustment, and the authors state these should be interpreted with caution. SPIRIT was terminated early, on 16 December 2019, by the sponsor.
cards.watchOut: A safety trial with a 3:3:1 allocation and roll-over patients already selected for tolerating fevipiprant: its exploratory efficacy signals cannot rehabilitate the failed LUSTER and ZEAL primaries.
cards.source: Maspero J et al. Long-term safety and exploratory efficacy of fevipiprant in patients with inadequately controlled asthma: the SPIRIT randomised clinical trial. Respir Res. 2021. PMID: 34895218. Registry ID: NCT03052517 (ClinicalTrials.gov, as listed in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: target engagement without clinical benefit — a stopped programme, answered 'no' at phase 3
cards.summary: Synthesis: target engagement without clinical benefit — a stopped programme, answered 'no' at phase 3
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Adolescents and adults with uncontrolled asthma on standard controller therapy.
cards.result: Four phase 3 trials (LUSTER-1/2 on exacerbations; ZEAL-1/2 on lung function) failed their primary endpoints; the one positive result in the programme is a 61-patient sputum-eosinophil biomarker effect. Long-term safety was placebo-like. Stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) for benefit — in plain terms, no demonstrated clinical benefit, and development was stopped.
cards.watchOut: This shelf answers a historical/guideline-era question; fevipiprant is not an available treatment option, and the shelf should not be read as a prescribing recommendation in either direction.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–4 (PMIDs 32979986, 33997741, 27503237, 34895218), all fetched from PubMed this session.

shelves.title: Sputum-eosinophil-guided asthma management: titrating treatment to the sputum eosinophil count cut severe exacerbations in two small randomised trials (35 vs 109 events in the first), and a Cochrane synthesis favoured the strategy — but the trials are old, small and single-programme, and sputum induction exists in few clinics
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe asthma, does treatment titrated to sputum eosinophil counts versus guideline/symptom-based management reduce severe exacerbations?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Two randomised trials asked whether titrating asthma treatment to normalise the induced sputum eosinophil count beats symptom/guideline-based care. Green et al. (Lancet 2002, n=74) found far fewer severe exacerbations with sputum management (35 vs 109 events; p=0.01) and fewer hospital admissions (1 vs 6 patients), at no higher corticosteroid dose. Jayaram et al. (Eur Respir J 2006, n=117, 2 years) found the same direction: fewer exacerbations needing prednisone (5 vs 15) and a 49% relative reduction in the risk of a first exacerbation, driven by fewer eosinophilic exacerbations — the sputum strategy did not change the frequency of non-eosinophilic exacerbations, which were the majority. The Cochrane synthesis (Petsky 2017; six studies, 374 participants randomised) pooled an odds ratio of 0.57 (0.38–0.86) for having any exacerbation — a relative measure; the absolute risks printed in the review were 82% (control) vs 62% (sputum) for one or more exacerbations over 16 months, NNTB 6. The honest limits: the trials are small, old and from specialist centres with sputum laboratories; sputum induction is not available in most clinics, so this shelf supports the strategy where the assay exists, not as a general practice recommendation. This is a different biomarker question from FeNO-guided management (live #1728, pack #5904), which is not duplicated here.

cards.headline: Green 2002 (Lancet): sputum-guided management cut severe exacerbations to 35 vs 109 events and admissions to 1 vs 6 patients, at the same corticosteroid dose (n=74)
cards.summary: Green 2002 (Lancet): sputum-guided management cut severe exacerbations to 35 vs 109 events and admissions to 1 vs 6 patients, at the same corticosteroid dose (n=74)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (single-centre)
cards.people: 74 patients with moderate-to-severe asthma from hospital clinics, randomised to management by British Thoracic Society guidelines or by normalisation of the induced sputum eosinophil count plus symptom reduction, assessed nine times over 12 months; sputum results were used only in the sputum group and not disclosed in the guideline group.
cards.result: The sputum eosinophil count was 63% lower (95% CI 24–100) over 12 months in the sputum group (p=0.002). Severe exacerbations numbered 35 in the sputum group vs 109 in the guideline group (p=0.01), and 1 vs 6 patients were admitted to hospital with asthma (p=0.047). Average daily inhaled or oral corticosteroid dose did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: 74 patients from one specialist centre with a sputum laboratory; exacerbation counts are events, not patients, so a few frequent exacerbators weigh heavily. The result supports the strategy where sputum induction exists — it does not show the assay can be delivered in ordinary clinics.
cards.source: Green RH et al. Asthma exacerbations and sputum eosinophil counts: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2002. PMID: 12480423. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jayaram 2006: over 2 years the sputum strategy delayed the first exacerbation (by 213 days) and cut prednisone-treated exacerbations to 5 vs 15 — benefit confined to eosinophilic exacerbations (n=117)
cards.summary: Jayaram 2006: over 2 years the sputum strategy delayed the first exacerbation (by 213 days) and cut prednisone-treated exacerbations to 5 vs 15 — benefit confined to eosinophilic exacerbations (n=117)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (2-year effectiveness study)
cards.people: 117 adults with asthma in a multicentre randomised parallel-group effectiveness study over 2 years: a clinical strategy (symptoms and spirometry) versus a sputum strategy (corticosteroid therapy titrated to keep sputum eosinophils ≤2%, with symptoms/spirometry for other decisions). Patients were blind to sputum counts in both strategies and physicians were blind in the clinical strategy.
cards.result: In phase 2, 126 exacerbations occurred: 79 (62.7%) in the clinical group and 47 (37.3%) in the sputum group; 80.1% were mild, and most exacerbations with a pre-treatment sputum sample were non-eosinophilic. Time to first exacerbation was longer in the sputum group (by 213 days; by 490 days in patients needing a long-acting beta2-agonist), the relative risk of a first exacerbation was lower by 49% (a relative measure), and exacerbations needing prednisone numbered 5 vs 15. Cumulative corticosteroid dose was similar. The sputum strategy did not influence the frequency of non-eosinophilic exacerbations.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is real but narrow: it operates on eosinophilic exacerbations, while most exacerbations in the trial were non-eosinophilic and unaffected. Two-phase design (treatment minimisation, then maintenance) makes the headline counts harder to map onto ordinary practice.
cards.source: Jayaram L et al. Determining asthma treatment by monitoring sputum cell counts: effect on exacerbations. The European respiratory journal. 2006. PMID: 16507847. cards.headline: Cochrane synthesis (Petsky 2017): pooled odds ratio 0.57 for any exacerbation with sputum-tailored treatment; absolute risks 62% vs 82% over 16 months, NNTB 6 — evidence graded moderate to low
cards.summary: Cochrane synthesis (Petsky 2017): pooled odds ratio 0.57 for any exacerbation with sputum-tailored treatment; absolute risks 62% vs 82% over 16 months, NNTB 6 — evidence graded moderate to low
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Cochrane)
cards.people: Six randomised studies (five in adults, one in children/adolescents) of asthma treatment tailored to sputum eosinophils versus clinical symptoms with or without lung function; 374 participants randomised, 333 completing. Studies were clinically and methodologically heterogeneous (medications, eosinophil cut-offs, exacerbation definitions).
cards.result: Pooled odds ratio for the occurrence of any exacerbation was 0.57 (95% CI 0.38 to 0.86) favouring sputum tailoring — a relative measure. The review's absolute risks: one or more exacerbations over 16 months in 82% of controls vs 62% (95% CI 49% to 74%) in the sputum arm, number needed to treat to benefit 6 (95% CI 4 to 13). Hospitalisation risk over 16 months was 24% (control) vs 8% (sputum). Symptoms, quality of life, spirometry and mean inhaled corticosteroid dose did not differ significantly. GRADE quality ranged from moderate (exacerbations, hospitalisation) to low (inhaled corticosteroid dose). Sputum induction was not always possible; no adverse events were recorded in the included studies.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate leans heavily on the two adult trials carded above — it is a synthesis of the same small evidence base, not independent confirmation. One included study was unblinded (high risk of bias), though excluding it in sensitivity analysis left the primary result significant.
cards.source: Petsky HL et al. Tailored interventions based on sputum eosinophils versus clinical symptoms for asthma in children and adults. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real exacerbation reduction where sputum induction exists — POSSIBLE, capped by small old trials and by the assay's scarcity
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real exacerbation reduction where sputum induction exists — POSSIBLE, capped by small old trials and by the assay's scarcity
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Green 2002 (74 patients), Jayaram 2006 (117 patients) and the Cochrane synthesis (six studies, 374 randomised) of sputum-eosinophil-guided versus symptom/guideline-based asthma management.
cards.result: All three reports point the same way: titrating anti-inflammatory treatment to the sputum eosinophil count reduces exacerbations — most clearly severe and eosinophilic ones (35 vs 109 events; prednisone-treated exacerbations 5 vs 15; pooled odds ratio 0.57, a relative measure, with absolute risks 62% vs 82%) — without increasing total corticosteroid dose. The cap at POSSIBLE is set by the evidence structure, not by disagreement: two small, old, specialist-centre trials plus their own synthesis, and a monitoring test (induced sputum) that most clinics cannot perform. FeNO-guided management is a separate, already-homed question (live #1728, pack #5904) and none of its references is carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not read the pooled odds ratio as an absolute benefit: the review's own absolute risks (62% vs 82% over 16 months) are the honest scale, in trial populations with frequent exacerbations.
cards.source: Synthesis of Green RH et al. Lancet. 2002 (PMID: 12480423), Jayaram L et al. Eur Respir J. 2006 (PMID: 16507847) and Petsky HL et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017 (PMID: 28837221).

shelves.title: Rituximab added to mycophenolate in NSIP-pattern ILD: EVER-ILD improved FVC by 3.60% predicted versus mycophenolate alone — one positive trial, supported by an SSc-ILD meta-analysis and a small rescue cohort; the rituximab-versus-cyclophosphamide head-to-head lives on pack #3950 and is not re-carded here
shelves.question: In adults with connective-tissue-disease-associated ILD or idiopathic interstitial pneumonia with an NSIP pattern, does adding rituximab to mycophenolate mofetil slow FVC decline compared with mycophenolate alone?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), for the add-on question only. PREMISE CORRECTION recorded at build: the slate row's lead anchor, RECITAL (rituximab vs intravenous cyclophosphamide in CTD-ILD), is already carded as the whole question of pack #3950, and its PMID is on this wave's gate list — it is therefore NOT carded here; pack #3950 is the home for rituximab versus cyclophosphamide, and this shelf cross-points to it rather than duplicating it. What remains genuinely unasked is the add-on question. EVER-ILD (double-blind, n=122, NSIP-pattern ILD on background mycophenolate) found rituximab improved percent-predicted FVC by a between-group 3.60% (95% CI 0.41–6.80; p=0.0273) at 6 months, with better progression-free survival (crude HR 0.47 — a relative measure) and similar serious adverse event rates (41% vs 39%), at the cost of more infections (9 vs 4 reports, including viral). A 2025 meta-analysis in systemic-sclerosis ILD (six studies, two randomised) found rituximab reduced FVC decline versus conventional treatment (SMD 0.65, 0.08–1.22). A small retrospective rescue cohort (18 transplant-listing-grade patients) is carded as labelled observational support only. The two comparisons in the original slate question (versus cyclophosphamide; as add-on to mycophenolate) are not merged into one claim: the first lives on #3950, the second is answered here, capped at POSSIBLE because it rests on a single trial.

cards.headline: EVER-ILD 2023: rituximab added to mycophenolate improved FVC by 3.60% predicted at 6 months (p=0.0273) and progression-free survival HR 0.47 — with more infections (n=122)
cards.summary: EVER-ILD 2023: rituximab added to mycophenolate improved FVC by 3.60% predicted at 6 months (p=0.0273) and progression-free survival HR 0.47 — with more infections (n=122)
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial (EVER-ILD)
cards.people: 122 randomised patients with connective-tissue-disease-associated ILD or idiopathic interstitial pneumonia (with or without autoimmune features) and an NSIP pattern, all on mycophenolate mofetil 2 g daily, assigned to rituximab 1000 mg (63 patients) or placebo (59 patients) on days 1 and 15, followed for 6 months.
cards.result: Least-squares mean change in percent-predicted FVC at 6 months was +1.60 (SE 1.13) with rituximab plus mycophenolate vs −2.01 (SE 1.17) with placebo plus mycophenolate: between-group difference 3.60% predicted (95% CI 0.41 to 6.80; p=0.0273). Progression-free survival was better with rituximab (crude hazard ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.96; p=0.03 — a relative measure). Serious adverse events occurred in 26 (41%) rituximab patients vs 23 (39%) placebo patients; nine infections were reported in the rituximab group (five bacterial, three viral, one other) vs four bacterial infections in the placebo group.
cards.watchOut: A single trial with a 6-month primary endpoint and a modest absolute FVC difference; the population mixes CTD-ILD with idiopathic NSIP-pattern disease, so the result is a class-level answer for NSIP-pattern ILD on mycophenolate, not proof for every CTD-ILD subtype. The trial's 1-year follow-up report was not carded: its fetched record carried no abstract this session, so no numbers from it are printed.
cards.source: Mankikian J et al. Rituximab and mycophenolate mofetil combination in patients with interstitial lung disease (EVER-ILD): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. The European respiratory journal. 2023. PMID: 37230499. Registry ID: NCT02990286 (ClinicalTrials.gov, as listed in the record). cards.headline: SSc-ILD meta-analysis 2025: rituximab reduced FVC decline versus conventional treatment (SMD 0.65, 0.08–1.22) across six studies — only two of them randomised
cards.summary: SSc-ILD meta-analysis 2025: rituximab reduced FVC decline versus conventional treatment (SMD 0.65, 0.08–1.22) across six studies — only two of them randomised
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of comparative studies of rituximab in adults with systemic-sclerosis-associated ILD: six studies included (two randomised, four non-randomised), with change in forced vital capacity versus conventional treatments as the primary outcome; standardised mean differences were used because study durations varied.
cards.result: Rituximab reduced FVC decline compared with conventional treatment (standardised mean difference 0.65; 95% CI 0.08 to 1.22; P=.03). No significant differences were found in diffusing capacity or modified Rodnan skin score. Rituximab showed a significantly lower incidence of leukopenia compared with cyclophosphamide (P=.02) and a non-significant trend toward fewer pneumonias and urinary tract infections.
cards.watchOut: Four of the six pooled studies are non-randomised, durations varied enough to force standardised mean differences, and the confidence interval (0.08–1.22) nearly touches no effect — supportive synthesis, not independent randomised confirmation. It covers systemic-sclerosis ILD only.

cards.headline: Rescue cohort 2020 (observational, labelled): in 18 patients with transplant-grade progressive CTD lung disease, DLCO rose 12.4% at 1 year on rituximab after a year of decline — no comparator
cards.summary: Rescue cohort 2020 (observational, labelled): in 18 patients with transplant-grade progressive CTD lung disease, DLCO rose 12.4% at 1 year on rituximab after a year of decline — no comparator
cards.type: Retrospective observational cohort (no comparator)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of 18 patients with progressive connective-tissue-disease-related lung disease meeting lung-transplant listing criteria (FVC <60% and/or DLCO <40%) who started rituximab for progression: systemic sclerosis 7, rheumatoid arthritis 5, systemic lupus erythematosus 4, Sjögren syndrome 1, antisynthetase syndrome 1; radiologic patterns included NSIP in 9. Observational evidence, labelled as such.
cards.result: In the year before rituximab, FVC changed by −3.8% (p=0.095) and DLCO by −8.4% (p=0.004). After treatment, DLCO improved significantly (+12.4%, p<0.001 at 1 year; +15.3%, p=0.001 at 2 years). Six patients (33.3%) had adverse events related to rituximab. No patient required lung transplant or died during the study period.
cards.watchOut: Observational, uncontrolled and small (n=18): patients were selected for progression, so regression to the mean and survivor effects can mimic benefit. Carded as labelled supporting evidence only; it cannot carry the shelf's claim, which rests on EVER-ILD.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the add-on answer is POSSIBLE; the cyclophosphamide head-to-head is a different shelf (#3950) and is deliberately not re-carded here
cards.summary: Synthesis: the add-on answer is POSSIBLE; the cyclophosphamide head-to-head is a different shelf (#3950) and is deliberately not re-carded here
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: EVER-ILD (122 randomised patients, NSIP-pattern ILD on mycophenolate), a six-study SSc-ILD meta-analysis, and an 18-patient retrospective rescue cohort.
cards.result: For the question this shelf asks — rituximab added to mycophenolate in NSIP-pattern ILD — the one double-blind trial is positive on FVC (+3.60% predicted difference) and on progression-free survival (HR 0.47, a relative measure), the SSc-ILD synthesis points the same way on FVC, and the small uncontrolled cohort is consistent. That concordance earns POSSIBLE (benefit), no higher: one trial, 6 months, more infections with the combination. The slate row's other comparison — rituximab versus intravenous cyclophosphamide (RECITAL) — is the whole question of pack #3950, where RECITAL is carded; under the one-home rule it is cross-pointed, not duplicated, and RECITAL's gated PMID is not carded on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the two rituximab comparisons into one pooled claim: versus-cyclophosphamide (#3950, null on FVC with a tolerability edge) and added-to-mycophenolate (this shelf, positive on FVC) are different questions with different answers.

shelves.title: Transbronchial lung cryobiopsy versus surgical lung biopsy for ILD diagnosis: agreement was 70.8% histopathologically and 76.9% at multidisciplinary discussion (COLDICE), and a cryobiopsy-first step-up strategy matched surgical yield (89% vs 88%) with far fewer serious adverse events (4% vs 50%) — agreement is not identity, and low-confidence cryobiopsy diagnoses still need surgery
shelves.question: In adults with undiagnosed interstitial lung disease needing tissue, does transbronchial lung cryobiopsy (including a cryobiopsy-first step-up strategy) versus surgical lung biopsy achieve comparable diagnostic yield at multidisciplinary discussion with fewer serious adverse events?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), as a test-strategy shelf. COLDICE (n=65, both biopsies under one anaesthetic) found histopathological agreement between cryobiopsy and surgical biopsy of 70.8% (weighted κ 0.70) and multidisciplinary-discussion (MDD) agreement of 76.9% (κ 0.62) — good, not identical; where the cryobiopsy MDD diagnosis was high-confidence (60% of cases) it matched surgery in 95%, but in the 40% with low-confidence or unclassifiable cryobiopsy diagnoses, surgery reclassified 23% to a definite alternative. The randomised COLD study (n=55) tested the strategy rather than the sample: cryobiopsy-first with surgery only if inconclusive reached an MDD diagnostic yield of 89% vs 88% for immediate surgery, with serious adverse events in 1 of 28 (4%) vs 12 of 24 (50%) and a hospital stay of 1 vs 5 days. Earlier prospective series are less tidy — Casoni 2014 (n=69) reported a 76% high-confidence pattern yield but pneumothorax in 28%, and a technique study (n=46) found yield depended on sampling two segments (69% for one sampling vs 96% with two-segment sampling) — the disagreement across cohorts on yield and complications is printed on the cards, not smoothed over. These are diagnostic-agreement and yield outcomes, not patient-outcome endpoints.

cards.headline: COLDICE 2020: cryobiopsy–surgery agreement 70.8% histopathologically and 76.9% at MDD; high-confidence cryobiopsy diagnoses matched surgery in 95%, low-confidence ones were reclassified in 23% (n=65)
cards.summary: COLDICE 2020: cryobiopsy–surgery agreement 70.8% histopathologically and 76.9% at MDD; high-confidence cryobiopsy diagnoses matched surgery in 95%, low-confidence ones were reclassified in 23% (n=65)
cards.type: Prospective multicentre diagnostic-accuracy study (paired biopsies)
cards.people: 65 patients with interstitial lung disease (mean age 66.1 years; 48% men; FVC 83.7% predicted) at nine Australian tertiary hospitals who, after centralised multidisciplinary discussion, underwent sequential transbronchial lung cryobiopsy and surgical lung biopsy under one anaesthetic, with masked pathologists and cases discussed twice at MDD (once with each biopsy) in random order.
cards.result: Histopathological agreement between cryobiopsy and surgical biopsy was 70.8% (weighted κ 0.70, 95% CI 0.55–0.86); diagnostic agreement at MDD was 76.9% (κ 0.62, 0.47–0.78). Cryobiopsy samples averaged 7.1 mm vs 46.5 mm for surgical samples. For cryobiopsy cases with high or definite diagnostic confidence at MDD (39 of 65, 60%), 37 (95%) were concordant with surgical diagnoses; in the 26 (40%) with low-confidence or unclassifiable cryobiopsy diagnoses, surgical biopsy reclassified six (23%) to alternative high-confidence or definite diagnoses. Mild–moderate airway bleeding occurred in 14 (22%) patients due to cryobiopsy. Ninety-day mortality was 2% (one of 65), following acute exacerbation of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
cards.watchOut: Agreement is not accuracy against a gold standard — both samples can be wrong together, and roughly a quarter of paired diagnoses disagreed. The reassuring 95% figure applies only to the 60% of cryobiopsies the MDD already found high-confidence.

cards.headline: COLD 2024 (randomised): cryobiopsy-first step-up matched surgical yield (89% vs 88%) with serious adverse events in 4% vs 50% and a 1-day vs 5-day stay (n=55)
cards.summary: COLD 2024 (randomised): cryobiopsy-first step-up matched surgical yield (89% vs 88%) with serious adverse events in 4% vs 50% and a 1-day vs 5-day stay (n=55)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial of diagnostic strategies (COLD)
cards.people: 55 patients with ILD and a multidisciplinary-team indication for lung biopsy, randomised at six Dutch hospitals to a step-up strategy (transbronchial cryobiopsy, then surgical biopsy only if inconclusive; n=28) or immediate surgical lung biopsy (n=27; three excluded), with 12 weeks of follow-up; patients, clinicians and pathologists were not masked.
cards.result: Unexpected chest-tube drainage (the primary endpoint) occurred in 3 of 28 (11%) step-up patients, while the chest tube could not be removed within 24 h in 11 of 24 (46%) surgical patients — an absolute risk reduction of 35% (95% CI 11–56%; p=0.0058). MDD diagnostic yield after cryobiopsy alone was 82% (64–92%), rising to 89% (73–96%) after step-up surgery for inconclusive cases, vs 88% (69–97%) with immediate surgery. Total in-hospital stay was 1 day (IQR 1–1) vs 5 days (IQR 4–6). One (4%) serious adverse event occurred in the step-up strategy vs 12 (50%) in the immediate-surgery strategy.
cards.watchOut: Small (55 patients) and unmasked, and the primary endpoint (chest-tube drainage) is partly built into the surgical procedure itself — the fair reading is lower procedural burden at equal yield, not a like-for-like safety contest. Yield confidence intervals are wide (73–96% vs 69–97%).
cards.source: Kalverda KA et al. Transbronchial cryobiopsy followed by as-needed surgical lung biopsy versus immediate surgical lung biopsy for diagnosing interstitial lung disease (the COLD study): a randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2024. PMID: 38640934. Registry ID: NL7634 (Dutch Trial Register, as stated in the record; no databank registry field in the record). cards.headline: Casoni 2014 (prospective series): cryobiopsy gave a high-confidence pattern in 76% — but pneumothorax occurred in 28% and one patient (1.4%) died of acute exacerbation (n=69)
cards.summary: Casoni 2014 (prospective series): cryobiopsy gave a high-confidence pattern in 76% — but pneumothorax occurred in 28% and one patient (1.4%) died of acute exacerbation (n=69)
cards.type: Prospective single-arm case series
cards.people: Prospective study of 69 cases of transbronchial lung cryobiopsy with a flexible cryoprobe in fibrotic diffuse parenchymal lung disease with non-diagnostic high-resolution CT features, assessed for safety, feasibility and diagnostic yield.
cards.result: Pneumothorax occurred in 19 patients (28%); one patient (1.4%) died of acute exacerbation. Adequate cryobiopsies were obtained in 68 cases (99%), median size 43.11 mm². Among adequate biopsies, pathologists were highly confident of a specific pattern in 52 patients (76%), including 36 of 47 with usual interstitial pneumonia (77%); in 11 UIP diagnoses confidence was low. Agreement between pathologists on UIP detection was very good (κ 0.83, 95% CI 0.69–0.97). By consensus clinicoradiologic–pathologic correlation, 32% (20/63) were classified as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, 30% (19/63) as possible IPF, 25% (16/63) as other fibrotic diseases and 13% (8/63) as unclassifiable.
cards.watchOut: No surgical comparator in the same patients, and a 28% pneumothorax rate is materially worse than the complication picture in COLDICE/COLD — centre experience and technique differ across cohorts, which is exactly the disagreement this shelf keeps on its face.
cards.source: Casoni GL et al. Transbronchial lung cryobiopsy in the diagnosis of fibrotic interstitial lung diseases. PloS one. 2014. PMID: 24586252. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Technique study 2017: cryobiopsy yield was 69% after a first sampling and reached 96% only when two samples came from two different segments (n=46)
cards.summary: Technique study 2017: cryobiopsy yield was 69% after a first sampling and reached 96% only when two samples came from two different segments (n=46)
cards.type: Prospective randomised technique-comparison study
cards.people: 46 prospectively enrolled patients with suspected diffuse parenchymal lung disease, randomised to cryobiopsy sampling strategy: group A, four samples from the same segment, or group B, two samples from one segment and two from a different segment of the same lobe; pathologists reformulated the histopathologic diagnosis as each sample was added.
cards.result: The mean diagnostic yield with only the first sampling (both groups combined) was 69%. Adding a second biopsy improved yield significantly only when the two samples came from two different segments (96%, group B).
cards.watchOut: A yield study of sampling strategy, not a cryobiopsy-versus-surgery comparison — carded because it explains part of the between-cohort yield disagreement: reported cryobiopsy performance depends on how the procedure is done, not only on the device.
cards.source: Ravaglia C et al. Transbronchial Lung Cryobiopsy in Diffuse Parenchymal Lung Disease: Comparison between Biopsy from 1 Segment and Biopsy from 2 Segments - Diagnostic Yield and Complications. Respiration; international review of thoracic diseases. 2017. PMID: 28245447. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: cryobiopsy-first is the lower-burden route to a near-surgical yield — POSSIBLE, with agreement limits and technique dependence printed
cards.summary: Synthesis: cryobiopsy-first is the lower-burden route to a near-surgical yield — POSSIBLE, with agreement limits and technique dependence printed
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: COLDICE (65 paired-biopsy patients), the COLD randomised strategy trial (55 patients), a 69-patient prospective series and a 46-patient technique study.
cards.result: The strategy answer is consistent: start with cryobiopsy and reserve surgery for inconclusive cases — diagnostic yield 89% vs 88%, serious adverse events 4% vs 50%, stay 1 vs 5 days (COLD). The sample answer is more qualified: cryobiopsy and surgical diagnoses agree in about three-quarters of cases (70.8% histopathological, 76.9% at MDD), high-confidence cryobiopsy diagnoses are reliable (95% concordant), and low-confidence ones are not a stopping point (23% reclassified by surgery). Yield and complications vary by cohort and technique (76% high-confidence yield with 28% pneumothorax in one series; 69%→96% yield by sampling strategy in another), so the stamp stays POSSIBLE and the shelf stays a diagnostic-strategy (GAP-E) shelf: no card shows that either route changes treatment outcomes or survival.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the 89% vs 88% yields without their confidence intervals, and do not convert diagnostic agreement into diagnostic accuracy — COLDICE measured concordance between two imperfect samples.
cards.source: Synthesis of Troy LK et al. Lancet Respir Med. 2020 (PMID: 31578168), Kalverda KA et al. Lancet Respir Med. 2024 (PMID: 38640934), Casoni GL et al. PLoS One. 2014 (PMID: 24586252) and Ravaglia C et al. Respiration. 2017 (PMID: 28245447).

shelves.title: Talc poudrage versus talc slurry for malignant pleural effusion: the randomised trials found no overall difference (TAPPS failure 22% vs 24%; Dresler success 78% vs 71%) — a lung-or-breast-primary subgroup favoured poudrage in the older trial, and the one positive comparative study allocated its sickest patients to slurry
shelves.question: In adults with malignant pleural effusion undergoing pleurodesis, does talc poudrage (thoracoscopic) versus talc slurry (bedside) differ in pleurodesis failure?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) for a poudrage advantage; the overall randomised answer is no difference. This is a PARTIAL shelf: live #816 asks indwelling pleural catheter versus talc pleurodesis (TIME2/AMPLE) and pack #3958 covers IPC-PLUS — the delivery-route comparison (poudrage vs slurry) is not asked in either, and none of #816's references is carded here. TAPPS (JAMA 2020, n=330, open-label) found 90-day pleurodesis failure in 22% with thoracoscopic poudrage vs 24% with bedside slurry (adjusted OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.54–1.55 — a relative measure; absolute difference −1.8%), with no significant difference in any of 24 prespecified secondary outcomes; the authors note the trial may have been underpowered for small differences. The older intergroup phase 3 trial (Dresler 2005, n=501 registered) likewise found no overall difference in 30-day success (78% vs 71%), but in the prespecified subgroup with lung or breast primaries success was 82% vs 67% favouring poudrage, while respiratory complications were more common after poudrage (14% vs 6%). The one clearly positive comparative study (Stefani 2006, n=109) was not randomised: patients at high anaesthetic risk or with short life expectancy were given slurry by design, so its poudrage advantage (life-long symphysis 81.9% vs 62.2%) is confounded by allocation and is carded as such.

cards.headline: TAPPS 2020: 90-day pleurodesis failure 22% with poudrage vs 24% with slurry (adjusted OR 0.91, NS) — no difference in any of 24 secondary outcomes (n=330)
cards.summary: TAPPS 2020: 90-day pleurodesis failure 22% with poudrage vs 24% with slurry (adjusted OR 0.91, NS) — no difference in any of 24 secondary outcomes (n=330)
cards.type: Open-label multicentre randomised clinical trial (TAPPS)
cards.people: 330 patients older than 18 years with confirmed malignant pleural effusion who could undergo thoracoscopy with local anaesthesia, randomised at 17 UK hospitals to talc poudrage during thoracoscopy under moderate sedation (166 patients; 4 g talc) or bedside chest-tube talc slurry (164 patients; 4 g talc); mean age 68 years, 55% women; 320 (97%) were included in the primary outcome analysis. Patients needing diagnostic thoracoscopy or with non-expandable lung were excluded.
cards.result: Pleurodesis failure at 90 days occurred in 36 of 161 patients (22%) in the poudrage group and 38 of 159 (24%) in the slurry group (adjusted odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.55; P=.74 — a relative measure; absolute difference −1.8%, 95% CI −10.7% to 7.2%). No statistically significant differences were noted in any of the 24 prespecified secondary outcomes, which included failure at 30 and 180 days, hospital nights, pain, dyspnoea, quality of life and mortality.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the confidence interval (−10.7% to +7.2% absolute) cannot exclude a small benefit either way — the authors themselves flag possible underpowering for small but potentially important differences. 'No significant difference' is the finding; exact equivalence is not proven.
cards.source: Bhatnagar R et al. Effect of Thoracoscopic Talc Poudrage vs Talc Slurry via Chest Tube on Pleurodesis Failure Rate Among Patients With Malignant Pleural Effusions: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020. cards.headline: Dresler 2005 (intergroup phase 3): no overall difference in 30-day success (78% vs 71%), but lung-or-breast-primary patients succeeded more with poudrage (82% vs 67%) — and respiratory complications were more frequent (14% vs 6%)
cards.summary: Dresler 2005 (intergroup phase 3): no overall difference in 30-day success (78% vs 71%), but lung-or-breast-primary patients succeeded more with poudrage (82% vs 67%) — and respiratory complications were more frequent (14% vs 6%)
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 intergroup trial
cards.people: 501 patients with documented malignant pleural effusion registered in a prospective randomised intergroup trial comparing thoracoscopy with talc insufflation (poudrage; 242 randomised) with thoracostomy and talc slurry (240 randomised); the primary endpoint was 30-day freedom from radiographic recurrence among surviving patients whose lungs initially re-expanded more than 90%. Demographics and primary malignancies were similar between arms.
cards.result: Overall 30-day success did not differ between arms (poudrage 78% vs slurry 71%). In the subgroup of patients with primary lung or breast cancer, success was higher with poudrage than slurry (82% vs 67%). Common morbidity included fever, dyspnoea and pain. Treatment-related mortality occurred in nine poudrage and seven slurry patients. Respiratory complications were more common after poudrage (14% vs 6%); respiratory failure occurred in 8% of poudrage vs 4% of slurry patients, accounting for six and five toxic deaths respectively. Quality-of-life measurement showed less fatigue with poudrage; patient ratings of comfort and safety were also higher with poudrage, with no difference in perceived value or convenience.
cards.watchOut: The lung/breast advantage is a subgroup result inside an overall-null trial — hypothesis-generating, not a proven indication — and it came with roughly double the respiratory complications. The primary endpoint was assessed only in surviving patients with >90% lung re-expansion, a selected denominator.
cards.source: Dresler CM et al. Phase III intergroup study of talc poudrage vs talc slurry sclerosis for malignant pleural effusion. Chest. 2005. PMID: 15764775. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Stefani 2006 (non-randomised, labelled): poudrage 'won' on immediate (87.5% vs 73%) and life-long (81.9% vs 62.2%) pleurodesis — but the sickest patients were assigned to slurry by design (n=109)
cards.summary: Stefani 2006 (non-randomised, labelled): poudrage 'won' on immediate (87.5% vs 73%) and life-long (81.9% vs 62.2%) pleurodesis — but the sickest patients were assigned to slurry by design (n=109)
cards.type: Prospective non-randomised comparative study
cards.people: 109 patients with malignant pleural effusion and lung re-expansion after drainage in a prospective, explicitly not randomised comparative study: 72 received videothoracoscopic talc poudrage under general anaesthesia (6 g talc) and 37 received bedside talc slurry through a chest tube (6 g talc). By protocol, patients at high risk for general anaesthesia, in poor general condition or with short life expectancy received slurry; all others received poudrage. Non-randomised evidence, labelled as such.
cards.result: Immediate successful pleurodesis occurred in 63 of 72 poudrage patients (87.5%) vs 27 of 37 slurry patients (73%) (p=0.049); at 90 days success was 88.3% vs 69.6% among those assessed, and life-long pleural symphysis was achieved in 59 (81.9%) vs 23 (62.2%) (p=0.023). Adverse effects were generally mild: chest pain in 36.1% (poudrage) vs 48.6% (slurry) and fever in 38.8% vs 35.1%, differences not significant. There was no acute respiratory failure and no procedure-related mortality.
cards.watchOut: Confounding by indication is built into the design: slurry was reserved for patients too sick for anaesthesia or with short life expectancy, who would be expected to fare worse with either technique. This study cannot overturn the two randomised nulls and is carded to show why the older literature looked more favourable to poudrage than the trials do.

cards.headline: Synthesis: on randomised evidence the delivery route (the treatment made no difference) — MAYBE (weak evidence) for the subgroup claim only; cross-point to live #816 for catheter versus talc
cards.summary: Synthesis: on randomised evidence the delivery route (the treatment made no difference) — MAYBE (weak evidence) for the subgroup claim only; cross-point to live #816 for catheter versus talc
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: TAPPS (330 randomised patients), the Dresler intergroup phase 3 trial (501 registered) and one non-randomised comparative study (109 patients).
cards.result: Two randomised trials, fifteen years apart, agree on the primary answer: thoracoscopic talc poudrage and bedside talc slurry produce closely similar pleurodesis outcomes overall (failure 22% vs 24% at 90 days in TAPPS; success 78% vs 71% at 30 days in Dresler). What keeps this shelf at MAYBE (weak evidence) rather than a flat 'no difference' stamp is the residue: a lung-or-breast-primary subgroup favouring poudrage in Dresler (82% vs 67%), TAPPS's own underpowering caveat, and a non-randomised study whose design guarantees a poudrage-favouring bias. Practical reading: choose the route by patient fitness, local expertise and whether thoracoscopy is needed anyway — not by an expectation of better pleurodesis. For the different question of catheter versus talc pleurodesis, see live #816 (TIME2/AMPLE); none of its references is carded here.
cards.watchOut: Subgroup and non-randomised signals are printed so they are not lost — and labelled so they are not upgraded. If a future trial confirms the lung/breast subgroup, this stamp should be revisited; on current evidence it is a hypothesis.

shelves.title: PHYSIOLOGY — Work of breathing and its oxygen cost: respiratory muscles take only a few percent of total oxygen consumption at rest in health, but the share rises steeply under load — ~16% of total VO2 at rest in morbid obesity (from the record's absolute values), an oxygen cost per litre of ventilation 3.5-fold higher in malnourished COPD, and an oxygen cost of breathing that predicted weaning failure better than the rapid-shallow-breathing index
shelves.question: In healthy humans and in patients with lung disease or critical illness, what fraction of total oxygen consumption do the respiratory muscles use at rest and under load, how is that cost measured, and how high does it rise in obstructive disease, obesity and failed weaning?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The textbook framing (West's Respiratory Physiology and Nunn's Applied Respiratory Physiology: at rest the respiratory muscles consume only a small fraction — of the order of a few percent — of total oxygen uptake, because the work of quiet breathing is small; the cost rises disproportionately when ventilation must increase or when the respiratory system becomes inefficient, until breathing itself becomes a major claimant on oxygen delivery) is supported by concordant primary human studies using the standard measurement: the fall in total oxygen consumption when the respiratory muscles are rested by mechanical ventilation, or the rise in oxygen consumption per litre of added ventilation. Kress 1999 showed that in morbid obesity the cost is already high at rest: total VO2 fell from 354.6 to 297.2 mL/min when obese patients were ventilated and paralysed (a 57.4 mL/min respiratory share, about 16% of total VO2 by the record's absolute values), while non-obese controls showed no significant fall (221.4 to 219.8 mL/min). Donahoe 1989 measured the oxygen cost of augmenting ventilation directly: 1.23 mL O2 per litre in controls, 2.61 in normally nourished COPD and 4.28 in malnourished COPD. Shikora 1994 found the oxygen cost of breathing predicted weaning outcome better than the respiratory-rate/tidal-volume ratio (sensitivity 100%, specificity 87% in 28 patients), and Shikora 1992 (N=8 patients, labelled sub-10 classic) showed pressure support titrated the cost down from 22% to 8% of VO2. Two slate anchors could not be carded and their refusal is reported on the Synthesis card: the fetched records for the 1957/1961 classics carried no abstract this session, so no numbers from them are printed anywhere on this shelf.

cards.headline: Kress 1999: in morbid obesity the respiratory muscles' share of VO2 was already large at rest — total VO2 fell from 354.6 to 297.2 mL/min on ventilation and paralysis, while controls showed no fall (221.4 to 219.8 mL/min)
cards.summary: Kress 1999: in morbid obesity the respiratory muscles' share of VO2 was already large at rest — total VO2 fell from 354.6 to 297.2 mL/min on ventilation and paralysis, while controls showed no fall (221.4 to 219.8 mL/min)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (before/after ventilation and paralysis)
cards.people: Morbidly obese patients measured immediately before gastric bypass surgery and again after intubation, mechanical ventilation and paralysis, compared with non-obese patients scheduled for elective abdominal surgery measured the same way. The oxygen cost of breathing (VO2RESP) is the fall in total oxygen consumption when the respiratory muscles are taken off work. The fetched record does not state the group sizes, so N is printed as not documented from the record.
cards.result: Baseline total VO2 was higher in the obese patients than controls (354.6 vs 221.4 mL/min; p=0.0001). On mechanical ventilation and paralysis, VO2 fell significantly in the obese patients (354.6 to 297.2 mL/min; p=0.0002) — a respiratory share of 57.4 mL/min, about 16% of total VO2 computed from the record's absolute values — but did not change in controls (221.4 to 219.8 mL/min; p=0.86), a respiratory share of about 1.6 mL/min. The authors conclude that morbidly obese patients dedicate a disproportionately high percentage of total VO2 to respiratory work even during quiet breathing, implying decreased ventilatory reserve.
cards.watchOut: The ~16% figure is arithmetic on the record's group-mean absolute values, not a per-patient percentage the paper reports in its abstract; and paralysis plus anaesthesia may lower non-respiratory VO2 as well, so the fall is an upper-bound estimate of the respiratory share. Group sizes are not in the fetched record and are not invented here.
cards.source: Kress JP et al. The impact of morbid obesity on oxygen cost of breathing (VO(2RESP)) at rest. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 1999. PMID: 10471613. cards.headline: Donahoe 1989: the oxygen cost of augmenting ventilation was 1.23 mL O2/L in controls, 2.61 in normally nourished COPD and 4.28 in malnourished COPD (26 subjects)
cards.summary: Donahoe 1989: the oxygen cost of augmenting ventilation was 1.23 mL O2/L in controls, 2.61 in normally nourished COPD and 4.28 in malnourished COPD (26 subjects)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (dead-space stimulation, cross-sectional)
cards.people: Nine normally nourished patients with COPD (>90% ideal body weight), 10 malnourished patients with COPD (<90% ideal body weight) and seven normal control subjects. The oxygen cost of breathing was measured with an open-circuit technique using dead-space stimulation of ventilation; resting energy expenditure was also measured and compared with predicted values. The malnourished group had more hyperinflation (RV/TLC 0.69 vs 0.55) and weaker inspiratory muscles (PImax 34 vs 51, units as reported in the record).
cards.result: The oxygen cost of augmenting ventilation was significantly higher in malnourished COPD patients (4.28 ± 0.98 mL O2 per litre of ventilation) than in normally nourished COPD patients (2.61 ± 1.07) and controls (1.23 ± 0.51) (p<0.001). Measured resting energy expenditure as a percentage of predicted was 94.57 ± 6.21% in controls, 105.5 ± 19.66% in normally nourished COPD and 119.4 ± 11.69% in malnourished COPD (p<0.005). The authors conclude that malnourished COPD patients have increased energy requirements specifically for augmenting ventilation, plausibly from increased mechanical load and/or reduced ventilatory muscle efficiency.
cards.watchOut: Small groups (7–10 per arm) and a cost-per-litre measure under stimulated ventilation, not the resting fractional share of VO2 — the two metrics answer different versions of the shelf's question and are not interchangeable. Malnutrition, hyperinflation and muscle weakness travel together in this cohort, so the design cannot separate their contributions.

cards.headline: Shikora 1994: the oxygen cost of breathing predicted weaning outcome with sensitivity 100% and specificity 87%, outperforming the respiratory-rate/tidal-volume ratio (40% and 52%) in 28 ventilated surgical patients
cards.summary: Shikora 1994: the oxygen cost of breathing predicted weaning outcome with sensitivity 100% and specificity 87%, outperforming the respiratory-rate/tidal-volume ratio (40% and 52%) in 28 ventilated surgical patients
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (prospective weaning-prediction comparison)
cards.people: 28 consecutive patients with chronic respiratory insufficiency requiring long-term mechanical ventilation in a surgical ICU. The oxygen cost of breathing and the respiratory rate to tidal volume ratio were measured during spontaneous breathing; patients extubated within 2 weeks were designated extubated (5 patients), and those not extubated within that period or requiring reintubation were designated not extubated (23 patients).
cards.result: The oxygen cost of breathing predicted successful extubation in all five patients who were extubated and failure in 20 of 23 who could not be extubated (sensitivity 100%; specificity 87%). The respiratory rate to tidal volume ratio predicted extubation in only two of five extubated patients and failure in only 12 of 23 (sensitivity 40%; specificity 52%). The authors conclude the oxygen cost of breathing was the more reliable predictor of both successful extubation and failure in this prolonged-ventilation group.
cards.watchOut: Only five successful extubations anchor the 100% sensitivity, in one surgical ICU's prolonged-ventilation population; the record does not print the actual oxygen-cost values or the cut-off used, so none is quoted on this shelf. A prediction result, not evidence that lowering the cost changes outcomes.

cards.headline: Shikora 1992 (physiology classic, N=8 patients — sub-10, labelled): raising pressure support steadily cut the oxygen cost of breathing from 22% to 8% of total VO2 (9 studies in 8 patients)
cards.summary: Shikora 1992 (physiology classic, N=8 patients — sub-10, labelled): raising pressure support steadily cut the oxygen cost of breathing from 22% to 8% of total VO2 (9 studies in 8 patients)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (pressure-support titration, N=8 — labelled classic)
cards.people: Eight ventilator-dependent patients in a surgical ICU whose weaning was limited by inability to sustain respiratory work, studied on nine occasions — N printed plainly: below the library's usual 10-human floor, carded only as a labelled physiology classic alongside the larger studies, per the physiology carve-out. Oxygen cost of breathing, tidal volume, respiratory rate and minute ventilation were measured at various levels of pressure support ventilation; the cost was calculated from the difference in oxygen consumption between mechanical and spontaneous ventilation.
cards.result: With increasing levels of pressure support, the oxygen cost of breathing steadily decreased from 22% to 8% of total oxygen consumption (p<0.001), with statistically significant increases in tidal volume and decreases in respiratory rate; minute ventilation was not influenced. The authors propose bedside oxygen-cost measurement as a method for titrating pressure support to optimise respiratory work.
cards.watchOut: Eight patients, nine studies, one centre, 1992 equipment — the 22% starting figure describes patients already failing to sustain respiratory work, not ordinary ventilated patients. Carded for the dose–response demonstration (unloading the muscles lowers their oxygen claim), not as a prevalence estimate.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a few percent at rest in health, a major claimant under load — ESTABLISHED; two classic anchors were refused at build and that refusal is recorded here
cards.summary: Synthesis: a few percent at rest in health, a major claimant under load — ESTABLISHED; two classic anchors were refused at build and that refusal is recorded here
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Kress 1999 (group sizes not documented in the fetched record), Donahoe 1989 (26 subjects), Shikora 1994 (28 patients) and Shikora 1992 (8 patients, labelled classic). Textbook framing: West's Respiratory Physiology and Nunn's Applied Respiratory Physiology, with Guyton & Hall's account of respiratory muscle metabolism.
cards.result: The measured pattern matches the textbook account. In health at rest the respiratory muscles' claim on oxygen is small (the non-obese control share in Kress was ~1.6 mL/min of a 221.4 mL/min total VO2; Donahoe's controls paid 1.23 mL O2 per litre of added ventilation). The claim rises exactly where the textbooks predict: with inefficiency (malnourished COPD paid 4.28 mL O2/L, 3.5-fold the control cost), with load at rest (morbid obesity: ~57 mL/min, about 16% of total VO2 by the records' absolute values), and at the edge of weaning failure (an oxygen cost high enough to predict failure with 87% specificity, and titratable down from 22% to 8% by pressure support in failing patients). REFUSALS RECORDED: two slate anchors were not carded. The fetched record for McGregor & Becklake (J Clin Invest 1961; PMID: 13773979) carried no abstract this session, and no verifiable abstract record for Campbell, Westlake & Cherniack (J Appl Physiol 1957) could be fetched this session; under the physiology build rules an anchor whose abstract is empty or unverifiable is refused, so no numbers from either classic appear anywhere on this shelf, and their textbook-era values are presented only as the textbooks' account in the framing above.
cards.watchOut: Two different metrics run through this shelf — fractional share of total VO2 and oxygen cost per litre of ventilation — and the cards keep them separate; merging them into one 'cost of breathing' number would be an error. All measurements come from small physiology-laboratory or single-ICU cohorts.

shelves.title: Sodium oxybate in paediatric narcolepsy: the child slice of the oxybate programme
shelves.question: In children and adolescents aged 7-16 with narcolepsy and cataplexy, does sodium oxybate, versus placebo (randomised withdrawal), maintain control of cataplexy and sleepiness?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Narcolepsy/drug therapy · Prospective Studies · Sodium Oxybate/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Withholding Treatment
shelves.balance: This is the paediatric slice of the oxybate question; the adult programme is homed at Shelf #921 (read alongside this shelf) and is not re-carded here. Within its own programme, the evidence is one trial in three reports: Plazzi 2018 randomised 63 stabilised children to continue oxybate or switch to placebo, and withdrawal cost a median 12.7 extra cataplexy attacks per week within 2 weeks (versus 0.3 on continued treatment, p<0.0001) — a maintenance effect in responders, shown by a withdrawal design, not an initiation effect. The open-label extension (95 entered) maintained control for up to a year, and a BMI report found percentiles falling over the first year before plateauing — in growing children, a monitoring signal as much as a benefit. The burden is real: enuresis in 21% of oxybate-naive children, nausea in 22%, twice-nightly dosing of a controlled substance. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, capped by the single-programme rule on the same precedent as Shelf #921 itself.

cards.headline: Plazzi 2018 (randomised-withdrawal RCT, 63 randomised): children switched to placebo gained a median 12.7 extra cataplexy attacks per week versus 0.3 on continued sodium oxybate (p<0.0001); enuresis in 21% of oxybate-naive children
cards.summary: Plazzi 2018 (randomised-withdrawal RCT, 63 randomised): children switched to placebo gained a median 12.7 extra cataplexy attacks per week versus 0.3 on continued sodium oxybate (p<0.0001); enuresis in 21% of oxybate-naive children
cards.type: Double-blind placebo-controlled randomised-withdrawal trial — N = 106 enrolled, 63 randomised
cards.people: Children and adolescents aged 7-16 with narcolepsy with cataplexy at 30 sites in 5 countries, either already taking sodium oxybate or oxybate-naive (titrated to an optimal dose); after a stable-dose period, 63 were randomised to continue oxybate (n=31) or switch to placebo (n=32) for 2 weeks, followed by open-label treatment for up to 1 year.
cards.result: Weekly cataplexy attacks rose by a median of 12.7 attacks (Q1, Q3: 3.4, 19.8) in children withdrawn to placebo versus 0.3 attacks (-1.0, 2.5) in those continuing oxybate (p<0.0001); a preplanned interim analysis (p=0.0002) stopped the placebo arm early on the data safety monitoring board's guidance. Common adverse events in oxybate-naive children included enuresis (15 of 72, 21%), nausea (16 of 72, 22%) and vomiting.
cards.watchOut: A randomised-withdrawal design measures maintenance in children already stabilised on the drug — it shows that stopping loses control, not how much starting helps a new patient, and the early stop for efficacy, while ethical, truncates the blinded contrast at 63 randomised children. This is one programme, not a literature.

cards.headline: Lecendreux 2022 (open-label extension of the same programme, 95 entered): cataplexy control and sleepiness scores were maintained for up to 47 further weeks; enuresis, nausea, vomiting, headache and decreased weight/appetite were the commonest events
cards.summary: Lecendreux 2022 (open-label extension of the same programme, 95 entered): cataplexy control and sleepiness scores were maintained for up to 47 further weeks; enuresis, nausea, vomiting, headache and decreased weight/appetite were the commonest events
cards.type: Open-label long-term extension report (same trial programme) — N = 106 enrolled, 95 entered the open-label period, 85 completed it
cards.people: The same children and adolescents (aged 7-16, narcolepsy with cataplexy) from the randomised-withdrawal study, entering an open-label sodium oxybate period of up to 47 weeks after the blinded phase, with cataplexy attacks, cataplexy-free days and the Epworth Sleepiness Scale for Children and Adolescents (ESS-CHAD) as efficacy measures.
cards.result: Efficacy established before the blinded phase was maintained through the open-label period: median change in weekly cataplexy attacks from the stable-dose period to the end of the open-label period was 0.0 in both oxybate-naive and previously treated participants, and ESS-CHAD changes were likewise 0.0 and 1.0. Cataplexy-free days per week rose from a median 2.3 in week 1 to 3.8 in week 48. Treatment-emergent adverse events in at least 5% included enuresis, nausea, vomiting, headache, decreased weight, decreased appetite, nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infection and dizziness.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and uncontrolled: maintenance in children who stayed on a drug they were already tolerating is the expected pattern under several explanations besides drug effect, and 20 of 106 enrolled children did not complete the extension. It supports durability and longer-term tolerability; it is not a second efficacy trial.
cards.source: Lecendreux M et al. Long-term safety and maintenance of efficacy of sodium oxybate in the treatment of narcolepsy with cataplexy in pediatric patients. J Clin Sleep Med. 2022. cards.headline: Dauvilliers 2024 (BMI report, same programme): BMI percentile fell over the first year on sodium oxybate — in oxybate-naive children of normal weight, from a median 77.0 to 35.0 — then plateaued
cards.summary: Dauvilliers 2024 (BMI report, same programme): BMI percentile fell over the first year on sodium oxybate — in oxybate-naive children of normal weight, from a median 77.0 to 35.0 — then plateaued
cards.type: Randomised-withdrawal trial programme report on body mass index (same trial programme) — population as in the parent study
cards.people: Children and adolescents aged 7-16 with narcolepsy with cataplexy from the same study (oxybate-naive children titrated to twice-nightly dosing, and children already on oxybate at entry), followed through the open-label period to week 52 and an optional 1-2 year continuation, with BMI percentile categories tracked.
cards.result: Median BMI percentile decreased from baseline to week 52 in oxybate-naive participants who were normal weight at baseline (77.0 to 35.0) and in those overweight or obese at baseline (98.0 to 86.7); decreases were smaller in children already taking oxybate at entry. Category shifts included 9 of 10 overweight oxybate-naive children becoming normal weight, while a small number moved the other way (1 of 16 normal-weight children became obese). Decreases plateaued after about 1 year.
cards.watchOut: A secondary, descriptive analysis of the same single programme: BMI falls in growing children with narcolepsy may reflect the drug, the disease's own weight trajectory, or increased activity with better sleep — the design cannot separate them, and in children a falling BMI percentile is a monitoring signal (growth and nutrition), not automatically a benefit.
cards.source: Dauvilliers Y et al. Effect of sodium oxybate on body mass index in pediatric patients with narcolepsy. J Clin Sleep Med. 2024. PMID: 37942930. Registry ID: NCT02221869, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Dronabinol in obstructive sleep apnoea (PACE): an AHI signal the specialty academy advises against acting on
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe OSA, does dronabinol at bedtime, versus placebo, reduce the apnoea-hypopnoea index?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic/therapeutic use · Body Mass Index · Disorders of Excessive Somnolence/drug therapy · Dronabinol/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Lung · Male · Middle Aged · Pilot Projects · Sleep/drug effects · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive/drug therapy · Wakefulness/drug effects · Young Adult
shelves.balance: The signal is real and the shelf still lands low. PACE (n=73, the only randomised trial) found dronabinol lowered the apnoea-hypopnoea index by 10.7 events/hour at 2.5 mg and 12.9 at 10 mg versus placebo over 6 weeks, with self-reported sleepiness improved at the higher dose — but overnight oxygenation and objectively measured wakefulness did not change, and AHI is a surrogate for the outcomes that matter. The only other human data are a 17-patient uncontrolled pilot from the same group. Against that base, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2018 position statement — carded on the face, as it must be — advises that medical cannabis and its synthetic extracts should not be used to treat OSA. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): one small trial, one surrogate endpoint, one programme, and the specialty academy formally against.

cards.headline: PACE 2018 (phase 2 RCT, N = 73): dronabinol lowered AHI by 10.7 (2.5 mg) and 12.9 (10 mg) events/hour versus placebo at 6 weeks — but oxygenation and objective alertness were unchanged (the treatment made no difference to either)
cards.summary: PACE 2018 (phase 2 RCT, N = 73): dronabinol lowered AHI by 10.7 (2.5 mg) and 12.9 (10 mg) events/hour versus placebo at 6 weeks — but oxygenation and objective alertness were unchanged (the treatment made no difference to either)
cards.type: Phase 2 double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial — N = 73
cards.people: 73 adults with moderate or severe obstructive sleep apnoea (baseline AHI 25.9 +/- 11.3; mean age 53.6 years; mean BMI 33.4) randomised to placebo (n=25), dronabinol 2.5 mg (n=21) or dronabinol 10 mg (n=27) taken 1 hour before bedtime for up to 6 weeks.
cards.result: Dronabinol dose-dependently reduced AHI versus placebo by 10.7 +/- 4.4 events/hour at 2.5 mg (p=.02) and 12.9 +/- 4.3 at 10 mg (p=.003). At 10 mg, the Epworth Sleepiness Scale fell by 3.8 points from baseline and by 2.3 points versus placebo (p=.05). Maintenance of Wakefulness Test latencies, gross sleep architecture and overnight oxygenation parameters were unchanged in any group (the treatment made no difference to objective alertness or oxygenation). Adverse-event number and severity and adherence were equivalent across groups, and satisfaction was highest at 10 mg (p=.04).
cards.watchOut: AHI is a surrogate: a 13-event fall that leaves oxygenation and objectively measured wakefulness untouched has not been shown to prevent the cardiovascular or sleepiness outcomes that make OSA matter. Seventy-three patients, 6 weeks, one trial — and the field's own academy advises against use (card below).
cards.source: Carley DW et al. Pharmacotherapy of apnea by cannabimimetic enhancement, the PACE clinical trial: effects of dronabinol in obstructive sleep apnea. Sleep. 2018. PMID: 29121334. Registry ID: NCT01755091, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Prasad 2013 (proof-of-concept pilot, N = 17): AHI fell by 14.1 +/- 17.5 events/hour after 21 days of dose-escalated dronabinol (p=0.007) — single-centre, uncontrolled dose escalation
cards.summary: Prasad 2013 (proof-of-concept pilot, N = 17): AHI fell by 14.1 +/- 17.5 events/hour after 21 days of dose-escalated dronabinol (p=0.007) — single-centre, uncontrolled dose escalation
cards.type: Single-centre open-label dose-escalation pilot study — N = 17
cards.people: 17 adults with OSA (baseline AHI at least 15/hour) studied after a 7-day CPAP washout, receiving dronabinol starting at 2.5 mg daily and escalating weekly as tolerated to 5 mg then 10 mg, with polysomnography at baseline and on treatment nights 7, 14 and 21.
cards.result: Change in AHI from baseline to night 21 was -14.1 +/- 17.5 events/hour (p=0.007). No degradation of sleep architecture and no serious adverse events were noted at doses of 2.5-10 mg daily over the short term.
cards.watchOut: Seventeen patients, no control group, 3 weeks: the standard deviation (17.5) is larger than the mean effect, CPAP washout itself changes the baseline, and night-to-night AHI variability is notorious. This pilot justified the PACE trial; it is not independent confirmation of it, coming from the same investigative group.
cards.source: Prasad B et al. Proof of concept trial of dronabinol in obstructive sleep apnea. Front Psychiatry. 2013. PMID: 23346060. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.summary: AASM position statement 2018: medical cannabis and its synthetic extracts should NOT be used to treat OSA — unreliable delivery, insufficient evidence of effectiveness, tolerability and safety
cards.type: Professional-society position statement (American Academy of Sleep Medicine) — not a trial
cards.people: Issued by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine in 2018, reviewing the same early evidence base carded above (small pilot and proof-of-concept studies of dronabinol) for adults with obstructive sleep apnoea.
cards.result: The AASM position is that medical cannabis and/or its synthetic extracts should not be used for the treatment of OSA, because of unreliable delivery methods and insufficient evidence of effectiveness, tolerability and safety; it recommends OSA be excluded from state medical cannabis programme condition lists, and notes dronabinol is not FDA-approved for OSA, that cannabinoid composition in medical cannabis varies significantly and is unregulated, and that somnolence was reported in most patients in the early studies.
cards.watchOut: A position statement is guidance, not data — it is carded because the question's own specialty academy has formally advised against the intervention on this evidence base, and a shelf that printed only the positive AHI numbers would mislead. Its 2018 date means it predates nothing material here: PACE (carded above) is the trial it was written around, and no larger trial has followed in the record.
cards.source: Ramar K et al. Medical cannabis and the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine position statement. J Clin Sleep Med. 2018. PMID: 29609727. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small positive trial on a surrogate endpoint, one 17-patient pilot from the same group, and the specialty academy formally against — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small positive trial on a surrogate endpoint, one 17-patient pilot from the same group, and the specialty academy formally against — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: 73 randomised patients (PACE) and 17 pilot patients, all from one investigative programme, plus the AASM position statement on that same base.
cards.result: AHI fell by 10.7-12.9 events/hour versus placebo at 6 weeks in PACE, with self-reported sleepiness improved at 10 mg; objective alertness and oxygenation did not change (the treatment made no difference to either). No trial reports cardiovascular events, accidents, or durable sleepiness benefit. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a genuine pharmacological signal on a surrogate, in a thin single-programme base, against an explicit specialty-society recommendation not to use it.
cards.watchOut: Dronabinol is a defined pharmaceutical product; the AASM statement's warning about variable, unregulated cannabis preparations applies with full force to any read-across from this shelf to cannabis products generally. Positive airway pressure remains the effective standard treatment for OSA.
cards.source: Synthesis of Carley DW et al. 2018 (PMID: 29121334), Prasad B et al. 2013 (PMID: 23346060) and Ramar K et al. 2018 (PMID: 29609727), all carded above.

shelves.title: Dipyridamole in restless legs syndrome: a blinded positive from a single small programme
shelves.question: In adults with idiopathic RLS, does dipyridamole, versus placebo, reduce RLS severity (IRLS) and periodic limb movements?
shelves.mesh: Adenosine · Dipyridamole/administration & dosage · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Phosphodiesterase Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Polysomnography · Prospective Studies · Restless Legs Syndrome/drug therapy · Sleep Stages · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One Madrid group has built the whole record, and it is coherent but small. An open-label study (n=15) showed IRLS falling from 23.4 to 10.7 over 8 weeks; the double-blind crossover trial that followed (n=28, 2-week limbs) confirmed a real short-term effect under blinding — IRLS 11.1 on dipyridamole versus 18.7 on placebo (p<0.001), with periodic leg movements also sharply lower (index 8.2 versus 28.1). A 2025 post-hoc analysis of the same patients adds the key fence: those previously treated with dopaminergic drugs responded significantly worse, so the headline effect belongs mainly to untreated RLS. The adenosine hypothesis framing is the investigators' own and is labelled as such. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — total evidence base 43 patients, one centre, no long-term or comparative data.

cards.headline: Garcia-Borreguero 2018 (open-label study, N = 15): IRLS fell from 23.4 to 10.7 over 8 weeks on dipyridamole, and periodic leg movement index from 26.7 to 4.3 — uncontrolled, labelled as such
cards.summary: Garcia-Borreguero 2018 (open-label study, N = 15): IRLS fell from 23.4 to 10.7 over 8 weeks on dipyridamole, and periodic leg movement index from 26.7 to 4.3 — uncontrolled, labelled as such
cards.type: Prospective open-label uncontrolled clinical trial (observational design — labelled as such) — N = 15 enrolled, 13 completed
cards.people: 15 untreated patients with idiopathic restless legs syndrome at a single Madrid centre, starting dipyridamole 100 mg with up-titration to 400 mg if necessary (mean effective dose 281.8 mg/day at 8 weeks), with severity rated on the IRLS and CGI and polysomnography at baseline and 8 weeks.
cards.result: Mean IRLS improved from 23.4 (+/-4.6) at baseline to 10.7 (+/-4.5) at 8 weeks; 6 of 13 completers were full responders (at least 50% IRLS improvement) and 4 were partial responders. Mean periodic leg movement index fell from 26.7 (+/-7.2) to 4.3 (+/-1.9), and sleep variables improved. Main side effects were abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, dizziness and flushing. The authors classify this as class III evidence.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no comparator in a condition with large placebo and expectancy effects: this study's job was to justify the randomised trial carded next, and its effect size should be expected to shrink under blinding — it did (compare the crossover card). The adenosine hypothesis framing is the investigators' own hypothesis, labelled as such on this shelf.
cards.source: Garcia-Borreguero D et al. Treatment of restless legs syndrome/Willis-Ekbom disease with the non-selective ENT1/ENT2 inhibitor dipyridamole: testing the adenosine hypothesis. Sleep Med. 2018. PMID: 29680437. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Garcia-Borreguero 2021 (double-blind crossover RCT, N = 28): IRLS fell to 11.1 on dipyridamole versus 18.7 on placebo after 2 weeks (p<0.001); periodic leg movement index 8.2 versus 28.1
cards.summary: Garcia-Borreguero 2021 (double-blind crossover RCT, N = 28): IRLS fell to 11.1 on dipyridamole versus 18.7 on placebo after 2 weeks (p<0.001); periodic leg movement index 8.2 versus 28.1
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial — N = 29 recruited, 28 analysed
cards.people: 28 untreated patients with idiopathic restless legs syndrome receiving dipyridamole (up-titrated to a possible 300 mg; mean effective dose 217.8 mg/day) and placebo in random order for 2 weeks each, with weekly IRLS ratings and polysomnography after each phase.
cards.result: IRLS fell from 24.1 (+/-3.1) at baseline to 11.1 (+/-2.3) at the end of the dipyridamole phase, versus 23.7 (+/-3.4) to 18.7 (+/-3.2) on placebo (p<0.001). CGI, sleep-scale and immobilisation-test scores all improved (p<0.001), as did sleep variables; mean periodic leg movement index was 8.2 (+/-3.5) on dipyridamole versus 28.1 (+/-6.7) on placebo. Side effects on dipyridamole versus placebo included abdominal distension (18% versus 7%), dizziness (10.7% versus 7.1%), diarrhoea and asthenia (each 7.1% versus 3.6%).
cards.watchOut: Two-week treatment limbs in 28 patients at one centre: enough to show a short-term symptomatic effect, not durability, augmentation risk, or performance in the previously treated patients who dominate real RLS clinics — and the next card shows prior dopaminergic treatment blunting exactly this response.
cards.source: Garcia-Borreguero D et al. A randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study with dipyridamole for restless legs syndrome. Mov Disord. 2021. PMID: 34137476. Registry ID: EudraCT 2017-004580-12, from the record's databank fields.
