cards.headline: Garcia-Borreguero 2025 (post-hoc analysis of the crossover trials): patients previously treated with dopaminergic drugs responded significantly worse to dipyridamole than dopamine-naive patients
cards.summary: Garcia-Borreguero 2025 (post-hoc analysis of the crossover trials): patients previously treated with dopaminergic drugs responded significantly worse to dipyridamole than dopamine-naive patients
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of two randomised crossover trials (the dipyridamole trial carded above and a suvorexant trial) — dipyridamole limb N = 28
cards.people: The 28 dipyridamole-trial patients (10 previously treated with dopaminergic drugs, 18 dopamine-naive) and 40 suvorexant-trial patients, none meeting criteria for augmentation, re-analysed by prior dopaminergic exposure after a 2-week washout; the dipyridamole findings are the ones carded here.
cards.result: Compared with dopamine-naive patients, previously dopaminergic-treated patients responded significantly worse to dipyridamole on the IRLS, CGI-Severity, immobilisation-test and periodic-leg-movement measures; sleep parameters did not differ. The authors interpret this as prior long-term dopaminergic treatment inducing changes that impair later responses even before clinical augmentation appears.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc, small subgroups (10 versus 18), and the same 28 patients as the trial above — this is a refinement of the programme's own data, not independent evidence, and the suvorexant limb belongs to a different drug question. It matters clinically because it fences the headline result to largely untreated patients.
cards.source: Garcia-Borreguero D et al. Subclinical augmentation in relation to previous dopaminergic treatment in patients with restless legs syndrome: a post hoc analysis of two randomized, placebo-controlled, crossover trials. cards.headline: Synthesis: one centre, one group, 43 patients in total — a large short-term effect in untreated RLS that prior dopaminergic treatment appears to blunt — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: one centre, one group, 43 patients in total — a large short-term effect in untreated RLS that prior dopaminergic treatment appears to blunt — POSSIBLE
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: 43 patients across the programme's reports (15 open-label + 28 in the crossover trial; the 2025 post-hoc re-analyses the same 28).
cards.result: Blinded result: IRLS 11.1 on dipyridamole versus 18.7 on placebo at 2 weeks (p<0.001), with periodic leg movement index 8.2 versus 28.1. Open-label results were larger, as expected without blinding. Post-hoc: prior dopaminergic treatment significantly blunted response. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a properly blinded positive trial, but single-centre, single-group, 2-week limbs, and a total evidence base of 43 patients; the adenosine mechanism is the investigators' hypothesis, not an established account of RLS.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here addresses long-term use, augmentation on dipyridamole itself, or comparison against iron, gabapentinoids or dopaminergic standards; iron treatment for RLS is a separate shelf. Dipyridamole's homes elsewhere in this library (stroke prevention, coronary physiology) are different questions and are not evidence here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Garcia-Borreguero D et al. 2018 (PMID: 29680437), Garcia-Borreguero D et al. 2021 (PMID: 34137476) and Garcia-Borreguero D et al. 2025 (PMID: 40467956), all carded above.

shelves.title: Pharyngeal critical closing pressure (Pcrit) in sleep: −13 cmH₂O in normal sleepers, climbing through zero into apnea — with loop gain and arousal threshold as the other dials
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how collapsible is the upper airway during sleep — what is the pharyngeal critical closing pressure (Pcrit) in normal sleepers versus snorers and patients with sleep apnoea, and how large are ventilatory loop gain and arousal threshold in health?
shelves.mesh: Sleep Apnea Syndromes · Pharynx · Airway Obstruction · Respiration · Sleep · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for Pcrit as the measured index of upper-airway collapsibility, framed by Boron & Boulpaep / Ganong and Kryger (sleep physiology). The gradient is concordant across independent preparations: in natural NREM sleep, Pcrit was −13.3 ± 3.2 cmH₂O in 7 normal subjects (Schwartz), rising to −6.5 ± 2.7 in snorers, −1.6 ± 1.4 in obstructive hypopnea and +2.5 ± 1.5 in obstructive apnea (Gleadhill) — the airway becomes self-closing as Pcrit crosses zero. In the anaesthetised, paralysed passive pharynx (Isono), velopharyngeal closing pressure showed the same ordering at higher absolute values (−3.77 ± 3.44 normal vs +0.90 and +2.78 in sleep-disordered breathing), because that preparation removes neuromuscular compensation — values are carded per protocol and never merged. The phenotyping limb (Eckert/Wellman, 75 studied) qualifies the anatomy story: OSA Pcrit averaged +0.3 vs −6.2 cmH₂O in controls, but 36% of patients had high loop gain, 37% a low arousal threshold, and 19% obstructed with a near-normal Pcrit. The OSA treatment shelves ask different questions.

cards.headline: Schwartz 1988: the normal sleeping airway has a Pcrit of −13.3 ± 3.2 cmH₂O — occlusion had to be induced by driving nasal pressure below it (7 normal subjects)
cards.summary: Schwartz 1988: the normal sleeping airway has a Pcrit of −13.3 ± 3.2 cmH₂O — occlusion had to be induced by driving nasal pressure below it (7 normal subjects)
cards.type: Human sleep physiology study (nasal pressure-drop Pcrit in health), J Appl Physiol 1988
cards.people: Seven normal subjects studied during non-rapid-eye-movement (NREM) sleep with varying levels of subatmospheric pressure applied through a nasal mask, relating maximal inspiratory airflow to nasal pressure. Small physiology study: N = 7 printed on the face.
cards.result: Maximal inspiratory airflow fell in proportion to nasal pressure, and when nasal pressure fell below the critical closing pressure (Pcrit), subjects developed upper-airway occlusions terminated by arousals. In these normal sleepers the upper-airway Pcrit was −13.3 ± 3.2 (SD) cmH₂O — deeply negative, i.e. the healthy airway stays open unless upstream pressure is driven far below atmospheric. In the four subjects who stayed asleep with nasal pressure below Pcrit, recurrent occlusive apneas were demonstrated, and the Pcrit read off the airflow–pressure regression at the zero-flow intercept matched the experimentally observed value.
cards.watchOut: N = 7, NREM sleep, one laboratory's pressure-drop protocol — the reference value for the method, not a universal constant across protocols (see the Isono card's different, anaesthetised preparation).
cards.source: Schwartz AR, Smith PL, Wise RA, Gold AR, Permutt S. Induction of upper airway occlusion in sleeping individuals with subatmospheric nasal pressure. Journal of Applied Physiology. 1988. PMID: 3372411. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Gleadhill 1991: Pcrit climbs a continuum — snorers −6.5 ± 2.7, obstructive hypopnea −1.6 ± 1.4, obstructive apnea +2.5 ± 1.5 cmH₂O
cards.summary: Gleadhill 1991: Pcrit climbs a continuum — snorers −6.5 ± 2.7, obstructive hypopnea −1.6 ± 1.4, obstructive apnea +2.5 ± 1.5 cmH₂O
cards.type: Human sleep physiology study (Pcrit across the snoring–apnea spectrum), Am Rev Respir Dis 1991
cards.people: 10 asymptomatic snorers, 6 patients with obstructive hypopneas and 10 patients with obstructive apneas, studied during NREM sleep with Pcrit derived from the relationship between maximal inspiratory airflow and nasal pressure (the Schwartz pressure-drop method).
cards.result: Pcrit rose stepwise across the spectrum: −6.5 ± 2.7 cmH₂O in snorers, −1.6 ± 1.4 in obstructive hypopnea and +2.5 ± 1.5 in obstructive apnea (mean ± SD, P < 0.001) — in apnea the airway closes at a positive pressure, i.e. it closes on its own at atmospheric pressure. Higher Pcrit was associated with lower maximal inspiratory airflow during tidal breathing in sleep (P < 0.005). Small differences in collapsibility along a continuum thus separate normal snoring from hypopnea and apnea — there is no threshold jump, there is a gradient.
cards.watchOut: Groups of 10, 6 and 10; the gradient is the finding, and its absolute values belong to this laboratory's NREM pressure-drop protocol.
cards.source: Gleadhill IC, Schwartz AR, Schubert N, Wise RA, Permutt S, Smith PL. Upper airway collapsibility in snorers and in patients with obstructive hypopnea and apnea. cards.headline: Isono 1997: in the paralysed passive pharynx, velopharyngeal closing pressure was −3.77 ± 3.44 cmH₂O in normal subjects versus +0.90 and +2.78 in sleep-disordered breathing — and the velopharynx is where the airway closes
cards.summary: Isono 1997: in the paralysed passive pharynx, velopharyngeal closing pressure was −3.77 ± 3.44 cmH₂O in normal subjects versus +0.90 and +2.78 in sleep-disordered breathing — and the velopharynx is where the airway closes
cards.type: Human physiology study (passive pharynx mechanics under anaesthesia/paralysis), J Appl Physiol 1997
cards.people: 57 subjects under general anaesthesia with complete paralysis, divided by nocturnal oximetry into a normal group (n = 17), and two sleep-disordered-breathing groups (SDB-1, n = 18; SDB-2, n = 22), matched for age and body-mass index; the static pressure–area relationship of the passive pharynx was quantified segment by segment.
cards.result: The primary closure site was the velopharynx in 49 subjects and the oropharynx in only 8, with no difference in distribution between groups. Velopharyngeal closing pressure was −3.77 ± 3.44 cmH₂O in normal subjects, significantly lower than in SDB-1 (0.90 ± 1.34) and SDB-2 (2.78 ± 2.78) (P < 0.01), and maximal velopharyngeal area was larger in normals (2.10 ± 0.85 cm²) than in SDB-1 (1.15 ± 0.46) and SDB-2 (1.06 ± 0.75). Velopharyngeal closing pressure was the only mechanical variable highly correlated with the oxygen desaturation index. The passive pharynx is thus narrower and more collapsible in sleep-apneic patients — measured here with muscle activity abolished, which is why its normal closing pressure (−3.8) sits well above the sleeping, muscle-intact Schwartz value (−13.3): protocol is part of the number.
cards.watchOut: Anaesthetised and paralysed by design — this is the passive anatomical limb of collapsibility, deliberately stripped of the neuromuscular compensation that operates in natural sleep; do not merge its closing pressures with sleep Pcrit values.
cards.source: Isono S, Remmers JE, Tanaka A, Sho Y, Sato J, Nishino T. Anatomy of pharynx in patients with obstructive sleep apnea and in normal subjects. Journal of Applied Physiology. 1997. cards.headline: Eckert & Wellman 2013: phenotyping 75 people — OSA airways averaged Pcrit +0.3 versus −6.2 cmH₂O in controls, but 36% of patients had high loop gain and 37% a low arousal threshold, and 19% had a fairly non-collapsible airway
cards.summary: Eckert & Wellman 2013: phenotyping 75 people — OSA airways averaged Pcrit +0.3 versus −6.2 cmH₂O in controls, but 36% of patients had high loop gain and 37% a low arousal threshold, and 19% had a fairly non-collapsible airway
cards.type: Human sleep physiology study (OSA trait phenotyping: Pcrit, loop gain, arousal threshold), Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2013
cards.people: 75 men and women with and without obstructive sleep apnea, aged 20–65, studied on three nights: polysomnography, then measurement of anatomic (passive Pcrit) and non-anatomic traits — genioglossus muscle responsiveness, arousal threshold and respiratory control stability (loop gain).
cards.result: Traits varied substantially. Overall the OSA airway was more collapsible (Pcrit 0.3 [−1.5 to 1.9] vs −6.2 [−12.4 to −3.6] cmH₂O in controls, P < 0.01), yet 19% of patients had a relatively non-collapsible airway (Pcrit −2 to −5 cmH₂O) similar to many controls — and in those patients loop gain was almost twice as high as in patients with Pcrit above −2 (−5.9 vs −3.2 in the record's signed dimensionless presentation, P = 0.01). Among patients, 36% had minimal genioglossus responsiveness, 37% a low arousal threshold, 36% high loop gain and 28% multiple non-anatomic features; the authors estimate non-anatomic traits play an important role in 56% of OSA. Collapsibility is therefore one dial among several, and in a fifth of patients it is barely abnormal at all.
cards.watchOut: A phenotyping framework measured in a research sleep laboratory over three nights; loop-gain and arousal-threshold values are method-defined traits, not routine clinical measurements.
cards.source: Eckert DJ, White DP, Jordan AS, Malhotra A, Wellman A. Defining phenotypic causes of obstructive sleep apnea. Identification of novel therapeutic targets. American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine. 2013. PMID: 23721582. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the healthy airway closes only far below atmospheric pressure; disease is Pcrit climbing through zero — with loop gain and arousal threshold deciding who actually obstructs
cards.summary: Synthesis: the healthy airway closes only far below atmospheric pressure; disease is Pcrit climbing through zero — with loop gain and arousal threshold deciding who actually obstructs
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human records above (the Schwartz pressure-drop programme, the Gleadhill spectrum study, the Isono passive-pharynx programme and the Eckert/Wellman phenotyping cohort), framed by Boron & Boulpaep / Ganong on upper-airway mechanics in sleep and by Kryger's sleep-medicine account as framing.
cards.result: The Pcrit gradient is the settled core, concordant across two independent preparations: in natural NREM sleep the normal airway's Pcrit is deeply negative (−13.3 ± 3.2 cmH₂O), snorers sit at −6.5, hypopnea at −1.6 and apnea at +2.5 — the airway becomes self-closing as Pcrit crosses zero; in the paralysed passive pharynx the same ordering appears at higher absolute pressures (normals −3.8, disordered breathing +0.9 to +2.8 cmH₂O), because the preparation removes neuromuscular compensation — protocol is part of every Pcrit number, and this shelf never merges values across protocols. The phenotyping limb adds the modern qualification: Pcrit is one trait among several — loop gain and arousal threshold are abnormal in roughly a third of patients each, and about a fifth of patients obstruct despite a near-normal Pcrit, driven by those non-anatomic traits. Textbook framing (Boron & Boulpaep / Ganong; Kryger for the sleep context) presents the pharynx as a Starling resistor whose closing pressure is set by surrounding tissue pressure and wall compliance — the carded human measurements are that model's numbers. The OSA treatment shelves (CPAP, stimulation, myofunctional therapy) ask what to do about a collapsible airway; this shelf asks how collapsible it measurably is.
cards.watchOut: Pcrit values are protocol-bound (natural sleep vs anaesthesia/paralysis, nasal-mask pressure drops vs static pressure–area curves); the gradient across health and disease is the portable finding, not any single absolute value.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 3372411, 2048817, 9104871, 23721582), with Boron & Boulpaep, Ganong and Kryger textbook framing. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: The diaphragmatic tension-time index: above a critical zone of about 0.15-0.20 the human diaphragm fatigues — measured in small classic loaded-breathing experiments
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how does the tension-time index of the diaphragm (mean transdiaphragmatic pressure per breath as a fraction of maximum, multiplied by the inspiratory duty cycle) determine whether the diaphragm fatigues — what is the critical threshold above which fatigue is inevitable, and how was it measured?
shelves.mesh: Diaphragm/physiology · Humans · Male · Muscle Contraction · Pressure · Thorax/physiology · Time Factors · Adult · Electromyography · Inspiratory Capacity · Muscle Relaxation · Respiration · Tidal Volume · Abdominal Muscles/physiology · Immobilization · Movement · Physical Endurance · Physical Exertion · Ribs/physiology · Work of Breathing · Diaphragm/physiopathology · Lung Diseases, Obstructive/metabolism,physiopathology · Methods · Middle Aged · Pulmonary Ventilation · Rest
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the existence and approximate location of a diaphragmatic fatigue threshold, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology on respiratory-muscle energetics and blood-flow limitation. The tension-time index of the diaphragm (TTdi) is the mean transdiaphragmatic pressure per breath as a fraction of maximum, multiplied by the inspiratory duty cycle (TI/Ttot). In the founding experiment (4 normal subjects), the pattern that could be sustained beyond 45 minutes had a TTdi of about 0.15 — the critical TTdi — and above it, endurance time fell steeply as TTdi rose, consistent with diaphragmatic blood-flow limitation; textbook accounts (Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep framing) commonly quote the critical zone as about 0.15-0.18, and the upper part of that range is the textbook's account, not a value the carded records separately confirm. An independent 1983 study (4 male subjects) using relaxation-rate and electromyographic fatigue markers found those markers changed only at TTdi above 0.20 and not below it — bracketing the threshold from the other side. A 1985 exercise study (5 normal young men) adds the necessary caution: with rib-cage restriction, diaphragmatic fatigue occurred during heavy exercise at a TTdi of only 0.06 ± 0.02, which the authors attributed to the higher inspiratory flow rate and breathing frequency — the threshold is a property of the breathing task, not a universal constant. A 1986 critique further showed TTdi values run about 15% higher when the duty cycle is computed from the duration of diaphragmatic tension rather than from inspiratory airflow time. All founding studies are small classics, carded with their Ns on the face under the physiology labelling rule. One classic COPD report was refused as a card because its PubMed record carries no abstract and its claims could not be verified this session (see Synthesis).

cards.headline: Bellemare & Grassino 1982: the critical tension-time index is about 0.15 — patterns above it could not be sustained, endurance falling as TTdi rose (N = 4 normal subjects)
cards.summary: Bellemare & Grassino 1982: the critical tension-time index is about 0.15 — patterns above it could not be sustained, endurance falling as TTdi rose (N = 4 normal subjects)
cards.type: Human physiology experiment (classic, small N — printed on the face)
cards.people: Four normal subjects breathing with constant patterns for 45 minutes or until the target transdiaphragmatic pressure (Pdi) could no longer be sustained; Pdi ranged from 0.15 to 0.90 of maximum and inspiratory duty cycle (TI/Ttot) from 0.15 to 1.0, set by an inspiratory resistance and timing monitored from tidal volume.
cards.result: Endurance time (Tlim) was inversely related to both Pdi and TI/Ttot and therefore to their product, the tension-time index (TTdi), following a quadratic hyperbola. The breathing pattern that could be sustained for more than 45 minutes had a TTdi of about 0.15, termed the critical TTdi; above that value Tlim decreased as a function of TTdi. The authors read the pattern as consistent with Tlim being set by diaphragmatic blood-flow limitation.
cards.watchOut: N = 4 — a founding classic, carded under the physiology labelling rule with its N printed; the 45-minute cut-off defines 'sustainable' operationally, so 0.15 is the threshold for indefinite endurance under these resting, resistive-load conditions, not for every task.
cards.source: Bellemare F, Grassino A. Effect of pressure and timing of contraction on human diaphragm fatigue. J Appl Physiol Respir Environ Exerc Physiol. 1982. PMID: 7174413. cards.headline: Esau and colleagues 1983: relaxation-rate and EMG fatigue markers changed only at TTdi above 0.20, and not below it (N = 4 male subjects)
cards.summary: Esau and colleagues 1983: relaxation-rate and EMG fatigue markers changed only at TTdi above 0.20, and not below it (N = 4 male subjects)
cards.type: Human physiology experiment (classic, small N — printed on the face)
cards.people: Four male subjects in whom transdiaphragmatic pressure and inspiratory duty cycle were varied (tidal volume and total breath duration held constant, inspiratory resistances used to raise Pdi), with maximum relaxation rate and relaxation time constant of Pdi compared against the high-to-low frequency ratio of the diaphragmatic electromyogram.
cards.result: Baseline maximum relaxation rate relative to Pdi was 0.0100 ± 0.0004 per ms and baseline tau 53.2 ± 3.2 ms. At TTdi greater than 0.20, relaxation rate and the EMG high-to-low ratio fell and tau rose, with maximum changes at the highest TTdi; at TTdi less than 0.20 there was no change in any marker. Change in relaxation rate tracked the EMG marker under fatiguing conditions, making it as useful a predictor of diaphragmatic fatigue.
cards.watchOut: N = 4, and its no-change-below / change-above boundary sits at 0.20 rather than 0.15: read together with the founding study, the threshold is a zone (roughly 0.15-0.20 by these markers and tasks), not a single exact number.
cards.source: Esau SA et al. Changes in relaxation rate with diaphragmatic fatigue in humans. J Appl Physiol Respir Environ Exerc Physiol. 1983. PMID: 6863095. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hussain & Pardy 1985: during heavy exercise with rib-cage restriction the diaphragm fatigued at a TTdi of only 0.06 ± 0.02 — below the classic critical value (N = 5 normal young men)
cards.summary: Hussain & Pardy 1985: during heavy exercise with rib-cage restriction the diaphragm fatigued at a TTdi of only 0.06 ± 0.02 — below the classic critical value (N = 5 normal young men)
cards.type: Human physiology experiment (classic, small N — printed on the face)
cards.people: Five normal young men exercising on a cycle ergometer at 80% of maximum power output to exhaustion under three conditions: rib-cage restriction, abdominal-wall restriction (inelastic surgical corset), and no restriction; transdiaphragmatic, oesophageal and gastric pressures and diaphragmatic EMG high-to-low ratio measured, with maximum Pdi before and after exercise.
cards.result: Rib-cage restriction shortened endurance, progressively lowered the EMG high-to-low ratio and significantly reduced maximum Pdi after exercise (diaphragmatic fatigue); abdominal restriction produced none of these changes. The diaphragmatic TTdi in exercise was always less than the critical value of 0.15 from the resistive-loading experiments; the authors suggest the higher inspiratory flow rate and breathing frequency explain fatigue occurring at a TTdi of 0.06 ± 0.02 in this task.
cards.watchOut: N = 5. This card limits the threshold claim: TTdi alone does not fix fatigue risk when flow rate and frequency differ — a boundary condition the textbooks carry, and the reason the shelf states a task-dependent zone rather than a constant.
cards.source: Hussain SN, Pardy RL. Inspiratory muscle function with restrictive chest wall loading during exercise in normal humans. J Appl Physiol. 1985. PMID: 3159717. cards.headline: Roussos and colleagues 1986 (critique): TTdi computed from the duration of diaphragmatic tension runs about 15% higher than TTdi computed from inspiratory airflow time, in normal men and in COPD
cards.summary: Roussos and colleagues 1986 (critique): TTdi computed from the duration of diaphragmatic tension runs about 15% higher than TTdi computed from inspiratory airflow time, in normal men and in COPD
cards.type: Human methods critique (measurement study)
cards.people: Spontaneously breathing normal adult males and age-matched males with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, at rest and during treadmill exercise; TTdi computed both ways — duty cycle as the fraction of the cycle over which diaphragmatic tension is maintained (Tdi/TT) versus the fraction over which inspiratory airflow is maintained (TI/TT). Number of subjects not documented in the record's abstract — printed as such (N not documented).
cards.result: At rest and during exercise in both groups, Tdi/TT exceeded TI/TT, so TTdi values computed from tension duration were greater (P<0.05) than those computed from airflow time — but the difference was relatively small, approximately 15%.
cards.watchOut: A measurement caveat, not a threshold experiment: when comparing TTdi values across studies, the duty-cycle definition must match, or values differ by roughly 15% before any physiology is invoked.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a fatigue threshold zone around TTdi 0.15-0.20 at rest, task-dependent in exercise — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, on small classic studies with Ns printed
cards.summary: Synthesis: a fatigue threshold zone around TTdi 0.15-0.20 at rest, task-dependent in exercise — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, on small classic studies with Ns printed
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: three small human experiments (N = 4, N = 4, N = 5) and one methods critique (N not documented in its record), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology.
cards.result: The tension-time index multiplies how hard the diaphragm works each breath (mean Pdi as a fraction of maximum) by how much of each cycle it spends working (duty cycle). Sustained indefinitely at rest, it must stay near or below about 0.15; fatigue markers appear above about 0.20; between those values lies the practical threshold zone the textbooks quote (their 0.15-0.18 formulation is the textbook account). Exercise with high flow rates can fatigue the diaphragm well below 0.15, so the index predicts fatigue within a task family, not across all breathing. Refusal reported as required: a classic 1984 report on diaphragm fatigue and breathing strategy in COPD was NOT carded because its PubMed record carries no abstract, so its claims could not be verified from its own record this session. The stop-condition for this row was met: a further distinct human report of the threshold (the 1983 relaxation-rate study) was verified from its own record, in addition to the two slate anchors.
cards.watchOut: Animal diaphragm preparations and isolated-muscle tension-time work exist but are not carded: this shelf is human physiology only, per the PHYS rules.

shelves.title: Maximal inspiratory and expiratory mouth pressures: men exceed women, expiratory exceeds inspiratory, values fall with age — weakness begins below 62/83 cmH2O (inspiratory) and 81/109 cmH2O (expiratory)
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are maximal inspiratory and expiratory mouth pressures (MIP/MEP) by age, sex and height — the population reference equations — and where are the lower limits that define respiratory muscle weakness?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aging/physiology · Analysis of Variance · Female · Humans · Italy · Male · Maximal Voluntary Ventilation/physiology · Middle Aged · Mouth/physiology · Reference Values · Regression Analysis · Respiratory Function Tests/methods/statistics & numerical data · Sex Characteristics · Smoking/physiopathology · Aged, 80 and over · Brazil · Maximal Voluntary Ventilation · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Ventilation · Random Allocation · Respiratory Function Tests · Inspiratory Capacity/physiology · Mouth · Respiratory Muscles/physiology · Maximal Respiratory Pressures · Cross-Sectional Studies · Respiratory Insufficiency · Muscle Strength/physiology · Inhalation/physiology · Pressure · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): maximal inspiratory pressure (MIP, measured near residual volume) and maximal expiratory pressure (MEP, near total lung capacity) are the standard volitional tests of respiratory muscle strength, and a value is only interpretable against a reference equation for the person's age, sex and size. The fetched human data are concordant on the pattern and give the numbers. In the population sample of Bruschi 1992 (N = 625), MEP exceeded MIP at matched lung volumes, men's pressures exceeded women's, body surface area was the strongest size correlate, and age added a smaller downward effect; the authors' own conclusion was that pressures are most useful for following change within a patient, with equations as the interpretive frame. Neder 1999 (N = 100, randomly selected) built sex-specific equations in which age and anthropometry explained up to 56% of the variability — and found earlier reference studies systematically underestimated the MIP values actually observed, a warning that equations do not travel unchanged between populations. The Polish cohort of Adamiak-Kardas (N = 166) prints the scale directly: mean PImax/PEmax 60/87.5 cmH2O in women and 73.2/115.9 cmH2O in men. The largest uniform-methodology dataset, Lista-Paz 2023 (N = 610, 14 centres), supplies the weakness cut-offs this shelf exists to state: PImax below 62 cmH2O (women) or 83 cmH2O (men), and PEmax below 81 cmH2O (women) or 109 cmH2O (men), defined as 2.5 SD below the young-adult peak mean. The systematic review (Sclauser Pessoa 2014; meta-analysis n = 840) agrees on direction — MIP higher in men, falling from the 40- to 60-year range onward — while stressing that technique and participant characteristics move the values, which is why this shelf cards equations and cut-offs per study rather than one pooled norm. Inspiratory muscle TRAINING is an intervention question housed on its own shelves; this shelf is the normative measurement underneath it. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Population reference values (N = 625): expiratory pressures exceed inspiratory, men's exceed women's, and body surface area — not age — is the strongest correlate (Bruschi 1992)
cards.summary: Population reference values (N = 625): expiratory pressures exceed inspiratory, men's exceed women's, and body surface area — not age — is the strongest correlate (Bruschi 1992)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population-based reference-values study)
cards.people: 625 clinically and functionally normal subjects (266 men, 359 women) drawn from a sample representative of the general population (Italy); maximal inspiratory pressure measured near residual volume and functional residual capacity, maximal expiratory pressure near total lung capacity and functional residual capacity.
cards.result: MEP (near TLC and FRC) was significantly higher than MIP (near RV and FRC), and pressures in men were significantly higher than in women. MEP at TLC and at FRC were closely related, as were MIP near RV and near FRC. Among body-size variables, body surface area had the highest correlation with all parameters. Stepwise regression equations used body surface area, sex, age and interaction terms; all variables were highly significant but R2 values were relatively low, so much variability remained unexplained. Age's influence was smaller than body surface area's, though age did reduce unexplained variance. The authors conclude MIP/MEP are most useful for monitoring change within each patient, supported by reliable reference equations.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports patterns and equations, not a table of mean pressures — the absolute scale on this shelf comes from the Polish cohort and the 2023 cut-off study; low R2 means an individual value well inside the population spread can still be abnormal for that person, which is why within-patient change carries the authors' endorsement.
cards.source: Bruschi C et al. The American review of respiratory disease. 1992. PMID: 1519865. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sex-specific prediction equations from a randomly selected sample (N = 100): age and anthropometry explained up to 56% of MIP/MEP variability — and earlier studies systematically underestimated observed MIP (Neder 1999)
cards.summary: Sex-specific prediction equations from a randomly selected sample (N = 100): age and anthropometry explained up to 56% of MIP/MEP variability — and earlier studies systematically underestimated observed MIP (Neder 1999)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (reference-values / prediction-equation study)
cards.people: 100 healthy non-smoking Brazilian adults (50 men, 50 women), 20-80 years old, prospectively selected at random from more than 8,000 individuals; maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures and maximal voluntary ventilation measured.
cards.result: Gender-specific linear prediction equations for MIP, MEP and maximal voluntary ventilation were developed by multiple regression: age and, secondarily, anthropometric measurements explained up to 56% of the variability. The most cited previous studies, in Caucasian and non-Caucasian samples, systematically underestimated the MIP values observed in this sample (P < 0.05). Self-reported regular physical activity and maximum aerobic power correlated strongly with both respiratory and peripheral muscle strength (P < 0.01).
cards.watchOut: A single-population equation set: the study's own headline caution is that reference values imported from other populations misclassify — equations must match the population and technique being tested.
cards.source: Neder JA et al. Brazilian journal of medical and biological research = Revista brasileira de pesquisas medicas e biologicas. 1999. PMID: 10412550. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: The absolute scale in 166 healthy adults: mean PImax/PEmax 60/87.5 cmH2O in women and 73.2/115.9 cmH2O in men (Adamiak-Kardas 2002)
cards.summary: The absolute scale in 166 healthy adults: mean PImax/PEmax 60/87.5 cmH2O in women and 73.2/115.9 cmH2O in men (Adamiak-Kardas 2002)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative mouth-pressure measurements)
cards.people: 166 clinically normal subjects (79 women, 87 men); maximal inspiratory (PImax) and expiratory (PEmax) mouth pressures measured directly.
cards.result: In women, PImax ranged 38-104 cmH2O (mean 60 cmH2O) and PEmax ranged 46-140 cmH2O (mean 87.5 cmH2O). In men, PImax ranged 40-120 cmH2O (mean 73.2 cmH2O) and PEmax ranged 46-140 cmH2O (mean 115.9 cmH2O). PImax and PEmax correlated positively with weight in both sexes, and with height in the whole group (P = 0.00019). The author concludes normal values should be qualified individually for the population studied, and that equipment manufacturers' recommended norms may be inadequate.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre Polish cohort with wide within-sex ranges (e.g. men's PEmax 46-140 cmH2O): the means give the scale, but the ranges are the reason a fixed universal cut-off misleads — compare the equation- and T-score-based cut-offs in the 2023 study.
cards.source: Adamiak-Kardas M Polski merkuriusz lekarski : organ Polskiego Towarzystwa Lekarskiego. 2002. PMID: 12053582. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Weakness cut-offs from the largest uniform dataset (N = 610): PImax below 62 cmH2O (women) / 83 cmH2O (men) and PEmax below 81 / 109 cmH2O define respiratory muscle weakness (Lista-Paz 2023)
cards.summary: Weakness cut-offs from the largest uniform dataset (N = 610): PImax below 62 cmH2O (women) / 83 cmH2O (men) and PEmax below 81 / 109 cmH2O define respiratory muscle weakness (Lista-Paz 2023)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (multicentre reference equations and weakness cut-offs)
cards.people: 610 healthy non-smoking volunteers aged 18-80 years (314 women) recruited across 14 Spanish centres, stratified by sex and age; PImax/PEmax assessed with uniform methodology according to international standards.
cards.result: Sex-specific reference equations for PImax and PEmax included body mass index and a squared term of age as independent variables for both sexes (P < 0.01). Cut-off points for respiratory muscle weakness, set at T-scores ≥2.5 SD below the peak mean value achieved at a young age, were 62 and 83 cmH2O for PImax and 81 and 109 cmH2O for PEmax in females and males respectively. The authors describe this as the largest dataset collected in a European population using uniform methodology.
cards.watchOut: Cut-offs are statistical (2.5 SD below the young peak), not outcome-validated thresholds: a value just above the line in a patient with neuromuscular symptoms is not reassurance, and the equations are European-population derived.
cards.source: Lista-Paz A et al. Archivos de bronconeumologia. 2023. PMID: 37839949. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Systematic review (labelled synthesis): across 22 studies, MIP is higher in men and begins falling in the 40- to 60-year range (Sclauser Pessoa 2014)
cards.summary: Systematic review (labelled synthesis): across 22 studies, MIP is higher in men and begins falling in the 40- to 60-year range (Sclauser Pessoa 2014)
cards.type: Systematic review / meta-analysis of reference-value studies (labelled synthesis)
cards.people: Systematic review of maximal inspiratory pressure reference values; 22 articles included, with MIP data synthesised by age group and sex from six reports (n = 840; 426 men, 414 women; ages 18-83 years) in the meta-analyses. Labelled synthesis — not a primary study.
cards.result: MIP began to decrease with age in the 40- to 60-year age range and continued to fall progressively thereafter; for the same age group, men tended to have higher MIPs than women. Mean methodological quality (QUADAS) was 3.5 of 7, and sensitivity analysis identified one study contributing disproportionately to heterogeneity in some age groups. The authors conclude the meta-analysis provides normative MIP values from the broadest participant representation available, while participant characteristics and measurement technique influence values.
cards.watchOut: Review-level card: pooled normative values inherit the technique differences (mouthpiece, lung volume, instruction) of the primary studies — the per-study equations and cut-offs above govern interpretation for an individual patient.
cards.source: Sclauser Pessoa IM et al. Canadian respiratory journal. 2014. PMID: 24137574. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: MEP exceeds MIP, men exceed women, values fall with age — and weakness begins below 62/83 cmH2O (PImax) and 81/109 cmH2O (PEmax) in women/men
cards.summary: Synthesis: MEP exceeds MIP, men exceed women, values fall with age — and weakness begins below 62/83 cmH2O (PImax) and 81/109 cmH2O (PEmax) in women/men
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human studies and the one systematic review above.
cards.result: The concordant picture the textbooks (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep) frame and the fetched records support: maximal expiratory pressure exceeds maximal inspiratory pressure at matched lung volumes, men's pressures exceed women's (means 73.2 vs 60 cmH2O inspiratory and 115.9 vs 87.5 cmH2O expiratory in the Polish cohort), and pressures decline with age — detectably from the 40- to 60-year range in the pooled review, and modelled with a squared age term in the 2023 equations. Size matters (body surface area in 1992; body mass index in 2023) but equations leave much variance unexplained (up to 56% explained in Neder 1999), and equations imported from other populations systematically misestimate (Neder 1999). The operational lower limits are the 2023 T-score cut-offs: PImax 62 (women) / 83 (men) cmH2O and PEmax 81 (women) / 109 (men) cmH2O. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the pattern, the sex ordering and the cut-off framework; the exact predicted value for any individual remains equation- and population-specific.
cards.watchOut: All values are volitional and technique-sensitive (lung volume at measurement, mouthpiece seal, coaching): a low single measurement is an indication to repeat under standard conditions, not a diagnosis of weakness.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bruschi C et al. The American review of respiratory disease. 1992 (PMID: 1519865); Neder JA et al. Brazilian journal of medical and biological research. 1999 (PMID: 10412550); Adamiak-Kardas M. Polski merkuriusz lekarski. 2002 (PMID: 12053582); Lista-Paz A et al. Archivos de bronconeumologia. 2023 (PMID: 37839949); Sclauser Pessoa IM et al. Canadian respiratory journal. 2014 (PMID: 24137574). synthesis synthesis of the four primary human studies and the one systematic review above. the concordant picture the textbooks (guyton & hall; boron & boulpaep) frame and the fetched records support: maximal expiratory pressure exceeds maximal inspiratory pressure at matched lung volumes, men's pressures exceed women's (means 73.2 vs 60 cmh2o inspiratory and 115.9 vs 87.5 cmh2o expiratory in the polish cohort), and pressures decline with age — detectably from the 40- to 60-year range in the pooled review, and modelled with a squared age term in the 2023 equations. size matters (body surface area in 1992; body mass index in 2023) but equations leave much variance unexplained (up to 56% explained in neder 1999), and equations imported from other populations systematically misestimate (neder 1999). the operational lower limits are the 2023 t-score cut-offs: pimax 62 (women) / 83 (men) cmh2o and pemax 81 (women) / 109 (men) cmh2o. physiology — established for the pattern, the sex ordering and the cut-off framework; the exact predicted value for any individual remains equation- and population-specific. all values are volitional and technique-sensitive (lung volume at measurement, mouthpiece seal, coaching): a low single measurement is an indication to repeat under standard conditions, not a diagnosis of weakness. synthesis of bruschi c et al. the american review of respiratory disease. 1992 (pmid: 1519865); neder ja et al. brazilian journal of medical and biological research. 1999 (pmid: 10412550); adamiak-kardas m. polski merkuriusz lekarski. 2002 (pmid: 12053582); lista-paz a et al. archivos de bronconeumologia. 2023 (pmid: 37839949); sclauser pessoa im et al. canadian respiratory journal. 2014 (pmid: 24137574). textbook framing: guyton & hall textbook of medical physiology; boron & boulpaep medical physiology.

shelves.title: Lung clearance index: ~6.2 in healthy children (upper limit 7.0-7.9 by method), flat through school age, then rising with adult age to a mean of 8.8 by age 90 — repeatable within about 5%
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the lung clearance index (and related multiple-breath washout indices) by age — the Global Lung Function Initiative reference values for nitrogen and SF6 washout — and how repeatable is LCI within a person?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Reference Values · Aged · Middle Aged · Adult · Functional Residual Capacity/physiology · Aged, 80 and over · Young Adult · Adolescent · Child · Respiratory Function Tests/standards/instrumentation · Lung/physiology · Child, Preschool · Healthy Volunteers · Breath Tests/instrumentation/methods · Tidal Volume/physiology · Equipment Design · Lung Diseases/diagnosis · Prospective Studies · Reproducibility of Results · Breath Tests · Functional Residual Capacity · Lung · Respiratory Function Tests · Schools · Switzerland · Age Factors · Anthropometry · Cross-Sectional Studies · Lung Diseases, Obstructive/physiopathology · Smokers · Sulfur Hexafluoride/analysis
shelves.balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): even in healthy lungs, ventilation is not perfectly uniform, and the multiple-breath washout quantifies that heterogeneity — the lung clearance index (LCI) is the number of functional residual capacity (FRC) turnovers needed to wash an inert tracer gas (resident nitrogen, or inhaled sulfur hexafluoride, SF6) down to 1/40 of its starting concentration, so a higher LCI means more uneven ventilation. The fetched human data give the scale. In healthy children the index sits near 6: Fuchs 2009 measured mean LCI 6.2 (SD 0.4) with an upper limit of normal of 7.0 on the EasyOne Pro ultrasonic system, with within-test repeatability of 5.1% and short- and long-term reproducibility of 4.2-5.1% — the test is stable within a person. The school-age nitrogen-washout norms (Anagnostopoulou 2020, Exhalyzer D) set a fixed upper limit of 7.91 for LCI at the 2.5% endpoint, because the age rise across 6-18 years was negligible (0.04 units per year). In adults the picture changes: with SF6, Trinkmann 2021 found age explained 47% of LCI variance, mean LCI rising from 6.3 (upper limit 7.4) at age 20 to 8.8 (upper limit 9.9) at age 90. The Global Lung Function Initiative equations (Ramsey 2024; 1,579 unique healthy observations, ages 2-81) pool the field: LCI prediction needs age alone, FRC needs height, age and sex, and — at the level of the prediction equations — equipment type, tracer gas and dead space did not significantly change the equations. The device-specific upper limits on the cards below (7.0 vs 7.91 vs age-dependent SF6 limits) are therefore not a contradiction of the GLI pooling but its practical boundary: interpret a patient's LCI against the reference set for their method and age. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Global Lung Function Initiative reference equations: 1,579 healthy observations, ages 2-81 — LCI predicted by age alone, FRC by height, age and sex (Ramsey 2024)
cards.summary: Global Lung Function Initiative reference equations: 1,579 healthy observations, ages 2-81 — LCI predicted by age alone, FRC by height, age and sex (Ramsey 2024)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (international reference-equation programme)
cards.people: Multiple-breath washout data from healthy individuals collated from 23 sites (3,647 test occasions); reference equations derived from 1,579 unique observations from participants aged 2-81 years, re-analysed with the latest software versions.
cards.result: Reference equations for lung clearance index and functional residual capacity were derived with the lambda-mu-sigma method (generalised additive models of location, scale and shape). Reference equations for LCI include age as the only predictor, whereas sex-specific reference equations for FRC included height and age. Equipment type, inert tracer gas and equipment dead space volume did not significantly affect the prediction equations for either LCI or FRC.
cards.watchOut: The abstract states the equations' structure, not numeric LCI values at each age — the numeric norms on this shelf come from the device- and age-specific studies below; a pooled equation that is statistically insensitive to equipment does not abolish the different upper limits those studies report.
cards.source: Ramsey KA et al. The European respiratory journal. 2024. PMID: 39326920. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Healthy children: mean LCI 6.2 (SD 0.4), upper limit of normal 7.0 — and the index barely moves on retesting (5.1% within-test, 4.2% at 1 hour, 5.1% at 6-15 months) (Fuchs 2009)
cards.summary: Healthy children: mean LCI 6.2 (SD 0.4), upper limit of normal 7.0 — and the index barely moves on retesting (5.1% within-test, 4.2% at 1 hour, 5.1% at 6-15 months) (Fuchs 2009)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative values and repeatability in children/adolescents)
cards.people: 44 healthy volunteers aged 5.3-20.3 years tested with nitrogen multiple-breath washout using the sidestream ultrasonic flow sensor (EasyOne Pro MBW Module, ndd Medical Technologies); 22 retested after 1 hour and 34 retested 6-15 months later.
cards.result: Mean LCI (SD) was 6.2 (0.4) at the first test, 6.3 (0.4) at the second (1 hour later) and 6.0 (0.4) at follow-up 6-15 months later; the upper limit of normal was 7.0 for all subjects. Within-test repeatability was 5.1%. Short-term reproducibility was 4.2% with a mean difference of -0.13 (95% CI -0.350 to 0.087); long-term reproducibility was 5.1%. The authors conclude the low within- and between-test variability demonstrates the reliability of the equipment, protocol and technique.
cards.watchOut: Device-specific norms (EasyOne Pro ultrasonic sensor): the upper limit of 7.0 belongs to this system and age range and should not be transplanted to other devices or to older adults, in whom LCI rises with age (see the SF6 adult study).

cards.headline: Nitrogen washout in school-age children (N = 180): upper limits fixed at 7.91 (LCI 2.5%) and 5.73 (LCI 5%) because the age rise was negligible — 0.04 units per year (Anagnostopoulou 2020)
cards.summary: Nitrogen washout in school-age children (N = 180): upper limits fixed at 7.91 (LCI 2.5%) and 5.73 (LCI 5%) because the age rise was negligible — 0.04 units per year (Anagnostopoulou 2020)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative nitrogen-washout data, school-aged children)
cards.people: 180 healthy Caucasian children aged 6-18 years from four experienced centres (485 trials analysed); nitrogen multiple-breath washout on an ultrasonic flowmeter (Exhalyzer D, Eco Medics AG), analysed with Spiroware version 3.2.1.
cards.result: While LCI increased with age, the increase was negligible (0.04 units per year for LCI at the 2.5% endpoint), so fixed upper limits of normal were defined for this age group: 7.91 for LCI2.5%, 5.73 for LCI5%, 1.75 for the moment ratio M1/M0 and 6.15 for M2/M0. Height and weight were independent predictors of functional residual capacity, for which a prediction equation was generated.
cards.watchOut: Method-specific values: nitrogen washout on the Exhalyzer D gives a higher upper limit (7.91) than the EasyOne Pro paediatric study (7.0) — gas, device and software generation must match the reference set used, exactly the per-method caution this shelf is built around.

cards.headline: SF6 washout in adults (N = 100, ages 20-88): age drives LCI — mean 6.3 (upper limit 7.4) at age 20 rising to 8.8 (upper limit 9.9) at age 90 (Trinkmann 2021)
cards.summary: SF6 washout in adults (N = 100, ages 20-88): age drives LCI — mean 6.3 (upper limit 7.4) at age 20 rising to 8.8 (upper limit 9.9) at age 90 (Trinkmann 2021)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (SF6 washout reference values across adult age)
cards.people: 100 pulmonary-healthy adults (never-smokers and smokers; mean age 51 years, SD 20, range 20-88) undergoing triplicate sulfur hexafluoride multiple-breath washout; LCI, acinar (Sacin) and conductive (Scond) heterogeneity derived at the 2.5% and 5% stopping points; upper limit of normal defined as the 95th percentile.
cards.result: Age was the only meaningful parameter influencing SF6 washout parameters, explaining 47% (95% CI 33% to 59%) of the variance in LCI, 32% (18% to 47%) in Sacin and 10% (2% to 22%) in Scond. Mean LCI increased from 6.3 (upper limit 7.4) to 8.8 (upper limit 9.9) between ages 20 and 90 years. Smoking accounted for only 2% (0% to 8%) of LCI variability, and no influence of height, weight or sex was seen.
cards.watchOut: SF6 (inhaled tracer) values in adults are not interchangeable with nitrogen (resident gas) values in children: the adult age rise means a single paediatric-style upper limit near 7 would mislabel healthy older adults as abnormal.
cards.source: Trinkmann F et al. Thorax. 2021. PMID: 33593931. Registry ID: NCT04099225. cards.headline: Synthesis: healthy LCI is ~6 in childhood with an upper limit near 7-8 depending on method, stays flat through school age, then climbs with adult age to ~8.8 by age 90 — and repeats within ~5% in the same person
cards.summary: Synthesis: healthy LCI is ~6 in childhood with an upper limit near 7-8 depending on method, stays flat through school age, then climbs with adult age to ~8.8 by age 90 — and repeats within ~5% in the same person
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human studies above.
cards.result: The concordant account, framed by the textbooks (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep) as a measure of ventilation heterogeneity: a healthy child's lung clears tracer in about six FRC turnovers (mean LCI 6.2, SD 0.4; Fuchs 2009), the school-age rise is negligible (0.04 units/year; Anagnostopoulou 2020), and the adult rise is the dominant fact (age explaining 47% of variance; mean 6.3 at 20 years to 8.8 at 90 years on SF6; Trinkmann 2021). Upper limits are method-bound: 7.0 (EasyOne Pro, children), 7.91 at the 2.5% endpoint (nitrogen, Exhalyzer D, school age), and age-dependent on SF6 (7.4 at 20 years, 9.9 at 90 years). The GLI equations (Ramsey 2024) unify reporting — LCI from age alone, FRC from height, age and sex — without erasing those method-specific limits. Within a person the measurement is tight (repeatability/reproducibility ~4-5%), so a change well beyond ~5% is signal, not noise. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: LCI values across gases (nitrogen vs SF6), devices and software versions are cousins, not twins: longitudinal follow-up of a patient should stay on one system, and cross-system comparisons should use each system's own reference equations.

shelves.title: Diaphragm ultrasound in health: end-expiratory thickness lower limits 1.3 mm (men) / 1.1 mm (women) seated, thickening-fraction lower limits ~39–48%, deep-breathing excursion ~5 cm supine
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are diaphragm thickness, thickening fraction and excursion on ultrasound at rest and during deep breathing, by sex and posture — the reference values and limits of normality?
shelves.mesh: Diaphragm · Ultrasonography · Reference Values · Muscle Strength · Respiratory Function Tests
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for thickness and thickening in healthy adults, framed by Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep on the diaphragm and respiratory mechanics as textbook framing, not as an evidence card. Two large healthy cohorts measured in different postures converge on the same muscle: seated, end-expiratory thickness has a lower limit of normality of 1.3 mm in men and 1.1 mm in women, with thickening-fraction lower limits around 39–48% by side and sex (Boussuges 2021, N = 200); supine, mean end-expiratory thickness is 0.14 ± 0.05 cm (1.4 mm) rising to 0.29 ± 0.10 cm at end-inspiration, with quiet-breathing excursion 1.68 ± 0.37 cm and deep-breathing excursion 5.06 ± 1.40 cm (Zhang 2024, N = 212). Women have thinner diaphragms than men in both cohorts, while thickening fraction does not differ by sex — the pattern is consistent across posture and centre. A smaller study (N = 64) ties the ultrasound measures to function: deep-breathing mobility, total-lung-capacity thickness and thickening fraction correlate with lung function and inspiratory strength, including inspiratory gastric pressure in a 40-person subgroup (Cardenas 2018). Posture and breathing manoeuvre move the numbers, so each card names its own; the values are not pooled across postures. Cross-point, not duplicated: the mouth-pressures shelf (MIP/MEP reference values) measures the same muscle system by pressure rather than by imaging.

cards.headline: Boussuges 2021: seated reference values in 200 healthy volunteers — end-expiratory thickness lower limit 1.3 mm (men) / 1.1 mm (women); thickening-fraction lower limits 39–48%
cards.summary: Boussuges 2021: seated reference values in 200 healthy volunteers — end-expiratory thickness lower limit 1.3 mm (men) / 1.1 mm (women); thickening-fraction lower limits 39–48%
cards.type: Human ultrasound reference-values study (diaphragm, seated), Front Med 2021
cards.people: Two hundred healthy volunteers (100 men, 100 women) with normal pulmonary function tests, studied seated; diaphragm thickness was measured on both sides at the zone of apposition during quiet breathing at end-expiration and end-inspiration and after maximal inspiration, and the thickening ratio, thickening fraction and an end-inspiration/deep-breathing thickness ratio were derived.
cards.result: Women had thinner hemidiaphragms than men on both sides at all breathing times. The lower limit of normality for end-expiratory thickness was 1.3 mm in men and 1.1 mm in women, on both sides. Thickening fraction did not differ significantly between sexes: observed ranges in men were 60–260% (left) and 57–200% (right), in women 58–264% (left) and 60–229% (right); its lower limits of normality were 40% (right) and 39% (left) in men, and 39% (right) and 48% (left) in women. The upper limit of normal for the mean-of-both-sides ratio of thickness at end-inspiration to thickness at deep breathing was 0.78 in women and 0.79 in men.
cards.watchOut: Seated values at the zone of apposition — posture and measurement site are part of the number; do not apply these limits to supine ICU measurements without the posture difference in view.
cards.source: Boussuges A, Rives S, Finance J, Chaumet G, Vallée N, Risso JJ, Brégeon F. cards.headline: Zhang 2024: supine multimodal values in 212 healthy subjects — thickness 0.14 ± 0.05 cm at end-expiration, 0.29 ± 0.10 cm at end-inspiration; excursion 1.68 cm quiet, 5.06 cm deep breathing
cards.summary: Zhang 2024: supine multimodal values in 212 healthy subjects — thickness 0.14 ± 0.05 cm at end-expiration, 0.29 ± 0.10 cm at end-inspiration; excursion 1.68 cm quiet, 5.06 cm deep breathing
cards.type: Human ultrasound reference-values study (diaphragm, supine, multimodal), Int J Gen Med 2024
cards.people: Two hundred and twelve subjects (105 men, 107 women) with normal spirometry, studied supine with multimodal ultrasound: contraction and motion parameters plus shear-wave velocity; effects of sex, age, body mass index and lifestyle were analysed.
cards.result: Diaphragm thickness at end-expiration was 0.14 ± 0.05 cm and at end-inspiration 0.29 ± 0.10 cm, with thickening fraction 1.11 ± 0.54 (printed as a ratio in the record). Excursion was 1.68 ± 0.37 cm with velocity 1.45 ± 0.41 cm/s during calm breathing, and 5.06 ± 1.40 cm with velocity 3.20 ± 1.18 cm/s during deep breathing. Longitudinal shear modulus averaged 16.72 ± 4.07 kPa. Male thickness exceeded female (P < 0.05) with no sex difference in thickening fraction; thickness rose weakly with age, calm-breathing excursion fell with age and body mass index, and deep-breathing excursion and velocity correlated with lifestyle.
cards.watchOut: Supine values — excursion and thickness differ from the seated card by posture, kept separate on this shelf. Thickening fraction is printed as a ratio (1.11 ± 0.54) in this record versus percentages in the seated record; the two are the same quantity in different dress and are not averaged.

cards.headline: Cardenas 2018: in 64 healthy subjects, deep-breathing ultrasound mobility, thickness and thickening fraction correlate with lung function and inspiratory strength — quiet-breathing measures do not separate the sexes, deep-breathing measures do
cards.summary: Cardenas 2018: in 64 healthy subjects, deep-breathing ultrasound mobility, thickness and thickening fraction correlate with lung function and inspiratory strength — quiet-breathing measures do not separate the sexes, deep-breathing measures do
cards.type: Human ultrasound–function correlation study (diaphragm in healthy subjects), Ultrasound Med Biol 2018
cards.people: Sixty-four healthy subjects (30 men) with lung function and inspiratory strength (maximal inspiratory pressure and sniff nasal inspiratory pressure) measured; gastric and oesophageal pressures were measured in a subgroup of 40. Ultrasound characterised mobility in quiet and deep breathing and thickness at functional residual capacity and total lung capacity, with thickening fraction calculated.
cards.result: During quiet breathing, ultrasound measures were similar between sexes; during deep breathing, women had lower mobility, thickness and thickening fraction than men. Deep-breathing mobility, thickness at total lung capacity and thickening fraction correlated significantly with lung function and inspiratory strength, and ultrasound measures correlated with inspiratory gastric pressure — the imaging tracks the muscle's pressure-generating function when the muscle is actually loaded, which is during deep breathing rather than at rest.
cards.watchOut: Correlations are reported as significant in the record without coefficients in its abstract — this card claims the direction and significance the record states, not effect sizes it does not print. N = 64 (pressure subgroup 40).

cards.headline: Synthesis: diaphragm thickness ~1.1–1.4 mm at end-expiration with thickening-fraction lower limits near 40% and deep-breathing excursion ~5 cm — thinner in women, fraction sex-independent, all posture- and manoeuvre-specific
cards.summary: Synthesis: diaphragm thickness ~1.1–1.4 mm at end-expiration with thickening-fraction lower limits near 40% and deep-breathing excursion ~5 cm — thinner in women, fraction sex-independent, all posture- and manoeuvre-specific
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human studies above (Boussuges 2021; Zhang 2024; Cardenas 2018), framed by the Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep account of diaphragmatic mechanics as textbook framing, not as an evidence card.
cards.result: The concordant picture across 476 healthy subjects in three cohorts: a thin muscle at rest (end-expiratory thickness means/limits around 1.1–1.4 mm depending on sex and posture) that roughly doubles in thickness and shortens by about 1.7 cm in quiet breathing and about 5 cm in deep breathing; thickening fraction, with lower limits of normality near 39–48%, is the sex-independent index, while absolute thickness is not. The functional card explains why deep-breathing measures carry the signal — they correlate with inspiratory strength and gastric pressure where quiet-breathing measures do not. Posture (seated vs supine) and side are part of every number and are named on each card rather than pooled away. No refusals on this shelf: all three slated anchors verified from abstract-present records. No animal data are carded.
cards.watchOut: Reference limits come from healthy volunteers with normal spirometry/pulmonary function; applying them to critically ill or neuromuscular populations is a clinical extrapolation the shelf does not make.

shelves.title: Rademikibart in moderate-to-severe uncontrolled asthma: one phase 2b trial (322 patients) — FEV1 rose 140–189 mL over placebo at week 12; all three reports are of that single trial
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe persistent uncontrolled asthma, does rademikibart (anti-IL-4R-alpha monoclonal antibody, 150 mg or 300 mg every other week after a loading dose) versus placebo improve lung function and asthma control over 24 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Asthma/drug therapy/physiopathology · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Adult · Treatment Outcome · Forced Expiratory Volume/drug effects · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Severity of Illness Index · Double-Blind Method · Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — SINGLE-TRIAL FLAG, printed plainly: every card on this shelf is a report of ONE phase 2b randomised trial of 322 adults with moderate-to-severe uncontrolled asthma (rademikibart 150 mg or 300 mg every other week after a 600 mg loading dose, versus placebo, for 24 weeks). There is no second trial and no phase 3 report; a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. In that trial, trough FEV1 at week 12 improved over placebo by 140 mL (150 mg) and 189 mL (300 mg), gains appeared in week 1 and held to week 24, and asthma control scores improved. The proportion with one or more exacerbations through week 24 was 7.5% (150 mg) and 9.3% (300 mg) versus 16.7% on placebo — absolute differences of about 9 and 7 percentage points, i.e. roughly 55% and 44% relative reductions — but a 24-week phase 2b trial is not powered to settle exacerbation benefit, and the shelf does not claim it. Exploratory subgroup reports found the largest gains where type 2 biomarkers were high (baseline eosinophils at least 300 cells/microlitre and FeNO at least 25 ppb), and a dedicated eosinophil analysis found counts fell slightly rather than rising, unlike the hypereosinophilia seen with some IL-4R-alpha blockade — an exploratory safety observation, not a settled class distinction. Rademikibart is a single-source investigational product (developed as CBP-201); it is not an approved asthma treatment.

cards.headline: Phase 2b primary (Kerwin 2025): FEV1 at week 12 improved 140 mL (150 mg, P=0.005) and 189 mL (300 mg, P<0.001) over placebo; exacerbations in 7.5% and 9.3% versus 16.7% on placebo
cards.summary: Phase 2b primary (Kerwin 2025): FEV1 at week 12 improved 140 mL (150 mg, P=0.005) and 189 mL (300 mg, P<0.001) over placebo; exacerbations in 7.5% and 9.3% versus 16.7% on placebo
cards.type: Phase 2b, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial — the only trial of this programme
cards.people: 322 adults with moderate-to-severe, persistent, uncontrolled asthma were randomised 1:1:1 to subcutaneous rademikibart 150 mg or 300 mg every other week (after a 600 mg loading dose) or placebo for 24 weeks. Primary endpoint: prebronchodilator (trough) FEV1 at week 12.
cards.result: Least squares mean FEV1 change above placebo at week 12 was 140 mL (95% CI 44 to 236; P=0.005) for 150 mg and 189 mL (95% CI 92 to 286; P<0.001) for 300 mg. Improvements began in week 1, were sustained through week 24, and were greatest with high baseline blood eosinophils (at least 300 cells/microlitre: placebo-adjusted week-24 gain 420 mL, 95% CI 239 to 600, in the 300 mg group). Percent predicted FEV1 and Asthma Control Questionnaire scores also improved significantly. Through week 24, one or more exacerbations occurred in 7.5% (150 mg) and 9.3% (300 mg) versus 16.7% (placebo) — absolute differences of about 9 and 7 percentage points (roughly 55% and 44% relative reductions). Eighty-eight percent completed treatment; treatment-emergent adverse events were generally similar to placebo, injection site reactions were mostly mild, the commonest events (10–12%) were cough, COVID-19 and dyspnoea, and no eosinophilia was observed.
cards.watchOut: A 24-week phase 2b trial sized for FEV1, not exacerbations — the exacerbation proportions are a secondary observation with few events. Patients with screening eosinophils above 1500 cells/microlitre were excluded, so the highest-eosinophil population is untested here.
cards.source: Kerwin E et al. Rademikibart Treatment for Moderate-to-Severe Uncontrolled Asthma: A Phase 2B Randomized Clinical Trial. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2025. PMID: 39998473. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04773678, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Type 2 biomarker subgroups of the same trial (Wechsler 2026): week-24 placebo-adjusted FEV1 gain 519 mL where eosinophils and FeNO were both high, falling to 159 mL in the lowest subgroup; exacerbations fell by at least 63% (relative) per subgroup
cards.summary: Type 2 biomarker subgroups of the same trial (Wechsler 2026): week-24 placebo-adjusted FEV1 gain 519 mL where eosinophils and FeNO were both high, falling to 159 mL in the lowest subgroup; exacerbations fell by at least 63% (relative) per subgroup
cards.type: Exploratory, predominantly post hoc subgroup analysis of the same single phase 2b trial — not an independent trial
cards.people: The same 322 trial patients, divided into up to eight baseline eosinophil-count (EOS) and fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) subgroups; the five focus subgroups were EOS at least 300 cells/microlitre and FeNO at least 25 ppb (N=80), FeNO at least 25 ppb (N=142), EOS at least 300 (N=129), EOS at least 150 (N=247), and EOS 150 to under 300 (N=118). All patients were on medium-to-high dose inhaled corticosteroids with at least one reliever/controller.
cards.result: FEV1 rose significantly at week 1 and was sustained to week 24, with the largest gains where both biomarkers were elevated. At week 24 on 300 mg, placebo-adjusted FEV1 increases were 519 mL (both high), 401 mL (FeNO at least 25 ppb), 394 mL (EOS at least 300), 287 mL (EOS at least 150) and 159 mL (EOS 150 to under 300). Exacerbations decreased by at least 63% per subgroup — a relative reduction as reported, without arm-level absolute rates printed in this report. Rademikibart was well tolerated; no eosinophilia was reported, and grade 1 eosinophil count increases (n=2) did not stop treatment.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory and largely post hoc: eight subgroups carved from 322 patients invite chance findings, subgroup Ns overlap (the same patients appear in several subgroups), and the exacerbation figure is a relative reduction with no absolute rates in this report — it must not be read as an absolute benefit.
cards.source: Wechsler ME et al. Rademikibart for Asthma With Type 2 Biomarkers: Exploratory Subgroup Analyses From a Phase 2b Randomized Clinical Trial. Allergy. 2026. PMID: 42717393. cards.headline: Eosinophil analysis of the same trial (Wechsler 2026): mean eosinophil counts fell slightly on rademikibart (-30 and -97 cells/microlitre at week 24) versus -23 on placebo; no hypereosinophilia signal
cards.summary: Eosinophil analysis of the same trial (Wechsler 2026): mean eosinophil counts fell slightly on rademikibart (-30 and -97 cells/microlitre at week 24) versus -23 on placebo; no hypereosinophilia signal
cards.type: Exploratory analysis of the same single phase 2b trial — not an independent trial
cards.people: The same 322 randomised patients (baseline mean eosinophil counts 268, 320 and 299 cells/microlitre in the 150 mg, 300 mg and placebo groups); patients with screening counts above 1500 cells/microlitre had been excluded. Counts were followed through 24 weeks of treatment and 8 weeks off treatment.
cards.result: Mean eosinophil counts changed by -8, -25 and +2 cells/microlitre at week 12 and by -30, -97 and -23 cells/microlitre at week 24 in the 150 mg, 300 mg and placebo groups respectively. Among patients with baseline counts of at least 500 cells/microlitre, counts above 1500 occurred in 10.0% on rademikibart (n=3) versus 18.8% on placebo (n=3); below 500 at baseline, in 1.1% versus 1.1%. One patient exceeded 3000 cells/microlitre during off-treatment follow-up (150 mg group). Two patients on 300 mg had nonserious grade 1 events of increased eosinophil count/percentage. No clear differences in infection or cardiovascular events.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory, with very small event counts (the key contrast is 3 patients versus 3 patients) and an exclusion of the highest-eosinophil patients at screening — the authors themselves say larger confirmatory analyses are required before any class-effect conclusion.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, three reports — real lung-function gains, exacerbation and biomarker claims still exploratory — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, three reports — real lung-function gains, exacerbation and biomarker claims still exploratory — POSSIBLE
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: all report the single phase 2b trial of 322 adults with moderate-to-severe uncontrolled asthma (rademikibart 150 mg or 300 mg every other week versus placebo, 24 weeks). No other trial of rademikibart in asthma has reported.
cards.result: The primary report shows dose-ordered, rapid and sustained FEV1 gains (140 and 189 mL over placebo at week 12) with improved asthma control and numerically fewer exacerbations (7.5% and 9.3% versus 16.7%). The two companion reports are exploratory cuts of the same patients: benefit concentrated in type 2-high subgroups, and no hypereosinophilia signal.
cards.watchOut: SINGLE-TRIAL structure: three publications do not multiply the evidence base — it remains 322 patients from one phase 2b trial, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. A phase 3 programme would be needed to test exacerbations and confirm the biomarker gradient.

shelves.title: CPAP versus non-invasive ventilation in obesity hypoventilation syndrome (Pickwick): the two treatments matched on symptoms and long-term heart changes; NIV edged ahead on blood gases, lung function and early heart measures, and neither beat lifestyle advice on hospital days without severe sleep apnoea
shelves.question: In adults with obesity hypoventilation syndrome (with and without severe obstructive sleep apnoea), is long-term non-invasive ventilation superior to CPAP — or to lifestyle modification alone — for gas exchange, cardiovascular outcomes and survival?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Exercise Test · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Health Promotion/methods · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Life Style · Male · Middle Aged · Noninvasive Ventilation · Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome/therapy · Polysomnography · Spirometry · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — and the split runs exactly where the Pickwick programme itself split it: by whether severe obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is present, and by endpoint. All four cards come from the one Spanish Pickwick programme (a single registry entry covering its trials and their secondary reports); the reports share populations and must not be counted as independent trials. In patients WITH severe OSA (221 randomised), 2 months of non-invasive ventilation (NIV) and CPAP both beat lifestyle modification on symptoms and sleep measures; NIV improved daytime PaCO2 and bicarbonate most, with a significant difference against lifestyle but not against CPAP, while spirometry, 6-minute walk and some quality-of-life measures improved more with NIV. At 2 months only NIV lowered systolic pulmonary artery pressure (-3.4 mm Hg versus control) and left ventricular mass index; over 3 years, however, pulmonary pressure and diastolic function improved to the same degree on both treatments. In patients WITHOUT severe OSA (98 randomised, median follow-up about 5 years), NIV versus lifestyle modification made no difference to hospital days per year (2.71 versus 2.60; adjusted rate ratio 1.07, 95% CI 0.44 to 2.59) — the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint — though blood gases, quality of life and sleepiness improved more on NIV. No card here shows a mortality advantage for either device. Practical reading: CPAP is a reasonable first treatment when severe OSA dominates; NIV earns its place on gas-exchange and functional grounds, not on hospitalisation or survival.

cards.headline: Pickwick main trial (Masa 2015): in OHS with severe OSA, NIV improved PaCO2 most — significantly versus lifestyle, not versus CPAP; symptoms and sleep measures improved similarly on NIV and CPAP
cards.summary: Pickwick main trial (Masa 2015): in OHS with severe OSA, NIV improved PaCO2 most — significantly versus lifestyle, not versus CPAP; symptoms and sleep measures improved similarly on NIV and CPAP
cards.type: Randomised, multicentre, controlled trial (Pickwick Study) — 2-month efficacy report, severe-OSA population
cards.people: 351 patients with obesity hypoventilation syndrome and severe sleep apnoea were screened and 221 randomised to non-invasive ventilation (NIV), CPAP, or lifestyle modification (control) for 2 months. Main outcome: daytime PaCO2; symptoms, quality of life, polysomnography, spirometry, 6-minute walk, compliance and side effects were also assessed, by intention to treat with compliance-adjusted analyses.
cards.result: NIV yielded the greatest improvement in PaCO2 and bicarbonate, significantly different from the control group but not from the CPAP group. CPAP's PaCO2 improvement differed significantly from control only after adjustment for CPAP compliance. Clinical symptoms and polysomnographic parameters improved similarly with NIV and CPAP relative to control, but some health-related quality-of-life assessments, spirometry and 6-minute-walk distance improved more with NIV than CPAP. Dropouts were similar between groups, and compliance and side effects were similar between NIV and CPAP.
cards.watchOut: Two months is short, the lifestyle arm is not a blinded comparator, and the headline PaCO2 contrast (NIV versus CPAP) was not significant — the NIV edge is in secondary functional measures. This is one programme's population; the echocardiographic cards below re-report these same patients.

cards.headline: Pickwick long-term trial without severe OSA (Masa 2020): hospital days per year 2.71 on NIV versus 2.60 on lifestyle advice (adjusted rate ratio 1.07, P=.882) — the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint
cards.summary: Pickwick long-term trial without severe OSA (Masa 2020): hospital days per year 2.71 on NIV versus 2.60 on lifestyle advice (adjusted rate ratio 1.07, P=.882) — the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint
cards.type: Randomised, multicentre, open-label, parallel-group trial (Pickwick) — long-term report, population without severe OSA
cards.people: 98 stable ambulatory patients with untreated obesity hypoventilation syndrome and an apnoea-hypopnoea index below 30 events/hour (no severe OSA) were randomised at 16 Spanish sites to NIV (n=49) or lifestyle modification (n=49); 48 per group were analysed over a median follow-up of 4.98 years. Primary endpoint: hospitalisation days per year. The trial stopped early in its eighth year because this phenotype was hard to recruit.
cards.result: Mean hospital days per year were 2.60 (SD 5.31) on lifestyle modification and 2.71 (4.52) on NIV (adjusted rate ratio 1.07, 95% CI 0.44 to 2.59; P=.882) — no difference. NIV did produce significant longitudinal improvement in PaCO2, pH, bicarbonate, physical quality of life and daytime sleepiness versus control, and per-protocol analysis favoured NIV for time to first emergency department visit; patients with high NIV adherence had longer time to the composite of admission, emergency visit and death than low-adherence patients. Adverse events were similar between arms.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, stopped early, and only 98 patients — the confidence interval (0.44 to 2.59) cannot exclude a worthwhile effect in either direction, so this is an imprecise null, not proof of equivalence. The adherence subgroup contrast is not randomised and is confounded by whatever makes patients adhere.
