cards.headline: Pickwick long-term echocardiography (Masa 2020): over 3 years, systolic pulmonary artery pressure fell about 5–6 mm Hg on both CPAP (40.5 to 35.3) and NIV (41.5 to 35.5), with no significant difference between treatments
cards.summary: Pickwick long-term echocardiography (Masa 2020): over 3 years, systolic pulmonary artery pressure fell about 5–6 mm Hg on both CPAP (40.5 to 35.3) and NIV (41.5 to 35.5), with no significant difference between treatments
cards.type: Prespecified secondary echocardiographic analysis of the long-term Pickwick trial — same programme and overlapping patients as the other cards, not an independent trial
cards.people: 196 patients with obesity hypoventilation syndrome and coexistent severe OSA from the Pickwick trial (102 CPAP, 94 NIV) with echocardiography at baseline and annually for 3 years; echocardiographers were blinded to allocation.
cards.result: Systolic pulmonary artery pressure decreased from 40.5 (SE 1.47) mm Hg at baseline to 35.3 (1.33) at 3 years on CPAP, and from 41.5 (1.56) to 35.5 (1.42) on NIV (P<0.0001 for the within-group change in both arms), with no significant differences between groups. NIV and CPAP similarly improved left ventricular diastolic dysfunction and reduced left atrial diameter, and both improved respiratory function and dyspnoea.
cards.watchOut: A within-programme secondary analysis: the falls in pulmonary pressure are within-group changes in treated patients (there is no untreated long-term comparator here), so they show the heart improving on treatment, not that either device beats the other — on that question the result is no difference.

cards.headline: Pickwick 2-month echocardiography (Corral 2018): only NIV lowered systolic pulmonary artery pressure (-3.4 mm Hg versus control) and left ventricular mass index (-5.7 g/m2) at 2 months; NIV alone improved 6-minute walk (+32 m)
cards.summary: Pickwick 2-month echocardiography (Corral 2018): only NIV lowered systolic pulmonary artery pressure (-3.4 mm Hg versus control) and left ventricular mass index (-5.7 g/m2) at 2 months; NIV alone improved 6-minute walk (+32 m)
cards.type: Secondary echocardiographic analysis of the Pickwick main trial — same 221 patients as the first card, not an independent trial
cards.people: The 221 Pickwick patients with OHS and severe OSA (NIV n=71, CPAP n=80, lifestyle control n=70) with echocardiograms at baseline and 2 months; 55% had pulmonary hypertension and 51% left ventricular hypertrophy at baseline. Echocardiographers were blinded; analysis was intention to treat.
cards.result: NIV, but not CPAP, lowered systolic pulmonary artery pressure (-3.4 mm Hg, 95% CI -5.3 to -1.5; adjusted P=0.025 versus control and P=0.033 versus CPAP), with a larger fall in patients with baseline pulmonary hypertension (-6.4 mm Hg, 95% CI -9 to -3.8). Only NIV reduced left ventricular mass index (-5.7 g/m2, 95% CI -11.0 to -4.4; adjusted P=0.015 versus control) and only NIV significantly improved 6-minute walk distance (32 m, 95% CI 19 to 46).
cards.watchOut: Two-month surrogate cardiac measures in the same patients as the main trial card — and the 3-year echocardiographic card above shows CPAP catching up, so the early NIV advantage on these measures did not persist as a between-treatment difference.

cards.summary: Synthesis: one programme, two phenotypes — NIV wins some physiology, neither device wins hospital days or survival — SPLIT
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the four cards above: all are reports of the single Spanish Pickwick programme — 221 randomised patients with OHS and severe OSA (2-month and 3-year reports) and 98 randomised patients with OHS without severe OSA (long-term report). The populations overlap between reports and are not independent trials.
cards.result: With severe OSA: NIV and CPAP improved symptoms and sleep similarly; NIV improved blood gases, lung function, walk distance and 2-month heart measures more, but 3-year heart changes were equal. Without severe OSA: NIV improved gases, sleepiness and quality of life but made no difference to hospital days per year (rate ratio 1.07). No mortality benefit is shown for either treatment anywhere in the programme.
cards.watchOut: SPLIT by phenotype and endpoint, as the programme itself split it. Do not pool the reports into a single NIV-versus-CPAP verdict, and do not count the four publications as four trials — they are one programme with two randomised populations.

shelves.title: Solithromycin for community-acquired bacterial pneumonia: non-inferior to moxifloxacin in both phase 3 trials (early response 78.2% versus 77.9% oral; 79.3% versus 79.7% intravenous-to-oral) — and never approved, over liver-safety concerns
shelves.question: In adults with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, is solithromycin (oral, or intravenous-to-oral) non-inferior to moxifloxacin for early clinical response and clinical success?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Community-Acquired Infections/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Europe · Female · Fluoroquinolones/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Latin America · Macrolides/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Moxifloxacin · North America · Pneumonia, Bacterial/drug therapy · South Africa · Triazoles/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE on the narrow non-inferiority question — with the failure printed on the face: solithromycin is a FAILED programme. It met non-inferiority against moxifloxacin in both of its phase 3 pneumonia trials, yet it was never approved — regulators refused it over hepatotoxicity concerns — and it is not an available treatment. This shelf is a completeness record, not a treatment option. In SOLITAIRE-ORAL (860 adults), early clinical response was 78.2% on oral solithromycin versus 77.9% on oral moxifloxacin (difference 0.29 percentage points, 95% CI -5.5 to 6.1; 10% non-inferiority margin). In SOLITAIRE-IV (863 adults), intravenous-to-oral solithromycin gave early response in 79.3% versus 79.7% (difference -0.46, 95% CI -6.1 to 5.2), with investigator-assessed clinical success at short-term follow-up of 84.6% versus 88.6%. A meta-analysis of three randomised trials (1855 patients) found no significant difference in early response (odds ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.24) or adverse-event outcomes. Within the trials, short-course safety looked similar to moxifloxacin — but the trials were short and sized for efficacy, and the liver-safety record that stopped the programme sits outside them: infusion-site events were commoner with intravenous solithromycin, a paediatric trial run by the sponsor was stopped early by the sponsor before completion, and the regulatory refusal over liver concerns is the defining fact of this drug's history. Non-inferiority to moxifloxacin also deserves its plain meaning: as good as an existing drug within a 10% margin, not better.

cards.headline: SOLITAIRE-ORAL (Barrera 2016): early clinical response 78.2% on oral solithromycin versus 77.9% on oral moxifloxacin (difference 0.29, 95% CI -5.5 to 6.1) — non-inferior within the 10% margin
cards.summary: SOLITAIRE-ORAL (Barrera 2016): early clinical response 78.2% on oral solithromycin versus 77.9% on oral moxifloxacin (difference 0.29, 95% CI -5.5 to 6.1) — non-inferior within the 10% margin
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled non-inferiority trial (114 centres)
cards.people: 860 adults (at least 18 years) with clinically and radiographically confirmed community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, PORT risk class II, III or IV, randomised to oral solithromycin (800 mg day 1, 400 mg days 2–5, placebo days 6–7; n=426) or oral moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 7 days (n=434). Primary outcome: early clinical response at 72 hours (improvement in at least two of four symptoms with no worsening), analysed by intention to treat. Sponsor: Cempra.
cards.result: Solithromycin was non-inferior to moxifloxacin: early clinical response in 333 (78.2%) solithromycin patients versus 338 (77.9%) on moxifloxacin (difference 0.29 percentage points, 95% CI -5.5 to 6.1). Safety profiles were similar: drug-related treatment-emergent adverse events in 43 (10%) of 155 events on solithromycin versus 54 (13%) of 154 on moxifloxacin; the commonest events were gastrointestinal (diarrhoea 4% versus 6%, nausea 4% versus 4%, vomiting 2% versus 2%) and headache (4% versus 3%).
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority within a generous 10% margin against an active comparator shows the drug works about as well as moxifloxacin over 5–7 days — it cannot detect uncommon liver injury, which is what later stopped the programme, and this trial's short follow-up (to days 28–35) is not a liver-safety verdict.
cards.source: Barrera CM et al. Efficacy and safety of oral solithromycin versus oral moxifloxacin for treatment of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia: a global, double-blind, multicentre, randomised, active-controlled, non-inferiority trial (SOLITAIRE-ORAL). Lancet Infect Dis. 2016. PMID: 26852726. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01756339, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: SOLITAIRE-IV (File 2016): intravenous-to-oral solithromycin non-inferior — early response 79.3% versus 79.7% (difference -0.46, 95% CI -6.1 to 5.2); clinical success 84.6% versus 88.6%
cards.summary: SOLITAIRE-IV (File 2016): intravenous-to-oral solithromycin non-inferior — early response 79.3% versus 79.7% (difference -0.46, 95% CI -6.1 to 5.2); clinical success 84.6% versus 88.6%
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, multicentre non-inferiority trial
cards.people: 863 adults with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (PORT class II–IV) randomised 1:1 to intravenous-to-oral solithromycin or moxifloxacin for 7 once-daily doses; all patients received 400 mg intravenously on day 1 and could switch to oral dosing when clinically indicated. Primary objective: non-inferiority (10% margin) in early clinical response at 3 days in the intention-to-treat population.
cards.result: Early clinical response was achieved by 79.3% of solithromycin patients and 79.7% on moxifloxacin (treatment difference -0.46 percentage points, 95% CI -6.1 to 5.2); in the microbiological intention-to-treat population, 80.3% versus 79.1% (difference 1.26, 95% CI -8.1 to 10.6). Investigator-assessed clinical success at short-term follow-up (5–10 days post-therapy) was 84.6% versus 88.6%. Mostly mild-to-moderate infusion events made overall adverse events commoner in the solithromycin group; other adverse events were comparable.
cards.watchOut: The point estimate for clinical success at follow-up actually favours moxifloxacin by 4 percentage points, inside the non-inferiority margin — 'non-inferior' here means 'not unacceptably worse', and the infusion reactions are the visible cost of the intravenous formulation.
cards.source: File TM Jr et al. SOLITAIRE-IV: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Multicenter Study Comparing the Efficacy and Safety of Intravenous-to-Oral Solithromycin to Intravenous-to-Oral Moxifloxacin for Treatment of Community-Acquired Bacterial Pneumonia. Clin Infect Dis. 2016. PMID: 27448679. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01968733, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Meta-analysis of the randomised trials (Wen 2019): early clinical response odds ratio 1.00 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.24) across 1855 patients; no significant difference in adverse events or mortality
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of the randomised trials (Wen 2019): early clinical response odds ratio 1.00 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.24) across 1855 patients; no significant difference in adverse events or mortality
cards.type: Meta-analysis / systematic review of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: Three randomised trials totalling 1855 patients with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia comparing solithromycin monotherapy with other antibiotics (the two phase 3 moxifloxacin trials above plus one further randomised trial), pooled for early clinical response, clinical success at short-term follow-up, and safety outcomes in intention-to-treat and microbiological populations.
cards.result: No statistically significant differences between solithromycin and comparator antibiotics: early clinical response odds ratio 1.00 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.24; P=0.99) and clinical success at short-term follow-up odds ratio 0.78 (95% CI 0.60 to 1.01; P=0.06) in the intention-to-treat population; microbiological-population results were likewise null (early response OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.27; success OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.31). Treatment-emergent, drug-related and serious adverse events and mortality did not differ significantly. These are odds ratios — relative measures; the underlying absolute response rates are those on the trial cards (about 78–80% in both arms).
cards.watchOut: The pooled clinical-success estimate (OR 0.78) leans toward the comparators and nearly reaches significance — pooling does not strengthen the case beyond 'about as good'. The pool is dominated by the two sponsor phase 3 trials, so it is not independent confirmation.
cards.source: Wen J et al. Solithromycin monotherapy for treatment of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia: A meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Int J Clin Pract. 2019. PMID: 30810253. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: an effective antibiotic that does not exist as a treatment — non-inferiority proven, programme failed on liver safety — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: an effective antibiotic that does not exist as a treatment — non-inferiority proven, programme failed on liver safety — POSSIBLE
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: two phase 3 non-inferiority trials (860 and 863 adults) and a meta-analysis of 1855 randomised patients, all against moxifloxacin-based comparators in community-acquired bacterial pneumonia.
cards.result: Solithromycin matched moxifloxacin on early clinical response in both formulations (differences of +0.29 and -0.46 percentage points) and pooled analysis found no efficacy or short-term safety difference. None of that made it a medicine: approval was refused over hepatotoxicity concerns and the programme ended.
cards.watchOut: Read this shelf as history and as a lesson in what non-inferiority trials cannot show: rare liver injury emerges at regulatory review and wider exposure, not in 860-patient efficacy trials. Solithromycin cannot be prescribed; the gonorrhoea programme is a separate question and is not built into this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Barrera CM et al. Lancet Infect Dis. 2016 (PMID: 26852726), File TM Jr et al. Clin Infect Dis. 2016 (PMID: 27448679), Wen J et al. Int J Clin Pract. 2019 (PMID: 30810253). Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01756339, NCT01968733.

shelves.title: GLI-2012 spirometry: continuous FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC equations for ages 3–95 from 97,759 healthy nonsmokers — FEV1/FVC is virtually ancestry-independent, and the race-neutral GLI Global (2022) equations fit about as well with wider limits of normal
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are the reference values for forced spirometry (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC) across the 3–95-year age range — the Global Lung Function Initiative 2012 multi-ethnic equations — including the lower limit of normal and how predicted values differ by ancestry group and by the newer race-neutral (GLI Global) equations?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Child · Ethnicity · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Male · Reference Values · Spirometry/methods, standards · Vital Capacity
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep's respiratory-mechanics account and Guyton & Hall ch. 37 (spirometric volumes as the measurable expression of lung and chest-wall mechanics), named as textbook framing; the numbers below are the primary measurement literature. The GLI-2012 programme (Quanjer 2012) pooled 97,759 records of healthy nonsmokers and derived continuous LMS equations for ages 3–95 in four ancestry groups, with age-dependent lower limits of normal; FEV1 and FVC differed proportionally between groups while FEV1/FVC remained virtually independent of ancestry — so the ratio is the most portable index and the volumes are the equation-sensitive ones. The race-neutral re-analysis (Bowerman 2023) built GLI Global (2022) equations from 74,185 GLI records: fit was similar to the GLI-2012 'other' equations but limits of normal were wider, and sitting height did not explain between-group differences in NHANES III. An independent primary dataset (Madanhire 2020, 712 Zimbabwean children — a population GLI-2012 did not sample) found the African-American equations fit well (all z-score means within ±0.5). Equation choice changes who is labelled abnormal: that dependence is the core teaching content of this shelf.

cards.headline: Quanjer 2012 (GLI-2012): equations for ages 3–95 derived from 97,759 healthy nonsmokers in 33 countries — FEV1/FVC virtually independent of ethnic group
cards.summary: Quanjer 2012 (GLI-2012): equations for ages 3–95 derived from 97,759 healthy nonsmokers in 33 countries — FEV1/FVC virtually independent of ethnic group
cards.type: Human normative programme (pooled multi-centre spirometry reference equations), Eur Respir J 2012
cards.people: 97,759 records of healthy nonsmokers aged 2.5–95 years (55.3% female) collated from 72 centres in 33 countries; after exclusions, reference equations were derived for ages 3–95 in Caucasians (n=57,395), African-Americans (n=3,545), North East Asians (n=4,992) and South East Asians (n=8,255), with a composite 'other' equation averaged across groups.
cards.result: Prediction equations were derived by the LMS method, modelling mean, coefficient of variation and skewness simultaneously, giving continuous predicted values and age-dependent lower limits of normal across the whole 3–95-year range. FEV1 and FVC differed between ethnic groups proportionally to the Caucasian values, such that the FEV1/FVC ratio remained virtually independent of ethnic group. The authors noted that data from the Indian subcontinent, Arabic, Polynesian and Latin American countries and Africa would further improve the equations.
cards.watchOut: A pooled-equation programme, not a single cohort: 23,572 records were discarded, mostly because they could not be combined with other ethnic or geographic groups, and several world regions were unrepresented at derivation — the composite 'other' equation is an interim average, labelled as such by its authors.
cards.source: Quanjer PH et al. Multi-ethnic reference values for spirometry for the 3-95-yr age range: the global lung function 2012 equations. Eur Respir J. 2012. PMID: 22743675. cards.headline: Bowerman 2023 (GLI Global): race-neutral 2022 equations from 74,185 GLI records fit similarly to GLI-2012 'other' equations, with wider limits of normal
cards.summary: Bowerman 2023 (GLI Global): race-neutral 2022 equations from 74,185 GLI records fit similarly to GLI-2012 'other' equations, with wider limits of normal
cards.type: Human normative re-analysis (race-neutral reference equations), Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2023
cards.people: Re-analysis of the original GLI dataset (n=74,185) using inverse-probability weights to create race-neutral equations, alongside a re-analysis of NHANES III data (n=6,984) testing sitting height and the Cormic index as predictors.
cards.result: Including sitting height slightly improved the statistical precision of reference equations over standing height alone but did not explain the observed differences in spirometry between NHANES III race and ethnic groups. The race-neutral GLI Global (2022) equations, which do not require selecting a race or ethnicity, had a similar fit to the GLI-2012 'other' equations and wider limits of normal — so a single global equation classifies a somewhat different (wider-normal) population as within limits than the ancestry-specific equations do.
cards.watchOut: Wider limits of normal cut both ways — fewer false 'abnormal' labels but less sensitivity near the boundary; the authors themselves caution that GLI Global interpretation requires careful consideration of symptoms and history for clinical, employment and insurance decisions.
cards.source: Bowerman C et al. A Race-neutral Approach to the Interpretation of Lung Function Measurements. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2023. PMID: 36383197. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Madanhire 2020: in 712 healthy Zimbabwean children aged 7–13, the GLI-2012 African-American equations fit well (all z-score means within ±0.5) and beat the locally used Polgar equations
cards.summary: Madanhire 2020: in 712 healthy Zimbabwean children aged 7–13, the GLI-2012 African-American equations fit well (all z-score means within ±0.5) and beat the locally used Polgar equations
cards.type: Human normative validation cohort (primary population dataset), BMC Pulm Med 2020
cards.people: 712 healthy urban and peri-urban black-Zimbabwean school children aged 7–13 years (344 girls; mean age 10.5 years, SD 1.81) in Harare, with acceptable spirometry; children with respiratory disease history or symptoms, or BMI z-score below −2, were excluded.
cards.result: Spirometry z-scores from the African-American GLI-2012 equations were reasonably normally distributed, with all means lower than zero but within ±0.5 — the conventional criterion for a good fit — and the African-American module gave the distribution closest to normal of the GLI-2012 modules. No systematic bias was seen across age, height, BMI or school (socioeconomic proxy), and the GLI-2012 equations fit better than the Polgar equations then in use in Zimbabwe.
cards.watchOut: Children only (7–13 years), one city, and the fit is to a borrowed ancestry module — Sub-Saharan African populations were not in the GLI-2012 derivation data, so this is external validation, not representation; girls' z-scores deviated more than boys'.
cards.source: Madanhire T et al. Validation of the global lung initiative 2012 multi-ethnic spirometric reference equations in healthy urban Zimbabwean 7-13 year-old school children: a cross-sectional observational study. BMC Pulm Med. 2020. PMID: 32111226. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Synthesis: one continuous 3–95-year equation family, an ancestry-sensitive volume and an ancestry-robust ratio — and the equation you choose decides who is 'abnormal'
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human reports above (Quanjer 2012; Bowerman 2023; Madanhire 2020), framed by Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall ch. 37 as textbook framing.
cards.result: GLI-2012 replaced the patchwork of local spirometry equations with continuous LMS equations and age-dependent lower limits of normal for ages 3–95 (Quanjer). Within that family, FEV1/FVC is the robust quantity — virtually independent of ethnic group — while FEV1 and FVC predicted values shift proportionally by ancestry group. The race-neutral GLI Global (2022) equations (Bowerman) remove the ancestry selection step at the cost of wider limits of normal and similar overall fit, and body proportions (sitting height) did not explain away group differences. External validation in an unsampled population (Madanhire, Zimbabwean children) showed a borrowed module can still fit within ±0.5 z — reassuring, but a validation, not a derivation. The practical rule the evidence supports: report the equation set beside every predicted value and lower limit, because the same lungs can cross the abnormal line when the equation changes.
cards.watchOut: No carded record here supplies a single bedside table of predicted litres by age and height — the equations are LMS functions implemented in software, and any printed litre value without its equation set named beside it violates this shelf's own rule.
cards.source: Synthesis of Quanjer PH et al., Eur Respir J 2012 (PMID: 22743675); Bowerman C et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2023 (PMID: 36383197); Madanhire T et al., BMC Pulm Med 2020 (PMID: 32111226). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Static lung volumes: GLI-2021 equations from 7,190 Europeans aged 5–80 — plethysmography reads higher than dilution in the elderly, and borrowed middle-aged equations misclassify up to 62.5% of healthy older women as below the TLC lower limit
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are normal static lung volumes — total lung capacity, functional residual capacity, residual volume and RV/TLC — by body plethysmography and gas dilution, per the Global Lung Function Initiative 2021 reference values?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Child · Female · Humans · Lung Volume Measurements · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Total Lung Capacity · Vital Capacity
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep's lung-volumes account and Guyton & Hall ch. 37, named as textbook framing. The GLI-2021 technical standard (Hall 2021) derived sex-specific equations for TLC, FRC, RV, inspiratory capacity, vital capacity, expiratory reserve volume and RV/TLC from 7,190 observations in people of European ancestry aged 5–80, combining plethysmography and dilution FRC after finding physiologically insignificant differences between techniques in the pooled data. The independent cohorts qualify that pooling: in 321 healthy never-smokers aged 65–85 (Garcia-Rio 2009), plethysmography gave higher values than helium dilution for all volumes with wide limits of agreement, and extrapolated middle-aged equations branded 17.9–62.5% of healthy women and 12.5–42.2% of healthy men as below the TLC lower limit of normal. In 5,371 healthy Austrians (Mraz 2024), the GLI equations themselves fit poorly (mean z-scores above +0.5 for RV, RV/TLC and TLC in both sexes), prompting population-derived equations. Method and population both move the 'normal' line — values are carded per-method and per-population.

cards.headline: Hall 2021 (GLI-2021): static lung volume equations from 7,190 observations, ages 5–80, European ancestry — plethysmographic and dilution FRC combined after showing physiologically insignificant differences
cards.summary: Hall 2021 (GLI-2021): static lung volume equations from 7,190 observations, ages 5–80, European ancestry — plethysmographic and dilution FRC combined after showing physiologically insignificant differences
cards.type: Human normative programme (ERS technical standard, pooled reference equations), Eur Respir J 2021
cards.people: 7,190 observations from healthy participants of European ancestry aged 5–80 years, collated from 17 centres, measured by body plethysmography and gas dilution; data from non-European ancestry populations were insufficient to derive multi-ethnic equations.
cards.result: Sex-specific LMS reference equations including height and age were derived for total lung capacity, functional residual capacity, residual volume, inspiratory capacity, vital capacity, expiratory reserve volume and RV/TLC. FRC measured by plethysmography and by dilution showed physiologically insignificant differences and the techniques were combined. The derived equations were similar to previously published equations for FRC and TLC, agreeing more closely in childhood and adolescence than in adulthood; overweight and obesity effects on the ranges were assessed.
cards.watchOut: European ancestry only — the multi-ethnic aim was not met because non-European data were insufficient; and the technique-pooling decision is a pooled-data average that the elderly cohort card below shows does not hold at older ages.
cards.source: Hall GL et al. Official ERS technical standard: Global Lung Function Initiative reference values for static lung volumes in individuals of European ancestry. Eur Respir J. 2021. PMID: 33707167. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Garcia-Rio 2009: in 321 healthy never-smokers aged 65–85, plethysmography exceeded helium dilution for every volume, and middle-aged equations put up to 62.5% of healthy women below the TLC lower limit
cards.summary: Garcia-Rio 2009: in 321 healthy never-smokers aged 65–85, plethysmography exceeded helium dilution for every volume, and middle-aged equations put up to 62.5% of healthy women below the TLC lower limit
cards.type: Human normative cohort (independent plethysmography and dilution cohort), Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2009
cards.people: 321 healthy never-smoker subjects aged 65–85 years, randomly selected from the general population; spirometry and lung volumes measured by both body plethysmography and multibreath helium equilibration following ATS/ERS recommendations.
cards.result: Reference values with lower and upper limits of normal were derived by a piecewise polynomial model, confirming age- and body-size dependence of lung volumes in older subjects beyond height. Plethysmography provided higher values than the dilution method for all lung volumes, with wide limits of agreement. Practically all equations extrapolated from middle-aged adults overpredicted the true volumes: middle-aged reference equations classified between 17.9% and 62.5% of the women and between 12.5% and 42.2% of the men in this healthy sample as below the total lung capacity lower limit of normal.
cards.watchOut: The misclassification percentages are ranges across several published middle-aged equation sets, not one equation's error rate; the cohort is European elderly only, and the plethysmography–dilution gap widens exactly where airway disease also widens it, so method must be recorded with every clinical volume.
cards.source: Garcia-Rio F et al. Lung volume reference values for women and men 65 to 85 years of age. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2009. PMID: 19745204. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mraz 2024 (LEAD, Austria): in 5,371 healthy people aged 6–80, GLI static-volume equations fit poorly — mean z-scores above +0.5 for RV, RV/TLC and TLC in both sexes — so population-derived equations were built
cards.summary: Mraz 2024 (LEAD, Austria): in 5,371 healthy people aged 6–80, GLI static-volume equations fit poorly — mean z-scores above +0.5 for RV, RV/TLC and TLC in both sexes — so population-derived equations were built
cards.type: Human normative cohort (population validation and re-derivation), Respir Res 2024
cards.people: 5,371 respiratory-healthy subjects aged 6–80 years from the Austrian LEAD study, with spirometry and body plethysmography; fit to the GLI equations was judged by z-scores and distribution within the limits of normality, and LEAD reference equations were then created by the same LMS/GAMLSS approach.
cards.result: Good fit (mean z-scores between −0.5 and +0.5) was not observed for the GLI static lung volume equations: mean z-scores exceeded +0.5 for residual volume, RV/TLC and total lung capacity in both sexes, and for expiratory reserve volume and inspiratory capacity in females, with distributions shifted toward the upper limit. The population-derived LEAD equations showed superior fit and reproducible results in this cohort.
cards.watchOut: A single-country validation: poor fit in Austria does not prove poor fit everywhere, but it is direct evidence that the GLI-2021 line is population-sensitive — the opposite of a universal constant — and the female misfit was the largest.
cards.source: Mraz T et al. Updated reference values for static lung volumes from a healthy population in Austria. Respir Res. 2024. PMID: 38570835. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: GLI-2021 is the shared standard for ages 5–80, but technique (plethysmography vs dilution) and population each move the normal line enough to mislabel healthy people
cards.summary: Synthesis: GLI-2021 is the shared standard for ages 5–80, but technique (plethysmography vs dilution) and population each move the normal line enough to mislabel healthy people
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human reports above (Hall 2021; Garcia-Rio 2009; Mraz 2024), framed by Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall ch. 37 as textbook framing.
cards.result: The GLI-2021 equations (Hall) give one continuous, sex-specific standard for TLC, FRC, RV and RV/TLC across ages 5–80 in European-ancestry populations, pooling plethysmography and dilution FRC on pooled-data equivalence. The independent cohorts bound that standard from both sides: at older ages the two techniques diverge systematically (Garcia-Rio — plethysmography higher for every volume, wide limits of agreement) and borrowed middle-aged equations misclassify large fractions of healthy elderly as restrictive; and in a large unselected healthy population the GLI line itself sat high for RV, RV/TLC and TLC (Mraz), requiring local re-derivation. Read together: a static volume is only interpretable with its method and its equation set attached — the same discipline as spirometry on the neighbouring shelf.
cards.watchOut: GLI-2021 covers European ancestry only; no carded record here supports applying these limits to other ancestry groups, and obstructed lungs widen the plethysmography–dilution gap beyond anything in these healthy cohorts.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hall GL et al., Eur Respir J 2021 (PMID: 33707167); Garcia-Rio F et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2009 (PMID: 19745204); Mraz T et al., Respir Res 2024 (PMID: 38570835). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: DLCO reference values: GLI-2017 equations from 12,660 measurements (ages 5–85, Caucasians) — haemoglobin-uncorrected at derivation, and older national equations read up to 111% of predicted against them
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are the reference values for lung diffusing capacity (DLCO / transfer factor) and transfer coefficient (KCO) by age, sex, height and haemoglobin — the GLI-2017 equations — and what lower limit of normal do they define?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Carbon Monoxide/blood, metabolism · Child · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pulmonary Diffusing Capacity/physiology · Reference Standards · Respiratory Function Tests · Spirometry
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep's gas-transfer account and Guyton & Hall ch. 40, named as textbook framing. This shelf is the measurement slice only: how DLCO changes with posture and exercise, and what drives that change, is a different question, already homed in the diffusing-capacity posture-and-exercise shelf (pack #6259) — it is cross-pointed here in prose and none of its studies is re-carded. The GLI-2017 standard (Stanojevic 2017) pooled 12,660 transfer-factor measurements from 19 centres and derived Caucasian reference values for ages 5–85 for TLCO, KCO and alveolar volume — with all data uncorrected for haemoglobin at derivation, so haemoglobin handling belongs on the face of any clinical use. Independent population datasets show why equation vintage matters: in 282 healthy Danes the combined DLCO/DLNO method produced its own equations with haemoglobin built into the CO conductance term (Munkholm 2018), and in 631 healthy Finns the 1982 national values under-predicted so far that mean measured DLCO ran at 111.0% of predicted in men and 104.4% in women (Kainu 2017). Altitude and haemoglobin corrections are part of the measurement, not afterthoughts.

cards.headline: Stanojevic 2017 (GLI-2017): TLCO, KCO and alveolar-volume reference values for Caucasians aged 5–85 from 12,660 measurements in 19 centres — derived uncorrected for haemoglobin
cards.summary: Stanojevic 2017 (GLI-2017): TLCO, KCO and alveolar-volume reference values for Caucasians aged 5–85 from 12,660 measurements in 19 centres — derived uncorrected for haemoglobin
cards.type: Human normative programme (ERS technical standard, pooled reference equations), Eur Respir J 2017
cards.people: 12,660 single-breath transfer factor measurements from asymptomatic lifetime nonsmokers submitted by 19 centres in 14 countries; 85% of the data were from Caucasians, and reference values were derived for Caucasians aged 5–85 years.
cards.result: Using the LMS method and GAMLSS modelling, the GLI derived the first global all-age reference values for the carbon monoxide transfer factor (TLCO), the transfer coefficient (KCO) and alveolar volume, with their lower limits of normal. All data were uncorrected for haemoglobin concentration; before pooling, datasets were adjusted for elevation above sea level, gas concentration and the assumptions used to calculate anatomic dead-space volume, after which there was a high degree of overlap between datasets.
cards.watchOut: Caucasian derivation only, and the haemoglobin point is structural: because the pooled data were uncorrected for haemoglobin, an anaemic or polycythaemic patient's percent-predicted shifts with the correction convention the laboratory applies — the correction must be named with the result.
cards.source: Stanojevic S et al. Official ERS technical standards: Global Lung Function Initiative reference values for the carbon monoxide transfer factor for Caucasians. Eur Respir J. 2017. PMID: 28893868. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Munkholm 2018: in 282 healthy adults aged 18–97, combined DLCO/DLNO single-breath equations for DLCO, DLNO, membrane capacity and capillary volume — with haemoglobin inside the CO conductance formula
cards.summary: Munkholm 2018: in 282 healthy adults aged 18–97, combined DLCO/DLNO single-breath equations for DLCO, DLNO, membrane capacity and capillary volume — with haemoglobin inside the CO conductance formula
cards.type: Human normative cohort (primary population dataset, combined-gas method), Eur Respir J 2018
cards.people: 282 healthy individuals aged 18–97 years; combined diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide and nitric oxide measured by the single-breath technique with a 5-second breath-hold (true apnoea period).
cards.result: Reference equations were established for DLCO and DLNO and for the calculated membrane diffusing capacity (Dm) and pulmonary capillary blood volume (Vc), with age, sex, height and age-squared as independent variables. The calculation fixed the nitric-oxide conductance at 4.5 mL NO per mL blood per min per mmHg, the DmNO/DmCO ratio at 1.97, and made the red-cell CO conductance explicitly haemoglobin-dependent — 1/θCO scaled by 14.6 divided by the haemoglobin concentration in g/dL — a worked example of the haemoglobin correction the GLI derivation left to the user.
cards.watchOut: The 5-second breath-hold and the fixed conductance constants are method choices, not universals — DLNO-derived Dm and Vc values are only as portable as those constants, and this single-country Caucasian cohort does not extend the GLI ancestry range.
cards.source: Munkholm M et al. Reference equations for pulmonary diffusing capacity of carbon monoxide and nitric oxide in adult Caucasians. Eur Respir J. 2018. PMID: 29903858. cards.headline: Kainu 2017: in 631 healthy nonsmoking Finns, the 1982 national equations under-predicted DLCO (mean 111.0% of predicted in men, 104.4% in women) and ECSC values split by sex — new Finnish equations proposed
cards.summary: Kainu 2017: in 631 healthy nonsmoking Finns, the 1982 national equations under-predicted DLCO (mean 111.0% of predicted in men, 104.4% in women) and ECSC values split by sex — new Finnish equations proposed
cards.type: Human normative cohort (primary population dataset), Scand J Clin Lab Invest 2017
cards.people: 631 healthy non-smoking Finnish volunteers (41.5% male); single-breath DLCO, alveolar volume, DLCO/VA and lung volumes measured to the updated ATS/ERS standards, with reference models by linear regression.
cards.result: The previously used Finnish (1982) reference values produced too-low predicted values: mean measured DLCO was 111.0% of predicted in males and 104.4% in females, and DLCO/VA 103.5% and 102.7% respectively. With the European (ECSC) reference values there was a significant sex difference in DLCO/VA — mean predicted 105.4% in males versus 92.8% in females (P < 0.001). New reference values for DLCO, DLCO/VA, alveolar volume and vital capacity were proposed to replace the outdated national set.

cards.headline: Synthesis: GLI-2017 is the shared DLCO standard — but it is Caucasian-derived, haemoglobin-uncorrected, and national cohorts keep showing that equation vintage moves percent-predicted by ~10 points
cards.summary: Synthesis: GLI-2017 is the shared DLCO standard — but it is Caucasian-derived, haemoglobin-uncorrected, and national cohorts keep showing that equation vintage moves percent-predicted by ~10 points
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human reports above (Stanojevic 2017; Munkholm 2018; Kainu 2017), framed by Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall ch. 40 as textbook framing. The posture-and-exercise behaviour of DLCO is homed in pack #6259 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Three legs, one discipline. The GLI-2017 equations (Stanojevic) give continuous reference values and lower limits for TLCO, KCO and alveolar volume for ages 5–85 from the largest normative collection assembled (12,660 measurements) — explicitly for Caucasians and explicitly uncorrected for haemoglobin. The combined-gas cohort (Munkholm) shows the haemoglobin term doing real work inside the calculation and extends the partition into membrane capacity and capillary volume under stated constants. The Finnish cohort (Kainu) shows the cost of stale equations: a generation-old national set read healthy people at 104–111% of predicted, and a continental set split the sexes by 12.6 points on DLCO/VA. A DLCO result without its equation set, haemoglobin handling and altitude context is not yet an interpretable number.
cards.watchOut: This shelf deliberately does not cover how DLCO moves with posture, exercise or disease — those are other shelves' questions (posture/exercise: pack #6259); mixing a reference-value percent-predicted with a within-person physiological change is the error this split exists to prevent.
cards.source: Synthesis of Stanojevic S et al., Eur Respir J 2017 (PMID: 28893868); Munkholm M et al., Eur Respir J 2018 (PMID: 29903858); Kainu A et al., Scand J Clin Lab Invest 2017 (PMID: 28218012). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Respiratory impedance by oscillometry: height drives the adult equations, women run higher resistance than men, and the 1994 equations still in laboratory use misread healthy older adults by −34% to +76%
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are normal respiratory impedance values by impulse oscillometry / forced oscillation (resistance at 5 and 20 Hz, reactance, area of reactance) by age, height and sex — and how do values differ between devices and populations?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cohort Studies · Electric Impedance · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Oscillometry/methods · Reference Values · Respiratory Function Tests
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing for oscillometry specifically is thin in Boron & Boulpaep's respiratory-mechanics chapters — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature and says so. Three primary cohorts from three populations agree on the structure: in 567 healthy Chinese adults from 19 hospitals (Liang 2021), height — not age — was the dominant predictor, and both the equations and the manufacturer's ranges in routine use mis-stated the normal limits; in 397 never-smoking lung-healthy adults aged 45–91 from the population-based KORA cohorts (Schulz 2013), women had higher resistance and lower low-frequency reactance than men, R5−R20, reactance area and resonant frequency rose with age, and the Vogel & Smidt 1994 equations in widespread use erred by −34% to +76% where the new equations erred by −1% to +5% (relative differences); in 75 asymptomatic Norwegians over 70 (Aarli 2013), within-breath impedance (the inspiratory–expiratory reactance difference at 5 Hz) gained its first elderly reference values, with higher resistance than earlier studies reported. Values are carded per-device and per-population: IOS and FOT generations and their signal processing are not interchangeable.

cards.headline: Liang 2021: reference equations from 567 healthy Chinese adults (19 hospitals) — height, not age, drives IOS indices, and the manufacturer's normal ranges clearly differ from the derived limits
cards.summary: Liang 2021: reference equations from 567 healthy Chinese adults (19 hospitals) — height, not age, drives IOS indices, and the manufacturer's normal ranges clearly differ from the derived limits
cards.type: Human normative cohort (multicentre primary population dataset), J Thorac Dis 2021
cards.people: 567 healthy adults with acceptable impulse oscillometry data, drawn from 1,318 subjects measured at 19 general hospitals across China between 2016 and 2018, with measurements performed to European Respiratory Society recommendations; the study was registered as part of a larger study (NCT03467880).
cards.result: Sex-specific reference equations with lower and upper limits of normal were developed for the impulse oscillometry indices by multiple linear regression. Height, but not age, was the most influential contributor to the indices. The reference equations then in laboratory use predicted higher R5 and X5 than the new equations, and the normal ranges for R5 and X5 recommended by the equipment manufacturer were clearly different from the upper and lower limits derived from this population — so the device defaults and the population data disagree about who is normal.
cards.watchOut: One population and one device family: the equations are Chinese-adult IOS values, and the headline lesson — manufacturer ranges ≠ population limits — means these numbers must not be exported to other devices or ancestries without local validation.
cards.source: Liang XL et al. Reference values of respiratory impedance with impulse oscillometry in healthy Chinese adults. J Thorac Dis. 2021. PMID: 34277060. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03467880, from the record's databank fields. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Schulz 2013 (KORA): in 397 lung-healthy adults aged 45–91, women had higher resistance and lower reactance than men; the 1994 Vogel & Smidt equations erred by −34% to +76% (relative) where new equations erred by −1% to +5%
cards.summary: Schulz 2013 (KORA): in 397 lung-healthy adults aged 45–91, women had higher resistance and lower reactance than men; the 1994 Vogel & Smidt equations erred by −34% to +76% (relative) where new equations erred by −1% to +5%
cards.type: Human normative cohort (population-based primary dataset, advanced age), PLoS One 2013
cards.people: 397 never-smoking, lung-healthy subjects with normal spirometry (243 women, 154 men), identified within a population-based sample of 1,990 subjects aged 45–91 years from the KORA cohorts (Augsburg, Germany); sex-specific quantile regression models used age, height and body weight as predictors.
cards.result: Women showed higher resistance values than men, while reactance at low frequencies (up to 20 Hz) was lower (P < 0.05). A significant age dependency was found for R5−R20 (the difference between resistance at 5 and 20 Hz), the integrated low-frequency reactance area (AX) and resonant frequency in both sexes, and for reactance at 5 Hz (X5) in women only. Against the healthy subjects, mean differences between observed and predicted resistance (5 and 20 Hz) and reactance (5 Hz) ranged from −1% to +5% (relative) with the new model, versus −34% to +76% (relative) with the then-current Vogel & Smidt 1994 equations.
cards.watchOut: The error ranges are relative differences between observed and predicted values in this cohort, printed with that meaning; the cohort is Caucasian and aged 45+, so the equations fill the older-age gap rather than replacing adult equations at younger ages.
cards.source: Schulz H et al. Reference values of impulse oscillometric lung function indices in adults of advanced age. PLoS One. 2013. PMID: 23691036. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Aarli 2013: first within-breath impedance reference values in 75 asymptomatic elderly over 70 — whole-breath and inspiratory/expiratory reactance at 5 Hz by forced oscillation
cards.summary: Aarli 2013: first within-breath impedance reference values in 75 asymptomatic elderly over 70 — whole-breath and inspiratory/expiratory reactance at 5 Hz by forced oscillation
cards.type: Human normative cohort (within-breath FOT/IOS, elderly), Clin Respir J 2013
cards.people: 75 healthy non-smoking participants aged over 70 years with normal spirometry and at least two valid forced-oscillation measurements, selected from 148 elderly participants drawn as an age- and sex-stratified random sample from the population of Bergen, Norway; measurements used an impulse oscillometry system.
cards.result: Predictive equations for men and women were created for whole-breath and within-breath impedance parameters by linear multiple regression, including the within-breath reactance difference at 5 Hz (ΔX5 — the inspiratory-to-expiratory swing used to detect expiratory flow limitation). Resistance measurements were higher than those reported in previous studies, and frequency dependence of resistance was significantly larger in this elderly sample.
cards.watchOut: N = 75 after validity filtering from 148 selected — a small, single-city elderly sample; within-breath indices are device- and algorithm-specific (the ΔX5 method derives from the Dellacà forced-oscillation work), so these values travel with the technique, not across oscillometry platforms.
cards.source: Aarli BB et al. Reference values for within-breath pulmonary impedance parameters in asymptomatic elderly. Clin Respir J. 2013. PMID: 22822726. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: oscillometry norms are real but local — height- and sex-structured, age-sensitive in the reactance indices, and only valid for the device and population that produced them
cards.summary: Synthesis: oscillometry norms are real but local — height- and sex-structured, age-sensitive in the reactance indices, and only valid for the device and population that produced them
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human cohorts above (Liang 2021; Schulz 2013; Aarli 2013). Boron & Boulpaep framing for oscillometry is thin, as flagged in the balance; the forty-year review of adult impedance reference values in the wider literature is consistent with this per-population picture but is a review and is not carded.
cards.result: The three cohorts triangulate one discipline. Structure: resistance falls and reactance rises with height (Liang — height the dominant adult predictor), women run higher resistance and lower low-frequency reactance than men (Schulz), and the frequency-dependence and reactance indices (R5−R20, AX, resonant frequency, X5) drift with age even when R5 itself does not (Schulz; Aarli's elderly within-breath values). Validity: in every cohort the inherited standard failed somewhere measurable — manufacturer ranges (Liang), the 1994 equations' −34% to +76% relative errors in older adults (Schulz), absent within-breath norms over 70 (Aarli). REFUSAL, recorded per the standing rule: a verified Indian-adult IOS reference cohort (Moitra et al., Int J Tuberc Lung Dis 2020) was refused as an evidence card this session because its PubMed record carries an EMPTY abstract and its numbers cannot be verified from the record; it is named here as refused, not carded, pending a full-text pull.
cards.watchOut: Never pool IOS and FOT values or apply one population's limits to another: device generation, signal processing and population each shift the normal range, which is this shelf's central finding rather than a caveat.
cards.source: Synthesis of Liang XL et al., J Thorac Dis 2021 (PMID: 34277060); Schulz H et al., PLoS One 2013 (PMID: 23691036); Aarli BB et al., Clin Respir J 2013 (PMID: 22822726). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: FeNO in healthy people: upper limits run 24–54 ppb by age and height in never-smokers, the prediction equations explain only ~10% of the variation, and atopy and male sex push values up while current smoking breaks the equations
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the distribution of fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO at 50 mL/s) — its geometric mean and upper reference limit in lifelong never-smokers, and how much do atopy, height, age, sex and current smoking shift it?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Biomarkers/analysis · Body Height/physiology · Breath Tests · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nitric Oxide/analysis · Reference Values
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing for FeNO is thin in Boron & Boulpaep (airway nitric-oxide signalling) — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature and says so. This shelf is the measurement slice only: whether FeNO should guide asthma treatment is a different, management question, already homed in the live adolescent shelf (#1728) and the adult FeNO-guided-treatment pack (#5904) — cross-pointed here in prose, with none of their studies re-carded. In healthy lifelong never-smokers (Olin 2007, n=1,131), FeNO at 50 mL/s is predicted from height and age, but the equations explain only 9–11% of the variation and the upper limit spans 24.0–54.0 parts per billion across age and height. The larger general-population study (Torén 2017, n=3,378 after exclusions) found never- and former smokers similar enough to merge, built sex-specific equations with atopy included — and found current smokers' values so unstable to model that fixed cut-off limits are proposed instead. In 166 healthy Korean adults (Kim 2010), male sex and atopy independently raised FeNO, with group means from 24.1 ppb (nonatopic women) to 37.3 ppb (atopic men). Analyser type matters: the Swedish cohorts used chemiluminescence (NIOX) analysers, and values from electrochemical devices are not assumed interchangeable.

cards.headline: Olin 2007: in 1,131 healthy lifelong never-smokers, FeNO upper limits range from 24.0 to 54.0 ppb by age and height — and height/age equations explain only 9–11% of the variation
cards.summary: Olin 2007: in 1,131 healthy lifelong never-smokers, FeNO upper limits range from 24.0 to 54.0 ppb by age and height — and height/age equations explain only 9–11% of the variation
cards.type: Human normative cohort (primary population dataset, chemiluminescence), Chest 2007
cards.people: 1,131 healthy lifelong never-smokers (845 nonatopic, 286 atopic) remaining from 3,376 adults after excluding physician-diagnosed asthma, asthma symptoms, ever wheezing, dry cough and inhaled-steroid use; FeNO at 50 mL/s measured by chemiluminescence analyser to ATS/ERS guidelines, with atopy defined by specific IgE.
cards.result: The proposed reference equation for healthy never-smoking adults was ln(FeNO) = 0.057 + 0.013 × height (cm) + 0.0088 × age (years), with residual SD 0.51 and explanatory value 9%; in nonatopic subjects alone the equation was ln(FeNO) = −0.0026 + 0.013 × height + 0.010 × age (residual SD 0.48, explanatory value 11%). Because so little variation is explained, the authors' most important finding is the spread of the upper limit itself: 24.0 to 54.0 parts per billion depending on age and height.
cards.watchOut: A single 'normal FeNO' cut-off does not exist in this data — the upper limit more than doubles across the age/height range, and with ~90% of variation unexplained by the equation, an individual's predicted value is a weak anchor; Swedish population, chemiluminescence device.

cards.headline: Torén 2017: in 3,378 respiratory-healthy adults, never- and former smokers merge into one reference population, atopy enters the sex-specific equations — and current smokers get fixed cut-offs because their models were unstable
cards.summary: Torén 2017: in 3,378 respiratory-healthy adults, never- and former smokers merge into one reference population, atopy enters the sex-specific equations — and current smokers get fixed cut-offs because their models were unstable
cards.type: Human normative cohort (general-population primary dataset, chemiluminescence), BMC Pulm Med 2017
cards.people: 3,378 subjects aged 25–75 years remaining from 5,265 general-population participants after excluding asthma, chronic bronchitis, spirometric airway obstruction and current cold; FeNO measured with a chemiluminescence (NIOX) analyser to ATS/ERS guidelines, atopy by Phadiatop IgE testing.
cards.result: FeNO levels were similar in never-smokers and former smokers, so the two groups were merged as 'non-smokers' and sex-specific reference equations with 5th and 95th percentiles were generated from age, height and atopy. Regression models for current smokers were unstable, so no equation is offered for them: the proposed reference values for current smokers are based on the univariate distribution, as fixed cut-off limits — direct evidence that current smoking shifts FeNO in a way the standard determinants do not capture.
cards.watchOut: The record does not print the smokers' numeric cut-offs in its abstract, so none is claimed here; the unstable-models finding is itself the carded result. Same Swedish chemiluminescence tradition as Olin — device portability to electrochemical analysers is not established by these two cohorts.
cards.source: Torén K et al. Reference values of fractional excretion of exhaled nitric oxide among non-smokers and current smokers. BMC Pulm Med. 2017. PMID: 28841881. cards.headline: Kim 2010: in 166 healthy nonsmoking Korean adults, FeNO was independently higher in men (P = 0.008) and in atopic subjects (P = 0.044) — group means 24.1 ppb (nonatopic women) to 37.3 ppb (atopic men)
cards.summary: Kim 2010: in 166 healthy nonsmoking Korean adults, FeNO was independently higher in men (P = 0.008) and in atopic subjects (P = 0.044) — group means 24.1 ppb (nonatopic women) to 37.3 ppb (atopic men)
cards.type: Human normative cohort (primary population dataset, Asian adults), J Asthma 2010
cards.people: 166 nonsmoking healthy Korean adults; FeNO measured alongside spirometry, with atopic status by skin-prick testing and age, height, weight and respiratory symptoms recorded; associations tested by multivariate linear regression adjusting for age, height, weight, FEV1 and chronic rhinitis.
cards.result: FeNO levels were positively and independently associated with male gender (P = 0.008) and atopy (P = 0.044). Mean FeNO was highest in atopic men (37.3 ± 12.1 ppb), followed by nonatopic men (33.9 ± 14.3 ppb), atopic women (28.6 ± 17.7 ppb) and nonatopic women (24.1 ± 10.6 ppb) — the sex gap within a population is as large as the atopy gap, and both sit inside the Swedish never-smoker upper-limit range on the neighbouring card.
cards.watchOut: N = 166 — the smallest cohort on this shelf, single-country, and its standard deviations are wide (up to ±17.7 ppb), so the group means order the determinants rather than fix precise limits; atopy here is skin-prick defined, versus IgE-defined in the Swedish cohorts.
cards.source: Kim SH et al. Reference values and determinants of exhaled nitric oxide in healthy Korean adults. J Asthma. 2010. PMID: 20536283. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: healthy FeNO is a wide, determinant-shifted distribution — height, age, sex and atopy each move it, smoking breaks the model, and no single cut-off survives the data
cards.summary: Synthesis: healthy FeNO is a wide, determinant-shifted distribution — height, age, sex and atopy each move it, smoking breaks the model, and no single cut-off survives the data
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human cohorts above (Olin 2007; Torén 2017; Kim 2010). Whether FeNO should guide asthma treatment is homed in live shelf #1728 and pack #5904 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Across 1,131 Swedish never-smokers, 3,378 general-population adults and 166 Korean adults, the same structure repeats: FeNO at 50 mL/s rises with height and age (Olin's equations), is higher in men and in atopic people (Kim's adjusted associations; Torén's atopy-inclusive equations), is indistinguishable between never- and former smokers (Torén), and resists equation modelling altogether in current smokers (Torén). The honest summary statistic is a range, not a point: upper limits of 24.0–54.0 ppb across age and height in never-smokers (Olin), with ~90% of individual variation unexplained by the standard determinants. Any clinic cut-off is therefore a convention laid over this distribution — useful, but not a property of the biology.
cards.watchOut: All three cohorts predate widespread electrochemical-analyser use and two of three are Swedish chemiluminescence data; paediatric FeNO distributions are a separate literature and are not covered by this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Olin AC et al., Chest 2007 (PMID: 17565022); Torén K et al., BMC Pulm Med 2017 (PMID: 28841881); Kim SH et al., J Asthma 2010 (PMID: 20536283). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: SNIP norms: healthy adults sniff harder than they can suck — mean 76.8 cm H₂O in Japanese men and 60.0 in women (lower limits 32.9 and 28.8), children aged 6–17 already reach adult-range values, and SNIP complements rather than replaces mouth pressure
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is sniff nasal inspiratory pressure (SNIP) — its mean and lower limit of normal by age and sex — and how does it compare with maximal inspiratory mouth pressure as a measure of inspiratory muscle strength?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Female · Humans · Inhalation/physiology · Male · Middle Aged · Pressure · Reference Values · Respiratory Muscles/physiology · Sex Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framing follows Guyton & Hall ch. 37 and Boron & Boulpaep's mechanics of breathing, named as textbook framing. This shelf is the nose-measured manoeuvre only; mouth-pressure (MIP/MEP) reference values are a neighbouring question (Slate 8's S8-4-27) and are not duplicated here. Three cohorts from three age bands agree: in 160 healthy adults aged 20–80 (Uldry & Fitting 1995), maximal SNIP fell with age, was the same sitting and supine, and equalled or exceeded maximal inspiratory mouth pressure in 107 of 160 subjects (mean SNIP/PImax ratio 1.08 in men, 1.17 in women) — with agreement low enough that the authors call the two tests complementary, not interchangeable. In 223 healthy Japanese adults (Kamide 2009), mean SNIP was 76.8 ± 28.9 cm H₂O in men and 60.0 ± 20.0 in women, with lower limits of normal of 32.9 and 28.8 cm H₂O. In 180 healthy children aged 6–17 (Stefanutti & Fitting 1999), SNIP was already 104 ± 26 cm H₂O in boys and 93 ± 23 in girls — adult-range values, higher than mouth pressure at the same lung volume.

cards.headline: Uldry & Fitting 1995: in 160 healthy adults aged 20–80, maximal SNIP fell with age, matched sitting and supine, and equalled or beat PImax in 107 of 160 — mean ratio 1.08 (men) and 1.17 (women)
cards.summary: Uldry & Fitting 1995: in 160 healthy adults aged 20–80, maximal SNIP fell with age, matched sitting and supine, and equalled or beat PImax in 107 of 160 — mean ratio 1.08 (men) and 1.17 (women)
cards.type: Human normative cohort (classic primary dataset, adults), Thorax 1995
cards.people: 160 healthy subjects (80 men) aged 20–80 years with FVC above 80%, FEV1/FVC above 85% of predicted and BMI 18–31; SNIP measured from functional residual capacity through a catheter plugging one nostril during 10 maximal sniffs, sitting and supine, and PImax measured from FRC with a flanged mouthpiece over four manoeuvres.
cards.result: For both men and women, maximal SNIP was negatively correlated with age and was similar in the sitting and supine positions. In the sitting position, maximal SNIP was greater than or equal to PImax in 107 of 160 subjects; the mean (SD) SNIP/PImax ratio was 1.08 (0.22) in men and 1.17 (0.29) in women. Normal SNIP values can be predicted from age and sex — but the low level of agreement between SNIP and PImax means the two manoeuvres are not interchangeable, only complementary.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract does not print the absolute mean SNIP values by decade, so none is claimed from this card — its carded content is the age relation, the posture equivalence and the SNIP–PImax comparison; absolute means come from the Japanese and paediatric cards.
cards.source: Uldry C, Fitting JW. Maximal values of sniff nasal inspiratory pressure in healthy subjects. Thorax. 1995. PMID: 7785009. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Kamide 2009: in 223 healthy Japanese adults, mean SNIP was 76.8 ± 28.9 cm H₂O in men and 60.0 ± 20.0 in women, with lower limits of normal of 32.9 and 28.8 cm H₂O
cards.summary: Kamide 2009: in 223 healthy Japanese adults, mean SNIP was 76.8 ± 28.9 cm H₂O in men and 60.0 ± 20.0 in women, with lower limits of normal of 32.9 and 28.8 cm H₂O
cards.type: Human normative cohort (primary population dataset with lower limits), Respiration 2009
cards.people: 223 healthy Japanese volunteers (112 men, 111 women) aged 18–69 years with no history of pulmonary, heart, neuromuscular or sinus disease; SNIP measured with a nasal plug in one nostril, mouth closed, as short sharp maximal sniffs from functional residual volume, with good reproducibility by intraclass correlation in both sexes.
cards.result: Mean SNIP was 76.8 ± 28.9 cm H₂O in men and 60.0 ± 20.0 cm H₂O in women — significantly higher in men (P < 0.01). On stepwise multiple regression, SNIP was negatively related to age in men and positively related to body mass index in women. The lower limits of normal were 32.9 cm H₂O in men and 28.8 cm H₂O in women — roughly 40–45% of the sex-specific means (relative comparison), which is how wide the healthy spread is.
cards.watchOut: The study exists because ethnic differences were expected — these are Japanese-population values and the authors' premise is that they should not be assumed to transfer unchanged to other populations; standard deviations near ±29 cm H₂O make any single cut-off a blunt instrument.
cards.source: Kamide N et al. Sniff nasal inspiratory pressure in healthy Japanese subjects: mean values and lower limits of normal. Respiration. 2009. PMID: 18957838. cards.headline: Stefanutti & Fitting 1999: in 180 healthy children aged 6–17, SNIP was 104 ± 26 cm H₂O in boys and 93 ± 23 in girls — adult-range values, and higher than PImax at the same lung volume in most children
cards.summary: Stefanutti & Fitting 1999: in 180 healthy children aged 6–17, SNIP was 104 ± 26 cm H₂O in boys and 93 ± 23 in girls — adult-range values, and higher than PImax at the same lung volume in most children
cards.type: Human normative cohort (primary population dataset, children), Am J Respir Crit Care Med 1999
cards.people: 180 unselected healthy children aged 6–17 years studied in a school setting, all with FVC above 80% of predicted and FEV1/FVC above 85% of predicted; SNIP measured sitting, via a catheter occluding one nostril during maximal sniffs from FRC, with PImax measured from FRC and residual volume and PEmax from FRC and total lung capacity.
cards.result: All children could perform the sniff manoeuvre easily. SNIP was 104 ± 26 cm H₂O in boys and 93 ± 23 cm H₂O in girls (P < 0.005) — values similar to those previously measured in healthy adults. SNIP correlated with age, weight and height in boys but not in girls, and in both sexes SNIP exceeded PImax measured at the same lung volume (FRC) (P < 0.0001), equalling or exceeding it in 73 of 93 boys and 79 of 87 girls.
cards.watchOut: Children's means exceeding the Japanese adult means on the neighbouring card is a cross-population, cross-laboratory comparison (Caucasian schoolchildren vs Japanese adults, same senior author's laboratory tradition) — it shows children are not simply small adults on this test, not that one population is stronger.
cards.source: Stefanutti D, Fitting JW. Sniff nasal inspiratory pressure. Reference values in Caucasian children. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 1999. PMID: 9872826. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SNIP is an easy, posture-independent sniff that usually exceeds mouth pressure — with age- and sex-structured norms, wide healthy spread, and lower limits near 30 cm H₂O in adults
cards.summary: Synthesis: SNIP is an easy, posture-independent sniff that usually exceeds mouth pressure — with age- and sex-structured norms, wide healthy spread, and lower limits near 30 cm H₂O in adults
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human cohorts above (Uldry & Fitting 1995; Kamide 2009; Stefanutti & Fitting 1999), framed by Guyton & Hall ch. 37 and Boron & Boulpaep as textbook framing.
cards.result: One manoeuvre, three age bands, consistent findings. Performance: every child studied could do it (Stefanutti), it needs no mouthpiece seal, and posture does not change it (Uldry — sitting equals supine, unlike mouth pressure). Magnitude: healthy values centre near 77 cm H₂O in adult men and 60 in adult women with lower limits of normal at 32.9 and 28.8 (Kamide), and children aged 6–17 already average 93–104 (Stefanutti). Relation to mouth pressure: SNIP usually exceeds PImax (ratios 1.08–1.17 in adults; higher at FRC in most children) yet agrees with it too loosely to substitute for it (Uldry) — the two tests are complementary windows on inspiratory muscle strength, and a low value on either deserves the other test before it is believed.
cards.watchOut: Norms are population-specific by the Japanese authors' own premise, and the healthy standard deviations are so wide that SNIP discriminates weakness at the low tail (near the ~30 cm H₂O lower limits) far better than it grades strength in the middle of the range.
cards.source: Synthesis of Uldry C, Fitting JW, Thorax 1995 (PMID: 7785009); Kamide N et al., Respiration 2009 (PMID: 18957838); Stefanutti D, Fitting JW, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 1999 (PMID: 9872826). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Cough flows rest on a thin base: three small healthy-volunteer studies (N = 52, 30 and 40) — peak cough flow agrees between pneumotachograph and portable meter above 270 L/min, the meter over-reads below it, and no GLI-style normative programme exists
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are voluntary cough flows and cough aerodynamics — peak cough flow by sex and age, glottic compression-phase behaviour and expulsive-phase flow — and how reproducible is peak cough flow measurement between pneumotachograph and portable peak-flow meter?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Cough/diagnosis · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Peak Expiratory Flow Rate/physiology · Reference Values · Respiratory Function Tests/methods · Sex Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — stamped emerging, not established, because the base is genuinely thin and this shelf says so on its face: there is NO GLI-style normative programme for cough flow. Framing follows Guyton & Hall ch. 37 (the cough reflex and airway mechanics) and Boron & Boulpaep's respiratory mechanics, named as textbook framing. The entire healthy-human distribution is assembled from three small volunteer studies, their Ns printed here and on every card: cough aerodynamics in 52 healthy adults (Feinstein 2017 — peak airflow rose with height, peak pressure was greater in men, expiratory rise time was longer in women); a device-agreement study with 30 healthy subjects alongside 32 neuromuscular patients (Sancho 2004 — pneumotachograph and portable meter agreed closely overall, r = 0.95, but the meter overestimated flows below 270 L/min); and airflow features of cough versus throat clearing in 40 healthy participants (Mootassim-Billah 2025 — throat clearing is aerodynamically a weaker manoeuvre than cough, P < 0.001). The widely used clinical peak-cough-flow thresholds in neuromuscular care rest on this thin base — that thinness is the teaching content of this shelf, and nothing here inflates it.

cards.headline: Feinstein 2017: cough aerodynamics in 52 healthy adults (N = 52) — peak airflow rose with height, peak pressure was greater in men and rose with height, expiratory rise time was longer in women
cards.summary: Feinstein 2017: cough aerodynamics in 52 healthy adults (N = 52) — peak airflow rose with height, peak pressure was greater in men and rose with height, expiratory rise time was longer in women
cards.type: Human physiological study (healthy-volunteer cough aerodynamics, N = 52), Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol 2017
cards.people: 52 healthy subjects (29 women, 23 men; mean age 51.6 years in women and 52.3 in men) recruited from an outpatient clinic, performing maximal voluntary cough with measurements recorded on a pneumotachograph; outcomes were cough peak airflow, peak pressure and expiratory rise time, stratified by age, gender and height. N = 52 — a small healthy-volunteer study, printed plainly.
cards.result: Peak airflow differed significantly across age, gender and height, increasing with increasing height. Peak cough pressure also increased with height and was significantly greater in males than females. Expiratory rise time — the time from glottal opening to peak airflow, the measurable signature of the compression-to-expulsive phase transition — did not vary with age or height but was statistically significantly longer in women. The authors present these as normative reference data for future studies of laryngotracheal disorders; the record's abstract does not print the absolute flow values, so none is claimed here.
cards.watchOut: N = 52 from a single outpatient clinic, and the stratification findings are directional (the abstract reports significance, not the stratum values) — this card establishes which variables a cough-flow norm must condition on, not the conditioned values themselves.
cards.source: Feinstein AJ et al. Measurement of Cough Aerodynamics in Healthy Adults. Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol. 2017. PMID: 28397558. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sancho 2004: peak cough flow by pneumotachograph vs portable meter in 30 healthy subjects and 32 neuromuscular patients — overall agreement r = 0.95, but the meter overestimated flows below 270 L/min
cards.summary: Sancho 2004: peak cough flow by pneumotachograph vs portable meter in 30 healthy subjects and 32 neuromuscular patients — overall agreement r = 0.95, but the meter overestimated flows below 270 L/min
cards.type: Human physiological study (device agreement, healthy N = 30 plus patient limb), Am J Phys Med Rehabil 2004
cards.people: 30 healthy subjects and 32 medically stable patients with neuromuscular disease (62 people in total); every subject performed maximal cough efforts from total lung capacity through an oronasal mask connected, in randomised order, to a pneumotachograph and to a portable peak flow meter (asmaPLAN+, Vitalograph). The healthy N is 30 — printed plainly; the agreement statistics below are for the combined study population as the record reports them.
cards.result: Peak cough flow by pneumotachograph was 377.70 ± 179.28 L/min and by portable meter 377.50 ± 172.98 L/min (not significant), with the two measurements correlated at r = 0.95 (P < 0.001) and a random error of 9.37%; the mean difference was 0.20 L/min with limits of agreement of ±109.78 L/min. Across flow ranges there were no significant differences overall — except below 270 L/min, where in 14 patients the meter read significantly higher than the pneumotachograph (213.93 ± 55.92 vs 180.86 ± 57.22 L/min, P < 0.01). The authors conclude the portable meter is reproducible and reasonably accurate above 270 L/min, with caution required at lower flows.
cards.watchOut: The headline means pool healthy subjects and neuromuscular patients exactly as the record reports them — they are agreement data, not healthy norms; and the low-flow over-reading occurred in patients, which is precisely the range where neuromuscular thresholds are applied, so the caution lands where it matters most.
cards.source: Sancho J et al. Comparison of peak cough flows measured by pneumotachograph and a portable peak flow meter. Am J Phys Med Rehabil. 2004. PMID: 15277962. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mootassim-Billah 2025: in 40 healthy participants (N = 40), voluntary throat clearing produced significantly lower peak expiratory flow and expired volume than voluntary cough and induced reflexive cough (P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Mootassim-Billah 2025: in 40 healthy participants (N = 40), voluntary throat clearing produced significantly lower peak expiratory flow and expired volume than voluntary cough and induced reflexive cough (P < 0.001)
cards.type: Human physiological study (healthy-volunteer cough and throat-clearing airflow, N = 40), Int J Lang Commun Disord 2025
cards.people: 40 healthy participants; airflow measured for single voluntary throat clearings, single voluntary coughs and the first two induced reflexive coughs of a reflexive cough epoch, as peak expiratory flow rate (L/s) and cough expired volume (L) per manoeuvre. N = 40 — a small healthy-volunteer study, printed plainly. Registered as ISRCTN16540497.
cards.result: Voluntary throat clearing displayed lower airflow feature values than both voluntary cough and induced reflexive cough (P < 0.001 for the comparisons) — throat clearing is aerodynamically a distinct, weaker airway-protective manoeuvre, not a quiet cough, even though the two can be confused by ear during a clinical swallowing evaluation. The record's abstract reports the direction and significance of the differences rather than the absolute flow values, so none is claimed here.
cards.watchOut: N = 40, exploratory by the authors' own description, and framed around dysphagia assessment — its contribution here is the within-person manoeuvre comparison in healthy people, not a normative flow distribution.
cards.source: Mootassim-Billah S et al. Airflow Features Obtained From Voluntary Throat Clearing Compared to Voluntary Cough and Induced Reflexive Cough in a Healthy Population. Int J Lang Commun Disord. 2025. PMID: 41246892. Registry ID: ISRCTN16540497, from the record's databank fields.
