cards.headline: Synthesis: the honest state of cough-flow physiology — three small studies, device agreement that fails exactly at the clinically decisive low flows, and no normative programme behind the thresholds in routine use
cards.summary: Synthesis: the honest state of cough-flow physiology — three small studies, device agreement that fails exactly at the clinically decisive low flows, and no normative programme behind the thresholds in routine use
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human studies above (Feinstein 2017, N = 52; Sancho 2004, healthy N = 30; Mootassim-Billah 2025, N = 40), framed by Guyton & Hall ch. 37 and Boron & Boulpaep as textbook framing.
cards.result: What is actually known: cough peak airflow scales with height and differs by sex, peak pressure is greater in men, and the glottal compression-to-expulsive timing (expiratory rise time) is longer in women (Feinstein). A portable peak-flow meter reproduces pneumotachograph peak cough flow well at higher flows (r = 0.95 overall) but over-reads below 270 L/min (Sancho) — the very range in which neuromuscular cough thresholds are applied. And the manoeuvre matters: throat clearing is not a weak cough but a measurably different, lower-flow act (Mootassim-Billah). What is not known is just as definite: no large, multi-population, GLI-style reference programme for cough flow exists in the carded literature, so every 'normal peak cough flow' figure in clinical use traces back to small volunteer samples like these three (combined healthy N = 122). This shelf is stamped PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING for exactly that reason.
cards.watchOut: Do not cite this shelf as normative reference values: two of its three records do not print absolute healthy flow distributions in their abstracts, and the third is a device-agreement study. It documents the structure of the evidence and its thinness — a builder with full texts could deepen it, but the thin-base warning would remain.
cards.source: Synthesis of Feinstein AJ et al., Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol 2017 (PMID: 28397558); Sancho J et al., Am J Phys Med Rehabil 2004 (PMID: 15277962); Mootassim-Billah S et al., Int J Lang Commun Disord 2025 (PMID: 41246892). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Ventilatory efficiency: the VE/VCO2 slope rises ~0.12–0.13 units per year of age and runs higher in women — about 24–26 in healthy 20-somethings, with the ventilatory-equivalent nadir at 24.2 (men) to 27.0 (women)
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is ventilatory efficiency during exercise — the VE/VCO2 slope and the ventilatory equivalent nadir — by age and sex, and how much does the slope rise with normal ageing?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Anaerobic Threshold · Carbon Dioxide/physiology · Exercise Test · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen Consumption/physiology · Pulmonary Ventilation/physiology · Reference Values · Sex Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep's control-of-breathing and exercise account and Guyton & Hall ch. 84, named as textbook framing. The slope-distribution question is this shelf's own: the mathematical coupling between ventilatory efficiency and the dead-space fraction is analysed in the physiological dead-space shelf (pack #6258), which homes the Sun and colleagues 2002 ventilatory-efficiency analysis — cross-pointed here in prose only; that analysis is not re-carded and no number from it is used. The distribution itself rests on three free-standing cohorts. In 101 healthy volunteers (Habedank 1998), the exercise VE vs VCO2 slope rose linearly with age — slope = 0.13 × age + 19.9 in men and 0.12 × age + 24.4 in women — and resting ventilatory equivalent was higher in women (57.6 vs 50.5). In 529 healthy Japanese adults (Ashikaga 2021), the slope in the 20s was 24.4 ± 3.2 (men) and 25.7 ± 3.2 (women) and the minimum VE/VCO2 (the nadir) was 24.2 ± 2.3 and 27.0 ± 2.8, both rising with age. The FRIEND registry analysis (Nevill 2021) supplies sex-by-age centile curves for ages 20–80 from treadmill testing, so an individual slope can be placed on a population centile rather than against a single cut-off.

cards.headline: Habedank 1998: in 101 healthy volunteers aged 16–75, the VE vs VCO2 slope rose 0.13 units/year in men (slope = 0.13 × age + 19.9) and 0.12/year in women (0.12 × age + 24.4)
cards.summary: Habedank 1998: in 101 healthy volunteers aged 16–75, the VE vs VCO2 slope rose 0.13 units/year in men (slope = 0.13 × age + 19.9) and 0.12/year in women (0.12 × age + 24.4)
cards.type: Human normative cohort (classic primary dataset, exercise gas exchange), Eur J Appl Physiol 1998
cards.people: 101 healthy volunteers (56 men) aged 16–75 years; ventilation and gas exchange measured at rest (n = 64) and during exercise on a modified Naughton protocol (n = 101), with ventilatory efficiency at rest defined as the VE:VCO2 ratio and during exercise as the slope of the linear VE–VCO2 relationship.
cards.result: Ventilatory efficiency at rest was largely independent of age but smaller (better) in men than women: VE:VCO2 50.5 (SD 8.8) versus 57.6 (SD 12.6) (P < 0.05). During exercise, efficiency declined significantly with age in both sexes: VE vs VCO2 slope = 0.13 × age + 19.9 in men and 0.12 × age + 24.4 in women — so a healthy 70-year-old's expected slope sits roughly 6–7 units above a healthy 20-year-old's on the same sex line. For context within the same cohort, VO2 at the anaerobic threshold was reached at 58 (SD 9)% of VO2max, and breathing reserve at end-exercise was 41%, independent of sex and age.
cards.watchOut: The authors state plainly that normal values for ventilatory efficiency had not been established before this study — these are first-generation equations from 101 volunteers on one (treadmill, Naughton) protocol; ergometer type and slope-fitting window move the number, so the equations travel with their protocol.
cards.source: Habedank D et al. Ventilatory efficiency and exercise tolerance in 101 healthy volunteers. Eur J Appl Physiol Occup Physiol. 1998. PMID: 9562292. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Ashikaga 2021: in 529 healthy Japanese adults, VE/VCO2 slope in the 20s was 24.4 ± 3.2 (men) and 25.7 ± 3.2 (women), minimum VE/VCO2 was 24.2 ± 2.3 and 27.0 ± 2.8 — both rose with age
cards.summary: Ashikaga 2021: in 529 healthy Japanese adults, VE/VCO2 slope in the 20s was 24.4 ± 3.2 (men) and 25.7 ± 3.2 (women), minimum VE/VCO2 was 24.2 ± 2.3 and 27.0 ± 2.8 — both rose with age
cards.type: Human normative cohort (primary population dataset, ramp CPET), J Cardiol 2021
cards.people: 529 healthy Japanese subjects aged 20–78 years undergoing cardiopulmonary exercise testing on a cycle ergometer with ramp protocols; tidal volume and minute ventilation at rest, anaerobic threshold and peak exercise, the VE vs VCO2 slope, the minimum VE/VCO2 and the oxygen uptake efficiency slope were determined.
cards.result: In subjects in their 20s, the VE vs VCO2 slope was 24.4 ± 3.2 in men and 25.7 ± 3.2 in women (P = 0.035) and the minimum VE/VCO2 — the ventilatory-equivalent nadir — was 24.2 ± 2.3 in men and 27.0 ± 2.8 in women (P < 0.001). The slope and the minimum VE/VCO2 both increased with age while the oxygen uptake efficiency slope decreased; peak tidal volume and peak ventilation fell with age and rose with weight and height. The study establishes the normal ranges for a healthy Japanese population as reference values for interpreting cardiopulmonary exercise tests.
cards.watchOut: Cycle-ergometer ramp values in a Japanese population: the 20s means sit close to the Habedank treadmill equations' young-adult predictions, which is reassuring cross-protocol agreement at young ages, but the two should not be averaged into a single 'normal slope' — protocol and population stay attached to each number.
cards.source: Ashikaga K et al. Ventilatory efficiency during ramp exercise in relation to age and sex in a healthy Japanese population. J Cardiol. 2021. PMID: 32768174. cards.headline: Nevill 2021 (FRIEND registry): sex-by-age centile curves for VE/VCO2 slopes, ages 20–80, from treadmill cardiopulmonary testing — placing an individual on a population centile instead of a single cut-off
cards.summary: Nevill 2021 (FRIEND registry): sex-by-age centile curves for VE/VCO2 slopes, ages 20–80, from treadmill cardiopulmonary testing — placing an individual on a population centile instead of a single cut-off
cards.type: Human normative analysis (registry reference centiles), ERJ Open Res 2021
cards.people: Cardiopulmonary exercise testing data (treadmill protocol) from the Fitness Registry and the Importance of Exercise National Database (FRIEND Registry), for males and females aged 20–80 years, for whom reference centiles for VE/VCO2 slopes had recently been published; this analysis refitted those slopes as centile curves. The record's abstract does not state the registry N, so none is claimed here.
cards.result: Centile curves for VE/VCO2 slope were fitted with generalised additive models for location, scale and shape (GAMLSS), giving a more precise estimate of where an individual's slope falls within the population than reference tables. Allometric (log-linear) models gave more normal, homoscedastic residuals and superior goodness of fit over traditional ANCOVA (Akaike information criterion 14,671 versus 15,008) — the methodological point being that ventilatory-efficiency comparisons across age and body size need size-aware modelling, the same lesson as the spirometry shelves.
cards.watchOut: A modelling paper over registry data, treadmill protocol: it refines how the FRIEND centiles are read rather than adding a new measured cohort, and its abstract reports fit statistics rather than the centile values themselves — the curves, not this abstract, carry the numbers.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ventilatory efficiency worsens measurably with normal ageing (~0.12–0.13 slope units per year) and is sex-offset throughout — an unadjusted 'abnormal slope' cut-off will mislabel healthy older adults
cards.summary: Synthesis: ventilatory efficiency worsens measurably with normal ageing (~0.12–0.13 slope units per year) and is sex-offset throughout — an unadjusted 'abnormal slope' cut-off will mislabel healthy older adults
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human reports above (Habedank 1998; Ashikaga 2021; Nevill 2021), framed by Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall ch. 84 as textbook framing. The dead-space coupling of ventilatory efficiency is homed in pack #6258 (physiological dead space), whose carded Sun 2002 analysis is cross-pointed here in prose only and contributes no number to this shelf.
cards.result: Two measured cohorts a generation and a continent apart tell the same story: the VE/VCO2 slope starts near 24–26 in healthy people in their 20s (Ashikaga's measured means; Habedank's equations at age 20), runs consistently higher in women than men at every age, and climbs roughly 0.12–0.13 units per year of age (Habedank), with the ventilatory-equivalent nadir rising in parallel (Ashikaga: 24.2 in young men, 27.0 in young women). The FRIEND centiles (Nevill) turn that structure into the modern reporting form — a sex-by-age centile, not a threshold. The clinical consequence is arithmetic, not opinion: a fixed slope cut-off derived from young or mixed-age patients will classify healthy 70-year-olds as ventilatory-inefficient at a predictable rate, exactly as borrowed spirometry and lung-volume equations mislabel the elderly on the neighbouring shelves.
cards.watchOut: Slope values depend on the fitting window (to the respiratory compensation point vs whole exercise) and ergometer; the carded records use their own conventions, so cross-study numbers are compared as patterns and young-adult anchors, not pooled into one meta-value.
cards.source: Synthesis of Habedank D et al., Eur J Appl Physiol Occup Physiol 1998 (PMID: 9562292); Ashikaga K et al., J Cardiol 2021 (PMID: 32768174); Nevill AM et al., ERJ Open Res 2021 (PMID: 34322548). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Multiple Sleep Latency Test in health: wide spread, protocol-dependent, and the 8-minute line is a convention not a percentile
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what is normal daytime sleep propensity on the Multiple Sleep Latency Test — mean sleep latency by age and sex, the spread around the mean, and how protocol choices (nap number, prior sleep, the 8-minute convention) move the result?
shelves.mesh: Sleep/physiology · Sleep Stages/physiology · Disorders of Excessive Somnolence/diagnosis · Reference Values · Circadian Rhythm
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — framed by Kryger's Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine (the named framing source for this row) with Guyton & Hall ch. 60 as secondary framing, and resting on primary healthy-cohort MSLT data plus the AASM practice parameters: in 100 healthy adults (MSLT-30, five 30-minute naps) mean latency to sleep was 13.9 ± 6.9 minutes with a quadratic age pattern, shortest in middle age; in 176 healthy adults (four naps) latency ranged from 2 to 20 minutes within each age group and young adults were sleepier; and in 55 normal young adults sleepiness was better captured by sleep-onset frequency, peaking around 14:00. The evidence base is thin, protocol-sensitive and old — and the 8-minute 'pathological sleepiness' line is a convention, not a percentile of any of these distributions, so the stamp is EMERGING. Cross-point: overnight sleep architecture and ageing (pack #6204) is a different measurement — overnight structure, not daytime propensity.

cards.headline: Geisler 2006: the MSLT-30 normative study — 100 healthy adults, five 30-minute naps, mean latency 13.9 ± 6.9 minutes, shortest in middle age (quadratic age pattern)
cards.summary: Geisler 2006: the MSLT-30 normative study — 100 healthy adults, five 30-minute naps, mean latency 13.9 ± 6.9 minutes, shortest in middle age (quadratic age pattern)
cards.type: Human normative cohort (MSLT-30), Sleep 2006
cards.people: 100 subjects with no complaint of sleep disturbance or daytime sleepiness, 10 men and 10 women from each of five age decades (20–69 years), tested in a sleep laboratory with the MSLT-30 (a Multiple Sleep Latency Test variant with a fixed 30-minute duration for each of 5 test sessions), plus mood, subjective and objective sleepiness measures.
cards.result: Mean latency to sleep stage 1 or any other sleep stage was 13.9 ± 6.9 minutes. Latency showed a clear quadratic association with age, with the shortest latencies in the middle age groups — reconciling earlier reports of long latencies in adolescents and rising latencies with age in adults. There was no correlation between mean latency and sociodemographic variables, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, vigilance test, mood scales, sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index) or amount of prior sleep.
cards.watchOut: MSLT-30 uses 30-minute nap opportunities, not the standard 20-minute MSLT — its latencies run longer than the classic test's and are not interchangeable with them; sex effects are explicitly absent here, despite the row's by-sex framing.
cards.source: Geisler P et al. The influence of age and sex on sleep latency in the MSLT-30--a normative study. Sleep. 2006. PMID: 16774159. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Levine 1988: in 129 healthy young adults (18–29) and 47 healthy older adults (30–80), mean MSLT latency ranged from 2 to 20 minutes within each group — young adults were sleepier
cards.summary: Levine 1988: in 129 healthy young adults (18–29) and 47 healthy older adults (30–80), mean MSLT latency ranged from 2 to 20 minutes within each group — young adults were sleepier
cards.type: Human healthy-cohort MSLT study, Sleep 1988
cards.people: 129 healthy young adults aged 18–29 years with no sleep-wake complaints and 47 healthy, normal-sleeping adults aged 30–80 years, each spending 8 hours in the laboratory overnight and receiving the Multiple Sleep Latency Test the next day, with sleep latency measured at 10:00, 12:00, 14:00 and 16:00.
cards.result: Mean sleep latency ranged from 2 to 20 minutes within each group, but the shape of the distribution differed between groups: the mean latency of young subjects (particularly college students) was shorter than that of the older subjects, with the differences occurring between the sleepiest 80% of each distribution. Among college students, those with higher nocturnal sleep efficiencies were sleepier the next day than those with lower efficiencies — suggesting the increased sleepiness of average young adults reflects mild sleep restriction.
cards.watchOut: A classic pre-standardisation dataset (four naps, overnight lab sleep first): it reports the range and the age contrast, not a group mean, so its contribution here is the wide within-group spread (2–20 minutes) and the young-adult sleepiness signal, not a single reference value.
cards.source: Levine B et al. Daytime sleepiness in young adults. Sleep. 1988. PMID: 3363268. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Clodoré 1990: in 55 normal young adults, sleep-onset frequency — not latency — captured diurnal sleepiness, with a peak around 14:00 and high alertness morning and evening
cards.summary: Clodoré 1990: in 55 normal young adults, sleep-onset frequency — not latency — captured diurnal sleepiness, with a peak around 14:00 and high alertness morning and evening
cards.type: Human healthy-cohort MSLT study (time-of-day effects), Sleep 1990
cards.people: 55 young good sleepers undergoing a Multiple Sleep Latency Test procedure; 11 of them also took part in a Repeated Test of Sustained Wakefulness procedure. MSLT results were analysed as a function of both the number of sleep onsets per day and the time of day.
cards.result: Diurnal sleepiness was better appreciated by sleep-onset frequency than by the traditional latency criterion: sleep-onset frequency, unlike latency, was influenced by usual sleep duration, morning/evening score and the sustained-wakefulness procedure. The time-of-day effect was a decrease in sleep tendency at the beginning and at the end of the day (fewer sleep onsets, longer latencies) with a peak of sleepiness around 14:00 — the morning and evening periods of high alertness may anchor the coupling of sleep/wake and temperature rhythms.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-five young adults and no mean latency in the record's abstract — the card is used for what it verifies (frequency beats latency as a sleepiness measure, and the 14:00 peak), not as a source of a reference value; the small sustained-wakefulness limb (n = 11) is printed as such.
cards.source: Clodoré M et al. The Multiple Sleep Latency Test: individual variability and time of day effect in normal young adults. Sleep. 1990. PMID: 2287850. cards.headline: Littner 2005 (AASM practice parameters): the protocol-defining synthesis — MSLT is indicated for suspected narcolepsy evaluation, not routinely for OSA diagnosis or CPAP response
cards.summary: Littner 2005 (AASM practice parameters): the protocol-defining synthesis — MSLT is indicated for suspected narcolepsy evaluation, not routinely for OSA diagnosis or CPAP response
cards.type: AASM practice parameters (protocol-defining synthesis), Sleep 2005
cards.people: A Task Force of content experts appointed by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine performed a comprehensive literature review and graded the evidence for the clinical use of the Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) and the Maintenance of Wakefulness Test (MWT); recommendations replaced the 1992 American Sleep Disorders Association position paper and were approved by the Standards of Practice Committee and the AASM Board of Directors.
cards.result: The MSLT is indicated as part of the evaluation of patients with suspected narcolepsy and may be useful for suspected idiopathic hypersomnia; it is not routinely indicated in the initial evaluation and diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnoea, or in assessment of change following treatment with nasal CPAP, nor routinely for sleepiness in medical and neurological disorders (other than narcolepsy), insomnia or circadian rhythm disorders. The parameters include recommendations for MSLT and MWT protocols, a discussion of the normative data available for both tests, and a description of issues needing further study. The record's abstract does not state an 8-minute threshold — that figure is a convention from the wider literature, not a value this record prints.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis and protocol document, not a primary normative dataset — it is carded for the protocol and indications, and the normative claims of this shelf rest on the three primary cohorts above, not on it.
cards.source: Littner MR et al. Practice parameters for clinical use of the multiple sleep latency test and the maintenance of wakefulness test. Sleep. 2005. PMID: 15700727. cards.headline: Synthesis: healthy daytime sleep propensity is wide and protocol-dependent — a mean near 14 minutes on the 30-minute variant, a 2–20 minute range on the classic test — and the 8-minute line is a convention, not a percentile
cards.summary: Synthesis: healthy daytime sleep propensity is wide and protocol-dependent — a mean near 14 minutes on the 30-minute variant, a 2–20 minute range on the classic test — and the 8-minute line is a convention, not a percentile
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded records (the 100-subject MSLT-30 normative study, the 176-subject young/older cohort, the 55-subject time-of-day study, and the AASM practice parameters), framed by Kryger's Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine and Guyton & Hall ch. 60.
cards.result: Normal daytime sleep propensity has no single number: on the MSLT-30 (30-minute naps) healthy adults average 13.9 ± 6.9 minutes with the shortest latencies in middle age (a quadratic age pattern, no sex effect, no correlation with the Epworth scale or prior sleep amount); on the classic four-nap test, healthy latencies span 2–20 minutes within every age group, with young adults sleepier than older ones. Time of day matters (peak sleepiness around 14:00), and sleep-onset frequency may capture diurnal sleepiness better than latency. Against that spread, the 8-minute line used to call sleepiness 'pathological' is a convention, not a percentile of these distributions — a healthy young adult can fall below it by being mildly sleep-restricted, and a healthy middle-aged adult can sit well above it. Prior sleep, nap number and nap duration all move the result, so protocol must be named beside any value.
cards.watchOut: The normative base is old (1988–2006) and small (331 healthy subjects across the three primary cohorts, by different protocols), and the 8-minute convention's origin is not itself a carded record here — it is stated as a convention on the row's authority and on the practice parameters' protocol discussion, not as a value extracted from a fetched record.
cards.source: Synthesis of Geisler P et al. Sleep. 2006 (PMID: 16774159); Levine B et al. Sleep. 1988 (PMID: 3363268); Clodoré M et al. Sleep. 1990 (PMID: 2287850); Littner MR et al. shelves.title: AHI in unselected adults: common, higher in men, and the scoring rule halves or doubles who counts
shelves.question: In unselected general-population adults, how common are raised apnoea–hypopnoea index values on polysomnography — the AHI distribution by age and sex in the HypnoLaus and Wisconsin cohorts — and how much does the hypopnoea scoring rule (3% desaturation/arousal vs 4% desaturation) change who counts as having sleep apnoea?
shelves.mesh: Sleep Apnea Syndromes/epidemiology · Polysomnography · Prevalence · Age Distribution · Sex Distribution
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Kryger's Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine (epidemiology/scoring chapters) with Guyton & Hall ch. 60 as secondary framing, and resting on two large population cohorts plus a scoring-rule analysis of the same HypnoLaus data: in the HypnoLaus general population (2,121 with polysomnography), median AHI was 6.9 events/h in women and 14.9 in men, and moderate-to-severe sleep-disordered breathing (AHI ≥15) was present in 23.4% of women and 49.7% of men; the Wisconsin cohort's US estimates are lower but the same order of magnitude (AHI ≥15 in 10–17% of men and 3–9% of women by age band) and rose by a relative 14–55% over two decades with obesity. The scoring rule is the core content: in HypnoLaus, median AHI was 10.9, 4.4 or 10.1 events/h under the AASM 1999, 2007 and 2012 hypopnoea definitions respectively, and AHI ≥15 prevalence was 39.3%, 18.8% or 36.6% — the rule more than doubles who counts. This is a measurement/prevalence shelf: it carries no CPAP or device content (those homes are live #635/#923 and the OSA treatment family), and no treatment claim is carded here.

cards.headline: Heinzer 2015 (HypnoLaus): in 2,121 people from the general population, median AHI was 6.9 events/h in women and 14.9 in men — moderate-to-severe sleep-disordered breathing (≥15) in 23.4% of women and 49.7% of men
cards.summary: Heinzer 2015 (HypnoLaus): in 2,121 people from the general population, median AHI was 6.9 events/h in women and 14.9 in men — moderate-to-severe sleep-disordered breathing (≥15) in 23.4% of women and 49.7% of men
cards.type: Human population cohort (HypnoLaus, in-home polysomnography), Lancet Respir Med 2015
cards.people: 2,121 people (48% men; median age 57 years, range 40–85; mean BMI 25.6 kg/m²) with complete in-home polysomnography, from 3,043 consecutive participants of the CoLaus/PsyCoLaus cohort invited between September 2009 and June 2013 in Lausanne, Switzerland, with extensive phenotyping for diabetes, hypertension, metabolic syndrome and depression.
cards.result: Median apnoea–hypopnoea index was 6.9 events/h (interquartile range 2.7–14.1) in women and 14.9/h (7.2–27.1) in men. Prevalence of moderate-to-severe sleep-disordered breathing (≥15 events/h) was 23.4% (95% CI 20.9–26.0) in women and 49.7% (46.6–52.8) in men. After multivariable adjustment, the upper AHI quartile (>20.6 events/h) was independently associated with hypertension (odds ratio 1.60), diabetes (2.00), metabolic syndrome (2.80) and depression (1.92). The authors attribute the high prevalence partly to the increased sensitivity of current recording techniques and scoring criteria.

cards.headline: Peppard 2013 (Wisconsin Sleep Cohort): US prevalence of moderate-to-severe sleep-disordered breathing (AHI ≥15) was 10–17% in men and 3–9% in women, up by a relative 14–55% over two decades
cards.summary: Peppard 2013 (Wisconsin Sleep Cohort): US prevalence of moderate-to-severe sleep-disordered breathing (AHI ≥15) was 10–17% in men and 3–9% in women, up by a relative 14–55% over two decades
cards.type: Human population cohort (Wisconsin Sleep Cohort, modelled US prevalence), Am J Epidemiol 2013
cards.people: 1,520 participants aged 30–70 years with baseline polysomnography in the Wisconsin Sleep Cohort, an ongoing community-based study established in 1988 with participants randomly selected from an employed Wisconsin population, invited for repeat studies at 4-year intervals; prevalence was modelled by age, sex and BMI and extrapolated to US BMI distributions from NHANES, for 1988–1994 and 2007–2010.
cards.result: Current prevalence estimates for moderate-to-severe sleep-disordered breathing (AHI ≥15 events/h) were 10% (95% CI 7–12) among 30–49-year-old men, 17% (15–21) among 50–70-year-old men, 3% (2–4) among 30–49-year-old women and 9% (7–11) among 50–70-year-old women — substantial increases over the previous two decades, with relative increases of between 14% and 55% depending on the subgroup (relative increases, printed beside the absolute prevalences they describe).
cards.watchOut: Modelled estimates, not counted cases: they extrapolate Wisconsin data to US BMI distributions, so they inherit both the cohort's employed-population selection and the obesity epidemic's trajectory — and they use the Wisconsin scoring rules of their era, not the HypnoLaus criteria.
cards.source: Peppard PE et al. Increased prevalence of sleep-disordered breathing in adults. American Journal of Epidemiology. 2013. PMID: 23589584. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hirotsu 2019: the same HypnoLaus data re-scored under three hypopnoea definitions — median AHI 10.9, 4.4 or 10.1 events/h, and AHI ≥15 prevalence 39.3%, 18.8% or 36.6%
cards.summary: Hirotsu 2019: the same HypnoLaus data re-scored under three hypopnoea definitions — median AHI 10.9, 4.4 or 10.1 events/h, and AHI ≥15 prevalence 39.3%, 18.8% or 36.6%
cards.type: Human scoring-rule re-analysis (HypnoLaus), J Clin Sleep Med 2019
cards.people: 2,162 participants (51% women, 57 ± 19 years) from the HypnoLaus study with in-home full polysomnography, re-analysed with AHI calculated under three hypopnoea definitions: AASM1999 (≥50% airflow decrease, or lower reduction with ≥3% desaturation or an arousal), AASM2007 (≥30% reduction with ≥4% desaturation) and AASM2012 (≥30% reduction with ≥3% desaturation or an arousal). Same HypnoLaus programme as the Heinzer card — labelled, not an independent cohort.
cards.result: Median AHI was 10.9, 4.4 and 10.1 events/h under the 1999, 2007 and 2012 criteria respectively. OSA prevalence at AHI ≥5, ≥15 and ≥30 was 74.5%, 39.3% and 16.3% under AASM1999; 46.9%, 18.8% and 6.8% under AASM2007; and 72.2%, 36.6% and 14.9% under AASM2012. Different AHI thresholds were associated with hypertension (11.5, 4.8, 10.7 events/h), diabetes (15.7, 7.1, 14.4) and metabolic syndrome (12.8, 5.5, 11.8) under the three criteria — roughly a twofold difference in threshold between the 2007 rule and the other two.
cards.watchOut: A re-scoring of the same participants, not new people: its contribution is methodological — it shows the 4%-desaturation rule roughly halves prevalence and halves the comorbidity-associated threshold — and it cannot be pooled with the Heinzer card as if it were a second population.
cards.source: Hirotsu C et al. Effect of Three Hypopnea Scoring Criteria on OSA Prevalence and Associated Comorbidities in the General Population. Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine. 2019. cards.headline: Synthesis: raised AHI is common in unselected adults — and who counts as having sleep apnoea depends on the scoring rule as much as on the sleeper
cards.summary: Synthesis: raised AHI is common in unselected adults — and who counts as having sleep apnoea depends on the scoring rule as much as on the sleeper
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human records (the HypnoLaus population prevalence study, the Wisconsin Sleep Cohort US estimates, and the three-rule re-scoring of HypnoLaus), framed by Kryger's Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine and Guyton & Hall ch. 60.
cards.result: In unselected adults, raised AHI is not rare: the HypnoLaus median was 6.9 events/h in women and 14.9 in men, with AHI ≥15 in 23.4% of women and 49.7% of men (2012-era scoring); the Wisconsin US estimates are lower — 10–17% of men and 3–9% of women by age band — and rising with obesity (a relative 14–55% increase over two decades). Men run higher than women at every age, and AHI rises with age and BMI. But the decisive quantity is the rule: under AASM2007 (≥4% desaturation) the HypnoLaus median AHI was 4.4 events/h and AHI ≥15 prevalence 18.8%, against 10.9 and 39.3% under AASM1999 and 10.1 and 36.6% under AASM2012. Every prevalence figure on this shelf is therefore printed beside its scoring rule and cohort, and no figure is presented as 'the' prevalence of sleep apnoea. No treatment evidence is carded here.
cards.watchOut: AHI counts events per hour of sleep, not disease: the comorbidity associations are cross-sectional, and nothing here establishes what AHI threshold, if any, should trigger treatment — that question belongs to the OSA treatment shelves, which are deliberately not drawn on.
cards.source: Synthesis of Heinzer R et al. Lancet Respiratory Medicine. 2015 (PMID: 25682233); Peppard PE et al. American Journal of Epidemiology. 2013 (PMID: 23589584); Hirotsu C et al. Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 30736872), all carded above, with Kryger / Guyton & Hall textbook framing. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Handheld peak flow has its own equations (Nunn & Gregg 15-85; NHATS past 65), published formulae disagree by up to 229 L/min, and a healthy day's swing is only ~6-7%
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is peak expiratory flow — the reference equations for adults (Nunn & Gregg) and for older US adults — how do the many published prediction formulas disagree, and how large is diurnal PEF variability in people without asthma?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Aged · Aging/physiology · Body Height · Female · Forced Expiratory Flow Rates · Humans · Lung/physiology · Male · Middle Aged · Peak Expiratory Flow Rate · Reference Values · Regression Analysis · Sex Factors · Peak Expiratory Flow Rate/physiology · Aged, 80 and over · United States · Spirometry/standards,methods,instrumentation · Nutrition Surveys · Cohort Studies · Adolescent · Adult · Algorithms · Asthma/classification,diagnosis · Body Weight · Child · Forecasting · Population Surveillance · Practice Guidelines as Topic · Reference Standards · Reproducibility of Results · Circadian Rhythm/physiology · Confidence Intervals · India · Respiratory Mechanics · Circadian Rhythm · Cotinine/urine · Data Interpretation, Statistical · Lung Diseases, Obstructive/physiopathology,urine · Pneumoconiosis/physiopathology,urine · Smoking/metabolism,physiopathology · Spirometry · Tobacco Smoke Pollution
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep (respiratory mechanics/forced expiration); Guyton & Hall, ch. 37. Distinct from laboratory spirometry (pack #7150): this is handheld-meter PEF, the asthma self-management measurement, with its own devices and scales (Wright vs EU/EN13826 values differ). The adult reference standard is Nunn & Gregg's 1989 age-and-height regression equations for ages 15-85, derived from strictly normal lifelong non-smokers with an added older cohort (23 men, 29 women). For older US adults, NHATS handheld-meter equations from 1,740 healthy adults aged 65+ validate in a later cohort, whereas spirometry-based NHANES equations overestimate handheld PEF by ~29.3 L/min in men and ~10.1 L/min in women (Donahue 2024). Formula choice is not academic: across published formulae, one young man's 100% predicted spans 501-730 L/min (Radeos & Camargo 2004). Healthy diurnal variability is small — amplitude 7.23% of the mean in 152 young adults (Aggarwal 2000) and 6.26% of the daily mean by cosinor in healthy men (Casale & Pasqualetti 1997) — with a morning nadir and afternoon peak. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Nunn & Gregg 1989: new peak-flow regression equations for ages 15-85, built by adding 23 older men and 29 older women to the original strictly-normal cohort
cards.summary: Nunn & Gregg 1989: new peak-flow regression equations for ages 15-85, built by adding 23 older men and 29 older women to the original strictly-normal cohort
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (PEF reference equations for adults 15-85)
cards.people: Lifelong non-smokers meeting strict normality criteria: the original adult cohort plus an additional 23 men and 29 women aged 55 or over, recruited because the earlier equations lacked older men (over 55) and women (over 65); combined data modelled as PEF regressed on age and height, separately by sex.
cards.result: The new equations predict peak expiratory flow for men and women aged 15-85. For younger ages (men under 55, women under 65) the predicted values were almost identical to those previously published — the revision's purpose was to extend trustworthy prediction into old age and so enhance the accuracy of testing in the elderly. The fetched record states the equations' scope and validation, not their coefficients, and this card claims no numeric predicted values.
cards.watchOut: The reference population is deliberately super-normal (lifelong non-smokers, strict criteria): predicted values describe healthy lungs, which is exactly what a reference equation should do — and why symptomatic clinic populations fall below them.
cards.source: Nunn AJ et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 1989. PMID: 2497892. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Handheld-meter reference equations for older US adults (NHATS healthy subsample, N = 1,740, age 65+): handheld PEF runs below spirometry predictions — NHANES equations overestimate it by ~29 L/min in men and ~10 L/min in women (Donahue 2024)
cards.summary: Handheld-meter reference equations for older US adults (NHATS healthy subsample, N = 1,740, age 65+): handheld PEF runs below spirometry predictions — NHANES equations overestimate it by ~29 L/min in men and ~10 L/min in women (Donahue 2024)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population reference equations for handheld PEF in older adults)
cards.people: Healthy subsample of the National Health and Aging Trends Study 2011 cohort: 1,740 US adults aged 65+ (68.9% female; mean age 77.0, SD 7.9 years); PEF measured with a handheld flow meter; sex-specific equations from height and age, validated against the NHATS 2015 cohort.
cards.result: Applying the 2011 equations to the 2015 cohort, measured and predicted PEF did not differ significantly (P > 0.05) — the equations validate. By contrast, spirometry-based NHANES PEF equations tended to overestimate handheld measurements in the 2015 cohort, by an average of 29.3 L/min in males and 10.1 L/min in females. The authors conclude handheld-meter equations are comparable in performance and can serve the traditionally undersampled oldest population with a low-cost measure.
cards.watchOut: Handheld-meter PEF is its own measurement family (device and scale dependent), validated here only in US adults 65+: do not apply these equations to younger adults or read spirometer PEF from them.
cards.source: Donahue PT et al. Respiratory medicine. 2024. PMID: 39305967. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Formula comparison (labelled analysis): the same 18-year-old man is '100% predicted' at anywhere from 501 to 730 L/min depending on the published formula — enough to flip asthma severity class (Radeos & Camargo 2004)
cards.summary: Formula comparison (labelled analysis): the same 18-year-old man is '100% predicted' at anywhere from 501 to 730 L/min depending on the published formula — enough to flip asthma severity class (Radeos & Camargo 2004)
cards.type: Synthesis — comparison of published PEF prediction formulae (labelled analysis)
cards.people: Analysis of published PEF prediction formulae in the literature, applied to hypothetical patients at the 50th percentile for height and weight, with percent-predicted values classified into asthma guideline severity groups. Labelled analysis of prior equations — not a new cohort.
cards.result: Predicted PEF varied widely across formulae: for an 18-year-old man, 100% predicted ranged from 501 to 730 L/min (a 229 L/min spread). For a 35-year-old woman, the choice of formula alone classified the same measured value as severe (46% predicted) under one formula and moderate (57%) under another. The authors conclude formula choice may alter guideline-based care and propose recently published population-based equations as the reference standard for future guidelines.
cards.watchOut: Hypothetical-patient arithmetic, deliberately so: it sizes the disagreement between equations rather than measuring any population — the measured-population anchors are the Nunn & Gregg and NHATS cards.
cards.source: Radeos MS et al. The American journal of emergency medicine. 2004. PMID: 15666252. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Diurnal PEF variation in 152 healthy young adults: mean amplitude 7.23% of the mean (SD 3.48) over three days — morning nadir, late-afternoon peak in 74.6% (Aggarwal 2000)
cards.summary: Diurnal PEF variation in 152 healthy young adults: mean amplitude 7.23% of the mean (SD 3.48) over three days — morning nadir, late-afternoon peak in 74.6% (Aggarwal 2000)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (diurnal PEF variability in healthy young adults)
cards.people: 152 healthy volunteers aged 20-40 years; peak expiratory flow recorded over three days, variability expressed as amplitude percent mean (A%M) and standard deviation percent mean (SD%M).
cards.result: The commonest pattern (74.6%) was a nadir on waking, a progressive rise to late afternoon, then a plateau or small fall at bedtime. On the third day, mean diurnal variation was 7.23% (SD 3.48) by A%M and 2.98% (SD 1.31) by SD%M. Both the variation and its calculated upper limits of normality were lower than previously reported for Western subjects — the authors note this baseline is what gives PEF monitoring in asthma its meaning.
cards.watchOut: Young Indian adults over three days: the ~7% figure is this population's amplitude-percent-mean; other metrics (amplitude percent mesor, morning-evening difference) give different numbers for the same rhythm, as the cosinor card shows.
cards.source: Aggarwal AN et al. The Indian journal of chest diseases & allied sciences. 2000. PMID: 10851817. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cosinor analysis in 30 healthy never-smoking men: PEF amplitude 6.26% of the daily mean (95% limits 4.57-7.95), peaking in the early afternoon — passive smokers similar, heavy smokers double (Casale & Pasqualetti 1997)
cards.summary: Cosinor analysis in 30 healthy never-smoking men: PEF amplitude 6.26% of the daily mean (95% limits 4.57-7.95), peaking in the early afternoon — passive smokers similar, heavy smokers double (Casale & Pasqualetti 1997)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (circadian PEF rhythm and amplitude in healthy men and comparison groups)
cards.people: 30 clinically healthy never-smoking men (group A), compared with 30 passive smokers, 30 heavy smokers, 30 COPD patients and 15 interstitial lung disease patients, comparable for age, weight and height; PEF by portable spirometer at 11 time points across a whole day of normal life; cosinor analysis with amplitude expressed as percent of the mesor (daily mean). Only the healthy-group values anchor the norms here.
cards.result: All groups showed significant circadian PEF rhythms peaking in the early afternoon, without significant timing differences between groups. Healthy controls' amplitude percent mesor was 6.26% (95% confidence limits 4.57-7.95) — statistically indistinguishable from passive smokers (7.79%) but significantly below heavy smokers (12.60%) and COPD (17.19%), whose daily mean (mesor) was also significantly lower. The authors propose increased diurnal variability as an early index of smoke damage, and caution that smoking habit must be considered when studying PEF variability.
cards.watchOut: Men only, one day of recording, portable spirometer: the 6.26% amplitude-percent-mesor is metric-specific — it corroborates, and must not be averaged with, the amplitude-percent-mean metric of the Aggarwal card.
cards.source: Casale R et al. Respiration; international review of thoracic diseases. 1997. PMID: 9257358. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: healthy PEF needs its own equations per age span and device — Nunn & Gregg for 15-85, NHATS for handheld meters past 65 — because published formulae disagree by up to 229 L/min, and healthy diurnal swing is only ~6-7% against asthma's much larger variability
cards.summary: Synthesis: healthy PEF needs its own equations per age span and device — Nunn & Gregg for 15-85, NHATS for handheld meters past 65 — because published formulae disagree by up to 229 L/min, and healthy diurnal swing is only ~6-7% against asthma's much larger variability
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human studies and the one labelled formula analysis above.
cards.result: Framed by Boron & Boulpaep (respiratory mechanics/forced expiration) and Guyton & Hall (ch. 37). This shelf is deliberately distinct from the laboratory spirometry reference shelf (pack #7150, slate row S9-4-09): PEF here is the handheld-meter measurement of asthma self-management, with its own devices, scales (Wright vs EU/EN13826 readings differ) and equations. The adult standard remains Nunn & Gregg's age-and-height regressions for ages 15-85 from strictly normal lifelong non-smokers (1989); for the oldest adults, NHATS handheld-meter equations (N = 1,740, age 65+) validate prospectively, while spirometry-derived NHANES equations overestimate handheld PEF by ~29 L/min (men) and ~10 L/min (women) (Donahue 2024). The need for that care is sized by the formula comparison: 100% predicted for one hypothetical young man spans 501-730 L/min across published formulae, enough to flip guideline severity class (Radeos & Camargo 2004). Healthy diurnal variability — the baseline asthma monitoring is judged against — is modest and consistent across metrics and continents: amplitude ~7.23% of the mean in 152 young Indian adults (Aggarwal 2000) and 6.26% of the mesor in healthy Italian men (Casale & Pasqualetti 1997), with a morning nadir and early/late-afternoon peak. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Percent-predicted PEF is meaningless without naming the equation, the meter and its scale; a patient's own best remains the practical comparator in asthma diaries precisely because population equations disagree this much.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nunn AJ et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 1989 (PMID: 2497892); Donahue PT et al. Respiratory medicine. 2024 (PMID: 39305967); Radeos MS et al. Respiration; international review of thoracic diseases. 1997 (PMID: 9257358). Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (respiratory mechanics); Guyton & Hall, ch. 37.

shelves.title: Inhaled levofloxacin in cystic fibrosis: SPLIT — FEV1 and Pseudomonas density improved and noninferior to tobramycin, but the placebo phase 3 trial (n=330) missed its exacerbation endpoint
shelves.question: In people with cystic fibrosis (≥12 years in the phase 3 trials) and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa airway infection, does levofloxacin inhalation solution (240 mg twice daily, 28-day cycles) versus placebo — or versus tobramycin inhalation solution — improve lung function and delay exacerbation?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Cystic Fibrosis · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Levofloxacin · Ofloxacin · Pseudomonas Infections · Pseudomonas aeruginosa · Respiratory Function Tests · Solutions · Sputum · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT. Levofloxacin inhalation solution (the tested product — development names MP-376 / APT-1026, marketed in the EU as Quinsair; named under the clarification exception) reduced sputum Pseudomonas density and improved FEV1 in the phase 2 trial (n=151), and was noninferior to tobramycin inhalation solution on FEV1 in a phase 3 trial (n=282), with an open-label extension (n=88) showing continued tolerability. But the placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (n=330) MISSED its primary endpoint — there was no statistically significant difference in time to exacerbation versus placebo — although FEV1 % predicted improved (mean difference 1.31%). Dysgeusia (taste distortion) was the most frequent adverse event in both phase 3 trials. The shelf therefore supports a lung-function / bacterial-density effect and comparability with inhaled tobramycin, not an exacerbation-prevention claim. Tobramycin and dornase alfa in CF have their own homes and are cross-pointed, not re-carded.

cards.headline: Phase 2 RCT (Geller 2011): inhaled levofloxacin (MP-376) 240 mg twice daily reduced sputum Pseudomonas density versus placebo (0.96 log difference, P=0.001) and improved FEV1 over 28 days
cards.summary: Phase 2 RCT (Geller 2011): inhaled levofloxacin (MP-376) 240 mg twice daily reduced sputum Pseudomonas density versus placebo (0.96 log difference, P=0.001) and improved FEV1 over 28 days
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial, 28 days
cards.people: 151 patients with cystic fibrosis and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, heavily treated, were randomised to MP-376 (levofloxacin inhalation solution) 120 mg once daily, 240 mg once daily, 240 mg twice daily, or placebo for 28 days. The primary endpoint was change in sputum Pseudomonas density.
cards.result: All MP-376 doses reduced sputum Pseudomonas density at day 28; the 240 mg twice-daily dose showed a 0.96 log difference versus placebo (P=0.001). FEV1 increased dose-dependently, with a difference of 8.7% between the 240 mg twice-daily group and placebo (P=0.003). The need for other anti-Pseudomonas antimicrobials fell by a relative 61–79% across the MP-376 groups versus placebo. MP-376 was generally well tolerated relative to placebo.
cards.watchOut: A 28-day trial with microbiological and lung-function endpoints in a heavily treated population: it establishes short-term antibacterial and FEV1 effects, not exacerbation prevention.
cards.source: Geller DE et al. Levofloxacin inhalation solution (MP-376) in patients with cystic fibrosis with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine. 2011. PMID: 21471106. Registry ID: NCT00677365. cards.headline: Phase 3 placebo-controlled RCT (Flume 2016): levofloxacin inhalation solution MISSED its primary endpoint — no significant difference in time to exacerbation — though FEV1 % predicted improved (mean difference 1.31%)
cards.summary: Phase 3 placebo-controlled RCT (Flume 2016): levofloxacin inhalation solution MISSED its primary endpoint — no significant difference in time to exacerbation — though FEV1 % predicted improved (mean difference 1.31%)
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre multinational randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, one 28-day course
cards.people: 330 subjects aged 12 years or older with cystic fibrosis and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection were randomised 2:1 to levofloxacin inhalation solution (APT-1026) 240 mg twice daily (n=220) or placebo for 28 days. Time to exacerbation was the primary endpoint; FEV1 % predicted and quality of life were secondary endpoints.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant difference in protocol-defined pulmonary exacerbations between treatment arms — the primary endpoint was missed. The relative change in FEV1 % predicted from baseline was significantly greater on levofloxacin inhalation solution than on placebo (mean difference 1.31%, P=0.01, 95% CI 0.27 to 2.34). The treatment was well tolerated, with dysgeusia the most frequent adverse event. The authors noted significantly more patients randomised to levofloxacin had experienced multiple exacerbations in the prior year, a baseline imbalance that may have contributed to the primary-endpoint result.
cards.watchOut: The largest placebo-controlled trial missed its primary (exacerbation) endpoint — secondary FEV1 findings must not be converted into the headline claim. A single 28-day course also limits what a time-to-exacerbation endpoint could show.
cards.source: Flume PA et al. A phase 3, multi-center, multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of levofloxacin inhalation solution (APT-1026) in stable cystic fibrosis patients. Journal of Cystic Fibrosis. 2016. PMID: 26852040. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Phase 3 noninferiority RCT (Stuart Elborn 2015): levofloxacin inhalation solution was NONINFERIOR to tobramycin inhalation solution on FEV1 over three 28-day cycles (mean difference 1.86% predicted)
cards.summary: Phase 3 noninferiority RCT (Stuart Elborn 2015): levofloxacin inhalation solution was NONINFERIOR to tobramycin inhalation solution on FEV1 over three 28-day cycles (mean difference 1.86% predicted)
cards.type: Phase 3 multinational open-label randomised noninferiority trial vs tobramycin inhalation solution, three 28-day on/off cycles
cards.people: 282 subjects aged 12 years or older with cystic fibrosis and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection were randomised 2:1 to levofloxacin inhalation solution (APT-1026) or tobramycin inhalation solution over three 28-day on/off cycles. The primary endpoint was relative change in FEV1 % predicted at day 28.
cards.result: Noninferiority was demonstrated: the mean FEV1 difference was 1.86% predicted (95% CI −0.66 to 4.39) in favour of levofloxacin inhalation solution. Levofloxacin was well tolerated, with dysgeusia (taste distortion) the most frequent adverse event.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and a noninferiority comparison against an established inhaled antibiotic on a lung-function endpoint: it shows levofloxacin is a comparable alternative to tobramycin, not that it is superior or that it prevents exacerbations.
cards.source: Stuart Elborn J et al. A phase 3, open-label, randomized trial to evaluate the safety and efficacy of levofloxacin inhalation solution (APT-1026) versus tobramycin inhalation solution in stable cystic fibrosis patients. Journal of Cystic Fibrosis. 2015. PMID: 25592656. Registry ID: NCT02109822. cards.headline: Open-label extension (Elborn 2016): prolonged levofloxacin inhalation solution treatment in 88 patients was well tolerated with no new safety signals — a programme report of the tobramycin-comparison trial, not a new trial
cards.summary: Open-label extension (Elborn 2016): prolonged levofloxacin inhalation solution treatment in 88 patients was well tolerated with no new safety signals — a programme report of the tobramycin-comparison trial, not a new trial
cards.type: Open-label extension study of the phase 3 tobramycin-comparison trial (same programme — not independent comparative evidence)
cards.people: 88 patients who completed the multinational randomised levofloxacin-versus-tobramycin trial carded above enrolled in an open-label extension in which all received three additional cycles of levofloxacin inhalation solution 240 mg twice daily for 28 days, followed by 28 days off drug.
cards.result: Extended treatment was well tolerated, with no new safety signals, and the report describes positive effects on FEV1 and quality of life (the abstract reports no numerical effect sizes). Time to pulmonary exacerbation was among the endpoints assessed.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled extension in trial completers (88 of the parent trial's 282): it informs longer-term tolerability only and adds no comparative efficacy evidence.
cards.source: Elborn JS et al. Safety and efficacy of prolonged levofloxacin inhalation solution (APT-1026) treatment for cystic fibrosis and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa airway infection. cards.headline: Synthesis: inhaled levofloxacin lowers Pseudomonas density and improves FEV1 and matches tobramycin — but the placebo-controlled phase 3 trial missed its exacerbation endpoint, so no exacerbation claim is supported
cards.summary: Synthesis: inhaled levofloxacin lowers Pseudomonas density and improves FEV1 and matches tobramycin — but the placebo-controlled phase 3 trial missed its exacerbation endpoint, so no exacerbation claim is supported
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Across the programme (phase 2 n=151; phase 3 placebo n=330; phase 3 tobramycin-comparison n=282; extension n=88), levofloxacin inhalation solution consistently improved FEV1 and, in phase 2, sputum Pseudomonas density, and was noninferior to tobramycin inhalation solution. The one placebo-controlled test of the clinical endpoint that matters most — time to exacerbation — was not significant. Dysgeusia was the most frequent adverse event. The supported claim is a short-term lung-function/antibacterial effect and comparability with inhaled tobramycin in patients aged 12 and over with chronic Pseudomonas infection.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Laninamivir for influenza treatment: single inhaled dose noninferior to 5-day oseltamivir in three Japanese trials (73.0 vs 73.6 hours in adults) — treatment only, Japan only
shelves.question: In children and adults with influenza, is a single inhaled dose of laninamivir octanoate non-inferior to a 5-day course of oseltamivir for time to illness alleviation?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Antiviral Agents · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Guanidines · Humans · Influenza A Virus, H1N1 Subtype · Influenza A Virus, H3N2 Subtype · Influenza B virus · Influenza, Human · Male · Middle Aged · Oseltamivir · Pyrans · Sialic Acids · Viral Load · Zanamivir
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) versus oseltamivir — that is what these noninferiority trials were designed to show, and they showed it: a single inhaled dose of laninamivir octanoate gave times to illness alleviation similar to a 5-day course of oral oseltamivir in adults (median 73.0 hours on laninamivir 40 mg vs 73.6 hours on oseltamivir, n=996 analysed) and in patients with chronic respiratory diseases (64.7 vs 59.7 hours, n=201 analysed). The paediatric trial (184 children analysed) found an advantage only against oseltamivir-resistant A(H1N1)2009 virus (a 2009-era context, printed on the card), with no significant differences for A(H3N2) or B. This shelf is confined to TREATMENT: the laninamivir post-exposure-prophylaxis programme is a separate question and is deliberately NOT folded in. Laninamivir is licensed in Japan only, and all three trials are Japanese, oseltamivir-controlled noninferiority designs. Other influenza antivirals (baloxavir, peramivir, oseltamivir itself) have their own homes and are cross-pointed, not re-carded.

cards.headline: Adult phase 3 noninferiority RCT (Watanabe 2010): single inhaled laninamivir was NONINFERIOR to 5-day oseltamivir — median time to illness alleviation 73.0 hours (40 mg) vs 73.6 hours (oseltamivir)
cards.summary: Adult phase 3 noninferiority RCT (Watanabe 2010): single inhaled laninamivir was NONINFERIOR to 5-day oseltamivir — median time to illness alleviation 73.0 hours (40 mg) vs 73.6 hours (oseltamivir)
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind randomised noninferiority trial, single inhaled laninamivir vs 5-day oral oseltamivir, adults
cards.people: 1,003 patients aged 20 years or older with febrile influenza symptoms for no more than 36 hours were randomised to a single inhalation of laninamivir octanoate 40 mg or 20 mg, or oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily for 5 days; 996 were included in the primary analysis (40 mg n=334, 20 mg n=326, oseltamivir n=336). The primary endpoint was time to illness alleviation, with a prespecified noninferiority margin of 18 hours.
cards.result: Median time to illness alleviation was 73.0 hours (laninamivir 40 mg), 85.8 hours (20 mg) and 73.6 hours (oseltamivir). The difference versus oseltamivir was −0.6 hours (95% CI −9.9 to 6.9) for the 40 mg dose and 12.2 hours (95% CI −1.5 to 17.2) for the 20 mg dose; the upper confidence limits were below the 18-hour noninferiority margin for both doses. The proportion of patients shedding virus at day 3 was significantly lower in the 40 mg laninamivir group than on oseltamivir (P=0.006).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority against oseltamivir — itself a treatment of modest effect — in a single-dose-versus-5-day comparison: the trial shows the two are similar, not that either shortens illness by the full median times quoted, and there is no placebo arm.
cards.source: Watanabe A et al. Long-acting neuraminidase inhibitor laninamivir octanoate versus oseltamivir for treatment of influenza: A double-blind, randomized, noninferiority clinical trial. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2010. PMID: 20936975. Registry ID: NCT00803595. cards.headline: Paediatric RCT (Sugaya, Ohashi 2010): laninamivir shortened illness versus oseltamivir ONLY in oseltamivir-resistant A(H1N1) infection (by about 61–66 hours); no significant differences for A(H3N2) or B
cards.summary: Paediatric RCT (Sugaya, Ohashi 2010): laninamivir shortened illness versus oseltamivir ONLY in oseltamivir-resistant A(H1N1) infection (by about 61–66 hours); no significant differences for A(H3N2) or B
cards.type: Randomised double-blind controlled trial, single inhaled laninamivir vs 5-day oral oseltamivir, children ≤9 years
cards.people: Children aged 9 years and under with febrile influenza symptoms of no more than 36 hours' duration were randomised to a single inhalation of laninamivir octanoate 40 mg or 20 mg, or oseltamivir 2 mg/kg orally twice daily for 5 days; the primary analysis included 184 patients (61, 61 and 62 per group). The primary endpoint was time to alleviation of influenza illness.
cards.result: In children infected with oseltamivir-resistant influenza A (H1N1) virus, laninamivir markedly reduced the median time to illness alleviation versus oseltamivir — by 60.9 hours (40 mg group) and 66.2 hours (20 mg group). For influenza A (H3N2) or B infection there were no significant differences between the laninamivir groups and oseltamivir. Laninamivir was well tolerated; the most common adverse events were gastrointestinal.
cards.watchOut: The headline paediatric advantage is confined to the oseltamivir-resistant A(H1N1)2009 virus of that season — a dated, strain-specific context — and the authors themselves state further study is needed for A(H3N2) and B, where no significant difference was found.
cards.source: Sugaya N, Ohashi Y. Long-acting neuraminidase inhibitor laninamivir octanoate (CS-8958) versus oseltamivir as treatment for children with influenza virus infection. Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy. 2010. PMID: 20368393. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chronic respiratory disease RCT (Watanabe 2013): laninamivir showed similar efficacy and safety to oseltamivir — median time to illness alleviation 64.7 vs 59.7 hours (difference 5.0 hours, 95% CI −13.6 to 16.1)
cards.summary: Chronic respiratory disease RCT (Watanabe 2013): laninamivir showed similar efficacy and safety to oseltamivir — median time to illness alleviation 64.7 vs 59.7 hours (difference 5.0 hours, 95% CI −13.6 to 16.1)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind controlled trial, single inhaled laninamivir vs oseltamivir, adults with chronic respiratory diseases
cards.people: 203 patients aged 20 years or older with influenza and chronic respiratory diseases were randomised to laninamivir octanoate (single inhalation) or oseltamivir; the full analysis set included 201 patients (laninamivir n=101, oseltamivir n=100). Most patients had underlying bronchial asthma and 170 were infected with influenza A(H1N1)2009. The primary endpoint was time to illness alleviation.
cards.result: Median time to illness alleviation was 64.7 hours on laninamivir and 59.7 hours on oseltamivir, a difference of 5.0 hours (95% CI −13.6 to 16.1). No adverse events specific to laninamivir were observed, and bronchospasm — reported with other inhaled drugs related to laninamivir — did not occur. The authors concluded laninamivir showed similar efficacy and safety to oseltamivir in this population, including for A(H1N1)2009 infection.
cards.watchOut: A small trial (203 randomised) dominated by asthma patients and A(H1N1)2009 infection; the confidence interval around the 5-hour difference is wide, so this is similarity within wide bounds, not precision equivalence.

cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (treatment question only).
cards.result: Three Japanese noninferiority trials (996, 184 and 201 patients analysed) consistently found no meaningful difference in time to illness alleviation between single-dose inhaled laninamivir octanoate and 5-day oral oseltamivir; the convenience difference is the single inhalation versus ten oral doses. The paediatric trial's resistant-virus finding dates from the 2009 pandemic strain and does not generalise to susceptible strains. This shelf deliberately does not cover laninamivir for post-exposure prophylaxis, which is a separate question with its own programme, per the commissioning row.

shelves.title: High-dose rifampicin in pulmonary TB: SPLIT — faster culture conversion (35 mg/kg HR 1.78, relative) but 50 mg/kg intolerable and 4-month high-dose regimens failed noninferiority in RIFASHORT
shelves.question: In adults with newly diagnosed rifampicin-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis, does rifampicin at doses above the standard 10 mg/kg (20–35 mg/kg, or fixed 1200–1800 mg/day in shortened regimens) versus standard dosing improve culture conversion and treatment success without unacceptable toxicity?
shelves.mesh: Adamantane · Adult · Antitubercular Agents · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Ethambutol · Ethylenediamines · Female · Fluoroquinolones · Humans · Isoniazid · Male · Moxifloxacin · Pyrazinamide · Rifampin · South Africa · Tanzania · Tuberculosis, Pulmonary
shelves.balance: SPLIT, with the three design limbs kept separate. (1) Dose-ranging / bactericidal-activity limb: in PanACEA HIGHRIF1's final cohorts, early bactericidal activity rose with dose, but 50 mg/kg was not tolerated (all 17 patients had adverse events; 11 withdrew or stopped) while 40 mg/kg (n=15) was selected for further study — small cohorts, Ns printed on the card, and a surrogate endpoint. (2) Regimen-selection limb: in the PanACEA multi-arm multi-stage trial (n=365), 35 mg/kg rifampicin speeded liquid-media culture conversion versus standard dosing (median 48 vs 62 days; adjusted hazard ratio 1.78, a relative measure), with no difference on solid media. (3) Treatment-shortening limb — the outcome that matters: RIFASHORT (672 enrolled) found 4-month regimens with rifampicin 1200 mg or 1800 mg/day FAILED to meet noninferiority against the 6-month standard (favourable responses 93% control vs 90% and 87%), though grade 3–4 adverse events were similar (about 4% in each group). The meta-analysis card (8 RCTs, 1,897 subjects) is a synthesis card, not a primary trial: week-8 culture conversion was higher with high doses (83.7% vs 80.6%; relative risk 1.06, relative) with no significant difference in treatment failure. Faster culture conversion has not translated into a proven shorter or more successful regimen. Intensified rifampicin in tuberculous meningitis is a different population and question (pack #1707) — cross-pointed, not re-carded.

cards.headline: PanACEA MAMS RCT (Boeree 2017): rifampicin 35 mg/kg speeded liquid-media culture conversion versus standard 10 mg/kg (median 48 vs 62 days; adjusted hazard ratio 1.78, relative) — no difference on solid media
cards.summary: PanACEA MAMS RCT (Boeree 2017): rifampicin 35 mg/kg speeded liquid-media culture conversion versus standard 10 mg/kg (median 48 vs 62 days; adjusted hazard ratio 1.78, relative) — no difference on solid media
cards.type: Multi-arm multi-stage open-label randomised regimen-selection trial (PanACEA), high-dose rifampicin arms vs standard-dose control
cards.people: 365 patients with newly diagnosed, rifampicin-sensitive, previously untreated pulmonary tuberculosis at seven sites in South Africa and Tanzania were randomised (1:1:1:1:2) to: rifampicin 35 mg/kg with ethambutol (n=63); rifampicin 10 mg/kg with SQ109 (n=59); rifampicin 20 mg/kg with SQ109 (n=57); rifampicin 10 mg/kg with moxifloxacin (n=63); or standard control (rifampicin 10 mg/kg, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol; n=123) — all experimental arms also received isoniazid and pyrazinamide for 12 weeks, then 14 weeks of isoniazid plus rifampicin 10 mg/kg. The primary endpoint was time to culture conversion in liquid media within 12 weeks.
cards.result: Time to stable culture conversion in liquid media was faster in the 35 mg/kg rifampicin group than in controls (median 48 vs 62 days; adjusted hazard ratio 1.78, 95% CI 1.22 to 2.58; P=0.003 — a relative measure), but not in the other experimental arms, and there was no difference in any group in time to culture conversion on solid media. Recruitment to the SQ109 arms was stopped early when prespecified efficacy thresholds were not met at interim analysis. Eleven patients had treatment failure or recurrent disease in post-treatment follow-up (one in the 35 mg/kg arm, none in the moxifloxacin arm). Grade 3–5 adverse events were reported by 45 of 365 patients (12%), in similar proportions across arms.
cards.watchOut: A regimen-selection trial with a microbiological (culture-conversion) primary endpoint and combination arms — the 35 mg/kg signal is about speed of conversion in liquid media only, and the design mixes rifampicin dose with companion-drug changes in other arms. Open-label (orange discoloration of body fluids made masking impossible).
cards.source: Boeree MJ et al. High-dose rifampicin, moxifloxacin, and SQ109 for treating tuberculosis: a multi-arm, multi-stage randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. Infectious Diseases. 2017. PMID: 28100438. Registry ID: NCT01785186. cards.headline: PanACEA HIGHRIF1 final cohorts (Te Brake 2021) — SMALL Ns printed on the face (n=15 and n=17): bactericidal activity was highest at 50 mg/kg, but that dose was NOT tolerated; 40 mg/kg was selected for further study
cards.summary: PanACEA HIGHRIF1 final cohorts (Te Brake 2021) — SMALL Ns printed on the face (n=15 and n=17): bactericidal activity was highest at 50 mg/kg, but that dose was NOT tolerated; 40 mg/kg was selected for further study
cards.type: Dose-escalation early-bactericidal-activity study, final cohorts (PanACEA HIGHRIF1) — SMALL cohorts, n=15 and n=17
cards.people: Treatment-naive adult smear-positive tuberculosis patients received, in consecutive cohorts, rifampicin 40 mg/kg once daily (n=15) or 50 mg/kg once daily (n=17) as monotherapy on days 1–7, supplemented with standard-dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol on days 8–14. Outcomes were safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and 7- and 14-day early bactericidal activity.
cards.result: In the 40 mg/kg cohort (n=15), 13 patients had 36 adverse events during monotherapy, with one treatment discontinuation. In the 50 mg/kg cohort (n=17), all patients had adverse events (93 in total) and 11 withdrew or stopped study medication; events were mostly mild/moderate and tolerability-related (gastrointestinal disorders, pruritus, hyperbilirubinaemia, jaundice). Early bactericidal activity increased with dose and was highest at 50 mg/kg (14-day EBA −0.427 log10 CFU·mL−1·day−1, 95% CI −0.500 to −0.355). The authors concluded 50 mg/kg was not well tolerated and selected 40 mg/kg for a phase IIc treatment-shortening trial.
cards.watchOut: SMALL cohorts (n=15, n=17) and a 14-day surrogate (early bactericidal activity): this card defines the tolerability ceiling of rifampicin dosing, not treatment efficacy. Do not read the dose–EBA gradient as evidence that 50 mg/kg treats tuberculosis better — patients could not stay on it.
cards.source: Te Brake LHM et al. Increased bactericidal activity but dose-limiting intolerability at 50 mg·kg-1 rifampicin. The European Respiratory Journal. 2021. PMID: 33542056. cards.headline: RIFASHORT RCT (Jindani 2023): 4-month high-dose rifampicin regimens (1200 mg or 1800 mg/day) FAILED to meet noninferiority versus the 6-month standard — favourable responses 87–90% vs 93%
cards.summary: RIFASHORT RCT (Jindani 2023): 4-month high-dose rifampicin regimens (1200 mg or 1800 mg/day) FAILED to meet noninferiority versus the 6-month standard — favourable responses 87–90% vs 93%
cards.type: Randomised noninferiority trial (RIFASHORT), 4-month high-dose rifampicin regimens vs 6-month standard control
cards.people: 672 adults with rifampicin-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis in six countries were enrolled and assigned to a 6-month control regimen (n=191), a similar 4-month regimen with rifampicin 1200 mg/day (study regimen 1, n=192), or a 4-month regimen with rifampicin 1800 mg/day (study regimen 2, n=195). The primary endpoint was a composite of treatment failure and relapse in participants smear-positive at baseline; the noninferiority margin was 8 percentage points.
cards.result: Noninferiority was not shown. Favourable response rates were 93% (control), 90% (1200 mg) and 87% (1800 mg); the country-adjusted absolute risk difference comparing the 1800 mg regimen with control was 6.3 percentage points (90% CI 1.1 to 11.5), against the 8-point noninferiority margin under the trial's ordered testing. Grade 3 or 4 adverse events occurred in 4.0%, 4.5% and 4.4% of the control, 1200 mg and 1800 mg groups respectively — the high doses did not produce dose-limiting toxicity, but the shorter regimens were not shown to be as effective.
cards.watchOut: The only carded trial that tests the actual clinical prize — a shorter regimen — and it failed its noninferiority test despite the higher doses being tolerable. Its question is the 4-month regimen as a whole, not rifampicin dose in isolation.
cards.source: Jindani A et al. Four-Month High-Dose Rifampicin Regimens for Pulmonary Tuberculosis. NEJM Evidence. 2023. PMID: 38320155. Registry ID: NCT02581527. MeSH: Humans · Rifampin · Antitubercular Agents · Isoniazid · Drug Therapy, Combination · Tuberculosis, Pulmonary

cards.headline: Meta-analysis — synthesis card (Onorato 2021), not a primary trial: high-dose rifampicin raised week-8 culture conversion (83.7% vs 80.6%; relative risk 1.06, relative) with no significant difference in treatment failure across 8 RCTs (1,897 subjects)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis — synthesis card (Onorato 2021), not a primary trial: high-dose rifampicin raised week-8 culture conversion (83.7% vs 80.6%; relative risk 1.06, relative) with no significant difference in treatment failure across 8 RCTs (1,897 subjects)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis — synthesis card (pools 8 RCTs; not a primary trial, and its component trials are not separately carded here beyond the primaries above)
cards.people: Eight randomised controlled trials (1,897 subjects) comparing standard rifampicin dosing (10 mg/kg) with higher doses in treatment-naive patients with pulmonary tuberculosis, pooled for 8-week sputum culture conversion, treatment failure and safety outcomes.
cards.result: At week 8, culture conversion was higher with high-dose rifampicin (83.7% vs 80.6%; relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.12; P=0.028 — a relative effect on a 3.1-percentage-point absolute difference), confirmed in the subgroup receiving at least 20 mg/kg but not at 11–19 mg/kg. Treatment failure did not differ significantly (relative risk 0.84, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.21). Grade 3–4 liver toxicity (7.2% vs 5.4%; relative risk 1.19, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.73) and adverse drug reactions leading to discontinuation (1.5% vs 0.6%; relative risk 2.31, 95% CI 0.65 to 8.21) were not significantly different. Risk of bias was low in three of the eight trials, intermediate in three and high in two.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis of mostly small, short trials whose positive outcome is a microbiological surrogate at week 8; it pools doses from just above standard to very high, and its own failure outcome — the one closest to cure — was not significantly different.
cards.source: Onorato L et al. Standard versus high dose of rifampicin in the treatment of pulmonary tuberculosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Microbiology and Infection. 2021. cards.headline: Synthesis: higher rifampicin doses speed culture conversion (relative risk 1.06 for week-8 conversion in the meta-analysis; hazard ratio 1.78 for liquid conversion at 35 mg/kg), but 50 mg/kg is intolerable and the 4-month high-dose regimens failed noninferiority — no proven shorter or better regimen yet
cards.summary: Synthesis: higher rifampicin doses speed culture conversion (relative risk 1.06 for week-8 conversion in the meta-analysis; hazard ratio 1.78 for liquid conversion at 35 mg/kg), but 50 mg/kg is intolerable and the 4-month high-dose regimens failed noninferiority — no proven shorter or better regimen yet
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The bactericidal-activity limb (HIGHRIF1, n=15 and n=17 cohorts) sets a tolerability ceiling near 40 mg/kg. The regimen-selection limb (PanACEA, n=365) shows faster liquid-media conversion at 35 mg/kg. The treatment-shortening limb (RIFASHORT, 672 enrolled) — the only test of a patient-level outcome strategy — did not show the 4-month high-dose regimens to be noninferior to 6 months of standard treatment. The meta-analysis (8 RCTs, 1,897 subjects) agrees with the surrogate signal and finds no significant difference in treatment failure. High-dose rifampicin remains a promising but unproven route to shorter tuberculosis treatment.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
