shelves.title: Vornorexant in insomnia (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 patient reports): 2-week RCT showed ~10 min subjective latency gain vs placebo; 52-week open-label tolerability, Japan only
shelves.question: In adults with insomnia disorder, does the dual orexin receptor antagonist vornorexant (5–10 mg nightly), versus placebo, improve subjective sleep onset and maintenance, and is it safe over 52 weeks? (FLOOR-RISK: the patient-population base is exactly two reports, both from Japan.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Double-Blind Method · Japan · Orexin Receptor Antagonists · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders · Sleep Latency · Treatment Outcome · Oxazines · Pyrazoles · Pyridines · East Asian People
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on a FLOOR-RISK base, stated plainly: the entire patient-population evidence for vornorexant (Vorzzz, Taisho) in insomnia is exactly TWO reports, both Japanese — one 2-week placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (n=596) and one 52-week open-label dose-randomised study (n=371) with no placebo arm. The phase 3 trial showed statistically significant but modest subjective benefits at week 2: sleep latency improved by least-squares mean differences of −10.6 minutes (5 mg) and −10.1 minutes (10 mg) versus placebo, and subjective sleep efficiency by +3.41% and +2.94%. The long-term study observed sustained diary improvements to 52 weeks (subjective latency changes of −31.8 and −44.0 minutes) with nasopharyngitis and somnolence as the commonest adverse events and no withdrawal or rebound signal in a 1-week placebo run-out — but without a control arm those long-term changes cannot be separated from expectancy and natural history. Vornorexant is approved in Japan; it is not FDA- or EMA-approved. A driving-simulator trial in healthy volunteers (cross-point card) found no clinically meaningful next-morning impairment at 10–20 mg. No phase 2 dose-finding report in insomnia patients could be verified, so the base stays at two patient reports.

cards.headline: Phase 3 RCT (Uchiyama 2026): vornorexant in Japanese insomnia patients — subjective sleep latency improved by −10.6 min (5 mg) and −10.1 min (10 mg) versus placebo at week 2 (n=596)
cards.summary: Phase 3 RCT (Uchiyama 2026): vornorexant in Japanese insomnia patients — subjective sleep latency improved by −10.6 min (5 mg) and −10.1 min (10 mg) versus placebo at week 2 (n=596)
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, vornorexant 5 or 10 mg vs placebo in insomnia (patient report 1 of 2)
cards.people: 596 Japanese patients with insomnia, randomised 1:1:1 double-blind to vornorexant 5 mg, vornorexant 10 mg or placebo nightly for 2 weeks, after a 2-week placebo run-in and followed by a 1-week placebo run-out. Endpoints were subjective (sleep-diary) sleep latency (primary) and subjective sleep efficiency (key secondary).
cards.result: At week 2, subjective sleep latency improved significantly versus placebo: least-squares mean differences of −10.6 min (95% CI −14.2 to −7.0; P<.001) for 5 mg and −10.1 min (95% CI −13.8 to −6.5; P<.001) for 10 mg. Subjective sleep efficiency also improved significantly: +3.41% (95% CI 1.87 to 4.96; P<.001) and +2.94% (95% CI 1.40 to 4.48; P<.001) respectively. The most common adverse event was somnolence (5 mg 3.1%, 10 mg 3.6%, placebo 1.5%). No cataplexy, falls, muscular weakness, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations or excessive daytime sleepiness were reported, and no withdrawal symptoms or rebound insomnia were observed in the run-out week.
cards.watchOut: Two weeks long, subjective diary endpoints only, and a single-country (Japanese) population after a placebo run-in that enriches for placebo nonresponders. The absolute gains — about 10 minutes of subjective latency and about 3% of sleep efficiency — are modest.
cards.source: Uchiyama M et al. Efficacy and safety of vornorexant in Japanese patients with insomnia: a randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 pivotal study. Sleep. 2026. PMID: 41001841. Registry ID: NCT05453136. cards.headline: 52-week open-label study (Uchimura 2026): vornorexant 5 vs 10 mg in Japanese insomnia patients (n=371 randomised by dose, NO placebo arm) — diary improvements sustained to 52 weeks; nasopharyngitis and somnolence the commonest events
cards.summary: 52-week open-label study (Uchimura 2026): vornorexant 5 vs 10 mg in Japanese insomnia patients (n=371 randomised by dose, NO placebo arm) — diary improvements sustained to 52 weeks; nasopharyngitis and somnolence the commonest events
cards.type: 52-week open-label randomised-by-dose long-term study (no placebo control), vornorexant in insomnia (patient report 2 of 2)
cards.people: 371 Japanese patients with insomnia randomised open-label to vornorexant 5 mg or 10 mg for an initial 26 weeks with an optional 26-week extension (up to 52 weeks), followed by a 1-week single-blind placebo run-out. 38 patients discontinued during the initial period and 8 during the extension. This is patient report 2 of 2 — there is no third patient-population report.
cards.result: The most common adverse events were nasopharyngitis (10.9% on 5 mg, 8.2% on 10 mg) and somnolence (5.4% and 12.0%). No withdrawal symptoms or rebound insomnia of clinical concern were detected at run-out. Mean change from baseline in subjective sleep latency was −31.2 min (5 mg) and −38.9 min (10 mg) at week 26 and −31.8 and −44.0 min at week 52; subjective sleep efficiency changed by +14.07% and +17.63% at week 26 and +15.56% and +20.40% at week 52. Changes were generally similar across age and sex subgroups; psychiatric-comorbidity subgroup analyses were underpowered.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and uncontrolled: the large diary improvements cannot be attributed to the drug rather than expectancy, regression to the mean or natural history. Its usable content is long-term tolerability (including the dose-related somnolence split, 5.4% vs 12.0%) and the absence of a withdrawal/rebound signal.
cards.source: Uchimura N et al. Long-term safety and efficacy of vornorexant in Japanese patients with insomnia: A 52-week open-label, randomized trial. Sleep medicine. 2026. PMID: 42731338. cards.headline: Cross-point only — next-morning driving-simulator RCT in HEALTHY volunteers (Miyazaki 2025): vornorexant 10 and 20 mg produced no clinically meaningful driving impairment after single or repeated dosing (not an insomnia-patient report; not counted toward the evidence floor)
cards.summary: Cross-point only — next-morning driving-simulator RCT in HEALTHY volunteers (Miyazaki 2025): vornorexant 10 and 20 mg produced no clinically meaningful driving impairment after single or repeated dosing (not an insomnia-patient report; not counted toward the evidence floor)
cards.type: Cross-point companion report: randomised double-blind crossover driving-simulator trial in healthy volunteers (residual-effects question only — not insomnia efficacy evidence)
cards.people: 61 healthy Japanese participants randomised (55 completed) in a four-way double-blind crossover: vornorexant 10 mg, vornorexant 20 mg and placebo for eight consecutive nights, with zopiclone on days 1 and 8 as the active reference. Driving was assessed 9 hours post-dose on days 2 and 9 by standard deviation of lateral position (SDLP) in a validated simulator.
cards.result: Mean drug–placebo changes in SDLP for vornorexant 10 mg were +0.767 cm on day 2 and −0.422 cm on day 9, and for 20 mg +2.132 cm and −0.040 cm, versus approximately 6 cm for zopiclone; all upper bounds of the 90% confidence intervals were below the predefined clinically significant threshold, and symmetry analysis found no excess of participants crossing the threshold on 10 mg (either day) or 20 mg (day 9). Plasma concentrations were consistent between single and repeated dosing.
cards.watchOut: Healthy volunteers, a simulator, and doses up to twice the insomnia dose: reassuring for next-morning residual effects, but it says nothing about whether vornorexant treats insomnia, and it is not counted in this shelf's two-report patient base. The phase 1 pharmacokinetic studies in healthy Japanese participants (PMID 37563858) are likewise not carded as efficacy evidence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly two patient reports exist (one 2-week placebo-controlled trial, one 52-week open-label study, both Japanese); vornorexant improved subjective sleep onset and efficiency modestly in the controlled trial and was tolerated over a year
cards.summary: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly two patient reports exist (one 2-week placebo-controlled trial, one 52-week open-label study, both Japanese); vornorexant improved subjective sleep onset and efficiency modestly in the controlled trial and was tolerated over a year
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (two insomnia-patient reports plus one healthy-volunteer cross-point report that is not counted as efficacy evidence).
cards.result: Vornorexant (Vorzzz, Taisho; approved in Japan, not FDA- or EMA-approved) beat placebo over 2 weeks in 596 Japanese insomnia patients on subjective sleep latency (−10.6 and −10.1 min at 5 and 10 mg) and subjective sleep efficiency (+3.41% and +2.94%), with somnolence the commonest adverse event (3.1–3.6% vs 1.5%). Over 52 weeks open-label (n=371), tolerability held (somnolence 5.4% at 5 mg vs 12.0% at 10 mg; nasopharyngitis ~8–11%) with no withdrawal or rebound signal, but the sustained diary improvements in that study are uncontrolled. No phase 2 dose-finding report in insomnia patients could be verified from its own record this session, so the patient base remains exactly two reports — this shelf is built under its floor-risk flag with that count on its face, and should be revisited if a third patient report appears. Other orexin-antagonist and insomnia questions are homed at live #572, #231 and #1500 and pack #2420 and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Aclidinium bromide in COPD: better lung function (+124 to +128 mL trough FEV1), cardiovascularly non-inferior and fewer exacerbations in ASCENT-COPD (rate ratio 0.78)
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe COPD, does twice-daily inhaled aclidinium bromide (400 μg) versus placebo improve lung function and reduce exacerbations — and is it cardiovascularly safe in patients at increased cardiovascular risk?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Muscarinic Antagonists · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Quality of Life · Spirometry · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome · Tropanes
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). Two short placebo-controlled trials showed aclidinium 400 μg twice daily improving trough FEV1 by 124 mL at 12 weeks (ACCORD COPD I) and 128 mL at 24 weeks (ATTAIN), with better symptom and health-status scores. The large ASCENT-COPD trial (3630 patients at increased cardiovascular risk, up to 3 years) showed cardiovascular non-inferiority (major events 3.9% versus 4.2%; hazard ratio 0.89, against a wide 1.8 margin) and fewer first-year moderate-to-severe exacerbations (0.44 versus 0.57 per year; rate ratio 0.78 — a 22% relative reduction, absolute difference 0.13 per year). The efficacy trials are 12–24 weeks with lung-function primary endpoints — the exacerbation and cardiovascular claims rest on ASCENT alone, and this shelf says so.

cards.headline: ACCORD COPD I RCT (Kerwin 2012): aclidinium 400 μg twice daily improved trough FEV1 by 124 mL and peak FEV1 by 192 mL versus placebo at week 12 in 561 patients
cards.summary: ACCORD COPD I RCT (Kerwin 2012): aclidinium 400 μg twice daily improved trough FEV1 by 124 mL and peak FEV1 by 192 mL versus placebo at week 12 in 561 patients
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ACCORD COPD I), aclidinium 200/400 μg twice daily vs placebo, 12 weeks
cards.people: 561 patients with moderate-to-severe COPD (mean age 64 ± 9 years; mean baseline FEV1 1.36 ± 0.54 L, 47.2% predicted) randomised 1:1:1 to inhaled aclidinium 200 μg, aclidinium 400 μg or placebo twice daily for 12 weeks.
cards.result: At week 12, aclidinium 200 μg and 400 μg improved trough FEV1 versus placebo by 86 mL (95% CI 45 to 127) and 124 mL (95% CI 83 to 164), and peak FEV1 by 146 mL and 192 mL (all P≤0.0001). Both doses also significantly improved St George's Respiratory Questionnaire scores, Transitional Dyspnea Index and almost all COPD symptom scores (P<0.05). Adverse-event incidences were similar across groups; anticholinergic events were low (dry mouth 0.5–1.6%; constipation 0–1.1%).
cards.watchOut: A 12-week lung-function trial: it cannot speak to exacerbations or cardiovascular safety — those claims rest on ASCENT-COPD alone (below), as this shelf's balance states.
cards.source: Kerwin EM et al. Efficacy and safety of a 12-week treatment with twice-daily aclidinium bromide in COPD patients (ACCORD COPD I). COPD. 2012. PMID: 22320148. Registry ID: NCT00891462. cards.headline: ATTAIN RCT (Jones 2012): aclidinium 400 μg twice daily improved trough FEV1 by 128 mL versus placebo at week 24 in 828 patients, with better health status and dyspnoea scores
cards.summary: ATTAIN RCT (Jones 2012): aclidinium 400 μg twice daily improved trough FEV1 by 128 mL versus placebo at week 24 in 828 patients, with better health status and dyspnoea scores
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ATTAIN), aclidinium 200/400 μg twice daily vs placebo, 24 weeks
cards.people: 828 patients with moderate-to-severe COPD randomised to twice-daily aclidinium 200 μg, aclidinium 400 μg or placebo for 24 weeks; primary endpoint was change in trough FEV1 at week 24.
cards.result: At week 24, trough FEV1 improved versus placebo by 99 mL (200 μg) and 128 mL (400 μg) (both P<0.0001), and peak FEV1 by 185 mL and 209 mL (both P<0.0001); day-1 peak improvements were comparable with week 24. Aclidinium improved St George's Respiratory Questionnaire total score by −3.8 (200 μg) and −4.6 units (400 μg) versus placebo (P<0.001 and P<0.0001) and Transitional Dyspnea Index focal score by 0.6 and 1.0 units. Anticholinergic adverse events were low and similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: A 24-week trial with a lung-function primary endpoint; symptom and health-status gains are secondary endpoints, and there is still no exacerbation or safety-outcome evidence at this duration.
cards.source: Jones PW et al. Efficacy and safety of twice-daily aclidinium bromide in COPD patients: the ATTAIN study. The European respiratory journal. 2012. PMID: 22441743. cards.headline: ASCENT-COPD RCT (Wise 2019): aclidinium 400 μg twice daily was non-inferior to placebo for major cardiovascular events over up to 3 years (3.9% versus 4.2%; hazard ratio 0.89) and reduced moderate-to-severe exacerbations in year 1 (rate ratio 0.78 — a 22% relative reduction; absolute rates 0.44 versus 0.57 per year)
cards.summary: ASCENT-COPD RCT (Wise 2019): aclidinium 400 μg twice daily was non-inferior to placebo for major cardiovascular events over up to 3 years (3.9% versus 4.2%; hazard ratio 0.89) and reduced moderate-to-severe exacerbations in year 1 (rate ratio 0.78 — a 22% relative reduction; absolute rates 0.44 versus 0.57 per year)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled cardiovascular-safety and exacerbation trial (ASCENT-COPD), aclidinium 400 μg twice daily vs placebo, up to 3 years
cards.people: 3630 patients with moderate-to-very-severe COPD and either cardiovascular disease history or at least 2 atherothrombotic risk factors, randomised at 522 North American sites to aclidinium 400 μg (1812) or placebo (1818) twice daily for up to 3 years (until at least 122 major adverse cardiovascular events); 3589 were analysed (mean age 67.2 years, 58.7% men) and 2537 (70.7%) completed.
cards.result: Major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 69 (3.9%) aclidinium versus 76 (4.2%) placebo patients (hazard ratio 0.89, 1-sided 97.5% CI 0 to 1.23; non-inferiority margin 1.8 — met). The expanded cardiovascular definition gave 168 (9.4%) versus 160 (8.9%) (hazard ratio 1.03). Annual moderate-to-severe exacerbation rates in year 1 were 0.44 versus 0.57 (rate ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.89; P<0.001 — a 22% relative reduction, absolute difference 0.13 exacerbations per year), and exacerbations requiring hospitalisation 0.07 versus 0.10 per year (rate ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.89; P=0.006 — a 35% relative reduction). Commonest adverse events were pneumonia (6.1% versus 5.8%), urinary tract infection (5.2% versus 5.0%) and upper respiratory infection (4.8% versus 5.6%).
cards.watchOut: The non-inferiority margin for cardiovascular events was wide (hazard ratio 1.8), so 'non-inferior' here excludes only a large excess; and the exacerbation benefit is a first-year endpoint in a high-cardiovascular-risk population — it is the only exacerbation evidence for aclidinium monotherapy, as the row directs the shelf to state.
cards.source: Wise RA et al. Effect of Aclidinium Bromide on Major Cardiovascular Events and Exacerbations in High-Risk Patients With Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: The ASCENT-COPD Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2019. cards.headline: Programme report — post-hoc analysis of ASCENT-COPD (Wise 2021): aclidinium did not increase major cardiovascular events or mortality in any baseline-therapy subgroup, with exacerbation reductions largest on background LABA (43% relative reduction) — a report OF the ASCENT trial, not a separate trial
cards.summary: Programme report — post-hoc analysis of ASCENT-COPD (Wise 2021): aclidinium did not increase major cardiovascular events or mortality in any baseline-therapy subgroup, with exacerbation reductions largest on background LABA (43% relative reduction) — a report OF the ASCENT trial, not a separate trial
cards.type: Programme report: post-hoc subgroup analysis of the ASCENT-COPD randomised trial (same trial as the card above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The 3589 analysed ASCENT-COPD patients, grouped post hoc by baseline maintenance therapy: LABA alone (227), inhaled corticosteroid alone (290), LABA + inhaled corticosteroid (2058), or no maintenance therapy (1130).
cards.result: Aclidinium did not increase the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events or all-cause mortality versus placebo in any subgroup. Reductions in moderate-to-severe exacerbation rates with aclidinium versus placebo were 43% relative (P=0.046) on LABA, 25% relative (P=0.202) on inhaled corticosteroid, 22% relative (P=0.003) on LABA + inhaled corticosteroid and 18% relative (P=0.130) with no maintenance therapy — relative reductions from a post-hoc analysis, with two of four subgroups not statistically significant. Aclidinium improved morning trough FEV1 irrespective of baseline therapy.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and subgroup-based: hypothesis-generating only. Carded, labelled as a programme report, to complete the ASCENT record — it adds no independent trial.
cards.source: Wise RA et al. Efficacy of Aclidinium Bromide According to Baseline Therapy: Post-Hoc Analysis of ASCENT-COPD Randomized Trial. Advances in therapy. 2021. PMID: 34528220. cards.result: ACCORD COPD I (561 patients, 12 weeks) and ATTAIN (828 patients, 24 weeks) consistently showed aclidinium 400 μg twice daily improving trough FEV1 by about 124–128 mL versus placebo, with better symptom and health-status scores and placebo-like tolerability. The exacerbation and cardiovascular claims rest on ASCENT-COPD alone (3630 randomised, up to 3 years, in patients at increased cardiovascular risk): major cardiovascular events 3.9% versus 4.2% (hazard ratio 0.89, meeting a wide 1.8 non-inferiority margin) and first-year moderate-to-severe exacerbation rates of 0.44 versus 0.57 per year (rate ratio 0.78 — a 22% relative reduction). The 2021 post-hoc subgroup analysis is a report of ASCENT, not a further trial. Aclidinium is also marketed in a formoterol combination; that combination question is a different shelf and is not folded in here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Nebulised revefenacin in COPD: trough FEV1 up 146–147 mL versus placebo at 12 weeks — a single programme (two replicate trials plus one 52-week safety trial), labelled on the face
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-very-severe COPD, does once-daily nebulised revefenacin (175 μg) versus placebo improve lung function over 12 weeks and maintain benefit and safety over 52 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Adrenergic beta-Agonists · Aged · Benzamides · Bronchodilator Agents · Carbamates · Clinical Trials, Phase III as Topic · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Lung · Male · Middle Aged · Muscarinic Antagonists · Nebulizers and Vaporizers · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recovery of Function · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a SINGLE PROGRAMME, labelled as such. Revefenacin (nebulised solution, marketed as Yupelri — the nebulised delivery is the point of the question) rests on one development programme: two replicate 12-week placebo-controlled trials (Studies 0126/0127, reported together) showing day-85 trough FEV1 advantages of 146–147 mL for the 175 μg once-daily dose, and one 52-week safety trial (1055 patients, versus open-label tiotropium) showing comparable tolerability and maintained exploratory lung-function gains. The AUC substudy, maintained-effect and subgroup papers are reports of those same trials, carded and labelled as programme reports — not independent trials. Endpoints are lung function and health status; there is no exacerbation-outcome trial.

cards.headline: Primary replicate-trial report (Ferguson 2019): revefenacin 175 μg once daily improved day-85 trough FEV1 versus placebo by 146 mL in Study 0126 and 147 mL in Study 0127 — the two replicate 12-week phase 3 trials of this single programme, reported together in one paper
cards.summary: Primary replicate-trial report (Ferguson 2019): revefenacin 175 μg once daily improved day-85 trough FEV1 versus placebo by 146 mL in Study 0126 and 147 mL in Study 0127 — the two replicate 12-week phase 3 trials of this single programme, reported together in one paper
cards.type: Primary report of two replicate randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (Studies 0126 and 0127) reported together, revefenacin 88/175 μg once-daily nebulised vs placebo, 12 weeks
cards.people: Patients aged 40 or over with moderate-to-very-severe COPD in two double-blind parallel-group replicate studies (Study 0126, NCT02459080, and Study 0127, NCT02512510), randomised to revefenacin 88 μg, revefenacin 175 μg or placebo once daily by standard jet nebuliser for 12 weeks; the total randomised number across the two studies is not stated in the fetched abstract.
cards.result: At day 85, revefenacin 88 μg and 175 μg improved trough FEV1 versus placebo in Study 0126 by 79 mL (P=0.0003) and 146 mL (P<0.0001), and in Study 0127 by 160 mL and 147 mL (both P<0.0001). In pooled data, revefenacin 88 μg and 175 μg increased overall treatment effect on trough FEV1 by 115 mL and 142 mL (both P<0.001) and peak FEV1 by 127 mL and 129 mL (both P<0.0001). Revefenacin 175 μg showed greater FEV1 improvements in patients on concomitant long-acting beta-agonists and in more severe patients. Adverse events were minor and revefenacin was generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: This one paper is the primary report for BOTH replicate trials — the programme's 12-week efficacy evidence is these two trials, and the pooled, subgroup and AUC papers carded below are reports of the same trials, not additional trials. Lung function is the endpoint; no exacerbation-outcome trial exists in this programme.

cards.headline: Programme report — AUC spirometry substudy (LeMaster 2024): in the 24-hour serial-spirometry substudy of the same replicate trials, revefenacin's FEV1 advantage over placebo was sustained across the whole dosing interval at day 84 (AUC differences 205–282 mL) — a report OF the replicate trials, not a separate trial
cards.summary: Programme report — AUC spirometry substudy (LeMaster 2024): in the 24-hour serial-spirometry substudy of the same replicate trials, revefenacin's FEV1 advantage over placebo was sustained across the whole dosing interval at day 84 (AUC differences 205–282 mL) — a report OF the replicate trials, not a separate trial
cards.type: Programme report: post-hoc area-under-the-curve spirometry substudy of the two replicate phase 3 trials (same trials as the primary card above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: A substudy of the same two replicate 12-week phase 3 trials (NCT02459080/NCT02512510): 50 revefenacin and 47 placebo patients underwent 24-hour serial spirometry at day 84, with FEV1 area-under-the-curve assessed over 0–2, 0–12, 12–24 and 0–24 hours.
cards.result: At day 84, least-squares mean differences versus placebo were 282 mL for FEV1 AUC0–2h, 220 mL for AUC0–12h, 205 mL for AUC12–24h and 212 mL for AUC0–24h (all P<0.001), supporting sustained bronchodilation over the 24-hour dosing interval.
cards.watchOut: A post-hoc substudy of under 100 patients with serial spirometry: it describes the shape of the bronchodilator effect in the same trials and adds no independent efficacy evidence. Carded, labelled as a programme report, to complete the single-programme record.

cards.headline: 52-week safety trial (Donohue 2019): revefenacin was generally well tolerated over 52 weeks in 1055 patients, with treatment-emergent adverse events in 72.2% (175 μg), 74.7% (88 μg) and 77.2% (open-label tiotropium)
cards.summary: 52-week safety trial (Donohue 2019): revefenacin was generally well tolerated over 52 weeks in 1055 patients, with treatment-emergent adverse events in 72.2% (175 μg), 74.7% (88 μg) and 77.2% (open-label tiotropium)
cards.type: Randomised 52-week phase 3 safety and tolerability trial (Study 0128), revefenacin 88/175 μg (double-blind) vs open-label tiotropium
cards.people: 1055 participants with moderate-to-very-severe COPD in a randomised parallel-group 52-week trial (Study 0128, NCT02518139), receiving double-blind revefenacin 88 μg or 175 μg once daily by nebuliser, or open-label active-control tiotropium.
cards.result: Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 272 patients (74.7%) on revefenacin 88 μg, 242 (72.2%) on 175 μg and 275 (77.2%) on tiotropium. COPD exacerbations were numerically fewer with revefenacin 175 μg (73 patients, 21.8%) than with 88 μg (107, 29.4%) or tiotropium (100, 28.1%) — percentages of patients, from a safety trial not designed as an exacerbation-efficacy comparison. Serious adverse events were 15.9% (88 μg), 12.8% (175 μg) and 16.3% (tiotropium), and mortality was low. Concurrent long-acting beta-agonist use slightly raised adverse-event incidence in the 88 μg and tiotropium groups but not the 175 μg group.
cards.watchOut: A safety trial with an open-label comparator: the numerically fewer exacerbations on the 175 μg dose are an observation within a safety study, not a demonstrated exacerbation benefit — do not promote them into an efficacy claim.
cards.source: Donohue JF et al. Revefenacin, a once-daily, lung-selective, long-acting muscarinic antagonist for nebulized therapy: Safety and tolerability results of a 52-week phase 3 trial in moderate to very severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Respiratory medicine. 2019. PMID: 31150963. Registry ID: NCT02518139. cards.headline: Programme report — maintained effect in the same 52-week trial (Donohue 2019): trough FEV1 improvements with revefenacin 175 μg ranged from 52.3 to 124.3 mL over 52 weeks, comparable with tiotropium's 79.7 to 112.8 mL — a second report OF Study 0128, not a separate trial
cards.summary: Programme report — maintained effect in the same 52-week trial (Donohue 2019): trough FEV1 improvements with revefenacin 175 μg ranged from 52.3 to 124.3 mL over 52 weeks, comparable with tiotropium's 79.7 to 112.8 mL — a second report OF Study 0128, not a separate trial
cards.type: Programme report: exploratory efficacy/health-outcomes report of the same 52-week trial (Study 0128) as the safety card above — not independent evidence
cards.people: The same 1055 participants of the 52-week trial (Study 0128, NCT02518139) carded above — revefenacin 88 μg or 175 μg double-blind, or open-label tiotropium — with exploratory efficacy and health-outcome endpoints.
cards.result: Over 52 weeks, both revefenacin doses and tiotropium significantly improved trough FEV1 from baseline (all P<0.0003); the least-squares mean change profile ranged from 52.3 to 124.3 mL for revefenacin 175 μg and 79.7 to 112.8 mL for tiotropium. Effects were comparable in patients taking concomitant long-acting beta-agonists (with or without inhaled corticosteroids) and in those not taking them. All measured health-status outcomes (St George's Respiratory Questionnaire, COPD Assessment Test, Clinical COPD Questionnaire, dyspnoea index) improved significantly from 3 months onward in all arms.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory endpoints in a safety trial, reported without a placebo arm (the comparator was open-label tiotropium): within-group improvements from baseline cannot separate drug effect from trial effects. Carded, labelled as a programme report of the same trial.
cards.source: Donohue JF et al. Maintained therapeutic effect of revefenacin over 52 weeks in moderate to very severe Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). Respiratory research. 2019. PMID: 31666076. Registry ID: NCT02518139. cards.headline: Programme report — prespecified subgroup analysis (Sethi 2020): revefenacin improved day-85 trough FEV1 versus placebo similarly with and without concomitant LABA/ICS-LABA (placebo-adjusted 139.2 mL and 150.9 mL) — a report OF the phase 3 programme, not a separate trial
cards.summary: Programme report — prespecified subgroup analysis (Sethi 2020): revefenacin improved day-85 trough FEV1 versus placebo similarly with and without concomitant LABA/ICS-LABA (placebo-adjusted 139.2 mL and 150.9 mL) — a report OF the phase 3 programme, not a separate trial
cards.type: Programme report: prespecified subgroup analysis of the phase 3 programme (Studies 0126/0127/0128 — same trials as the cards above, not independent evidence)
cards.people: Patients from the same programme: efficacy data from the two 12-week replicate placebo-controlled trials (Studies 0126/0127) and pooled safety data from those trials plus the 52-week tiotropium-controlled trial (Study 0128), analysed by concomitant long-acting beta-agonist use (the LABA subgroup includes ICS/LABA users).
cards.result: Placebo-adjusted least-squares mean change in day-85 trough FEV1 was 150.9 mL (95% CI 110.3 to 191.6) in the non-LABA subgroup and 139.2 mL (95% CI 82.9 to 195.5) in the LABA subgroup (both P<0.0001 versus placebo); St George's Respiratory Questionnaire changes were −3.3 and −3.4 respectively. Revefenacin was well tolerated, with more adverse events reported in the LABA than the non-LABA subgroup.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup analysis of already-carded trials: it answers 'does background LABA change the effect?' for the same programme and must not be counted as further confirmation. Carded, labelled as a programme report, to complete the single-programme record.

shelves.title: Zileuton in asthma: better lung function and fewer steroid-requiring exacerbations in 1990s trials (6.1% vs 15.6%) — short trials, no outcomes trial, liver monitoring required
shelves.question: In patients with mild-to-moderate chronic asthma, does zileuton versus placebo — or versus theophylline — improve lung function and asthma control?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Agonists · Adult · Analysis of Variance · Asthma · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Monitoring · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Glucocorticoids · Humans · Hydroxyurea · Lipoxygenase Inhibitors · Liver · Liver Function Tests · Male · Peak Expiratory Flow Rate · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Four 1990s trials in mild-to-moderate asthma show zileuton improving lung function versus placebo (FEV1 +0.32 L versus +0.05 L over 4 weeks at 2.4 g/day) and, in the largest (401 patients, 13 weeks), fewer corticosteroid-requiring exacerbations (6.1% versus 15.6% — absolute difference 9.5 percentage points); against theophylline it appeared comparable, and responders maintained control on reduced dosing frequency. All trials are short (≤3 months of randomised treatment, one 6-month responder study), with lung-function and symptom endpoints — no exacerbation-outcome trial exists. Hepatotoxicity monitoring is part of the drug's real-world use and is on this shelf's face: liver-enzyme elevations over three times normal occurred on zileuton 600 mg four times daily in the largest trial and reversed on withdrawal. Original dosing was four times daily (later extended-release), stated as the publications give it.

cards.headline: Zileuton Clinical Trial Group RCT (Israel 1996): over 3 months, corticosteroid-requiring exacerbations occurred in 6.1% on zileuton 600 mg four times daily versus 15.6% on placebo, and FEV1 improved more with zileuton
cards.summary: Zileuton Clinical Trial Group RCT (Israel 1996): over 3 months, corticosteroid-requiring exacerbations occurred in 6.1% on zileuton 600 mg four times daily versus 15.6% on placebo, and FEV1 improved more with zileuton
cards.type: Randomised double-blind parallel-group trial (Zileuton Clinical Trial Group), zileuton 400/600 mg four times daily vs placebo, 13 weeks
cards.people: 401 patients with mild-to-moderate asthma (FEV1 40–80% predicted) whose only treatment was inhaled beta-agonists, randomised after a 10-day placebo lead-in to zileuton 600 mg, zileuton 400 mg or placebo, each four times daily, for 13 weeks (132 patients in the 600 mg group and 135 on placebo in the figures reported).
cards.result: Only 8 (6.1%) of 132 patients on zileuton 600 mg four times daily required corticosteroid treatment for an exacerbation versus 21 (15.6%) of 135 on placebo (P=0.02) — an absolute difference of 9.5 percentage points; the report expresses the placebo-versus-zileuton contrast as a relative risk of 2.6. At expected peak drug concentration, average FEV1 improved 15.7% with zileuton 600 mg versus 7.7% with placebo (P=0.006) — percentage improvements in lung function, printed beside the absolute exacerbation rates. Quality of life improved significantly in the 600 mg group and not on placebo (P=0.007 overall). Liver-function-test elevations over three times normal, all reversing on drug withdrawal, occurred in 5 patients on zileuton 600 mg (P=0.03 versus placebo), 3 on 400 mg (P=0.12) and none on placebo.
cards.watchOut: A 1990s trial in patients using only inhaled beta-agonists — a treatment context far from modern inhaled-corticosteroid-based care — and the liver-enzyme signal (5 patients with elevations over three times normal on the 600 mg dose) is why hepatotoxicity monitoring belongs on this shelf's face.
cards.source: Israel E et al. Effect of treatment with zileuton, a 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor, in patients with asthma. A randomized controlled trial. Zileuton Clinical Trial Group. JAMA. 1996. PMID: 8598621. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: 5-lipoxygenase inhibition RCT (Israel 1993): zileuton 2.4 g/day increased FEV1 by 0.32 L versus 0.05 L on placebo over 4 weeks, with fewer symptoms and less beta-agonist use
cards.summary: 5-lipoxygenase inhibition RCT (Israel 1993): zileuton 2.4 g/day increased FEV1 by 0.32 L versus 0.05 L on placebo over 4 weeks, with fewer symptoms and less beta-agonist use
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, zileuton 1.6/2.4 g/day vs placebo, 4 weeks
cards.people: 139 persons with mild-to-moderate asthma (FEV1 40–75% predicted) not treated with inhaled or oral steroids, randomised double-blind to zileuton 2.4 g/day, zileuton 1.6 g/day or placebo for 4 weeks.
cards.result: Zileuton produced a 0.35 L increase in FEV1 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.45) within 1 hour of administration (P<0.001 versus placebo), a 14.6% increase from baseline. After 4 weeks, the 2.4 g/day group's FEV1 had increased by 0.32 L (95% CI 0.16 to 0.48), a 13.4% increase, versus 0.05 L (95% CI −0.10 to 0.20) on placebo (P=0.02); symptoms and beta-agonist use also fell most in the 2.4 g/day group. Urinary leukotriene E4 fell by 39.2 pg/mg creatinine (2.4 g/day) and 26.5 pg/mg (1.6 g/day) versus a slight rise on placebo. No difference in adverse-event numbers was noted between groups.
cards.watchOut: A short (4-week), small mechanistic-efficacy trial from 1993: it establishes that 5-lipoxygenase inhibition changes airway function, not that zileuton improves long-term asthma outcomes.
cards.source: Israel E et al. The effect of inhibition of 5-lipoxygenase by zileuton in mild-to-moderate asthma. Annals of internal medicine. 1993. PMID: 8239223. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Head-to-head RCT versus theophylline (Schwartz 1998): zileuton appeared as effective as slowly absorbed theophylline over 13 weeks in 377 randomised patients, with comparable adverse events
cards.summary: Head-to-head RCT versus theophylline (Schwartz 1998): zileuton appeared as effective as slowly absorbed theophylline over 13 weeks in 377 randomised patients, with comparable adverse events
cards.type: Randomised double-blind active-comparator trial, zileuton 400/600 mg four times daily vs titrated theophylline, 13 weeks
cards.people: 471 eligible patients with chronic asthma (FEV1 40–80% predicted, documented reversibility, age 18–60) at 38 centres, of whom 377 were randomised to 13 weeks of titrated slowly absorbed theophylline (trough 8–15 μg/mL) or zileuton 400 mg or 600 mg four times daily, after washout and a 1-week placebo lead-in; 313 completed.
cards.result: On first-dose administration all groups improved FEV1 by 11–13% within 30 minutes. Zileuton 400 mg gave significantly greater improvement than theophylline at several time points; the range of long-term maximum FEV1 improvement was 30–34% across groups (P=0.40 for zileuton 600 mg and P=0.90 for zileuton 400 mg versus theophylline). The theophylline group initially improved more in symptom scores, beta-agonist use and peak flow, but at maximal effect there was no significant difference; all groups improved quality of life significantly, with no overall difference between zileuton doses and comparable adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is theophylline — itself a marginal, monitoring-heavy asthma drug — so 'as effective as theophylline' is a low bar, and 64 of 377 randomised patients did not complete. There is no comparison with inhaled corticosteroids, the modern standard.
cards.source: Schwartz HJ et al. A randomized controlled trial comparing zileuton with theophylline in moderate asthma. The Zileuton Study Group. Archives of internal medicine. 1998. PMID: 9448552. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Reduced-dosing-frequency RCT (DuBuske 1997): patients who had responded to zileuton 600 mg four times daily maintained lung function and symptom control when stepped down to three-times- then twice-daily dosing over 6 months
cards.summary: Reduced-dosing-frequency RCT (DuBuske 1997): patients who had responded to zileuton 600 mg four times daily maintained lung function and symptom control when stepped down to three-times- then twice-daily dosing over 6 months
cards.type: Randomised double-blind dose-frequency reduction trial in prior responders (after an open-label run-in), 6 months total
cards.people: 278 patients with chronic asthma aged 16–70 (FEV1 35–75% predicted, reversible disease) at 25 US centres: an 8-week open-label period on zileuton 600 mg four times daily, then responders were randomised double-blind to zileuton 600 or 800 mg three times daily for 8 weeks and re-randomised to 600 or 800 mg twice daily for a further 8 weeks.
cards.result: Patients who had improved on zileuton 600 mg four times daily showed minimal decreases in FEV1 and comparable peak flow, symptom control, beta-agonist use and systemic-corticosteroid rescue when treated at lower total doses and/or less frequent dosing. The authors concluded responders may be able to reduce dose and/or frequency while maintaining symptom control.
cards.watchOut: A responder-enriched design: only patients who had already improved on four-times-daily zileuton entered the randomised phase, so this answers a maintenance-of-response question in selected patients — it is not a fourth independent efficacy trial in unselected asthma. The original dosing was four times daily (a later extended-release form exists); dosing is stated as the publications give it.
cards.source: DuBuske LM et al. Randomized trial of zileuton in patients with moderate asthma: effect of reduced dosing frequency and amounts on pulmonary function and asthma symptoms. Zileuton Study Group. The American journal of managed care. 1997. PMID: 10169531. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: 1990s trials show zileuton improving lung function and, in one trial, fewer steroid-requiring exacerbations versus placebo, and matching theophylline — short trials, surrogate endpoints, no exacerbation-outcome trial, with a liver-enzyme signal
cards.summary: Synthesis: 1990s trials show zileuton improving lung function and, in one trial, fewer steroid-requiring exacerbations versus placebo, and matching theophylline — short trials, surrogate endpoints, no exacerbation-outcome trial, with a liver-enzyme signal
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: All four reports are 1990s trials of at most 3 months' randomised treatment (the dosing-frequency study runs 6 months in prior responders), in mild-to-moderate asthma managed without modern inhaled-corticosteroid-based regimens. Versus placebo, zileuton improved FEV1 (0.32 L versus 0.05 L over 4 weeks at 2.4 g/day; 15.7% versus 7.7% peak improvement in the 3-month trial) and, in the largest trial, reduced corticosteroid-requiring exacerbations (6.1% versus 15.6% over 13 weeks, absolute difference 9.5 percentage points). Against theophylline it looked comparable. No exacerbation-outcome trial exists. Hepatotoxicity is part of the drug's real-world use — liver-enzyme elevations over three times normal occurred on zileuton in the largest trial, reversing on withdrawal — and liver monitoring belongs on the face of any zileuton answer. Original dosing was four times daily (later extended-release); doses are stated as the publications give them.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Zafirlukast in asthma: better symptoms and lung function versus placebo over 13 weeks (symptom-free days 7.0 vs 3.7/month) — 1990s programme, and low-dose fluticasone beat it on bronchial hyper-responsiveness
shelves.question: In patients with mild-to-moderate asthma, does zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily versus placebo improve symptoms and lung function, and how does it compare with low-dose inhaled corticosteroid?
shelves.mesh: Absenteeism · Adult · Anti-Asthmatic Agents · Asthma · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Health Services · Humans · Indoles · Leukotriene Antagonists · Male · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Phenylcarbamates · Sleep Wake Disorders · Sulfonamides · Surveys and Questionnaires · Tosyl Compounds · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Two 13-week placebo-controlled trials in mild-to-moderate asthma showed zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily improving symptoms and lung function: in the 762-patient trial, daytime symptom scores fell 26.5% and FEV1 rose 6.3% versus placebo; in the 146-patient trial, symptom-free days were 7.0 versus 3.7 per month in absolute terms (an 89% relative increase) with 55% fewer health-care contacts in relative terms (18.5 versus 40.7 per 100 per month). Against an inhaled corticosteroid, the only comparison is a small 30-patient, 2-week mechanistic crossover in which low-dose fluticasone improved bronchial hyper-responsiveness more — not an ICS-equivalence verdict. This is a 1990s programme with symptom/lung-function endpoints and no exacerbation trial.

cards.headline: RCT (Suissa 1997): zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily gave 89% more symptom-free days than placebo (7.0 versus 3.7 days per month) and 55% fewer health-care contacts over 13 weeks in 146 patients
cards.summary: RCT (Suissa 1997): zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily gave 89% more symptom-free days than placebo (7.0 versus 3.7 days per month) and 55% fewer health-care contacts over 13 weeks in 146 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind multicentre placebo-controlled trial, zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily vs placebo, 13 weeks
cards.people: 146 patients aged 12 or over with mild-to-moderate asthma (FEV1 at least 55% predicted, demonstrated bronchial hyperresponsiveness, symptomatic in the 7-day run-in) at 28 outpatient clinics: 103 received zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily and 43 placebo twice daily for 13 weeks, all with as-needed inhaled beta-agonists.
cards.result: The zafirlukast group had 89% more days without symptoms (adjusted rates 7.0 versus 3.7 days per month; P=0.03), 89% more days without beta-agonist use (11.3 versus 6.0 days per month; P=0.001) and 98% more days without asthma episodes (10.1 versus 5.1 days per month; P=0.003) — the percentages are relative increases, printed beside the absolute day rates. Health-care contacts were 55% fewer in relative terms (18.5 versus 40.7 per 100 per month; P=0.007) and days absent from work or school 55% fewer in relative terms (15.6 versus 35.0 per 100 per month; P=0.04). Beta-agonist canister use was 17% lower (P=0.17, not significant).
cards.watchOut: A small trial (146 patients, only 43 on placebo) framed around clinical and economic effectiveness in a pre-modern-controller era; its headline percentages are relative and shrink to a few extra symptom-free days per month in absolute terms, as printed on the card.
cards.source: Suissa S et al. Effectiveness of the leukotriene receptor antagonist zafirlukast for mild-to-moderate asthma. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Annals of internal medicine. 1997. PMID: 9027267. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zafirlukast Trialists Group RCT (Fish 1997): zafirlukast decreased daytime symptom scores by 26.5% and beta-agonist use by 22.3% versus placebo, and increased FEV1 by 6.3%, over 13 weeks in 762 patients
cards.summary: Zafirlukast Trialists Group RCT (Fish 1997): zafirlukast decreased daytime symptom scores by 26.5% and beta-agonist use by 22.3% versus placebo, and increased FEV1 by 6.3%, over 13 weeks in 762 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-masked placebo-controlled parallel-group trial, zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily vs placebo, 13 weeks
cards.people: 762 patients aged 12–76 with mild-to-moderate asthma (cumulative daytime symptom score at least 8 over 7 consecutive days before randomisation) randomised to zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily or placebo for 13 weeks, maintained on as-needed beta-agonist therapy.
cards.result: Versus placebo, zafirlukast significantly decreased daytime asthma symptom scores (−26.5%), night-time awakenings (−19.8%), mornings with asthma (−29.0%) and beta-agonist use (−22.3%), and increased morning peak expiratory flow (6.9%) and FEV1 (6.3%) — percentage changes as reported by the trial, on symptom and lung-function endpoints. Changes appeared within 2 days and continued throughout the trial. Zafirlukast was well tolerated; pharyngitis and headache were the commonest adverse events, at similar frequency to placebo, with no clinically significant laboratory, physical-examination or electrocardiographic changes.
cards.watchOut: The programme's largest trial still runs only 13 weeks on symptom and lung-function endpoints in patients on as-needed beta-agonists alone — it does not test exacerbations, and it does not position zafirlukast against inhaled corticosteroids.
cards.source: Fish JE et al. Zafirlukast for symptomatic mild-to-moderate asthma: a 13-week multicenter study. The Zafirlukast Trialists Group. Clinical therapeutics. 1997. PMID: 9377612. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Head-to-head crossover RCT versus low-dose fluticasone (Westbroek 2000): fluticasone propionate 100 μg twice daily improved bronchial hyper-responsiveness more than zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily (difference 0.77 doubling doses of histamine PC20, P=0.037) in 30 patients
cards.summary: Head-to-head crossover RCT versus low-dose fluticasone (Westbroek 2000): fluticasone propionate 100 μg twice daily improved bronchial hyper-responsiveness more than zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily (difference 0.77 doubling doses of histamine PC20, P=0.037) in 30 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind double-dummy crossover trial, zafirlukast vs low-dose inhaled fluticasone, 2 weeks per period — a mechanistic bronchial-hyper-responsiveness comparison
cards.people: 30 patients (9 men, 21 women; mean age 45) with mild-to-moderate asthma (FEV1 over 50% predicted, salbutamol reversibility at least 15%) in a single-centre double-blind double-dummy crossover study: two successive 2-week treatment periods (fluticasone propionate 100 μg twice daily; zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily), each preceded by a 2–4 week single-blind placebo period.
cards.result: After 2 weeks, mean histamine PC20 was 1.61 mg/mL (SD 2.34) on fluticasone and 0.99 mg/mL (SD 1.74) on zafirlukast; adjusting for baseline, the difference favoured fluticasone by 0.77 doubling doses (95% CI 0.05 to 1.50; P=0.037). Morning peak flow was significantly higher on fluticasone in the second treatment week (by 17 L/min; P=0.049). Both treatments were well tolerated, and the authors judged low-dose fluticasone to offer greater clinical benefit.
cards.watchOut: A small (30 patients), 2-week mechanistic trial: it compares the two drugs on bronchial hyper-responsiveness, not on symptoms over time or exacerbations — do not present it as an inhaled-corticosteroid-equivalence verdict, as the commissioning row directs.
cards.source: Westbroek J et al. Effects of 2 weeks of treatment with fluticasone propionate 100 mcg b.d. by comparison with zafirlukast 20 mg b.d. on bronchial hyper-responsiveness in patients with mild to moderate asthma. Respiratory medicine. 2000. PMID: 10714415. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: zafirlukast improved symptoms and lung function versus placebo over 13 weeks in two 1990s trials, and was outperformed by low-dose inhaled fluticasone on bronchial hyper-responsiveness in a small 2-week mechanistic crossover
cards.summary: Synthesis: zafirlukast improved symptoms and lung function versus placebo over 13 weeks in two 1990s trials, and was outperformed by low-dose inhaled fluticasone on bronchial hyper-responsiveness in a small 2-week mechanistic crossover
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The placebo-controlled record is two 13-week 1990s trials in mild-to-moderate asthma on as-needed beta-agonists: the 762-patient Trialists Group trial showed better symptom scores, less beta-agonist use and higher FEV1/peak flow with zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily, and the 146-patient effectiveness trial showed more symptom-free days (7.0 versus 3.7 per month in absolute terms; the 89% figure is the relative increase) and fewer health-care contacts. The only inhaled-corticosteroid comparison is a 30-patient, 2-week crossover on bronchial hyper-responsiveness, in which low-dose fluticasone did better (0.77 doubling doses) — a mechanistic result, not an equivalence verdict. Endpoints throughout are symptoms and lung function; no exacerbation-outcome trial exists. This is one of three separate leukotriene-pathway shelves (zileuton, zafirlukast, montelukast), cross-pointed, not merged.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Montelukast in chronic asthma (adolescents/adults): better than placebo (FEV1 +7.4% vs +0.7%), less than inhaled beclomethasone (+13.1%); largest effect in aspirin-intolerant asthma
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with chronic asthma, does once-daily oral montelukast versus placebo — alone, versus inhaled beclomethasone, or added to inhaled corticosteroid — improve lung function and asthma control, including in aspirin-intolerant asthma?
shelves.mesh: Acetates · Administration, Inhalation · Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analysis of Variance · Anti-Asthmatic Agents · Asthma · Beclomethasone · Blood Cell Count · Cyclopropanes · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Eosinophils · Female · Humans · Leukotriene Antagonists · Male · Middle Aged · Peak Expiratory Flow Rate · Placebos · Quality of Life · Quinolines · Sulfides
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). In adolescents and adults with chronic asthma, once-daily oral montelukast 10 mg was better than placebo on lung function and symptoms in a 895-patient phase 3 trial (FEV1 +7.4% vs +0.7% over 12 weeks), but inhaled beclomethasone was better still (+13.1%, P<0.01 versus montelukast). Added to inhaled beclomethasone in 642 incompletely controlled patients, montelukast gave significant additional benefit on FEV1, daytime symptoms and nocturnal awakenings. In aspirin-intolerant asthma (80 patients, most already on moderate-to-high-dose glucocorticosteroids) the effect was large: a 10.2% between-group FEV1 difference and 54% fewer exacerbations as reported. Limits printed on the cards: the pivotal trials are from 1999, before modern ICS/LABA standard care, and current US labelling for montelukast carries a boxed warning about serious neuropsychiatric events, which belongs in any prescribing decision. This shelf is confined to chronic asthma in adolescents and adults — preschool episodic wheeze (pack #1426) and allergic rhinitis (pack #2666) stay in their own homes, and acute-exacerbation montelukast is a different question, not folded in.

cards.headline: Malmstrom 1999 (Montelukast/Beclomethasone Study Group): montelukast beat placebo on FEV1 (+7.4% vs +0.7%) but inhaled beclomethasone beat montelukast (+13.1%) over 12 weeks in 895 patients
cards.summary: Malmstrom 1999 (Montelukast/Beclomethasone Study Group): montelukast beat placebo on FEV1 (+7.4% vs +0.7%) but inhaled beclomethasone beat montelukast (+13.1%) over 12 weeks in 895 patients
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind double-dummy placebo-controlled trial, montelukast vs inhaled beclomethasone vs placebo
cards.people: 895 patients aged 15 to 85 years with chronic asthma and FEV1 50% to 85% of predicted, in a randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, placebo-controlled parallel-group 12-week study at 36 sites worldwide: montelukast 10 mg once daily at bedtime, inhaled beclomethasone 200 µg twice daily via spacer, or placebo. Primary endpoints: daytime asthma symptom score and FEV1.
cards.result: Average percentage change in FEV1 over 12 weeks: 13.1% with beclomethasone, 7.4% with montelukast and 0.7% with placebo (P<0.001 for each active treatment versus placebo; P<0.01 for beclomethasone versus montelukast). Daytime symptom score change: −0.62 beclomethasone, −0.41 montelukast, −0.17 placebo, with the same significance pattern. Both active treatments improved peak flow and quality of life, reduced nocturnal awakenings and asthma attacks, and decreased days with exacerbations versus placebo; montelukast had a faster onset and greater initial effect, while beclomethasone had the larger mean benefit. Tolerability of both agents was similar to placebo over 12 weeks.
cards.watchOut: 1999 trial, before modern ICS/LABA standard care: it positions montelukast against low-dose inhaled beclomethasone and placebo, not against today's controller combinations. Endpoints are lung function and symptoms over 12 weeks.
cards.source: Malmstrom K et al. Oral montelukast, inhaled beclomethasone, and placebo for chronic asthma. A randomized, controlled trial. Montelukast/Beclomethasone Study Group. Annals of internal medicine. 1999. PMID: 10075616. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Laviolette 1999 (additivity trial): adding montelukast to inhaled beclomethasone significantly improved FEV1, daytime symptoms and nocturnal awakenings in 642 incompletely controlled patients
cards.summary: Laviolette 1999 (additivity trial): adding montelukast to inhaled beclomethasone significantly improved FEV1, daytime symptoms and nocturnal awakenings in 642 incompletely controlled patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind double-dummy add-on / blinded-withdrawal trial, montelukast added to inhaled beclomethasone
cards.people: 642 patients with chronic asthma (FEV1 50 to 85% of predicted, predefined symptom level) incompletely controlled on inhaled beclomethasone 200 µg twice daily during a 4-week run-in, randomised double-blind double-dummy to: montelukast 10 mg plus continuing beclomethasone; placebo tablet plus continuing beclomethasone; montelukast plus inhaled placebo (blinded beclomethasone withdrawal); or placebo tablet plus inhaled placebo (blinded withdrawal).
cards.result: Montelukast provided significant (P<0.05) additional clinical benefit on top of inhaled beclomethasone, improving FEV1, daytime asthma symptom scores and nocturnal awakenings (the fetched abstract reports significance without printing the effect sizes). Blinded removal of beclomethasone on placebo tablets worsened asthma control, confirming the steroid was contributing; blinded removal on montelukast worsened control less, but not to the placebo level — montelukast did not fully substitute for the inhaled steroid. Clinical and laboratory adverse experiences were generally similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: The abstract gives P values but no effect sizes, so the size of the add-on benefit cannot be quantified from this record — the claim carded is direction and significance only. Also a 1999 beclomethasone-era trial.
cards.source: Laviolette M et al. Montelukast added to inhaled beclomethasone in treatment of asthma. Montelukast/Beclomethasone Additivity Group. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 1999. PMID: 10588598. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dahlén 2002: in aspirin-intolerant asthma, adding montelukast gave a 10.2% FEV1 advantage and 28.0 L morning peak-flow advantage over placebo in 4 weeks (80 patients)
cards.summary: Dahlén 2002: in aspirin-intolerant asthma, adding montelukast gave a 10.2% FEV1 advantage and 28.0 L morning peak-flow advantage over placebo in 4 weeks (80 patients)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in aspirin-intolerant asthma, montelukast add-on vs placebo
cards.people: 80 aspirin-intolerant patients with asthma randomised double-blind to oral montelukast 10 mg once daily at bedtime or placebo for 4 weeks; 90% were already treated with moderate-to-high doses of glucocorticosteroids. Pulmonary function was measured weekly in clinic (FEV1) and daily at home (morning and evening peak expiratory flow).
cards.result: From equal baselines, the mean between-group difference over the 4-week treatment period was 10.2% for FEV1 and 28.0 L for morning peak flow (P<0.001 for both), favouring montelukast; the placebo group showed no change. The montelukast group used 27% less rescue bronchodilator (P<0.05), had 1.3 more nights of sleep per week, and had 54% fewer asthma exacerbations as reported (P<0.05; absolute exacerbation counts are not printed in the record), with improved asthma-specific quality of life (P<0.05). Response did not correlate with baseline urinary leukotriene E4.
cards.watchOut: A specific, leukotriene-driven phenotype and only 80 patients over 4 weeks — the large effect here should not be read onto unselected chronic asthma, where the pivotal trial showed a smaller benefit than inhaled steroid.
cards.source: Dahlén SE et al. Improvement of aspirin-intolerant asthma by montelukast, a leukotriene antagonist: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2002. PMID: 11779723. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: montelukast works versus placebo in chronic asthma, is outperformed by inhaled beclomethasone head-to-head, adds benefit on top of inhaled steroid, and shows its largest effect in aspirin-intolerant asthma
cards.summary: Synthesis: montelukast works versus placebo in chronic asthma, is outperformed by inhaled beclomethasone head-to-head, adds benefit on top of inhaled steroid, and shows its largest effect in aspirin-intolerant asthma
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (895, 642 and 80 patients).
cards.result: Across the three carded trials the direction is consistent: montelukast 10 mg daily improves FEV1 and symptoms versus placebo, adds significant benefit to inhaled beclomethasone in incompletely controlled patients, and is clearly inferior on average to inhaled beclomethasone as monotherapy in the one head-to-head trial. The aspirin-intolerant trial is a phenotype-specific limb, not the general estimate. No carded trial tests exacerbation or mortality outcomes over modern ICS/LABA care, and the current neuropsychiatric boxed warning is part of the real-world answer.

shelves.title: Levalbuterol vs racemic albuterol in asthma: SPLIT — modest chronic bronchodilator edge, no advantage in acute asthma (meta-analysis of 1,625) and one acute trial favouring racemic albuterol
shelves.question: In children and adults with asthma — chronic use and acute exacerbations — does levalbuterol (the (R)-enantiomer) versus racemic albuterol improve bronchodilation and reduce hospitalisation or adverse effects?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Albuterol · Asthma · Bronchodilator Agents · Child · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Risk Assessment · Stereoisomerism
shelves.balance: SPLIT. The limbs point different ways and are kept separate. Chronic nebulised dosing (Nelson 1998, 362 patients): levalbuterol gave a larger first-dose peak FEV1 response than racemic albuterol (combined groups 0.92 vs 0.82 L, P=0.03), with the week-4 difference similar but not significant, and levalbuterol 0.63 mg matching racemic albuterol 2.5 mg with fewer beta-adrenergic side effects. Paediatric MDI (173 children): levalbuterol significantly beat placebo on peak FEV1 change (25.6% vs 16.8%) while racemic albuterol's 21.8% did not reach significance versus placebo — not a demonstrated head-to-head superiority. Acute asthma is the opposite limb: a continuous-nebulisation ED trial (99 children) found racemic albuterol SUPERIOR on FEV1 and asthma score, and a meta-analysis of 7 acute-asthma trials (1,625 participants) found no significant efficacy or safety difference and concluded levalbuterol should not be used over albuterol for acute asthma. No hospitalisation claim is pooled across these limbs — the carded records do not support one. Product naming under the clarification exception: levalbuterol is the single-(R)-enantiomer product (marketed as Xopenex), named as the publications name it.

cards.headline: Nelson 1998: chronic nebulised levalbuterol gave a larger first-dose peak FEV1 response than racemic albuterol (0.92 vs 0.82 L, P=0.03); the week-4 difference was not significant (362 patients)
cards.summary: Nelson 1998: chronic nebulised levalbuterol gave a larger first-dose peak FEV1 response than racemic albuterol (0.92 vs 0.82 L, P=0.03); the week-4 difference was not significant (362 patients)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind parallel-group trial, nebulised levalbuterol vs racemic albuterol vs placebo, chronic dosing
cards.people: 362 patients aged 12 years or older with moderate-to-severe asthma in a randomised double-blind parallel-group trial of nebulised levalbuterol 0.63 mg or 1.25 mg, equivalent amounts of levalbuterol given as racemic albuterol, or placebo, three times daily for 28 days. Primary endpoint: peak change in FEV1 after 4 weeks.
cards.result: Peak FEV1 response to the first dose was significantly greater in the combined levalbuterol group than the combined racemic albuterol group (0.92 vs 0.82 L; P=0.03); after 4 weeks the results were similar but not significant (0.84 vs 0.74 L). Levalbuterol 0.63 mg matched racemic albuterol 2.5 mg, levalbuterol 1.25 mg gave the greatest increase (especially in severe asthma), and racemic albuterol 1.25 mg was weakest, particularly after chronic dosing. Beta-adrenergic side effects with levalbuterol 0.63 mg were reduced relative to levalbuterol 1.25 mg or racemic albuterol 2.5 mg. All active treatments were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A bronchodilation trial over 28 days, not an exacerbation or hospitalisation trial; the significant difference is the first-dose response, and the prespecified week-4 primary comparison did not reach significance.
cards.source: Nelson HS et al. Improved bronchodilation with levalbuterol compared with racemic albuterol in patients with asthma. The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology. 1998. PMID: 9847435. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Berger 2006 (paediatric MDI): levalbuterol significantly beat placebo on peak FEV1 change (25.6% vs 16.8%, P<0.001); racemic albuterol (21.8%) did not reach significance versus placebo — 173 children aged 4–11
cards.summary: Berger 2006 (paediatric MDI): levalbuterol significantly beat placebo on peak FEV1 change (25.6% vs 16.8%, P<0.001); racemic albuterol (21.8%) did not reach significance versus placebo — 173 children aged 4–11
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo- and active-controlled trial, levalbuterol MDI vs racemic albuterol MDI vs placebo in children
cards.people: 173 children aged 4–11 years with asthma in a multicentre randomised double-blind 28-day trial of four-times-daily levalbuterol MDI 90 µg, racemic albuterol MDI 180 µg, or placebo (2:1:1). Primary endpoint: double-blind average peak percent change in FEV1 from visit pre-dose, primary comparison against placebo.
cards.result: Least-square mean peak percent change in FEV1: levalbuterol 25.6% ± 1.3% (P<0.001 versus placebo), racemic albuterol 21.8% ± 1.8% (not significant versus placebo), placebo 16.8% ± 1.9%. No levalbuterol-treated patient had a peak FEV1 change under 10%, versus 15.8% on racemic albuterol and 30.3% on placebo. Adverse events: 43.4% levalbuterol, 56.4% racemic albuterol, 51.4% placebo; asthma attacks were similar (10.5%, 12.8%, 14.3%); both active treatments reduced rescue medication use versus placebo (P<0.01).
cards.watchOut: The powered comparison is against placebo, not head-to-head: 'levalbuterol significant, racemic not significant' versus placebo is not itself proof levalbuterol beats racemic albuterol in children. Spirometry endpoints over 28 days only.

cards.headline: Wilkinson 2011 (acute continuous nebulisation, ED): racemic albuterol was SUPERIOR to levalbuterol on FEV1 (P=0.043) and asthma score (P=0.01) after 1 hour — 99 children with acute exacerbations
cards.summary: Wilkinson 2011 (acute continuous nebulisation, ED): racemic albuterol was SUPERIOR to levalbuterol on FEV1 (P=0.043) and asthma score (P=0.01) after 1 hour — 99 children with acute exacerbations
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial, continuous nebulised racemic albuterol vs levalbuterol in acute paediatric asthma
cards.people: 99 children aged 6–17 years presenting to an emergency department with an acute asthma exacerbation and initial FEV1 under 70% predicted, randomised double-blind to continuous nebulisation of racemic albuterol 7.5 mg (44 patients) or levalbuterol 3.75 mg (55 patients) over 1 hour, plus standard asthma therapies, with a second hour of the same drug if needed.
cards.result: The racemic albuterol group had a greater improvement in FEV1 (P=0.043) and in asthma scores (P=0.01) after 1 hour than the levalbuterol group; the asthma-score advantage was maintained after the second hour (P=0.008) but the FEV1 difference was not (P=0.57). There were no differences between groups in heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, or rates of admission. The authors conclude that at the doses used, racemic albuterol appears superior to levalbuterol on FEV1 and asthma score, with no difference in admission rates or side-effect profile.
cards.watchOut: The racemic group had a higher baseline asthma score, and the doses compared (7.5 mg racemic vs 3.75 mg levalbuterol over 1 hour) are the trial's chosen equipotent pairing — a different dose pairing could read differently. Single ED trial in children.

cards.headline: Jat 2013 (meta-analysis, acute asthma): 7 trials, 1,625 participants — no significant difference between levalbuterol and albuterol on respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, FEV1 change or asthma score; authors advise against preferring levalbuterol
cards.summary: Jat 2013 (meta-analysis, acute asthma): 7 trials, 1,625 participants — no significant difference between levalbuterol and albuterol on respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, FEV1 change or asthma score; authors advise against preferring levalbuterol
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials in acute asthma
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials comparing levalbuterol versus albuterol for acute asthma in all age groups (PubMed and Cochrane databases); 7 trials including 1,625 participants met eligibility.
cards.result: No significant between-group differences: respiratory rate mean difference 0.35 (95% CI −0.81 to 1.51), oxygen saturation −0.29 (95% CI −0.68 to 0.10), percentage change in FEV1 −28.3 (95% CI −59.95 to 3.33) and clinical asthma score −1.01 (95% CI −5.30 to 3.28). Side effects did not differ significantly. The authors conclude levalbuterol was not superior to albuterol for efficacy or safety in acute asthma and suggest levalbuterol should not be used over albuterol for acute asthma. Data were unavailable for two probably eligible trials, and some calculated values and assumptions were used.
cards.watchOut: Confined to acute asthma — it does not pool the chronic-dosing bronchodilation trials carded above, and must not be read as a verdict on them. Two probably eligible trials contributed no data.
cards.source: Jat KR et al. Levalbuterol versus albuterol for acute asthma: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Pulmonary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2013. PMID: 23207739. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT by setting — a modest chronic-dosing bronchodilator edge for levalbuterol in two trials, and no advantage (one trial favouring racemic albuterol) in acute asthma
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT by setting — a modest chronic-dosing bronchodilator edge for levalbuterol in two trials, and no advantage (one trial favouring racemic albuterol) in acute asthma
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (362 adults/adolescents, 173 children, 99 acute paediatric patients, and a 1,625-participant acute-asthma meta-analysis).
cards.result: Chronic use: levalbuterol produced somewhat greater peak bronchodilation than racemic albuterol in the 1998 nebulised trial (significant on first dose only) and beat placebo where racemic albuterol did not reach significance in the paediatric MDI trial. Acute use: the one continuous-nebulisation trial favoured racemic albuterol, and the acute-asthma meta-analysis found no significant difference on any pooled outcome. Admission rates did not differ in the acute trial, and no carded record supports a hospitalisation advantage for either drug.

shelves.title: Zanamivir for influenza treatment: symptoms relieved a median 1.5 days earlier (MIST, 455 patients) and 2.5 days earlier in high-risk patients — pre-2000 trial base
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with influenza A or B, does inhaled zanamivir (10 mg twice daily for 5 days) versus placebo shorten illness and reduce complications, including in high-risk patients?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adolescent · Adult · Antiviral Agents · Double-Blind Method · Enzyme Inhibitors · Guanidines · Humans · Influenza A virus · Influenza B virus · Influenza, Human · Neuraminidase · Pyrans · Safety · Sialic Acids · Treatment Outcome · Zanamivir
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Two pre-2000 placebo-controlled trials in largely healthy adolescents and adults found inhaled zanamivir 10 mg twice daily for 5 days shortened influenza illness by about 1 to 1.5 days: GG167 (417 randomised, 262 with confirmed influenza) — median time to alleviation of all major symptoms 4 versus 5 days, and 4 versus 7 days in patients febrile at entry or treated within 30 hours; MIST (455 patients) — symptoms relieved a median 1.5 days earlier (intention-to-treat), 2 days earlier if febrile at entry, and 2.5 days earlier in the high-risk subgroup, with fewer complications in high-risk patients (P=0.004). The high-risk evidence beyond that subgroup is a retrospective pooled analysis (2,751 recruited across the programme, 321 high-risk, 154 on zanamivir): 2.5 days' benefit, return to normal activities 3.0 days earlier, and a 43% relative reduction in complications requiring antibiotics (absolute incidences are not printed in that record). Cross-point: the Cochrane neuraminidase-inhibitor review (PMID 24718923) is already carded inside live shelf #583 (the oseltamivir shelf) and is deliberately NOT re-carded here. This shelf is treatment only; zanamivir prophylaxis is a separate question and is not folded in.

cards.headline: Hayden 1997 (GG167): inhaled zanamivir shortened confirmed influenza by 1 day overall (4 vs 5 days to alleviation of all major symptoms), and by 3 days in febrile or early-treated patients (4 vs 7 days)
cards.summary: Hayden 1997 (GG167): inhaled zanamivir shortened confirmed influenza by 1 day overall (4 vs 5 days to alleviation of all major symptoms), and by 3 days in febrile or early-treated patients (4 vs 7 days)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials (North American and European studies), inhaled/intranasal zanamivir vs placebo
cards.people: 417 adults with influenza-like illness of 48 hours' duration or less, randomised across 38 North American and 32 European centres (1994–1995 season) to zanamivir 6.4 mg intranasal plus 10 mg inhaled, zanamivir 10 mg inhaled plus placebo spray, or placebo by both routes, self-administered twice daily for 5 days; 262 patients (63%) had confirmed influenza-virus infection.
cards.result: Among confirmed-influenza patients, median time to alleviation of all major symptoms was 4 days in both zanamivir groups versus 5 days on placebo (88 patients inhaled+intranasal, P=0.02; 85 inhaled alone, P=0.05; 89 placebo). Among infected patients febrile at enrolment or starting treatment within 30 hours of symptom onset, median time was 4 days in both zanamivir groups versus 7 days on placebo (P≤0.01). Viral titres in nasal washings were significantly lower with inhaled+intranasal zanamivir than placebo. Topically administered zanamivir was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The headline benefit is in the 262 confirmed-influenza patients, not all 417 randomised with influenza-like illness; one zanamivir arm also used an intranasal formulation that is not the marketed inhaled product. A 1994–95-season trial in largely healthy adults.
cards.source: Hayden FG et al. Efficacy and safety of the neuraminidase inhibitor zanamivir in the treatment of influenzavirus infections. GG167 Influenza Study Group. cards.summary: MIST 1998: zanamivir relieved symptoms a median 1.5 days earlier overall and 2.5 days earlier in high-risk patients, with fewer complications in high-risk patients (P=0.004) — 455 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (MIST), inhaled zanamivir vs placebo
cards.people: 455 patients aged 12 years and older with influenza-like symptoms of 36 hours' duration or less in Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, randomised to inhaled zanamivir 10 mg (227) or placebo (228) twice daily for 5 days, with diary-card symptom recording. Analyses: intention-to-treat, influenza-positive, and high-risk populations.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, zanamavir relieved influenza symptoms a median of 1.5 days earlier in the intention-to-treat population (P=0.011) and the influenza-positive population (P=0.004), and 2 days earlier in patients febrile at entry. In high-risk patients, symptoms were alleviated a median of 2.5 days earlier (P=0.048), fewer had complications (P=0.004), and fewer used complication-associated antibiotics (P=0.025). Adverse event profiles were similar for zanamivir and placebo. The authors note the high-risk complication findings need confirmation because the number of high-risk patients was limited.
cards.watchOut: The byline in the fetched record is the MIST Study Group (no individual first author is listed in the record). The complication benefit rests on the small high-risk subgroup and is flagged by the authors themselves as needing confirmation.
