cards.headline: Cochrane 2019 (Altmann): across 10 placebo-controlled studies (993 participants), fibrinolysis showed no mortality difference (odds ratio 1.16, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.91) and fewer surgical interventions (odds ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.68, low certainty) — but the surgery benefit disappeared in the low/unclear risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis
cards.summary: Cochrane 2019 (Altmann): across 10 placebo-controlled studies (993 participants), fibrinolysis showed no mortality difference (odds ratio 1.16, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.91) and fewer surgical interventions (odds ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.68, low certainty) — but the surgery benefit disappeared in the low/unclear risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis (updated version), intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy vs placebo or a different fibrinolytic agent
cards.people: Updated Cochrane review of 12 randomised trials in adults with post-pneumonic empyema or complicated parapneumonic effusions (excluding tuberculous effusions, prior surgery or trauma): 10 studies compared a fibrinolytic agent (streptokinase, alteplase or urokinase) versus placebo (993 participants), one compared streptokinase with urokinase (50 participants) and one alteplase with urokinase (99 participants); searches to 28 August 2019. Fibrinolytic-plus-DNase combination therapy was explicitly beyond this review's scope.
cards.result: No evidence of a mortality difference for fibrinolytic versus placebo (odds ratio 1.16, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.91; 8 studies, 867 participants; moderate certainty). Surgical intervention was reduced (odds ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.68; 8 studies, 897 participants; low certainty) and overall treatment failure reduced (odds ratio 0.16, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.58; 7 studies, 769 participants; very low certainty, I²=88%) — but in the sensitivity analysis confined to studies at low or unclear risk of bias, the reductions in surgical referral and treatment failure disappeared. In a moderate-risk population the review translates this to 115 fewer surgical interventions and 19 more deaths (36 fewer to 59 more) per 1,000 people treated. No clear increase in adverse effects was shown, though an increase could not be excluded (odds ratio 1.28, 95% CI 0.36 to 4.57). Head-to-head, streptokinase versus urokinase showed no clear difference in surgery requirement, and alteplase versus urokinase showed more serious adverse events, mainly bleeding, with alteplase (odds ratio 5.61, 95% CI 1.16 to 27.11).
cards.watchOut: This updated version supersedes the 2008 Cochrane card above in coverage and also includes MIST1; its headline pooled benefits carry low to very low certainty, high heterogeneity for treatment failure (I²=88%), and vanish when restricted to low/unclear risk-of-bias trials. DNase combination studies are out of its scope by design.

cards.headline: Synthesis: for fibrinolytic therapy ALONE, the largest trial (MIST1, 454 randomised) is negative on death, surgery and hospital stay, while pooled syntheses find fewer surgical interventions driven by smaller older trials — a benefit that disappears in low-bias sensitivity analysis; no synthesis finds a mortality benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: for fibrinolytic therapy ALONE, the largest trial (MIST1, 454 randomised) is negative on death, surgery and hospital stay, while pooled syntheses find fewer surgical interventions driven by smaller older trials — a benefit that disappears in low-bias sensitivity analysis; no synthesis finds a mortality benefit
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: MIST1 (streptokinase 250,000 IU twice daily for 3 days) found death or surgical drainage in 31% versus 27% (relative risk 1.14, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.54). The 2008 Cochrane review (7 trials, 761 participants) and the 2019 update (10 placebo-controlled studies, 993 participants) both report reduced surgical intervention in pooled analyses and no mortality effect, and both flag the discordance with MIST1; the 2019 low/unclear-bias sensitivity analysis removes the pooled benefits. The two Cochrane versions are one synthesis lineage (2019 updates 2008) and both include MIST1, so this shelf's independent base is MIST1 plus the small older trials inside the syntheses. Intrapleural tPA plus DNase (MIST2) is a different, combination question homed at live #816 — cross-pointed here only, never re-carded on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data, and no MIST2 study is carded on this shelf.

shelves.title: Ciclesonide in chronic asthma: better lung function and control than placebo, and prednisone dose cut 47-63% in severe asthma — over 8-12 weeks only, with no exacerbation trial
shelves.question: In adults (and adolescents) with persistent asthma — including severe oral-steroid-dependent asthma — does once-daily inhaled ciclesonide versus placebo improve lung function and asthma control, and can it replace oral corticosteroids?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for lung function, asthma control and oral-steroid sparing over 8-12 weeks. The Cochrane review (18 trials, 6,343 participants) found ciclesonide improved lung function, symptoms and rescue inhaler use versus placebo at 100-400 µg/day in mild-to-moderate asthma, with no dose-response. Two adult switch-off-steroid trials (n=329 and n=311) showed morning peak flow maintained on ciclesonide while it fell on placebo, and in severe prednisone-dependent asthma (n=141) ciclesonide 640 and 1,280 µg/day cut prednisone dose by 47% and 63% versus a 4% rise on placebo. The limits are printed on the face: all horizons are 8-12 weeks, there is NO exacerbation-outcome or mortality trial, and the Cochrane review could not assess the safety profile from the reported adverse-event data.

cards.headline: Cochrane review (Manning 2008): 18 trials, 20 comparisons, 6,343 participants — ciclesonide improved lung function, symptoms and rescue inhaler use versus placebo at 100-400 µg/day in mild-to-moderate asthma, with no usable data on exacerbations or safety
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Manning 2008): 18 trials, 20 comparisons, 6,343 participants — ciclesonide improved lung function, symptoms and rescue inhaler use versus placebo at 100-400 µg/day in mild-to-moderate asthma, with no usable data on exacerbations or safety
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review, ciclesonide vs placebo in chronic asthma (adults and children)
cards.people: 18 trials reporting 20 study comparisons in adults and children with chronic asthma; 18 group comparisons with data available covered 6,343 participants, of whom 1,692 were children.
cards.result: At doses of 100 µg/day or less up to 400 µg/day in mild-to-moderate asthma, ciclesonide improved lung function, asthma symptoms and rescue inhaler use compared with placebo. Dose-response comparisons (100 vs 200, 100 vs 400 and 400 vs 800 µg/day) showed no significant differences in lung function. The short duration of the included studies meant there was a lack of data on the impact of ciclesonide on asthma exacerbations, and adverse-event data were not available in sufficient detail to assess the safety profile.
cards.watchOut: This review pools adults and children, and this shelf's question is the adult/adolescent one — the paediatric ciclesonide reports are not folded in. Its own conclusion flags the missing exacerbation and safety data.
cards.source: Manning P et al. Ciclesonide versus placebo for chronic asthma in adults and children. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2008. PMID: 18425941. cards.headline: Maintenance RCT (Chapman 2005): after switching from prior inhaled steroid, morning peak flow held on ciclesonide 160 or 640 µg once daily but fell on placebo (P<0.0001); lack of efficacy 30-31% on ciclesonide vs 63% on placebo over 12 weeks
cards.summary: Maintenance RCT (Chapman 2005): after switching from prior inhaled steroid, morning peak flow held on ciclesonide 160 or 640 µg once daily but fell on placebo (P<0.0001); lack of efficacy 30-31% on ciclesonide vs 63% on placebo over 12 weeks
cards.type: 12-week double-blind randomised placebo-controlled maintenance trial, ciclesonide 160/640 µg once daily
cards.people: 329 adults with persistent asthma randomised after a 2-week baseline on their current inhaled corticosteroid to ciclesonide 160 µg (n=107) or 640 µg (n=112) once daily in the morning, or placebo (n=110), for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Morning peak expiratory flow remained stable on either ciclesonide dose but decreased on placebo (P<0.0001 for both doses vs placebo); FEV1 and forced vital capacity decreased significantly on placebo (P<0.005) but were unchanged on ciclesonide. Lack of efficacy was significantly greater on placebo (63%) than on ciclesonide 160 µg (30%) or 640 µg (31%) (both P<0.0001 vs placebo). There were no significant differences between the two ciclesonide doses in efficacy or safety. Serum and 24-hour urine cortisol were unaffected, and there were no cases of oral candidiasis.
cards.watchOut: A withdrawal-style design — patients were switched off their existing inhaled steroid, so part of the placebo group's decline is loss of prior treatment; 12 weeks, with lung function and lack-of-efficacy endpoints, not exacerbations.
cards.source: Chapman KR et al. Maintenance of asthma control by once-daily inhaled ciclesonide in adults with persistent asthma. Allergy. 2005. PMID: 15679718. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Oral-steroid-sparing RCT (Bateman 2006): in severe prednisone-dependent asthma, prednisone dose fell 47% on ciclesonide 640 µg/day and 63% on 1,280 µg/day versus a 4% rise on placebo over 12 weeks
cards.summary: Oral-steroid-sparing RCT (Bateman 2006): in severe prednisone-dependent asthma, prednisone dose fell 47% on ciclesonide 640 µg/day and 63% on 1,280 µg/day versus a 4% rise on placebo over 12 weeks
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind placebo-controlled oral-steroid-sparing trial in severe persistent asthma
cards.people: 141 adult and adolescent patients (aged 12 years or over) with severe, persistent, oral steroid (prednisone)-dependent asthma, randomised to ciclesonide 640 or 1,280 µg/day in divided doses or placebo for 12 weeks, with weekly review against preset criteria for prednisone dose reduction.
cards.result: Prednisone dose was significantly reduced by 47% (640 µg/day) and 63% (1,280 µg/day) versus an increase of 4% on placebo (both P ≤ 0.0003) at week 12. By week 12 prednisone had been discontinued by approximately 30% of patients in the ciclesonide groups versus 11% on placebo (both P ≤ 0.04). FEV1 improved significantly at week 12 on ciclesonide versus placebo (P<0.03). Local and systemic adverse events were comparable between all treatment groups.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks only: steroid sparing over one quarter is not evidence that oral steroids can be stopped long term, and the trial was not powered for exacerbations or adrenal outcomes.
cards.source: Bateman E et al. Ciclesonide reduces the need for oral steroid use in adult patients with severe, persistent asthma. Chest. 2006. PMID: 16685007. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mild-to-moderate asthma RCT (Adachi 2007): morning peak flow was maintained on ciclesonide 100, 200 and 400 µg once daily (+4.23, +3.75 and -0.40 L/min) while it fell -24.95 L/min on placebo over 8 weeks
cards.summary: Mild-to-moderate asthma RCT (Adachi 2007): morning peak flow was maintained on ciclesonide 100, 200 and 400 µg once daily (+4.23, +3.75 and -0.40 L/min) while it fell -24.95 L/min on placebo over 8 weeks
cards.type: 8-week double-blind placebo-controlled trial in mild-to-moderate asthma (Japanese multicentre)
cards.people: 311 adults with mild-to-moderate asthma, after a 4-week baseline on beclomethasone dipropionate 400 µg/day, randomised to once-daily ciclesonide 100, 200 or 400 µg or placebo for 8 weeks without a spacer.
cards.result: Changes in morning peak expiratory flow (least-squares mean) at the end of the study were +4.23 L/min (100 µg), +3.75 L/min (200 µg) and -0.40 L/min (400 µg), each P<0.001 as compared with -24.95 L/min on placebo; in the ciclesonide groups peak flow remained at the baseline-period level. No large differences in safety were observed between the placebo and ciclesonide groups.
cards.watchOut: Like the maintenance trial, this is a switch-off-active-steroid design (all patients came off beclomethasone at randomisation), there is no dose-response across 100-400 µg, and the horizon is 8 weeks.
cards.source: Adachi M et al. Efficacy and safety of once-daily inhaled ciclesonide in adults with mild to moderate asthma: a double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Respirology (Carlton, Vic.). 2007. PMID: 17587424. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ciclesonide beats placebo on lung function and asthma control over 8-12 weeks in mild-to-moderate asthma, maintains control after switching from another inhaled steroid, and halves or better the prednisone dose in severe steroid-dependent asthma — with no trial evidence on exacerbations or long-term safety

cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The Cochrane pool (18 trials, 6,343 participants, adults and children) found better lung function, symptoms and rescue inhaler use than placebo at 100-400 µg/day, no dose-response, and insufficient data on exacerbations or adverse events. The adult primaries agree: morning peak flow held on ciclesonide and fell on placebo in both switch-off-steroid trials (n=329 over 12 weeks; n=311 over 8 weeks), and in severe prednisone-dependent asthma (n=141) prednisone fell 47% and 63% on ciclesonide versus a 4% rise on placebo. Ciclesonide is a prodrug activated in the lung, but this shelf's safety framing rests on the trials' own data — cortisol unaffected and no oral candidiasis in the 12-week maintenance trial, adverse events comparable across arms in the steroid-sparing trial — not on the prodrug rationale.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Pranlukast in asthma: better than placebo and a useful beclomethasone add-on in tiny old trials, but switching off inhaled steroid to pranlukast left fewer patients controlled (72.2% vs 90%)
shelves.question: In patients with mild-to-severe asthma, does oral pranlukast (a cysteinyl-leukotriene receptor antagonist) versus placebo — or added to inhaled beclomethasone, or substituted for low-dose inhaled corticosteroid at step-down — improve lung function and symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Anti-Asthmatic Agents · Asthma · Chromones · Double-Blind Method · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Leukotriene Antagonists · Lung · Male · Middle Aged · Peak Expiratory Flow Rate · Time Factors
shelves.balance: SPLIT — benefit in the placebo and add-on limbs, against the switch in the step-down limb, on a small, old, short base that must be printed with its Ns. Versus placebo over 4 weeks (1997, N not documented in the record) pranlukast improved morning peak flow and trough FEV1 by 210-340 mL. Added to inhaled beclomethasone in two protocols of only 41 and 39 patients, pranlukast 450 mg/day performed like doubling the beclomethasone dose in moderate asthma and helped severe asthma not on oral steroids, but not severe asthma already on prednisolone. In the only step-down trial (n=40), switching well-controlled patients off low-dose inhaled steroid to pranlukast left 72.2% controlled at 6 months versus 90% on reduced-dose inhaled steroid, with FeNO significantly increased. Pranlukast is licensed in Japan and a few other markets, not in the US/UK. No exacerbation or mortality evidence exists.

cards.headline: First European placebo-controlled trial (Barnes 1997): pranlukast 337.5 mg twice daily improved morning home peak flow at all time points over 4 weeks (mean increase 10.8 to 18.6 L/min vs a slight deterioration on placebo) and raised trough FEV1 by 210-340 mL
cards.summary: First European placebo-controlled trial (Barnes 1997): pranlukast 337.5 mg twice daily improved morning home peak flow at all time points over 4 weeks (mean increase 10.8 to 18.6 L/min vs a slight deterioration on placebo) and raised trough FEV1 by 210-340 mL
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial, pranlukast 225/337.5 mg twice daily, 4 weeks (N not documented in the record)
cards.people: Patients with mild-to-moderate asthma in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group multicentre 4-week study of oral pranlukast 225 or 337.5 mg twice daily. The fetched abstract does not state the number randomised — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Morning home peak expiratory flow improved significantly at all time points on pranlukast 337.5 mg twice daily, and at weeks 1 and 2 on 225 mg twice daily, versus placebo; mean morning home peak flow increased by 10.8 to 18.6 L/min (95% CI 0.2 to 29.3 L/min) on pranlukast compared with a slight deterioration on placebo. FEV1 increased within one hour of the first dose and the increase was maintained for eight hours; trough FEV1 increases of 210 to 340 mL (95% CI 60 to 500 mL) were statistically significant for the 225 mg group versus placebo at week 4. Summary symptom and night-time asthma scores improved, and rescue bronchodilator use fell. Pranlukast was well tolerated with no drug-related changes in haematological or biochemical variables.
cards.watchOut: A 4-week trial from 1997 with the participant count not stated in the fetched record: peak-flow and FEV1 endpoints only, no exacerbation or control outcome, and no N on the face of the record to weigh it by.
cards.source: Barnes NC et al. Pranlukast, a novel leukotriene receptor antagonist: results of the first European, placebo controlled, multicentre clinical study in asthma. Thorax. 1997. PMID: 9227718. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Add-on protocols (Tomari 2001): pranlukast 450 mg/day added to inhaled beclomethasone — two small randomised protocols (41 and 39 patients); effective in moderate asthma and in severe asthma not on oral steroids, but not in severe asthma already on prednisolone
cards.summary: Add-on protocols (Tomari 2001): pranlukast 450 mg/day added to inhaled beclomethasone — two small randomised protocols (41 and 39 patients); effective in moderate asthma and in severe asthma not on oral steroids, but not in severe asthma already on prednisolone
cards.type: Two small randomised protocols, pranlukast added to inhaled beclomethasone in moderate/severe asthma (n=41 and n=39)
cards.people: Protocol 1: 41 patients with moderate asthma, divided between beclomethasone dipropionate 1,600 µg/day or 800 µg/day plus pranlukast 450 mg/day after a 2-week observation period. Protocol 2: 39 patients — moderate asthma on beclomethasone 800 µg/day (group I), severe asthma on 1,600 µg/day (group II), and severe asthma on 1,600 µg/day plus prednisolone 5-20 mg (group III) — all additionally treated with pranlukast.
cards.result: Protocol 1: both regimens improved each clinical parameter (morning peak flow, symptom score, beta2-agonist use, daily peak-flow variability), with no significant differences between the two regimens — that is, halving the beclomethasone dose with pranlukast added performed like the full dose. Protocol 2: pranlukast was effective in groups I and II but not in group III (severe asthma already on oral prednisolone), and tended to be more effective when beclomethasone had been introduced within the first year of asthma onset.
cards.watchOut: Very small protocols (39-41 patients each) with no placebo arm in protocol 2 — the add-on comparisons are between dose regimens and severity groups, so these reports support, and cannot carry, this shelf.
cards.source: Tomari S et al. Effects of pranlukast, a cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1 antagonist, combined with inhaled beclomethasone in patients with moderate or severe asthma. Annals of allergy, asthma & immunology : official publication of the American College of Allergy, Asthma, & Immunology. 2001. PMID: 11527250. Registry ID: none in the record. two small randomised protocols, pranlukast added to inhaled beclomethasone in moderate/severe asthma (n=41 and n=39) protocol 1: 41 patients with moderate asthma, divided between beclomethasone dipropionate 1,600 µg/day or 800 µg/day plus pranlukast 450 mg/day after a 2-week observation period. protocol 2: 39 patients — moderate asthma on beclomethasone 800 µg/day (group i), severe asthma on 1,600 µg/day (group ii), and severe asthma on 1,600 µg/day plus prednisolone 5-20 mg (group iii) — all additionally treated with pranlukast. protocol 1: both regimens improved each clinical parameter (morning peak flow, symptom score, beta2-agonist use, daily peak-flow variability), with no significant differences between the two regimens — that is, halving the beclomethasone dose with pranlukast added performed like the full dose. protocol 2: pranlukast was effective in groups i and ii but not in group iii (severe asthma already on oral prednisolone), and tended to be more effective when beclomethasone had been introduced within the first year of asthma onset. very small protocols (39-41 patients each) with no placebo arm in protocol 2 — the add-on comparisons are between dose regimens and severity groups, so these reports support, and cannot carry, this shelf. tomari s et al. effects of pranlukast, a cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1 antagonist, combined with inhaled beclomethasone in patients with moderate or severe asthma. annals of allergy, asthma & immunology : official publication of the american college of allergy, asthma, & immunology. 2001. pmid: 11527250. registry id: none in the record. mesh: administration, inhalation · anti-asthmatic agents · anti-inflammatory agents · asthma · beclomethasone · chromones · drug therapy, combination · humans · leukotriene antagonists · membrane proteins · peak expiratory flow rate · receptors, leukotriene · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Step-down switch RCT (Harada 2016): switching well-controlled patients from low-dose inhaled steroid to pranlukast left fewer patients controlled at 6 months (72.2% vs 90% on reduced-dose inhaled steroid) and raised FeNO, though the difference was not statistically significant
cards.summary: Step-down switch RCT (Harada 2016): switching well-controlled patients from low-dose inhaled steroid to pranlukast left fewer patients controlled at 6 months (72.2% vs 90% on reduced-dose inhaled steroid) and raised FeNO, though the difference was not statistically significant
cards.type: Randomised step-down trial, switch to pranlukast vs inhaled-steroid dose reduction, 6 months (n=40)
cards.people: 40 adults with mild persistent asthma, well controlled for at least 3 months on low-dose inhaled corticosteroid, randomly assigned to inhaled-steroid dose reduction or a switch to pranlukast for 6 months.
cards.result: The percentage of patients with controlled asthma was 72.2% in the pranlukast group and 90% in the inhaled-steroid dose-reduction group; there was no statistically significant difference between the groups in treatment failure, and no significant differences in lung function at the endpoint. FeNO levels were significantly increased in the pranlukast group over the inhaled-steroid group, and 27.8% of the pranlukast group failed to maintain good control. The authors state the study was limited by its small sample size and should be considered preliminary.
cards.watchOut: Only 40 patients and explicitly preliminary: it cannot prove pranlukast step-down is worse, but it is the only direct step-down evidence and it points against the switch, with a rising FeNO signal.
cards.source: Harada S et al. Evaluation of switching low-dose inhaled corticosteroid to pranlukast for step-down therapy in well-controlled patients with mild persistent asthma. shelves.title: Bambuterol in asthma: a full 24 hours of bronchodilation versus placebo in a 487-patient trial — a 1990s oral beta-agonist, never US-licensed, with no outcome evidence
shelves.question: In adults with asthma — including nocturnal asthma and elderly patients — does once-daily oral bambuterol versus placebo improve 24-hour lung function and reduce rescue bronchodilator use?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adrenergic beta-Agonists · Asthma · Bronchodilator Agents · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Peak Expiratory Flow Rate · Spirometry · Terbutaline
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for 24-hour lung function only, in a 1990s pre-LABA-era programme that must not read as a modern treatment option. The one large trial (n=487, 4 weeks) found bambuterol 10 mg once daily raised mean daily morning and evening peak flow by 11 L/min versus placebo throughout the study, and 20 mg improved FEV1 as well. A 29-patient crossover showed 24-hour mean FEV1 of 3.2-3.4 L on bambuterol versus 2.9 L on placebo, with evening dosing best for lung function on awakening. A one-week dose-finding crossover in elderly patients (N not documented in the record) showed dose-related peak-flow improvement and reduced night-time rescue use, with tremor and palpitations mild and dose-related — the systemic beta-agonist harms of an oral drug. No exacerbation, hospitalisation or mortality evidence exists, and bambuterol was never licensed in the US.

cards.headline: One-month multicentre RCT (Persson 1995): bambuterol 10 and 20 mg once daily in the evening gave a significant 24-hour effect — 10 mg raised mean daily morning and evening peak flow by 11 L/min versus placebo throughout the study, and 20 mg improved FEV1 as well (n=487)
cards.summary: One-month multicentre RCT (Persson 1995): bambuterol 10 and 20 mg once daily in the evening gave a significant 24-hour effect — 10 mg raised mean daily morning and evening peak flow by 11 L/min versus placebo throughout the study, and 20 mg improved FEV1 as well (n=487)
cards.type: Double-blind randomised parallel-group placebo-controlled multicentre trial, bambuterol 10/20 mg once daily, 4 weeks
cards.people: 487 patients with asthma (mean age 45 years; mean baseline FEV1 2.05 L, 62% of predicted) randomised after a one-week placebo run-in with oral bronchodilators withdrawn, to placebo, bambuterol 10 mg or bambuterol 20 mg once daily in the evening for 4 weeks.
cards.result: Administration of bambuterol 10 mg resulted in a significant 24-hour effect duration, expressed as an increase in mean daily morning and evening peak expiratory flow (+11 L/min, adjusted means) throughout the study compared with placebo. Bambuterol 20 mg gave a significant 24-hour effect in both FEV1 and morning and evening peak flow compared with placebo. Adverse events during the study were relatively few and mild.
cards.watchOut: One month of treatment in the pre-LABA-inhaler era, with peak-flow and FEV1 endpoints only — no exacerbation, hospitalisation or safety outcome over any longer horizon.
cards.source: Persson G et al. One month treatment with the once daily oral beta 2-agonist bambuterol in asthmatic patients. The European respiratory journal. 1995. PMID: 7744191. cards.headline: Morning-versus-evening crossover RCT (D'Alonzo 1995): 24-hour mean FEV1 was higher on bambuterol 20 mg than placebo whether dosed in the morning (3.2 L) or evening (3.4 L) versus 2.9 L, with the maximum effect at 4 AM and evening dosing best for lung function on awakening (n=29)
cards.summary: Morning-versus-evening crossover RCT (D'Alonzo 1995): 24-hour mean FEV1 was higher on bambuterol 20 mg than placebo whether dosed in the morning (3.2 L) or evening (3.4 L) versus 2.9 L, with the maximum effect at 4 AM and evening dosing best for lung function on awakening (n=29)
cards.type: Double-blind crossover placebo-controlled trial, bambuterol 20 mg morning vs evening dosing, 24-hour spirometry (n=29)
cards.people: 29 diurnally active patients with asthma in a double-blind, crossover, randomised, placebo-controlled study of bambuterol 20 mg once daily given at 7 AM versus 10 PM, with 39-hour inpatient assessments and a 7-day washout between treatments.
cards.result: Mean 24-hour plasma terbutaline concentration was comparable for morning and evening dosing (13.2 vs 14.0 nmol/L). The 24-hour mean FEV1 was greater (P<0.001) on bambuterol (morning 3.2 L; evening 3.4 L) than placebo (2.9 L), as were FVC, FEF25-75% and peak flow, with the maximum effect at 4 AM independent of medication time. Evening dosing gave the greatest 7 AM (awakening) FEV1, FEF25-75 and peak flow (P<0.03). Improvement in FEV1 at the end of the 24-hour dosing interval versus placebo was 0.34 L (13.5%) with evening dosing and 0.35 L (15.9%) with morning dosing. Side effects were greater on bambuterol than placebo, but not significantly so.
cards.watchOut: Only 29 patients in an inpatient physiological crossover — it answers a dosing-time and 24-hour-duration question, not whether bambuterol improves asthma outcomes.
cards.source: D'Alonzo GE et al. Bambuterol in the treatment of asthma. A placebo-controlled comparison of once-daily morning vs evening administration. Chest. 1995. PMID: 7842769. cards.headline: Elderly dose-finding crossover (Sitar 1993): peak flow rose with dose on bambuterol 10 and 20 mg once daily in patients aged 64-82, night-time rescue inhaler use fell, and tremor and palpitations were mild and dose-related (N not documented in the record)
cards.summary: Elderly dose-finding crossover (Sitar 1993): peak flow rose with dose on bambuterol 10 and 20 mg once daily in patients aged 64-82, night-time rescue inhaler use fell, and tremor and palpitations were mild and dose-related (N not documented in the record)
cards.type: Randomised crossover double-blind placebo-controlled dose-finding study in elderly asthma, one week per dose (N not documented in the record)
cards.people: Elderly patients with asthma aged 64 to 82 years in a randomised, crossover, double-blind study receiving placebo and bambuterol 5 mg, 10 mg and 20 mg tablets once daily for a week at each dose. The fetched abstract does not state the number of patients — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Plasma concentration of the active metabolite terbutaline increased linearly with bambuterol dose (P<0.001). Peak expiratory flow increased with dose in the morning (P<0.001 for the 10 mg and 20 mg doses) and afternoon, and differed from placebo for the 10 mg/day and 20 mg/day regimens. Supplemental inhaled beta2-agonist use during the night was reduced on 10 mg (P<0.05) and 20 mg (P<0.01) versus placebo. No significant effects on blood pressure or pulse were shown. Tremor and palpitations were mild and related to the dose.
cards.watchOut: One week per dose, dose-finding in design, and the participant count is not documented in the fetched record — this card is supporting physiology, never load-bearing for the shelf.
cards.source: Sitar DS et al. A placebo-controlled dose-finding study with bambuterol in elderly patients with asthma. Chest. 1993. PMID: 8449067. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: once-daily oral bambuterol bronchodilates for a full 24 hours — in the one large trial (n=487, 4 weeks) both 10 mg and 20 mg beat placebo on peak flow, with 20 mg also improving FEV1; a 29-patient crossover confirms the overnight effect, and a one-week elderly dose-finding study shows the same dose-response with dose-related tremor and palpitations

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: This is a 1990s oral beta-agonist programme from the pre-LABA-inhaler era: bambuterol is a prodrug of terbutaline taken by mouth, so its beta-agonist effects are systemic, and the dose-related tremor and palpitations in the elderly study belong on the face of the shelf. No trial measured exacerbations, hospitalisations or mortality, and treatment lasted one week to one month. Bambuterol was never licensed in the US. The shelf records that the drug does what a long-acting oral bronchodilator should do to lung function; it must not be read as a modern treatment recommendation.

shelves.title: High-dose inhaled flunisolide in acute asthma: helped airflow in the ED, matched steroids in a tiny inpatient trial, and did nothing after discharge — a split record
shelves.question: In adults presenting with acute severe asthma, does high-dose inhaled flunisolide — added to salbutamol in the emergency department, substituted for systemic corticosteroids after initial intravenous treatment, or continued after ED discharge — improve airflow and outcomes versus placebo or systemic corticosteroids?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Inhalation · Adolescent · Adrenergic beta-Agonists · Adult · Albuterol · Analysis of Variance · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Asthma · Bronchodilator Agents · Chi-Square Distribution · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Emergencies · Female · Fluocinolone Acetonide · Follow-Up Studies · Forced Expiratory Volume · Glucocorticoids · Heart Rate · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nebulizers and Vaporizers · Peak Expiratory Flow Rate · Placebos
shelves.balance: SPLIT — three acute settings, three different answers, never pooled. Added to salbutamol in the emergency department (n=94), high cumulative-dose inhaled flunisolide separated from placebo on FEV1 and peak flow at 90-180 minutes, mainly in patients whose attack had lasted 24 hours or more. Substituted for systemic corticosteroids after 48 hours of intravenous steroids in hospital (n=40), it performed comparably over 7 days — a trial far too small to establish equivalence. Continued after ED discharge on top of 5 days of prednisone (n=104 randomised, 28% lost to follow-up), it gave no benefit at 24 days and more nocturnal wheezing (48% vs 18%). This is the acute question only; the chronic-asthma flunisolide base is not folded in, and flunisolide inhaler availability is now limited.

cards.headline: ED add-on RCT (Rodrigo 1998): high cumulative-dose inhaled flunisolide added to salbutamol separated from placebo on FEV1 and peak flow at 90-180 minutes, the benefit concentrated in patients whose attack had lasted 24 hours or more before arrival (n=94)
cards.summary: ED add-on RCT (Rodrigo 1998): high cumulative-dose inhaled flunisolide added to salbutamol separated from placebo on FEV1 and peak flow at 90-180 minutes, the benefit concentrated in patients whose attack had lasted 24 hours or more before arrival (n=94)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind ED trial, cumulative inhaled flunisolide plus salbutamol vs salbutamol plus placebo, 3 hours
cards.people: 94 patients presenting to an emergency department with an acute asthma exacerbation, assigned double-blind to salbutamol plus placebo (n=47) or salbutamol plus flunisolide (n=47), both given successively by metered-dose inhaler and spacer every 10 minutes for 3 hours (salbutamol 400 µg and flunisolide 1 mg per round).
cards.result: FEV1 and peak expiratory flow improved significantly over baseline in both groups (P<0.01). Results in the flunisolide group were significantly different from the placebo group at 90, 120, 150 and 180 minutes. Analysed by duration of attack before presentation, the placebo group with symptoms for 24 hours or more had a significantly lower FEV1 at 120, 150 and 180 minutes (P=0.041) than the remaining groups — that is, the flunisolide advantage lay mainly in patients with a prolonged attack.
cards.watchOut: A 3-hour airflow endpoint in a single ED, with the headline separation driven by the subgroup whose symptoms had already lasted at least 24 hours — not an admission, intubation or relapse outcome.

cards.headline: Inpatient substitution RCT (Lee-Wong 2002): after 48 hours of intravenous steroids, high-dose inhaled flunisolide performed comparably to continuing systemic corticosteroids over 7 days — peak flow 190 to 379 L/min versus 207 to 347 L/min (n=40)
cards.summary: Inpatient substitution RCT (Lee-Wong 2002): after 48 hours of intravenous steroids, high-dose inhaled flunisolide performed comparably to continuing systemic corticosteroids over 7 days — peak flow 190 to 379 L/min versus 207 to 347 L/min (n=40)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled inpatient substitution trial, inhaled flunisolide vs systemic corticosteroids after IV steroids (n=40)
cards.people: 40 patients aged 18 to 55 years hospitalised for a severe asthma exacerbation, all after eight doses of intravenous corticosteroids, randomised double-blind to high-dose inhaled flunisolide (250 µg per activation, eight puffs twice daily) or systemic corticosteroids alone, with outcomes at day 1 and day 7.
cards.result: From day 1 to day 7, mean peak expiratory flow increased from 190 to 379 L/min in the flunisolide group and from 207 to 347 L/min in the systemic corticosteroid group (P=0.95; 95% CI -66.3 to infinity). Mean FEV1 increased from 1.6 to 2.3 L on flunisolide and from 1.4 to 2.1 L on systemic corticosteroids (P=0.33). Changes in symptom scores were -0.7 and -0.9 respectively (P=0.39). Hospital readmission rates on day 7 were zero in both groups. The authors concluded high-dose inhaled corticosteroids are as effective as systemic corticosteroids during the 7 days following admission.
cards.watchOut: Only 40 patients and a one-sided confidence interval running to infinity: 'comparable' here means no difference was detected in a very small trial, not that equivalence was established. Every patient had already received 48 hours of intravenous steroids.
cards.source: Lee-Wong M et al. Comparison of high-dose inhaled flunisolide to systemic corticosteroids in severe adult asthma. Chest. 2002. PMID: 12377843. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ED-discharge RCT (Brenner 2000): high-dose inhaled flunisolide after discharge, on top of 5 days of prednisone, gave NO benefit at 24 days (percent predicted peak flow 87% vs 83%, P=0.36) and more nocturnal wheezing (48% vs 18%, P=0.01), with 28% lost to follow-up (n=104)
cards.summary: ED-discharge RCT (Brenner 2000): high-dose inhaled flunisolide after discharge, on top of 5 days of prednisone, gave NO benefit at 24 days (percent predicted peak flow 87% vs 83%, P=0.36) and more nocturnal wheezing (48% vs 18%, P=0.01), with 28% lost to follow-up (n=104)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled ED-discharge trial, inhaled flunisolide vs placebo, both arms on prednisone
cards.people: 104 patients (of 551 eligible) aged 18 to 50 years discharged from one inner-city ED after acute asthma, all given prednisone 40 mg/day for 5 days and inhaled beta-agonists as needed, randomised to high-dose inhaled flunisolide 2 mg/day (n=51) or placebo (n=53), followed to 24 days.
cards.result: Despite precautions, 28% of patients (16 on flunisolide, 13 on placebo) were completely lost to follow-up, 2 on flunisolide withdrew because of medication-related bronchospasm, and 4 patients in each group relapsed. Among the 63 remaining patients there was no difference at day 24 in percent predicted peak flow (87% vs 83%, P=0.36; difference 4%, 95% CI -5% to 13%). Nocturnal wheezing and nocturnal albuterol use were higher on flunisolide at day 24 (48% vs 18% for nocturnal wheezing, P=0.01; 3.8 vs 1.4 nocturnal albuterol puffs, P=0.03). Dyspnoea, cough and overall well-being were similar between groups. The authors concluded adding high-dose inhaled flunisolide does not benefit inner-city patients in the first 24 days after ED discharge.
cards.watchOut: Only 104 of 551 eligible patients took part and 28% were then lost to follow-up, so the analysis rests on 63 patients — the negative result is the largest and longest of the three settings, but it is attrition-limited.
cards.source: Brenner BE et al. Randomized trial of inhaled flunisolide versus placebo among asthmatic patients discharged from the emergency department. Annals of emergency medicine. 2000. cards.headline: Synthesis: split verdicts across three different acute settings, presented plainly — positive on airflow when added to salbutamol in the ED over 3 hours (n=94), indistinguishable from continuing systemic steroids after 48 hours of IV treatment in a 40-patient inpatient trial, and negative after ED discharge over 24 days (n=104 randomised, 63 analysed)
cards.summary: Synthesis: split verdicts across three different acute settings, presented plainly — positive on airflow when added to salbutamol in the ED over 3 hours (n=94), indistinguishable from continuing systemic steroids after 48 hours of IV treatment in a 40-patient inpatient trial, and negative after ED discharge over 24 days (n=104 randomised, 63 analysed)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: These are three different questions wearing one drug's name, and they are not pooled. The ED add-on trial's separation appeared at 90-180 minutes and was concentrated in patients whose attack had lasted at least 24 hours. The substitution trial is too small (n=40, confidence interval to infinity) to establish equivalence. The discharge trial — the only one with a post-discharge horizon — found no benefit and more nocturnal wheezing on flunisolide. This shelf is the acute question only; the chronic-asthma flunisolide base did not verify at three adult reports and is not folded in. Flunisolide inhaler availability is now limited.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: IV aminophylline in acute asthma (adults): no added bronchodilation or fewer admissions in the Cochrane pool of 17 trials — and more vomiting and arrhythmias
shelves.question: In adults with acute asthma treated in the emergency department or hospital, does adding intravenous aminophylline to inhaled beta-2 agonists (with systemic corticosteroids) improve lung function, admission and outcomes versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Adrenergic beta-Agonists · Adult · Aminophylline · Asthma · Bronchodilator Agents · Drug Therapy, Combination · Emergency Service, Hospital · Hospitalization · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference) — with more harm. The Cochrane 2012 update (17 trials) found adding intravenous aminophylline to inhaled beta-2 agonists produced no statistically significant additional bronchodilation at any time point and no significant reduction in hospital admission (OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.12; 6 studies, n=315), and no subgroup — by baseline airflow limitation or corticosteroid use — in which it worked better. It did produce more vomiting (OR 4.21, 95% CI 2.20 to 8.07) and palpitations/arrhythmias (OR 3.02, 95% CI 1.15 to 7.90): about 20 extra patients vomiting and 15 extra with arrhythmias or palpitations per 100 treated. The named primaries are small and old, with their Ns on the face — one positive inpatient trial of 21 adults and one negative trial of 59 — and they do not outweigh the pool. Aminophylline's narrow therapeutic index belongs on the face. Adults only.

cards.headline: Cochrane review, 2012 update (Nair 2012): 17 trials — adding IV aminophylline to inhaled beta-2 agonists gave no significant bronchodilation and no significant reduction in hospital admission (OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.12; 6 studies, n=315), with more vomiting and palpitations/arrhythmias
cards.summary: Cochrane review, 2012 update (Nair 2012): 17 trials — adding IV aminophylline to inhaled beta-2 agonists gave no significant bronchodilation and no significant reduction in hospital admission (OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.12; 6 studies, n=315), with more vomiting and palpitations/arrhythmias
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (2012 update; the 2000 version, PMID 11034753, is not carded — one version only), IV aminophylline added to inhaled beta-2 agonists in adults with acute asthma
cards.people: Adults with acute asthma treated in the emergency department with inhaled beta-2 agonists, in randomised trials of intravenous aminophylline versus placebo (patients could also receive corticosteroids or other bronchodilators if not part of the randomised treatment). Fifteen studies were in the previous version and two new studies were added in the 2012 update, though the new data could not be pooled.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant advantage from adding intravenous aminophylline for hospital admissions (OR 0.58; 95% CI 0.30 to 1.12; 6 studies; n=315), and no statistically significant effect on airflow outcomes at any time period. Peak flow values were similar at 12 hours (mean difference 8.30 L/min; 95% CI -20.69 to 37.29 L/min) and 24 hours (22.20 L/min; 95% CI -56.65 to 101.05 L/min). Subgroup analyses by baseline airflow limitation and by corticosteroid use found no subgroup in which aminophylline was more effective. Aminophylline-treated patients reported more palpitations/arrhythmias (OR 3.02; 95% CI 1.15 to 7.90; 6 studies; n=249) and vomiting (OR 4.21; 95% CI 2.20 to 8.07; 7 studies; n=321), with no significant difference in tremor. For every 100 people treated with aminophylline an additional 20 had vomiting and 15 had arrhythmias or palpitations. The reviewers concluded the risk-benefit balance of intravenous aminophylline is unfavourable. Overall study quality was moderate; allocation concealment was clearly adequate in only seven of the trials.
cards.watchOut: This shelf's weight rests on this pool, as the commissioning row directs — and the pool is heterogeneous, with aminophylline doses, co-medications and asthma severity varying between studies, and only seven trials with clearly adequate allocation concealment.
cards.source: Nair P et al. Addition of intravenous aminophylline to inhaled beta(2)-agonists in adults with acute asthma. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2012. PMID: 23235591. cards.headline: Hospitalised-patient RCT (Huang 1993): aminophylline added to nebulised albuterol and IV methylprednisolone improved FEV1 more at 3 hours (29% vs 10% improvement, P=0.023) and at 48 hours, and patients needed fewer albuterol nebulisations — in 21 adults
cards.summary: Hospitalised-patient RCT (Huang 1993): aminophylline added to nebulised albuterol and IV methylprednisolone improved FEV1 more at 3 hours (29% vs 10% improvement, P=0.023) and at 48 hours, and patients needed fewer albuterol nebulisations — in 21 adults
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled double-blind inpatient trial, IV aminophylline (as theophylline) added to albuterol and methylprednisolone (n=21)
cards.people: 21 adults (22 to 48 years) admitted to an inpatient service of a tertiary-care university hospital for an acute asthma exacerbation — 10 in the aminophylline group and 11 on placebo — all receiving nebulised albuterol and intravenous methylprednisolone 60 mg every 6 hours, with individualised aminophylline doses or placebo for 48 hours.
cards.result: Baseline FEV1 was 49% ± 19% of predicted in the aminophylline group and 43% ± 13% on placebo. Improvement in FEV1 at 3 hours was greater on aminophylline (29% ± 23% vs 10% ± 10%; mean difference 19 percentage points; 95% CI 3 to 35; P=0.023). At 48 hours FEV1 was 75% ± 19% of predicted on aminophylline versus 58% ± 15% on placebo (mean difference 17 percentage points; 95% CI 0.2 to 34.8; P=0.048). Aminophylline patients required fewer albuterol nebulisations (10.3 ± 3.8 vs 16.4 ± 5.3) and less total albuterol (34 ± 16 mg vs 70 ± 34 mg; P=0.02). No statistical differences were observed in symptom scores or frequency of adverse effects, with serum concentrations maintained in the therapeutic range.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-one patients: the positive primary on this shelf, and far too small to overturn the Cochrane pool. Its 48-hour P value is 0.048 with a confidence interval whose lower bound is 0.2 percentage points.
cards.source: Huang D et al. Does aminophylline benefit adults admitted to the hospital for an acute exacerbation of asthma? Annals of internal medicine. 1993. PMID: 8239245. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ED/inpatient RCT (Coleridge 1993): continuous aminophylline infusion conferred NO benefit on peak flow or hospital stay in acute severe asthma treated with IV steroids and inhaled bronchodilators — 59 patients treated, 31 discharged from the ED within 12 hours and 28 admitted
cards.summary: ED/inpatient RCT (Coleridge 1993): continuous aminophylline infusion conferred NO benefit on peak flow or hospital stay in acute severe asthma treated with IV steroids and inhaled bronchodilators — 59 patients treated, 31 discharged from the ED within 12 hours and 28 admitted
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, continuous IV aminophylline infusion in acute severe asthma (n=59 treated)
cards.people: Patients with acute severe asthma treated in the emergency department and inpatient wards, randomised double-blind to continuous aminophylline infusion (adjusted to maintain therapeutic levels) or placebo; all received nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium bromide, intravenous hydrocortisone 250 mg six-hourly and oxygen. Thirty-one patients improved enough to be discharged home from the ED within 12 hours; the remaining 28 were admitted for a total trial duration of 48 hours.
cards.result: No significant difference was found between the placebo and treatment groups for measurements of peak expiratory flow, or for the duration of hospital stay. The study had 80% power for a 25% to 33% difference at the 5% significance level. Presentation values of peak flow and arterial blood gases did not predict which patients would require admission and which could be discharged from the ED.
cards.watchOut: A negative trial, but also small — 59 patients split between ED discharge and admission pathways; it agrees with the Cochrane pool rather than proving the null on its own.
cards.source: Coleridge J et al. Intravenous aminophylline confers no benefit in acute asthma treated with intravenous steroids and inhaled bronchodilators. shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for arterial blood gases and acid–base status — pH, PaCO2, PaO2, bicarbonate and the alveolar–arterial oxygen difference — by age (including older adults) and sex, at sea level and at moderate altitude, and how much do analyser and sampling conditions move them?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, respiration and acid–base chapters, and Boron & Boulpaep, respiratory physiology. This is the reference-INTERVALS slice only: pack #6349 homes the alveolar gas EQUATION and what determines the A–a gradient (a mechanism question, which cards one elderly-Japanese ABG dataset as a supporting card) — cross-pointed here, its dataset not re-carded, and no intervals are derived there. Three independent free datasets are carded: reference equations from 96 healthy lifetime nonsmokers at sea level and 243 at 1,400 m (Crapo 1999); non-parametric intervals from 182 medical students plus health professionals aged 21-76 on a named Radiometer ABL analyser (Klaestrup 2011), in which PaO2 fell by 0.29 kPa (about 2.2 mmHg) per decade; and an elderly cohort aged over 70 (Epshtein 2025) whose HEALTHY subgroup — subgroup N not printed in the fetched record — had mean PaCO2 36.9 ± 4.2 mmHg, inside the conventional range. The stamp is graded down: the largest dataset publishes equations rather than printed intervals, the elderly healthy subgroup N is not printed, and altitude rests on a single dataset. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

cards.headline: Crapo 1999: reference equations for PaO2, PaCO2, pH and AaPO2 from 96 healthy lifetime nonsmokers at sea level and 243 at 1,400 m — barometric pressure improved prediction
cards.summary: Crapo 1999: reference equations for PaO2, PaCO2, pH and AaPO2 from 96 healthy lifetime nonsmokers at sea level and 243 at 1,400 m — barometric pressure improved prediction
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (arterial blood-gas reference equations, sea level and 1,400 m altitude)
cards.people: 339 healthy lifetime nonsmokers aged 18-81 years (166 men, 173 women): 96 studied at sea level and 243 at an altitude of 1,400 m; arterial samples were analysed in duplicate on two separate blood gas analysers and CO-oximeters at each site, with variables PaO2, PaCO2, pH, calculated alveolar–arterial PO2 difference (AaPO2), haemoglobin, carboxyhaemoglobin, methaemoglobin and SaO2.
cards.result: Reference equations were fitted two ways — best-fit models and simple equations using only variables explaining at least 3% of variance — as sea-level-only equations and as combined equations with barometric pressure as an independent variable. The equation including barometric pressure predicted PaO2 slightly better at sea level than the sea-level-specific equation, and including barometric pressure allows prediction of reference values at sea level and at altitudes up to 1,400 m. The decline in PaO2 with age at each altitude was consistent with most previous studies; comparisons with earlier studies revealed small but significant differences. The fetched record prints the equations' construction and performance, not a table of interval limits, and this card claims no numeric limits from it.
cards.watchOut: Altitude values are a separate limb, never merged into sea-level intervals: the 1,400 m limb is this one dataset of 243 people. The product is equations, so an individual's expected PaO2 must be computed for their age and pressure, not read off a single range.
cards.source: Crapo RO et al. Arterial blood gas reference values for sea level and an altitude of 1,400 meters. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 1999. PMID: 10556115. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Klaestrup 2011: adult arterial reference intervals on a Radiometer ABL analyser — women had higher pH and lower PaCO2, PaO2 fell 0.29 kPa (about 2.2 mmHg) per decade, lactate upper limit 2.5 mmol/L (about 23 mg/dL)
cards.summary: Klaestrup 2011: adult arterial reference intervals on a Radiometer ABL analyser — women had higher pH and lower PaCO2, PaO2 fell 0.29 kPa (about 2.2 mmHg) per decade, lactate upper limit 2.5 mmol/L (about 23 mg/dL)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (arterial blood-gas and electrolyte reference intervals, named analyser)
cards.people: Healthy adults in two groups — 182 medical students aged 20-32 years and a group of health professionals aged 21-76 years (the second group's N is not printed in the fetched abstract); arterial samples analysed on the Radiometer ABL blood gas analyser, with reference intervals calculated non-parametrically and age and sex dependency examined for all analytes.
cards.result: Women had significantly higher pH and lower PaCO2, base excess, and plasma standard and actual bicarbonate than men (p<0.01), but the differences were minor and common reference intervals were also determined, generally at the same level as previously published. Lactate values were similar between the sexes but with a high upper limit of 2.5 mmol/L (about 23 mg/dL). PaO2 values were similar in non-smoking women and men, but PaO2 decreased with age by 0.29 kPa per decade (95% CI for the slope -0.11 to -0.47 kPa; about 2.2 mmHg per decade). The authors concluded sex and age dependency is generally without clinical importance, except for lower PaCO2 in women and decreasing PaO2 with age.
cards.watchOut: Analyser-specific by design — the intervals are for the Radiometer ABL platform named in the record; the younger group (medical students, n=182) dominates the sample, so the older-age intervals rest on the smaller health-professional group whose N the abstract does not print.
cards.source: Klaestrup E et al. Reference intervals and age and gender dependency for arterial blood gases and electrolytes in adults. Clinical chemistry and laboratory medicine. 2011. PMID: 21619466. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Epshtein 2025: in elderly patients over 70, the healthy subgroup's mean PaCO2 was 36.9 ± 4.2 mmHg — inside the conventional range; venous–arterial pCO2 bias was +10.0 mmHg with wide limits of agreement
cards.summary: Epshtein 2025: in elderly patients over 70, the healthy subgroup's mean PaCO2 was 36.9 ± 4.2 mmHg — inside the conventional range; venous–arterial pCO2 bias was +10.0 mmHg with wide limits of agreement
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (elderly blood-gas ranges; healthy subgroup carded only)
cards.people: 130 participants aged over 70 years in a single-centre cohort, divided into four categories — healthy patients, stable chronic pulmonary disease, hospitalised acute respiratory illness, and hospitalised patients without respiratory disease — with paired arterial and venous blood gases on a point-of-care analyser. Only the healthy category is carded here, as the row directs; its subgroup N is not printed in the fetched record.
cards.result: Mean PaCO2 was 36.9 ± 4.2 mmHg in the healthy control group, 37.0 ± 4.8 mmHg in the stable chronic respiratory group, 37.0 ± 5.0 mmHg in the non-respiratory hospitalisation group and 42.3 ± 11.4 mmHg in the respiratory hospitalisation group (Kruskal–Wallis p<0.0025). Mean bias between venous and arterial CO2 was +10.0 mmHg, with 95% limits of agreement from 2.7 to -22.8 mmHg as published. The authors concluded that in elderly patients the PaCO2 range was similar to the accepted normal range in clinical practice, and that the venous–arterial pCO2 gradient had high bias and wide limits of agreement.
cards.watchOut: Mixed-population dataset carded for its healthy subgroup only, exactly as published: the healthy subgroup's N is not printed in the fetched record, so this card supports the PaCO2 centre in healthy over-70s and nothing more; the venous values are a bias/agreement limb, not arterial intervals.

shelves.title: Suplatast tosilate in asthma (Japanese programme): Lancet trial — deterioration on steroid halving significantly worse on placebo; small mechanistic limbs (n=28/25/20) show eosinophilic inflammation falling
shelves.question: In adults with asthma — steroid-dependent asthma undergoing inhaled-steroid reduction, mild-to-moderate asthma, and cough-variant asthma — does oral suplatast tosilate versus placebo improve lung function and symptoms, permit inhaled-corticosteroid reduction, and reduce eosinophilic airway inflammation?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Administration, Oral · Anti-Allergic Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Arylsulfonates/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Asthma/drug therapy · Beclomethasone/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Circadian Rhythm · Cytokines/antagonists & inhibitors · Double-Blind Method · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Peak Expiratory Flow Rate · Sulfonium Compounds/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Th2 Cells
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a Japanese programme whose load-bearing report is one Lancet trial. In steroid-dependent asthma (85 randomised, 77 analysed), suplatast tosilate 100 mg three times daily improved pulmonary function and symptoms during a 4-week add-on phase and, when inhaled beclomethasone was halved over the next 4 weeks, pulmonary function, symptoms and beta-agonist use deteriorated significantly more on placebo than on suplatast. Three smaller randomised reports (n=28, n=25, n=20 — printed on their cards) support an anti-eosinophilic mechanism: blood and sputum eosinophils, exhaled nitric oxide and airway responsiveness fell; bronchial-biopsy goblet-cell metaplasia measures fell; and in cough-variant asthma the capsaicin cough threshold rose from 2.72 to 39.7 μM with sputum eosinophil cationic protein falling. JAPANESE PROGRAMME FLAG: suplatast is licensed in Japan and not in the US/UK. Endpoints are lung function, symptoms and inflammatory markers over 4 weeks to 3 months; there is no exacerbation-outcome or mortality trial. The paediatric suplatast reports are not folded into this adult shelf.

cards.headline: Lancet double-blind RCT in steroid-dependent asthma (Tamaoki 2000): during inhaled-steroid halving, pulmonary function, symptoms and beta-agonist use deteriorated significantly more on placebo than on suplatast tosilate
cards.summary: Lancet double-blind RCT in steroid-dependent asthma (Tamaoki 2000): during inhaled-steroid halving, pulmonary function, symptoms and beta-agonist use deteriorated significantly more on placebo than on suplatast tosilate
cards.type: Double-blind randomised parallel-group multicentre trial (Tokyo Joshi-Idai Asthma Research Group), suplatast tosilate vs placebo during inhaled-steroid reduction
cards.people: 85 patients with moderate-to-severe steroid-dependent asthma taking high-dose inhaled beclomethasone dipropionate (≥1500 μg/day), assigned to suplatast tosilate 100 mg three times daily or placebo for 8 weeks (4-week add-on phase with other medication unchanged, then 4 weeks with the beclomethasone dose halved); data were available from 77 patients.
cards.result: During the add-on phase, suplatast versus placebo was associated with higher forced expiratory volume in 1 s (mean between-group difference for change from baseline at week 4, 0.20 L [95% CI 0.16 to 0.24], P=0.043), higher morning peak expiratory flow (18.6 L/min [14.1 to 23.1], P=0.037), less diurnal peak-flow variation and lower asthma symptom scores, and lower serum eosinophil cationic protein and IgE. In the steroid-reduction phase, pulmonary function, asthma symptoms and beta2-agonist use deteriorated significantly more in the placebo group than in the suplatast group. The authors concluded suplatast improves control and allows inhaled-corticosteroid dose reduction without significant side-effects.
cards.watchOut: The load-bearing report of this shelf — but an 8-week trial with 77 analysed patients and surrogate/symptom endpoints; 8 of 85 randomised patients contributed no data. Japanese programme; suplatast is not licensed in the US/UK.

data were available from 77 patients. during the add-on phase, suplatast versus placebo was associated with higher forced expiratory volume in 1 s (mean between-group difference for change from baseline at week 4, 0.20 l [95% ci 0.16 to 0.24], p=0.043), higher morning peak expiratory flow (18.6 l/min [14.1 to 23.1], p=0.037), less diurnal peak-flow variation and lower asthma symptom scores, and lower serum eosinophil cationic protein and ige. in the steroid-reduction phase, pulmonary function, asthma symptoms and beta2-agonist use deteriorated significantly more in the placebo group than in the suplatast group. the authors concluded suplatast improves control and allows inhaled-corticosteroid dose reduction without significant side-effects. the load-bearing report of this shelf — but an 8-week trial with 77 analysed patients and surrogate/symptom endpoints; cards.headline: Randomised AHR/inflammation study (Yoshida 2002; n=28): blood and sputum eosinophils, exhaled nitric oxide and airway responsiveness all fell on suplatast over 28 days; no such change without suplatast
cards.summary: Randomised AHR/inflammation study (Yoshida 2002; n=28): blood and sputum eosinophils, exhaled nitric oxide and airway responsiveness all fell on suplatast over 28 days; no such change without suplatast
cards.type: Randomised controlled study (treatment vs no suplatast treatment), suplatast tosilate in mild-to-moderate asthma
cards.people: 28 patients with mild-to-moderate asthma, randomised into two groups with or without suplatast tosilate treatment (100 mg three times daily for 28 days); blood eosinophil counts, eosinophilic cationic protein, sputum eosinophil count, exhaled nitric oxide and airway responsiveness were measured before and after treatment.
cards.result: In the suplatast group, blood and sputum eosinophil counts decreased significantly after treatment, and exhaled nitric oxide level and airway responsiveness (measured using an Astograph) also decreased; there were no such significant changes in the group without suplatast. The authors concluded oral suplatast suppresses airway hyperresponsiveness by reducing eosinophilic inflammation. (The fetched abstract prints no numeric effect sizes, and none are claimed here.)
cards.watchOut: Small mechanistic limb (n=28) with a no-treatment rather than placebo comparator and no printed effect sizes — supporting evidence only, never load-bearing.

cards.headline: Double-blind goblet-cell-metaplasia biopsy study (Hoshino 2005; n=25): AB/PAS and MUC5AC stained area in bronchial epithelium fell significantly on suplatast over 3 months (both P<0.01)
cards.summary: Double-blind goblet-cell-metaplasia biopsy study (Hoshino 2005; n=25): AB/PAS and MUC5AC stained area in bronchial epithelium fell significantly on suplatast over 3 months (both P<0.01)
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled bronchial-biopsy study, suplatast tosilate vs placebo
cards.people: 25 patients with asthma, given oral suplatast 300 mg daily or placebo for 3 months in a double-blind parallel-group study; bronchial biopsy specimens before and after treatment were assessed for alcian blue/periodic acid–Schiff (AB/PAS) and MUC5AC staining, interleukin-4- and interleukin-13-positive cells, and inflammatory cells in the lamina propria.
cards.result: The percentage of AB/PAS-stained area (P<0.01) and MUC5AC-stained area (P<0.01) decreased significantly in the suplatast group, accompanied by significant decreases in IL-4-positive and IL-13-positive cells and in infiltrating eosinophils and CD4-positive T cells. The authors concluded suplatast prevents goblet-cell metaplasia through modulation of Th2 cytokine production and recruitment of eosinophils and CD4-positive T cells.
cards.watchOut: Small mechanistic biopsy limb (n=25): a tissue-marker endpoint, not a clinical outcome — supporting evidence only, never load-bearing.
cards.source: Hoshino M et al. Effect of suplatast tosilate on goblet cell metaplasia in patients with asthma. Allergy. 2005. PMID: 16197471. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cough-variant asthma double-blind RCT (Shioya 2002; n=20): capsaicin cough threshold rose from 2.72 to 39.7 μM and sputum eosinophil cationic protein fell from 435 to 56 μg/l on suplatast over 6 weeks
cards.summary: Cough-variant asthma double-blind RCT (Shioya 2002; n=20): capsaicin cough threshold rose from 2.72 to 39.7 μM and sputum eosinophil cationic protein fell from 435 to 56 μg/l on suplatast over 6 weeks
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial, suplatast tosilate vs placebo in cough-variant asthma
cards.people: 20 patients with cough-variant asthma, assigned to suplatast tosilate 100 mg three times daily or placebo for 6 weeks in a double-blind randomised study; cough and medication scores, pulmonary function, methacholine responsiveness, capsaicin cough threshold, and sputum eosinophil percentage and eosinophilic cationic protein (ECP) were evaluated.
cards.result: In the suplatast group, cough scores and medication scores decreased significantly over time; sputum eosinophils fell from 53.5 ± 5.6% to 13.6 ± 2.6%; capsaicin cough threshold improved from 2.72 ± 3.41 μM to 39.7 ± 22.7 μM; sputum ECP fell from 435 ± 123 μg/l to 56 ± 34 μg/l; and methacholine responsiveness changed from 8.45 ± 3.43 to 11.4 ± 3.76 units. The authors reported no significant side effects.
cards.watchOut: Very small limb (n=20, 6 weeks) in the cough-variant subtype — its within-group changes support the mechanism and the cough indication, but it is never load-bearing for asthma control generally.
cards.source: Shioya T et al. Effect of suplatast tosilate, a Th2 cytokine inhibitor, on cough variant asthma. European journal of clinical pharmacology. 2002. PMID: 12107601. cards.headline: Synthesis: one load-bearing Lancet steroid-reduction trial (n=85) plus three small mechanistic randomised reports (n=28, n=25, n=20) pointing the same anti-eosinophilic way — a Japanese programme with no exacerbation-outcome trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: one load-bearing Lancet steroid-reduction trial (n=85) plus three small mechanistic randomised reports (n=28, n=25, n=20) pointing the same anti-eosinophilic way — a Japanese programme with no exacerbation-outcome trial
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Suplatast tosilate permitted inhaled-steroid halving with significantly less deterioration than placebo in steroid-dependent asthma, and the three smaller reports consistently show reduced eosinophilic airway inflammation (blood/sputum eosinophils, exhaled nitric oxide, biopsy goblet-cell and Th2-cytokine measures, and cough threshold in cough-variant asthma). A 2-year monotherapy pilot versus low-dose fluticasone from this programme is a cross-point only and is not carded. Suplatast is licensed in Japan, not in the US/UK; endpoints across the programme are lung function, symptoms and inflammatory markers over 4 weeks to 3 months, and no trial measured exacerbations or mortality. Paediatric suplatast reports are a different population and are not folded in.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards; the three smaller Ns (28, 25, 20) are printed on their faces and those limbs are supporting, never load-bearing.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Seratrodast (AA-2414 — one drug) in asthma (Japanese programme): symptoms and PEF variability improved in two small trials (n=45, n=31), FEV1 unchanged in one; phase II report is PK/PD only
shelves.question: In patients with mild-to-moderate asthma, does oral seratrodast (AA-2414, thromboxane A2 receptor antagonist) versus placebo improve symptoms, peak-flow variability and airway inflammation/hyperresponsiveness?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/pharmacology · Asthma/physiopathology · Benzoquinones/pharmacology · Double-Blind Method · Heptanoic Acids/pharmacology · Humans · Middle Aged · Mucociliary Clearance/drug effects · Respiratory Mechanics · Sputum/chemistry/metabolism · Viscosity
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a mechanistic, short and dose-inconsistent Japanese programme — presented as such. Seratrodast is the thromboxane A2 receptor antagonist developed as AA-2414 — the two names are ONE drug, and this shelf states that identity so they are not read as two agents. In the multicentre placebo-controlled trial (45 patients with sputum-producing asthma, 40 mg/day for 6 weeks), diurnal peak-flow variation, daytime symptoms and rescue beta-agonist use fell significantly versus placebo and sputum amount and viscosity fell — but FEV1 and peak-flow changes did NOT differ between groups. In the bronchial-biopsy trial of AA-2414 (31 patients, 80 mg/day for 4 months), symptom score, peak flow, diurnal variation and bronchial responsiveness improved versus placebo with reduced submucosal eosinophils and chemokine-expressing cells. The phase II report (183 patients) is a population pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic analysis of its trial, not a conventional efficacy report, and is labelled as such. Seratrodast is licensed in Japan, not in the US/UK. Endpoints are symptoms, peak-flow variability and biopsy/sputum markers; no exacerbation-outcome trial exists.

cards.headline: Multicentre double-blind RCT (Tamaoki 2000; n=45): seratrodast 40 mg/day for 6 weeks reduced diurnal PEF variation (P=0.034), daytime symptoms (P=0.030), rescue beta-agonist use (P=0.032) and sputum amount and viscosity vs placebo — but FEV1 and PEF changes did not differ
cards.summary: Multicentre double-blind RCT (Tamaoki 2000; n=45): seratrodast 40 mg/day for 6 weeks reduced diurnal PEF variation (P=0.034), daytime symptoms (P=0.030), rescue beta-agonist use (P=0.032) and sputum amount and viscosity vs placebo — but FEV1 and PEF changes did not differ
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial, seratrodast vs placebo in sputum-producing mild-to-moderate asthma
cards.people: 45 patients with mild-to-moderate asthma who had been continuously expectorating sputum (>20 g/day), assigned after a 2-week run-in to seratrodast 40 mg/day or placebo for 6 weeks; patients with current pulmonary infection or taking oral corticosteroids, antibiotics or mucolytic agents were excluded.
cards.result: Changes in FEV1 and peak expiratory flow (PEF) were not different between the groups, but diurnal variation of PEF (P=0.034), frequency of daytime asthma symptoms (P=0.030) and daytime supplemental beta2-agonist use (P=0.032) fell significantly on seratrodast. Sputum amount (P=0.005), dynamic viscosity (P=0.007) and albumin concentration (P=0.028) decreased on seratrodast, with no effect on elastic modulus or fucose concentration; nasal saccharin-particle clearance time was shortened at weeks 4 (P=0.031) and 6 (P=0.025). The authors concluded thromboxane A2 blockade has minimal effects on pulmonary function but may improve mucociliary clearance by decreasing secretion viscosity.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=45), short (6 weeks) and sputum-selected — and negative on its lung-function measures; the positive findings are symptom, variability and secretion measures. Print both halves.
cards.source: Tamaoki J et al. Effect of a thromboxane A(2) antagonist on sputum production and its physicochemical properties in patients with mild to moderate asthma. Chest. 2000. PMID: 10893362. cards.headline: Bronchial-biopsy trial of AA-2414 — seratrodast's development code, the same drug (Hoshino 1999; n=31): symptom score, PEF, diurnal variation and bronchial responsiveness improved vs placebo over 4 months at 80 mg/day, with reduced submucosal eosinophils
cards.summary: Bronchial-biopsy trial of AA-2414 — seratrodast's development code, the same drug (Hoshino 1999; n=31): symptom score, PEF, diurnal variation and bronchial responsiveness improved vs placebo over 4 months at 80 mg/day, with reduced submucosal eosinophils
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled bronchial-biopsy trial, AA-2414 (seratrodast) vs placebo
cards.people: 31 asthmatic subjects, treated orally with AA-2414 (seratrodast) 80 mg/day or matched placebo for 4 months in a double-blind manner; bronchial biopsy specimens were examined by immunohistochemistry before and after treatment, and symptom score, peak expiratory flow, lung function and methacholine responsiveness were measured.
cards.result: After treatment, symptom score (P<0.05), PEF (P<0.01), diurnal variation of PEF (P<0.01) and bronchial responsiveness (P<0.01) improved significantly in the AA-2414 group compared with placebo, accompanied by a significant decrease in submucosal EG2-positive eosinophils (P<0.05) and reductions in cells expressing RANTES and macrophage inflammatory protein-1alpha in the epithelium and monocyte chemotactic protein-3, RANTES, MIP-1alpha and eotaxin in the submucosa. The number of EG2-positive eosinophils correlated with chemokine-expressing cell counts, and its change correlated negatively with the increase in bronchial responsiveness (rs=−0.65, P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Small mechanistic biopsy limb (n=31) at 80 mg/day — twice the dose of the sputum trial's 40 mg/day; the dose inconsistency across this programme is printed, not smoothed over.
cards.source: Hoshino M et al. Effect of AA-2414, a thromboxane A2 receptor antagonist, on airway inflammation in subjects with asthma. The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology. 1999. PMID: 10359886. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Phase II programme report (Samara 1997; n=183): a population PK/PD analysis of a 15-centre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial — FEV1 increase at 120 mg/day was linearly correlated with seratrodast plasma concentration; this is NOT a conventional efficacy report
cards.summary: Phase II programme report (Samara 1997; n=183): a population PK/PD analysis of a 15-centre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial — FEV1 increase at 120 mg/day was linearly correlated with seratrodast plasma concentration; this is NOT a conventional efficacy report
cards.type: Programme report: phase II population pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic analysis of a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, seratrodast vs placebo
cards.people: 183 patients with mild-to-moderate asthma in a phase II, randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled 15-centre study, assigned to placebo or seratrodast 80 mg or 120 mg daily for 8 weeks; pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic modelling used the population approach.
cards.result: Seratrodast pharmacokinetics were linear after single and multiple dosing; population oral clearance was 8.5 ml/hr/kg and apparent volume of distribution 43.3 ml/kg, with residual variability of 30%. Seratrodast 120 mg daily produced an increase in FEV1 from baseline linearly correlated with plasma concentrations (average concentration-effect slope 0.222% per μg/ml after single dosing and 0.470% per μg/ml after multiple dosing); interpatient variability in response was mainly affected by initial disease severity, with lower percent-predicted FEV1 (more severe obstruction) associated with higher slopes.
cards.watchOut: Labelled as what it is: a PK/PD modelling report of a trial, with a concentration-effect relationship — it carries no conventional placebo-adjusted efficacy estimate and must not be counted as a third efficacy trial.

cards.result: Seratrodast (AA-2414 — one drug, two names) improved daytime symptoms, diurnal peak-flow variation and rescue-medication use versus placebo in sputum-producing asthma, without differing on FEV1 or peak-flow change; improved symptom score, peak flow, diurnal variation and bronchial responsiveness in the biopsy trial, with reduced submucosal eosinophils and chemokine expression; and showed a concentration-correlated FEV1 increase in the phase II PK/PD analysis. An earlier 4-day hyperresponsiveness study from this programme (n=15) is sub-floor in size and duration — it is a cross-point only, is not carded, and is never load-bearing. Seratrodast is licensed in Japan, not in the US/UK; no exacerbation-outcome or mortality trial exists in this base.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards; doses differ across the programme (40 mg vs 80 mg vs 80/120 mg) and endpoints are symptoms, peak-flow variability and tissue/secretion markers.
