shelves.title: Zolpidem in chronic insomnia: ER 12.5 mg 'helped me sleep' 92.3% vs 59.7% at 24 weeks (n=1,018); IR 10 mg worked over 35 nights in a small trial (n=75); ER 6.25 mg improved polysomnography in older adults
shelves.question: In adults with chronic primary insomnia, does zolpidem — immediate-release nightly, or extended-release taken 3–7 nights per week — improve sleep onset and maintenance versus placebo, and what happens on discontinuation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Chronic Disease · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives/administration & dosage,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Polysomnography · Psychomotor Performance/drug effects · Pyridines/administration & dosage,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Sleep/drug effects · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/drug therapy · Zolpidem
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for sleep onset and maintenance over the periods tested, on three randomised trials carded separately by formulation. Immediate-release zolpidem 10 mg (n=75, 35 nights, sleep-laboratory) improved latency to persistent sleep and sleep efficiency from week 1 with no tolerance and no post-treatment difference from placebo; 15 mg added nothing and reduced REM sleep at weeks 3–4. Extended-release 12.5 mg taken 3–7 nights per week (n=1,018, 24 weeks) beat placebo on every subjective measure — the primary endpoint was the patient's global impression that the drug 'helped me sleep' (89.8% vs 51.4% at week 12; 92.3% vs 59.7% at week 24) — with no rebound over the first 3 discontinuation nights; commonest adverse events were headache, anxiety and somnolence. In older adults (n=205, mean age 70.2), zolpidem ER 6.25 mg improved polysomnographic wake after sleep onset, latency and total sleep time over 3 weeks, with some polysomnographic measures worsening for a single night after abrupt discontinuation and no next-morning residual effects detected. The 1994 trial is small (n=75) and labelled as such; the weight rests on the two ER trials. None of the carded trials reports falls, fractures or complex sleep behaviours as outcomes — those harms are not measured in this evidence base and are not claimed either way here.

cards.headline: Immediate-release zolpidem 10 mg for 35 nights (Scharf 1994, n=75): latency to persistent sleep and sleep efficiency improved from week 1 and were maintained, with no tolerance and no post-treatment difference from placebo; 15 mg reduced REM sleep and added nothing
cards.summary: Immediate-release zolpidem 10 mg for 35 nights (Scharf 1994, n=75): latency to persistent sleep and sleep efficiency improved from week 1 and were maintained, with no tolerance and no post-treatment difference from placebo; 15 mg reduced REM sleep and added nothing
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, immediate-release zolpidem 10 mg and 15 mg, 35 nights (sleep-laboratory)
cards.people: 75 patients with chronic insomnia in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group multicentre sleep-laboratory trial of zolpidem 10 mg, zolpidem 15 mg or placebo nightly for 35 nights, with a 3-night post-treatment period. This trial is small (n=75) and is labelled as such; it is not the load-bearing card of this shelf.
cards.result: Within the first week, zolpidem 10 mg significantly improved latency to persistent sleep and sleep efficiency, and efficacy was maintained throughout the 35 nights. There was no evidence of tolerance at either dose, no residual effect at 10 mg, and no significant difference between the 10 mg group and placebo in latency to persistent sleep or sleep efficiency during the post-treatment period. Stage 3–4 sleep was preserved at both doses; the 15 mg dose significantly decreased REM sleep at weeks 3 and 4 versus placebo and provided no clinical advantage over 10 mg. Treatment-emergent adverse-event rates in the zolpidem groups were similar to placebo, and psychomotor performance was not detrimentally affected.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=75 across three arms) and from 1994, before current regulatory harm framing existed: it cannot exclude uncommon harms, and its 'no rebound' finding is a 3-night post-treatment comparison in a small sample. The row's weight rests on the two extended-release trials below.
cards.source: Scharf MB et al. A multicenter, placebo-controlled study evaluating zolpidem in the treatment of chronic insomnia. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 1994. PMID: 8071269. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zolpidem extended-release 12.5 mg, 3–7 nights per week for 24 weeks (Krystal 2008, n=1,018): 'helped me sleep' 89.8% vs 51.4% at week 12 and 92.3% vs 59.7% at week 24; all subjective sleep measures favoured zolpidem ER; no rebound on discontinuation
cards.summary: Zolpidem extended-release 12.5 mg, 3–7 nights per week for 24 weeks (Krystal 2008, n=1,018): 'helped me sleep' 89.8% vs 51.4% at week 12 and 92.3% vs 59.7% at week 24; all subjective sleep measures favoured zolpidem ER; no rebound on discontinuation
cards.type: Phase IIIb multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, zolpidem extended-release 12.5 mg self-administered 3–7 nights/week, 24 weeks
cards.people: 1,018 adults aged 18–64 with DSM-IV chronic primary insomnia (≥3 months of difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep or nonrestorative sleep), randomised to zolpidem extended-release 12.5 mg (n=669) or placebo (n=349), self-administered from a minimum of 3 to a maximum of 7 nights per week for 24 weeks (25-week phase IIIb multicentre study).
cards.result: The primary endpoint — Patient Global Impression item 1, scored favourable ('helped me sleep') — was met by 89.8% on zolpidem ER versus 51.4% on placebo at week 12 and 92.3% versus 59.7% at week 24 (P<0.0001 at both). Zolpidem ER was significantly superior to placebo at every time point for the other global-impression items and Clinical Global Impression–Improvement, and for diary-measured total sleep time, wake after sleep onset and quality of sleep (P<0.0001), sleep onset latency (P≤0.0014) and number of awakenings (months 2–6). Morning sleepiness and ability to concentrate also improved. The most frequent adverse events on zolpidem ER were headache, anxiety and somnolence. No rebound effect was observed during the first 3 nights of discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is subjective — a patient's global impression that the tablet 'helped me sleep' — not polysomnography; the very large placebo response (51.4% favourable at week 12) is part of the result and is printed on the face. Intermittent self-administration (3–7 nights/week, patient's choice) is the tested regimen, not fixed nightly dosing.
cards.source: Krystal AD et al. Long-term efficacy and safety of zolpidem extended-release 12.5 mg, administered 3 to 7 nights per week for 24 weeks, in patients with chronic primary insomnia: a 6-month, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, multicenter study. Sleep. 2008. PMID: 18220081. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zolpidem extended-release 6.25 mg in older adults (Walsh 2008, n=205, mean age 70.2): polysomnographic wake after sleep onset, latency and total sleep time all improved over 3 weeks; some measures worsened for one night after abrupt discontinuation; no next-morning residual effects detected
cards.summary: Zolpidem extended-release 6.25 mg in older adults (Walsh 2008, n=205, mean age 70.2): polysomnographic wake after sleep onset, latency and total sleep time all improved over 3 weeks; some measures worsened for one night after abrupt discontinuation; no next-morning residual effects detected
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in elderly primary insomnia, zolpidem extended-release 6.25 mg nightly, 3 weeks (polysomnographic endpoints)
cards.people: 205 patients (117 women, 88 men; mean age 70.2 ± 4.5 years) with DSM-IV primary insomnia, randomised to 3 weeks of nightly zolpidem extended-release 6.25 mg or placebo; 198 completed the study. Outcomes were polysomnographic (PSG) and self-reported.
cards.result: Versus placebo, zolpidem ER 6.25 mg significantly decreased PSG wake time after sleep onset during the first six hours of the night; PSG latency to persistent sleep was reduced and PSG total sleep time increased at nights 1/2 and 15/16. Patient self-report measures were significantly better on zolpidem ER throughout treatment. Some PSG measures indicated a worsening of sleep for a single night after abrupt discontinuation. No next-morning residual effects were observed, and the overall incidence and nature of adverse events was comparable between the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Only 3 weeks of treatment in older adults — the population in whom hypnotic harms matter most — and the single-night worsening of some PSG measures after abrupt discontinuation qualifies the 'no rebound' message of the other two cards: it is formulation-, dose- and measure-dependent, not a blanket property.
cards.source: Walsh JK et al. Efficacy and safety of zolpidem extended release in elderly primary insomnia patients. The American journal of geriatric psychiatry : official journal of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry. 2008. PMID: 18165461. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three randomised trials, two formulations — immediate-release 10 mg works over 35 nights in a small sleep-laboratory trial (n=75), and extended-release works over 24 weeks of intermittent use in a large trial (n=1,018) and over 3 weeks by polysomnography in older adults (n=205)
cards.summary: Synthesis: three randomised trials, two formulations — immediate-release 10 mg works over 35 nights in a small sleep-laboratory trial (n=75), and extended-release works over 24 weeks of intermittent use in a large trial (n=1,018) and over 3 weeks by polysomnography in older adults (n=205)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Every carded trial favoured zolpidem over placebo on its sleep endpoints, with no tolerance signal over 35 nights (immediate-release) or 24 weeks (extended-release, 3–7 nights/week). The honest limits are printed on the cards: the largest trial's primary endpoint is a subjective global impression with a placebo response above 50%; the immediate-release trial randomised only 75 patients; the elderly trial lasted 3 weeks and showed a single night of polysomnographic worsening after abrupt discontinuation; and the 15 mg immediate-release dose reduced REM sleep without added benefit. Falls, fractures and complex sleep behaviours were not outcomes in any carded trial, so this shelf makes no claim about them in either direction.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Procaterol in asthma (bronchodilator programme, Japan/Asia licensing): matched albuterol over 12 weeks with longer action; matched nebulised salbutamol in acute asthma; cough benefit added to budesonide
shelves.question: In patients with asthma, does procaterol — oral, inhaled or nebulised — versus placebo or another short-acting beta-2 agonist improve lung function and symptoms, in chronic use, in moderate acute asthma, and as an adjunct in cough-variant asthma?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Airway Obstruction · Albuterol · Asthma · Bronchodilator Agents · Child · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Ethanolamines · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Procaterol · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit — bronchodilation only): this is a bronchodilator programme, not an outcomes programme, and it is presented as such. The load-bearing reports are three: a 333-patient 12-week double-blind trial in which procaterol aerosol matched albuterol aerosol on FEV1 with a longer duration of action (effect maintained 4–7 hours versus 3–6 hours, and more patients controlled three times daily); a 140-patient emergency-department trial in moderate acute asthma in which nebulised procaterol matched nebulised salbutamol on peak flow and asthma score; and a 159-patient 8-week trial in cough-variant asthma in which procaterol added to inhaled budesonide improved cough scores more than budesonide plus placebo — a combination (adjunct) limb, labelled as such. The remaining three cards are small or short pharmacodynamic crossovers (n=20, n=20, and one whose fetched abstract states no N — printed as 'N not documented'), labelled and never load-bearing. Endpoints throughout are FEV1/PEF, symptom and cough scores over single doses to 12 weeks; there is no exacerbation, hospitalisation or mortality trial. Procaterol is licensed in Japan and parts of Asia, not in the US/UK.

cards.headline: 12-week parallel trial (Mazza 1992): procaterol aerosol matched albuterol aerosol on FEV1 in 333 outpatients — with a longer action (4–7 hours vs 3–6 hours) and more patients controlled three times daily
cards.summary: 12-week parallel trial (Mazza 1992): procaterol aerosol matched albuterol aerosol on FEV1 in 333 outpatients — with a longer action (4–7 hours vs 3–6 hours) and more patients controlled three times daily
cards.type: Double-blind randomised parallel trial, procaterol aerosol vs albuterol aerosol, 12 weeks
cards.people: 333 outpatients with reversible bronchial airway obstruction, treated with procaterol aerosol (10 µg per inhalation) or albuterol (salbutamol) aerosol (100 µg per inhalation), two inhalations three or four times daily, over 12 weeks in a double-blind randomised parallel study.
cards.result: Pulmonary function tests showed similar improvement in both groups; clinically significant improvement in mean FEV1 was maintained for four to seven hours post-dose for procaterol and three to six hours for albuterol. A significantly higher percentage of procaterol patients (59%) continued on a three-times-daily schedule rather than four times daily, compared with albuterol (48%; P<0.05). Adverse experiences were reported in 15% of procaterol-treated and 17% of albuterol-treated patients, headache and tremor being most frequent, with no significant between-group differences.
cards.watchOut: Active-comparator trial with no placebo arm: it shows procaterol performs like albuterol with a somewhat longer action — it does not by itself quantify benefit against no treatment. Bronchodilator endpoints only; no exacerbation or mortality outcomes.
cards.source: Mazza JA et al. Evaluation of procaterol and albuterol (salbutamol) aerosol in the treatment of asthma. Annals of allergy. 1992. PMID: 1532117. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Acute asthma trial (Mangunnegoro 2011): nebulised procaterol matched nebulised salbutamol in 140 emergency-department patients with moderate acute asthma
cards.type: Randomised double-blind parallel-group trial, nebulised procaterol vs nebulised salbutamol in moderate acute asthma
cards.people: 140 patients with moderate acute asthma (by modified GINA 1998 criteria) attending the emergency department of Persahabatan Hospital, Jakarta, randomised double-blind to three doses of nebulised procaterol or nebulised salbutamol; 68 and 69 patients respectively were analysed for the primary outcome.
cards.result: After treatment there was significant improvement in percentage predicted peak expiratory flow rate (P<0.001) and in asthma score (P<0.001) in both groups, and procaterol and salbutamol produced similar efficacy on both measures; the fetched abstract prints no numeric between-group difference and none is claimed here. Both treatments were well tolerated; palpitation and sinus tachycardia occurred with low incidence.
cards.watchOut: Active-comparator trial in a single emergency department, short-term peak-flow and score endpoints only — no admission, relapse or mortality outcomes are reported in the fetched abstract.

cards.headline: Cough-variant asthma adjunct trial (Bao 2013): procaterol ADDED to inhaled budesonide improved cough scores more than budesonide plus placebo in 159 patients over 8 weeks — a combination limb, not monotherapy evidence
cards.summary: Cough-variant asthma adjunct trial (Bao 2013): procaterol ADDED to inhaled budesonide improved cough scores more than budesonide plus placebo in 159 patients over 8 weeks — a combination limb, not monotherapy evidence
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial, procaterol + budesonide vs placebo + budesonide in cough-variant asthma (adjunct limb)
cards.people: 159 patients aged 18–75 with cough-variant asthma in a prospective randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial in China, receiving inhaled budesonide 100 µg twice daily plus either oral procaterol 25 µg or placebo twice daily for 8 weeks (80 and 78 participants per group after one exclusion).
cards.result: Daily cough score was lower in the budesonide/procaterol group at 8 weeks (0.44 versus 0.73) and 10 weeks (0.36 versus 0.69) (P<0.05). The proportion with a cough-score reduction of 3 points or more was 66% versus 42%, and the proportion scoring 0 points was 63% versus 51% (both P<0.05). Leicester Cough Questionnaire improvement at 8 weeks was superior with procaterol (38.94 versus 32.71 points of improvement as printed; P<0.05). The combination was well tolerated, as the report states.
cards.watchOut: Adjunct limb: procaterol was added to inhaled budesonide in cough-variant asthma — a different population and design from the monotherapy bronchodilator cards, and it must not be pooled with them. Cough scores are symptom endpoints.
cards.source: Bao W et al. Efficacy of procaterol combined with inhaled budesonide for treatment of cough-variant asthma. Respirology (Carlton, Vic.). 2013. PMID: 24188204. cards.headline: Oral crossover versus salbutamol and placebo (Tukiainen 1988): both agents bronchodilated versus placebo on PEF in 20 patients — a small short-period study, never load-bearing
cards.summary: Oral crossover versus salbutamol and placebo (Tukiainen 1988): both agents bronchodilated versus placebo on PEF in 20 patients — a small short-period study, never load-bearing
cards.type: Double-dummy crossover study, oral procaterol vs salbutamol and placebo, 4-day periods (n=20)
cards.people: 20 patients with bronchial asthma in a double-dummy crossover study of oral procaterol 0.1 mg twice daily and oral salbutamol 4 mg three times daily, over four consecutive 4-day treatment periods including two periods of plain placebo.
cards.result: A significant direct bronchodilating effect of both procaterol and salbutamol versus placebo was seen in peak expiratory flow measured four times daily (P<0.01 for both); procaterol was slightly superior to salbutamol, although the doses were not equivalent. Afternoon and evening PEF values during the procaterol period did not differ from placebo. Tremor was significantly more frequent on procaterol than placebo (P<0.01), and both agents produced more palpitation than placebo (P<0.05). The authors concluded the duration of procaterol's effect on twice-daily dosing did not seem long enough in all patients.
cards.watchOut: 20 patients and 4-day periods: a small pharmacodynamic study, labelled and never load-bearing. Its duration finding (effect not lasting the full dosing interval in all patients) runs against the longer-duration reading of the 12-week aerosol trial and is kept on the face for that reason.
cards.source: Tukiainen H et al. Comparison between oral procaterol and salbutamol in patients with bronchial asthma. Current medical research and opinion. 1988. PMID: 2975204. shelves.title: Modafinil for excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy: wakefulness improved in three randomised reports, including a labelled withdrawal trial
shelves.question: In patients with narcolepsy, does modafinil (200–400 mg/day) improve objective and subjective daytime sleepiness versus placebo, and does the benefit persist under randomised withdrawal?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Benzhydryl Compounds · Central Nervous System Stimulants · Circadian Rhythm · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Modafinil · Narcolepsy · Placebos · Reaction Time · Sleep · Sleep Stages · Treatment Outcome · Wakefulness
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). Three randomised reports with three labelled designs agree. Broughton (75 patients, crossover): modafinil 200 and 400 mg increased Maintenance of Wakefulness Test sleep latency by 40% and 54% versus placebo (relative measures), reduced Epworth scores equally at both doses, and did not disturb nocturnal sleep; nausea and nervousness increased only at 400 mg. The U.S. multicentre trial (283 randomised, 9 weeks): modafinil significantly reduced every subjective and objective sleepiness measure and improved global impression, with few, dose-dependent, mostly mild-to-moderate adverse experiences. Moldofsky (labelled randomised withdrawal after 16 weeks open-label): continuing modafinil held MWT latency at 16.4 versus 9.7 minutes and Epworth at 13.2 versus 15.4 versus switching to placebo — evidence the benefit persists on treatment and is lost on stopping, not a fresh placebo contrast.

cards.headline: Broughton 1997 crossover RCT: modafinil 200 and 400 mg increased mean Maintenance of Wakefulness Test sleep latency by 40% and 54% versus placebo (relative measures), with Epworth scores reduced equally at both doses and no effect on nocturnal sleep
cards.summary: Broughton 1997 crossover RCT: modafinil 200 and 400 mg increased mean Maintenance of Wakefulness Test sleep latency by 40% and 54% versus placebo (relative measures), with Epworth scores reduced equally at both doses and no effect on nocturnal sleep
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial, modafinil 200 or 400 mg for excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy
cards.people: 75 patients meeting international diagnostic criteria for narcolepsy, enrolled in a 6-week three-period randomised crossover placebo-controlled trial; patients received placebo, modafinil 200 mg or modafinil 400 mg in divided doses (morning and noon), each for 2 weeks, with evaluations at baseline and at the end of each period.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, modafinil 200 and 400 mg significantly increased mean sleep latency on the Maintenance of Wakefulness Test by 40% and 54% respectively (relative increases, as published), with no significant difference between the two doses. Both doses also reduced the combined number of daytime sleep episodes and periods of severe sleepiness in sleep logs, and the likelihood of falling asleep on the Epworth Sleepiness Scale was equally reduced at both dose levels. There were no effects on nocturnal sleep initiation, maintenance or architecture, on sleep apnoea or periodic leg movements, and neither dose interfered with the ability to nap voluntarily or with nocturnal sleep quantity or quality. Modafinil produced no changes in blood pressure or heart rate in normotensive or hypertensive patients. The only significant adverse effects were at 400 mg, which brought more nausea and more nervousness than placebo or 200 mg.
cards.watchOut: A crossover with 2-week periods in 75 patients — the percentage latency gains are relative to placebo-period values, and the trial cannot address long-term use. No registry ID is in the PubMed record (pre-registration era).
cards.source: Broughton et al. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of modafinil in the treatment of excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy. Neurology. 1997. PMID: 9270575. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: U.S. Modafinil in Narcolepsy Multicenter Study Group RCT (1998): modafinil 200 or 400 mg for 9 weeks significantly reduced every subjective and objective sleepiness measure (Epworth, MSLT, MWT) and improved global impression versus placebo, in 283 randomised patients
cards.summary: U.S. Modafinil in Narcolepsy Multicenter Study Group RCT (1998): modafinil 200 or 400 mg for 9 weeks significantly reduced every subjective and objective sleepiness measure (Epworth, MSLT, MWT) and improved global impression versus placebo, in 283 randomised patients
cards.type: Placebo-controlled double-blind randomised parallel-group multicentre trial (U.S. Modafinil in Narcolepsy Multicenter Study Group), modafinil 200 or 400 mg in narcolepsy
cards.people: 283 subjects with narcolepsy at 18 centres, randomised in a placebo-controlled double-blind parallel-group study to daily modafinil 200 mg, modafinil 400 mg or placebo for 9 weeks, followed by an open-label treatment period. Subjective sleepiness was measured with the Epworth Sleepiness Scale; objective sleepiness with the Multiple Sleep Latency Test and the Maintenance of Wakefulness Test; level of illness with the Clinical Global Impression of Change.
cards.result: Modafinil significantly reduced all measures of sleepiness and was associated with significant improvements in level of illness, as reported in the record (the abstract reports significance without printing the per-measure values). Medication-related adverse experiences were few, dose-dependent and mostly rated mild to moderate. In the open-label extension, efficacy was maintained and the safety profile remained excellent for up to 40 weeks, which the authors read as suggesting tolerance will not develop with long-term use.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports that all measures improved significantly but does not print the numerical effect sizes, so none are claimed on this card. The 40-week tolerance statement comes from an uncontrolled open-label extension and is the authors' interpretation, not a randomised comparison. No registry ID is in the PubMed record.

cards.headline: Moldofsky 2000 — RANDOMISED-WITHDRAWAL design, labelled: after 16 weeks of open-label modafinil, patients randomised to continue modafinil held MWT latency at 16.4 versus 9.7 minutes and Epworth at 13.2 versus 15.4 versus those switched to placebo for 2 weeks
cards.summary: Moldofsky 2000 — RANDOMISED-WITHDRAWAL design, labelled: after 16 weeks of open-label modafinil, patients randomised to continue modafinil held MWT latency at 16.4 versus 9.7 minutes and Epworth at 13.2 versus 15.4 versus those switched to placebo for 2 weeks
cards.type: Randomised double-blind withdrawal trial after 16 weeks of open-label modafinil in narcolepsy — labelled randomised-withdrawal design
cards.people: 69 patients with narcolepsy who had completed a 6-week crossover study of modafinil continued on open-label modafinil (300 ± 100 mg) for 16 weeks; 63 were then randomised double-blind for 2 weeks to continue modafinil at the same dose (n=30) or switch to placebo (n=33). Labelled randomised-withdrawal design: everyone randomised had already been taking, and tolerating, modafinil.
cards.result: A mean modafinil dose of 330 mg continued to produce significantly less excessive daytime somnolence than withdrawal to placebo: Maintenance of Wakefulness Test latency 16.4 ± 13.7 minutes on continued modafinil versus 9.7 ± 7.9 on placebo (P=0.009); Epworth Sleepiness Scale 13.2 ± 5.7 versus 15.4 ± 5.8 (P=0.023); and episodes of severe somnolence and sleep in patient diaries 4.2 ± 5.2 versus 8.2 ± 7.2 (P=0.017). Modafinil had no significant effects on nocturnal sleep, blood pressure, heart rate, the electrocardiogram, weight or mood. MeSH: none in the record for this report.
cards.watchOut: A withdrawal design shows loss of effect on stopping in patients already established on the drug — it is not a fresh placebo contrast in untreated patients and will tend to flatter the drug. The randomised phase lasted only 2 weeks. MeSH: none in the record.
cards.source: Moldofsky et al. A randomized trial of the long-term, continued efficacy and safety of modafinil in narcolepsy. Sleep medicine. 2000. PMID: 10767651. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: modafinil improves daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy across three randomised reports with three different designs — a crossover trial (MWT latency up 40% at 200 mg and 54% at 400 mg versus placebo, relative measures), a 283-patient parallel-group trial (all subjective and objective measures significantly improved), and a labelled randomised-withdrawal trial (continuing modafinil held MWT latency at 16.4 vs 9.7 minutes after 16 weeks of open-label treatment) — with no disruption of nocturnal sleep and harms largely confined to nausea and nervousness at 400 mg

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: Broughton 1997 (75 patients, crossover), the U.S. Modafinil in Narcolepsy Multicenter Study Group trial (283 randomised) and Moldofsky 2000 (63 randomised in the withdrawal phase).
cards.result: The three designs are not interchangeable and are labelled on their cards; the withdrawal report in particular must not be read as a third placebo-controlled efficacy trial in untreated patients. See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Presatovir for RSV in transplant recipients: positive only in the healthy-volunteer challenge model — all three patient trials missed their primary endpoints
shelves.question: In patients with respiratory syncytial virus infection — haematopoietic-cell transplant recipients with upper or lower respiratory tract infection, and lung transplant recipients — does oral presatovir (GS-5806) versus placebo reduce nasal viral load, progression to lower respiratory tract complications, oxygen requirement, respiratory failure and death; and in experimentally infected healthy adults, does it reduce viral load and symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antiviral Agents/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation/adverse effects · Humans · Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections/drug therapy · Respiratory Tract Infections/drug therapy · Transplant Recipients
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no benefit) in patients — a single development programme whose signal never left the challenge model. Four randomised trials, one programme: the human challenge trial in healthy adults (54 infected participants in cohorts 1–4) was clearly positive — viral-load AUC 250.7 versus 757.7 log₁₀ PFUe·hours/mL, mucus weight 6.9 versus 15.1 g, symptom scores lower. All three patient trials then missed their primary endpoints: in HCT recipients with upper respiratory tract infection (189 randomised) the coprimary endpoints were not met at the prespecified α=0.01 (viral-load difference −0.33 log₁₀ copies/mL, P=.040; lower-respiratory complications 11.2% vs 19.5%, P=.11); in HCT recipients with lower respiratory tract infection (60 randomised) the viral-load difference was −0.02 log₁₀ copies/mL, P=.94, with no difference in oxygen-free days, respiratory failure or mortality, and resistance-associated fusion substitutions emerged in 6 of 29 presatovir-treated patients; in lung transplant recipients (61 randomised) the viral-load difference was 0.10 log₁₀ copies/mL, P=0.72, with no benefit on symptoms or lung function. The one positive post-hoc finding (fewer complications in the lymphopenia subgroup, 13.3% vs 64.3%) is hypothesis-generating only. Presatovir was never marketed; development stopped — printed plainly, this is a failed programme, not an antiviral that works in transplant patients.

cards.headline: Human challenge trial (DeVincenzo 2014): presatovir (GS-5806) cut viral-load AUC to 250.7 versus 757.7 log₁₀ PFUe·hours/mL and halved mucus weight in experimentally infected healthy adults — the programme's only positive trial
cards.summary: Human challenge trial (DeVincenzo 2014): presatovir (GS-5806) cut viral-load AUC to 250.7 versus 757.7 log₁₀ PFUe·hours/mL and halved mucus weight in experimentally infected healthy adults — the programme's only positive trial
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled human challenge trial (GS-5806 / presatovir) in healthy adults experimentally infected with RSV
cards.people: Healthy adults inoculated intranasally with a clinical challenge strain of RSV and monitored for 12 days; on a positive RSV test or 5 days after inoculation they were randomised to GS-5806 or placebo in seven sequential cohorts with differing dose schedules (cohorts 1–4: 50 mg first dose then 25 mg daily for 4 days; later cohorts used shorter, single-dose or lower-dose regimens chosen after an interim analysis). The primary analysis population was the 54 participants in cohorts 1–4 who were infected with RSV.
cards.result: Among the 54 infected participants in cohorts 1–4, active treatment gave a lower viral-load AUC (adjusted mean 250.7 vs 757.7 log₁₀ plaque-forming-unit equivalents × hours per millilitre; P<0.001), lower total mucus weight (mean 6.9 g vs 15.1 g; P=0.03) and a lower AUC for change from baseline in symptom scores (adjusted mean −20.2 vs 204.9 × hours; P=0.005). Results were similar in cohorts 5, 6 and 7. Adverse events, including low neutrophil counts and increased alanine aminotransferase levels, were more common among participants receiving GS-5806.
cards.watchOut: An experimental-infection model in healthy young adults, treated at first positive test: it proves antiviral activity against a challenge strain under ideal timing, and it is the only positive trial of the programme — all three trials in actual patients (next cards) missed their primary endpoints.
cards.source: DeVincenzo JP et al. Oral GS-5806 activity in a respiratory syncytial virus challenge study. The New England journal of medicine. 2014. PMID: 25140957. Registry ID: NCT01756482. cards.headline: Phase 2 in HCT recipients with RSV upper respiratory tract infection (Chemaly 2020): coprimary endpoints NOT met — viral-load difference −0.33 log₁₀ copies/mL (P=.040 against a prespecified α=0.01) and lower-respiratory complications 11.2% vs 19.5% (P=.11)
cards.summary: Phase 2 in HCT recipients with RSV upper respiratory tract infection (Chemaly 2020): coprimary endpoints NOT met — viral-load difference −0.33 log₁₀ copies/mL (P=.040 against a prespecified α=0.01) and lower-respiratory complications 11.2% vs 19.5% (P=.11)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of presatovir in HCT recipients with RSV upper respiratory tract infection
cards.people: 189 haematopoietic-cell transplant recipients with RSV upper respiratory tract infection (96 presatovir, 93 placebo), randomised and stratified by lymphopenia (<200/µL) and ribavirin use, to oral presatovir 200 mg or placebo on days 1, 5, 9, 13 and 17, followed through day 28 (January 2015 to June 2017).
cards.result: Presatovir did not significantly affect either coprimary endpoint at the prespecified α=0.01: the time-weighted average decline in nasal RSV viral load from day 1 to 9 (treatment difference −0.33 log₁₀ copies/mL, 95% CI −0.64 to −0.02; P=.040) or progression to lower respiratory tract complications (11.2% vs 19.5%; odds ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.22 to 1.18; P=.11). In a post-hoc analysis among patients with lymphopenia, presatovir decreased complication development by day 28 (2/15 [13.3%] vs 9/14 [64.3%]; P=.008). Adverse events were similar between arms, and the authors concluded presatovir had a favourable safety profile but did not achieve the coprimary endpoints.
cards.watchOut: The lymphopenia result (15 versus 14 patients) is post-hoc and hypothesis-generating only — it was not a prespecified endpoint and cannot rescue a trial that missed both coprimaries at its own prespecified threshold.
cards.source: Chemaly RF et al. cards.headline: Phase 2b in HCT recipients with RSV lower respiratory tract infection (Marty 2020): no virologic or clinical benefit — viral-load difference −0.02 log₁₀ copies/mL (P=.94); resistance substitutions emerged in 6 of 29 presatovir-treated patients
cards.summary: Phase 2b in HCT recipients with RSV lower respiratory tract infection (Marty 2020): no virologic or clinical benefit — viral-load difference −0.02 log₁₀ copies/mL (P=.94); resistance substitutions emerged in 6 of 29 presatovir-treated patients
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial of presatovir in HCT recipients with RSV lower respiratory tract infection
cards.people: 60 patients with confirmed RSV in the upper and lower respiratory tract and new chest X-ray abnormalities (31 presatovir, 29 placebo), randomised 1:1 and stratified by supplemental oxygen and ribavirin use, to oral presatovir 200 mg or placebo every 4 days for 5 doses at 17 centres (January 2015 to March 2017); 59 received study treatment (50 allogeneic, 9 autologous HCT).
cards.result: In the efficacy population (29 presatovir, 28 placebo), presatovir did not significantly reduce the time-weighted average change in nasal viral load through day 9 (−1.12 vs −1.09 log₁₀ copies/mL; treatment difference −0.02 log₁₀ copies/mL, 95% CI −0.62 to 0.57; P=.94), median supplemental oxygen-free days (26 vs 28 days; P=.84), incident respiratory failure (10.3% vs 10.7%; P=.98) or all-cause mortality (0% vs 7.1%; P=.19). Adverse events were similar (80% vs 79%). Resistance-associated substitutions in the RSV fusion protein emerged in 6 of 29 presatovir-treated patients.

cards.headline: Phase 2b in lung transplant recipients (Gottlieb 2023): presatovir did not improve nasal viral load (difference 0.10 log₁₀ copies/mL, P=0.72), symptoms or lung function
cards.summary: Phase 2b in lung transplant recipients (Gottlieb 2023): presatovir did not improve nasal viral load (difference 0.10 log₁₀ copies/mL, P=0.72), symptoms or lung function
cards.type: Phase 2b international randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of presatovir in lung transplant recipients with RSV infection
cards.people: 61 adult lung transplant recipients with symptomatic confirmed RSV infection for ≤7 days, randomised 2:1 to oral presatovir 200 mg on day 1 and 100 mg daily on days 2 to 14 (40 patients) or placebo (20 patients; 61 randomised in total as the record reports), with follow-up through day 28 in an international trial; 54 patients were included in the efficacy analyses.
cards.result: Presatovir did not significantly improve the primary endpoint — time-weighted average change in nasal RSV load from day 1 to 7 — in the full analysis set (treatment difference 0.10 log₁₀ copies/mL, 95% CI −0.43 to 0.63; P=0.72) or in the shorter symptom-duration subgroup (−0.12, 95% CI −0.94 to 0.69; P=0.76). Secondary endpoints — respiratory infection symptoms on the Influenza Patient-Reported Outcomes questionnaire and lung function by spirometry — were not different between groups. Presatovir was generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The programme's last patient trial, published 2023, six years after enrolment in the HCT trials: again no benefit on viral load, symptoms or lung function. The record reports 61 randomised with 40 presatovir and 20 placebo recipients named; the remaining patient's allocation is not stated in the fetched abstract and none is invented here.

cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: One programme, four trials, one positive result — and the positive one is the experiment, not a patient trial. Presatovir clearly reduced viral load, mucus weight and symptoms in healthy adults experimentally infected with RSV (54 infected participants in the primary cohorts). In every real patient population it was then tried in — HCT recipients with upper respiratory infection (n=189), HCT recipients with lower respiratory infection (n=60, with resistance emerging in 6/29 treated), and lung transplant recipients (n=61) — it missed its primary endpoints and showed no clinical benefit. The programme's two drug-resistance reports are secondary reports of these same trials, are not carded as independent trials, and do not change the count. Presatovir was never marketed and development stopped: the shelf records a failed programme whose signal never left the challenge model.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Inhaled liposomal ciprofloxacin (ORBIT) in non-CF bronchiectasis: the phase 3 twins split — ORBIT-4 positive (HR 0.72), ORBIT-3 null (HR 0.99), pooled estimate non-significant
shelves.question: In adults with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa lung infection and frequent exacerbations, does once-daily inhaled liposomal ciprofloxacin (ARD-3150, dual-release liposomal/free formulation) versus placebo prolong time to first pulmonary exacerbation and reduce sputum bacterial density (the ORBIT-2, ORBIT-3 and ORBIT-4 programme)?

shelves.balance: SPLIT — the twin phase 3 trials disagree, and the split is printed wherever this programme is summarised. This shelf cards only the liposomal formulation slice (the dual-release liposomal/free ciprofloxacin product ARD-3150, as the publications name it): the class home, pack #2784, cards only the dry-powder RESPIRE programme plus a meta-analysis, and the two products are not interchangeable. ORBIT-2 (phase 2, 42 adults) cut sputum Pseudomonas density by a mean 4.2 log₁₀ CFU/g versus −0.08 on placebo at day 28 (P=0.002) — a bacterial-density surrogate. ORBIT-4 (304 patients) prolonged median time to first exacerbation (230 vs 158 days; hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.97; P=0.032), while its concurrent twin ORBIT-3 (278 patients) was flatly null on the same endpoint (214 vs 136 days; HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.38; P=0.97), and the pooled estimate was non-significant (HR 0.82, P=0.074). No pooled headline is printed without that split. The programme did not lead to an approved bronchiectasis therapy.

cards.headline: ORBIT-2 phase 2 (Serisier 2013): dual-release liposomal ciprofloxacin cut sputum Pseudomonas density by a mean 4.2 log₁₀ CFU/g versus −0.08 on placebo at day 28 (P=0.002) in 42 adults
cards.summary: ORBIT-2 phase 2 (Serisier 2013): dual-release liposomal ciprofloxacin cut sputum Pseudomonas density by a mean 4.2 log₁₀ CFU/g versus −0.08 on placebo at day 28 (P=0.002) in 42 adults
cards.type: Phase 2 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ORBIT-2), dual-release liposomal ciprofloxacin vs placebo
cards.people: 42 adults with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, at least 2 pulmonary exacerbations in the prior 12 months and ciprofloxacin-sensitive Pseudomonas aeruginosa at screening, in an Australian/New Zealand multicentre trial; dual-release ciprofloxacin for inhalation (liposomal plus free ciprofloxacin) or placebo in three treatment cycles of 28 days on / 28 days off over 24 weeks.
cards.result: The primary outcome — change in sputum P. aeruginosa bacterial density to the end of cycle 1 (day 28) — fell by a mean (SD) 4.2 (3.7) log₁₀ CFU/g on liposomal ciprofloxacin versus −0.08 (3.8) on placebo (P=0.002). Time to first pulmonary exacerbation was delayed (median 134 vs 58 days; P=0.057 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis, P=0.046 per protocol). The treatment was well tolerated, with a similar incidence of systemic adverse events to placebo but fewer pulmonary adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A 42-patient phase 2 trial whose primary endpoint is a sputum bacterial-density surrogate: it establishes antipseudomonal activity of the formulation, never an exacerbation benefit — that claim rests on the phase 3 twins, which split (next cards).
cards.source: Serisier DJ et al. Inhaled, dual release liposomal ciprofloxacin in non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis (ORBIT-2): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Thorax. 2013. PMID: 23681906. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ORBIT-3 phase 3 (Haworth 2019, twin trial 1 of 2): liposomal ciprofloxacin ARD-3150 was flatly null on time to first exacerbation — median 214 vs 136 days, hazard ratio 0.99 (P=0.97)
cards.summary: ORBIT-3 phase 3 (Haworth 2019, twin trial 1 of 2): liposomal ciprofloxacin ARD-3150 was flatly null on time to first exacerbation — median 214 vs 136 days, hazard ratio 0.99 (P=0.97)
cards.type: Phase 3 international randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ORBIT-3), inhaled liposomal ciprofloxacin (ARD-3150) vs placebo, 48 weeks
cards.people: 278 patients in the full analysis population of ORBIT-3 (183 received at least one dose of ARD-3150, 95 placebo), adults with non-CF bronchiectasis, at least two antibiotic-treated pulmonary exacerbations in the previous 12 months and chronic P. aeruginosa lung infection; ARD-3150 (3 mL liposome-encapsulated ciprofloxacin 135 mg plus 3 mL free ciprofloxacin 54 mg) or 6 mL placebo, self-administered once daily for six 56-day treatment cycles over 48 weeks, randomised 2:1.
cards.result: Median time to first pulmonary exacerbation was 214 days on ARD-3150 versus 136 days on placebo — a non-statistically significant difference of 78 days, hazard ratio 0.99 (95% CI 0.71 to 1.38; P=0.97): despite the longer median, the hazard estimate is exactly null. The numbers of adverse events and serious adverse events were similar in both groups. (ORBIT-3 and ORBIT-4 were reported together in one publication; they are carded separately here because they are two distinct trials with opposite results.)
cards.watchOut: One of two concurrent, near-identical phase 3 trials of the same product in the same population — and it found nothing. The contrast between the 78-day median difference and the null hazard ratio is a reminder that medians alone do not summarise a time-to-event result.

cards.headline: ORBIT-4 phase 3 (Haworth 2019, twin trial 2 of 2): liposomal ciprofloxacin ARD-3150 prolonged median time to first exacerbation — 230 vs 158 days, hazard ratio 0.72 (P=0.032) — while the pooled twin estimate was non-significant
cards.summary: ORBIT-4 phase 3 (Haworth 2019, twin trial 2 of 2): liposomal ciprofloxacin ARD-3150 prolonged median time to first exacerbation — 230 vs 158 days, hazard ratio 0.72 (P=0.032) — while the pooled twin estimate was non-significant
cards.type: Phase 3 international randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ORBIT-4), inhaled liposomal ciprofloxacin (ARD-3150) vs placebo, 48 weeks
cards.people: 304 patients in the full analysis population of ORBIT-4 (206 received at least one dose of ARD-3150, 98 placebo), with the same eligibility, product, regimen and 48-week design as ORBIT-3 (previous card), run concurrently in similar geographical regions; 514 patients were screened for ORBIT-3 and 533 for ORBIT-4.
cards.result: Median time to first pulmonary exacerbation was 230 days on ARD-3150 versus 158 days on placebo — a statistically significant difference of 72 days (hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.97; P=0.032), a relative measure. But in the pooled analysis of ORBIT-3 and ORBIT-4 together, median time to first exacerbation was 222 versus 157 days and the difference was non-significant (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.02; P=0.074). Adverse and serious adverse event numbers were similar between groups in both trials, and the authors concluded that the inconsistency between the trials requires further research.
cards.watchOut: The programme's one positive phase 3 result cannot be quoted without its twin: ORBIT-3 (previous card) was null (HR 0.99) and the pooled estimate across both trials did not reach significance. This is a split programme, not a proven therapy, and it led to no approved bronchiectasis treatment.

cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The liposomal slice of inhaled ciprofloxacin in non-CF bronchiectasis is three trials: ORBIT-2 (n=42) proved sputum bacterial-density reduction, a surrogate; ORBIT-4 (n=304) significantly prolonged time to first exacerbation (HR 0.72); ORBIT-3 (n=278) found no effect at all (HR 0.99); and the pooled phase 3 estimate was non-significant (HR 0.82, P=0.074). The ORBIT symptom report and the 2025 endotype analysis are secondary reports of ORBIT-3/4 — programme support, not independent trials, and not carded. The dry-powder ciprofloxacin programme and the class-level question stay homed at pack #2784, aztreonam at pack #4254 and colistin PROMIS at pack #6683; the tested product here, ARD-3150 (dual-release liposomal/free ciprofloxacin), is not interchangeable with the dry-powder product.

cards.search: synthesis synthesis in adults with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, chronic pseudomonas aeruginosa lung infection and frequent exacerbations, does once-daily inhaled liposomal ciprofloxacin (ard-3150, dual-release liposomal/free formulation) versus placebo prolong time to first pulmonary exacerbation and reduce sputum bacterial density (the orbit-2, orbit-3 and orbit-4 programme)? synthesis all reports carded on this shelf. the liposomal slice of inhaled ciprofloxacin in non-cf bronchiectasis is three trials: orbit-2 (n=42) proved sputum bacterial-density reduction, a surrogate; orbit-4 (n=304) significantly prolonged time to first exacerbation (hr 0.72); orbit-3 (n=278) found no effect at all (hr 0.99); and the pooled phase 3 estimate was non-significant (hr 0.82, p=0.074). the orbit symptom report and the 2025 endotype analysis are secondary reports of orbit-3/4 — programme support, not independent trials, and not carded. the dry-powder ciprofloxacin programme and the class-level question stay homed at pack #2784, aztreonam at pack #4254 and colistin promis at pack #6683; the tested product here, ard-3150 (dual-release liposomal/free ciprofloxacin), is not interchangeable with the dry-powder product. see the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Inhaled ciclesonide for COVID-19: six trials, no primary endpoint met anywhere — and one imaging-defined pneumonia-progression harm signal
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with COVID-19 — non-hospitalised with symptoms, hospitalised with mild disease, or hospitalised on oxygen — does inhaled ciclesonide versus placebo, usual care or control shorten symptoms or oxygen therapy, and reduce worsening, emergency visits, admission and pneumonia progression?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adolescent · Adult · Ambulatory Care Facilities · COVID-19 · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucocorticoids · Humans · Male · Metered Dose Inhalers · Middle Aged · Outpatients · Pregnenediones · COVID-19 Drug Treatment
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference) — a consistently negative programme: six randomised trials across three care settings (outpatients, hospitalised mild disease, hospitalised patients on oxygen), and no primary endpoint was met anywhere. The single positive reading is a secondary endpoint (fewer emergency visits or admissions, odds ratio 0.18) inside a primary-negative US trial. The Japanese RACCO trial is a harm limb: pneumonia progressed more often on ciclesonide (39.0% versus 18.8%; relative risk 2.08) on an imaging endpoint, without worse clinical symptoms. Settings and eras are not pooled: pre-vaccination 2020-21 outpatient trials, a hospitalised-on-oxygen trial, and a 2026 trial in a 96%-vaccinated Omicron population are separate limbs. Inhaled budesonide for COVID-19 is a different agent, homed at pack #2213, and is cross-pointed only — its trials are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: US phase 3 outpatient RCT (Clemency 2022): ciclesonide did NOT shorten time to alleviation of all symptoms (median 19.0 days in both arms) — primary endpoint not met
cards.summary: US phase 3 outpatient RCT (Clemency 2022): ciclesonide did NOT shorten time to alleviation of all symptoms (median 19.0 days in both arms) — primary endpoint not met
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre double-blind randomised trial, inhaled ciclesonide vs placebo, non-hospitalised symptomatic COVID-19
cards.people: 400 non-hospitalised adolescents and adults with symptomatic COVID-19 (197 ciclesonide, 203 placebo; mean age 43.3 years), randomised double-blind at 10 US centres (June-November 2020) to ciclesonide metered-dose inhaler 640 micrograms/day or placebo for 30 days.
cards.result: Median time to alleviation of all COVID-19-related symptoms was 19.0 days in both arms, and there was no difference in resolution of all symptoms by day 30 (odds ratio 1.28, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.97). On a secondary endpoint, subsequent emergency-department visits or hospital admissions for COVID-19 were fewer on ciclesonide (odds ratio 0.18, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.85). No participant died.
cards.watchOut: The programme's only positive reading sits in this trial's secondary endpoint while its primary endpoint was flatly negative — the secondary result must not be promoted over the primary. Pre-vaccination 2020 population.
cards.source: Clemency BM et al. Efficacy of Inhaled Ciclesonide for Outpatient Treatment of Adolescents and Adults With Symptomatic COVID-19: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2022. PMID: 34807241. Registry ID: NCT04377711. cards.headline: CONTAIN phase 2 RCT (Ezer 2021): inhaled plus intranasal ciclesonide did not significantly increase symptom resolution by day 7 (40% vs 35%) — stopped early
cards.summary: CONTAIN phase 2 RCT (Ezer 2021): inhaled plus intranasal ciclesonide did not significantly increase symptom resolution by day 7 (40% vs 35%) — stopped early
cards.type: Phase 2 double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (CONTAIN), inhaled + intranasal ciclesonide vs placebo, adult outpatients
cards.people: 203 adults with PCR-confirmed COVID-19 presenting with fever, cough or dyspnoea in three Canadian provinces (modified intention-to-treat: 105 ciclesonide, 98 placebo; median age 35 years, mainly younger adults without comorbidities), treated for 14 days.
cards.result: Resolution of symptoms by day 7 occurred in 42/105 (40%) on ciclesonide versus 34/98 (35%) on placebo — an absolute adjusted risk difference of 5.5% (95% CI -7.8 to 18.8), not significant. The trial was stopped early and may have been underpowered.
cards.watchOut: The intervention combined inhaled AND intranasal ciclesonide — it is labelled as a combined-route limb, not silently folded into the inhaled-only trials. Stopped early; a mainly young, healthy population.
cards.source: Ezer N et al. Inhaled and intranasal ciclesonide for the treatment of covid-19 in adult outpatients: CONTAIN phase II randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2021. PMID: 34728476. cards.headline: COVERAGE RCT (Duvignaud 2022): the ciclesonide arm was halted for futility — day-14 worsening composite 13.2% on ciclesonide versus 11.3% on control
cards.summary: COVERAGE RCT (Duvignaud 2022): the ciclesonide arm was halted for futility — day-14 worsening composite 13.2% on ciclesonide versus 11.3% on control
cards.type: Open-label randomised controlled trial (COVERAGE), inhaled ciclesonide vs control, at-risk outpatients — arm halted for futility
cards.people: 217 at-risk outpatients with documented COVID-19 and symptoms for 7 days or fewer (110 ciclesonide, 107 control; median age 63 years, 72.4% with at least one comorbidity), in an open-label randomised platform trial.
cards.result: The trial's Safety Monitoring Board recommended halting the ciclesonide arm for futility at the first interim analysis. By day 14, the composite primary endpoint (hospitalisation, home oxygen therapy or death) was reached by 14/106 (13.2%) on ciclesonide versus 12/106 (11.3%) on control. Over 28 days, 2 participants died (both control), 4 received home oxygen and 24 were hospitalised (14 ciclesonide, 10 control). Secondary outcomes were similar in both arms.
cards.watchOut: Open-label platform limb stopped for futility: the point estimate favoured control. This is the older, comorbid outpatient population — a different limb from the younger CONTAIN population, and the two are not pooled.
cards.source: Duvignaud A et al. Inhaled ciclesonide for outpatient treatment of COVID-19 in adults at risk of adverse outcomes: a randomised controlled trial (COVERAGE). Clinical Microbiology and Infection. 2022. PMID: 35304280. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: HALT COVID-19 hospitalised RCT (Brodin 2023): ciclesonide did not shorten oxygen therapy (median 5.5 vs 4 days; hazard ratio 0.73) — stopped early for slow enrolment
cards.summary: HALT COVID-19 hospitalised RCT (Brodin 2023): ciclesonide did not shorten oxygen therapy (median 5.5 vs 4 days; hazard ratio 0.73) — stopped early for slow enrolment
cards.type: Multicentre randomised open-label trial (HALT COVID-19), inhaled ciclesonide vs standard care, hospitalised patients on oxygen
cards.people: 98 adults hospitalised with COVID-19 and receiving oxygen therapy at 9 Swedish hospitals (48 ciclesonide, 50 standard care; median age 59.5 years, 68% men), treated with inhaled ciclesonide 320 micrograms twice daily for 14 days versus standard care in an open-label trial (June 2020-May 2021).
cards.result: Median duration of oxygen therapy was 5.5 days on ciclesonide versus 4 days on standard care (hazard ratio for termination of oxygen therapy 0.73, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.11 — a relative measure). The authors calculated that the trial ruled out, with 0.95 confidence, an effect larger than a 1-day reduction in oxygen-therapy duration. Three participants in each group died or received invasive mechanical ventilation (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.15 to 5.32). The trial was discontinued early due to slow enrolment.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and stopped early; the point estimate favoured standard care. This is the hospitalised-on-oxygen limb — it answers a different question from the outpatient trials.
cards.source: Brodin D et al. Inhaled ciclesonide in adults hospitalised with COVID-19: a randomised controlled open-label trial (HALT COVID-19). BMJ Open. 2023. PMID: 36813503. cards.headline: RACCO trial (Terada-Hirashima 2022) — HARM LIMB: pneumonia progressed more often on ciclesonide (39.0% vs 18.8%; relative risk 2.08) on an imaging endpoint
cards.summary: RACCO trial (Terada-Hirashima 2022) — HARM LIMB: pneumonia progressed more often on ciclesonide (39.0% vs 18.8%; relative risk 2.08) on an imaging endpoint
cards.type: Multicentre open-label randomised trial (RACCO), inhaled ciclesonide vs control, hospitalised asymptomatic/mild COVID-19 — imaging-defined harm limb
cards.people: 89 patients admitted to 22 Japanese hospitals with asymptomatic or mild COVID-19 and no signs of pneumonia on chest X-ray, randomised open-label to ciclesonide 400 micrograms three times daily for 7 days or control.
cards.result: Exacerbated pneumonia within 7 days — the primary endpoint, defined on imaging — occurred in 16 patients (39.0%) on ciclesonide versus 9 (18.8%) on control: relative risk 2.08 (95% CI 1.15 to 3.75), a relative measure. The signal was larger in participants with fever on admission and in those aged 60 or older. The authors state the imaging worsening occurred without worsening clinical symptoms.
cards.watchOut: HARM LIMB, labelled as such: the endpoint is pneumonia progression on images, not clinical deterioration — symptoms did not worsen. It is a harm signal to print on the face, not proof of clinical harm, and it comes from a small open-label trial.
cards.source: Terada-Hirashima J et al. Impact of inhaled ciclesonide on asymptomatic or mild COVID-19: A randomized trial. Drug Discoveries & Therapeutics. 2022. PMID: 36288939. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · SARS-CoV-2 · Pregnenediones · Hospitalization · Treatment Outcome · COVID-19 Drug Treatment

cards.headline: Community placebo-controlled RCT (Wark 2026): in a 96%-vaccinated Omicron-era population, time to first recovery was identical (median 7 days in both arms; recovery rate ratio 1.04)
cards.summary: Community placebo-controlled RCT (Wark 2026): in a 96%-vaccinated Omicron-era population, time to first recovery was identical (median 7 days in both arms; recovery rate ratio 1.04)
cards.type: Double-blind placebo-controlled community randomised trial, inhaled ciclesonide vs placebo, vaccinated Omicron-era population
cards.people: 189 people randomised in a community-based double-blind trial (185 completed treatment; 96% COVID-19 vaccinated, Omicron era) to inhaled ciclesonide 320 micrograms daily or matching placebo for 14 days.
cards.result: There was no difference in time to first recovery from all symptoms within 28 days: recovery rate ratio 1.04 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.40 — a relative measure), with median time to recovery 7 days in both arms (P=0.84). No significant differences appeared in secondary outcomes, including time to sustained recovery and respiratory symptoms. Treatment was safe and well tolerated. The authors conclude these results, with the combined placebo-controlled evidence, do not support inhaled corticosteroids for acute COVID-19.
cards.watchOut: Era limb: a highly vaccinated Omicron population is not the 2020-21 pre-vaccination setting of the earlier trials — the null result here closes the modern-era version of the question rather than replicating the earlier limbs.
cards.source: Wark P et al. Inhaled Ciclesonide for Community-Based COVID-19: A Placebo-Controlled Randomised Trial. Respirology. 2026. PMID: 41054293. Registry ID: ACTRN12620000566932. cards.headline: Synthesis: six randomised trials, no primary endpoint met anywhere; one secondary-endpoint positive, one futility stop, and one imaging-defined harm signal
cards.summary: Synthesis: six randomised trials, no primary endpoint met anywhere; one secondary-endpoint positive, one futility stop, and one imaging-defined harm signal
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Outpatients (US phase 3, CONTAIN, COVERAGE, and the 2026 community trial), hospitalised mild disease (RACCO) and hospitalised patients on oxygen (HALT COVID-19) all failed to show a primary-endpoint benefit from inhaled ciclesonide. The US trial's fewer emergency visits/admissions were a secondary endpoint; COVERAGE halted its ciclesonide arm for futility; RACCO found more imaging-defined pneumonia progression on the drug. Budesonide's COVID-19 record (pack #2213) belongs to a different agent and does not transfer.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Camostat for COVID-19: four double-blind trials, all null — no benefit on improvement, viral clearance or symptoms, even at 4–8 times the clinical dose
shelves.question: In adults with COVID-19 — hospitalised, or non-hospitalised with mild-to-moderate disease — does oral camostat mesilate versus placebo speed clinical improvement or viral clearance and reduce hospitalisation and death?
shelves.mesh: none in the record
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a uniformly negative programme, presented as one. Four double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trials of oral camostat mesilate in COVID-19 — two hospitalised (n=205; n=155) and two in mild-to-moderate / non-hospitalised disease (n=342; n=216) — met no primary endpoint anywhere: clinical improvement, viral clearance and symptom resolution were the same on camostat as on placebo, including at four to eight times the Japanese clinical dose in the CANDLE study, which closes the 'underdosed' objection. Camostat was not notably unsafe; it simply did not work. Endpoints, variants and vaccination eras differed per trial and are labelled, never pooled.

cards.headline: Danish hospitalised RCT (Gunst 2021): camostat did not speed clinical improvement — median 5 days in both groups; 30-day mortality hazard ratio 0.82 (0.24–2.79)
cards.summary: Danish hospitalised RCT (Gunst 2021): camostat did not speed clinical improvement — median 5 days in both groups; 30-day mortality hazard ratio 0.82 (0.24–2.79)
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial (hospitalised COVID-19), camostat vs placebo
cards.people: 205 patients hospitalised with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection in Denmark, randomised within 48 hours of admission 2:1 to camostat mesilate 200 mg three times daily for 5 days (137) or placebo (68), double-blind.
cards.result: Median time to clinical improvement (discharge or ≥2-point improvement on a 7-point ordinal scale) was 5 days in both groups (camostat IQR 3–7; placebo IQR 2–10; P=0.31). The hazard ratio for 30-day mortality was 0.82 (95% CI 0.24–2.79; P=0.75) — a relative measure whose confidence interval spans from large benefit to large harm on very few deaths. Adverse events were similar. The day-5 viral-load fall was numerically LARGER on placebo (−0.82 log10 copies/mL) than on camostat (−0.22 log10 copies/mL).
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint was not met, and the viral-load reading must not be softened: it favoured placebo numerically. Era flag: enrolled April–December 2020, an early-variant, pre-vaccination landscape.
cards.source: Gunst JD et al. Efficacy of the TMPRSS2 inhibitor camostat mesilate in patients hospitalized with Covid-19-a double-blind randomized controlled trial. EClinicalMedicine. 2021. PMID: 33903855. Registry ID: NCT04321096. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: CANDLE study (Kinoshita 2022): camostat at 4–8 times the Japanese clinical dose did not speed viral clearance — median time to two consecutive negative tests 11.0 days in both groups
cards.summary: CANDLE study (Kinoshita 2022): camostat at 4–8 times the Japanese clinical dose did not speed viral clearance — median time to two consecutive negative tests 11.0 days in both groups
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial (CANDLE, hospitalised COVID-19), high-dose camostat vs placebo — virological endpoint
cards.people: 155 patients hospitalised in Japan within 5 days of COVID-19 symptom onset (or of a positive test if asymptomatic), excluding severe cases requiring oxygenation/ventilation; camostat mesilate 600 mg four times daily (78) or placebo (77) for up to 14 days, double-blind. The camostat dose was four to eight times the clinical dose used in Japan.
cards.result: Median time to the first of two consecutive negative SARS-CoV-2 tests was 11.0 days in both groups (camostat 95% CI 9.0–12.0; placebo 95% CI 10.0–13.0). Conversion to negative viral status by day 14 occurred in 45 of 74 patients (60.8%) on camostat versus 47 of 74 (63.5%) on placebo. Neither the primary (Bayesian) nor the secondary (frequentist) analysis found a significant difference. No additional safety concerns beyond those already known were identified.
cards.watchOut: This is the dose-escalation limb and it closes the 'underdosed' objection: even at a supratherapeutic dose there was no virological benefit. Patients with severe disease were excluded, so the result speaks to mild-to-moderate hospitalised disease.

cards.headline: Korean phase 2 RCT (Kim 2023): camostat (DWJ1248) did not meet its primary endpoint in mild-to-moderate COVID-19 — median time to clinical improvement 7 vs 8 days, hazard ratio 1.09 (0.84–1.43), P=0.50
cards.summary: Korean phase 2 RCT (Kim 2023): camostat (DWJ1248) did not meet its primary endpoint in mild-to-moderate COVID-19 — median time to clinical improvement 7 vs 8 days, hazard ratio 1.09 (0.84–1.43), P=0.50
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (mild-to-moderate COVID-19), camostat DWJ1248 vs placebo
cards.people: 342 patients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 in South Korea, randomised to oral camostat mesylate (DWJ1248) or placebo for 14 days, double-blind. The primary endpoint was time to clinical improvement of symptoms within 14 days on a subjective 4-point Likert scale.
cards.result: Median time to clinical improvement was 7 days on camostat versus 8 days on placebo — hazard ratio 1.09 (95% CI 0.84–1.43), P=0.50, a relative measure; the primary endpoint was not met. Post-hoc and high-risk subgroup readings (clinical improvement by day 7: 45.8% [50/109] vs 38.4% [40/104]; odds ratio 1.33, 95% CI 0.77–2.31, P=0.31) also did not reach significance. Adverse events were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint was subjective (a symptom Likert scale) and was not met; the nominally favourable high-risk readings are post-hoc/subgroup and non-significant — they do not rescue the trial. Product naming: the tested product was DWJ1248 (camostat mesylate), named as the publication gives it.

cards.headline: ACTIV-2 phase 2 RCT (Jilg 2023): one week of oral camostat in non-hospitalised adults — median time to symptom improvement 9 days in both arms, P=0.99; hospitalisation 5.6% vs 4.7%
cards.summary: ACTIV-2 phase 2 RCT (Jilg 2023): one week of oral camostat in non-hospitalised adults — median time to symptom improvement 9 days in both arms, P=0.99; hospitalisation 5.6% vs 4.7%
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (ACTIV-2, non-hospitalised COVID-19), camostat vs pooled placebo
cards.people: 216 non-hospitalised adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 in the ACTIV-2/A5401 platform trial (109 camostat for 7 days, 107 pooled placebo); median age 37 years; 45% had 5 or fewer days of symptoms at entry and 26% met the protocol definition of higher risk of progression.
cards.result: Median time to symptom improvement was 9 days in both arms (P=0.99). There were no significant differences in the proportion with SARS-CoV-2 RNA below the lower limit of quantification on days 3, 7 or 14. Through day 28, 6 participants (5.6%) on camostat and 5 (4.7%) on placebo were hospitalised; one camostat participant subsequently died. Grade ≥3 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 10.1% on camostat versus 6.5% on placebo (P=0.35).
cards.watchOut: A phase 2 platform-trial limb with a pooled placebo arm and a young population (median age 37) at mostly low risk of progression — event counts are small, but the symptom and viral-clearance results are flatly null, consistent with the other three trials.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a uniformly negative programme — four double-blind placebo-controlled trials, hospitalised and outpatient, and no primary endpoint met anywhere, including at supratherapeutic dose
cards.summary: Synthesis: a uniformly negative programme — four double-blind placebo-controlled trials, hospitalised and outpatient, and no primary endpoint met anywhere, including at supratherapeutic dose
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
cards.result: Synthesis: all four double-blind randomised trials carded above were null on their primary endpoints — time to clinical improvement 5 days in both groups in hospitalised Danish patients (n=205); time to viral negativity 11.0 days in both groups at 4–8 times the clinical dose in CANDLE (n=155); time to symptom improvement 7 vs 8 days, hazard ratio 1.09, P=0.50, in Korean mild-to-moderate disease (n=342); and 9 days in both arms with hospitalisation 5.6% vs 4.7% in non-hospitalised ACTIV-2 participants (n=216). The in-vitro TMPRSS2 rationale did not translate. The shelf's value is the closed question, and it is presented as one: camostat for COVID-19 did not work in any setting or dose tested. Populations, variants, vaccination landscapes (2020–22) and endpoints differed per trial; the trials are labelled, never pooled.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Inhaled interferon beta-1a (SNG001) in hospitalised COVID-19: FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials — phase 2 (n=101) positive, SPRINTER phase 3 (n=623) primary not met
shelves.question: In adults hospitalised with COVID-19, does nebulised interferon beta-1a (SNG001) added to standard care versus placebo improve clinical status, speed recovery and prevent progression to severe disease or death?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adult · Aged · Antiviral Agents · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Interferon beta-1a · Male · Middle Aged · Nebulizers and Vaporizers · Treatment Outcome · COVID-19 Drug Treatment
shelves.balance: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 efficacy reports, stated on the face. The phase 2 pilot (101 randomised, UK, spring 2020, pre-vaccination era) found greater odds of improvement on the WHO Ordinal Scale at day 15/16 (odds ratio 2.32, a relative measure) and faster recovery (hazard ratio 2.19, relative), with 3 deaths on placebo and 0 on SNG001. The SPRINTER phase 3 trial (623 randomised, hospitalised patients requiring oxygen, later era) met NOTHING: median time to discharge 7.0 versus 8.0 days (hazard ratio 1.06, p=0.51), time to recovery 25.0 days in both groups (hazard ratio 1.02), and progression to severe disease or death 10.7% versus 14.4% (odds ratio 0.71, p=0.161 — the abstract's '25.7% relative risk reduction' is a non-significant relative measure and is never printed without its confidence interval and p-value). Serious adverse events were 12.6% versus 18.2%. The arc — a small positive phase 2 followed by a phase 3 six times its size that met no endpoint — is the shelf's answer. Results apply to the tested nebulised SNG001 formulation and do not transfer to systemic interferon preparations.

cards.headline: Phase 2 pilot (Monk 2021, 101 randomised): SNG001 gave greater odds of improvement on the WHO Ordinal Scale (odds ratio 2.32, relative) and faster recovery (hazard ratio 2.19, relative); 3 deaths on placebo, 0 on SNG001
cards.summary: Phase 2 pilot (Monk 2021, 101 randomised): SNG001 gave greater odds of improvement on the WHO Ordinal Scale (odds ratio 2.32, relative) and faster recovery (hazard ratio 2.19, relative); 3 deaths on placebo, 0 on SNG001
cards.type: Phase 2 pilot randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, nebulised SNG001 vs placebo, hospitalised COVID-19
cards.people: 101 adults admitted to hospital with COVID-19 at nine UK sites, March-May 2020, randomly assigned to inhaled nebulised interferon beta-1a (SNG001, 6 MIU daily for 14 days; 50 assigned, 48 treated) or placebo (51 assigned, 50 treated); 67% required oxygen at baseline. Primary outcome was change in clinical condition on the WHO Ordinal Scale for Clinical Improvement during dosing.
cards.result: Patients receiving SNG001 had greater odds of improvement on the ordinal scale at day 15 or 16 (odds ratio 2.32, 95% CI 1.07-5.04; p=0.033 — a relative measure) and were more likely to recover to no limitation of activities during treatment (hazard ratio 2.19, 95% CI 1.03-4.69; p=0.043 — a relative measure). The most frequent treatment-emergent adverse event was headache (15% on SNG001 versus 10% on placebo). There were three deaths in the placebo group and none in the SNG001 group — three events in a 101-patient pilot, not a mortality finding.
cards.watchOut: A 101-patient pilot run in the pre-vaccination, pre-standard-antiviral era (spring 2020); its positive ordinal-scale readings are the small-trial limb of a two-report arc whose large limb is negative — never read alone.
cards.source: Monk PD et al. Safety and efficacy of inhaled nebulised interferon beta-1a (SNG001) for treatment of SARS-CoV-2 infection: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial. cards.headline: SPRINTER phase 3 (Monk 2023, 623 randomised): primary objective NOT met — time to discharge hazard ratio 1.06 (p=0.51), time to recovery 25.0 days in BOTH groups; progression to severe disease or death 10.7% vs 14.4% (odds ratio 0.71, p=0.161, non-significant)
cards.summary: SPRINTER phase 3 (Monk 2023, 623 randomised): primary objective NOT met — time to discharge hazard ratio 1.06 (p=0.51), time to recovery 25.0 days in BOTH groups; progression to severe disease or death 10.7% vs 14.4% (odds ratio 0.71, p=0.161, non-significant)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (SPRINTER), nebulised SNG001 vs placebo, hospitalised COVID-19 requiring oxygen
cards.people: 623 adults hospitalised with COVID-19 who required oxygen via nasal prongs or mask, randomised double-blind to SNG001 (309) or placebo (314) once daily for 14 days plus standard of care. Primary objective was recovery, in terms of time to hospital discharge and time to recovery to no limitation of activity.
cards.result: Median time to hospital discharge was 7.0 days on SNG001 and 8.0 days on placebo (hazard ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.89-1.27; p=0.51 — a relative measure); time to recovery was 25.0 days in both groups (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.81-1.28; p=0.89). There were no significant differences for the key secondary endpoints; progression to severe disease or death occurred in 10.7% versus 14.4% (odds ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.44-1.15; p=0.161) — described in the abstract as a 25.7% relative risk reduction, a non-significant relative measure printed here only with its confidence interval and p-value. Serious adverse events were reported by 12.6% on SNG001 and 18.2% on placebo. The authors state the primary objective was not met, with a favourable safety profile.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK limb: this is one of exactly 2 efficacy reports for this question. SPRINTER ran later than the phase 2 pilot, against evolved standard care — the era difference is labelled, and the two trials are never pooled.

cards.headline: Era and formulation facet (drawn only from the two reports carded above — not a third report): a spring-2020 pilot against a later-era phase 3, testing one specific nebulised formulation
cards.summary: Era and formulation facet (drawn only from the two reports carded above — not a third report): a spring-2020 pilot against a later-era phase 3, testing one specific nebulised formulation
cards.type: Facet card drawn only from the two reports carded above (era, formulation and safety reading) — explicitly not an independent report
cards.people: The same 724 randomised patients in the two trials carded above (101 in phase 2; 623 in SPRINTER). No additional patients and no additional efficacy report are introduced by this card.
cards.result: The phase 2 pilot enrolled in March-May 2020, before vaccination and before standard antivirals, when 67% of its patients required oxygen at baseline; SPRINTER enrolled hospitalised patients requiring oxygen via nasal prongs or mask in a later treatment era. Both trials tested the same intervention — recombinant interferon beta-1a (SNG001) delivered to the lungs by nebuliser, 6 MIU daily for 14 days in phase 2 and once daily for 14 days in SPRINTER — added to standard care. Safety readings were favourable in both (headache the commonest event in phase 2; serious adverse events 12.6% versus 18.2% in SPRINTER), so the phase 3 failure is an efficacy failure, not a tolerability failure. A 2026 viral-evolution report of SNG001 in the separate ACTIV-2 trial (a different, non-hospitalised setting) is a virology report, not an efficacy report for this question, and is not counted or carded here.
cards.watchOut: This card exists to keep the era and formulation facts on the face of a two-report shelf; it adds no evidence. The shelf's efficacy base remains exactly 2 reports.
