cards.headline: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 efficacy reports exist (phase 2, n=101, positive; SPRINTER phase 3, n=623, primary not met), and the arc is the answer
cards.summary: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 efficacy reports exist (phase 2, n=101, positive; SPRINTER phase 3, n=623, primary not met), and the arc is the answer
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the phase 2 pilot (101 randomised) and the SPRINTER phase 3 trial (623 randomised), plus one facet card drawn only from those two reports.
cards.result: A 101-patient phase 2 pilot found greater odds of ordinal-scale improvement (odds ratio 2.32, relative) and faster recovery (hazard ratio 2.19, relative). The 623-patient phase 3 trial that followed met neither its discharge nor its recovery objective (hazard ratios 1.06 and 1.02, relative) and no key secondary endpoint, including progression to severe disease or death (10.7% versus 14.4%; odds ratio 0.71, p=0.161, non-significant). On this two-report base there is no demonstrated efficacy for nebulised SNG001 in hospitalised COVID-19, and the favourable safety profile does not change that. There is no third hospitalised efficacy report to card.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK stated exactly: 2 reports. If either trial had failed to verify this session, this pack would not have been built. See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Nasal nitric oxide reference values by technique: healthy controls 304.6 ± 118.8 nl/min (PCD cut-off 77 nl/min) vs 426.76 ± 143.27 ppb by tidal breathing — never pooled
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference values for nasal nitric oxide — the mean, spread and upper range by measurement technique (breath-hold / velum-closure sampling in nl/min vs tidal-breathing NIOX MINO measurement in ppb) — which subject factors (sex, age, body size, lung function, blood eosinophils) move the value, and how far below the healthy range does the primary-ciliary-dyskinesia cut-off (77 nl/min) sit?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep have no nasal-nitric-oxide reference chapter — this shelf rests on the primary reference literature alone, and says so. Three independent datasets, carded per technique because technique is destiny in this literature: velum-closure aspiration values in nl/min and tidal-breathing NIOX MINO values in ppb are different quantities and are never converted or pooled. The dedicated reference study (Antosova 2017; 141 healthy adults, NIOX MINO per ATS/ERS recommendations) derived reference values and studied the affecting factors, but its fetched record prints no numeric nasal NO values, and none is claimed from it. The numeric anchor in nl/min comes from the healthy-control arm of the primary-ciliary-dyskinesia standardisation study (Leigh 2013; 78 healthy controls, mean 304.6 ± 118.8 nl/min, range 125.5–867.0) — a control group inside a diagnostic study, not a dedicated interval derivation, printed as such — against which the PCD cut-off of 77 nl/min (sensitivity 0.98, specificity >0.999) sits roughly fourfold below the healthy mean. The tidal-breathing dataset (Gelardi 2016; 32 healthy subjects) gives 426.76 ± 143.27 ppb with a wide interval, its small N and width printing beside any range claim. Fractional EXHALED nitric oxide (FeNO, the lower-airway measurement, pack #7154) is a cross-point only — the two are never merged. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (see proposedStamp).

cards.headline: Dedicated reference-values study (Antosova 2017): 141 healthy adults measured by NIOX MINO per ATS/ERS recommendations, affecting factors studied — the record prints no numeric nasal NO values
cards.summary: Dedicated reference-values study (Antosova 2017): 141 healthy adults measured by NIOX MINO per ATS/ERS recommendations, affecting factors studied — the record prints no numeric nasal NO values
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (dedicated reference-values derivation, NIOX MINO)
cards.people: 141 healthy adult volunteers; nasal nitric oxide measured by NIOX MINO (Aerocrine, Sweden) according to ATS & ERS recommendations. Studied as potential variables influencing nasal NO levels: sex, age, height, body weight, waist-to-hip ratio, FEV1/FVC, PEF, and numbers of leukocytes, eosinophils, basophils and monocytes.
cards.result: The study derived reference values for nasal NO in this healthy population and identified the individual parameters that modulate levels, creating a homogeneous group for nasal NO monitoring; its data are offered as reference data for the given variables. There was a significant correlation between nasal NO and exhaled NO, which the authors read as supporting the 'one airway — one disease' concept. The fetched record prints no numeric nasal NO mean, spread or interval, and this card claims none — the numeric values on this shelf come from the two datasets carded below, each bound to its own technique.
cards.watchOut: The only dedicated reference derivation on the shelf is also the one whose record carries no numbers: it establishes that reference values and affecting-factor data exist for a defined young healthy population under an ATS/ERS-conformant protocol, and it must not be quoted for any value.
cards.source: Antosova M et al. Nasal nitric oxide in healthy adults - reference values and affecting factors. Physiological research. 2017. PMID: 28937239. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: PCD standardisation study's healthy controls (Leigh 2013): 78 healthy controls at 304.6 ± 118.8 nl/min (range 125.5–867.0) — the PCD cut-off of 77 nl/min sits far below, at sensitivity 0.98 and specificity >0.999
cards.summary: PCD standardisation study's healthy controls (Leigh 2013): 78 healthy controls at 304.6 ± 118.8 nl/min (range 125.5–867.0) — the PCD cut-off of 77 nl/min sits far below, at sensitivity 0.98 and specificity >0.999
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (healthy-control arm of a multicentre diagnostic standardisation study; nl/min)
cards.people: Multicentre standardisation study (lead site plus six validation sites). At the lead site, nasal NO was measured prospectively in 78 healthy control subjects and 146 disease controls (asthma n = 37, cystic fibrosis n = 77, COPD n = 32), against 149 confirmed primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) patients (143 by ciliary ultrastructural defects, 6 by DNAH11 mutations). The healthy arm is a control group inside a diagnostic standardisation study, not a dedicated interval derivation, and prints as such.
cards.result: Healthy-control nasal NO was 304.6 ± 118.8 nl/min (range 125.5–867.0), against PCD at 20.7 ± 24.1 nl/min (range 1.5–207.3), asthma at 267.8 ± 103.2, COPD at 223.7 ± 87.1 and cystic fibrosis at 134.0 ± 73.5 nl/min — the healthy range overlapped the disease-control ranges but only rarely the PCD range. The disease-specific cut-off was defined at 77 nl/min (sensitivity 0.98; specificity >0.999), roughly a quarter of the healthy mean; at the six other sites this cut-off identified 70 of 71 (98.6%) participants with confirmed PCD. All values are in nl/min under the study's standardised velum-closure protocol.
cards.watchOut: The 77 nl/min figure is a disease-specific diagnostic cut-off for PCD derived against these controls, not a lower reference limit for healthy adults; and the healthy mean comes from a control arm assembled for comparison, measured under one standardised protocol — centres using other protocols or units cannot adopt it directly.
cards.source: Leigh MW et al. Standardizing nasal nitric oxide measurement as a test for primary ciliary dyskinesia. Annals of the American Thoracic Society. 2013. PMID: 24024753. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tidal-breathing NIOX MINO dataset (Gelardi 2016): 32 healthy subjects at 426.76 ± 143.27 ppb (95% CI 160.22–733.30, as published) — men 446.76, women 403.80 ppb
cards.summary: Tidal-breathing NIOX MINO dataset (Gelardi 2016): 32 healthy subjects at 426.76 ± 143.27 ppb (95% CI 160.22–733.30, as published) — men 446.76, women 403.80 ppb
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (dedicated normal-range derivation, tidal-breathing technique; ppb)
cards.people: 32 healthy subjects measured with the NIOX MINO Nasal device (Aerocrine AB, Solna, Sweden) using the tidal-breathing technique with velum closure — a different measurement quantity (ppb) from the nl/min aspiration values of the Leigh dataset, and never converted or pooled with them.
cards.result: The measured normal nasal NO values were 426.76 ± 143.27 ppb, with a 95% confidence interval of 160.22–733.30 as published. Men averaged 446.76 ± 133.63 ppb (interval 178.64–714.02 as published) and women 403.80 ± 154.90 ppb (interval 94.00–713.60 as published). The authors conclude the study establishes the normal range of nitric oxide produced in the nasal/sinus cavities of healthy individuals using this device and the tidal-breathing velum-closure manoeuvre, consistent with values in the international literature.
cards.watchOut: Small (N = 32) and the published interval is very wide (160.22–733.30 ppb around a mean of 426.76): the dataset exceeds the ~10-human reference floor but its range claim carries that width, and its ppb values answer a different measurement question from the nl/min values on the card above.
cards.source: Gelardi M et al. Standardization procedure for the nasal nitric oxide measurement method using Niox MINO® and the tidal-breathing technique with velum-closure. Journal of biological regulators and homeostatic agents. 2016. PMID: 27655510. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: healthy nasal NO sits far above the 77 nl/min PCD cut-off in nl/min terms (healthy mean 304.6), but reference values are technique-bound — nl/min (velum-closure aspiration) and ppb (tidal breathing) are different quantities and are never pooled
cards.summary: Synthesis: healthy nasal NO sits far above the 77 nl/min PCD cut-off in nl/min terms (healthy mean 304.6), but reference values are technique-bound — nl/min (velum-closure aspiration) and ppb (tidal breathing) are different quantities and are never pooled
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by the primary reference literature alone — neither Guyton & Hall nor Boron & Boulpaep carries a nasal-nitric-oxide reference chapter. Antosova 2017 (141 healthy adults, NIOX MINO per ATS/ERS) derived dedicated reference values and studied sex, age, body size, lung function and leukocyte subsets as affecting factors, with a significant nasal–exhaled NO correlation; its record prints no numeric values. Leigh 2013 supplies the nl/min anchor from 78 healthy controls (304.6 ± 118.8 nl/min, range 125.5–867.0) inside the PCD standardisation study, against a disease cut-off of 77 nl/min (sensitivity 0.98, specificity >0.999). Gelardi 2016 supplies the ppb anchor from 32 healthy subjects (426.76 ± 143.27 ppb) under tidal-breathing velum-closure measurement. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the three datasets are independent and mutually consistent in direction (healthy values far above the PCD range), but each is bound to its device and manoeuvre, one prints no numbers in its record, one is a diagnostic study's control arm, and the smallest has N = 32 with a very wide interval. Fractional exhaled NO (FeNO) is the lower-airway measurement, built at pack #7154 — cross-point only, never merged with nasal NO.
cards.watchOut: Never convert ppb to nl/min or average across techniques: sampling flow and manoeuvre define the quantity. A value below 77 nl/min is a PCD-test result under the Leigh protocol, not a statement that any low nasal NO value, on any device, carries the same meaning.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Pleconaril for picornavirus colds: a median 1-day shortening, only in virus-confirmed colds with susceptible isolates — 2 trials in 1 primary publication, plus 1 labelled secondary analysis; never marketed after CYP3A induction
shelves.question: In adults with a naturally acquired common cold, does oral pleconaril started early versus placebo shorten illness — and is any benefit confined to patients whose infecting picornavirus is drug-susceptible?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Antiviral Agents · Common Cold · Diarrhea · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Nausea · Oxadiazoles · Oxazoles · Picornaviridae · Picornaviridae Infections · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — narrowly. One programme: 2 trials reported in 1 primary publication found a median 1-day shorter illness (P<.001) among 1,363 picornavirus-infected participants, with no effect in participants without picornavirus infection; the labelled susceptibility analysis confines the benefit to infections with drug-susceptible isolates (median 1.9–3.9 days gained) and documents resistance emergence in 10.7% of treated patients. Pleconaril induces CYP3A (the oral-contraceptive interaction) and was never marketed. The withdrawn Cochrane version (PMID 17636705) is fenced and not used.

cards.headline: Primary publication — 2 parallel trials (Hayden 2003): among 1,363 picornavirus-infected participants in the two trials combined, median time to alleviation of illness was 1 day shorter on pleconaril (P<.001); NO treatment effect in participants without picornavirus infection
cards.summary: Primary publication — 2 parallel trials (Hayden 2003): among 1,363 picornavirus-infected participants in the two trials combined, median time to alleviation of illness was 1 day shorter on pleconaril (P<.001); NO treatment effect in participants without picornavirus infection
cards.type: Primary publication reporting 2 parallel randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials of oral pleconaril for picornavirus colds
cards.people: Adults with naturally acquired common colds in 2 parallel randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of oral pleconaril started early; 1,363 participants (65% of those enrolled across the two studies) had picornavirus infection — the virology-confirmed limb is the analysed population for the headline result.
cards.result: Among picornavirus-infected participants, the median time to alleviation of illness was 1 day shorter for pleconaril than placebo recipients (P<.001); cold symptom scores were lower and culturable virus was lost faster by day 2. No treatment effects were seen in those without picornavirus infection. Pleconaril was associated with more nausea (6% vs 4%) and diarrhoea (9% vs 7%) and small increases in mean serum cholesterol and platelet counts. A subsequent 6-week prophylaxis study found pleconaril induces cytochrome P-450 3A enzymes, which metabolise many drugs including ethinyl estradiol — the interaction that ended the programme's regulatory path.
cards.watchOut: The entire treatment effect is a median 1-day shortening in the subset with confirmed picornavirus infection, in a self-limiting illness with patient-reported symptom endpoints. This card reports TWO trials in ONE publication — the count is stated in exactly those terms and the publication is never counted twice.
cards.source: Hayden FG et al. Efficacy and safety of oral pleconaril for treatment of colds due to picornaviruses in adults: results of 2 double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2003. PMID: 12802751. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Labelled secondary analysis of the same two trials (Pevear 2005): benefit correlated with baseline isolate susceptibility — median 1.9–3.9-day reduction for highly susceptible viruses (EC50 ≤0.38 µg/mL), NO benefit for less susceptible isolates; reduced-susceptibility or resistant isolates recovered from 10.7% of treated patients
cards.summary: Labelled secondary analysis of the same two trials (Pevear 2005): benefit correlated with baseline isolate susceptibility — median 1.9–3.9-day reduction for highly susceptible viruses (EC50 ≤0.38 µg/mL), NO benefit for less susceptible isolates; reduced-susceptibility or resistant isolates recovered from 10.7% of treated patients
cards.type: Secondary analysis (virological susceptibility) OF the two pleconaril trials — same programme, never counted as a third trial
cards.people: 827 baseline culture-positive nasal samples from the same two trials carded above (420 placebo, 407 pleconaril) — a susceptibility analysis of the primary programme's participants, not a new trial.
cards.result: Pleconaril treatment was associated with more rapid loss of culturable virus (culture-positive samples by day 3: 202 on pleconaril vs 282 on placebo, P<0.0001). Clinical benefit correlated strongly with baseline isolate susceptibility: patients infected with highly susceptible viruses (EC50 ≤0.38 µg/mL) gained a median 1.9- to 3.9-day reduction in symptom duration vs placebo, while patients whose isolates were less susceptible did not benefit. Post-baseline isolates with reduced susceptibility were recovered from 10.7% and fully resistant isolates from 2.7% of pleconaril-treated patients, who shed low virus levels with no unusual clinical outcomes.
cards.watchOut: A secondary analysis of the same patients: it refines WHO benefits (susceptible isolates only) and documents on-treatment resistance emergence in about 1 in 10 treated patients cultured — it adds no independent efficacy evidence.
cards.source: Pevear DC et al. Relationship of pleconaril susceptibility and clinical outcomes in treatment of common colds caused by rhinoviruses. Antimicrobial agents and chemotherapy. 2005. cards.headline: Labelled support — Cochrane review, non-withdrawn version (Jefferson 2001): a multi-agent review of antivirals for the common cold; pleconaril appears among several compounds with antiviral properties — support only, never a trial, and the later WITHDRAWN version of this review (PMID 17636705) is fenced and is NOT carded or cited here

cards.type: Support only: Cochrane systematic review (2001, non-withdrawn version) of antivirals for the common cold — a multi-agent review, not pleconaril trial evidence
cards.people: 241 studies in 230 reports of randomised and quasi-randomised trials of antivirals (interferons, interferon inducers and other compounds) for prevention and treatment of experimental and naturally occurring common colds — a class-level review, of which pleconaril is one small part.
cards.result: The review concluded there are no licensed effective antivirals for the common cold. Pleconaril was listed among compounds that 'appear to have important antiviral properties and are well-tolerated' (protective efficacy against experimental colds 71%, 95% CI 15% to 90% — a relative protective-efficacy measure from experimental-challenge data), with further assessment recommended. Intranasal interferons, the review's largest evidence base, were judged to have no place in everyday use because prolonged administration causes symptoms indistinguishable from a cold.
cards.watchOut: FENCE: the withdrawn version of this Cochrane review (PMID 17636705) is never carded or cited on this shelf; only this earlier non-withdrawn version is carded, as labelled support. A 241-study multi-agent review cannot substitute for pleconaril-specific trial evidence.

shelves.title: Doxofylline vs theophylline and placebo in asthma: 5 reports covering at least 4 and at most 5 distinct trials (the 2002 trial and DOROTHEO 1 may be the same trial reported twice) — theophylline-like lung-function effects with fewer adverse events and drop-outs
shelves.question: In patients with asthma (and, in the older literature, reversible chronic airways obstruction), does oral doxofylline versus placebo — or versus theophylline — improve lung function and asthma events, and does its safety profile differ from theophylline's?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit — a tolerability claim, not an efficacy-superiority claim). Counted as REPORTS, exactly as printed: 5 randomised reports in asthma / obstructive airways disease covering at least 4 and at most 5 distinct trials — the 2002 trial and DOROTHEO 1 may be the same trial reported twice (identical designs, no registry number for either), and they are never presented here as independent confirmations. Wherever doxofylline and theophylline were compared, lung-function effects were similar, with a consistently smaller adverse-event and drop-out burden on doxofylline. No trial was powered on exacerbations or hospitalisation; endpoints are spirometry, symptom/event diaries and rescue use over 28 days to 6 months, on 1989–2002-era background therapy. The DOROTHEO pooled publication is one publication covering two trials, never counted as two. Labelled limbs (COPD crossover; paediatric steroid-sparing pilot) are carded separately and never folded into the asthma count.

cards.headline: 2002 placebo-controlled trial (Goldstein 2002): 346 patients randomised — FEV1 change differed significantly for doxofylline 400 mg and for theophylline against placebo, with few significant differences for the 200 mg dose; significantly more patients interrupted treatment for adverse events on theophylline than on doxofylline 400 mg (p = 0.001)
cards.summary: 2002 placebo-controlled trial (Goldstein 2002): 346 patients randomised — FEV1 change differed significantly for doxofylline 400 mg and for theophylline against placebo, with few significant differences for the 200 mg dose; significantly more patients interrupted treatment for adverse events on theophylline than on doxofylline 400 mg (p = 0.001)
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled multicentre trial, doxofylline (200/400 mg three times daily) vs theophylline vs placebo in chronic reversible asthma
cards.people: 346 patients with chronic reversible bronchial asthma, randomly assigned to 12 weeks of oral doxofylline 400 mg three times daily (high dose), doxofylline 200 mg three times daily (low dose), theophylline 250 mg three times daily (active control) or placebo, in a double-blind randomised placebo-controlled multicentre trial.
cards.result: Changes in FEV1 2 hours after treatment versus baseline differed significantly between doxofylline 400 mg and placebo and between theophylline and placebo, with similar differences on FVC, peak flow and FEF25-75; asthma attack rate and albuterol use decreased remarkably with doxofylline 400 mg and theophylline. There were few statistically significant differences between doxofylline 200 mg and placebo. Significantly more patients had to interrupt treatment because of adverse events under theophylline than under doxofylline 400 mg (p = 0.001); with doxofylline 400 mg, the number treated to spare one drop-out due to theophylline was 5.
cards.watchOut: OVERLAP WARNING (load-bearing): DOROTHEO 1's design (doxofylline 200/400 mg, theophylline 250 mg, placebo, three times daily) is identical to this 2002 trial's design, and the two may be the same trial reported twice — no registry number exists for either (pre-registration era) to settle it. This shelf counts REPORTS: 5 asthma / obstructive-airways reports covering at least 4 and at most 5 distinct trials. The 2002 trial and DOROTHEO 1 are never presented as two independent confirmations.

cards.headline: DOROTHEO pooled report (Calzetta 2018): ONE publication pooling two trials (DOROTHEO 1 and 2), 483 patients pooled — both active drugs significantly increased FEV1 and reduced asthma events and salbutamol use vs placebo (p < 0.01), with no significant difference between doxofylline and theophylline; adverse-event risk was significantly higher on theophylline than placebo but not on doxofylline
cards.summary: DOROTHEO pooled report (Calzetta 2018): ONE publication pooling two trials (DOROTHEO 1 and 2), 483 patients pooled — both active drugs significantly increased FEV1 and reduced asthma events and salbutamol use vs placebo (p < 0.01), with no significant difference between doxofylline and theophylline; adverse-event risk was significantly higher on theophylline than placebo but not on doxofylline
cards.type: Pooled analysis (one publication) of two randomised placebo-controlled trials, DOROTHEO 1 and DOROTHEO 2 — doxofylline vs theophylline vs placebo in asthma
cards.people: Pooled analysis of two multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trials, DOROTHEO 1 and 2, in asthmatic patients aged ≥16 years with FEV1 ≥50% and <80% predicted and ≥15% post-bronchodilator increase; 483 patients pooled on the doxofylline 400 mg / theophylline 250 mg / placebo arms (all treatments oral, immediate-release, three times daily). The two DOROTHEO trials have no separate indexed primary reports — this pooled publication is their only report.
cards.result: Both doxofylline 400 mg and theophylline 250 mg significantly increased FEV1, reduced the rate of asthma events and reduced use of salbutamol as rescue medication compared with placebo (p < 0.01). No significant differences were detected between doxofylline 400 mg and theophylline 250 mg. Doxofylline 400 mg did not significantly (p > 0.05) increase the risk of adverse events compared with placebo, whereas in patients treated with theophylline 250 mg the risk of adverse events was significantly (p < 0.05) greater than with placebo.
cards.watchOut: This pooled publication is ONE report covering two trials — never counted as two publications. OVERLAP WARNING (load-bearing): DOROTHEO 1's design (doxofylline 200/400 mg, theophylline 250 mg, placebo, three times daily) is identical to this 2002 trial's design, and the two may be the same trial reported twice — no registry number exists for either (pre-registration era) to settle it. This shelf counts REPORTS: 5 asthma / obstructive-airways reports covering at least 4 and at most 5 distinct trials. The 2002 trial and DOROTHEO 1 are never presented as two independent confirmations.

cards.headline: 1989 head-to-head trial (Melillo 1989): 139 patients randomised, no placebo arm — both drugs significantly increased spirometry and reduced salbutamol use; unwanted effects 12 on doxofylline vs 37 on theophylline, drop-outs for side effects 5 vs 10
cards.summary: 1989 head-to-head trial (Melillo 1989): 139 patients randomised, no placebo arm — both drugs significantly increased spirometry and reduced salbutamol use; unwanted effects 12 on doxofylline vs 37 on theophylline, drop-outs for side effects 5 vs 10
cards.type: Double-blind randomised multicentre head-to-head trial (no placebo arm), doxofylline vs slow-release theophylline in reversible chronic airways obstruction
cards.people: 139 patients (86 males, 53 females) aged 17–77 years with reversible chronic airways obstruction, in a double-blind randomised multicentre trial of doxofylline 400 mg twice daily (n = 69) vs slow-release theophylline 300 mg twice daily (n = 70) for 28 days, after a one-week wash-out; inhaled salbutamol on demand was allowed throughout.
cards.result: Both drugs significantly increased spirometric parameters (p < 0.001 for all tests) and significantly reduced salbutamol consumption (p < 0.001 for both drugs). Doxofylline was better tolerated than theophylline, considering either the number of unwanted side-effects (doxofylline 12; theophylline 37) or the number of drop-outs due to side-effects (doxofylline 5; theophylline 10). Average serum levels at days 14 and 28 were doxofylline 7.5 and 8.5 micrograms/mL and theophylline 10.4 and 7.95 micrograms/mL.
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm — this report compares the two xanthines only. The 1989 population ('reversible chronic airways obstruction') predates modern asthma/COPD separation and is labelled as such.
cards.source: Melillo G et al. Treatment of reversible chronic airways obstruction with doxofylline compared with slow-release theophylline: a double-blind, randomized, multicentre trial. International journal of clinical pharmacology research. 1989. PMID: 2699466. Registry ID: none in the record. double-blind randomised multicentre head-to-head trial (no placebo arm), doxofylline vs slow-release theophylline in reversible chronic airways obstruction 139 patients (86 males, 53 females) aged 17–77 years with reversible chronic airways obstruction, in a double-blind randomised multicentre trial of doxofylline 400 mg twice daily (n = 69) vs slow-release theophylline 300 mg twice daily (n = 70) for 28 days, after a one-week wash-out; inhaled salbutamol on demand was allowed throughout. both drugs significantly increased spirometric parameters (p < 0.001 for all tests) and significantly reduced salbutamol consumption (p < 0.001 for both drugs). doxofylline was better tolerated than theophylline, considering either the number of unwanted side-effects (doxofylline 12; theophylline 37) or the number of drop-outs due to side-effects (doxofylline 5; theophylline 10). average serum levels at days 14 and 28 were doxofylline 7.5 and 8.5 micrograms/ml and theophylline 10.4 and 7.95 micrograms/ml. no placebo arm — this report compares the two xanthines only. the 1989 population ('reversible chronic airways obstruction') predates modern asthma/copd separation and is labelled as such. melillo g et al. treatment of reversible chronic airways obstruction with doxofylline compared with slow-release theophylline: a double-blind, randomized, multicentre trial. international journal of clinical pharmacology research. 1989. pmid: 2699466. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · albuterol/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · delayed-action preparations · double-blind method · female · humans · lung diseases, obstructive/drug therapy/physiopathology · male · middle aged · multicenter studies as topic · randomized controlled trials as topic · respiratory function tests · theophylline/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use

cards.headline: Indian add-on pilot (Rajanandh 2014): 167 recruited, 123 completed — among budesonide add-ons, FEV1 improvement ranked formoterol first, then doxofylline, then montelukast, then tiotropium at day 90
cards.summary: Indian add-on pilot (Rajanandh 2014): 167 recruited, 123 completed — among budesonide add-ons, FEV1 improvement ranked formoterol first, then doxofylline, then montelukast, then tiotropium at day 90
cards.type: Randomised four-arm pilot comparison of budesonide add-ons (formoterol, doxofylline, montelukast, tiotropium) in mild-to-moderate persistent asthma
cards.people: Patients with mild-to-moderate persistent asthma, randomly allocated to four groups receiving budesonide 400 µg with formoterol 12 µg, doxofylline 400 mg, montelukast 10 mg or tiotropium 18 µg for 3 months; 167 patients were recruited and 123 completed the study.
cards.result: Significant within-group improvement in FEV1 was observed in all groups. At day 90, the between-group difference showed improvement in FEV1 was significantly (P < 0.05) highest for budesonide plus formoterol, followed by budesonide plus doxofylline, budesonide plus montelukast and lastly budesonide plus tiotropium. Within-group comparison also showed a significant (P < 0.05) reduction in rescue medication use in all groups, most intense in the formoterol group, followed by doxofylline, montelukast and tiotropium.
cards.watchOut: An unblinded comparison against other controllers with budesonide in every arm — not a placebo-controlled doxofylline test. This report and the 2015 report below come from one group with near-identical designs and may share a programme lineage; they are counted as two reports with that flag, never silently as independent confirmations.
cards.source: Rajanandh MG et al. Pulmonary function assessment in mild to moderate persistent asthma patients receiving montelukast, doxofylline, and tiotropium with budesonide: a randomized controlled study. Clinical therapeutics. 2014. PMID: 24650447. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Indian add-on trial (Rajanandh 2015): 297 patients completed 6 months — among the second-line options, montelukast improved outcomes fastest, ahead of doxofylline and tiotropium
cards.summary: Indian add-on trial (Rajanandh 2015): 297 patients completed 6 months — among the second-line options, montelukast improved outcomes fastest, ahead of doxofylline and tiotropium
cards.type: Randomised comparison of budesonide add-ons (formoterol, montelukast, doxofylline, tiotropium) in mild-to-moderate persistent asthma
cards.people: Patients with mild-to-moderate persistent asthma, all concurrently using inhaled budesonide 400 µg, treated for 6 months with formoterol 12 µg, montelukast 10 mg, doxofylline 400 mg or tiotropium 18 µg; 297 patients completed the study.
cards.result: In all four groups, significant improvements were observed in all outcome measures, with formoterol having greater and earlier improvements than the other three second-line controller medications with budesonide. Among the second-line treatments, montelukast improved FEV1 from day 45 (P < 0.01), St George's Respiratory Questionnaire scores from day 30 (P < 0.0001), daytime and nighttime symptom scores from day 30, and rescue medication use from day 15 (P < 0.0001) at a faster rate than doxofylline or tiotropium with budesonide. No patients discontinued treatment because of adverse reactions. The authors note that further studies with blinding techniques are likely to be useful.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded, budesonide in every arm, and doxofylline was not the leading second-line option here — montelukast was faster. Same group and near-identical design as the 2014 pilot above: counted as two reports with that lineage flag, never silently as independent confirmations.
cards.source: Rajanandh MG et al. Assessment of montelukast, doxofylline, and tiotropium with budesonide for the treatment of asthma: which is the best among the second-line treatment? A randomized trial. Clinical therapeutics. 2015. PMID: 25577543. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: LABELLED LIMB — COPD crossover (Saiphoklang 2025): 20 patients randomised — doxofylline improved post-bronchodilator flow measures vs procaterol but not dyspnoea, CAT score or walk distance; neurological adverse events 35% vs 5% (p = 0.044)
cards.summary: LABELLED LIMB — COPD crossover (Saiphoklang 2025): 20 patients randomised — doxofylline improved post-bronchodilator flow measures vs procaterol but not dyspnoea, CAT score or walk distance; neurological adverse events 35% vs 5% (p = 0.044)
cards.type: LABELLED LIMB (stable COPD, active-comparator crossover) — doxofylline vs procaterol; never folded into the asthma count
cards.people: 20 patients with clinically stable COPD in a crossover randomised controlled trial, receiving doxofylline or the oral beta-agonist procaterol for 4 weeks each, with a 1-week washout; mean age 71.7 ± 9.4 years.
cards.result: After four weeks, the doxofylline group showed significantly greater improvement in post-bronchodilator peak expiratory flow and post-bronchodilator forced expiratory flow 25–75 compared with procaterol. There were no significant differences in modified Medical Research Council dyspnoea scores, COPD Assessment Test scores or 6-minute walking distance. More neurological adverse events were observed with doxofylline than procaterol (35% vs 5%, p = 0.044).
cards.watchOut: A labelled COPD limb, not asthma evidence: 20 patients, an active comparator, spirometry-only benefit, and a neurological adverse-event excess on doxofylline in this small crossover — the tolerability advantage seen against theophylline does not extend to this comparison.
cards.source: Saiphoklang N et al. Effects of Oral Doxofylline and Procaterol on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: A Randomized Crossover Study. Medical sciences (Basel, Switzerland). 2025. PMID: 40407544. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: LABELLED LIMB — paediatric steroid-sparing pilot (González-Díaz 2024): 61 children randomised in an open-label crossover pilot — every child received doxofylline, so the comparison is of steroid dose, not of doxofylline against control
cards.summary: LABELLED LIMB — paediatric steroid-sparing pilot (González-Díaz 2024): 61 children randomised in an open-label crossover pilot — every child received doxofylline, so the comparison is of steroid dose, not of doxofylline against control
cards.type: LABELLED LIMB (paediatric steroid-sparing pilot, open-label crossover) — doxofylline plus standard-dose vs reduced-dose budesonide sequences; never folded into the asthma count
cards.people: 61 Mexican children aged 6–16 years with asthma, treated with inhaled corticosteroids for at least 8 weeks before enrolment, randomised in a 10-week open-label crossover pilot to sequences of doxofylline 18 mg/kg/day plus standard-dose budesonide and doxofylline plus reduced-dose budesonide (group A n = 31, group B n = 30), 4 weeks per period.
cards.result: Combined use of doxofylline and inhaled corticosteroids may allow children with asthma to reduce their daily dose of inhaled corticosteroids while maintaining lung function and improving asthma control (p = 0.008). There were few asthma exacerbations and only one patient required treatment with systemic corticosteroids. Rescue medication use decreased significantly in patients receiving doxofylline plus standard-dose budesonide during the first 4-week period. The authors state that longer-term, controlled studies are needed to confirm these observations.
cards.watchOut: A labelled paediatric limb, not asthma efficacy evidence for doxofylline: every child received doxofylline, so the comparison is of budesonide dose; open-label pilot, 4-week periods.
cards.source: González-Díaz SN et al. Doxofylline as a steroid-sparing treatment in Mexican children with asthma. The Journal of asthma : official journal of the Association for the Care of Asthma. 2024. PMID: 38153316. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: 5 reports covering at least 4 and at most 5 distinct trials — doxofylline performs like theophylline on lung function wherever the two were compared, with a consistently smaller adverse-event and drop-out burden: a tolerability claim, not an efficacy-superiority claim
cards.summary: Synthesis: 5 reports covering at least 4 and at most 5 distinct trials — doxofylline performs like theophylline on lung function wherever the two were compared, with a consistently smaller adverse-event and drop-out burden: a tolerability claim, not an efficacy-superiority claim
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the 2002 placebo-controlled trial (346 randomised), the DOROTHEO pooled publication (one publication covering two trials, 483 pooled), the 1989 head-to-head trial (139 randomised, no placebo arm) and the two Indian budesonide add-on reports from one group (167 recruited / 123 completed; 297 completed) — 5 reports, at least 4 and at most 5 distinct trials. Two labelled limbs (COPD crossover, n = 20; paediatric steroid-sparing pilot, n = 61) are carded separately and never counted.
cards.result: Never counted on this shelf: the LESDA study (a one-year open-label single-arm safety cohort), the 2023 COPD adjuvant study (explicitly non-randomised) and the terbutaline-plus-doxofylline study (a combination question). Neighbouring xanthine homes — low-dose theophylline in COPD (pack #2519), intravenous aminophylline in acute asthma (pack #7418) and zileuton versus theophylline in chronic asthma (pack #7281) — ask different questions and share no anchor. OVERLAP WARNING (load-bearing): DOROTHEO 1's design (doxofylline 200/400 mg, theophylline 250 mg, placebo, three times daily) is identical to this 2002 trial's design, and the two may be the same trial reported twice — no registry number exists for either (pre-registration era) to settle it. This shelf counts REPORTS: 5 asthma / obstructive-airways reports covering at least 4 and at most 5 distinct trials. The 2002 trial and DOROTHEO 1 are never presented as two independent confirmations.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Peginterferon lambda for COVID-19 — SPLIT by limb: TOGETHER (outpatients) found hospitalisation or prolonged emergency care in 2.7% vs 5.6% (relative risk 0.49, relative), the small outpatient trials split, and the hospitalised trial was null and stopped early; all trials are pre-Omicron era
shelves.question: In outpatients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19, and in hospitalised patients with COVID-19, does peginterferon lambda versus placebo prevent clinical events (hospitalisation or prolonged emergency care), speed viral clearance, or shorten symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Bayes Theorem · COVID-19/therapy · Double-Blind Method · Interferon Lambda/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Polyethylene Glycols/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · SARS-CoV-2 · Treatment Outcome · COVID-19 Drug Treatment · Ambulatory Care · Injections, Subcutaneous · Antiviral Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · COVID-19 Vaccines/therapeutic use · Vaccination
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the limb split is the answer, and this shelf is never readable as 'peginterferon lambda treats COVID-19' without it. Outpatient limb: the one large trial (TOGETHER, 1,951 assigned) is positive on clinical events — hospitalisation or emergency-department visit >6 h within 28 days in 2.7% vs 5.6% (relative risk 0.49, a relative measure beside its absolute rates) — while the two small outpatient trials are split (a viral-load signal with a non-significant unadjusted primary in Toronto; fully null on shedding and symptoms at Stanford). Hospitalised limb: null, in a trial stopped prematurely (WHO-severity global odds ratio 0.76 [95% CI 0.35–1.66], p = 0.49). ERA FLAG (load-bearing): all four trials ran in the pre-Omicron / early-vaccine era against variants that no longer circulate, in populations whose vaccination and prior-infection status differs from today's. Peginterferon lambda is investigational for this use; generic name only.

cards.headline: TOGETHER (Reis 2023): 933 patients assigned to pegylated interferon lambda and 1,018 to placebo — the primary outcome (hospitalisation or emergency-department visit >6 h within 28 days) occurred in 2.7% vs 5.6%; relative risk 0.49 (95% Bayesian credible interval 0.30–0.76), a relative measure beside its absolute rates
cards.summary: TOGETHER (Reis 2023): 933 patients assigned to pegylated interferon lambda and 1,018 to placebo — the primary outcome (hospitalisation or emergency-department visit >6 h within 28 days) occurred in 2.7% vs 5.6%; relative risk 0.49 (95% Bayesian credible interval 0.30–0.76), a relative measure beside its absolute rates
cards.type: Randomised controlled adaptive platform trial (TOGETHER), single-dose pegylated interferon lambda vs placebo in predominantly vaccinated COVID-19 outpatients
cards.people: Predominantly vaccinated adults (83% vaccinated) with acute symptomatic COVID-19 in Brazil and Canada, presenting within 7 days of symptom onset, randomised in an adaptive platform trial to a single subcutaneous injection of pegylated interferon lambda 180 µg (933 assigned, 931 analysed after 2 exclusions) or placebo (1,018 assigned; single injection or oral placebo).
cards.result: A total of 25 of 931 patients (2.7%) in the interferon group had a primary-outcome event, compared with 57 of 1018 (5.6%) in the placebo group — relative risk 0.49 (95% Bayesian credible interval 0.30 to 0.76; posterior probability of superiority to placebo >99.9%), a relative measure printed beside its absolute rates (2.7% vs 5.6%). Secondary outcomes were generally consistent, including Covid-19-related hospitalisation or death (hazard ratio 0.59; 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.35 to 0.97, also a relative measure) and time to hospitalisation for Covid-19 (hazard ratio 0.57; 0.33 to 0.95). Effects were consistent across dominant variants and independent of vaccination status, and patients with a high baseline viral load had lower viral loads by day 7 on interferon lambda. The incidence of adverse events was similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Design flags, printed as reported: TOGETHER's placebo arm mixed injected and oral placebo, and its analysis is Bayesian (credible intervals, not confidence intervals). cards.headline: Toronto phase 2 (Feld 2021): 60 outpatients randomised — viral-load decline was greater on peginterferon lambda from day 3 (difference 2.42 log copies/mL at day 7, p = 0.0041), but day-7 undetectable virus was 80% vs 63% (p = 0.15): the primary endpoint was not significant unadjusted
cards.summary: Toronto phase 2 (Feld 2021): 60 outpatients randomised — viral-load decline was greater on peginterferon lambda from day 3 (difference 2.42 log copies/mL at day 7, p = 0.0041), but day-7 undetectable virus was 80% vs 63% (p = 0.15): the primary endpoint was not significant unadjusted
cards.type: Phase 2 double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial, single-dose peginterferon lambda in COVID-19 outpatients (Toronto)
cards.people: 60 outpatients (30 per group) with laboratory-confirmed mild-to-moderate COVID-19, randomly assigned double-blind to a single subcutaneous injection of peginterferon lambda 180 µg or placebo within 7 days of symptom onset or first positive swab if asymptomatic, between May and September 2020.
cards.result: The decline in SARS-CoV-2 RNA was greater in those treated with peginterferon lambda than placebo from day 3 onwards, with a difference of 2.42 log copies per mL at day 7 (p = 0.0041). By day 7, 24 of 30 (80%) participants in the peginterferon lambda group had an undetectable viral load, compared with 19 of 30 (63%) in the placebo group (p = 0.15) — the primary endpoint, not significant in the unadjusted intention-to-treat analysis. After controlling for baseline viral load in the prespecified adjusted analysis, patients on peginterferon lambda were more likely to have undetectable virus by day 7 (odds ratio 4.12 [95% CI 1.15–16.73; p = 0.029], a relative measure). Peginterferon lambda was well tolerated; mild and transient aminotransferase increases were more frequent on peginterferon lambda, with one grade 3 increase in each group.
cards.watchOut: A viral-load signal in 60 patients whose unadjusted primary endpoint (day-7 undetectable virus) was not significant — the adjusted analysis is printed as the prespecified analysis it was, never as a rescued primary. cards.headline: Stanford phase 2 (Jagannathan 2021): 120 outpatients randomised, single-blind — median time to cessation of viral shedding was 7 days in both arms (hazard ratio 0.81 [95% CI 0.56–1.19]) and symptoms resolved in 8 vs 9 days (hazard ratio 0.94 [95% CI 0.64–1.39]): null on both endpoints; liver-transaminase elevations 15/60 vs 5/60 (p = 0.027)
cards.summary: Stanford phase 2 (Jagannathan 2021): 120 outpatients randomised, single-blind — median time to cessation of viral shedding was 7 days in both arms (hazard ratio 0.81 [95% CI 0.56–1.19]) and symptoms resolved in 8 vs 9 days (hazard ratio 0.94 [95% CI 0.64–1.39]): null on both endpoints; liver-transaminase elevations 15/60 vs 5/60 (p = 0.027)
cards.type: Randomised single-blind placebo-controlled trial, single-dose peginterferon lambda-1a in outpatients with uncomplicated COVID-19 (Stanford)
cards.people: 120 outpatients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19, randomised single-blind to a single 180 µg subcutaneous dose of peginterferon lambda-1a (n = 60) or placebo (n = 60) within 72 hours of diagnosis; the primary endpoint was duration of viral shedding and the secondary endpoint was symptom duration.
cards.result: In both groups the median time to cessation of viral shedding was 7 days (hazard ratio 0.81; 95% CI 0.56 to 1.19 — a relative measure). Symptoms resolved in 8 days on peginterferon lambda and 9 days on placebo, with no significant difference (hazard ratio 0.94; 95% CI 0.64 to 1.39). Both treatments were well tolerated, though liver transaminase elevations were more common in the peginterferon lambda arm (15/60 vs 5/60; p = 0.027). The authors concluded that a single dose neither shortened viral shedding nor improved symptoms in outpatients with uncomplicated COVID-19.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind, not double-blind — printed as reported. A complete null on both endpoints in the same outpatient setting where TOGETHER later found a clinical-event benefit: the limbs and endpoints differ (shedding/symptoms here, hospitalisation events there), and neither result cancels the other. ERA FLAG (load-bearing): all four trials on this shelf ran in the pre-Omicron / early-vaccine era against variants that no longer circulate, in populations whose vaccination and prior-infection status differs from today's.

cards.headline: Hospitalised-patient trial (Kandel 2025): 97 patients enrolled, 94 contributing outcomes — WHO-severity global odds ratio 0.76 (95% CI 0.35–1.66), p = 0.49, and the probability of a >1-day shorter hospital stay was 0.04; the trial was stopped prematurely as the pandemic changed
cards.summary: Hospitalised-patient trial (Kandel 2025): 97 patients enrolled, 94 contributing outcomes — WHO-severity global odds ratio 0.76 (95% CI 0.35–1.66), p = 0.49, and the probability of a >1-day shorter hospital stay was 0.04; the trial was stopped prematurely as the pandemic changed
cards.type: Phase 2 placebo-controlled randomised trial (stopped prematurely), two-dose peginterferon λ in hospitalised patients with COVID-19
cards.people: 97 individuals admitted to hospital with COVID-19, within 10 days of symptom onset and receiving <6 L/min of supplemental oxygen, recruited at seven sites in Canada and Brazil (November 2020 to December 2022) and randomised to two 180 µg subcutaneous doses of peginterferon λ (at enrolment and day 5) or placebo; 94 contributed outcome information for the day-14 WHO COVID severity scale primary outcome.
cards.result: The global odds ratio of peginterferon λ leading to improved outcomes according to the WHO severity scale was 0.76 (95% CI 0.35–1.66; p = 0.49) — a relative measure with no significant difference. Clinical trajectories were similar between the groups, and the probability that peginterferon λ, compared with placebo, led to a >1-day reduction in duration of hospitalisation was 0.04. No safety concerns were identified. The trial was stopped prematurely due to the changing conditions of the pandemic, and the authors concluded that no apparent benefit was identified in hospitalised patients.
cards.watchOut: The hospitalised limb is null and the trial stopped early — it is never pooled with the outpatient limb. This record carries no registry ID, and its source line says so. ERA FLAG (load-bearing): all four trials on this shelf ran in the pre-Omicron / early-vaccine era against variants that no longer circulate, in populations whose vaccination and prior-infection status differs from today's.

shelves.title: Pimodivir for influenza A (one programme: 4 reports covering 5 trials): viral-load primaries consistently met, but the phase 3 hospital study was null and the outpatient phase 3 gain was 12.5 hours of symptom time
shelves.question: In patients with influenza A infection — challenged healthy volunteers, uncomplicated outpatients, hospitalised patients, and high-risk outpatients — does pimodivir (alone or with oseltamivir) versus placebo (with or without oseltamivir) reduce viral load, shorten symptoms, or prevent complications?

shelves.balance: One programme only — 4 publications covering 5 trials (challenge study, TOPAZ, OPAL, and two phase 3 studies in one publication) — stated in exactly those terms. The virologic arc is consistent: pimodivir significantly reduced viral shedding in the challenge model and viral-load AUC to day 8 in TOPAZ (combination −8.6 day·log10 copies/mL [95% CI −12.0 to −5.1]). The clinical arc is thin and split: OPAL's symptom and complication readings are secondary readings of a pharmacokinetic-primary trial; the phase 3 hospital study showed no clinical benefit on the day-6 Hospital Recovery Scale (common odds ratio 0.943 [95% CI 0.609–1.462], P = .397 — a relative measure), while the phase 3 outpatient study found median time to resolution of 7 symptoms 92.6 h vs 105.1 h (P = .0216) — a 12.5-hour difference. The programme was discontinued. Pimodivir (development code JNJ-63623872) is an investigational antiviral that was never marketed — stated plainly under the clarification exception. Every positive primary in this programme is a viral-load endpoint; symptom and complication readings are secondary or trend-only.

cards.headline: Challenge study (Trevejo 2018): pimodivir significantly reduced viral shedding in 104 inoculated volunteers (pooled P = 0.036); in the 1,200/600 mg group, qRT-PCR shedding AUC was 0.45 vs 18.4 log10 copies/mL·day for pooled placebo (P = 0.014) — a challenge-model limb
cards.summary: Challenge study (Trevejo 2018): pimodivir significantly reduced viral shedding in 104 inoculated volunteers (pooled P = 0.036); in the 1,200/600 mg group, qRT-PCR shedding AUC was 0.45 vs 18.4 log10 copies/mL·day for pooled placebo (P = 0.014) — a challenge-model limb
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase IIa human challenge study, pimodivir in experimentally inoculated healthy volunteers
cards.people: 104 healthy volunteers inoculated with influenza A/Wisconsin/67/2005 (H3N2) challenge virus; 72 received pimodivir and 32 placebo, dosed once daily for 5 days from 24 h after inoculation at four dose levels (100 mg, 400 mg, loading dose 900/600 mg, loading dose 1,200/600 mg).
cards.result: Pimodivir significantly reduced viral shedding AUC (by cell culture assay) versus placebo in the pooled analysis (P = 0.036). In the 1,200/600 mg group, viral shedding AUC by qRT-PCR was 0.45 vs 18.4 log10 copies/mL·day for pooled placebo (P = 0.014). Reductions in influenza-like and clinical symptoms were also seen, significantly so for the 1,200/600 mg group. No serious adverse events or adverse events leading to discontinuation were reported.
cards.watchOut: A challenge model in healthy volunteers, not natural infection in patients — a virologic proof-of-concept limb, never an efficacy confirmation in clinical influenza.

cards.headline: TOPAZ (Finberg 2019): viral-load AUC to day 8 significantly decreased on pimodivir 300 mg (−3.6), 600 mg (−4.5) and pimodivir + oseltamivir (−8.6 day·log10 copies/mL) vs placebo; only a trend for shorter symptom resolution; trial stopped early because the virologic primary was met
cards.summary: TOPAZ (Finberg 2019): viral-load AUC to day 8 significantly decreased on pimodivir 300 mg (−3.6), 600 mg (−4.5) and pimodivir + oseltamivir (−8.6 day·log10 copies/mL) vs placebo; only a trend for shorter symptom resolution; trial stopped early because the virologic primary was met
cards.type: Randomised double-blind phase 2b trial (TOPAZ), pimodivir alone or with oseltamivir in acute uncomplicated influenza A
cards.people: 292 patients randomised with acute uncomplicated influenza A; 223 were treated and had confirmed influenza A infection. Twice-daily treatment for 5 days: placebo, pimodivir 300 mg, pimodivir 600 mg, or pimodivir 600 mg plus oseltamivir 75 mg.
cards.result: Viral-load AUC from baseline to day 8 significantly decreased in all active groups vs placebo: 300 mg −3.6 day·log10 copies/mL (95% CI −7.1 to −0.1), 600 mg −4.5 (95% CI −8.0 to −1.0), combination −8.6 (95% CI −12.0 to −5.1). The combination yielded a significantly lower viral load over time than placebo and a trend only for shorter time to symptom resolution. The most commonly reported adverse event was mild or moderate diarrhoea. The trial was stopped early because the primary endpoint was met.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is viral load, a surrogate — the clinical reading (symptom resolution) was a trend only. Early stopping on a met virologic primary truncates the clinical evidence this trial can give.
cards.source: Finberg RW et al. Phase 2b Study of Pimodivir (JNJ-63623872) as Monotherapy or in Combination With Oseltamivir for Treatment of Acute Uncomplicated Seasonal Influenza A: TOPAZ Trial. cards.headline: OPAL (O'Neil 2022): a pharmacokinetic-primary trial in hospitalised patients — symptom resolution numerically shorter (72.45 h vs 94.15 h) and influenza-related complications 7.9% vs 15.6% on pimodivir + oseltamivir vs placebo + oseltamivir are secondary readings, labelled as such
cards.summary: OPAL (O'Neil 2022): a pharmacokinetic-primary trial in hospitalised patients — symptom resolution numerically shorter (72.45 h vs 94.15 h) and influenza-related complications 7.9% vs 15.6% on pimodivir + oseltamivir vs placebo + oseltamivir are secondary readings, labelled as such
cards.type: Randomised phase 2b study (OPAL), pimodivir + oseltamivir in hospitalised influenza A — pharmacokinetic primary endpoint
cards.people: Hospitalised patients with influenza A infection randomised 2:1 to pimodivir 600 mg plus oseltamivir 75 mg or placebo plus oseltamivir 75 mg, twice daily for 7 days, in elderly (65–85 years) and nonelderly (18–64 years) adults. The abstract does not state the total randomised number, and none is claimed here.
cards.result: The primary objective was pharmacokinetic: pimodivir exposure was similar in elderly and nonelderly patients. As secondary readings, time to influenza symptom resolution was numerically shorter with pimodivir (72.45 hours) than placebo (94.15 hours), and influenza-related complications occurred in 7.9% vs 15.6%. Treatment was generally well tolerated. The authors state a larger study is needed to test whether the differences are clinically significant.
cards.watchOut: Do not read the symptom or complication numbers as efficacy findings: this trial was designed and powered on pharmacokinetics, and its own conclusion is that a larger trial is needed.
cards.source: O'Neil B et al. A Phase 2 Study of Pimodivir (JNJ-63623872) in Combination With Oseltamivir in Elderly and Nonelderly Adults Hospitalized With Influenza A Infection: OPAL Study. The Journal of infectious diseases. 2022. PMID: 32604406. Registry ID: NCT02532283. cards.headline: Two phase 3 studies in one publication (Leopold 2025): hospital study NULL on the day-6 Hospital Recovery Scale (common odds ratio 0.943 [95% CI 0.609–1.462], P = .397 — a relative measure); outpatient study positive on symptom resolution, 92.6 h vs 105.1 h (P = .0216) — a 12.5-hour difference
cards.summary: Two phase 3 studies in one publication (Leopold 2025): hospital study NULL on the day-6 Hospital Recovery Scale (common odds ratio 0.943 [95% CI 0.609–1.462], P = .397 — a relative measure); outpatient study positive on symptom resolution, 92.6 h vs 105.1 h (P = .0216) — a 12.5-hour difference
cards.type: Two randomised phase 3 trials reported in one publication, pimodivir + standard of care in hospitalised and in high-risk outpatient influenza A
cards.people: Two phase 3 studies in adolescents and adults with laboratory-confirmed influenza A: hospitalised patients (NCT03376321) and high-risk outpatients (NCT03381196), randomised 1:1 to pimodivir 600 mg twice daily plus investigator-chosen standard of care (for most patients, oseltamivir) or placebo plus standard of care for 5 days. The abstract does not state the total randomised numbers, and none are claimed here.
cards.result: Hospital study: pimodivir + standard of care showed no clinical benefit over placebo + standard of care on the Hospital Recovery Scale at day 6 (common odds ratio 0.943; 95% CI 0.609–1.462; P = .397 — a relative measure). Outpatient study: median time to resolution of 7 symptoms was 92.6 hours (95% CI 77.6–104.2) with pimodivir vs 105.1 hours (95% CI 92.7–128.6) with placebo (P = .0216) — a 12.5-hour difference, printed as such.
cards.watchOut: One publication, two trials — never counted as one pooled result: the hospital limb is null on its clinical primary and the outpatient limb's gain is half a day of symptom time. This is the programme's decisive clinical evidence, and it is split.
cards.source: Leopold L et al. Efficacy and Safety of Pimodivir Combined With Standard of Care in Hospitalized and Nonhospitalized High-Risk Adolescents and Adults With Influenza A Infection. The Journal of infectious diseases. 2025. PMID: 39172627. Registry ID: NCT03376321 and NCT03381196. cards.headline: Synthesis: one programme, 4 reports covering 5 trials — pimodivir met its viral-load primaries in the challenge study and TOPAZ, gave only secondary symptom/complication signals in the pharmacokinetic-primary OPAL trial, and in phase 3 was null in hospitalised patients while shortening outpatient symptom resolution by 12.5 hours (92.6 vs 105.1 h)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one programme, 4 reports covering 5 trials — pimodivir met its viral-load primaries in the challenge study and TOPAZ, gave only secondary symptom/complication signals in the pharmacokinetic-primary OPAL trial, and in phase 3 was null in hospitalised patients while shortening outpatient symptom resolution by 12.5 hours (92.6 vs 105.1 h)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The balance is a tested antiviral whose clinical benefit never cleared the hospital bar: consistent virologic activity, thin and split clinical effects, and a discontinued programme. Pimodivir (JNJ-63623872) was never marketed. The genotypic/phenotypic resistance characterisation of trial isolates is a secondary analysis and is not counted as a report on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: Every positive primary here is a viral-load (surrogate) endpoint. Never present the OPAL secondary readings or the TOPAZ symptom trend as clinical efficacy, and never merge the two phase 3 studies into a single verdict.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Denufosol for cystic fibrosis lung disease: a borderline 24-week FEV1 positive followed by a fully null 48-week phase 3 in 466 patients
shelves.question: In patients with cystic fibrosis and normal-to-mildly impaired lung function, does inhaled denufosol tetrasodium 60 mg three times daily versus placebo improve FEV1 over 24–48 weeks and reduce pulmonary exacerbations? (Era flag on the face: programme 2007–2012, before CFTR modulators; population FEV1 ≥75% predicted only.)
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Cough/chemically induced · Cystic Fibrosis/drug therapy · Deoxycytosine Nucleotides/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Lung Volume Measurements · Male · Middle Aged · Nebulizers and Vaporizers · Purinergic P2 Receptor Agonists · Treatment Outcome · Uridine/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: The arc is the answer: a positive 28-day phase 2 and a borderline 24-week phase 3 (p = 0.047, +45 mL difference, every secondary endpoint null) were followed by a fully null 48-week phase 3 in 466 patients — this shelf presents a tested-and-failed airway-hydration programme, not a promising one, and the 24-week p-value must never be printed without the 48-week null beside it. Population flag: all three trials enrolled patients with FEV1 ≥75% predicted (early/mild disease, age ≥5 years) — nothing here addresses moderate-to-severe CF lung disease. Era flag: the programme ran 2007–2012, before CFTR modulators changed background therapy in this population — stated on the face. Product naming under the clarification exception: denufosol tetrasodium is an investigational inhaled P2Y2 agonist that was never marketed — stated plainly. All primaries are FEV1-only, with exacerbation secondaries null throughout.

cards.headline: Report 1 of 3 — phase 2 trial (2007, N = 89 randomised): pooled denufosol arms (20/40/60 mg three times daily for 28 days) had significantly higher changes from baseline than placebo in FEV1 (p = 0.006), FEF25–75% (p = 0.008) and FVC (p = 0.022); cough was the commonest adverse event (47% on denufosol vs 52% on placebo)
cards.summary: Report 1 of 3 — phase 2 trial (2007, N = 89 randomised): pooled denufosol arms (20/40/60 mg three times daily for 28 days) had significantly higher changes from baseline than placebo in FEV1 (p = 0.006), FEF25–75% (p = 0.008) and FVC (p = 0.022); cough was the commonest adverse event (47% on denufosol vs 52% on placebo)
cards.type: Primary report — randomised double-blind phase 2 trial, 28 days
cards.people: 89 patients with mild cystic fibrosis (FEV1 ≥75% predicted, not treated with inhaled antibiotics for the past 30 days) randomised to denufosol tetrasodium 20, 40 or 60 mg or placebo (normal saline), three times daily for 28 days; 94% completed and 98% were compliant with dosing.
cards.result: Denufosol patients (pooling active doses) had significantly higher changes from baseline in FEV1 (P = 0.006), FEF25–75% (P = 0.008), FVC (P = 0.022) and FEV1/FVC (P = 0.047) than placebo at the end of the study. All treatments were generally well tolerated with no dose-response trends in safety; 5 patients discontinued early for adverse events (2 placebo, 3 denufosol).
cards.watchOut: A 28-day, pooled-dose phase 2 signal in 89 patients with mild disease — preliminary by the authors' own wording, and the programme's later, larger trials are the test of it (cards 2 and 3).
cards.source: Deterding et al. Phase 2 randomized safety and efficacy trial of nebulized denufosol tetrasodium in cystic fibrosis. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2007. PMID: 17446337. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Report 2 of 3 — 24-week phase 3 trial (2011, N = 352 randomised): mean FEV1 change at week 24 was +0.048 L on denufosol 60 mg vs +0.003 L on placebo (p = 0.047) — a small, borderline-significant primary — with no significant differences on any secondary endpoint, including exacerbation rate
cards.summary: Report 2 of 3 — 24-week phase 3 trial (2011, N = 352 randomised): mean FEV1 change at week 24 was +0.048 L on denufosol 60 mg vs +0.003 L on placebo (p = 0.047) — a small, borderline-significant primary — with no significant differences on any secondary endpoint, including exacerbation rate
cards.type: Primary report — phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 24 weeks
cards.people: 352 patients aged ≥5 years with cystic fibrosis and FEV1 ≥75% predicted randomised to inhaled denufosol 60 mg (n = 178) or placebo (n = 174) three times daily for 24 weeks, in a phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
cards.result: Mean change from baseline to the week 24 endpoint in FEV1 was 0.048 L on denufosol versus 0.003 L on placebo (P = 0.047). No significant differences between groups were observed for secondary endpoints including exacerbation rate and other measures of lung function. Denufosol was well tolerated, with adverse-event and growth profiles similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: Borderline means borderline: p = 0.047 on a +45 mL difference with every secondary endpoint null. This reading must never be printed without the fully null 48-week phase 3 beside it (card 3).

cards.headline: Report 3 of 3 — 48-week phase 3 trial (2012, N = 466 randomised): adjusted mean FEV1 change was +40 mL on denufosol vs +32 mL on placebo, treatment effect 8 mL (95% CI −40 to 56 mL) — null on the primary endpoint; pulmonary exacerbation was 21% on denufosol vs 26% on placebo with no difference in time to first event
cards.summary: Report 3 of 3 — 48-week phase 3 trial (2012, N = 466 randomised): adjusted mean FEV1 change was +40 mL on denufosol vs +32 mL on placebo, treatment effect 8 mL (95% CI −40 to 56 mL) — null on the primary endpoint; pulmonary exacerbation was 21% on denufosol vs 26% on placebo with no difference in time to first event
cards.type: Primary report — phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 48 weeks
cards.people: 466 patients (233 per arm) aged ≥5 years with mild lung-function impairment, randomised at 102 centres to denufosol 60 mg or placebo via inhalation three times daily for 48 weeks; the primary endpoint was change in FEV1 from day 0 to week 48.
cards.result: The adjusted mean change in FEV1 was 40 mL for denufosol and 32 mL for placebo, a treatment effect of 8 mL (95% CI −0.040 to 0.056 L). The average rate of change in FEV1 percent predicted over 48 weeks was −2.30% on denufosol versus −3.04% on placebo (a difference of 24% relative to placebo — a relative measure, as reported). The incidence of pulmonary exacerbation was 21% on denufosol versus 26% on placebo with no differences in time to first event. Treatments were well tolerated with no systemic safety signal. The authors concluded 48 weeks of denufosol did not improve pulmonary function or reduce exacerbations.
cards.watchOut: This is the programme's definitive test and it is null on its primary and on exacerbations. The 24% figure in this abstract is a relative difference in the rate of FEV1-percent-predicted decline, not an absolute benefit, and it does not rescue the null primary.

shelves.title: Nemiralisib (inhaled PI3Kδ inhibitor) for COPD: the 938-patient exacerbation trial was null on every clinical endpoint; positives are small surrogate and mechanistic trials only
shelves.question: In patients with COPD — stable disease, or an acute exacerbation treated with standard care — does inhaled nemiralisib versus placebo improve lung function, imaging airway volume, or sputum neutrophil phenotype, and does it reduce re-exacerbations? (GAP-T: one programme — 3 publications covering 4 randomised trials, labelled on the face.)
shelves.mesh: Bronchodilator Agents/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Indazoles · Indoles · Oxazoles/pharmacology,therapeutic use · Phosphatidylinositol 3-Kinases/pharmacology,therapeutic use · Piperazines · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/diagnosis,drug therapy
shelves.balance: GAP-T — one programme, labelled: this shelf rests on one programme's reports — 3 publications covering 4 randomised trials (one large null exacerbation trial, one small imaging trial, and two small mechanistic trials reported together) — and the face states the count in exactly those terms. The arc is the answer: the only adequately sized trial (N = 938) is null on lung function, re-exacerbations and symptoms; every positive reading comes from a small trial with a surrogate (imaging airway volume) or mechanistic (sputum transcriptomics) primary — a biologically active inhaled anti-inflammatory that did not translate, not a candidate therapy. The positive trials use Bayesian credible intervals and posterior probabilities, printed as reported. Post-inhalation cough is a recurring, dose-related harm (35% vs 3% on placebo in the imaging trial) and belongs in the balance. Product naming under the clarification exception: nemiralisib (development code GSK2269557) is an investigational inhaled PI3Kδ inhibitor that was never marketed — stated plainly. The danirixin CXCR2 programme in the same territory is a different programme and is not merged or carded here.

cards.headline: Report 1 of 3 — acute-exacerbation dose-ranging trial (2021, N = 938 randomised — the programme's largest trial): no difference in change from baseline in post-bronchodilator FEV1 at week 12 (posterior adjusted median difference, 750 µg vs placebo, −0.004 L [95% credible interval −0.051 to 0.042]) and no differences in re-exacerbations or patient-reported outcomes — null on every clinical endpoint

cards.type: Primary report — double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial in acute exacerbation (one programme)
cards.people: 938 patients aged 40–80 with a current moderate/severe acute COPD exacerbation requiring standard-of-care treatment, randomised to inhaled nemiralisib 12.5–750 µg or placebo for 12 weeks, with an exploratory 12-week follow-up; the primary endpoint was change from baseline in post-bronchodilator FEV1 at week 12.
cards.result: There was no difference in FEV1 change at week 12 between nemiralisib and placebo, and no differences in secondary endpoints including rate of re-exacerbations and patient-reported outcomes (EXACT, CAT, SGRQ-C). Plasma pharmacokinetics increased in a dose-proportional manner. The most common adverse event for nemiralisib was post-inhalation cough, which appeared dose-related.
cards.watchOut: This is the only adequately sized trial in the programme and it is null on every clinical endpoint — it outweighs the small surrogate and mechanistic positives below, which must never be printed without it.

cards.headline: Report 2 of 3 — acute-exacerbation imaging trial (2021, N = 126 randomised): primary endpoint specific imaging airway volume at day 28 showed an 18% placebo-corrected increase (95% credible interval −1% to 42%), with a 96% posterior probability of a true effect >0% and a posterior median FEV1 improvement of 107.3 mL at day 84 (95% credible interval −2.1 to 215.5) — a surrogate imaging primary in a small trial, labelled as such
cards.summary: Report 2 of 3 — acute-exacerbation imaging trial (2021, N = 126 randomised): primary endpoint specific imaging airway volume at day 28 showed an 18% placebo-corrected increase (95% credible interval −1% to 42%), with a 96% posterior probability of a true effect >0% and a posterior median FEV1 improvement of 107.3 mL at day 84 (95% credible interval −2.1 to 215.5) — a surrogate imaging primary in a small trial, labelled as such
cards.type: Primary report — double-blind placebo-controlled imaging trial in acute exacerbation (one programme)
cards.people: 126 patients aged 40–80 with an acute COPD exacerbation and post-bronchodilator FEV1 ≤80% predicted, randomised 1:1 to inhaled nemiralisib 1 mg or placebo once daily for 84 days added to standard care; 55 on active treatment and 49 on placebo completed. The primary endpoint was specific imaging airway volume (siVaw) at day 28, analysed with a Bayesian repeated-measures model.
cards.result: An 18% placebo-corrected increase from baseline in distal siVaw was observed at day 28 (95% credible interval −1% to 42%), with a 96% posterior probability that the true treatment ratio was >0%. Improvements were observed across all lung lobes, and the posterior median FEV1 improvement versus placebo at day 84 was 107.3 mL (95% credible interval −2.1 to 215.5). Adverse events were reported by 49 patients on nemiralisib and 41 on placebo, the most common being post-inhalation cough on nemiralisib (35%) versus placebo (3%).
cards.watchOut: A surrogate imaging primary in 126 patients, reported with Bayesian credible intervals whose FEV1 interval (−2.1 to 215.5 mL) crosses zero — a mechanistic signal, never an efficacy confirmation, and it does not outweigh the null 938-patient trial.
cards.source: Cahn et al. An Inhaled PI3Kδ Inhibitor Improves Recovery in Acutely Exacerbating COPD Patients: A Randomized Trial. International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. 2021. cards.headline: Report 3 of 3 — mechanistic two-trial report (2021, one publication covering two randomised trials: stable COPD N = 28 and acute exacerbation N = 44): sputum neutrophil migration-phenotype changes were seen in stable COPD but not in the exacerbation trial, while a placebo-corrected FEV1 improvement of 136 mL (95% credible interval −46 to 315) was seen in the exacerbation trial with imaging endpoints unchanged — a mechanistic report, never an efficacy confirmation
cards.summary: Report 3 of 3 — mechanistic two-trial report (2021, one publication covering two randomised trials: stable COPD N = 28 and acute exacerbation N = 44): sputum neutrophil migration-phenotype changes were seen in stable COPD but not in the exacerbation trial, while a placebo-corrected FEV1 improvement of 136 mL (95% credible interval −46 to 315) was seen in the exacerbation trial with imaging endpoints unchanged — a mechanistic report, never an efficacy confirmation
cards.type: Primary report — two mechanistic randomised trials in one publication (one programme)
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials reported in one publication: stable COPD (N = 28, randomised 3:1) and acute exacerbation of COPD (N = 44, randomised 1:1), both receiving inhaled nemiralisib 1 mg; primary endpoints were induced-sputum transcriptomics, with inflammatory mediators, functional respiratory imaging and spirometry also measured.
cards.result: In stable COPD, nemiralisib was associated with sputum neutrophil transcriptomic changes suggestive of improved migration phenotype and with inhibition of sputum inflammatory mediators; the same effects were not observed in the exacerbation trial. In the exacerbation trial, a placebo-corrected FEV1 improvement of 136 mL (95% credible interval −46 to 315) was observed, with functional respiratory imaging endpoints unchanged.
cards.watchOut: N = 28 and N = 44 mechanistic trials with transcriptomic primaries: they show biological activity in stable COPD, not clinical benefit, and their FEV1 interval (−46 to 315 mL) is wide and crosses zero. Counted as one publication covering two trials, never as two publications.
