shelves.title: VV116 (deuremidevir) for mild-to-moderate COVID-19: shorter time to symptom resolution vs placebo and non-inferior to nirmatrelvir–ritonavir — China, Omicron era, symptom-duration claims only
shelves.question: In adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19, does a 5-day course of oral VV116 versus placebo — or versus nirmatrelvir–ritonavir — shorten time to sustained clinical recovery or symptom resolution, and how often do viral-load and symptom rebound occur after treatment? (GAP-T: one programme, 3 randomised trials. Era/setting flag on the face: all trials in China, Omicron era, mild-to-moderate disease. Name-collision fence: VV116 / deuremidevir is not azvudine.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · COVID-19 · SARS-CoV-2 · COVID-19 Vaccines · China/epidemiology · Double-Blind Method · Adenosine/analogs & derivatives
shelves.balance: GAP-T — one programme, labelled: this shelf rests on one programme's reports — 3 distinct randomised trials (versus placebo, versus nirmatrelvir–ritonavir, and a rebound trial) — and the face states the count in exactly those terms. Era/setting flag (load-bearing, on the face): every trial ran in China during the Omicron era, in mild-to-moderate disease; the active-comparator trial recorded zero deaths or progressions to severe disease in either arm, so this base says nothing about preventing severe outcomes — its claims are symptom-duration claims only. Endpoint flag: the positive results are time-to-symptom-resolution hazard ratios (a relative time measure, printed with their confidence intervals as reported), not reductions in hospitalisation or death. Name-collision fence: VV116 (deuremidevir) is NOT azvudine — a different China-developed antiviral — and is not remdesivir itself; VV116 is a deuterated remdesivir-parent nucleoside. Name flag: VV116's generic name is deuremidevir (hydrobromide); the shelf uses the name the trials publish under (VV116) with the generic name stated, per the clarification exception for a product marketed only in China and not FDA-approved. No onset-prevention claim is made anywhere in this base, so delay-not-prevention wording has no application here.

cards.headline: Trial 1 of 3 — placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (2024, China, Omicron era; 1,369 patients randomly assigned, 1,347 treated): time to sustained clinical symptom resolution hazard ratio 1.21 (95% CI 1.04–1.40; p = 0.0023) at interim analysis and 1.17 (95% CI 1.04–1.33; p = 0.0009) at final analysis — hazard ratios for a time-to-resolution outcome, printed as reported; adverse events 35.9% on VV116 vs 42.1% on placebo
cards.summary: Trial 1 of 3 — placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (2024, China, Omicron era; 1,369 patients randomly assigned, 1,347 treated): time to sustained clinical symptom resolution hazard ratio 1.21 (95% CI 1.04–1.40; p = 0.0023) at interim analysis and 1.17 (95% CI 1.04–1.33; p = 0.0009) at final analysis — hazard ratios for a time-to-resolution outcome, printed as reported; adverse events 35.9% on VV116 vs 42.1% on placebo
cards.type: Primary report — multicentre double-blind phase 3 randomised controlled trial vs placebo, China (one programme)
cards.people: 1,369 adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 in hospitals in China, with symptom onset ≤3 days before first dose and a score ≥2 for any target symptom, randomly assigned 1:1 to oral VV116 (0.6 g every 12 hours on day 1, 0.3 g every 12 hours on days 2–5) or placebo on the same schedule; 1,347 received treatment (674 VV116, 673 placebo). The primary endpoint was time to clinical symptom resolution for 2 consecutive days, in a modified intention-to-treat population (interim n = 1,229; final n = 1,296).
cards.result: At interim analysis VV116 was superior to placebo in reducing time to sustained clinical symptom resolution (hazard ratio 1.21, 95% CI 1.04–1.40; p = 0.0023); at final analysis the hazard ratio was 1.17 (95% CI 1.04–1.33; p = 0.0009). The incidence of adverse events was similar between groups (242 [35.9%] of 674 on VV116 versus 283 [42.1%] of 673 on placebo), with no observed safety concerns reported by the authors.
cards.watchOut: China, Omicron era, mild-to-moderate disease with symptoms ≤3 days: a symptom-duration result (a relative time measure), not evidence about hospitalisation or death, and not evidence outside this setting and variant era.

cards.headline: Trial 2 of 3 — active-comparator phase 3 trial (2023, China, Omicron B.1.1.529 outbreak; 822 participants randomised, 771 treated): non-inferiority to nirmatrelvir–ritonavir established for time to sustained clinical recovery (hazard ratio 1.17 [95% CI 1.01–1.35] in the primary analysis; median 4 vs 5 days in the final analysis); no participant in either group died or progressed to severe Covid-19 by day 28 — a zero-event severity base, labelled as such; adverse events 67.4% vs 77.3%
cards.summary: Trial 2 of 3 — active-comparator phase 3 trial (2023, China, Omicron B.1.1.529 outbreak; 822 participants randomised, 771 treated): non-inferiority to nirmatrelvir–ritonavir established for time to sustained clinical recovery (hazard ratio 1.17 [95% CI 1.01–1.35] in the primary analysis; median 4 vs 5 days in the final analysis); no participant in either group died or progressed to severe Covid-19 by day 28 — a zero-event severity base, labelled as such; adverse events 67.4% vs 77.3%
cards.type: Primary report — phase 3 non-inferiority observer-blinded randomised trial vs nirmatrelvir–ritonavir, China (one programme)
cards.people: 822 symptomatic adults with mild-to-moderate Covid-19 at high risk of progression, randomised during the Omicron B.1.1.529 outbreak to a 5-day course of VV116 or nirmatrelvir–ritonavir; 771 received treatment (384 VV116, 387 nirmatrelvir–ritonavir). The primary end point was time to sustained clinical recovery through day 28, with non-inferiority defined as a lower 95% confidence bound for the hazard ratio above 0.8 (a hazard ratio >1 indicating shorter time to recovery on VV116).
cards.result: Non-inferiority was established in the primary analysis (hazard ratio 1.17; 95% CI 1.01 to 1.35) and maintained in the final analysis (median 4 days with VV116 and 5 days with nirmatrelvir–ritonavir; hazard ratio 1.17; 95% CI 1.02 to 1.36). Time to sustained symptom resolution and to a first negative SARS-CoV-2 test did not differ substantially between groups in the final analysis. No participant in either group had died or progressed to severe Covid-19 by day 28. Adverse events were lower on VV116 (67.4% versus 77.3%).
cards.watchOut: Zero deaths and zero progressions in both arms means this trial cannot compare the drugs on severe outcomes at all — the comparison is time to recovery only, in high-risk but mild-to-moderate Omicron-era patients in China.
cards.source: Cao et al. VV116 versus Nirmatrelvir-Ritonavir for Oral Treatment of Covid-19. The New England journal of medicine. 2023. PMID: 36577095. Registry ID: NCT05341609. cards.headline: Trial 3 of 3 — rebound trial (2024, single-centre Shanghai, China; 345 participants in the full analysis set): viral-load rebound occurred in 20.0% on VV116 vs 21.7% on nirmatrelvir–ritonavir (p = 0.70) and symptom rebound in 25.6% vs 24.5% (p = 0.82) — rebound was common and did not differ between the two antivirals
cards.summary: Trial 3 of 3 — rebound trial (2024, single-centre Shanghai, China; 345 participants in the full analysis set): viral-load rebound occurred in 20.0% on VV116 vs 21.7% on nirmatrelvir–ritonavir (p = 0.70) and symptom rebound in 25.6% vs 24.5% (p = 0.82) — rebound was common and did not differ between the two antivirals
cards.type: Primary report — single-centre investigator-blinded randomised rebound trial, Shanghai (one programme)
cards.people: 345 adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 within 5 days of SARS-CoV-2 infection, enrolled at a single centre in Shanghai between December 20, 2022 and January 19, 2023 and randomised to VV116 (n = 165) or nirmatrelvir–ritonavir (n = 180) for 5 days, followed every other day to day 28 and weekly to day 60. The primary outcome was viral-load rebound (a half-log increase in viral RNA copies/mL versus treatment completion); symptom rebound was an increase of more than 2 points in symptom score versus treatment completion.
cards.result: Viral-load rebound occurred in 33 patients (20.0%) on VV116 and 39 (21.7%) on nirmatrelvir–ritonavir (P = .70). Symptom rebound occurred in 41 of 160 patients (25.6%) on VV116 and 40 of 163 (24.5%) on nirmatrelvir–ritonavir (P = .82). Viral whole-genome sequencing of 24 rebound cases showed the same lineage at baseline and at rebound in each case. The authors suggest prolongation of treatment duration might be investigated to reduce rebound.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and smaller than the other two trials: its finding is that rebound after a standard 5-day course is common (~1 in 5 viral-load, ~1 in 4 symptom) and indistinguishable between these two antivirals — not that either drug prevents rebound.
cards.source: Yang et al. COVID-19 Rebound After VV116 vs Nirmatrelvir-Ritonavir Treatment: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA network open. 2024. PMID: 38477921. Registry ID: ChiCTR2200066811. shelves.title: Tralokinumab for severe, uncontrolled asthma — one programme, 4 publications covering 5 trials: every primary endpoint was null, and the one positive biomarker subgroup did not replicate
shelves.question: In patients with severe, uncontrolled asthma despite inhaled corticosteroids and a long-acting β2-agonist, does subcutaneous tralokinumab 300 mg every 2–4 weeks versus placebo reduce the annual asthma exacerbation rate over 52 weeks, improve lung function and asthma control, or spare oral corticosteroids in patients who require them?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal/chemistry/therapeutic use · Asthma/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Immunoglobulin G/therapeutic use · Interleukin-13/metabolism · Male · Middle Aged · Models, Statistical · Respiratory Function Tests · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/administration & dosage · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage · Asthma/drug therapy/physiopathology/psychology · Bronchodilator Agents/therapeutic use · Disease Progression · Fluticasone/therapeutic use · Forced Expiratory Volume/drug effects · Quality of Life · Salmeterol Xinafoate/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Child · Severity of Illness Index · Administration, Inhalation · Administration, Oral · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/administration & dosage · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: One programme, counted exactly: 4 publications covering 5 randomised trials. The arc is the answer — tralokinumab improved FEV1 modestly and repeatedly but never improved its primary endpoint in any population: asthma control was null in phase 2 (ACQ-6 p = 0.375), exacerbations were null in phase 2b (rate changes 6% and −2% vs placebo — relative measures) and in STRATOS 1 all-comers (7.0% relative reduction, rate ratio 0.93, p = 0.59), the FENO-high subgroup positive in STRATOS 1 (44.0% relative reduction, p = 0.028) did not replicate in STRATOS 2 (15.8%, p = 0.47), and oral-corticosteroid sparing was null in TROPOS (37.62% vs 29.85% dose reduction, p = 0.271). Tralokinumab was never marketed for asthma — the asthma programme was discontinued (it is marketed for atopic dermatitis, homed at pack #1650, cross-point only).

cards.headline: Piper 2013 — phase 2: the asthma-control primary was NULL (ACQ-6 change −0.76 on tralokinumab vs −0.61 on placebo, p = 0.375); FEV1 rose modestly with a dose-response
cards.summary: Piper 2013 — phase 2: the asthma-control primary was NULL (ACQ-6 change −0.76 on tralokinumab vs −0.61 on placebo, p = 0.375); FEV1 rose modestly with a dose-response
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised placebo-controlled trial (Piper 2013) — publication 1 of 4 in one programme covering 5 trials
cards.people: 194 subjects with moderate-to-severe uncontrolled asthma despite controller therapies, randomised to subcutaneous tralokinumab 150, 300 or 600 mg or placebo every 2 weeks; primary endpoint was change in ACQ-6 at week 13 for the combined tralokinumab doses vs placebo.
cards.result: ACQ-6 change at week 13 was −0.76 ± 1.04 on combined tralokinumab vs −0.61 ± 0.90 on placebo (p = 0.375) — the primary endpoint was not improved. FEV1 increased 0.21 ± 0.38 L vs 0.06 ± 0.48 L (p = 0.072) with a dose-response, rescue β2-agonist use fell (p = 0.020), and the FEV1 increase remained evident 12 weeks after the final dose. No serious adverse events were related to tralokinumab.
cards.watchOut: A symptom-control primary that missed, with a lung-function signal — the pattern the whole programme then repeated at larger size. The FEV1 difference itself did not reach significance here (p = 0.072).
cards.source: Piper E et al. A phase II placebo-controlled study of tralokinumab in moderate-to-severe asthma. European Respiratory Journal. 2013. PMID: 22743678. cards.headline: Brightling 2015 — phase 2b: the exacerbation primary was NULL at both regimens (rate changes 6% and −2% vs placebo, both relative measures as reported); FEV1 improved on the every-2-weeks regimen only
cards.summary: Brightling 2015 — phase 2b: the exacerbation primary was NULL at both regimens (rate changes 6% and −2% vs placebo, both relative measures as reported); FEV1 improved on the every-2-weeks regimen only
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Brightling 2015) — publication 2 of 4 in one programme covering 5 trials
cards.people: 452 patients aged 18–75 with severe asthma and 2–6 exacerbations in the previous year, randomised to tralokinumab 300 mg every 2 weeks (n = 150), every 4 weeks (n = 151) or placebo (n = 151) for 1 year, all on high-dose fluticasone/salmeterol plus other controllers; 383 (85%) completed 52 weeks.
cards.result: Annual exacerbation rates were 0.91 (every 2 weeks), 0.97 (every 4 weeks) and 0.90 (placebo) per patient-year; percentage changes vs placebo were 6% (95% CI −31 to 33; p = 0.709) and −2% (−46 to 29; p = 0.904) — relative measures as reported, both non-significant. Prebronchodilator FEV1 improved vs placebo on the every-2-weeks regimen only (7.3% [2.6–12.0], p = 0.003). The positive high-reversibility subgroup readings rest on a post-hoc subgroup of n = 33 vs n = 48 and are labelled post-hoc.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc biomarker/reversibility subgroups of a null trial generated the phase 3 hypothesis — they are not findings. The exacerbation rates themselves (0.91/0.97 vs 0.90) show no separation at all.
cards.source: Brightling CE et al. Efficacy and safety of tralokinumab in patients with severe uncontrolled asthma: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2b trial. cards.headline: Panettieri 2018 — STRATOS 1 and STRATOS 2 (ONE publication covering TWO trials, never counted as two publications): the all-comers primary was null, and the FENO-high subgroup positive in STRATOS 1 did NOT replicate in STRATOS 2
cards.summary: Panettieri 2018 — STRATOS 1 and STRATOS 2 (ONE publication covering TWO trials, never counted as two publications): the all-comers primary was null, and the FENO-high subgroup positive in STRATOS 1 did NOT replicate in STRATOS 2
cards.type: Phase 3 report covering STRATOS 1 and STRATOS 2 (Panettieri 2018) — publication 3 of 4 in one programme covering 5 trials; one publication, two trials
cards.people: Two phase 3 trials in one publication. STRATOS 1: 1,207 participants randomised (1,202 treated) aged 12–75 with severe uncontrolled asthma on inhaled corticosteroids plus a long-acting β2-agonist (maintenance oral corticosteroids excluded). STRATOS 2: 856 randomised (849 treated), testing the biomarker-positive population identified in STRATOS 1. Tralokinumab 300 mg or placebo subcutaneously every 2 or 4 weeks (STRATOS 1) or every 2 weeks (STRATOS 2) for 52 weeks.
cards.result: In STRATOS 1 all-comers, every-2-weeks tralokinumab reduced the annualised exacerbation rate by 7.0% (95% CI −20.8 to 28.4; rate ratio 0.93 [0.72–1.21], p = 0.59) — a relative measure, non-significant; the primary was null. In the STRATOS 1 FENO ≥37 ppb subgroup, the reduction was 44.0% (6.0–66.0; rate ratio 0.56 [0.34–0.94], p = 0.028; n = 97 vs 102) — relative, labelled. In STRATOS 2's FENO-high population the same comparison gave a 15.8% reduction (−33.7 to 47.0; rate ratio 0.84 [0.53–1.34], p = 0.47; n = 108 vs 121) — the subgroup finding did not replicate.
cards.watchOut: The single nominally positive reading in this programme is a subgroup of a null trial that failed its own prospective replication — never print the STRATOS 1 FENO-high result without the STRATOS 2 result beside it. STRATOS excluded maintenance-OCS patients; that population is covered only by the TROPOS card below.

cards.headline: Busse 2019 — TROPOS, the oral-corticosteroid-sparing trial: primary NULL (OCS dose reduction 37.62% on tralokinumab vs 29.85% on placebo, p = 0.271) and no secondary endpoint differed
cards.summary: Busse 2019 — TROPOS, the oral-corticosteroid-sparing trial: primary NULL (OCS dose reduction 37.62% on tralokinumab vs 29.85% on placebo, p = 0.271) and no secondary endpoint differed
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind oral-corticosteroid-sparing trial, TROPOS (Busse 2019) — publication 4 of 4 in one programme covering 5 trials
cards.people: 140 patients (70 per arm) with severe uncontrolled asthma requiring maintenance oral corticosteroids plus inhaled corticosteroids/long-acting β2-agonists, randomised to tralokinumab 300 mg or placebo every 2 weeks for 40 weeks.
cards.result: The percentage reduction in average OCS dose at week 40 was 37.62% on tralokinumab vs 29.85% on placebo (p = 0.271) — the primary endpoint was not met, and there were no significant between-treatment differences for any secondary endpoint. Upper respiratory tract infections were more frequent on tralokinumab (35.7% vs 14.3%); there were no cases of pneumonia.
cards.watchOut: This is the programme's only trial in the OCS-dependent population, and it is 140 patients. A near-8-point difference in dose reduction that is non-significant at this size is absence of demonstrated effect, not a trend to quote.
cards.source: Busse WW et al. Tralokinumab did not demonstrate oral corticosteroid-sparing effects in severe asthma. European Respiratory Journal. 2019. PMID: 30442714. cards.people: One programme: 4 publications covering 5 randomised trials (phase 2 N = 194; phase 2b N = 452; STRATOS 1 N = 1,207 and STRATOS 2 N = 856 in a single publication; TROPOS N = 140). Tralokinumab is marketed for atopic dermatitis but was never marketed for asthma; the asthma programme was discontinued.
cards.result: The arc is the answer: IL-13 neutralisation improved FEV1 modestly and repeatedly but never improved its primary endpoint in any population — not asthma control (phase 2), not exacerbations (phase 2b; STRATOS 1 all-comers), not the biomarker-enriched replication (STRATOS 2), and not steroid-sparing (TROPOS). Every percentage reduction printed on this shelf is a relative measure and is labelled as such beside its rate ratio. This shelf presents a completed, negative programme — not a candidate therapy.

shelves.title: Losmapimod for COPD — one programme, 3 randomised reports: a biomarker effect (fibrinogen −11%) with no clinical benefit on any endpoint, and an exacerbation trial stopped early for futility
shelves.question: In patients with moderate-to-severe COPD, does oral losmapimod versus placebo reduce systemic/airway inflammation (sputum neutrophils, plasma fibrinogen), improve exercise tolerance (6-minute walk distance), or reduce moderate/severe exacerbations?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Albuterol/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Androstadienes/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Cyclopropanes/pharmacology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Female · Fibrinogen/metabolism · Fluticasone-Salmeterol Drug Combination · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neutrophils/drug effects · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/blood/drug therapy/metabolism · Pyridines/pharmacology · Sputum/cytology · p38 Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinases/antagonists & inhibitors · Acute Disease · Adult · Cyclopropanes/therapeutic use · Exercise Tolerance/drug effects · Forced Expiratory Volume/drug effects · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/drug therapy/physiopathology · Pyridines/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Vital Capacity/drug effects · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/therapeutic use · Bronchodilator Agents/therapeutic use · Cyclopropanes/administration & dosage/pharmacology · Disease Progression · Eosinophils · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/drug therapy/metabolism/physiopathology · Pyridines/administration & dosage/pharmacology · Respiratory Function Tests/methods · Risk
shelves.balance: One programme, counted exactly: 3 publications covering 3 trials. The arc is the answer — losmapimod reduced plasma fibrinogen by 11% (ratio of effect 0.89 [95% CI 0.83–0.96], p = 0.002 — a relative ratio as reported) yet produced no clinical benefit on any endpoint in any trial: sputum neutrophils (its first primary) unchanged, 6-minute walk distance numerically worse than placebo at all three doses (−6.7, −4.7, −3.4 m), and exacerbations numerically more frequent (rate ratio 1.04) in a trial terminated early at a planned interim analysis for low probability of success, with only 24 of 184 randomised subjects completing. Losmapimod (GW856553) was never marketed.

cards.headline: Lomas 2012 — biomarker trial: the primary endpoint (sputum neutrophils) was NULL on losmapimod and on inhaled combination therapy alike; plasma fibrinogen fell 11% (ratio 0.89, a relative ratio as reported)
cards.summary: Lomas 2012 — biomarker trial: the primary endpoint (sputum neutrophils) was NULL on losmapimod and on inhaled combination therapy alike; plasma fibrinogen fell 11% (ratio 0.89, a relative ratio as reported)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind biomarker trial (Lomas 2012) — report 1 of 3 in one programme
cards.people: 302 individuals with GOLD stage II COPD randomised to oral losmapimod 7.5 mg twice daily, inhaled salmeterol/fluticasone combination, or placebo for 12 weeks in a double-blind double-dummy study.
cards.result: Neither losmapimod nor the inhaled combination changed the primary endpoint, sputum neutrophils. Losmapimod reduced plasma fibrinogen by 11% (−0.4 g/L; ratio of effect 0.89 [95% CI 0.83–0.96], p = 0.002 — a relative ratio as reported) with non-significant reductions in IL-6, IL-8 and CRP. There was evidence of improvement in hyperinflation vs placebo (overall P = .02).
cards.watchOut: A systemic biomarker effect (fibrinogen) with a null airway primary is a mechanism–outcome dissociation, not clinical benefit — the distinction this whole shelf turns on.
cards.source: Lomas DA et al. An oral inhibitor of p38 MAP kinase reduces plasma fibrinogen in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. 2012. cards.headline: Watz 2014 — exercise-tolerance trial: 6-minute walk distance was NULL at every dose, with point estimates favouring placebo (−6.7, −4.7 and −3.4 m)
cards.summary: Watz 2014 — exercise-tolerance trial: 6-minute walk distance was NULL at every dose, with point estimates favouring placebo (−6.7, −4.7 and −3.4 m)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled exercise-tolerance trial (Watz 2014) — report 2 of 3 in one programme
cards.people: 602 patients enrolled and treated, aged ≥40 with moderate-to-severe COPD and 6-minute walk distance <350 m, randomised to losmapimod 2.5, 7.5 or 15 mg or placebo twice daily for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Differences in mean 6-minute-walk change vs placebo were −6.7 m (95% CI −18.2 to 4.9) at 2.5 mg, −4.7 m (−16.1 to 6.8) at 7.5 mg and −3.4 m (−15.1 to 8.2) at 15 mg — not significant at any dose, all numerically favouring placebo. Drug-related adverse events were more common on losmapimod 7.5 mg (13%) and 15 mg (13%) than placebo (7%).
cards.watchOut: The largest trial in the programme, and its point estimates run the wrong way at all three doses. There is no dose at which a walk-distance claim can be printed.

cards.headline: Pascoe 2017 — exacerbation trial STOPPED EARLY for futility: exacerbation-rate ratio 1.04 (95% credible interval 0.63–1.73), posterior probability of any benefit 0.44 against a >0.90 success criterion
cards.summary: Pascoe 2017 — exacerbation trial STOPPED EARLY for futility: exacerbation-rate ratio 1.04 (95% credible interval 0.63–1.73), posterior probability of any benefit 0.44 against a >0.90 success criterion
cards.type: Randomised double-blind exacerbation trial terminated early at interim analysis (Pascoe 2017) — report 3 of 3 in one programme
cards.people: 184 subjects randomised (94 placebo, 90 losmapimod 15 mg) with moderate-to-severe COPD at exacerbation risk and ≥2% blood eosinophils at screening, for a planned 26–52 weeks. A planned interim analysis terminated the study early for low probability of success; only 14 placebo and 10 losmapimod subjects completed the study.
cards.result: The adjusted posterior median annualised exacerbation-rate ratio was 1.04 (95% credible interval 0.63–1.73) — null, with the point estimate favouring placebo — and the posterior probability of any benefit was 0.44 against a >0.90 success criterion. A week-26 post-bronchodilator FEV1 reading (p = 0.007) is a secondary reading from this terminated trial and is labelled as such. Health-status (SGRQ) changes were similar in both groups, and no new safety signals were identified.
cards.watchOut: A trial that randomised 184 and completed 24 subjects cannot support any efficacy reading: its FEV1 p-value must never be printed as evidence of benefit. The trial's own Bayesian success criterion was missed by a wide margin (0.44 vs >0.90).
cards.source: Pascoe S et al. Biological effects of p38 MAPK inhibitor losmapimod does not translate to clinical benefits in COPD. Respiratory Medicine. 2017. PMID: 29206629. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One programme: 3 publications covering 3 trials (N = 302, 602 and 184 randomised). Losmapimod (development code GW856553) is an investigational drug that was never marketed.
cards.result: The arc is the answer: p38 MAPK inhibition produced a measurable systemic biomarker effect (plasma fibrinogen −11% as a ratio of effect 0.89 — a relative ratio, labelled) and no clinical benefit on any endpoint in any trial — sputum neutrophils unchanged, walk distance numerically worse at every dose, and exacerbations numerically more frequent in a trial stopped early for futility. This shelf presents a clean mechanism–outcome dissociation, not a candidate therapy.
cards.watchOut: The post-hoc subgroup analysis of the exercise-tolerance trial and the population-pharmacokinetic report are not counted as reports. Do not merge this programme with the nemiralisib row (pack #7772) or other inhaled/oral anti-inflammatory COPD programmes — different mechanisms, separate bases.

shelves.title: Bemnifosbuvir for COVID-19 — one programme, 3 randomised reports (only 1 a full report; N not documented for the other two): every trial was discontinued early or missed its primary endpoint
shelves.question: In patients with COVID-19 — ambulatory adults with mild-to-moderate disease, or hospitalised adults with moderate disease — does oral bemnifosbuvir 550–1,100 mg twice daily for 5 days versus placebo reduce nasopharyngeal viral load, alleviate symptoms faster, or prevent hospitalisation and death?
shelves.mesh: Humans · COVID-19 · Antiviral Agents/adverse effects · SARS-CoV-2 · Treatment Outcome · Hepatitis C, Chronic
shelves.balance: One programme, composition on the face: 3 randomised reports, of which only one (MOONSONG, phase 2, N = 100) is a full report; the other two survive only as short summary-level reports whose abstracts state no participant count — N not documented for both. The arc is the answer: no trial met its primary endpoint — MOONSONG's viral-load primary was null at both doses (−0.25 and −0.08 log10, p = 0.426 and 0.808), MORNINGSKY (phase 3) was discontinued prematurely and missed its symptom primary, and the hospital study ended early and missed its primary. The one positive clinical claim — fewer hospitalisations in MORNINGSKY — is a secondary reading from a discontinued trial, expressed as a 71% relative risk reduction (labelled relative) with no viral-load reduction. Bemnifosbuvir (AT-527) was never marketed for COVID-19.

cards.headline: Boffito 2023 (MOONSONG) — the programme's only full report: the primary endpoint was NOT met at either dose (day-7 viral-RNA differences −0.25 log10 [p = 0.426] at 550 mg and −0.08 log10 [p = 0.808] at 1,100 mg)
cards.summary: Boffito 2023 (MOONSONG) — the programme's only full report: the primary endpoint was NOT met at either dose (day-7 viral-RNA differences −0.25 log10 [p = 0.426] at 550 mg and −0.08 log10 [p = 0.808] at 1,100 mg)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind trial, MOONSONG (Boffito 2023) — report 1 of 3 in one programme, and its only full report
cards.people: Ambulatory patients with mild/moderate COVID-19 randomised to bemnifosbuvir 550 mg or placebo (cohort A) and bemnifosbuvir 1,100 mg or placebo (cohort B), all twice daily for 5 days, in a phase 2 double-blind trial. The modified intention-to-treat infected population comprised 100 patients (550 mg n = 30; 1,100 mg n = 30; cohort A placebo n = 30; cohort B placebo n = 10). The primary endpoint was change in nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was not met: the day-7 viral-RNA difference vs placebo was −0.25 log10 copies/mL (80% CI −0.66 to 0.16, P = 0.4260) at 550 mg and −0.08 log10 copies/mL (80% CI −0.48 to 0.33, P = 0.8083) at 1,100 mg. Bemnifosbuvir did not show meaningful antiviral activity on nasopharyngeal viral load in the primary analysis.
cards.watchOut: Viral load is a surrogate endpoint — and here it was null at both doses, with the higher dose numerically worse. Nothing in this trial supports a clinical-outcome claim.

cards.people: Outpatient adults/adolescents with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 randomised 2:1 to bemnifosbuvir or placebo in a phase 3 study whose primary outcome was time to symptom alleviation/improvement. This report survives only as a short summary-level report whose abstract states no participant count — N not documented for this report, per the standing labelling rule.
cards.result: The study was discontinued prematurely and did not meet its primary endpoint. As reported, bemnifosbuvir treatment resulted in fewer hospitalisations — expressed by its authors as a 71% relative risk reduction, labelled relative — and fewer COVID-19-related medically attended hospital visits and complications, with no reduction in viral load. The proportion of patients with adverse events was similar between groups and no deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: The hospitalisation claim is a secondary reading from a discontinued, primary-missing trial, expressed only as a relative reduction with no absolute rates and no N in its abstract — it must never be printed without the discontinuation and the missed primary beside it.

cards.people: Hospitalised high-risk adults with moderate COVID-19 randomised 1:1 to bemnifosbuvir or placebo in a phase 2 study, amended to two parts after an interim analysis, with part B enrolment limited owing to evolving standard of care. This report survives only as a short summary-level report whose abstract states no participant count — N not documented for this report, per the standing labelling rule.
cards.result: The study ended early and did not meet its primary efficacy endpoint. Bemnifosbuvir was well tolerated and did not contribute to all-cause mortality. Compared with placebo, bemnifosbuvir resulted in a 0.61 log10 greater viral-load mean change on day 2, a trend sustained through day 8. Treatment-emergent adverse events were similar in both groups and mostly mild/moderate and unrelated to study drug.
cards.watchOut: A day-2 viral-load difference in an early-ended, primary-missing study is a surrogate signal, not progression benefit — the authors' own framing ('a potential role') goes no further, and neither does this shelf. The evolving-standard-of-care reason for ending early is part of the result.

shelves.title: Zaleplon versus placebo in insomnia (adults and older adults): sleep-latency efficacy over 2–4 weeks without the rebound seen with zolpidem in the same trials — four double-blind reports of ONE 1999–2000 programme, plus one open-label extension labelled as such
shelves.question: In adults — including older adults — with insomnia, does zaleplon (5–20 mg, a short-half-life pyrazolopyrimidine hypnotic) shorten sleep latency versus placebo over 2–4 weeks, does it maintain sleep, and what happens on discontinuation? (Four double-blind reports of ONE development programme, 1999–2000, plus one open-label extension labelled as such — counted as a programme, never as four independent confirmations.)

shelves.balance: One development programme (1999–2000), four double-blind reports, counted as a programme — never as four independent confirmations. The efficacy signal is sleep latency: in the adult pivotal (615 outpatients, 28 nights), median latency was significantly lower than placebo on zaleplon 10 and 20 mg in all 4 weeks (5 mg, weeks 1–3); the adult confirmatory (Fry et al. — sample size NOT documented in its abstract, labelled as such on its card) found latency shorter at week 1 on all doses, persisting to week 4 only at 20 mg. Maintenance is weak, exactly as the drug's ~1-hour half-life predicts: sleep duration increased only at 20 mg in adults and only in week 1 at 10 mg in the older-adult pivotal (549 patients ≥65, 14 nights). Discontinuation is the programme's distinguishing claim and is printed whole, including its internal contrast: no rebound insomnia or withdrawal after zaleplon in the adult pivotal, the adult confirmatory and the older-adult pivotal — whereas the zolpidem comparator arms in the same trials showed significantly more withdrawal symptoms and rebound indications — BUT the older-adult confirmatory reports a weak indication of rebound after the 10 mg dose, which qualifies the cleaner picture and prints beside it. Every efficacy outcome is subjective (morning questionnaires); no report rests on polysomnography — printed on the face. Treatment durations are 2–4 weeks; the only long-term data are the 1-year open-label extension in older patients, which itself states placebo-controlled trials are needed. These trials predate the modern class safety record for Z-drugs (complex sleep behaviours, next-day impairment warnings): no 1999–2000 adverse-event table on this shelf stands as a current safety statement.

cards.headline: Adult pivotal (Elie 1999, N = 615): median sleep latency significantly lower than placebo on zaleplon 10 and 20 mg during all 4 weeks (5 mg, weeks 1–3); NO rebound insomnia or withdrawal after zaleplon — while the zolpidem arm in the same trial showed significantly more withdrawal symptoms and a rebound indication
cards.summary: Adult pivotal (Elie 1999, N = 615): median sleep latency significantly lower than placebo on zaleplon 10 and 20 mg during all 4 weeks (5 mg, weeks 1–3); NO rebound insomnia or withdrawal after zaleplon — while the zolpidem arm in the same trial showed significantly more withdrawal symptoms and a rebound indication
cards.type: Double-blind randomised trial — adult pivotal report of the zaleplon programme (zolpidem active comparator)
cards.people: 615 adult outpatients with DSM-III-R insomnia randomised double-blind to zaleplon 5, 10 or 20 mg, zolpidem 10 mg (active comparator) or placebo for 28 nights, followed by 3 nights of placebo; sleep assessed by morning questionnaires.
cards.result: Median sleep latency was significantly lower with zaleplon 10 and 20 mg than placebo during all 4 weeks, and with 5 mg for the first 3 weeks. Zaleplon 20 mg also significantly increased sleep duration in all but week 3. There was no evidence of rebound insomnia or withdrawal symptoms after discontinuation of zaleplon. Zolpidem 10 mg decreased latency, increased duration and improved quality at most timepoints, but after its discontinuation the incidence of withdrawal symptoms was significantly greater than with placebo and there was an indication of significant rebound insomnia in some patients. Adverse-event frequency on active treatment did not differ significantly from placebo.
cards.watchOut: One programme, not an independent confirmation of the other reports on this shelf. All outcomes subjective (morning questionnaires) — no polysomnography. The zolpidem discontinuation contrast is part of this shelf's balance and prints whole.

cards.people: Adult outpatients with insomnia in a 4-week double-blind trial of zaleplon 5, 10 and 20 mg vs placebo, with zolpidem 10 mg as active comparator; post-sleep questionnaires. N not documented in the abstract — labelled per the standing rule, and this report is never load-bearing for any N-dependent claim.
cards.result: During week 1, sleep latency was significantly shorter with zaleplon 5, 10 and 20 mg than placebo; the decrease persisted through week 4 with 20 mg and was again evident with 10 mg at week 3. Zaleplon 20 mg also significantly improved sleep duration, number of awakenings and sleep quality vs placebo. No pharmacological tolerance developed, and there were no indications of rebound insomnia or withdrawal after discontinuation. Zolpidem 10 mg improved latency, duration and quality, but with a significantly greater incidence of withdrawal symptoms and a suggestion of rebound insomnia vs placebo. Adverse-event frequency did not differ significantly between active treatment and placebo.
cards.watchOut: BINDING: this report carries 'N not documented' labelling (its abstract states no sample size). One programme with the other reports — never counted as an independent confirmation.

cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial — older-adult pivotal report of the zaleplon programme (zolpidem active comparator)
cards.people: 549 patients aged ≥65 with DSM-IV insomnia in a multicentre randomised placebo-controlled outpatient trial: zaleplon 5 or 10 mg vs zolpidem 5 mg vs placebo for 14 nights, assessed by morning questionnaires, with 7 placebo nights after discontinuation. This report's PubMed record carries no MeSH terms ('none in the record' in its source line).
cards.result: Zaleplon 10 mg and zolpidem 5 mg significantly reduced sleep latency during both weeks; zaleplon 5 mg reduced latency only during week 2. Sleep duration increased with zolpidem in both weeks and with zaleplon 10 mg during week 1 only — the maintenance weakness expected from a ~1-hour half-life. No clinically significant rebound insomnia was observed after zaleplon discontinuation, whereas evidence of rebound effects was seen with zolpidem. Neither zaleplon dose differed significantly from placebo in the frequency of any central-nervous-system adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Two weeks only, subjective outcomes only. One programme with the other reports on this shelf.

cards.people: Patients aged ≥65 with primary insomnia in a multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled 2-week outpatient trial of zaleplon 5 and 10 mg; subjective sleep variables from post-sleep questionnaires. (The report's abstract does not state the enrolled N in the fetched record.)
cards.result: Zaleplon significantly reduced subjective sleep latency during both weeks at both the 5 mg and 10 mg doses. Subjective sleep quality improved for significantly more patients on zaleplon 10 mg than placebo during both weeks. There was a weak indication of rebound insomnia after discontinuation of the 10 mg dose, but no significant difference in common treatment-emergent adverse events across groups.
cards.watchOut: The weak rebound indication at 10 mg prints beside the other reports' 'no rebound' findings — never silently dropped. Two weeks only; subjective outcomes only.

cards.headline: Supportive, NOT a double-blind report: 1-year open-label extension in older patients — maintained subjective benefit and no rebound on discontinuation, with the report itself stating placebo-controlled trials are needed to confirm long-term effects
cards.summary: Supportive, NOT a double-blind report: 1-year open-label extension in older patients — maintained subjective benefit and no rebound on discontinuation, with the report itself stating placebo-controlled trials are needed to confirm long-term effects
cards.type: Open-label extension report — supportive only, not counted among the programme's double-blind reports
cards.people: Older patients from two randomised double-blind zaleplon trials self-administered zaleplon 5 or 10 mg nightly for 6–12 months in open-label extension phases, followed by a 7-day single-blind placebo run-out. The fetched abstract does not state the extension N.
cards.result: The safety profile over the long term was similar to that in the short-term trial in an equivalent population. Long-term therapy produced and maintained statistically significant improvement in time to persistent sleep onset, duration of sleep and number of nocturnal awakenings (P < 0.001 for each) for durations up to 12 months, and discontinuation was not associated with rebound insomnia. The authors conclude the open-label data suggest safety and effectiveness and that placebo-controlled double-blind trials are needed to confirm them.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, self-administered, no placebo control: supportive only. It is the programme's only long-term data and cannot carry a long-term efficacy claim.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one 1999–2000 programme — zaleplon shortens subjective sleep latency for 2–4 weeks, barely maintains sleep, and (one weak contrary signal aside) stops without the rebound its zolpidem comparators showed
cards.summary: Synthesis: one 1999–2000 programme — zaleplon shortens subjective sleep latency for 2–4 weeks, barely maintains sleep, and (one weak contrary signal aside) stops without the rebound its zolpidem comparators showed
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Four double-blind reports of ONE programme (adult pivotal N = 615; older-adult pivotal N = 549; the Fry confirmatory's N is not documented in its abstract) plus one open-label extension labelled as such. Counted as a programme, never as four independent confirmations.
cards.result: Latency: consistently and significantly shortened (10–20 mg in adults across 4 weeks; 5–10 mg in older adults across 2 weeks). Maintenance: narrow — duration gains only at 20 mg (adults) and week 1 only at 10 mg (older adults), as a ~1-hour half-life predicts. Discontinuation: no rebound/withdrawal in three reports, a weak rebound indication at 10 mg in the fourth; zolpidem arms in the same trials did show rebound/withdrawal. All outcomes subjective; durations 2–4 weeks; the adverse-event tables predate the modern Z-drug class safety record and are not a current safety statement.
cards.watchOut: Never present the four reports as independent confirmations, and never let the 1999–2000 safety tables stand as current class-safety evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Ataluren for nonsense-mutation cystic fibrosis — one programme, 4 publications covering 4 studies; both phase 3 primaries null
shelves.question: In patients aged ≥6 years with cystic fibrosis caused by a nonsense (premature stop-codon) CFTR mutation, does oral ataluren (10, 10 and 20 mg/kg/day in three divided doses) versus placebo over 48 weeks preserve percent-predicted FEV1 and reduce pulmonary exacerbations?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (no benefit) — one programme, stated in exactly those terms: 4 publications covering 4 studies, of which only the two phase 3 trials (238 + 279 patients) are clinical-efficacy reports; the two phase 2 reports measure nasal chloride transport, a pharmacodynamic surrogate. The arc is the answer, and it is unusually clean: phase 2 pharmacodynamic activity was real and reproducible, the first phase 3 missed its primary endpoint (difference 3.0%, p = 0.12), its rescue hypothesis was a POST-HOC subgroup of patients not using chronic inhaled tobramycin (5.7% difference, nominal p = 0.0082), and the sponsor then ran the correct experiment — a second phase 3 (ACT CF) restricted to that exact population — which was also null on every endpoint (difference 0.6, p = 0.54). The post-hoc 5.7% figure is never printed without the ACT CF result beside it. Ataluren was never approved for cystic fibrosis and the CF programme was discontinued after ACT CF (clarification, not promotion); its Duchenne muscular dystrophy question stays homed at pack #4316 — cross-point only, under diagnosis-first. A chest-CT secondary analysis of the first phase 3 trial exists in the programme and is never counted as a fifth report.

cards.headline: Kerem 2014: first phase 3 missed its primary endpoint — FEV1 relative change −2.5% on ataluren vs −5.5% on placebo (difference 3.0% [95% CI −0.8 to 6.3], p = 0.12); exacerbations did not differ (rate ratio 0.77 [0.57–1.05], p = 0.0992, a relative measure)
cards.summary: Kerem 2014: first phase 3 missed its primary endpoint — FEV1 relative change −2.5% on ataluren vs −5.5% on placebo (difference 3.0% [95% CI −0.8 to 6.3], p = 0.12); exacerbations did not differ (rate ratio 0.77 [0.57–1.05], p = 0.0992, a relative measure)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (48 weeks)
cards.people: 238 patients randomly assigned at 36 sites (116 per arm with a valid post-baseline spirometry measurement), aged ≥6 years with nonsense-mutation CF.
cards.result: Relative change in percent-predicted FEV1 at week 48 was −2.5% on ataluren vs −5.5% on placebo (difference 3.0% [95% CI −0.8 to 6.3], p = 0.12) — primary endpoint null. Pulmonary exacerbations did not differ significantly (rate ratio 0.77 [95% CI 0.57–1.05], p = 0.0992 — a relative measure). Increased creatinine (acute kidney injury) occurred in 18 (15%) on ataluren vs 1 (<1%) on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The POST-HOC subgroup not using chronic inhaled tobramycin showed a 5.7% difference [1.5–10.1] (nominal p = 0.0082) — a post-hoc reading of a null trial. It designed the next trial; it is not evidence of benefit, and ACT CF (carded next) tested it prospectively and was null.
cards.source: Kerem E et al. Ataluren for the treatment of nonsense-mutation cystic fibrosis: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial. Lancet Respir Med. 2014. PMID: 24836205. Registry ID: NCT00803205. cards.headline: Konstan 2020 (ACT CF): the confirmatory phase 3 in the exact post-hoc population was null — FEV1 difference 0.6 [95% CI −1.3 to 2.5], p = 0.54; exacerbations 0.95 vs 1.13 per 48 weeks (rate-ratio p = 0.40)
cards.summary: Konstan 2020 (ACT CF): the confirmatory phase 3 in the exact post-hoc population was null — FEV1 difference 0.6 [95% CI −1.3 to 2.5], p = 0.54; exacerbations 0.95 vs 1.13 per 48 weeks (rate-ratio p = 0.40)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled confirmatory phase 3 trial (48 weeks)
cards.people: 279 subjects enrolled at 75 sites (138 ataluren, 136 placebo evaluable for efficacy), restricted to patients NOT receiving chronic inhaled aminoglycosides — the population the first trial's post-hoc analysis had nominated.
cards.result: Average percent-predicted FEV1 treatment difference to weeks 40/48 was 0.6 [95% CI −1.3 to 2.5], p = 0.54 — primary endpoint null. Pulmonary exacerbation rates did not differ (0.95 vs 1.13 per 48 weeks, rate-ratio p = 0.40).
cards.watchOut: This is the prospective test of the first trial's post-hoc subgroup, and it failed on every endpoint. Any presentation of the 5.7% post-hoc figure without this result beside it misstates the programme.
cards.source: Konstan MW et al. Efficacy and safety of ataluren in patients with nonsense-mutation cystic fibrosis not receiving chronic inhaled aminoglycosides: The international, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Ataluren Confirmatory Trial in Cystic Fibrosis (ACT CF). cards.summary: Wilschanski 2011: ataluren improved nasal chloride transport in 19 adults (combined mean change −5.4 mV, p < 0.001) — a pharmacodynamic activity study with no placebo arm, not a clinical-efficacy report
cards.type: Phase 2 activity study (12 weeks, lower vs higher dose, no placebo arm)
cards.people: 19 patients (aged 19–57) took ataluren at lower (4/4/8 mg/kg) or higher (10/10/20 mg/kg) dose.
cards.result: The endpoint was nasal total chloride transport, a pharmacodynamic measure: combined mean change −5.4 mV (p < 0.001), with on-treatment responses (≥ −5 mV improvement) in 61% of patients.
cards.watchOut: A mechanistic activity study, labelled as such: the surrogate responded and the clinical endpoints at phase 3 did not. Never counted as clinical efficacy.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ataluren in nonsense-mutation CF — LIKELY no benefit; a complete failed programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: ataluren in nonsense-mutation CF — LIKELY no benefit; a complete failed programme
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional population.
cards.result: One programme: 4 publications covering 4 studies. The two phase 3 trials (238 and 279 patients) both missed their primary endpoints; the second was purpose-built to test the first trial's post-hoc subgroup and was null on every endpoint. The two phase 2 reports show genuine pharmacodynamic activity on nasal chloride transport that did not translate into clinical benefit. Ataluren was never approved for CF; the Duchenne question stays at pack #4316.
cards.watchOut: Never print the post-hoc 5.7% subgroup figure without ACT CF beside it, and never count the phase 2 pharmacodynamic reports — or the first trial's secondary CT analysis — as clinical-efficacy evidence.

shelves.title: Nemonoxacin versus levofloxacin for community-acquired pneumonia — non-inferiority met in 3 trials, exclusively East Asian base
shelves.question: In adults with community-acquired pneumonia, is nemonoxacin 500 mg once daily for 7–14 days — oral, or intravenous — non-inferior to levofloxacin 500 mg once daily for clinical cure at the test-of-cure visit?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Community-Acquired Infections/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Haemophilus influenzae/drug effects · Humans · Levofloxacin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Mycoplasma pneumoniae/drug effects · Pneumonia, Bacterial/drug therapy/microbiology · Quinolones/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Streptococcus pneumoniae/drug effects · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult · Administration, Oral · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/pharmacology · Levofloxacin/administration & dosage/adverse effects/pharmacology · Microbial Sensitivity Tests · Microbial Viability/drug effects · Pneumonia, Bacterial/drug therapy · Quinolones/administration & dosage/adverse effects/pharmacology · Safety · Levofloxacin/therapeutic use/adverse effects/administration & dosage · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Quinolones/therapeutic use/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Administration, Intravenous · Infusions, Intravenous · Pneumonia/drug therapy · Aged, 80 and over
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (non-inferior to levofloxacin) — the non-inferiority framing is load-bearing: every trial in this base (3 randomised reports, 1,244 patients randomised as reported) is an active-comparator non-inferiority trial against levofloxacin; there is NO placebo-controlled evidence, and 'non-inferior to levofloxacin' must never be printed as 'effective' without the comparator and design beside it. Setting flag: all three trials were conducted in China/Taiwan populations, and local pneumococcal fluoroquinolone-resistance epidemiology is part of the result. Safety flag: in the intravenous trial, drug-related adverse events were more frequent on nemonoxacin (37.1% vs 22.2%), including QT prolongation and transaminase elevation, mostly mild. Nemonoxacin is a non-fluorinated quinolone, structurally distinct from the fluoroquinolones it was compared against — it must not be merged into a fluoroquinolone class shelf. It is approved in China and Taiwan and is NOT FDA-approved (named for clarification, not promotion). An integrated phase II/III safety summary pools these same trials and is never counted as a fourth report.

cards.headline: Liu 2017: oral nemonoxacin was non-inferior to levofloxacin — clinical cure 93.3% (500 mg) and 87.3% (750 mg) vs 88.5% in the full analysis set
cards.summary: Liu 2017: oral nemonoxacin was non-inferior to levofloxacin — clinical cure 93.3% (500 mg) and 87.3% (750 mg) vs 88.5% in the full analysis set
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind multicentre non-inferiority trial (7–10 days)
cards.people: 192 patients randomised to nemonoxacin 500 mg, nemonoxacin 750 mg or levofloxacin 500 mg once daily; full analysis set n = 168.
cards.result: Clinical cure was 93.3% / 87.3% / 88.5% respectively, with non-inferiority of both nemonoxacin doses shown in the full analysis set. Bacteriological success was 83.3% in both nemonoxacin groups vs 80.0% on levofloxacin.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against an active comparator in a Chinese population — there is no placebo arm anywhere in this base.
cards.source: Liu Y et al. A randomized, double-blind, multicenter Phase II study comparing the efficacy and safety of oral nemonoxacin with oral levofloxacin in the treatment of community-acquired pneumonia. J Microbiol Immunol Infect. 2017. PMID: 26748734. Registry ID: NCT01537250. cards.headline: Yuan 2019: phase 3 oral nemonoxacin non-inferior to levofloxacin — cure 94.3% (300/318) vs 93.5% (143/153), difference 0.9% [95% CI −3.8 to 5.5]; adverse events comparable (33.1% vs 33.3%)
cards.summary: Yuan 2019: phase 3 oral nemonoxacin non-inferior to levofloxacin — cure 94.3% (300/318) vs 93.5% (143/153), difference 0.9% [95% CI −3.8 to 5.5]; adverse events comparable (33.1% vs 33.3%)
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind double-dummy active-controlled non-inferiority trial (7–10 days)
cards.people: 527 patients randomised and treated (356 nemonoxacin, 171 levofloxacin); modified intention-to-treat cure population 318 vs 153.
cards.result: Clinical cure at test-of-cure was 94.3% (300/318) on nemonoxacin vs 93.5% (143/153) on levofloxacin (difference 0.9% [95% CI −3.8 to 5.5]) — non-inferiority met. Microbiological success 92.1% vs 91.7%. Overall adverse-event incidence was comparable (33.1% vs 33.3%).
cards.watchOut: The cure rates are modified-ITT readings from a non-inferiority design; the randomised denominators (356/171) and the mITT denominators (318/153) are both printed so the rates are not misread.
cards.source: Yuan J et al.
